This study examines brake orbits within the three-body problem, defined as trajectories where all velocities momentarily vanish. Drawing from a recent database of 30 non-collision periodic brake orbits for the equal-mass three-body problem compiled by Li and Liao, we identify and resolve both a paradox and a mystery, concluding by proposing an open question.

Quantum computers are approaching a size capable of breaking most existing encryption and signature schemes, including those used in human interface devices and IoT nodes. This paper compares signature schemes currently under standardization by NIST. After explaining the underlying reasons for their differences, I will evaluate which available implementations are best suited for IoT applications. The discussion will focus on the most promising schemes, FALCON and Dilithium, which differ in a significant aspect that makes FALCON less efficient for signing but superior for verification.

This paper establishes a Gauss-Bonnet formula for the renormalized area of Graham-Witten minimal hypersurfaces within 5-dimensional Poincaré-Einstein manifolds. The derived formula expresses this area as integrals of local geometric invariants. Furthermore, we demonstrate a theorem linking the total integral of the Laplacian of the squared norm of the second fundamental form to the conformal geometry at infinity.

We examine the likelihood that an $m\times n$ matrix, formed by extending a given $k\times n$ integer primitive matrix $A$ (whose entries are bounded by $\lambda$ and which can be completed to an $n\times n$ unimodular matrix), remains primitive. This is achieved by selecting $m-k$ additional vectors uniformly at random from the set $\{0, 1, \ldots, \lambda-1\}$. We provide a rigorous, complete proof demonstrating that for $m\le n-4$, this probability is bounded below by a constant. This result advances prior work by Maze et al. (2011), which only addressed the natural density in the limit as $\lambda\rightarrow\infty$ with $k=0$. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a fast Las Vegas algorithm capable of completing a $k\times n$ primitive matrix $A$ into an $n\times n$ unimodular matrix in expected $\tilde{O}(n^{\omega}\log \|A\|)$ bit operations, where $\tilde{O}$ denotes big-$O$ complexity excluding logarithmic factors, $\omega$ represents the exponent for matrix multiplication arithmetic operations, and $\|A\|$ is the maximum absolute entry value of $A$.

Since the discovery of spontaneous scalarization in black holes, scalar-tensor theories featuring a scalar field coupled to the Gauss-Bonnet invariant have garnered significant attention. This work extends the existing literature by providing a comprehensive analysis of spontaneously scalarized neutron stars (NSs) within a specific model characterized by a massive scalar field and a quadratic coupling function. Our investigation examines spherical NS configurations alongside their perturbative characteristics—specifically tidal deformability and moment of inertia—using a unified and extensible approach based on spherical decomposition. We observe that while the mass, radius, and moment of inertia of these scalarized NSs deviate only moderately from their general relativity (GR) counterparts, their tidal deformability displays substantial discrepancies for certain parameter values in the scalar-Gauss-Bonnet framework. Consequently, the renowned universal relation linking the moment of inertia and tidal deformability of neutron stars is violated. Given that gravitational waves from binary NS mergers can yield measurements of mass and tidal deformability, X-ray satellites can constrain the radius, and high-precision pulsar timing can determine the moment of inertia, future multi-messenger observations will allow for direct comparison with theoretical predictions, thereby offering essential data to develop theories extending beyond GR.

This letter presents both theoretical analysis and experimental measurements regarding split-ring resonators (SRRs) incorporating high-Q capacitors and nonlinear varactors. We show that the resonance frequency $f_m$ of these nonlinear SRRs is adjustable through increased incident power. Specifically, $f_m$ shifts toward lower frequencies when a single varactor is used, whereas it shifts toward higher frequencies with two back-to-back varactors. At high incident power levels, we observe bistable tunable metamaterials along with hysteresis effects. Additionally, the interaction between two nonlinear SRRs is examined.

Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in computer vision, manually designing them remains time-consuming and prone to errors. Among the various Neural Architecture Search (NAS) approaches aimed at automating high-performance CNN design, differentiable NAS and population-based NAS have garnered significant interest due to their distinct characteristics. To leverage the strengths of both methods while mitigating their weaknesses, this paper introduces RelativeNAS, a novel NAS framework. Central to its efficiency is a pairwise joint learning strategy that trains fast-learners (networks with higher accuracy) alongside slow-learners. Furthermore, because RelativeNAS relies only on low-fidelity performance estimates to differentiate between these pairs, it significantly reduces the computational costs associated with training candidate architectures. RelativeNAS offers several key advantages: (1) it achieves state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet with a top-1 error rate of 24.88%, surpassing DARTS and AmoebaNet-B by 1.82% and 1.12% respectively; (2) it discovers cells in just nine hours using a single 1080Ti GPU, making it 3.75 times faster than DARTS and 7,875 times faster than AmoebaNet; (3) it demonstrates that cells discovered on CIFAR-10 can be directly applied to object detection, semantic segmentation, and keypoint detection, yielding competitive results of 73.1% mAP on PASCAL VOC, 78.7% mIoU on Cityscapes, and 68.5% AP on MSCOCO. The RelativeNAS implementation is accessible at https://github.com/EMI-Group/RelativeNAS.

This study tackles the longstanding and contentious issue regarding the statistical characteristics of integrable quantum systems by examining the paradigmatic Lieb-Liniger model. This one-dimensional many-body system of interacting bosons permits the rigorous calculation of energy spectra using the Bethe ansatz method, with our focus being on determining if Poisson statistics define this model. Through combined analytical and numerical investigations, we demonstrate that spectral properties are heavily contingent on whether the analysis covers the complete energy spectrum or is restricted to a single subset with a fixed total momentum. We establish that a Poisson distribution of nearest-neighbor energy spacings arises exclusively within a set of levels possessing fixed total momentum, under conditions of moderate interaction strength (neither too strong nor too weak) and at sufficiently high energies. Conversely, when examining long-range correlations between energy levels, we observe significant deviations from the predictions expected of a Poisson process.

This study investigates inverse Cauchy problems associated with specific elliptic partial differential equations, where the goal is to reconstruct missing information on an inaccessible boundary using measurements from an accessible boundary, a task known to be severely ill-posed. By employing the coupled complex boundary method (CCBM), which unifies Dirichlet and Neumann data into a unified Robin boundary condition, the problem is reformulated as an operator equation. Utilizing this new framework, the existence of solutions for the reduced problem with noisy data is analyzed. To solve the operator equation iteratively, a Golub-Kahan bidiagonalization (GKB) process combined with Givens rotation is applied. Theoretical proofs establish the regularizing properties and convergence rates of the proposed CCBM-GKB method under an a posteriori stopping criterion. Furthermore, a linear finite element method facilitates the numerical implementation of CCBM-GKB. Numerical experiments confirm that CCBM-GKB functions as an accelerated iterative regularization technique, demonstrating significantly faster performance compared to the traditional Landweber method.

Dialogue state tracking (DST) serves as a critical component of task-oriented dialogue systems, with recent research heavily relying on deep neural models. However, these models demand extensive training data and struggle to generalize to new domains because they are typically trained to mimic specific datasets. To address this, we introduce Schema Encoding for Transferable Dialogue State Tracking (SETDST), a neural approach designed to facilitate effective transfer across domains. By employing a schema encoder to comprehend the underlying dataset structure rather than merely imitating it, SETDST enables the model to adapt to new domains through the encoding of new schemas within multi-domain settings. This transferable DST capability supports dialogue system development even when target domains have limited data. Experimental results on MultiWOZ 2.1 demonstrate that SETDST achieves a 1.46-point improvement in joint accuracy.

The impact of compound drops onto solid surfaces holds significant industrial relevance in fields like combustion, food processing, and drug encapsulation. A notable aspect of this phenomenon is the formation of singular jets, which can reach velocities dozens of times greater than the initial impact speed. These jets fragment into micro-droplets that generate aerosols and influence the quality of printing processes. This study examines the jetting behavior following the impact of a coaxial water-in-oil compound drop on a glass substrate, varying parameters such as release height and volumetric ratio. Post-impact, the water core spreads and retracts, producing an initial vertical oil jet. Under specific impact velocities, singular jets characterized by high speed and extreme thinness are observed. The number of velocity peaks (one or two) depends on the volumetric ratio and is driven by the contraction dynamics of a deep, cylindrical cavity. The time evolution of the collapse for the first singularity regime adheres to a $1/2$ power law, consistent with bubble pinch-off theory. Conversely, the collapse associated with the second peak follows a $2/3$ power law, resulting from a balance between inertial and capillary forces.

Monopole-dipole interactions arising from scalar couplings between a spin and a massive particle, which can be mediated by axions, violate both parity (P) and time-reversal (T) symmetries. To investigate this, we employed a $^{129}$Xe-$^{131}$Xe-Rb atomic cell comagnetometer to measure the ratio of precession frequencies between the two xenon isotopes, specifically searching for variations correlated with the distance between the cell and a non-magnetic bismuth germanate (BGO) crystal. A modulated Rb polarization technique was implemented to reduce systematic effects by two orders of magnitude. The null results obtained from this search enhance the upper limit on the coupling strength $g_{s}^Ng_{p}^{n}$ within the interaction range of 0.11 to 0.55 mm, achieving a maximum improvement factor of 30 at 0.24 mm. Consequently, the newly excluded region corresponds to a propagator mass range of 0.36 to 1.80 meV.

This study addresses Upper Domination, defined as identifying the smallest dominating set with the largest possible cardinality. While few exact algorithms exist for this problem, no binary programming formulations have previously been documented in the literature, despite their proven effectiveness in other domination contexts. We present two such binary programming models and evaluate their performance across different graph types. Our results indicate that the first formulation generally outperforms the second, except in the case of very sparse graphs where the second excels. Additionally, we provide a concise proof demonstrating that the upper domination number of any generalized Petersen graph P(n,k) is exactly n.

The "Amplituhedron program," which describes the geometric architecture of the S-matrix, is increasingly evident even within non-supersymmetric quantum field theories. Building upon the foundational research of Arkani-Hamed, Bai, He, and Yan, it is now established that for a broad range of scalar quantum field theories, tree-level amplitudes correspond to canonical forms defined on polytopes called accordiohedra. Likewise, higher-loop scalar integrands map to canonical forms associated with type-D cluster polytopes for cubic interactions, or with a recently identified class of polytopes termed pseudo-accordiohedra for higher-order scalar interactions. In this study, we further investigate the universality of these geometric structures across an expanded class of scalar quantum field theories. Specifically, we identify novel realizations of the associahedron within planar kinematic space; the canonical forms of these geometries generate (colour-ordered) tree-level S-matrix elements for external massless particles featuring $n-4$ massless poles and a single massive pole at $m^{2}$. These amplitudes arise from a potential of the form $\lambda_{1}\, \phi_{1}^{3}\, +\, \lambda_{2}\, \phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}$, where $\phi_{1}$ and $\phi_{2}$ represent massless and massive scalar fields with bi-adjoint colour indices, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in the "decoupling limit" (defined by $m \rightarrow \infty$ and $\lambda_{2} \rightarrow \infty$ such that $g := \frac{\lambda_{2}}{m}$ remains finite), these associahedra project onto a specific subset of accordiohedra. These accordiohedra are recognized as positive geometries describing amplitudes generated by the potential $\lambda \phi_{1}^{3} + g \phi_{1}^{4}$.

We apply a divide-and-concur iterative projection method for inferring context-free grammars. In contrast to most state-of-the-art natural language processing models, our approach relies on a relatively small set of discrete parameters, ensuring the resulting grammar is directly interpretable; users can easily read the solution to understand how to construct grammatically valid sentences. Additionally, our method can derive meaningful grammatical rules from just a few sentences, whereas many other models require hundreds of gigabytes of training data. We demonstrate various applications of our approach, including word classification and de novo grammar inference, refining existing grammar categories and rules, and expanding a grammar's lexicon as it processes new words in incoming data.

Recent years have seen significant efforts to constrain the initial phase-space coordinates of Milky Way (MW) dwarf galaxies for backward orbital integration. However, assumptions regarding the gravitational potential experienced by these dwarfs over time are equally critical, particularly as the MW currently accretes the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). Utilizing a dark matter-only zoom-in simulation, this study evaluates whether standard parametric potential models are sufficient for accurately integrating subhalo orbits from their current positions back to their origins. By parametrizing recovered orbits and comparing them with simulation data, we demonstrate that simple, symmetric parametric potentials fail to capture the true potential's complexities and inhomogeneities. Specifically, approximating a recent massive accretion event like the LMC's as a sum of two spherical parametric potentials introduces substantial errors in the recovered orbital parameters. These errors are comparable to those arising from a 30% uncertainty in the MW's virial mass or from failing to model the potential of recently accreted massive satellites. Consequently, our findings suggest that uncertainties in the parameters of recovered orbits for certain MW dwarfs may be underestimated, and researchers must characterize the uncertainties inherent to their integration techniques and potential assumptions against cosmological zoom-in simulations of the MW that include a recently accreted LMC.

This study presents above-barrier fusion cross-sections for oxygen isotopes ($A=16-19$) bombarding a $^{12}$C target, comparing experimental results against both static and dynamic microscopic models. These calculations fail to account for the observed $\sim$37% rise in average above-barrier fusion cross-sections for $^{19}$O relative to $\beta$-stable oxygen isotopes. This discrepancy indicates that time-dependent Hartree-Fock methods underestimate the significance of dynamical effects at energies near the barrier for neutron-rich nuclei. Consequently, high-precision measurements of above-barrier fusion across an isotopic chain of increasingly neutron-rich nuclei serve as a valuable tool for investigating fusion dynamics.

A significant hurdle in reinforcement learning involves training agents capable of solving diverse tasks. When tasks are interdependent—such as mastering walking before running—curriculum learning accelerates the process by prioritizing the most suitable next task. This study investigates curriculum learning within the complex, visually demanding environment of Minecraft, known for its difficult exploration challenges. We identify that learning progress, quantified as a shift in task success probability, serves as a robust metric for automatically designing effective curricula. We propose a learning-progress-driven curriculum and evaluate it on the "Simon Says" task, a complex reinforcement learning scenario where an agent must acquire specific goal items, many of which rely on prerequisite skills. Experimental results indicate that: (1) adding an intra-episode exploration bonus for discovering new items enhances performance; (2) dynamically modulating this bonus during training to apply only to items the agent currently struggles with yields further improvements; (3) the proposed curriculum naturally aligns with the agent's learning trajectory; and (4) integrating this curriculum with dynamic exploration bonuses leads to significantly greater efficiency and higher performance compared to uniform baselines. These findings suggest that combining intra-episode and cross-training exploration incentives with learning progress offers a promising approach for automated curriculum generation, potentially greatly advancing our ability to train more capable, general-purpose intelligent agents.

Recent measurements of two-particle transverse momentum differential correlators in Pb-Pb collisions at LHC energies offer a valuable method for probing particle production mechanisms and determining transport properties, such as the shear viscosity-to-entropy density ratio, of the created medium. Notably, longitudinal long-range correlations and significant azimuthal anisotropy observed at low transverse momenta in small collision systems like pp and p-Pb resemble collective behavior, suggesting that locally equilibrated matter may also form in these smaller systems, akin to Pb-Pb collisions. This study applies the same two-particle transverse momentum differential correlators to pp and p-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 7$ TeV and $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV, respectively, to search for signs of viscous effects. By analyzing the strength and shape of these correlators as a function of particle multiplicity, the work aims to detect evidence for longitudinal broadening indicative of viscosity in these smaller systems. Furthermore, the measured correlators and their evolution from pp and p-Pb to Pb-Pb collisions are compared with predictions from Monte Carlo event generators, with a discussion on the potential presence of viscous effects.

This study investigates a two-dimensional system of Active Brownian Particles (ABPs) that interact through a repulsive potential featuring two distinct length scales: a soft shell and a hard core. The system exhibits two distinct regimes depending on the ratio between the soft shell barrier strength and the activity level. When this ratio is significantly greater or less than one, the behavior aligns with ABPs governed by a single length-scale potential. However, when the ratio is approximately one, both length scales significantly influence structural and dynamical properties. Structurally, during motility-induced phase separation, the dense phase displays novel and more intricate arrangements compared to the hexatic phase seen in single length-scale systems. Dynamically, this work represents the first known instance of anomalous dynamics in active particles.

Smart contracts are compact yet security-sensitive programs that facilitate wallets, token mechanisms, auctions, crowdfunding, elections, and other multi-party transactions on the blockchain. While various techniques exist to verify functional correctness, these contracts often must also adhere to specific hyperproperties, including symmetry, determinism, or information flow policies. This paper demonstrates a synthesis method for smart contracts that guarantees compliance with such desired hyperproperties. Building upon a recent synthesis approach utilizing temporal logic (TSL), we introduce HyperTSL, an extension designed to specify hyperproperties for infinite-state software. We also detail a preprocessing technique to identify when a hyperproperty can be equivalently expressed as a simpler trace property. Finally, we outline a refinement process to ensure the synthesized contract strictly adheres to its HyperTSL specification.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC utilized 139 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV to analyze Higgs boson production cross-sections via the diphoton decay channel. This analysis employed machine-learning techniques to define 101 unique signal regions. The resulting inclusive signal strength for the diphoton channel is measured at $1.04^{+0.10}_{-0.09}$. Reported cross-sections cover gluon-gluon fusion, vector-boson fusion, associated production with $W$ or $Z$ bosons, and top-associated production. An upper limit, corresponding to 10 times the Standard Model (SM) prediction, was established for the associated production of a Higgs boson with a single top quark, offering distinct sensitivity to the sign of the top quark Yukawa coupling. Additionally, Higgs production was characterized using Simplified Template Cross-Sections (STXS), with measurements taken across 28 STXS regions. These STXS cross-sections align with SM predictions, yielding a $p$-value of 93%. The data further constrain Higgs coupling strengths and potential new interactions within an effective field theory framework. No significant deviations from SM expectations were observed, although these measurements demonstrate substantial improvements in sensitivity over prior ATLAS results.

We investigate how well interacting Bosonic systems can be approximated by a classical field as the total occupation number grows, utilizing our publicly accessible code repository, QIBS, which serves as a massively parallel solver for such systems. By analyzing various toy models established in existing literature, we monitor the onset of quantum corrections to the classical field description, defining this threshold as the quantum breaktime. This approach enables us to evaluate assertions in the literature concerning the convergence rates of these systems toward classical evolution. Our study examines diverse initial conditions, including coherent states, number eigenstates, and field number states. We observe that among these, only number eigenstates fail to converge to classical evolution as the occupation number increases. Furthermore, systems resembling scalar field dark matter display a logarithmic enhancement in the quantum breaktime relative to the total occupation number, whereas systems featuring contact interactions, field number state initial conditions, or linear dispersions show a power law enhancement. Ultimately, we conclude that the scaling of the breaktime is contingent upon both the model's interactions and its initial conditions.

We present evidence of oscillatory reactions within ultra-cold chemistry involving atom-molecular Bose-Einstein condensates. Nonlinear oscillations in mean-field dynamics emerge within a specific range of elliptic modulus, producing both in-phase and out-phase modulations of atom-molecule population densities. The velocity of the reaction front is governed by photoassociation, which simultaneously regulates condensate density. We identify two distinct pairs of in-phase bright localized gap solitons as exact solutions, noting that the existence of one pair necessitates a background. Cnoidal atomic density waves in a plane-wave molecular background are observed across both attractive and repulsive domains. Furthermore, the influence of intra- and inter-species interactions on the existence and stability of these systems is detailed in the context of photoassociation.

Current state-of-the-art radial velocity (RV) exoplanet surveys are constrained by stellar magnetic activity. Since magnetically active features—such as spots, plages, and network regions—affect observed spectral lines differently, they induce varying shifts in the apparent stellar RV. Consequently, distinguishing the coverage or filling factors of these active regions is essential to separate activity-induced RV signals from those caused by planetary Doppler shifts. This study introduces a method to estimate feature-specific magnetic filling factors using solely spectroscopic and photometric data. We apply both linear and neural network versions of this method to observations from the HARPS-N solar telescope, the Mt. Wilson HK Project, and the SORCE Total Irradiance Monitor. Comparisons with direct Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) measurements show that both implementations produce filling factor estimates highly correlated with observed values. Modeling solar RVs with these factors successfully replicates the expected contributions from convective blueshift suppression and rotational imbalance caused by brightness inhomogeneities. Furthermore, both methods reduce the total activity-driven RMS RV from 1.64 m/s to 1.02 m/s, achieving a 1.28 m/s reduction in RMS variation. This represents an additional 0.41 m/s improvement over traditional activity indicators.

Investigating search spaces represents one of the most unpredictable challenges that has captured researchers' attention for decades. To manage this unpredictability, it is essential to characterize these spaces and adapt actions accordingly; a well-characterized space facilitates mapping problem states to operators that generate new ones. This paper examines a landscape analysis-based set of features using prominent machine learning techniques to identify the optimal feature set. Nevertheless, addressing problem complexity and fostering cross-domain experience transfer necessitates selecting the most representative features. Consequently, the proposed approach evaluates the predictivity of various features to determine the best categorization.

We establish an inequality applicable to any finitely generated group equipped with a fixed finite symmetric generating set, which connects the expansion of successive balls with the mean length of elements within those balls. This result extends recent refinements of the Coulhon-Saloff-Coste inequality. By recasting the inequality using the Følner function, we derive, for amenable groups with exponential growth, an explicit formula for the optimal (outer) constant in the Coulhon-Saloff-Coste isoperimetric inequality, based on the growth rate and the asymptotic properties of the Følner function.

We introduce a technique for identifying bifurcations by pinpointing the zeros of a signed variant of the minimum singular value of the Jacobian. This approach allows for the application of quadratically convergent root-bracketing methods or Chebyshev interpolation to locate these bifurcation points. Although only positive singular values need calculation, the method assumes the presence of an analytic or smooth singular value decomposition (SVD). By utilizing the determinant of the Jacobian—calculated during the bidiagonal reduction phase of the SVD algorithm—the method removes slope discontinuities at the zeros of the smallest singular value. We applied this method to identify spatially quasi-periodic traveling water waves emerging from large-amplitude periodic waves. The water wave equations were formulated using a conformal mapping framework to streamline the computation of the quasi-periodic Dirichlet-Neumann operator. Our findings include pure gravity waves with zero surface tension and overhanging gravity-capillary waves; in both instances, the waves exhibit two spatial quasi-periods with an irrational ratio. We utilized numerical continuation to trace secondary branches beyond the linearization region around primary branch solutions, yielding traveling water waves defined over the real line where no two crests or troughs share an identical shape. The pure gravity wave problem holds significance for oceanography, where capillary effects are negligible; such waves exist only through secondary bifurcation and do not persist at zero amplitude. Furthermore, the gravity-capillary wave problem illustrates the efficacy of employing the signed smallest singular value as a test function for multi-parameter bifurcation issues, a function that achieves mesh independence once the discretization is sufficiently refined.

The enhanced sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors has led to a surge in both astrophysical signal detections and "glitches," which are transient, non-Gaussian noise events. The temporal overlap of these signals and glitches poses a significant challenge for inference analyses that typically rely on the assumption of purely Gaussian detector noise. In this study, we extensively evaluate a recently proposed approach that models glitches using sine-Gaussian wavelets while simultaneously fitting signals with compact-binary waveform templates. By examining a broad spectrum of glitch families and signal morphologies, we demonstrate that jointly modeling glitches and signals—using wavelets and templates, respectively—allows for reliable separation of the two components. Our findings indicate that the glitches most detrimental to parameter estimation are precisely those well-represented by such wavelets, owing to their compact time-frequency signatures. Furthermore, we test the robustness of this methodology against waveform systematics, such as those resulting from the omission of higher-order modes and spin-precession effects. The analysis yields estimates for signal parameters, identifies the glitch waveform to be subtracted from the data, and assesses whether detected excess power corresponds to a glitch, a signal, or a combination of both. Specifically, our investigation of low-significance triggers (191225_215715 and 200114_020818) reveals that both are consistent with glitches overlapping high-mass signals.

Thermal emission usually arises from a blackbody at any temperature above absolute zero, exchanging energy with its surroundings via radiation. This standard emission is predominantly incoherent in both space and time. However, nanophotonics principles have enabled the demonstration of thermal emission with properties that significantly deviate from those of a blackbody. Specifically, by utilizing the intrinsic attributes of novel materials or through nanostructuring at sub-wavelength or wavelength scales, researchers can manipulate the directionality, temporal coherence, and other unique traits of thermal radiation. Yet, these characteristics are generally static once the device is fabricated. Achieving dynamic control necessitates the use of external mechanisms to actively modulate radiative properties. Such control offers benefits for numerous applications, including solar energy harvesting, thermo-photovoltaic conversion, radiative cooling, sensing, spectroscopy, imaging, and thermal camouflage. This tutorial explores thermal emission across two domains: the near-field and the far-field, while outlining experimental methods for probing radiation in both regimes. Furthermore, we examine strategies for tailoring the spatial and temporal coherence of thermal emission and review existing mechanisms for actively tuning these features.

Black-box adversarial attacks can deceive image classifiers into misclassification without needing access to the model's internal structure or weights. Recent advancements in this area have achieved success rates exceeding 95% using fewer than 1,000 queries, raising concerns about the vulnerability of IoT devices that depend on cloud APIs for image analysis. While previous studies have mainly focused on maximizing success rates and minimizing query counts, this research highlights that the time required to execute an attack is another critical factor. By targeting cloud APIs directly instead of local models, this paper avoids several errors found in earlier work. Additionally, it leverages load balancing to facilitate distributed black-box attacks, which reduce the time needed for both local search and gradient estimation methods by approximately fivefold.

Recent investigations into the Galactic gamma-ray flux to identify dark matter annihilation signals have yielded controversial outcomes without definitive confirmation. In this study, we analyze the radio flux density profile of the M31 galaxy, suggesting it may reveal a potential dark matter annihilation signature. By comparing the likelihoods of archival radio flux density observations against predicted profiles from dark matter and stellar emission, we constrain relevant dark matter parameters. Specifically, for thermal annihilation through the $b\bar{b}$ channel, the best-fit dark matter mass is approximately 30 GeV, aligning with findings from numerous recent studies. We anticipate that this approach will serve as a valuable complementary method for constraining dark matter, alongside traditional radio analyses and other indirect detection techniques.

Building large-scale liquid scintillator detectors is challenging because photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) must be isolated from the scintillation region to mitigate their inherent radioactivity. Traditionally, acrylic or nylon barriers achieve this separation, but their own radioactivity can significantly reduce the fiducial volume available for low-energy (MeV) studies, and constructing these barriers becomes increasingly costly and difficult as detector sizes grow. This paper introduces an initial simulation of an alternative design called SLIPS (Stratified LIquid Plane Scintillator), which seeks to eliminate physical barriers altogether by employing layers of lipophobic liquids to separate the PMTs from the scintillation medium.

In three spatial dimensions ($N=3$), the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation admits solutions that develop singularities, meaning they diverge to infinity at a specific point within a finite time frame. In 1972, Zakharov notably studied this finite-time blow-up phenomenon as a representation of the spatial collapse of Langmuir waves in plasma, which constitutes the most prevalent form of matter in the universe. Zakharov postulated that the blow-up of solutions to the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLS) follows a self-similar and radially symmetric pattern, modelable by a solution to an associated self-similar complex ordinary differential equation (ODE). This ODE includes a parameter $a > 0$, with the dependent variable $Q$ satisfying initial conditions $(Q(0), Q'(0)) = (Q_0, 0)$ where $Q(0) > 0$. A crucial mathematical advancement requires establishing, for the case $N=3$, whether there exist values of $a > 0$ and $Q_0 > 0$ such that $Q$ also fulfills the physically significant "zero-energy" integral constraint. This question has remained unresolved since 1972. In this work, we settle the matter by demonstrating that for all $a > 0$ and $Q(0) > 0$, the function $Q$ indeed satisfies the "zero-energy" integral constraint.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have shown promise in recovering realistic details for single image super-resolution (SISR). To enhance the visual quality of these results, the PIRM2018-SR Challenge utilized perceptual metrics like PI, NIQE, and Ma to evaluate perceptual fidelity, which correlates strongly with human ratings. However, current approaches struggle to directly optimize these non-differentiable metrics. To solve this, we introduce RankSRGAN, a Super-Resolution GAN designed to optimize the generator based on various perceptual metrics. Our approach involves first training a Ranker to mimic the behavior of these metrics and then implementing a novel rank-content loss to improve perceptual quality. A key advantage of this method is its ability to integrate the strengths of different super-resolution techniques to produce superior results. Additionally, we extend the framework to multiple Rankers, providing multi-dimensional constraints for the generator. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RankSRGAN yields visually appealing outcomes and achieves state-of-the-art performance in both perceptual metrics and overall quality. Project page: https://wenlongzhang0517.github.io/Projects/RankSRGAN

The ALICE experiment measured the $p_\mathrm{T}$-differential production cross sections for prompt and non-prompt (originating from beauty-hadron decays) D mesons at midrapidity ($|y|<0.5$) during proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=5.02~\mathrm{TeV}$. This analysis utilized a dataset with an integrated luminosity of $(19.3\pm0.4)~\mathrm{nb^{-1}}$. D mesons were identified via the decays $\mathrm{D^0 \to K^-\pi^+}$, $\mathrm{D^+\to K^-\pi^+\pi^+}$, and $\mathrm{D_s^+\to \phi\pi^+\to K^-K^+\pi^+}$, along with their charge conjugates. Relative to earlier studies in this rapidity range, the cross sections for prompt $\mathrm{D^+}$ and $\mathrm{D_s^+}$ mesons now cover an extended $p_\mathrm{T}$ range, with total uncertainties reduced by factors between 1.05 and 1.6, depending on $p_\mathrm{T}$. This improvement enables a more precise calculation of their $p_\mathrm{T}$-integrated cross sections. The observed results align well with perturbative QCD predictions. Additionally, the ratio of heavy quark fragmentation into strange mesons versus non-strange mesons, $f_\mathrm{s}/(f_\mathrm{u}+f_\mathrm{d})$, is consistent for both charm and beauty quarks and matches previous measurements across various centre-of-mass energies and collision systems. Based on non-prompt D-meson data, the $\mathrm{b\overline{b}}$ production cross section per rapidity unit at midrapidity is determined to be $\mathrm{d}\sigma_\mathrm{b\overline{b}}/\mathrm{d} y|_\mathrm{|y|<0.5} = 34.5 \pm 2.4 (\mathrm{stat.}) ^{+4.7}_{-2.9} (\mathrm{tot. syst.})~\mu\mathrm{b}$. This value agrees with prior measurements at the same centre-of-mass energy and with theoretical perturbative QCD cross-section predictions.

To ensure safety, particularly during interactions involving potential physical contact, robots must navigate legibly around humans. Handovers exemplify such tasks, necessitating implicit communication regarding the timing and location of object transfer. This study investigates how the trajectory model employed by a robot during its reaching phase influences human perceptions during robot-to-human handovers. A user study involving 32 participants examined three objects using four distinct trajectory models: three variations of a minimum jerk trajectory and one based on ellipse fitting. While the starting position remained constant across all trajectories, the endpoint varied randomly within a ±3 cm range along all axes. Results indicated no significant differences in participant responses concerning safety, predictability, naturalness, or other subjective metrics. Although these findings appear to refute the hypothesis that trajectory shapes affect human perception of handovers, they suggest avenues for future research into other variables, including robot speed, transfer location, object orientation, and explicit communicative cues like gaze and speech.

This research examines holographic subregion complexity within a spatially anisotropic field theory that models a confinement-deconfinement phase transition. The corresponding holographic dual is a five-dimensional anisotropic model exhibiting a Van der Waals-like transition between small and large black holes. We introduce a novel informational framework to distinguish between stable and unstable thermodynamic solutions, positing that states requiring more or less information to define correspond to unstable or stable configurations, respectively. Furthermore, we propose a criterion based on computational resources, where solution stability is determined by whether the required computational power increases or decreases with rising temperature. Our findings indicate that anisotropy exerts a diminishing effect on holographic subregion complexity. This reduction can be understood by viewing the system and its environment as a closed whole, where the complexity of the mixed state declines while the environment's complexity rises.

A vast array of machine learning models relies on solving large-scale optimization problems. Recently, sub-sampled Newton methods have gained significant traction due to their iterative efficiency, addressing the primary drawback of the standard Newton method: its high per-iteration cost despite maintaining a rapid convergence rate. This paper introduces two novel, efficient Newton-type algorithms, termed Refined Sub-sampled Newton and Refined Sketch Newton. These methods offer substantial improvements over existing sub-sampled approaches, particularly when Hessian-vector products can be computed efficiently. Specifically, the proposed algorithms demonstrate superlinear convergence in general scenarios and quadratic convergence under slightly stronger assumptions. Furthermore, these methods can be extended to a unified framework for proving the convergence of various existing sub-sampled Newton techniques, thereby uncovering novel convergence characteristics. Finally, empirical evaluations on several standard datasets reveal consistent gains in computational efficiency.

**Context.** NGC 1851 is among the globular clusters where distinct subgiant branch populations and metallicity variations have been clearly established, yet a consensus on the sum of A(C+N+O) abundances remains elusive. This metric is vital for understanding the cluster's formation history, as the subgiant branch separation relies on age and/or A(C+N+O) differences. **Aims.** The primary objective was to measure carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen abundances in evolved giants within NGC 1851 to verify whether the double stellar populations share the same age. **Methods.** We analyzed high-resolution spectra obtained via the FLAMES-UVES spectrograph on the ESO VLT using a differential model atmosphere technique. **Results.** Abundances for up to 29 chemical elements were derived for a sample of 45 giants in NGC 1851. These stars divide into two populations distinguished by a 0.07 dex difference in mean metallicity, 0.3 dex in mean C/N, and 0.35 dex in mean [s/Fe] ratios. However, no significant differences were found in the mean A(C+N+O) values or in abundance ratios relative to iron for carbon, alpha-, and iron-peak elements, as well as for europium. **Conclusions.** The lack of difference in averaged A(C+N+O) values between the two groups supports the hypothesis that NGC 1851 consists of two coalesced clusters, with the metal-rich component being approximately 0.6 Gyr older than the metal-poor one. Furthermore, the overall properties and detailed chemical abundances suggest the cluster formed within a dwarf spheroidal galaxy subsequently accreted by the Milky Way.

Although Reinforcement Learning (RL) has achieved significant progress in tackling complex challenges, numerous algorithms remain fragile when faced with minor environmental shifts. Contextual Reinforcement Learning (cRL) offers a rigorous theoretical framework to model these variations, facilitating flexible, accurate, and interpretable task definition and creation. Consequently, cRL serves as a vital formalization for investigating generalization within RL. This study examines both the theoretical and practical aspects of solving cRL. We demonstrate that theoretically optimal performance in contextual Markov Decision Processes necessitates explicit context data. Furthermore, we empirically investigate context-driven task generation by incorporating context during training and introduce cGate, a state-modulating policy architecture. To support this, we present CARL, the inaugural benchmark library tailored for generalization studies based on cRL extensions of established benchmarks. In summary: Context is crucial!

For integers $t$ and $k$ satisfying $2 \leq t \leq k$, we examine $k$ set families $\mathcal{A}_j$ (where $1 \leq j \leq k$) defined on $[n]$ with sets $A_{j,i} \subseteq [n]$ for $1 \leq i \leq m$. The condition is that the intersection $|A_{1,i_1} \cap \cdots \cap A_{k,i_k}|$ is even precisely when at least $t$ of the indices $i_j$ are distinct. We establish that $m = O(n^{1/\lfloor k/2 \rfloor})$ for the case $t=k$, and $m = O(n^{1/(t-1)})$ when $2t-2 \leq k$, demonstrating that both bounds are tight. Furthermore, by restricting the scenario to identical families $\mathcal{A}_1 = \cdots = \mathcal{A}_k = \mathcal{A}$, we derive a variant of the classical oddtown problem.

With the growing prevalence of collaborative learning and outsourced data collection, malicious actors attempting to subvert the learning process encounter a new challenge: they must compete with one another. In backdoor attacks, where adversaries poison models by injecting malicious samples, the presence of additional attackers can inadvertently undermine individual success rates. This paper examines a multi-agent backdoor scenario involving non-colluding adversaries who craft and insert triggered samples into a shared dataset used by a defender model. We identify a distinct "backfiring" effect, where increasing the number of attackers reduces each attacker's Attack Success Rate (ASR). Leveraging this phenomenon, we propose two defense strategies to minimize collective attacker ASR and maximize the defender's robustness: (i) artificially inflating the number of attackers, and (ii) indexing to exclude the attackers' sub-datasets during model inference.

This study presents a grant-free non-orthogonal multiple-access (GF-NOMA) framework enhanced by a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS). To satisfy the power reception differences inherent in power-domain NOMA (PD-NOMA), we introduce a method that jointly optimizes user clustering and RIS assignment/alignment. This approach maximizes the network sum rate by strategically pairing user equipments (UEs) with varying channel gains, allocating RISs to appropriate clusters, and adjusting RIS phase shifts to benefit the members with the highest cluster sum rate. After being notified of their cluster index, UEs can immediately access their resource blocks (RBs) without needing additional grants from the base station (BS) or power control, as all devices transmit at a uniform power level. Consequently, the proposed method achieves implicit over-the-air power control with minimal signaling overhead between the BS and UEs. Numerical results demonstrate that this scheme can boost the network sum rate by up to 20% compared to benchmark GF-NOMA and optimal grant-based PD-NOMA systems, depending on specific network parameters. Furthermore, the analysis evaluates how UE density, RIS deployment, and hardware specifications influence the overall performance of the RIS-aided GF-NOMA architecture.

This study investigates whether two distinct black holes (BHs) can produce identical shadows. Under spherical symmetry, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for a static BH to be shadow-degenerate with the Schwarzschild solution: the dominant photon spheres of both must share the same impact parameter, adjusted for the varying redshifts experienced by observers in different spacetimes. We categorize these shadow-degenerate geometries into two groups. The first group, termed shadow-equivalent, includes metrics where constant (areal) radius hypersurfaces are isometric to those of Schwarzschild, exemplified by the Simpson and Visser (SV) metric. The second group comprises spacetimes with distinct redshift profiles, for which we present an explicit family of metrics. In the stationary, axisymmetric regime, we identify a sufficient condition for a metric to be shadow-degenerate with the Kerr solution as observed from far away. We also define two classes of examples here. The first class features metrics whose constant (Boyer-Lindquist-like) radius hypersurfaces are isometric to the Kerr geometry, illustrated by a rotating extension of the SV metric derived via a modified Newman-Janis algorithm. The second class involves black holes lacking the standard north-south $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry yet remaining shadow-degenerate with Kerr. These latter cases sharply demonstrate that a shadow does not uniquely probe horizon geometry. Collectively, these examples confirm that non-isometric black hole spacetimes can cast identical shadows, although the resulting lensing effects generally differ.

We have discovered a new structure within the Milky Way: the leading part of the Smith High Velocity Cloud, currently traversing the Galactic plane near a longitude of 25 degrees. Utilizing fresh 21cm HI observations from the Green Bank Telescope (GBT), we analyzed the characteristics of dozens of clouds belonging to this formation. Their kinematics align with those of the Smith Cloud, exhibiting a VLSR that surpasses the limits allowed by circular rotation in their direction. Evidence of interaction with disk gas is present in most clouds within the Leading Component, enabling us to estimate the site of these interactions. This component intersects the Galactic plane at a distance of 9.5 kpc from the Sun, roughly 4.5 kpc from the Galactic Center. Its HI mass could reach up to 10^6 Solar masses, similar to the neutral mass of the Smith Cloud, although only a portion of this mass resides in clouds resolved by the GBT data. Like the Smith Cloud, the Leading Component seems to be contributing mass and angular momentum to the inner Galaxy's ISM. We propose that the Smith Cloud is not an isolated entity but rather a segment of a larger structure spanning over 40 degrees (approximately 7 kpc) across the sky, consisting of two pieces separated by a gap of about 1 kpc.

We investigate the phenomenological influence of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) on a two-component Bose-Einstein condensate of particles undergoing Lévy flights within one- and two-dimensional frameworks. The governing coupled Gross-Pitaevskii equations feature fractional kinetic-energy operators defined by the Lévy index $\alpha < 2$, with the standard kinetic energy corresponding to $\alpha = 2$. In the two-dimensional setting, SOC terms with strength $\lambda$ induce significant effects, generating families of stable semi-vortex (SV) and mixed-mode (MM) solitons for $1 < \alpha < 2$. In this parameter range, stable solitons are otherwise impossible due to supercritical collapse when SOC is absent. As $\lambda$ approaches zero, the amplitudes of these solitons diminish proportionally to $\lambda^{1/(\alpha - 1)}$.

We demonstrate that each unstable equivariant minimal surface in $\mathbb{R}^n$ generates a maximal representation of a surface group into $\prod_{i=1}^n\textrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{R})$, accompanied by an unstable minimal surface within the associated product of closed hyperbolic surfaces. This is achieved by lifting the $\mathbb{R}^n$ surface to a surface in a product of $\mathbb{R}$-trees and subsequently deforming it into a surface in a product of closed hyperbolic surfaces. Furthermore, we establish that instability in one setting necessitates instability in the other two.

This study examines state-dependent delay equations (SDDEs) derived by introducing delays into a planar ordinary differential equation (ODE) that possesses a limit cycle. Such scenarios arise in various physical models where minor delay effects are incorporated. Although these delays are small, they constitute highly singular perturbations because the natural phase space of an SDDE is infinite-dimensional. We demonstrate that these SDDEs admit solutions analogous to those of the ODE; specifically, a periodic solution exists alongside a two-parameter family of solutions whose evolution converges to this periodic orbit. Despite the SDDE's function-space phase space, we identify initial conditions yielding solutions similar to the ODE.

Our proof strategy circumvents standard theories regarding the existence, uniqueness, and parameter dependence of SDDEs. Instead, we focus on function classes with well-defined behaviors (such as periodic or asymptotically periodic) and derive functional equations characterizing their solutions. Utilizing functional analysis, we establish an "a posteriori" result: given an approximate solution to the functional equation with favorable condition numbers, we prove the existence of a true solution nearby. This approach enables the validation of numerical computations and yields practical algorithms, with implementation details and representative results discussed in a companion paper. A distinct advantage of this method is its ability to establish smooth parameter dependence for periodic solutions and their slow stable manifolds without requiring the study of the flow's smoothness—a challenging issue for SDDEs where current optimal flow smoothness results are limited to $C^1$.

This study examines an inverse problem aimed at identifying the right-hand side of a subdiffusion equation featuring a Caputo fractional derivative, where the elliptic component takes its most general form on an N-dimensional torus. Utilizing the Fourier method, the authors establish theorems regarding the existence and uniqueness of classical solutions for the initial-boundary value problem, as well as the unique reconstruction of the unknown source term. Furthermore, specific requirements for the initial function and additional conditions are defined to ensure the applicability of the classical Fourier method to this particular inverse problem.

While certain words are crucial for a sentence's meaning, named entities (NEs) pose significant challenges for neural models. Despite their importance, S2T translation research has often overlooked their accurate handling, with recent studies indicating that S2T models struggle notably with locations and person names due to spelling difficulties. This work investigates how utilizing dictionaries of NEs likely to appear in a specific context can enhance S2T model performance. Our experiments demonstrate that NEs likely present in an utterance can be reliably detected from S2T encoder outputs, and we show that this detection quality is sufficient to improve translation accuracy, specifically reducing person name errors by 31%.

A promising approach to continuously lower the energy consumed per operation involves redesigning functionality to manage uncertainty by embracing computational methods inherently robust to such unpredictability. This necessitates a fresh perspective on data formats, operations, circuits, and the materials and substrates that facilitate them. The path forward may lie in combining 3D integrated nanotechnologies with new brain-inspired computing paradigms capable of rapid learning and fault tolerance. Given the vast scale of neural circuits, hyperdimensional (HD) computing represents neural activity as points within a high-dimensional space, utilizing hypervectors—large, randomly generated patterns. Fundamentally, HD computing revolves around manipulating and comparing these patterns directly within memory. Emerging nanotechnologies, such as carbon nanotube field-effect transistors (CNFETs) and resistive RAM (RRAM), along with their monolithic 3D integration, provide avenues for hardware-based HD computing by tightly coupling logic and memory, enhancing energy efficiency, and leveraging unique device traits. We present and characterize an end-to-end HD computing nanosystem constructed via the monolithic 3D integration of CNFETs and RRAM. Using this system, we successfully demonstrated language classification for 21 languages, achieving up to 98% accuracy on over 20,000 sentences (6.4 million characters) trained on a single text sample (~100,000 characters) per language. Furthermore, the system maintained 98% accuracy even when 78% of the hardware errors affected the HD representation (with outputs stuck at 0 or 1). By capitalizing on the distinct properties of these nanotechnologies, we show that HD computing implemented with monolithic 3D integration can achieve up to 420 times greater energy efficiency and utilize 25 times less area compared to conventional silicon CMOS implementations.

In recent years, numerous pre-trained language models designed for source code have been introduced to capture code context and act as foundations for various downstream code intelligence tasks, including code completion, search, and summarization. Built upon Transformer architectures and utilizing masked pre-training, these models have yielded encouraging outcomes. Nevertheless, significant progress remains elusive regarding the interpretability of current pre-trained code models; specifically, the reasons behind their effectiveness and the feature correlations they capture remain unclear. This paper performs a comprehensive structural analysis to offer interpretations of pre-trained language models for source code (such as CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT) through three distinct lenses: attention analysis, word embedding probing, and syntax tree induction. Our thorough investigation uncovers several insightful findings to guide future research: (1) attention mechanisms strongly align with code's syntactic structure; (2) code-specific pre-trained language models retain code's syntax structure within the intermediate representations of each Transformer layer; and (3) these models possess the capability to induce syntax trees. These results indicate that integrating code's syntax structure into the pre-training process could enhance the quality of code representations.

We introduce a novel exclusion limit for axion-like particle dark matter featuring axion-photon couplings exceeding $10^{-13}$ $\mathrm{GeV^{-1}}$, established across a frequency span of 4796.7--4799.5 MHz. This range targets axion masses centered near 19.84 $\mu$eV. This study marks the inaugural use of a Josephson Traveling Wave Parametric Amplifier (JTWPA) within a dark matter search context. Operated inside the Axion Dark Matter eXperiment (ADMX), the JTWPA functioned as an independent receiver connected to a 0.588-liter cavity. The device's capacity to provide substantial gain across a broad 3 GHz bandwidth has sparked significant interest among researchers pursuing the long-standing objective of broadband axion searches.

Simulating electronic structures on quantum computers necessitates mapping fermionic systems onto qubits. While standard encoding approaches convert a system of $N$ spin-orbitals into an $N$-qubit system, they often include fermionic configurations that violate the system's necessary symmetries and conditions. Consequently, these methods result in a qubit Hilbert space containing unphysical states, preventing full utilization of the available space. We introduce a generalized qubit-efficient encoding (QEE) scheme where the required number of qubits scales only logarithmically with the count of configurations adhering to the specified conditions and symmetries. Specifically, when restricting the analysis to particle-conserving and singlet configurations, we lower the qubit requirement to an upper bound of $\mathcal O(m\log_2N)$, with $m$ representing the particle count. This QEE approach was validated on an H$_2$ molecule (6-31G basis set) and a LiH molecule (STO-3G basis set), utilizing fewer qubits than conventional encoding techniques. Ground-state energy surfaces were computed using a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) paired with a hardware-efficient ansatz; this choice was made because our scheme predominantly spans the desired configurations, making heuristic eigenstate searches appropriate. Simulations were executed on IBM Quantum devices and the Qiskit simulator, incorporating a noise model derived from actual IBM Quantum hardware. By applying measurement error mitigation and error-free linear extrapolation, we demonstrated that the distributions of extrapolated energies from our QEE scheme align with exact results from Hamiltonian diagonalization within the specified basis sets, achieving chemical accuracy. These findings and our proposed methodology highlight the viability of quantum simulations for larger molecular systems during the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era.

V392 Persei, a recognized dwarf nova (DN) that experienced a classical nova outburst in 2018, has been monitored via ground-based optical, Swift UV/X-ray, and Fermi-LAT gamma-ray observations for nearly three years post-eruption. Among the fastest-evolving novae observed, V392 Per exhibits a $t_2$ decline time of just 2 days. Early spectral data indicate multiple, interacting mass ejections, with shocks from these events driving both the initial optical brightness and gamma-ray emission. The system entered solar conjunction shortly after the eruption; upon re-emergence, the nova had transitioned into the nebular phase, revealing the tail end of the super-soft X-ray stage. Later optical observations tracked the fading ejecta and a persistent narrow-line emission spectrum originating from the accretion disk. Continued hard X-ray emission suggests a standing accretion shock within an intermediate polar. Optical analysis determined an orbital period of 3.230 $\pm$ 0.003 days, with no detected white dwarf spin period. Data point toward a high-mass white dwarf, an evolved donor star indicated by the pre-nova spectral energy distribution (SED), and a high accretion rate inferred from the post-nova SED. Post-eruption, the system maintained a nova-like high-mass transfer state instead of reverting to the pre-nova low-mass transfer configuration typical of dwarf novae, a high state likely driven by donor irradiation from the nova event. In numerous aspects, V392 Per resembles the extensively studied nova and dwarf nova system GK Persei.

This research introduces the concepts of weak partial $b$-metric spaces and weak partial Hausdorff $b$-metric spaces. Furthermore, we aim to extend Nadler's theorem within the framework of weak partial $b$-metric spaces by employing weak partial Hausdorff $b$-metric spaces. To demonstrate the validity of our findings, a non-trivial example is provided.

This survey provides a historical overview and systematic generalization of how machine learning tackles this challenge. Our objective is to consolidate information regarding both traditional methods and recent advancements. We begin by defining systematic generalization, followed by an introduction to the Classicist and Connectionist frameworks. Subsequently, we examine various types of Connectionist models and their specific approaches to generalization, alongside discussions on two critical issues: variable binding and causality. The survey further explores systematic generalization within the domains of language, vision, and visual question answering (VQA), before addressing recent improvements from multiple perspectives. Given the extensive history of systematic generalization in artificial intelligence, we acknowledge that only a fraction of its contributions can be covered. Ultimately, we hope this paper serves as a foundational background to inspire future research.

Training deep neural networks demands growing computational resources across numerous data centers, often relying on brute-force methods for hyperparameter tuning. This work aims to (1) improve upon this by implementing second-order optimization techniques that require fewer hyperparameters for large-scale networks and (2) conduct a survey of performance optimizers to recommend the most suitable options for specific tasks. We present a new second-order optimization approach that only necessitates the Hessian-vector product, thereby circumventing the prohibitive costs associated with explicitly constructing the Hessian matrix for large models. We evaluate this proposed method against two state-of-the-art optimizers across five representative neural network challenges, ranging from regression to very deep architectures in computer vision and variational autoencoders. For the most extensive experiment, we utilized Horovod to efficiently parallelize the optimizers on an 8-GPU NVIDIA P100 (DGX-1) system.

We report the initial BVR photometry, period variations, and light-curve analysis for two eclipsing binaries, V1321 Cyg and CR Tau, which have received little prior study. Data collection took place between November 2017 and January 2020 at the Uzhhorod National University observatory, incorporating both newly observed and previously published eclipse timings. The light-curve analysis and derivation of photometric parameters were performed using the recently developed ELISa code. Our findings indicate that V1321 Cyg is a close detached system with a low mass ratio ($q=0.28$), implying it is a post-mass-transfer binary, with no significant period changes observed. Conversely, CR Tau is a semi-detached system where the secondary nearly fills its Roche lobe. We identified a long-term period increase of $1.49 \times 10^{-7} d/y$, which supports a scenario of mass transfer from the lower-mass secondary to the more massive primary.

The demand for expanded millikelvin cooling systems stems from the requirement to accommodate an increasing number of cryogenic qubits within quantum computing architectures. As a project under the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab, supported by the Department of Energy's National Quantum Initiative, we are constructing a cryogenic infrastructure designed to achieve millikelvin temperatures within an experimental volume measuring roughly 2 meters in diameter and 1.5 meters in height. This platform is engineered to support a three-dimensional qubit architecture utilizing superconducting radiofrequency accelerator cavity technologies. The following paper outlines the baseline design of this system and details its anticipated key performance metrics.

The swift dissemination of information across social media significantly impacts quantitative trading and investment strategies. The rising trend of speculative trading in highly volatile assets, such as cryptocurrencies and meme stocks, introduces new complexities to the financial sector. Examining these "bubbles"—defined as periods of sudden, anomalous market behavior—is essential for comprehending investor psychology and market dynamics. Nevertheless, the combination of extreme volatility and vast amounts of chaotic social media text, particularly regarding under-researched assets like cryptocurrencies, complicates existing analytical methods. Addressing this gap, we introduce CryptoBubbles, a novel multi-span identification task for bubble detection, along with a publicly available dataset comprising over 400 cryptocoins from nine exchanges across a five-year period, totaling more than two million tweets. Additionally, we propose a suite of sequence-to-sequence hyperbolic models tailored for this multi-span identification task, leveraging the power-law dynamics inherent in cryptocurrency and social media user behavior. We further evaluate our models' efficacy in zero-shot scenarios using a test set of Reddit posts related to 29 "meme stocks," which experience surges in trading volume driven by social media hype. Through comprehensive quantitative, qualitative, and zero-shot analyses spanning Reddit and Twitter data for both cryptocurrencies and meme stocks, we demonstrate the practical utility of the CryptoBubbles framework and hyperbolic modeling approaches.

Primary-backup database systems often utilize asynchronous replication to enhance availability and handle read-only workloads. To manage both incoming writes from the primary and serve read-only queries, backups employ a cloned concurrency control protocol. This protocol ensures that read-only transactions receive a state snapshot that previously existed on the primary, thereby forcing the backup to mirror the primary's commit order exactly. Current cloned protocols achieve this by restricting the backup's parallelism, which causes the primary to process certain workloads with higher parallelism than the backup can match. This discrepancy creates a "parallelism gap," leading to unbounded replication lag where writes may take indefinitely to replicate; this issue has caused severe failures in production environments. This paper introduces C5, the first cloned concurrency protocol capable of guaranteeing bounded replication lag. We implemented two versions of C5: evaluations in MyRocks, a widely used database, confirm C5 achieves bounded lag, while tests in Cicada, a modern in-memory database, show that C5 can keep pace with the fastest primary systems.

This study elucidates the rainbow distinguished point method introduced in our prior publication (DOI: 978-3-319-02726-5\_21), presenting updated theoretical and experimental findings that demonstrate its performance is inferior to other time-memory tradeoff techniques.

We introduce a hybrid quantum repeater architecture utilizing qubit repetition and Calderbank-Shor-Steane codes. Specifically, for repetition codes, we detail an explicit implementation of the quantum error-correction protocol. Furthermore, we examine the entangled-pair distribution rate of the encoded hybrid repeater, clearly delineating a three-way trade-off among code efficiency, memory decoherence duration, and local gate errors. Finally, we demonstrate that even with reasonable imperfections, our system can achieve approximately 24 Hz per memory at a 20 km spacing, reaching a total distance of 1280 km with a final fidelity near 0.95.

Medical image analysis is essential to precision medicine, enabling clinicians to detect anatomical irregularities and serving as a standard component of clinical evaluations. Within quantitative medical image analysis, the curation and pre-processing of medical images are vital steps that substantially influence model outcomes. This paper presents a precision-medicine toolbox designed for researchers to execute data curation, image pre-processing, handcrafted radiomics extraction (utilizing Pyradiomics), and feature exploration in Python. By offering this open-source solution, we seek to resolve challenges related to data preparation and exploration, unify currently fragmented software packages, and enhance the reproducibility of quantitative medical imaging research.

We introduce a method for characterizing Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking (SSB) that bypasses the order-parameter-dependent free energy typical of Landau theory. Instead, we employ the Functional Renormalization Group (FRG) evolution of an explicitly broken theory, utilizing a truncation scheme consistent with Ward identities. To signify the symmetry breaking, we define a "Ward ratio," which equals zero in the symmetric phase and one in the broken phase. This framework allows for a unified scale evolution of the effective potential across both phases, with the notable feature that the scale evolution accelerates within the critical regime.

Chain event graphs (CEGs) represent a modern class of probabilistic graphical models that offer a compelling alternative to Bayesian networks (BNs) for representing asymmetric processes, such as those involving context-specific independencies or structural asymmetries like zeros and missing values. Model selection for CEGs relies on staged trees as an intermediate framework, employing score-based methods akin to those used in BNs. Since a CEG is uniquely determined by its staged tree, and given that the Bayesian Dirichlet equivalent uniform (BDeu) score is widely favored in BNs for its theoretical advantages—including straightforward hyperparameter selection, maintained effective sample size, and score equivalence—it is logical to define an analogous BD score function for staged trees and CEGs under standard assumptions. Despite this theoretical possibility, research regarding how hyperparameter choices in the BD score function affect these models remains limited. This paper derives a BDeu score specifically for staged trees and CEGs and investigates the connection between this score and the BD sparse (BDs) score, which was designed for BNs with unobserved variable configurations. By establishing this relationship, we highlight the advantageous properties of CEGs when modeling processes characterized by sparsity or asymmetry.

Based on a deep 700 ks Chandra observation, we analyzed the X-ray imaging and spectral properties of the Spiderweb galaxy at z=2.16, covering both its nucleus and surrounding diffuse emission. After characterizing the nuclear source and correcting for instrumental PSF wing contamination, we quantified the extended emission within a 12" radius. Our results indicate that the Spiderweb galaxy harbors a mildly absorbed quasar exhibiting modest but significant variability over approximately one year. In the jet regions, the emission follows a power law with a spectral index of Gamma~2-2.5, consistent with inverse Compton (IC) scattering of CMB photons by relativistic electrons. Additionally, we detected roughly symmetric, diffuse emission within ~100 kpc. This emission aligns with thermal bremsstrahlung from a hot intracluster medium (ICM) with a temperature of kT=2.0_{-0.4}^{+0.7} keV and metallicity Z<1.6Z_sun. The average electron density within 100 kpc is n_e=(1.51+-0.24+-0.14)E-2 cm^{-3}, implying an upper limit on the total ICM mass of <=(1.76+-0.30+-0.17)E+12 M_sun (errors represent 1 sigma statistical and systematic uncertainties). Applying hydrostatic equilibrium yields a total gravitational mass of M(<100 kpc)=(1.5^{+0.5}_{-0.3})E+13 M_sun, with an extrapolated mass of M_{500}=(3.2^{+1.1}_{-0.6})E+13 M_sun within r_{500}=(220+-30) kpc. We conclude that the Spiderweb protocluster exhibits significant diffuse emission within 12 arcsec, primarily driven by IC scattering from radio jets. Beyond the jet regions, we identified thermal emission within ~100 kpc, suggesting the presence of hot, diffuse baryons that likely constitute the embryonic virialized halo of the forming cluster.

Typically, the ultrafast dynamics of resonantly excited molecules are studied and calculated within the molecular frame, whereas experiments occur in the laboratory frame. This work introduces a formalism using a laboratory frame density matrix to bridge quantum dynamics between these two frames, establishing a direct connection between theoretical computation and experimental observation. The approach demonstrates that molecular frame dynamics differ across various molecular orientations and that specific coherences, though potentially observable, are filtered out by the orientation-averaged reduced vibronic density matrix. Consequently, Molecular Angular Distribution Moments (MADMs) are proposed as a more precise descriptor of experimentally accessible data. Additionally, the formalism defines molecular frame quantum tomography and outlines the necessary conditions to execute such measurements, thereby enabling the experimental imaging of molecular frame vibronic dynamics. Successfully completing these measurements would fully characterize the molecular frame quantum dynamics for molecules at any orientation within the laboratory frame.

Although elastic collisions between free particles cannot produce bound states due to conservation of momentum and energy, the presence of an external trapping potential in ultracold experiments can couple center-of-mass and relative motions, thereby facilitating bound-state formation. We report the observation of weakly bound molecular states created between a single ultracold $^{87}$Rb atom and a trapped $^{88}$Sr$^+$ ion within a linear Paul trap. Our results demonstrate that bound states form efficiently during binary collisions, significantly enhancing inelastic process rates. By analyzing electronic spin-exchange rates, we investigated how these states depend on collision energy and magnetic field, deriving an average binding energy of $E_{\textrm{bind}}=0.7(1)$ mK$\cdot k_B$ and a mean molecular lifetime of $\tau=0.3(1)\,\mu$s, both of which align well with molecular-dynamics simulations. These simulations further predict a highly atypical power-law distribution of molecular lifetimes, where the mean is dominated by rare, long-lived events. The ability to tune molecular properties through trapping parameters offers new pathways for studying and controlling ultracold collisions.

Genome annotation is a critical area in biology that has traditionally relied on gene prediction methods and manual experiments requiring specialized biological knowledge. However, the advancement and increased precision of Next Generation Sequencing technologies enable a novel approach: segmenting RNA-Seq data to identify gene boundaries. Given the algorithm's near-linear complexity, we propose adapting the Pruned Dynamic Programming (PDP) algorithm—previously validated for CGH arrays—to Seq-experiment outputs. This adaptation involves modifying the algorithm to fit a negative binomial distribution for modeling the data. We demonstrate that when signal dispersion is known, the PDP algorithm is applicable and provide an estimator for this dispersion. Furthermore, we propose estimating the number of segments, corresponding to coding or non-coding genomic regions, using an oracle penalty. We validate our approach with a real dataset, demonstrating its robust performance, and our algorithm is now available as an R package on the CRAN repository.

The increasing prevalence of sharing news and content via social media and the internet is significantly reshaping our understanding of truth, thereby influencing perspectives on politics, economics, relationships, and desires. This shift stems from the proliferation of misinformation and disinformation, disseminated intentionally or inadvertently by various actors. Consequently, society faces serious political, social, ethical, and privacy challenges. These issues are exacerbated by two main factors: first, the rapid advancement of Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) algorithms capable of generating highly realistic yet fraudulent digital media (text, images, videos); and second, the capacity to personalize content feeds and foster polarized "filter bubbles" through big data. Given these concerns, there is an urgent ethical imperative to curb the spread of fake content. This paper addresses key aspects of this challenge by introducing TRUSTD, a blockchain and collective signature-based ecosystem designed to empower content creators with community validation and assist users in assessing the credibility and accuracy of digital content.
