Detecting individual, traveling microwave photons is crucial for both emerging quantum technologies and fundamental research in quantum thermodynamics regarding heat transport. A recent study by W. Khan et al. (Nat. Commun. 12, 5130, 2021) demonstrated that a double quantum dot (DQD) linked to a microwave resonator functions as an efficient, continuous photodetector, transforming incoming photon streams into an electrical photocurrent. While that experiment analyzed average photon and electron flows, this work theoretically investigates the photocurrent fluctuations within the same setup under a coherent microwave drive. We examine both low-frequency full counting statistics and finite-frequency noise (FFN). Our analysis combines numerical results and analytical expressions for limiting cases with a mean-field approach that ignores dot-resonator correlations, offering a clear physical understanding of the photocurrent statistics. We observe that ideal detection with unity efficiency yields charge current fluctuations matching the Poisson statistics of the incoming photons, whereas non-ideal detection results in sub-Poissonian statistics. Additionally, FFN reveals how detector short-time properties depend on system parameters. These findings provide new insights into microwave photon-electron interactions in hybrid dot-resonator systems and guide future experiments on the continuous detection of single microwave photons.

In the frequency-amplitude domain, Gravitational Waves (GWs) originating from cosmic strings exhibit a flat plateau at high frequencies, a feature resulting from string loop dynamics during the standard radiation-dominated post-inflationary era. However, if the primordial dark age preceding Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) follows non-standard cosmic histories, the spectrum might display a sudden upward or downward shift beyond a characteristic turning frequency $f_*$. We propose that a spectral break accompanied by an increase in GW amplitude—arising from a post-inflationary equation of state ($\omega>1/3$) stiffer than the standard radiation value ($\omega=1/3$)—could serve as a significant indicator of leptogenesis within the seesaw framework for neutrino masses. Specifically, the dynamical generation of right-handed (RH) neutrino masses via a gauged $U(1)$ symmetry breaking creates a cosmic string network that emits stochastic GWs. Furthermore, a gravitational interaction between the lepton current and an operator of the form $\partial_\mu R j^\mu$—which emerges at the two-loop level in the seesaw model through RH neutrino mediation—naturally favors a stiffer equation of state to efficiently generate a baryon asymmetry proportional to $1-3\omega$. We explore how GWs with sufficiently strong amplitudes, alongside signals from neutrino-less double beta decay, could investigate the transition to the most recent radiation domination and determine the mass of the lightest RH neutrino at intermediate energy scales.

International relations research frequently utilizes dyadic data, yet conventional analytical methods often overlook the statistical dependence that arises when dyads share a common member. To address this clustering issue, recent advancements have introduced dyadic clustering robust standard errors (DCRSEs). Applying this method, we reexamined all empirical studies featuring dyadic data published in *International Organization* from January 2014 to January 2020. Our analysis reveals that the standard errors reported in these articles are, on average, roughly twice as large as those derived using DCRSEs, indicating that dyadic clustering causes researchers to significantly underestimate uncertainty. Nevertheless, 67% of the originally significant findings remain robust when DCRSEs are applied. We conclude that correcting for dyadic clustering is both essential and practical, and we provide accompanying R and Stata software to support its implementation in future work.

It is now firmly established that galaxy interactions and mergers are fundamental to the hierarchical development of cosmic structure. These mergers not only facilitate the creation of elliptical and larger disk galaxies but also drive evolution via star formation and nuclear activity. As galaxies merge, their cores draw near, eventually forming double-nuclei galaxies (DNGs). Despite the frequency of mergers, detecting DNGs remains rare and largely accidental. However, identifying them is critical, as their characteristics illuminate the origins of supermassive black hole (SMBH) binaries, dual active galactic nuclei (DAGN), and related feedback mechanisms. Consequently, a systematic, automated survey is essential for discovering these objects. Leveraging the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) as our target catalog, we developed a new algorithm named "Gothic" (Graph-bOosTed iterated HIll Climbing) to identify images exhibiting the specific traits of DNGs (ASCL entry 2707). Testing this method on a random sample of 100,000 galaxies from the SDSS Stripe 82 region yielded a maximum detection rate of 4.2%, achieved through a careful selection of the input catalog.

We investigate the chirality of the cosmological medium arising from parity-violating decays of standard model particles, using tau leptons as a case study. However, the resulting non-trivial chirality is insufficient to generate a significant cosmological magnetic field through the chiral-magnetic effect.

Gold nanoparticles are highly sought after for various technological applications because their tunable properties depend on the size and shape of the individual particles. While many heuristic approaches exist for controlling these morphological traits, the fundamental mechanisms governing size and shape remain poorly understood, largely due to the vast number of possible synthesis parameter combinations. Data-driven methods could provide valuable insights into these mechanisms if sufficient synthesis data were available. To enable data mining in this area, we have created and made publicly accessible a dataset of codified gold nanoparticle synthesis protocols and outcomes. Extracted directly from the materials science literature using natural language processing and text-mining, this dataset comprises 5,154 records, each representing a single synthesis article filtered from a database of 4,973,165 publications. Each record includes codified synthesis procedures and extracted morphological details derived from 7,608 experimental and 12,519 characterization paragraphs.

Constructing a benchmark dataset for hate speech detection involves significant hurdles. Primarily, the scarcity of hate speech makes random tweet sampling inefficient for annotation. While previous datasets often rely on tweets containing known "hate words" to mitigate this, such a reliance on a fixed vocabulary risks excluding real-world instances of hate speech. A second obstacle is the inherent subjectivity and variability in defining hate speech, which can lead to annotator disagreements and difficulties in adhering to labeling guidelines. Our central insight is that the rarity and subjectivity of hate speech mirror those of relevance in information retrieval (IR), suggesting that established IR test collection methodologies can enhance hate speech benchmark creation. To efficiently and intelligently select tweets for annotation, we employ standard IR techniques like {\em pooling} and {\em active learning}. Furthermore, to boost annotation consistency and value, we utilize {\em task decomposition} and {\em annotator rationale} methods. We introduce a new Twitter-based hate speech detection benchmark that offers broader coverage than prior datasets and demonstrates a substantial decline in accuracy for existing models when evaluated on these expanded forms of hate. The collected annotator rationales not only validate labeling choices but also facilitate future research in dual-supervision and explanation generation. Additional details regarding our approach are available in the supplementary materials.

We introduce the BrainScaleS-2 mobile system, a compact analog inference engine built on the BrainScaleS-2 ASIC, showcasing its ability to classify a medical electrocardiogram dataset. The ASIC's analog network core executes the multiply-accumulate operations required for a convolutional deep neural network. Operating at a system power of 5.6W, the ASIC consumes 192uJ of total energy and achieves a classification time of 276us per ECG patient sample. Atrial fibrillation is accurately detected with a rate of (93.7${\pm}$0.7)% and a false positive rate of (14.0${\pm}$1.0)%. Thanks to its compact form factor, power efficiency, and flexible I/O, the system is immediately suitable for edge inference, enabling the BrainScaleS-2 ASIC to function reliably outside specialized laboratory environments. Future deployments on this single neuromorphic platform will facilitate the integration of conventional machine learning layers with online learning in spiking neural networks.

This study reports findings from an ALMA survey covering 10 square degrees of the Serpens star-forming region, targeting 320 young stellar objects, of which 302 are probable Serpens members (classified as 16 Class I, 35 Flat spectrum, 235 Class II, and 16 Class III). Analysis of the 1.3 mm continuum data reveals disk dust masses that consistently decrease from Class I through Flat spectrum to Class II sources. When grouped by evolutionary stage, these disk mass distributions resemble those found in other young regions ($<3$ Myr), suggesting that the broad environment of a star-forming region does not significantly influence overall disk dust mass characteristics. These inter-population comparisons further support earlier findings that disks in the Ophiuchus star-forming region exhibit unusually low masses across all evolutionary phases. Furthermore, we identify a single deeply embedded protostar previously undocumented in the literature and catalog 15 protostellar outflows derived from the $^{12}$CO ($J=2-1$) line observations.

A graph is defined as one-regular when its automorphism group acts regularly on the set of its arcs. This paper presents a classification of 4-valent one-regular graphs with order $5p^2$, where $p$ represents a prime number.

With the proliferation of IoT devices, Bluetooth has become increasingly vital. However, most existing research on Bluetooth simulation prioritizes network protocol performance while overlooking privacy safeguards mandated by the BLE standard, such as MAC address randomization. Although this technique is designed to protect device identity, recent studies highlight persistent challenges, particularly the correlation between public packets and their sources. Unfortunately, current simulation tools like NS-3 lack the necessary functionality to replicate this standard, rendering it impossible to effectively test device-fingerprinting solutions due to the absence of ground truth for large-scale scenarios involving randomized addresses. This paper addresses these gaps by introducing a standard-compliant MAC address randomization module for NS-3, capable of emulating real BLE devices and generating authentic traces. Furthermore, to mitigate the exponential growth in simulation run-time associated with trace collection, we implement an optimization that linearizes public packet sniffing, making large-scale data gathering practically feasible. Finally, leveraging these generated traces and ground truth, we conduct a case study evaluating a generic MAC address association method found in literature. Our results indicate that nearly 90% of randomized addresses can be correctly linked, even in highly dense and dynamic environments.

When analyzing clustered units within repeated measures factorial designs, researchers often employ parametric approaches like linear mixed-effects models to address within-subject correlations. Nevertheless, the strict parametric requirements of continuity and normality are frequently unmet, and verifying homoscedasticity proves difficult in practice. These constraints become particularly unrealistic when data are non-metric, a common scenario in outcomes such as Quality of Life. This article introduces nonparametric effect-size measures tailored for pre-post measurements in clustered factorial designs. These measures offer intuitive, probabilistic comparisons of treatment and time effects, accommodating arbitrary dependence structures within clusters across different treatment groups. The study details the effect-size estimators, their asymptotic properties, and methods for calculating confidence intervals and conducting hypothesis tests. Additionally, ANOVA-type statistics utilizing a $\chi^2$ approximation are explored, maintaining optimal asymptotic performance even in small samples. The methodology allows for mixed cluster types within treatment groups, distinguishing between those with both pre- and post-intervention data (complete clusters) and those with data from only one period (incomplete clusters). The proposed methods demonstrate particular efficacy under multiple clustering forms. Finally, the developed nonparametric techniques are applied to data from a three-arm Randomized Trial assessing indoor wood smoke reduction to alleviate asthma symptoms in children living in homes heated by wood stoves.

In lossless periodic structures exhibiting appropriate symmetry, transmission and reflection spectra frequently display peaks and dips that are exactly $100\%$ and $0\%$, respectively. These idealized features, characterized by full peaks and null dips, typically emerge near resonant frequencies and remain robust against structural perturbations that maintain the necessary symmetry. However, existing theoretical frameworks regarding the occurrence of these phenomena are both incomplete and challenging to apply. To address this, we introduce a new theory for periodic structures containing bound states in the continuum (BIC), which elucidates the conditions for real transmission and reflection zeros corresponding to spectral zero dips. This proposed theory is notably simpler, comprehensive, and user-friendly. Numerical examples are provided to confirm the validity of this new approach.

We have explored a method to determine Majorana type-phases by analyzing the time evolution of lepton family numbers. These phases correspond to the orientation of the unitarity triangles within the Pontecorvo-Maki-Nakagawa-Sakata (PMNS) matrix and are associated with the Majorana phases $\alpha_{21}$ and $\alpha_{31}$. By computing the second-order time derivatives of the expectation values for lepton family numbers, we can isolate the dependencies on the summation of these Majorana type-phases, thereby enabling the extraction of both the unitarity triangle orientations and the specific Majorana phases. Our investigation examines the extraction of these phases and the lightest neutrino mass in scenarios involving three massive neutrinos, as well as cases where one neutrino is massless ($m_{1,3}=0$). Our findings offer a complementary approach to neutrinoless double-beta decay for determining the orientation of PMNS unitarity triangles and the Majorana phases.

Recently, the Maximal Coding Rate Reduction (MCR$^2$) principle has been introduced as a training objective designed to learn intrinsic low-dimensional structures within high-dimensional data, offering greater robustness compared to standard methods like cross-entropy minimization. Despite its demonstrated benefits, MCR$^2$ incurs a substantial computational burden because it requires evaluating and differentiating numerous log-determinant terms, a count that increases linearly with the number of classes. By leveraging variational representations of matrix spectral functions, we reformulate the MCR$^2$ objective into a scalable version that maintains training accuracy. Experiments in image classification show that this new formulation significantly accelerates optimization compared to directly optimizing the original MCR$^2$ objective and frequently yields superior learned representations. Additionally, this approach holds independent value for other models necessitating log-determinant calculations, such as system identification and normalizing flow models.

This study determines the dipole within the Pantheon+ dataset. We observe that although the dipole's amplitude aligns reasonably well with the cosmic microwave background (CMB) dipole—typically attributed to the solar system's motion relative to the cosmic rest frame—their directions diverge with very high significance. While the amplitude fluctuates based on the lower redshift cutoff, the direction remains remarkably stable. However, for redshift thresholds of approximately $z_{\rm cut} \simeq 0.05$ or higher, the dipole can no longer be detected with high statistical significance. It appears that corrections for peculiar velocities play a crucial role in these findings.

We establish a correspondence between Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning (MaxEnt RL) and Markovian processes conditioned on rare events. Within the long-time limit, this relationship enables the derivation of analytical formulas for the optimal policy, system dynamics, and initial state distributions across the general case of stochastic dynamics in MaxEnt RL. Our findings demonstrate that soft-$\mathcal{Q}$ functions in MaxEnt RL can be extracted from the Perron-Frobenius eigenvalue and its associated left eigenvector of a regular, non-negative matrix constructed from the underlying Markov Decision Process (MDP). These theoretical results facilitate the development of new algorithms for both model-based and model-free MaxEnt RL, which we verify through numerical simulations. The mapping introduced herein paves the way for applying innovative analytical and computational methods to further challenges in MaxEnt RL. Our code is accessible at: https://github.com/argearriojas/maxent-rl-mdp-scripts

Short gamma-ray burst (GRB) light curves frequently exhibit an "internal plateau" followed by a rapid decline, where the plateau is typically attributed to dipole radiation from a supra-massive magnetar and the subsequent drop suggests its collapse into a black hole (BH). Post-collapse, fallback accretion onto the nascent BH can sustain prolonged activity through the Blandford-Znajek (BZ) mechanism. In this model, magnetic flux accumulates near the BH and remains trapped by the accretion disk until declining accretion rates allow the field to halt gas inflow, forming a magnetically-arrested disk (MAD). Under these conditions, the BZ process generates two characteristic X-ray profiles: Type I features an extended plateau followed by a power-law decay with slopes between 5/3 and 40/9, requiring lower magnetic field strengths, whereas Type II displays a single power-law decay with a 5/3 slope, indicative of higher field values. We identified two candidates, GRB 101219A (Type II) and GRB 160821B (Type I), within a sample of short GRBs showing internal plateaus, demonstrating that our model accurately reproduces the observed data.

Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (MNMT) systems utilize diverse language pairs during training to enhance translation performance for low-resource languages by leveraging knowledge from high-resource ones. This study evaluates a domain-adapted MNMT model within the medical field for English-Romanian translation, employing both automatic metrics and a human-annotated error typology that categorizes terminology-specific mistakes. We contrast the out-of-domain MNMT model against its in-domain adapted counterpart. Results indicate that the in-domain MNMT model surpasses the out-of-domain model across all automatic metrics and generates fewer terminology errors.

Over the last few years, cryptocurrencies have transitioned from an obscure niche to a prominent asset class, with investment interest growing significantly. Nevertheless, these assets entail substantial risk due to their extreme volatility. This study defines criteria based on historical data to characterize returns and risks across varying short-term horizons (specifically 7 and 15 days), subsequently analyzing the importance of these criteria through multiple methods and evaluating their impact. Ultimately, the research outlines a future roadmap to leverage these insights for selecting investment portfolios by employing multi-criteria decision-making techniques.

Ensembles of deep neural networks leveraging model diversity have proven effective in enhancing predictive accuracy and robustness across various applications. Recent findings indicate that sparse subnetworks derived from dense models can achieve comparable performance while simultaneously boosting robustness and reducing complexity. However, traditional ensembling methods typically demand multiple parallel, computationally expensive evaluations and are largely designed for deterministic models, whereas sparsity is often achieved through ad-hoc pruning. We introduce a framework for sequentially ensembling dynamic Bayesian neural subnetworks that systematically lowers model complexity via sparsity-inducing priors and generates diverse ensembles within a single forward pass. This strategy comprises an exploration phase to identify high-performing parameter regions, followed by multiple exploitation phases that leverage the compactness of sparse models to rapidly converge to distinct minima in the energy landscape, thereby producing diverse subnetworks. Empirical results on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and their corrupted variants (CIFAR10-C, CIFAR100-C) demonstrate that our approach outperforms baseline dense frequentist and Bayesian ensembles in prediction accuracy, uncertainty estimation, and out-of-distribution robustness. Additionally, our method yields the most diverse ensembles among those using a single forward pass and, in certain cases, surpasses even those utilizing multiple forward passes.

This work investigates the general characteristics of moduli spaces for SO(3) vortices on orbifold Riemann surfaces, leveraging these findings to describe solutions to the SO(3) monopole equations on Seifert manifolds, thereby extending the approach pioneered by Mrowka, Ozsváth, and Yu. Additionally, we examine SO(3) monopole solutions on S¹ × (Riemann Surface) to inspire the development of "framed monopole Floer homology," a construct analogous to the instanton Floer homology framework established by Kronheimer and Mrowka. Furthermore, SO(3) vortex moduli spaces serve as an effective illustrative model for recent research by Feehan and Leness on a natural Morse-Bott function defined over the moduli space of SO(3) monopoles on Kähler manifolds; specifically, we calculate the Morse-Bott indices for this function.

Let $F$ denote a global function field and $G$ a semisimple algebraic group. Consider a prime $\ell$ that differs from the characteristic of $F$ and is sufficiently large with respect to the root datum of $G$. For a continuous representation $\bar{\rho} \colon \Gamma_{F} \to G(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell})$, we establish that $\bar{\rho}$ admits a lift to a $G$-compatible system of Galois representations featuring Zariski-dense images, provided certain conditions are met regarding the image of $\bar{\rho}$. This result relies primarily on a lifting theorem by Fakhruddin, Khare, and Patrikis, along with L. Lafforgue's contributions to the Langlands correspondence for function fields. As a consequence, we demonstrate new cases of the inverse Galois problem for finite groups of Lie type within the context of function fields.

The primary scientific objective of the Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is to observe Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) arising from the mergers of binary compact stars and the collapse of massive stars, both of which can generate gravitational waves. To evaluate the GECAM Gamma-Ray Detectors' (GRDs) response to high-energy bursts and validate the satellite's in-flight trigger and localization software prior to launch, a portable GRB simulator was developed using grid-controlled X-ray tube (GCXT) and direct digital synthesis (DDS) technologies. This simulator modulates X-ray flux powered by high voltage up to 20 kV, achieving a time jitter (FWHM) of approximately 0.9 $\mu$s. Before the December 2020 launch, both GECAM satellites were exposed to various GRB types—including short and long durations—generated by this device. The light curves recorded by the GECAM/GRDs matched the programmed input functions within statistical uncertainties, confirming the reliable performance of both the detectors and the simulator.

To advance a novel alternative methodology, we introduce a distinct convex reformulation for a broad category of stochastic quadratically constrained quadratic optimization problems. Drawing inspiration from Burer's approach, this reformulation elevates variables into a significantly lower-dimensional space by leveraging a generalization of the set-completely positive matrix cone. By approximating this cone using both inner and outer bounds, we derive upper and lower estimates that can potentially eliminate the optimality gap. Consequently, this enables the certification of exactness for these sparse reformulations even beyond conventional sufficient conditions. Furthermore, numerical experiments are presented to evaluate the efficacy of these inner and outer approximations, demonstrating their capacity to close the optimality gap in various significant scenarios.

Cyber-physical systems (CPS) must adhere to safety requirements across diverse fields, including robotics, industrial manufacturing, and power grids. Faults and cyberattacks can breach these safety limits, potentially damaging infrastructure and threatening human life. To mitigate these risks, resilient architectures have been introduced, utilizing strategies such as redundancy and safe-state restarts to maintain system integrity. However, current resilient designs employ disparate mechanisms, lacking a unified approach for comparison, and methodologies developed for one architecture are difficult to transfer to others. This paper introduces a timing-based framework capable of analyzing and designing various resilient CPS architectures. Leveraging the insight that cyber subsystems operate within a finite set of statuses, we first construct a hybrid system model applicable to any of these architectures. Subsequently, we formulate a method for jointly computing control policies and timing parameters to satisfy specific safety constraints, deriving sufficient conditions for their existence. Based on these conditions, we present an algorithm to calculate the necessary control policies and timing parameters for a given architecture. Furthermore, our solution is applicable to a broad class of CPS with polynomial dynamics and accommodates new architectural designs. We validate this framework through a case study on adaptive cruise control systems.

This article examines the history of Korean space missions, with a specific focus on astronomy and astrophysics. For every mission discussed, we analyze the scientific motivations and achievements alongside technical program details, including schedules. The review covers ongoing and approved missions, as well as planned future endeavors. Concluding with the review, and acknowledging the limitations of the authors' viewpoint, we offer insights into the future trajectory of Korea's space program in the fields of astronomy and astrophysics.

Salient object detection demands a comprehensive and scalable receptive field to identify visually prominent objects within images. While recent advancements in visual transformers and multi-branch architectures have markedly improved neural networks' capacity to perceive objects across various scales, these approaches present specific challenges. Traditional transformer backbones are computationally expensive, and multi-branch modules often suffer from identical error backpropagation during training, hindering the extraction of discriminative features. To address these issues, we introduce a bilateral network integrating both transformers and CNNs to simultaneously expand local details and global semantic information. Furthermore, we propose a Multi-Head Boosting (MHB) strategy to increase the specificity of distinct network branches. By evaluating the errors of different prediction heads, this approach enables each branch to focus more intensely on pixels that other branches mispredict. Unlike standard multi-path parallel training, MHB employs a boosting mechanism that randomly selects a single branch for gradient backpropagation at each step. Additionally, an Attention Feature Fusion Module (AF) is developed to merge two feature types based on their unique characteristics. Extensive experiments across five benchmark datasets confirm that the proposed method yields significant performance gains compared to state-of-the-art solutions.

Let $p$ be a prime, $K$ a discretely valued extension of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, and $A_{K}$ an abelian $K$-variety possessing semistable reduction. Building upon the work of Kim and Marshall, which addressed the case where $p>2$ and $K/\mathbb{Q}_p$ is unramified, we establish an $l=p$ complement to Grothendieck's Galois cohomological formula concerning the $l$-primary component of the N\'eron component group of $A_{K}$. Our methodology constructs, for every integer $m \geq 0$, a finite flat $\mathscr{O}_K$-group scheme whose generic fiber corresponds to the maximal 1-crystalline submodule of $A_{K}[p^{m}]$. Consequently, we provide a novel proof of the Coleman-Iovita monodromy criterion regarding the good reduction of abelian $K$-varieties.

We restrict the light CP-odd Higgs boson $A_{1}^{0}$ within the NMSSM framework by examining the rare decay $\pi^{0}\to e^{+}e^{-}$. Our analysis demonstrates that the $3\sigma$ tension between theory and the recent KTeV measurement of ${\cal B}({\pi}^{0}\to e^+ e^-)$ remains unresolved when incorporating constraints from $\Upsilon\to\gamma A_1^0$, the muon anomalous magnetic moment $a_{\mu}$, and $\pi^{0}\to \gamma \gamma$. Additionally, these combined constraints rule out the scenario where $m_{A_1^0}=214.3$ MeV, a mass value proposed to account for the $\Sigma^{+}\to p \mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ anomaly observed by the HyperCP Collaboration.

This article investigates semigroups of composition operators acting on the $BMOA_p$ spaces and their corresponding "little oh" counterparts, $VMOA_p$. Introduced by R. Zhao within the broader $F(p,q,s)$ family, $BMOA_p$ represents the Möbius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces $D^p_{p-1}$. The study focuses on identifying the maximal subspace of strong continuity by establishing a sufficient condition on the infinitesimal generator of ${\phi}$ such that $[{\phi}_t,BMOA_p]=VMOA_p$, alongside a related necessary condition when the Denjoy-Wolff point lies within $\mathbb{D}$. Furthermore, the paper characterizes semigroups satisfying $[{\phi}_t, BMOA_p]=VMOA_p$ using the resolvent operator of the infinitesimal generator of $T_t$. It also elucidates the relationship between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and Volterra-type operators $T_g$. Specifically, the symbols $g$ are characterized for which $T_g$ maps $BMOA$ boundedly or compactly into $BMOA_1$, thereby extending prior results to the $p=1$ case. Finally, it is demonstrated that for $1<p<2$, the compactness of $T_g$ on $BMOA_p$ is equivalent to its weak compactness.

Addressing the generalization difficulties neural networks face when predicting molecular properties from scarce 3D structural data, this paper introduces a novel pre-training method based on denoising. By leveraging extensive datasets of equilibrium 3D molecular structures, the approach learns robust representations that enhance performance on downstream tasks. Exploiting the established connection between denoising autoencoders and score-matching, we demonstrate that the denoising objective effectively trains a molecular force field by approximating the Boltzmann distribution using a mixture of Gaussians directly from equilibrium data. Experimental results indicate that this pre-training strategy significantly boosts accuracy across various benchmarks, establishing a new state-of-the-art on most targets within the QM9 dataset. Furthermore, our analysis offers practical guidance on how dataset size, model architecture and scale, and the selection of upstream and downstream datasets influence pre-training outcomes.

Energy reconstruction in calorimeters at high-luminosity particle colliders presents a significant challenge due to the pile-up effect, where overlapping pulses from the front-end compromise energy estimation unless signal disentanglement is performed. While recent approaches utilizing signal deconvolution have been suggested for both online and offline contexts, online processing is constrained by demands for speed, memory efficiency, and cost-effectiveness. Conversely, offline reconstruction can leverage Sparse Representation theory to execute advanced iterative deconvolution algorithms. This paper introduces Iterative Deconvolution methods grounded in Sparse Representation that achieve computational efficiency suitable for online deployment. Validation using simulated data compares these proposed techniques against current standards in online environments. The analysis indicates that, despite higher computational costs relative to conventional methods, the performance gains justify their adoption, particularly for the Separable Surrogate Functional, which demonstrates feasibility for implementation on modern FPGAs.

Multi-view data analysis has become increasingly popular due to the frequent occurrence of such data in machine learning tasks. A straightforward yet promising technique for clustering multi-view data is multi-view clustering (MVC), which has been widely developed to group subjects by learning latent common features shared across multiple views. Among current methods, graph-based multi-view clustering (GMVC) attains state-of-the-art results by utilizing a unified matrix as a shared graph structure. However, existing approaches, including GMVC, fail to explicitly handle inconsistent components within input graph matrices, leading to suboptimal clustering performance. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a novel GMVC method that integrates both consistent and inconsistent parts across multiple views, termed CI-GMVC. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets confirm the effectiveness of the proposed CI-GMVC approach.

The "coming and going" phenomenon in projectile motion, analyzed under linear air resistance, reveals through both approximate and numerical methods that a specific critical angle and an intriguing geometric property of the trajectory shift in response to changes in the linear air resistance coefficient.

A newly created self-healing diffusion Monte Carlo algorithm [PRB 79, 195117] has been adapted for computing excited states. This approach relies on a mixed estimator for excited-state probability density and an excited-state fixed-node approximation. To determine the fixed-node ground-state wave-functions of distinct nodal pockets concurrently, a recursive method is employed. Decay into lower-energy states is mitigated through two strategies: first, by eliminating the projection of the enhanced trial-wave function onto previously computed eigenstates; and second, by adjusting the reference energy for each nodal pocket. This adjustment introduces a kink in the global fixed-node wave-function that, upon local smoothing, expands the volume of higher-energy pockets at the cost of lower-energy ones until all pocket energies equalize. This reference energy technique aims to identify nodal structures representing local minima for arbitrary node fluctuations within a specific nodal topology. Finally, the algorithm's convergence to many-body eigenstates in both fermionic and bosonic scenarios is demonstrated using a model system.

Resource Constrained Project Scheduling Problems (RCPSPs) lacking preemption represent established NP-hard combinatorial optimization challenges. A valid RCPSP solution involves a time-sequenced arrangement of jobs and their specific execution modes, adhering to both precedence and resource limitations. This study introduces a cutting plane method designed to separate five distinct cut families, alongside an innovative preprocessing procedure to reinforce resource-based constraints. The approach utilizes enhanced versions of standard precedence and cover inequalities. During each iteration, a dense conflict graph is constructed based on feasibility and optimality criteria to identify cliques, odd-holes, and strengthened Chvátal-Gomory cuts. These strategies significantly enhance linear relaxation bounds, enabling a state-of-the-art mixed-integer linear programming solver to determine provably optimal solutions for 754 previously unresolved instances across various RCPSP variants, a feat unachievable with original linear programming formulations.

This research examines the propagation of charm quarks during the initial phase of high-energy nuclear collisions at the RHIC and LHC. A key innovation is the inclusion of the color current carried by heavy quarks moving through the evolving Glasma (Ev-Glasma), which drives energy loss through medium polarization. We calculate the transverse momentum broadening, $\sigma_p$, of charm quarks during the pre-thermalization period and assess how this diffusion influences the nuclear modification factor in nucleus-nucleus collisions. While the overall energy loss effect remains negligible in this early stage, the analysis is extended by computing the coordinate spreading, $\sigma_x$, and comparing findings with Langevin dynamics. In the Ev-Glasma framework, $\sigma_p$ exceeds the predictions of standard Langevin dynamics by the end of the pre-hydro regime. We attribute this discrepancy to the quark's memory of the color force, resulting in a $\sigma_p\propto t^2$ dependence. Furthermore, the observation that $\sigma_x\propto t^2$ during the pre-hydro stage indicates that charm quarks in the Ev-Glasma undergo ballistic diffusion.

The ellipsoid embedding function of a symplectic four-manifold quantifies the scaling required for its symplectic form to accommodate an ellipsoid with varying eccentricity, thereby generalizing both the Gromov width and ball packing numbers. Within the family of one-point blowups of the complex projective plane, a dense open set of symplectic forms allows for a complete description of their ellipsoid embedding functions via finitely many obstructions; conversely, a Cantor set of forms requires infinitely many obstructions, a phenomenon termed an "infinite staircase." This paper identifies a novel infinite staircase when the target is a four-dimensional polydisk, expanding upon a countable family previously discovered by Usher in 2019. Furthermore, our findings suggest a proof strategy for a conjecture proposed by Usher.

Recent research indicates that heavy tails can arise in stochastic optimization and are connected to generalization error. Although these findings have illuminated interesting facets of generalization in modern contexts, they depended on stringent topological and statistical regularity assumptions that are difficult to verify in practice. Additionally, empirical evidence suggests that the relationship between heavy tails and generalization may not always be monotonic, contradicting established theoretical conclusions. In this study, we establish new connections between tail behavior and the generalization properties of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) using algorithmic stability as a framework. We analyze a quadratic optimization problem and employ a heavy-tailed stochastic differential equation to model the heavy-tailed dynamics observed in SGD. Our proof of uniform stability bounds yields three key insights: (i) Without exotic assumptions, we demonstrate that SGD lacks stability when measured with squared loss ($x\mapsto x^2$), but achieves stability when measured with a surrogate loss ($x\mapsto |x|^p$) for some $p<2$. (ii) Depending on data variance, there exists a specific "threshold of heavy-tailedness" where generalization error decreases as tails become heavier, provided the tails remain lighter than this threshold, indicating that the heavy tail-generalization relationship is not globally monotonic. (iii) We derive matching lower bounds on uniform stability, confirming that our bounds are tight regarding the heaviness of the tails. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on both synthetic data and real neural networks.

This study introduces a novel framework enabling autonomous drone flight by utilizing image inputs, specifically designed to handle uncertainties and noisy indoor conditions. To enhance stability amidst such disturbances, a new Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) controller equipped with a derivative filter is developed, leveraging object and depth detection capabilities. The underlying mathematical model achieves high fidelity by resolving issues related to non-linearity, coupling, and uncertainties. Furthermore, the PIDA controller is optimized using the Stochastic Dual Simplex Algorithm (SDSA) to facilitate autonomous operations. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that integrating deep learning-based image understanding methods, specifically RetinaNet with ant colony optimization and PSMNet, allows the controller to successfully generate and track target points despite environmental disruptions.

Born-Infeld (BI) electrodynamics was developed to address the issue of infinite self-energy inherent to point charges in Maxwell electrodynamics. By imposing an upper limit $b$ on the electric field, BI theory constrains this self-energy. This review outlines the motivation for the BI Lagrangian and derives the corresponding field equations. Additionally, we determine the stress-energy tensor within BI theory, compute the potential generated by a point charge, and identify wave solutions of order $b^{-2}$ in $1+1$ dimensions. Finally, we analyze BI plane waves striking a mirror at normal incidence.

This work generalizes the holographic Schwinger-Keldysh framework from arXiv:1812.08785 to charged black branes, aiming to investigate Hawking radiation within these geometries. This approach is equivalent to analyzing real-time fluctuations of a dual CFT maintained at finite temperature and chemical potential. We validate the prescription by employing charged Dirac probe fields and solving the Dirac equation using a boundary derivative expansion that builds upon the findings in arXiv:2011.07039. The resulting Schwinger-Keldysh correlators inherently fulfill the requisite KMS conditions, incorporating Fermi-Dirac statistical factors.

This study numerically investigates the scalar curvature tensor within a two-dimensional discrete space. A continuous two-sphere metric is discretized into a lattice via two distinct slicing methods: the first employs two integer coordinates, whereas the second assumes one coordinate is ignorable. The numerical outcomes from both scenarios are subsequently compared against the anticipated values in the continuous limit as the lattice cell count approaches infinity.

Automatic parsing of anatomical structures in X-ray imagery is vital for various clinical uses, especially for image-guided interventions and workflow automation. Current deep learning models depend heavily on extensive labeled datasets. However, acquiring precise pixel-level annotations for X-rays is challenging, as it requires skilled clinicians to navigate complex textures and significant anatomical overlaps. Conversely, 3D CT scans offer distinct organ structures with sharper boundaries, making delineation straightforward. This paper introduces a novel framework to learn automatic X-ray parsing using labeled CT data. First, a Dense Image-to-Image network (DI2I) for multi-organ segmentation is trained on Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs (DRRs) synthesized from 3D CT volumes. Next, a Task Driven Generative Adversarial Network (TD-GAN) is employed to perform simultaneous style transfer and parsing on unseen real X-ray images. The TD-GAN integrates a modified Cycle-GAN substructure for translating between DRRs and X-rays with an additional module that utilizes the pre-trained DI2I to ensure segmentation consistency. This framework is versatile and adaptable to other learning tasks. Experimental validation on 815 DRRs and 153 topograms demonstrates that while the standard DI2I fails completely on topograms without adaptation, the proposed model requires no topogram labels and achieves a promising average Dice score of 85%, matching the accuracy of supervised training (88%).

This study investigates the efficacy of deep learning for diagnosing lung cancer within medical image analysis. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have gained prominence in pattern recognition and computer vision due to their ability to generate robust high-level image representations. We introduce a novel deep learning architecture designed to achieve high classification accuracy with reduced variance in binary medical image classification by learning discriminative compact features at the network's initial layers. Our proposed model is evaluated using the Kaggle Data Science Bowl 2017 dataset and benchmarked against other related works from the competition.

Speech enhancement and separation are foundational components of robust speech processing, where the former aims to suppress background noise and the latter isolates target speech from interfering sources. Although numerous supervised learning-based methods have been developed with strong performance, research into applying self-supervised learning (SSL) to these tasks remains scarce. This paper assesses 13 SSL upstream models across speech enhancement and separation downstream tasks. Experiments conducted on the Voicebank-DEMAND and Libri2Mix datasets demonstrate that certain SSL representations consistently surpass baseline features, such as short-time Fourier transform (STFT) magnitude and log Mel filterbank (FBANK) representations. Additionally, we investigate the challenges hindering the application of current SSL frameworks to these domains and identify the specific representation properties required for both tasks. This study serves as the official benchmark for speech enhancement and separation within the SUPERB framework.

This study introduces a hybrid collocation technique combining finite differences with Haar wavelets to address nonlocal hyperbolic partial differential equations. Creating an efficient and precise numerical solution for such problems is challenging due to nonlocal boundary conditions. The proposed approach excels by effectively managing integral boundary conditions using available data. Leveraging the advantageous traits of Haar wavelets—including closed-form expressions, compact support, and orthonormality—we apply them for spatial discretization, while utilizing second-order finite differences for temporal discretization. We also examine stability and derive error estimates to guarantee the method's convergence. Furthermore, numerical results are benchmarked against existing solutions, demonstrating that our proposed method yields superior outcomes.

This paper investigates Ricci pseudosymmetric $(LCS)_n$-manifolds equipped with a Ricci soliton metric. We establish the conditions under which Ricci solitons on concircular, projective, $W_{3}$, conharmonic, and conformal Ricci pseudosymmetric $(LCS)_n$-manifolds are shrinking, steady, or expanding. Furthermore, we provide an example of a concircular Ricci pseudosymmetric $(LCS)_3$-manifold whose metric constitutes a Ricci soliton.

Indexes enable rapid data retrieval in databases by pre-building structures that accelerate query response times; however, their creation and continuous updates incur significant overhead. In-memory databases typically outperform disk-based systems in query processing, making them ideal for real-time applications, yet they urgently require methods to lower the costs associated with index creation and updates. Database cracking is currently an effective technique for reducing initialization time, though existing algorithms primarily address simple columnar structures rather than the complex indexes found in in-memory systems. To demonstrate the feasibility of cracking indexes for in-memory databases and encourage further research, this paper presents a case study on the Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), a widely used tree-based index. Following a detailed analysis of ART construction overhead, the study proposes an algorithm that leverages auxiliary data structures to efficiently crack ART indexes.

Although condensed matter physics encompasses both fermionic and bosonic quasi-particles, the reliable prediction and experimental confirmation of topological states remain well-established only for fermionic electronic systems, whereas topological bosonic excitations have been investigated only sporadically. This gap is significant because bosonic systems, such as those involving phonons, provide a unique avenue to study spinless band structures where nodal lines can emerge without relying on special symmetries to counteract spin-orbit coupling. In this work, we integrate first-principles calculations with meV-resolution inelastic x-ray scattering to report the first observation of parity-time reversal ($\mathcal{PT}$) symmetry-protected helical nodal lines within the phonon spectrum of MoB$_{2}$. This phenomenon is distinct to phononic systems, as the spin-orbit coupling inherent in electronic systems typically disrupts degeneracy away from high-symmetry points. Our findings establish a robust protocol for accurately identifying topological bosonic excitations, thereby opening new pathways to investigate exotic topological states in crystalline materials.

This study examines how constraints on cosmological and astrophysical parameters ($\Omega_{\rm m}$, $\sigma_{8}$, $A_{\rm SN1}$, $A_{\rm SN2}$) change when leveraging data from multiple cosmological fields. Utilizing a convolutional neural network, we extract key features from various combinations of field maps within the IllustrisTNG simulation of the CAMELS project. The specific fields analyzed include neutral hydrogen (HI), gas mass density (Mgas), magnetic fields (B), and gas metallicity (Z). Predictive uncertainty is quantified using Monte Carlo dropout as a Bayesian approximation. Our results indicate that model performance for all parameters improves as the number of input channels increases. Compared to prior research, our approach achieves up to $5\%$ higher accuracy in predicting astrophysical parameters. In the optimal configuration utilizing all four fields (Mgas-HI-B-Z), the model attains an $R^{2} > 0.96$ across all parameters. Furthermore, we observe that total uncertainty, primarily driven by aleatoric uncertainty, generally diminishes as more fields are incorporated into the training. However, the predictive uncertainty derived from dropout variational inference is initially overestimated for all parameters, with values significantly exceeding the actual squared error. Following calibration via a simple $\sigma$ scaling method, the maximum average deviation between total uncertainty and actual error reduces to $25\%$ (observed for $A_{\rm SN1}$).

Current advancements in Natural Language Processing (NLP), fueled by pretrained models trained on vast datasets, have primarily advantaged the world's political and economic leaders, leaving technologically marginalized languages behind due to a scarcity of resources. However, hundreds of these underserved languages possess valuable data in the form of interlinear glossed text (IGT) generated by language documentation initiatives. Despite this, IGT remains largely untapped in NLP research, likely because its annotations are semi-structured and often specific to individual languages. This paper argues that IGT can be effectively utilized in NLP when supported by target language expertise, specifically through collaboration with documentary linguists. We outline a strategic roadmap for such projects: first, identifying feasible NLP tasks and their benefits to the speech community; second, meticulously converting data into standard structured formats with the aid of linguistic expertise; and third, conducting task- and user-specific evaluations to ensure the resulting tools genuinely serve the community. These steps are demonstrated through a case study on creating a morphological reinflection system for the Gitksan language.

The relentless pursuit of knowledge remains humanity's enduring objective. Over the last century, scientific literature—the primary conduit for sharing knowledge among researchers—has experienced exponential expansion. Although numerous tangible metrics, such as citations, impact factors, and the g-index, are frequently employed to quantify paper influence and scientific productivity from various angles, the relationship between productivity and the actual volume of knowledge remains poorly understood. Specifically, it is unclear how the knowledge value and quantity of papers evolve as a discipline develops, raising the critical question of whether high scientific productivity necessarily equates to a large knowledge base. Addressing this, we leverage extensive literature on academic journals and conferences to compile a dataset of 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines from 1970 to 2020. We construct a citation network research area to map the flow of knowledge from cited authors to citing authors within each specific domain. The resulting structure, which evolves over time, implicitly reveals how knowledge flows between nodes and how these dynamics shift as literature volume (productivity) increases. By utilizing Structural entropy in structured high-dimensional space and Shannon entropy in unstructured probability space, we introduce the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI). Defined as the difference between these two entropy types, KQI reflects the extent of disorder (knowledge amount) generated by structural order. Using KQI, our analysis indicates that while published literature has grown explosively, the actual knowledge contained within it has noticeably decelerated; however, a threshold exists beyond which knowledge growth begins to accelerate.

As a recently established professional role, research software engineers (RSEs) bridge the gap between software engineering and scientific research. However, they face ambiguous pathways for development and training, especially regarding mentorship. This paper examines mentorship in the context of RSEs' specific requirements and suggests strategies for organizations and institutions to foster effective mentor-mentee relationships for this group.

The monoidal category of twisted modules for a Vertex Operator Algebra $V$ is constructed and simplified to its 2-group of invertible objects, denoted $G_\alpha$. This structure is characterized by a 3-cocycle $\alpha$ defined on the 0-truncation $G$ with values in the unit group $A$ of the field over which $V$ is defined, where $\alpha$ functions as the associator. Furthermore, this cocycle defines the classifying morphism for an $\infty$-group extension of $G$ by the delooping $BA$. Inspired by this connection, it is demonstrated that an $\infty$-group extension classified by a 3-cocycle $\alpha$ is represented by the skeletal 2-group $G_\alpha$ equipped with $\alpha$ as its associator. These findings are contextualized within recent advancements in Moonshine theory and $(\infty,1)$-topos theory.

Cross-domain knowledge integration is a fundamental aspect of human cognition. Paradigms such as transfer learning, meta-learning, and multi-task learning emulate this process by leveraging prior knowledge to accelerate learning and enhance generalization on new tasks. This article offers a comprehensive examination and comparative analysis of these approaches. While individual weaknesses in one algorithm often complement the strengths of another—leading to their frequent combination in existing literature—many prior studies have focused exclusively on each paradigm in isolation. In contrast, this survey specifically reviews research that synthesizes two or more of these learning strategies. It outlines how these combined techniques address challenges across diverse fields, including computer vision, natural language processing, and hyperspectral imaging, within supervised learning frameworks. Consequently, the paper introduces the Global Generic Learning Network, which amalgamates meta-learning, transfer learning, and multi-task learning, while also highlighting open research questions and future directions in the multi-task domain.

This study examines linear elliptic systems arising in composite materials, where coefficients vary with the shape and may exhibit discontinuities across subregions. We introduce a function linked to the gradient of weak solutions that achieves local Hölder continuity, improving upon prior local piecewise Hölder continuity. Using this derived function, we estimate the gradient of weak solutions and establish local piecewise gradient Hölder continuity, confirming results previously obtained.

This paper outlines an efficient model-based diagnostic approach for systems where component inputs and outputs exhibit causal relationships. The process begins by identifying a set of likely faulty components and then determining the most informative probe point within each candidate group. Both steps operate with a worst-case time complexity of ${\cal O}(n^2)$, where $n$ represents the number of components; however, if component connectivity is low, the complexity reduces to linear time. The study also demonstrates the applicability of this method to dynamic systems and those containing feedback loops. Specifically, when diagnosing dynamic systems, there is an option to either detect intermittent faults or enhance diagnostic accuracy by assuming faults are non-intermittent.

Jet tagging represents a vital but difficult classification challenge within particle physics. Although deep learning has revolutionized this field and boosted performance, the absence of extensive public datasets limits further progress. This study introduces JetClass, a comprehensive new dataset comprising 100 million jets, which is approximately 100 times larger than current public resources. The dataset simulates 10 distinct jet types, covering several categories previously unexplored for tagging. Leveraging this extensive data, we developed the Particle Transformer (ParT), a novel Transformer-based architecture. By integrating pairwise particle interactions into its attention mechanism, ParT outperforms standard Transformers and exceeds the prior state-of-the-art, ParticleNet, by a significant margin. Additionally, fine-tuned pre-trained ParT models substantially improve results on two widely used jet tagging benchmarks. The dataset, source code, and models are publicly accessible at https://github.com/jet-universe/particle_transformer.

This paper investigates physical layer security (PLS) within a dual-hop orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) wireless communication framework. Initially, the study focuses on a single-user, single-relay configuration, addressing a joint power optimization problem at the source and relay under individual power constraints for both nodes, with the goal of maximizing the end-to-end secrecy rate through optimal power allocation across sub-carriers. Subsequently, the research expands to a more complex multi-user, multi-relay scenario. Utilizing a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) approximation for the end-to-end secrecy rate, an optimization problem is defined to jointly optimize power allocation at the base station, relay selection, sub-carrier assignment to users, and power loading at each relay node. The objective is to enhance overall system security while adhering to independent power budget limits at each transmitter and exclusive sub-carrier allocation constraints inherent to OFDMA. A joint optimization solution is derived using duality theory, where dual decomposition enables the application of convex optimization techniques to determine power loading at source and relay nodes. Additionally, the paper examines an optimization for relay power loading, relay selection, and sub-carrier assignment given a fixed base station power allocation. Finally, a sub-optimal scheme exploring joint power allocation across all transmitting nodes with fixed sub-carrier and relay assignments is analyzed. Simulation results are provided to validate the performance of the proposed schemes.

This paper establishes a second main theorem in Nevanlinna theory for meromorphic mappings involving arbitrary families of hypersurfaces within projective varieties by introducing the concept of a "distributive constant." This new theorem extends and refines prior findings concerning hypersurfaces, specifically addressing algebraically degenerate mappings and those in subgeneral position. Additionally, analogous results are provided for holomorphic curves with finite growth indices mapping from a complex disc into a projective variety, as well as for meromorphic mappings defined on a complete K\"{a}hler manifold. To achieve this final objective, we prove a Schmidt's subspace theorem applicable to arbitrary families of homogeneous polynomials, serving as the number-theoretic counterpart to our main theorem. Collectively, these findings represent significant generalizations and enhancements of all previous results in the field.

This paper tackles privacy-preserving federated neural network training involving $N$ users by introducing Hercules, a high-precision and efficient framework capable of withstanding collusion among up to $N-1$ users. Building upon the POSEIDON framework by Sav et al. (NDSS'21), Hercules achieves a significant performance leap through two key contributions: (i) a novel parallel homomorphic computation method for matrix operations that facilitates rapid Single Instruction and Multiple Data (SIMD) operations on ciphertexts, reducing the computational complexity of multiplying two $h\times h$ matrices from $O(h^3)$ to $O(h)$, thereby substantially enhancing training efficiency given that convolution operations dominate ciphertext computation; and (ii) an efficient sign function approximation utilizing composite polynomial approximation to model non-polynomial functions like ReLU and max with optimal asymptotic complexity. Extensive experiments across various benchmark datasets (BCW, ESR, CREDIT, MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100) demonstrate that Hercules outperforms POSEIDON by achieving up to a 4% increase in model accuracy while reducing both computation and communication costs by up to 60$\times$.

This work investigates coalgebraic modal logic to define behavioral equivalence within contexts involving side effects, specifically when coalgebras are situated in (co)Kleisli or Eilenberg-Moore categories. Our objective is to establish a unified framework utilizing indexed categories or fibrations that applies across these categories. Specifically, we demonstrate that the coalgebraic concept of behavioral equivalence stems from relation liftings—a particular type of indexed morphism—and provide a general method for constructing such liftings in the three specified scenarios. Finally, we utilize this framework to derive logical characterizations for (weighted) language equivalence and conditional bisimilarity.

This study examines mean-field dynamo models featuring a fluctuating $\alpha$ effect, analyzing scenarios both with and without shear. The $\alpha$ effect is modeled as Gaussian white noise with a zero mean and a specified covariance. Analytical results demonstrate that while the mean magnetic field does not increase, the mean-squared magnetic field in an infinitely large domain exhibits exponential growth for the fastest growing mode; this growth rate is proportional to the shear rate. These findings align with previous numerical simulations by Yousef et al. (2008) and recent analytical work by Heinemann et al. (2011), which employed a distinct methodology. In the absence of shear, an incoherent $\alpha^2$ dynamo remains a possibility. Furthermore, explicit calculations of the growth rates for the third and fourth moments of the magnetic field confirm that the probability density function of the mean magnetic field produced by this dynamo is non-Gaussian.

This study examines a dusty plasma system comprising nonthermally distributed inertialess electrons, warm inertial ions, and positively charged stationary dust. Using the reductive perturbation method, the fundamental characteristics of subsonic and supersonic modified ion-acoustic solitary and shock waves within this system were analyzed. The findings indicate that positively charged dust species facilitate the creation of subsonic solitary and shock waves. Conversely, the ion fluid temperature (denoted by $\sigma$) and the electron nonthermal parameter (denoted by $\alpha$) act to inhibit subsonic wave formation; however, once these parameters exceed specific thresholds, they promote the emergence of supersonic solitary and shock waves. Furthermore, it was demonstrated that surpassing a critical value of the nonthermal parameter $\alpha$ results in the formation of both subsonic and supersonic solitary and shock waves characterized by negative potential. The potential applications of these theoretical findings for both space and laboratory dusty plasma environments are also highlighted.

To determine the inertial range power spectrum of compressible turbulence, we utilize an analytic model for steady-state conditions. We posit that in homogeneous turbulence, the timescales governing energy injection from smaller to a specific wavenumber are identical across all spatial components. Nevertheless, because longitudinal energy is siphoned off into compression, the turbulent viscosity rate responsible for transferring energy to larger wavenumbers is diminished. This mechanism yields an inertial range characterized by a power law with an index of -2, a pattern confirmed by observations in diverse astrophysical environments and numerical simulations.

This review examines recent experimental and theoretical/phenomenological advances concerning the phase structure of strongly interacting matter. It details the evolution of net-proton number fluctuations with collision energy, as observed by various experiments, and outlines their implications for the QCD phase diagram. Furthermore, it presents theoretical calculations regarding correlations among conserved charges and discusses prospects for their experimental investigation.

This paper examines various invariants closely linked to Dirac operators defined on odd-dimensional manifolds with boundaries, under the action of a compact isometry group $H$. Specifically, we prove the equivalence among equivariant winding numbers, spectral flow, and Maslov indices. Additionally, we analyze equivariant $\eta$-invariants, which are essential for the equivariant version of Getzler's spectral flow formula. As a result, we derive a connection between these equivariant $\eta$-invariants and equivariant Maslov triple indices arising from the splitting of manifolds.

A novel approach for simulating a binary homogeneous Markov process on a quantum computer has been introduced, leveraging key quantum mechanical attributes such as superposition, entanglement, and probability computation. Executing this method necessitates a specialized two-qubit logic gate capable of generating entanglement; this gate applies a specific X-axis rotation to the target qubit, where the rotation magnitude corresponds to the transient probabilities of the Markov process, but only activates when the control qubit is in the |1> state. Developing an algorithm that intuitively utilizes transient probability distributions to determine these X-axis offsets is essential. While it is feasible to construct a quantum controlled n-th root of X gate using standard basic gates available on cloud platforms, current hardware noise levels significantly inflate measurement errors. Among the tested devices, IBM's Yorktown 'bow-tie' architecture demonstrated superior quantum fidelity compared to the 5-qubit T-shaped and 14-qubit Melbourne processors. Simulation results on real quantum hardware achieved the highest fidelity, nearing 0.82 via the Hellinger metric, on the 5-qubit Vigo and Yorktown back-ends. Ultimately, optimizing fidelity requires selecting a quantum circuit that aligns with the specific hardware constraints, including topology, size, and timing properties.

This research examines proof systems that extend resolution with inference rules capable of deriving clauses from a conjunctive normal form formula $\Gamma$. These derived clauses may not be logical consequences of $\Gamma$, but adding them to $\Gamma$ maintains satisfiability. While allowing new variables yields systems equivalent to extended resolution, this study focuses on versions restricted to the original variables, termed BC${}^-$, RAT${}^-$, SBC${}^-$, and GER${}^-$, which stand for blocked clauses, resolution asymmetric tautologies, set-blocked clauses, and generalized extended resolution, respectively. Each system formalizes a constrained form of the "without loss of generality" assumption often used to simplify proofs. Although SBC${}^-$ is an exception, the other systems are known to be exponentially weaker than extended resolution. However, they are all equivalent to extended resolution under a relaxed simulation model that permits translating both the formula and the proof when moving between systems. Leveraging this equivalence, we construct formulas that separate RAT${}^-$ from GER${}^-$ and vice versa, and similarly separate SBC${}^-$ from RAT${}^-$. Furthermore, we provide polynomial-size SBC${}^-$ proofs for the pigeonhole principle, separating SBC${}^-$ from GER${}^-$ based on an existing lower bound. These findings also distinguish these three systems from BC${}^-$, as they all simulate it. Consequently, we present an almost comprehensive overview of their relative strengths.

Let $\Gamma$ denote a Fuchsian group of the first kind. For any even integer $m \ge 4$, we characterize the space $H^{m/2}\left(\mathfrak R_\Gamma\right)$ of $m/2$-holomorphic differentials by identifying it with a subspace $S_m^H(\Gamma)$ within the space of cuspidal holomorphic modular forms $S_m(\Gamma)$. This result extends the classical isomorphism $S_2(\Gamma)\simeq H^{1}\left(\mathfrak R_\Gamma\right)$. We examine the properties of $S_m^H(\Gamma)$ and apply this analysis to detail the algorithm in SAGE used to determine whether a cusp at $\infty$ on a non-hyperelliptic curve $X_0(N)$ constitutes a $\frac{m}{2}$-Weierstrass point.

Neuromorphic hardware platforms can substantially reduce the energy consumption associated with machine learning inference. This work presents a design-technology tradeoff analysis for executing such inference tasks on the processing elements (PEs) of Non-Volatile Memory (NVM)-based neuromorphic systems. Through detailed circuit-level simulations using scaled process nodes, we demonstrate that technology scaling negatively affects information-processing latency, thereby degrading the quality-of-service (QoS) in embedded ML systems. Specifically, latency within a PE is determined by two factors: delays caused by parasitic components on current paths and the variable sensing times for different resistance states in NVM cells. Based on these findings, we offer three key contributions. First, at the technology level, we propose an optimization strategy that maps the NVM resistance state with the longest sensing time to current paths with minimal delay, and vice versa, thereby lowering average PE latency and enhancing QoS. Second, at the architecture level, we introduce isolation transistors within each PE to divide it into regions capable of individual power gating, which reduces both latency and energy usage. Finally, at the system-software level, we develop a mechanism to exploit these technological and architectural improvements during the implementation of ML inference tasks on neuromorphic PEs. Evaluations using a recent neuromorphic hardware architecture indicate that our proposed design-technology co-optimization approach enhances both performance and energy efficiency for machine learning inference without incurring a high cost-per-bit.

Quantum Darwinism explains how classical, objective features typically observed at macroscopic scales emerge from microscopic quantum properties. This process occurs when a quantum system interacts with its environment, redundantly spreading information across many environmental components, thereby making the information accessible and objective to various observers. However, since direct probing of the quantum system is impossible and only its environment can be accessed, determining whether an unknown quantum property is truly objective remains a challenge. We introduce a probabilistic framework to address this issue, demonstrating that objectivity necessitates the satisfaction of a Bell-like inequality. Our analysis reveals quantum violations of this inequality, providing a device-independent proof that certain quantum correlations are non-objective. We term the resulting phenomenon "collective hallucination," where observers examining different parts of the environment may agree on a measurement outcome for a specific observable, yet that outcome remains entirely uncorrelated with the actual property of the quantum system being measured. Furthermore, we present a photonic experiment utilizing the temporal degree of freedom of photons as the quantum system and their polarization as the environment. By employing a fully black-box approach, we achieve a violation of a Bell inequality, thereby certifying the non-objectivity of the underlying quantum dynamics within a completely device-independent framework.

This paper investigates a class of conservative bandit problems (CBPs) subject to sample-path reward constraints, requiring the learner's performance to remain at least as high as a specified baseline at every time step. We introduce a unified One-Size-Fits-All approach for CBPs and demonstrate its applicability to three related domains: conservative multi-armed bandits (CMAB), conservative linear bandits (CLB), and conservative contextual combinatorial bandits (CCCB). Unlike prior research that typically imposes high-probability constraints on expected rewards, our method focuses on constraints applied to the actual received rewards, yielding superior theoretical guarantees—specifically, $T$-independent additive regrets rather than $T$-dependent ones—and enhanced empirical performance. Additionally, we generalize these findings to address a novel conservative mean-variance bandit problem (MV-CBP), which evaluates learning performance based on both expected reward and variability. For this extension, we develop a new algorithm achieving $O(1/T)$ normalized additive regrets (equivalent to $T$-independent cumulative regrets), a result confirmed through empirical evaluation.

We investigate the effects of applying random, repeated resets to the initial condition on the paradigmatic Kuramoto model, which features interacting oscillators with distributed natural frequencies and exhibits spontaneous collective synchronization in its stationary state. Although resetting can occur from a synchronized state, the system may desynchronize between two consecutive resets, a phenomenon contingent upon the duration of the random interval separating them. This study reveals how such a stochastic resetting protocol fundamentally alters the phase diagram of the original model, notably enabling the emergence of a synchronized phase even in parameter regimes where the unresetted model fails to sustain it. Our findings rely on an exact analytical approach utilizing the celebrated Ott-Antonsen ansatz for Lorentzian frequency distributions, complemented by numerical simulations for Gaussian distributions. Ultimately, this work presents a straightforward method to induce global synchrony within the system via stochastic resetting.

In recent years, high-energy vector meson photoproduction has garnered significant attention owing to the distinctive kinematic ranges accessible through LHC experiments. Both the ALICE and LHCb collaborations have delivered measurements of this process on both proton and nuclear targets, specifically involving p, Pb, and Xe. The extensive datasets from LHC Run 2 now enable more granular differential analyses.

Recently, ALICE and LHCb have reported measurements of coherent $\jpsi$ production in ultra-peripheral collisions (UPC) within $\PbPb$ interactions. Notably, ALICE has presented the first study of the $|t|$-dependence for coherent $\jpsi$ in $\PbPb$ collisions and has also measured coherent $\rhozero$ photoproduction off Pb and Xe targets, marking the inaugural investigation into the A-dependence of this process.

Furthermore, ALICE and LHCb have observed vector meson photoproduction in peripheral $\PbPb$ collisions, offering a robust method to determine photonuclear cross sections at a low Bjorken-$x$ value of approximately $10^{-5}$. Finally, the text briefly explores the potential of ultra-peripheral collisions for searching for tetraquarks.

Monocular visual odometry estimates an agent's position using images from a single camera, a technique utilized in autonomous vehicles, medical robotics, and augmented reality. Nevertheless, these systems are hindered by scale ambiguity, stemming from the absence of depth cues in two-dimensional frames. This paper introduces the application of a dense prediction transformer model to address scale estimation within monocular visual odometry. Experimental findings demonstrate that this model significantly mitigates scale drift by generating accurate depth maps, thereby achieving performance that rivals current state-of-the-art results on visual odometry benchmarks.

Quantum coherence arising from a physical process can only be considered a valuable resource if it remains detectable at a later stage. Recently, the concept of non-coherence-generating-and-detecting (NCGD) dynamics was introduced and linked to the classical nature of statistics observed in sequential measurements across different times. For a dynamics to qualify as NCGD, its propagators must fulfill a specific set of conditions for every triple of consecutive time points. Assuming a time-independent generator, we simplify this requirement to a finite set of $d(d-1)$ conditions, where $d$ represents the dimension of the quantum system. Additional constraints are established for the more complex scenario involving time-dependent generators. Applying these findings to qubit dynamics clarifies the specific types of noise responsible for non-coherence-generation-and-detection.

Recently, pre-trained language models like BERT have been utilized in document ranking for information retrieval, typically involving pre-training on large unlabeled corpora followed by fine-tuning on expert-labeled relevance datasets.
