Recent research highlights that local conserved quantities are pivotal in regulating the relaxation dynamics of OTOCs in non-integrable systems, particularly causing slow scrambling when observables overlap with these quantities. Notably, an observable might not overlap directly with the Hamiltonian but rather with the Hamiltonian raised to a power greater than one. This study demonstrates that such higher exponents lead to faster, albeit algebraic, relaxation rates, with these exponents capable of increasing without bound. These analytical findings are corroborated by numerical simulations.

A one-dimensional model has been developed to investigate sub-femtosecond experiments involving metal surfaces. This model incorporates key system characteristics, including the pseudopotential governing electron motion within the metal bulk, the sharp decline of the external electromagnetic field normal to the surface inside the bulk, the finite mean free path of electrons, and the influence of a stationary, screened positive hole on ejected electrons. The findings indicate that the streaking effect depends on the final energy of the ejected electron. However, the dependence on the nature of the initial state—whether localized or delocalized—is even more significant. This insight may offer an additional mechanism for interpreting the results of recent experiments, specifically those by Cavalieri et al. (Nature 449, 1029-1032, 2007).

The COVID-19 crisis accelerated the spread of research and preprints concerning the virus and the disease. Although the complexity of the situation requires a multidisciplinary strategy, the urgency of the emergency and social distancing constraints posed distinct hurdles for scientific collaboration. To address this, we utilized Manubot to implement a large-scale, open online publishing model. By leveraging GitHub, a team of collaborators summarized and critiqued existing literature to draft a review manuscript. Manubot automatically gathered citation data from diverse sources, including clinical trials, journals, websites, and preprints. Nightly continuous integration workflows fetched the latest data from online repositories, automatically regenerating specific figures and statistics. The system also rendered the manuscript into PDF, HTML, LaTeX, and DOCX formats, instantly updating the online version whenever new content was integrated. This initiative coordinated over 50 scientists from varied disciplines who assessed more than 1,500 sources to produce seven literature reviews. While the computational community has largely focused on mining COVID-19 data, our project demonstrates how open publishing can mobilize both technical and non-expert scientists to effectively aggregate and share information during an evolving crisis.

Stochastic games integrate controllable and adversarial non-determinism with probabilistic dynamics, serving as a fundamental framework for controlling, verifying, and synthesizing reactive systems under uncertainty. Multi-objective stochastic games are particularly applicable when multiple, potentially conflicting performance metrics—such as time and energy usage—are involved; the literature predominantly focuses on conjunctive combinations of these objectives. In contrast, this paper addresses the dual disjunctive problem. Specifically, we examine turn-based, two-player stochastic games on graphs where the winning condition requires guaranteeing at least one reachability or safety goal from a provided set of alternatives. We offer a detailed analysis of the strategy and computational complexity associated with these disjunctive queries (DQs) and establish new lower and upper bounds for various problem variants, substantially advancing prior research. Furthermore, we introduce a novel value iteration-based algorithm designed to approximate the set of Pareto optimal thresholds for a given DQ.

This paper explores the extension of the bubble transform to differential forms. Previously, the authors introduced this transform for scalar functions (zero-forms) as a novel instrument for analyzing finite element spaces with arbitrary polynomial degrees. This study applies a similar approach to differential forms. Starting from a simplicial mesh of the domain, we construct a mapping that breaks down piecewise smooth $k$-forms into a sum of local bubbles supported on specific macroelements. The decomposition is characterized by its commutativity with the exterior derivative and its ability to maintain the piecewise polynomial nature of standard finite element spaces for $k$-forms. Additionally, the transform is bounded within $L^2$ and on the corresponding subspace of $k$-forms whose exterior derivatives also belong to $L^2$.

**Aims.** This study analyzes how the galaxy number density in input data influences the detection of filaments using the Bisous filament finder and evaluates the method's reliability to ensure result robustness.

**Methods.** The Bisous filament finder was applied to MultiDark-Galaxies data with varying magnitude cuts to examine the impact of different galaxy number densities and model parameters. Structures were compared based on the fraction of galaxies within filaments and the volume they occupy, while similarities across different cuts were assessed via the overlap of detected filamentary networks. Additionally, the finder was run 200 times on identical data with fixed parameters to evaluate stochasticity, and correlations between these runs were computed.

**Results.** Multiple samples indicate that galaxies located in filaments tend to have higher luminosities. Analysis reveals a 97% probability that a galaxy identified in a filament will also be found in one with more complete data, and approximately 85% of filaments persist when higher-density inputs are used. Lower galaxy number densities result in fewer detected filaments, yet those found remain persistent even with more complete data. The correlation coefficient between 200 independent Bisous runs on the same input was calculated to be 0.98.

**Conclusions.** The findings confirm that higher galaxy number densities are essential for obtaining a comprehensive view of the cosmic web. To address limitations in spectroscopic surveys, the Bisous model will be further developed to apply this tool to combined spectroscopic and narrow-band photometric redshift surveys, such as J-PAS.

Currently, data-driven discovery in biological sciences focuses on identifying segmentation strategies within multivariate data that yield meaningful descriptions. While clustering is one such approach, it often falls short due to challenges in determining appropriate cutoffs, deciding the optimal number of clusters, or failing to maintain the topological properties of the original system. This work demonstrates how a straightforward metric for evaluating connectivity clustering can lead to an optimized segmentation of biological data. The innovation lies in developing a simple optimization method for clustering dense datasets, where the approach relies solely on metrics derived from the clustering's inherent properties. This new method promotes optimized clustering through an implementation that is both accessible and easy to adopt. We examine how this clustering optimization strategy aligns with the viable information content produced by the final segmentation and further elaborate on how the optimal clustering results correspond to prior knowledge across three distinct datasets.

The High Luminosity LHC necessitates dipole orbit correctors housed within double-aperture magnet assemblies, which generate a 3.1 T field at 100 A within a 70 mm aperture. While the current standard utilizes a classical cosine-theta configuration constructed from ribbon cable, the insulation of this cable lacks sufficient radiation resistance for the anticipated operational loads of the LHC. Consequently, a replacement design employing a radiation-hardened cable with polyimide insulation is required to succeed the existing orbit correctors at the end of their lifecycle. This new magnet must integrate seamlessly into current positions and remain compatible with existing busbars, passive quench protection systems, and power supplies. We propose a self-protected canted-cosine-theta (CCT) design, leveraging this opportunity to refine CCT concepts into a cost-effective, high-quality solution that promotes sustainable resource use. The proposed design satisfies stringent field quality requirements while adhering to the original mechanical volume and maximum excitation current limits.

To achieve this, a partnership between Swedish universities and industry has been established to develop and manufacture a prototype magnet using concurrent engineering (CE) methodologies to accelerate production timelines. The prototype features a 1-meter-long CCT dipole arrangement comprising two coils. It utilizes commercially available 0.33 mm superconducting wire with polyimide insulation, wound into a 6-around-1 cable configuration. The coil formers are machined with channels accommodating two layers of five cable strands each. With a total of 70 windings, the design ensures the coil current remains below 100 A. This presentation will detail the comprehensive design and offer preliminary quench simulations.

A primary unresolved issue in Descriptive Complexity concerns the existence of a logic capable of characterizing deterministic polynomial time (PTIME) over relational structures. To address this, we introduce a logic derived from first-order logic with fixed points (FO(FP)) through specific transformations, such as limiting logical connectives and incorporating a dynamic variant of Hilbert's Choice operator, Epsilon. This formalism functions dually as an algebra of binary relations and a linear-time modal dynamic logic, where algebraic expressions representing "proofs" or "programs" are embedded within modalities. We demonstrate how the logic axiomatizes counting, reachability, and hybrid cases involving linear equations modulo two, as well as the encoding of arbitrary PTIME Turing machines. While model checking for any fixed Choice function falls within PTIME, the potential number of such functions is exponential. A pivotal inquiry is identifying the syntactic constraints on algebraic terms that render the verification of a single Choice function sufficient. Resolving this demands an investigation into computational symmetries. Consequently, this paper establishes the necessary mathematical foundations for such research using algebraic and automata-theoretic methods.

Current terrestrial networks struggle to maintain strong communication links with unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) because access points (APs) are down-tilted to prioritize ground user equipment (GUEs). While tilting AP antennas upward or increasing transmit power could address this, such measures degrade downlink (DL) rates for GUEs. This paper proposes leveraging a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) to boost UAV communication without altering the standard downward antenna tilt, potentially enhancing GUE DL performance as well. We demonstrate that, utilizing conjugate beamforming (CB) precoding and an optimal power allocation between GUEs and the UAV, an RIS configured to reflect signals toward the UAV can substantially increase UAV DL throughput while simultaneously benefiting GUEs. Numerical simulations across varying RIS element counts, UAV altitudes, and power split factors confirm that this RIS-assisted approach can meet the UAV's data rate requirements while outperforming conventional CF-MIMO systems (without RIS or UAV) in terms of GUE DL performance.

This paper revisits the challenge of calculating control invariant sets for linear discrete-time systems using a data-driven methodology, a technique essential for ensuring safe control operations. The approach involves recording sample points along convergent trajectories from linear Model Predictive Control (MPC), where the convex hull of these points constructs the control invariant set. To approximate this convex hull across multiple samples, a convex piecewise linear (PWL) fitting framework is introduced, producing a polyhedral approximation with a user-defined complexity level. Additionally, a descent algorithm tailored for convex PWL fitting is developed, ensuring convergence to a local optimum. This strategy offers flexibility in computing control invariant sets for high-dimensional systems while maintaining a predefined complexity. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed data-driven approximation achieves high accuracy in determining the control invariant set with relatively low computational expense.

The widespread adoption of continuous monitoring systems, equipped with an expanding array of sensors, has permeated numerous application areas. Although the resulting data is often high-dimensional and complex to interpret, it is theorized to exist within a lower-dimensional manifold. While many deep learning (DL) models attempt to uncover this manifold, they frequently fail to enforce structure or ensure interpretability. We introduce the SOM-CPC model, which simultaneously optimizes Contrastive Predictive Coding (CPC) and a Self-Organizing Map (SOM) to discover an organized manifold. We tackle a previously underexplored and challenging set of scenarios involving high-rate time series, demonstrating through synthetic data as well as real-world medical and audio datasets that SOM-CPC surpasses robust baseline models combining DL with SOMs. With its ability to reveal latent patterns in high-frequency data streams, SOM-CPC holds significant promise for enhancing our understanding of diverse processes and systems.

We provide a detailed analysis of the proposal that time serves as the conjugate variable to the constants of nature, a concept where distinct times correspond to distinct constants, a hallmark of "relational time" frameworks. Specifically, we demonstrate how, in regions governed by a single constant, the Hamiltonian constraint can be recast as a Schrödinger equation within the associated time. This equation is solved in the connection representation using outgoing, monochromatic plane waves that propagate through a "space" extending the Chern-Simons functional. Our discussion places particular emphasis on unitarity and the choice of measure for the inner product. We construct normalizable superpositions, encompassing solitons, "light-rays," and coherent or squeezed states that satisfy the Heisenberg uncertainty relation between constants and their conjugate times. A robust classical limit emerges for factorizable coherent states in both mono-fluid and multi-fluid scenarios. For multi-fluid cases, we address transition regions where control shifts from one time to another, investigating the behavior of the subdominant clock. In this context, minisuperspace is optimally viewed as a dispersive medium where wave packets travel at a group speed differing from the phase speed. We confirm that the motion of these packet peaks accurately reproduces the classical limit, even during transitions and after the subdominant clock becomes negligible, although deviations from the coherent or semi-classical limit are anticipated in these instances. Given our recent cosmic shift from deceleration to acceleration, this proposal offers potential testability, a point explored in related work.

This paper explores various aspects of the symmetries inherent in the Duflo-Serganova functor. Specifically, we present novel constructions of Lie superalgebras, Lie supergroups, and associative superalgebras that act upon this functor. Our work builds upon a calculation by Heidersdorf and Weissauer regarding $DS_x$ for maximal rank $x$ acting on Kac-modules of $GL(n|n)$, extending these concepts and findings to the context of $P(n)$.

This paper investigates Time Series Extrinsic Regression (TSER), a regression task focused on modeling the connection between time series data and continuous scalar values. This objective is closely linked to time series classification (TSC), which instead predicts categorical class labels. TSER generalizes time series forecasting (TSF) by removing the constraint that predictions must correspond to future values or rely primarily on recent data. The authors motivate and explore this task, benchmarking existing solutions and TSC adaptations against a newly compiled archive of 19 TSER datasets. Results indicate that the state-of-the-art TSC algorithm, Rocket, when adapted for regression, outperforms other TSC adaptations and leading machine learning methods like XGBoost, Random Forest, and Support Vector Regression in overall accuracy. Crucially, the study highlights the necessity for further research to enhance the performance of ML models in this domain and suggests that future work holds significant promise for surpassing these current baseline approaches.

Earlier singer identification methods relied exclusively on either isolated monophonic vocals or mixed recordings containing multiple instruments, creating a semantic divide between these audio domains. This paper introduces a system that learns a unified embedding space for both monophonic and mixed singing tracks. By employing a metric learning technique, we ensure that tracks from the same singer across both domains are mapped closer together than those from different singers. The system is trained on a large synthetic dataset generated through music mashups to mirror real-world recordings. Our approach enables new cross-domain applications, such as retrieving mixed recordings of a specific singer when provided with a monophonic query, all without requiring additional vocal enhancement steps like source separation. We demonstrate the system's effectiveness for singer identification and query-by-singer tasks in both same-domain and cross-domain scenarios.

Since the inception of task automation, autonomous vehicles have garnered significant attention. Human drivers are susceptible to fatigue and exhibit delayed reaction times, compounding the inherent dangers of driving, which currently results in approximately 1.35 million fatalities annually from road accidents. Consequently, the potential for autonomous systems to mitigate global traffic incidents has driven extensive research interest. Presently, self-driving cars employ diverse algorithms to address specific sub-problems in achieving autonomy. This study concentrates on reinforcement learning techniques, specifically Q-learning and NeuroEvolution of Augmenting Topologies (NEAT)—a hybrid of evolutionary algorithms and artificial neural networks—to train an agent capable of navigating a designated path. The primary objective of this paper is to compare these two distinct algorithms.

Isochronous mass spectrometry (IMS) within heavy-ion storage rings serves as a potent instrument for measuring the masses of short-lived nuclei. In IMS, mass values are derived from high-precision measurements of ion revolution times; however, this method fails to distinguish between particles possessing nearly identical mass-to-charge (m/q) ratios. To address this constraint and accurately determine revolution times for ion pairs with closely matched m/q values, our earlier research on particle identification examined the amplitudes of timing signals generated by secondary electron emission. We have further refined this analytical approach by incorporating signal amplitudes, detection efficiencies, and the quantity of stored ions. The introduction of a Z-dependent parameter sensitive to these factors significantly enhanced the resolution of $^{34}$Ar$^{18+}$ and $^{51}$Co$^{27+}$ (A/Z=17/9). Consequently, the mean revolution times for these species were successfully deduced despite a time difference as minute as 1.8 ps, whereas their uncorrected, overlapping peak exhibited a full width at half maximum of 7.7 ps. The resulting mass excess for $^{51}$Co was calculated as -27332(41) keV, which aligns with the previously established value of -27342(48) keV.

Text-based games serve as rigorous environments for assessing virtual agents' capabilities in language comprehension, multi-step reasoning, and common-sense logic. However, existing systems are hindered by slow performance, limited to roughly 300 steps per second, primarily because of outdated infrastructure. We introduce TextWorldExpress, a high-performance framework implementing three standard text game benchmarks that boosts simulation speed by a factor of 1,000, achieving more than one million steps per second on standard desktops. This dramatic improvement drastically cuts experiment duration, allowing researchers to conduct billion-step simulations within a single day.
We establish the connectedness of the locus consisting of degree-$d$ branched self-coverings of $S^2$ that possess two critical points of order $d$, with one such point being $n$-periodic.

To characterize intricate emotional conditions, psychologists have introduced various emotion descriptors, including sparse facial action units, continuous metrics like valence and arousal, and discrete class labels such as happiness and anger. Ekman and Friesen (1969) theorize that facial action units function as sign vehicles transmitting emotional signals, whereas discrete and continuous descriptors represent the messages humans perceive and express. In this study, we developed an architecture for estimating multiple emotion descriptors as part of the ABAW3 Challenge. Drawing on Ekman and Friesen's framework, we constructed separate architectures to evaluate sign vehicles (facial action units) and messages (discrete emotions, valence, and arousal), accounting for their distinct characteristics. Quantitative experiments on the ABAW3 dataset demonstrate that our approach outperforms two baseline models.

This paper investigates a time-fractional initial-boundary value problem of Kirchhoff type featuring a memory term for non-homogeneous materials. By employing an energy argument, we establish a priori bounds on the solution, thereby proving the existence and uniqueness of the weak solution. We maintain the time variable in its continuous form while discretizing the spatial domain using a conforming Finite Element Method (FEM) to derive a semi-discrete formulation. The error analysis for this semi-discrete scheme utilizes a modified standard Ritz-Volterra projection operator. To achieve an efficient numerical solution, we introduce a new linearized L1 Galerkin FEM, which demonstrates a convergence rate of $O(h+k^{2-\alpha})$, where $\alpha$ ($0<\alpha<1$) represents the fractional derivative exponent and $h$ and $k$ denote the spatial and temporal discretization parameters, respectively. Furthermore, we propose a novel linearized L2-1$_{\sigma}$ Galerkin FEM to enhance the convergence rate in the time direction, achieving an accuracy of $O(h+k^{2})$. Finally, numerical experiments are performed to verify these theoretical results.

Simulating real-sized plasmonic nanostructures at the fully atomistic level is computationally intensive, which typically restricts calculations to small or medium-sized systems. Nevertheless, plasmonic characteristics are highly sensitive to the specific dimensions and geometry of these samples. This study significantly broadens the scope of classical, fully atomistic methods by leveraging advanced iterative Krylov-based numerical techniques. Specifically, we examine the recently developed $\omega$FQ model applied to carbon nanotubes, graphene-based nanostructures, and metal nanoparticles. We evaluate the performance of Generalized Minimal Residual (GMRES) and Quasi-Minimum Residual (QMR) algorithms, with particular attention to how convergence rates vary with system size (reaching up to one million atoms) and the physical parameters inherent to the atomistic framework.

Current computer vision approaches to art style analysis primarily target image generation by optimizing the recognition of low-level features like brushstrokes. However, capturing and controlling higher-level artistic qualities demands fundamentally distinct computational techniques. This study examines style representations learned by neural networks that incorporate these advanced characteristics. We observe that style features vary when trained using triplets annotated by art historians to indicate stylistic similarity. Additionally, networks utilizing statistical priors or pre-trained on photographic datasets like ImageNet can extract meaningful visual representations of artwork. We correlate the influence of expert human knowledge, statistical assumptions, and photo-realism priors on these representations with established art historical research, subsequently applying them to zero-shot artist classification. To support this research, we introduce the first large-scale dataset of portraits specifically curated for computational analysis.

This document provides an overview of derived nonhomogeneous Koszul duality over a field, primarily drawing from the author's memoir (arXiv:0905.2621). It aims to offer a pedagogical introduction and summary of the covariant duality linking DG-algebras and curved DG-coalgebras, alongside the triality connecting DG-modules, CDG-comodules, and CDG-contramodules. The text also incorporates personal reflections within its historical discussion.

Simulating RNA folding at an atomic level remains a significant challenge due to the limitations of current force fields and the computational difficulty of sampling rare conformational changes. To address these hurdles, we adapted an enhanced path sampling technique, previously effective for proteins, to RNA systems. This approach utilizes a soft, history-dependent biasing force informed by the RNA's native structure, which is combined with the atomistic force field to facilitate the generation of productive folding pathways. We present results from explicit solvent simulations of RNA molecules ranging from 20 to 47 nucleotides in length and varying degrees of topological complexity. Statistical analysis of the folding trajectories reveals that, unlike proteins, the free energy landscape of RNA is markedly frustrated, even in relatively short chains with simple topologies. The observed folding mechanisms and thermodynamic properties align with experimental data and certain coarse-grained models. This methodology offers a fully microscopic description of RNA folding, linking transition kinetics and dynamics to the chain's chemistry and solvent environment. Consequently, it establishes a transferable framework poised for future translational applications.

Recent years have seen a surge in interest for segmentation, which is now applied across diverse fields including fraud detection, public health anomaly detection, and intrusion detection. This work details an ablation study of FgSegNet_v2, evaluating its three core stages: the Encoder, the Feature Pooling Module, and the Decoder. Based on these findings, we propose a modified version of the method that outperforms current state-of-the-art benchmarks. The model was tested on three datasets: CDNet2014, SBI2015, and Cityscapes. On CDNet2014, our approach achieved overall improvements over existing methods, particularly within the LowFrameRate subset. Furthermore, the proposed method demonstrates promising potential by delivering results comparable to state-of-the-art performance on SBI2015 and Cityscapes under varying conditions, such as differing lighting environments.

Spin susceptibility serves as a crucial tool for determining the symmetry of the order parameter in unconventional superconductors. Recently, nonunitary triplet superconductors have garnered significant interest, particularly in the pursuit of topological superconductivity. In this work, we establish a general expression for the spin susceptibility of nonunitary triplet superconductors based on a single-band model applicable to non-magnetic, centrosymmetric materials exhibiting strong spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, we apply this formula to rigorously evaluate experimental assertions regarding nonunitary triplet superconductivity in specific materials.

To address the scarcity of options for node-level tasks in graph kernels, we introduce a new, generalized graph kernel designed for semi-supervised learning with node features. Derived from a regularization framework that models both graph structure and feature data as distinct Hilbert spaces, our design encompasses numerous existing graph-based kernel models. This approach yields a kernel with transductive properties, enhancing learning efficiency with limited training data and improving performance on highly non-Euclidean data. We validate these benefits using synthetic datasets where global graph distributions inform label patterns. Furthermore, by incorporating a flexible polynomial of the graph Laplacian, the model achieves effective semi-supervised classification across graphs with varying degrees of homophily.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated significant promise for integration into commercial network control and management systems. Early applications of GNNs have revealed an exceptional ability to learn from various network features inherently modeled as graphs, such as topology, routing configurations, and traffic patterns across nodes. Unlike prior Machine Learning (ML) approaches, GNNs can generate precise predictions even on networks that were not present during the training phase. Currently, GNNs are a prominent subject in the Machine Learning community, driving substantial efforts to apply their capabilities across diverse domains like chemistry, physics, and social networks. However, the Graph Neural Networking challenge 2021 highlighted a critical limitation of existing GNN-based networking solutions: their inability to generalize effectively to larger networks. This paper addresses the scalability issue by proposing a GNN-based approach capable of efficiently scaling to larger networks with increased link capacities and aggregated link traffic.

Influenza type A is recognized as a highly pathogenic virus capable of infecting various species, frequently resulting in fatal outcomes for its hosts. The Haemagglutinin (HA) gene represents a critical target for antiviral drug development, contingent upon the precise identification of its subtypes and associated host ranges. This study presents and evaluates a method designed to accurately predict the capacity of Influenza type A viruses to infect humans using solely the HA gene sequence. The proposed approach involves three primary stages: (i) converting protein sequences into numerical signals via the EIIP amino acid scale, (ii) analyzing these sequences through Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) to extract relevant features, and (iii) applying an Artificial Neural Network model trained on the DFT-derived features. Data were sourced from the Influenza Research Database, comprising 30,724 human, 18,236 avian, and 8,157 swine HA protein sequences. Based on 10-fold cross-validation, the model achieved a training accuracy of 97.36% (+- 0.04%) and a validation accuracy of 97.26% (+- 0.26%), with a precision of 0.978 (+- 0.004), recall of 0.963 (+- 0.005), and a Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of 0.945 (+- 0.005). Leveraging one of the most extensive datasets available, this method produces promising results that facilitate early species detection and support the development of preventative strategies against potential human infections.

This study tackles the challenge of patient heterogeneity in biomedical prediction tasks. We introduce a systematic hypothesis testing framework to identify whether patient subgroups exist and, if so, to estimate the number of such subgroups. To model the link between disease outcomes and patient characteristics—including clinical factors and targeted biomarker profiles—we employ a mixture of generalized linear models. We develop a test statistic grounded in the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm and establish its asymptotic distribution under the null hypothesis. A key computational benefit of this test is that parameter estimates under the complex alternative hypothesis can be derived via a limited number of EM iterations, avoiding the need to optimize the objective function directly. We validate the test's finite sample performance regarding type-I error rates and power through comprehensive simulation studies. Furthermore, the method's practical utility is demonstrated using a multi-center prostate cancer dataset.

Interactions between cosmic rays (CRs) and the dense gas within Giant Molecular Clouds (GMCs) generate neutral pions, which subsequently decay into gamma rays. Consequently, gamma-ray emission from GMCs serves as a direct indicator of both the matter density and the cosmic ray density within these clouds. Detecting enhanced TeV emission from GMCs—significantly exceeding levels predicted by average Galactic cosmic rays—could signal variations in local cosmic ray density, potentially caused by a nearby recent accelerator. While such observations are vital for mapping cosmic ray distribution across the Galaxy, they remain challenging for current-generation Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes (IACTs). These studies struggle to distinguish between the cloud's emission, the strong cosmic-ray induced background, and large-scale diffuse emission due to the limited field of view of existing IACTs. This contribution utilizes 16 years of H.E.S.S. data to search for TeV emission from GMCs located in the Galaxy's inner molecular ring. We employ a 3D field-of-view likelihood technique to simultaneously model the hadronic background, galactic diffuse emission, and contributions from known very-high-energy sources, aiming to identify any excess TeV gamma-ray emission originating from GMCs.

We present Perceval, an open-source, evolving platform designed for simulating and interfacing with discrete variable photonic quantum computers, outlining its primary components and features. Its Python interface enables the construction of photonic circuits using fundamental elements such as photon sources, beam splitters, phase shifters, and detectors. The system supports multiple computational back-ends optimized for various applications, employing state-of-the-art techniques for both weak (sampling) and strong simulations. We demonstrate Perceval's capabilities by reproducing diverse photonic experiments and simulating implementations of quantum algorithms, ranging from Grover's and Shor's to quantum machine learning examples. Perceval serves as a versatile toolkit for experimentalists aiming to model, design, simulate, or optimize photonic experiments, as well as for theoreticians developing algorithms and applications for discrete-variable photonic quantum computing.

Integrated photonic active beamforming offers a significant reduction in both size and cost for coherent imagers used in LiDAR and medical imaging. However, existing architectures suffer from a linear increase in the complexity of electronic and photonic circuits as imaging resolution improves. We introduce a novel photonic transceiver architecture leveraging co-prime sampling to overcome this limitation, enabling a full, radiating-element-limited field-of-view (FOV) for a 2D aperture using a single-frequency laser. By employing only an order-of-N radiating elements, this design matches the beamwidth and side-lobe level (SLL) performance of a conventional transceiver with order-of-N-squared elements spaced at half-wavelength intervals. Additionally, we integrate a pulse amplitude modulation (PAM) row-column drive approach that reduces the required electrical drivers from an order of N to the order of the square root of N. A silicon photonics prototype utilizing two 64-element apertures for transmission and reception necessitates only 34 PAM electrical drivers. This implementation achieves an SLL of -11.3 dB, supports 1,026 total resolvable spots, and delivers a 0.6-degree beamwidth across a 23×16.3-degree FOV.

This study examines a functional equation analogous to that governing the generating function of a quarter-plane lattice walk model. A notable characteristic of this equation is that its orbit sum vanishes, yet its solution is non-algebraic. This solution corresponds to the generating function for lattice walks on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ originating at $(-1,-1)$, with the constraint that coordinate axes may be crossed only in a single direction. Furthermore, we analyze several variants of this equation, all of which appear to yield transcendental solutions; in one instance, the solution may not even be D-finite.

In 2013, a dynamical technique for calculating mass ratios in dwarf novae was introduced, utilizing stage A (growing) superhumps. This approach depends exclusively on celestial mechanics rather than experimental calibration. Since its inception, over 100 objects have been analyzed using this method. This paper presents an updated overview of the technique. When compared to modern eclipse modeling, regarded as the gold standard, the two methods demonstrate excellent agreement, confirming that the stage A superhump method is equally accurate and reliable. Currently, the number of objects studied via the superhump method is several times greater than those analyzed by eclipse modeling, making the former essential for investigating the terminal evolution of cataclysmic variables. Furthermore, I demonstrate that previous studies by other groups utilized incorrect fractional superhump excess relations, leading to evolutionary biases. Additionally, a new empirical relation for stage B superhumps has been derived. The updated evolutionary tracks near the period minimum indicate that angular momentum loss is approximately 1.9 times higher than predictions based on gravitational wave radiation alone. These measurements rely heavily on international collaborations between amateurs and professionals, a dynamic comparable to ornithology in fostering global unity through observation exchange. I summarize these collaborative efforts, explore the parallels between astronomy and ornithology, and outline prospects for future multidisciplinary integration between these distinct scientific fields.

This work introduces a novel anisotropic mesh adaptation strategy designed for solving elliptic differential equations via the finite element method. The approach constructs anisotropic adaptive meshes that appear quasi-uniform within a specific metric space, where the metric tensor is derived from a posteriori error estimates outlined in \cite{YinXie}. Unlike existing methods, this new metric tensor captures a more comprehensive understanding of the anisotropy inherent in the true solution. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the method effectively handles Poisson equations and steady convection-dominated problems. Furthermore, comparisons across various complex two-dimensional simulations illustrate that the proposed metric tensor achieves superior accuracy and efficiency relative to other approaches.

Quantum noise, specifically radiation pressure (RP) noise, restricts the sensitivity of laser interferometric gravitational wave (GW) detectors at lower frequencies. We proposed a potential RP noise cancellation technique involving the injection of phase-flipped ponderomotive-squeezed light (FPSL) onto free-mass mirrors within interferometer arms. This study examines the feasibility of this approach for space-based GW detectors operating in a broad frequency band below 1 Hz, without relying on long optical cavities. By analyzing various configurations in a single-path small-scale scenario to generate FPSL, we demonstrated that no viable setup exists for this specific case.

In quantum field theory, a time-dependent external agent breaks time-translational invariance, triggering particle creation and creating ambiguities in defining the quantum vacuum within canonical quantization. This study examines how the evolution of the created particle count varies with these ambiguities specifically under spatially homogeneous external conditions. We extend the standard quantum Vlasov equation to incorporate various vacuum choices, including adiabatic ones. Consequently, we propose a novel physical criterion, more stringent than the unitary implementation of dynamics, aimed at resolving quantization ambiguities.

This work employs adversarial domain adaptation within an unsupervised framework to mitigate sample bias in training a supervised high-energy physics event classifier. By utilizing a neural network architecture that integrates both event and domain classifiers connected by a gradient reversal layer, the approach simultaneously performs signal versus background discrimination and minimizes discrepancies in network responses to background samples derived from different Monte Carlo models through adversarial domain classification loss. We demonstrate the method's efficacy in eliminating bias using simulated LHC events for the classification of $t\bar{t}H$ signals against $t\bar{t}b\bar{b}$ backgrounds, while also addressing the method's implications and constraints.

Noisy 3D point clouds frequently appear in various applications, stemming from inaccuracies during image-based model construction or inherent imprecision in depth sensors. By leveraging graphs derived from point similarity to impose geometrical structure, this paper proposes a denoising technique that combines this graph structure with convex optimization. Additionally, the work briefly explores how these methods naturally extend to time-varying data, such as sequences of 3D point clouds.

A closed analytical framework for relativistic multipole moments within axistationary electrovac spacetimes is established. This work provides a comprehensive characterization of the Ernst potentials along the symmetry axis in terms of these arbitrary multipole moments and explores several specific applications.

Future ground-based and satellite experiments aim to detect the faint signature of primordial tensor fluctuations by observing large-scale $B$-mode polarisation in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). However, achieving this necessitates a precise and reliable separation of the signal from polarised Galactic foregrounds. We introduce a component separation technique for multi-frequency CMB data that integrates the strengths of both map-based and power-spectrum-based approaches, proving effective even with realistic foregrounds and instrumental noise. Our results show that the method can suppress Galactic foreground contamination to an equivalent tensor-to-scalar ratio of $r_{\rm FG}\lesssim5\times10^{-4}$, meeting the stringent requirements of next-generation observatories across various foreground complexities. This reduction in bias comes with a modest $\sim20-30\%$ increase in statistical uncertainties and remains valid for extensive sky areas, covering both the reionisation and recombination peaks in the $B$-mode power spectrum.

To achieve mid-century CO2 reduction targets, the existing electric power and natural gas (NG) infrastructure must undergo rapid transformation. This shift demands long-term planning for integrated power-NG systems that accounts for representative demand and supply scenarios, operational limits, and policy factors. Driven by the computational and practical hurdles of solving the generation and transmission expansion problem (GTEP) for these coupled systems, this study focuses on efficiently deriving a set of representative days from power and NG data to alleviate the computational load. We introduce the Graph Autoencoder for Multiple time resolution Energy Systems (GAMES), designed to capture spatio-temporal demand patterns in interdependent networks while handling variations in data temporal resolution. These generated embeddings feed into a clustering algorithm to identify representative days. We assess our method by solving a GTEP formulation tailored for the New England power-NG system, which incorporates physical interdependencies and joint emissions constraints. Our findings demonstrate that the GAMES-derived representative days enable the tractable solution of the GTEP formulation while simultaneously reducing the costs associated with joint planning decisions.

Frouros is a Python library designed to detect drift in machine learning tasks. It offers a blend of traditional and modern drift detection algorithms, supporting supervised, unsupervised, and semi-supervised approaches. The library is built to seamlessly integrate with scikit-learn by adhering to its application programming interface. Developed using established best practices for coding and continuous integration, Frouros ensures maintainability and extensibility. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/IFCA/frouros.

We interpret a subset of the experimental findings from Shwartz-Ziv and Tishby [2017]. Drawing inspiration from these results, we formulated a conjecture regarding the operational dynamics of deep neural networks. This conjecture provides an explanation for the corresponding findings reported by Saxe et al. [2018].

Learning dynamic state representations is a critical component of robot learning. Latent spaces capable of encoding dynamic information offer broad utility in accelerating model-free reinforcement learning, bridging the simulation-to-reality gap, and simplifying motion planning. However, existing methods struggle to scale effectively on complex dynamic systems, such as deformable objects, and fail to directly incorporate well-defined simulation functions into their training processes. We introduce DiffSRL, a pipeline for dynamic state representation learning that leverages differentiable simulation to embed complex dynamics models within an end-to-end training framework. Furthermore, we integrate differentiable dynamic constraints into the pipeline to incentivize the latent state to recognize dynamical limitations. We also establish a benchmark for state representation learning using the soft-body simulation environment, PlasticineLab. Our model demonstrates superior performance in capturing long-term dynamics and reward prediction compared to existing approaches.

The prevalence of code-mixed content on social media among the new generation necessitates a robust translation system to serve monolingual users and facilitate understanding by language processing models. This study introduces a translation framework employing a translation-transliteration approach to convert code-mixed data into their monolingual equivalents. To enhance fluency, the output is reordered using a target language model. A key advantage of this framework is that it operates without requiring a code-mixed to monolingual parallel corpus at any stage. Upon testing, the framework achieved BLEU and TER scores of 16.47 and 55.45, respectively. Given the framework's modular nature, we examine the significance of each component, analyze errors, and propose strategies for improvement.

This study examines Hom-Lie algebras characterized by non-invertible, equivariant twist maps, deriving their central extensions and demonstrating the preservation of these properties. Conditions are established to ensure that such extensions possess an invariant metric relative to their Hom-Lie product, rendering the twist map self-adjoint when the original algebra is equipped with a similar metric. Algebras satisfying these criteria are termed quadratic Hom-Lie algebras. The work illustrates how a quadratic Hom-Lie algebra generates a quadratic Lie algebra, and how the Lie algebra corresponding to the central extension of the Hom-Lie algebra acts as a central extension of the latter. Furthermore, it is proven that if the 2-cocycle defining the central extension is not a coboundary, a non-abelian, non-associative algebra exists whose commutator product exactly matches the Hom-Lie product of the extension. Additionally, if the associated Lie algebra is nilpotent, the algebra realizing this Hom-Lie product via its commutator is shown to be simple. The paper concludes with the provision of non-trivial examples.

This work investigates the thermodynamics of a moving Schwarzschild black hole, determining its temperature and entropy within a relativistic context. We establish a framework linking invariant geometric quantities across global spacetime transformations with the system's dispersion relation. Subsequently, we extend this analysis to accommodate more general dispersion relations and define criteria for their exclusion.

This study introduces and examines a cut finite element approach for weakly enforcing Neumann boundary conditions within the Darcy problem framework. Utilizing Raviart-Thomas mixed elements on both triangular and quadrilateral grids, the proposed method builds upon the Nitsche formulation detailed in [10.1515/jnma-2021-0042], representing an initial effort to extend this technique to unfitted scenarios. The core mechanism involves incorporating two ghost penalty operators to stabilize the velocity and pressure fields. We provide a rigorous proof that the stabilized formulation is well-posed and establish a priori error estimates for both velocity and pressure. Additionally, we demonstrate an upper bound for the stiffness matrix's condition number, supported by numerical examples that validate the theoretical findings.

Gaseous detectors have historically served particle physics experiments, whether located at beamlines or operating independently. Recently, their low momentum threshold has made them attractive as active targets for long baseline neutrino studies. To enhance statistics while maintaining this low threshold, pressurized Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) have been suggested; the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is currently evaluating the construction of one for its near detector complex. Gas Monitoring Chambers function as miniature TPCs designed to characterize gas properties. A system capable of testing both standard and novel drift gas mixtures can offer valuable insights for designing new high-pressure TPCs. This work details the construction of a High Pressure Gas Monitoring Chamber capable of operating at pressures up to 10 bar and sustaining a maximum drift field of approximately 1000 V/cm.

This study investigates $CP$ and $P$ violation in charmless four-body $B^{0} \to p \bar{p} K^{+} \pi^{-}$ decays by analyzing triple-product asymmetry observables. The analysis utilizes proton-proton collision data from the LHCb experiment, recorded at center-of-mass energies of 7, 8, and 13 TeV, totaling an integrated luminosity of 8.4 fb$^{-1}$. Measurements of $CP$- and $P$-violating asymmetries are conducted across the entire phase space as well as within specific regions. While no evidence for $CP$ violation is found, $P$-parity violation is detected with a significance of 5.8 standard deviations.

Concentrated Animal Feeding Operations (CAFOs) present significant threats to air, water, and public health, yet remain difficult to regulate. A primary obstacle identified by the U.S. Government Accountability Office is the absence of comprehensive location data for these facilities. This study leverages the USDA's National Agricultural Imagery Program (NAIP), featuring 1-meter resolution aerial photography, to detect poultry CAFOs throughout the continental United States. By training convolutional neural network (CNN) models to recognize individual poultry barns, we applied the most effective model to over 42 TB of imagery, generating the first national, open-source dataset of poultry CAFOs. We validated the model's predictions using a held-out test set comprising hand-labeled poultry CAFO locations from ten counties in California, demonstrating that this methodology holds substantial promise for addressing gaps in environmental monitoring.

Modeling hand-object interactions serves as the central challenge in egocentric video understanding. While standard architectures like CNNs and Vision Transformers, which process RGB frames, achieve strong results, their performance can be further enhanced by incorporating additional inputs such as object detections, optical flow, and audio. However, the necessity for specialized modules to handle these diverse modalities often renders such models impractical for real-world deployment. This work aims to match the efficacy of multimodal methods while relying exclusively on RGB images during inference. Our strategy employs multimodal knowledge distillation, utilizing a teacher model trained on a combination of object detections, optical flow, and RGB frames, to train a student model that accepts only RGB input. Preliminary findings indicate that this distilled model substantially outperforms both a standard baseline RGB model (trained without distillation) and a variant trained jointly on all modalities, achieving superior results in both standard and compositional action recognition tasks.

This short letter establishes several identities connecting conformal Killing-Yano tensors (CKYTs) with geometric quantities. We subsequently apply these identities to build covariantly conserved "currents." Our findings indicate that rank-$n$ currents, which are linear in rank-$n$ CKYTs $k$ and second-order in derivatives, must adopt a straightforward expression involving $dk$. Furthermore, utilizing the Plebański-Demiański and Kerr-Newman metrics, we demonstrate how these currents can define charges. By design, these currents remain covariant under any general conformal rescaling of the metric.

During LHC Run 2 at 13 TeV, the Precision Proton Spectrometer (PPS) for the CMS and TOTEM experiments recorded 107.7 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data. This article outlines the essential aspects of PPS alignment and optical calibration, the methodology for proton reconstruction, and evaluates both detector efficiency and simulation performance. These components are verified using a dataset of (semi)exclusive dilepton events. The results confirm that the PPS successfully demonstrates the viability of running a near-beam proton spectrometer continuously at a high-luminosity hadron collider.

The Lagrangian-Hamiltonian unified formalism introduced by R. Skinner and R. Rusk was initially formulated for autonomous dynamical systems in classical mechanics. Subsequently, it was extended to cover non-autonomous first-order mechanical systems and both first-order and higher-order field theories. Nevertheless, a comprehensive generalization for higher-order mechanical systems remains undeveloped. This paper reviews the natural geometric framework and the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formalisms applicable to higher-order autonomous mechanical systems. Building on this review, we construct a complete generalization of the Skinner-Rusk formalism for such systems and apply it to examine several physical models from this novel perspective.

Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is a prevalent imaging technique for diagnosing coronary artery disease, often enhanced by attenuation correction (AC) using computed tomography (CT)-derived attenuation maps (u-maps) to boost diagnostic precision. However, the sequential acquisition of SPECT and CT in clinical settings frequently leads to misregistration between the scans. While convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are effective for medical image registration, existing cross-modality approaches typically rely on early fusion via direct concatenation or late fusion using separate CNN modules, failing to fully capture or integrate cross-modality information. Furthermore, deep-learning-based rigid registration for cardiac SPECT and CT-derived u-maps has not been previously explored. This paper introduces a Dual-Branch Squeeze-Fusion-Excitation (DuSFE) module designed for registering cardiac SPECT and CT-derived u-maps. By integrating knowledge from multiple modalities, DuSFE recalibrates both channel-wise and spatial features for each modality and can be embedded at various convolutional layers to facilitate feature fusion across different spatial dimensions. Clinical data analysis indicates that networks incorporating DuSFE produce significantly lower registration errors, resulting in more accurate AC SPECT images compared to prior methods.

Using LHCb data from $pp$ collisions at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 3.0 fb$^{-1}$, the $CP$ asymmetry in $B^-\to D_s^-D^0$ and $B^-\to D^-D^0$ decays has been measured. The obtained values are $A^{CP}(B^-\to D_s^-D^0)=(-0.4\pm 0.5\pm 0.5)\%$ and $A^{CP}(B^-\to D^-D^0)=( 2.3\pm 2.7\pm 0.4)\%$, where the first uncertainties represent statistical errors and the second systematic ones. This study marks the first measurement of $A^{CP}(B^-\to D_s^-D^0)$ and provides the most precise determination to date for $A^{CP}(B^-\to D^-D^0)$. Neither outcome indicates any evidence of $CP$ violation.

Colorectal cancer (CRC) represents a leading cause of cancer and cancer-related deaths globally. Timely colon cancer screening is essential for early detection, with colonoscopy serving as the primary diagnostic method. Despite its importance, the miss rate for polyps, adenomas, and advanced adenomas remains alarmingly high. Detecting polyps at their precancerous stage can significantly lower mortality rates and the associated economic burden. Deep learning-based computer-aided diagnosis (CADx) systems can assist gastroenterologists in identifying polyps that might otherwise be overlooked, thereby enhancing detection rates. Furthermore, these CADx systems offer a cost-effective approach to improving long-term CRC prevention. This study introduces Transformer ResU-Net (TransResU-Net), a deep learning architecture designed for automatic polyp segmentation. Built upon residual blocks with a ResNet-50 backbone, the model leverages transformer self-attention mechanisms and dilated convolutions. Experiments conducted on two public polyp segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that TransResU-Net achieves a highly promising Dice score with real-time processing speed. Given its strong performance metrics, TransResU-Net is established as a robust benchmark for developing real-time systems for the early diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of colorectal cancer. The source code for TransResU-Net is publicly accessible at https://github.com/nikhilroxtomar/TransResUNet.

Using the Palomar Cosmic Web Imager (PCWI) on the Hale (P200) telescope, we have identified the host galaxy of a damped Ly$\alpha$ system (DLA) toward the background quasar SDSS J011852+040644 at $z \approx 3.0091$. This DLA exhibits a hydrogen column density of $\log N(\text{HI}) [\text{cm}^{-2}] = 21.0 \pm 0.10$. We detected Ly$\alpha$ emission within the dark core of the DLA trough at a $3.3\sigma$ significance level, with a luminosity of $L_{\rm Ly\alpha} = (3.8 \pm 0.8) \times 10^{42}\ \text{erg s}^{-1}$. Assuming a minimum Ly$\alpha$ escape fraction of $f_{esc}^{\text{Ly}\alpha} \sim 2\%$, this luminosity implies a star formation rate of $\gtrsim 2\ \text{M}_{\odot}\ \text{yr}^{-1}$, a value consistent with Lyman break galaxies at similar redshifts. The observed Ly$\alpha$ emission is blueshifted relative to the systemic redshift inferred from metal absorption lines by $281 \pm 43$ km/s. The associated galaxy lies at an impact parameter of $\lesssim 12$ kpc from the background quasar, aligning with the established anticorrelation between column density and impact parameter found in spectroscopic studies of DLA host environments.

Smart Metering Infrastructure (SMI) serves as the fundamental element of the Smart Grid (SG), facilitating bidirectional communication between utility providers and consumers to oversee energy usage data. However, while SMIs leverage Information and Communication Technology (ICT), their reliance on public networks introduces novel security vulnerabilities, necessitating robust authentication and key agreement mechanisms to meet SG security standards. To address these challenges, this paper proposes "LiSA," a lightweight and secure authentication protocol designed specifically to protect SMIs within SG environments. Built upon Elliptic Curve Cryptography, LiSA ensures mutual authentication, anonymity, replay protection, session key security, and resistance to various attacks by utilizing the hardness of the Elliptic Curve Qu Vanstone (EVQV) certificate mechanism, alongside the Elliptic Curve Diffie Hellman Problem (ECDHP) and Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP). The protocol is engineered to offer superior security compared to existing solutions while minimizing computational and communication overhead. Specifically, LiSA completes execution in approximately 11.826 ms for smart meters and 0.992 ms for service providers, requiring only 544 bits of message transmission per session.

Although deep learning has advanced many computer vision tasks, it depends heavily on extensive annotated datasets, leaving the challenge of modeling real-world data's unconstrained nature unresolved. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) mitigates annotation expenses by leveraging large volumes of unlabeled data alongside labeled examples. Traditional SSL methods assume unlabeled samples share the same distribution as labeled ones, whereas the emerging "open-world" SSL framework acknowledges that unlabeled data may include instances from unseen classes. This paper introduces a novel pseudo-labeling strategy designed for open-world SSL. Central to our method is the integration of sample uncertainty with prior knowledge regarding class distributions to produce reliable, distribution-aware pseudo-labels for both known and unknown classes. Comprehensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the approach's efficacy, achieving significant performance gains over current state-of-the-art methods on seven diverse datasets, including ~17% improvement on CIFAR-100, ~5% on ImageNet-100, and ~9% on Tiny ImageNet. Furthermore, we illustrate the method's adaptability for novel class discovery, its robustness against data imbalance, and provide a technique to estimate the count of new classes.

Addressing multi-modal, multi-objective optimization problems (MMOPs) involves not only approximating the Pareto-optimal front in the objective space but also discovering all equivalent Pareto-optimal subsets in the decision space. This dual requirement is practically significant for decision-makers seeking alternative designs with comparable performance. Although recent years have seen substantial research into efficient algorithms for MMOPs, current methods often demand a prohibitive number of function evaluations—even for problems with just two objectives and two variables. These algorithms typically rely on complex, customized mechanisms requiring extra parameters to manage diversity and convergence. In this letter, we present a steady-state evolutionary algorithm designed for MMOPs that features a simple architecture and requires no additional user-defined tuning parameters compared to a standard evolutionary algorithm. We evaluate its performance across 21 MMOPs from widely used benchmark suites using a computational budget of only 1,000 function evaluations. The proposed method is benchmarked against six state-of-the-art algorithms (MO Ring PSO SCD, DN-NSGAII, TriMOEA-TA&R, CPDEA, MMOEA/DC, and MMEA-WI). Results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms these counterparts significantly across established metrics such as IGDX, PSP, and IGD. We hope this study will inspire the development of simple, efficient, and generalized algorithms to enhance their adoption in practical applications.

RCSEDv2 (https://rcsed2.voxastro.org/), the second Reference Catalog of Spectral Energy Distributions for galaxies, contains the most extensive homogeneously processed photometric dataset compiled from multiple wide-field surveys, covering 4 million galaxies. This paper details the methodology used to homogenize the photometric data. The process begins by correcting all measurements for foreground Galactic extinction, followed by converting them into our adopted standard photometric system (comprising GALEX, SDSS, UKIDSS, and WISE). We calculated aperture corrections for various pre-defined apertures by utilizing published galaxy sizes and light profiles alongside the image quality of each survey. Additionally, we applied k-corrections using our own analytic approximations. This resulting homogeneous photometric catalog enables the construction of fully calibrated SEDs for galaxies within our sample (identified by the availability of their spectra) and facilitates direct scientific analysis of this unique extragalactic dataset.

Connection calculi facilitate highly compact implementations of goal-directed proof search. This overview presents our contributions to connection tableaux calculi: we demonstrate optimized functional implementations for both clausal and nonclausal proof search, featuring a Skolemisation procedure consistent with machine learning applications. Furthermore, we introduce two machine learning-based guidance strategies—reordering proof steps using Naive Bayesian probabilities and expanding proof search trees via Monte Carlo Tree Search. Finally, we provide a translation mechanism that converts connection proofs into LK format, thereby enabling proof certification and automatic proof search within interactive theorem provers.

This study presents the inaugural experimental observation of a dust acoustic solitary wave reflecting from a potential barrier within a dusty plasma environment. Conducted in an inverted $\Pi$-shaped Dusty Plasma Experimental (DPEx) device under a DC glow discharge, the solitary wave was generated by superimposing a short negative Gaussian pulse onto the discharge voltage. The wave propagated toward a potential barrier formed by the sheath surrounding a biased wire, reflected, and returned. Key parameters—including amplitude, width, and velocity—were tracked over time. Experiments were conducted across various potential barrier strengths and initial soliton amplitudes. Results indicate that the minimum distance between the soliton and the barrier's center increases as the barrier strength rises or the initial wave amplitude diminishes. Additionally, an emissive probe measured sheath potential and thickness by analyzing the axial plasma potential profile across different resistances connected to the biased wire. Finally, a modified Korteweg-de Vries equation was derived and solved numerically to qualitatively interpret the experimental data.

We employ the coordinate transformation method to investigate electron propagation where spinor orientability varies. Topological Insulators are defined by an odd number of orientability reversals within the Brillouin zone, whereas defects exhibit such reversals along closed orbits in real space; both scenarios involve nontrivial spin connections. Leveraging this approach, we determine the specific form of spin connections for topological defects in three-dimensional Topological Insulators. Specifically, an edge dislocation on the surface of a Topological Insulator generates a spin connection governed by torsion. Our findings indicate that electrons propagate along two-dimensional regions and confined circular paths. Additionally, we calculate the tunneling density of states for these edge dislocations. Finally, we observe that edge dislocations break parity symmetry, leading to a measurable current represented by the in-plane spin component on the surface.

According to Alexa, YouTube ranks as the second most visited website, making it an attractive target for scammers. However, the inherent computational complexity of analyzing multimedia content makes detecting scams on YouTube more challenging than on text-based platforms. Consequently, existing research offers limited understanding of the prevalence, duration, and operational tactics of scammers on the site. This paper presents a preliminary investigation into scam videos on YouTube. The authors started by identifying 74 search terms likely to surface scam content based on their own browsing experiences. Through a manual review of the results, they identified 668 scams across 3,700 videos. A detailed analysis of the classifications and metadata revealed that these scam videos have a median lifespan of nearly nine months, with many relying on external sites for monetization. Furthermore, the study explored whether metadata alone could detect scams, concluding that it lacks sufficient predictive power to differentiate between fraudulent and legitimate videos. Ultimately, this work confirms that scams pose a genuine threat to YouTube users, thereby highlighting the need for future research in this area.

Inspired by the LHCb Collaboration's identification of the fully open-flavor tetraquark states $X_0(2900)$ and $X_1(2900)$, this study calculates the magnetic dipole moment of the $J^{P} = 1^{-}$ $X_1(2900)$ state within the diquark-antidiquark framework using light-cone sum rules. The calculated value is $\mu_{X_1}=0.79^{+0.36}_{-0.39}\,\mu_N$. Hadronic magnetic moments provide critical insights into internal charge and magnetization distributions, enhancing our understanding of their geometric structures and quark-gluon configurations. As the first two fully open-flavor multiquark states observed, $X_0(2900)$ and $X_1(2900)$ offer a new avenue for exploring exotic hadrons. Consequently, the findings of this research may guide future theoretical and experimental investigations into the properties of fully open-flavor multiquark states.

GW190521 stands as the most massive binary black hole merger ever recorded, possessing unique characteristics. Its exceptionally loud ringdown makes it an ideal target for searching for gravitational wave echoes, a potential signature of the quantum structure of black hole horizons. We conducted an unprecedented, multi-method search for these echoes using two independent, well-established pipelines: a template-based search for stimulated Hawking radiation (Boltzmann echoes) and the model-agnostic coherent WaveBurst (cWB) search. Stimulated Hawking radiation is predicted to produce post-merger echoes at a horizon mode frequency of approximately 50 Hz (for quadrupolar radiation), repeating roughly every second due to partial reflection from the Planckian quantum structure of the horizon. Dynamic nested sampling analysis yielded a Bayesian evidence of $7 \pm 2$ (90% confidence level) for this signal following GW190521, indicating an energy excess of $10^{+9}_{-7}\%$ relative to the main event. Similarly, the cWB-reconstructed waveform of the first echo shows an energy excess of $13^{+16}_{-7}\%$. After accounting for "look-elsewhere" effects, the cWB pipeline estimates a false detection p-value of $5.1 \times 10^{-3}$ (2.6$\sigma$), though the sky co-localization of the echo and the main event remains inconclusive. Although the current evidence for stimulated Hawking radiation falls short of the $5\sigma$ gold standard, the results align with expectations given current detector sensitivities, suggesting that next-generation gravitational wave observatories will be able to definitively determine the quantum nature of black hole horizons.

We provide a critical examination of evidence suggesting New Physics, based on potential lepton universality violations in the LHCb experiment's $R_K$ and $R_{K^*}$ ($\mu/e$) ratios and the $g-2$ lepton anomalies. The study starts with a detailed theoretical analysis of these $\mu/e$ ratios and the $B_s \rightarrow \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay, incorporating complex Wilson coefficients to constrain their real and imaginary components. Following this, we conduct an extensive comparison with experimental data. Our findings indicate that fitting a single Wilson coefficient yields a $4.7\sigma$ deviation from the Standard Model using only hadronic-insensitive observables, which rises to $6.1\sigma$ when hadronic-sensitive ones are included. When all relevant Wilson coefficients are active and both types of data are combined, the deviation peaks at $7.2\sigma$, though it drops to $4.9\sigma$ if the central values for $R_K$ and $R_{K^{\ast}}$ are assumed to be unity. We also evaluate unaccounted Standard Model contributions, demonstrating that their inclusion still necessitates New Physics to reconcile the data. Furthermore, we incorporate recent $g-2$ lepton anomalies and $W$-mass measurements, exploring various theoretical models capable of explaining these discrepancies. Finally, we project the influence of upcoming data from LHCb (Run 3) and Belle II, once the latter accumulates approximately $5~ab^{-1}$.

Restricting the distribution of small-scale structures in the universe enables us to test alternatives to the cold dark matter model. Strong gravitational lensing provides a distinctive means to investigate low-mass dark matter halos ($<10^{10} M_\odot$), as these objects generate lensing signals regardless of whether they contain luminous galaxies. We generated extensive datasets of strong lensing images incorporating realistic low-mass halos, Hubble Space Telescope (HST) observational characteristics, and galaxy light derived from the HST COSMOS field. By employing a simulation-based inference pipeline, we trained a neural posterior estimator for the subhalo mass function (SHMF) and imposed constraints on lens populations created with distinct galaxy source sets. Our results demonstrate that integrating our network with a hierarchical inference framework allows for the reliable determination of the SHMF across various configurations while scaling efficiently to populations comprising hundreds of lenses. Through precise inference on large, complex simulated datasets, this approach establishes a groundwork for deriving dark matter constraints from future wide-field optical imaging surveys.

In 2007, Grytczuk conjectured that for any sequence of alphabets of size 3, there exists an infinite square-free word where the $i$-th letter is chosen from the $i$-th alphabet. While Thue's 1906 result guarantees such a word when all alphabets are identical, Grytczuk, Przybyło, and Zhu later demonstrated in 2011 that the conjecture also holds for alphabets of size 4. This article first establishes that if the alphabets have size 4, the number of square-free words is at least $2.45^n$, improving upon the previous bound of $2^n$. Our primary result shows that a square-free word can be constructed when the alphabets are size-3 subsets of a single alphabet of size 4. This proof also implies there are at least $1.25^n$ such words of length $n$ for any such assignment. The argument relies on a set of coefficients verified by computer, and we suspect the full conjecture could be resolved using this method with a significantly more powerful computer, though such hardware may not be available for several decades.

Dark matter simulations rely on statistical methods to accurately identify and categorize their halos and structures. While nonparametric approaches generate catalogs of these formations, they lack the modeling capabilities of algorithm-based methods and may incorrectly classify particles during mergers. By utilizing mixture models, it becomes possible to fit multiple density profiles simultaneously to the halos detected in dark matter simulations. In this study, we apply the Einasto profile (Einasto 1965, 1968, 1969) to model halos within a sample from the Bolshoi simulation (Klypin et al. 2011), determining their location, dimensions, shape, and mass. The code, developed within the R statistical environment, is available at https://github.com/LluisHGil/darkmix.

Annually, our reliance on wearable technology for collecting personalized metrics—such as movement patterns, heart rate, and breathing—continues to increase. These devices utilize sensors like accelerometers and gyroscopes to detect environmental changes and transmit data to support informed decision-making. While these sensors are expected to function consistently across various devices, this is not always true. This case study examines accelerometers from three distinct devices recording identical actions to assess whether observed discrepancies stem from variability within a single device or between different units. Our findings indicate that the most substantial variations occur between devices with differing specifications, including sensitivity and sampling frequency. Consequently, even when data is collected from the same individual, during the same activity, and using the same sensor type, variance in the data must be anticipated.

This research investigates the inclusive production of $\Xi^-$ hyperons via antikaon-induced cascades on $^{12}$C and $^{184}$W targets near the production threshold, utilizing a nuclear spectral function framework. The methodology accounts for incoherent direct production through elementary ${K^-}p \to {K^+}\Xi^-$ and ${K^-}n \to {K^0}\Xi^-$ interactions, while incorporating the effects of scalar and Coulomb potentials from $K^-$, $K^+$, $K^0$, and $\Xi^-$ within the nuclear medium. Absolute differential and total cross sections for $\Xi^-$ production were computed for laboratory angles up to 45$^{\circ}$ using $K^-$ beams with momenta of 1.0 and 1.3 GeV/c, which are proximate to the 1.05 GeV/c threshold for free nucleon targets. Additionally, the momentum dependence of the transparency ratio for the $^{184}$W/$^{12}$C system was evaluated at these beam energies. Our findings indicate that both differential and total (absolute and relative) $\Xi^-$ cross sections at these initial momenta exhibit significant sensitivity to variations in the scalar $\Xi^-$ nuclear potential at saturation density ($\rho_0$), particularly within the low-momentum range of 0.1--0.6 GeV/c. Furthermore, at the subthreshold beam momentum of 1.0 GeV/c, the transparency ratio demonstrates strong sensitivity to changes in the $\Xi^-$ nuclear potential across all outgoing $\Xi^-$ momenta. Consequently, dedicated measurements of these absolute and relative observables at J-PARC would yield crucial insights into $\Xi^-$ in-medium properties, offering complementary data to those derived from inclusive ($K^-$,$K^+$) reactions at incident momenta of 1.6--1.8 GeV/c in the $\Xi^-$ bound and quasi-free regimes.

Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) supports diverse applications ranging from environmental monitoring to biotechnology. However, existing snapshot HSI methods face a compromise between spatial and spectral resolution, preventing simultaneous high performance in both areas. Furthermore, these approaches are resource-inefficient due to significant photon loss caused by spectral filtering. This study introduces a snapshot HSI method that leverages the strong spectro-temporal correlations of entangled photons via a modified quantum ghost spectroscopy setup. In this system, the target is directly imaged using one photon, while spectral data is retrieved through ghost spectroscopy from its partner photon. Since only a minimal number of edge pixels on the camera function as the spectrometer, spatial resolution is virtually unaffected. Additionally, the elimination of spectral filtering ensures that every photon contributes to the imaging process, significantly enhancing resource efficiency.

This study introduces a multimodal emotion recognition framework utilizing hybrid fusion to categorize emotions expressed through paired speech and visual inputs into discrete classes.
