Our central finding is that certified regression can be reduced to certified classification when employing the median as the primary decision mechanism. By integrating this reduction with established certified classifiers, we present six new provably robust regressors. To our knowledge, this is the inaugural work to certify the robustness of individual regression predictions without relying on assumptions regarding data distribution or model architecture. Furthermore, we demonstrate that current state-of-the-art certified classifiers often rely on excessively pessimistic assumptions that weaken their provable guarantees. We propose a refined analysis of model robustness that yields significantly stronger certified guarantees in many scenarios. Finally, empirical evaluations on both regression and classification datasets show that our methods guarantee accuracy for up to 50% of test predictions under 1% training corruption and up to 30% under 4% corruption. Our source code is accessible at https://github.com/ZaydH/certified-regression.
We demonstrate that semi-simple Lie algebras are uniquely defined by their maximal nilpotent subalgebra, which coincides with the nilpotent radical of a Borel subalgebra.

The robust formulation of the Vafa-Witten theorem is found to be invalid, as direct calculations of the order parameter reveal a zero condensate indicative of a symmetric vacuum. Consequently, the theorem's applicability depends on its weaker counterpart, which stipulates that Goldstone bosons do not emerge in vector-like gauge theories where the $\theta$-angle is zero. This weak version remains consistent with the presence of a charged $\rho$-meson condensate in QCD under strong magnetic fields, even though such a condensate breaks electromagnetic gauge symmetry.

This study models a two-dimensional binary mixture of passive and active Brownian particles by employing the effective interaction between passive particles immersed in an active bath. The system's behavior is governed by two control parameters: the activity level of the active particles and the size ratio between the two particle types. By calculating the average force exerted on a pair of particles by the surrounding active bath, we determine the effective interaction, which can manifest as either attractive or repulsive depending on specific system conditions. Consequently, passive particles organize into four distinct structural states—disorder (D), disordered cluster (DC), ordered cluster (OC), and poly-crystalline order (PC)—dictated by the nature of this effective interaction. These four structures are further validated through comprehensive microscopic simulations of the active-passive mixture. Ultimately, this research provides insights into the diverse collective behaviors observed in non-equilibrium systems.

Inspired by the intermediate Lang conjectures regarding hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish novel finiteness theorems for non-constant maps from a fixed variety to another fixed variety over a number field, utilizing Faltings's finiteness theorems on moduli spaces of maps.

The radiative type-I seesaw mechanism has previously been utilized to account for the lightness of Majorana neutrinos alongside both Majorana and Dirac heavy fermions, as well as for Dirac neutrinos paired with Dirac heavy fermions. This study introduces a minimal realization of the radiative type-I seesaw featuring light Dirac neutrinos and heavy Majorana fermions. The dark sector, safeguarded by an Abelian fermiophobic gauge symmetry that simultaneously prevents tree-level mass terms for all light neutrinos, is composed of an inert doublet and a complex singlet scalar. Additionally, a fermion vector-like extension is proposed, allowing light right-handed neutrinos to thermalize within the primordial plasma and enabling the direct production of the extra gauge boson at colliders. Specifically, the current upper limit on $\Delta N_{\text{eff}}$ from PLANCK suggests large ratios of $M_{Z'}/g'\gtrsim 40\ \text{TeV}$, which could rival collider constraints if $g'$ is sufficiently close to Standard Model values, whereas future cosmic microwave background experiments might be capable of probing all the non-minimal models discussed.

The Weak Gravity Conjecture is conventionally defined as a limit on the mass-to-charge ratio of particles within a theory, though it has also been suggested that its fundamental form concerns the existence of a particle that experiences self-repulsion under all long-range interactions. We introduce a related yet distinct proposal: the conjecture should instead apply to particles possessing non-negative self-binding energy. This perspective is especially significant in anti-de Sitter (AdS) space, as it admits a straightforward conformal field theory (CFT) dual. Specifically, if $\Delta(q)$ represents the scaling dimension of the lowest-dimension operator carrying charge $q$ under a global $U(1)$ symmetry, then $\Delta(q)$ must be a convex function of $q$. Unlike formulations relying on holographic dual forces or spacetime locality, this approach allows us to boldly conjecture that charge spectrum convexity applies to any unitary CFT, extending beyond those with weakly coupled and weakly curved gravitational duals. We term this the Charge Convexity Conjecture and note its generalization to larger global symmetry groups. Testing this via perturbation theory, $1/N$ expansions, and semi-classical methods in examples where anomalous dimensions are calculable confirms the conjecture in all cases examined. However, the underlying CFT reason for this validity remains unclear.

We introduce a straightforward technique for selecting a limited set of reference optical turbulence and wind profiles from extensive datasets, specifically designed for single-conjugate and extreme adaptive optics simulations. These profiles serve as representative models of atmospheric variability within slow, end-to-end adaptive optics simulations. The approach relies on the premise that system performance correlates with integrated atmospheric metrics: $r_0$, $\theta_0$, and $\tau_0$. Consequently, profiles are chosen from a large dataset to simultaneously match the distributions of these parameters, thereby capturing the atmospheric variations encountered by the AO system. Additionally, we adapt the equivalent layers method for profile compression to incorporate wind profiles. This methodology was applied to stereo-SCIDAR data from ESO Paranal to derive five turbulence and wind profiles spanning a wide spectrum of atmospheric conditions. Analytical adaptive optics simulations demonstrate that these profiles correspond to an equivalent range of AO-corrected Strehl ratios.

The mammalian nervous system utilizes diverse synaptic plasticity mechanisms, operating alone or in concert across extensive timescales, to govern learning and memory. To replicate biological cognition in artificial intelligence, neuromorphic computing requires synthetic synapses capable of accurately reproducing these intricate plasticity rules and dynamic behaviors. While specific plasticity rules have previously been simulated using complex CMOS and memristive circuits, there has been a lack of hardware implementations that integrate multiple plasticity types—such as long-term (LTP) and short-term plasticity (STP) with adjustable dynamics—into single, low-power nanoscale devices. In this work, we present a phase-change memtransistive synapse that exploits the non-volatility of memristors and the volatility of transistors to couple LTP with both homo- and heterosynaptic STP effects. We demonstrate that these biomimetic synapses can support advanced cognitive frameworks, including short-term spike-timing-dependent plasticity (ST-STDP) and stochastic Hopfield neural networks. Furthermore, we show that, similar to the mammalian brain, these emulations can identify temporal relationships within data streams to facilitate sequential learning and combinatorial optimization.

This study presents a new method for classifying pulsars in time-domain radio astronomy by employing a Born machine, also known as a quantum neural network. We demonstrate that utilizing a single-qubit architecture effectively maps the pulsar classification task onto the Bloch sphere, achieving accuracy levels comparable to classical machine learning techniques. Furthermore, we propose a novel single-qubit encoding scheme for the pulsar data, which performs equivalently to multi-qubit QAOA encoding.

To visually characterize individuals across a decade, this study introduces the Faces Through Time dataset, comprising more than a thousand portrait images per decade from the 1880s to today. Leveraging this collection, we propose a framework for resynthesizing portraits across different eras, allowing us to imagine how a specific portrait from one decade would appear if captured in another. Our approach optimizes a family of per-decade generators that capture subtle distinctions between decades—such as variations in hairstyles and makeup—while preserving the original subject's identity. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art image-to-image translation techniques, as well as attribute-based and language-guided portrait editing models, in resynthesizing portraits across time. The code and data will be accessible at https://facesthroughtime.github.io.

Knowledge graph embedding is a representation learning method that maps entities and relations within a knowledge graph into continuous vector spaces. These embeddings have become widely adopted for link prediction and various downstream tasks. Typically, existing approaches are assessed on individual tasks or specific task groups to gauge overall performance, focusing primarily on task-specific effectiveness. However, there is a significant lack of understanding regarding the specific information these embedding methods actually learn to represent.

To address this gap, we introduce the DLCC (Description Logic Class Constructors) benchmark, a resource designed to evaluate embedding approaches based on the types of classes they can represent. This benchmark includes two gold standards: one derived from the real-world DBpedia knowledge graph and another synthetic standard. Additionally, we provide an evaluation framework that implements an experimental protocol, enabling researchers to directly utilize these gold standards. By applying these standards to compare multiple embedding approaches, we demonstrate the utility of DLCC. Our findings reveal that many Description Logic (DL) constructors on DBpedia are often learned by identifying correlated patterns distinct from those defined in the gold standard. Furthermore, we observe that specific DL constructors, such as cardinality constraints, pose particular challenges for most embedding approaches to learn effectively.

The performance and behavior of large-scale distributed applications are significantly shaped by network characteristics like latency, bandwidth, packet loss, and jitter. Engineers often need to investigate specific scenarios, such as how increased latency impacts response times, how shifting clusters across geographical regions influences throughput, or how network dynamics affect stability. However, answering these questions systematically and reproducibly is challenging due to the inherent variability and lack of control over real-world networks. Current state-of-the-art solutions suffer from significant limitations: tools like MiniNet scale poorly, CrystalNet focuses solely on the control plane, and EmuLab neglects network dynamics. Kollaps addresses these gaps as a fully distributed network emulator. It relies on two core insights. First, applications care primarily about emergent end-to-end properties (e.g., latency, bandwidth, loss, jitter) rather than the internal states of routers and switches; this insight enables a simpler, dynamically adaptable model that avoids maintaining full network state. Second, this streamlined model supports fully decentralized maintenance, allowing the emulation to scale with the number of application machines. Kollaps is fully decentralized, language-agnostic, transport-protocol-agnostic, capable of scaling to thousands of processes, and accurate when benchmarked against bare-metal deployments or full-state emulation approaches. The system demonstrates its ability to replicate results from existing literature and accurately predict the behavior of complex, unmodified distributed systems, such as Cassandra, under various deployment configurations.

Ultrafast electron diffraction and time-resolved serial crystallography form the foundation of a revolution in observing molecular structural dynamics at the atomic scale. Yet, most current experiments rely on traditional "ball-and-stick" representations, omitting crucial information about molecular quantum states like the density matrix. This study presents a framework for preparing rotational wave packets and performing ultrafast coherent diffraction, alongside a novel variant of quantum state tomography for ultrafast electron diffraction to characterize these quantum states. Reconstructing the density matrix for molecules with arbitrary degrees of freedom will offer an unprecedented clarity of molecular quantum states, allowing for the visualization of effects driven by quantum dynamics.

Missing data frequently arises in practical applications, prompting the development of numerous imputation methods. However, many of these techniques, particularly multiple imputation strategies, struggle to scale with high-dimensional datasets, a trend that is increasingly common. To address this, we introduce Principal Component Analysis Imputation (PCAI), a streamlined and adaptable framework leveraging PCA to accelerate imputation and mitigate memory constraints inherent in existing methods, all while maintaining imputation quality measured by Mean Squared Error (MSE). Furthermore, PCAI remains effective even when dealing with categorical missing features or a high volume of missing variables. We also present PCA Imputation-Classification (PIC), an adapted version of PCAI designed for classification tasks. Experimental validation across diverse scenarios demonstrates that both PCAI and PIC can be integrated with various imputation algorithms, including state-of-the-art solutions. These approaches significantly enhance imputation speed while delivering competitive MSE and classification accuracy compared to direct imputation methods.

Quantum coherence and entanglement represent distinct manifestations of the superposition principle. This article demonstrates that the separable basis is the appropriate choice for estimating quantum coherence. Coherence calculated using the Bell basis fails to accurately reflect the system's true coherence because it includes artifacts arising from the specific basis state selection. The study begins by calculating entanglement, coherence, and mixedness for two-qubit mixed states derived from Bell states and a computational basis state, utilizing the $l_1$-norm for coherence, concurrence for entanglement, and linear entropy for mixedness. These metrics are then evaluated within the Bell basis to confirm that coherence must be measured only in a separable basis, whereas entanglement and mixedness are basis-independent. Furthermore, the research computes teleportation fidelity for these mixed states, identifying regions where fidelity exceeds classical limits. The study also investigates Bell-CHSH inequality violations to confirm quantum nonlocal correlations. Additionally, these analyses are extended to bipartite states generated by tracing out a qubit from tripartite systems. Results indicate that quantum teleportation can occur even when the Bell-CHSH inequality is not violated, proving that nonlocality is not a requisite condition for teleportation.

Quantum circuit dynamics incorporating local projective measurements can generate a diverse range of entangled states in quantum matter. Inspired by the physics of the Kitaev quantum spin liquid [1], we investigate such dynamics in (2+1)-dimensions, where monitored trajectories exhibit either (i) a phase characterized by topological quantum order or (ii) a "critical" phase marked by a logarithmic breach of area-law entanglement entropy scaling and extensive long-range tripartite entanglement. By employing a Majorana parton framework that extends the out-of-equilibrium parton description of the Kitaev honeycomb model, we achieve an analytical understanding of the universal characteristics of these two phases. This includes the steady-state entanglement properties, the system's evolution toward equilibrium, and the phase transition between the states. In the topologically-ordered phase, two logical qubits initialized in the system can be encoded and protected for a duration scaling exponentially with the system's linear size, whereas no robust quantum information encoding survives in the critical phase. Comprehensive numerical simulations of these monitored dynamics validate our analytical findings.

This paper introduces a suboptimal active disturbance rejection controller (S-ADRC) designed for second-order systems characterized by unknown, time-varying nonlinear dynamics. Utilizing a high-gain observer to estimate both main and extended state variables, the proposed output-feedback controller employs dynamic control gains to ensure global convergence toward an optimal solution. The efficacy of this approach is validated through three numerical examples, which compare its performance against fixed-gain conventional ADRC and various model-based optimal and suboptimal controllers across both linear and nonlinear systems.

CePtSi2 displays antiferromagnetic ordering below T*=1.8 K at ambient pressure, undergoes a valence transition near 1.2 GPa, and becomes superconducting between 1.4 and 2.1 GPa, peaking at 0.14 K [T. Nakano et al., Phys. Rev. B 79, 172507 (2009)]. To investigate its magnetic structure under varying pressures, we conducted neutron diffraction studies on both polycrystalline and single-crystal samples. At ambient pressure and below T_{SDW}~1.25 K, we observed incommensurate magnetic peaks with a propagation vector of (0.32, 0, 0.11). These peaks indicate a spin-density-wave order with the easy axis aligned along the c-axis and an average ordered moment of 0.45(5) μ_B, implying the existence of an intermediate phase between T* and T_{SDW}. Upon applying pressure, the magnetic propagation vector remained unchanged, yet the magnetic order vanished around 1.0 GPa—significantly below the critical pressure required for superconductivity. These findings suggest that factors other than magnetic fluctuations likely drive the primary mechanism of superconducting pairing.

This paper presents a general min-max characterization for the eigenvalues located within a gap of the essential spectrum of a self-adjoint unbounded operator. We establish an abstract theorem and subsequently apply it to Dirac operators featuring a Coulomb-like potential. The resulting characterization is optimal for the Coulomb potential. An erratum is included at the end of the LaTeX source.

In the context of Fourier restriction theory, the cone and the paraboloid serve as model surfaces. Wolff initially established the sharp bilinear restriction estimate for the cone, with Tao later determining the endpoint. Regarding the paraboloid, Tao achieved the sharp $L^2$ bilinear restriction estimate, yet the endpoint case remained unresolved. This paper resolves that open problem by proving the endpoint $L^2$ bilinear restriction estimate for the paraboloid.

Adaptive designs evolve dynamically as data accumulates, yet this flexibility can introduce small-sample bias into estimates. In the fields of psychometrics and psychophysics, a prevalent research focus is assessing a subject's task performance relative to stimulus intensity—the quantity or clarity of information provided. This relationship is modeled by a psychometric function. Standard experiments in these areas utilize adaptive designs that determine subsequent stimulus intensities based on prior performance and intensity levels, aiming to sample points that maximize information gain regarding the psychometric function. Comparable approaches are frequently employed in drug trials to dynamically assign doses based on previous responses and dosages. This paper examines how adaptation impacts statistical inference concerning the psychometric function, specifically regarding estimation methods. It evaluates both parametric and non-parametric estimators under fixed and adaptive designs, accounting for both within-subject independence and dependence via random effects. The study employs analytical methods centered on a latent class model to derive results under random effects, alongside a numerical simulation study. Findings indicate that while the asymptotic properties of estimators remain intact under adaptive designs, the adaptive structure generates small-sample bias, particularly affecting the slope parameter of the psychometric function. Consequently, the use of adaptive designs presents a dilemma: researchers must balance the efficiency of optimized sampling against the necessity of increasing sample sizes to mitigate this small-sample bias.

Richard Feynman's proposal to utilize quantum systems for simulating other quantum systems established the field of quantum simulation. Although present-day quantum computers remain susceptible to decoherence and depend on error correction, the creation of hybrid algorithms combining classical and quantum processing enables quantum simulation tasks. Notably, the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) has facilitated the investigation of the electronic structures of basic atoms and molecules by applying the Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle. This study presents the implementation of the VQE algorithm, using the Python Qiskit library, to determine the ground state energy of the hydrogen molecule.

Although recommenders for e-commerce and entertainment have garnered significant focus, educational recommenders remain underexplored despite the immense potential of intelligent tutors to enhance learning outcomes. A primary obstacle in this field is the lack of large, publicly accessible datasets. To address this, we introduce PEEK (Personalised Educational Engagement with Knowledge Topics), a novel, large-scale dataset featuring learners interacting with real-world educational videos. As the first public resource of its kind, PEEK links video lectures to Wikipedia concepts, offering an intuitive content taxonomy. We anticipate that combining fine-grained engagement metrics with rich content representations will enable powerful personalization algorithms, transforming both educational and informational recommendation systems. To achieve this, we: 1) created a new dataset from a major video lecture platform, 2) selected benchmark algorithms for modeling engagement, and 3) conducted extensive experiments on PEEK to validate its utility. Our results indicate strong potential for developing robust informational recommenders. The dataset and accompanying code are now publicly available.

Current Entity Linking (EL) systems suffer from a popularity bias, and no existing dataset addresses tail and emerging entities in non-English languages. To fill this gap, we introduce Hansel, a new Chinese benchmark designed to tackle few-shot and zero-shot EL challenges outside of English. The Hansel test set features human-annotated and reviewed data, generated via a novel approach for assembling zero-shot EL datasets. It encompasses 10,000 diverse documents from news, social media, and web articles, utilizing Wikidata as the target Knowledge Base. Our results indicate that state-of-the-art EL systems perform inadequately on Hansel, achieving only a 36.6% R@1 in Few-Shot scenarios. In response, we established a robust baseline that reaches 46.2% R@1 in Few-Shot and 76.6% in Zero-Shot settings. Furthermore, this baseline demonstrates competitive performance on the TAC-KBP2015 Chinese Entity Linking task.

Magnetization transfer contrast magnetic resonance fingerprinting (MTC-MRF) represents a new quantitative imaging method capable of simultaneously assessing multiple tissue parameters related to semisolid macromolecules and free bulk water. This study introduces an Only-Train-Once MR fingerprinting (OTOM) framework designed to estimate both free bulk water and MTC parameters from MR fingerprints irrespective of the specific MRF schedule used. This approach eliminates the need for time-consuming procedures, such as generating training datasets and training networks for every distinct MRF schedule. A recurrent neural network is specifically developed to handle two types of MRF schedule variations: differing lengths and varying patterns. Experimental results using both digital phantoms and in vivo data confirm that the method achieves accurate quantification of water and MTC parameters across multiple MRF schedules. Furthermore, the proposed technique shows excellent agreement with conventional deep learning and fitting methods. Consequently, the flexible OTOM framework serves as an efficient tool for tissue quantification across various MRF protocols.

The solar spectrum provides the primary means for diagnosing stellar processes. While understanding these spectra is essential for their application, their formation is intricate due to the non-local interactions between matter and radiation across space, wavelength, and time within the solar atmosphere. This complexity is outlined and demonstrated through classic literature, ultimately converging in the formation of the chromospheric spectrum.

Neural networks can be analyzed using two distinct duality frames: parameter-space and function-space. We show that symmetries inherent in network densities can be identified through dual computations of network correlation functions, even without knowledge of the specific density or assuming network equivariance. This approach, termed symmetry-via-duality, leverages the invariance properties of correlation functions, which arise from the selection of network parameter distributions. By determining input and output symmetries of these densities, we recover established Gaussian process results in the infinite width limit. Furthermore, this mechanism can identify symmetries during training when parameters are correlated, as well as symmetries within the Neural Tangent Kernel. Our findings indicate that the degree of symmetry in the initialization density influences the accuracy of networks trained on Fashion-MNIST, and that symmetry breaking yields improvements only when aligned with the ground truth.

We develop a kinetic framework for quantum information scrambling within a paradigmatic model of interacting electrons near a superconducting phase transition. By rigorously deriving a system of coupled partial differential equations, we describe information propagation dynamics across generic dimensions. These equations yield traveling wave solutions that are discontinuous at the light cone's boundary and maintain a strictly causal structure, ensuring no influence extends beyond the light cone.

In a capital market, the social structure comprises traders whose individual actions are driven by the desire to affiliate with and gain approval from their peers. When making decisions, individuals align their own requirements with those of the group, allowing any two agents to interact through costly information exchange. Agents are assumed to cite the source of information upon request, enabling others to verify private data. Drawing on Rivier's methods, Hudak analyzed the social behavior of these agents, characterizing information verification as a quantity that increases an agent's risk aversion. An agent's investment mix within a specific cell, defined by a risk aversion measure A, is determined by minimizing the average cell objective function $<FM>$. The absolute minimum of this function represents an optimal state where information exchange is balanced given market expectations. This aversion constant A incorporates both collective and individual contributions to risk aversion. The model examines stable and metastable market states across varying values of expected return (E), expected risk (EV), and the constant b (which influences the contribution of quantity $<f>$ to risk aversion). Furthermore, the variance of n for the distribution of irreducible subgroups is calculated, illustrating how the model captures intermediary process effects.

We introduce the concept of hitting time for a Markov decision process (MDP). This definition diverges from the hitting time of the Markov process naturally induced by the MDP, primarily because the latter might lack a stationary distribution. Furthermore, even if such a distribution exists, it does not necessarily align with the MDP's normalized occupancy measure. By identifying a connection between the MDP and PageRank, we construct a Markov process whose stationary distribution exactly matches the MDP's normalized occupancy measure. Consequently, we define the MDP's hitting time as the hitting time of this newly constructed Markov process.

One perspective on quantum non-locality is that information within a composite system can be encoded such that it remains inaccessible via local measurements, even when aided by classical communication. Unlike classical scenarios, quantum many-body systems can contain information that cannot be retrieved locally. However, we demonstrate a striking exception: two-dimensional subspaces do not exhibit this behavior. Regardless of entanglement or multipartite structure, any physically permissible measurement on information encoded within such a subspace can be executed locally. This process requires only local measurements and the feed-forward of classical information, which is readily achievable across various experimental platforms. Applying these findings to quantum secret sharing, we propose a modification of a well-known quantum information splitting protocol. This approach ensures that no single recipient can access the complete transmitted state, necessitating collaboration among parties to perform measurements on it. These results hold practical significance for measuring encoded qubits in contexts such as quantum secret sharing and quantum error correction, while also highlighting a fundamental property unique to two-dimensional subspaces.

Theories of decision-making, including Fuzzy-Trace Theory (FTT), indicate that individuals prioritize gist, or the essential meaning, of text when making choices. This paper outlines the creation of GisPy, a Python-based open-source utility designed to calculate the Gist Inference Score (GIS). Testing GisPy across three benchmarks from news and scientific domains reveals that its generated scores effectively differentiate between texts with low and high gist. The tool is freely accessible at: https://github.com/phosseini/GisPy.

The origins of metal production in the Universe are located within galaxy clusters, specifically inside their Intra-Cluster Medium (ICM). The X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU), scheduled for launch on the next-generation European X-ray observatory Athena in the 2030s, will offer a critical advancement in spatially-resolved spectroscopy needed to unravel the complex processes driving this chemical enrichment. This paper examines the prospective capabilities of the X-IFU for analyzing hot gas in galaxy clusters. Utilizing a test sample of four clusters from cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, we present extensive synthetic observations spanning various redshifts (up to z = 2) and enclosed within the R500 radius, generated via the SIXTE instrument simulator. With exposure times of 100 ks, we show that the X-IFU will enable spatially-resolved mapping of ICM physical properties with minimal bias (<5%) and well within statistical limits. Furthermore, detailed analysis of abundance profiles and ratios within R500 underscores the instrument's capacity to constrain diverse enrichment models. By simulating observations out to z = 2, we quantify the X-IFU's precision in tracking chemical elements across cosmic history, allowing for an investigation into the evolution of metal production mechanisms and their connection to the stellar initial mass function. Ultimately, this study highlights the X-IFU's unparalleled ability to reveal ICM properties while emphasizing the data analysis challenges that future high-resolution X-ray missions like Athena will encounter.

This study conducts a detailed analysis of the potential neutrino mass ($M_
u$) limits obtainable by merging future spectroscopic galaxy surveys with cosmic microwave background (CMB) observations, specifically highlighting the roles of CMB lensing and galaxy-CMB lensing. While CMB lensing can assist in resolving the $M_
u$-curvature degeneracy when paired with baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data alone, we show that this approach discards substantial constraining power because the broadband power spectrum shape significantly influences the results. Furthermore, building on prior research, we illustrate how cosmology-independent $M_
u$ constraints can be derived by combining the scale-dependent features in the power spectrum induced by neutrino free-streaming with the comprehensive capabilities of upcoming CMB missions. These free-streaming-based limits are independent of the CMB optical depth ($	au$) and remain competitive with BAO constraints for extended cosmological models, even when both are supplemented by CMB and galaxy-CMB lensing.

As the deployment of robots in unpredictable and unstructured settings gains traction, there is a heightened focus on integrating risk assessment into safety-critical control development. The authors argue that this consideration must also extend to the verification of such controllers. To address the need for sample-efficient verification methods for uncertain black-box systems, we first outline a technique for estimating the Value-at-Risk of arbitrary scalar random variables without prior knowledge of their distribution. Subsequently, we recast the uncertain verification problem as a Value-at-Risk estimation task, leveraging our initial findings. This approach establishes fundamental sampling requirements to bound, with high confidence, the volume of states and parameters in a black-box system that could lead to unsafe outcomes. Furthermore, we demonstrate through Robotarium simulations that this procedure remains effective regardless of system complexity.

Let $V$ denote an infinite-dimensional vector space over a field with a characteristic other than 2. We examine and categorize the ideals within the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$, which consists of all linear transformations acting on $V$.

GRS 1915+105 marked the first instance of a stellar-mass black hole in our galaxy exhibiting a superluminal radio jet, a phenomenon previously associated only with active galactic nuclei hosting supermassive black holes. It was hypothesized that instabilities within the accretion disc drive this radio emission by ejecting inner disc material into the jet. This study demonstrates a robust correlation between the radio flux (originating from the jet) and the iron emission line flux (emerging from the disc), as well as between the temperature of the X-ray corona (which generates high-energy X-rays via inverse Compton scattering) and the amplitude of high-frequency variability from the innermost accretion flow. Conversely, the radio flux and iron line flux show a strong anti-correlation with both the corona's temperature and the variability amplitude. These relationships have remained consistent over approximately 10 years, despite significant fluctuations in the source's X-ray and radio characteristics. These findings offer definitive proof that the energy powering this system is directed either toward the X-ray corona or the jet: when energy heats the corona, less remains to fuel the jet, causing radio flux to decrease, and vice versa. Combined with variability modeling, this evidence conclusively indicates that in GRS 1915+105, the X-ray corona transforms into the jet.

Predicting nuclear properties in regions distant from experimental data is inherently uncertain due to incomplete knowledge of nuclear forces and the complexities of modeling quantum many-body interactions in strongly coupled systems. Although model bias can be directly computed where experimental data exists, it can only be estimated when such data is missing. Existing methods for estimating this bias rapidly lose reliability when extrapolating variables like proton or neutron numbers, leading to uncontrolled errors in applications such as nucleosynthesis simulations. This letter introduces a novel technique to identify the optimal input variables for machine learning algorithms to generate robust bias estimates. Our method selects features based on their probability distributions across the entire nuclear chart. We demonstrate this approach by quantifying model bias in nuclear binding energies derived from Density Functional Theory (DFT), showing that systematic feature selection enhances theoretical predictions without increasing uncertainty.

When reliable prior information regarding an object is available, its phase can be accurately estimated from a single diffracted intensity image. Such priors encompass amplitude bounds, object support, sparsity in spatial or transform domains, deep image priors, and deep neural networks trained on labeled datasets. While deep learning achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction quality, it necessitates extensive labeled datasets (ground truth-measurement pairs captured under identical experimental conditions) for training. To address this data scarcity, this letter introduces a zero-shot learning approach. It demonstrates that an object prior learned by a deep neural network during a denoising task can effectively support phase retrieval, provided the diffraction physics are strictly enforced on the network's output. Furthermore, the study shows that integrating total variation into this zero-shot framework enables reconstruction of comparable quality in significantly less time (approximately an 8.5-fold reduction, as reported in the test case within this letter).

This study demonstrates the manipulation of both static and dynamic magnetic properties through photostriction in an extrinsic multiferroic composite, utilizing visible blue light. The composites are fabricated by coupling magnetostrictive Fe$_{81}$Ga$_{19}$ thin films (with thicknesses of 2.5, 5, or 10 nm) to a (011)-Pb(Mg$_{1/3}$Nb$_{2/3}$)O$_3$-Pb(Zr,Ti)O$_3$ piezoelectric substrate. Under the converse magneto-photostrictive effect (CMPE), angular-dependent magnetization reversal characteristics are significantly either enhanced or suppressed. To quantify this phenomenon, a new physical parameter, the converse magneto-photostrictive coupling coefficient, is introduced as a general method for analyzing and comparing various extrinsic multiferroics. Analysis reveals that CMPE strength diminishes substantially as the Fe$_{81}$Ga$_{19}$ film thickness increases. Furthermore, ferromagnetic resonance measurements on the thinnest sample provide experimental proof of the CMPE's ability to control dynamic magnetic properties. Ultimately, this research establishes CMPE as an efficient strategy for regulating both static and dynamic magnetic behaviors in extrinsic multiferroic systems.

We propose a model-space framework for quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to facilitate the stable estimation of both ground and excited states on quantum computers. Model-space QITE (MSQITE) maintains orthogonality while propagating the model space toward the exact space, allowing it to describe multiple states at once. To enhance convergence, the quantum Lanczos (QLanczos) algorithm is adapted for MSQITE. Our scheme demonstrates superior performance compared to both standard QLanczos and the recently introduced folded-spectrum QITE when simulating excited states. Furthermore, we show that spin contamination can be effectively mitigated by shifting the imaginary time propagator, enabling the efficient capture of excited states with specific spin quantum numbers without erroneously converging to lower-energy states of different spins. Finally, we examine how varying levels of the unitary approximation utilized in MSQITE influence the outcomes.

This study examines the frequentist characteristics of the variational sparse Gaussian Process regression framework, specifically focusing on the theoretical implications of using spectral features as inducing variables. We establish both the guarantees and constraints regarding the frequentist coverage of the derived variational credible sets. Furthermore, we determine sufficient and necessary lower bounds for the quantity of inducing variables needed to attain minimax posterior contraction rates, illustrating the consequences of these findings across various prior distributions. Finally, our numerical analysis explores a broader spectrum of inducing variable methods, revealing comparable behaviors that extend beyond the specific scope of our theoretical results.

For every double poset (a finite set equipped with two partial orders) and any weight function on its underlying set, a quasisymmetric function is defined. This construction extends established mathematical objects such as monomial and fundamental quasisymmetric functions, (skew) Schur functions, dual immaculate functions, and quasisymmetric $\left(P, \omega\right)$-partition enumerators. We establish a formula for the antipode of this function that applies under specific conditions—conditions met when the second partial order is total, as well as in additional scenarios. This result restates a finding by Malvenuto and Reutenauer in a manner we find more intuitive, supported by a novel and self-contained proof. Furthermore, we extend this result to a broader framework where a group acts on the double poset via automorphisms.

This paper introduces a centroid-based clustering algorithm designed to group data points with n-features without requiring the number of clusters to be predefined. The algorithm's fundamental mechanism relies on a similarity metric that determines whether an incoming data point should be assigned to an existing cluster or used to form a new one. This approach is tailored for specific applications involving the clustering analysis of data streams, where a data point is associated with a cluster only if its similarity to that cluster exceeds a predefined Level-of-Similarity threshold.

The IceCube Observatory has measured the diffuse cosmic neutrino flux across TeV to PeV energy ranges. We demonstrate that refining the characterization of this flux at lower energies, specifically the sub-TeV and TeV bands, provides model-independent insights into the nature of astrophysical neutrino sources. Most notably, such analysis could validate current suggestions that these neutrinos arise from cosmic environments optically thick to GeV-TeV gamma rays. This conclusion would become certain if observations in the TeV region reveal a steeper or continuous neutrino power law. In these gamma-ray obscured sources, the gamma rays inherently produced alongside cosmic neutrinos would cascade down to MeV-GeV energies. The condition that this cascaded gamma-ray flux must not surpass the observed diffuse gamma-ray background imposes constraints on the radiation field's peak energy and density within the sources. Calculations based on current data suggest that a portion of the observed diffuse MeV-GeV gamma-ray background may stem from neutrino sources possessing intense radiation fields that hide the high-energy gamma-ray emission associated with the neutrinos.

This paper presents a generalized investigation of abelian gauge field theory involving rank-one fields $T_{\mu}$ within an $n$-successive rotor model set in $D$-dimensional flat spacetime. The theory describes interactions among massless elementary spin-1 particles, a requirement to maintain gauge symmetry. We prove that $n$ rotors introduce contributions proportional to $\Box^n T^{\mu}$ in the action via the integration-by-parts method. This mathematical structure corresponds to transforming the gauge field as $T^{\mu} \rightarrow \Box^n T^{\mu}$ and the field strength as $G_{\mu\nu} \rightarrow \Box^n G_{\mu\nu}$. When $n=0$, the framework reduces to standard abelian gauge theory. Furthermore, we analyze the equations of motion and the Noether conserved current associated with this extended theory.
This paper examines the distribution of zeros for specific nonlinear difference polynomials derived from entire functions of finite order.

Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) has recently garnered significant interest for its ability to learn transferable visual representations. Nevertheless, semantic gaps within datasets cause CLIP's pre-trained image-text alignment to become sub-optimal on downstream tasks, severely degrading its transfer performance. To better adapt the cross-modality embedding space, we propose enhancing CLIP with Visual-guided Texts, termed VT-CLIP. Specifically, we direct textual features of various categories to adaptively identify informative regions within images and aggregate visual features using attention mechanisms. Consequently, texts become visual-guided, exhibiting stronger semantic correlation with downstream images, which significantly improves the category-wise matching process. In few-shot scenarios, we evaluate VT-CLIP across 11 established classification datasets to demonstrate its efficacy.

This research investigates a quantum trimer composed of coupled two-level systems, extending analysis beyond the single-excitation regime to include complex phases within the coherent coupling constants. By adopting an open quantum systems framework that incorporates both losses and gain, we demonstrate that the mean state populations are significantly influenced by the accumulated phase throughout the trimer. Specifically, nontrivial accumulated phases induce notable nonreciprocal behavior in both singly and doubly excited manifolds regarding population dynamics and steady states. Moreover, while the loop's accumulated phase primarily dictates the direction of the resulting chiral current, the flow's sign can also be altered by variations in coupling strength and gain levels. These findings provide a foundation for experimental investigations into nanoscale chiral currents, where complex hopping parameter phases are tuned via magnetic or synthetic magnetic fields. (14 pages)

This paper introduces a novel stabilization technique for the discontinuous Galerkin method, grounded in the Dafermos entropy rate criterion. The method functions by solving linear or nonlinear optimization problems at each timestep to correct the standard discontinuous Galerkin scheme. This enforcement of the Dafermos criterion enhances stability relative to the basic approach while maintaining the method's order of accuracy, as confirmed by numerical experiments. Additionally, modifying the optimization problem enables the enforcement of classical entropy inequalities. Consequently, this proposed stabilization offers an alternative to existing shock capturing techniques such as flux-differencing, finite-volume subcells, artificial viscosity, and modal filtering.

We introduce the formalism for general continuum models that explicitly incorporates boundary conditions and apply it to a system possessing the minimal degrees of freedom required for a well-defined boundary: a two-component wave function governed by a linear-in-momentum Hamiltonian. We derive the most general Hamiltonians and boundary conditions (Class A) for one-dimensional (insulator), two-dimensional (quantum anomalous Hall insulator), and three-dimensional (Weyl node) scenarios, followed by an analytical investigation of the resulting bound, edge, and surface-state structures. In the 1D case, a single bound state emerges within half of the $\text{U}(1)$ parameter space defined by possible boundary conditions. By analyzing multiple dimensions simultaneously, we unify these models and reveal critical interconnections among them. We formulate a comprehensive version of the bulk-boundary correspondence that fully characterizes the neighborhood of a Weyl point, establishing that the chirality of the surface-state spectrum along a path encircling the projected Weyl point equals the Chern number of that point. Furthermore, we demonstrate how symmetries are naturally integrated into this framework by deriving the most general model form for chiral symmetry (Class AIII). We show that the seemingly unexpected presence of persistent bound states in the topologically trivial 1D Class-A model is not coincidental, offering at least two topological interpretations: relating it to the topologically nontrivial 2D Class-A system (viewed as an effective 2D quantum anomalous Hall system) and the 1D Class-AIII system (via deviations from chiral symmetry in the parameter space). We identify this phenomenon as a systematic "propagation effect," wherein bound states from topologically nontrivial classes—where they are protected and guaranteed to exist—propagate to related, topologically trivial classes that are adjacent in terms of dimension or symmetry.

Inspired by the mathematical foundations of superstring theory, we propose a novel equation defined on balanced, Hermitian manifolds with a vanishing first Chern class. Solutions to this equation yield, within every Bott-Chern cohomology class, a Hermitian Ricci-flat balanced metric, effectively extending the classical Calabi-Yau equation to the level of differential forms. We demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of these solutions on complex tori and establish specific uniqueness and openness results for general Kähler manifolds.

The emergence of $\pi$-stacked layered metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) has created new possibilities for developing compact MOF-based devices, combining unique electrical conductivity with permanent porosity and exceptionally high surface areas. Leveraging the modular nature of these electrically conductive (EC) MOFs allows for the creation of an unlimited variety of materials suitable for electronic applications, including battery electrodes, supercapacitors, and spintronics. By permuting structural building blocks such as various metal nodes and organic linkers, researchers can generate novel systems with unprecedented and unexplored physical and chemical properties. With the ultimate goal of establishing a platform for accelerated materials design and discovery, this work lays the groundwork for the first comprehensive database of EC-MOFs using an experimentally guided approach. The initial phase of this database, designated EC-MOF/Phase-I, includes 1,061 bulk and mono-layer structures derived from all possible combinations of experimentally reported organic linkers, functional groups, and metal nodes. A high-throughput screening (HTS) workflow has been established to perform density functional theory calculations under periodic boundary conditions, optimizing structures and calculating key relevant properties. Given that EC-MOF research has historically lacked appropriate initial crystal structures, all geometric and property data are now made available to the community via an online platform developed during this project. This database offers comprehensive physical and chemical data on EC-MOFs, facilitating the selection of suitable materials for specific applications and thereby accelerating the design and discovery of compact EC-MOF-based devices.

Q-Stars, alternatively known as gray holes possessing a radius twice that of the corresponding Schwarzschild radius for an equivalent mass, belong to the compact neutron star category and exhibit extremely high density. These structures were derived by employing a generalization of $q$-deformed fermions, utilizing two parameters, $q$ and $p$, as the stellar constituents. Since the deformation parameters within $q,p$-fermions regulate particle interactions more directly than a complex interaction Lagrangian, the study identifies the parameter values that maximize Q-Star pressure between interacting stellar particles. Numerical solutions of the TOV equations were applied to analyze both cold and hot Q-Stars at temperatures of $T=0$, $T=40\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and $T=60\ \mathrm{MeV}$. The results indicate that Q-Stars can attain masses up to $13$ solar masses and radii of $75$ km. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that as a star cools, both its total mass and radius increase, leading to a significantly denser state.

A primary objective of self-supervised learning is to allow model pre-training to leverage nearly boundless datasets. Yet, a recently popular technique, masked image modeling (MIM), is often believed to fail when scaled with larger data. This study disproves that assumption through comprehensive experiments spanning data volumes from 10% of ImageNet-1K to the entirety of ImageNet-22K, model capacities from 49M to 1B parameters, and training durations from 125K to 500K iterations. Our analysis demonstrates three key points: (i) MIM requires substantial data; specifically, very large models tend to overfit when trained on relatively small datasets. (ii) Training duration is critical; large models employing MIM can effectively utilize more data if the training period is extended. (iii) Pre-training validation loss serves as a reliable predictor of a model's fine-tuning performance across various tasks, enabling early evaluation without the need for expensive downstream trial-and-error testing. We anticipate these insights will deepen the understanding of MIM's scaling capabilities.

The digitization of scanned receipts involves extracting text from images and organizing it into structured documents, a process typically divided into text localization and optical character recognition (OCR). Conventional OCR models generally rely on cropped text instances, necessitating a separate detection model to provide bounding box coordinates. However, adding a detector is inefficient, and instance-level OCR models often struggle with full-document accuracy when handling complex layouts containing multiple text lines. To address this, we introduce a localization-free, document-level OCR model capable of transcribing all characters in a receipt image into an ordered sequence in an end-to-end manner. Specifically, we adapt the pretrained Transformer-based instance-level model TrOCR by finetuning it with randomly cropped image chunks and progressively increasing the chunk size to extend recognition capabilities from individual instances to entire pages. Experiments on the SROIE dataset demonstrate that our strategy yields a 64.4 F1-score and a 22.8% Character Error Rate (CER), significantly outperforming baseline results of 48.5 F1-score and 50.6% CER. The optimal configuration, which divides the full image into 15 equal chunks, achieves an 87.8 F1-score and a 4.98% CER with minimal additional pre- or post-processing. Furthermore, the generated document-level sequences maintain correct reading order, making the approach highly practical for real-world applications.

In a three-dimensional spacetime with conformal flatness, the linearised higher-spin Cotton tensor $\mathfrak{C}_{\alpha(n)}(h)$ represents the sole conserved conformal current that arises as a gauge-invariant descendant of the conformal gauge prepotential $h_{\alpha(n)}$. While the explicit structure of $\mathfrak{C}_{\alpha(n)}(h)$ is established in Minkowski space, this work addresses its extension to anti-de Sitter (AdS) space, yielding a closed-form expression using AdS Lorentz covariant derivatives. We demonstrate that every conformal higher-spin action $S_{\text{CS}}^{(n)}[h]\propto \int\text{d}^3x\, e \, h^{\alpha(n)}\mathfrak{C}_{\alpha(n)}(h)$ decomposes into a product of $(n-1)$ first-order operators linked to the spin-$n/2$ partially massless AdS values. These results significantly simplify the on-shell analysis of massive higher-spin gauge-invariant actions in AdS$_3$, and the findings are further generalized to $\mathcal{N}=1$ AdS supersymmetry, providing concise formulas for the higher-spin super-Cotton tensors in AdS$_3$.

The Multi-speaker Multi-style Voice Cloning Challenge (M2VoC) is designed to offer a substantial, standardized dataset and an equitable evaluation environment for benchmarking voice cloning technologies. Specifically, the challenge focuses on adapting average Text-to-Speech (TTS) models to match target voices in both identity and style using limited speaker data. The competition is divided into two main tracks: the few-shot track, requiring cloning from 100 samples, and the one-shot track, requiring cloning from just 5 samples. Each track includes two sub-tracks: Sub-track A restricts participants to using only the training data provided by the organizers to ensure fair strategy comparison, while Sub-track B permits the use of any publicly available data. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the challenge's tasks and datasets, along with a summary of submitted systems and their evaluation results.

We introduce a novel method to achieve longitudinal coherence in X-ray Free-Electron Laser (FEL) outputs, utilizing a series of undulators and delay chicanes alongside precise initial electron beam conditioning with time-dependent focusing. Simulations of a simplified FEL model indicate that this approach is effective.

This paper investigates non-Einstein Bach-flat gravitational instantons, which serve as the conformal gravity extension of the Taub-NUT/Bolt and Eguchi-Hanson solutions found in Einstein gravity. The resulting geometries encompass non-Einstein spaces that are either asymptotically locally flat (ALF) or asymptotically locally Anti-de Sitter (AlAdS). However, we also identify solutions with distinct asymptotic behaviors, specifically those exhibiting a weakened AlAdS asymptotic condition characteristic of the low decaying modes in conformal gravity. These findings allow us to determine a simple Neumann boundary condition that isolates the Einstein solution within the broader class of conformal gravity solutions, mirroring the behavior seen in the asymptotically AdS sector. All identified geometries possess non-zero Hirzebruch signature and Euler characteristic, classifying them as single-centered instantons. Furthermore, we calculate the topological and Noether charges for the Taub-NUT/Bolt and Eguchi-Hanson spacetimes, confirming their finiteness and thereby facilitating an analysis of their thermodynamic properties.

Progresses in material architecture have allowed for the integration of exotic properties into materials, expanding beyond traditional mechanical engineering capabilities. This study focuses specifically on twisting, a mechanism in which metamaterials convert static axial loads into rotational motion. To investigate the longitudinal-to-twist (L-T) conversion in a chiral tetragonal-beam metamaterial, we utilize finite element method computations supported by an analytical framework based on Lagrange's equations applied to a monoatomic spring-mass system. First, an eigenvalue analysis incorporating polarization states is conducted to underscore the potential role of the longitudinal mode in this conversion. We then compare the twisting dynamics of the chiral cell against those of homogeneous media, octagonal-tube structures, and non-chiral cells. Furthermore, both time-domain and frequency-domain analyses are employed to illustrate how the cell's chirality affects L-T conversion. Results demonstrate that a significant portion of longitudinally propagating waves transforms into twist across a wide frequency spectrum, achieving near-total conversion at specific frequencies.

Given the daily surge in new publications, analyzing authorship in scientific texts—whether single or multi-authored—presents a compelling challenge. However, current datasets are often deficient, lacking either scientific content or essential metadata. To address this, we introduce SMAuC, a novel, metadata-enriched corpus tailored for scientific authorship analysis. Containing over three million papers across diverse scientific fields, SMAuC represents the largest publicly available resource for this purpose to date. It integrates a broad spectrum of texts from both the humanities and natural sciences with meticulously curated metadata, featuring unique and disambiguated author identifiers. We anticipate that SMAuC will substantially advance research and development in scientific authorship analysis.

Error-correcting codes (ECC) enable senders to transmit messages to receivers such that the receiver can recover the original information even when a constant fraction of the bits are corrupted. Given their significance and foundational role, ECCs have been widely investigated, with a primary objective of maximizing the fraction of errors they can withstand. For adversarial erasure errors over a binary channel, the maximum resilience of an ECC is limited to one-half of the transmitted bits. This work overcomes that $\frac12$ limitation by proposing interactive error-correcting codes (iECC) and constructing an iECC capable of tolerating adversarial erasure of $\frac35$ of the total communicated bits. We highlight that the adversary may corrupt both the sender and the receiver, with the adversary's budget accounting for rounds from both parties. Additionally, we establish an impossibility (upper) bound of $\frac23$ for the maximum resilience of any binary iECC against adversarial erasures, and a bound of $\frac27$ in the bit-flip scenario.

Advancements in aerial photography and precise 3D reconstruction of cityscapes have heightened focus on the automated analysis of urban zones. This study investigates two critical components enabling live analysis of building structures within city models using oblique aerial imagery: automatic building extraction via Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and selective real-time depth estimation from aerial photos. By leveraging transfer learning, we trained the Faster R-CNN method for real-time deep object detection, integrating a extensive ground-based dataset for urban scene comprehension with a limited set of aerial images. On a chosen evaluation set, our building extraction approach achieved an average precision (AP) of approximately 80%. Our assessment covers both dataset-specific learning and transfer learning strategies. Additionally, we introduce an algorithm capable of real-time multi-view depth estimation from aerial imagery. Utilizing the Semi-Global Matching (SGM) optimization strategy ensures sharp edges are maintained at object boundaries. When paired with Faster R-CNN, this enables the selective reconstruction of buildings, identified as Regions of Interest (RoIs), from oblique aerial imagery.

We recently established the "Newman-Penrose map," a new correspondence linking specific solutions of Einstein's equations to self-dual vacuum Maxwell solutions, a connection closely tied to the classical double copy. In this work, we provide an alternative definition of this map using quantities naturally defined on twistor space and a shear-free null geodesic congruence in Minkowski space, whose twistorial properties are described by the Kerr theorem. This reformulation offers a purely geometric perspective, explicitly invariant under both spacetime diffeomorphisms and projective transformations on twistor space. Although the original formulation may remain more practical for explicit computations, our proposed twistorial version likely holds greater theoretical significance.

This study utilized linear algebra and functional analysis to establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for stable, oscillation-free solutions in both linear and nonlinear parabolic partial differential equations. By applying singular value decomposition and Fourier analysis to diverse finite difference schemes, we identified patterns within the eigenfunctions (represented by sampled eigenvectors) and the structure of their eigenspectra. Leveraging these findings, we analyzed how initial and boundary conditions influence the frequency and long-term behavior of numerical oscillations, as well as pinpointed the solution regions most vulnerable to such instabilities.

The emerging novel Coronavirus (COVID-19) has infected millions globally since its initial detection. Establishing efficient short-term forecasting models is crucial for predicting future case numbers, enabling public health systems to create strategic plans that can prevent fatalities. This study evaluates several techniques—including Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), Cubist (CUBIST), Random Forest (RF), Ridge Regression (RIDGE), Support Vector Regression (SVR), and Stacking Ensemble Learning—for forecasting one-, three-, and six-day-ahead cumulative confirmed cases in ten Brazilian states with high daily incidence. In the stacking ensemble approach, Cubist, RF, RIDGE, and SVR served as base learners, with Gaussian Process (GP) acting as the meta-learner. Model performance was assessed using the improvement index, Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error (SMAPE). Across most scenarios, SVR and the stacking ensemble outperformed the other models according to these metrics. Generally, the developed models produced accurate forecasts, with error rates ranging from 0.87% to 3.51% for one-day, 1.02% to 5.63% for three-day, and 0.95% to 6.90% for six-day predictions. The final model ranking across all scenarios was SVR, followed by stacking ensemble learning, ARIMA, CUBIST, RIDGE, and RF. These models are recommended for forecasting and monitoring the ongoing spread of COVID-19, as they provide valuable support for managerial decision-making.

Matter along the line of sight of relic photons induces subtle yet measurable distortions in the angular distribution of Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) temperature fluctuations. The Planck Collaboration has recently provided an estimated convergence map, representing the integrated large-scale matter distribution responsible for the weak gravitational lensing (WL) signals detected in Planck CMB data. We conducted comprehensive analyses of this convergence map, computing variance across both small and large sky regions while excluding areas masked by galactic foregrounds, and compared these findings against simulated convergence maps also supplied by Planck. Our objective was to identify sky regions exhibiting anomalous WL signatures in the variance estimator, detected via $\chi^2$ analysis at a statistically significant level. In our local analysis of the Planck convergence map, we identified eight sky patches that deviated by more than $2\sigma$ from the average of the simulations. Conversely, the large-scale region analysis revealed no statistically significant discrepancies; however, the areas with the highest $\chi^2$ values were notably concentrated around the ecliptic poles. Overall, our results align well with the features predicted by the $\Lambda$CDM concordance model as represented in the simulations. Nevertheless, the presence of outlier regions may indicate residual contamination, such as noise, potentially arising from over- or under-estimation of systematic effects within the simulation dataset.

Observations of electromagnetic and gravitational waves reveal a scarcity of compact objects with masses between approximately $2.5$ and $5~{\rm M_\odot}$, a phenomenon known as the "mass gap." This gap is potentially connected to the supernova mechanisms responsible for creating neutron stars (NSs) and black holes (BHs). However, the confirmed existence of a few mass-gap compact objects, including some identified as BHs, challenges conventional theories regarding black hole formation. This study explores the formation of BHs through the accretion-induced collapse (AIC) of NSs within X-ray binaries, specifically examining the effects of super-Eddington accretion. Recent data from ultraluminous X-ray pulsars suggest that their observed luminosities likely represent the actual accretion rates, which can exceed the Eddington limit by factors greater than 100. Consequently, NSs undergoing super-Eddington accretion could rapidly evolve into BHs in intermediate or low-mass X-ray binaries. Utilizing super-Eddington accretion disk models alongside binary population synthesis and detailed stellar evolution calculations, we analyzed the evolution of these systems. Our results indicate that super-Eddington accretion is crucial for NS mass growth, with the final BH masses heavily influenced by the NS magnetic field strength, the donor star's metallicity, and the binary's bifurcation period. The AIC of NSs may explain certain observed mass-gap BHs, such as GRO J0422+32. Furthermore, we present parameter distributions for potential mass-gap BHs in a Milky Way-like galaxy and suggest that future space-based gravitational wave observations could provide significant tests or constraints on the AIC formation channel.

This study focuses on moduli spaces of rank 2 logarithmic connections on elliptic curves featuring two poles. To achieve this, we examine specific rank 2 logarithmic connections on the Riemann sphere and establish a transformation rule to lift them onto an elliptic curve. The process involves taking an elliptic curve $C$ with an elliptic quotient $\pi\colon C\to{\mathbb P}^1$ and a logarithmic connection $(E,\nabla)$ on ${\mathbb P}^1$; by pulling back the connection, we derive a new connection $(\pi^*E, \pi^*\nabla)$ on $C$. Following appropriate birational modifications, the connection is reduced to a specific normal form. Since this entire transformation respects bundle automorphisms, it induces a mapping between the respective moduli spaces of connections. The primary objective of this paper is to characterize these moduli spaces and derive explicit formulas for the aforementioned map, specifically when the target space consists of rank 2 logarithmic connections on an elliptic curve $C$ with two simple poles and a trivial determinant.

Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is revolutionizing the AI landscape by bolstering end-user trust in automated systems. With the continuous expansion of connected devices, the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem must remain reliable for its users; however, current literature lacks a systematic and comprehensive review of XAI applications within IoT. To fill this gap, this paper examines XAI frameworks, emphasizing their specific attributes and suitability for IoT environments. We showcase prevalent XAI services deployed in IoT sectors, including security reinforcement, the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), Industrial IoT (IIoT), and Internet of City Things (IoCT), while providing implementation recommendations supported by concrete examples and key insights for future research. Furthermore, we highlight advancements in edge-based XAI architectures and their integration with sixth-generation (6G) communication services for IoT, concluding with critical takeaways. Ultimately, this work offers the first all-encompassing compilation detailing XAI frameworks designed to meet the evolving demands of future IoT scenarios.

This paper reviews existing literature on discrimination theories, with a primary emphasis on recent advancements. Contemporary models extend traditional frameworks of taste-based and statistical discrimination by incorporating specific aspects of learning and signaling environments, frequently employing innovative information and mechanism-design terminology. These theories also examine algorithmic learning and decision-making processes while accounting for agents exhibiting behavioral biases and incorrect beliefs. Furthermore, this survey seeks to bridge the divide between economic perspectives on discrimination and its broader treatment in social science. In doing so, I first contribute by delineating a category of models regarding discriminatory institutions, encompassing both discriminatory social norms and institutional design. Additionally, I explore the distinction between direct and systemic discrimination, comparing these classifications to other concepts found within economic literature.

The rising need for search and rescue operations has created a critical demand for detecting objects of interest within large-scale images captured by Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), a task that is particularly difficult due to the extremely small size of these objects. While most current approaches utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN) to enhance shallow layer features by integrating deep contextual information, the inconsistency in gradient computation across different layers prevents the full exploitation of shallow layers for detecting tiny objects. To address this, we introduce the Scale Selection Pyramid Network (SSPNet) specifically designed for tiny person detection. This architecture comprises three key components: the Context Attention Module (CAM), which generates hierarchical attention heatmaps by considering contextual information; the Scale Enhancement Module (SEM), which emphasizes features at specific scales across various layers to direct the detector toward target objects rather than background noise; and the Scale Selection Module (SSM), which leverages relationships between adjacent layers to facilitate appropriate feature sharing between deep and shallow layers, thereby resolving gradient computation inconsistencies. Additionally, we propose a Weighted Negative Sampling (WNS) strategy to guide the detector in selecting more representative samples. Experimental results on the TinyPerson benchmark demonstrate that our method surpasses other state-of-the-art detectors.

Kostanek and Waszkiewicz extended the Edalat and Heckmann formal ball model, originally designed for metric spaces, to ${\sf Q}$-categories. This paper investigates how the internal structure of the quantale ${\sf Q}$ affects the relationship between Yoneda completeness in ${\sf Q}$-categories and the directed completeness of their corresponding sets of formal balls. Specifically, when ${\sf Q}$ is the unit interval $[0,1]$ endowed with a continuous t-norm $\&$, the authors demonstrate that Yoneda completeness for every ${\sf Q}$-category is equivalent to the directed completeness of its set of formal balls if and only if the t-norm $\&$ satisfies the Archimedean property.

Deep neural networks currently dominate natural language processing (NLP), yet they suffer from systematicity deficits that constrain both performance and data efficiency. These limitations are evident even in simple, artificial tasks using synthetic data, particularly in abstract pattern learning where generalization to unseen data is difficult. Abstract patterns, defined by relational properties like equality rather than specific values, highlight the struggle of neural networks to acquire systematic knowledge. This study introduces Embedded Relation Based Patterns (ERBP), a novel method that embeds a relational inductive bias to facilitate learning of equality and distance-based relations. Building upon Relation Based Patterns (RBP), ERBP functions as a Bayesian prior on network weights and is applied as a regularization term within standard training procedures. It integrates seamlessly into existing architectures without compromising learning capacity. Experimental results demonstrate that ERBP priors achieve near-perfect generalization on abstract patterns derived from synthetic, noise-free sequences. Furthermore, ERBP enhances NLP models at the word and character levels, as well as pitch prediction in melodies using RNN, GRU, and LSTM architectures. The method also yields improvements in complex tasks such as graph edit distance learning and compositional sentence entailment. Consistently outperforming both RBP and standard networks, ERBP proves effective at enabling abstract pattern learning, thereby boosting performance in natural language applications.

The prediction and management of spreading dynamics within social networks (SNs) depend heavily on their inherent connectivity structures. Unlike previous research that primarily examines positive interactions, the influence of contagion on the temporal development of signed social networks (SSNs)—which feature both friendly and hostile ties—remains largely underinvestigated. This study investigates the interaction between social link polarity and the spread of viral phenomena, factoring in user alertness. Specifically, we introduce a new energy model grounded in Heider's balance theory, which links the stochastic susceptible-alert-infected-susceptible (SAIS) epidemic framework to the structural balance of SSNs to highlight the trade-off between social tension and epidemic propagation. Furthermore, we analyze how hostile connections contribute to the creation of separate clusters of alerted and infected users within friendly groups. Leveraging three real-world SSN datasets, we also develop a time-efficient algorithm to accelerate energy calculations within our Monte-Carlo simulation approach. These efforts reveal significant insights into the efficacy and logical soundness of user awareness and initial network configurations in achieving both local and global structurally balanced energy states.

Quantization-based model compression offers a high-performance, rapid inference solution, producing significantly more compact models than full-precision floating-point versions. The most aggressive form utilizes 1-bit parameters with only two possible values, typically -1 or +1, which allows ubiquitous dot products to be executed efficiently using solely additions. This work introduces a method to smooth the combinatorial challenge of selecting binary weight vectors that minimize expected loss via empirical risk minimization and backpropagation. This is accomplished by approximating a multivariate binary state over weights through a deterministic, differentiable transformation of continuous, real-valued parameters. The proposed approach incurs minimal training overhead, integrates seamlessly into original architectures without substantial modifications, avoids adding saturating nonlinearities or auxiliary losses, and permits the use of other activation binarization techniques. Contrary to common claims in the literature, it is shown that binary weighted networks train effectively using standard optimization methods and hyperparameters similar to those of full-precision models, specifically momentum SGD with large learning rates and $L_2$ regularization. Experimental results demonstrate the method's remarkable performance across various inductive image classification tasks and architectures compared to their full-precision equivalents. The source code is publicly accessible at https://bitbucket.org/YanivShu/binary_weighted_networks_public.

The rapid expansion of the meal delivery sector has intensified concerns regarding the labor rights of riders. Existing dispatch strategies employed by these platforms primarily prioritize customer satisfaction or cost reduction through minimizing rider numbers, with scant attention given to enhancing rider working conditions via algorithmic design.
