The remarks section explores factorial Schur polynomials, the dual Cauchy identity, and the connection to the Newton interpolation formula.

Mental health conditions in online users are identified through their social media posts. A primary obstacle in this field is obtaining ethical approval to utilize user-generated content from these platforms. Academic researchers have also highlighted the scarcity of insufficient and unlabeled data for mental health classification. To address this, we investigated the impact of data augmentation techniques on domain-specific user-generated text aimed at improving mental health classification. Among established methods, we selected Easy Data Augmentation (EDA), conditional BERT, and Back Translation (BT) as promising approaches to generate additional text and enhance classifier performance. Furthermore, we employed three distinct classifiers—Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Logistic Regression (LR)—to evaluate the effects of data augmentation on two publicly available social media datasets. The experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in classifier performance when trained on augmented data.

We investigate the challenge of identifying edge correlations between two random graphs containing $n$ unlabeled vertices. This issue is framed as a hypothesis test: under the null hypothesis, the graphs are generated independently, whereas under the alternative, they share identical marginal distributions but exhibit edge correlation based on a hidden node mapping. We establish the precise threshold for optimal testing error probability undergoing a phase transition from zero to one as $n$ grows large for both Gaussian-weighted complete graphs and dense Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi graphs (with edge probability $n^{-o(1)}$). For sparse Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi graphs with edge probability $n^{-\Omega(1)}$, we derive the threshold up to a constant factor. The proofs of impossibility rely on the conditional second-moment method, which bounds the truncated second moment of the likelihood ratio by conditioning on the typical properties of the intersection graph (edges present in both observed graphs) and considering the cycle structure of the resulting random permutation on edges. Specifically, in the sparse regime, this approach utilizes the pseudoforest structure of subcritical Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi graphs alongside a detailed enumeration of subpseudoforests formed from short orbits of the edge permutation.

Epistemic frameworks often face significant challenges, especially when measurement protocols lack clear definition. In contrast, ontological models posit that measurement outcomes remain independent of the specific procedures employed to derive them. Quantum mechanics, however, is widely recognized as ambiguous in this respect. If we stipulate that all measurement results must be reducible to pointer readings, then any functional ontology requires an unambiguous specification of object positions. Yet, defining pointer positions becomes problematic in numerous relativistic and cosmological contexts. A promising avenue for resolution lies in the solutions to the Wheeler-DeWitt equation formulated by Hartle and Hawking. This article introduces a model where these solutions constitute the ontology. We demonstrate that for any model treating these solutions as beables, the simultaneous preservation of global Lorentz invariance and global determinism is impossible. Nevertheless, we also argue that an Everettian-style interpretation—where all possible mappings of matter fields to geometry and all corresponding foliations of these mappings are equally real—may offer a solution to this conflict.

Recent advancements in graph generative models have achieved notable success in creating increasingly realistic graphs, evaluated by global metrics like degree distribution, density, and clustering coefficients. Furthermore, deep generative models have significantly improved by better capturing local topological correlations, which aids in predicting unseen elements such as missing links or node classes based on nearby observed components. A comprehensive understanding of graph data requires addressing both global and local structures. This paper introduces a joint model treating these as complementary objectives within a Graph VAE framework. Global structure is modeled by integrating graph kernels into a probabilistic approach where the loss function approximates the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between the global structures of input and reconstructed graphs. The derived ELBO objective combines a standard local link reconstruction term with an MMD regularization term. Experimental results show a substantial enhancement in the realism of generated graph structures, often improving global metrics by one to two orders of magnitude compared to leading Graph VAE and GAN models, while also frequently boosting local link reconstruction performance.

Current text-to-SQL semantic parsers are often tailored for specific scenarios—such as multi-table, multi-domain, or multi-turn queries—rendering them ineffective when transferred to other contexts. We introduce UniSAr (Unified Structure-Aware Autoregressive Language Model), which leverages a standard off-the-shelf language model architecture to achieve consistently high performance across diverse settings. Specifically, UniSAr adapts existing autoregressive models through three non-invasive, structure-aware enhancements: (1) inserting structure markers to encode database schemas, conversation history, and their interrelations; (2) employing constrained decoding to generate well-formed SQL queries aligned with the schema; and (3) utilizing SQL completion to infer missing JOIN relationships based on the schema. Evaluated on seven prominent text-to-SQL datasets spanning multi-domain, multi-table, and multi-turn tasks, UniSAr matches or surpasses the performance of specialized state-of-the-art models. Crucially, our approach is non-invasive, allowing other core advancements in text-to-SQL to integrate these extensions to further boost results.

Over the last few years, several "dark" binaries containing non-luminous compact objects have been identified. By analyzing astrometric and radial velocity data from the luminous companion, researchers can determine the post-supernova orbital parameters of these systems. This paper introduces a statistical framework to deduce the pre-supernova orbital elements and the natal kick generated by the supernova (SN) using such measurements. We apply this method to VFTS 243, a recently discovered X-ray quiet binary hosting a black hole in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Under the assumption of an isotropic, Maxwellian natal kick distribution and employing broad, non-informative mass priors, we constrain the kick velocity to less than $V_k < 56$ km/s and the dispersion of the kick distribution to $\sigma_k < 66$ km/s at 90% confidence. Furthermore, assuming a natal kick occurred, we infer with 90% confidence that the supernova resulted in a mass loss of at least approximately $0.6 M_{\odot}$. Finally, the pre-supernova orbital separation is robustly determined to be roughly $0.43$ AU.

Reports indicate widespread growth patterns in confirmed COVID-19 cases, characterized by abrupt shifts among three distinct dynamical regimes: exponential, superlinear, and sublinear. By combining analytical and numerical methods, a new framework has been created to leverage these signatures. Drawing on a well-established physics approach, the study identifies shared dynamical characteristics while disregarding variations in other variables. These identified features and their corresponding scaling laws serve as an effective instrument to determine where analytical models are valid, reveal qualitative shifts in disease progression, and estimate critical infection parameters. Ultimately, this integrated analytical and numerical framework for empirically observed growth trends offers a foundational understanding of how infections evolve under stringent control measures, with applicability to both COVID-19 and future outbreaks of other infectious diseases.

Although Reinforcement Learning (RL) has achieved empirical success in contact-rich manipulation, its model-based underpinnings remain poorly understood, primarily due to three challenges: (i) the combinatorial explosion of contact modes, (ii) stiff, non-smooth dynamics leading to discontinuous or exploding gradients, and (iii) the non-convexity of planning. While RL's stochastic nature mitigates (i) and (ii) through sampling and averaging, model-based approaches have addressed these issues by analytically smoothing contact dynamics. This work first establishes a theoretical and empirical equivalence between these two strategies for simple and complex systems, respectively. To further address (ii), we introduce a convex, differentiable, quasi-dynamic formulation of contact dynamics compatible with smoothing schemes, demonstrating its efficacy in contact-rich planning. Finally, we resolve (iii) by showing that classical sampling-based motion planners can effectively handle global planning when contact modes are smoothed. Applied to challenging manipulation tasks, our method enables efficient model-based planning to match RL performance with significantly reduced computational cost. The concepts of cause and effect are extensively utilized in scientific inquiry. This discussion explores why and how these notions are grounded in thermodynamics. Specifically, the entropy gradient (i) clarifies the direction in which interventions influence the future instead of the past, and (ii) forms the basis for the time orientation of the knowing subject as a physical entity. Through these two distinct mechanisms, it is this gradient alone that serves as the origin of causal time orientation, ensuring that causes precede their effects.

This study introduces a differential equations model where the spread of a contagious disease is influenced by the contagious fear of the disease itself and the contagious fear of control measures, specifically vaccination. These three contagions are interconnected. The two types of fear evolve and interact, shaping distancing behaviors, vaccine adoption rates, and their subsequent relaxation. These behavioral dynamics can either amplify or suppress disease transmission, creating a feedback loop that further influences behavior. The model uncovers several coupled contagion mechanisms driving multiple epidemic waves. Methodologically, the paper enhances infectious disease modeling by incorporating human behavioral adaptation, utilizing insights from neuroscience regarding fear learning, extinction, and transmission.

Recent research indicates that the Milky Way's Dark Matter halo may be significantly tilted relative to its central stellar disk, potentially reflecting its formation history. This study introduces a technique to constrain the orientation of the halo's minor axis by utilizing angle and frequency variables, serving as a complementary approach to conventional methods like orbit fitting. We initially validate this method using a simulated tidal stream from the FIRE cosmological simulation, demonstrating that the action-angle-frequency formalism accurately describes streams within a realistic cosmological potential. By analyzing the slopes of lines in angle and frequency space, we identify that the correct rotation frame produces minimal slope differences, thereby enabling constraints on the minor axis position. Applying this approach to Sagittarius stream's leading arm, we find the Milky Way's Dark Matter halo is oblate with a flattening parameter of $q\sim0.7-0.9$ and a minor axis oriented toward $(\ell,b) = (42^{o},48^{o})$. Our derived constraint on the minor axis is weak and conflicts with previous estimates; we attribute this discrepancy partly to observational uncertainties and partly to the gravitational influence of the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Retrieval serves as a foundational element for open-domain NLP, where the coexistence of multiple entities sharing the same name makes disambiguation an intrinsic yet insufficiently investigated challenge. To address this, we introduce the Ambiguous Entity Retrieval (AmbER) sets, a benchmark designed to evaluate the disambiguation proficiency of retrieval systems. An AmbER set consists of entities sharing a specific name alongside related queries, providing a rigorous test of disambiguation by covering polysemous terms. We constructed these sets for three prominent open-domain applications: fact-checking, slot filling, and question answering, and assessed a variety of retrievers. Our findings reveal a distinct popularity bias, where systems significantly struggle with rarer entities sharing a name; for instance, queries targeting the less popular entity under the same name result in erroneous document retrieval twice as often as those for the more popular counterpart. These experiments demonstrate the utility of AmbER sets as an evaluation metric while exposing critical limitations in current retrieval systems.

This work demonstrates that in any prime nonassociative Novikov algebra, all nonzero ideals are inherently nonassociative. Furthermore, it is proven that within finite-dimensional Novikov algebras over a field of characteristic zero or an algebraically closed field of odd characteristic, the Baer (and Andrunakievich) radical is identical to the left quasiregular radical. Additionally, the study establishes the non-existence of a right quasiregular radical in finite-dimensional Novikov algebras.

Network topology identification (TI) serves as a critical capability for Distributed Energy Resources Management Systems (DERMS), enabling the coordination and operation of extensive distributed energy resources (DERs). This paper introduces a TI function based on discriminant analysis (DA) that utilizes exclusively the data accessible to DERMS. The proposed methodology effectively determines network switching configurations and the status of protective devices. Subsequently, to enhance TI resilience against communication channel interruptions, a quadratic programming optimization technique is introduced to reconstruct missing signals. By integrating this data recovery method with Bayes' theorem, a benchmark is established to detect anomalous measurements, thereby securing the TI function against cyber-attacks. Due to its minimal computational demand, this approach is computationally efficient and suitable for real-time deployment. Finally, a sensitivity analysis is conducted to evaluate the influence of various measurement types, system load characteristics, and loading levels on the performance of the proposed solution.

This article examines the finite exceptional groups of Lie type $E_6$ and $^2E_6$, demonstrating that the inductive blockwise Alperin weight condition is satisfied for unipotent $l$-blocks of $E_6^{\varepsilon}(q)$ provided that $2,3\nmid q$ and $l\geq 5$.

We examine Lifshitz-type scalar field theories characterized by anisotropic scaling near the ultraviolet fixed point and explicit Lorentz symmetry breaking. It is demonstrated that for actions with an anisotropy parameter $z=3$ in 3+1 dimensions, discarding all momentum-dependent vertex operators yields quantum corrections that violate Lorentz symmetry but are suppressed by inverse powers of momentum, effectively restoring the symmetry in the infrared limit. In the ultraviolet regime, the singular nature of these corrections is significantly softened; only logarithmic divergences emerge, resulting in negligible coupling variations across vast momentum ranges. Specifically, when all couplings are identical, the theory adopts a Liouville-like potential, allowing quantum corrections to be summed exactly and yielding an asymptotically free model. Nevertheless, the observed reduction in divergences does not eliminate the need for fine-tuning the mass parameter at extremely high energy scales to achieve a physically viable mass in the infrared.

This study investigates novel backdoor vulnerabilities in HyperNet-based personalized federated learning (HyperNetFL) via poisoning attacks. Leveraging these findings, we introduce HNTROJ, a pioneering model transfer attack capable of propagating a locally poisoned model to all legitimate and personalized local models generated by HyperNetFL. This is achieved by calculating consistent and effective malicious gradients across every compromised client throughout the entire training phase. Consequently, HNTROJ minimizes the number of required compromised clients to execute the attack successfully while maintaining the model's utility on legitimate data, rendering the intrusion stealthy with no observable degradation or sudden shifts. To counter HNTROJ, we integrated various backdoor-resistant federated learning training algorithms into the HyperNetFL framework. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that HNTROJ significantly surpasses traditional data poisoning and model replacement attacks and successfully evades robust training defenses.

This paper investigates the period of the linear map $T:\textbf{Z}_m^n\rightarrow\textbf{Z}_m^n$, defined by $(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1})\mapsto(a_0+a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}+a_0)$, as a function of $m$ and $n$, where $\textbf{Z}_m$ denotes the ring of integers modulo $m$. As a variant of the Ducci map, several established results are adapted to this context. The central theorem establishes that the period modulo $m$ can be determined from the prime factorization of $m$ and the periods corresponding to its prime factors, alongside several other notable properties.

We develop a phase space for a three-dimensional cellular complex featuring edge and face decorations by utilizing crossed modules (strict 2-groups) endowed with a non-trivial Poisson structure. Rather than employing the most general form of crossed modules, we restrict our approach to those with a trivial target map. Specifically, this framework demonstrates that deformations of the Poincaré group can be extended to deformations of the Poincaré 2-group. The $\kappa$-deformation scenario offers a natural candidate for modeling discrete geometries characterized by curved edge decorations while maintaining flat face decorations. Furthermore, our construction extends the classical phase space defined in reference [5] for a 3D triangulation, which was originally formulated using an undeformed Poincaré 2-group.

Deep Forest is a leading machine learning algorithm renowned for its forecasting precision. Unlike deep neural networks, it requires minimal multiplication operations and performs well on small datasets; however, its deep architecture and extensive forest size lead to significant computational and memory demands. This paper introduces the first FPGA-based hardware accelerator for Deep Forest models. To enhance inference speed, a specialized node computing unit (NCU) is developed. Building on the NCU, an efficient architecture and adaptive dataflow are proposed to mitigate node computing imbalances during classification. Additionally, an optimized storage strategy improves both hardware utilization and power efficiency. Implemented on an Intel Stratix V FPGA board, the design was evaluated using the ADULT and Face Mask Detection datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed accelerator achieves approximately a 40x speedup compared to a 40-core high-performance x86 CPU.

The hypothesis that a constant density of two-level systems (TLS) underpins certain universal low-temperature phenomena in glasses has been proposed. This work investigates whether such TLS are essential for accounting for the universal density of quasi-localized modes (QLM) in these materials at ultra-low temperatures. A detailed analysis of QLM within a generic atomistic model of a glass-forming substance identifies at least two distinct types, each characterized by a unique density of states scaling as $\omega^3$ and $\omega^4$, respectively. We examine the glassy energy landscape responsible for these modes, elucidating the analytical features that generate these two families of QLM. While adjacent energy wells undoubtedly exist within the complex landscape of glasses, the significance of TLS in explaining the universal density of QLM is called into question.

Creating truly human-like open-ended dialogue systems remains a challenging objective. We suggest that current Natural Language Generation (NLG) methods fail to achieve this because they rely on end-to-end architectures that do not sufficiently replicate how humans generate language. To address this, we separated the generation process into two distinct stages: planning and realization. During the planning stage, two specialized planners are trained to create response plans, while the realization stage utilizes these plans to formulate the final responses. Rigorous evaluations, including both automated metrics and human assessments, confirm that this decoupled planning-and-realization approach outperforms traditional end-to-end models.

Planktonic communities exhibit remarkable diversity, encompassing a multitude of rare species. While individual-based models best capture the dynamics of these rare populations, they encounter significant challenges due to the immense number of individuals needed for realistic simulations. This paper investigates planktonic diversity using a spatial coalescence model that accounts for oceanic current transport. A primary benefit of this method is that it requires simulating only as many individuals as exist in the target sample, rather than the entire community. Through theoretical analysis and simulations, we examine the conditions under which this coalescence model mirrors individual-based dynamics. Applying our model, we predict how chaotic advection by ocean currents influences biodiversity. Ultimately, we conclude that the coalescent approach enables the simulation of marine microbial communities far more efficiently than traditional individual-based models.

We investigate the oscillation modes of differentially rotating remnants from binary neutron star inspirals by modeling them as incompressible Riemann ellipsoids characterized by the ratio $f$ of internal circulation to rotation frequency. This study examines the impacts of viscosity and gravitational wave radiation on these modes, demonstrating that such bodies display generic instabilities driven by gravitational wave emission, similar to the Chandrasekhar--Friedman--Schutz instabilities observed in uniformly rotating stars. Specifically, odd-parity modes are unstable across all values of $f$ (excluding the spherical case and deformations), while even-parity unstable modes emerge only in highly eccentric ellipsoids. We quantify how varying the model mass and viscosity magnitude alters these modes; however, the modes show weak dependence on the mass ranges pertinent to binary neutron star mergers. Furthermore, large turbulent viscosity can suppress gravitational wave instabilities, whereas kinematical viscosity exerts a negligible influence on both the modes and their damping timescales.

We have conducted a systematic investigation of the low-temperature specific heat in BaFe$_{2-x}$Ni$_x$As$_2$ single crystals across the entire superconducting dome. By utilizing the nonsuperconducting, heavily overdoped sample (x = 0.3) as a baseline for phonon contributions, we determined that the electronic specific heat in the normal state of superconducting samples exhibits a nonlinear temperature dependence, contradicting earlier findings in electron-doped Ba-122 iron-based superconductors. Furthermore, a model incorporating ferromagnetic spin fluctuations accounts for the data between x = 0.1 and x = 0.15, highlighting the critical influence of Fermi-surface topology on the normal-state electronic properties.

Recent years have seen extensive development of video-based automatic depression analysis, offering a rapid, objective, and repeatable method for self-assessment. Although depression indicators can manifest in human facial behaviors across various temporal scales, most current methods focus exclusively on either short-term or video-level facial cues. To address this, we introduce a two-stage framework designed to model depression severity by integrating both multi-scale short-term and video-level facial behaviors. In the first stage, the short-term behavior modeling module utilizes deep learning to extract depression-related facial features from multiple short temporal intervals. This stage incorporates a Depression Feature Enhancement (DFE) module, which amplifies depression-specific signals across all temporal scales while filtering out non-depression noise. The second stage, dedicated to video-level behavior modeling, introduces two novel graph encoding strategies: Sequential Graph Representation (SEG) and Spectral Graph Representation (SPG). These strategies re-encode short-term features from the target video into a comprehensive video-level graph representation, effectively summarizing multi-scale temporal information. Consequently, the resulting graph representations enable the prediction of depression severity by leveraging both short-term and long-term facial behavior patterns. Experimental evaluations on the AVEC 2013 and AVEC 2014 datasets demonstrate that the proposed DFE module consistently improves depression severity estimation across various CNN architectures, while SPG outperforms other video-level modeling techniques. Furthermore, the overall two-stage framework delivers robust and promising performance when compared to widely adopted one-stage modeling approaches.

We present AirWare, an in-air hand-gesture recognition system that leverages the built-in speaker, microphone, and infrared proximity sensors found in most electronic devices. Designed to interpret gestures performed above touchscreens or mobile phones, AirWare employs convolutional neural networks to classify a diverse vocabulary of hand movements by analyzing multi-modal audio Doppler signatures and infrared (IR) sensor data. Unlike existing solutions that rely on high-frequency Doppler radars or depth cameras, AirWare operates without the need for any external sensors. For our evaluation, we utilized open APIs to access the audio and proximity sensors on a Samsung Galaxy S5 for data collection. Our analysis revealed that AirWare lacks the reliability required for a deployable interaction system when attempting to classify a set of 21 gestures, achieving an average true positive rate of only 50.5% per gesture. To enhance performance, we trained AirWare to recognize subsets of the 21-gesture vocabulary tailored to specific usage scenarios. Consequently, we found that AirWare can identify three distinct gesture sets with an average true positive rate exceeding 80%, each containing 4–7 gestures, covering a total vocabulary of 16 unique in-air gestures.

This research investigates how rotation influences the spectrum of bound states for dust cores that generate (quantum) black holes, as previously detailed in Eur. Phys. J. C 82 (2022) 10. The model assumes the dust ball rotates as a rigid body with a sufficiently low angular velocity to permit the use of perturbation theory. It is demonstrated that, analogous to total mass, both the total angular momentum and the horizon area are quantized in terms of Planck units. Furthermore, when the outermost layer comprises a sufficiently small fraction of the total mass, the model supports ground states capable of spinning rapidly enough within the perturbative framework to represent regular rotating objects instead of black holes.

This study introduces a system utilizing a hyperspectral camera and a specialized deep neural network architecture to assess fruit ripeness. The proposed architecture surpasses competitive baseline models in predicting the ripeness state of fruit. To support this, we have recorded and made publicly available a dataset of ripening avocados and kiwis. Additionally, we detail the data collection methodology in a way that facilitates easy adaptation for other fruit types. The trained network is empirically validated, and we examine the learned features. Furthermore, we present a technique for visualizing the ripening process.

Steerable needles enable precise targeting of hard-to-access clinical sites by navigating around sensitive anatomical structures, thereby reducing the invasiveness of various medical procedures. However, their curved insertion paths introduce perpendicular forces from the needle shaft that can cause lateral shearing and significant tissue damage, adversely impacting patient outcomes. This study introduces a novel tissue and needle force model grounded in a Cosserat string formulation, which calculates normal and frictional forces along the shaft based on the planned trajectory, friction parameters, and tip piercing force. We propose this model, alongside an associated cost function, as a safer and more clinically pertinent alternative to existing metrics for motion planning. The model was fitted and validated using physical needle robot experiments within a gel phantom. Applying this force model to define a bottleneck cost function for motion planning, we evaluated its performance against the traditional path-length cost function across hundreds of randomly generated 3-D environments. Results indicate that plans utilizing the force-based cost function achieve a 62% reduction in peak modeled tissue force with only a 0.07% average increase in path length compared to path-length-based planning. Furthermore, we demonstrated the capability to plan motions in a lung tumor biopsy scenario using segmented CT data. By explicitly minimizing modeled needle-to-tissue forces, our method generates needle paths that lower the risk of substantial tissue damage while successfully reaching intended targets.

This study introduces EvoK, a novel approach to combat social isolation and loneliness by facilitating heart rate sharing and feedback between individuals and their close contacts. The system comprises two wearable prototypes: a sender headband and a receiver wristwatch. The sender features an aesthetically pleasing design for continuous heart rate monitoring to ensure high social acceptance, while the receiver is an unobtrusive wristwatch equipped with multi-modal notifications to convey the loved one's continuous heart rate data.

This research examines how gene frequencies evolve within a spatially distributed population where individual dispersal is non-uniform across space. By adapting the \slfv to this context, we analyze a scenario where individuals propagate their offspring further in one halfspace than in the other at each generation. We investigate the large-scale dynamics of this process, demonstrating that ancestral lineages move asymptotically like a family of skew Brownian motions that coalesce upon collision in one dimension but never meet in higher dimensions. Consequently, we extend Nagylaki's findings on the scaling limits of gene frequencies: while non-uniform dispersal creates a discontinuity in the slope of gene frequencies at the interface, the frequencies themselves remain continuous across it.

Microservices have emerged as the standard architectural pattern, enabling independent development through the partitioning of software into finer-grained modules. This approach offers significant advantages in cloud deployment, allowing for dynamic resource allocation based on demand. Consequently, enterprises transitioning to the cloud are increasingly refactoring monolithic applications into microservices, where each service encapsulates a set of software entities responsible for a specific functionality. Since graphs naturally model software systems by representing entities as nodes and their dependencies as links, the refactoring challenge can be framed as a graph-based clustering problem. This work introduces a novel method that adapts recent advances in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for code analysis, enhancing software understanding and optimizing the clustering process. Additionally, the approach identifies graph outliers that correspond directly to high-priority refactoring candidates. Our solution demonstrates superior performance compared to existing techniques from both software engineering and graph representation domains.

The Unruh-DeWitt detector, a simple yet potent model, describes a two-level system interacting with a field, treating detected particles as field excitations. Existing research typically employs either a fully classical description of the detector's external degrees of freedom or a comprehensive field-theoretic approach where the detector itself is modeled as a field. Recently, significant attention has shifted toward the quantum properties of the detector's center of mass, whether depicted as moving in superposition along semiclassical paths or evolving dynamically via a non-relativistic Hamiltonian. However, fundamental processes like the absorption or emission of field quanta inherently alter the detector's rest mass by the energy of those quanta; neither previous model accounts for this. In this work, we integrate the quantization of the detector's mass-energy into the Unruh-DeWitt framework. We demonstrate that internal energy shifts resulting from emission or absorption remain significant even in the lowest energy limit. Specifically, corrections to transition rates arising from the detector's changing mass cannot be disregarded unless the entire center-of-mass dynamics are also neglected. Consequently, our findings indicate that a consistent model of the Unruh-DeWitt detector as a massive particle must include mass-energy equivalence.

We establish S. Thomass\'e's conjecture by demonstrating that for any (potentially infinite) digraph $ D $, one can iteratively reverse directed cycles to obtain a final reorientation $ D^{*} $ with a dichromatic number of at most two, ensuring that every edge is flipped only a finite number of times. Furthermore, we ensure that within every strong component of $ D^{*} $, all local edge-connectivities remain finite and that no edge undergoes reversal more than twice.

The Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) features the Kilometer Square Array (KM2A), which is designed to survey the northern gamma-ray sky with exceptional sensitivity at energies exceeding 10 TeV. Gamma-ray detection has historically been a premier method for searching for dark matter, particularly because heavy dark matter particles might decay into high-energy gamma-rays. This study presents the inaugural dark matter analysis utilizing LHAASO-KM2A, incorporating 340 days of data from the 1/2-KM2A sub-array and 230 days from the 3/4-KM2A sub-array. By examining multiple regions of interest, we searched for a signal while accounting for residual cosmic-ray backgrounds following gamma/hadron separation. No excess indicative of dark matter was detected; consequently, we establish some of the most stringent gamma-ray constraints to date on the lifetime of heavy dark matter particles with masses ranging from 10^5 to 10^9 GeV. Our findings from LHAASO are robust and hold significant implications for interpreting the diffuse astrophysical high-energy neutrino flux in the context of dark matter.

This paper establishes a conjecture by Angella, Otal, Ugarte, and Villacampa, which posits that for a compact Hermitian manifold, if the Strominger connection (also referred to as the Bismut connection) is K\"ahler-like—meaning its curvature tensor shares all the symmetries of a K\"ahler manifold's curvature—then the metric must be pluriclosed. In fact, we demonstrate that the condition of being Strominger K\"ahler-like is equivalent to the metric being pluriclosed and the torsion being parallel, even in the absence of the compactness assumption.

This study investigates the production of vector-like quark pairs, specifically T$\overline{\mathrm{T}}$ (charge 2/3) or Y$\overline{\mathrm{Y}}$ (charge -4/3), from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. Data collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC in 2016, amounting to an integrated luminosity of 35.8 fb$^{-1}$, are analyzed. The analysis assumes that both T and Y quarks decay exclusively into a W boson and a bottom quark. The search focuses on events characterized by a single isolated electron or muon, significant missing transverse momentum, and at least four jets with high transverse momentum. Kinematic reconstruction of the final state allows for the detection of a potential signal as a narrow mass peak with an approximate 7% resolution. The observed event count aligns with standard model predictions. Under the assumption of strong pair production and a 100% branching ratio to bW, a lower mass limit of 1295 GeV is established for the T and Y quarks at the 95% confidence level.

Experimentally resolving Weyl Fermions (WFs) in the type-II Weyl Semimetal WTe$_2$ is challenging due to the extremely narrow dispersion of Weyl bands within the (E-k) space. By employing DFT-assisted high-resolution $^{125}$Te solid-state NMR (ssNMR) across a temperature range of 50K to 700K, we successfully detected low-energy WF excitations and tracked their thermal evolution. Notably, WFs seem to emerge around 120K, whereas WTe$_2$ exhibits metallic behavior at lower temperatures. This surprising transition from metal to WSM is driven by a sharp increase in the Fermi level with temperature. In the low-temperature metallic phase, this shift traverses only the electron and hole pockets; however, for temperatures exceeding 120K, it crosses the Weyl bands near the nodal points—a necessary condition for WF emergence.

This note leverages a specific functional equation of the dilogarithm function to establish nontrivial lower bounds for the $p$-adic valuation (where $p$ is a prime) of certain rational numbers containing harmonic numbers. Subsequently, we apply these estimates to prove the integrality of specific sequences of rational numbers that are not immediately evident from their definitions.

Bohmian mechanics and Bell's interpretations of quantum foundations exhibit significant parallels with the modern Primitive Ontology framework and the minimalist ontology proposed by Esfeld and Deckert. These programs collectively prioritize ontological clarity as a prerequisite for theoretical validity, advocate for scientific realism within the quantum realm, and enhance the explanatory capacity of quantum theory. Despite these shared goals, they diverge substantially due to their reliance on distinct metaphysical principles, which generate conflicting worldviews. The primary objective of this essay is to elucidate both the connections and the key distinctions among these approaches, relations that are frequently overlooked in existing literature. It is common to find Bell's views erroneously equated with the PO programme, or the latter conflated with Esfeld and Deckert's specific proposal. Consequently, this work aims to resolve such misconceptions.

This study marks the initial exploration of Graphcore Intelligence Processing Units (IPUs) for their suitability and performance in deep learning tasks within cosmology. It benchmarks a Nvidia V100 GPU against a Graphcore MK1 (GC2) IPU across three specific cosmological scenarios: a classical deep neural network and a Bayesian neural network (BNN) for estimating galaxy shapes, alongside a generative network for producing galaxy images. The findings indicate that IPUs may offer a promising solution to the growing computational demands in the field of cosmology.

The dynamic nature of the electricity sector demands updated and novel ancillary services to ensure system security and reliability. Yet, current assessments and policy guidance on market design and ancillary services often fail to account for the intricate interactions between markets and services. To address this gap, this paper introduces an open-source agent-based model designed to evaluate design options for electricity markets and ancillary services. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model (ASAM) integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA toolbox for power system analysis. This model offers adjustable design parameters for both markets and agents, alongside detailed clearing algorithms for day-ahead markets, intra-day continuous trading, redispatch, and imbalances. Additionally, ASAM features extensive policy performance indicators, including new metrics for price mark-ups and redispatch efficiency. A stylized simulation scenario was used to validate the model and explore a specific redispatch design issue. The findings regarding multi-period all-or-none order types in redispatch markets reveal three key implications: (1) The order design minimizes risk for market participants by ensuring full order clearance. (2) Large orders can create dispatch ramps before and after delivery periods, potentially triggering ramp-risk mark-ups and necessitating extra intra-day imbalance trading. (3) In liquid market conditions, an all-or-none design leads to grid operator over-procurement of redispatch because partial order activation is impossible; furthermore, incomplete activation often forces grid operators to introduce system imbalances, as upward and downward redispatch volumes become unequal.

We present SketchySGD, a stochastic quasi-Newton technique that leverages sketching to estimate the curvature of the loss function. While quasi-Newton methods are highly effective in traditional optimization due to their rapid convergence compared to first-order approaches like SGD, they are often deemed inferior in modern deep learning because of high per-iteration costs and sensitivity to inexact gradients. SketchySGD overcomes these limitations through an innovative integration of subsampling, randomized low-rank approximation, and dynamic regularization. In convex scenarios, we demonstrate that SketchySGD with a fixed stepsize converges to a small neighborhood of the optimum faster than SGD on ill-conditioned problems. For non-convex cases, the method achieves linear convergence under two supplementary assumptions: interpolation and the Polyak-Lojaciewicz condition, which is likely satisfied in wide neural networks. Empirical results on image and tabular datasets confirm that SketchySGD offers superior reliability and speed in deep learning tasks compared to standard optimizers like SGD and Adam, as well as existing quasi-Newton methods.

This work provides a theoretical investigation into the low-temperature behavior of the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model with half-integer spin $S$ on a Kagome lattice exhibiting significant trimerization. We construct a low-energy effective model for arbitrary $S$ using spin and nematicity operators within triangular units, then analyze their low-temperature correlations for $S=3/2$ via classical Monte Carlo simulations. While prior research on the $S=1/2$ case [M. Ferrero et al., Phys. Rev. B 68, 214431 (2003)] identified a low-temperature spin liquid state driven by the glassy behavior of isolated dimer and trimer nematicities, our findings for $S=3/2$ reveal that these nematicity dimers and trimers are linked by weak connections to create a defective planar network. At extremely low temperatures, nematicities exhibit glassy slow dynamics, whereas cluster spins persist in fluctuating against a nonperiodically frozen nematicity background. Furthermore, the characteristic timescale of this glassy dynamics follows a power-law dependence on temperature.

The "magic texture" represents a successful form of the flavor neutrino mass matrix for Majorana neutrinos. This paper demonstrates that two additional types of magic textures are also compatible with neutrino oscillation data, cosmic microwave background observations, and neutrinoless double beta decay experiments. Furthermore, the relationship between these new magic textures and the leptogenesis scenario explaining the baryon asymmetry of the Universe is explored.

The European Commission's climate and energy goals strive to establish Europe as the world's first climate-neutral continent by 2050. As low-carbon, net-neutral energy systems increasingly rely on variable renewable generation, significant challenges have emerged regarding market integration, revenue cannibalization, and cost recovery for wind and solar photovoltaics. While traditional merit-order effect theories suggest wholesale prices in a fully renewable system would oscillate between extreme highs and lows, this study offers a distinct, technology-specific analysis of the cross-sectoral demand bidding effect on price formation in low-carbon markets. Utilizing the SCOPE SD cross-sectoral market modelling framework, we build upon a stylized market arrangement to progressively incorporate all relevant technologies, thereby constructing and quantifying cross-sectoral demand bidding effects in future European power markets. Our primary contribution involves a detailed explanation and substantiation of how new market participants influence market clearing. We specifically examine hybrid heat supply systems—comprising combined heat and power plants, fuel boilers, thermal storage, and electrical backup—to derive their opportunity costs. Additionally, we analyze the impacts of cross-border integration within a large-scale European net-neutral energy scenario. Ultimately, the granular insights into market clearing mechanisms enable us to assess the resulting revenues for all major technology categories in future electricity markets.

The ALICE detector at the LHC has measured the production yield of the $\Lambda(1520)$ baryon resonance at mid-rapidity in Pb-Pb collisions occurring at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 2.76 TeV. This analysis, conducted using the $\Lambda(1520)\rightarrow {\rm pK}^{-}$ decay channel (along with its charge conjugate), examines the data across varying transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) and collision centrality. In central collisions, the $p_{\rm T}$-integrated production rate of $\Lambda(1520)$ relative to $\Lambda$ is suppressed by approximately a factor of two compared to peripheral collisions. This study represents the first observation of baryonic resonance suppression at the LHC and provides the first $3\sigma$ evidence of $\Lambda(1520)$ suppression within a single collision system. Furthermore, the observed $\Lambda(1520)/\Lambda$ ratio in central collisions falls below the predictions of the statistical hadronisation model. The EPOS3 Monte Carlo event generator successfully reproduces both the shape of the measured $p_{\rm T}$ distribution and the centrality-dependent suppression. These findings reinforce the hypothesis that a dense hadronic phase forms in the final stages of fireball evolution in heavy-ion collisions, persisting long enough to significantly reduce the observable yields of short-lived resonances.

We investigate the Page curve for the four-dimensional asymptotically flat eternal Garfinkle-Horowitz-Strominger dilaton black holes using the "quantum extremal surface" prescription. Our findings show that in the absence of an island, the entanglement entropy of Hawking radiation grows linearly with time and diverges at late stages. However, when considering an island that extends slightly beyond the event horizon, the entanglement entropy ceases to increase and saturates at a value equal to twice the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, aligning with the finiteness of the von Neumann entropy for eternal black holes. Additionally, we examine how the parameter $n$ and charge $Q$ influence the Page time. The effect of $n$ is negligible when the charge-to-mass ratio ($Q/M$) is sufficiently small, whereas the charge $Q$ significantly affects the Page time. Crucially, in the extremal limit, the Page time either diverges or vanishes, indicating that semiclassical theory requires further investigation in this regime.

Diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) consist of hundreds of absorption features within the interstellar medium (ISM), primarily found in the optical range but also present in the infrared. Using CRIRES at a resolution of R=50,000 and signal-to-noise ratios in the hundreds, we observed 76 early-type stars. We detected DIBs at wavelengths including 1318, 1527, 1561, 1565, 1567, 1574, and/or 1624 nm. Our analysis identified six confirmed DIB features alongside 17 probable stellar features, supported by CMFGEN modeling. Additionally, we measured the 1318 nm and 1527 nm DIBs using X-shooter toward ten Cepheid variables with extinction values of 3.2 < E(B-V) < 6.5, as well as four stars with low water vapor content.

Comparisons between near-infrared DIB equivalent widths and E(B-V) yielded correlation coefficients ranging from 0.73 to 0.96. When comparing near-infrared and optical DIBs (5705, 5780, 6203, 6283, and 6269 Å), correlations exceeded r > 0.8, whereas the 5797 Å DIB showed a weaker correlation with near-infrared DIBs. Furthermore, the "C60+" DIB at 9632 Å did not correlate well with the 1318 nm DIB. Partial correlation coefficients, using E(B-V) as a covariate, were also calculated. For stars earlier than spectral type B2, the 1318 nm DIB exhibits an emission line on its blue wing, likely of stellar origin, though an interstellar or circumstellar cause cannot be entirely excluded. The 1318 nm DIB displays a red wing and is reasonably well-fitted by two Gaussians; however, neither the component ratios nor their separation correlates with the 5780/5797 Å ratio or E(B-V). The equivalent width of the 1318 nm DIB correlates with HI, while the ratio EW(1318 nm)/E(B-V) decreases as the fraction of molecular hydrogen (f(H2)) increases.

Five star pairs separated by 1 astronomical unit display similar 1318 nm DIB profiles, with variations noted in the HD 145501/145502 and HD 168607/168625 pairs. We analyzed CRIRES data for 17 stars separated by 6–14 months and two X-shooter sightlines separated by 9.9 years. No time variability was detected in the 5780, 5797 Å, 1318 nm, or 1527 nm DIBs. However, tentative time variability was observed in the C60+ DIBs at 9577 and 9632 Å toward HD 183143, although these signals are close to the noise level and require confirmation.

Although a significant portion of the community maintains that general relativity requires the cosmological constant $\Lambda$ to remain uniform, Bianchi identities indicate that $\Lambda$ can develop local characteristics when matter is present, transforming into $\Lambda(x^\mu)$. This paper extends that insight further by demonstrating that a non-uniform vacuum energy does not necessitate the presence of any additional matter-energy forms or theories beyond general relativity, particularly in extreme conditions such as those near a black hole.

This study attempts to enhance a model describing particle transport in astrophysical plasma outflows and develops corresponding algorithms. We first validate the method's reliability and efficacy using numerical simulations of well-known Galactic microquasars, specifically SS 433 and Cyg X-1. Subsequently, we focus on forecasting associated emissions, particularly high-energy neutrinos and gamma rays, from the extra-galactic X-ray binary M33 X-7 in the Messier 33 galaxy, a system that has not yet been modeled in detail. Within our framework, particle and radiation energy distributions arising from magnetized astrophysical jets are attributed to decay and scattering processes involving secondary particles generated when relativistic protons in the jet collide with thermal protons (the p-p interaction mechanism). These distributions are calculated by solving a system of coupled integro-differential transport equations for multi-particle reaction chains following inelastic proton-proton collisions. To detect these high-energy neutrinos and multi-wavelength emissions (spanning radio, X-ray, and gamma-ray bands), highly sensitive instruments such as CTA, IceCube, ANTARES, KM3NeT, IceCube-Gen-2, and various space telescopes are either currently operational or under development.

Let $X$ be a Polish space equipped with a Borel probability measure $\mu$, and let $G$ be a Borel graph defined on $X$ that contains no odd cycles and has a maximum degree of $\Delta(G)$. We demonstrate that the Baire measurable edge chromatic number of $G$ does not exceed $\Delta(G)+1$; furthermore, if $G$ is $\mu$-hyperfinite, the $\mu$-measurable edge chromatic number satisfies the same upper bound. More broadly, we establish that the Borel edge chromatic number of $G$ is bounded by $\Delta(G)$ plus its asymptotic separation index.

We examine a Bose-Josephson junction (BJJ) composed of a binary mixture of ultracold atoms to explore how coherent collective dynamics influence ergodicity and quantum scars, thereby establishing a link between these phenomena. By adjusting both inter- and intra-species interactions, we reveal a diverse range of Josephson dynamics and their transitions, which are essential for regulating overall ergodic behavior. The entanglement spectrum exposes the signatures of underlying classicality and clarifies the emergence of quantum scars associated with unstable steady states and periodic orbits that result in athermal behavior. Furthermore, the extent of ergodicity within the energy band and scarring effects can be investigated through the auto-correlation function and condensate phase fluctuations, findings that hold significance for cold atom experiments.

Human-robot collaboration, particularly close physical human-robot interaction (pHRI), represents a prevailing trend in both industry and science. Existing safety guidelines mandate two operational modes: (i) restricting power and force, and (ii) monitoring speed and separation. This study investigates the viability of utilizing robots outfitted with artificial sensitive skin and a surrounding protective safety zone (peripersonal space) to ensure safe pHRI.

The field of video understanding has garnered significant research interest, particularly following the release of large-scale video benchmarks. This paper tackles the challenge of multi-label video classification. We begin by noting a substantial disparity between human and machine learning processes: while current machine learning methods, including deep neural networks, primarily focus on data representations, humans often utilize external knowledge beyond the immediate data to enhance decision-making. To bridge this gap, we propose integrating external knowledge graphs into video classification. Specifically, we introduce a novel end-to-end framework that unifies traditional "knowledge-agnostic" machine learning models with knowledge graphs. This framework is adaptable and compatible with most existing video classification algorithms, including leading deep learning models. Finally, we perform extensive experiments on YouTube-8M, the largest public video dataset. The results are highly encouraging, achieving improvements in mean average precision of up to 2.9%.

Optical transition-edge sensors (TES) have demonstrated the capability to resolve incident photon counts at telecommunication wavelengths, yet biological imaging and microscope spectroscopy demand even higher energy resolution. This study reports a Au/Ti (10/20 nm) bilayer TES that achieved superior energy resolution by reducing the critical temperature ($T_c$) to 115 mK. At 0.8 eV, this resulted in an energy resolution of 67 meV full width at half maximum (FWHM). Given that typical optical TESs operate at $T_c = 300$ mK with resolutions around 150 meV, lowering $T_c$ to 115 mK theoretically predicts a resolution of 30 meV FWHM. To bridge the gap between this theoretical limit and the measured 67 meV, we analyzed the device's complex impedance and current noise, identifying excess Johnson noise. Specifically, an excess Johnson term $M$ of 1.5 was observed at a bias point where resistance was 10% of the normal value. For comparison, this device was evaluated against a reference TES with typical resolution (156 meV FWHM), and we will discuss the factors contributing to the improved resolution as well as the likely limiting factors.

We deliver high-precision predictions for muon and tau pair production in photon-photon collisions by incorporating a comprehensive set of one-loop scattering amplitudes, which include electroweak (EW) corrections alongside both soft and hard QED radiation. Consequently, we offer a thorough numerical analysis, focusing specifically on pure QED and genuinely weak corrections. We also examine how angular distributions and initial beam polarizations influence production rates, noting that production rates improve by a factor of two when using oppositely polarized photons. Our findings demonstrate that one-loop EW radiative corrections increase the Born cross section, with the total relative correction reaching approximately ten percent for both production channels. Furthermore, achieving percent-level accuracy necessitates the inclusion of full EW corrections for the process $\gamma \gamma \to \ell^- \ell^+$.

Ensuring the reliability of learning models is essential for the effective implementation of machine learning across diverse sectors. Developing resilient models that withstand adversarial attacks necessitates a thorough grasp of adversarial examples, yet this phenomenon is challenging to articulate due to the intricate complexities inherent in machine learning. As a result, numerous studies attempt to explore the phenomenon by introducing simplified models of its occurrence and validating them through specific predictions. Although these efforts address various characteristics of adversarial examples, they have yet to achieve a holistic geometric and analytic framework. This paper introduces a formal framework rooted in learning theory, leveraging complex analysis and holomorphicity to establish a robust learning rule for artificial neural networks. By employing complex analysis, we can seamlessly transition between geometric and analytic viewpoints, gaining deeper insights by uncovering the phenomenon's connection to harmonic functions. Utilizing this model allows us to elucidate key features of adversarial examples, such as their transferability, and opens pathways for innovative strategies to mitigate their impact.

Feature selection is a critical component of data mining, essential for managing the high volume of features that can overwhelm learning algorithms computationally. Its importance extends beyond resource constraints, as it enhances the accuracy of machine learning tasks, a point further explored in subsequent sections. This review examines various feature selection methods and their relationships with different machine learning algorithms.

Quantum embedding offers a promising strategy for decomposing large, interacting quantum systems into smaller auxiliary "cluster" problems to leverage the locality of correlated physical phenomena. This study provides a critical review of methods used to recombine these fragmented solutions for calculating non-local expectation values, such as total energy. Building upon the democratic partitioning of expectation values found in density matrix embedding theory, we introduce and evaluate several alternative methodologies. Numerical results demonstrate that these new approaches offer greater efficiency and enhanced accuracy regarding both energetics and non-local two-body observables in molecular and solid-state systems as cluster sizes increase. These methods address the $N$-representability of expectation values by employing an implicit global wavefunction across clusters and by incorporating contributions that span multiple fragments simultaneously, thus mitigating the fundamental locality approximation inherent in embedding schemes. We explicitly show that these new functionals enable the reliable extraction of observables and ensure robust, systematic convergence with increasing cluster size, allowing for the use of significantly smaller clusters to achieve target accuracy compared to traditional *ab initio* wavefunction quantum embedding techniques.

High-density materials like metal implants and dental fillings often generate severe streak artifacts in computed tomography (CT) scans, significantly hindering diagnostic accuracy. While numerous deep learning approaches have been developed for metal artifact reduction (MAR), they frequently underperform due to insufficient utilization of global context within the sinogram domain, the creation of secondary artifacts in the image domain, and the necessity for accurate metal masks. To overcome these limitations, this study investigates fast Fourier convolution for MAR across both sinogram and image domains, introducing a Fourier dual-domain network called FD-MAR. First, we develop a Fourier sinogram restoration network capable of utilizing wide-range receptive fields to reconstruct metal-corrupted areas from adjacent uncorrupted regions, ensuring robustness against metal traces. Second, we introduce a Fourier refinement network operating in the image domain that enhances reconstructed images by integrating local and global context information. Consequently, FD-MAR effectively leverages extensive receptive fields in both domains for artifact reduction. Optimized with a composite loss function, extensive experiments confirm that FD-MAR outperforms state-of-the-art MAR techniques based on both quantitative metrics and visual assessments. Importantly, FD-MAR eliminates the need for precise metal masks, a critical advantage for routine clinical applications.

This study examines supersymmetric composite generalized quantum integrable models that are solvable via the algebraic Bethe ansatz. By employing a coproduct within the bialgebra of monodromy matrix elements and their action on Bethe vectors, explicit formulas for Bethe vectors in these supersymmetric composite models—constructed from the super-Yangians $Y[\mathfrak{gl}(2|1)]$ and $Y[\mathfrak{gl}(1|2)]$—are derived.

Fine-tuning pre-trained language models like BERT has become a standard approach that dominates performance rankings across numerous NLP tasks. However, despite its recent achievements and widespread use, this process remains unstable when training data is scarce, often evidenced by high sensitivity to random seeds. This paper addresses this issue by leveraging the noise stability properties of deep neural networks, a concept explored in recent studies (Arora et al., 2018; Sanyal et al., 2020). Specifically, we present a new and effective regularization technique called Layer-wise Noise Stability Regularization (LNSR) to enhance fine-tuning for NLP tasks. We expand upon existing theories regarding input noise, demonstrating that our method provides a more stable regularization effect. Experimental results confirm that high-performing models exhibit low noise sensitivity, and fine-tuning with LNSR significantly improves both generalizability and stability. Additionally, our approach outperforms other state-of-the-art algorithms, including L2-SP (Li et al., 2018), Mixout (Lee et al., 2020), and SMART (Jiang et al., 2020).

We introduce the Convolutional Variational Recurrent Neural Network, a model designed to extract musical features and synthesize original music sequences. Leveraging an encoder-decoder framework with latent probabilistic links, this approach captures the underlying structure of music to generate sequential data. By utilizing a sequence-to-sequence architecture, our generative model draws from prior distributions to produce extended musical sequences. We evaluated our proposed model against other neural network architectures using the Information Rate metric, implemented via the Variable Markov Oracle, which facilitates the statistical analysis of musical information dynamics and motif detection. Our findings indicate that the proposed model exhibits a superior statistical alignment with the training data's musical structure, thereby enhancing the generation of new music that mimics the style of the originals.

It can be argued that the standard description of a reversible quantum process linking two one-to-one correlated measurement results is insufficient because it fails to specify the direction of causality, thereby permitting causal structures that contradict the time symmetry inherent in reversible processes. Consequently, this description can be completed by applying time-symmetrization, which mandates that both the initial and final measurements equally contribute to selecting their correlated outcome pair. While this approach leaves the original description unchanged, it reveals that the phenomenon arises from a quantum superposition of unobservable, time-symmetrized instances with fully defined causal structures. Each such instance forms a causal loop: the final measurement propagates backward in time to alter the input state of the unitary transformation, effectively modifying the state immediately preceding it. Previous research has demonstrated that these loops precisely account for quantum computational speedup and nonlocality. In this study, we demonstrate that they also provide a completion of the anthropic principle, enabling a model of universe evolution that incorporates quantum speedup.

This work presents multiple enhancements to conic fitting within Geometric Algebra by embedding specific constraints into the optimization framework. Each added constraint enforces distinct geometric characteristics on the resulting conic, such as positioning the center at the origin, aligning the axes with the coordinate system, or combining both features. The paper details the underlying algebraic and optimization principles for each derived algorithm, alongside their MATLAB implementations. Furthermore, we provide illustrative examples using a sample dataset and discuss potential applications for these methods.

The nullity of a graph corresponds to the multiplicity of zero within its spectrum. A signed graph consists of a graph where each edge is assigned a sign. This paper derives a coefficient theorem for the characteristic polynomial of signed graphs and provides two formulas for calculating the nullity of signed graphs containing cut-points. Utilizing these findings, we examine the nullity of the bicyclic signed graph $\Gamma(\infty(p,q,l))$, derive the nullity set for unbalanced bicyclic signed graphs, and consequently establish the nullity set for all bicyclic signed graphs.

We expand the EUCLID framework, originally designed for unsupervised automated discovery of material laws, to address materials with unknown behavioral classes. By utilizing the theory of generalized standard materials, which covers a wide range of constitutive models, we demonstrate that EUCLID can automatically identify the two defining scalar thermodynamic potentials—Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential—using solely full-field kinematic data and net reaction forces. The inherent convexity constraint on these potentials ensures the resulting model is both stable and thermodynamically consistent. In the absence of stress-strain labeled pairs, the balance of linear momentum serves as a fundamental constraint, while sparsity-promoting regularization automatically selects a minimal subset of candidate features, yielding a parsimonious and interpretable model. Crucially, this sparse regression simultaneously selects the necessary internal variables for an accurate yet simple description of material behavior. A fully automated procedure also determines the hyperparameter for the regularization weight, balancing model accuracy against simplicity. Validation using synthetic data with artificial noise confirms that EUCLID can successfully recover the true hidden material model from a vast catalog of constitutive classes, including elasticity, viscoelasticity, elastoplasticity, viscoplasticity, and various hardening mechanisms.

Machine learning is transforming image-based diagnostics within radiology and pathology. Although ML models have demonstrated significant promise in research, their clinical adoption has been hindered by interoperability challenges. DICOM serves as the standard for defining and communicating digital medical images and their associated annotations; however, the standard's complexity acts as a barrier for the machine learning community, necessitating specialized tools to manage DICOM datasets. We introduce `highdicom`, a Python library offering a high-level API that abstracts the standard's intricate details, allowing for the encoding and decoding of image-derived information with minimal code. By integrating with the broader Python ecosystem for image processing and machine learning, `highdicom` simplifies the creation and parsing of DICOM-compliant files. This facilitates interoperability with medical imaging systems that store training data and host model deployments, ensuring seamless communication and storage of outputs for clinical use. Experimental results using slide microscopy and computed tomography demonstrate that `highdicom` bridges these two ecosystems, enabling developers to train and evaluate state-of-the-art models in pathology and radiology while maintaining full DICOM compliance and clinical interoperability throughout the workflow. To foster standardization in ML research and streamline development and deployment, the library is provided as free and open-source software.

Thul et al. (2020) highlighted issues emerging when chronometric experiments utilizing specific factorial designs are analyzed via generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs), particularly when factor smooths are employed to account for trial-to-trial dependencies. Based on simulations incorporating these dependencies, they concluded that GAMMs are unsuitable for between-subject designs, arguing that the models offer excessive flexibility and recommending the linear mixed model (LMM) as an alternative. This paper addresses the concerns raised by Thul et al. (2020), acknowledging their demonstration that problems do occur when combining factor smooths with factorial designs. However, we demonstrate that these issues do not manifest when utilizing by-smooths. Additionally, we identified a bug in the factor smooths implementation within the mgcv package, which has been resolved in version 1.8-36 and later. To illustrate the accuracy of current GAMM estimates, we present simulation studies featuring various by-subject longitudinal effects. Results indicate that the maximal LMM is slightly conservative compared to GAMMs, while GAMMs yield coefficient estimates with lower variability across simulation runs. We also examine two datasets where time-varying effects interact meaningfully with numerical predictors. Furthermore, we contend that the extensive toolkit offered by GAMMs across scientific domains does not lead to uncontrolled researcher degrees of freedom when applied to specific psycholinguistic datasets. We also propose a distinction between replicable and non-replicable non-linear effects. Ultimately, we conclude that GAMMs constitute an excellent and reliable instrument for analyzing experimental data, including chronometric data characterized by time-varying effects.

This paper investigates distributed maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) for dependent quantized data, assuming a known joint probability density function (pdf) structure with unknown deterministic parameters. These parameters encompass distinct vector parameters for marginal pdfs and those characterizing inter-sensor observation dependencies. Given that MLE using a single quantizer is vulnerable to threshold selection uncertainties arising from pdf ambiguity, we focus on MLE employing multiple quantizer groups (established via prior information or heuristic methods) to mitigate risks associated with poor or outlier quantizers. Under specific regularity conditions, we prove the asymptotic efficiency of this multi-quantizer MLE scheme and derive its asymptotic variance as the inverse of a weighted linear combination of Fisher information matrices derived from the various quantizers, thereby demonstrating the method's robustness. To illustrate this, we analyze an estimation problem involving a bivariate non-Gaussian pdf relevant to distributed constant false alarm rate (CFAR) detection systems. Simulation results confirm the robustness of the proposed MLE approach, particularly when the count of quantized measurements is low.

**Aims.** Molecular masers, particularly methanol masers and hydroxyl masers in excited rotational states (ex-OH masers), serve as vital instruments for investigating star-forming regions; consequently, identifying new maser sources in these areas is highly significant. While extensive surveys of ex-OH masers have focused on the southern celestial hemisphere, the northern hemisphere has received far less attention. The primary objective of this study is to address this imbalance.

**Methods.** We observed star-forming regions in the northern hemisphere that already host known active methanol masers to search for new ex-OH maser sources using the 32 m and 16 m radio telescopes at the Ventspils International Radio Astronomy Centre (VIRAC).

**Results.** We detected three excited-state OH maser lines at 6035 MHz within three northern hemisphere star-forming regions. The source 189.030+0.783 was previously identified, but we propose it may be variable. Additionally, we corroborated recent detections of the ex-OH masers 85.41+0.00 and 90.92+1.49 reported by other researchers. By analyzing the splitting between right circular polarization (RCP) and left circular polarization (LCP) pairs, we estimated the magnetic field strength in the masering regions. The high-velocity resolution of our observations allowed us to determine comparatively weak magnetic field strengths for the star-forming regions associated with 189.030+0.783 and 90.92+1.49.

Optimum filters are increasingly recognized as essential instruments for parametric estimation across numerous scientific and technical domains. The DPLMS method, introduced approximately two decades ago, stands out among synthesis algorithms because it generates optimum filters directly from experimental signal and noise waveforms. This paper presents two novel extensions of the DPLMS technique. The first extension accelerates the synthesis process and enhances energy estimation by employing automatically designed flat-top lengths for the optimum filters. The second extension refines parameter estimation quality in multi-channel systems by leveraging inter-channel noise correlations. The discussion begins by reviewing the theoretical and functional foundations of the DPLMS method for optimum filter synthesis. Subsequently, the two new DPLMS extensions are explained theoretically and evaluated from an application standpoint. The DPLMS filters were tested on simulated signals featuring varying noise levels and characteristics, as well as on experimental waveforms obtained from a solid-state Germanium detector. Results were analyzed both absolutely and comparatively against more traditional, suboptimal filters, demonstrating the efficacy of the two new DPLMS extensions. For single-channel energy estimation, the optimum filters yielded superior results compared to alternative methods. Furthermore, DPLMS multi-channel filters improved estimation quality beyond single-channel filters when non-negligible inter-channel noise correlations were present. The robustness and effectiveness of the DPLMS method in synthesizing high-quality filters for energy estimation are set to be validated in upcoming leading-edge multi-channel physics experiments.

Divisibility sequences are characterized by the condition that if an index divides another, the corresponding sequence terms also divide one another. Those satisfying a linear recurrence relation, such as the Fibonacci sequence, are generated by polynomials that divide their compositions with any positive integer power. We fully characterize these polynomials by expressing them as products of cyclotomic polynomials via labeled Hasse diagrams and use this approach to construct novel integer divisibility sequences. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, in contrast to the Fibonacci numbers, these non-classical sequences lack the property of strong divisibility.

Topological approaches are seldom employed in structural dynamics or structural health monitoring (SHM), particularly regarding the structure and topology of observed data. However, these methods offer a means to develop novel metrics and scrutiny techniques that might otherwise be ignored. This study introduces a technique for quantifying data shape through topological data analysis (TDA), with persistent homology serving as its primary instrument. Persistent homology quantifies data shape across varying length scales, and the necessary background along with a computation method for it are briefly outlined here. Applying TDA concepts to a Z24 Bridge case study, the research scrutinizes different data partitions categorized by collection conditions. A metric derived from TDA is utilized to compare these partitions. The results indicate that damage presence significantly alters the manifold shape more than the effects caused by temperature variations.

Sequential neuronal activity drives numerous brain functions, with evidence for such sequences found across diverse domains including perception, motor control, speech, spatial navigation, and memory. Consequently, various dynamical principles have been suggested as mechanisms for generating these sequences. By integrating experimental data with computational frameworks like the Bayesian brain hypothesis and predictive coding, we uncover the intriguing possibility that the brain's predictive and inferential processes rely on generative mechanisms that preserve sequential structure. Although probabilistic inference regarding ongoing sequences serves as a valuable computational model for analyzing neuroscientific data and solving problems in artificial recognition and motor control, research in this area remains limited and fragmented across neuroscience disciplines. This review examines key findings on neuronal sequences and connects them to the concept of online sequence inference as a model for sensory-motor processing and recognition. We propose that characterizing sequential neuronal activity as probabilistic inference over sequences could yield new insights into brain function. Furthermore, it is highly promising to apply this core concept of probabilistic sequence inference to machine learning to tackle challenges in real-time speech and human motion recognition.

This article, serving as the initial installment in a series dedicated to the comprehensive analysis of the radio pulsar death line, investigates the potential for generating secondary particles at extended pulsar periods. We re-evaluate the potential drop required to initiate secondary plasma within the inner gap above the magnetic polar caps. Our findings allow for a refined understanding of the conditions necessary for secondary plasma formation, specifically regarding particle multiplicity and spatial distribution. Furthermore, we provide a more quantitative examination of how the feasibility of secondary plasma generation depends on various parameters, including the angle between the magnetic and rotation axes, the dimensions of the polar cap, and the configuration of the magnetic field.
