Additionally, we are evaluating a new readout element with a 215 {\mu}m pitch to enhance spatial resolution and a {\mu}NID variant employing a boron-based neutron converter to boost rate capabilities.

The recent detection of magnetic field switchbacks or deflections within the solar wind by the Parker Solar Probe has sparked significant interest in modeling their origins and formation mechanisms. Various hypotheses have been proposed, spanning from reconnection events in the lower solar atmosphere to manifestations of solar wind turbulence. This study investigates potential formation mechanisms for these switchbacks in the lower solar atmosphere using three-dimensional magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) numerical simulations. The model simulates an intense flux tube within an open magnetic field region, representing a magnetic bright point transitioning into an open coronal structure, such as a coronal hole. The simulation is driven by diverse photospheric plasma flows, including fast upward jets and shearing flows caused by vortex motions or torsional oscillations. Across all tested scenarios, magnetic switchbacks form in regions corresponding to chromospheric heights. Consequently, plasma flows around the footpoints of intense flux tubes appear to be viable drivers for generating switchbacks in the lower solar atmosphere. However, within the current model, these switchbacks fail to propagate into coronal heights. Ultimately, based on these simulations, switchbacks observed in the solar wind are unlikely to originate from photospheric or chromospheric dynamics.

This study investigates the thermal impacts of vacuum Cherenkov radiation within a framework of Lorentz- and CPT-violating electrodynamics. Utilizing the Thermofield Dynamics approach, we calculate the thermal component of the Cherenkov radiation rate. Because the model allows for consistent canonical quantization and satisfies the necessary physical conditions for this vacuum process, it serves as an ideal system for analyzing the phenomenon at finite temperatures. We provide a detailed evaluation of the instantaneous energy loss rate for a charged particle, demonstrating that the radiation rate undergoes significant modification at extremely high temperatures. Remarkably, we also find that as the temperature approaches infinity, the radiation rate diminishes to zero, despite the process remaining kinematically feasible.

Recent experiments and simulations involving oscillatory deformation of amorphous solids have revealed unexpected dynamics: at small strain amplitudes, the system can exhibit reversibility, challenging the conventional view of plasticity as inherently irreversible. This reversibility enables the system to enter limit-cycles where plastic events repeat indefinitely under the driving force. While reaching these reversible limit-cycles may require many driving cycles, it was previously assumed that plastic events occurring during the transient phase were unique and thus irreversible. However, by utilizing a graph representation of stable configurations and the plastic events linking them, we demonstrate that the concept of reversibility is more nuanced. Our findings indicate that reversible plastic events are plentiful and that a significant fraction of events observed during the transient period are actually reversible, meaning they can participate in a reversible deformation path. We observe that the transition graph decomposes into clusters of configurations connected by reversible transitions; these clusters correspond to the graph's strongly connected components and exhibit a power-law distribution in size. The largest clusters reside within regions of reversibility, which are bounded by regions of irreversibility that multiply as strain increases. These results explain the irreversibility transition—specifically, the divergence of the transient period at a critical forcing amplitude. Long transients arise from the system transitioning between clusters of reversibility while searching for one large enough to sustain a limit-cycle of a given amplitude. For sufficiently large amplitudes, this search time becomes extremely long because the required limit-cycle sizes exceed the dimensions of the available reversible regions.

We have recently employed a compact Penning trap to capture and isolate highly-charged ions extracted from an Electron Beam Ion Trap (EBIT) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Specifically, isolated charge states of highly-stripped neon and argon ions, possessing total charges $Q \geq 10$ and extracted at energies reaching up to $4\times 10^3\,Q$ eV, were successfully confined within a trap featuring well depths of approximately $(4\, {\rm to}\, 12)\,Q$ eV. This study details the optimization of velocity tuning, capture, and storage procedures within a unitary Penning trap specifically engineered to facilitate easy radial access for atomic or laser beams during charge exchange or spectroscopic experiments. Such capabilities are pertinent to proposed investigations involving one-electron ions in Rydberg states or optical transitions of metastable states in multiply-charged ions. Under near-optimal conditions, ions isolated and captured in these rare-earth Penning traps exhibit an initial energy distribution roughly 60 times narrower than that typically observed in an EBIT. This significant reduction in thermal energy is achieved passively, requiring no active cooling scheme within the ion-capture trap.

This study examines $S$-adic shifts arising from sequences of constant-length morphisms. We define such a sequence as torsion-free if every prime factor of any morphism's length divides infinitely many subsequent lengths. We demonstrate that shifts generated by these torsion-free directive sequences possess the property of quasi-recognizability, which serves as a viable alternative to standard recognizability. Specifically, any quasi-recognizable directive sequence can be substituted with a recognizable one. Leveraging this, we provide a more detailed characterization of the spectrum of shifts produced by torsion-free sequences over alphabets of bounded size, utilizing extensions of the concepts of height and column number. Throughout, we support our findings with examples that clarify the nuances involved.

Solid-state semiconductor detectors play a critical role in high-energy physics, medical technology, and space exploration. Accurately characterizing these devices and understanding their performance requires a precise understanding of the electric fields within their fundamental cells. These fields dictate charge propagation, which in turn defines the signal's magnitude and quality, making electric field simulation essential for sensor analysis. However, the specific field configuration depends on the unique fabrication and growth details of the device, information that is often commercially confidential or incompatible with current technology computer-aided design (TCAD) tools. Consequently, reconstructing the field is practically unfeasible without some prior knowledge. This study demonstrates that by integrating public beam-test data with limited, publicly available TCAD insights, we can effectively reconstruct the three-dimensional electric field within the pixel cell of the ALPIDE sensor, a widely used monolithic active pixel sensor (MAPS). Although the ALPIDE sensor is globally prevalent, its field data remains proprietary and inaccessible to the broader community. We present the derived 3D effective field function for the ALPIDE sensor and explain the methodology using the Allpix$^2$ software. Furthermore, we discuss how this approach can be applied to characterize other similar devices.

Bayesian linear mixed-effects models are becoming common in cognitive science for conducting null hypothesis tests, which compare the hypothesis of no effect against one where an effect exists. Although software for calculating Bayes factors is readily available, correctly specifying models and data remains unclear. Many researchers advocate aggregating data by subject to compute these factors, yet simulations show this approach can produce biased results. Specifically, if random slope variances differ (violating sphericity), Bayes factors from aggregated data become overly conservative for low-variance contrasts and overly liberal for high-variance ones. Additionally, ignoring random item variance while aggregating by subject leads to biased (too liberal) Bayes factors. Frequentist analyses confirm these issues are well-known in traditional tools. These biases can be avoided by analyzing non-aggregated data, such as individual trials, and by explicitly modeling the complete random effects structure. Reproducible code is available at https://osf.io/mjf47/.

Although the loss landscapes of deep neural networks significantly influence training, they have primarily been investigated theoretically because of computational limitations. This study drastically cuts the time needed to calculate these landscapes and leverages them to analyze winning lottery tickets discovered through iterative magnitude pruning. Furthermore, we present findings that challenge previously asserted links between specific loss landscape projection techniques and a model's trainability or generalization error.

Conjectures are fundamental to theoretical physics, particularly those proposing upper limits for dimensionless ratios of physical quantities. This paper presents a novel conjecture establishing an upper bound for the ratio of magnetic moment to angular momentum. Additionally, we examine the current state of various established bounds on both dimensionless and dimensional quantities across arbitrary spatial dimensions. Specifically, our new conjecture posits that the dimensionless Schuster-Wilson-Blackett number, defined as $c\mu / \sqrt{JG}$ (where $\mu$ represents the magnetic moment and $J$ the angular momentum), is capped by a value of order unity. We confirm that this bound applies to charged rotating black holes in theories with known exact solutions, including Einstein-Maxwell theory, Kaluza-Klein theory, the Kerr-Sen black hole, and the STU family of charged rotating supergravity black holes. Furthermore, we address the present status of the Maximum Tension Conjecture, the Dyson Luminosity Bound, and Thorne's Hoop Conjecture.

Real-world collectives, such as living cells, grains, and active particles, are inherently heterogeneous, consisting of individuals with varying properties that interact to produce emergent group-level effects. A common objective is to deduce these intrinsic individual differences by analyzing observed movement patterns. However, true individual characteristics are often obscured by these collective emergent behaviors. This study addresses the inference challenge within a bidisperse system comprising two distinct agent types, aiming to classify them based on collective motion. Since phenomena like jamming and clustering influence individual trajectories, an agent's isolated movement lacks sufficient data for accurate classification; consequently, simple algorithms relying solely on individual velocities fail to estimate system heterogeneity correctly and frequently misidentify agents. We introduce a novel classification method that explicitly incorporates collective influences on motion. By leveraging insights from the physics of collective dynamics, we quantify neighborhood impacts through a specific parameter. This approach successfully distinguishes between two agent types even when their observed motions are identical, offering significantly more accurate estimates of heterogeneity and marked improvements in classification performance. Our findings demonstrate that explicitly accounting for neighborhood effects is frequently essential for correctly inferring the intrinsic properties of individuals.

We revive the notorious harmonic mean estimator used for calculating marginal likelihood (Bayesian evidence) and resolve its critical issue of high variance. As a fundamental element of Bayesian model selection, marginal likelihood is essential for determining model posterior probabilities, yet computing it remains difficult. Originally introduced by Newton and Raftery in 1994, the harmonic mean estimator calculates the harmonic mean of the likelihood using posterior samples. However, it was quickly recognized that this method can fail disastrously due to excessively large or infinite variance. Although several variants have been developed to mitigate this problem, none have been entirely satisfactory. We introduce the learnt harmonic mean estimator, an improved variant that eliminates the large variance problem. By viewing the estimator through the lens of importance sampling and defining a novel target distribution, we learn an approximation of the optimal yet unattainable target to minimize estimator variance. Because it relies solely on posterior samples, the method is independent of the sampling strategy employed. We validate our approach across various numerical experiments, including pathological cases where the original estimator collapses. In every instance, the learnt harmonic mean estimator demonstrates high accuracy. Furthermore, the estimator is computationally scalable, capable of handling problems with dimensions up to $\mathcal{O}(10^3)$ and beyond, and the implementation code is publicly available.

Traditionally, language prediction research has relied on straightforward designs comparing neural reactions to anticipated versus unexpected words in a categorical manner. However, these methods have faced criticism for being "prediction encouraging," potentially overstating the role of prediction in language comprehension. Recent studies have started to address these concerns by employing model-based techniques to examine linguistic predictability within naturalistic contexts, such as continuous narratives. Yet, these earlier investigations were limited to very local prediction forms, utilizing models that considered no more than the preceding two words. In this work, we expand upon this methodology by applying a cutting-edge neural language model capable of incorporating approximately 500 times more linguistic context. Predictability estimates derived from this neural network align significantly better with EEG data from participants listening to natural narratives than simpler models do, uncovering strong surprise responses comparable to the P200 and N400 components. These findings indicate that predictability effects in language are not merely artifacts of simple experimental designs and highlight the practical application of recent AI advancements in the cognitive neuroscience of language.

Training visual control policies from scratch for a new robot usually necessitates generating substantial robot-specific data. To address this, we investigate how pre-collected data from other robots can minimize or eliminate the need for such new data. We introduce a "robot-aware control" framework that utilizes existing knowledge about the robot's mechanics. This approach is implemented through a robot-aware model-based reinforcement learning policy, which employs modular dynamics models combining a transferable, robot-aware world dynamics component with a robot-specific, potentially analytical, robot dynamics component. This structure also allows for visual planning costs that distinctly evaluate the robot agent and the environment. Experiments involving tabletop manipulation tasks with both simulated and physical robots show that these plug-in enhancements significantly improve the transferability of visual model-based RL policies, enabling zero-shot transfer of visual manipulation skills to new robots. Project website: https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~hued/rac

This study evaluates the evolutionary states of 24 post-AGB stars using Gaia DR3 data, all of which possess parallaxes with uncertainties under 3σ and RUWE values below 1.4. Utilizing the Gaia-derived distances, absolute luminosities were calculated; for 14 stars, these values corroborate their post-AGB classification. Conversely, V1027 Cyg, formerly identified as a post-AGB star, exhibits a higher luminosity, suggesting it is likely an evolved, massive, pulsating semi-regular variable star of spectral type G7Ia. Additionally, the luminosities of 9 stars fall below 1000 L☉, implying that several are post-RGB or post-HB stars. Although this research was finalized over four months ago, its publication has been delayed.

Recent years have witnessed a surge in interest regarding transfer learning (TL) within natural language processing (NLP), driven by the remarkable capacity of pre-trained models to adapt to new tasks. This work evaluates three primary strategies for leveraging multiple supervised datasets during fine-tuning: Sequential Task-In-Label Transfer (STILTs), which involves training on an intermediate task before the target task; pairwise Multi-Task Learning (MTL), where the target and a supplementary task are trained jointly; and MTL-ALL, which trains on all available datasets simultaneously. Through a comprehensive analysis of the GLUE dataset suite, we identify a straightforward heuristic for selecting the optimal method: pairwise MTL outperforms STILTs when the target task contains fewer instances than the supporting task, and vice versa. This rule proved accurate in over 92% of applicable scenarios on GLUE and was further validated through experiments manipulating dataset sizes. The surprising simplicity and efficacy of this heuristic suggest a need for further investigation by the TL community. Additionally, our findings indicate that MTL-ALL underperforms compared to pairwise approaches in nearly all instances. We anticipate that this study will assist researchers in selecting appropriate TL methods for NLP applications.

The dark matter sector remains entirely enigmatic, making it essential to remain open to its potential nature and interactions. Specifically targeting Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs), this study concretizes that broad philosophy by applying contemporary machine learning methods to dark matter direct detection. We achieve this by employing a convolutional variational autoencoder to encode and decode the graphical representations of background events from the XENONnT experiment. Our methodology leverages an anomaly score derived from the reconstruction loss of the autoencoder, alongside a pre-trained standard convolutional neural network, within a semi-supervised framework. We find that optimal performance is achieved only when both unsupervised and supervised anomaly scores are combined. Events with a higher proportion of anomaly scores are flagged as anomalous and warrant further scrutiny. Unlike classical analyses, this approach utilizes all available event information in principle, thereby avoiding unnecessary data loss. Finally, we demonstrate the efficacy of learning-driven anomaly detection by comparing our results with classical inference, showing that, when properly tuned, these techniques hold the potential to surpass likelihood-based methods.

We demonstrate a method for integrating Bayes nets and game theory to forecast the actions of hybrid systems comprising both humans and automated elements. This new framework, termed "Semi Network-Form Games," is illustrated through the prediction of pilot behavior during potential near mid-air collisions. Currently, collision avoidance systems in aircraft cockpits provide pilots with instructions to prevent collisions at the onset of such events. However, research on mid-air encounters reveals significant inconsistency in how pilots respond to these advisories. Specifically, pilots seldom execute the recommended maneuvers with perfect accuracy, even though the system's efficacy depends on their compliance. Instead, pilots determine their actions by synthesizing all accessible information, including advisories, instrument data, and visual cues. We detail how to incorporate this dynamic into a semi network-form game model of the encounter and subsequently present computational simulations of the resulting framework.

The magnetospheres of the outer planets, especially Jupiter and Saturn, have been investigated via both remote sensing and in-situ measurements. Interpreting these data frequently requires concurrent knowledge of the solar wind conditions impacting the magnetosphere. Lacking an upstream monitor, solar wind context is usually supplied by models initialized with coronal outputs constrained by magnetograms or, more frequently, by in-situ data from 1 AU. Although 1-AU observations directly measure solar wind conditions, they represent single points and must be interpolated to feed outer-heliosphere models. This study evaluates various interpolation techniques using synthetic 1-AU data representing evolving solar wind structures. The basic "corotation" approach assumes a steady state rotating with the Sun, yet it creates discontinuities as new data arrives. While corotating backward and forward mitigates these breaks, it still generates significant errors in stream magnitude and timing. We demonstrate that the dynamic time warping (DTW) algorithm can enhance solar wind inputs for outer-heliosphere models by approximately an order of magnitude when using near-1 AU in-situ observations. This work aims to establish a foundation for future efforts to validate and refine methods for improving inner-boundary conditions in outer-heliosphere models, specifically addressing solar wind transients and quantifying gains for Saturn and Jupiter.

The emergence of moiré superlattices has made fractal Hofstadter bands widely accessible, enabling investigations into interaction effects within these systems. In this study, we utilize a renormalization group (RG) approach to show that repulsive interactions, combined with a tunable set of Van Hove singularities, create a novel pathway to unconventional superconductivity in Hofstadter bands. Specifically, adjusting the flux per unit cell and electronic filling allows control over the number of Van Hove singularities at the Fermi energy, triggering instabilities that lead to nodal superconductivity and chiral topological superconductivity with a Chern number $\mathcal{C} = \pm 6$. The latter state exhibits a self-similar fixed trajectory in the RG flow and an emerging self-similarity symmetry in the order parameter. These findings position Hofstadter quantum materials, such as moiré heterostructures, as promising candidates for realizing new reentrant Hofstadter superconductors.

The soil water retention curve (SWRC) is the primary relationship utilized in unsaturated soil research. This study examines the influence of porosity on the SWRC through numerical modeling of unsaturated soil using the Shan-Chen multiphase Lattice Boltzmann Method. The simulated SWRC shapes are compared with predictions from the van Genuchten model, showing a strong agreement except at low saturation levels. Additionally, the results indicate that the air-entry value increases as porosity decreases.

Operating in uncertain environments, space free-flyers such as the Astrobee robots on the International Space Station must account for inherent system uncertainties. Quantifying parametric uncertainties, specifically mass and moment of inertia, is critical for these safety-critical systems, as they can shift significantly during events like on-orbit cargo handling where unknown payloads alter system dynamics. By cautiously learning these uncertainties during operation, missions can potentially avoid fuel- and time-intensive maneuvers dedicated solely to system identification. Acknowledging this, the proposed RATTLE algorithm is an online, information-aware motion planner that integrates parametric model learning with real-time replanning, leveraging improved system models to enhance performance. The approach employs a two-tiered planner (global and local), a low-level model predictive controller, and an online parameter estimator that determines the robot's inertial properties to inform control and replanning; all components utilize models that update online. Simulation results of RATTLE controlling an Astrobee robot grappling an uncertain payload are presented, alongside hardware demonstration data that highlights the system's ability to actively promote parametric learning while executing useful motions.

Quotient gradings play a crucial role in calculating the intrinsic fundamental group $\pi_1(A)$ of an algebra $A$. To investigate quotient gradings within finite-dimensional semisimple complex algebras, it suffices to analyze those of twisted gradings. We determine the graded structure of these quotients by employing Mackey's obstruction class. Furthermore, for matrix algebras $A=M_n(\mathbb{C})$, we unify the notions of braces, group-theoretic Lagrangians, and elementary crossed products. Additionally, we successfully compute the intrinsic fundamental group for the diagonal algebras $A=\mathbb{C}^4$ and $A=\mathbb{C}^5$.

Ensuring that neural networks meet specific performance criteria by validating their input-output behaviors is a critical but challenging task, especially given the widespread adoption of neural networks in various engineering fields. This study leverages concepts from probability theory within the frequency domain to establish probabilistic verification guarantees for ReLU neural networks. Specifically, we model a deep feedforward neural network as a discrete dynamical system operating over a finite horizon, which transforms the distributions of initial states. By employing characteristic functions, we propagate the distribution of input data through the network and apply the inverse Fourier transform to derive the cumulative distribution function for the output set. This allows us to verify whether the network performs as intended for any random input point. Notably, our method does not depend on the existence of well-defined moments or moment generating functions. We validate the proposed approach using two case studies and compare its efficacy against related methods.

We examine stochastic inflation through a general framework of exponential coarse-graining filters. This approach yields inflaton-Langevin equations driven by colored noise correlated in $e$-fold time. Initially, we analyze the dynamics within the slow-roll regime for simple potentials using first-order perturbative, semi-analytical methods, which are subsequently validated against numerical simulations. Later calculations incorporate exponentially correlated noise, representing a leading-order correction to the full slow-roll noise correlations of the form $\big\langle \xi(N)\xi(N') \big\rangle_{(n)}\sim\left( \cosh\left[ n(N-N')+1 \right] \right)^{-1}$. Our results indicate that the curvature perturbation power spectrum $\mathcal{P}_{\zeta}$ is suppressed during early $e$-folds, with the degree of suppression governed by $n$. Additionally, employing this leading-order exponentially correlated noise, we conduct a first passage time analysis to determine the statistics of the stochastic $e$-fold distribution $\mathcal{N}$ and obtain an approximate formula for the mean number of $e$-folds $\big\langle \mathcal{N} \big\rangle$. By comparing our analytical findings with numerical simulations of inflaton dynamics, we demonstrate that the leading-order noise correlation function serves as an excellent approximation for the exact noise, which is computationally more challenging to simulate.

Advanced and adaptable computational tools are vital for designing and optimizing accelerator systems and their associated experiments. This work provides a concise overview of current capabilities and identifies necessary developments in accelerator software. Specifically for the FCC-ee project, it is crucial to incorporate effects such as beamstrahlung, beam-beam interactions, machine imperfections, and sources of beam-induced backgrounds relevant to experimental analysis, alongside the potential for beam polarization. The paper describes Key4hep, a software initiative aiming to establish a unified stack for future experiments, and explores extending this framework to machine-level codes. Furthermore, we examine strategies for efficiently and flexibly interfacing accelerator and experiment codes to optimize the FCC-ee interaction region design, including the feasibility of utilizing shared data formats as a connection mechanism.

Earth System Models (ESMs) serve as the principal instruments for exploring future planetary conditions over timescales ranging from decades to centuries, particularly concerning human-induced greenhouse gas emissions. Current advanced ESMs can replicate observed global mean temperature anomalies from the past 150 years; however, they require further enhancements, primarily addressing: (i) the significant variation in estimated climate sensitivity, (ii) modeled spatial distributions of critical variables like temperature and precipitation, (iii) the depiction of extreme weather phenomena, and (iv) the portrayal of multistable Earth system components and their capacity to forecast sudden transitions. We contend that rendering ESMs automatically differentiable holds immense promise for overcoming these specific limitations. First, automatic differentiability would facilitate objective model calibration, enabling the optimization of numerous free parameters via cost functions, a process currently reliant on manual tuning. Second, recent strides in Machine Learning (ML) and the growing volume, accuracy, and resolution of observational data offer solutions to several of these challenges, as ML can integrate additional observational insights into ESMs. Automatic differentiability is a fundamental component for developing such hybrid models, which merge process-based ESMs with ML elements. We present recent findings demonstrating the potential of automatic differentiation to create a new generation of significantly improved, data-driven ESMs.

We theoretically introduce a multidimensional spectroscopic method enhanced by biphoton entanglement to investigate dissipative polariton dynamics within the ultrafast regime. This technique is applied to a cavity-confined monomeric photosynthetic complex, serving as a model for multi-site excitonic quantum aggregates. The proposed approach exhibits high sensitivity to inter-manifold polariton coherence across the one-excitation and two-excitation subspaces. It is capable of tracking the dynamic influence of cavity-mediated excitonic correlations and dephasing processes occurring alongside phonon-induced dissipation. Furthermore, the non-classical nature of the entangled biphoton sources amplifies the signal's ultrafast and broadband correlation features, providing insights into the state correlations driving long-range cavity-assisted exciton migration.

We propose and analyze a novel general parameterization involving eight mixing parameters among the Z boson, the photon (gamma), and an additional neutral gauge boson Z'. Beyond the standard Weinberg angle ($\theta_W$), the most comprehensive description of Z-gamma-Z' mixing requires seven other phenomenological parameters: $G'$, $\xi$, $\eta$, $\theta_l$, $\theta_r$, $r$, and $l$. Specifically, the parameter $G'$ emerges from an extra Stueckelberg-type mass coupling, while the remaining six ($\xi$, $\eta$, $\theta_l - \theta'$, $\theta_r - \theta'$, $r$, and $l$) result from general kinetic mixings. When combined with the conventional Z-Z' mass mixing angle $\theta'$, these eight parameters allow for the determination of both $\theta'$ and the mass ratio $M_Z/M_{Z'}$. This framework is grounded in a model-independent extended electroweak chiral Lagrangian (EWCL) previously introduced by us. Furthermore, we demonstrate that there are eight corresponding independent theoretical coefficients within our EWCL, which are entirely constrained by the eight phenomenological mixing parameters. Finally, we find that the experimental accessibility of these eight parameters does not depend on an extended neutral current for the Z', but rather relies on the Z-Z' mass ratio.

This study investigates the theoretical characteristics of a stochastic formulation of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, situated within the modeling framework of location uncertainty (LU). Constructed via a stochastic adaptation of the Reynolds transport theorem, this approach integrates specific transport noise and distinct features, including a large-scale diffusion term comparable to traditional subgrid models and a modified advection term resulting from the spatial heterogeneity of small-scale velocity fields. While previous numerical investigations have focused on geophysical flow approximations and data assimilation, this work concentrates on a rigorous theoretical examination. Using standard arguments, we establish the existence of martingale solutions for the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations in the LU framework and demonstrate their pathwise uniqueness for two-dimensional flows. Furthermore, we prove that as noise intensity vanishes, these solutions converge, up to a subsequence in three dimensions, to solutions of the deterministic Navier-Stokes equations. Analogous to the grid convergence observed in established large-eddy simulation techniques, this finding provides assurance regarding the interpretation of the LU Navier-Stokes equations as a consistent large-scale representation of the deterministic system.

Visual Object Tracking (VOT) can be regarded as an advanced iteration of Few-Shot Learning (FSL). Although FSL has been utilized in tracking before, existing methods are often customized for specific algorithms, frequently compromising execution speed. This study introduces a generalized two-stage framework designed to accommodate a wide range of FSL algorithms while enhancing adaptation velocity. The initial stage employs a Siamese Regional Proposal Network to efficiently identify potential candidates, which are then passed to the second stage where the task is reframed as a few-shot classification problem. By following this coarse-to-fine approach, the first stage supplies informative sparse samples that allow diverse FSL algorithms to operate more conveniently and efficiently. To validate the second stage, we systematically evaluate several optimization-based few-shot learners from prior research, varying their objective functions, optimization techniques, and solution spaces. Furthermore, our framework facilitates the direct application of most other FSL algorithms to visual tracking, fostering cross-disciplinary communication between these fields. Comprehensive experiments across major benchmarks—including VOT2018, OTB2015, NFS, UAV123, TrackingNet, and GOT-10k—demonstrate both significant performance improvements and real-time processing speeds.

The development of dark matter halos depends on the Universe's expansion rate and the gravitational collapse of structures. As these halos virialize, they heat the intra-cluster gas to extreme temperatures, resulting in significant X-ray photon emission. This summary outlines advancements in using X-ray surveys of galaxy clusters to constrain cosmological models. It reviews recent findings derived from cluster volume abundance, spatial clustering, standard candle properties, and statistics of extreme objects, alongside pertinent theoretical frameworks. Additionally, the text explores galaxy clusters as tools for testing gravitational theories and provides a perspective on future research directions.

State-of-the-art cross-lingual summarization models typically utilize a multi-task learning approach featuring a shared vocabulary module and self-attention mechanisms to process tokens across two languages. However, the correlations captured by self-attention are often implicit and loose, rendering them inefficient for extracting essential cross-lingual representations. This issue is exacerbated when dealing with languages that possess distinct morphological or structural characteristics, complicating cross-lingual alignment and causing performance degradation. To address this, we introduce a novel Knowledge-Distillation-based framework for cross-lingual summarization. This approach explicitly constructs cross-lingual correlations by transferring knowledge from a monolingual summarization teacher to a cross-lingual summarization student. Because the teacher and student operate in separate vector spaces, we employ a Knowledge Distillation loss based on Sinkhorn Divergence—an optimal transport distance—to measure the discrepancy between their representations. Leveraging the intuitive geometric properties of Sinkhorn Divergence, the student model effectively aligns its cross-lingual hidden states with monolingual ones, thereby establishing robust correlations even between distant languages. Experiments across various cross-lingual summarization datasets involving distant language pairs confirm that our method surpasses state-of-the-art models in both high and low-resourced scenarios.

Record linkage algorithms connect records from disparate databases that correspond to the same real-world entity by utilizing direct and/or quasi-identifiers like name, address, age, and gender. Because these identifiers typically contain personal identifiable information (PII), such algorithms must incorporate privacy constraints, a field known as privacy-preserving record linkage (PPRL). Numerous studies have explored performing linkage on encoded or encrypted identifiers, often combining differential privacy (DP) with computationally efficient methods such as Bloom filter encoding to ensure provable privacy guarantees. However, standard DP fails to address critical constraints, specifically fairness-bias and the computational cost measured by the number of record pairs compared. This work introduces new concepts of fairness-constrained DP and combined fairness and cost-constrained DP for PPRL, alongside a framework integrating these notions with Bloom filter encoding. We provide theoretical proofs for these new DP definitions and experimentally evaluate them using two datasets containing person-specific data. Our results demonstrate that these new DP notions enable PPRL to achieve superior performance compared to standard DP, effectively balancing privacy, cost, and fairness constraints.

In information retrieval (IR) systems, shifting user interests and temporal trends can alter both query distributions and the content available for recommendation. Because neural ranking methods rely heavily on training data, it is essential to evaluate their long-term transferability when facing new domains. This paper introduces a dataset derived from the MS-MARCO corpus, designed to simulate continuous topic streams and IR property-driven controlled environments. We subsequently conduct a detailed analysis of recent neural IR models' capacity for continual learning within these streams. Our empirical investigation identifies specific scenarios where catastrophic forgetting arises—such as varying task similarity, text length characteristics, and model learning strategies—to guide future model design directions.

The observation of gravitational waves from the binary neutron star merger GW170817, along with its electromagnetic counterparts GRB170817 and AT2017gfo, launched the era of gravitational wave multimessenger astronomy. While the optically red to near-infrared emission ("red" component) of AT2017gfo was successfully attributed to the decay of freshly synthesized nuclei via rapid neutron capture (a kilonova), the origin of the dominant early-time (up to 1.5 days) ultraviolet to blue emission ("blue" component) remains debated. Two primary hypotheses exist: radiation from lanthanide-poor ejecta or shock interaction (cocoon emission). This study simulates AT2017gfo-like light curves and employs Bayesian analysis to determine if an ultraviolet satellite designed for rapid gravitational wave follow-up can differentiate between the physical mechanisms driving the early "blue" component. Our findings indicate that a Dorado-like ultraviolet satellite, featuring a 50 square degree field of view and a limiting magnitude (AB) of 20.5 for a 10-minute exposure, can distinguish radiation components out to at least 160 Mpc if observations commence within 3.2 or 5.2 hours for two specific light curve scenarios. Additionally, we assessed how well model parameters can be constrained using the resulting photometry. We determined that while ultraviolet data alone restricts parameters related to outer ejecta properties, combining ground-based optical and space-based ultraviolet data enables tight constraints on all but one kilonova model parameter up to 160 Mpc. These results suggest that an ultraviolet mission such as Dorado would offer unique insights into the early post-merger evolution and the physics driving its emission.

This study presents and analyzes the initial light curves of CSS J022914.4+044340 across the B-, V-, Rc-, and Ic bands. The results identify the system as a deep contact binary with a low mass ratio of 0.198 ± 0.005 and a depth of 63.7 ± 7.9%, suggesting it resides at the final stage of tidally-locked evolution driven by magnetized winds. Due to its complete eclipsing nature, the derived photometric solutions are considered highly reliable. Spectroscopic observations yield a temperature of 5855 ± 15 K and a metallicity of [Fe/H] = -0.842 ± 0.031. Utilizing the Gaia EDR3 parallax, the physical parameters are estimated as follows: M1 = 1.44 (+0.25, -0.22) M☉, M2 = 0.29 (+0.05, -0.05) M☉, R1 = 1.26 (+0.08, -0.06) R☉, R2 = 0.65 (+0.03, -0.04) R☉, L1 = 1.718 (+0.186, -0.191) L☉, and L2 = 0.416 (+0.039, -0.050) L☉. By incorporating the 54% light contribution from a third body identified through photometric analysis, its luminosity is calculated at 2.705 L☉, implying it is likely a subgiant. This configuration explains why the primary component possesses a higher mass relative to similar systems and exhibits such low metallicity.

We introduce a novel approach utilizing quantum imaging and communication tools to investigate physics beyond the Standard Model. This method targets "dark spontaneous parametric down-conversion" (dSPDC), a process where pump photons generate a signal photon and a new, non-interacting particle from the dark sector instead of the conventional idler. Although this dark particle does not interact directly, its existence can be deduced by analyzing the signal photon's properties, with potential candidates including dark photons and axion-like particles. We demonstrate that incorporating an optical medium expands the phase space for this decay process, enabling events that are otherwise forbidden in a vacuum. Our proposed search strategies utilize optical spectroscopy and imaging of the signal photons. Notably, the signal rate in this scheme scales with the square of the weak coupling to new physics, offering a significant advantage over light-shining-through-wall experiments, which scale with the fourth power. We further evaluate the specific optical media characteristics required to enhance dSPDC and estimate the resulting rates. Finally, we present a tabletop experiment using a Skipper-CCD to perform high-resolution ghost imaging, thereby validating its potential utility for dSPDC searches.

Applying simple symmetry arguments to the third generation yields a prediction for the existence of new sequential Higgs doublets with masses around or below 5 TeV. These doublets feature approximately universal Higgs-Yukawa coupling constants of $g\sim 1$, a value calibrated by the known Higgs boson mass, the top quark's coupling, and the $b$-quark mass. Specifically, a new massive weak-isodoublet, $H_b$, coupled to the $b$-quark with $g\sim 1$, is forecasted; it could be detectable at the LHC operating at 13 TeV and would certainly be accessible at the upgraded 26 TeV facility. Extending this framework to leptons predicts a new $H_\tau$ and potentially an $H_{\nu_\tau}$ doublet, though the detectability of the latter hinges on whether the $\tau$-neutrino mass is Dirac or Majorana in nature.

Deep learning models have achieved state-of-the-art results across numerous applications, largely due to well-trained classifiers on benchmark datasets serving as backbone feature extractors for downstream tasks. However, the widely used cross-entropy loss function often induces severe overfitting in deep neural networks (DNN) unless mitigated by techniques like data augmentation. This paper demonstrates that minimizing cross-entropy essentially trains DNNs to learn the conditional entropy of the data distribution—representing the remaining uncertainty in labels given the input. To address this, we propose a mutual information learning framework that trains DNNs by optimizing the mutual information between inputs and labels. Theoretically, we establish a lower bound for population error probability based on mutual information. Furthermore, we derive both lower and upper bounds for mutual information and corresponding error probability lower bounds within a specific binary classification model in $\mathbb{R}^n$. We also determine the sample complexity required to accurately estimate mutual information from empirical data. Empirical evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets validate our theoretical findings. The resulting Mutual Information Learned Classifiers (MILCs) demonstrate significantly superior generalization compared to state-of-the-art methods, with testing accuracy improvements exceeding 10\%.

We examine conformal field theory on the plane using the conformal bootstrap methodology. This overview presents the core concepts of the bootstrap approach within quantum field theory and illustrates their application to two-dimensional theories possessing local conformal symmetry. We outline the mathematical frameworks inherent to these theories, ranging from the Virasoro algebra and its representations to BPZ equations and conformal blocks. Specific examples covered include Liouville theory, (generalized) minimal models, free bosonic theories, the $H_3^+$ model, and the $SU_2$ and $\widetilde{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ WZW models. Furthermore, we explore the interconnections among these models and analyze their behavior in limiting cases where the central charge and/or conformal dimensions approach specific values.

This work reports initial findings for the masses of the proton, neutron, and $\Omega^-$ baryons derived from QCD+QED lattice simulations employing four dynamical quarks and C$^*$ boundary conditions. These findings contribute to the RC${}^*$ collaboration's ongoing project, detailed in accompanying proceedings, and were generated using a single ensemble characterized by a renormalised electromagnetic coupling of $\alpha_{\text{em}}\sim 0.04$, a physical volume of $L\sim 1.7$ fm, and four dynamical quark masses tuned to the $U$--spin symmetric point ($m_d=m_s$). We show that, even on this unphysical ensemble, baryon masses can be computed with sufficient accuracy when incorporating QED without relying on gauge-fixing or perturbation theory. This success instills confidence that the proposed strategy will remain effective for simulations approaching the physical point.

Wetlands provide multiple ecosystem services, including water filtration and carbon sequestration. Since wetlands consist of numerous open water bodies, mapping these areas is an effective way to monitor their expansion. An affordable, albeit indirect, strategy for mapping these bodies involves using geo-computational techniques on satellite imagery. This study introduces the flexible Beta regression (FBR) model to forecast open water fractions based on water index measurements. We analyzed data from two MODIS images captured during the 2008 dry season in Marismas Nacionales, a wetland on Mexico's northwestern Pacific coast. A Bayesian estimation framework is detailed, specifically outlining a nested Metropolis-Hastings and Gibbs sampling algorithm for parameter inference. Results indicate that the FBR model generates reliable predictions of water fractions, outperforming standard models. Additionally, we have developed supporting software in R, which is accessible via a GitHub repository.

We compare manually and automatically parallelized NAS Benchmarks to pinpoint divergent code sections, discuss prospects for improving automatic parallelizers, and identify ten patterns that challenge current parallelization technology. Additionally, we quantify the potential impact of advanced techniques capable of performing necessary transformations automatically. While some findings are unsurprising yet difficult to achieve—requiring compilers to better detect parallelism in outermost loops and loops with function calls—other opportunities are within reach and could make a significant difference, such as merging loops into parallel regions, mitigating load imbalance, and enhancing reduction parallelization. Studying hand-optimized code is an essential pathway for advancing compilers and pushing the boundaries of compiler research; however, few recent papers have pursued this objective. This work aims to address that gap.

Over the past few years, there has been increasing interest in using radiative transfer codes to post-process cosmological simulations and predict observable fluxes for simulated galaxies. While effective, this approach is computationally slow and relies on assumptions when simulations fail to resolve the interstellar medium (ISM). Although zoom-in simulations offer superior resolution of ISM structure and the geometry of stars and gas, their statistical utility is limited by the high cost of simulating even a single halo. This study utilizes high-resolution, cosmological zoom-in simulations of massive ($M_* > 10^{10.5} M_{\odot}$) star-forming galaxies at $z=2$ from the FIRE suite. We apply the SKIRT radiative transfer code to hundreds of snapshots spanning the redshift range $1.5 < z < 5$ to calibrate a power-law scaling relation connecting dust mass, star formation rate, and 870 $\mu$m flux density. The resulting relation demonstrates encouraging consistency with observational data from the sub-millimeter-selected AS2UDS sample. Extending this work to other wavelengths, we derive scaling relations linking dust mass, stellar mass, star formation rate, redshift, and sub-millimeter flux density across observed-frame wavelengths from 340 $\mu$m to 870 $\mu$m. These relations are subsequently applied to galaxies selected from EAGLE, a large-volume cosmological simulation. We demonstrate that these scaling relations accurately predict EAGLE sub-millimeter number counts, aligning well with prior results obtained through significantly more computationally intensive radiative transfer methods. Consequently, our scaling relations can be employed across various simulations and semi-analytical or semi-empirical models to produce robust and efficient predictions for sub-millimeter number counts.

Let $C$ and $K$ be centrally symmetric convex bodies in ${\mathbb R}^n$. We demonstrate that if $C$ is isotropic, then for all $s \geq 1$ and ${\bf t}=(t_1,\ldots ,t_s)\in {\mathbb R}^s$, the following inequality holds:
$$ \|{\bf t}\|_{C^s,K}=\int_{C}\cdots\int_{C}\Big\|\sum_{j=1}^st_jx_j\Big\|_K\,dx_1\cdots dx_s \leq c_1L_C(\log n)^5\,\sqrt{n}M(K)\|{\bf t}\|_2, $$
where $L_C$ denotes the isotropic constant of $C$ and $M(K)$ is defined as $\int_{S^{n-1}}\|\xi\|_Kd\sigma (\xi)$. This result transforms a question posed by V.~Milman into the task of establishing an upper bound for the parameter $M(K)$ of an isotropic convex body. The proof relies on an insight integrating findings by Eldan, Lehec, and Klartag regarding the slicing problem: specifically, if $\mu $ is an isotropic log-concave probability measure on ${\mathbb R}^n$, then for any centrally symmetric convex body $K$ in ${\mathbb R}^n$, the inequality $$I_1(\mu ,K):=\int_{{\mathbb R}^n}\|x\|_K\,d\mu(x)\leq c_2\sqrt{n}(\log n)^5\,M(K)$$ is satisfied. We conclude by demonstrating additional applications of this inequality.

We introduce a method for learning single-view 3D object pose estimation by leveraging a novel data source: in-the-wild videos featuring rotating objects. These videos are common in real-world scenarios, such as vehicles in roundabouts or aircraft near runways, and are straightforward to gather. Our findings demonstrate that combining classical structure-from-motion algorithms with recent progress in instance detection and feature matching yields surprisingly precise relative 3D pose estimation for such footage. We present a multi-stage training framework that initially learns a canonical pose from a video collection before supervising a model for single-view pose estimation. This approach achieves performance comparable to current state-of-the-art methods on standard 3D pose estimation benchmarks without relying on any pose labels during training. Additionally, we release the Accidental Turntables Dataset, a challenging benchmark comprising 41,212 images of cars amidst cluttered backgrounds, motion blur, and varying illumination, designed to advance 3D pose estimation research.

This research investigates efficient and precise shortest path algorithms for road networks incorporating realistic traffic data. In navigation contexts, both current live traffic conditions and forecasts of future flow are critical. Although preprocessing methods have proven effective for handling live traffic or predictions separately, integrating both presents substantial hurdles: predicted traffic demands costly preprocessing, whereas live traffic necessitates rapid updates for frequent adjustments. We introduce an A*-based solution that addresses these issues by extending A* potentials to account for time dependency, meaning the estimated distance from a vertex to the destination varies based on the visit time. This innovation yields significantly faster query times than previously achieved. Our evaluation demonstrates that the proposed method supports interactive query performance on continental-scale road networks while permitting live traffic updates within less than a minute. Furthermore, our approach delivers a speedup of at least two orders of magnitude compared to Dijkstra's algorithm and up to one order of magnitude over current state-of-the-art time-independent A* potentials.

This paper investigates the calculation of charged moments for the reduced density matrix of two disjoint intervals within the $1+1$-dimensional free compactified boson conformal field theory (CFT) by analyzing the four-point correlation function of fluxed twist fields. We derive the exact scaling function for this four-point function and examine its decompactification limit. Utilizing this scaling function, we compute the charged moments of the partial transpose, termed charged Rényi negativity. These charged moments, along with those of the partial transpose, play a crucial role in the symmetry decomposition of associated entanglement measures. Furthermore, we validate our analytic expressions against precise numerical results from the complex harmonic chain, observing perfect agreement.

We demonstrate that incorporating quantum gravity renders uncertainty in the causal structure of field theory unavoidable, including the ill-defined nature of lightcones. While this effect remains negligible in the effective field theory regime—where it is independent of the UV completion—it escalates with energy, introducing an unknown uncertainty for generic UV completions. We provide specifics regarding the causality uncertainty within a particular UV completion, namely quadratic gravity, and discuss how the mechanisms identified in both the effective field theory and quadratic gravity contexts may represent common features of quantum gravity.

Numerous machine learning challenges depend on multi-task learning (MTL), which involves solving several interconnected tasks at once. This approach is especially vital for privacy-conscious domains like healthcare, finance, and IoT, where data from diverse sources must be shared to facilitate learning. This study formalizes client-level privacy within MTL using joint differential privacy (JDP), a relaxed form of differential privacy tailored for distributed optimization and mechanism design. We subsequently introduce an algorithm for mean-regularized MTL—an objective frequently employed in personalized federated learning—constrained by JDP. Our analysis of both the objective and the solver offers certifiable assurances regarding privacy and utility. Empirical results demonstrate that our method achieves superior privacy/utility trade-offs compared to global baselines across standard federated learning benchmarks.

While frozen, uncorrelated random on-site potentials in interacting quantum systems drive a transition from an ergodic to a localized phase known as many-body localization (MBL), this study numerically investigates how auto-correlated disorder affects the static and dynamical properties of a one-dimensional MBL system. By employing standard metrics for energy level repulsion and the localization of energy eigenstates, we demonstrate that strong correlations between on-site potentials in the one-dimensional spin-1/2 Heisenberg model suppress the MBL phase. However, at low disorder strengths, level repulsion is weakened even though energy eigenstates remain well-extended. These results are particularly evident in the time domain, which serves as our primary focus, as illustrated by the temporal evolution of experimentally relevant observables such as the return probability and the spin auto-correlation function.

Short superconducting segments can link quantum dots through elastic co-tunneling (ECT) and crossed Andreev reflection (CAR), hosting Majorana bound states if the ECT-to-CAR ratio is adjustable. While metallic superconductors have previously mediated these processes with restricted tunability, this work demonstrates that Andreev bound states within semiconductor-superconductor heterostructures can facilitate CAR and ECT across mesoscopic distances. Because these bound states contain both electron and hole components, they generate complex interference patterns that enable deterministic control over the ECT and CAR ratio. Additionally, we show that combining intrinsic spin-orbit coupling in InSb nanowires with an external magnetic field offers a powerful mechanism to further tune the ECT-CAR ratio and enhance the coupling strength between adjacent quantum dots.

Particle acceleration during magnetic reconnection remains a critical area of study in solar, astrophysical, and space plasmas. Recent three-dimensional (3D) particle-in-cell simulations reveal that particles can escape flux ropes via 3D field-line chaos, granting them access to further acceleration zones, enhanced energy gains through Fermi acceleration, and the formation of power-law energy distributions. These 3D dynamics are absent in conventional two-dimensional (2D) simulations, where particle motion across field lines is restricted, artificially trapping them within magnetic islands. Although comprehensive 3D simulations are computationally prohibitive for many investigations, this study proposes replicating 3D outcomes in 2D models by applying ad hoc pitch-angle scattering to a subset of particles. Our results demonstrate that scattered particles successfully exit 2D islands, undergo more efficient Fermi acceleration, and exhibit a marked rise in energetic particle flux. Furthermore, we examine how scattering frequency impacts nonthermal particle spectra, contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of particle acceleration mechanisms in magnetic reconnection.

Current self-supervised deep learning methods capable of segmenting images into a fixed set of hard labels, similar to the k-means algorithm, remain underdeveloped. We present the k-textures algorithm, which performs self-supervised segmentation of 4-band images (RGB-NIR) into $k$ distinct classes. We demonstrate its application on high-resolution Planet satellite imagery. Our approach proves that discrete search is viable when utilizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and gradient descent. The model identifies $k$ hard clustering classes, represented as $k$ discrete binary masks and their corresponding $k$ independently generated textures, which together simulate the original image. The similarity loss is calculated as the mean squared error between features of the original and simulated images; these features are extracted from the penultimate convolutional block of a Keras 'imagenet' pretrained VGG-16 model and a custom feature extractor trained on Planet data. The primary advancements of the k-textures model include: first, obtaining $k$ discrete binary masks within the model via gradient descent, facilitated by a novel method employing a hard sigmoid activation function. Second, it delivers hard clustering classes where each pixel belongs to exactly one class. Third, unlike k-means which treats pixels independently, this approach incorporates contextual information, associating each class not only with similar color channel values but also with specific textures. This methodology is designed to simplify the generation of training samples for satellite image segmentation, and the k-textures architecture can be adapted to handle varying numbers of bands and more complex tasks such as object self-segmentation. The model's code and weights are accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6359859.

Globally, cardiovascular diseases represent the leading cause of death. Identifying atrial fibrillation (AF) during its asymptomatic phase is crucial for stroke prevention and enables timely clinical interventions, such as administering anticoagulant therapy. This clinical imperative has spurred numerous recent studies focused on detecting AF within electrocardiogram (ECG) signals, many of which utilize machine learning algorithms. However, ECG datasets containing AF samples often exhibit severe class imbalance; failing to address this issue can significantly degrade the performance of classification models. Data augmentation is a widely adopted strategy to mitigate this challenge. This study examines the effectiveness of various augmentation techniques—including oversampling, Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs), and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)—in resolving class imbalance. These methods were quantitatively and qualitatively assessed, compared, and analyzed in depth. The findings indicate that deep learning approaches for AF classification derive greater benefit from GMMs and GANs than from oversampling. Specifically, GANs yielded an average classification accuracy improvement of approximately 3% compared to baseline methods, while achieving an f1-score comparable to that of GMMs.

This study investigates the model-theoretic characteristics of Kac-Moody groups, with a specific emphasis on elementary equivalence. We demonstrate that for untwisted affine Kac-Moody groups, elementary equivalence necessitates both identical generalized Cartan matrices and isomorphic ground fields. Furthermore, we establish that for arbitrary Kac-Moody groups over finite fields, elementary equivalence entails the equality of these fields and an isomorphism between their twin root data. A comparable result is proven for Kac-Moody groups defined over infinite subfields of the algebraic closures of finite fields.

Extended stellar halos offer vital insights into galaxy assembly and evolution. This study examines the resolved stellar populations and extended halo of NGC 5128 across varying galactocentric distances. Utilizing HST imagery, we resolved individual red giant branch (RGB) stars in 28 distinct pointings. Surface density distributions were derived from deep VI color-magnitude diagrams extending at least 1.5 magnitudes below the RGB tip. Contamination from Milky Way stars was evaluated using a novel control field, modeling techniques, and a combination of optical and near-infrared photometry. We also provide a new calibration of WFC3 F606W+F814W photometry relative to the ground-based VI system. Our photometric results indicate that NGC 5128's stellar halo is dominated by old RGB stars present in all observed fields. The V-band surface brightness decreases from 23 to 32 mag/arcsec$^2$ between 8.3 kpc and the outermost halo fields, which lie 140 kpc along the major axis and 92 kpc along the minor axis. Within approximately 30 kpc, we detect a 2–3 Gyr old population traced by bright asymptotic giant branch stars; this group accounts for up to 10% of the total stellar mass if 2 Gyr old, but requires a 30–40% contribution if 3 Gyr old. The stellar surface density profile is well described by an $r^{1/4}$ law or a power law of $\sim r^{-3.1}$ across the full radial range, showing no significant slope break but exhibiting substantial field-to-field scatter. While the inner halo's ellipticity measured from integrated light is $e=(b/a)=0.77$, it flattens to $e=0.54 \pm 0.02$ beyond 30 kpc. Accounting for this outer halo flattening, the projection of the elliptical isophote on the semimajor axis extends to nearly 30 effective radii in our most distant field. [abridged]

We introduce a cost-effective framework that derives the Inverse Seesaw mechanism from the spontaneous breaking of a local $U(1)_{B-L}$ symmetry, where sterile neutrino Majorana masses arise radiatively from the dark sector. This model extends the Standard Model by incorporating neutral scalars and fermionic singlets, alongside a gauge group augmented with $U(1)_{B-L}$ and a discrete $\mathbb{Z}_4$ symmetry. Beyond dynamically generating the Inverse Seesaw to yield small active neutrino masses, the framework provides two viable dark matter candidates—one scalar and one fermionic—stabilized by a residual $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry. Furthermore, the model satisfies experimental constraints from direct dark matter detection, invisible Higgs decays, and $Z'$ collider searches for dark sector particles at the TeV scale.

This study examines the dark Higgs inflation model incorporating curvature corrections and investigates whether particle physics experiments at the LHC can verify its predictions. Our findings indicate that this model, enhanced by curvature corrections, is strongly supported by current cosmological data. The model's cosmological forecasts, which account for quantum corrections to dark Higgs coupling constants and uncertainties in reheating temperature estimation, yield a dark Higgs mass of $m_{\phi}=0.919 \pm 0.211$ GeV and a mixing angle of $\theta = 1.492 \pm 0.045$ (at 68% CL). We assessed the sensitivity of the FASER and MAPP-1 experiments to detect the dark Higgs inflaton mass and mixing angle within the 95% CL cosmological confidence region, assuming an integrated luminosity of 3 ab$^{-1}$ at 13 TeV at the LHC and 100% detection efficiency. Ultimately, we conclude that the dark Higgs inflation model with curvature corrections represents a compelling inflation scenario grounded in particle physics theory, favored by existing cosmological measurements, and one that leaves detectable signatures in searches for the dark Higgs boson at the LHC.

Inductive biases such as translational invariance and rotational equivariance are crucial for graph neural networks processing 3D atomistic structures like molecules. Drawing inspiration from the widespread success of Transformers across different fields, this study explores integrating these specific biases into Transformer architectures. We introduce Equiformer, a graph neural network that combines the power of Transformers with $SE(3)/E(3)$-equivariant features derived from irreducible representations (irreps). These irreps features embed equivariant data within channel dimensions, avoiding the need to complicate the graph topology. This straightforward approach allows for the direct substitution of standard operations with their equivariant equivalents. Furthermore, to better suit Transformers for 3D graphs, we develop a new equivariant graph attention mechanism that accounts for both content and geometric details, such as relative positions found in irreps features. To enhance attention expressivity, we substitute dot-product attention with multi-layer perceptron attention and introduce non-linear message passing. We evaluate Equiformer on two quantum property prediction datasets, QM9 and OC20. On QM9, Equiformer outperforms other models trained on identical data partitions on 11 of the 12 regression tasks. On OC20, when trained using IS2RE data with optional IS2RS data, Equiformer surpasses existing state-of-the-art models. The code to reproduce all primary results will be made available shortly.

The World Trade Web (WTW) represents the network of global trade connections between nations. Developing a single model that effectively characterizes both the local trade volumes and the global topological structure of the WTW remains an unresolved challenge. Although the traditional Gravity Model (GM) accurately replicates observed trade volumes by utilizing macroeconomic factors like GDP and geographic distance, it fails to produce a realistic network topology by predicting a fully connected system. To address this limitation, two distinct modeling frameworks have emerged in econometrics and statistical physics. Econometric methods treat the traditional GM as the expected value of an arbitrary, testable probability distribution. Conversely, statistical physics approaches derive maximum-entropy probability distributions for weighted graphs based on selected measurable structural constraints. This study compares and integrates these two methodologies by employing a class of maximum-entropy models that incorporate macroeconomic properties typical of standard econometric analyses. The findings indicate that this integrated approach outperforms purely econometric models. These results imply that maximum-entropy construction offers a robust econometric framework where extensive and intensive margins can be independently regulated by combining topological constraints with dyadic macroeconomic variables.

Quantum many-body systems display a variety of phases defined by distinct correlation types. While established tools exist to investigate whether a phase is gapped or gapless, methods for probing whether a phase supports a well-defined quasi-particle description remain underdeveloped. We introduce a protocol that examines many-body correlations by dynamically ramping a Hamiltonian parameter to a fixed target value at varying speeds. The first-order correction arising from finite ramping velocities beyond the adiabatic limit is universal and independent of the path, effectively revealing the correlations of equilibrium phases at the target point. We designate this approach as non-adiabatic linear response and validate it experimentally using the Bose-Hubbard model within ultracold atom setups. Both theoretical analysis and experimental results confirm that this non-adiabatic linear response is substantial in the quantum critical regime where quasi-particles are ill-defined, yet it becomes negligibly small deep within superfluid and Mott insulator phases that possess well-defined quasi-particles.

Tau-based finite-energy sum-rule (FESR) studies typically presume that the scale $s_0 \sim m_\tau^2$ is sufficiently large to ignore integrated duality violations (DVs) and to treat non-perturbative OPE condensate contributions of dimension $D$ as scaling with $(\Lambda_{\rm QCD}/m_\tau )^D$, thereby permitting truncation of the OPE series at low dimensions. However, the assumption regarding truncation is questionable because the OPE series does not converge, and the neglect of DVs is suspect given experimental data on the electromagnetic $I=1$ vector ($V$), axial vector ($A$), and $V+A$ spectral functions, which exhibit DV oscillations with magnitudes comparable to $\alpha_s$-driven perturbative terms around $s\sim2-3$ GeV$^2$. This discussion introduces novel tools for evaluating the numerical impact of omitted higher-$D$ OPE terms. When applied to the "truncated OPE" approach utilized in Refs.[1,2] and previous studies by the same group, these tools reveal that such a strategy produces unreliable determinations of the strong coupling from hadronic $\tau$ decays.

We have developed multiple language models for Icelandic, such as IceBERT, which attain state-of-the-art results across various downstream tasks, including part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, grammatical error detection, and constituency parsing. Our training process relies on the Icelandic Common Crawl Corpus (IC3), a newly introduced dataset comprising high-quality online texts filtered by the Icelandic top-level domain (TLD), alongside other public sources to form a total of 16GB of Icelandic text. To improve evaluation standards and elevate baselines for Icelandic, we adapted and translated the WinoGrande dataset for co-reference resolution. These initiatives demonstrate that a well-cleaned crawled corpus is adequate for achieving state-of-the-art performance in NLP applications for low- to medium-resource languages, comparable to models trained on curated corpora. Additionally, we show that initializing models with existing multilingual architectures can yield state-of-the-art results on specific downstream tasks.

We investigate the link between galaxy star formation quenching and their position in cluster outskirts within the redshift interval $z=[0,2]$ by calculating the proportion of red galaxies. Specifically, we compare galaxies entering clusters isotropically against those arriving along filaments. Our study utilizes a galaxy sample derived from the semi-analytic model SAG applied to the MultiDark {\textsc{mdpl2}} simulation. Consistent with observational data, we observe that infalling regions exhibit intermediate star formation rates, situated between those of cluster and field galaxies. Furthermore, within the redshift range [0-0.85], we demonstrate that quenching is more pronounced in filamentary regions than in isotropic infall zones. Analyzing the fraction of red galaxies relative to the normalized distance from the cluster center, we find that at radii $R/R_{200}>3$, the filamentary regions contain a significantly higher fraction of red galaxies compared to isotropic infall regions. By examining the properties of the main progenitors of $z=0$ galaxies, we identify that evolutionary behaviors vary with stellar mass and environment. These findings support observational evidence indicating that cluster infall regions are crucial for galaxy pre-processing throughout much of their evolutionary history.

The distribution of LIGO black hole binaries (BBHs) exhibits an intermediate-mass range that aligns with the Salpeter Initial Mass Function (IMF) for black holes formed via core-collapse supernovae, provided binary pairing is maintained. These systems are effectively described by a mean mass $\mu$, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of $r = 0.93\,\pm\,0.06$ for the secondary-to-primary mass ratio, and a mean mass-ratio $\bar{q}\simeq 0.67$ ($q=M_2/M_1$), a finding consistent with the scarcity of intermediate-mass X-ray binaries. The mass function of LIGO BBHs is well-modeled by a broken power-law featuring a tail where $\mu\gtrsim 31.4M_\odot$, with the mean binary mass defined as $\mu=\left(M_1+M_2\right)/2$. The power-law index derived from this tail, $\alpha_{B,true}=4.77\pm 0.73$, approaches the upper limit of $2\alpha_S=4.7$ for uncorrelated binary initial mass functions, based on the Salpeter stellar IMF index of $\alpha_S=2.35$. The observed minimal scatter in BBH mass ratios indicates that mass transfer during binary evolution prior to black hole formation tends to equalize masses. Furthermore, at the progenitor redshift $z^\prime$, the power-law index satisfies $\alpha_B^\prime>\alpha_B$ within a flat $\Lambda$CDM cosmology. Consequently, the constraint $\alpha_{B,true}^\prime \lesssim 2\alpha_S$ rules out formation at arbitrarily high redshifts ($z^\prime \gg1$), a conclusion that can be refined and strengthened with expanded BBH surveys from future LIGO O4-5 observations.

Pre-stellar cores define the starting parameters for star formation. While these initial conditions have been thoroughly studied in nearby low-mass star-forming regions, they remain largely unexplored in massive star-forming regions. This study reports the discovery of a cluster of low-mass starless and pre-stellar core candidates within the massive star protocluster NGC6334S. Utilizing ALMA observations with a spatial resolution of approximately 0.02 pc, we identified 17 low-mass starless core candidates lacking any signs of protostellar activity. These candidates exhibit small velocity dispersions, elevated fractional abundances of NH$_{2}$D, high NH$_{3}$ deuterium fractionations, and remain completely invisible in infrared wavelengths ranging from 3.6 to 70 $\mu$m. In these regions, turbulence has significantly dissipated, and gas kinematics are governed primarily by thermal motions. Of the 17 cores, nine are gravitationally bound and thus classified as pre-stellar core candidates. The embedded cores in NGC6334S display a broad diversity in mass and evolutionary stage.

Backdoor attacks aim to implant concealed triggers within deep neural networks (DNNs), allowing the models to function correctly on normal inputs while producing malicious outputs when specific attacker-defined triggers are present. This vulnerability arises when the training process lacks full oversight, such as when utilizing third-party datasets or models, presenting a significant and realistic security risk. Although research into backdoor learning is expanding rapidly, a systematic review of the field has been notably absent. This paper addresses that gap by offering the first comprehensive survey of backdoor learning. We categorize existing attacks and defenses based on their attributes and propose a unified framework for analyzing poisoning-based backdoor threats. Furthermore, we examine the connections between backdoor attacks and related domains, including adversarial attacks and data poisoning, while summarizing commonly used benchmark datasets. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions based on the reviewed literature and provides a curated list of backdoor-related resources at \url{https://github.com/THUYimingLi/backdoor-learning-resources}.

We introduce a straightforward deterministic dynamic equation to uncover the mechanism behind the large-scale, perpetual evolution of spatial density inhomogeneity within active nematics. These phase regions are determined analytically. The interaction between density, the magnitude of nematic order, and the nematic director is essential for driving long-wavelength instabilities and generating apparently fluctuating collective movements. Furthermore, ordered nematic domains can continuously absorb particles, expand, and undergo endless division. These findings broaden our comprehension of large-scale, seemingly fluctuated organization in active fluids.

I present a straightforward illustration of how time series data from searches for ultralight bosonic dark matter (DM), such as axions, can distinguish between coherent and incoherent quantum states. Although this example is conceptually simple, I hope that explicitly working through it will stimulate experimental investigation.
