In a standard coherent state, the number density undergoes $\mathcal{O}(1)$ oscillations over the coherence time, $\tau_c = h/mv^2$, where $m$ represents the particle mass and $v$ the galactic virial velocity; this leads to a diminished constraining power for experiments with durations $T < \tau_c$ because of the unknown global phase. Conversely, if the DM is incoherent, such pronounced number oscillations do not occur, as the ensemble average over particles in various streams results in an effective phase averaging. Consequently, if a signal is detected, time series analysis spanning the coherence time can determine whether the DM is coherent or incoherent. This insight is observationally significant for DM masses ranging from $10^{-17}\text{ eV}$ to $10^{-11}\text{ eV}$ (corresponding to coherence times from roughly a year down to 100 seconds), and can be probed by experiments such as CASPEr, DMRadio, and AION. While coherence might also be measurable at higher masses within the microwave regime, that possibility has not been explored here.

Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) for semantic segmentation has become highly popular due to its ability to facilitate Sim2Real transfer by significantly reducing the need for labor-intensive pixel-level annotations in real-world settings. This paper introduces a novel extension of this task: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Video Semantic Segmentation. Given the ease of acquiring large-scale video labels via simulation, maximizing Sim2Real knowledge transferability is proposed as a key strategy to address the inherent data scarcity in video processing. To solve this, we propose a new two-phase adaptation framework. In the initial phase, we comprehensively extract knowledge from the source domain using supervised losses, while simultaneously employing Video Adversarial Training (VAT) to align source and target features by leveraging video context. In the second phase, we utilize Video Self-Training (VST) focused exclusively on target data. To generate robust pseudo-labels, we exploit temporal information within videos—a factor rarely considered in prior image-based self-training methods. Our approach achieves strong baseline results in the 'VIPER to CityscapeVPS' adaptation scenario. Furthermore, our method significantly outperforms previous image-based UDA techniques across both image-level (mIoU) and video-level (VPQ) evaluation metrics.

The detection of low-frequency gravitational waves generated by merging supermassive black hole binaries is a primary goal of pulsar timing experiments. While existing theories largely rely on the plane-wave formalism, this study introduces the more comprehensive Fresnel formalism. We demonstrate that incorporating Fresnel corrections into gravitational wave timing residual models enables new measurements, including the direct determination of source distance from the timing residual's phase and frequency, as well as the direct measurement of chirp mass from monochromatic sources. Investigating these Fresnel corrections will necessitate future pulsar timing arrays utilizing distant Galactic pulsars (preferably at Magellanic Cloud distances) with timing precisions under 100 ns and distance uncertainties reduced to the scale of the gravitational wavelength. Our findings indicate that sources with chirp masses around $10^9 \ \mathrm{M}_\odot$ and orbital frequencies exceeding 10 nHz are optimal for probing these effects. When these criteria are satisfied, source distance uncertainties can be minimized to less than 10% of the total distance for objects up to ~100 Mpc away, sky localization can achieve sub-arcminute accuracy, and volume localization can reach better than $1 \ \text{Mpc}^3$ for sources extending to 1-Gpc distances.

Behavioral indicators are fundamental to human interaction and cognitive understanding. Across many professional fields, recruitment strategies are designed to evaluate both technical competencies and personality characteristics. Hiring interviews are specifically structured to comprehensively assess a candidate's fit for a role, examining their qualifications, interpersonal abilities, and capacity to handle critical, stressful, and resource-constrained situations. Consequently, applicants must understand their own strengths and weaknesses while remaining vigilant about behavioral signals that could hinder their success. This paper introduces a multimodal analytical framework designed to evaluate candidates during interviews and offer feedback on specific metrics such as engagement, speaking pace, and eye contact. The proposed method conducts a thorough examination of the interviewee's facial expressions, speech, and prosodic features by utilizing video, audio, and text transcripts from recorded sessions. These diverse data sources are integrated into a composite representation to train machine learning classifiers for predicting target labels. This analytical process ultimately generates constructive guidance for candidates regarding their body language and behavioral cues. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed methodology yields promising outcomes.

Realist accounts of quantum mechanics rely on the assumption that elements of reality exist independently of the measurements used to uncover them. This perspective is contested by various no-go theorems demonstrating that quantum correlations cannot be accounted for by non-contextual ontological models, which posit that physical properties exist prior to and apart from the act of measurement. Nevertheless, these contextuality arguments typically depend on a conventional understanding of causal structure, where influence moves from the past to the future in line with standard dynamical laws. Consequently, it remains an open question whether the observed contextuality in quantum mechanics merely reflects an unusual causal structure, such as retrocausality (future affecting past) or correlations arising from non-local constraints. In this work, we demonstrate that quantum predictions necessitate a more profound form of contextuality: even when allowing for any possible causal structure, no model can explain quantum correlations based on non-contextual ontological properties of the world, whether these be initial states, dynamical laws, or global constraints.

Current deep neural networks in artificial intelligence (AI) have yet to replicate key attributes of biological intelligence, such as abstraction, causal learning, and energy efficiency. Although expanding model size has enhanced performance for existing tasks, achieving brain-like capabilities likely requires novel theoretical frameworks and design methodologies for AI. We propose that re-evaluating insights derived from the brain should foster collaboration between AI research and theory-driven computational neuroscience (CN). To establish a biological foundation for neural computation, we introduce a dynamical perspective on intelligence, expanding on concepts like structural sparsity, temporal dynamics, and interactive learning. Specifically, we argue that temporal dynamics—manifested through neural synchrony, nested oscillations, and adaptable sequences—offer a potent computational mechanism for accessing and updating hierarchical models stored within long-term memory networks. Furthermore, adopting agent-centered approaches in both AI and CN will expedite our comprehension of the intricate dynamics and behaviors essential for constructing functional world models. The convergence of AI and CN theories and goals will uncover the dynamical principles underlying intelligence in both biological brains and engineered systems. This work stems from a symposium on dynamical neuroscience and machine learning held at the 6th Annual US/NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting.

Despite the administration of billions of COVID-19 vaccines, significant vaccine hesitancy persists, largely attributed to misinformation spreading on social media. However, merely encountering such misinformation does not confirm that individuals have adopted it. This paper introduces a novel framework for detecting stance toward misinformation based on attitude consistency and its characteristics. We utilize a new neural architecture that leverages the interplay between attitude consistency, the adoption or rejection of misinformation, and the content of microblogs, organizing the resulting stances within a knowledge graph. This approach achieves state-of-the-art results in identifying attitudes toward COVID-19 vaccine misinformation. Our experiments employ the CoVaxLies dataset, a new collection of misinformation regarding COVID-19 vaccines gathered from recent Twitter discourse. Given that CoVaxLies includes a taxonomy of this misinformation, we can determine which specific types are most frequently adopted versus rejected.

This paper introduces a novel, distinct from standard deterministic partial differential equation (PDE) approaches, low regularity theory for the three-dimensional Burgers equation under the influence of a linear multiplicative stochastic force. The proposed methodology and findings are broadly applicable to other deterministic PDEs and stochastic hydrodynamic models. Furthermore, we derive a random maximum principle for stochastic 3D Burgers equations, a crucial instrument for analyzing these systems. While obtaining moment estimates for highly nonlinear stochastic hydrodynamic equations is notoriously challenging, such estimates are vital for understanding the probabilistic characteristics and long-term dynamics of stochastic systems. By leveraging the random maximum principle, we successfully secure key moment estimates for the 3D stochastic Burgers equation, thereby establishing a robust foundation for future research in this area.

Liquids represent a highly complex state of matter characterized by the interplay of strong kinetic and interaction effects, making them more difficult to comprehend than either gases or solids. In weakly interacting gases, kinetic factors prevail, whereas low-temperature solids typically exhibit minimal fluctuations around their ground state. Despite their intricacy, aside from quantum fluids and supercooled liquids, many aspects of standard liquid dynamics, such as dynamic viscosity, are frequently modeled using simple, Arrhenius-type activated equations with nearly constant, temperature-independent energy barriers. This study experimentally analyzes the viscosities of numerous liquids measured well above their equilibrium melting points to evaluate the validity of this assumption. Our findings reveal significant deviations from simple activated dynamics for the examined liquids. Even at temperatures far exceeding the equilibrium melting point, viscosity increases more rapidly as temperature drops than predicted by activated dynamics based on a single, uniform energy barrier. For metallic fluids, the magnitude of the prefactors in the best-fitting Arrhenius models for viscosity is generally consistent with the product $nh$, where $n$ denotes number density and $h$ represents Planck's constant. In various fluids investigated, $nh$ serves as a lower bound scale for viscosity. Furthermore, scaling the temperature axis alongside viscosity results in a partial collapse of temperature-dependent viscosity data across different fluids; this scaling supports a functional dependence of viscosity on temperature that, while incorporating the Arrhenius form, is far more general. Finally, we speculate on connections between non-Arrhenius dynamics and thermodynamic observables.
We settle a conjecture by Cox and Martin by establishing the asymptotic maximum count of $C_{2k}$ copies in an $n$-vertex planar graph for every $k\ge 2$.

We apply deep learning techniques to two critical phases of product search at JD.com, a global e-commerce giant. Specifically, we detail a deep learning architecture capable of retrieving semantically relevant items in milliseconds, alongside a pairwise deep re-ranking mechanism designed to capture nuanced user preferences. Compared to conventional search systems, these methods excel in both semantic retrieval and personalized ranking, delivering substantial performance gains.

The Sombor index, a vertex-degree-based topological index for simple graphs with n vertices, was recently proposed by I. Gutman. This paper calculates the Sombor index for m-splitting and m-shadow graphs, and it establishes the relationship between energy and Sombor energy for these graph types when derived from k-regular graphs.

Attosecond science aims to uncover the most basic electronic dynamics within matter and can advance by achieving two interconnected technological objectives concerning high-order harmonic sources: increased photon flux (to enable the measurement of low cross-section processes) and enhanced spectral tunability (for selective addressing of specific electronic transitions). Progress is driven by parametric waveform synthesis, which offers control over the shape of high-energy electric field transients, facilitating the generation of highly tunable isolated attosecond pulses through high-harmonic generation. This study demonstrates that the central energy, spectral bandwidth and shape, and temporal duration of these attosecond pulses can be manipulated by shaping the laser pulse waveform using two critical parameters: the relative phase between the two halves of the multi-octave optical spectrum and the overall carrier-envelope phase. These findings not only suggest expanded experimental capabilities in attosecond science but also illustrate the coherent strong-field control of free-electron trajectories via tailored optical waveforms.

To ensure reproducibility, image features must remain stable despite variations in positioning, acquisition, and segmentation. While radiomic models relying solely on robust features can effectively analyze new images, those incorporating non-robust features may yield inaccurate predictions. Although test-retest imaging is the standard for evaluating robustness, it is often unavailable for specific phenotypes. Consequently, this study evaluated 18 alternative methods for assessing feature robustness through image perturbations. The performance of test-retest and perturbation-based robustness was compared across 4,034 features derived from gross tumour volumes in two computed tomography cohorts: one comprising 31 patients with non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and another with 19 patients suffering from head-and-neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Robustness was quantified using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), with a threshold of $\geq0.90$ defining robust features. The NSCLC cohort exhibited a significantly higher proportion of robust features in test-retest scenarios compared to the HNSCC cohort ($73.5\%$ versus $34.0\%$). Furthermore, a specific perturbation sequence involving noise addition, affine translation, volume scaling, and supervoxel-based contour randomization identified the lowest rate of false positive robust features ($3.3\%$ for NSCLC and $10.0\%$ for HNSCC). Therefore, this perturbation chain serves as a viable method for assessing feature robustness.

Computed eclipse epochs (C) are derived from the orbital period ephemerides of eclipsing binaries. However, ephemerides constructed from historical data fail to accurately forecast future observed eclipse epochs (O). Removing linear or quadratic trends from the O-C dataset enhances this predictability. Strictly periodic variations in O-C data arise from light-time travel effects induced by additional companions within the binary system. Hajdu et al. (2019) recently calculated that the likelihood of identifying periods for two new companions using O-C data is merely 0.00005. This study applies the novel Discrete Chi-square Method (DCM) to 236 years of O-C data for the eclipsing binary Algol ($\beta$ Persei), revealing tentative signals for at least five companion candidates with periods ranging from 1.863 to 219.0 years. The weakest of these five signals does not indicate a "new" companion, as its $680.4 \pm 0.4$ day period differs from the established $679.85 \pm 0.04$ day orbital period of Algol~C by only $1.4 \sigma$. These signals are also present in the initial 226.2 years of the dataset and provide an excellent prediction for the subsequent 9.2 years. Since no variations have been detected in Algol's eclipses, the orbital planes of Algol~C and the identified companion candidates are likely co-planar. Furthermore, the 2.867-day orbital period has remained constant since Goodricke's determination in 1783.

This study investigates probing techniques for the broader challenge of calculating the trace of a permuted inverse matrix, denoted as $PA^{-1}$. The primary motivation stems from Lattice QCD, where constructing "disconnected diagrams" is essential for extracting flavor-separated Generalized Parton distributions. In the context of Lattice QCD's 4D toroidal lattice, these non-local operators manifest as $PA^{-1}$, with $P$ representing a permutation associated with a displacement vector $\vec{p}$ across one or more dimensions. While our analysis concentrates on displacements within a single dimension ($p$), the proposed methods remain broadly applicable. We demonstrate that standard probing on $A^k$ or $(PA)^k$ fails to eliminate the largest magnitude elements. To address this, we introduce a displacement-based probing strategy applied to $PA^k$, utilizing a novel coloring scheme that operates directly on suitably displaced lattice neighborhoods. We establish theoretical lower bounds for the required number of colors and evaluate the scheme's impact on variance reduction through both theoretical analysis and experimental validation on actual Lattice QCD computations. Our approach yields speedups by orders of magnitude compared to both unprobed and naively probed alternatives.

PyECLOUD is a recently developed tool designed to simulate electron cloud (EC) formation in particle accelerators. Written almost entirely in Python, it largely relies on the same physical models as the original ECLOUD code but achieves markedly better performance in accuracy, speed, reliability, and flexibility through the integration of new, optimized algorithms. These enhanced capabilities have already been extensively utilized to investigate EC phenomena observed in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and its injector chain, as well as to project results for high-luminosity upgrade scenarios.

We present high-precision measurements of the Deeply Virtual Compton Scattering (DVCS) cross section at elevated Bjorken $x_B$ values. Since DVCS offers insight into the nucleon's Generalized Parton Distributions (GPDs), which describe its internal structure in three dimensions, we utilized an exact analytic formula for the cross section covering all polarization configurations of the initial and final electrons, nucleons, and photons. This work marks the first experimental determination of all four helicity-conserving Compton Form Factors (CFFs) as a function of $x_B$, with the systematic inclusion of helicity flip amplitudes. Notably, the high precision of our data reveals sensitivity to several previously poorly understood CFFs.

A primary objective in speech recognition is to minimize the discrepancy between training and evaluation data, a challenge frequently caused by variations among speakers. Speaker adaptation methods are essential for mitigating this mismatch. However, model-based approaches typically demand substantial amounts of target speaker data to maintain robustness; when such data is scarce, these methods are susceptible to overfitting and fail to generalize effectively. To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces a full Bayesian learning framework for Deep Neural Network (DNN) speaker adaptation, designed to capture uncertainty in speaker-dependent (SD) parameters even with limited adaptation data. The study evaluates three Bayesian DNN adaptation variants: Bayesian learning of hidden unit contributions (BLHUC), Bayesian parameterized activation functions (BPAct), and Bayesian hidden unit bias vectors (BHUB). In all three methods, fixed SD parameters are substituted with latent variable posterior distributions, with their parameters estimated efficiently via variational inference. Experimental results on 300-hour speed-perturbed Switchboard corpus trained LF-MMI TDNN/CNN-TDNN systems indicate that these Bayesian approaches consistently surpass deterministic adaptation on the NIST Hub5'00 and RT03 test sets. Specifically, using only the first five utterances per speaker for adaptation yielded significant word error rate reductions of up to 1.4% absolute (7.2% relative) on the CallHome subset. Furthermore, the effectiveness of these proposed Bayesian techniques is validated by comparing them against state-of-the-art performance on the same task achieved with the latest systems reported in the literature.

This paper presents multiple findings regarding the expected complexity of the convex hull formed by $n$ points selected uniformly and independently from a convex shape.
(i) We demonstrate that the expected number of vertices for the convex hull of $n$ points chosen from a disk is $O(n^{1/3})$, while for a convex polygon with $k$ sides, it is $O(k \log{n})$. Although these findings are established (see \cite{rs-udkhv-63,r-slcdn-70,ps-cgi-85}), we contend that the elementary proof provided here is more straightforward and intuitive.
(ii) Given a set of directions $\D$ in the plane, we introduce a generalized concept of convexity based on $\D$, which encompasses both standard and rectilinear convexity. We establish that the expected complexity of the $\D$-convex hull of $n$ points, selected uniformly and independently from a disk, is $O(n^{1/3} + \sqrt{n\alpha(\D)})$, where $\alpha(\D)$ denotes the maximum angle between consecutive vectors in $\D$. This result generalizes existing bounds for standard and rectilinear convexity.
(iii) Let $\B$ be an axis-parallel hypercube in $\Re^d$. We prove that the expected number of points lying on the boundary of the quadrant hull of a set $S$ of $n$ points, chosen uniformly and independently from $\B$, is $O(\log^{d-1}n)$. The quadrant hull extends rectilinear convexity to higher dimensions; notably, this count exceeds both the number of maxima in $S$ and the number of vertices in the standard convex hull of $S$. These bounds were previously known \cite{bkst-anmsv-78}, but we believe our new proof offers greater simplicity.

Ensuring algorithmic fairness is crucial in machine learning, often achieved by applying fairness constraints during the learning process. However, datasets frequently suffer from imbalances in specific label categories (such as "healthy") and sensitive subgroups (like "older patients"). Empirical evidence shows that such imbalances hinder the generalizability of both classification performance and fairness metrics, particularly within over-parameterized models. For instance, while fairness-aware training might satisfy Equalized Odds (EO) on training data, this fairness is often not maintained for new users. This paper introduces Imbalance-Fairness-Aware (FIFA), a theoretically grounded yet flexible method designed to promote generalization in both classification and fairness. FIFA can be adaptably integrated with numerous existing fair learning techniques that utilize logits-based losses. Although the primary focus is on EO, the approach can also be directly applied to Equalized Opportunity (EqOpt) and, under specific conditions, other fairness definitions. We demonstrate FIFA's effectiveness by combining it with a widely used fair classification algorithm, resulting in significantly improved fairness generalization across several real-world datasets.

The non-local correlations linking a completely characterized quantum system to an untrusted black box device are characterized by an assemblage of conditional quantum states. These assemblages constitute a convex set, where the extremal points hold significance in numerous operational scenarios. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for an assemblage to be extremal based on linear independence criteria and present an algorithm to decompose any generic assemblage into its extremal components. A Matlab implementation of this algorithm is included in the supplementary material.

Using first-principles quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods, we investigate the ground-state characteristics of the narrowest zigzag graphene nanoribbon featuring an infinite linear acene structure. Our findings indicate that this quasi-one-dimensional system exhibits correlation, with its ground state composed of localized $\pi$ electrons arranged in an antiferromagnetic (AFM) order. The QMC calculations predict significant AFM stabilization energy (36(3) meV per carbon atom) and absolute magnetization (1.13(1) $\mu_\textrm{B}$ per unit cell), implying that antiferromagnetic correlations persist above room temperature. These results can only be partially replicated by density functional theory (DFT) when strong interactions are incorporated via the DFT+U approach or hybrid functionals. Consequently, based on our QMC data, we determine the appropriate Hubbard repulsion strength for DFT+U within this class of systems.

This study investigates a system comprising $n$ ordinary differential equations coupled with a single reaction-diffusion equation within a bounded $N$-dimensional domain subject to no-flux boundary conditions, specifically in the context of pattern formation. While such initial boundary value problems can yield various stationary solutions, our previous work demonstrated that although sufficiently smooth stationary solutions exist, they are entirely unstable. The objective of this research is to construct discontinuous stationary solutions for general reaction-diffusion-ODE systems and to establish sufficient conditions under which these solutions remain stable.

Neural abstractive summarization models often produce outputs that contradict the factual content of their source documents. While prior research has framed identifying these inconsistencies as a downstream natural language inference (NLI) task, current state-of-the-art NLI models struggle in this domain due to a lack of generalization. This study demonstrates that NLI models can successfully address this issue when trained on high-quality, task-specific augmented data. We present Falsesum, a data generation pipeline that utilizes a controllable text generation model to perturb human-annotated summaries, thereby introducing diverse and plausible factual inconsistencies. Unlike existing document-level NLI datasets, Falsesum offers examples that are both varied and realistic. Our experiments reveal that training NLI models on this augmented dataset significantly boosts state-of-the-art performance across four benchmarks for detecting factual inconsistencies in summarization. The code for generating the dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/joshbambrick/Falsesum.

The Planck scale, corresponding to a timescale of approximately $10^{-44}\,\mathrm{s}$, represents an uncharted physical domain. While it is commonly assumed that investigating Planck time will remain beyond reach for the foreseeable future, we propose an experiment to test the discreteness of time at this scale and suggest that the necessary technology is not far from current capabilities.

This research examines the impact of a first-order phase transition within a confining $SU(N)$ dark sector containing heavy dark quarks, where the sector's baryons serve as the dark matter candidate. During the confinement transition, these heavy quarks become confined within isolated, contracting pockets of the deconfined phase, triggering a secondary annihilation stage that significantly reduces the dark quark population. The final abundance depends on the local accidental asymmetry present in each pocket. The resulting dark matter density matches observational requirements for dark quark masses in the $\mathcal{O}(1-100)$ PeV range, surpassing the standard unitarity limit.

Extensive research has explored domain wall dynamics in magnetic nanostrips due to their versatile non-linear physics and promising applications in data storage; however, most prior work has concentrated on out-of-plane or in-plane head-to-head (and tail-to-tail) configurations. In this study, we numerically investigate the field-driven motion of in-plane side-by-side domain walls within ferromagnetic strips that exhibit stable behavior under an in-plane easy-axis anisotropy transverse to the strip direction. At low fields, these domain walls exhibit rigid-body motion, whereas at high fields, they display complex Walker breakdown phenomena. Specifically, we observe a multi-step Walker breakdown involving vortex nucleation in wide strips. Furthermore, in the presence of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI), the field required for the first Walker breakdown initially decreases and then increases with interfacial DMI, while it continues to increase with bulk DMI. These results enhance the current understanding of domain wall dynamics.

This study investigates the behavior of a freely falling chain. Specifically, we analyze an inextensible chain with free ends suspended by a fixed pulley under gravity. When the system becomes unbalanced, the chain accelerates and may eventually detach from the pulley. Our findings indicate that once liftoff occurs, the chain's motion mimics that of a whip, causing the tip speed to diverge. The curved section of the chain is critical to this process, facilitating the lift-off. Although the chain is in free fall, it displays whip-like dynamics, with one end snapping upward periodically as it descends. We have performed experiments to validate this phenomenon.

We investigate ultra-diffuse galaxy (UDG) populations across isolated, satellite, and cluster environments using the Romulus25 and RomulusC simulations, examining variations based on UDG definitions and viewing angles. Based on a standard UDG definition, isolated UDGs exhibit significantly larger semi-major (b/a) and smaller semi-minor (c/a) axis ratios compared to non-UDGs, indicating they are more oblate or disk-like. This aligns with prior studies using the same definition, which suggested that isolated UDGs form through early, high-spin mergers. However, the specific UDG definition chosen can drastically alter the subset of dwarfs classified as UDGs, shifting the count by up to ~45% of the dwarf population. Additionally, we find that UDG classification depends on viewing orientation, though this dependence diminishes as environmental density increases. Overall, we conclude that while certain UDG definitions in the literature isolate specific formation mechanisms for isolated dwarfs, less restrictive definitions obscure this link. Therefore, the definition of UDG populations must be carefully considered to understand their formation and evolution.

We propose a paradigm shift in supporting the Free/Libre and Open Source Software (FLOSS) ecosystem, moving from an emphasis on individual projects to monitoring the entire organic FLOSS system, which we term software meta-maintenance. We explore the challenges involved in constructing a global source code management system, a global issue management system, and a FLOSS human capital index, all grounded in blockchain technologies.

The double copy connects scattering amplitudes in momentum space between gauge and gravity theories. While this concept has been extended to classical solutions—sometimes allowing for an exact double copy defined directly through products of fields in position space—this appears contradictory to its momentum-space foundations. Consequently, the reasons behind the feasibility of exact position-space double copies and the conditions under which they fail have remained unclear. This paper addresses that gap by employing a recently developed twistorial framework for the double copy. We demonstrate that for specific vacuum type-D solutions, the double copies in momentum space, twistor space, and position space are equivalent and linked via integral transforms. Furthermore, we establish that locality in position space arises from the unique structure of momentum-space three-point amplitudes, thereby validating the hypothesis that local position-space double copies occur only in spacetimes with highly special algebraic properties.

In the design of safety-critical systems, engineers rely on architecture patterns like Firewalls and Watchdogs to mitigate identified threats and failures. However, implementing safety patterns can inadvertently introduce security vulnerabilities, and vice versa, where security measures might create new failure points. Consequently, a co-design approach is essential to analyze these interdependencies and trade-offs for optimal system architecture. Currently, pattern descriptions and their implications are expressed in natural language, necessitating a manual deployment process that is both time-intensive and susceptible to human error, particularly within highly complex systems. We propose utilizing semantically enriched architecture patterns to facilitate automated safety and security co-design through Knowledge Representation and Reasoning (KRR). Leveraging a domain-specific language, we define reasoning principles as logic specifications formatted as answer-set programs. KRR engines then automate co-engineering tasks, such as recommending suitable architecture patterns for specific failures or threats and predicting the resulting consequences. We validate this methodology using a case study derived from the ISO 21434 standard.

Gravitational waves from massive black hole binaries within the LISA frequency range are susceptible to gravitational lensing. When the lens's Schwarzschild radius is smaller than the radiation's wavelength, wave-optics phenomena become critical; these frequency-dependent features could allow for the determination of lens parameters even from a solitary detection. This study evaluates the detectability of such wave-optics effects using LISA via an information-matrix analysis based on analytical solutions for both point-mass and singular isothermal sphere lenses. By employing gravitational-waveform models that incorporate mergers, ringdown phases, higher harmonics, and aligned spins, we investigate how model choices and source parameters influence measurement uncertainties regarding lens properties. Our findings indicate that prior research underestimated the observability of these wave-optics effects, suggesting that LISA can identify lensed signals even at higher impact parameters and with lower lens masses.

This research addresses the challenge of forecasting the probability distribution across various potential future paths individuals take through diverse visual environments. We present two primary contributions. First, we introduce a novel dataset generated within a realistic 3D simulator; this dataset is derived from real-world trajectory data and expanded by human annotators to simulate different latent objectives, establishing the inaugural benchmark for quantitatively evaluating multi-future trajectory prediction models. Second, we propose a new architecture for generating multiple plausible future paths, featuring innovative designs such as multi-scale location encodings and convolutional RNNs operating on graphs. We designate this model as Multiverse. Our experiments demonstrate that Multiverse achieves superior performance on our proposed dataset as well as on the real-world VIRAT/ActEV dataset, which currently supports only single-future predictions.

This paper presents findings from a survey distributed within the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, focusing on researcher opinions regarding shared tasks, specifically concerning their organization and participation. Based on 175 responses containing both favorable and critical feedback, we conducted a comprehensive analysis that results in the proposal of a Shared Task Organisation Checklist. Designed to be flexible and adaptable to the diverse nature of shared tasks in our field, this checklist aims not to be prescriptive but to act as a tool that encourages organizers to prioritize ethical conduct, starting with the key issues identified by respondents. Utilizing this checklist would facilitate reflection on critical aspects of shared tasks and foster greater transparency within the community.

Generating code automatically from natural language descriptions remains a difficult challenge. Recently, there has been substantial advancement in creating code generation systems for domain-specific languages (DSLs) using sequence-to-sequence deep learning methods. This paper focuses on generative models for the \textsc{AlgoLisp} DSL, demonstrating significant dataset bias through various adversarial examples. We also evaluate two Transformer-based model variants that surpass all current \textsc{AlgoLisp} baselines. Like existing state-of-the-art systems, our proposed models struggle in adversarial scenarios. Consequently, we introduce several dataset augmentation techniques to mitigate this bias and validate their effectiveness through rigorous experimentation.

Automatic cover detection, which involves identifying all covers of one or more query tracks within an audio database, has long been regarded as a significant theoretical challenge for the MIR community and a pressing practical issue for authors and composer societies. While original algorithms demonstrated high accuracy on small datasets, they failed to scale to modern, real-world audio corpora. Conversely, faster methods designed to handle thousands of pairwise comparisons sacrificed accuracy, rendering them impractical. This work introduces a neural network architecture trained to represent each track as a single embedding vector. This design shifts the computational load to the embedding extraction phase, which can be performed offline and stored, reducing the pairwise comparison step to a straightforward Euclidean distance calculation. Furthermore, we propose generating each track's embedding from its dominant melody representation, derived via a separate neural network trained specifically for this purpose. We demonstrate that this architecture achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on both small and large datasets while scaling efficiently to query databases containing thousands of tracks within seconds.

This study presents magnetic optical second-harmonic generation (SHG) polarimetry and imaging applied to Sr$_2$Cu$_3$O$_4$Cl$_2$, enabling the direct visualization of the mesoscopic antiferromagnetic (AFM) architecture in a parent cuprate. Investigations into the temperature- and magnetic-field-dependent SHG reveal extensive domains oriented at 90$^{\circ}$ relative to one another, stabilized by a synergy of uniaxial magnetic anisotropy and the Earth's magnetic field. Below a critical temperature $T_R$ of approximately 97 K, an anomalous 90$^{\circ}$ spin reorientation transition occurs, potentially driven by competing magnetic anisotropies within the two copper sublattices; this transition exchanges AFM domain states while maintaining the overall domain structure. Consequently, deterministic switching of AFM states becomes achievable through thermal or laser heating. Close to $T_R$, domain walls exhibit heightened sensitivity to applied magnetic fields, with the Earth's field alone being sufficient to fully expel them from the crystal. These results open new avenues for investigating the mesoscopic AFM dynamics of parent cuprates and assessing their viability for AFM-based technologies.

The Schrijver graph $S(n,k)$ is defined for integers $n$ and $k$ where $n \geq 2k$. Its vertices consist of all $k$-subsets of $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ that contain no two consecutive elements under modular arithmetic, with adjacency defined by disjointness. Schrijver established that the chromatic number of $S(n,k)$ is $n-2k+2$ (Nieuw Arch. Wiskd., 1978). The computational Schrijver problem involves receiving a coloring of $S(n,k)$ using only $n-2k+1$ colors and identifying a monochromatic edge. This problem is recognized as $\mathsf{PPA}$-complete. We demonstrate that it admits a randomized algorithm with a running time of $n^{O(1)} \cdot k^{O(k)}$, proving that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by $k$.

Spin-orbit coupling (SOC) plays a fundamental role in topological materials, spanning both conventional systems and those based on quantum gases. Engineered SOC in ultracold atom systems offers a unique advantage due to their exceptional experimental controllability and measurement capabilities, presenting a significant opportunity to explore and comprehend topological phenomena. In this work, we both experimentally demonstrate and theoretically analyze a method for manipulating SOC within a two-component Bose-Einstein condensate via amplitude-modulated Raman coupling.

A significant hurdle for autonomous vehicles is ensuring safe and fluid interactions with other road users. A promising solution involves equipping these vehicles with Interaction-Aware Controllers (IACs), which utilize driver models to forecast how human drivers will react to the autonomous vehicle's maneuvers. However, the predictive accuracy of the driver models underpinning IACs is seldom validated, potentially restricting their effectiveness beyond simple simulation environments. This paper argues that, alongside assessing interactive capabilities, the underlying driver models must be validated against natural human driving behavior. We introduce a validation workflow featuring scenario-based data extraction and a two-stage evaluation process (tactical and operational) grounded in human factors research. Applying this workflow to a case study involving an inverse-reinforcement-learning-based driver model from an existing IAC revealed that the model exhibited correct tactical behavior in only 40% of predictions, with operational behavior that did not align with observed human actions. This case study underscores the necessity of a rigorous evaluation framework. We contend that our proposed workflow will aid in developing suitable driver models for future automated vehicles.

CodexDB is an SQL processing engine that allows customization through natural language instructions. Built upon OpenAI's GPT-3 Codex, which converts text into code, CodexDB serves as a framework that breaks down intricate SQL queries into a sequence of straightforward processing steps described in natural language. These steps are enhanced with user-supplied instructions and details regarding database characteristics, which Codex then translates into executable query processing code. An early prototype of CodexDB successfully generates correct code for most queries in the WikiSQL benchmark and supports various customization options.

Large-scale AI training clusters, which employ thousands of domain-specific accelerators (DSAs), are essential for training ever-more-complex deep learning models. These clusters depend on a data storage and ingestion (DSI) pipeline tasked with storing exabytes of data and delivering it at speeds reaching tens of terabytes per second. As DSAs drive up training efficiency and throughput, the DSI pipeline has emerged as the primary bottleneck limiting overall training performance and capacity. Consequently, there is an urgent need for innovations that enhance DSI system and hardware efficiency, which requires a profound understanding of DSI characteristics within large-scale infrastructure.

This paper details Meta's end-to-end DSI pipeline, featuring a central data warehouse on distributed storage and a scalable Data PreProcessing Service designed to prevent data stalls. We analyze how hundreds of models are jointly trained across geographically distributed datacenters through varied and continuous training jobs. These jobs read and heavily filter vast, evolving datasets, generating popular features and samples utilized across multiple training tasks. We also quantify the substantial network, memory, and compute resources each training job consumes during sample preprocessing. Finally, we derive key insights from our production infrastructure analysis, including the identification of hardware bottlenecks, exploration of heterogeneous DSI hardware opportunities, advocacy for research in datacenter scheduling and benchmark datasets, and the integration of lessons learned for optimizing DSI infrastructure.

The 2021 Fermilab findings regarding the muon anomalous magnetic moment (AMM) failed to significantly diminish the persistent $4\sigma$ discrepancy from the Standard Model (SM) prediction. Explaining this gap through new particles places numerous physics models under pressure due to conflicting null results from direct LHC searches. This study examines the CP-violating Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM), both with and without an inverse seesaw mechanism. We calculate one-loop supersymmetric contributions to the AMM and two-loop Barr-Zee diagrams involving effective Higgs-photon couplings to determine leptonic electric dipole moments (EDMs). The extended (s)neutrino sector may substantially influence the muon AMM and the mass of the SM-like Higgs boson, while complex phases play a critical role in the AMM but are constrained by strict EDM limits. Our computations are available via the public Fortran codes NMSSMCALC and NMSSMCALC-nuSS. Beyond calculating leptonic AMMs and EDMs, these tools also determine Higgs masses, mixings, decay widths, and branching ratios, incorporating the latest higher-order corrections for the NMSSM with and without the inverse seesaw mechanism.

We calculate one-loop corrections to the $\sigma(e^+ e^- \to Z h)$ cross-section within representative extended Standard Model scalar sectors. Based on the new scalar $\mathrm{SU(2)_L}$ representations, we examine models featuring inert doublets, real and complex triplets, quintuplets, and septuplets. Given the anticipated sub-percent precision of future $e^+e^-$ collider measurements for the Higgsstrahlung process, these studies will probe the extended scalar particle spectrum and interactions in a way that complements direct searches at the Large Hadron Collider and potential future proton-proton colliders. We further compare these findings with the sensitivity of future measurements regarding the Higgs diphoton decay rate. Our results indicate that the complementarity between $\sigma(e^+ e^- \to Z h)$ and $\Gamma(h\to\gamma\gamma)$ is especially significant for the complex triplet model.

This paper derives the Noether current from the surface term of the Einstein-Hilbert action. We demonstrate that the associated charge, evaluated on the horizon, corresponds to the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy. Furthermore, utilizing this charge, the same entropy is recovered through the Virasoro algebra and Cardy formula method. In this framework, the pertinent diffeomorphisms are identified by enforcing a straightforward physical criterion: that diffeomorphisms must leave the horizon structure invariant. These findings complement previous results (arXiv:1204.1422) derived from the York-Gibbons-Hawking surface term. Finally, we examine the technical advantages and simplifications offered by this approach compared to earlier attempts, along with discussing several significant physical implications.

Recent advancements demonstrate that pre-trained language models significantly enhance task-oriented dialogue (TOD) systems. However, current approaches typically treat this as a cascaded generation problem, resulting in error propagation across sub-tasks and increased annotation costs. This study introduces PPTOD, a unified plug-and-play architecture designed for TOD. We also propose a novel multi-task pre-training strategy that enables the model to acquire core TOD completion skills from diverse dialogue corpora. Our model was rigorously evaluated on three standard benchmarks: end-to-end dialogue modeling, dialogue state tracking, and intent classification. Results indicate that PPTOD achieves state-of-the-art performance across all tasks in both high-resource and low-resource settings. Additionally, human evaluations reveal that PPTOD generates responses that are more factually accurate and semantically coherent compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.

Emerging data indicates that SARS-CoV-2 infection can trigger a range of neurological symptoms. This study introduces a theoretical framework explaining these neurological consequences of COVID-19 using a non-equilibrium thermodynamic method, which connects neuronal electric potential to pH changes induced by the virus. Our theoretical results advocate for additional experimental research into therapeutically correcting electrolyte imbalances, specifically involving Na$^+$ and K$^+$, to mitigate the neurological impacts of SARS-CoV-2.

Let $N(a, b; n)$ denote the count of ways to express a non-negative integer $n$ as a sum of squares using coefficients of 1 or 3, specifically with $a$ ones and $b$ threes. Similarly, $N^*(a,b; n)$ represents the number of representations of $n$ as a sum of odd squares under the same coefficient constraints. It is established that $N^*(a,b;8n+a+3b)$ equals the number of representations of $n$ as a sum of triangular numbers with $a$ ones and $b$ threes. For cases where $1\leq a+3b \leq 7$, the relationship is given by:
$$ N^*(a,b;8n+a+3b)= \frac{2}{2+{a\choose4}+ab} N(a,b;8n+a+3b) $$
When $a+3b=8$, the formula becomes:
$$ N^*(a,b;8n+a+3b) = \frac{2}{2+{a\choose4}+ab} \left( N(a,b;8n+a+3b) - N(a,b; (8n+a+3b)/4) \right) $$
(Note: This corresponds to the specific case $t(8,0;{n}) = \frac{1}{36} \left( N(8,0;8n+8) - N(8,0;2n+2) \right)$.) These exact identities remain unproven for $a+3b>8$. In this work, we demonstrate asymptotic equivalences of similar formulas for general $a$ and $b$ where $a+b$ is even, as $n$ approaches infinity. A primary contribution of this paper is extending a theorem by Bateman, Datskovsky, and Knopp, which previously addressed only the case $b=0$ with general $a$. Unlike their approach, which relied on the circle method and singular series, our methodology explicitly computes the Eisenstein components of the generating functions for both $N^*(a,b;8n+a+3b)$ and $N(a,b;8n+a+3b)$. This technique is versatile and can be applied to investigate the asymptotic behavior of other representation numbers involving general coefficients.

This study investigates the Bouton-Lie group invariants associated with the Navier-Stokes equations (NSE) governing incompressible fluids. By applying Bouton's theory to the general scaling transformations permitted by the NSE, the article derives all self-similar solutions. Based on these solutions, it analyzes the criticality of the standard NSE system and establishes corresponding criticality criteria. Furthermore, the Beale-Kato-Majda theorem is utilized to exclude blow-up scenarios for a specific subset of Bouton's self-similar solutions. Regarding a subset of Leray's self-similar solutions, the cavitation number is identified as a scale-invariant, conserved quantity. Finally, by extending Bouton's analysis to higher-dimensional manifolds, additional conserved quantities are discovered, which may offer deeper insights into the physics of fluid turbulence.

We report ALMA Band 5 (~170 GHz) observations of the merging ultraluminous infrared galaxy "Superantennae" (IRAS 19254-7245) at redshift z=0.0617, identified as hosting a luminous, obscured active galactic nucleus (AGN). Alongside dense molecular line emissions (HCN, HCO+, and HNC J = 2-1), we identify a highly luminous (~6e4 Lsun) 183 GHz H2O 3(1,3)-2(2,0) line. We attribute this strong H2O emission primarily to maser amplification within dense, warm molecular gas illuminated by the AGN, supported by three key factors: (1) the emission's compact spatial scale (<220 pc), contrasting with the resolved (>500 pc) dense molecular gas; (2) a distinct velocity profile; and (3) a significantly higher flux ratio compared to dense molecular lines. While H2O maser emission beyond the well-known 22 GHz 6(1,6)-5(2,3) line is anticipated to reveal crucial physical properties of gas near a central mass-accreting supermassive black hole (SMBH) due to its unique excitation energy, we demonstrate here that sensitive ALMA observations can detect millimeter 183 GHz H2O masers out to distances exceeding 270 Mpc. This capability opens a new avenue for investigating molecular gas properties around accreting SMBHs far beyond the local universe.

This study addresses continual learning in large-scale pretrained neural machine translation models without requiring access to prior training data or employing model separation. We contend that conventional regularization-based approaches, which utilize auxiliary losses for multi-objective learning, often encounter misestimation issues and fail to adequately balance performance on old and new tasks. To address this, we introduce a two-stage training strategy grounded in the local characteristics of the actual loss function. Initially, we identify low-forgetting-risk regions that allow the model to maintain previous task performance during parameter updates, thereby mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Subsequently, the model is fine-tuned exclusively on new data within this safe region to adapt to new tasks. Specifically, we develop two techniques for locating these regions: one based on loss curvature and the other on the influence of parameters on model outputs. Experiments conducted on domain adaptation and more complex language adaptation tasks demonstrate that our approach yields significant improvements over several robust baselines.

This paper investigates the zero dissipation limit of the one-dimensional full compressible Navier-Stokes equations, assuming temperature-dependent viscosity and heat-conduction coefficients. We demonstrate that for a given rarefaction wave with a one-sided vacuum state in the full compressible Euler equations, a sequence of solutions to the full compressible Navier-Stokes equations can be constructed; these solutions converge to the aforementioned rarefaction wave as viscosity and heat conduction vanish. Furthermore, we establish a uniform convergence rate. The primary challenge in our proof arises from the degeneracies of density, temperature, and temperature-dependent viscosities within the vacuum region during the zero dissipation limit.

This study analyzes the Overton policy document database, detailing the composition of its indexed materials and the manner in which they reference academic literature. The report covers multiple data dimensions, including expansion rates, geographic distribution, language diversity, the variety of policy source types, and the presence of citation links. Through longitudinal analysis using established journal classification systems, we assess the scale and disciplinary focus of citations to evaluate the potential for creating field-normalized citation indicators. We also compare self-reported funding outcomes from UK funders with Overton's indexed data and investigate the correlation between the UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) 2014 peer-review assessments and derived citation metrics. Our results indicate that for specific domains—such as health, economics, social care, and the environment—Overton holds a substantial collection of policy documents with robust citation connections to academic works, supporting citation analyses useful for research evaluation, impact assessment, and policy review. Furthermore, the indexed data aligns with self-reported funding information and demonstrates correlation with peer-reviewed impact assessments in certain disciplines.

Achieving greater efficiency, speed, and compatibility with low-end hardware in deep networks relies heavily on network compression. However, current compression techniques face two significant challenges: the absence of a theoretical framework to determine the maximum achievable compression rate, and the risk of over-pruning certain layers, which leads to a notable decline in performance. To address these issues, this study introduces a method based on gradient-matrix singularity analysis to estimate the upper limit of network redundancy. Utilizing this estimated maximum rate, a new and efficient hierarchical pruning algorithm has been developed to maximize the condensation of the neural network structure while maintaining performance levels. Extensive experiments across various advanced convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. Compared to existing methods, the proposed algorithm achieves state-of-the-art results; at equivalent or similar compression ratios, it delivers superior prediction accuracy.

We introduce a unified framework for evaluating the representation quality of self-supervised learning (SSL) models without requiring supervised labels, remaining independent of specific architectures, learning algorithms, or data preprocessing techniques. We posit that representations should be assessed based on their expressiveness and learnability. To quantify expressiveness, we utilize Intrinsic Dimension (ID), and to measure learnability, we propose Cluster Learnability (CL), defined as the convergence speed of a KNN classifier trained on labels derived from K-means clustering of the representations. By integrating CL and ID, we develop a combined predictor called CLID. Extensive empirical analysis across a diverse range of SSL algorithms demonstrates that CLID correlates more strongly with in-distribution model performance than other recent evaluation methods. Furthermore, we benchmark CLID on out-of-domain generalization, where it effectively predicts the transfer performance of SSL models across multiple classification tasks, outperforming competing baselines.

The majority of existing research on task-oriented dialog modeling relies on written text, yet practical systems often receive speech input. These systems typically employ Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) to convert speech to text, a process that introduces errors and fails to account for the distinct differences between written and spoken language. This field is further hindered by the absence of a public corpus. To address these issues, we organized a speech-aware dialog state tracking challenge aimed at creating a public dataset to examine the performance gap between written and spoken inputs, develop models to bridge this gap, and determine if Text-to-Speech (TTS) serves as a viable alternative to labor-intensive human data collection. We generated three spoken variants of the established written-domain MultiWoz task: (a) TTS-Verbatim, where written inputs were converted to speech waveforms via TTS; (b) Human-Verbatim, where humans read inputs exactly as written; and (c) Human-paraphrased, where humans rephrased the inputs. Additionally, to broaden participation among teams lacking state-of-the-art ASR, we provided various ASR outputs, including transcripts, word timestamps, and latent audio representations. This paper details the corpus, presents results from participating teams, offers preliminary analyses of those outcomes, and summarizes the current state-of-the-art in this domain.

This study examines a dynamic client selection challenge for multiple federated learning (FL) services within a wireless network, characterized by clients providing variable datasets for concurrent training and service requesters operating under limited financial budgets. The issue is modeled as a non-cooperative Markov game across training iterations. To optimize joint client selection and payment strategies while preventing action conflicts, we introduce a multi-agent hybrid deep reinforcement learning algorithm. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this proposed approach substantially enhances training performance.

We demonstrate that transcendental curves within $\mathbb R^n$, whether compact or not, possess a limited number of rational points with bounded height, contingent upon the curves exhibiting specific well-behaved properties relative to algebraic sets and admitting parametrizations via functions from a designated algebra of infinitely differentiable functions. Illustrative instances of these curves encompass logarithmic spirals and the solutions to Euler equations of the form $x^2y''+xy'+cy=0$ where $c>0$.

3D perception utilizing point clouds is revolutionizing the capabilities of next-generation intelligent machines. However, point cloud algorithms often suffer from irregular memory access patterns, causing severe inefficiencies in the memory subsystem and creating a bottleneck for overall performance. This paper introduces Crescent, an algorithm-hardware co-design framework designed to regularize these irregularities in deep point cloud analytics without sacrificing high accuracy. To achieve this, we employ two approximation strategies: approximate neighbor search and selective bank conflict elision, which streamline DRAM and SRAM memory accesses. Although these approximations inherently introduce some accuracy degradation, we counteract this through a novel network training procedure that embeds approximation directly into the training process. Specifically, our method trains models conditioned on specific approximation settings, thereby maintaining high accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that Crescent achieves double the performance and halves energy consumption compared to an optimized baseline accelerator, with less than 1% accuracy loss. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/horizon-research/crescent.

The straightforward analytic framework of meson scattering amplitudes within the large-$N_c$ limit, coupled with the positivity of the spectral density, yields precise predictions for low-energy observables. Extending prior research, we investigate the permissible domains for chiral Lagrangian parameters and meson-pion couplings. Our analysis uncovers a pattern of kinks across all orders of the chiral expansion and establishes analytical methods demonstrating that these kinks invariably signify amplitudes featuring a single light pole. We construct scalar- and vector-less deformations of the Lovelace-Shapiro and Coon UV-complete amplitudes, finding they reside near the theoretical boundaries. Furthermore, crossing-symmetry constraints indicate that meson-pion couplings diminish as spin increases, offering an explanation for the efficacy of Vector Meson Dominance and holographic QCD. We examine the sensitivity of these findings to assumptions regarding high-energy amplitude behavior and conclude by highlighting the synergistic relationship between our results and Lattice computations in probing large-$N_c$ QCD.

The proposed future CLIC high-energy linear $e^+ e^-$ collider places stringent performance requirements on its detector system. Specifically, the vertex and tracking detectors must integrate precise measurements with resilience against the anticipated high rates of beam-induced backgrounds. Achieving a spatial resolution of a few microns, a material budget of no more than 0.2\% of a radiation length per vertex-detector layer, and a time-stamping accuracy of a few nanoseconds is essential. These goals are being pursued through an ambitious detector R\&D program that leverages innovative technologies, encompassing hardware development alongside detailed device and Monte Carlo simulations using TCAD, Geant4, and Allpix-Squared. Several fine-pitch hybrid silicon pixel detector technologies are currently being explored for the CLIC vertex detector. The CLICpix and CLICpix2 readout ASICs, featuring a \SI{25}{\micro\meter} pixel pitch, have been fabricated in a \SI{65}{\nano\meter} commercial CMOS process and are bump-bonded to planar active edge sensors or capacitively coupled to High-Voltage (HV) CMOS sensors. For the large surface ($\approx$ \SI{140}{\meter\squared}) CLIC tracker, fully monolithic silicon tracking detectors are planned. Prototypes in High-Resistivity (HR) CMOS, HV-CMOS, and Silicon on Insulator (SOI) technologies are currently under development. Recent prototypes have benefited from laboratory and beam tests facilitated by the CaRIBou universal readout system. This talk provides an overview of the CLIC pixel-detector R\&D program, highlighting recent test-beam data and simulation outcomes.

Educators across various levels often struggle to teach physics within real-world scenarios. This article introduces three Context-Rich Problems tailored for higher education, utilizing the Beirut explosion as a case study. These tasks necessitate the retrieval and examination of authentic data while leveraging technology as a learning instrument, specifically through the analysis of images, videos, maps, and audio files. Designed to foster active engagement with classical mechanics and cultivate collaborative abilities, these activities enable classroom discussions grounded in scientific evidence based on the outcomes of each problem.

Drawing inspiration from the works of Piterbarg (2004) and H\"{u}sler (2004), this study examines the asymptotic relationship between the maximum of a continuous dependent homogeneous Gaussian random field and the maximum obtained by sampling this field at discrete intervals. The analysis reveals that in the weakly dependent scenario, the two maxima are asymptotically independent on sparse grids, dependent on Pickands grids, and coincident on dense grids. Conversely, under strong dependence, the maxima are asymptotically totally dependent when the discrete grid is sufficiently dense, whereas they remain asymptotically dependent if the grid points are sparse or follow a Pickands configuration.

This study examines interactions between agents performing driving tasks by modeling them as general-sum games, which feature multiple equilibria and thus present challenges regarding equilibrium selection. While identifying the most socially efficient equilibrium is often computationally infeasible, this work investigates the inefficiency of any equilibrium the agents might adopt. Specifically, we constrain this inefficiency by framing driving scenarios as a specific form of congestion game involving spatio-temporal resources. Our analysis yields new guarantees that sharpen existing bounds on the Price of Anarchy (PoA) based on problem-specific parameters, such as the trade-off between proximity costs and individual goals like comfort and progress. Although these theoretical guarantees apply to open-loop trajectories, we demonstrate that efficient equilibria persist even when agents utilize closed-loop policies trained through decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning.

When an electron beam strikes a conversion target, it generates positrons characterized by a broad energy spectrum and a wide range of trajectory angles relative to the system axis. To ensure compatibility with an adjacent accelerator, the angular divergence of the positron bunch must be reduced. The Adiabatic Matching Device (AMD) is identified as an optimal apparatus for modifying the positron bunch's phase portrait. This paper outlines a concise theoretical framework for the AMD, demonstrating that reducing the angular spread through the transformation of the transverse phase volume inevitably leads to bunch elongation. Furthermore, analytical expressions for both longitudinal and transverse probability density functions are derived, with these results confirmed through numerical simulations.

We evaluate the current and prospective experimental capabilities regarding lepton flavor violation (LFV) in muon and tau decays into a light, invisible axion-like particle (ALP), denoted as $a$. We introduce a novel configuration for the MEG II experiment, termed MEGII-fwd, which incorporates a forward calorimeter positioned downstream of the muon stopping target. In the search for $\mu \to e a$ decays, MEGII-fwd achieves maximum sensitivity to LFV ALPs provided they possess non-zero couplings to right-handed leptons. This setup mitigates Standard Model background in the forward direction by regulating the polarization purity of the muon beam. We compare the projected reach of MEGII-fwd against existing constraints, as well as the potential sensitivities of Mu3e and Belle-II in $\tau \to \ell a$ decays. Our analysis demonstrates that a dedicated experimental effort at MEG II and Mu3e targeting LFV muon decays into ALPs could explore an uncharted region of the ALP parameter space, extending far beyond current astrophysical limits. Furthermore, we examine the implications of these searches for representative LFV ALP models, where a light ALP is motivated by neutrino masses, the strong CP problem, and/or the Standard Model flavor puzzle. Specifically, we discuss the majoron within low-scale seesaw frameworks and introduce the LFV QCD axion, LFV axiflavon, and leptonic familon, with special focus on scenarios where LFV ALPs serve as cold dark matter.

Cassini's extended mission to Saturn enabled infrared spectroscopy to track the seasonal development and decay of large, warm vortices located poleward of approximately $75^\circ$ latitude in the stratosphere; these features peak in summer and vanish in winter. This study constrains the formation and dissipation timescales for vortices in both hemispheres, focusing on the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV), characterized by higher temperatures and increased hydrocarbon levels at millibar pressures. While the NPSV began forming in late northern spring, it lacked the distinct thermal and compositional contrasts observed at the south pole during its southern summer by the end of Cassini's observations, shortly after the northern summer solstice. The newly formed NPSV was defined by a steepening thermal gradient near $78^\circ$N. Its hexagonal boundary suggests that the Rossby wave responsible for Saturn's persistent polar hexagon—previously thought to remain in the troposphere—can impact stratospheric temperatures roughly 300 km above the cloud tops.

Cellular elastomeric metamaterials hold significant promise for applications like soft robotics due to their ability to undergo multiple microstructural pattern transformations, each displaying distinct mechanical properties. Previous numerical research indicated that pattern formation is confined to boundary layers in thick specimens, leading to pronounced mechanical size effects. This study seeks to experimentally verify these observations using miniaturized samples suitable for practical use, while also examining how increased geometric and material imperfections from miniaturization affect performance. Consequently, cellular metamaterial specimens of varying scale ratios were fabricated, subjected to in-situ micro-compression tests paired with digital image correlation to capture full-field kinematics, and benchmarked against complementary numerical simulations. The results demonstrate strong agreement between experimental and numerical data regarding global behavior, including pre-buckling stiffness, buckling strain, and post-buckling stress. Furthermore, local behaviors such as pattern transformation and boundary layer formation align well between the two methods. By comparing these findings with idealized literature models, the study highlights the impact of real-world boundary conditions—such as lateral confinement—on mechanical responses, particularly concerning size effects and boundary layer dynamics in cellular metamaterials.

Conceptual models serve to visually depict entities and their interconnections within an information system. An effective model must balance simplicity with the ability to convey adequate information, as managing this trade-off between complexity and clarity is vital for preventing information system development failures. Previous research suggested that more expressive models enhance performance on tasks assessing deep user understanding by reducing the cognitive workload experienced. To test this hypothesis, this study measured users' EEG brain activity while they interacted with various conceptual models. Thirty participants were split into two groups: one utilizing a low ontologically expressive model (LOEM) and the other a high ontologically expressive model (HOEM). Cognitive workload was quantified using the EEG Engagement Index, calculated as the ratio of beta band power to the combined power of alpha and theta bands. Results showed no significant difference in cognitive workload between the LOEM and HOEM groups, indicating that both models required equivalent cognitive processing for comprehension. The primary contribution of this research lies in introducing neurophysiological measures as an objective method for quantifying cognitive workload within the domains of conceptual modeling and information systems.
An expression for the subdifferential of the joint numerical radius is derived, and its applications to best approximation problems within this context are examined.

Complex fluids display diverse, unusual flow characteristics under high stress, including shear thickening and shear jamming. While rheology effectively characterizes these behaviors across the bulk fluid, it lacks the capability to resolve them spatially. This study employs high-speed imaging and the free-surface dynamics of drop impacts to investigate the flow of colloidal suspensions. For the first time, we document the coexistence of solid and liquid phases resulting from impact-induced shear jamming. Beyond observing Newtonian-like spreading and bulk shear jamming, we identify a transition between these states manifested as localized patches of jammed suspension within the spreading drop. We capture the instantaneous occurrence of shear jamming through a solidification front propagating from the impact site, demonstrating that the velocity of this front depends on the degree to which impact conditions exceed the shear thickening threshold.

We present in situ measurements of an electron diffusion region (EDR) alongside its neighboring separatrix. Significant magnetic field fluctuations near the lower hybrid frequency were detected, moving perpendicular to the reconnection plane. Furthermore, strong electron-scale gradients adjacent to the EDR display notable oscillations at comparable frequencies. Since such oscillations are inconsistent with a trajectory through a static 2D EDR, they suggest a complex motion of the reconnection plane driven by current sheet kinking that propagates out of the reconnection plane. Consequently, a full three-dimensional analysis is required to account for the observed disturbances during the EDR crossing.

This paper examines the stable marriage problem through Monte Carlo simulations, focusing on how correlations within preference lists influence simulation outcomes such as relaxation time and the distribution of these times. Additionally, the study incorporates individual attractiveness, various types thereof, and personal taste.

Acquiring a risk-aware policy is crucial yet difficult for unstructured robotic tasks, where safe reinforcement learning (RL) methods offer promising solutions. However, traditional conservative policy updates often hinder sufficient exploration and desirable performance in complex, data-intensive environments. To address this, we introduce a dual-agent safe RL strategy comprising a baseline agent and a safe agent. This decoupled architecture provides high flexibility, data efficiency, and inherent risk awareness for RL-based control. Specifically, the baseline agent maximizes rewards under standard RL conditions, remaining compatible with existing off-the-shelf techniques for unconstrained optimization, exploration, and exploitation. Meanwhile, the safe agent mimics the baseline for policy improvement while learning to satisfy safety constraints through off-policy RL tuning. Unlike training from scratch, correcting policies safely requires significantly fewer interactions to achieve near-optimal performance. The dual policies can be optimized either synchronously using a shared replay buffer or by treating the pre-trained model or a non-learning controller as a fixed baseline. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach can learn feasible skills without prior knowledge and generate risk-averse versions from pre-trained unsafe policies. Furthermore, the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art safe RL algorithms on challenging robot locomotion and manipulation tasks, excelling in both safety constraint satisfaction and sample efficiency.

We examine the influence of magnetic fields generated by laser pulses on XUV ionization assisted by lasers. Through numerical solutions of the three-dimensional time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation, we observe that the IR streaking field's magnetic component distorts the photoelectron momentum distribution. This distortion produces a longitudinal momentum shift in electrons that varies with both transverse momentum and time delay, a finding further validated analytically using the nondipole-corrected strong field approximation. Although the streaking spectrum is visibly modified by this momentum shift, we demonstrate that the extracted time delay remains unaffected by the magnetic field. Ultimately, our study elucidates the time-resolved nondipole effects of laser pulses via attosecond streaking.

Liger is a next-generation adaptive optics (AO) fed integral field spectrograph (IFS) and imager for the W. M. Keck Observatory, specifically designed to leverage the upgraded Keck All-Sky Precision Adaptive-optics (KAPA) system. This instrument aims to surpass current IFS capabilities by offering higher spectral resolving power (R$\sim$4,000-10,000), broader wavelength coverage ($\sim$0.8-2.4 $\mu$m), and a larger field of view. We detail the design and analysis of a custom dewar chamber intended to characterize Liger's opto-mechanical system. This chamber facilitates the testing and assembly of Liger's imaging camera and slicer IFS components while remaining adaptable for future experiments. Operating under a vacuum below $10^{-5}$ Torr, the system utilizes a cold shield maintained at temperatures below 90 K. The dewar is mounted on an optical vibration isolation platform and decoupled from cryogenic and vacuum systems via bellows. A custom cart supports the cold head and vacuum components, housing the necessary electronics and computers for experimental interfacing. Ultimately, this test chamber offers an efficient solution for calibrating, characterizing, and conducting future experiments with the Liger instrument.

This study utilizes the genomic structure as a second-order Markov process, defined by the distributions of consecutive base triplets, to address two bioinformatics challenges: detecting outliers in genome databases and classifying reads in metagenomics, employing real-world data from coronaviruses and adenoviruses.

Automatically identifying personality traits can benefit numerous applications, including mental health assessment and human resource management. While most existing datasets for personality detection analyze individuals in isolation, personality is deeply connected to social behavior. Moreover, research into personality analysis using low-resource languages remains surprisingly limited.
