We develop and resolve a generalized inverse Navier-Stokes problem designed to simultaneously reconstruct joint velocity fields and segment boundaries from noisy flow images. Utilizing a Bayesian framework with Gaussian random fields for regularization, we estimate uncertainties in the unknowns by approximating their posterior covariance via a quasi-Newton method. Initial tests on synthetic 2D flow images with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 3 demonstrate the method's success in reconstructing and segmenting these noisy images. Subsequently, we perform a magnetic resonance velocimetry (MRV) experiment on an axisymmetric flow to evaluate performance at low ($\simeq 6$) and high ($>30$) SNRs. Our results indicate that the method effectively reconstructs and segments low-SNR images, yielding noiseless velocity fields and smooth segmentations with negligible errors relative to high-SNR counterparts, thereby reducing total scanning time by a factor of 27. Furthermore, the approach provides additional physical insights, such as pressure distributions, and mitigates MRV limitations like low spatial resolution and partial volume effects, which otherwise impede accurate wall shear stress estimation. While the current implementation is limited to 2D steady planar and axisymmetric flows, the underlying formulation readily extends to 3D steady flows and naturally accommodates 3D periodic and unsteady scenarios.

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a flexible and data-integrable alternative to conventional methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). Although PINNs have demonstrated success across diverse PDE applications, their computational efficiency remains a challenge. One strategy to address this is optimizing training point generation. While residual-based adaptive sampling and quasi-uniform sampling have individually improved PINN training, we propose the Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation (RANG) approach to leverage the strengths of both. RANG utilizes a variable density nodal distribution technique derived from RBF-FD and incorporates a memory mechanism to enhance training stability. Experimental evaluations on six PDEs—comprising three linear and three nonlinear cases—using various node generation strategies numerically confirm that RANG achieves superior accuracy and efficiency compared to standard uniform sampling.

Calculating the free energy of large molecules using quantum mechanical energy functions has long been a significant challenge. We present a method capable of estimating harmonic contributions to the thermodynamics of molecular systems of unprecedented size at the quantum mechanical level with modest computational cost. Applying this approach, we computed the vibrational thermodynamics of various diamond nanocrystals, demonstrating that the error per atom diminishes as system size increases in the limit of large systems. Furthermore, we show that it is possible to derive vibrational contributions to the binding free energies of prototypical protein-ligand complexes where exact computations are too expensive to be practical. Our work suggests the potential for routine quantum mechanical estimation of thermodynamic quantities in complex systems.

Balanced homodyne interferometry is a widely recognized method for the sensitive analysis of light fields. Typically, a homodyne interferometer functions by using an active feedback loop to lock the relative phase between the reference and signal beams. In contrast, a less common approach involves slowly and continuously modulating the length of the reference arm to average all relative phases throughout the measurement. In this work, we demonstrate both theoretically and experimentally that this quadrature averaging offers benefits when estimating parameters of a resonant optical cavity. We show that averaging converts the transduction function—relating cavity frequency fluctuations to the interferometer signal—into a straightforward function of laser detuning that notably remains independent of parameters associated with any non-resonant channels in the system. This method eliminates the need for active feedback and yields results that are easily interpretable. Furthermore, phase-averaged measurements enable the characterization of the absolute magnitude of cavity frequency modulation.

Correlation Clustering is a significant clustering task with numerous practical applications. This work investigates its reconstruction variant, where the objective is to recover a latent clustering obscured by both random noise and adversarial alterations. While existing literature typically employs a "post-adversarial" framework where adversarial changes occur after noise introduction, we propose and analyze a novel "pre-adversarial" model in which adversarial modifications precede the noise. The goal is to reconstruct the latent clustering almost perfectly and with high probability given inputs generated by this semi-adversarial process. Focusing on scenarios where hidden clusters are of nearly equal size, we demonstrate that in the pre-adversarial setting, spectral algorithms are optimal; they achieve reconstruction up to the information-theoretic limit, beyond which recovery is impossible. This contrasts with the post-adversarial setting, where spectral algorithms fall short of this threshold, a gap that SDP-based algorithms optimally bridge. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized robustness in spectral algorithms, indicating they are less fragile than previously believed.

Solar active regions (ARs) are central to driving numerous geo-effective eruptions that extend throughout the Solar System; however, we currently lack the ability to reliably forecast their emergence location and timing by detecting pre-emergence indicators in observables like Doppler velocity, excluding helioseismic techniques. This study seeks to identify the earliest point at which Horizontal Divergent Flow (HDF) signatures can be robustly detected using SDO/HMI data. Building on prior research that employed a thresholding approach to find significant increases in pixels exhibiting specific line-of-sight velocities, we expanded this method to include multiple velocity windows and conducted a parameter study to assess the impact of data cadence on the results. Our findings align with previous work, confirming that HDF is present in 37.5% of ARs with an average lead time of 58 minutes before flux emergence. Furthermore, we introduce a new potential signature characterized by cadence-independent transient disruptions in the amplitudes across several velocity windows, which allowed us to recover pre-emergence indicators for 10 out of 16 studied ARs, yielding lead times ranging from 60 to 156 minutes. Various factors can influence the estimated timing for both HDF and flux emergence, suggesting that combining Doppler and magnetic field data may be necessary to establish a reliable indicator of continued flux emergence.

This work introduces novel algebraic instruments designed to analyze concurrent behaviors represented through Mazurkiewicz traces and asynchronous automata. These tools capture the distributed essence of traces, along with the inherent causality and concurrency among events, thereby enabling genuine reasoning about true concurrency. They extend the efficacy of methods previously used to understand, categorize, and reason about word languages. Specifically, we present an asynchronous variant of the wreath product and delineate the trace languages identified by this operation, establishing what is known as the asynchronous wreath product principle. Furthermore, we propose a decomposition theorem for recognizable trace languages, mirroring the Krohn-Rhodes theorem, and validate this result for acyclic architectures. Additionally, we define and examine two distributed automata-theoretic operations: the local cascade product, which directly implements the asynchronous wreath product, and global cascade sequences, which, while conceptually similar, rely on a more intricate asynchronous approach utilizing the Mukund and Sohoni gossip automaton. These developments yield significant insights into characterizing trace languages definable in first-order logic; such languages are accepted either by a restricted local cascade product of the gossip automaton and 2-state asynchronous reset automata, or by a global cascade sequence of 2-state asynchronous reset automata. Moreover, for distributed alphabets satisfying the asynchronous Krohn-Rhodes theorem, a local cascade product of these automata suffices, subsequently allowing for the identification of a simple temporal logic that is expressively complete for these alphabets.

We introduce a real-space approach and implementation of Kohn-Sham Density Functional Theory specifically designed for twisted geometries, utilizing it to analyze torsional deformations in X (X = C, Si, Ge, Sn) nanotubes. This method relies on high-order finite difference discretization within helical coordinates, employs ab initio pseudopotentials, and inherently accounts for both rotational (cyclic) and screw (helical) symmetries. We examine various facets of the computational technique, covering the governing equations, numerical implementation details, and its convergence, accuracy, and efficiency.

This approach is ideally suited for first-principles simulations of quasi-one-dimensional structures and their deformations, allowing the investigation of many relevant systems using small simulation cells with only a few atoms. We systematically apply the method to single-wall zigzag and armchair group-IV nanotubes under twisting conditions. For the deformations studied, the mechanical response aligns largely with isotropic linear elasticity, where torsional stiffness scales with the cube of the nanotube radius. Additionally, for a fixed radius, carbon nanotubes exhibit the highest stiffness, tin nanotubes the lowest, while silicon and germanium nanotubes show intermediate values that are similar to one another. We also detail the changes in electronic properties during twisting. Specifically, similar to armchair carbon nanotubes, armchair nanotubes of silicon, germanium, and tin display bandgaps that vary periodically with the twist rate, with this periodicity scaling inversely with the square of the tube radius.

This work investigates the interplay of quasiperiodic disorder, driving forces, and interactions within the periodically kicked Aubry-Andr\'{e} model. In the absence of interactions, analysis of quasienergy spectrum statistics confirms a dynamical localization transition in the high-frequency regime. Conversely, low-frequency statistics become complex due to the appearance of extended/localized-to-multifractal edges that demarcate multifractal states from extended (localized) ones. Upon introducing interactions, we observe that the periodically kicked incommensurate potential induces a transition from an ergodic phase to a many-body-localization phase in the high-frequency region. However, in the low-frequency region, the many-body localization phase disappears even under strong quasiperiodic disorder. These findings highlight the rich dynamical behaviors of the model and underscore that driving frequency is as critical as disorder strength in governing many-body localization.

Digital Twins serve as digital counterparts of Internet of Things (IoT) systems, frequently relying on AI models trained on data from those systems. Semantic models are increasingly employed to connect datasets across various stages of the IoT lifecycle and to automatically configure AI modeling pipelines. Integrating semantic models with AI pipelines operating on external datasets presents unique challenges, especially when deployed at scale. This paper examines the specific requirements for applying semantic graphs to automate Digital Twins across diverse practical scenarios. We introduce the DTBM benchmark dataset, which embodies these characteristics, and analyze the scaling challenges associated with different knowledge graph technologies. Leveraging these insights, we propose a reference architecture currently utilized in multiple IBM products and derive lessons learned for scaling knowledge graphs to configure AI models for Digital Twins.

Surface termination significantly influences the physical properties of materials, making it essential to understand its impact on the metal-insulator transition (MIT) in V$_2$O$_3$ films for both theoretical insights and practical applications. By adjusting growth conditions, we generated various surface terminations in V$_2$O$_3$ films, which were analyzed using low energy electron diffraction (LEED) and photoemission spectroscopy. Our findings indicate that the MIT can be partially or completely suppressed near the surface, depending on the specific termination. This suppression arises from distinct electron filling levels in surface and sub-surface layers relative to the bulk, as well as alterations in the screening length. Across the transition, we observed a significant redistribution of spectral weight, transferring from high to low binding energy regimes over a broad energy scale. Notably, the total spectral weight in the low-energy regime is not conserved across the MIT, signaling a violation of spectral weight sum rules—a hallmark of strongly correlated systems. These spectral changes likely stem from variations in hybridization, lattice volume (effectively carrier density), and spin degrees of freedom during the transition. Our results confirm that the MIT in this system is driven by strong correlations, with electron-electron interactions playing a central role. Furthermore, these findings offer deeper insight into the electronic structure of strongly correlated materials and underscore the necessity of considering surface effects when interpreting physical property data obtained through surface-sensitive techniques like surface resistivity.

Recent interest has surged in using deep learning for jet classification, yet these models often sacrifice interpretability for performance. We introduce an interpretable network trained on the jet spectrum $S_{2}(R)$, defined as the two-point correlation function of jet constituents. This spectrum arises from the functional Taylor series of any arbitrary jet classifier acting on energy flows, and an interpretable model can be constructed by truncating this series. The network's intermediate feature is an infrared and collinear safe C-correlator, which quantifies the significance of a $S_{2}(R)$ deposit at an angular scale R for classification purposes. While the architecture's performance rivals that of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on jet images, it requires significantly fewer inputs and is structurally simpler. We demonstrate this approach with two cases: distinguishing two-prong jets based on the mother particle's color charge, and comparing jets generated by Pythia 8 versus Herwig 7.

Clemens' conjecture asserts that the count of rational curves within a generic quintic threefold is finite. Should this conjecture prove false, we demonstrate that specific periods associated with rational curves in such a threefold must be zero. Our approach relies on extending the proof of Max Noether's theorem through the application of infinitesimal variation of Hodge structures, which is then recast using integrals and the Gauss-Manin connection.

Two distinct AI paradigms, neural networks and symbolic systems, have demonstrated significant success across various applications; however, neither has yet attained the general reasoning capabilities necessary for human-like intelligence. This limitation is often attributed to inherent flaws within each approach. Fortunately, these weaknesses are complementary, as symbolic systems excel where neural networks struggle, and vice versa. Consequently, the emerging field of neural-symbolic AI aims to leverage this asymmetry by integrating neural networks with symbolic AI into unified systems, frequently achieved by embedding symbolic knowledge within neural networks. Despite numerous proposed methods for this integration, a standardized definition for comparing encoding techniques remains absent. This study addresses that gap by proposing a semantic framework for neural-symbolic AI, which proves sufficiently broad to encompass a wide range of existing systems. Through various examples and proofs, we demonstrate how this framework applies to the neural encoding of diverse knowledge representations and network structures. Although these methods initially appear disparate, they all conform to the framework's formal definition of semantic encoding in neural-symbolic AI.

We introduce a newly developed thread pool compatible with modern C++17, engineered specifically for high-performance scientific computing. Designed as a single, lightweight, and self-contained class, it relies exclusively on the C++17 standard library, ensuring maximum portability without dependencies on OpenMP or other high-level multithreading frameworks. This approach grants programmers precise low-level control over parallelization details, enabling more robust optimizations. The implementation has undergone extensive testing on AMD and Intel CPUs featuring up to 40 cores and 80 threads. This paper details the motivation behind the design, provides comprehensive usage instructions, and presents performance evaluation results.

This paper introduces several new classes of logarithmically completely monotonic functions, all of which are defined using the $q$-gamma and $q$-digamma functions. Leveraging these findings, we derive various inequalities for both the $q$-gamma and $q$-digamma functions. Furthermore, some of our results extend theorems previously established by Alzer and Berg, as well as by C.-P. Chen and F. Qi.

Morphological measures are employed to investigate the intricate process of shock wave interaction within porous materials, specifically characterizing the geometric and topological features of pixelized maps for state variables such as temperature. The study reveals their connection to material thermodynamics and simulates various experimental conditions. Numerical findings indicate that shock wave reactions in porous media generate a complex sequence of compressions and rarefactions. The rate of increase in the total fractional white area, $A$, approximately corresponds to the velocity $D$ of the compressive wave series; however, specifying $D$ requires defining the associated threshold contour-level of the state variable. As this threshold level rises, $D$ decreases. During the initial phase, area $A$ grows parabolically with time $t$. In three specific scenarios—(i) as porosity $\delta$ approaches 1, (ii) as the initial shock intensity increases, and (iii) as the contour-level nears the minimum state variable value—the $A(t)$ curve transitions back to linearity. Furthermore, high-temperature regions may continue to expand even after early compressive waves reach the downstream free surface and rarefactive waves return to the target body. In the case of energetic materials... (see the full text).

This study investigates continuous gravitational waves from seven pulsars that have not previously been included in Advanced LIGO continuous wave searches. We examine emission at precisely twice the pulsar's rotation frequency, as well as within a narrow frequency band surrounding this value. The search targeting the exact double frequency assumes the gravitational wave quadrupole remains phase-locked with the pulsar's rotation, whereas the broader frequency range search accommodates differential rotation between the radio-emitting component and the gravitational wave source, such as between the core and the crust or magnetosphere. Timing data from the Arecibo 327-MHz Drift-Scan Pulsar Survey (AO327) were utilized for these analyses. No signals were detected, leading to established upper limits on gravitational wave amplitude. For one specific pulsar, we constrained intrinsic gravitational wave amplitudes to be only 3.8 times above the spin-down limit, assuming a canonical moment of inertia of $10^{38}$ kg m$^2$. Our most stringent ellipticity limit is $1.5 \times 10^{-8}$, a value consistent with the structural support capabilities of a neutron star crust.

This study examines the use of Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) within intelligent reflecting surface (IRS)-enabled unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) assisted non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) downlink networks. Equipping a UAV with an IRS is crucial because it greatly enhances IRS flexibility, particularly benefiting users lacking a line-of-sight (LoS) connection to the base station (BS). Consequently, this letter aims to maximize the sum rate by jointly optimizing base station power allocation, IRS phase shifting, and the UAV's horizontal location. Since the resulting optimization problem is non-convex, the DDPG algorithm is employed to solve it. Computer simulations demonstrate that the proposed DDPG-based algorithm achieves superior performance.

Current tools for navigating the NASA Astrophysics Data System (ADS) offer powerful features like similar and trending operators, yet they do not yet fully support semantic search. For instance, a query such as "results from the Planck mission" currently fails to automatically distinguish between the various entities named Planck (e.g., a person, a mission, a constant, or an institution) without additional user input. To address this, ADS is employing modern machine learning and natural language processing techniques on a dataset of recent astronomical publications to train astroBERT, a deeply contextual language model inspired by Google's research. By leveraging astroBERT, we aim to enhance the ADS dataset and improve overall discoverability, specifically through the development of a custom named entity recognition tool. This paper presents our preliminary findings and key takeaways.

This paper develops a Bass-Serre theory within the groupoid framework and establishes a corresponding structure theorem. It demonstrates that any edge-action on a forest by a groupoid, provided it avoids inversion, induces a graph of groupoids. Conversely, any graph of groupoids meeting specific criteria admits a canonical fundamental groupoid and an associated Bass-Serre forest, upon which the fundamental groupoid acts. The structure theorem asserts that these two processes are mutually inverse.

We derive constraints on GUP parameters for two distinct GUP formulations by analyzing gravitational wave data from events GW150914 and GW190521. Within a curved spacetime framework modified by GUP, we calculate the propagation speeds of photons and gravitons, assuming these particles possess small masses. The observational limits on the velocity difference between these particles are then converted into bounds for the GUP parameters, representing some of the most stringent results to date in quantum gravity phenomenology.

Shifting between topics is an inherent aspect of human-to-human conversation. Despite decades of research into topic transitions in dialogue, only a limited number of corpus-based studies have examined their nuances. Consequently, this study annotates 215 dialogues from the Switchboard corpus to analyze the relationship between variables such as transition length, frequency, shared transitions, and transitions per turn. This work offers an empirical investigation of topic transitions within the Switchboard corpus, followed by a model achieving 83% precision on an in-domain test set and 82% on ten out-of-domain test sets. It is anticipated that these findings will facilitate the emulation of human-like topic transitions in open-domain dialogue systems.

Tensor network representations serve as essential tools for analyzing strongly correlated quantum many-body states, particularly those where local correlations and ground states adhering to entanglement area laws are prominent. For interacting fermionic systems, selecting an appropriate basis or set of orbitals significantly lowers tensor bond dimensions and accelerates computations. We present a basis transformation strategy utilizing unitary gates derived by compressing fermionic Gaussian states into quantum circuits compatible with various tensor network structures. These circuits effectively diminish ground state entanglement entropy, thereby enhancing the efficiency of algorithms like the density matrix renormalization group. We demonstrate the method's utility in boosting computational performance and clarifying impurity physics through a study of the 1D single impurity Anderson model. Additionally, fermionic Gaussian circuits exhibit promise in suppressing entanglement growth during the time evolution of low-lying excited states, which are crucial for calculating impurity Green's functions. Finally, we explore Gaussian multi-scale entanglement renormalization ansatz (GMERA) circuits that hierarchically compress fermionic Gaussian states, examining the resulting emergent coarse-grained models regarding their entanglement characteristics and aptness for time evolution tasks.

This research investigates the eigenvalue distribution of almost-Hermitian random matrices derived from the classical Gaussian and Laguerre unitary ensembles. Building on the framework introduced by Fyodorov, Khoruzhenko, and Sommers for the GUE, our study focuses on a regime where eigenvalues deviate from the real axis, acquiring imaginary components that form a narrow band of height proportional to $1/N$ around the real line, with $N$ representing the matrix dimension. We analyze vertical slices of the 1-point density and examine microscopic scaling limits, benchmarking these findings against recent literature. Our methodology relies on Ward's equation and a novel concept termed "cross-section convergence," which connects the large-$N$ behavior of eigenvalue density cross-sections to the equilibrium densities of their Hermitian counterparts: specifically, the semi-circle law for GUE and the Marchenko-Pastur law for LUE.

The electrostatic theory governing magnetoplasmons in a semi-infinite magnetized electron gas is extended to encompass mixed Faraday-Voigt configurations. This analysis identifies a novel class of electrostatic surface waves characterized by strong directionality, which could potentially be observed in narrow-gap semiconductors within the terahertz frequency range. A comprehensive formula for the dispersion relation is provided, detailing its sensitivity to both the strength and orientation of the external magnetic field. Notably, the group velocity of these magnetoplasmons is consistently orthogonal to their phase velocity. The study offers an in-depth examination of the resulting velocity and energy characteristics. Furthermore, under specific limiting conditions, the established magnetoplasmons found in the higher-symmetry Faraday and Voigt configurations are successfully retrieved.

This study demonstrates that the q-Heun equation and its variants emerge within the linear q-difference equations linked to certain q-Painlevé equations, specifically through the analysis of blow-ups in their initial-value spaces. Furthermore, we derive the first degenerated Ruijsenaars-van Diejen operator from the linear q-difference equation corresponding to the q-Painlevé equation of type $E_8$.

We present an analysis of indefinite causal orders within relativistic quantum mechanics, utilizing Feynman's electron-positron framework where negative-energy electrons travel backward in time. Our findings demonstrate that true realizations of the quantum switch, which typically violate causal inequalities and maintain a fixed temporal sequence, become feasible under extreme external electromagnetic field conditions that permit closed time-like curves.

This study evaluates the efficacy of deep learning in handling tabular data. While decision trees and their ensembles are currently regarded as the dominant approaches in this field, often relegating deep neural networks to computer vision and audio tasks, this paper argues that deep networks' core capability—constructing gradient-based hierarchical representations—makes them uniquely suited for processing generic structured data, not merely images or spectrograms. The analysis is conducted through the lens of the Yandex Shifts Weather Prediction challenge, a regression problem involving tabular data that also addresses critical issues of generalization and uncertainty in machine learning. The authors propose an end-to-end regression algorithm with uncertainty estimation for tabular data, built upon four key concepts: deep ensembles of self-normalizing neural networks, treating regression as parameter estimation of a Gaussian error distribution, hierarchical multitask learning, and straightforward data preprocessing. Three variants of this algorithm secured the top three positions on the Yandex Shifts Weather leaderboard. The paper posits that this success stems from the fundamental properties of the deep learning architecture and seeks to substantiate this claim.

We introduce a systematic method termed the Clebsch canonization, which derives a canonical Hamiltonian system linked to a given Lie-Poisson equation through a momentum map. This approach is detailed in both coordinate and geometric forms, with the latter reportedly presented here for the first time. Furthermore, we identify an additional momentum map such that the two maps form a dual pair under specific conditions. This dual pair offers a concrete implementation of the collectivization of Lie-Poisson systems. Consequently, applying symplectic Runge-Kutta methods to solve the canonized system produces collective Lie-Poisson integrators that exactly preserve coadjoint orbits and Casimirs. We illustrate these concepts with several examples, including the Kida vortex and the heavy top on a movable base with controls, which correspond to Lie-Poisson systems defined on $\mathfrak{so}(2,1)^{*}$ and $(\mathfrak{se}(3) \ltimes \mathbb{R}^{3})^{*}$, respectively.

Although deception profoundly impacts human society and only 54% of people can accurately detect it, Machine Learning systems for automated Deception Detection (DD) remain impractical for real-world use due to a scarcity of data. The limited number of public DD datasets and the difficulty in creating new ones stem from the theoretical divide between low-stakes and high-stakes lies; this distinction suggests that datasets of one type cannot effectively train models for the other. While low-stakes deception is easier to gather through simulated, controlled environments, it lacks the depth and significance of high-stakes lies, which are harder to obtain but crucial for practical DD applications. To assess the validity of this distinction, we conducted experiments comparing high-stakes and low-stakes datasets using a Deep Learning classifier based solely on video input. Our results showed that a network trained on low-stakes data achieved higher accuracy when classifying high-stakes deception than when classifying low-stakes deception; however, using low-stakes data as an augmentation technique for the high-stakes dataset ultimately reduced accuracy.

We introduce the Correlation-Locking Optimization SchEme (CLOSE), a real-time adaptive filtering method designed for integrator-controlled adaptive optics (AO) systems. CLOSE utilizes the temporal autocorrelation of modal signals within controller telemetry to dynamically adjust the gains of the integral command law within a closed servo-loop. Configured with only a few scalar parameters, this supervisory loop automatically tunes modal gains to approximate transfer functions that achieve minimum variance control. The efficacy of this optimization is validated across the noise and atmospheric seeing conditions pertinent to AO operations. Developed in preparation for high-order AO systems on extremely large telescopes, CLOSE specifically addresses the optical gain (OG) phenomenon—a sensitivity reduction caused by on-sky residuals—which is a critical challenge for pyramid wavefront sensors (PWFS). Building on the previously demonstrated linear modal compensation approach for OG, which has significantly enhanced correction in high-order PWFS systems, CLOSE operates via multiplicative increments on modal gains. This naturally mitigates recurring issues related to unaccounted sensitivity factors within the AO loop. We present end-to-end simulations of the MICADO instrument's single-conjugate AO to illustrate CLOSE's performance and capabilities. These results demonstrate that a single configuration can efficiently and versatilely optimize the modal integrator, simultaneously compensating for OG and providing substantial robustness against transient effects that impact PWFS sensitivity.

Pedestrian crossing prediction has become a focal point of research, yielding numerous algorithmic advancements. Although assessing overall progress has become increasingly established through new public benchmarks and standardized metrics, a critical gap remains: understanding how existing predictors perform on unseen data. This assessment is vital because reliable predictors must operate effectively across diverse scenarios without jeopardizing pedestrian safety due to errors. Consequently, we conducted a study utilizing direct cross-dataset evaluation. Our findings reveal that current state-of-the-art predictors generalize poorly in cross-dataset settings, even when they appear robust in standard train-test splits. Based on these observations, we argue that the future of pedestrian crossing prediction should move beyond tailoring models trained on limited data for classical evaluation, with the intent of inferring real-world behavior. Instead, the focus must shift to evaluating models in cross-dataset contexts while accounting for uncertainty estimates under domain shift.

Arbitrary conditioning represents a significant challenge in unsupervised learning, aiming to model conditional densities $p(\mathbf{x}_u \mid \mathbf{x}_o)$ for all possible non-overlapping subsets $o, u \subset \{1, \dots , d\}$. Yet, most density estimation techniques concentrate solely on the joint distribution $p(\mathbf{x})$, leaving critical conditional dependencies between features obscure. We introduce a straightforward and versatile framework named Posterior Matching, which allows Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to execute arbitrary conditioning without any internal modifications. By applying to the wide range of existing VAE-based joint density estimation methods, Posterior Matching avoids the need for the specialized architectures previously required for arbitrary conditioning. Our results demonstrate that Posterior Matching matches or exceeds the performance of current state-of-the-art methods across various tasks when utilizing different VAE variants, including discrete, hierarchical, and VaDE models.

Accurately forecasting geomagnetic storms is critical for numerous space weather applications. This study evaluates the performance of the StormFocus service, launched in 2011 by SpaceWeather.Ru, which estimates storm intensity via the $Dst$ index several hours in advance. Utilizing hourly updates based on real-time L1 solar wind and interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) data, the service operated during the weak solar maximum of cycle 24 (2011–2016), meaning most statistical data reflects moderate storm events. We assessed the reliability of the selection criteria and compared the quality of real-time input data against final archived values. During live operations, 87% of storms were correctly predicted, whereas a reanalysis using complete OMNI data achieved a 97% success rate. Consequently, the primary sources of prediction errors stem from discrepancies between real-time and final data regarding the $Dst$ index, solar wind, and IMF, caused by processing inaccuracies and dataset-specific characteristics.

Geometric dispersion is a critical factor in integrated microresonators for nonlinear optics, particularly at short wavelengths, where it counteracts the inherent normal material dispersion. By engineering geometric confinement, researchers can induce anomalous dispersion, facilitating the creation of microcombs capable of entering the dissipative Kerr soliton (DKS) regime. Because soliton-induced dispersive wave generation processes make broadband DKS combs highly sensitive to higher-order dispersion—and because this dispersion depends on nanometer-scale ring dimensions—precise control is essential. For microrings with a rectangular cross-section, the primary adjustable parameters for achieving target dispersion are ring width and thickness. While width can be readily adjusted via lithography mask variations, thickness is determined by the film growth of the initial material stack and may vary significantly (by a few percent) across a single wafer. This letter demonstrates that controlled dry-etching enables fine-tuning of the device layer (silicon nitride) thickness at the wafer level, supporting multi-project wafers for different wavelength bands and post-fabrication trimming of air-clad ring devices. Furthermore, we show that this dry-etching process does not adversely impact silicon nitride surface roughness or the optical quality of the devices, thereby allowing for precise adjustment of dispersion and the spectral characteristics of the resulting DKS states.

This research investigates the thermoelectric (Seebeck and Nernst) response in heavily overdoped, non-superconducting La$_{1.67}$Sr$_{0.33}$CuO$_4$. Despite the electron-like curvature of its Fermi surface, the Seebeck coefficient remains positive at low temperatures. This phenomenon, previously noted in copper, silver, gold, and lithium, stems from a non-trivial energy dependence of the scattering time. We contend that this indicates a pronounced asymmetry in the lifetimes of occupied versus unoccupied states along the zone diagonals, and that such electron-hole asymmetry hinders the formation of Cooper pairs along the nodal direction within the superconducting ground state observed at lower doping levels.

This paper introduces a novel correspondence linking acyclic orientations to the coloring of signed graphs. Building on the bivariate chromatic polynomial $\chi_G(k,l)$ defined by Goodall et al.—which enumerates signed colorings using colors $0,\pm1,\dots,\pm k$ and $l-1$ symmetric colors $0_1,\dots,0_{l-1}$—we demonstrate that the value $|\chi_G(-1,2)|$ corresponds to the number of acyclic orientations of the signed graph, considering orientations equivalent if they differ only by swapping sources and sinks. We provide three distinct proofs for this result: one utilizing toric hyperplane arrangements, another employing the deletion-contraction method, and a third direct proof.

This paper introduces the concept of an N-ideal within a BE-algebra by utilizing N-structures and establishes the necessary conditions for an N-structure to qualify as an N-ideal. To derive a broader definition, the study proposes a point N-structure that is (k-conditionally) applied within an N-structure. Leveraging these concepts, the paper redefines the N-ideal and examines its associated properties, characterizing it as a generalized form of the N-ideal and discussing its specific characterizations.

This work offers a non-technical overview of tensor field theories and their corresponding renormalization group, emphasizing the conceptual drivers from quantum gravity over specific technicalities. Specifically, we examine how the asymptotic freedom inherent in these theories exemplifies a natural "quantum relativity" principle: in the deep ultraviolet limit, physics becomes increasingly independent of any specific Hilbert basis chosen for the universe's state space.

Deuteron production in high-energy collisions, typically modeled via a coalescence mechanism, reflects the space-time evolution of the collision system. For the first time, we report on jet-associated deuteron production in proton-proton ($\text{p p}$) collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, offering a new test of the established deuteron production framework in events involving hard scattering. By utilizing a high transverse-momentum ($p_{\rm T}>5$ GeV/$c$) trigger particle as a proxy for a midrapidity jet, we detect a significant population of deuterons near the jet proxy. The deuteron yield measured within a narrow angular window around the trigger particle deviates from the uncorrelated background by 2.4 to 4.8 standard deviations. These observations are consistent with PYTHIA model calculations that incorporate baryon coalescence.

The density of states, defined as a Borel probability measure on the real line, is derived from the solution to the Dyson equation within any fixed $C^\ast$-probability space, given a selfadjoint offset and a $2$-positive linear map. Leveraging methods from free noncommutative function theory, we establish explicit Hölder bounds for the Lévy distance between two such measures as any parameter varies. Central to our proof, and of independent significance, are the demonstration that solutions to the Dyson equation possess strong analytic properties and evolve along any $C^1$-path of $2$-positive linear maps in accordance with an operator-valued formulation of the inviscid Burgers equation.

We have concluded the analysis of all 2018 sub-prime-field microlensing planetary candidates detected by the KMTNet AnomalyFinder. Among the nine events with clear planetary interpretations that were previously unpublished, six are definitively planetary (KMT-2018-BLG-0030, KMT-2018-BLG-0087, KMT-2018-BLG-0247, OGLE-2018-BLG-0298, KMT-2018-BLG-2602, and OGLE-2018-BLG-1119), whereas the other three remain ambiguous. Additionally, the AnomalyFinder algorithm identified eight previously published sub-prime field planets. Combined with a companion study (Gould et al. 2022) covering 2018 prime-field planets, this research establishes the foundation for the first statistical examination of the planet mass-ratio function using KMTNet data. Consistent with prior expectations (Zhu et al. 2014), half (17 out of 33) of the 2018 planets suitable for mass-ratio analysis exhibit non-caustic-crossing anomalies. However, among the five non-caustic anomalies with a planet-host mass ratio $q<10^{-3}$, only one was found visually, compared to seven of the twelve with $q>10^{-3}$, highlighting the critical role of the semi-automated AnomalyFinder search.

This study investigates the existence and non-existence of solutions for a specific class of elliptic problems defined over the entire space, featuring the $N$-Laplacian operator. The analysis centers on a nonlinearity exhibiting critical Trudinger-Moser growth. Employing a non-variational methodology, we tackle a broad spectrum of issues absent from existing literature. Notably, despite the failure of the embedding $W^{1,N}(\mathbb{R}^N)\hookrightarrow L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N)$, we demonstrate that for any solution $u$, the inequality $\|u_{\lambda}\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N)} \leq C \|u\|_{W^{1,N}(\mathbb{R}^N)}^{\Theta}$ holds (where $\Theta>0$ and $C$ is a constant). Finally, we examine various asymptotic characteristics.

We suggest analyzing two decay channels, $\bar{B}^0 \to K^0 D^{+} K^-$ and $\bar{B}^0 \to K^{*0} D^{*+} K^-$, which have already been observed at Belle, to investigate the $J^P=0^+$ $X_0(2866)$ state and its $1^+$ partner, hypothesized to have a molecular $D^*\bar{K}^*$ structure. This investigation focuses on the $D^+ K^-$ and $D^{*+} K^-$ invariant mass spectra, respectively. We predict distinct peaks rising clearly above the background and calculate the production branching ratios to assist in estimating the required statistics for observation. Given that the $K^{*0} K^-$ mass distribution, derived from accumulated events across various reactions, is already accessible, it suggests that sufficient statistics exist to detect peaks in the $D^{(*)+} K^-$ mass distributions, which have not yet been analyzed.

Ellis-Bronnikov (EB) wormholes necessitate a violation of null energy conditions at the throat. This issue was resolved by modifying the "shape function" to include a new parameter $m \ge 2$, where $m=2$ recovers the original EB model, thereby creating a generalized (GEB) framework. This study examines a model embedding GEB wormhole geometry within a five-dimensional warped background. We conducted a detailed analysis of all energy conditions for both the EB and GEB embeddings, presenting our findings both analytically and graphically. Notably, a decaying warp factor enables the satisfaction of weak energy conditions even in the EB geometry, while improving the status of all other energy conditions compared to the four-dimensional scenario. Beyond offering a novel method to circumvent the need for exotic matter to sustain a wormhole passage, our work highlights another significant benefit of utilizing warped extra dimensions.

We introduce an optimization algorithm tailored for Bayesian learning in complex models. Our method utilizes natural gradient updates within a general black-box framework, enabling efficient training with minimal model-specific derivations. This approach is applicable to exponential-family variational posterior distributions, with a detailed focus on the Gaussian case, where the update rules are notably straightforward. Our Quasi Black-box Variational Inference (QBVI) framework is easily implementable and broadly applicable to various Bayesian inference tasks. Crucially, the updates for the variational posterior avoid calculating gradients regarding model parameters and do not require specifying the Fisher information matrix. We explore QBVI under different assumptions concerning the posterior covariance matrix, address implementation details to ensure robustness and feasibility, and present several real-world applications to validate its efficacy.

We demonstrate that a specific eventually homological isomorphism between module categories leads to triangle equivalences among their singularity categories, Gorenstein defect categories, and stable categories of Gorenstein projective modules. Furthermore, we establish that both the Auslander-Reiten conjecture and the Gorenstein symmetry conjecture can be reduced via these eventually homological isomorphisms. By applying these findings to vertex and arrow removal operations, we characterize Gorenstein projective modules over certain non-monomial algebras and confirm the Auslander-Reiten conjecture for specific algebraic structures.

This work offers a systematic investigation of the $^{10-14}\text{C}$ isotopes using the \textit{ab initio} no-core shell model framework. Four distinct realistic nucleon-nucleon interactions are employed: (i) the charge-dependent Bonn 2000 (CDB2K) potential, (ii) the inside non-local outside Yukawa (INOY) potential, (iii) the next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order (N$^3$LO) potential, and (iv) the optimized next-to-next-to-leading order (N$^2$LO$_{opt}$) potential. The study details the low-lying energy spectra and level structures for both positive and negative parity states across these isotopes. Furthermore, electromagnetic properties, including transition strengths and quadrupole and magnetic moments, are calculated. The analysis examines the dependence of point-proton radii on the harmonic oscillator frequency and basis space, while also presenting translation-invariant one-body density matrix calculations within the no-core shell model to explore isotopic trends in density distributions. The calculations utilize a maximum basis space of $10 \hbar \Omega$ for $^{10}\text{C}$ and $8 \hbar \Omega$ for $^{11-14}\text{C}$, reaching a peak M-scheme dimension of $1.3 \times 10^{9}$ for $^{10}\text{C}$. Results indicate that although the INOY interaction provides the most accurate description of ground state energies, the N$^3$LO interaction yields the best reproduction of point-proton radii.

Let $G$ be a finite group and $\chi$ an irreducible character of $G$. The codegree of $\chi$ is defined as $\cod(\chi) = |G:\kernel(\chi)|/\chi(1)$. The set of all codegrees of $G$ is denoted by $\cod(G) = \{ \cod(\chi) \mid \chi \in \Irr(G) \}$. For any $d \in \cod(G)$, $m'_G(d)$ represents the count of irreducible characters in $G$ with codegree $d$. A finite group $G$ is termed a $T'_k$-group for an integer $k \geq 1$ if there exists a specific $d_0 \in \cod(G)$ such that $m'_G(d_0) = k$, while $m'_G(d) = 1$ for all other $d \in \cod(G) \setminus \{d_0\}$. This note provides a complete characterization of finite $T'_k$-groups for any integer $k \geq 1$.

This work examines classical and quantum oscillations in metals possessing complex Fermi surfaces, specifically near magnetic field directions ($\, {\bf B} \, $) where the topological structure of the dynamical system governing the semiclassical motion of quasiparticles along the Fermi surface undergoes transformation. Crossing the boundaries of these structural changes results in abrupt shifts in the oscillation patterns, with the resulting form being critically dependent on the specific topological nature of the reconstruction. We outline the primary characteristics of these transitions for all elementary topological types and explore the potential for experimentally identifying these types through their distinct signatures.

Point cloud upsampling is crucial for high-fidelity augmented reality, virtual reality, and telepresence systems, primarily because current capture, processing, and communication technologies face inherent limitations. While densifying point cloud coordinates through geometry upsampling has received significant attention, enhancing color attributes has largely been neglected. This paper introduces CU-Net, the inaugural deep-learning model designed for point cloud color upsampling, which delivers low-latency performance with high visual fidelity. By utilizing a sparse convolution-based feature extractor and a neural implicit function-driven color prediction module, CU-Net achieves linear time and space complexity. Consequently, it is theoretically assured to surpass the efficiency of most existing methods, which typically exhibit quadratic complexity. Experimental findings show that CU-Net can generate photo-realistic point clouds containing nearly one million points in real time, outperforming baseline methods in visual quality. Furthermore, the model adapts to arbitrary upsampling ratios and unseen objects without requiring retraining. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/UMass-LIDS/cunet.

Research on Wigner matrices perturbed by a single rank-one term, defined as $P=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A+\theta vv^T$ where $A$ is a symmetric matrix with i.i.d. centered standard normal entries and $v$ is a unit vector, has been extensive. It is established that the largest eigenvalue, $\lambda_1(P)$, undergoes a phase transition at $\theta_0=1$: for $\theta \leq 1$, it converges almost surely to 2, while for $\theta > 1$, it converges almost surely to $\theta+\theta^{-1}$. Under broader conditions, the normalized limiting behavior of $\lambda_1(P)$ is known to be Gaussian when $||v||_{\infty}=o(1)$, or a convolution of the entry distribution with a Gaussian when $v$ is concentrated on a single entry; these results typically require a finite fourth moment. This paper investigates scenarios where this condition is violated. Specifically, for symmetric entries $a_{11}$ with heavy tails characterized by an index $\alpha \in (0,4)$, fluctuations are shown to be universal, depending on $\theta$ but independent of $v$. In the critical case $\alpha=4$, a specific subfamily exhibits characteristics of both light- and heavy-tailed regimes: two distinct limiting laws arise depending on whether $v$ is localized, each featuring a continuous phase transition at $\theta_0=1$ for $\theta_0 \in [1,\frac{128}{89}]$. These findings extend our prior work analyzing the asymptotic behavior of $\lambda_1(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A)$ within this same subfamily.

Ensuring successful multimedia service provisioning in next-generation networks like 5G and 6G relies heavily on Quality of Experience (QoE) management, a domain where machine learning (ML) is essential for monitoring, predicting quality, and managing resources. This paper serves as a tutorial on creating and implementing supervised learning-based ML models for measuring and predicting QoE in video streaming. First, it outlines a comprehensive pipeline for developing these models, encompassing data collection, feature engineering, model training and optimization, as well as testing and evaluation. Second, it explores deploying ML-driven QoE prediction and measurement within 5G/6G environments by proposing a reference architecture that leverages enabling technologies such as Software-Defined Networking (SDN), Network Function Virtualization (NFV), and Mobile Edge Computing (MEC). Finally, the paper offers a comparative analysis of state-of-the-art supervised learning models for video streaming QoE prediction, assessing them against various performance metrics.

This study assesses two image clustering goals—k-means and correlation clustering—within the framework of Triplet Loss-driven feature embeddings. We train a convolutional neural network to acquire discriminative features by optimizing two established Triplet Loss variants, aiming to analyze their clustering behavior under noisy label conditions. Furthermore, we introduce a novel, straightforward Triplet Loss formulation that exhibits favorable alignment with formal clustering objectives and surpasses current methods. All three Triplet Loss variants are evaluated for both K-means and correlation clustering on the CIFAR-10 dataset.

The eROSITA X-ray telescope, part of the Spectrum-Roentgen-Gamma (SRG) mission, is designed to detect and characterize approximately 100,000 galaxy clusters and 3 million active galactic nuclei across the entire sky. To effectively analyze the statistical outcomes of this extensive survey, an accurate estimation of the selection function is essential. We have generated full-sky light-cones utilizing the MultiDark and UNIT dark matter-only N-body simulations. Additionally, we introduce a new approach to forecast the X-ray emission from galaxy clusters. By inputting specific dark matter halo attributes—including mass, redshift, ellipticity, and offset parameters—we generate corresponding X-ray emissivity profiles and images for every halo within the light-cones. Adhering to the eROSITA scanning strategy, we compile a comprehensive list of X-ray photons covering the full sky. Our model yields scaling relations for these synthetic clusters that align well with existing literature, and the predicted cluster number density as a function of flux matches prior observations. Furthermore, we calculate a scatter of 0.21 (with ranges of 0.07 and 0.25) for the X-ray luminosity–mass, temperature–mass, and luminosity–temperature scaling relations. We also release catalogs containing model photons from both clusters and active galactic nuclei, which will support the end-to-end simulation workflow for eROSITA, specifically enhancing source detection and cataloging methodologies.

This study examines a class of linear Boltzmann transport equations designed to model the transport of charged particles. The proposed equation serves as an approximation of the original exact transport equation, which features hyper-singular integrals within its collision terms. These hyper-singular integrals are approximated by combining partial differential operators with partial integral operators, yielding the equation under consideration. Such approximations are utilized, for instance, in radiation therapy dose calculations. The associated transport problem is formulated as an initial inflow boundary value problem, and the regularity of its solutions is verified using scales of relevant anisotropic Sobolev spaces.

The Keldysh formalism effectively models the driven-dissipative dynamics of open quantum systems as nonunitary effective field theories that may deviate from thermodynamics, frequently revealing novel physical phenomena. In this work, we present a generalized Keldysh action that strictly adheres to Weinbergian principles, encompassing locality, Poincaré invariance, and two specific "$CPT$" conditions: complete positivity with trace preservation, alongside charge, parity, and time-reversal symmetries. Our analysis reveals that the perturbative Lindblad term governing driven-dissipative dynamics takes the natural form of a double-trace deformation, $\mathcal{O}^2$. In the large $N$ limit, this deformation can generate a new nonthermal conformal fixed point. Depending on the scaling dimension $\Delta$ of $\mathcal{O}$ relative to half the spacetime dimension $d$, this fixed point appears either in the infrared (when $\Delta < d/2$) or the ultraviolet (when $\Delta > d/2$). The existence of a UV fixed point not prohibited by Weinbergian constraints suggests its potential reality and self-consistency, challenging the conventional view that dissipation is invariably infrared-relevant. This insight indicates that driven-dissipative dynamics is significantly more complex than thermodynamics, differing not only in its violation of thermodynamic symmetries like the fluctuation-dissipation relation but also in its distinct UV/IR relevance. We further investigate specific examples, including a $(0+1)$-dimensional harmonic oscillator subjected to continuous measurement and a $(4-\epsilon)$-dimensional classical $O(N)$ vector model featuring quartic interactions.

This study investigates the influence of temperature on the anomalous viscosity of the Graphene Hall fluid using quantum many-vortex hydrodynamics, focusing on filling fractions $\nu$ where $0 < \nu < 2$. We derive an expression for temperature-dependent anomalous viscosity that incorporates a geometric parameter known as the Hall expansion coefficient. This viscosity stems from two sources: a pseudo-magnetic field generated by strain and an anomalous component in vortex velocity, the latter driving the re-normalization of vortex-vortex interactions. Our findings indicate that both factors significantly alter the anomalous viscosity and enhance the detection of weakly observed fractional states. Specifically, non-zero expansion coefficients yield constant or infinite viscosity values across varying temperatures; these infinities correspond to energy gaps and point to temperatures where new stable fractional quantum Hall fractions may emerge. Consequently, we apply this phenomenon to estimate the energy gaps of previously measured fractional quantum Hall states in Graphene.

This study reveals several novel features regarding the exact non-equilibrium dynamics of quantum double dark-soliton states within the Lieb-Liniger model for a one-dimensional Bose gas with repulsive interactions. We further demonstrate an exact finite-size scaling of the Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) fraction in the ground state, which characterizes the quasi-BEC assumed to exist in these states under weak coupling conditions. First, we utilize the Bethe ansatz to present the exact time evolution of the density profile for the quantum double dark-soliton state. Second, we derive an effective macroscopic quantum wave-function by precisely calculating the square amplitude and phase profiles of the field operator matrix elements between these states; these profiles closely resemble those of dark-solitons, especially in the weak-coupling regime. Additionally, we provide an exact demonstration of the scattering between two notches in the quantum double dark-soliton state. Based on these findings, we suggest that quasi-BEC plays a crucial role in the dynamics of such states. Specifically, if the condensate fraction approaches unity, the quantum state can be well approximated by a quasi-BEC state where the mean-field description remains valid.

Although recent advances in quantum computing herald the dawn of a quantum information era, managing quantum states remains a significant challenge, and the energy requirements for large-scale applications have received insufficient attention. Resolving these challenges demands a thorough investigation into the most energy-efficient execution of fundamental quantum operations. This analysis demonstrates that the optimal control problem can be addressed using the robust framework of quantum speed limits. Specifically, we establish state-independent lower bounds on energetic costs, thereby identifying the universally optimal implementation of unitary quantum gates for both single-qubit and N-qubit operations.

Current acoustic event detection (AED) paradigms often fail to account for the natural variability of organic sounds and typically impose constraints on the number of concurrent sources, frequently assuming only a single source or one of each type is active. These limitations are particularly problematic for applications like bird population monitoring. We present a straightforward approach that models the onsets, durations, and offsets of acoustic events, thereby eliminating inherent restrictions on polyphony and inter-event timing patterns. Evaluated on a dataset comprising over 3,000 zebra finch calls, this method demonstrates superior accuracy in event recovery and greater robustness in estimating calling rates compared to a Hidden Markov Model (HMM)-based approach.

A liquid helium target apparatus was engineered and constructed to execute a high-precision measurement of the parity-violating neutron spin rotation in helium, which arises from the nucleon-nucleon weak interaction. This experiment utilized a low-energy neutron beam traversing a crossed polarizer-analyzer setup, with the liquid helium target positioned between them. Variations in the target's state induced corresponding changes in the beam's transmission through the polarizer-analyzer system, allowing the magnitude of the parity-violating spin rotation to be derived from the observed transmission asymmetries. Given that the anticipated spin rotation is on the order of $10^{-6}$ radians, the target design faced stringent requirements. Specifically, distinguishing the parity-odd spin rotation from a significantly larger background rotation induced by magnetic fields necessitated a nonmagnetic cryostat and target assembly supported within magnetic shielding, while simultaneously permitting the nonmagnetic movement of liquid helium between isolated target chambers. This article offers a comprehensive account of the target system's design, operational principles, and performance.

This study examines the behavior of linear and nonlinear, third-order-in-time sound waves within thermally relaxing fluids and gases as sound diffusivity approaches zero. Nonlinear acoustic propagation is represented by the Jordan--Moore--Gibson--Thompson equation in both its Westervelt and Kuznetsov-type formulations, which incorporate quadratic nonlinearities of the forms $(u^2)_{tt}$ and $(u_t^2 + |\nabla u|^2)_t$. It is demonstrated that sufficiently smooth solutions to these equations converge to the solutions of the corresponding inviscid models in the energy norm at a linear rate, a finding supported by numerical experiments.

Achieving efficient and robust policy transfer remains a critical hurdle for reinforcement learning to be practically viable in real-world robotics. Current approaches, such as warm initialization, imitation, and interacting with diverse randomized agents, have successfully addressed various reinforcement learning tasks. However, these methods diverge significantly from biological skill transfer, where humans and animals rapidly adapt learned behaviors to similar tasks and acquire new skills in novel situations. This study investigates whether integrating adaptation and exploration can enhance the efficiency of policy transfer across domains. We propose a principled "Adapt-to-Learn" mechanism that adjusts source policies to effectively solve target tasks characterized by substantial transition differences and uncertainties. Our results demonstrate that this method seamlessly combines learning derived from adaptation and exploration, yielding a robust policy transfer algorithm that significantly reduces sample complexity when transferring skills between related tasks.

Vehicle-to-vehicle communication is crucial for maintaining road safety, with emergency alerts typically distributed via broadcasting. However, high traffic density and rapid mobility often hinder this process, causing issues like broadcast storms and reduced packet reception rates. To address these challenges, this study introduces a solution combining federated learning with blockchain technology. Drawing parallels to incentive-based Proof-of-Work consensus, the proposed Proof-of-Federated-Learning (PoFL) mechanism embeds a consensus protocol within blockchain smart contracts, allowing vehicles to compete for relay node status by processing PoFL. The paper offers both theoretical and practical evaluations of this approach. Results indicate that the blockchain-integrated federated learning system encourages a higher volume of vehicle model uploads within a specific timeframe, potentially yielding a more accurate model faster than non-blockchain alternatives. Furthermore, it surpasses other blockchain-based dissemination methods by cutting consensus time delay by 65.2%, boosting the message delivery rate by at least 8.2%, and enhancing the privacy protection of neighboring vehicles. Finally, the study analyzes an economic incentive model for vehicle participation in federated learning and message dissemination using a Stackelberg game framework.

This paper introduces a framework for modeling and analyzing the dynamics of multi-domains within ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs). The periodic domain texture results in an oscillatory conduction band profile in the device's electrostatics. To accurately represent these oscillations, we solve a coupled 2-D system comprising Poisson's equation and the net ferroelectric energy density equation (which includes gradient, free, and depolarization energies). Domain dynamics are simulated by minimizing this net energy to achieve thermodynamic stability. We demonstrate that moving domain walls generate local bound charge densities in the ferroelectric region, thereby inducing the negative capacitance (NC) effect, with the NC strength governed by the material's gradient energy. Consequently, FeFETs display drain current variability tied to the domain period due to this intrinsic NC effect. The study also examines how soft-to-hard domain wall transitions influence electrostatics and transport, while the model successfully captures both domain nucleation and wall motion. Finally, the proposed model is rigorously validated through comparisons with experimental data and phase-field simulations.

We examine lepton-number-violating processes in $\Lambda_b$ and $\Lambda_c$ decays driven by on-shell sterile neutrinos at the GeV scale. We compute the branching ratios for the channels $\Lambda_b^{0} \rightarrow \mathcal{B}^+ \mu^{-}\mu^- \pi^+$ (where $\mathcal{B}^+$ denotes either a $\Lambda_c^+$ or a proton) and $\Lambda_c^{+} \rightarrow \Lambda \mu^{+}\mu^+ \pi^-$, as functions of the sterile neutrino mass $m_N$ and the heavy-light mixing parameter $|U_{\mu N}|^2$ from the extended PMNS matrix. Our calculations account for finite detector resolution. By comparing the theoretical effective branching ratios with the projected sensitivity of the LHCb experiment, we derive upper limits on $|U_{\mu N}|^2$ across the ($|U_{\mu N}|^2$-$m_N$) plane. These decay modes yield constraints comparable to those from alternative search strategies at facilities such as Belle, NuTeV, DELPHI, and BEBC within the mass range $0.25 \text{ GeV} \lesssim m_N \lesssim 4.5 \text{ GeV}$, offering particularly stringent limits for $2 \text{ GeV} < m_N < 4.5 \text{ GeV}$.

This study proposes a wireless sensor network designed for participatory sensing, featuring IoT devices specifically engineered to monitor and forecast air quality as a cost-effective alternative to traditional meteorological stations. The system, named pmSensing, focuses on measuring particulate matter. Its validation involved comparing prototype-collected data with readings from established stations, revealing closely aligned results that support the viability of low-cost solutions. Furthermore, the system incorporates predictive analysis using Long Short-Term Memory Recurrent Neural Networks (LSTM-RNN), which demonstrated high accuracy when compared to actual data.

Dots-and-Boxes is a well-known children's game whose winning strategies have been explored by researchers such as Berlekamp, Conway, and Guy. This article examines two related variations, Dots-and-Triangles and Dots-and-Polygons, which share the same lattice board structure as the original game. The combination of these variations and the lattice format makes it possible to use Pick's theorem to determine the claimed area. Furthermore, strategies analogous to those found in Dots-and-Boxes are employed to analyze these new game variants.

This study investigates the strong decays of $\Xi$ baryons within the N=2 shell using a chiral quark model, which provides a reasonable description of these well-known ground decuplet baryons. First, $\Xi(1690)$ and $\Xi(1820)$ are likely candidates for the $J^P=1/2^-$ and $J^P=3/2^-$ states defined by $|70,^{2}{8},1,1,1/2^->$ and $|70,^{2}{8},1,1,3/2^->$, respectively, with possible slight configuration mixing. Second, $\Xi(1950)$ may represent multiple resonances: broad states ($\Gamma\sim 100$ MeV) in the $\Xi\pi$ channel could be either a pure $J^P=5/2^-$ octet or a mixed $J^P=1/2^-$ state, while moderate-width states ($\Gamma\sim 60$ MeV) might correspond to a $J^P=1/2^+$ excitation. Narrow states in the $\Lambda \bar{K}$ channel could potentially be the second orbital excitation or a mixed state, though their spin-parity assignments conflict with moment analysis data. Third, $\Xi(2030)$ cannot be attributed to $J^P=7/2^+$ or pure $J^P=5/2^+$ configurations; although it favors the $|70,^{2}8,2,2,3/2^+>$ assignment, its spin contradicts moment analysis results. To discover additional $\Xi$ resonances, future observations in the $\Xi(1530)\pi$ and $\Sigma(1385) \bar{K}$ channels are required.

This paper introduces a rapid Monte Carlo approach for additive processes. We conduct a detailed analysis of numerical error origins and suggest a method to mitigate the two primary sources of inaccuracy. Additionally, we benchmark our findings against a standard technique: jump simulation using Gaussian approximation. The proposed method is applied to additive normal tempered stable processes, a category capable of exactly calibrating the implied volatility surface. The numerical outcomes demonstrate that the algorithm serves as a precise instrument for pricing path-dependent options with discrete monitoring, achieving errors of one basis point or less. Furthermore, the scheme is highly efficient, with computational requirements comparable to standard algorithms used for Brownian motions.

This paper introduces an experiment utilizing deep learning and transfer learning for emotion analysis in tweets, along with a method to interpret the resulting deep learning models. Our proposed emotion analysis approach integrates a Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) network with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). We then extend this framework to predict emotion intensity using transfer learning. Additionally, we present a visualization technique to highlight the importance of individual words within tweets, facilitating a deeper understanding of the model. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed models surpass state-of-the-art performance in emotion classification while achieving competitive outcomes in emotion intensity prediction.

This article investigates the asymptotic behavior of a finite volume scheme applied to one-dimensional linear kinetic equations, utilizing either a Fokker-Planck or linearized BGK collision operator. Leveraging suitable uniform estimates, we demonstrate that the scheme is Asymptotic-Preserving within the diffusive limit. Furthermore, we extend the hypocoercivity method introduced by Dolbeault, Mouhot, and Schmeiser (2015) to the discrete setting to prove that the approximate solution returns to equilibrium exponentially, with decay rates that remain uniformly bounded as the diffusive limit is approached. Finally, we detail an efficient implementation of these numerical schemes and conduct extensive simulations to evaluate their accuracy and efficiency in reproducing the correct asymptotic dynamics of the models.

Recent years have seen extensive research into deep learning-based code summarization. Existing models typically rely on the encoder-decoder framework inspired by neural machine translation, where an encoder extracts semantic features from source code and a decoder converts these features into human-readable descriptions of code functionality. Although these approaches have achieved state-of-the-art results, they often struggle with generating fluent summaries or accurately capturing core functionality because they rely on a single type of code representation. To address this, we introduce GypSum, a novel deep learning model that leverages hybrid representations through graph attention networks and pre-trained programming-natural language models. Our approach integrates control-flow-specific edges into the abstract syntax tree for graph construction and employs two distinct encoders to process both the graph and the token sequence. Furthermore, we adapt the Transformer decoder's sublayer to fuse these representations and implement a dual-copy mechanism to enhance summary generation. Experimental findings confirm that GypSum outperforms current code summarization models.

Beginning in 2021, the International Maritime Organization imposed stricter $\text{NO}_\text{x}$ emission limits for vessels operating in the Baltic and North Seas. However, because current compliance monitoring methods are expensive and require physical proximity to ships, continuous global surveillance of emission standards has remained unfeasible. A viable solution lies in remote sensing using the newly launched TROPOMI/S5P satellite, whose exceptional spatial resolution enables the visual identification of $\text{NO}_\text{2}$ plumes from individual ships. To implement a compliance system based on TROPOMI data, an automated method for attributing $\text{NO}_\text{2}$ to specific vessels is necessary; yet, this task is highly challenging due to an extremely low signal-to-noise ratio, interference from stronger external sources, and a lack of ground truth data. This study presents the first application of supervised learning for segmenting emission plumes from individual ships, marking a crucial step toward automated global monitoring via remote sensing. We developed a feature construction technique that facilitates the use of multivariate models on spatial data, applied and benchmarked several supervised-learning models against existing unsupervised solutions for ship-plume segmentation with TROPOMI data. Our results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly improves plume segmentation and exhibits a strong correlation with theoretical measures of a ship's emission potential.

This study considers a nonparametric regression framework where signals consist of the sum of a smooth function and a piecewise constant function. To identify change-points and estimate the regression functions, we introduce PCpluS, a method that integrates fused Lasso with kernel smoothing. Unlike prior techniques, PCpluS explicitly leverages the decomposition assumption of the signal into smooth and piecewise constant components for change-point detection, a strategy grounded in various applications and theoretical findings regarding partial linear models. We select tuning parameters via cross-validation and contend that minimizing L1-loss outperforms L2-loss in this context. Furthermore, we discuss critical implications for cross-validation within piecewise constant change-point regression. Simulation results indicate that our approach achieves low average mean square error and accurately detects change-points. We also apply the methodology to genome sequencing data to identify copy number variations. Finally, we showcase the method's adaptability by merging it with smoothing splines and extending it to handle multivariate and filtered data.

Domain adaptation is a key strategy for addressing domain shift, a common challenge in large-scale land use and land cover mapping, as well as the lack of pixel-level ground truth essential for supervised semantic segmentation. While existing research on adversarial domain adaptation through source domain re-styling using generative adversarial networks has shown mixed results, these approaches often struggle with semantic inconsistencies, visual artifacts, and a high demand for target domain samples. This letter introduces a novel unsupervised domain adaptation method for semantic segmentation of very high-resolution images that achieves three main objectives: (i) producing semantically consistent and noise-free images, (ii) functioning with only a single target domain sample (one-shot learning), and (iii) utilizing a fraction of the parameters required by state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, we propose an image-to-image translation framework based on an encoder-decoder architecture that mixes latent content representations across domains, enhanced by a perceptual network module and loss function to ensure semantic consistency. Comparative experiments across different cities demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing domain adaptation techniques. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/Sarmadfismael/LRM_I2I}.

Robotics in laboratory settings presents a promising solution to free scientists from repetitive duties and speed up the discovery of new materials, which is critical for addressing global challenges like climate change and disease. Although many workflows are automated, sample preparation often remains manual due to the complex motor skills needed to handle heterogeneous materials involving various chemicals, tools, and glassware. In chemical research, crystallization is a key process, particularly for polymorph screening to determine a molecule's three-dimensional structure. Success in this area depends on maximizing sample recovery, as synthesizing molecules is both time-consuming and expensive. Traditionally, chemists manually scrape vials to retrieve contents before imaging, a step that is difficult to automate because it requires precise, fine-grained movements within the confined space of a vial, going beyond simple insertion tasks. Inspired by human techniques, this work introduces a model-free reinforcement learning approach to develop a scraping policy for fully autonomous sample retrieval. First, a simulation environment featuring a Panda Franka Emika robot and a laboratory scraper was created to demonstrate successful policy learning. Subsequently, the method was tested on a real robotic arm in a lab setting, proving its ability to autonomously scrape powder across diverse configurations.

This paper reviews recent progress in computing standard errors and test statistics for statistical inference.
