Although the past twenty years in economics have largely prioritized generating unbiased coefficients, recent years have witnessed significant strides in correcting for non-standard standard errors. We synthesize these advances in tackling obstacles to conventional inference, including heteroskedasticity, clustering, serial correlation, and multiple hypothesis testing. Additionally, we examine improvements in numerical techniques such as the bootstrap, wild bootstrap, and randomization inference. We offer three specific recommendations: first, applied economists must clearly identify the challenges to statistical inference present in their data and their sources; second, given modern computing capabilities and statistical software, there is no excuse for failing to calculate standard errors and test statistics correctly; and third, due to the complexity of sampling strategies and research designs that complicate formula derivation, we advocate for bootstrapping as a standard practice for achieving asymptotic refinements in estimator and test statistic distributions. Throughout, we reference both built-in and user-written Stata commands that facilitate the rapid calculation of accurate standard errors and relevant test statistics.

This study investigates how outer stellar companions influence the frequency of giant planets identified via radial velocities. We examined a volume-limited sample of solar-type stars within 25 parsecs, searching for both stellar and planetary companions using adaptive optics imaging from the Lick 3m and Palomar 200" Telescopes. This imaging allowed us to characterize the multiplicity of our sample stars down to the lower end of the main sequence, confirming existing field star multiplicity statistics from prior surveys. We combined three decades of radial velocity data from the California Planet Search with new observations from Keck/HIRES and APF/Levy to search for planets within these same systems. By utilizing an updated catalog of stellar and planetary companions alongside injection/recovery tests to assess sensitivity, we calculated the occurrence rate of planets in both single and multiple star systems. Our results indicate that planets with masses between 0.1 and 10 $M_{Jup}$ and semi-major axes between 0.1 and 10 AU occur at a rate of $0.18^{+0.04}_{-0.03}$ per single star and $0.12\pm0.04$ per binary primary. Only one planet-hosting binary in our sample had a separation less than 100 AU, and none were closer than 50 AU. For binaries with separations greater than 100 AU, the planet occurrence rate was $0.20^{+0.07}_{-0.06}$ per star, whereas for those with separations less than 100 AU, it was $0.04^{+0.04}_{-0.02}$ per star. The comparable occurrence rates around single stars and wide binary primaries suggest that wide binary systems should host more planets overall than single star systems due to having more potential host stars. We estimated a system-wide planet occurrence rate of 0.3 planets per wide binary system for binaries with separations exceeding 100 AU. Finally, our findings provide evidence that giant planets in binary systems exhibit a different semi-major axis distribution compared to those in single star systems.

The LHCb experiment analyzed a dataset from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 1.0 fb$^{-1}$, to search for lepton-flavour violating decays of $B^0_s \to e^{\pm} \mu^{\mp}$ and $B^0 \to e^{\pm} \mu^{\mp}$. The number of observed candidates for both decay modes aligns with background predictions, leading to upper limits on their branching fractions of $BR(B^0_s \to e^{\pm} \mu^{\mp}) < 1.1 \,(1.4) \times 10^{-8}$ and $BR (B^0 \to e^{\pm} \mu^{\mp}) < 2.8 \,(3.7) \times 10^{-9}$ at 90% and 95% confidence levels, respectively. These constraints represent a twenty-fold improvement over previous experimental limits. Additionally, lower limits on the masses of Pati-Salam leptoquarks were derived as $M_{\rm LQ} (B^0_s \to e^{\pm} \mu^{\mp}) > 107$ TeV/c$^2$ and $M_{\rm LQ} (B^0 \to e^{\pm} \mu^{\mp}) > 126$ TeV/c$^2$ at 95% C.L., which are twice as stringent as earlier bounds.

This study establishes specific criteria for a Young function $\Phi$ and a one-parameter family of Young functions $\{\Psi_q\}$ such that the Orlicz norms corresponding to each $\Psi_q$ satisfy a particular property for all $f \in L^\Phi(X,\mu)$:
\[
\lim_{q\rightarrow \infty}\|f\|_{L^{\Psi_q}(X,\mu)}=C\|f\|_{L^\infty(X,\mu)}.
\]
The constant $C$ remains independent of $f$, relying solely on the family $\{\Psi_q\}$. Furthermore, these conditions are proven to be both necessary and sufficient when $f \in L^1(X,\mu)$. The paper includes several examples of one-parameter families that meet these requirements, alongside counterexamples demonstrating cases where the conditions fail. Additionally, applications within the field of partial differential equations are explored.

Contemporary online platforms depend on distributed data stores that replicate data across geographically dispersed centers. Enforcing strict consistency in these environments leads to high latency and susceptibility to network partitions, whereas relaxing consistency compromises essential correctness guarantees. A viable middle ground involves supporting multiple coexisting consistency levels. This paper introduces UniStore, the inaugural fault-tolerant and scalable data store that unifies causal and strong consistency. The primary challenge UniStore addresses is maintaining liveness during data center failures, specifically preventing scenarios where a strong transaction relies on a causal transaction that is subsequently lost due to a failure. UniStore ensures such conflicts never occur while incurring durability costs for causal transactions only when required. Evaluated on Amazon EC2 through microbenchmarks and a sample application, the results demonstrate that UniStore effectively and scalably integrates both consistency models.

Complex topological materials can be chemically doped to create novel electronic systems with unique physical properties. Specifically, molybdenum ditelluride (MoTe$_2$), a type-II Weyl semimetal candidate, exhibits significantly enhanced superconductivity reaching 4.1 K when rhenium (Re) substitutes molybdenum sites. Through bulk transport measurements and local scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), we demonstrate that Re doping in Re$_{0.2}$Mo$_{0.8}$Te$_2$ also induces a potential charge density wave (CDW) phase. Furthermore, the tunneling current-voltage ($I-V$) curves reveal non-linearity and hysteresis, which aligns with the observed hysteresis in tip-height ($z$) variations relative to applied voltage ($V$). These findings suggest an electric field-driven hysteretic switching mechanism, indicative of both piezoelectric and potential ferroelectric behaviors.

Eigenvector perturbation analysis is crucial across numerous data science domains. However, existing research has predominantly concentrated on $\ell_{2}$ bounds for eigenvector perturbations, which often fail to capture the fine-grained dynamics required by specific tasks. This paper advances the field by investigating the perturbation of linear functions of an unknown eigenvector. Targeting two core problems—matrix denoising and principal component analysis under Gaussian noise—we establish a comprehensive statistical framework that characterizes how arbitrary linear functions of an unknown eigenvector are affected by perturbations. To address the significant bias present in standard "plug-in" estimators, we introduce de-biased estimators that (1) attain minimax lower bounds across a range of scenarios (up to logarithmic factors) and (2) are computable in a data-driven fashion without requiring sample splitting. Remarkably, these proposed estimators remain nearly minimax optimal even when the corresponding eigen-gap is significantly smaller than the thresholds typically demanded by previous statistical theories.

Visual inspection software is now a critical component for quality control and process monitoring in manufacturing, with semantic segmentation models becoming increasingly vital for their precision. However, these models demand extensive, well-annotated image datasets to achieve high accuracy, a requirement often unmet in specialized production settings where data is scarce or poorly labeled. While data augmentation is a standard technique for expanding datasets, it typically offers limited variation. This article proposes a novel strategy to augment small datasets, specifically applied to carbon fiber surface monitoring. The study employs two distinct methods for generating binary labels: a custom trigonometric function and a WGAN model. These labels are then converted into color images via pix2pix to train a U-Net. Results indicate that the trigonometric function outperforms the WGAN model; yet, detailed analysis reveals that both WGAN and image-to-image translation yield segmentation results that closely align with traditional data augmentation. Ultimately, this research investigates the application of generative adversarial networks for data synthesis in industrial monitoring systems.

Keywords: Image-to-Image Translation, Carbon Fiber, Data Augmentation, Computer Vision, Industrial Monitoring, Adversarial Learning.

This work introduces, investigates, and computes solutions for a category of optimal control problems involving hyperbolic conservation laws and their viscous regularizations, using the barotropic compressible Navier--Stokes equations (BNS) as a primary model. Initially, we apply the entropy-entropy flux-metric condition to BNS by selecting an appropriate entropy function and reformulating the equations as a sum of flux and the metric gradient of entropy. Subsequently, we construct a metric variational problem for BNS, where the critical points yield a primal-dual BNS system. A finite difference scheme is designed for this variational system, featuring implicit time approximations for the conservation laws. The variational problem is solved using an algorithm derived from the primal-dual hybrid gradient method, which incorporates a novel approach for handling implicit time approximations in conservation laws that appears to be unconditionally stable. Several numerical examples are provided to illustrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm.

Semantic segmentation remains a difficult endeavor because it demands significantly more low-level spatial details than other computer vision tasks. Pixel-level classification accuracy is often hindered by various factors, including imaging constraints and the ambiguity of object boundaries. Traditional approaches typically leverage deep neural networks (DNNs) to process three-channel RGB images from the visible spectrum. However, thermal imaging can greatly enhance segmentation performance, as infrared cameras capture details regardless of weather or lighting conditions. The application of infrared spectra in semantic segmentation offers numerous practical benefits across fields such as autonomous driving, healthcare, agriculture, and defense. Consequently, developing precise segmentation algorithms utilizing infrared data is a critical challenge. One strategy involves fusing visible and infrared images as dual inputs, which improves accuracy through enriched data but incurs the overhead of aligning and processing multiple streams. Alternatively, relying solely on thermal images reduces hardware requirements, making it suitable for smaller-scale applications. Despite the existence of various surveys on semantic segmentation, there is a notable absence of a comprehensive review specifically dedicated to infrared-based methods. This work seeks to address that gap by surveying existing literature and categorizing these algorithms based on their input modalities.

This study examines an isolated ion within a neutral buffer gas, establishing an analytical model that fully characterizes both the dynamic behavior and steady-state characteristics of the ions. By adapting mathematical methods from financial theory, an extended version of this model elucidates recent findings regarding non-Maxwellian statistical distributions in such systems. Collectively, these insights provide a resolution to persistent challenges related to the sympathetic cooling of ions via neutral buffer gases.

Currently, there is limited understanding of the Cargo ecosystem's architecture and the risks associated with vulnerability propagation. Numerous empirical studies apply third-party dependency governance strategies from one software ecosystem to others, often overlooking structural differences; this hinders the direct transfer of security strategies to Cargo. To address this gap, this paper constructs a dependency vulnerability knowledge graph for Cargo using related techniques. As the first large-scale empirical study in this domain, it investigates vulnerability propagation within Cargo. The research introduces a parsing algorithm for dependency-vulnerability knowledge graphs to identify propagation paths and scope, alongside an empirical analysis of vulnerability characteristics, propagation ranges, and contributing factors. Findings indicate that Cargo security vulnerabilities are predominantly memory-related. Specifically, 18% of affected libraries remain vulnerable even in their latest versions, and the vulnerability propagation impacts 19.78% of versions across the entire ecosystem. By examining vulnerability characteristics and triggering factors, this study offers practical resolution strategies for Cargo administrators, developers managing third-party libraries, and library maintainers, thereby providing new approaches to enhance the overall security of the Cargo ecosystem.

This study examines an obscure facet of the Klein paradox, revealing that a Klein-Gordon boson can traverse a supercritical rectangular barrier without reflection while spending a negative duration within it. Although this transmission mechanism is clearly acausal, efforts to formulate a corresponding causal solution to the Klein-Gordon equation are unsuccessful. We connect the causal solution to a divergent series of multiple reflections and demonstrate that the issue is resolved for a smooth barrier; in this case, pair production at half the barrier's height is amplified but remains finite.

We examine an inhomogeneous Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random graph ensemble characterized by exponentially decaying disconnection probabilities driven by an i.i.d. field of heavy-tailed variables with infinite mean, associated with the graph's vertices. Recently, this model appeared in physics literature~\cite{GMD2020} as a scale-invariant random graph within network renormalization frameworks. Mathematically, it belongs to the class of scale-free inhomogeneous random graphs, whose asymptotic geometric properties have recently garnered significant attention. While many results exist for such graphs when vertex variables possess a finite mean, this work focuses on the case of one-sided stable variables, which inherently have an infinite mean. To facilitate our analysis, we assume these variables follow a Pareto distribution with parameter $\alpha\in(0,1)$. We begin by characterizing the asymptotic distributions of typical degrees and related observables. Specifically, we demonstrate that, after appropriate scaling, the degree of a vertex converges in distribution to a mixed Poisson law. Furthermore, we establish that while correlations between the degrees of different vertices do not vanish asymptotically, a form of asymptotic tail independence emerges when examining the joint Laplace transform near zero. Finally, we report initial findings regarding the asymptotic density of wedges and triangles, and we identify a cross-over point concerning the existence of dust (disconnected nodes) within the ensemble.

A recent proposal formalized the olfactory circuit of a fruit-fly as a locality-sensitive hash (Flyhash) and bloom filter (FBF), which were subsequently adapted for machine learning tasks like similarity search, outlier detection, and text embeddings. This work introduces a novel adaptation of these hash and bloom filter mechanisms to emulate a canonical nearest neighbor classifier (NNC) within the demanding Federated Learning (FL) framework, where training and test data remain distributed across parties without leaving their local environments. By employing Flyhash and FBF to construct the FlyNN classifier, we theoretically define conditions under which FlyNN achieves parity with NNC. We demonstrate that FlyNN can be trained precisely in an FL setting with minimal communication costs to generate FlyNNFL, while also supporting differential privacy. Empirical evaluations reveal that (i) FlyNN attains NNC-level accuracy across 70 OpenML datasets, and (ii) FlyNNFL training scales efficiently with low communication overhead, delivering up to an $8\times$ speedup when utilizing 16 parties.

This study introduces a novel time-domain finite-element method for modeling thin sheets using hyperbolic basis functions, which are adapted from the standard steady-state solution of the linear flux diffusion equation. By integrating solutions across various operating frequencies, the magnetic field formulation effectively captures the temporal evolution of field quantities. The proposed method is demonstrated on a planar shielding scenario, handling both harmonic and time-dependent simulations for materials exhibiting either linear or nonlinear properties. Results for both local and global metrics demonstrate strong alignment with reference solutions derived from the conventional finite element method on a comprehensive discretization of the region subjected to a time-varying magnetic field.

This study investigates a hierarchy of equivalence classes concerning quasi-random properties of Boolean functions. Specifically, we establish an equivalence among various attributes, such as balanced influences, spectral discrepancy, local strong regularity, homomorphism counts in colored or weighted graphs and hypergraphs linked to Boolean functions, and the $k$th-order strict avalanche criterion, among others. Additionally, we develop families of quasi-random Boolean functions that demonstrate the properties outlined in our equivalence theorem and distinguish between the tiers of this hierarchy.

This study investigates the steady, two-dimensional nonlinear flow of a fluid past a submerged body beneath an elastic sheet. The mathematical framework utilizes velocity potential theory, incorporating fully nonlinear boundary conditions on both the fluid surface and the elastic sheet, which are integrated throughout the numerical process. To derive the complex velocity potential, the integral hodograph method is applied, explicitly representing the velocity magnitude along the interface. This approach reduces the coupled problem to a system of nonlinear equations regarding the unknown interface velocity magnitude, which is resolved via a collocation method. Case studies covering both subcritical and supercritical flow regimes are conducted, presenting results for interface geometry, bending moments, and pressure distributions across extensive ranges of Froude numbers and submergence depths. Based on the dispersion equation, two distinct waves emerge on the interface: a primary, long gravity-induced wave and a secondary, shorter wave generated by the elastic sheet. The solution demonstrates a strongly nonlinear interaction between these waves over the submerged body. Furthermore, it is observed that near the critical Froude number, a specific range of submergence depths yields non-convergent solutions.

The spanning tree congestion problem involves finding a spanning tree $T$ in a connected graph $G$ that minimizes the maximum edge congestion, defined as the count of adjacent vertex pairs in $G$ whose $T$-path crosses a specific edge $e$. Although this problem is NP-hard, its approximability remains largely unclear, with no known efficient approximation ratio better than $o(n)$. In the decision variant, STC-$K$, the goal is to ascertain whether a spanning tree exists with congestion no greater than $K$. Previously, it was established that STC-$K$ is NP-complete for $K\ge 8$, yielding a $1.125$ lower bound for the approximation ratio. While the $3$-STC case is solvable in polynomial time, the complexity for $K \in \{4,5,6,7\}$ was an open question. This study significantly advances prior hardness results by demonstrating that STC-$K$ is NP-complete for $K\ge 5$. Consequently, only the $K=4$ case remains unresolved, and the lower bound for the approximation ratio is improved to $1.2$.

The SNO+ experiment operated as a low-threshold water Cherenkov detector from September 2017 through July 2019. Using an Am-Be calibration source, the experiment measured the 2.2-MeV $\gamma$ rays resulting from neutron capture on hydrogen; this source emits neutrons that are largely accompanied by a 4.4-MeV $\gamma$. By analyzing the delayed coincidence between these two gamma rays, researchers determined a neutron detection efficiency centered near 50% with a variation of only 1% throughout the detector's inner region, marking the highest efficiency recorded for a pure water Cherenkov detector to date. Furthermore, the neutron capture time constant was measured and translated into a thermal neutron-proton capture cross section of $336.3^{+1.2}_{-1.5}$ mb.

We introduce an extended microcanonical Lanczos method (MCLM) designed for the direct calculation of the diffusion constant and its frequency dependence within the disordered Anderson model of noninteracting particles. This approach enables the investigation of systems comprising more than $10^6$ sites on hypercubic lattices across dimensions $d = 3$ to $7$. Below the localization transition, where we validate dynamical scaling behavior, a broad regime of incoherent diffusion emerges, exhibiting characteristics similar to percolation phenomena and interacting many-body localized systems.

This study proposes a new cause-effect relationship within Markov decision processes based on the probability-raising principle. It begins by treating sets of states as both causes and effects, later expanding this framework to include regular path properties in those roles. The paper establishes the mathematical basis for these relations and evaluates their algorithmic characteristics. This evaluation encompasses algorithms for verifying cause conditions given a specific effect and determining the existence of probability-raising causes. Since the definition permits sub-optimal coverage, the research investigates quality metrics for causes derived from statistical analysis, such as recall, coverage ratio, and f-score. Additionally, the computational complexity associated with identifying optimal causes according to these metrics is examined.

This study investigates the decay-time-dependent charge-parity ($CP$) asymmetry in $D^0 \to K^+K^-$ and $D^0 \to \pi^+\pi^-$ decays using LHCb data from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 5.4 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis selects $D^0$ mesons produced in semileptonic $b$-hadron decays, where the muon's charge determines the initial flavor of the neutral $D$ meson. The measured asymmetries in the effective decay widths are $A_{\Gamma}(K^+K^-) = ( -4.3 \pm 3.6 \pm 0.5 )\times 10^{-4}$ and $A_{\Gamma}(\pi^+\pi^-) = ( 2.2 \pm 7.0 \pm 0.8)\times 10^{-4}$, with statistical and systematic uncertainties listed respectively. These findings are consistent with $CP$ symmetry; combining them with prior LHCb measurements results in $A_{\Gamma}(K^+K^-) = ( -4.4 \pm 2.3 \pm 0.6 )\times 10^{-4}$ and $A_{\Gamma}(\pi^+\pi^-) = ( 2.5 \pm 4.3 \pm 0.7)\times 10^{-4}$.

We present new mathematical and computational methodologies to construct a comprehensive and efficient algorithm for determining the non-properness set of polynomial maps defined on the plane. This specific subset of $\mathbb{K}^2$ (where $\mathbb{K}$ is either $\mathbb{C}$ or $\mathbb{R}$), termed the \emph{Jelonek set}, identifies regions where a dominant polynomial map $f: \mathbb{K}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{K}^2$ fails to be proper. Distinct from prior methods, our approach requires no assumptions regarding the map $f$. The algorithm leverages the sparsity of the polynomials by relying on the Minkowski sums of their Newton polytopes. Additionally, as a secondary contribution, we offer a more refined representation of the non-properness set as a union of algebraic or semi-algebraic sets associated with the edges of the Newton polytope, a result of independent significance. We also provide a detailed Boolean complexity analysis of the algorithm alongside a prototype implementation in \maple.

We examine the second-quantized entanglement Hamiltonian (EH) for diverse subregions within the ground states of multiple interacting lattice fermion and spin systems. While the connection between the EH and the underlying model Hamiltonian remains an open question for generic local ground states, this letter demonstrates that the EH is effectively local. Its primary components mirror those of the model Hamiltonian, modified by a smooth, spatially varying temperature. This holds true even for discrete lattice systems, models lacking emergent conformal or Lorentz symmetry, and subsystems with non-flat boundaries, despite relatively strong interactions. Furthermore, we establish that this local temperature decays inversely with the distance from the subsystem's boundary. Additionally, we identify subdominant EH terms, showing they are strongly suppressed away from the boundaries and remain relatively small near them.

This note addresses a significant barrier to realizing dS observer patch holography within string/M theory, uncovering a novel function for averaging in quantum gravity. The recently developed solvable $T\bar T(+\Lambda_2)$ deformation has enabled a precise microstate enumeration of the $dS_3$ cosmic horizon, successfully matching the refined Gibbons-Hawking entropy derived by Anninos et al. and yielding the accurate radial bulk geometry. On the gravitational side, this deformation positions the boundary immediately exterior to a black hole horizon, rendering it indistinguishable from the dS cosmic horizon and allowing a smooth transition to a bounded dS region. In the context of string/M theory, linking AdS/CFT to dS requires uplifts that alter internal topology, such as substituting an internal sphere $\mathbb{S}$ with a hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}$ while adjusting warp and conformal factors. We bridge these methodologies by demonstrating that internal averaging, occurring in the presence of a timelike boundary near the horizon, effectively neutralizes the discrepancies in extra dimensions between AdS black holes and dS solutions. This insight encourages a deeper exploration of timelike boundaries in (A)dS frameworks within string/M theory and initiates efforts to generalize Liouville walls as a viable approach.

Since lung cancer ranks among the most lethal diseases, early detection and diagnosis are vital for patient survival. However, traditional diagnosis is labor-intensive, demands specialist expertise, and suffers from notable inaccuracy. This study aims to develop a system that accurately detects, classifies, and segments lung lesions in CT scans. The proposed method automatically extracts features from CT images and classifies them using Ensemble Gradient Boosting algorithms. Furthermore, if a lesion is identified, it is segmented via a hybrid technique combining Fuzzy Clustering and Level Set methods. To train and evaluate the models, a dataset of CT images from patients in Mashhad, Iran, was assembled. The results demonstrate 96% accuracy on this dataset, suggesting that this approach can aid clinicians in diagnosing lung abnormalities and minimizing diagnostic errors.

The Iron Calorimeter (ICAL), a 51 kton magnetized detector planned for the India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO), is specifically engineered to detect muons with energies between 1 and 20 GeV. Its magnetic field allows for the separate measurement of $\mu^-$ and $\mu^+$ momenta arising from the charge current interactions of $\nu_\mu$ and $\bar\nu_\mu$ within the iron, a capability essential for determining neutrino mass ordering and other key ICAL objectives. Consequently, achieving high precision in magnetic field measurement is critical. Mini-ICAL, an 85-ton operational prototype located in Madurai, South India, serves as the testbed for this work. This paper details the initial measurement of the magnetic field in Mini-ICAL using Hall sensor printed circuit boards (PCBs). A dedicated calibration setup utilizing an electromagnet was developed for the Hall probes. The readout architecture, based on an Arduino Nano, manages channel selection for the PCB-mounted probes and converts analog voltage signals to digital outputs. Measurements were conducted in the small gaps between iron plates in the top layer of Mini-ICAL and in the air immediately outside the detector. The system achieved a precision exceeding 3%, with a sensitivity reaching approximately 0.03 kGauss for detecting small fringe fields external to the detector.

We employ a newly established high-resolution coherent probe spectroscopy technique to examine the dispersion of collective excitations within a polaritonic quantum fluid. By measuring the dispersion relation with exceptional energy and wavenumber precision, we calculate the fluid's speed of sound and confirm the role of the excitonic reservoir. We document the creation of collective excitations at negative energies along the ghost branch of the dispersion curve and identify signs of impending dynamical instabilities. These methodologies pave the way for accurate investigations into the quantum hydrodynamics of quantum fluids of light.

Wandering poses significant safety risks for individuals with dementia, often resulting in dangerous scenarios. To address this, we propose a method for the real-time automatic detection of wandering episodes that lead to getting lost. This approach utilizes GPS data to identify frequent locations and movement trajectories, employing a step that converts GPS coordinates into geohash sequences. By analyzing historical data to establish frequent and normal movement patterns, the system can subsequently detect anomalies in new, ongoing sequences. We evaluated the method using synthetic data to assess its capability in identifying frequent locations and compared its results against a leading alternative approach. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed method successfully identifies frequent locations and achieves superior performance, reaching an AUC of up to 0.99 with specific parameter configurations, thereby outperforming the state-of-the-art baseline.

This paper introduces a methodology for estimating actuator and sensor faults in nonlinear systems. The approach involves augmenting the system dynamics with an approximated ultra-local model, represented as a finite chain of integrators, for the fault vector, alongside the construction of a Nonlinear Unknown Input Observer (NUIO) for these augmented dynamics. Consequently, fault reconstruction is recast as a robust state estimation problem within the augmented state space, which comprises both the true state and the fault-related state. We establish sufficient conditions ensuring the existence of the observer and the stability of the estimation error dynamics, specifically guaranteeing asymptotic stability at the origin when no faults are present and Input-to-State Stability (ISS) in the presence of faults. Furthermore, the synthesis of observer gains is formulated as a semidefinite program that minimizes the L2-gain from model mismatch—arising from the approximated fault model—to the fault estimation error. Finally, simulations are provided to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methodology.

We introduce Scrybe, an example-driven synthesis tool for statically-typed functional languages that integrates $\lambda^2$-style top-down deductive reasoning with Smyth-style live bidirectional evaluation. During the synthesis process, example constraints are passed through sketches to prune and direct the search, allowing Scrybe to more effectively utilize available contextual functions. To assess the tool's performance, it was tested on a merged set of largely disjoint benchmarks from $\lambda^2$ and Myth. The results show that Scrybe successfully synthesizes the majority of the combined benchmark tasks.

The inflationary epoch of our Universe is characterized as semi-classical, describable within four-dimensional Einstein gravity augmented by quantum corrections motivated by string theory. These corrections encompass higher-order gravitational terms, such as Gauss-Bonnet and Chern-Simons contributions. This study investigates inflationary phenomenology driven by a scalar field incorporating quadratic curvature terms, specifically in light of the GW170817 observations. We derived the equations of motion directly from the gravitational action, resulting in a complex system of differential equations concerning the Hubble parameter and the inflaton field that resists analytical solution, even under minimal coupling conditions. Utilizing the GW170817 constraint that the speed of primordial gravitational waves equals the speed of light, alongside slow-roll approximations and the neglect of string corrections, we simplified these equations. Our analysis demonstrates that inflationary dynamics involving a Gauss-Bonnet term remain compatible with recent observational data. Furthermore, we show that the Chern-Simons term induces asymmetric generation and evolution of the two circular polarization states of gravitational waves. Finally, we present viable inflationary models consistent with observational limits, briefly exploring the possibility of a blue-tilted tensor spectral index.

Successfully applying enhanced sampling techniques in molecular dynamics simulations typically demands prior knowledge of an approximate reaction coordinate that captures the system's key mechanisms. This study demonstrates that the recently developed artificial intelligence-driven State Predictive Information Bottleneck (SPIB) method can learn such a coordinate as a deep neural network, even when data is derived from under-sampled trajectories. We illustrate the utility of this approach by achieving over 40 orders of magnitude in acceleration for two test biophysical systems using well-tempered metadynamics biased along the SPIB-derived reaction coordinate. These systems include chirality transitions from left- to right-handed forms in the synthetic protein (Aib)₉ and the permeation of asymmetric benzoic acid through a symmetric synthetic phospholipid bilayer. Beyond significantly speeding up dynamics and enabling transitions between different metastable states, the SPIB-based reaction coordinate also provides mechanistic insights into the processes governing these two critical challenges.

This brief note outlines a model that generalizes the Harmonic explorer [6], which may be of interest but is not intended for journal publication. The conjectured continuous model is expected to share the same left-passage probability as SLE$_k$, though it may generate a different curve.

The framework of Higgs inflation can be seamlessly integrated into the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM). In this setup, a specific linear combination of the two Higgs-doublet fields serves as the inflaton, featuring a non-minimal coupling to gravity. This coupling manifests within the low-energy effective superpotential, thereby altering the model's phenomenology at the electroweak scale. Although the field content remains identical to that of the standard NMSSM, the inflation-inspired variant introduces an additional contribution to the $\mu$ term beyond the singlet's vacuum expectation value. We investigate this expanded parameter space, identifying scenarios that exhibit distinct phenomenological features compared to the pure NMSSM. Particular emphasis is placed on electroweak vacuum stability and the parameter dependencies governing the Higgs and neutralino sectors. We highlight regions that produce a $125\,$GeV Higgs boson consistent with experimental data and align with constraints from searches for extra Higgs bosons. Finally, we examine how the non-minimal gravitational coupling influences Higgs mixing and subsequently affects the decay channels of Higgs bosons within this model.

This study investigates the one-loop dilatation operator within the holomorphic 3-scalar sector of the dynamical fishnet theory. Because the underlying field theory is non-unitary, this operator, referred to as the eclectic spin chain Hamiltonian, cannot be diagonalized. Consequently, the resulting spectrum of Jordan blocks generates logarithms in two-point functions, a hallmark of logarithmic conformal field theories. Earlier conjectures suggested that under specific filling conditions and generic couplings, the eclectic model's spectrum matches that of a simpler system known as the hypereclectic spin chain. We offer additional support for this conjecture and present a generating function that completely describes the Jordan block spectrum of the simplified model. Derived through purely combinatorial methods, this function is directly related to the q-binomial coefficient.

Legendre initially provided a proof attempt for the Law of Quadratic Reciprocity, but his 1797 version contained a flaw. Approximately 125 years later, Herman Teege offered the first rigorous demonstration of the hypothesis underlying that gap. Forty-eight years after Teege's work, Kenneth Rogers presented a second proof, albeit an implicit one. These contributions ultimately elevated Legendre's original attempt to the status of a complete proof. However, the literature lacks a detailed exposition of these specific demonstrations, a void that our paper aims to fill.

Based on a proton-proton collision dataset from the LHCb experiment with an integrated luminosity of 8.5 fb$^{-1}$, a new excited $\Xi_b^0$ resonance decaying into the $\Xi_b^-\pi^+$ final state has been observed. This state, identified as $\Xi_b(6227)^0$, exhibits a measured mass of $m(\Xi_b(6227)^0) = 6227.1^{\,+1.4}_{\,-1.5}\pm0.5$ MeV and a natural width of $\Gamma(\Xi_b(6227)^0) = 18.6^{\,+5.0}_{\,-4.1}\pm1.4$ MeV, with uncertainties accounting for both statistical and systematic effects. The production rate of the $\Xi_b(6227)^0$ relative to the $\Xi_b^-$ baryon, within the kinematic range of $2<\eta<5$ and $p_{\rm T}<30$ GeV, is determined to be $\frac{f_{\Xi_b(6227)^0}}{f_{\Xi_b^-}}{\mathcal{B}}(\Xi_b(6227)^0\to\Xi_b^-\pi^+) = 0.045\pm0.008\pm0.004$, where ${\mathcal{B}}$ denotes the branching fraction and $f$ represents fragmentation fractions. Additionally, refined measurements for the mass and natural width of the previously observed $\Xi_b(6227)^-$ state, as well as the mass of the $\Xi_b^-$ baryon, are provided. These updated values are notably more precise than prior reports and remain consistent with them.

Drawing on six years of evaluation data, this study examines the medium- and long-term effects of university-mentored projects focused on advanced space science, astronomy, and particle physics on students, teachers, and schools. After completing six-month-long projects, 14- to 18-year-old students reported significantly heightened confidence in scientific topics and methods, a finding supported by teacher observations. While the projects notably boosted aspirations in physics, general science aspirations—which were already high—remained stable or were reinforced. A follow-up evaluation three years later indicated that these experiences were lasting, with students utilizing the benefits in their subsequent university studies. Data on student destinations reveals that participation in research made them more likely to pursue physics and STEM degrees than anticipated. Furthermore, instances of co-created novel physics research within the PRiSE program had a profound impact on both student co-authors and peers from other schools. Teachers also benefited, experiencing improvements in their knowledge, skills, and pedagogy, with positive ripple effects throughout their wider schools. These outcomes suggest that similar "research in schools" initiatives could effectively increase the uptake and diversity of physics and STEM in higher education while significantly enhancing the STEM environment within schools.

This study examines multivariate second-order stochastic mappings indexed by an abstract set $\Lambda$, focusing on their relationship with operator covariance functions. It provides characterizations of the associated normal Hilbert modules or Hilbert spaces using reproducing kernel structures. These characterizations aim to unify various concepts within the field and offer a framework for extending the well-established theory of multivariate second-order stochastic processes and random fields to include multivariate second-order random distribution fields and stochastic measures. Specifically, the paper discusses an extension of the general Wold-type decomposition within this context.

Coded-caching offers a promising approach to mitigate peak backhaul link demands during periods of high traffic. This letter investigates the impact of adaptive transmission on coded-caching networks, with a specific focus on alleviating backhaul congestion. We propose adaptive rate and power allocation strategies designed to maximize the network's successful transmission probability—the likelihood that all cache nodes correctly decode their intended signals. Additionally, we analyze how various message decoding and buffering schemes influence system performance. Our findings demonstrate that the efficacy of coded-caching networks is significantly influenced by both rate/power allocation and the chosen decoding/buffering mechanisms.

Higher-order moments of net-baryon distributions serve as valuable indicators for the QCD critical point and associated fluctuations in relativistic heavy ion collisions. Using a simplified model, we examine how net-proton distributions in the central rapidity region vary with collision energy and centrality. This model incorporates baryon stopping and pair production effects, with dependencies on these factors parameterized based on physical reasoning. We present predictions for net-proton distributions in Au+Au and Pb+Pb collisions at various centralities and energies ($\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 39 and 2760 GeV, respectively) derived from the parameterized model. Finally, we suggest that the validity of this model can be tested by analyzing net-proton distributions in non-central rapidity regions across different collision centralities and energies.

We introduce a practical approach to radiometrically calibrate cameras using readily accessible gaseous tritium light sources (betalights). By combining the known photon flux of these sources with measurements of gain (conversion factor) and read noise, we can accurately determine quantum efficiency. This setup is easily reproducible using a 3D printer and three low-cost components. As it is compatible with standard image sensors, we believe this method holds significant potential as a valuable tool for both microscopy facilities and optical laboratories.

This study examines magnetic field measurements from the initial six Parker Solar Probe (PSP) encounters, alongside three Helios fast streams and two Ulysses south polar passes, spanning heliocentric distances of $0.1\lesssim R\lesssim 3$ au. Utilizing this dataset, we statistically investigate how switchbacks of varying periods and amplitudes evolve with distance from the Sun. Our analysis compares the radial trends in magnetic field variances against the mean square amplitudes of switchbacks and quantifies the radial progression of cumulative switchback counts per kilometer. We observe that switchback amplitudes diminish more rapidly than general turbulent fluctuations, a pattern consistent with the radial decline of the mean magnetic field. This behavior may indicate amplitude saturation or serve as a signature of decay processes affecting large-amplitude Alfvénic fluctuations in the solar wind. Furthermore, we identify that the evolution of switchback occurrence is scale-dependent: the proportion of longer-duration switchbacks rises with distance, while that of shorter ones falls. This suggests that switchback dynamics in the inner heliosphere involve a complex interplay between in-situ generation and decay. Finally, while we confirm that solar wind expansion can generate switchbacks, we cannot exclude the possibility that other types of switchbacks originate closer to the Sun.

A central challenge in the prediction theory of discrete-time second-order stationary processes $X(t)$ involves characterizing the asymptotic behavior of the optimal linear mean squared error when predicting $X(0)$ based on observations $X(t)$ for $-n \le t \le -1$ as $n$ approaches infinity. This behavior relies on the regularity (specifically whether the process is deterministic or nondeterministic) and the dependence structure of the observed process $X(t)$. This paper addresses the problem for both deterministic and nondeterministic cases, reviewing recent findings with a specific emphasis on the less-explored domain of deterministic processes. We find that for nondeterministic processes, the asymptotic prediction error is governed by the dependence structure of $X(t)$ and the differential characteristics of its spectral density $f$, whereas for deterministic processes, it is dictated by the geometric properties of the spectrum of $X(t)$ and the singularities of its spectral density $f$.

We calculate the quantum variance of holomorphic cusp forms along vertical geodesics using smooth, compactly supported test functions. This variance corresponds to an averaged shifted-convolution problem, which we assess asymptotically. Our analysis reveals an off-diagonal term that precisely aligns with a specific diagonal term, a characteristic reminiscent of $L$-function moments.

This study investigates the structural, electronic, magnetic, and transport characteristics of the equiatomic quaternary alloy NbVTiAl. X-ray diffraction (XRD) data, specifically the lack of (111) and (200) peaks, verifies an A2-type structure. Magnetization results reveal a high Curie temperature alongside a negligible magnetic moment ($\sim 10^{-3} \mu_B/f.u.$), suggesting fully compensated ferrimagnetism. Resistivity measurements as a function of temperature confirm the material's metallic nature. While ab-initio calculations on a fully ordered NbVTiAl structure predict nearly half-metallic behavior with approximately 90% spin polarization and a net magnetic moment of 0.8 $\mu_B/f.u.$, these findings starkly contrast with experimental observations. A primary goal of this work is to address and elucidate the persistent gap between theory and experiment regarding magnetization in V-based quaternary Heusler alloys. To achieve deeper insight, we simulated various disordered states and analyzed their impact on magnetic and electronic properties. We attribute the discrepancy to A2 disorder, evidenced by our XRD data, which also introduces finite states at the Fermi level, thereby altering the system's spin polarization.

We demonstrate the reliable ignition of helium-diluted hydrogen-oxygen mixtures at high pressures (exceeding 20–30 bar) using an unfocused Nd:YAG laser. These results achieve ignition at laser irradiances several orders of magnitude lower than the minimum thresholds previously reported in literature. By installing a mirror within a cylindrical vessel and pressurizing it to 100 bar with non-combustible H₂-He or O₂-He mixtures, we measured the pressure-dependent absorptivity of the combustible He-H₂-O₂ blend. Our findings indicate no detectable laser signal absorption by the medium across the entire pressure range, limited only by the experimental apparatus sensitivity (approximately 1% of the laser irradiance). These results support the theory that ignition is initiated by seed electrons generated through autofocusing ionization of dust or impurities within the gas.

Data analysis tasks seldom happen in isolation. In intelligence analysis, where experts build a shared understanding, clear communication of how insights evolve is essential to align collaborators. Provenance offers a promising method for conveying analytic sensemaking by detailing interactions and summarizing the steps taken to reach conclusions. However, there are currently no universal guidelines for communicating provenance across different contexts. This study examines how presenting provenance information influences the conclusions drawn and the strategies employed by novice analysts. Through a 30-minute, open-ended textual exploration scenario, we qualitatively assessed how varying types of provenance—specifically data coverage and interaction history—impact analysts' confidence in their conclusions, their tendency to repeat work, data filtering, identification of relevant information, and general investigation strategies. Our findings indicate that data coverage (tracking what was interacted with) provides necessary context without restricting individual investigative freedom. Conversely, while interaction history (tracking when items were interacted with) does not significantly increase mimicry, it requires more time to comprehend comfortably, evidenced by lower confidence in conclusions and reduced effectiveness in gathering relevant information. These results provide empirical evidence on how provenance summarizations shape analyst behavior.

Continuous sign language recognition (cSLR) is a critical task that converts sign language videos into ordered sequences of glosses. Given the lack of explicit alignment between video frames and glosses, it is essential to capture fine-grained gloss-level details. While previous research has successfully utilized one-dimensional convolutional networks (1D-CNNs) to temporally fuse sequential frames, CNNs inherently ignore similarity or dissimilarity, limiting their ability to capture consistent semantics within adjacent frames. To overcome this limitation, we propose adaptively fusing local features based on temporal similarity. Specifically, we introduce the Multi-scale Local-Temporal Similarity Fusion Network (mLTSF-Net), which operates in three steps: first, for each video frame, we identify similar neighboring frames using multi-scale receptive fields to handle varying gloss durations; second, we apply position-aware convolution to temporally process each scale of selected frames to ensure temporal consistency; and third, we generate an enhanced frame-wise representation by fusing multi-scale results through a content-dependent aggregator. Trained in an end-to-end manner, our model achieves competitive performance on the RWTH-PHOENIX-Weather 2014 dataset, matching or exceeding several state-of-the-art approaches.

When robots operate alongside other intelligent entities, such as humans or fellow robots, they must infer the actions of their neighbors to successfully complete assigned tasks. However, due to limited computational power, these agents often act irrationally. Consequently, predicting optimal behaviors is both computationally expensive and prone to error. Addressing this, we discard the assumption of perfect rationality and integrate the concept of bounded rationality, viewed through information theory, into game-theoretic models. This enables robots to anticipate and respond to sub-optimal behaviors within their own resource constraints. Specifically, bounded rationality quantifies an agent's information processing capacity as the Kullback-Leibler divergence between nominal and optimized stochastic policies, with the resulting bounded-optimal policy derived via efficient importance sampling. Validated through both simulated and real-world multi-robot navigation experiments, this framework demonstrates the ability to model varying degrees of rationality in other agents and compute feasible strategies under computational limits.

Boosting functions as an ensemble technique within the PAC learning framework that transforms weak learners into strong ones. Freund and Schapire created the Godel prize-winning AdaBoost algorithm, which boosts learners producing binary hypotheses. Recently, Arunachalam and Maity introduced the first quantum boosting algorithm, QAdaBoost, offering comparable theoretical assurances. As a quantum variant of AdaBoost restricted to binary hypotheses, QAdaBoost provides a quadratic speedup regarding the VC-dimension of the weak learner's hypothesis class, though it performs polynomially worse concerning the learner's bias. Izdebski et al. raised an open question about boosting quantum weak learners that output non-binary hypotheses. This study addresses that challenge by developing QRealBoost, inspired by the classical RealBoost algorithm. The primary difficulty lay in establishing provable guarantees for convergence, generalization, and quantum acceleration, accounting for the noise and probabilistic nature of quantum subroutines. We demonstrate that QRealBoost maintains the quadratic advantage of QAdaBoost over AdaBoost while additionally achieving a polynomial speedup over QAdaBoost in terms of learner bias and the time required to learn the target concept class. Finally, empirical evaluations on quantum simulators using subsets of the MNIST and Breast Cancer Wisconsin datasets compare QRealBoost's convergence performance against QAdaBoost, AdaBoost, and RealBoost, yielding encouraging results.

Analyzing EEG signals for clinical use remains difficult, and existing methods have largely ignored sex-specific differences. This study utilizes machine learning to investigate sex-related variations in EEG data, validating the existence of these effects through successful classification of resting-state signals based on brain connectivity. Specifically, coherence between particular sensor channels was identified as a strong predictor of sex.

In 1993, Coifman, Lions, Meyer, and Semmes inquired if the Jacobian operator and related compensated compactness measures map their natural domains onto the real-variable Hardy space $\mathcal{H}^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$. This work offers an axiomatic, Banach space geometric methodology to address this question specifically for quadratic operators. Furthermore, we advance understanding of the primary unresolved case concerning the Jacobian equation in two dimensions.

Analyzing customer behaviors embedded within transactional data holds significant commercial potential for the grocery retail sector. Daily, consumers execute millions of transactions to fulfill distinct shopping requirements. Because product availability fluctuates by location based on local supply and demand, it is crucial to examine transactions within their specific store and regional contexts. Topic modeling serves as a robust analytical tool for this purpose, uncovering frequently co-purchased items and representing transactions as combinations of topics. This study employs the Segmented Topic Model (STM) to isolate customer behaviors nested within individual stores. Beyond generating topics and transaction summaries, STM produces store-level topical summaries that help identify regional patterns. We summarized the STM posterior distribution by processing multiple samples and selecting semantic modes as recurrent topics. Furthermore, we applied linear Gaussian process regression to model topic prevalence across the United Kingdom, incorporating spatial autocorrelation. Applied to a dataset from a major UK grocery chain, our approach demonstrates that shopping behaviors exhibit regional variation, with nearby stores often showing similar demand patterns.

TinyML has gained significant traction amidst the ubiquity of data, yet the most valuable datasets require stringent privacy and security protections. Furthermore, deploying TinyML hardware in practical scenarios faces substantial memory and communication limitations that conventional machine learning approaches cannot adequately resolve. Addressing these hurdles, we introduce TinyFedTL, marking the inaugural implementation of federated transfer learning on a resource-constrained microcontroller.

Complex Event Processing systems are limited by the expressive capabilities of their respective languages; some support only instantaneous events, others only durative ones, and while a few exceptions support both, they typically omit interval relations found in Allen's interval algebra. This paper introduces a novel logic-based temporal language designed specifically for Complex Event Processing, enabling the representation of both instantaneous and durative phenomena along with their temporal relationships. We validate the language's expressiveness through a maritime use case involving events of interest and analyze its execution semantics for stream processing, culminating in the presentation of the `Phenesthe` implementation prototype.

This note introduces a novel family of quasi-symmetric functions known as LLT cumulants and examines their characteristics. By employing an algebraic framework for conditional cumulants, we define these functions and demonstrate that Macdonald cumulants possess an explicit positive expansion in terms of LLT cumulants associated with ribbon shapes, thereby extending the classical decomposition of Macdonald polynomials. Furthermore, we establish a natural combinatorial interpretation where the LLT cumulant of a specific directed graph corresponds to a weighted generating function for the colorings of its subgraphs. Utilizing this graph-theoretic perspective, we prove several positivity results, including monomial positivity, positivity within fundamental quasisymmetric functions, and related positivity regarding the coefficients of Schur polynomials indexed by hook shapes. Additionally, we establish $e$-positivity for vertical-shape LLT cumulants following the variable shift $q \to q+1$, which refines a recent finding by Alexandersson and Sulzgruber. Collectively, these findings support our conjecture regarding the Schur-positivity of LLT cumulants; we further show that this conjecture would imply the Schur-positivity of Macdonald cumulants. Finally, we provide additional evidence for the conjecture by proving it for LLT cumulants of melting lollipops, a result that refines recent work by Huh, Nam, and Yoo.

Sequence-to-sequence automatic speech recognition (ASR) models demand vast datasets to achieve high performance, which has recently sparked significant interest in unsupervised and semi-supervised training approaches. Building on recent findings that highlight the benefits of cycle-consistency and related methods for semi-supervised learning, this study introduces a novel semi-supervised loss function. This approach integrates ASR with Text-to-Speech (TTS) models to create training procedures and losses that effectively utilize unpaired speech and/or text data. Specifically, the proposed method combines an end-to-end differentiable ASR$\rightarrow$TTS loss with a TTS$\rightarrow$ASR loss. By leveraging both unpaired speech and text modalities, the technique surpasses recently proposed related methods in terms of Word Error Rate (%WER). We present extensive analyses examining the effects of data volume and the interplay between speech and text modalities, demonstrating consistent improvements across the WSJ and Librispeech corpora. The accompanying code is available within ESPnet to facilitate the reproduction of these experiments.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly the focus of research due to their capacity for delivering flexible and cost-effective ubiquitous connectivity. To enhance UAV performance further, they must integrate with advanced technologies such as non-orthogonal multiple access (NOM A) and millimeter wave (mmWave), both of which offer high spectral efficiency (SE). Since traditional model-based techniques struggle to manage UAVs effectively, artificial intelligence (AI) has become an essential innovation for their operation. However, designing an AI-driven approach that adaptively allocates radio resources and positions UAVs in 3D space to satisfy specific communication goals remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces ProSky, a framework based on the Neuroevolution of Augmenting Topologies (NEAT), designed to manage NOMA-mmWave-UAV networks. ProSky demonstrates substantial performance gains compared to model-based methods. Furthermore, it surpasses a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) scheme by learning 5.3 times faster while achieving superior spectral efficiency (SE) and energy efficiency (EE) with reasonable fairness. The ProSky source code is available at: https://github.com/Fouzibenfaid/ProSky.

Probabilistic model checking determines probabilities and expected values concerning specific behaviors within Markov models. As a formal verification method used for critical systems, it is assumed that these checkers produce accurate outcomes. However, to ensure scalability and efficiency, they rely on finite-precision floating-point arithmetic, which introduces rounding errors that can accumulate and interact in unpredictable manners. This paper demonstrates how to achieve both speed and correctness in probabilistic model checking by leveraging hardware capabilities to manage the direction of rounding in floating-point operations. We discuss the challenges of implementing correct rounding from high-level programming languages, present our solution within the 'mcsta' model checker of the Modest Toolset, and illustrate the balance between performance and accuracy through extensive experiments across various operating systems and CPU architectures.

This paper introduces a technique for estimating an acoustic field from discrete microphone data, utilizing a kernel-interpolation approach previously applied in various contexts. While this method allows for the integration of prior knowledge regarding source directions via a directional weighting kernel to enhance estimation precision, previous research has relied on empirically determined weighting parameters. To address scenarios where source direction information is uncertain, we propose an optimization method that adjusts these parameters based on observation values. The algorithm achieves this by discretizing the parameters and representing the kernel function as a weighted sum of sub-kernels, with an investigation into two regularization types for the weights: $L_1$ and $L_2$. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this proposed approach yields superior estimation accuracy compared to methods lacking kernel learning.

This work offers a thorough classification of knot and link invariants linked to irreducible representations of \uqslN{} under the condition that the quantization parameter $q$ is a root of unity. We show that, beyond the standard HOMFLY-PT invariants tied to representations with highest and lowest weights, non-trivial invariants arise exclusively from nilpotent representations involving specific parameters. Furthermore, we define these invariants and examine their connections to standard invariants at distinct parameter values.

This research examines the fluctuations and limiting distributions of free energy in mean-field spin glass models featuring Ising spins subjected to weak external fields. We demonstrate that at high temperatures, the strength of the external field, defined as $h \approx \rho N^{-\alpha}$ where $\rho, \alpha \in (0,\infty)$, divides the system into three distinct sub-regimes. In the super-critical regime ($\alpha < 1/4$), the variance of the log-partition function scales approximately as $N^{1-4\alpha}$. At the critical threshold ($\alpha = 1/4$), fluctuations remain of constant order but are dependent on $\rho$. Conversely, in the sub-critical regime ($\alpha > 1/4$), the variance stabilizes at $\Theta(1)$ and becomes independent of $\rho$. We explicitly derive the asymptotic mean and variance across all three regimes and establish Gaussian central limit theorems. Our methodology relies on two primary strategies. The first employs quadratic coupling and Guerra's interpolation scheme for Gaussian disorder, a technique extendable to various spin glass models, though it is currently limited to very high temperatures. The second utilizes a cluster-based approach for general symmetric disorders, originally introduced by Aizenman, Lebowitz, and Ruelle for the zero-field case. Previously, it was thought this method failed when an external field was present; however, we show that with a novel cluster structure, it remains effective provided the field is not excessively strong. Specifically, we prove the central limit theorem up to the critical temperature for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) model when $\alpha \ge 1/4$. Furthermore, we explore the versatility of this cluster-based method by deriving analogous results for both the multi-species SK model and the diluted SK model.

We investigate two-dimensional soliton solutions within the $CP^2$ nonlinear $\sigma$-model featuring a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. Initially, we establish this model as the continuous limit of an $SU(3)$ tilted ferromagnetic Heisenberg model defined on a square lattice. By incorporating an additional potential term into the resulting Hamiltonian, we derive exact soliton solutions for specific parameter configurations, where the vacuum state corresponds to a spin nematic phase. Furthermore, for a broader spectrum of coupling constants, we generate numerical solutions that exhibit asymptotic decay characteristics identical to the exact analytical solutions, converging toward the same spin nematic state.

This article offers an elementary introduction to the theory of minimal surfaces in Euclidean spaces $\mathbb R^n$ for $n\ge 3$, utilizing solely basic calculus of functions of several variables suitable for a standard second-year undergraduate analysis course for Mathematics students at European universities. No prior understanding of differential geometry is required.

Traditional image compression techniques generally prioritize pixel-level fidelity, often overlooking the efficacy of subsequent AI applications. To address this limitation, we introduce Semantic-Assisted Image Compression (SAIC), designed to preserve semantic consistency and thereby enhance downstream AI task performance. This is achieved by training the compression network with a semantic-level loss function, specifically utilizing a gradient-based semantic weights (GSW) mechanism that directly incorporates the perceptual outcomes of downstream AI tasks. Furthermore, we propose a semantic-level distortion metric to quantify the retention of semantic information throughout compression. Experimental findings demonstrate that SAIC retains superior semantic information and delivers improved results for downstream AI tasks compared to both traditional deep learning approaches and advanced perceptual methods at equivalent compression ratios.
This pedagogical review examines the perturbative use of field-theoretic and path-integral techniques to compute moments of the probability density function for stochastic differential equations.

We examine the algebra $\dot\Sigma(\mathcal L)$, which arises from inner-limit derivations acting on the ${\rm GICAR}$ algebra of a fermion gas occupying an aperiodic Delone set $\mathcal L$. Assuming standard physical conditions—specifically finite interaction range, Galilean invariance, and continuity with respect to the aperiodic lattice—we show that the Fock representation image of $\dot \Sigma(\mathcal L)$ can be completed to form a groupoid-solvable pro-$C^\ast$-algebra. This finding represents the initial step toward applying $K$-theoretic methods for separable $C^\ast$-algebras to the study of interacting fermions.

Online music platforms host tens of millions of tracks, encompassing a vast array of musical genres alongside non-musical audio like podcasts and radio dramas. This immense scale and diversity make it challenging for users to locate relevant content, rendering precise recommendations essential for a high-quality user experience. This paper introduces a method for calculating track-to-track similarities by combining collaborative filtering signals with side information. Evaluated on a dataset from the music streaming service SoundCloud, our approach surpasses the widely used implicit matrix factorization technique. The implementation of this method is open-sourced and can be utilized for related item-item recommendation tasks that incorporate side information.

Detecting lepton number ($L$) violation by two units at particle colliders would confirm the Majorana nature of neutrinos. This study investigates $L$-violating signals within two prominent neutrino mass frameworks: the type-II seesaw model, where small masses emerge at tree level, and the Zee model, where they arise at one-loop level. Specifically, we examine $L$-violation signatures at the LHC resulting from the process $pp \to \ell^{\pm}\ell^{\prime \pm}$ + jets in these scenarios. Our analysis indicates that the high-luminosity LHC, with an integrated luminosity of $3~\text{ab}^{-1}$, could probe $L$-violation in the type-II seesaw model for triplet scalar masses up to 700 GeV and in the Zee model for charged scalar masses up to 4.8 TeV.

In any arbitrary D-dimensional spacetime, we demonstrate that the classical gauge symmetry transformations of the St$\ddot u$ckelberg-modified massive Abelian 3-form theory are generated by first-class constraints. These classical transformations are elevated to their quantum equivalents, the Becchi-Rouet-Stora-Tyutin (BRST) and anti-BRST symmetries, which remain invariant under coupled (yet equivalent) Lagrangian densities. Utilizing Noether's theorem, we establish the conserved and nilpotent (anti-)BRST charges. Furthermore, we confirm the existence of ghost-scale symmetry, derive the associated conserved ghost charge, and deduce the standard BRST algebra. A key contribution of this study is the derivation of (anti-)BRST invariant Curci-Ferrari (CF) type restrictions, which arise from the necessity of absolute anticommutativity among the conserved, nilpotent (anti-)BRST charges and the direct equivalence of the coupled (anti-)BRST invariant Lagrangian densities.

Digital keys are a cornerstone of numerous hardware and software security systems, yet they are constrained to binary values and remain vulnerable when stored in conventional memory. This paper introduces pHGen, a novel key generation mechanism based on emerging technology that exploits chemical reactions to induce potential shifts in ion-sensitive field-effect transistors (ISFETs). By immersing these transistors in specific pH buffer solutions (the keys), the ISFETs' threshold voltages are adjusted accordingly. To ensure effective detection of this chemical data, we developed a dedicated readout circuit designed for stable voltage threshold monitoring. We validated the practicality of this approach by applying pHGen to logic locking, a method for protecting hardware integrity. This technique transcends binary limitations, marking the initial step toward leveraging the multi-valued voltage thresholds of ISFETs governed by chemical inputs. Ultimately, the pHGen method represents a significant advancement in utilizing sophisticated, bio-inspired analog keys to secure future electronic systems.

The filamentary structure of accretion streams surrounding embedded sources indicates that protostellar disks undergo heterogeneous infall from their star-forming environment, aligning with accretion patterns observed in top-down star-cluster formation simulations. This process is expected to generate disk substructures—such as rings, gaps, and spirals—that high-resolution imaging surveys continue to detect in both embedded Class 0/I and later Class II sources. We conduct a parameter study on anisotropic infall, utilizing properties of accretion flows onto protostellar cores derived from numerical simulations, while varying the specific angular momentum and geometric configuration of incoming material. Our findings demonstrate that anisotropic infall disrupts the disk and efficiently triggers the Rossby wave instability (RWI), creating vortices at the boundaries of the infall zone where matter accumulates. These vortices induce spiral waves and facilitate angular momentum transport; in certain models, this generates stresses equivalent to a viscosity parameter of $\alpha \sim 10^{-2}$. The resulting azimuthal shear establishes robust pressure bumps that impede the radial drift of dust grains, a finding supported by post-processing simulations of drift-dominated dust evolution. Furthermore, we explore how a self-consistent anisotropic infall model explains the formation of millimeter rings in outer disks and the creation of compact dust disks, both of which are consistent with observations of embedded sources.

Spiral waves represent widespread spatiotemporal patterns found across diverse excitable systems. In cardiac tissue, their emergence is linked to dangerous arrhythmias, making the analysis of their dynamics crucial. By tracking the spiral-wave tip (TT), researchers can uncover key dynamical characteristics, including periodicity and susceptibility to instability. This study demonstrates the application of a data-driven spectral-decomposition technique known as dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) to identify spiral tip trajectories in three scenarios: (1) homogeneous media, (2) heterogeneous media, and (3) environments with external noise. Our results indicate that the DMD-based TT approach (DMDTT) performs as well as or superior to the conventional isopotential-intersection method (IIM) across all three settings. Specifically: (1) Both methods capture TT patterns at small image-sampling intervals ($\tau$), yet IIM exhibits greater sensitivity to variations in $\tau$ than DMDTT. (2) While IIM produces TT patterns in heterogeneous media, it is often accompanied by scattered noisy points, an issue effectively suppressed by DMDTT. (3) DMDTT demonstrates superior robustness against external noise compared to IIM. Finally, we illustrate that DMD enables the reconstruction and prediction of the spatiotemporal evolution of spiral waves within the studied models.

Since irreducibility is essential for analyzing the ergodicity of stochastic dynamical systems, this paper establishes the irreducibility of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations subject to pure jump noise. Our findings are dimension-independent, and the requirements imposed on the driving noises are minimal. These results rely significantly on criteria previously developed by the authors and T. Zhang regarding irreducibility in stochastic equations driven by pure jump noise. As an application, we derive the ergodicity of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations, noting that our result encompasses the weakly dissipative case involving pure jump degenerate noise.

This paper investigates a specific class of stochastic differential equations driven by fractional Brownian motions with a Hurst parameter $H \in (1/2, 1)$, where the equations depend on their distributions. We first demonstrate the well-posedness of these equations and subsequently derive a general Bismut formula for the Lions derivative utilizing Malliavin calculus. As applications, we present Bismut formulas for both non-degenerate and degenerate scenarios, yielding estimates for the Lions derivative and the total variation distance between the probability laws of two solutions.

The Persistent Fault Attack (PFA), introduced at CHES 2018, is a novel Fault Attack (FA) technique capable of recovering the complete AES secret key even in Single-Byte-Fault conditions. Research indicates that traditional FA defenses, including Dual Modular Redundancy (DMR) and masking, fail to stop PFA. To address this, we introduce a rapid detection and fault correction algorithm designed to mitigate PFA. This method utilizes a fixed input-output pair for swift fault identification and employs two additional redundant tables to map adjacent S-box element relationships, enabling the correction of faulty S-box values. Experimental findings demonstrate that our approach effectively counters PFA in both Single-Byte-Fault and Multiple-Bytes-Fault scenarios. Compared to classical FA countermeasures, our algorithm offers superior protection against PFA with a time overhead 40% lower than existing solutions.

We define a full linearisation functor that maps a graded bundle of degree $k$—a specific type of graded manifold—to a $k$-fold vector bundle. We provide a complete characterization of this functor's image, demonstrating that it yields a subcategory of $k$-fold vector bundles comprising symmetric structures equipped with a family of morphisms indexed by the symmetric group ${\mathbb S}_k$. Notably, in the degree 2 case, this added structure defines a symplectical double vector bundle, representing the skew-symmetric counterpart to a metric double vector bundle. Furthermore, we examine the related scenario of fully linearising $N$-manifolds and illustrate how the full linearisation functor enables the "superisation" of a graded bundle.

This research combines potential energy formulations with deep learning to address partial differential equations related to the deformation of hyperelastic and viscoelastic materials. The proposed Deep Energy Method (DEM) is a self-contained, meshfree approach that accurately models three-dimensional mechanical behavior without needing time-consuming training data generation typically required by classical numerical techniques like the finite element method. After appropriate training, the method can predict responses almost instantaneously at any spatial coordinate within the physical domain. Consequently, DEM emerges as a promising standalone solution for solving partial differential equations describing mechanical deformation in materials and structural systems, as well as other physical phenomena.

Accurately forecasting the likelihood of non-performing loans is essential for banks to mitigate credit risk and make informed lending decisions. Traditionally, these choices rely on credit assessments, industry standards, repayment histories, and client demographics. This study evaluates the performance of various machine learning models—including Random Forest, Decision Trees, KNN, SVM, and XGBoost—using a dataset from a private bank in Ethiopia. Furthermore, inspired by this evaluation, we investigate different feature selection techniques to identify the most impactful variables for the bank. Our results indicate that XGBoost achieved the highest F1 score when applied to KMeans SMOTE over-sampled data. Additionally, we determined that an applicant's age, years of employment, and total income are the most significant predictors of credit risk, outweighing collateral-related features.

This paper describes the methodology employed in Task 1 of the 2018 ISIC Skin Lesion Analysis Towards Melanoma Detection challenge.
