A U-Net architecture was utilized for segmentation, with training strategies focused on two critical aspects: modifying the loss function to address the imbalance between background and foreground pixels, and implementing post-processing steps to refine the predicted contours.

Link prediction remains a critical challenge within graph-structured data. Capitalizing on the recent advancements of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), numerous GNN-based approaches have been developed to address this task. These models utilize the message-passing paradigm to derive node representations, heavily relying on existing link connectivity. However, a fundamental issue arises in link prediction: training links are observed, whereas testing links are absent, creating a disconnect in connectivity patterns and introducing bias into the learned representations. This phenomenon causes a dataset shift that significantly hampers model performance. This paper first highlights the dataset shift issue in link prediction and offers theoretical insights into the vulnerability of current methods. Subsequently, we introduce FakeEdge, a model-agnostic technique designed to bridge the topological gap between training and testing sets. Comprehensive experiments across diverse domains and datasets validate the effectiveness and superiority of FakeEdge.

This paper introduces the $\bar{N}(p,q)$ summable sequence spaces and derives fundamental results concerning them. We establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for infinite matrices $A$ to map these spaces into $X$, where $X$ represents $c_0$, $c$, or $\ell_{\infty}$. Furthermore, by employing the Hausdorff measure of noncompactness, we determine the necessary and sufficient conditions for the compactness of linear operators acting on these spaces.

This study explores the dark sector within a supersymmetric axion framework, featuring late-decaying gravitino or axino dark matter alongside axion dark radiation. In the early universe, the decay of the saxion—the scalar superpartner of the axion—generates significant entropy. This extra entropy serves two purposes: it dilutes the abundance of gravitino/axino dark matter to prevent the universe from overclosing and loosens the constraints on the post-inflation reheating temperature $T_{R}$. Concurrently, axion dark radiation produced by the saxion decay elevates the effective number of neutrino species ($N_{\rm eff}$), offering a potential resolution to the cosmological Hubble tension. In the late universe, the decay of these long-lived dark matter particles yields axions with MeV-scale kinetic energy. We examine the feasibility of detecting such energetic axions via the inverse Primakoff process ($a+A \to \gamma+ A$) in neutrino observatories like Hyper-Kamiokande.

This introductory editorial seeks to engage researchers and inspire innovative work within the interconnected domains of sociophysics and computational social science. We outline key challenges and potential avenues for future inquiry regarding social phenomena, specifically emphasizing opinion dynamics. The primary goal of this special issue is to provide a platform for physicists, mathematicians, engineers, and social scientists to present their ongoing research interests in social dynamics, while also gathering recent advancements and novel methodologies for analyzing social systems.

This study investigates sufficient conditions that guarantee the enhanced solvability of strong vector equilibrium problems through a variational framework. In this context, enhanced solvability refers not only to the existence of solutions that are strong relative to the partial ordering but also includes inequalities that estimate the distance to the solution set, known as error bounds. These estimates are vital for the first-order (tangential) approximation of the solution set and for deriving optimality conditions in mathematical programming with equilibrium constraints (MPEC). The methodology characterizes solutions as zeros or global minimizers of specific merit functions linked to the original problem. Consequently, the conventional use of KKM theory is supplanted by imposing appropriate conditions on the slopes of these merit functions. To ensure these conditions are verifiable, tools from nonsmooth analysis are utilized. Ultimately, this approach yields several conditions for the enhanced solvability of strong equilibrium problems, formulated using generalized (Bouligand) derivatives, convex normals, and various (Fenchel and Mordukhovich) subdifferentials.

We establish algorithmic findings demonstrating that several natural parameterized problems fall within the restricted-space classes Para-L and FPT+XL. The Para-L class includes problems solvable in $f(k)n^{O(1)}$ time with $g(k) + O(\log n)$ bits of space, where $k$ denotes the parameter, $n$ the input size, and $f$ and $g$ are computable functions. The FPT+XL class encompasses problems meeting the same time constraint but utilizing $g(k) \log n$ bits of space. While previous research on these classes has primarily addressed their structural properties and connections to other classes, our work complements this by providing Para-L and FPT+XL algorithms for a restricted Hitting Set problem, various graph deletion problems involving target classes with infinite forbidden set characterizations, multiple problems parameterized by vertex cover number, and the Feedback Vertex Set problem.

This study adapts a multi-person pose estimation architecture for deployment on edge devices. We adopt the bottom-up approach from OpenPose, the 2016 COCO Keypoints Challenge winner, due to its robustness and high quality across varying numbers of people in a frame. With our proposed network design and optimized post-processing, the complete solution achieves 28 fps on an Intel NUC 6i7KYB mini PC and 26 fps on a Core i7-6850K CPU. The network features 4.1M parameters and 9 GFLOPs of complexity, representing approximately 15% of the computational cost of the baseline two-stage OpenPose while maintaining nearly identical performance. Both the code and model are included in the Intel OpenVINO Toolkit.

We re-examine heavy neutral lepton models, specifically neutrissimos featuring transition magnetic moments, as candidates for the $4.8\sigma$ electron-like event excess observed by MiniBooNE. Through a comprehensive Monte Carlo analysis, we reassess the favored parameter space regions capable of explaining MiniBooNE's results, while also accounting for possible sterile neutrino oscillations at the eV scale. Subsequently, we establish stringent constraints on the model using neutrino-electron elastic scattering data from MINERvA. Our findings indicate that while MINERvA excludes a significant portion of the parameter space, viable solutions remain at the $2\sigma$ confidence level. Furthermore, a specialized MINERvA analysis would likely have the sensitivity to explore the entire MiniBooNE-preferred region within this theoretical framework.

The initial observation of an anomalous Josephson effect occurs in mesoscopic superconductor-normal metal-superconductor (SNS) junctions configured as a cross-shaped Andreev Interferometer, without the magnetic fields or spin-orbit interactions typically needed to break time-reversal and inversion symmetries. By analyzing conductance data from the out-of-equilibrium weak link, we identify a voltage-controlled spontaneous phase that mimics a $\varphi_0$-junction. The combined temperature and voltage dependencies, along with a dissipative component in the current-phase relationship, strongly indicate that the observed phenomenon is driven by electron-hole asymmetries.

We introduce a method for online speaker diarization that integrates incremental clustering with local diarization operating on a 500ms rolling buffer. Each stage of this pipeline leverages the robust capabilities of a newly developed end-to-end overlap-aware segmentation model to identify and isolate simultaneous speakers. Specifically, we adapt the statistics pooling layer from the x-vector architecture to reduce the influence of frames where the segmentation model detects concurrent speakers. Additionally, we extract cannot-link constraints from the initial segmentation phase to ensure that the incremental clustering step does not incorrectly merge distinct local speakers. Finally, we demonstrate how the system's latency can be tuned between 500ms and 5s to suit specific application needs, accompanied by a comprehensive analysis of how latency variations impact performance across the AMI, DIHARD, and VoxConverse datasets.

This study employs Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to resolve the radiative transfer equation and generate a synthetic spectrum for the Type Ia supernova SN 2011fe. The model operates under Local Thermodynamic Equilibrium (LTE) assumptions and incorporates nine chemical elements, accounting for physical processes such as approximate radiative equilibrium, bound-bound transitions, and the Doppler effect. Radioactive decay energy deposition is handled via a PINN-based gamma-ray scattering approximation. The resulting synthetic spectrum is evaluated against observed data, a spectrum produced by the Monte-Carlo radiative transfer code TARDIS, and the formal solution of the radiative transfer equation. We examine both the challenges and the potential of this deep-learning approach to solving radiative transfer equations. Specifically, PINNs hold the promise of simultaneously determining the radiation field and thermal state across spacetime for atmospheric problems. Our calculations represent initial progress toward this goal, though they currently rely on several approximations to remain computationally feasible given the nascent stage of PINN applications in atmospheric modeling.

Cognitive radio offers a viable approach to addressing the impending spectrum shortage. By employing spectrum sensing, these systems can locate unused spectrum gaps. Achieving high-resolution detection ensures that even the tiniest inactive spectral segments are efficiently exploited. This paper introduces a spectrum hole detection method that begins with coarse sensing to simultaneously identify occupied channels. Subsequently, a fine sensing technique pinpoints spectrum holes within those occupied bands. The proposed architecture utilizes a two-stage Frequency Response Masking (FRM) filter positioned between two Pascal structure-based sampling rate converters, enabling arbitrary bandwidth variation. This flexibility allows for high-resolution spectrum sensing through fine-grained hole detection. Notably, the proposed method achieves this high resolution without escalating hardware complexity. When compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions, the hardware complexity of this approach is found to be substantially lower.

It is established that the optimal Noether inequality $\mathrm{vol}(X) \ge \frac{4}{3}p_g(X) - \frac{10}{3}$ applies to all general type $3$-folds $X$ where $p_g(X) \ge 11$. This paper presents a full classification of such $3$-folds satisfying the equality by detailing the explicit structure of their relative canonical models; notably, this model aligns with the canonical model when $p_g(X) \ge 23$. Furthermore, we derive the second and third optimal Noether inequalities for $3$-folds of general type with $p_g(X) \ge 11$. These findings resolve two open questions posed by J. Chen, M. Chen, and C. Jiang, as well as an open problem in dimension three raised by J. Chen and C. Lai. A new phenomenon emerges, revealing a one-to-one correspondence between the three Noether inequalities and the three possible residues of $p_g(X)$ modulo $3$.

This study examines scalar decentralized average-cost infinite-horizon LQG problems involving two controllers, specifically targeting the fast-dynamics regime where the system's scalar eigenvalue is large. It is demonstrated that the performance of the best linear controllers can degrade by an arbitrary factor compared to the optimal performance. To address this, we propose a collection of finite-dimensional nonlinear controllers, proving that this set includes an easily identifiable solution that achieves a cost within a constant ratio of the optimal quadratic cost. The rationale for these nonlinear strategies stems from uncovering the connection between control information flow and wireless information transmission. Specifically, we establish a strong link between the high-SNR limit in wireless communications and the fast-dynamics scenario in decentralized control, arguing that the proposed nonlinear strategy leverages the generalized degree-of-freedom gain found in wireless theory. To rigorously substantiate this argument, we develop novel mathematical tools and concepts. Furthermore, to elucidate the relationship between infinite-horizon problems and generalized MIMO Witsenhausen's counterexamples, we introduce the concept of geometric slicing. Finally, to evaluate the performance of the nonlinear strategy, we employ an approximate-comb-lattice model for the pertinent random variables.

Recent anomalies observed in the LHCb lepton flavour universality measurements and the Fermilab muon anomalous magnetic moment suggest promising indications of new physics within the lepton sector. Given the tau lepton's significantly larger mass and shorter lifetime compared to the muon, it is theorized to interact more strongly with potential physics beyond the Standard Model. While tau leptons have traditionally been studied via their decay products due to their brief existence, at high energy scales, a substantial fraction of these leptons can experience time dilation, resulting in lifetimes long enough to travel visible distances ranging from centimeters to kilometers. This extended range offers a unique opportunity to probe new physics and high-energy cosmic rays. This article demonstrates the potential of tau physics by utilizing long-lived taus as both a "microscope" and a "macroscope" to measure the tau's anomalous magnetic moment with unprecedented precision and to detect high-energy cosmic neutrinos across the 1 TeV to 1 PeV energy spectrum.

We examine the circular velocity profiles of seven isolated, gas-rich ultradiffuse galaxies (UDGs). By assuming their dark matter halos follow either a Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) profile or a Read profile (which permits constant-density cores), we find that the resulting halo concentrations are consistently lower than the cosmological median, dropping as much as $-0.6$ dex (approximately $5\sigma$) in certain instances. Alternatively, comparable fits can be achieved using a density profile that scales approximately as $1/r^2$ at radii beyond a few kiloparsecs. Both scenarios necessitate that the radius of peak circular velocity ($R_{\rm max}$) be significantly larger than the median expectation. Surprisingly, IllustrisTDM dark-matter-only simulations reveal an overabundance of such large-$R_{\rm max}$ halos relative to Gaussian predictions; these halos form later and possess higher spins than median halos of similar mass. Notably, the inner densities of the most extreme late-forming halos exceed those of their NFW equivalents, producing a $\sim 1/r^2$ profile. However, the two well-resolved UDGs in our sample strongly favor lower central dark matter densities compared to the simulations. Furthermore, when compared to IllustrisTNG hydrodynamical simulations, there is a tension in simultaneously achieving sufficiently low circular velocities and sufficiently high halo masses to match the observations. Consequently, our findings suggest that gas-rich UDGs pose a substantial challenge to current galaxy formation models.

Recently, Simultaneously Transmitting and Reflecting Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (STAR-RISs) have emerged as a promising technology that enables sustainable communication by offering 360-degree coverage, new degrees of freedom for signal manipulation, and support for simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT). Drawing inspiration from these capabilities, this paper introduces a novel secure SWIPT system utilizing STAR-RIS assistance for downlink Multiple-Input Single-Output (MISO) Rate-Splitting Multiple Access (RSMA) networks. In this setup, the transmitter delivers information to legitimate receivers (IRs) while transmitting energy to untrusted energy receivers (UERs), which are also capable of eavesdropping on the IR streams. The study assumes perfect channel state information (CSI) for the IRs at the transmitter, whereas only imperfect CSI (ICSI) is available for the UERs. The primary objective is to maximize the worst-case sum secrecy rate (WCSSR) of the IRs, subject to total transmit power limits, a sum energy constraint for the UERs, and constraints on transmission and reflection coefficients. This is achieved through the joint optimization of precoders and STAR-RIS beamforming vectors. Since the resulting problem is non-convex with tightly coupled variables, the paper proposes a suboptimal two-step iterative algorithm based on the Sequential Parametric Convex Approximation (SPCA) method, where precoders and beamforming vectors are optimized alternately. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed RSMA-based algorithm enhances both the secrecy of confidential data and the overall spectral efficiency within STAR-RIS-aided networks.

Coordinated cyberattacks have recently become increasingly prevalent online. A notable example occurred in May 2017, when the WannaCry ransomware compromised over 300,000 systems across 150 nations within days, severely disrupting critical infrastructure. Current threat-sharing platforms struggle to keep pace with evolving attack strategies, even as enterprises increasingly deploy machine learning tools for local threat detection. This paper addresses the question of what data defenders can exchange between multiple networks to enable machine learning models to better adapt to new coordinated attacks. We introduce three information-sharing methodologies across two networks and demonstrate how this shared data enhances a machine-learning network-traffic model's capacity to detect evasive, self-propagating malware.

Recent observational data on neutron stars following the GW170817 event have significantly advanced our understanding of nuclear symmetry energy at high densities. Key findings include: (1) Twenty-four new analyses determine the slope parameter $L$ of nuclear symmetry energy at saturation density $\rho_0$ to be approximately $L\approx 57.7\pm 19$ MeV at 68\% confidence, a result consistent with its fiducial value; (2) Sixteen new analyses estimate the curvature $K_{\rm{sym}}$ at roughly $K_{\rm{sym}}\approx -107\pm 88$ MeV; (3) Nine new analyses of neutron star observables extract the magnitude of nuclear symmetry energy at $2\rho_0$ as $E_{\rm{sym}}(2\rho_0)\approx 51\pm 13$ MeV at 68\% confidence, aligning with previous heavy-ion reaction results and state-of-the-art nuclear many-body theory predictions; (4) Although canonical neutron star data alone do not tightly constrain nuclear symmetry energy above approximately $2\rho_0$, NICER's recent observation of PSR J0740+6620 (mass $2.08\pm 0.07$ $M_{\odot}$, radius $12.2-16.3$ km) establishes a tight lower limit for the radius ($R_{2.01}=12.2$ km) at 68\% confidence, thereby setting a strict lower bound for the symmetry energy at densities exceeding $2\rho_0$; (5) Bayesian inferences incorporating models with a first-order hadron-quark phase transition suggest that such a phase transition shifts both $L$ and $K_{\rm{sym}}$ to higher values, albeit with increased uncertainties; and (6) The high-density behavior of nuclear symmetry energy significantly influences the minimum frequency required to rotationally support the secondary component of GW190814, which has a mass between 2.50 and 2.67 $M_{\odot}$, representing the fastest and most massive pulsar identified to date.

High-energy dual-energy X-ray Digital Radiography (DR) is primarily employed for cargo material identification. This paper outlines the technology's evolution and underlying principles, detailing our system's data processing workflow. The system transforms raw data into dual-energy transparency images, where material categories at every pixel are determined using a classification curve linked to the X-ray energy spectrum. To calibrate this curve, our approach combines a fundamental calibration step with a real-time correction mechanism to boost classification precision. Furthermore, image segmentation and denoising techniques are utilized to refine the visuals, while colorization enriches the informational content. Preliminary results indicate that our methods successfully achieve the intended outcomes.

This exposition introduces quantum permutation groups by proposing an alternative to the traditional 'Gelfand picture' for compact quantum groups. Drawing inspiration from algebraic quantum mechanics, this perspective interprets states on the algebra of continuous functions defined on a quantum permutation group as quantum permutations themselves. Such an interpretation facilitates discussions regarding elements within a compact quantum permutation group and clarifies the distinctions between deterministic, random, and quantum permutations. The approach is demonstrated through examples including the Kac-Paljutkin quantum group, the duals of finite groups, and other phenomena associated with finite quantum groups.

Recent observations have identified numerous systems containing Earth-mass planets orbiting late M dwarfs, where most orbits are near commensurabilities, indicating that planets were likely trapped in resonant chains during the formation around low-mass stars. This study examines the formation of such resonant multiple-planet systems around low-mass stars using a time-evolution model based on pebble accretion in the early disk phase, adapting the TRAPPIST-1 formation model proposed by Ormel et al. (2017). Our simulations demonstrate that the protoplanet appearance timescale is critical for determining both the total number of planets and their specific trapped resonances: longer timescales result in fewer planets that settle into more widely spaced resonances. We identify a specific range of protoplanet appearance timescales required to form stable multiple-planet systems in resonant chains, a range that varies with stellar mass and disk size. Consequently, we propose that the protoplanet appearance timescale is a fundamental parameter for understanding the formation of resonant multiple-planet systems around low-mass stars, and we also address the composition of the planets within our model.

Systems can be represented either as operational models, which explicitly define states and state transitions, or as axiomatic models, which are defined solely by a collection of invariants. Most formal verification techniques, such as IC3 and invariant synthesis, are tailored for operational models and are generally not applicable to axiomatic ones. Additionally, since no prior approach exists for automatically converting axiomatic models into operational ones, researchers have had to manually construct these equivalents and verify their consistency. This paper advances the state of the art in automating this conversion. We demonstrate that general axioms within the $\mu$spec framework cannot be translated into equivalent finite-state operational models. Instead, we identify specific constraints on $\mu$spec axioms that allow for the feasible generation of such operational equivalents. Practically, we present a methodology for automatically translating $\mu$spec axioms into finite-state automata-based operational models. The effectiveness of our approach is validated by using the generated models to verify ordering properties in three RTL designs.

Primordial black holes (PBHs) are theorized to arise from the collapse of overdense regions created by significant scalar curvature perturbations during the radiation-dominated epoch. Despite numerous independent observations over the last few decades, the fundamental nature of dark matter (DM) remains elusive. Recently, PBHs as a candidate for DM have gained attention because they offer a compelling explanation for the binary black hole merger events detected by LIGO/VIRGO and may play a crucial role in the DM sector. During their formation, PBHs generate gravitational waves sourced by linear scalar perturbations at second order, known as scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs), which present a novel method for detecting PBH DM. This review primarily examines the physics governing SIGWs produced alongside the formation of PBH dark matter.

We investigate axisymmetric solutions to the wave equation on extremal Kerr backgrounds and derive integrated local energy decay, known as Morawetz estimates, using an analysis strictly confined to physical space. While Aretakis originally established the boundedness of energy and Morawetz estimates for axisymmetric waves in extremal Kerr by constructing frequency-localized currents to address trapping degeneracy, this work extends a method introduced by Stogin for the sub-extremal case to the extremal setting. Furthermore, our approach simplifies Aretakis's derivation of Morawetz estimates by relying solely on purely classical currents.

Recent years have seen the proposal of Joint Radar and Communication (RadCom) systems to merge radar and communication functions onto a single platform for spectrum sharing. However, these integrated systems introduce clutter modulation and degrade radar performance, making performance enhancement a critical design requirement. This paper addresses clutter mitigation in joint RadCom systems using spatial modulation. The embedding of communication information creates variations in transmit beampatterns within a coherent processing interval (CPI), leading to clutter modulation and spectral spreading. To counter this, the study proposes a Reduced Dimension Spatial-Temporal Adaptive Processing (RD-STAP) method that applies time-domain filtering followed by spatial-domain filtering. For the time-domain stage, extended clutter is mitigated via subspace projection (SP), and a more efficient Power method-based eigen-decomposition algorithm is introduced to derive clutter subspace basis vectors, outperforming traditional Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Following clutter suppression, a matched filter is applied to reveal moving targets, while receive beamforming handles spatial-domain filtering. Simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of both the proposed RD-STAP method and the enhanced eigen-decomposition algorithm.

This research examines the core tension between privacy and welfare when aggregating privatized individual preferences, specifically quantifying the exact rate at which welfare diminishes as privacy levels rise. While previous studies have explored trade-offs regarding privacy versus accuracy or fairness, this work introduces concepts of welfare and probabilistic influence to precisely address how privacy constraints impact other system choices. We focus on social choice functions aggregating preferences between two candidates, where adding differential privacy noise to a voting system can alter power balances and render previously ideal deterministic functions suboptimal, potentially necessitating alternative aggregation methods. By employing two distinct proof techniques—first principles from combinatorics and probability, and Fourier analysis of Boolean functions—we connect privacy with welfare and influence. Furthermore, we evaluate the accuracy of private mechanisms across various social choice functions, ultimately bridging the gap between social choice theory and differential privacy.

In numerous online learning and multi-armed bandit scenarios, the selected actions or pulled arms must follow an ordinal sequence that is monotone over time. Illustrative cases include dynamic pricing, where firms employ markup strategies to attract early adopters and discourage strategic delays, and clinical trials, where dose allocation typically adheres to escalation principles to avoid toxicities. This work examines the continuum-armed bandit problem under the constraint of a monotone arm sequence. We demonstrate that if the unknown objective function is Lipschitz continuous, the regret scales as $O(T)$. Furthermore, when the objective function is additionally unimodal or quasiconcave, the regret achieves a rate of $\tilde O(T^{3/4})$ using the proposed algorithm, which represents the optimal rate for this setting. This result contrasts with the standard optimal rate of $\tilde O(T^{2/3})$ found in general continuous-armed bandit literature, highlighting the efficiency penalty imposed by the monotonicity requirement.

This paper tackles makeup transfer, a task designed to apply makeup from a reference image to a source image while maintaining the source's identity. Although current methods produce realistic results, they often struggle with color accuracy and spatial alignment. To resolve these limitations, we introduce the Facial Attribute Transformer (FAT) and its specialized variant, Spatial FAT, for superior makeup transfer. Inspired by NLP Transformers, FAT captures semantic relationships and interactions between the two faces to accurately estimate and transfer facial attributes. Furthermore, we incorporate Thin Plate Splines (TPS) into FAT to enhance the deformation of facial regions, resulting in Spatial FAT—the first approach capable of transferring both geometric attributes alongside color and texture. Comprehensive experiments confirm the effectiveness and superiority of our proposed models in four key areas: (1) achieving high-fidelity color transfer, (2) enabling geometric transformations of facial features, (3) managing facial variations like poses and shadows, and (4) generating high-resolution faces.

Assistive robotic manipulators are gaining significant importance for individuals with disabilities, particularly for teleoperating them during routine daily activities. Rather than manually guiding the robot through every action, utilizing self-recorded motion skills offers a substantial advantage for repetitive tasks. Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMP) represent a robust approach to skill learning; however, this specific application requires a straightforward heuristic to define start and stop points without relying on extra sensors. This paper introduces the concepts of local, global, and hybrid skills, establishing a modular framework that simplifies the composition of single-handed tasks. Special emphasis is placed on detailing the mathematical foundations to enable custom implementations for assistive robotic arms. Experimental results validate these methods through tasks such as scratching an itchy spot, sorting desk objects, and feeding a piggy bank with coins. An open-source implementation is available at https://github.com/fzi-forschungszentrum-informatik/ArNe.

We conducted shell model calculations for $^{48}$Cr using the GXPF1A and FPD6 interactions, adjusting the single-particle energies. Our results reveal a scaling behavior indicating that numerous interaction sets, despite having significantly different single-particle energies, yield nearly identical outcomes for the yrast spectrum of $^{48}$Cr.

Manycore computing platforms that employ self-adaptive runtime resource management typically rely on a system model reflecting the target architecture or software organization. However, the growing heterogeneity of resource types and their complex interactions create significant obstacles for coordinated, model-based decision-making under dynamic workloads. Reflective resource managers offer solutions to these challenges for emerging heterogeneous manycore processing (HMP) platforms by enabling self-awareness. Yet, as HMP architectures evolve rapidly, porting self-aware decision logic across diverse hardware remains difficult, necessitating frequent updates to resource manager models and platform-specific interfaces. To address this, we introduce MARS (Middleware for Adaptive and Reflective Systems), a cross-layer, multi-platform framework designed to facilitate the flexible and coordinated composition of system models and resource management policies, thereby simplifying the creation of resource managers. MARS features a generic user-level sensing and actuation interface for portable policy design, alongside a reflective system model for coordinating multiple policies. We validate MARS's cross-layer interactions using a dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) policy example, demonstrating its ability to operate on any Linux-based HMP computing platform.

Recent progress in reinforcement learning (RL) has allowed roboticists to automatically train sophisticated policies within simulated settings; however, the high sample complexity of these techniques makes applying them to real-world data difficult. This paper presents a new cost-shaping approach designed to minimize the data required for learning stabilizing controllers. By incorporating a Control Lyapunov Function (CLF)—an "energy-like" metric from model-based control—into standard cost functions, the method achieves theoretical guarantees that smaller discount factors yield stabilizing controllers, a strategy known to lower sample complexity. Additionally, the inclusion of the CLF term "robustifies" the search process, ensuring system stability even when policies are highly sub-optimal. Experimental validation on hardware, including a cartpole and an A1 quadruped, demonstrates that stabilizing controllers can be learned with merely seconds to a few minutes of fine-tuning data. Furthermore, simulation benchmarks reveal that optimizing the proposed costs requires orders of magnitude less data than traditional cost designs to achieve stabilizing policies.

We present an in-depth analysis of the maps linked to spectral interlacing, specifically addressing rank-one perturbations and bordering operations within symmetric and Hermitian matrices. The proofs utilize conventional methods from nonlinear analysis.

Although significant advancements have been made in pre-trained language models, a unified framework for pre-trained sentence representations remains absent. Consequently, various pre-training methods must be tailored to specific scenarios, often limiting the models' universality and representation quality. This study extends the recently introduced RetroMAE strategy, which follows the Masked Autoencoder (MAE) paradigm, to effectively support a broad spectrum of sentence representation tasks. The proposed framework operates in two stages, both utilizing RetroMAE. The initial stage trains the base model on generic corpora, such as Wikipedia and BookCorpus. The second stage continues training on domain-specific datasets, like MS MARCO and NLI, employing both RetroMAE and contrastive learning. The outputs from these two stages cater to distinct applications, with their efficacy validated through extensive experiments. Specifically, the base model demonstrates strong performance in zero-shot retrieval, achieving notable results on the BEIR benchmark. The subsequently fine-tuned models further enhance performance on downstream tasks, including domain-specific dense retrieval on MS MARCO and Natural Questions, as well as improving sentence embedding quality for standard STS and transfer tasks evaluated via SentEval. The empirical findings of this work are expected to guide future designs in sentence representation pre-training. Our pre-trained models and source code will be made publicly available.

The $\mathcal MQ$ problem, involving the solution of $m$ multivariate quadratic equations in $n$ variables, represents a primary challenge in algebraic cryptanalysis. The XL algorithm is a leading method for addressing this problem through linearization over a coefficient field, while the hybrid XL (h-XL) approach refines this by pre-guessing certain variables. This paper introduces a new variant of h-XL termed polynomial XL (PXL). In PXL, the $n$ variables are partitioned into $k$ fixed variables and $n-k$ "main" variables; consequently, the Macaulay matrix is constructed over a polynomial ring defined by the $k$ fixed variables. By eliminating specific columns within this polynomial ring prior to guessing the $k$ variables, the computational effort per guessed value is significantly reduced. Complexity analysis demonstrates that PXL is particularly efficient for systems where $n \approx m$. For instance, in systems over ${\mathbb F}_{2^8}$ with $n=m=80$, the estimated number of operations for h-XL, Wiedemann XL, and PXL are $2^{252}$, $2^{234}$, and $2^{220}$, respectively.

This study examines the information content of the maximum ranked set sampling procedure with unequal samples (MRSSU) using Tsallis entropy, a nonadditive extension of Shannon entropy. We derive multiple findings regarding Tsallis entropy, including bounds, monotonic properties, stochastic orders, and sharp bounds under specific conditions. Furthermore, we contrast the uncertainty and information content of MRSSU with those of simple random sampling (SRS). Finally, we establish characterization results based on cumulative and residual Tsallis entropy for both MRSSU and SRS data.

This study examines a one-dimensional degenerate wave equation featuring drift and a non-divergence-form leading operator. The analysis imposes homogeneous Dirichlet conditions at the point of degeneracy and boundary damping at the opposite endpoint, establishing specific criteria for the uniform exponential decay of solutions to the associated Cauchy problem.

We report new near-infrared observations of molecular hydrogen (H2) line emission from 18 Class I and flat-spectrum low-mass protostars, mostly located in the Tau-Aur and rho Oph dark clouds. For most of these objects, the emission extends over several arcseconds (hundreds of AU) and remains stable night-to-night relative to the continuum point source. The flux ratios of the H2 v = 2-1 S(1) and v = 1-0 S(1) lines suggest that jets or winds are the source in many cases. However, most objects exhibit only minor offsets (less than 10 km s-1) between their H2 and photospheric radial velocities. While no objects show line ratios exclusively indicative of UV excitation, UV or X-ray excitation alongside circumstellar dust may explain the H2 emission in several targets. Additionally, some objects in the sample display velocities and fluxes consistent with quiescent, non-mechanical origins for their H2 emission. In summary, the H2 emission characteristics of these protostars align with those previously observed in T Tauri star surveys.

We introduce type-aware operator mutation, a straightforward yet highly effective method for testing SMT solvers. This approach generates well-typed mutant formulas by mutating operators within seed formulas that adhere to specific types, which are then employed as test cases. We implemented this technique in the OpFuzz tool to rigorously evaluate Z3 and CVC4, two leading SMT solvers. The method proves exceptionally effective: over the course of one year of extensive testing with OpFuzz, we identified 1,092 bugs on the GitHub issue trackers for Z3 and CVC4. Of these, 819 were confirmed as unique bugs, and 685 were subsequently fixed by the developers. The discovered bugs exhibit significant diversity, spanning various types (including soundness issues, invalid model errors, and crashes), logics, and solver configurations. An in-depth analysis of the OpFuzz findings reveals high-quality bugs, many of which impact core components of the solvers' codebases and necessitated substantial fixes. Among the 819 confirmed bugs, 184 were soundness bugs—the most critical class of errors in SMT solvers—and 489 occurred in the solvers' default modes. Notably, OpFuzz uncovered 27 critical soundness bugs in CVC4, a solver renowned for its stability.
A summary of the JENAM 2008 Symposium 9, titled "Star Formation from Spitzer (Lyman) to Spitzer (Space Telescope) and Beyond," which took place in Vienna from September 10-12, 2008.

The Virtual Element Method (VEM) represents a novel class of numerical techniques designed to approximate partial differential equations, accommodating highly general polytopal mesh geometries. This study aims to adapt the Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) preconditioner to address the saddle-point linear systems generated by a VEM discretization of the two-dimensional Stokes equations. Provided that specific assumptions regarding the selection of primal unknowns are met, the preconditioned system becomes symmetric and positive definite, making the preconditioned conjugate gradient method applicable for solving it. The paper presents a theoretical convergence analysis that bounds the condition number of the preconditioned system. Various numerical experiments confirm these theoretical findings, demonstrating the method's scalability, quasi-optimality, and robust performance across diverse polygonal mesh element shapes. Additionally, the results indicate that convergence can be accelerated through the implementation of a slightly larger coarse space, which remains straightforward to construct and exceeds the minimal requirements outlined in the theory.

Colloidal gels made from small, attractive particles are frequently employed in formulations to suspend larger components. Nevertheless, although unfilled gels have been extensively studied, the impact of larger inclusions on the system's phase behavior and microstructure remains poorly understood. This study utilizes numerical simulations to investigate how larger "granular" particles modify gel transition phase boundaries. The results reveal two distinct regimes, contingent on both filler size and the original gel structure: a "passive" regime where fillers occupy existing voids with minimal effect on the transition, and an "active" regime where fillers are too large for these voids and disrupt the native structure. In this latter regime, the phase boundary is governed by an effective colloidal volume fraction determined by the available free volume.

Utilizing small droplets to compartmentalize reagents offers a promising avenue for simplifying procedures and enhancing conversion efficiency in numerous biphasic chemical reactions. This study employed surface nanodroplets, defined as having a maximal height under 100 nm, to quantitatively investigate how droplet size influences chemical reaction rates. In these systems, a surface-active reactant within pure or binary nanodroplets reacted with a bulk flow reactant, while the resulting product was continuously removed from the droplet surface. By analyzing the lateral size over time, the shrinkage rate was characterized; under specific flow conditions, the droplet size was governed exclusively by the chemical reaction rate governing reactant transport and product removal. Our findings reveal that overall kinetics accelerate rapidly as the droplet's lateral radius (R) decreases, following a relationship of dR/dt ~ R^(-2). This acceleration is driven by the faster increase in product concentration within smaller droplets. Furthermore, the rate enhancement attributed to small droplet dimensions was validated even when a non-reactive compound was present inside the droplets, provided it did not alter the surface concentrations of the reactants or products. These results deepen the understanding of droplet-based chemical kinetics and underscore the potential of small droplets for designing and controlling enhanced chemical reactions across a wide range of applications.

Many organelles within eukaryotic cells, such as the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, consist of interconnected tubule networks that span the entire cell. These tubular structures support numerous biochemical pathways that depend on proteins diffusing through the network to find binding partners or specific localized targets. This study introduces both precise analytical techniques for calculating mean first passage times and streamlined kinetic Monte Carlo algorithms to model particle diffusion within such networks. By utilizing exact propagator functions to describe transition time distributions between nodes, our method enables the use of large simulation time steps dictated by the network's architecture. We apply this approach to both synthetic planar networks and actual organelle structures, highlighting critical characteristics like the variability of search times across different regions and the functional benefits of dispersing target sites widely throughout the network. These new algorithms establish a foundation for further investigating the relationship between tubular network architecture and biomolecular reaction kinetics.

This paper presents a timing and trigger control system built on a field programmable gate array (FPGA), designed for the Dynamic Compression Sector (DCS) at the Advanced Photon Source (APS) within Argonne National Laboratory. As a pioneering facility for dynamic compression science, the DCS laser shock station requires precise synchronization of its components—including x-ray choppers, single-shot shutters, internal laser triggers, and shot diagnostics—relative to the arrival of x-rays. The system utilizes a Zynq FPGA synchronized to the APS storage ring's 352 MHz radio frequency clock to generate low-jitter trigger signals for the laser and x-ray shutter stages. Its architecture comprises the FPGA, a debug card, line drivers, and a power supply. Trigger delays and offsets are finely tuned via a user-friendly graphical interface. The article details the system's architecture, timing specifications, firmware, software implementation, and performance evaluation, highlighting its ability to achieve 15.5 ps r.m.s. timing jitter relative to the 352 MHz clock, which aligns with the 50 ps r.m.s. x-ray bunch duration at the APS.

This technical note investigates Lyapunov-like conditions designed to guarantee predefined-time stability within a specific class of dynamical systems. A system's origin is considered predefined-time stable if it achieves fixed-time stability, with the settling-time upper bound selectable a priori by adjusting system parameters. The study demonstrates that the proposed conditions establish equivalence among existing Lyapunov theorems for predefined-time stability in autonomous systems. Furthermore, the derived Lyapunov-like theorem is extended to analyze predefined-time ultimate boundedness with a specified bound, a feature particularly valuable for uncertain dynamical systems. Consequently, these results provide a comprehensive framework for analyzing predefined-time stability, unifying a wide range of systems exhibiting this property. Additionally, the framework is applied to design robust controllers for affine control systems that induce predefined-time stability (or predefined-time ultimate boundedness of solutions) relative to a desired manifold. A simulation example is provided to illustrate the controller's performance, with a specific focus on settling time estimation.

Cosmological Collider Physics enables the investigation of high-energy physics by analyzing spacetime fluctuations produced during inflation and recorded in the cosmic microwave background. Essentially, this approach allows us to explore energy scales inaccessible to terrestrial accelerators through precise astronomical observations. This study examines a scenario where the Grand Unified Theory (GUT) scale is proximate to the inflationary energy scale, calculating the three-point function of the inflaton mediated by the exchange of a GUT Higgs boson at the tree level. Our findings indicate that the results align with current observational limits on non-Gaussianity without requiring extreme fine-tuning of parameters. Furthermore, depending on specific model parameters, signatures of the GUT Higgs boson could potentially be detected via the 21cm spectrum, future large-scale structure surveys, or upcoming cosmic microwave background missions.

This study examines the joint influence of string clouds and quintessence on the thermodynamics of Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black holes. Utilizing equivalent thermodynamic parameters that account for the interplay between the black hole and cosmological horizons, we extensively analyze the resulting phase transitions. Our findings demonstrate that, akin to Anti-de Sitter space-time, second-order phase transitions can occur under specific conditions, while first-order transitions are absent in charged de Sitter black holes influenced by string clouds and quintessence. We also quantitatively explore how various thermodynamic variables affect these transitions, offering a novel method for investigating the thermodynamic properties of unstable de Sitter space-time. By focusing on the entropy force arising from interactions between the two horizons and comparing it to the Lennard-Jones force between particles, our results reveal a profound degeneracy between the entropy force and the ratio of horizon positions, mirroring the relationship between the Lennard-Jones force and the ratio of particle positions. Consequently, investigating the entropy force between horizons not only aids in exploring the three modes of cosmic evolution but also enhances our understanding of the correlations between black hole microstates and those in standard thermodynamic systems.

Despite longstanding criticism regarding $n$-gram based metrics like BLEU and NIST for assessing Natural Language Generation (NLG) systems, they remain widely used, including for evaluating automatic question generation (AQG) from documents, knowledge graphs, and images. Given the growing prominence of AQG, it is crucial to objectively determine the suitability of these metrics for this specific task. Specifically, we must verify if these metrics prioritize question answerability by favoring questions that include all necessary details, such as question type, entities, and relations. This study demonstrates that current $n$-gram based evaluation metrics do not consistently align with human judgments concerning question answerability. To address this issue and initiate the development of superior AQG evaluation methods, we propose a scoring function designed to capture answerability. Our results indicate that integrating this function with existing metrics significantly improves their correlation with human assessments. The scripts and data created for this research are publicly accessible at https://github.com/PrekshaNema25/Answerability-Metric.

Image-based navigation is widely regarded as the next major advancement in minimally invasive surgery. It is anticipated to broaden access to reproducible, safe, and high-precision procedures at reasonable costs and effort levels, primarily because these techniques eliminate the need for specialized hardware and integrate smoothly into current workflows. Furthermore, image-based navigation is expected to be pivotal in facilitating mixed reality environments and autonomous robotic systems. A cornerstone of image guidance is 2D/3D registration, which estimates the spatial correspondence between 3D structures (such as volumetric images or tool models) and their 2D representations (like fluoroscopy or endoscopy). Although image-based 2D/3D registration is a mature technology, its clinical adoption has been hindered by well-documented challenges, including the fragility of optimization objectives, difficulties in hyperparameter selection and initialization, issues with inconsistencies or multiple objects, and limited performance with single views. These obstacles persist largely because analytical solutions are often insufficient given the complexity, variability, and high dimensionality of generic 2D/3D registration tasks. Recently, machine learning approaches that approximate desired functional mappings using highly expressive parametric models offer a promising path to address these longstanding issues. This manuscript reviews the impact of machine learning on 2D/3D registration to systematically summarize recent advances driven by this emerging technology. Based on these insights, we provide our perspective on critical needs, significant open problems, and potential future directions.

This study measures the coherent cross-sections for $J/\psi$ and $\psi(\mathrm{2S})$ production in ultra-peripheral PbPb collisions at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of $5.02\,\mathrm{TeV}$, utilizing a $228\pm10\,\mathrm{\mu b}^{-1}$ data sample from the LHCb experiment in 2018. Differential cross-sections are determined separately for both mesons as functions of transverse momentum and rapidity within the nucleus-nucleus center-of-mass frame. The integrated coherent cross-sections are found to be $\sigma^\mathrm{coh}_{J/\psi} = 5.965 \pm 0.059 \pm 0.232 \pm 0.262\,\mathrm{mb}$ and $\sigma^\mathrm{coh}_{\psi(\mathrm{2S})} = 0.923 \pm 0.086 \pm 0.028 \pm 0.040\,\mathrm{mb}$, with uncertainties listed as statistical, systematic, and luminosity-related, respectively. Additionally, the cross-section ratio is measured as $\sigma^\mathrm{coh}_{\psi(\mathrm{2S})}/\sigma^\mathrm{coh}_{J/\psi} = 0.155 \pm 0.014 \pm 0.003$, where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second is systematic. These findings align with theoretical predictions.

The task of Argument Unit Recognition and Classification involves detecting argument units within text and categorizing them as either supporting or opposing a claim. A key design decision in building systems for this task is determining whether to classify at the level of token segments or complete sentences. Prior research indicates that fine-tuning language models at the token level produces more robust sentence classification outcomes than training directly on sentences. This study replicates the original findings and further explores the specific advantages of token-based approaches over sentence-based ones. We created systematic tests to analyze the behavioral distinctions between these two system types. Our results demonstrate that token-based models exhibit greater robustness than sentence-based models, particularly when tested on manually perturbed examples and specific data subpopulations.

This study introduces methods and initial findings regarding two-pulse Direct Laser Acceleration within a Laser-Driven Plasma Accelerator. In this mechanism, a secondary co-propagating laser pulse overlaps with the wakefield bubble to further accelerate electrons, boosting energy at the expense of emittance compared to standard Laser Wakefield Acceleration (LWFA). We present a technique for controlling the time delay between these two pulses on a femtosecond scale. Our results demonstrate energy enhancement when the separation between the pulses approximates the bubble radius.

The proliferation of IoT devices in smart homes enhances convenience but introduces significant challenges, particularly regarding privacy. Issues arise from opaque data collection methods and concealed devices that transmit information to third parties without occupants' awareness. Landlords managing multiple properties face compounded difficulties when tenants forget the location or existence of such hidden devices, highlighting a mismatch between single-user device design and multi-user living environments. To address device discovery in shared spaces, we developed tags utilizing wireless protocols, buzzers, and LED indicators. Attached to IoT units during installation, these tags enable tenants to locate devices later. While similar to commercial trackers like Tile or AirTag, our solution is tailored for privacy-focused use cases; it eliminates the need for pairing and allows multiple users to interact with the tags via a dedicated Android app. Although existing research has explored discovery tools like thermal cameras or VR, none have employed wireless protocols as a primary solution. We evaluated the feasibility of our tags through performance metrics and a user study assessing comfort levels during object retrieval. Our findings confirm that wireless tags are a viable solution for tracking devices within residential properties.

Using nuclear parton distributions derived independently of fixed-target Drell-Yan data and an analytic quenching weight formula grounded in the BDMPS formalism, a next-to-leading order analysis was conducted on Drell-Yan differential cross-section ratios from the Fermilab E906 and E866 Collaborations. The study reveals that calculations accounting solely for nuclear parton distribution effects fail to align with the experimental data from E866 and E906, indicating that parton energy loss cannot be neglected in nuclear Drell-Yan processes. Predictions show that assuming a constant quark transport coefficient, the suppression attributed to target nuclear geometry effects amounts to approximately 19.24%. Consequently, the target nuclear geometry effect must be included when investigating Drell-Yan reactions on nuclear targets. By incorporating the atomic mass dependence alongside the scale and Bjorken variable ($x_2$) dependence of the quark transport coefficient, a global fit to the experimental data determined the coefficient as a function of atomic mass, $x_2$, and $Q^2$. This analysis yielded a constant factor $\hat{q}_0$ of $0.061 \pm 0.004 \, \text{GeV}^2/\text{fm}$. Furthermore, it was found that the atomic mass dependence significantly influences the constant factor $\hat{q}_0$ of the quark transport coefficient in cold nuclear matter.

Deep learning models frequently develop predictions dependent on sensitive social attributes such as race and gender, creating substantial fairness concerns in critical societal domains like criminal justice, hiring, and banking. Current approaches attempt to mitigate this by reducing the model's reliance on social attributes, yet the strong correlation between these attributes and the target task often forces a trade-off between bias reduction and prediction accuracy. Recognizing that model bias stems from the fact that learning features related to sensitive attributes aids in optimizing the target task, we investigate whether proxy features can substitute the function of bias features during optimization. Consequently, we introduce \emph{Proxy Debiasing}, a method that first transfers the model's learned bias information from actual bias features to artificial proxy features, followed by causal intervention to remove these proxies during inference. The core concept involves designing controllable proxy features that replace bias features in supporting the target task during training while remaining easily eliminable via intervention during inference. This approach ensures the removal of bias features without compromising target information, effectively resolving the fairness-accuracy paradox found in prior debiasing techniques. Evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that \emph{Proxy Debiasing} significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and fairness metrics.

We extend the concept of Erd\H{o}s-Ginzburg-Ziv constants to a "higher degree," following the approach previously used to generalize Davenport constants, and derive corresponding upper and lower bounds. These bounds are occasionally exact, particularly for specific finite commutative rings with a prime power number of elements. Furthermore, we examine the applicability of a theorem independently established by W.D.~Gao and the first author, which connects these two parameters, within this higher-degree context. Two illustrative examples demonstrate the core properties of these higher-degree constants. 1) Let $\nu_p(m)$ represent the $p$-adic valuation of an integer $m$. If integers $t$ and $n$ satisfy $t | {m \choose 2}$ and $n=t+2^{\nu_2(m)}$, then any sequence $S$ over ${\mathbb Z}_2$ with length $|S| \geq n$ includes a subsequence $S'$ of length $t$ such that $\sum_{a_{i_1},\ldots, a_{i_m} \in S'} a_{i_1}\cdots a_{i_m} \equiv 0 \pmod{2}$, and this bound is tight. 2) For $k=3^{\alpha}$ where $\alpha \geq 2$ is an integer, every sequence $S$ over ${\mathbb Z}_3$ of length $|S| \geq k+6$ possesses a subsequence $S'$ of length $k$ satisfying $\sum_{a_h, a_i, a_j \in S'} a_ha_ia_j \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$. These cases highlight that sufficiently long sequences over finite commutative rings must contain subsequences of a specified length on which certain symmetric polynomials vanish. The classical Erd\H{o}s-Ginzburg-Ziv Theorem represents the specific instance where a sequence of length $2n-1$ over ${\mathbb Z}_n$ contains a subsequence $S'=(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ of length $n$ that evaluates to zero under the linear symmetric polynomial $a_1+\cdots+a_n$.

This study investigates instabilities leading to Bose-Einstein condensation and the modulation of "displacements" within a two-state Bose-Hubbard model of quantum particles, accounting for interactions between displacements across different lattice sites. The analysis examines scenarios involving uniform particle displacement from equilibrium and modulations that double the lattice constant. Conditions for these instabilities and phase transitions into a superfluid (SF) phase or an "ordered" phase with frozen displacements are determined. The behavior of order parameters is analyzed, and phase diagrams are derived both analytically for the ground state and numerically at non-zero temperatures. Findings indicate that the SF phase can exist as an intermediate state between normal and "ordered" phases, whereas the supersolid phase is thermodynamically unstable and does not emerge. The implications of these results for systems with double-well local potentials are also discussed.

This study presents a mathematical model for generating unidirectional waves, which incorporates Laplace's equation within a semi-infinite two-dimensional water domain. The model integrates dynamic and kinematic boundary conditions at the free surface, a lateral condition on the wavemaker, and a fixed bottom wall. Specifically designed for a flap-type wavemaker common in hydrodynamic towing tanks, the model relies on several simplifying assumptions, treating the water as an ideal fluid. By applying linear wavemaker theory and focusing on monochromatic wave generation, the study derives the relationship between wavenumber, wave height, and wavemaker stroke.

We investigate factorization-breaking coefficients relating momentum-dependent and momentum-averaged flow vectors to examine flow fluctuations originating from initial-state variations in heavy-ion collisions. These coefficients, calculated for the squared flow vector and squared flow magnitude, can facilitate the extraction of flow angle decorrelations. Our model predictions are compared against preliminary experimental data, and we also provide forecasts regarding momentum-dependent correlations between mixed flow harmonics.

We introduce a new class of black strings that lack time-translation, axisymmetry, and translational invariance along the string, yet possess a helical Killing vector field. These solutions emerge from the superradiant instability of $D=6$ Myers-Perry black strings with equal angular momenta. We term these "black resonator strings" and demonstrate that, within the parameter range where both solution types coexist, they exhibit greater entropy than their Myers-Perry counterparts. Additionally, we construct horizonless Kaluza-Klein geons that share the same symmetries; unlike in other superradiant contexts, these geons are not merely the horizonless limit of black resonator strings but represent entirely distinct solutions.

Cell movement frequently involves collisions with other cells, triggering a halt in motion, repolarization, and redirection away from the contact point—a mechanism known as contact inhibition of locomotion (CIL). During CIL, the interplay between actomyosin contractility and cell-substrate adhesions is altered; however, mathematical frameworks that model stochastic migration and collision outcomes based on this coupling have yet to be established. In this study, we expand our prior stochastic model of individual cell migration to incorporate CIL. Our simulations elucidate, through the lens of modified contractility and adhesion dynamics, various experimentally observed phenomena associated with CIL, such as response modulation under external cues and changes in group migration when CIL is absent. Combined with our earlier results, this work provides a comprehensive explanation for a broad spectrum of observations concerning both solitary and collective cell migration.

The divergence chain rules for channels establish a relationship between the divergence of channel inputs and their corresponding outputs. A notable instance of this principle is the data-processing inequality, which asserts that applying the same channel to two inputs does not increase their divergence. Utilizing direct matrix analysis techniques, we derive multiple R\'enyi divergence chain rules within the quantum framework. These findings streamline and, in certain instances, extend prior derivations found in existing literature.

We identify all polynomial tau-functions within the CKP hierarchy and its $n$-reductions; notably, for the case where $n=3$, we determine all polynomial tau-functions of the Kaup-Kupershmidt hierarchy.

Facilitating information exchange among multiple agents relies heavily on effective communication, making the study of emergent communication a dynamic research area, particularly within discrete cheap-talk frameworks. However, because these environments permit arbitrary information encoding, learned protocols typically fail to generalize beyond their specific training partners. In contrast, this work introduces a new problem setting and the Quasi-Equivalence Discovery (QED) algorithm, which enables zero-shot coordination (ZSC)—the ability to discover protocols that function with independently trained agents. Real-world scenarios often feature costly communication channels, such as the physical effort robots expend moving their limbs, alongside non-uniform distributions of intents. We demonstrate that these factors produce unique optimal ZSC policies in referential games where agents transmit intent using message energy costs. While Other-Play was recently developed for learning optimal ZSC policies, it necessitates prior knowledge of the problem's symmetries. Conversely, QED can iteratively uncover these symmetries within the setting and converge to the optimal ZSC policy.

The way individuals link colors to concepts shapes how they decode color meanings in visualizations. While prior research suggested these effects apply only to concepts with strong, specific color associations, a concept's meaning can still be clarified within an encoding system even if it lacks a direct color link, provided it is distinct from other mapped concepts. This perspective is formalized as Semantic Discriminability Theory, a broad framework explaining when observers can infer meaning from visual cues. The theory defines semantic discriminability as the extent to which viewers can deduce a unique mapping between visual features and concepts. It posits that the ability to achieve semantic discriminability across a set of concepts depends on the statistical difference between their respective color-concept association distributions. The authors establish the formal properties of this theory and validate its predictions through two experiments. Experiment 1 confirms that the capacity to generate semantically distinct colors for a concept set is limited by the statistical distance between their color-concept association distributions. Furthermore, Experiment 2 demonstrates that people can successfully interpret colors in bar graphs as long as those colors remain semantically discriminable, even for concepts previously deemed unsuitable for color mapping. Collectively, these findings indicate that colors are more resilient and effective for visual communication than earlier assumptions suggested.

This paper constructs a general bright-dark soliton solution, expressed in Pfaffian form, for an integrable semi-discrete vector NLS equation using Hirota's bilinear method. Explicit one- and two-bright-dark soliton solutions are provided for the two-component semi-discrete NLS equation, alongside explicit two-bright-one-dark and one-bright-two-dark soliton solutions for the three-component semi-discrete NLS equation. Furthermore, the asymptotic behavior of these two-soliton solutions is analyzed.

Dwarf Irregular galaxies (dIrrs) represent the smallest stellar systems featuring extended neutral hydrogen (HI) discs. Analyzing the kinematics of these discs offers a potent method for estimating total matter distribution at minute scales. This study examines the HI kinematics of 17 galaxies selected from the LITTLE THINGS survey. Our methodology diverges from prior research by directly fitting three-dimensional models (incorporating two spatial dimensions and one spectral dimension) using the $^\text{3D}$BAROLO software, thereby maximizing the utility of HI datacubes. For each galaxy, we determine the geometric parameters of the HI disc (inclination and position angle), the radial surface density distribution, the velocity-dispersion ($\sigma_v$) profile, and the rotation curve. By correcting the rotation curve for asymmetric drift, we derive the circular velocity (V$_{\text{c}}$), which directly reflects the galactic potential. As a preliminary application, we demonstrate that these dIrrs conform to a baryonic Tully-Fisher relation with remarkable consistency with observations on larger scales. The study yields high-quality, ready-to-use kinematic data (V$_{\text{c}}$ and $\sigma_v$) made publicly available, which can facilitate dynamical investigations and enhance our comprehension of these low-mass galaxies.

We examine the horocyclic flow associated with a (topologically mixing) Anosov flow or diffeomorphism, proving that transverse quasi-invariant measures possessing Hölder Jacobians are unique. Within this framework, we provide a precise characterization of the equilibrium states for the hyperbolic system. We demonstrate that if there exists a family of Radon measures on the horocyclic foliation such that any probability measure (whether invariant or not) with conditionals defined by this family is necessarily the unique equilibrium state of the system.

Currently, the Standard Model (SM) exhibits inconsistencies with experimental data in various observables related to $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ and $b \to c \ell^- \bar{\nu}_\ell$ transitions, collectively known as the $B$-flavour anomalies. This review compiles data up to Moriond 2021 and explores new-physics interpretations from two perspectives: a model-independent effective field theory framework and the construction of specific theoretical models. We emphasize the complementary nature of these methodologies. Furthermore, we examine unified explanations for both sets of anomalies and introduce models capable of addressing additional issues, including dark matter, the muon $(g-2)$ anomaly, neutrino characteristics, and hadronic anomalies.

We present logit uncertainty, a novel, robust, and model-agnostic metric for assessing uncertainty in classification tasks by leveraging neural network logits. Our analysis demonstrates that this approach outperforms existing methods across various applications, such as out-of-distribution detection and identifying erroneous predictions. Furthermore, we examine the theoretical underpinnings of the measure, investigate its connection to high-density regions, and illustrate its application for testing uncertainty via intermediate outputs during generative adversarial network training. Finally, we propose two practical strategies for integrating logit-based uncertainty into real-world scenarios, confirming its superior performance.

Magic state distillation employs specialized codes to mitigate errors in input states, typically designed for Clifford-twirled error models. We introduce comprehensive measurement sequences for distillation protocols capable of suppressing arbitrary errors throughout the entire process, provided that errors are independent across qubits. Given input magic states, our protocol functions on a two-dimensional square grid by performing $ZZ$ measurements on horizontal qubit pairs, $XX$ measurements on vertical pairs, and $Z,X$ measurements on individual qubits.

By employing the ultra-spinning limit as a method to generate new solutions, researchers have derived a novel family of ultra-spinning charged black holes from Chow's rotating charged black hole, which features two equal-charge parameters within six-dimensional $\mathcal{N} = 4$ gauged supergravity. The study analyzes the thermodynamics of these solutions and confirms that all thermodynamic variables strictly satisfy both the differential first law and the Bekenstein-Smarr mass formula. Specifically, for the six-dimensional ultra-spinning Chow black hole with a single rotation parameter, it is demonstrated that the reverse isoperimetric inequality (RII) is not universally obeyed; consequently, the black hole can be either sub-entropic or super-entropic, contingent on the mass and, particularly, the charge parameters. This behavior contrasts sharply with the six-dimensional singly-rotating Kerr-AdS super-entropic black hole, which invariably violates the RII. Furthermore, regarding the six-dimensional doubly-rotating Chow black hole that is ultra-spinning along only one spatial axis, it is noted that the RII may be either satisfied or violated, allowing the solution to exist in both super-entropic and sub-entropic states generally.

A SCADA system functions as a distributed network of cyber-physical devices designed for the instrumentation and control of vital infrastructures, including electric power grids. As the smart grid evolves, these systems are increasingly integrated with open networks, making security paramount. Nevertheless, many existing SCADA systems were deployed decades ago without security considerations, leaving field devices susceptible to false command injection from compromised or malicious sources. Implementing cryptographic defenses on these legacy devices is difficult due to their limited computational capabilities. Consequently, protective solutions for such systems must operate as add-ons. This paper examines two add-on defense strategies for legacy SCADA systems—the data diode and the detect-and-respond approach—comparing their security assurances and suitable application scenarios. Additionally, a generic architectural framework for the detect-and-respond strategy is proposed, accompanied by an implementation example to demonstrate its practicality.

Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are prevalent and can cause severe outcomes such as kidney damage, mental status changes, sepsis, and mortality. Diagnosis primarily relies on laboratory tests like urinalysis and urine culture, which involve collecting and processing specimens to identify their chemical and cellular makeup. This workflow demands meticulous collection, safe handling of biohazardous material, controlled storage, and rapid transport to advanced lab equipment. Holographic lens-free imaging (LFI) offers a compact, simple optical method to analyze large urine volumes, potentially facilitating automatic bedside testing. We present an LFI system that successfully detects key clinical biomarkers—including red and white blood cells, crystals, casts, and *E. coli*—within urine phantoms. This method is sensitive to particle concentrations associated with conditions like hematuria, pyuria, and bacteriuria. Our results demonstrate that LFI can estimate bacterial concentrations across eight orders of magnitude, while blood cell measurements remain relatively unaffected by bacterial variations spanning seven orders of magnitude. Furthermore, LFI clearly distinguishes between UTI-positive and UTI-negative samples from human patients. Collectively, these findings indicate that LFI holds significant promise as a screening tool, potentially enabling early, point-of-care detection of UTIs and other pathological states.

This study examines a queueing model featuring limited processor sharing, where no more than $n$ jobs can be served concurrently. Such a system effectively models bandwidth allocation in wireless networks and service processes within computer networks. When the system is full and a new job arrives, that job is discarded, potentially interrupting an ongoing service which is also terminated. The research analyzes two specific policies for selecting which job to discard: one prioritizes the job with the shortest remaining service time. The paper establishes relationships between the state probabilities of this limited-capacity system and those of an analogous unlimited processor sharing system, enabling the calculation of the former's probabilities based on the latter. Specifically, under a Poisson arrival process, the probability of server capacity exhaustion equals the probability of job loss. For this scenario, explicit formulas are derived for stationary state probabilities and loss probabilities. Notably, these probabilities remain invariant with respect to the specific job length distribution, provided the mean job length remains constant.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) has recently delivered remarkable results across diverse speech applications by effectively leveraging vast amounts of unlabeled data for representation extraction. Nevertheless, the gains from SSL in speech separation (SS) and enhancement (SE) remain notably modest compared to speech recognition (ASR). Building upon HuBERT, this study explores strategies to enhance SSL models specifically for SS and SE tasks. Initially, we modify HuBERT's masked speech prediction (MSP) objective by incorporating separation and denoising components, creating a multiple pseudo-label pre-training framework. While this approach substantially boosts SS and SE performance, it inadvertently harms ASR results. To preserve ASR efficacy, we introduce an adapter-based architecture for the HuBERT Transformer encoder; this design fine-tunes only a limited number of parameters per layer for the multi-task MSP objective while keeping the remaining parameters frozen in their original HuBERT state. Empirical findings demonstrate that our proposed adapter-based, multi-pseudo-label HuBERT achieves consistent and significant improvements across SE, SS, and ASR tasks, all while accelerating pre-training and requiring only a marginal increase in parameters.

Let $L$ be a finite lattice and $I$ an ideal of $L$; then the restriction map acts as a bounded lattice homomorphism from the congruence lattice of $L$ to that of $I$. The authors demonstrated the converse of this statement in a 2009 paper. In 2012, G. Cz\'edli established a similar result for rectangular lattices. This paper presents a stronger version of Cz\'edli's finding alongside a concise, elementary, and direct proof.

Fine-grained sentiment analysis seeks to identify sentiment holders, targets, and polar expressions while clarifying their interrelationships; however, progress in this area is constrained by annotation challenges. In contrast, targeted sentiment analysis is a more limited task dedicated to extracting sentiment targets and determining their polarity.
