This study investigates whether integrating holder and expression data can enhance target extraction and classification, utilizing eight English datasets for experimentation. Our findings indicate that jointly predicting target and polarity BIO tags improves target extraction, and enriching input text with gold-standard expressions generally boosts targeted polarity classification. These results underscore the value of annotating expressions for fine-grained sentiment datasets. Nevertheless, our data also reveal that current models struggle to predict polar expressions effectively, which limits the practical utility of this information.

Jet quenching, a primary indicator of quark-gluon plasma (QGP) creation where jets dissipate energy while moving through the medium, represents a well-established set of observables in heavy-ion collisions. Nevertheless, significant uncertainties persist regarding the mechanisms responsible for this effect. Theoretical efforts aiming to resolve these open questions often utilize the path-length dependence of jet energy loss to elucidate the underlying physics. However, extracting explicit values for this dependence from experimental data remains a difficult challenge. These proceedings present recent findings from ALICE that aim to advance our comprehension of this phenomenon, covering event-shape engineered jet spectra, the jet-particle $v_{2}$, and correlation analyses between hard triggers and hadrons.

Transformer-based architectures have achieved state-of-the-art results across numerous deep learning tasks; however, their extensive parameter counts make fine-tuning for downstream applications computationally expensive and energy-intensive. While automatic mixed-precision (FP32/FP16) fine-tuning has previously reduced these resource demands, recent advancements in low-bit integer back-propagation offer opportunities for further reductions in computation and memory usage. This study introduces a novel integer training approach that applies integer arithmetic to the forward pass and gradient computation of linear, convolutional, layer normalization, and embedding layers within transformers. We also investigate various bit-widths to determine the minimum necessary precision for effective integer fine-tuning. Experiments fine-tuning BERT and ViT models on standard downstream tasks reveal that 16-bit integer models achieve performance parity with floating-point baselines. Dropping the bit-width to 10 results in an average score decrease of 0.5, while reducing it further to 8 leads to a 1.7-point average score drop.

We present Flux, a system demonstrating how logical refinements integrate seamlessly with Rust's ownership model to provide ergonomic, type-based verification for low-level pointer manipulation. Initially, we designed a new refined type system for Rust that indexes mutable locations while allowing pure (immutable) values within refinements. This system leverages Rust's ownership mechanisms to abstract sub-structural reasoning about locations inside polymorphic type constructors, all while supporting strong updates. We formally established the critical reliance on Rust's strong aliasing guarantees by utilizing the stacked borrows model to prove that well-typed programs with valid borrows never get stuck. Second, we implemented this type system in Flux, a Rust compiler plugin that uses the decomposition of complex invariants into types and refinements to efficiently synthesize loop annotations. These annotations include complex quantified invariants describing container contents, generated via liquid inference. Third, we evaluated Flux using a benchmark suite of vector manipulation programs and components of a verified secure sandboxing library, highlighting the benefits of refinement types over the program logics used in the state-of-the-art Prusti verifier. Although Prusti's expressive program logic can verify deep functional correctness, for the lightweight yet ubiquitous verification cases in our benchmarks, liquid typing significantly enhances ergonomics by reducing specification lines by half, cutting verification time by an order of magnitude, and eliminating annotation overhead, which previously ranged from up to 24% of code size (averaging 9%) down to zero.

Compressed bitmap indexes are widely utilized in search engines and databases. Although numerous compression methods exist, most depend heavily on run-length encoding (RLE). However, for unsorted data, a hybrid approach combining uncompressed bitmaps and packed arrays within a two-level tree structure offers superior performance; this method is known as Roaring and has been adopted by major production systems such as Apache Lucene, Spark, Kylin, and Druid. Nevertheless, run-length encoded bitmaps can sometimes be more compact than Roaring bitmaps, particularly when data is sorted, resulting in long compressible runs. To address this, we have developed an enhanced Roaring hybrid that integrates uncompressed bitmaps, packed arrays, and RLE-compressed segments, yielding a new format with improved compression ratios. Our optimized Roaring implementation achieves speeds several times faster—up to two orders of magnitude—compared to traditional RLE-based alternatives like WAH, Concise, and EWAH, while also providing better compression. We examine the design decisions and optimizations that enable these significant performance gains.

Neutrinoless double-beta decay (0$
u eta eta$) involves numerous intermediate forbidden nuclear transitions that are sensitive to the quenching of the axial vector coupling constant ($g_A/g_V$), a factor critical to the sensitivity of 0$
u eta eta$ experiments. This Letter reports measurements using a high-resolution LiInSe$_{2}$ bolometer in a "source=detector" setup to analyze the spectral shape of the 4-fold forbidden $ eta$-decay of $^{115}$In. By comparing experimental $ eta$ spectra with theoretical predictions—while accounting for simulated backgrounds and detector effects—we determine the $g_A/g_V$ value. Our results provide evidence for $g_A/g_V$ quenching at greater than $5\sigma$, yielding a model-dependent quenching factor of $0.655\pm0.002$ relative to the free-nucleon value within the Interacting Shell Model. Additionally, we measured the $^{115}$In half-life as [$5.18\pm0.06(	ext{stat.})^{+0.005}_{-0.015}(	ext{sys.})]	imes{10}^{14}$ yr under the Interacting Shell Model framework. This study highlights the bolometeric technique's capability for precision single-$ eta$ decay measurements, thereby aiding in the reduction of uncertainties associated with 0$
u eta eta$ nuclear matrix element calculations.

We introduce a sampling technique grounded in an ensemble approximation of second-order Langevin dynamics. By augmenting the log target density with a quadratic term involving an auxiliary momentum variable and incorporating damped-driven Hamiltonian dynamics, we derive a stochastic differential equation that maintains invariance to the Gibbs measure, ensuring the marginal distribution of position coordinates aligns with the target. A preconditioner, constructed from the covariance under the dynamics' law, preserves this invariance while accelerating convergence to the Gibbs measure. This approach yields mean-field dynamics that can be approximated via an ensemble method, producing a stochastic dynamical system that is both gradient-free and affine-invariant. Numerical experiments confirm its viability as a foundation for numerical sampling in Bayesian inverse problems.

We examine a set of exact solutions for a nonlinear reaction-diffusion model, derived through nonclassical symmetry analysis. Under specific limiting conditions, this model converges to the established Fisher-KPP equation, linking it to diverse applications such as tumor growth, tissue regeneration, and ecological spread. These exact solutions are mathematically significant because solutions to the Fisher-KPP equation are uncommon, typically limited to long-time traveling waves under specific speed parameters.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) demonstrates significant efficacy in environments where agents acquire policies through active interaction. Conversely, shifting to an offline paradigm, where policy updates rely solely on static datasets, introduces the critical challenge of distributional shift. To address this, we introduce Pessimistic Offline Reinforcement Learning (PessORL), an algorithm that guides the agent back to familiar regions by adjusting the value function. Our approach specifically targets out-of-distribution (OOD) states, imposing penalties on high value estimates for states absent from the training data. This strategy ensures the learned pessimistic value function serves as a lower bound for the true value across the entire state space. Evaluations across multiple benchmark tasks reveal that PessORL outperforms methods that only account for OOD actions, achieving superior results by explicitly managing OOD states.

This document outlines the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Conversational Telephone Speech (CTS) Superset, a large-scale dataset featuring uniform metadata designed to aid the research community in training and developing narrowband telephony speaker recognition systems. Comprising speech segments from over 6,800 speakers with durations uniformly distributed between 10 and 60 seconds, the Superset aggregates data from source corpora used in previous NIST Speaker Recognition Evaluations (SRE 1996–2012), including the Greybeard corpus, Switchboard, and Mixer series from the Linguistic Data Consortium (LDC). Beyond this description, the document also presents speaker recognition results from the NIST 2020 CTS Challenge, achieved using a system trained on the CTS Superset, serving as a reference baseline for the challenge.

This paper introduces a model-free, learning-based control framework designed to enhance the contact-aware locomotion of soft snake robots within cluttered environments. The proposed scheme integrates two cooperative controllers: a bio-inspired controller (C1) that manages both velocity and steering, and an event-triggered regulator (R2) that adjusts steering proactively and reactively to obstacle contacts. These controllers' outputs are combined and fed into a Matsuoka CPG network to produce smooth, rhythmic actuation signals. To facilitate stable and efficient training of both controllers, we employ a game-theoretic fictitious play algorithm using a shared potential-field reward function for goal tracking. Simulations demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms two baseline controllers in terms of locomotion efficiency within obstacle-rich settings.

The swift advancement of quantum computing has revealed distinct quantum advantages, including enhanced feature representation and stronger security for model parameters. This study introduces a vertical federated learning framework utilizing variational quantum circuits to showcase the competitive efficacy of a quantum-enhanced pre-trained BERT model for text classification. Specifically, the proposed hybrid classical-quantum architecture integrates a new random quantum temporal convolution (QTC) learning framework, which substitutes certain layers within the BERT-based decoder. Experiments on intent classification using the Snips and ATIS spoken language datasets demonstrate that the BERT-QTC model achieves comparable results. Notably, BERT-QTC improves the performance of existing quantum circuit-based language models by 1.57% and 1.52% relative gains on two text classification datasets. Additionally, BERT-QTC is viable for deployment on both commercially accessible quantum hardware and CPU-based interfaces to guarantee data isolation.

Legged robots excel at traversing complex environments where wheeled platforms struggle. While reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise in teaching quadruped locomotion, there is limited research on integrating rule-based human expertise to enhance this learning. This paper introduces RMLL, a method that utilizes Linear Temporal Logic formulas to encode human knowledge, thereby accelerating RL-based locomotion training and enabling the specification of various gaits. Notably, this approach achieves these goals without relying on reference trajectories, a common form of prior knowledge. By formulating the task using an automaton based on the recently developed Reward Machine (RM) framework, we demonstrate that simulation results confirm our RM-based strategy effectively leverages rule-based human knowledge compared to competitive baselines, including those that also access such information.

Recent research has increasingly focused on linking individual identities across various social platforms. Current methods typically map these identities as deterministic vectors into a shared latent space and subsequently train a classifier using available annotations. However, the inherent uncertainties in real-world social platforms render these deterministic approaches sub-optimal. Furthermore, gathering sufficient linkage annotations is challenging due to the vast disparities between platforms. While semi-supervised models offer a promising alternative by leveraging unlabeled data to capture intrinsic distributions, existing methods heavily depend on heuristically defined similarity metrics to connect labeled and unlabeled samples. These manually crafted assumptions often fail to align with actual linkage signals, potentially introducing noise. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the Noise-aware Semi-supervised Variational User Identity Linkage (NSVUIL) model. This approach first employs a novel supervised module to integrate available annotations, representing each social identity as a Gaussian distribution within Wasserstein space to simultaneously maintain fine-grained profiles and model identity uncertainty. Additionally, we design a noise-aware self-learning module that effectively augments limited annotations by filtering noise from pseudo-labels generated by the supervised component.

This study addresses the challenge of managing frequency in low-inertia power systems by utilizing inverter-based resources (IBRs) with weak grid connections. We introduce a new grid-forming approach, termed frequency shaping control, designed to modify the frequency response of synchronous generators (SGs) during load disturbances, thereby effectively halting abrupt frequency declines. This method relaxes multiple conventional assumptions found in existing literature and successfully balances the trade-offs between peak power demands and the extent of maximum frequency deviations. Furthermore, we evaluate the solution's robustness against inaccuracies in network parameter knowledge, emphasizing the critical need for precise parameter estimation.

A core principle of Federated Learning (FL)—a method that trains models without centralizing user data—is privacy. Yet, prior research indicates that gradient updates in FL can inadvertently expose user information. Although industrial FL applications predominantly involve text tasks, such as keystroke prediction, existing privacy attacks have primarily targeted simple image classifiers. We introduce a novel attack that exposes private user text by deploying malicious parameter vectors, a method that remains effective even with mini-batches, multiple users, and long sequences. Distinct from previous FL attacks, our approach leverages specific traits of both the Transformer architecture and token embeddings, separately isolating tokens and positional embeddings to reconstruct high-fidelity text. These findings suggest that text-based FL, long considered resistant to privacy breaches, is actually far more susceptible than previously believed.

Locating and understanding how data is retained within biological systems, such as genetic and neural networks, is a fundamental objective in molecular genetics and neuroscience. However, existing methodologies primarily examine network architecture rather than function. We present a novel information-theoretic approach called "information fragmentation analysis," which utilizes comprehensive phenotypic data to pinpoint information locations within complex networks, evaluate the degree to which information is dispersed across multiple nodes, and measure its encryption levels. By employing information fragmentation matrices, we generate flow graphs that depict the propagation of information through these systems. We demonstrate the utility of this method by examining artificial brains evolved in silico as they perform specific tasks, revealing deeper insights into their information processing and cognitive mechanisms. Furthermore, the derived metrics for information fragmentation and encryption quantify the complexity of information processing within these networks, highlighting differences between initial sensory exposure during early development and subsequent routine processing.

Creating high-quality artwork is typically labor-intensive and demands significant skill from human painters. To streamline this process, researchers have developed systems trained to "paint like humans," serving as digital assistants. However, existing methods often rely on a progressive grid-based approach where the image is subdivided into finer grids and painted in parallel, resulting in artificial sequences that confuse users. To overcome this, we introduce a novel method that learns to generate canvases with a more authentic human style. Our proposed pipeline, Intelli-Paint, features three key components: 1) a progressive layering strategy that renders a natural background before sequentially adding foreground objects; 2) a new sequential brushstroke guidance mechanism that enables the agent to shift attention across image regions in a semantically aware way; and 3) a brushstroke regularization technique that reduces the total brushstroke count by 60–80% without compromising visual quality. Quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate that Intelli-Paint agents not only improve generation efficiency but also produce a more natural style, better assisting humans in expressing their creative ideas through digital art.

This study examines the elastic scattering of electron Airy beams by potential fields, specifically focusing on a hydrogen atom in its ground state and a Yukawa potential. The results demonstrate that the scattering probability density generally exhibits azimuthal asymmetry. When the atom is located at a minimum of the Airy beam's probability density, this asymmetric pattern manifests as four distinct peaks. The analysis reveals that this behavior is highly sensitive to the precision of the relative positioning between the atom and the beam's minima. Furthermore, the impact of positional uncertainty, quantified by the transverse wave-packet size, on the observation of azimuthal asymmetry is investigated. Finally, the discussion extends to spatially localized targets, highlighting the challenges in detecting azimuthal asymmetry when target dimensions exceed a critical value defined by the beam parameters and the target's central position.

Differential Privacy (DP) offers a rigorous privacy guarantee that prevents adversaries accessing a machine learning model from inferring details about specific training samples. Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), the leading method for training deep learning models with DP, achieves this by adding noise during the training process. However, prior research indicates that DP-SGD frequently causes substantial performance drops on standard image classification tasks. Additionally, some researchers argue that DP-SGD is inherently ill-suited for large models because the noise magnitude required for privacy scales with the model's dimensionality. Conversely, we show that DP-SGD can outperform previous expectations when applied to over-parameterized models. By employing meticulous hyper-parameter tuning alongside straightforward techniques to facilitate signal propagation and accelerate convergence, we establish a new state-of-the-art result on CIFAR-10 without requiring additional data, achieving 81.4% accuracy under (8, 10^{-5})-DP with a 40-layer Wide-ResNet, surpassing the prior best of 71.7%. Furthermore, fine-tuning a pre-trained NFNet-F3 yields an impressive 83.8% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet under (0.5, 8*10^{-7})-DP. We also reach 86.7% top-1 accuracy under (8, 8 \cdot 10^{-7})-DP, falling only 4.3% short of the current non-private state-of-the-art for this task. We consider these findings a major advancement in narrowing the accuracy gap between private and non-private image classification.

This study analyzes four distinct simulation series: entangled model networks featuring either mono-disperse or poly-disperse weight distributions between crosslinks, non-entangled phantom model networks, and non-entangled model networks incorporating excluded volume interactions. Building on prior research regarding average residual bond orientations (RBO) in model networks [1], this work extends the analysis to characterize the RBO distribution within the entangled networks examined here. The phantom model effectively captures monomer fluctuations, average RBOs, and their distributions in systems lacking both entanglements and excluded volume effects. For networks with excluded volume but no entanglements, the phantom model's predictions are adjusted by accounting for incompletely screened excluded volume interactions. The results demonstrate that tube model parameters can be derived from monomer fluctuations and RBO data in polymer networks. A scaling relationship of RBO $\propto N^{-1/2}$ is identified in both mono-disperse and poly-disperse entangled networks, whereas non-entangled networks exhibit an RBO $\propto N^{-1}$ scaling. The RBO distribution in entangled samples is modeled by assuming a normal distribution of tube lengths, broadened by local fluctuations in tube curvature. Both monomer fluctuations and RBO align with slip link or slip tube models [2] for networks but contradict models that prevent monomer sliding along a confining tube.

This study evaluates six theoretical frameworks—comprising one baryonic model, two dark matter scenarios, two modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) approaches, and one modified gravity theory—in their ability to explain galaxy rotation curves. The dark matter models utilize either an NFW profile or a core-modified profile for the dark halo. The MOND models examine Milgrom's theory using both standard and simple interpolation functions, while the modified gravity analysis focuses on Moffat's MSTG theory. We fitted these models to the observed rotation curves of 18 galaxies, consisting of nine high-surface brightness (HSB) and nine low-surface brightness (LSB) systems. Model performance was assessed using the Bayesian and Akaike Information Criteria. Results indicate that no single model successfully fits all rotation curves. The baryonic model alone provides the best fit for two galaxies without invoking nonluminous dark matter. MOND yields the best fit for the largest number of galaxies, whereas the MSTG model achieves the best fit for only one. The core-modified profile effectively fits approximately half of the LSB galaxies but fails for HSB galaxies, while the NFW profile fits only a small fraction of HSB galaxies and none of the LSB galaxies. These findings suggest that the oversimplified NFW and core-modified profiles are insufficient to accurately represent the postulated dark matter halos.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently demonstrated significant efficacy in recommender systems, particularly for modeling collaborative relations. However, real-world recommendation graphs often contain diverse relationship types, such as movies sharing genres, directors, or actors. Utilizing a single, monolithic graph to represent all these connections can lead to excessive complexity. To mitigate this, we adopt a pre-training strategy based on a divide-and-conquer approach, decomposing the large graph into three distinct sub-graphs: the user graph, the item graph, and the user-item interaction graph. We construct multi-relational user and item graphs based on specific attributes and pre-train embeddings for users and items using these sub-graphs separately. To this end, we introduce a novel Reinforced Attentive Multi-relational Graph Neural Network (RAM-GNN) for pre-training these embeddings prior to the final recommendation phase. This model incorporates a relation-level attention mechanism to assess the significance of various relations and employs a Reinforced Neighbor Sampler (RNS) to optimize the filtering threshold for selecting top-k similar neighbors, thereby addressing the problem of over-smoothing. The recommendation model is then initialized with these pre-trained embeddings. Finally, an aggregation-based GNN learns from collaborative signals within the user-item interaction graph to generate recommendations. Experimental results indicate that RAM-GNN surpasses other state-of-the-art graph-based recommendation models and multi-relational graph neural networks.

This study introduces a lagged Metropolis-Hastings walk designed for sampling from simple undirected graphs based on specified stationary probabilities. We demonstrate the application of this technique using tailored graphs to sample spatial units. Furthermore, we show that this proposed graph-based spatial sampling method offers greater flexibility and enhanced design efficiency compared to current spatial sampling approaches.

A primary goal of the CREDO project is to investigate Cosmic-Ray Ensembles (CRE) \cite{homola2020cosmic}. Verifying these phenomena requires extensive observation of low-energy Extensive Air Showers (EAS) alongside the analysis of their temporal correlations. To facilitate this, a global network of widely distributed detectors must be established, utilizing inexpensive devices capable of long-term data collection. For individual detectors or small systems, determining the EAS detection probability is essential for accurate data analysis and interpretation. When dealing with numerous systems possessing varying characteristics, traditional detailed simulations become impractical; therefore, a more efficient method has been developed. By leveraging general EAS characteristics from broader simulations, required probabilities are calculated through specific parameterizations that account for the EAS spectrum, particle density energy dependence, and zenith angle variations. This approach enables the estimation of expected EAS events for sets of small detectors \cite{Karbowiak_2020}, allowing for a comparison between calculated results and actual measurements.

We present a new architecture for in-situ training of machine learning models embedded within smart sensors, demonstrating its application in distributed training scenarios for radio frequency (RF) spectrum sensing. Existing edge-based RF sensors typically lack the computational capacity required for practical, real-time intelligent signal classification. To address this, we propose Deepdelay Loop Reservoir Computing (DLR), a processing framework that enables machine learning on resource-limited edge devices by integrating delay-loop reservoir computing with specialized hardware. Compared to State-of-the-Art (SoA) neural networks, DLR significantly reduces form factor, hardware complexity, and latency. We validate DLR through two applications: RF Specific Emitter Identification (SEI) and wireless protocol recognition. This approach allows mobile edge platforms to authenticate and track emitters with rapid SEI retraining capabilities. By utilizing delay loops to separate data classes, the need for traditionally complex and power-intensive classification models is eliminated. Even when employing simple classifiers like Ridge Regression (RR), where complexity typically scales quadratically with input size, DLR surpasses SoA accuracy while further cutting power consumption through parallel (split) loop architectures. Furthermore, DLR supports distributed training across large regions to authenticate mobile devices, requiring minimal additional processing and communication overhead while preserving accuracy. We also demonstrate methods for merging locally trained DLR classifiers within relevant use cases.

For any $r \in (0,1)$, we establish both lower and upper bounds for the maximum density achievable when packing unit-radius discs with radius $r$ in the Euclidean plane. While the lower bounds are largely established results, our upper bounds enhance the best previously known values across the interval $r \in [0.11, 0.74]$. These refined bounds offer a more precise estimate of the exact maximum density for numerous $r$ values. Notably, we identify new ranges of $r$ where no packing can exceed the density of the hexagonal arrangement of identical discs.

Mobile robots serve diverse sectors, including industry, leisure, and defense. However, navigation systems relying solely on inertial sensors often suffer from time-based drift. This paper introduces the MoRPI framework, a pure inertial navigation method for mobile robots. Rather than following a straight-line path, the robot executes a periodic motion trajectory to facilitate peak-to-peak estimation. This strategy replaces the three integrations typical of classical inertial solutions with an empirical formula for distance calculation. Two variants of the MoRPI approach are presented: one utilizing both accelerometer and gyroscope data, and another relying exclusively on gyroscopes. Derived closed-form analytical solutions demonstrate that MoRPI yields lower position errors than traditional pure inertial methods. To validate this approach, field experiments were conducted using a robot equipped with two types of inertial sensors, resulting in the collection and evaluation of 143 trajectories spanning 75 minutes. The findings highlight the advantages of the proposed method. To support future development, the dataset and source code are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ansfl/MoRPI.

This study presents the first investigation of $Z$ boson events accompanied by a charm jet within the forward region of proton-proton collisions. Utilizing the LHCb detector, the analysis relies on a dataset with an integrated luminosity of $6 \, {\rm fb}^{-1}$ collected at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The fraction of charm jets is measured across different intervals of $Z$-boson rapidity, spanning $2.0 < y(Z) < 4.5$ in events containing a $Z$ boson and a jet. A notable increase is detected in the most forward rapidity interval, suggesting the possible presence of a valence-like intrinsic-charm component within the proton's wave function.

Current popular graph embedding techniques predominantly focus on fixed-order global structural features, neglecting hierarchical representations. To overcome this limitation, we introduce GraphCSC, a new algorithm that achieves classification by combining skeleton information derived from fixed-order structures learned via anonymous random walks with component information extracted from subgraphs of varying sizes. Since two graphs are deemed similar when both their skeletons and components match, our model integrates these elements into embeddings to characterize graph homogeneity. Evaluated across multiple datasets against a comprehensive set of state-of-the-art baselines, our experiments demonstrate that GraphCSC outperforms existing methods in real-world graph classification tasks.

Although neural network methods for Named-Entity Recognition have minimized the reliance on manually engineered features, current state-of-the-art systems typically discard lexical features except for gazetteers. This study argues that such an approach is unjustified, demonstrating that lexical features offer significant utility. We introduce a method that embeds both words and entity types into a low-dimensional vector space trained via distant supervision using Wikipedia data. From this, we generate offline feature vectors for each word. When integrated with a standard recurrent neural network, this representation delivers notable performance gains. Consequently, we achieve a new state-of-the-art F1 score of 87.95 on the ONTONOTES 5.0 dataset and match the best existing results with an F1 score of 91.73 on the widely studied CONLL-2003 benchmark.

The Square Kilometre Array (SKA) stands as the world's largest radio interferometer currently under development, and its high-precision, wide-field, and massive imaging capabilities present substantial challenges to constructing the SKA Science Data Processor (SDP). To address these difficulties, we introduce a hybrid imaging technique combining enhanced W-Stacking with snapshot methods. By fitting the snapshot $uv$ plane to constrain the $w$ range, we effectively boost the performance of the improved W-Stacking algorithm. This paper details the implementation of the WS-Snapshot approach and, through comprehensive SKA1-LOW simulations, evaluates its imaging quality and performance across various parameter configurations. The findings indicate that the WS-Snapshot method facilitates more efficient distributed processing and markedly cuts computational time overhead while maintaining acceptable accuracy, a factor vital for future SKA scientific research.

Consider a metric space $(\mathcal{X}, \rho)$ equipped with a Borel measure $\lambda$ defined on the $\sigma$-algebra of open sets, which assigns volumes to Borel subsets. The primary scenario involves $\mathcal{X} = \mathbb{R}^d$ with the Euclidean metric and $\lambda$ as the Lebesgue measure. This work does not focus on low dimensions, as constructing effective covering schemes for small $d$ can be achieved through brute-force optimization. Conversely, for medium to large dimensions (e.g., $d \geq 10$), meaningful progress is unlikely without a deep understanding of the fundamental principles required to build efficient covering designs.

From prehistoric eras to the present, sketches have served as a primary medium for visualizing objects. Recent years have seen a surge in sketch research, driven largely by the widespread adoption of touchscreen technology. A core assumption in this field is that sketches can universally convey visual concepts across diverse demographics, regardless of age, language, race, or background. Their interactive and detailed nature makes them suitable for a range of visual understanding tasks, including image retrieval, generation, editing, segmentation, and 3D modeling. Nevertheless, sketches remain highly abstract and subjective, varying based on individual perception. While they offer users fine-grained control in depicting objects, many find the process tedious compared to alternatives like text or tags, largely due to limited drawing skills. Additionally, the scarcity of fine-grained sketch-photo pairs poses a major obstacle to commercializing sketch-based applications. Consequently, this thesis seeks to advance sketch-based visual understanding toward greater practical utility.

This study examines the generation of electron-positron pairs by high-energy electrons traversing a medium, calculating the energy spectra for both direct and cascade production mechanisms while incorporating Coulomb corrections. Additionally, a novel formulation of the equivalent photons method is introduced to account for multiple scattering effects, demonstrating that these phenomena can be effectively investigated within this specific process.

Let $\sigma$ denote a permutation acting on a finite or infinite set $X$, where $F_X\left( \sigma^k\right)$ represents the count of fixed points resulting from the $k$th power of $\sigma$. This work details how the infinite sequence $\left(F_X\left( \sigma^k\right) \right)_{k=1}^{\infty}$ uniquely identifies the conjugacy class of $\sigma$ and establishes the arithmetic functions corresponding to fixed point sequences of permutations.

Modeling swarms in biological or engineering contexts presents significant challenges due to the system's inherently high dimensionality, even though their emergent dynamics often appear low-dimensional. While most current approaches rely on first principles and produce parameterizations specific to particular swarms that lack broad generalizability, this study employs a purely data-driven strategy. Specifically, we aim to (1) derive local interaction rules for homogeneous swarms from observational data and (2) replicate similar swarming behaviors using the resulting model. To achieve this, we developed and evaluated a modified technique called swarmDMD (dynamic mode decomposition with control) on the standard Vicsek swarm model. The objective is to utilize swarmDMD to identify inter-agent interactions responsible for observed collective behavior. Our results demonstrate that swarmDMD can accurately reconstruct swarm dynamics; furthermore, the learned model enables short-term data extrapolation, balancing prediction accuracy against the prediction horizon. Additionally, we conducted a thorough analysis of various observation data types, finding that inter-agent distance produces the most accurate models. We anticipate that the proposed swarmDMD approach will prove valuable for investigating multi-agent systems across biology, physics, and engineering.

Discrete element simulations explore a novel method for inducing avalanches by examining how randomly distributed vacancies can precipitate a global collapse. The study models a monolayer of identical spheres arranged in a hexagonal pattern on an inclined plane, bounded by a small fence to retain them, analogous to fruit storage in a market. A continuous, random removal of spheres is then simulated until the system collapses. This numerical experiment yielded a phase diagram illustrating avalanche occurrence due to vacancies as a function of the tilt angle and system size. Crucially, a specific sub-zone was identified where the critical number of extractions required to trigger an avalanche can be predicted. This prediction relies on an evolution model tracking the average coordination number and elastic energy, supplemented by an empirical link between initial and critical average elastic energy. The theoretical prediction holds true within a limited angular range, where avalanches occur at a specific critical packing fraction.

The Oscura experiment is poised to pioneer the hunt for low-mass dark matter particles by employing an extensive array of innovative silicon Charge Coupled Devices (CCDs) featuring a two-electron threshold and a cumulative exposure of 30 kg-yr. Launched in FY20, the research and development initiative is now in the design stage, aiming to commence construction by the end of 2024. Oscura promises unparalleled sensitivity to sub-GeV dark matter particles interacting with electrons, investigating both dark matter-electron scattering for masses as low as 500 keV and electron absorption of dark matter for masses down to 1 eV. Significant progress has been made on the experiment's primary technical hurdles, specifically securing new foundries for CCD sensor fabrication, creating a cold readout system, and characterizing experimental backgrounds.

Calculating feedback control via the Dynamic Programming equation is challenging because of the curse of dimensionality. A recently proposed approach, the tree structure algorithm, addresses this issue by computing the value function without requiring a spatial grid or interpolation techniques, relying instead on a discrete set of controls. However, the resulting control is constrained by the specific control set used during the tree computation. This paper extends and completes the method by selecting a finer control set for feedback calculation. This extension necessitates an interpolation method for scattered data, enabling the reconstruction of the value function at nodes outside the tree. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through a numerical example.

The minimum detectable feature size in x-ray imaging is typically limited by the system's spatial resolution. However, this constraint can be surpassed by utilizing the diffusive dark-field signal, which arises from unresolved phase effects or ultra-small-angle x-ray scattering caused by microscopic sample structures. Quantifying this signal offers valuable insights into microstructure dimensions and material composition, aiding applications in medical diagnostics, security screening, and materials science. We recently introduced a novel method to quantify the diffusive dark-field signal via a scattering angle using a single-exposure grid-based technique. This manuscript focuses on determining sample microstructure size from such single-exposure data. To achieve this, we measured the dark-field signal generated by polystyrene microspheres of five distinct sizes (1.0 $\mu$m to 10.8 $\mu$m) to analyze the relationship between signal strength and microstructure size ($S$). Furthermore, we examined the feasibility of single-exposure dark-field imaging by deriving a simple equation for the optimal propagation distance based on specific microstructure size and thickness, a formula that was successfully validated against experimental results. Our theoretical model indicates that the dark-field scattering angle is inversely proportional to $\sqrt{S}$, a finding that aligns with our experimental observations.

Despite significant advancements in image segmentation accuracy and robustness provided by deep models, achieving highly precise boundaries and fine structural details remains a difficult challenge. This paper introduces BASNet, a straightforward yet potent Boundary-Aware Segmentation Network designed for superior segmentation performance. BASNet employs a predict-refine framework and a hybrid loss function. The predict-refine architecture integrates a densely supervised encoder-decoder for initial prediction and a residual refinement module for enhancing the segmentation probability map. The hybrid loss combines binary cross-entropy, structural similarity, and intersection-over-union metrics to facilitate the learning of three hierarchical representations (pixel, patch, and map levels). Evaluations on two inverse tasks—salient object and camouflaged object segmentation—demonstrate that BASNet delivers competitive results with notably sharp boundaries. Furthermore, BASNet operates at over 70 frames per second on a single GPU, making it suitable for various real-world applications. Leveraging BASNet, we developed two near-commercial tools: AR COPY & PASTE, which uses augmented reality to copy and paste real-world objects, and OBJECT CUT, a web-based platform for automatic background removal. Both applications have garnered significant attention and practical impact. The source code and applications are publicly accessible at: https://github.com/NathanUA/BASNet.

Direct gravitational simulations of n-body systems exhibit a time complexity of O(n^2), becoming increasingly computationally demanding as the number of bodies grows. Offloading this workload across multiple cores substantially accelerates the process, forming the basis of parallel computing. This project evolved our solar system over the next millennium (from 2015 to 3015) using the BlueCrystal supercomputer. Gravitational bodies, including planets, moons, and asteroids, were successfully simulated, with initial states (mass, position, and velocity vectors) for solar system objects retrieved from NASA's JPL Horizons web interface. The study examined two parallel computing domains: shared and distributed memory systems.

The power graph $\mathcal{P}(G)$ of a group $G$ is defined as a simple graph where the vertex set corresponds to $G$, and two vertices are connected if one is a positive power of the other. This paper investigates the minimum degree $\delta(\mathcal{P}(G))$ for finite noncyclic nilpotent groups $G$. By examining conditions related to the prime factors of $|G|$ and the Sylow subgroups, we identify specific vertices linked to the generators of maximal cyclic subgroups, demonstrating that $\delta(\mathcal{P}(G))$ matches the degree of one such vertex. Furthermore, we apply these findings to determine $\delta(\mathcal{P}(G))$ for various classes of finite noncyclic abelian groups.

Research on probabilistic rewriting has extensively investigated termination and confluence across various systems. In our work involving a lambda calculus designed for quantum computation, we encountered a system featuring probabilistic rewriting rules and strongly normalizing terms. This study analyzes how minor adjustments regarding probabilistic rewriting, affine variables, and strategies impact confluence within this strongly normalizing probabilistic calculus.

This paper examines the Wandzura-Wilczek relation for the structure function $g_2$, focusing specifically on its relationship with Transverse Momentum Dependent factorization. We highlight that the relation is violated by two separate twist-3 contributions. Based on these results, we interpret existing experimental data on $g_2$, which suggests a violation magnitude of 20–40%, and outline methods for the individual measurement of these twist-3 terms.

Accurate regulation of quantum dynamics represents a pivotal engineering hurdle in quantum technology. While model-based optimal control methods prove highly effective when theoretical predictions align closely with experimental results, achieving high-fidelity quantum processes with such approaches demands rigorous device characterization. In cold-atom quantum processors, the Hamiltonian is typically well-defined; however, superconducting qubits operating at milli-Kelvin temperatures suffer from less precise Hamiltonian characterization. Factors such as unaccounted physical phenomena (mode discrepancies), coherent disturbances, and elevated noise levels undermine traditional model-based control strategies in these systems. This study introduces Model Predictive Control (MPC) for quantum control applications. As a closed-loop optimization framework, MPC offers three key advantages: (i) it inherently rejects disturbances through the integration of measurement feedback, (ii) it employs finite-horizon model-based optimizations to manage complex multi-input, multi-output dynamical systems while adhering to state and input constraints, and (iii) it remains sufficiently flexible to integrate synergistically with other modern control methodologies. We illustrate the application of MPC in generating practical, optimized control sequences for representative quantum state preparation scenarios. Specifically, we demonstrate that MPC enables successful model-based control for a standard qubit, a weakly-anharmonic qubit, and a system experiencing crosstalk, even when the underlying model is insufficient. These cases highlight why MPC constitutes a vital addition to the quantum engineering control toolkit.

Historically, Fontaine proposed conjectures—now established as theorems—connecting \'etale and de Rham cohomologies for algebraic varieties over $p$-adic fields. In previous research, we demonstrated that pro-\'etale and de Rham cohomologies of analytic varieties are also linked in two limiting scenarios: the proper and Stein cases. While comparison theorems for proper varieties mirror those for algebraic ones, those for Stein varieties differ significantly. This paper extends Fontaine's conjectures to general smooth dagger varieties, which bridge these two extremes, and proves them for "small" varieties, encompassing quasi-compact varieties, their naive interiors, and analytifications of algebraic varieties. Our proof relies on a "geometrization" of the relevant cohomologies via quasi-Banach-Colmez spaces (qBCs), where the "quasi-" prefix indicates relaxed finiteness conditions. The core of the argument is a nuanced induction beginning with affinoids and leveraging qBC properties during the inductive step; these properties are of independent interest and form a substantial portion of our analysis.

Recent findings from the BICEP and Keck collaborations have imposed tight constraints on numerous inflationary models, including several well-motivated ones. While these constraints are problematic if gravity adheres to Einstein's theory up to the inflationary scale, they can be circumvented by incorporating quadratic-in-curvature terms effective at that energy level. Recent developments have demonstrated that such terms can provide a UV-complete description of gravity while maintaining stability and unitarity. This work calculates the predictions of quadratic gravity and compares them with BICEP/Keck limits, focusing on inflationary scenarios that are theoretically compelling from a particle physics perspective but ruled out in standard Einstein gravity: specifically, (critical) Higgs inflation and natural inflation. The former represents the most economical approach by identifying the inflaton with the sole known elementary scalar in the Standard Model, utilizing the field's near-criticality to stay within the perturbative regime. The latter involves a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson driving inflation with a naturally flat potential. The analysis demonstrates that quadratic gravity successfully reconciles both scenarios with current observational constraints.

The hierarchical overlap graph (HOG) represents overlaps among a set $P$ of $n$ strings similarly to how an overlap graph does. While the most established algorithm builds the HOG in $O(||P|| \log n)$ time and $O(||P||)$ space—where $||P||$ denotes the total length of all strings in $P$—this paper introduces a new approach that achieves $O(||P||)$ time and space complexity. Consequently, the proposed method improves upon the overlap graph's construction requirements, which are $O(||P|| + n^2)$.

A single-cycle laser pulse traveling through plasma induces a controllable, asymmetric expulsion of plasma electrons, governed by the laser's carrier envelope phase (CEP), thereby creating an oscillating plasma bubble. This bubble's transverse wakefield displays periodic modulation. The study proposes an injection scheme for a laser wakefield accelerator that utilizes a co-propagating pair consisting of a single-cycle low-frequency pulse and a multi-cycle high-frequency pulse. This interaction generates a transversely oscillating wakefield that efficiently captures and accelerates background plasma electrons. By adjusting the initial CEP of the single-cycle pulse, the injection dynamics can be tuned independently of the multi-cycle pulse, allowing for precise control over the spatial profile of the resulting electron bunches.

Although Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems have advanced considerably in recent years, they continue to struggle with noisy and out-of-domain data, often producing transcripts riddled with substitution and deletion errors that severely hinder downstream task performance. To address this, we introduce PhonemeBERT, a BERT-inspired language model trained jointly on phoneme sequences and ASR transcripts to derive phonetic-aware representations resilient to ASR inaccuracies. PhonemeBERT enhances downstream applications by incorporating phoneme sequences as auxiliary features and remains effective in low-resource scenarios where only ASR transcripts are available. We conducted extensive evaluations by generating noisy datasets from Stanford Sentiment Treebank, TREC, and ATIS for sentiment analysis, question classification, and intent recognition, respectively. Our results demonstrate that PhonemeBERT comprehensively outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across all tested datasets.

In numerous real-world multi-agent cooperative scenarios, the high costs and risks associated with online interaction prevent agents from gathering environmental experiences during learning, forcing them to rely on offline datasets. However, transition probabilities derived from these datasets often diverge significantly from those induced by the learned policies of other agents, leading to substantial errors in value estimation. Furthermore, disparate behavior policies can cause the experience distributions across agents' datasets to vary drastically, resulting in significant discrepancies in value estimates among agents. Consequently, agents tend to develop uncoordinated, suboptimal policies. To address this, we introduce MABCQ, which leverages value deviation and transition normalization to adjust transition probabilities. Specifically, value deviation optimistically boosts the probabilities of transitioning to high-value next states, while transition normalization corrects biases in the probability distributions of subsequent states. Together, these mechanisms encourage agents to identify potential optimal and coordinated policies. We provide a mathematical proof demonstrating the convergence of Q-learning under the modified non-stationary transition probabilities. Empirically, MABCQ significantly outperforms baseline methods and effectively reduces the variance in value estimates between agents.

Graphene nanoribbons exhibit fascinating electronic characteristics stemming from the unique nature of their charge carriers, local confinement effects, and atomic-level structural specifics. The local work function serves as proof of these structural, electronic, and chemical variations at surfaces. Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) enables the measurement of the local contact potential difference (LCPD) between a probe tip and a surface, a value directly linked to the work function. In this study, we employed KPFM to map the LCPD of graphene nanoribbons grown on a Au(111) substrate. The resulting LCPD data indicates charge transfer occurring between the nanoribbons and the gold substrate. These findings are supported by density functional theory calculations, which confirm that the maps correspond to the doping of the nanoribbons. Consequently, our results enhance the understanding of the relationship between atomic structures and electronic properties.

Coinfection refers to the scenario where a host already infected by one pathogen contracts a second one later. The immune response triggered by an initial infection can suppress the host's defenses, thereby facilitating the spread of a subsequent emerging pathogen. Within a population, social interaction patterns can be represented using complex networks, and research indicates that these contact structures significantly shape disease dynamics. This study examines how contact clustering influences the coinfection dynamics of two pathogens spreading across a network. By employing generating function formulations to predict outbreak sizes for each pathogen, we numerically analyze the threshold conditions required for the coexistence of both strains. Our findings reveal that the impact of clustering on coinfection levels is determined by the specific details of the contact network topology.

We compute tree-level amplitudes for electrically neutral $2\to2$ scattering within the Standard Model, where the Higgs doublet is non-minimally coupled to the Ricci scalar, examining both the metric and Palatini formulations of gravity. We determine the partial wave unitarity limit for arbitrary background field values, confirming consistency with prior studies. In the electroweak vacuum, tree-level unitarity breaks down at approximately $M_\text{Planck}/\xi$ for the metric formulation and at $\sim M_\text{Planck}/\sqrt{\xi}$ for the Palatini formulation. Conversely, in an inflationary large-field background, the unitarity limit is $\sim M_\text{Planck}/\sqrt{\xi}$ for both approaches. We compare this violation energy scale to those pertinent to inflation and derive a direct collider constraint on $\xi$ for the Palatini case, yielding $\xi < 2.5 \times 10^{31}$.

Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) focuses on extracting high-level semantics from spoken utterances. While prior research has explored combining speech self-supervised models with textual pre-trained models, achieving reasonable gains, these approaches often require complex architectural designs due to the modality mismatch between audio signals and text tokens. This study introduces a straightforward yet effective unsupervised framework that links speech and textual pre-trained models, creating an unsupervised speech-to-semantic pre-trained model applicable to various SLU tasks. Specifically, we utilize unsupervised Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) as a bridge to connect these distinct modalities. Our experiments demonstrate that unsupervised ASR alone enhances representations derived from speech self-supervised models. More significantly, it serves as an efficient connector between speech and textual pre-trained models, boosting performance across five different SLU tasks. Notably, our approach achieves a state-of-the-art result on the challenging NMSQA benchmark for spoken question answering.

We introduce a new one-shot approach for object detection and 6-degree-of-freedom pose estimation that eliminates the need for training on target objects. During inference, the system accepts a target image and a textured 3D query model as inputs. The fundamental concept involves representing the 3D model through multiple 2D templates rendered from various perspectives, facilitating direct dense feature extraction and matching via CNNs. The process begins with 2D localization, followed by the estimation of the approximate viewpoint, and subsequently predicts dense 2D-3D correspondences. The final pose is calculated using the PnP algorithm. We assessed this method on the LineMOD, Occlusion, Homebrewed, YCB-V, and TLESS datasets, demonstrating highly competitive performance against state-of-the-art techniques trained on synthetic data, despite our method never being trained on the specific object models used for testing.

The cardinal characteristics $\mathfrak t$ (tower number) and $\mathfrak u$ (ultrafilter number) originate in set theory, derived from combinatorial properties of subsets of $\omega$ under the almost inclusion relation $\subseteq^*$. This work explores analogs of these cardinals within computability theory. We demonstrate that the mass problem involving ultrafilter bases is equivalent to computing a function dominating all computable functions; consequently, via Martin's characterization, it captures the property of highness. Conversely, the mass problem for maximal towers lies below that of computing a non-low set. Furthermore, we establish that while some, but not all, noncomputable low sets compute maximal towers—specifically, every noncomputable (low) c.e. set does, whereas no 1-generic $\Delta^0_2$ set does. Finally, we examine mass problems concerning maximal almost disjoint families and maximal independent families. We prove that the former is Medvedev equivalent to maximal towers, while the latter is Medvedev equivalent to ultrafilter bases.

In inhomogeneous media, electromagnetic rays diverge from the paths forecasted by leading-order geometrical optics. This phenomenon, known as the spin Hall effect of light, is often disregarded in ray-tracing software designed for plasma modeling. This study demonstrates that the spin Hall effect can substantially impact radiofrequency waves within toroidal fusion plasmas. For instance, an electron-cyclotron wave beam may shift by up to ten wavelengths (approximately 0.1 m) in the poloidal direction compared to the lowest-order ray path. We derived this displacement using gauge-invariant ray equations from extended geometrical optics and validated our theoretical findings against full-wave simulations.

This study examines the unique characteristics of interparticle interactions among methanol molecules in the vapor phase. The bare potential is defined as the combination of repulsive, dispersive, and electrostatic forces, with the assumption that hydrogen bonding is primarily electrostatic in nature, rendering the contribution from electronic shell overlap negligible. Dispersive interactions are estimated using London's formula, while electrostatic interactions are modeled via a multipole expansion extending up to the dipole-octupole term. Multipole moments are assigned values derived from either experimental data or quantum chemical computations. Repulsive forces are represented by a power potential, with parameters adjusted to match the second virial coefficient and dimer characteristics. In addition to the bare potential, the averaged interparticle interaction potential is also evaluated. Results indicate that the repulsive potential follows an exponent of $n=28$. Furthermore, the multipole potential detailed in this work is rigorously compared against the OPLS potential.

Security serves as a fundamental pillar for operational digital markets and communities; without trust in data protection, users will abandon these platforms. Despite corporate commitment to risk management, the high cost of specialized security knowledge and the varied nature of vulnerabilities present significant challenges. Consequently, both corporations and governments are increasingly adopting bug bounty programs (BBPs) to crowdsource cybersecurity efforts by compensating individuals for identifying system flaws. Although BBP adoption has surged recently, scholarly understanding of the market's participants and their motivations remains scarce. This paper applies transaction cost economics to analyze the incentives driving firms and researchers (often termed hackers) within BBPs. It highlights the critical function of centralized platforms that coordinate these initiatives. Through an examination of the HackerOne platform, utilizing a unique dataset covering more than 14,000 researchers, 125,000 reported vulnerabilities, and over 500 firms between 2014 and late 2021, the study demonstrates how such platforms establish a market for security flaws by mitigating information asymmetries and the resulting transaction costs.

Ultralight axions and similar bosons appear as dark matter candidates in numerous high-energy physics theories extending the Standard Model, with the string axiverse specifically predicting up to $\mathcal{O}(100)$ light scalar bosons within the dark sector. By analyzing a mixture of axions and cold dark matter, we derive upper limits for the axion relic density of $\Omega_a h^2 < 0.004$ for masses ranging from $10^{-31}\;\mathrm{eV}$ to $10^{-26}\;\mathrm{eV}$ at a 95% confidence level. Furthermore, we tighten existing constraints by factors exceeding 4.5 and 2.1 for axion masses of $10^{-25}$ eV and $10^{-32}$ eV, respectively. Utilizing Fourier-space galaxy clustering data from the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS), we illustrate how galaxy surveys resolve key degeneracies in the axion parameter space that the cosmic microwave background (CMB) cannot. We validate the effective field theory of large-scale structure for mixed ultralight axion dark matter by generating mock galaxy catalogs, revealing an anisotropic signature in the galaxy quadrupole. Additionally, our simulations show that allowing a $10^{-28}$ eV axion to constitute 5% of dark matter increases the linear galaxy bias from 1.8 to 2.4. Finally, we introduce an enhanced interpolation scheme that accelerates the calculation of the axion contribution to the linear matter power spectrum, reducing the computational cost of full Monte Carlo Markov chain analyses by 70%.

Buan and Zhou previously formulated a silting theorem that extends the classical Brenner-Butter tilting theorem. This paper presents an alternative proof of that result utilizing differential graded algebras.

The predict+optimize framework integrates machine learning for estimating problem coefficients with a combinatorial optimization task that relies on those predictions. Although this can be addressed in two distinct stages, directly minimizing the optimization loss is superior; however, this necessitates differentiating through a discrete, non-differentiable combinatorial function. Most current methods employ surrogate gradients to address this challenge. Demirovic et al. demonstrated how to formulate the optimization loss as a piece-wise linear function of predicted coefficients, yet their method is limited to problems solvable via dynamic programming. In contrast, this work introduces a novel divide-and-conquer algorithm capable of handling optimization problems without such restrictions while predicting coefficients based on the optimization loss. Additionally, we present a greedy variant of this approach that yields comparable results with reduced computational cost. Comparisons with other predict+optimize strategies demonstrate that our method effectively solves challenging combinatorial problems more successfully than existing alternatives.

We present a novel method, the grid algorithm, for constructing images of attractors within generalized iterated function systems on finite-dimensional spaces, and we evaluate its performance against the deterministic algorithm proposed by P. Jaros, L. Maslanka, and F. Strobin in [Algorithms generating images of attractors of generalized iterated function systems, Numer. Algorithms, 73 (2016), 477-499].

Real-world datasets frequently display long-tail distributions characterized by severe class imbalance, where dominant majority classes can skew training dynamics and distort the decision boundaries of underrepresented minority classes. Recent studies have explored supervised contrastive learning (SCL) for long-tail recognition, reporting significant performance improvements. However, this paper demonstrates that while SCL enhances accuracy, existing baselines struggle with non-uniform feature distributions caused by data imbalance, resulting in poor separability for minority class samples within the feature space. To resolve this, we introduce Targeted Supervised Contrastive Learning (TSC), which enforces uniformity in the feature distribution across the hypersphere. TSC operates by generating a set of targets uniformly scattered on a hypersphere and guiding features from different classes to converge toward these distinct, evenly distributed points during training. This mechanism compels all classes, particularly minority ones, to maintain a uniform distribution in the feature space, thereby sharpening class boundaries and enhancing generalization capabilities even under long-tail conditions. Empirical results across various datasets confirm that TSC achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-tail recognition tasks.

Numerous studies have demonstrated the danger of overfitting when selecting trading strategies solely based on strong in-sample (IS) performance, yet most have only identified this issue without proposing solutions to mitigate it. This paper introduces an approach to prevent overfitting by ensuring that a robust strategy remains effective when tested against paths generated according to the distribution of historical data. We employ a GAN combined with LSTM to learn and replicate the distribution of historical time series, subsequently backtesting trading strategies using these generated paths to circumvent overfitting. (Please note that this is a translated English version of a thesis originally written in Chinese in 2018, and some statements or claims may be outdated as of 2022.)

Stimulated Raman adiabatic passage (STIRAP) is a prevalent method for achieving robust, high-fidelity quantum control across diverse systems. Nevertheless, its application to superconducting qubits remains constrained by population leakage resulting from weak anharmonicity. In this work, we present an optimally controlled shortcut-to-adiabatic (STA) technique designed to accelerate the STIRAP protocol within a superconducting qudit. By adjusting the STIRAP pulse profiles, we experimentally achieved rapid (32 ns) and high-fidelity quantum state transfer. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this protocol exhibits robustness against perturbations in control parameters. Consequently, our stimulated Raman shortcut-to-adiabatic passage transition offers an efficient and practical solution for quantum information processing.

This chapter introduces low-energy beam transport systems, examining common magnetostatic components (solenoids, dipoles, and quadrupoles) alongside electrostatic ones (einzel lenses, dipoles, and quadrupoles). It covers fundamental topics such as ion beam emittance, space-charge effects, and the physics governing ion source extraction. Additionally, the text references standard computer codes for ion optical system design and provides a detailed description of the trajectory tracking method typically employed for extraction simulations.

Predicting Irregularly Sampled Time Series (ISTS) is a critical challenge in real-world applications, where improved accuracy relies on capturing more data characteristics. Unlike standard time series, ISTS features irregular intra-series intervals and varying inter-series sampling rates. However, current methods often yield suboptimal results by artificially introducing dependencies and biasedly learning relationships when modeling these traits. To address this, we introduce a novel Time Encoding (TE) mechanism that embeds temporal information as complex-domain vectors. TE possesses properties for absolute and relative distances across different sampling rates, effectively representing both irregularities. Furthermore, we develop the Time Encoding Echo State Network (TE-ESN), the first ESN-based architecture capable of processing ISTS data. By integrating long short-term memories and series fusion, TE-ESN captures both horizontal and vertical relationships. Experimental results on one chaotic system and three real-world datasets demonstrate that TE-ESN outperforms all baselines while exhibiting superior reservoir properties.

We present an unusual phenomenon in electron transport within a one-dimensional disordered ring, regardless of whether the disorder is random or correlated, under zero magnetic flux and in the presence of Rashba spin-orbit coupling. This system demonstrates a significantly larger circulating current than a perfect ring across a broad spectrum of spin-orbit coupling strengths, resulting in enhanced electrical conductivity, a finding confirmed through our Drude weight analysis.

Consider the binary form $F(x, y) = \prod_{k = 0}^{n - 1}(\delta_kx - \gamma_ky)$ of degree $n \geq 1$ with complex coefficients, expressed as a product of $n$ linear forms over $\mathbb C[x, y]$. Define the height of $F$ as $h_F = \prod_{k = 0}^{n - 1}\sqrt{|\gamma_k|^2 + |\delta_k|^2}$ and let $A_F$ represent the area of the fundamental region corresponding to $F$, specifically the set $\{(x, y) \in \mathbb R^2 \colon |F(x, y)| \leq 1\}$. It is demonstrated that the inequality $h_F^{2/n}A_F \geq \left(2^{1 + (r/n)}\right)\pi$ holds, where $r$ counts the multiplicity of the roots of $F$ lying on the real projective line $\mathbb R\mathbb P^1$.

**Introduction:** Accurately forecasting disease severity and mortality risk for individuals with COVID-19 is essential for enhancing care delivery and optimizing resource distribution. While various patient-specific factors, including pre-existing comorbidities, influence disease progression, the widespread availability of rapid automated analysis of peripheral blood samples prompted an investigation into whether such data could predict clinical outcomes.

**Methods:** We examined clinical datasets from COVID-19 patients with established outcomes by integrating statistical comparison and correlation techniques with diverse machine learning algorithms. These algorithms included decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting machine variants, support vector machines, K-nearest neighbors, and deep learning models.

**Results:** Our analysis identified specific clinical parameters measurable in blood samples that effectively distinguished between healthy individuals and those infected with COVID-19, while also demonstrating predictive capability for future symptom severity. Consequently, we developed several analytical methods achieving accuracy and precision exceeding 90% for predicting both disease severity and mortality.

**Conclusions:** In summary, we have established methodologies for analyzing routine patient clinical data to improve the prediction of COVID-19 outcomes. By leveraging standard hospital laboratory blood analyses, these approaches can identify high-risk patients likely to experience mortality, thereby facilitating optimized treatment strategies.

Building on the "REtrieval from MIxed Sampling" (REMIS) blocking methodology introduced by Anderson et al. (2016a), which aims to recover a high-frequency model from mixed-frequency data, this paper examines parameter identifiability within the Johansen (1995) vector error correction model for mixed-frequency settings. We demonstrate that the parameters of the high-frequency system are generically identified from the second moments of the differenced blocked process at lag N, where N represents the slower sampling rate. Furthermore, our analysis covers both stock and flow scenarios, as well as deterministic terms.

The effective permittivity of a vaterite matrix containing gold nanoparticles was determined using the extended Maxwell Garnett formalism. This approach incorporates the inherent anisotropy of vaterite alongside the dimensions, geometry, and alignment of the nanoparticles, employing size-dependent permittivity for the gold. Numerical analysis demonstrated that the permittivity parameters of the resulting homogenized composite are highly sensitive to variations in the nanoparticles' size, shape, orientation, and volume fraction.

We demonstrate that the singularities of the twisted Kähler–Einstein metric, which emerge either as the long-time limit of the Kähler–Ricci flow or within the collapsed limit of Ricci-flat Kähler metrics, are closely tied to the holomorphic sectional curvature of the underlying conical geometry. This approach offers an alternative derivation of the second-order estimate established by Gross, Tosatti, and Zhang, featuring explicit constants in the divisorial pole.

Interpretability methods seek to elucidate the reasoning behind a model's decisions, typically by offering either local explanations for specific predictions (e.g., diagnosing a particular patient) or global explanations for entire classes (e.g., general diagnostic patterns for a group). Although numerous approaches exist for each type individually, few frameworks deliver both consistently. This study integrates two robust existing techniques—Integrated Gradients for local analysis and Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV) for global analysis—to generate unified concept-based explanations. We initially validate this approach using two synthetic datasets with known ground truths, followed by demonstrations on a benchmark natural image dataset. Our evaluation covers various concepts, target classes, model architectures, and IG parameters (such as baselines). Results indicate that our method enhances global explanations compared to standard TCAV against ground truth data while yielding valuable local insights. Furthermore, a user study confirms the method's utility relative to using no explanations or only global ones. Ultimately, we aim to advance the integration of disparate local and global techniques to maximize their combined benefits.

We introduce dynamic algorithms capable of estimating the maximum matching size of graphs subject to edge insertions and deletions, achieving polylogarithmic update times and an approximation ratio strictly superior to $2$. Specifically, our methods deliver an approximation of $1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\epsilon \approx 1.707+\epsilon$ for bipartite graphs and $1.973+\epsilon$ for general graphs. These results affirmatively resolve the longstanding open question originally raised by Onak and Rubinfeld (STOC'10) and frequently reiterated in dynamic graph algorithm research. Furthermore, our randomized algorithms function effectively against adaptive adversaries, ensuring worst-case polylogarithmic update times with high probability. The core of our approach involves simulating novel two-pass streaming matching algorithms within a dynamic framework. Our primary innovation lies in utilizing Behnezhad's (FOCS'21) recent sublinear-time matching algorithm in a white-box fashion to efficiently emulate the second pass of these streaming algorithms, thereby circumventing the established vertex-update barrier.

The thermal architecture of protoplanetary disks is a defining feature with profound implications for both disk evolution and planet formation. This study determines the two-dimensional thermal structure of the TW Hya disk by analyzing seven carbon monoxide (CO) spectral lines. The analysis incorporates new ALMA data for the 12CO J=2-1 and C18O J=2-1 transitions, alongside archival ALMA observations covering 12CO J=3-2, 13CO J=3-2, 6-5, C18O J=3-2, and 6-5. We also replicate a Herschel measurement of the HD J=1-0 line flux and the spectral energy distribution, while integrating recent estimates of CO radial depletion within TW Hya. These datasets were simulated using the RAC2D thermochemical code, with our optimal model successfully reproducing all spatially resolved CO surface brightness profiles. The derived thermal profile indicates a disk mass of 0.025 solar masses and identifies a thin upper gas layer depleted of small dust, with a thickness approximately 1.2% of the local radius. Based on this thermal structure, we conclude that CO alone cannot serve as a reliable mass tracer because its abundance is degenerate with the total H2 surface density; various mass models can fit the CO line profiles under different abundance assumptions. Consequently, determining mass requires supplementary constraints, which we provide here through HD observations to derive the gas mass and corroborate the CO depletion hypothesis. Our final thermal structure validates HD as an effective tool for probing protoplanetary disk mass. Furthermore, the methodology presented offers a viable strategy for future extraction of disk temperatures and masses.

This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of the Brown-York and Hawking masses on surfaces that are nearly round at infinity within an asymptotically flat manifold. Since nearly round surfaces admit an intrinsic definition, our findings demonstrate that the ADM mass of an asymptotically flat 3-manifold can be estimated by specific geometric invariants derived from a sequence of such surfaces as they approach the manifold's boundary at infinity.

We present a visual model of qubits designed to make quantum computing accessible to a wide audience. This model is derived from physical devices we created to demonstrate concepts such as superposition, entanglement, measurement, phases, interference, and quantum gates. We further illustrate how this representation can be applied to explain quantum teleportation and the Bennett-Brassard quantum key agreement protocol.

Currently, dark matter (DM) is inferred solely through its gravitational effects on visible matter. Consequently, understanding these interactions is crucial for elucidating both the properties and dynamics of DM and the evolution of visible matter.
