This study examines the gravitational impact of DM on the stability of the interstellar medium (ISM)—the birthplace of stars and clusters—using an isothermal, self-gravitating gas model for the ISM and treating DM particles as entities interacting only gravitationally. Analytical results indicate that even a small population of fast-moving DM particles significantly expands the stable radius and mass of a gas cloud, whereas a higher relative DM density induces instability. Specifically, under typical ISM and DM parameters, the presence of DM increases the maximum stable mass of an isothermal cloud by a factor of four and its radius by five.

This paper explores the square integrable representations of the generalized Weyl-Heisenberg group. We examine its quasi-regular representation and derive a specific form for the admissible vectors associated with this representation. Finally, we present several examples to illustrate our theoretical findings.

In the consistent histories approach to quantum theory, collections of coarse-grained histories designated as "consistent" adhere to classical probability laws. These sets are often cited as capable of describing the semi-classical dynamics of closed quantum systems. However, since most physical situations allow for multiple distinct consistent sets, each can be interpreted as a unique context. Drawing inferences from propositions across different consistent sets generates paradoxes, such as the contradictory conclusions first identified by Kent [Phys. Rev. Lett. 78, 2874 (1997)]. Advocates of this framework contend that mixing propositions from disparate consistent sets in logical reasoning is invalid, and that such paradoxes merely reflect the standard contextuality of microscopic quantum systems, as established by the Kochen-Specker theorem.

This contribution employs consistent histories to model a macroscopic (semi-classical) system, demonstrating that contextuality paradoxes—arising from mixing different consistent sets—survive even in the semi-classical limit. This finding contrasts sharply with standard quantum theory, where contextuality paradoxes typically vanish in the semi-classical regime. Specifically, we examine various consistent sets regarding the arrival times of a semi-classical wave packet within an infinite square well. Surprisingly, these sets yield conflicting results concerning whether a system, initially confined to a subregion, ever departed from it. These results suggest a necessity for constraints beyond the standard consistency condition to properly recover the semi-classical limit, supporting the principle that while "all consistent sets are equal," "some consistent sets are more equal than others."

By accounting for viscous friction that fluctuates both spatially and temporally, general formulas for entropy production, free energy, and entropy extraction rates are established for Brownian particles moving in both overdamped and underdamped environments. Utilizing standard stochastic methods for these media, thermodynamic expressions are first formulated at the trajectory level before being extended to the ensemble level. To investigate non-equilibrium thermodynamic characteristics of a Brownian particle hopping through a medium with time-varying viscosity, the study examines a particle walking on a periodic isothermal medium, with or without an applied load. Exact analytical findings reveal that when no load is present ($f=0$), the entropy production rate ${\dot e}_{p}$ converges to the entropy extraction rate ${\dot h}_{d}=0$. This aligns with the expectation that a system in contact with a uniform temperature must satisfy the detailed balance condition over long timescales. Conversely, under a load where viscous friction decreases either spatially or temporally, the entropy $S(t)$ rises monotonically before saturating at a constant value as time progresses. In this scenario, the entropy production rate ${\dot e}_{p}$ declines over time, reaching a steady state where ${\dot e}_{p}={\dot h}_{d}>0$. In contrast, if viscous friction increases spatially or temporally, both the entropy production rate and the entropy extraction rate increase monotonically, indicating that such systems are fundamentally irreversible.

GitHub repositories contain extensive details regarding contributors, commit counts, releases, pull requests, programming languages, and issues. Despite this wealth of information, there is currently no systematic dataset of open-source projects that captures such repository details for knowledge acquisition and mining. To address this, we developed a tool called GitRepository, which generates a dataset based on a proposed schema. Starting with 1,680 repositories, the final dataset includes 620 repositories after applying basic filters for stars and forks, and 247 repositories after applying all pre-defined filters. The tool extracts repository information and stores the data in both CSV files and a database (.DB) file.

In low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGN), the vanishing accretion disc reveals a faint optical nuclear continuum whose origin remains controversial, largely due to significant observational constraints in the infrared to ultraviolet spectrum. By integrating multi-wavelength sub-arcsecond resolution data capable of isolating the true nuclear continuum with mid-infrared nebular emission lines, we indirectly investigated the extreme ultraviolet continuum shape. Our findings indicate that eight of the closest prototype LLAGN are consistent with emission from pure compact jets—comprising self-absorbed synchrotron radiation and its associated self-Compton component—across more than ten orders of magnitude in frequency. Compared to typical radio galaxies, LLAGN continua exhibit two distinct characteristics: $i)$ a steep spectral slope in the infrared-to-optical/UV range ($-3.7 < \alpha_0 < -1.3$; $F_\nu \propto \nu^{\alpha_0}$); and $ii)$ a very high turnover frequency ($0.2\text{--}30\,\rm{THz}$; $1.3\,\rm{mm}\text{--}10\,\rm{\mu m}$). These features can be accounted for if the synchrotron continuum is primarily driven by thermalized particles at the jet base or corona with significantly high temperatures, while only a minor fraction of energy ($\sim 20\%$) is allocated to the high-energy power-law tail of accelerated particles. Conversely, nebular gas excitation in LLAGN aligns with photo-ionization from inverse Compton radiation ($\alpha_{\rm x} \sim -0.7$), which would dominate the nuclear continuum at wavelengths shorter than $\sim 3000$ \r{A}. Our results suggest that the LLAGN continuum may be dominated across all wavelengths by undeveloped jets powered by a thermalized particle distribution, mirroring the behavior seen in compact jets of quiescent black hole X-ray binaries. This has significant implications for galaxy evolution, as LLAGN could represent a major yet underestimated source of kinetic feedback in galaxies.

**Introduction:** Determining sleep stages is critical for diagnosing sleep disorders and maintaining sleep health. Traditionally, this process occurs in clinical environments and demands labor-intensive manual labeling. We propose that robust four-class sleep staging can be achieved using raw photoplethysmography (PPG) time series data combined with contemporary deep learning (DL) techniques.

**Methods:** Our study utilized two public sleep databases containing raw PPG recordings from 2,374 patients spanning 23,055 hours. We created SleepPPG-Net, a DL model designed for four-class sleep staging directly from raw PPG signals. This end-to-end architecture integrates a residual convolutional network for automated feature extraction with a temporal convolutional network to model long-range dependencies. We evaluated SleepPPG-Net by comparing its performance against models utilizing the best-reported state-of-the-art (SOTA) algorithms.

**Results:** On a held-out test set, SleepPPG-Net achieved a median Cohen's Kappa ($\kappa$) score of 0.75, surpassing the best SOTA approach which scored 0.69. Furthermore, the model demonstrated strong generalization capabilities on an external database, reaching a $\kappa$ score of 0.74 following transfer learning.

**Perspective:** Collectively, SleepPPG-Net establishes new state-of-the-art benchmarks. Moreover, its performance levels are sufficient to facilitate the creation of wearables capable of meeting clinical requirements for diagnosing and monitoring conditions such as obstructive sleep apnea.

The recently introduced identifiable variational autoencoder (iVAE) framework offers a promising method for learning latent independent components (ICs). By utilizing auxiliary covariates to construct an identifiable generative pathway from covariates to ICs and finally to observations, iVAEs employ a posterior network to approximate ICs based on both observations and covariates. While the identifiability of this approach is attractive, we demonstrate that iVAEs can suffer from local minima where observations and the approximated ICs become independent given the covariates—a phenomenon we term the posterior collapse problem of iVAEs. To address this issue, we propose a novel method, covariate-informed iVAE (CI-iVAE), which incorporates a mixture of encoder and posterior distributions into the objective function. This adjustment prevents posterior collapse, yielding latent representations that retain more information from the observations. Moreover, CI-iVAEs generalize the original iVAE objective function into a broader class, selecting the optimal variant to achieve tighter evidence lower bounds than the standard iVAE. Experimental results on simulation datasets, EMNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and a large-scale brain imaging dataset confirm the efficacy of our proposed approach.

**Motivation:** The advancement of droplet-based technologies has generated vast amounts of single-cell transcriptome data, facilitating the analysis of cellular and molecular mechanisms at single-cell resolution and aiding in the comprehension of numerous biological phenomena. Although current state-of-the-art clustering techniques are utilized, they encounter specific limitations: (1) suboptimal clustering quality; (2) a reliance on prior knowledge regarding the number of clusters, which is often unavailable; and (3) a need for enhanced computational efficiency.

**Results:** To address these issues, we introduce the Parallel Split Merge Sampling on Dirichlet Process Mixture Model (Para-DPMM). Distinct from traditional DPMM approaches that sample individual data points, our method employs a split-merge mechanism operating at the cluster level, thereby significantly enhancing convergence and solution optimality. The model is designed for high parallelization, leveraging High-Performance Computing (HPC) clusters to enable efficient clustering of massive datasets. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that Para-DPMM surpasses widely used existing models in both clustering accuracy and processing speed.

**Availability:** The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/tiehangd/Para_DPMM/tree/master/Para_DPMM_package.

We report a chemodynamical analysis of the Grus I ultra-faint dwarf galaxy (UFD) utilizing medium-resolution ($R\sim11,000$) spectra from the Magellan/IMACS instrument for its individual stellar members. Based on low metallicities and consistent radial velocities, we confirm eight members of Grus I, while four additional candidates are identified based on velocity data alone. Unlike prior studies, our findings reveal an exceptionally low mean metallicity for Grus I, $\langle$[Fe/H]$\rangle = -2.62 \pm 0.11$ dex, classifying it as one of the most metal-poor UFDs. The galaxy exhibits a systemic radial velocity of $-143.5\pm1.2$ km s$^{-1}$ and a velocity dispersion of $\sigma_{\text{rv}} = 2.5^{+1.3}_{-0.8}$ km s$^{-1}$. These measurements yield a dynamical mass within the half-light radius of $M_{1/2} (r_h) = 8^{+12}_{-4} \times 10^5$ M$_{\odot}$ and a mass-to-light ratio of M/L$_V$ = $440^{+650}_{-250}$ M$_\odot$/L$_\odot$. Assuming dynamical equilibrium, our analysis confirms that Grus I is dominated by dark matter (M/L $> 80$ M$_\odot$/L$_\odot$), though no metallicity dispersion is detected ($\sigma_{\text{[Fe/H]}} < 0.44$ dex). Consequently, Grus I appears to be a fairly typical UFD, with properties aligning with established mass-metallicity and metallicity-luminosity trends for faint galaxies. This consistency implies that Grus I has not suffered significant mass loss due to tidal interactions with the Milky Way, a conclusion supported by its orbital parameters. Notably, Grus I possesses one of the lowest central densities ($\rho_{1/2} \sim 3.5_{-2.1}^{+5.7} \times 10^7$ M$_\odot$ kpc$^{-3}$) among UFDs not currently undergoing tidal disruption. Future models of UFD formation and evolution must account for the observed diversity in central densities, alongside variations in their outer regions.

Safe reinforcement learning (RL) addresses scenarios where an agent must maximize rewards while simultaneously avoiding unsafe regions. This study introduces CUP, a new policy optimization technique grounded in the Constrained Update Projection framework, which offers rigorous safety guarantees. A core component of CUP is the introduction of novel surrogate functions coupled with performance bounds. Compared to prior safe RL approaches, CUP offers three key advantages: first, it extends surrogate functions to the generalized advantage estimator (GAE), resulting in robust empirical results; second, it unifies performance bounds, enhancing the interpretability and understanding of existing algorithms; and third, it enables a non-convex implementation using only first-order optimizers, eliminating the need for strong convexity assumptions on objectives. To validate CUP, we benchmarked it against a comprehensive set of safe RL baselines across diverse tasks. Experimental results demonstrate CUP's effectiveness in both reward maximization and safety constraint adherence. The source code for CUP is available at https://github.com/zmsn-2077/ CUP-safe-rl.

Sum-Product Networks (SPNs) are highly expressive probabilistic models known for enabling exact and tractable inference through the exploitation of local independence. In contrast, Mixtures of Exchangeable Variable Models (MEVMs) are another class of tractable models that leverage the exchangeability of discrete random variables to ensure efficient inference. Since exchangeability is a natural feature of relational domains but has not yet been integrated into SPNs for efficient representation and inference, this paper introduces a new model called Exchangeability-Aware Sum-Product Networks (XSPNs). XSPNs generalize both SPNs and MEVMs as special cases, merging SPNs' capacity for learning deep probabilistic structures with MEVMs' ability to manage exchangeable variables efficiently. We propose a structure learning algorithm for XSPNs and demonstrate empirically that they achieve higher accuracy than standard SPNs when data consists of repeated, interchangeable components.

**Context.** The initial Stellar Potential Perturbers Database (StePPeD) was introduced in 2020 to provide current data on stars and systems capable of influencing the trajectories of long-period comets. This first compilation relied on Gaia DR2 data, using the minimal distance between stars and the Sun as the primary selection criterion to identify objects with close encounters within the Solar System.

**Aims.** Following the publication of the Gaia EDR3 data release, an update to the database became essential. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations were conducted to determine the uncertainties associated with the closest approach parameters for each object.

**Methods.** All close approach parameters from the previous StePPeD release were recalculated, a process that eliminated approximately one-third of the original entries. New candidates were then identified across the entire Gaia EDR3 catalogue. The study also addressed stellar duplicity and specifically searched for previously overlooked double stars passing near the Sun. Additionally, mass estimates were determined for new objects, and existing data for previously selected stars were updated.

**Results.** After rigorous verification of the collected data, a revised list comprising 155 potential stellar perturbers of long-period comets was compiled. A stricter threshold of 2 parsecs was applied for the minimum star-Sun distance. This final list includes 146 single stars and nine multiple systems, with uncertainty estimates calculated for the closest approach parameters of every object. Notably, HD 7977 was identified as a new potential strong past perturber, and the future influence of Gliese 710 was confirmed as plausible.

The chromatic symmetric function (CSF) for Dyck paths, as defined by Stanley, along with the Shareshian-Wachs $q$-analogue, exhibits significant links to Hessenberg varieties, diagonal harmonics, and LLT polynomials. Specifically, for abelian Dyck paths, these concepts are intriguingly associated with non-attacking rook placements, a connection established through the work of Stanley and Stembridge (1993) and Guay-Paquet (2013). For the $q$-analogue, these findings have been extended by Abreu and Nigro (2020) and Guay-Paquet (via private communication) by utilizing $q$-hit numbers, a variation of the original hit numbers introduced by Garsia and Remmel. A key contribution of this work is a novel proof of Guay-Paquet's refined identity, which represents $q$-CSFs within a CSF basis using $q$-hit coefficients. Additionally, we demonstrate that this identity is equivalent to the Abreu-Nigro identity, which expands the $q$-CSF in terms of elementary symmetric functions. This text serves as the extended abstract for FPSAC; the complete version is available at ArXiv:2104.07599.

This study examines the transport characteristics of a spherical active Brownian particle moving within a periodic potential under conditions of heavy damping. Due to the asymmetric nature of the potential, detailed balance is broken, causing the self-propelled particle to exhibit a non-zero drift velocity. The analysis calculates the average current and evaluates the particle's diffusivity through the effective diffusion coefficient. Specifically, for chiral active particles, increasing the angular velocity leads to a reduction in diffusivity, which confines the particle closer to its starting position and diminishes the average current.

The increasing accessibility of observational databases, such as electronic health records (EHR), offers exceptional opportunities for secondary biomedical research. Nevertheless, these datasets often contain errors and require validation prior to analysis. Validating entire databases is typically impractical due to resource limitations; therefore, a cost-effective solution involves a two-phase design that validates a subset of patient records enriched for the specific research question. This study addresses odds ratio estimation in the presence of differential misclassification for both outcomes and exposures. We propose optimal designs that minimize the variance of the maximum likelihood odds ratio estimator and develop a novel adaptive grid search algorithm to identify these designs in a computationally efficient and numerically accurate way. Since the optimal design relies on unknown parameters that cannot be specified without prior information, we introduce a multi-wave sampling strategy to approximate it in practice. Through extensive simulations and two large observational studies, we demonstrate the efficiency improvements of these proposed designs compared to existing methods. Finally, we provide an R package and a Shiny application to support the implementation of these optimal designs.

The time-integrated Dalitz plot for the three-body hadronic charmless decay ${{\overline{B}}^0 \to K_{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle S}}^0 \pi^+ \pi^-}$ is analyzed using a $pp$ collision dataset collected by the LHCb detector, with an integrated luminosity of $3.0\;\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$. The decay amplitude is modeled using an isobar approach. Measurements are taken of the relative contributions of these isobar amplitudes to the ${\overline{B}^0 \to K_{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle S}}^0 \pi^+ \pi^-}$ branching fraction, as well as the CP asymmetries of the flavor-specific amplitudes. The CP asymmetry in the decay rates between the conjugate processes ${\overline{B}^0 \to K^{*}(892)^{-}\pi^+}$ and ${\overline{B}^0 \to K^{*}(892)^{+}\pi^-}$ is found to be $-0.308 \pm 0.062$.

Mn$_3$Ge, a kagome lattice antiferromagnet, exhibits local hexagonal symmetry and a 120$^\circ$ ordered ground state. This non-colinear configuration generates a robust anomalous Hall effect. The primary objective of this study is to analyze how strain influences this response. We develop an effective model for the Hall vector, treating it as the system's order parameter. Utilizing this framework, we demonstrate that both intra- and inter-planar strains can invert the sign of the Hall response under a fixed magnetic field. Additionally, we examine the impact of strain on spin wave band gaps, revealing that strain can effectively manipulate these gaps to tune the magnon dynamics within the system.

We aim to automate molecular design based on targeted chemical properties. Our key contributions include a streamlined method for creating chemically valid SMILES strings, achieved by integrating a novel context-free grammar with specific masking techniques, and reframing molecular property optimization as a reinforcement learning task, specifically employing best-of-batch policy gradient within a Transformer architecture. This strategy requires significantly fewer model steps per atom compared to prior methods, facilitating the generation of larger molecules and outperforming previous state-of-the-art baselines by a wide margin. Furthermore, applying reinforcement learning to a custom context-free grammar enhanced with masking to enforce non-local constraints offers a versatile framework for optimizing any graph structure subject to both local and non-local constraints.

Planar graphs can be modeled as intersection graphs of various geometric shapes in two dimensions, such as circles (Koebe, 1936), line segments (Chalopin \& Gon{\c{c}}alves, 2009), and \textsc{L}-shapes (Gon{\c{c}}alves et al, 2018). In contrast, determining whether such representations exist for general graphs is frequently $NP$-hard. This paper examines apex graphs, defined as graphs that become planar upon the removal of a single vertex. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that deciding the existence of geometric representations for apex graphs is also $NP$-hard.

Specifically, we prove that for any positive integer $k$, recognizing any graph class $\mathcal{G}$ where $\textsc{PURE-2-DIR} \subseteq \mathcal{G} \subseteq \textsc{1-STRING}$ is $NP$-hard, even when restricted to apex graphs with a girth of at least $k$. In this context, $\textsc{PURE-2-DIR}$ refers to intersection graphs of axis-parallel line segments (with intersections occurring only between horizontal and vertical segments), while \textsc{1-STRING} denotes intersection graphs of simple curves (where curves intersect at most once) in the plane. These findings partially address an open question posed by Kratochv{\'\i}l \& Pergel (2007).

Unlike most existing $NP$-hardness reductions for these problems, which rely on variants of 3-SAT, our reduction is based on the \textsc{PLANAR HAMILTONIAN PATH COMPLETION} problem, utilizing a more intuitive concept of planarity. Consequently, our proof is significantly simpler and simultaneously covers multiple classes of geometric graphs.

This study introduces a pair of rate-diverse encoder and decoder designed for a two-user Gaussian multiple access channel (GMAC). The proposed approach allows users to transmit codewords of identical length but with varying coding rates, accommodating diverse channel conditions. To achieve this, we first propose the row-combining (RC) and row-extending (RE) methods to construct practical low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes for rate-diverse GMAC. Second, we develop an iterative rate-diverse joint user message decoding (RDJD) algorithm for GMAC, which decodes all user messages using a single parity-check matrix. Unlike conventional network-coded multiple access (NCMA) and compute-forward multiple access (CFMA) schemes, which recover a linear combination of transmitted codewords before decoding individual messages, this method decodes both user messages simultaneously. EXIT chart analysis and simulations demonstrate that RDJD can achieve up to a 1.0 dB gain over NCMA and CFMA in the two-user GMAC scenario. Specifically, we identify an optimal rate allocation for the two users that maximizes decoding performance based on channel conditions and sum rate.

This study introduces the application of conditional generative adversarial networks (CGANs) for generating generalized gravitational wave bursts within the time domain. As generative machine learning models, CGANs create new data by leveraging the characteristics of their training sets. In this work, the network is conditioned on five standard time-series signal classes used to characterize gravitational wave burst searches: sine-Gaussian, ringdown, white noise burst, Gaussian pulse, and binary black hole merger. We demonstrate that the model effectively replicates the features of these standard signal classes while also producing generalized burst signals through interpolation and class mixing. Furthermore, we present an application where a convolutional neural network (CNN) classifier is trained on bursts generated by our CGAN. Our results indicate that a CNN classifier trained exclusively on the five standard signal classes achieves lower detection efficiency compared to a CNN classifier trained on a diverse population of generalized burst signals derived from the combined signal class space.

This study examines second-order stochastic partial differential equations driven by additive noise within a bounded domain of $\mathbb R^n$, assuming the noise coefficients belong to $L^p$ spaces for sufficiently large $p$. It is established that the solutions are almost surely H\"older-continuous, and their corresponding H\"older norms possess finite moments of all orders.

General relativity serves as a foundational classical framework for understanding spacetime and gravity, having successfully withstood numerous empirical validations, particularly in weak-field scenarios and increasingly in strong-field contexts. Among the earliest extraterrestrial tools for probing gravity, radio pulsars—hosting highly self-gravitating neutron stars—occupy a singular position in investigating strong-field gravitational dynamics. The precision of radio timing for binary pulsars allows for accurate determination of system parameters, with the technology detecting minute alterations in orbital evolution. Consequently, any alternative gravity theory predicting deviations from general relativity in binary orbital dynamics can be rigorously tested against these timing observations. This chapter examines the fundamental principles of employing radio pulsars to test strong-field gravity, supported by recent case studies on gravitational dipolar radiation, massive gravity theories, and the strong equivalence principle. As more sensitive radio telescopes come into operation, pulsars are poised to deliver even more rigorous tests of strong gravity in the near future.

This study examines maximum entropy mechanisms governing information exchange between neural network-based agents and the macroscopic states of such societies across various scenarios. Key components emerging from entropy-based learning dynamics include the mathematical quantification of surprise, distrust toward other agents, and confidence in one's own opinions. The learning process is propelled by surprises, occurring when a receptor encounters concurrence from a distrusted agent or disagreement from a trusted one. Blame attribution for these surprises relies on the receiver's level of distrust toward the sender and the receiver's confidence in their own stance. The dynamics evolve through adjustments in either the receptor's opinion on the matter or its distrust of the emitter. In societies with $N$ agents exchanging binary opinions on multiple issues, behavior becomes complex and contingent upon the agenda's intricacy. For small sets of issues, the society stabilizes into polarized factions of antagonists, strictly adhering to balanced norms like "the friend of an enemy is an enemy." Conversely, with larger issue sets, societies may remain in spin-glass-like states for extended periods. Two forms of frustration—ideological and affective—exhibit dynamical annealing properties tied to the complexity of the questions discussed, resulting in a prolonged absence of sharply defined parties during transient phases.

Tilt-to-length (TTL) coupling refers to the technical phenomenon where angular or lateral jitter converts into an interferometric phase signal. As a significant noise source in high-precision interferometers, it arises from variations in optical path lengths or wavefront and clipping effects. This paper concentrates on geometric TTL coupling, breaking it down into various mechanisms accompanied by analytic formulas. We demonstrate that a purely geometric model does not always accurately predict TTL noise in an interferometer. Consequently, we explore how leveraging an understanding of these geometric effects enables noise reduction through intelligent design strategies and can also be utilized to mitigate total measured TTL noise in a system. These principles are applicable to a broad range of precision interferometers, including space-based gravitational wave detectors such as LISA.

Sensor data and Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication significantly enhance the situational awareness and safety of Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs). While data from local sensors like cameras and radar supports the Host Vehicle (HV) with immediate, short-range awareness, this information remains confined to the HV. Conversely, V2X enables CAVs to exchange safety-critical data, facilitating the creation of sophisticated local object maps. This paper presents a point-to-point Driver Messenger System (DMS) that continuously updates the HV's local object map to transmit Over-the-Air (OTA) Driver Intent Messages (DIMs) to nearby Target Vehicles (TVs) based on predefined traffic scenarios. Specifically, the study focuses on lane changes, where the DMS identifies the nearest TV in the adjacent lane using the local object map and alerts it via a DIM. The paper introduces a TV recognition algorithm within the DMS that leverages the HV's Path History (PH) to pinpoint the most relevant TV for receiving a DIM. Furthermore, the DMS functions as an advanced warning system, offering increased time and space headway measurements between the HV and TVs across various simulated lane change scenarios.

Loop acceleration serves to verify program safety, reachability, runtime constraints, and termination properties. While numerous acceleration methods have been developed, existing approaches are monolithic, meaning they cannot combine multiple techniques to accelerate a single loop. In contrast, this work introduces a calculus that enables the modular integration of various acceleration techniques and demonstrates how to incorporate many existing methods into this framework. Additionally, we propose two novel techniques that integrate seamlessly with our calculus. Since some of these methods apply exclusively to non-terminating loops, their combination with our calculus yields a new modular strategy for proving non-termination. Empirical results confirm the effectiveness of this approach for both loop acceleration and non-termination verification.

Next-generation multibeam satellites introduce a novel approach to satellite communication channel design, offering complete flexibility in bandwidth, transmit power, and beam coverage management. This paper leverages these flexible capabilities alongside user geographical distribution to enhance satellite-assisted edge caching performance. Our objective is to jointly optimize bandwidth allocation in multibeam systems and caching decisions at edge nodes to solve two critical issues: minimizing cache feeding time and maximizing cache hits. To address the non-convex nature of this joint optimization problem, we reformulate it into a difference-of-convex (DC) structure, which is then solved using a proposed iterative algorithm with a theoretical guarantee of convergence to at least a local optimum. Additionally, we evaluate the proposed design's effectiveness using the realistic beam coverage of the SES-14 satellite and the Movielens dataset. Numerical results demonstrate that our joint design reduces cache feeding time by 50% and improves the cache hit ratio (CHR) by 10% to 20% compared to existing solutions. Finally, we analyze the impact of multispot beams and multicarrier wide-beams on the joint design and discuss potential future research directions.

**Context.** In Object-Oriented programming, mechanisms such as inheritance and delegation are widely acknowledged as fundamental tools for software design. Beyond reducing maintenance and evolution efforts, they are also employed to mitigate the risk of defects in source code. Historically, research has relied on source code reuse metrics primarily for predictive tasks, such as defect prediction.

**Objective.** However, our study highlights two significant gaps in the existing literature. First, there is limited understanding of the extent to which developers utilize code reuse mechanisms over time. Second, it remains unclear how these mechanisms influence defect-proneness and maintenance effort during software evolution. This research aims to address this knowledge gap, as a deeper understanding could reveal the actual support these mechanisms provide and guide their application in predictive models.

**Method.** We propose an exploratory study with two main goals: (1) to evaluate how developers apply inheritance and delegation throughout software evolution, and (2) to statistically analyze the impact of these mechanisms on fault proneness and maintenance effort. The study will analyze commits from 17 Java projects within the DEFECTS4J dataset.

Measurements of charged hadron production in hadron-hadron collisions with a longitudinal momentum fraction (Feynman-x, x_F) ranging from 0.1 to 0.9 have not been conducted at the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings beyond a center-of-mass energy of 63 GeV. This paper outlines a method to perform such measurements at the Large Hadron Collider operating at 13 TeV—an energy level equivalent to 40,000 times that of fixed-target experiments—which is crucial for elucidating cosmic ray showers.

Geodetic Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) enables the precise measurement of light deflection induced by the gravitational fields of the Sun and major planets. According to general relativity, the Parametrized Post-Newtonian (PPN) parameter $\gamma$, derived from observations of reference radio sources near the Sun, must equal unity. We conducted multiple VLBI experiments tracking these sources at angular distances between 1 and 3 degrees from the Sun. The single-session mode yielded the highest formal accuracy for $\gamma$, achieving less than 0.01 percent, which surpasses the precision of global solutions incorporating all available observations regardless of solar elongation. Furthermore, we plan to initiate additional experiments starting in 2020, taking advantage of improved observing conditions during the upcoming minimum of the solar activity cycle.

Location-based services, already widely adopted by end users, are increasingly integrating into new wireless infrastructures and emerging business workflows. While Deep Learning (DL) techniques excel in wireless fingerprinting localization using extensive indoor radio data, their growing complexity makes them computationally demanding and energy-intensive for both training and operation. With mobile users projected to surpass 7.4 billion by 2025, and assuming an average of one localization per user per hour, current models would require approximately 65 trillion predictions annually. When accounting for tens of billions of additional connected devices requiring frequent location updates, it becomes evident that localization significantly contributes to carbon emissions unless more energy-efficient models are developed. This insight drove our research into a new DL-based architecture for indoor localization that offers superior energy efficiency compared to state-of-the-art methods with only negligible performance loss. Our evaluation demonstrates that the proposed model generates just 58% of the carbon footprint of an external state-of-the-art model while retaining 98.7% of its overall performance. Furthermore, we present a methodology for calculating the complexity of DL models to estimate their CO2 footprint during both training and operational phases.

Reinforcement Learning serves as a robust instrument for modeling decision-making, yet it hinges on the exploration-exploitation trade-off, which presents an ongoing challenge across numerous tasks. This study investigates model-free, neighboring state-based exploration, driven by the hypothesis that early-stage agents can derive superior actions by examining a localized region of nearby states. We introduce two algorithms that select exploratory actions through an analysis of adjacent states, demonstrating that our proposed ${\rho}$-explore method surpasses the Double DQN baseline by 49% in Eval Reward Return within a discrete environment.

This study introduces DyDiff-VAE, a new diffusion model designed to predict information spread on social media. By utilizing initial content and a sequence of forwarding users, DyDiff-VAE calculates the likelihood of propagation for other potential users and generates corresponding user rankings. The core of diffusion prediction relies on inferring user interests from diffusion data, as users typically share content they are interested in or that originates from individuals with similar interests. These interests shift over time due to dynamic social influences from neighbors and time-sensitive information from both within and outside the platform. Current methods struggle to capture the intrinsic evolution of user interests from diffusion data, often assuming these interests remain static. DyDiff-VAE advances the field through two key innovations: (i) a dynamic encoder that infers the evolution of user interests from observed diffusion data, and (ii) a dual attentive decoder that estimates propagation likelihood by combining information from the initial cascade content and the forwarding user sequence. Extensive experiments across four real-world datasets from Twitter and YouTube demonstrate the model's superiority, achieving an average 43.3% relative improvement over the best baseline. Additionally, it exhibits the lowest runtime compared to recurrent neural network-based models.

This study examines the vacuum expectation values (VEVs) of the squared field and energy-momentum tensor for a massless scalar field within the Milne universe across an arbitrary number of spatial dimensions. Since the vacuum state relies on the selection of mode functions during canonical quantization, we consider the field to be in the conformal vacuum. Initially, an integral representation is derived for the difference between the Wightman functions associated with the conformal and Minkowski vacua, leading to the calculation of the mean field squared and energy-momentum tensor in the coincidence limit. The results demonstrate that the Minkowski vacuum can be interpreted as a thermal state relative to the conformal vacuum, characterized by a Bose-Einstein thermal factor in odd spatial dimensions and a Fermi-Dirac factor in even spatial dimensions.

This study presents a search for pair-produced vector-like quarks utilizing events characterized by exactly one lepton ($e$ or $\mu$), a minimum of four jets (with at least one $b$-tagged jet), and substantial missing transverse momentum. The analysis employs data from proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV collected by the ATLAS detector at the LHC between 2015 and 2018, amounting to an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. The investigation considers vector-like partners $T$ and $B$ of the top and bottom quarks, along with a vector-like $X$ particle carrying a charge of +5/3, assuming decays into a $W$, $Z$, or Higgs boson accompanied by a third-generation quark. No significant discrepancies from Standard Model predictions were found. Consequently, upper limits on the production cross-sections for $T$ and $B$ quark pairs were established as a function of mass across various decay branching ratio scenarios. The most stringent lower mass limits are determined to be 1.59 TeV for mass-degenerate vector-like quarks under the weak-isospin doublet model, and 1.47 TeV (1.46 TeV) for exclusive $T \rightarrow Zt$ ($B/X \rightarrow Wt$) decays. Furthermore, lower mass limits for the $T$ and $B$ quarks were derived for all conceivable branching ratios.

We introduce a new modular anomaly equation for the unflavored Schur index within $\mathcal{N}=4$ $SU(N)$ super-Yang-Mills theory. The vanishing conditions imposed by this equation restrict the modular ambiguity ansatz sufficiently to enable the recursive calculation of exact Schur indices for all $SU(N)$ gauge groups. By interpreting these representations as MacMahon's generalized sum-of-divisors functions and Jacobi forms, we validate our proposal and clarify a general formula previously conjectured by Pan and Peelaers.

This study presents statistical modeling techniques for pneumothorax deformation based on paired cone-beam computed tomography (CT) scans. We developed a deformable mesh registration framework capable of handling non-linear deformation and rotation during lung shape changes. These registered meshes, which establish local correspondences, serve dual purposes: guiding thoracoscopic surgery and constructing statistical deformation models that account for inter-patient variability. Furthermore, we propose a kernel-based deformation learning framework to reconstruct the intraoperative deflated state of the lung from preoperative CT models. This paper details the findings regarding pneumothorax deformation and evaluates the performance of the proposed kernel-based framework.

This research examines Poincaré series linked to a finite set of divisors on two structures: a finite graph and a specific class of metric graphs known as chains of loops. The primary contributions are establishing the rationality of these series and developing computational algorithms for both scenarios. The proof of rationality relies on distinct tools for each case. For graphs, the approach involves analyzing a homomorphism from a finite-rank free Abelian group to the direct sum of the graph's Jacobian and the integers. Regarding chains of loops, the study utilizes an analogue of Lang's conjecture concerning Brill-Noether loci and adapts the proof strategy used for divisors on algebraic curves over algebraically closed fields of characteristic zero. The proposed algorithms derive from a deeper investigation of the components used in the rationality proofs, specifically focusing on calculating the fibers of particular homomorphisms and enumerating lattice points within rational polyhedra.

Pixelation is a common limitation in imaging systems that restricts spatial resolution. This issue is particularly prominent in quantum imaging involving correlated photons, where the number of pixels available for coincidence detection is frequently constrained by sensor capabilities or acquisition speed. In this work, we present a pixel super-resolution method grounded in the measurement of the complete spatially-resolved joint probability distribution (JPD) of spatially-entangled photon pairs. By requiring no optical element shifting or prior information, this approach doubles the imaging system's pixel resolution and allows for the recovery of spatial details lost due to undersampling. We validate the technique across several quantum imaging protocols utilizing photon pairs, such as quantum illumination, entanglement-assisted quantum holography, and a full-field variant of N00N-state quantum holography. This JPD-based super-resolution strategy offers significant advantages for any full-field imaging system constrained by sensor spatial resolution, encompassing both existing and future photon-correlation-based quantum imaging methods, thereby advancing their potential for practical real-world applications.

Initial pulse-to-pulse observations of a glitch in the Vela pulsar revealed a null pulse, suggesting a sudden disruption of the star's magnetosphere. To date, the sole physical model linking this glitch to the null pulse involves a starquake that either initiated or was triggered by the glitch itself. This null pulse was unique among over 50 years of Vela pulsar data until we identified five additional pulses, termed "quasi-nulls," occurring before and after the glitch at intervals of hundreds of seconds. We confirmed that such nulls do not appear in data collected away from the glitch event. We hypothesize that these quasi-nulls correspond to foreshocks and aftershocks analogous to terrestrial earthquakes. This suggests that the energy reservoir accumulating between glitches is not released instantaneously but rather over a span of minutes to hours surrounding the glitch.

A new medium manganese steel, designated Novalloy, with the composition Fe-8.3Mn-3.8Al-1.8Si-0.5C-0.06V-0.05Sn, was created and subjected to thermomechanical processing involving hot rolling and intercritical annealing. This steel achieved a yield strength of 1 GPa, a tensile strength of 1.13 GPa, and a ductility of 41%. To investigate how cold rolling following intercritical annealing impacts subsequent tensile properties, the material underwent an additional cold rolling process with up to 20% reduction. Results indicated that while the strain hardening rate rose steadily with increasing cold rolling reduction, ductility remained largely unaffected during later tensile testing. Microstructural analysis of the evolution during cold rolling was conducted to elucidate the mechanisms driving the enhanced TRIP effect. The study revealed that cold rolling triggered additional twinning systems, creating numerous potent nucleation sites that facilitated the formation of strain-induced martensite during subsequent tensile tests.

Theoretical analysis at low temperatures investigates the magnetic and thermodynamic characteristics of an anisotropic XYZ spin-1/2 finite chain subjected to both uniform and non-uniform magnetic fields. Employing the exact diagonalization (ED) technique, we examine magnetization, magnetic susceptibility, and specific heat for a model defined by a finite correlation length, considering three distinct field configurations: longitudinal, transverse, and staggered transverse fields. These properties are analyzed under two separate scenarios: I) the application of homogeneous magnetic fields, and II) the inclusion of finite inhomogeneities within the Hamiltonian for all applied fields. Our findings demonstrate that for finite-size XYZ chains at low temperatures, clear magnetization plateaus progressively evolve into quasi-plateaus as the transverse magnetic field strength increases. Furthermore, we provide a detailed account of how transverse and staggered transverse fields, along with their respective inhomogeneities, influence the magnetization process, susceptibility, and specific heat. Our precise results indicate that modifying inhomogeneity parameters causes magnetization plateaus to gradually transition into quasi-plateaus. Additionally, the specific heat exhibits Schottky-type maxima, double-peak structures, and triple-peak structures, with transformations between these forms occurring as the inhomogeneity parameters in the Hamiltonian are varied.

Low-temperature microcalorimeter arrays represent a transformative technology for X-ray astrophysics, specifically for imaging spectrometry. A camera featuring thousands of pixels, each capable of an energy resolution ($E/\Delta E$) of several thousand (FWHM) across a wide spectrum from 200 eV to 10 keV or beyond, would revolutionize the study of energetic astrophysical phenomena. Effective signal readout is the crucial enabling factor; multiplexed readout, which consolidates signals from multiple pixels into a single amplifier channel, permits kilo-pixel-scale microcalorimeter arrays to satisfy strict orbital constraints regarding power usage, mass, volume, and cooling capacity. This chapter examines three distinct multiplexed-readout approaches for transition-edge-sensor microcalorimeters: time-division multiplexing, frequency-domain multiplexing, and microwave-SQUID multiplexing. For each technique, the fundamental methodology, key design considerations, and current state-of-the-art performance are presented. The chapter concludes with an overview of future prospects.

We introduce a broad class of entropy inequalities expressed concisely through Gaussian comparisons. This primary result synthesizes numerous classical and contemporary findings, such as the Shannon-Stam, Brunn-Minkowski, Zamir-Feder, Brascamp-Lieb, Barthe, and Anantharam-Jog-Nair inequalities, among others.

**Context.** Astronomical difference images can reveal "light echoes"—the apparent movement of interstellar dust illuminated by supernova outbursts—but their rarity renders manual detection laborious. Searching for echoes from centuries-old supernovae often requires examining hundreds of subimages from wide-field imagers across numerous pointings. **Aims.** We present ALED, a Python package featuring (i) a capsule network designed to automatically flag images with a high likelihood of containing at least one supernova light echo, and (ii) routing path visualization to pinpoint these echoes or echo-like features within flagged images. **Methods.** We evaluated the performance of the ALED-m capsule network against various capsule and convolutional neural network architectures. Additionally, we applied ALED to a vast catalog of astronomical difference images, followed by manual inspection of candidates for verification. **Results.** ALED-m achieved 90% classification accuracy on the test set and precisely localized identified echoes using routing path visualization. Out of over 13,000 images analyzed, ALED discovered light echoes that were previously missed during manual classification. The package is accessible at github.com/LightEchoDetection/ALED.

Investigating the connection between magnetism and the second harmonic generation (SHG) effect holds both fundamental importance in condensed matter physics and practical value for experimental applications. In this study, we establish a complete and exclusive taxonomy of the SHG effect within magnetic materials, providing a direct method to examine this fascinating relationship and uncovering the underlying symmetries and origins of SHG. First, utilizing the isomorphic group method, we analyze the symmetries of SHG tensors across all magnetic point groups. Subsequently, by incorporating the symmetries of magnetic phases and their corresponding parent phases, we propose a comprehensive classification of the SHG effect into seven distinct types. We have also developed a tensor dictionary encompassing both SHG and the linear magneto-optic effect (LMO), alongside an established database of magnetic materials featuring SHG data. Notably, our classification identifies an anomalous SHG effect that is even in nature and arises solely from magnetism. Furthermore, this classification aids in determining magnetic structures through SHG analysis.

Neural networks have emerged as vital elements of reactive systems across diverse computer science fields. Although they deliver superior performance, their deployment introduces significant risks due to the difficulty in comprehending and reasoning about their internal operations. Consequently, several formal verification methods have been developed to address these risks; however, they frequently encounter scalability constraints. Recent studies suggest that abstraction-refinement techniques could effectively alleviate these issues, yet these methods often generate overly abstract networks that are ill-suited for verification. To resolve this challenge, we introduce CEGARETTE, a new verification mechanism that concurrently abstracts and refines both the system and the property. Our findings indicate that this dual approach yields compact yet sufficiently accurate abstract networks, enabling rapid verification and minimizing the number of required refinement steps. For assessment, we integrated CEGARETTE as an extension to the recently introduced CEGAR-NN framework. The results are highly encouraging, demonstrating substantial performance gains across various benchmarks.

Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (2D) and zero-dimensional quantum dots (QDs) exhibit distinct optical characteristics individually, notably high exciton binding energies. Investigating the hybridization of these systems is crucial for elucidating energy and charge transfer mechanisms as well as exciton dynamics. This manuscript details anomalous photoluminescence (PL) in a MoS₂-CdSe QD heterostructure. We detected multiple exciton emission peaks in this system when placed on an hBN substrate, a phenomenon absent on SiO₂. These findings raise inquiries regarding the underlying causes: does the local potential arising from lattice mismatch between MoS₂ and hBN influence the emission, or is the strain field between the layers responsible? Furthermore, the modified quantum potential of the QDs induced by the presence of both hBN and MoS₂ could also account for these multiple emission features.

Neural machine translation (NMT) typically relies on a standard training algorithm that is plagued by exposure bias, prompting the development of alternative approaches to address this issue, though the practical significance of exposure bias remains contested. This study connects exposure bias to the prevalent problem of generating hallucinations when models encounter domain shifts. Through experiments across three datasets with various test domains, we demonstrate that exposure bias contributes partially to hallucination rates and that adopting Minimum Risk Training—a method designed to circumvent exposure bias—can alleviate this issue. Our analysis clarifies why exposure bias becomes particularly detrimental under domain shift conditions and establishes a connection between exposure bias and beam search limitations, specifically the decline in performance as beam size increases. Ultimately, our findings offer a fresh rationale for techniques aimed at reducing exposure bias: even when such methods fail to enhance in-domain performance, they can significantly improve a model's robustness to domain shifts.

Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) excel at generating robust image representations, making them highly valuable for image recognition tasks; however, their internal mechanisms struggle to effectively model orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we introduce Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), which leverage proposed Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs) to enhance the robustness of learned features against orientation changes. By integrating LGFs into convolutional filters, OCNs remain compatible with any existing deep learning architecture. Specifically, LGFs function as a sparse Gabor filter bank: instead of using all $ n $ original filters, we select $ p $ (where $ p \ll n $) representative filters as "landmarks" and express the remaining filters as sparse linear combinations of these landmarks. Utilizing a matrix factorization framework, this approach combines local and global structural information through sparsity and low-rank constraints. This propagation of low-rank structure significantly promotes the sparsity required to represent the original Gabor filter bank. Experimental evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our method is less sensitive to orientation variations and achieves superior performance in both accuracy and computational cost compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, OCNs require fewer learnable parameters, substantially reducing the complexity of network training.

This note offers an informal, example-driven introduction to technical elements concerning the re-normalization of measures on orbital integrals, a topic central to the research of Langlands, Frenkel-Langlands-Ng\^o, and Altug on Beyond Endoscopy. Specifically, it reviews pertinent measures defined on algebraic tori and elucidates their relationship with Tamagawa numbers, while providing a comprehensive, detailed analysis of the $\mathrm{GL}_2$ case. Additionally, an appendix by Matthew Koster examines the correspondence between geometric measures on orbits and Kirillov's measures on co-adjoint orbits for the Lie algebras $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ and $\mathfrak{so}_3$.

Developing techniques to identify or neutralize malicious network activity demands access to varied, contemporary datasets featuring labeled malicious connections; without them, such methods cannot be effectively trained, tested, or evaluated. Synthetic data, consisting of fabricated or combined network traffic, offers limited utility because even basic machine learning algorithms can easily distinguish it from genuine traffic. While real-world network data is ideal, its widespread sensitivity and lack of ground truth labels constrain its applicability for machine learning research.

This paper introduces a comprehensive strategy for creating a dataset of labeled malicious connections integrated within anonymized traffic gathered from large-scale production networks. The approach involves "defanging" real-world malware and introducing it to simulated, secure nodes within these networks. This process generates realistic traffic while ensuring sufficient isolation to safeguard actual data and infrastructure. Network sensor data, encompassing this embedded malicious traffic, is then collected at the network edge and anonymized for research purposes.

Data was collected and generated using these methods at two major educational institutions. The outcome is a highly realistic, long-term, multi-institutional dataset containing over 1.5 trillion connections with embedded labels and more than a petabyte of sensor log data. The dataset's practicality is validated through its application in our artificial intelligence and machine learning research program.

Ensuring contract consistency is vital for maintaining legal validity. Frequently, contracts are drafted by completing blanks within pre-existing templates, a process prone to human error where identical or distinct values may be mistakenly assigned inconsistently. Such inconsistencies can critically undermine a contract's enforceability. While traditional approaches to detecting these errors depend on labor-intensive and expensive manual reviews, this study introduces a new Contract Inconsistency Checking (CIC) problem and proposes an end-to-end framework named Pair-wise Blank Resolution (PBR) to resolve it with high precision. The PBR model features an innovative BlankCoder designed to handle the challenge of modeling non-informative blanks; it utilizes a two-stage attention mechanism to effectively link these blanks with their relevant context while filtering out irrelevant words. Empirical results on real-world datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness, achieving a balanced accuracy of 94.05% and an F1 score of 90.90% for the CIC task.

This paper presents a new methodology for deductive databases designed to address the requirements of modern data integration applications. We extend the standard deductive database formalism into the realm of Four-valued logic to manage unknown, inconsistent, true, or false information under an open world assumption. In this framework, a database consists of a pair (E, R), where E represents the extension and R the set of rules. The extension comprises pairs of the form (f, v), with f denoting a fact and v representing a value that can be true, inconsistent, or false; notably, unknown facts are excluded from storage. The rules resemble standard Datalog{neg} rules but differ in that their heads may contain negative atoms. Our primary contributions include: (i) expressing first-degree entailment using alternative connectors and identifying a functionally complete set of basic connectors that do not rely on first-degree entailment; (ii) introducing a novel operator to manage this specific rule type, demonstrating that it is both monotonic and continuous, thereby offering an efficient mechanism for defining and computing database semantics; and (iii) arguing that our framework supports the definition of a new class of updates suitable for most standard data integration scenarios.

The 3$\alpha$ decay of the 16.62\,MeV (2$^-$, T=1) resonance in $^{12}$C has been investigated for almost a century, beginning with early nuclear reaction experiments at the Cavendish Laboratory in the 1930s. A decade ago, the most recent study employed a model derived from 1960s research to successfully explain a set of inclusive data; this model characterized the decay as an l=3 $\alpha$-particle transition populating the 2$^+$ state of $^8$Be. In this work, we present new exclusive data on the 3$\alpha$ decay of the 16.62\,MeV resonance and demonstrate that the decay is most accurately described by a model featuring predominantly l=1 emission with an admixture of l=3.
We introduce a technique for estimating the mean values of lengthy Dirichlet polynomials, which we apply to investigate the characteristics of the logarithmic derivative of the Riemann zeta function.

Multiplayer Online Battle Arena (MOBA) games have gained significant popularity in recent years, prompting numerous initiatives to develop pre-game and in-game predictions. Nevertheless, existing approaches are constrained by two primary issues: a scarcity of comprehensive in-game features and a lack of interpretability in their predictive outcomes. These shortcomings severely hinder the practical utility and industrial deployment of current solutions. To address this, we gather and release a large-scale dataset enriched with diverse in-game features from the popular MOBA title, *Honor of Kings*. We subsequently propose an interpretable framework to forecast four critical event types by attributing predictions to input features using two gradient-based methods: Integrated Gradients and SmoothGrad. Furthermore, we introduce a fidelity-based evaluation metric to assess the explanatory capabilities of various models and attribution techniques. Finally, we evaluate the accuracy and fidelity of several competing methods on our dataset to determine how effectively machines can predict events within MOBA games.

Every better quasi-order represents a Borel graph devoid of a shift graph copy. Although it is established that some better quasi-order encodes a Borel graph with infinite Borel chromatic number, no explicit construction of such an example currently exists. This paper demonstrates that standard techniques cannot produce these examples and reveals that the majority of known better quasi-orders do not satisfy this property. Consequently, this suggests the existence of an unexplored class of better quasi-orders possessing intriguing combinatorial characteristics, the members of which remain unidentified.

The bottom quark Yukawa coupling plays a pivotal role in the detailed investigation of Higgs boson properties at the Large Hadron Collider and in the search for new physics within the electroweak symmetry breaking sector. This study examines potential deviations from the Standard Model prediction for the $b\bar{b}h$ coupling, characterized by a modification factor $\alpha_b$, specifically in the context of associated $b\bar{b}$ production of the 125-GeV scalar at the high-luminosity LHC. Utilizing a gradient boosting algorithm for a next-to-leading order analysis, we enhance the statistical significance compared to traditional cut-based methods. Results indicate that with an integrated luminosity of ${\cal L} = 3000$ fb$^{-1}$ and a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV, it is feasible to probe values down to $\alpha_b = 3$ with a significance exceeding $5~\sigma$, while the achievable $95\%$ confidence level limit is $\pm 1.95$.

Deep Learning (DL) advancements are emerging at an accelerated rate; however, the absence of standardized specifications for DL tasks currently hinders the sharing, execution, replication, and comparison of these innovations. To resolve this issue, we introduce DLSpec, a DL specification framework that is independent of specific models, datasets, software, or hardware and comprehensively captures the various dimensions of DL tasks. This approach has been validated by defining and executing hundreds of DL tasks.

This study examines the $k$-Canadian Traveller Problem ($k$-CTP) within the learning-augmented framework introduced by Lykouris and Vassilvitskii. As an extension of the shortest path problem, $k$-CTP involves a traveler who initially knows the full graph structure and aims to navigate from a source vertex $s$ to a destination vertex $t$ via the shortest route, only to discover upon arrival that up to $k$ edges are blocked. An imperfect predictor provides information regarding the count and positions of these blocked edges. We introduce both deterministic and randomized online algorithms for the learning-augmented $k$-CTP, demonstrating a balance between consistency (performance when predictions are accurate) and robustness (performance in the presence of prediction errors). Furthermore, we establish a matching lower bound for the deterministic scenario, proving that the tradeoff between consistency and robustness is optimal, and derive a lower bound for the randomized approach. Additionally, we prove multiple deterministic and randomized lower bounds on the competitive ratio of $k$-CTP as a function of prediction error, providing corresponding upper bounds that match these limits in most instances.

The rapid proliferation of diverse mobile applications, particularly those powered by artificial intelligence, is igniting intense debate regarding the future trajectory of wireless communication. As 5G deployment continues globally, both industry and academia are already looking past it to conceptualize 6G. We anticipate that 6G will undergo a radical transformation, rendering it fundamentally distinct from previous wireless generations. Specifically, 6G will extend beyond the scope of mobile internet and must support AI-driven services, while AI itself will be pivotal in designing, optimizing, and operating 6G architectures and protocols. This article examines the defining characteristics of 6G, the challenges involved in its implementation, and AI-enabled methodologies for network design and optimization.

This paper proposes methods to enhance the computational efficiency of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) applied to point cloud learning. We analyze the standard graph convolution, which typically involves a $K$-nearest neighbor (KNN) search followed by a multilayer perceptron (MLP). Through mathematical analysis of these operations, we derive two key insights for optimization: (1) Since local geometric information in 3D representations propagates smoothly across the GCN, the reliance on multiple KNN searches can be simplified. (2) The order of graph feature gathering and MLP application can be shuffled without altering the resulting composite operations. Leveraging these findings, we optimize the GCN computational workflow. Experimental results demonstrate that the optimized networks achieve lower computational complexity, reduced memory usage, and faster inference speeds while maintaining accuracy comparable to the original models. The code will be made available at \url{https://github.com/ofsoundof/EfficientGCN.git}.

The reflectance characteristics of mixtures containing water ice and dust are influenced, among other factors, by the specific manner in which these components are combined, such as through intimate mixing, areal distribution, or coating (Clark et al. 1999). Consequently, when inverting reflectance spectra from planetary surfaces to quantify surface water ice abundance, it is essential to differentiate between various mixing modes. However, distinguishing these modes solely from reflectance spectra remains ambiguous. This study demonstrates how to identify specific water ice/soil mixing modes by analyzing defined spectral criteria and color metrics derived from laboratory mixtures. By recreating ice and dust mixtures, we observed that surface frost increases reflectance and flattens spectral slopes, while increasing water ice within intimate mixtures primarily affects absorption bands. Specifically, we provide laboratory data and spectral analysis to assist in interpreting ice and soil reflectance spectra originating from the Martian surface.

We develop $\alpha$-attractor variants of hybrid inflation models where the inflaton field $\varphi$'s potential is elevated by that of a second field $\chi$. This elevation ceases due to a tachyonic instability in $\chi$, triggered once $\varphi$ drops below a critical threshold $\varphi_{c}$. Within the large $N$ limit, these models yield standard universal $\alpha$-attractor forecasts, specifically $n_{s} = 1 - {2 \over N}$ for exponential attractors. However, in certain scenarios, the large $N$ regime is attained only beyond the horizon when $N \gtrsim 60$, potentially altering cosmological predictions. For a fixed $N$, we identify an alternative attractor yielding $n_s = 1$ in the limits of large uplift $V_{\rm up}$ or large $\varphi_{c}$. By adjusting $V_{\rm up}$ and $\varphi_{c}$, one can smoothly transition between the two predictions, $n_{s }= 1- {2 \over N}$ and $n_{s} = 1$. This offers considerable flexibility, which is valuable given the increasing volume and precision of cosmological data. Crucially, our primary finding extends beyond hybrid inflation; it applies generally to any inflationary framework where the inflaton potential is uplifted for specific reasons, causing inflation to terminate prematurely.

This paper investigates the structural characteristics of Nevanlinna measures, which are Borel measures emerging from the integral representation of Herglotz-Nevanlinna functions. Specifically, we offer a characterization of these measures using their Fourier transforms, identify measures supported on hyperplanes (including extremal cases), analyze the singular component's structure when certain variables are fixed, and derive estimates for the measure of expanding and shrinking cubes. These findings are also presented within the context of the polydisc where feasible, with several proofs relying on polydisc techniques.

Autonomous Driving (AD) systems depend on artificial intelligence (AI) modules to ensure safe and correct driving behavior. Unfortunately, current AI algorithms are inherently susceptible to adversarial attacks. However, for these component-level vulnerabilities to have a meaningful impact at the system level, they must bridge non-trivial semantic gaps between system-level attack inputs and AI component inputs, as well as between AI component-level impacts and system-level outcomes. In this paper, we designate this specific domain as "semantic AI security," distinguishing it from generic AI security. Over the last five years, research addressing these semantic challenges within the AD context has expanded, exhibiting an exponential growth trajectory.

This study presents the first systematic review of this rapidly evolving semantic AD AI security landscape. We collected and analyzed 53 relevant papers, organizing them into a taxonomy based on research aspects critical to the security field. Through quantitative comparisons both vertically among existing AD AI security studies and horizontally with related security domains, we identified six major scientific gaps. These findings offer insights and potential future directions spanning design, research goals, methodologies, and community engagement. To address the most critical gap regarding scientific methodology, we have developed PASS, an open-source, uniform, and extensible system-driven evaluation platform for the semantic AD AI security community. Furthermore, we utilize a prototype of this platform to demonstrate its capabilities and benefits through representative semantic AD AI attacks.

We re-examine a straightforward Learning-from-Scratch approach for visuo-motor control, which employs data augmentation and a shallow ConvNet. Our findings indicate that this baseline achieves performance comparable to recent techniques that utilize frozen visual representations derived from large-scale vision datasets.

Amidst the current era of Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, the practical application of quantum computing is hindered by the difficulty of isolating qubits from their surroundings to suppress computational errors. This study proposes a method that utilizes knowledge of a qubit's initial quantum state, alongside standard decoherence parameters, to mitigate noise occurring during single-qubit gate operations. We validated this protocol using cloud access to IBM quantum processors. Specifically, on the ibmq_rome device, we achieved a 38% reduction in the single-qubit error rate, lowering it from $1.6 \times 10^{-3}$ to $1.0 \times 10^{-3}$, contingent on knowing the input qubit's initial state. Furthermore, testing on ibmq_bogota confirmed that our protocol never diminishes gate fidelity, provided the system's $T_1$ and $T_2$ relaxation times have not drifted beyond 100 times their assumed values. This approach can be applied to reduce errors in quantum state preparation and enhance the fidelity of quantum circuits where intermediate qubit states can be inferred. Ultimately, this work outlines a strategy for leveraging information regarding noise levels and quantum state distributions to substantially lower error rates in quantum gates through optimized decomposition into native gates.

Magnetic clouds (MCs) are transient structures comprising large-scale magnetic flux ropes originating from solar eruptions. The twist of magnetic field lines around the rope axis provides insights into formation mechanisms and geoeffectiveness. As MCs propagate, their flux ropes can erode through reconnection with the surrounding solar wind; this erosion diminishes magnetic flux and helicity while altering cross-sectional twist distributions. This research correlates twist profiles in MC flux ropes observed at 1 AU with the degree of erosion experienced in interplanetary space. The study analyzes the twist profiles of two well-identified MC flux ropes linked to distinct post-eruption arcade signatures in the solar corona. To quantify erosion, the magnetic flux content of these ropes is estimated in the solar atmosphere and compared to values measured at 1 AU. The first MC exhibits a monotonically decreasing twist from the axis to the periphery, whereas the second shows high central twist, a rise near the edges, and lower twist in the intermediate region. The first MC demonstrates a greater reduction in magnetic flux between the Sun and 1 AU, indicating more significant erosion than the second. In the second cloud, the rising twist at the edges likely results from an envelope of overlying coronal field lines with relatively high twist, generated by reconnection beneath the erupting flux rope in the low corona. This high-twist envelope remained largely intact from the Sun to 1 AU due to minimal erosion. Conversely, the high-twist envelope of the first cloud was likely completely stripped away by erosion before reaching 1 AU.

The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), a leading application of variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) designed to find the ground state energy of Hamiltonian-based quantum systems on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, faces significant challenges regarding accuracy and trainability. These issues stem from barren plateaus, non-negligible gate errors, and restricted coherence times inherent to NISQ hardware. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a gradient-sensitive alternate framework utilizing a variable ansatz to improve VQE performance. The study first establishes a theoretical framework for Variable Ansatz VQE (VA-VQE) by alternately solving the original VQE and a multi-objective optimization problem defined by cost function values and gradient magnitudes. Subsequently, a novel implementation method is proposed, combining a double $\epsilon$-greedy strategy with a candidate tree and a modified multi-objective genetic algorithm. This approach successfully avoids local optima in both ansatz and parameter spaces while enhancing ansatz stability. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework reduces solution error by up to 87.9% compared to hardware-efficient ansatzes. Additionally, relative to full-randomized VA-VQE implementations, the new framework achieves up to 36.0% error reduction and 58.7% stability improvement while maintaining comparable quantum costs.

In \cite{AV99}, Antoine and Vandergheynst introduce a group-theoretic method for generating continuous wavelet frames on the sphere. This frame is derived from a single admissible function through the application of unitary operators linked to a representation of the Lorentz group, which is square-integrable modulo the nilpotent component of the Iwasawa decomposition. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for spherical functions that guarantee the resulting system forms a frame. Furthermore, we enhance a comparable result found in \cite{AV99} by offering a rigorous and comprehensive proof.

This work demonstrates an exact simulation of a one-dimensional transverse Ising spin chain using a quantum computer. We develop an efficient quantum circuit capable of diagonalizing the Ising Hamiltonian, enabling the retrieval of all eigenstates through the preparation of computational basis states. Using a specific circuit instance for $n=4$ spins, we calculate the ground state magnetization expectation value, simulate time evolution, and outline a method for thermal evolution. Furthermore, all circuits were executed on IBM and Rigetti quantum devices to facilitate qualitative testing and comparison.

Chu originally defined the Chu category, denoted as Chu(C, g), over a closed symmetric monoidal category C and an object g, characterizing it as a *-autonomous category generated from C. Bishop later introduced the category of complemented subsets of a set to address issues arising from negation in constructive measure theory. Shulman notes that Bishop's complemented subsets roughly align with the Chu construction. This paper elucidates that alignment by demonstrating a Chu representation, specifically a full embedding, of the category of complemented subsets of a set X into Chu(Set, X x X).
