We term this finding the Strong "No Free Lunch" Theorem, as it subsumes recent findings by Tsipras et al. (2018), Fawzi et al. (2018), and others as specific instances. Our theoretical bounds are validated using both simulated datasets and real-world data from MNIST. The paper concludes with speculation on potential avenues for future research.

I examined the definition and characteristics of polynomials within non-commutative algebras, noting that such polynomials can possess finite, infinite, or no roots. For example, the polynomial $p_1(x)=ix-xi-1$ has an empty set of roots, whereas $p_k(x)=ix-xi-k$ yields the root set $x=C_1+C_2i+\frac 12 j$. Additionally, I explored polynomial division involving remainders.

We introduce an extra-dimensional framework based on the orbifold $S^1/Z_2$ to explain the origins of fermion mass and mixing hierarchies. By embedding a flavor symmetry $G_F$ (composed of non-Abelian and Abelian components) and extra gauged $U(1)$ symmetries into the bulk, we localize Standard Model $SU(2)$ singlet and doublet fermions on distinct 3-branes, while allowing extra $SU(2)$ singlet flavored fermions in the bulk to couple with these SM fermions. These additional $U(1)$ symmetries are anomaly-free with respect to gravity, a feature essential for generating the desired fermion mass and mixing hierarchies and ensuring the flavored axion remains naturally light. Spontaneous breaking of $G_F$ on the two 3-branes is driven by singlet scalar fields known as flavons, while the bulk $SU(2)$ singlet flavored fermions are integrated out to produce effective Yukawa couplings for SM fermions that encode the $G_F$ breaking patterns from both sectors. Furthermore, a flavored axion arising from PQ symmetry is incorporated to address the strong CP problem and serve as a dark matter candidate within this model.

Although the backpropagation algorithm is essential for training artificial neural networks, its reliance on weight sharing makes it an implausible model of brain function. In this work, we introduce a training algorithm for a two-layer network that circumvents this issue by eliminating the need for explicit error computation and backpropagation. Additionally, this proposed algorithm aligns closely with the connectivity patterns and learning rules observed in the cortex. Empirical results demonstrate that our method performs comparably to backpropagation across various datasets.

Although it was previously thought that the $\pm J$ Ising spin-glass fails to exhibit ordering at any finite temperature in two dimensions ($d=2$), we rigorously demonstrate using a graphical representation and contour argument that a finite-temperature phase transition does occur for $d \geq 2$, with a critical temperature $T_c \geq 0.4$. In this low-temperature phase, the graphical representation reveals the coexistence of multiple infinite clusters, each characterized by a rigidly aligned spin-overlap state. These clusters exhibit negative correlations with one another and remain entropically stable without violating any global symmetry. Furthermore, such clusters can arise across a wide range of graph structures and disorder measures.

We introduce the Gentle Measurement Principle (GMP) as a foundational axiom of quantum mechanics. This principle states that any set of states distinguishable with high probability can be distinguished via a measurement that leaves them nearly unchanged, even when accounting for correlations with a reference system. Although GMP holds true in both classical and quantum frameworks, we demonstrate within the context of general probabilistic theories that it places stringent constraints on physical laws. Specifically, the measurement uncertainty of two observables cannot exceed the preparation uncertainty by a significant margin; consequently, CHSH nonlocality cannot reach its maximal strength, and the parameter characterizing stretched quantum theory—a broader family encompassing quantum mechanics—is similarly restricted. Furthermore, the conditional entropy derived from a data compression theorem satisfies the chain inequality. This condition not only enforces information causality and Tsirelson's bound but also uniquely isolates quantum theory from stretched quantum theory. Collectively, these findings indicate that GMP serves as a central principle underlying quantum mechanics.

We detail the derivation of the next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order (N$^3$LO) spin-orbit interaction within the current frontier of post-Newtonian (PN) gravity, utilizing the Effective Field Theory of spinning objects. This work encompasses the most extensive and complex set of Feynman diagrams ever addressed in spin sectors, covering all PN orders up to the third subleading level. Our calculations employ sophisticated multi-loop techniques, with a critical requirement being the transition to generic dimensions throughout the entire derivation—a necessity shared by N$^3$LO sectors. Furthermore, at this high order involving spin, we extend the formal procedure for reducing higher-order time derivatives of spin variables beyond linear order for the first time. We provide the complete interaction potentials in both Lagrangian and Hamiltonian forms for the first time, which facilitate the direct derivation of equations of motion for position and spin, investigations into the associated Poincaré algebra, and explorations of various effective-one-body models. Additionally, we derive gauge-invariant observables, including relationships between binding energy, angular momentum, and orbital frequency. Our results show complete agreement with binding energies for circular orbits and scattering angles for aligned spins obtained via traditional General Relativity methods. Unlike those derivations, our framework is independent and generic, offering autonomous results that are essential for establishing the state of the art and advancing the limits of high-order precision.

Significant variations in mobility data volume across regions degrade the performance of spatial recommender systems that depend on localized information. To address this, we introduce REFORMD, a novel transfer learning framework designed for continuous-time location prediction in regions with sparse check-in data. Our approach models user-specific check-in sequences within a region using a marked temporal point process (MTPP) enhanced by normalizing flows to capture inter-check-in intervals and geo-distributions. We then transfer spatial and temporal flow parameters trained on data-rich source regions to predict the next check-in time and location in target regions with limited data. To adapt MTPP and spatial-temporal flows to evolving region-specific dynamics, we maximize the joint likelihood of the next check-in across three channels: check-in category, check-in time, and travel distance. Extensive experiments on user mobility datasets from the U.S. and Japan demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods for modeling continuous-time sequences. Furthermore, we show that REFORMD can be readily adapted for product recommendation tasks involving sequences without spatial components.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) for brain-computer interface (BCI) classification are often assumed to learn generalizable features across diverse contexts that can later be fine-tuned for specific scenarios. Although some success has been achieved with this strategy, we argue that this view is limited and that a different approach would better exploit the vast, newly available public EEG datasets. We propose adapting techniques and architectures from language modeling (LM)—which excel at processing large data volumes—to develop encephalography modeling (EM) using DNNs. Specifically, we modify an approach widely used in automatic speech recognition, which similarly employs a self-supervised objective to learn compressed representations of raw signals. When adapted to EEG, this single pre-trained model demonstrates the ability to handle completely novel raw EEG sequences recorded using various hardware and involving different subjects performing distinct tasks. Moreover, both the model's internal representations and its full architecture can be fine-tuned for a range of downstream BCI and EEG classification tasks, surpassing previous methods in specific self-supervised applications such as sleep stage classification.

We examine entanglement entropy (EE) and charge fluctuations in systems where low-energy dynamics are described by massless Dirac fermions, specifically analyzing their response to flux insertion, a process often presumed to be universal regarding microscopic details. Using dimensional reduction from the tight-binding model to the one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, we analytically derive the EE and charge fluctuations for graphene. Our asymptotic EE results align with conformal field theory predictions, and the charge variance exhibits identical asymptotic behavior, differing only by a constant factor. To test universality, we numerically evaluate various models featuring different geometries, numbers of Dirac cones, and dimensions, including strictly 2D systems and gapless surface modes of 3D topological insulators. We demonstrate that flux response remains independent of the entangling surface geometry provided the flux is enclosed. Additionally, we investigate universal corner contributions to EE, finding that the Kitaev-Preskill subtraction scheme yields non-universal, geometry-dependent outcomes in the presence of corners.

Protecting against cyberattacks is an evolving area within fault-tolerant control. To circumvent the complexities of intricate mathematical modeling, model-free control (MFC) is proposed as an alternative to traditional methods. As a case study, the Load Frequency Control of a multi-area power network is examined. Simulations introduce load alteration attacks and Denial of Service (DoS) incidents within the communication network. The objective is to evaluate how cyberattacks affect control loops managed by classical controllers versus MFC under these conditions. Computational experiments demonstrate that MFC yields highly effective results.

Merge Resolution (MRes), introduced by Beyersdorff et al. in 2021, is a recent proof system designed for false Quantified Boolean Formulas (QBFs). It encodes countermodels using merge maps, which are deterministic branching programs allowing for efficient isomorphism checks; this characteristic makes MRes verifiable in polynomial time. This paper presents a broader family of proof systems, denoted as MRes-R, where countermodels are stored using any pre-defined complete representation $R$ rather than being restricted to merge maps. For each such $R$, the resulting MRes-R system is both sound and refutationally complete. To accommodate arbitrary strategy representations, the system replaces isomorphism checking with consistency checking rules, a modification that renders these proof systems non-polynomially verifiable. The authors argue that relying solely on merge maps is unnecessarily restrictive and that substituting them with arbitrary representations yields several significant proof systems.

An analysis of the proof-theoretic properties of MRes-R demonstrates that eFrege+$\forall$red can simulate all valid refutations generated by systems within the MRes-R family. To achieve this simulation of arbitrary representations, the steps utilized by MRes-R are first formalized as a new complete structure, enabling the corresponding proof system to simulate all other MRes-R systems. Subsequently, this simulation is realized via eFrege+$\forall$red by adapting techniques from Chew et al. (2021). Regarding lower bounds, the paper establishes that completion principle formulas, previously identified as hard for regular MRes by Beyersdorff et al. (2020) and Jonata et al. (2015), remain hard for any regular proof system within the MRes-R class. Thus, the study extends the lower bound established for regular MRes to the entire class of proof systems utilizing complete representations, including those not yet discovered.

This paper outlines a method for constructing metrics and matter models on end-periodic manifolds, which are crucial for investigating exotic smooth structures of $\mathbb{R}^4$. We present three specific examples, analyze their corresponding matter models by solving the Einstein equations, and assess their physical viability through an examination of energy conditions. Furthermore, we compare one of these models directly with established matter distribution models in extragalactic systems to underscore the potential of using exotic smooth structures to explain the existence and distribution of dark matter.

We introduce a predictive four-dimensional $SU(5)$ grand unified theory (GUT) model incorporating a $D_4$ flavor symmetry that excludes triplet irreducible representations. This framework derives quark and charged lepton Yukawa matrices from renormalizable superpotentials by integrating out heavy messenger fields, whereas neutrino masses arise via the type I seesaw mechanism. Theoretical ratios for Yukawa couplings, dictated by group factors from 24- and 45-dimensional Higgs fields, align with experimental data, and dangerous proton decay operators are significantly suppressed. Numerical analysis demonstrates that the model accurately reproduces quark sector mixing angles, Yukawa couplings, and the CP phase at the GUT scale. Neutrino masses are generated at the renormalizable level, predicting trimaximal mixing, though an additional effective operator is necessary to explain the baryon asymmetry of the universe (BAU). The model exhibits remarkable predictivity by permitting only the normal neutrino mass ordering and the lower octant for the atmospheric angle, while ruling out CP-conserving values for the Dirac CP phase $\delta_{CP}$. Furthermore, the predicted effective Majorana mass $m_{\beta \beta}$ is testable in upcoming neutrinoless double beta decay experiments. We conducted both analytical and numerical investigations into leptogenesis, focusing on parameter regions where the lightest right-handed neutrino successfully generates the BAU, revealing strong correlations between neutrino sector parameters and the observed baryon asymmetry.

This research examines the homology groups of elementary Petri nets utilized in pipeline systems. We demonstrate that the integral homology groups for these nets consist of the integer group in dimensions 0 and 1, while vanishing in all other dimensions. Furthermore, we establish that the directed homology groups of elementary Petri nets are trivial across all dimensions.

Recently, self-supervised learning has gained significant interest because of its exceptional capacity to derive meaningful representations for classification without relying on semantic labels. This study presents a self-supervised framework tailored for hyperspectral images, which are notoriously difficult to annotate. The proposed architecture utilizes a cross-domain CNN to learn representations from diverse hyperspectral images with varying spectral properties, even in the absence of pixel-level annotations. Within this framework, contrastive learning is employed to generate cross-domain representations by clustering neighboring spectral vectors from the same image together within a shared space that encompasses multiple images, while simultaneously separating spectral vectors from different images into distinct clusters. To validate the effectiveness of these learned representations in downstream applications, a classification task was conducted on hyperspectral data. The experimental findings highlight the superiority of the proposed self-supervised approach compared to models trained from scratch or alternative transfer learning methods.

Rank ordering is essential for cognitive functions and serves as a foundational element for executing arbitrary digital operations. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) utilize their collective nonlinear dynamics to identify the largest $k$ out of $N$ analog inputs, effectively performing $k$-winner-take-all (k-WTA) computations based on partial rank orderings. However, existing research typically fixes the value of $k$, frequently setting it to one. This study introduces a reconfigurable SNN framework where $k$ can be dynamically selected via a single global parameter. This network operates through pulse suppression driven by inhibitory pulse couplings; these couplings scale with each neuron's state variable (voltage), forming a simple yet distinct type of leaky integrate-and-fire model. Computation outcomes are encoded as stable periodic orbits, where exactly $k$ units fire at a specific frequency while others fire less frequently or remain silent. The stability of these orbits ensures that the analog-to-digital conversion remains robust against minor fluctuations in parameters and input signals. Furthermore, the process completes rapidly, requiring only a few spike emissions per neuron. These findings demonstrate that reconfigurable $k$-WTA computations can be efficiently realized in minimal hardware using basic dynamical units and spike interactions akin to simple current leakage to a common ground.

The formation and spectroscopic properties of ethanimine in the gas phase have been re-examined as a benchmark demonstrating the precision of modern quantum-chemical (QC) methods in astrochemistry. Our calculations indicate that the reaction between amidogen (NH) and ethyl (C$_2$H$_5$) radicals proceeds rapidly, approaching the gas-kinetic limit. While the dominant pathway under interstellar conditions produces methanimine and a methyl radical, our models predict that the two stereoisomers of ethanimine (E and Z) will constitute approximately 10% of the yield. Advanced QC and kinetic modeling suggest an [E-CH$_3$CHNH]/[Z-CH$_3$CHNH] ratio of about 1.4, which is marginally higher than prior computations but remains significantly lower than the ratio observed in astronomy (approximately 3). By accurately modeling the structure, energetics, and spectroscopic features of both ethanimine isomers and integrating these with millimeter-wave data up to 300 GHz, we have predicted their rotational spectra up to 500 GHz, thereby enabling future astronomical observations.

We introduce a new framework designed to learn functions that simultaneously estimate the decision-making processes of both sellers and buyers within an oligopoly market for price-sensitive goods. The seller network aims to determine an optimal price for a specific context that maximizes expected revenue while accounting for buyer satisfaction. Conversely, the buyer network is tasked with assigning a probability of purchase to offered prices to replicate real-world consumer behavior, specifically reflecting price sensitivity by declining excessively high prices. Functioning similarly to generative adversarial networks, this system operates as a minimax two-player game. Through experiments utilizing both simulated and real-world transaction data, we compared our approach against baseline models and validated its effectiveness using proposed evaluation metrics.

The NASA TESS mission \citep{tess} has delivered high-precision photometry for millions of stars. While most TESS observations span approximately 27 days, covering a single sector, a small fraction of targets—roughly 1–2\% of those in the Continuous Viewing Zone (CVZ) during the prime mission \citep{yield}—are monitored continuously for a year across multiple sectors. These long-baseline observations are crucial for determining stellar rotation periods, which serve as indicators of age. We introduce a pip-installable Python tool designed to extract these long-period rotation rates from TESS CVZ data while effectively correcting for instrumental systematics.

Embedding-based neural topic models can explicitly represent words and topics within a unified feature space, enhancing interpretability; however, the absence of explicit constraints during embedding training results in a vast optimization landscape, and a clear understanding of how embedding shifts affect model performance remains elusive. This paper introduces an embedding-regularized neural topic model that imposes specialized training constraints on both word and topic embeddings to constrain the parameter optimization space. To elucidate the evolution and function of embeddings, we adopt \textbf{uniformity} as an evaluation metric for the embedding space. Based on this, we analyze how embeddings evolve throughout training by tracking changes in uniformity. Additionally, ablation studies illustrate the impact of these embedding variations on embedding-based neural topic models. Experimental results on two prominent datasets demonstrate that our model significantly surpasses baseline approaches in balancing topic quality and document modeling. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first effort to leverage uniformity for investigating embedding dynamics and their consequent effects on model performance within this framework.

This note establishes characterization theorems for real derivations. Specifically, it proves the following result: If $\xi\colon \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$ is a differentiable function and $d\colon \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$ is an additive function such that the mapping $x\longmapsto d(\xi(x))-\xi'(x)d(x)$ is regular (for instance, measurable, continuous, or locally bounded), then $d$ can be expressed as the sum of a derivation and a linear function.

This study introduces a novel family of nonrelativistic, Newtonian, non-quantum equilibrium configurations for galactic halos, proposing strange quark matter conglomerates with masses exceeding approximately 8 GeV as potential dark matter constituents. Originally conceptualized to describe matter within neutron stars, these conglomerates could also emerge under the high-density and high-temperature conditions of the early Universe. By decoupling from ordinary baryonic matter, they would serve as the fundamental building blocks of dark matter, facilitating the creation of primordial gravitational potential wells and driving the evolution of cosmic structures. The calculated halo masses and radii align with the observed rotational velocity curves of the Galaxy. Furthermore, the average density of these dark matter halos closely matches that of dwarf spheroidal galaxies, suggesting that the latter are scaled-down versions of the former and pointing toward a shared origin for both types of cosmic structures.

We demonstrate the realization of a time crystal at the topologically protected edge states of a Kagome ferromagnet, driven by magnon amplification induced by a specifically designed electromagnetic field. This magnon amplification spontaneously breaks discrete time-translation symmetry, yielding a discrete time crystal with a period exactly double that of the driving electromagnetic field. We analyze the characteristics of these time-crystalline edge states and evaluate their robustness against perturbations anticipated in real quantum magnets. Furthermore, we suggest an experimental signature to definitively identify time-crystalline behavior and highlight two recently discovered quasi-2D magnets as promising candidates for hosting this phenomenon.

Recent reports from the CMS and ATLAS collaborations indicate a diphoton excess at 750 GeV during the LHC Run II at 13 TeV. Assuming a heavy fourth-generation quark doublet ($z, y$) with a mass of 380 GeV, where the width of the $z$ and $t$ quarks is significantly smaller than that of the $b$ quark, we demonstrate that the bound state $\eta_{zy}(1S)$, defined as $(z\bar{z} + y\bar{y})/\sqrt{2}$, contributes $5.6^{+5.6}_{-2.8} \text{ fb}$ to the diphoton cross-section via the process $\sigma(pp\to \eta_{zy}(1s)\to \gamma\gamma)$ at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV. This predicted contribution aligns with the 750 GeV diphoton excess observed by both CMS and ATLAS.

Based on deep cosmological observations within the $\Lambda$CDM model, the present universe consists of 5% baryonic matter and 25% non-baryonic cold dark matter of speculative origin. This dark matter may comprise quanta from scalar fields, such as the dilaton ($\phi$) arising from scale symmetry, and quanta from pseudoscalar fields linked to extra standard model symmetries, like the axion ($\phi'$) associated with the Peccei-Quinn mechanism. These fields interact with diphotons via dimension-5 operators. In a magnetized medium, they can potentially couple with the three degrees of freedom of a photon ($\gamma$)—two transverse modes ($A_{\parallel,\perp}$) and one longitudinal mode ($A_{L}$)—provided total spin is conserved. Given their zero intrinsic spin, both $\phi$ and $\phi'$ could theoretically interact with the longitudinal mode ($s_{z}=0$), yet only one of these fields actually couples to $A_{L}$. The ambient external magnetic field and the surrounding medium break the system's intrinsic Lorentz symmetry, while invoking Charge conjugation, Parity, and Time reversal symmetries. By analyzing the mixing dynamics of the $\phi\gamma$ and $\phi'\gamma$ systems, we identify structural differences in their mixing patterns, which result in distinct strengths of electromagnetic signals. We conclude by discussing the feasibility of detecting this difference in polarimetric observables of the Electromagnetic Spectrum (EMS) using current space-borne detectors.

We recently established a formalism for scattering analysis in linear and acyclic branched structures composed of mutually non-interacting sub-units, as detailed in Svaneborg and Pedersen (2012). In that framework, each sub-unit possessed specific reference points defining precise locations for linkage. This paper extends the formalism to scenarios where each reference point corresponds to a distribution of potential link positions. Additionally, we introduce a generalized diagrammatic representation of this approach. We derive scattering expressions necessary for modeling rods, polymers, loops, flat circular disks, rigid spheres, and cylinders. Finally, we apply these expressions to derive generic scattering formulas for micelles and bottle brush structures, demonstrating how varying choices of potential link positions influence the resulting scattering patterns.

Monte Carlo integration is a widely utilized method for calculating integrals that are otherwise intractable, yet it is often considered ineffective for very high-dimensional problems. Consequently, we investigate Monte Carlo integration by incorporating techniques from high-dimensional statistics, allowing the dimensionality of the integral to grow. By applying concentration inequalities, we establish non-asymptotic bounds for both relative and absolute approximation errors for a range of general functions. Our findings reveal that the number of sample points required to ensure a consistent estimate can scale anywhere from polynomially to exponentially, depending on the specific function, thereby demonstrating that Monte Carlo integration does not exhibit uniform behavior in high dimensions. Furthermore, our approach yields non-asymptotic confidence intervals for the Monte Carlo estimate that remain valid irrespective of the sample size.

Supercritical water desalination (SCWD) represents a zero-liquid discharge alternative capable of addressing numerous technical and environmental hurdles associated with conventional desalination. Recent techno-economic evaluations of process integration and intensification indicate that SCWD is a financially viable zero-liquid discharge option specifically for highly concentrated brines. Beyond these benefits, this study investigates the potential for the SCWD process to selectively recover industrially critical materials as co-products. Model feeds consisting of sodium chloride, neodymium chloride, and other sodium salts were analyzed at temperatures ranging from 25 to 450°C under 25 MPa pressure. Results showed that sodium levels in the effluent remained unaffected by the presence of other salts, whereas neodymium concentrations were sensitive. The addition of sodium acetate resulted in the formation of water-insoluble precipitates. Characterization via gas pycnometry, FT-IR, SEM/EDS, and XRD revealed that these deposits primarily consist of neodymium hydroxide along with minor impurities. Consequently, these findings suggest that SCWD has the capacity to simultaneously produce freshwater and recover essential critical materials.

In preference modelling, determining the quantity and arrangement of questions posed to decision-makers is crucial. This study focuses on incomplete pairwise comparison matrices. By identifying optimal patterns for filling these gaps, we achieve weight vectors that are, on average, closest to those derived from complete matrices. These findings stem from extensive numerical simulations involving large sample sizes. Optimal filling sequences, constructed from optimal or near-optimal patterns, are located within the graph of representing structures. Among spanning trees, the star graph emerges as optimal, while optimal graphs generally resemble bipartite ones. Additionally, regular graphs appear to correspond to optimal scenarios, as regularity is a consistent property where vertex degrees remain as uniform as possible. The practical significance of these results applies to situations where decision-makers may terminate the process at any stage, such as in online questionnaires. Nevertheless, these patterns hold potential utility across a broad spectrum of preference and information theory models.

Nova eruptions, which are thermonuclear explosions occurring on white dwarf (WD) surfaces, are now acknowledged as some of the most frequent shock-driven astrophysical transients. This study details the early detection and swift temporal evolution in ultraviolet (UV), optical, and infrared (IR) bands of AT 2019qyl, a recent nova located in the nearby Sculptor Group galaxy NGC 300. The observed light curve exhibits a rapid rise lasting less than one day, peaking at an absolute magnitude of $M_V = -9.2$ mag, followed by a steep decline that dims by 2 magnitudes within 3.5 days. A pronounced drop in brightness after 71 days and the swift decline timescale imply a low-mass ejection from a massive white dwarf with $M_{\rm WD} \gtrsim 1.2~M_{\odot}$. We offer an unprecedented look at the early spectroscopic evolution of this event, where three pre-peak spectra reveal a complex, multicomponent outflow causing internal collisions and shocks within the ejecta of an He/N-class nova. We also identify a coincident, IR-variable counterpart in extensive pre-eruption data, inferring a symbiotic progenitor system comprising an O-rich asymptotic-giant-branch donor star and evidence of a prior UV-bright outburst in 2014. We propose that AT 2019qyl is similar to a subset of Galactic recurrent novae with red-giant companions, such as RS Oph, and other embedded systems like V407 Cyg. Our findings provide new evidence that internal shocks between multiple distinct outflow components likely contribute to generating the shock-powered emission in such systems.

This paper investigates a bordism theory for pairs $(M, \xi)$, where $M$ is a closed, smooth, oriented manifold equipped with a stably trivial normal bundle, and $\xi$ is a virtual $\SU$-bundle of virtual dimension 1 defined over $M$. The primary achievement is the computation of the associated ring modulo torsion, along with a detailed characterization of its generators.

Let $[a_1(x),a_2(x),a_3(x),\cdots]$ denote the continued fraction expansion of a number $x$ in the interval $(0,1)$. This study focuses on specific sets of continued fractions characterized by non-decreasing partial quotients. The primary result establishes the Hausdorff dimension of the set \[\left\{x\in(0,1): a_1(x)\leq a_2(x)\leq \cdots,\ \limsup\limits_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log a_n(x)}{\psi(n)}=1\right\}\] for any function $\psi:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^+$ such that $\psi(n)$ approaches infinity as $n$ increases.

This paper investigates gender classification with constrained network data, specifically applied to Fotolog. We employ a heuristic method to automate gender inference by leveraging usernames, follower counts, and network topology. Evaluating our approach on a subset of 100,000 nodes reveals significant value in utilizing these limited data points, indicating strong potential for further development in this classification strategy.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a crucial medical imaging technique, yet it suffers from lengthy acquisition times. Although various methods have been introduced to shorten this duration, they have largely failed to produce images with distinct structures due to two primary issues. First, MR images contain numerous similar patches, a characteristic that most existing deep learning approaches overlook by relying solely on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to capture local features. Second, current methods only utilize clear images to define the upper bound of the solution space, leaving the lower bound unconstrained and preventing the optimization of network parameters. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the Contrastive Learning for Local and Global Learning MRI Reconstruction Network (CLGNet). Leveraging Fourier theory, which dictates that every value in the Fourier domain is derived from the entire spatial domain, we develop a Spatial and Fourier Layer (SFL). This layer enables the simultaneous extraction of local and global information from both the spatial and Fourier domains. Furthermore, the SFL demonstrates superior learning capabilities compared to self-attention mechanisms and transformers, delivering better performance more efficiently. Built upon the SFL, our model features a Spatial and Fourier Residual block as its core component. Additionally, to effectively constrain both the upper and lower bounds of the solution space, we incorporate contrastive learning, which draws reconstructed results closer to clear images while pushing them away from undersampled versions. Extensive experiments across various datasets and acceleration rates confirm that CLGNet achieves new state-of-the-art results.

We employ field-theoretic methods to investigate the $SU(3)$ counterpart of the anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg model on a triangular lattice, where each site carries a $p$-box symmetric representation. In the large-$p$ limit, the low-energy effective description is identified as a $(2+1)$-dimensional relativistic $SU(3)/U(1)^2$ nonlinear sigma model. Given that the target space possesses a nontrivial homotopy group $\pi_2(SU(3)/U(1)^2)\simeq \mathbb{Z}^2$, the theory supports two distinct types of magnetic skyrmions, generated and destroyed via monopole instantons. Through a detailed examination of the Wess-Zumino term within the spin-coherent path integral, we determine the Berry phase associated with these monopoles, leading to destructive interference. This phenomenon limits the allowable monopole operator perturbations in the effective Lagrangian, indicating that the valence-bond-solid (VBS) phase exhibits degenerate ground states whenever $p$ is not a multiple of 3. Furthermore, by calculating 't Hooft anomalies to restrict potential phases, we find that anomaly matching supports a direct phase transition between the Néel and VBS states.

This paper presents and investigates {\it Carlitz polyominoes}. Specifically, we demonstrate that as $n$ approaches infinity, the asymptotic counts for \begin{enumerate} \item column-convex Carlitz polyominoes with perimeter $2n$ are \beq \frac{9\sqrt{2}(14+3\sqrt{3})}{2704\sqrt{\pi n^3}}4^n. \feq \item convex Carlitz polyominoes with perimeter $2n$ are \beq \frac{n+1}{10}\left(\frac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^{n-2}. \feq \end{enumerate}

Gaseous time projection chambers (TPCs) featuring recoil imaging and directional sensitivity hold great promise for dark matter (DM) research. Detectors capable of reconstructing 3D nuclear recoil trajectories would be uniquely suited to identify the predicted dipole angular distribution of DM recoils, thereby definitively confirming the galactic origin of a signal and offering strong discrimination against solar neutrino backgrounds. However, realizing these benefits requires the effective suppression of electron recoil backgrounds induced by gamma rays. This study introduces a deep learning-based event classifier utilizing a 3D convolutional neural network (3DCNN) to distinguish event types based on their recoil images. We evaluate the electron background rejection capabilities of the 3DCNN against traditional track length discriminants and those derived from advanced shallow learning methods. The 3DCNN was trained on recoil charge distributions spanning ionization energies from 0.5 to 10.5 $\rm keV_{ee}$, simulated for a 25 cm drift length in an 80:10:10 mixture of $\rm He$:$\rm CF_4$:$\rm CHF_3$. While track length and shallow learning discriminants utilized a fine segmentation of $(100\times 100\times 100)$ $\rm\mu m^3$ bins, the 3DCNN employed a coarser rebinning of approximately $(850\times 850\times 850)$ $\rm\mu m^3$. Despite this reduced resolution, the 3DCNN demonstrated superior performance, reducing electron backgrounds by up to a factor of 1,000 compared to track length methods. This improvement effectively lowered the energy threshold of the simulated TPC by 30% for fluorine recoils and 50% for helium recoils. Furthermore, the 3DCNN outperformed shallow machine learning approaches by reducing electron backgrounds by up to a factor of 20, corresponding to a 2 $\rm keV_{ee}$ reduction in the energy threshold.

As music technology advances, numerous Electronic Dance Music (EDM) subgenres have emerged in recent years. Although distinguishing EDM from non-EDM is a well-studied aspect of genre classification, classifying specific EDM subgenres remains significantly less explored. Current state-of-the-art approaches rely on extremely randomized trees, which could benefit from deep learning techniques. This paper extends the advanced music auto-tagging model "short-chunkCNN+Resnet" for EDM subgenre classification by incorporating two mid-level tempo-based features: the Fourier tempogram and the autocorrelation tempogram. We investigate two fusion strategies—early and late fusion—to combine these tempogram representations. Evaluated on a large dataset of 75,000 songs covering 30 distinct EDM subgenres, our results demonstrate that integrating deep learning models with tempo features significantly enhances classification accuracy.

Isolated classical black holes with rotation or charge contain an internal boundary known as the Cauchy horizon, past which General Relativity fails to predict spacetime evolution deterministically. This study examines the impact of a quantum massless scalar field on the Cauchy horizon within an evaporating rotating (Kerr) black hole, where the field exists in the Unruh state due to Hawking radiation. By computing the flux components of the renormalized stress-energy tensor in Eddington coordinates as functions of black hole spin and polar angle, we determine that these fluxes are generally non-zero. Additionally, the sign of these fluxes varies with changes in spin and angle; these signs are crucial for predicting whether the Cauchy horizon expands or collapses when backreaction is considered. Despite these sign variations, our findings indicate that, in coordinate systems regular at the horizon, the flux components generically diverge. This represents the first conclusive demonstration of Cauchy horizon irregularity under semiclassical effects for four-dimensional spinning black holes.

The Explorer-Director game, originally proposed by Nedev and Muthukrishnan, involves two participants, the Explorer and the Director, who dictate the movement of a token across a graph's vertices. At every step, the Explorer selects a distance for the token to travel, aiming to maximize the total number of visited vertices, while the Director counter-strategically determines the token's new position to minimize this count. For a specific graph and starting vertex, the count of vertices reached under optimal play is represented as $f_d(G,v)$. This paper begins by reducing the analysis of $f_d(G,v)$ to identifying minimal sets of vertices that are \textit{closed} in a specific combinatorial manner, thereby offering a structural insight into each player's optimal strategies. We apply this approach to problems involving lattices and trees; notably, for trees, we present a complete solution even when the Explorer's strategy is restricted to being independent of the Director's responses. Furthermore, an additional companion note on arXiv will detail further findings regarding this game across various specific graph families.

We examine the thermoelectric (TE) characteristics of two-dimensional materials featuring a Dirac band and a nonlinear band within a three- (or two-) band framework, employing linearized Boltzmann transport theory and the relaxation time approximation. Our analysis of the three-band model reveals that pairing Dirac bands with heavy nonlinear bands—whether parabolic or pudding-mold shaped—yields negligible differences in TE performance. The primary distinction lies solely in the energy position of the nonlinear band, which dictates the peak figure of merit ($ZT$). Optimal $ZT$ is achieved when the nonlinear band intersects the Dirac bands close to the Fermi level. However, by eliminating the linear conduction band to transition from a three-band to a two-band model, we observe superior TE performance, characterized by higher $ZT$ values.

We examine the stochastic characteristics of the single-trajectory spectral density $S(\omega,\mathcal{T})$ across various Gaussian stochastic processes, including Brownian motion, the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, the Brownian gyrator model, and fractional Brownian motion, analyzing how they vary with frequency $\omega$ and observation time $\mathcal{T}$. Specifically, we assess the variance and frequency-frequency correlations of $S(\omega,\mathcal{T})$ for distinct $\omega$ values. Our findings demonstrate that these properties display unique behaviors depending on the specific physical scenario, making them effective sensitive indicators for distinguishing between different types of random motion. Consequently, these results could be highly valuable for interpreting experimental data.

Generally, non-rigid registration involves aligning two scans of a dynamic object captured at distinct moments. These scans may experience both rigid movements and non-rigid deformations. Because new object parts may become visible while others become occluded between captures, the overlapping region constitutes a subset of both scans. In the most general scenario, there is no prior template shape, and no markers or explicit feature correspondences are provided. Consequently, this is treated as a partial matching problem that assumes subsequent scans undergo minor deformations while maintaining a substantial area of overlap [28]. The specific challenge addressed by this thesis is the simultaneous localization of cameras within an environment and the mapping of deforming objects.

Variability in environmental conditions presents a significant hurdle for learned robotic controllers, often leading to failures caused by mismatches between training and evaluation settings. While training with demonstrations across diverse scenarios can reduce these failures, it cannot entirely eliminate them. Typically, learned controllers like neural networks lack an inherent sense of uncertainty, preventing them from identifying discrepancies between training and testing environments or initiating corrective actions. This study introduces the use of Bayesian Neural Networks, which possess this crucial capability to quantify uncertainty. We demonstrate that leveraging uncertainty enables the consistent detection of sub-optimal performance in high-dimensional robotic domains, both in simulation and real-world settings. Furthermore, we show that this uncertainty-based approach facilitates informed decisions regarding when to activate fallback mechanisms, such as requesting additional data. Our empirical results indicate that acquiring data only upon request significantly enhances data efficiency.

**Context.** A specific group of runaway stars travels at extraordinary velocities relative to their surroundings. The combination of their rapid motion, stellar winds, and the interaction between these winds and the surrounding medium can drive particle acceleration and produce non-thermal radiation.

**Aims.** Our objective is to analyze the dynamics of the interaction between the winds of these fast-moving stars and their environment, specifically to evaluate their capability as cosmic-ray accelerators and sources of non-thermal emission.

**Methods.** We simulate the hydrodynamics of the collision between stellar winds and ambient material. Using a multi-zone code, we self-consistently model the injection and transport of relativistic particles within the bow shock and calculate their broadband emission spanning from radio waves to gamma-rays.

**Results.** Both the forward and reverse shocks serve as favorable locations for particle acceleration; however, the radiative efficiency of these particles is low, resulting in generally faint expected fluxes.

**Conclusions.** We demonstrate that high-sensitivity radio observations can detect the non-thermal radiation generated by bow shocks from hypervelocity and semi-relativistic stars. While hypervelocity stars are anticipated to be modest sources of sub-TeV cosmic rays, they may contribute only approximately 0.1% to the total flux of galactic cosmic rays.

We establish sufficient criteria ensuring that a dynamical system possesses a set of irregular points exhibiting full topological entropy. These criteria are confirmed for specific nonuniformly hyperbolic systems, including surface diffeomorphisms with positive entropy and rational functions defined on the Riemann sphere.

We introduce IMS-Speech, a web-based platform designed for transcribing German and English speech to support research across disciplines that depend on lexical access in spoken language. Built upon a modern open-source software stack, cutting-edge speech recognition techniques, and public data resources, this tool is freely accessible to academic researchers. The employed models are engineered for genericity, ensuring competitive transcription accuracy across a wide range of tasks and conditions.

Recent studies have effectively applied path integral molecular dynamics to analyze the thermodynamics of single-component identical bosons and fermions. This work extends that methodology to simulate the thermodynamics, Green's functions, and momentum distributions of two-component bosons in three dimensions. To demonstrate the general approach, we investigate the thermodynamic properties of up to sixteen bosons confined in a three-dimensional harmonic trap. For noninteracting spinor bosons, our simulations reveal a distinct peak in the heat capacity; however, as repulsive interaction strength increases, this peak gradually vanishes. We propose that these findings can be experimentally verified using ultracold spinor bosons within optical lattices, where magnetic-field Feshbach resonance allows for precise tuning of inter-particle interactions. Additionally, we compute the Green's functions and momentum distributions for these spinor bosons. Our research advances the capability for exact numerical simulations of spinor bosons, addressing a significant challenge in the study of ultracold Bose gases.

Although a vast amount of health-related literature is now accessible online, the specialized language in scientific articles often remains incomprehensible to the general public. Consequently, translating expert-level content into plain language is essential for reliable public understanding. While Deep Learning offers a potential solution for automatic translation, effective evaluation requires gold-standard datasets. Existing datasets are limited, offering either document-level pairs or sentence-level pairs mined from texts, which creates a trade-off between inaccurate alignments and insufficient test sizes. To resolve this, we introduce the Plain Language Adaptation of Biomedical Abstracts dataset. As the first manually adapted resource featuring both document and sentence alignment, it comprises 750 abstracts containing 7,643 sentence pairs. In addition to detailing the dataset, we evaluate state-of-the-art Deep Learning methods for automatic adaptation, establishing performance baselines for future studies.

We show that low-energy positive muon ($\mu^+$) spin spectroscopy, acting as a local probe, allows for the direct determination of free charge carrier profiles within the accumulation and depletion surface regions of p- or n-type germanium (Ge) wafers. The presence of free holes is detected by observing how their interaction with the $\mu^+$ probe spin alters the measurable muon spin polarization. By adjusting the $\mu^+$ energy from 1 keV to 20 keV, the technique probes the near-surface depth ranging from 10 nm to 160 nm. Our results indicate hole depletion and electron accumulation in all samples with doping levels up to $10^{17}$ cm$^{-3}$, a behavior contrary to that of cleaved Ge surfaces. Light illumination enables controlled manipulation of hole carrier density in the depletion zone. Depending on the light wavelength ($\lambda$), this modulation can be either persistent ($\lambda = 405, 457$ nm) or non-persistent ($\lambda = 635$ nm) at temperatures below 270 K; this distinction arises from differences in photo-electron kinetic energy. Specifically, photo-electrons generated by red light lack the energy to surmount the surface potential barrier and become trapped in empty surface acceptor states. Unlike conventional macroscopic transport measurements, this contact-less local probe method offers the unique capability to directly measure carrier depth profiles and perform manipulation. Consequently, our approach yields significant microscopic insights on the nanometer scale for semiconductor device research.

Using the IllustrisTNG simulations, we investigate how galaxy formation physics influences the magnetization of the intergalactic medium (IGM). Our findings show that large-scale areas influenced by outflows from galaxies and clusters host magnetic fields that are orders of magnitude stronger than those in unaffected regions with identical electron densities. Furthermore, similar to magnetic fields amplified within galaxies, these external fields are independent of primordial seeds, meaning the initial conditions for field strength do not affect the outcome. We analyze the volume filling fraction of these intense field regions and their likelihood along random lines of sight. As a primary application, we utilize these results to constrain photon-axion conversion derived from CMB spectral distortions. Since photon-axion coupling increases with energy, stronger constraints on this phenomenon could potentially be achieved by analyzing gamma-ray photon propagation through the IGM. Finally, we briefly explore potential applications of our findings to Faraday Rotation measurements.

Intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) with masses $\geq\!10^5\,M_\odot$ are considered viable progenitors for supermassive black holes (SMBHs) reaching $\sim\!10^9\,M_\odot$ in the early universe at redshift $z\sim6$. While Chon & Omukai (2020) initially proposed that direct collapse black holes (DCBHs) form in metal-enriched atomic-cooling halos (ACHs)—thereby easing the standard formation requirements—Hirano et al. (2021) demonstrated that magnetic fields facilitate DCBH formation in metal-free ACHs. This study employs magnetohydrodynamical simulations to examine star formation within magnetized ACHs across metallicities of $Z/Z_\odot = 0$, $10^{-5}$, and $10^{-4}$. The results indicate that while mass accretion rates onto protostars are lower in metal-enriched environments compared to metal-free ones, numerous protostars still emerge from gravitationally and thermally unstable metal-enriched clouds. Consequently, magnetic fields intensify rapidly as protostellar spin winds field lines. Driven by protostellar orbital motion and the rotation of infalling gas, this amplified magnetic field expands outward, extracting angular momentum from the accreting material. This process encourages the coalescence of low-mass protostars and accelerates the mass growth of the primary star. We conclude that magnetic field amplification invariably occurs in metal-enriched ACHs, independent of initial magnetic strength, thus relaxing the DCBH formation criterion. Furthermore, unlike previous unmagnetized simulations, our findings reveal that the mass growth rate peaks in extremely metal-poor ACHs with $Z/Z_\odot = 10^{-5}$.

Blazar PG 1553+113 is hypothesized to host a supermassive black hole binary (SMBHB) system. A 2.2-year quasi-periodicity observed in its $\gamma$-ray light curve may stem from jet precession. Building on prior $\gamma$-ray studies, we examined X-ray light curves and spectra recorded between 2012 and 2020. This 2.2-year periodicity appears consistent with the recurrence of main flares in the X-ray data. Notably, periods of weak $\gamma$-ray rebrightening correspond to relatively strong brightenings in the X-ray band. Both main and weak X-ray flares exhibit a "harder-when-brighter" trend, whereas the quiescent state shows a weak "softer-when-brighter" behavior. We investigate whether X-ray variability can be explained by a two-jet precession model. By applying the relationship between jets and accretion discs, we estimate the primary black hole mass at $\simeq 3.47\times 10^8M_{\odot}$, the secondary mass at $\simeq 1.40\times 10^8M_{\odot}$, and a mass ratio of approximately 0.41.

This study investigates the asymptotic behavior of sojourn times in random fields featuring continuous sample paths. Within a highly general framework, we demonstrate a significant connection between the tail asymptotics of sojourn times and those of the supremum. Furthermore, we introduce a uniform double-sum method to derive the tail asymptotics for sojourn times. While previous literature, building on S. Berman's foundational work, has used sojourn times to determine the tail asymptotics of the supremum for Gaussian processes, this paper reveals that the reverse approach is equally productive: knowing the asymptotics of the supremum for random processes and fields (especially Gaussian ones) allows us to deduce the asymptotics of their sojourn times. We validate these results through examples involving: i) two-dimensional Gaussian random fields, ii) chi-processes derived from stationary Gaussian processes, and iii) stationary Gaussian queueing processes.

A primary challenge in Sequential Recommendation (SR) lies in effectively extracting and representing user preferences. While traditional SR approaches depend on the next item as a supervisory signal to guide this process, we introduce a novel strategy called "preference editing." This approach compels the SR model to distinguish between common and unique preferences across various user-system interaction sequences, thereby enhancing the model's ability to learn and represent these preferences accurately. We present MrTransformer (Multi-preference Transformer), a transformer-based SR architecture that appends special tokens to sequence inputs to encode multiple user preferences, ensuring distinct aspects are captured via a preference coverage mechanism. To train MrTransformer, we develop a preference editing-driven self-supervised learning framework comprising two core operations: preference separation and preference recombination. Preference separation isolates common and unique preferences for specific sequence pairs, while preference recombination swaps common preferences to generate new, recombined sequences for each user. Leveraging these operations, we define two self-supervised learning (SSL) losses that enforce similarity between recombined and original preferences, as well as proximity among common preferences. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate that MrTransformer with preference editing significantly surpasses state-of-the-art SR methods in Recall, MRR, and NDCG metrics. Our findings indicate that preference editing yields the greatest benefits for long sequences where extracting and representing user preferences is particularly difficult.

This paper introduces Point Cloud Color Constancy (PCCC), an algorithm for estimating illumination chromaticity that utilizes point cloud data. By combining depth data from a time-of-flight (ToF) sensor rigidly attached to an RGB sensor, we construct a 6D point cloud where each point includes spatial coordinates and RGB values (x,y,z,r,g,b). PCCC employs the PointNet architecture to solve color constancy by calculating an illumination vector for each point before determining the global illumination chromaticity. Experiments conducted on two standard RGB-D datasets—extended with illumination details—and a new benchmark demonstrate that PCCC achieves lower error rates than existing state-of-the-art methods. The proposed approach is both efficient and straightforward, requiring only 16×16 input size and achieving speeds exceeding 500 frames per second, inclusive of point cloud construction and network inference.

Machine learning tools have demonstrated significant potential in critical sectors like healthcare and finance by enabling valuable inferences. However, the sensitive nature of data in these domains raises inherent privacy concerns, motivating the field of Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning (PPML) to ensure data confidentiality. Since traditional ML techniques demand substantial computational resources, clients with limited infrastructure often turn to Secure Outsourced Computation (SOC), where powerful cloud servers handle tasks on a pay-per-use basis. This work investigates PPML techniques within the SOC framework for widely used algorithms, including Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, and Neural Networks.

We introduce BLAZE, a high-performance PPML framework designed for a three-server architecture that tolerates one malicious participant within a ring (\Z{\ell}). BLAZE provides a robust fairness guarantee, ensuring that all honest servers receive the output if a corrupt server does. By utilizing an input-independent preprocessing phase, BLAZE achieves a rapid online phase dependent on the input, leveraging efficient PPML primitives. These include: (i) a dot product protocol where online communication is independent of vector size, marking the first such achievement in a three-server setting; and (ii) a truncation method that avoids expensive Ripple Carry Adder (RCA) circuits, achieving constant round complexity. This represents an improvement over ABY3 (Mohassel et al., CCS 2018), which relies on RCA and incurs round complexity proportional to the circuit's depth. Extensive benchmarks of BLAZE on the specified ML algorithms over a 64-bit ring, conducted in both WAN and LAN environments, demonstrate substantial performance gains compared to ABY3.

This study examines the first eigenvalues associated with two closed eigenvalue problems of the bi-Beltrami-Laplacian defined on minimal embedded isoparametric hypersurfaces within the unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}(1)$. While numerous mathematicians have attempted to establish analogous results for the first eigenvalues of the bi-Beltrami-Laplacian, they have faced significant challenges in proving the limit theorem for this operator using the strategies proposed by I. Chavel and E. A. Feldman (Journal of Functional Analysis, 30 (1978), 198-222) and S. Ozawa (Duke Mathematics Journal, 48 (1981), 767-778). Consequently, to the author's knowledge, no results of the Tang-Yan type (Journal of Differential Geometry, 94 (2013) 521-540) currently exist. By employing a variational approach, we successfully surmount these obstacles and determine the first eigenvalues of the bi-Beltrami-Laplacian specifically for isoparametric hypersurfaces, noting that our proof is notably straightforward.

The two-phase model of galaxy formation posits that stellar mass growth is initially driven by in-situ star formation before shifting to accretion. Using the Magneticum hydrodynamical cosmological simulation, we analyzed the radial distribution of accreted stellar mass across approximately 500 galaxies. While our results generally align with other simulations regarding higher accreted fractions in massive galaxies, we predict elevated accretion fractions for low-mass systems. By examining the radial profiles of both in-situ and accreted components, we categorized galaxies into six classes ranging from fully accretion-dominated to fully in-situ-dominated, and measured the transition radii where these regions intersect for applicable galaxies. Approximately 70% of the sample exhibits a single transition radius; however, about 10% are accretion-dominated throughout, and roughly 13% display two transition radii, with both the center and outskirts dominated by accretion. We demonstrate a strong correlation between these classes and merger histories, particularly the cold gas fractions of merging events. Furthermore, high total in-situ fractions (indicating low accretion) correlate with lower-mass galaxies, reduced central dark matter concentrations, and larger transition radii. Finally, we conclude that dips in observed surface brightness profiles of early-type galaxies do not mark the shift from in-situ to accretion dominance, nor do they reflect true mass fractions; instead, these features encode information regarding the galaxies' dry minor merger assembly history.

This study introduces the first strong gravitational lens model of SMACS J0723, observed by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). We constructed a 'pre-JWST' model utilizing Hubble Space Telescope and Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE) data, which was subsequently refined using new JWST near-infrared imagery. To accurately reproduce the positions of multiple lensed images, our mass parameterization includes a cluster-scale component—primarily representing dark matter and cluster members—along with an external shear component. The pre-JWST model relies on 19 multiple images from six background sources, four of which have secure spectroscopic redshifts derived in this work. The JWST model significantly expands these constraints with 30 additional images from eleven other lensed sources, more than doubling the data points. Both models successfully match multiple image positions, with root-mean-square residuals ($\delta_{rms}$) of $0.39''$ for the pre-JWST model and $0.51''$ for the JWST model. Total mass estimates within a 128 kpc radius (approximately the Einstein radius) are $7.9_{-0.2}^{+0.3}\times 10^{13}\rm M_{\odot}$ for the pre-JWST model and $8.7_{-0.2}^{+0.2}\times 10^{13}\rm M_{\odot}$ for the JWST model. Our models predict redshifts for newly detected JWST sources, providing essential data for follow-up observations of systems lacking spectroscopic measurements. Notably, one JWST-detected source family is identified at a very high redshift ($z>7.5$ at 68% confidence), with one image exhibiting a magnification of $|\mu|=9.5_{-0.8}^{+0.9}$, presenting a compelling target for future research. We make the lens models, including magnification maps and estimated redshifts, publicly available alongside the complete MUSE spectroscopic redshift catalogue.

The behavior of statistical relational representations across varying domain sizes has emerged as a critical research topic from both modeling and complexity perspectives. Recently, the property of projectivity within a family of distributions has gained prominence for guaranteeing that marginal probabilities remain invariant to domain size. However, existing formalizations rely on the assumption that a domain is defined solely by its size. This work expands the concept of projectivity from families indexed by domain size to functors that utilize extensional database data, thereby making projectivity applicable to a wide array of applications involving structured inputs. We adapt established results on projective distribution families to this new framework, including a characterization of projective fragments across various statistical relational formalisms and a general representation theorem for such families. Additionally, we demonstrate a correspondence between projectivity and distributions over countably infinite domains, which serves to unify and extend prior research on statistical relational representations in infinite settings. Finally, leveraging this extended notion of projectivity, we introduce a stronger variant termed $\sigma$-projectivity, enabling the reuse of the same representation across different modes while maintaining projectivity.

Consider a closed symplectic manifold $(X,\omega)$. A loop $\phi: S^1 \to \mathrm{Diff}(X)$ induces a fibration $\pi: P_{\phi} \to S^2$. Utilizing Gromov-Witten theory on the moduli spaces of holomorphic sections of this fibration, Lalonde, McDuff, and Polterovich demonstrated that if $\phi$ lifts to the Hamiltonian group $\mathrm{Ham}(X,\omega)$, the rational cohomology of $P_{\phi}$ admits an additive splitting. We extend this result under identical assumptions, showing that the $\mathbb{E}$-generalised cohomology of $P_{\phi}$ splits additively for any complex-oriented cohomology theory $\mathbb{E}$, which specifically implies an additive splitting of the integral cohomology. This framework encompasses all complex projective varieties admitting a smooth morphism to $\mathbb{CP}^1$; for these cases, an analogous rational splitting was previously established by Deligne via Hodge theory. Our methodology relies on virtual fundamental cycles of section moduli spaces within Morava $K$-theory and findings from chromatic homotopy theory. Furthermore, our proof introduces a construction of independent significance: we construct global Kuranishi charts for moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic spheres in $X$ within a class $\beta \in H_2(X;\mathbb{Z})$, contingent upon selecting an integral symplectic form $\Omega$ on $X$ and an ample Hermitian line bundle over the moduli space of stable genus zero curves with a single marked point and degree $d = \langle \Omega,\beta\rangle$ in $\mathbb{CP}^d$.

We introduce a formulation of the RSK correspondence derived from the Pitman transform and geometric principles. This approach integrates ordinary RSK, dual RSK, and continuous RSK into a single framework. We demonstrate that this formulation acts as both a bijection and an isometry, two essential characteristics for analyzing the limits of last passage percolation models. Leveraging the bijective nature of this mapping, we provide a non-computational proof showing that dual RSK transforms Bernoulli walks into nonintersecting Bernoulli walks.

Detecting anomalous sounds for machine condition monitoring holds immense promise for advancing Industry 4.0, yet such anomalies are typically absent during normal operational phases. Consequently, training models must rely on normal acoustic data to learn representations that can identify deviations during testing. This article introduces a Self-Supervised Dual-Path Transformer (SSDPT) network designed for anomaly detection in machine monitoring. The SSDPT architecture segments acoustic features and utilizes multiple Dual-Path Transformer (DPT) blocks to model both temporal and frequency dimensions. These DPT blocks leverage attention mechanisms to alternately capture the interactive information between frequency and temporal components within the segmented features. To overcome the scarcity of anomalous sound data, we employ a self-supervised learning strategy that trains the network exclusively on normal sounds. This method involves randomly masking and reconstructing acoustic features while simultaneously classifying machine identity to enhance detection performance. We validated our approach using the DCASE2021 Task 2 dataset, and experimental results demonstrate that the SSDPT network significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of harmonic mean AUC scores for anomalous sound detection.

Markov-modulated fluids constitute a well-established class of Markov additive processes. Originally conceptualized in the 1950s to model dams and reservoirs, they gained significant traction in the 1980s as fluid queues for simulating telecommunication buffers. Today, they are also utilized in risk theory and environmental research. Within telecommunication modeling, the primary objective is to determine the stationary distribution of buffer content. While early methods relied on Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) resolution, modern approaches focus on the system's physical evolution, requiring only the solution of a Riccati equation to derive key metrics. Building on foundational algorithms from Applied Probability, numerical analysts have introduced refined techniques that offer superior convergence speed, accuracy, and applicability. This overview presents the matrix-analytic framework for fluid queues, touches upon computational challenges, and outlines recent extensions to more general processes.

This paper provides enumerative findings regarding holomorphic foliations by curves on $\mathbb{P}^n$ (where $n\geq 3$) that possess singularities of positive dimension. Several of these findings refine earlier work by Corrêa–Fernández-Pérez–Nonato Costa–Vidal Martins and Nonato Costa. Furthermore, we establish an enumerative result that bounds the count of isolated singularities within a projective subvariety invariant under a holomorphic foliation by curves on $\mathbb{P}^n$ featuring a singularity of positive dimension.

We present the initial findings of an investigation into the tidally perturbed galaxy system AM\,546-324, which consists of two principal galaxies, 2MFGC 04711 and AM\,0546-324 (NED02), previously identified as an interacting pair. This system was chosen to examine interactions between ellipticals within a moderately dense environment. Our work includes spectral characteristics and an observational analysis of how interaction influences the morphology, kinematics, and stellar populations of these galaxies. The study relies on long-slit spectrophotometric data spanning approximately 4500-8000 $\AA$, collected using the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS-S) at Gemini South. We employed the STARLIGHT stellar population synthesis code to analyze the star formation history, while a direct r-G0303 broad-band image from Gemini/GMOS-S was utilized to resolve fine morphological details. Radial velocities were determined from the main absorption lines in the spectra. Throughout the entire long-slit, the spectra of the newly discovered Shadowy galaxy, along with 2MFGC 04711 and AM\,0546-324 (NED02), resemble those of early-type galaxies. We calculated redshifts of z= 0.0696, z= 0.0693, and z= 0.0718 for the Shadowy galaxy, 2MFGC 04711, and AM\,0546-324 (NED02), respectively, corresponding to heliocentric velocities of 20\,141 km s$^{-1}$, 20\,057 km s$^{-1}$, and 20\,754 km s$^{-1}$.

Recent research demonstrates that logical background knowledge can enhance learning systems by mitigating the scarcity of labeled training data, often implemented through loss functions that encode such knowledge. However, this logic is frequently discarded post-training despite its utility during inference. To address this, we propose a method that ensures neural network outputs adhere to this knowledge by refining predictions through an additional computational stage. We introduce differentiable refinement functions capable of identifying corrected predictions that remain proximate to the original outputs. Our investigation focuses on the effective and efficient computation of these functions. Furthermore, we present a novel algorithm, Iterative Local Refinement (ILR), which combines these functions to derive refined predictions for logical formulas of arbitrary complexity. ILR achieves significant efficiency gains on complex SAT formulas, requiring fewer iterations and often succeeding where gradient descent fails. Finally, the method yields competitive performance on the MNIST addition task.

We present a catalog of 350 pulsating variable stars identified across four DECam fields (~12 sq. deg.) centered on the Antlia 2 satellite galaxy. This sample comprises 318 RR Lyrae stars and eight anomalous Cepheids belonging to the galaxy. By reclassifying several objects previously identified as RR Lyrae as anomalous Cepheids, we eliminate the obscuring foreground stars, thereby removing the necessity for extensive tidal disruption of the dwarf galaxy. This finding aligns with recent proper motion and pericenter measurements derived from Gaia EDR3. Additionally, the field contains several bright foreground RR Lyrae stars and two distant background variables situated approximately 45 kpc behind Antlia 2. The detection of RR Lyrae stars across the entire search area suggests the galaxy is extensive and likely extends beyond our observed region. In Antlia 2, RRab stars exhibit a mean period of 0.599 days, while RRc stars average 0.368 days, classifying the system as Oosterhoff-intermediate. Based on RR Lyrae stars, the distance to Antlia 2 is determined to be 124.1 kpc ($\mu_0=20.47$) with a dispersion of 5.4 kpc. We observed a distinct distance gradient along the galaxy's semi-major axis, with the South-East side located approximately 13 kpc farther away than the North-West side. This elongation along the line of sight is likely attributable to the ongoing tidal disruption of Antlia 2.

Understanding ionospheric dynamics and related physical processes at low latitudes, particularly near the magnetic equator and the Equatorial Ionization Anomaly (EIA), requires a systematic investigation of ionospheric scintillation. This study analyzes NavIC $S_{4_C}$ data collected over Indore and Hyderabad, alongside GPS $S_{4_C}$ observations from Indore, covering both disturbed and quiet periods between September 2017 and 2019 during the declining phase of solar cycle 24. The analysis utilized proxy parameters such as ROT and ROTI, drawing on data from three NavIC satellites (PRNs 2, 5, and 6). Results indicate that scintillation onset occurred at approximately 19:30 LT in Hyderabad and 20:30 LT in Indore, with $S_{4_C}$ peaks reaching between 22:00 LT and 23:00 LT. During quiet conditions, the reliability of NavIC was confirmed through scattering coefficients, which demonstrated strong correlation between signal pairs. Furthermore, amplitude scintillations in NavIC signals were found to conform to both Nakagami-m and $\alpha-\mu$ distributions, reflecting deep power fades induced by scintillation. This work presents the first systematic assessment of such studies in these regions, enhancing our comprehension of the low-latitude ionosphere's dynamic behavior under low solar activity.

Maximal extractable value (MEV), also known as miner extractable value, typically denotes the profit that privileged participants can secure by strategically sequencing, censoring, or inserting transactions within a blockchain. Since every blockchain network, or domain, possesses unique consensus, ordering, and block-generation protocols, it fosters distinct optimal strategies for MEV extraction. The actions of rational actors, termed "searchers," create MEV games that generate varying impacts and externalities across different domains. Various transaction ordering mechanisms have been proposed to restructure these games, aiming to organize MEV extraction while reducing negative externalities; notable examples include sealed-bid auctions, first-in-first-out (FIFO) systems, and private priority gas auctions. Nevertheless, a sufficiently formal and abstract definition of MEV games has yet to be established. This paper advances the formalization of MEV games by comparing different ordering mechanisms and their associated externalities. Specifically, we aim to define games stemming from common knowledge MEV opportunities, such as arbitrage and sandwich attacks. In constructing these definitions, we employ a theoretical framework that clarifies key roles and concepts, including searchers, sequencers, domains, and bundles. Furthermore, we introduce the "price of MEV," defined as the price of anarchy within MEV games, offering a formal metric to compare the efficiency of various ordering mechanisms.

We present a new method for dimensional reduction within classical field theory, drawing inspiration from noncommutative geometry. This approach establishes extended algebras of differential forms over space-time, alongside generalized exterior derivatives and connections, specifically tailored to space-times featuring discrete extra dimensions. When applied to gauge and gravitational field theories, our formalism naturally yields geometrical origins for the axion, dilaton, and Higgs fields.

We investigate a broad extension of the Holst action that incorporates torsion and nonmetricity within manifolds possessing timelike boundaries, utilizing both metric and tetrad formalisms. Our analysis demonstrates that the solution space of this generalized action coincides exactly with that of the Palatini action. Consequently, we establish that the metric component aligns perfectly with General Relativity as defined by the Einstein-Hilbert action. Furthermore, although both the Palatini and the generalized Holst Lagrangians yield identical solution spaces, they are not cohomologically equivalent; this implies that the presymplectic structures and associated charges derived via the Covariant Phase Space method could potentially differ. Nevertheless, by employing the relative bicomplex framework, we prove that the covariant phase spaces of both theories—and their respective charges—are equivalent, confirming their consistency with General Relativity and resolving existing ambiguities concerning dual charges across different theoretical formulations.

This paper details a study evaluating the performance of various base classifiers for recognizing handwritten characters of the modern Latin alphabet. Classification accuracy was improved through Viterbi error correction, which identifies the optimal Viterbi sequence. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) leverage intra-word letter relationships to determine the most probable character sequence. The research examines four base classifiers across eight feature sets extracted from a handwritten dataset. Following correction, the best classification performance achieved was 89.8%, with an average of 68.1%.

This study reports the observation of the Bc+ -> Bs0 pi+ decay, utilizing the Bs0 -> Ds- pi+ and Bs0 -> J/psi Phi decay modes. The analysis utilizes data from pp collisions recorded by the LHCb detector, comprising an integrated luminosity of 1 fb-1 at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV and 2 fb-1 at 8 TeV. The Bc+ -> Bs0 pi+ decay is detected with a significance exceeding five standard deviations in both channels independently.
