In the pseudorapidity interval 2 < eta(B) < 5, the measured product of the cross-section ratio and branching fraction is sigma(Bc+)/sigma(Bs0) x BR(Bc+ -> Bs0 pi+) = (2.37 \pm 0.31 (stat) \pm 0.11 (syst)^{+0.17}_{-0.13} (tau_Bc)) x 10^-3, where the uncertainties correspond to statistical, systematic, and Bc lifetime variations, respectively. This marks the first observation of a B meson decaying into another B meson through the weak interaction.

Let $F(y):=\int_t^TL(s, y(s), y'(s))\,ds$ denote a positive functional, potentially non-autonomous, defined on the Sobolev space $W^{1,p}([t,T]; \mathbb R^n)$ ($p\ge 1$), subject to one or two boundary conditions. For practical applications, it is crucial to approximate the infimum of $F$ using values derived from a sequence of Lipschitz functions that satisfy the same boundary constraints. However, this is not always feasible; when the Lavrentiev phenomenon arises, such approximation fails. A notable example is Mani\`a's Lagrangian $L(s,y,y')=(y^3-s)^2(y')^6$ with boundary data $y(0)=0, y(1)=1$, where the gap appears; conversely, the gap disappears if only the condition $y(1)=1$ is imposed. This paper investigates the specific conditions required to prevent the gap in problems involving either a single or both boundary conditions. Under minimal assumptions regarding the possibly extended-valued Lagrangian, we demonstrate that the Lavrentiev phenomenon does not occur when only one endpoint condition is enforced. Furthermore, we introduce an additional hypothesis, which holds when the Lagrangian is bounded on bounded sets, to guarantee validity for both endpoint conditions $y_h(t)=y(t)$ and $y_h(T)=y(T)$, thereby offering new insights even for autonomous cases.

We present a novel category of collider observables within conformal field theories, termed generalized event shapes. Defined as matrix elements of light-ray operators, these observables capture the longitudinal or time-dependent structure of states generated in collisions. They can be analyzed through both correlation functions and scattering amplitudes, are infrared finite, and continuously transition into standard event shapes. We calculate them in planar ${\cal N}=4$ super-Yang-Mills theory across weak and strong coupling regimes to investigate their physical characteristics. Our results demonstrate that at strong coupling, both stringy and quantum-gravitational corrections to energy-energy correlation induce longitudinal broadening, evidenced by long-time tails in the energy flux recorded by detectors.

Editing real-world facial images semantically is a critical application of generative models. While recent studies have utilized the latent structures of pre-trained GANs to achieve this, these methods often necessitate training an encoder, a process that is both time-consuming and resource-heavy. A viable alternative is styleALAE, a latent-space autoencoder capable of producing high-quality, photo-realistic images; however, its reconstructions fail to retain the identity of the original input, thereby restricting its utility for semantic face editing on images with known identities. Our approach leverages recent one-shot domain adaptation advancements to overcome this limitation, ensuring that the reconstructed image maintains the same identity as the source. Furthermore, we apply semantic modifications within the latent space of the pre-trained styleALAE model. Our results demonstrate that this method successfully generates semantic edits on any real-world facial image while preserving the subject's identity.

We introduce DM-power, a novel approach designed to accurately calculate the dispersion measure (DM) of radio bursts, which we apply to the Fast Radio Burst (FRB) source FRB 20180916B. Driven by the multi-scale complexity observed in FRBs, DM-power refines DM estimates by synthesizing measurements across various Fourier frequencies within the burst's power spectrum. Through optimal weighting of these frequency-specific measurements, the method extracts a burst DM that effectively integrates data from diverse timescales. We first validate this technique using single pulses from pulsar B0329+54 before applying it to eleven bursts from FRB 20180916B. The resulting DM measurements achieve a precision of approximately $\sigma_{\rm DM} \sim 0.01~{\rm pc~cm}^{-3}$, enabling the detection of statistically significant DM fluctuations over a roughly 2-hour period. Although such variations might stem from electron density changes along the line of sight, the observed shifts are more likely attributable to intrinsic, frequency-dependent burst structures that can simulate dispersive delays.

This paper investigates the transverse instability of line solitons with critical speed within the generalized Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation. We establish and validate a normal form reduction concerning the bifurcation of stationary solutions to the nonlinear KdV equation defined on the product space R × T.

Ransomware constitutes a malicious software category that leverages encryption to compromise system availability, keeping victim data locked until a ransom is paid. A prevalent strategy in crypto-ransomware detection involves monitoring file system activity to spot encrypted files written to disk, frequently relying on file entropy as a primary indicator. Nevertheless, existing descriptions of these methods often lack justification for selecting specific entropy calculation techniques over alternatives. Among these, the Shannon entropy method is the most widely adopted for identifying file encryption. Since properly encrypted data should resemble random data, validation tools designed for pseudo-random number generators—such as Chi-Square, Shannon Entropy, and Serial Correlation tests—are also appropriate for this analysis. This paper hypothesizes that distinct entropy methods yield different results and that selecting the optimal ones can enhance ransomware detection. Consequently, the study evaluates the accuracy of 53 distinct tests in distinguishing encrypted data from other file types through a two-phase process: first identifying potential candidates and then rigorously assessing them. To guarantee robustness, the research utilizes the NapierOne dataset, which includes thousands of samples of common file formats alongside files encrypted by various crypto-ransomware strains.

This paper examines prominent decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols, specifically Compound and Aave, which facilitate collateralized lending for cryptoasset holders. Recognized as key applications within the DeFi ecosystem, these platforms are analyzed using publicly accessible data on borrowing and lending rates, activity volumes, and account information. The study focuses on estimating ex-post margins to comprehensively capture the costs of financial intermediation. Results indicate that ex-post margins across all markets remain at 1% or lower for stablecoin markets. Furthermore, we develop quarterly indicators assessing solvency, asset quality, earnings, and market risk, mirroring metrics standard in traditional banking. This approach offers an initial perspective on applying these measures to DeFi protocols and highlights the parallels and challenges in understanding financial intermediation within these systems compared to conventional banking frameworks.

The architecture of our Galaxy has been investigated using ultraviolet (UV) star counts derived from the Ultra-Violet Imaging Telescope (UVIT) aboard the {\em AstroSat} satellite, covering both Near-UV (NUV) and Far-UV (FUV) wavelengths. Observations utilized the N263M (NUVB4) filter for the NUV band and the F154W (BaF2) filter for the FUV band. To distinguish point sources from extra-galactic sources in the UVIT data, an infrared (IR) color cut method was applied. The observed star counts align closely with simulations generated by the Besan\c{c}on stellar population synthesis model across various Galactic directions. Furthermore, the scale height of the thin disc and both the scale length and scale height of the thick disc were determined using the space density function and exponential density law for stars at intermediate Galactic latitudes. The results indicate that the thick disc's scale length spans 3.11 to 5.40 kpc, with a scale height between 530$\pm$32 pc and 630$\pm$29 pc. Meanwhile, the thin disc's scale height is estimated to range from 230$\pm$20 pc to 330$\pm$11 pc.

We investigate the propagation of isotropic, monochromatic photons emitted equatorially by sources traveling on future-directed timelike geodesics within the near-horizon extremal Kerr (NHEK) and near-horizon near-extremal Kerr (near-NHEK) geometries, tracking them to asymptotic infinity. Our analysis yields numerical data for the photon escaping probability (PEP) and analytical formulas for the maximum observable blueshift (MOB) of these escaping photons, with both metrics varying according to the emission radius and the emitter's proper motion. Specifically, we determine that for all anti-plunging or deflecting emitters capable of reaching infinity, the PEP exceeds $50\%$, whereas for plunging emitters it remains below $55\%$; for bounded emitters in the (near-)NHEK region, the PEP never surpasses $59\%$. Additionally, regarding emitters on unstable circular orbits in the near-NHEK region, the PEP declines from $55\%$ to $50\%$ as the orbital radius shrinks from that of the innermost stable circular orbit down to the horizon. Finally, we demonstrate how the emitter's motion orientation—whether radial or azimuthal—influences both the PEP and the MOB of the emitted radiation.

Achieving high spatial-temporal resolution and brightness remains a significant hurdle for imaging atomic movement and capturing molecular dynamics. However, major advances in compact ultrabright sources of x-rays, electrons, and lasers have made it possible to directly visualize evolving molecular structures during chemical reactions. Furthermore, recent experimental progress in generating ultrafast electron and laser pulses has equipped molecular imaging with femtosecond time resolution. This perspective provides an overview of diverse methods for imaging molecular dynamics. Techniques such as high-order harmonic generation and photoelectron diffraction rely on laser-induced ionization and rescattering. Coulomb explosion imaging extracts structural data by measuring the momentum vectors of fragmented ions, while diffraction imaging encodes both electronic and structural information in reciprocal space. Additionally, we discuss various applications of these ultrafast imaging techniques in resolving nuclear and electronic dynamics induced by lasers.

Topological semimetals represent a novel category of metallic materials that remain conductive even at band fillings where conventional theory predicts insulating behavior or compensated accidental semimetals with zero Luttinger volume. This metallicity arises from nontrivial topology within momentum space and specific crystal symmetries, allowing topological charges to be assigned to point-like band-touching nodes; these charges prevent the opening of an energy gap unless the protecting symmetries are broken. However, since these charges are derived from noninteracting band eigenstates, there is a concern that strong electron-electron interactions could qualitatively alter the physics of these materials. This study addresses whether such interactions can induce a gap in topological semimetals without violating protecting symmetries or generating topological order. We demonstrate that the answer is generally no, as the topological response—or quantum anomalies—inherently prevents gap opening. While the topological response in magnetic Weyl semimetals manifests as an anomalous Hall effect, analogous responses in other topological semimetals are more complex, involving both crystal symmetries and electromagnetic gauge fields. These responses are physically observable as fractional symmetry charges localized on specific gauge defects. We provide detailed discussions of type-I Dirac semimetals and time-reversal invariant Weyl semimetals. Specifically for type-I Dirac semimetals, we show that the anomaly vanishes in a nontrivial fashion if the momenta of the Dirac nodes satisfy particular exceptional conditions.

This article presents an algorithm designed for the efficient simulation of electrolytes near physical boundaries. Building upon prior work where the Discrete Ion Stochastic Continuum Overdamped Solvent (DISCOS) algorithm was established for triply periodic domains—validated via ion-ion pair correlation functions, Debye-Hückel-Onsager conductivity theory, and the Wien effect for strong fields—this study extends the method to accurately model physical boundaries. To achieve this, we first detail modifications to spreading and interpolation operators required to account for ion-boundary interactions. Next, we address updates to the electrostatic solver to manage charges near fixed potential or dielectric interfaces, while introducing a short-ranged potential to model ion-wall interactions. Furthermore, the dry diffusion term is adjusted to reflect reduced ion mobility near boundaries, necessitating an additional stochastic drift correction. Validation tests confirm the correct equilibrium ion distribution within a channel, and the methodology is applied to electro-osmosis and induced charge electro-osmosis, with results compared against theoretical predictions and other numerical approaches. Notably, the DISCOS approach demonstrates superior accuracy compared to continuum electrostatic simulation methods. Finally, we investigate the impact of under-resolving hydrodynamic effects via a "dry diffusion" approach, revealing that significant computational speedups can be attained with negligible loss in accuracy.

Monitoring blood pressure (BP) is crucial in routine healthcare, particularly for managing cardiovascular conditions. However, traditional contact-based methods are often cumbersome and unsuitable for continuous tracking. To address this, we introduce an efficient end-to-end network capable of estimating BP from facial videos, enabling remote monitoring in everyday settings. Our approach begins by generating a spatial-temporal map from short video clips (~15 seconds). Utilizing this map, a specialized blood pressure classifier predicts the BP range, while a dedicated calculator determines the precise value within that range. Furthermore, we implemented a novel oversampling strategy to mitigate data imbalance. The network was trained on the private ASPD dataset and evaluated on the public MMSE-HR dataset. The results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, achieving a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 12.35 mmHg for systolic and 9.5 mmHg for diastolic pressure, outperforming recent studies. These findings indicate that our method holds significant promise for real-world, camera-based BP monitoring.

The Tool SPECS employs an efficient automated method for addressing SPARQL query containment, and this paper establishes the correctness of that approach. We define the precise semantics for a core subset of the SPARQL language and outline the procedure for translating the query containment problem into a formal logical framework. We demonstrate that this reduction is sound and complete for conjunctive queries, as well as for specific instances of non-conjunctive queries involving union, optional, and subquery operators. Furthermore, the proofs of soundness and completeness are provided in both containment and subsumption contexts.

Tensor cores and tensor processing units constitute a specialized hardware acceleration technology tailored for deep neural network computations within artificial intelligence. While these cores offer remarkable speed and energy efficiency, they are engineered specifically for low-precision floating-point tensor contractions (matrix-matrix multiplications). Despite this limitation, we show that tensor cores can be utilized with high efficiency to address the complex and numerically sensitive challenges of quantum-based Born-Oppenheimer molecular dynamics. This application demands precise electronic structure optimizations and conservative force evaluations. Interatomic forces are computed dynamically from an electronic structure derived via a generalized deep neural network; this architecture leverages the exceptional processing power of tensor cores to achieve performance exceeding 100 Tflops on a single Nvidia A100 GPU. Stable molecular dynamics trajectories are produced using extended Lagrangian Born-Oppenheimer molecular dynamics, a framework that balances computational efficiency with long-term stability, even when dealing with approximate charge relaxations and force evaluations constrained by the numerical noise inherent to low-precision tensor core operations. Additionally, a canonical ensemble simulation scheme is introduced, where the extra numerical noise in force calculations is incorporated into a Langevin-like dynamics.

Using the bilinear Kadomtsev-Petviashvili hierarchy reduction method, we derive general higher-order breather and rogue wave (RW) solutions for the two-component long wave–short wave resonance interaction (2-LSRI) model, expressed as determinants. Under specific parameter settings, these breather solutions can evolve into homoclinic orbits or hybrid structures combining both. Three distinct families of RW solutions emerge, categorized by the root types of an associated algebraic equation from the dimension reduction process: a simple root, two simple roots, and a double root. The first family comprises $\frac{N(N+1)}{2}$ bounded fundamental RWs. The second family features $\frac{N_1(N_1+1)}{2}$ bounded fundamental RWs alongside another $\frac{N_2(N_2+1)}{2}$ fundamental RWs with distinct bounded states (where $N, N_1, N_2$ are positive integers). The third family contains ${[\widehat{N}_1^2+\widehat{N}_2^2-\widehat{N}_1(\widehat{N}_2-1)]}$ fundamental bounded RWs ($\widehat{N}_1,\widehat{N}_2$ being non-negative integers). The second family represents superpositions of the first, while the third family corresponds to a degenerate case of the first under specific parameter choices. These varied RW patterns are depicted graphically.

This research aims to construct a computational framework for simulating the transmission dynamics of the COVID-19 pandemic, specifically utilizing a system called ADRIANA with South Africa as the case study. The ADRIANA architecture integrates three sub-models to create a computational approach that advises government lockdown policies aimed at curbing virus transmission. Furthermore, the system's outputs assist healthcare administrators in forecasting peak resource demands for treating infected patients. While Agent-Based Modeling (ABM) is suitable for this research, we addressed its computational limitations by developing an SEIR compartmental model, a discrete event simulator, and an optimized surrogate model to constitute the ADRIANA system. We ensured the surrogate model's accuracy to deliver optimal solutions, employing a Genetic Algorithm (GA) to estimate the best hyperparameter configuration. The study concludes by evaluating the ADRIANA system's solutions, which fulfill the primary objective of providing optimal guidance for government lockdown policies and hospital resource management.

Runners of algebraic effects, or comodels, serve as a mathematical framework for resource management. We demonstrate that they enable a programming paradigm capable of modeling top-level external resources and allowing developers to modularly design their own intermediate "virtual machines." We formalize the fundamental principles of runner-based programming within an equational calculus, $\lambda_{\mathsf{coop}}$, which features a sound and coherent denotational semantics ensuring linear resource usage and the proper execution of finalization code. Alongside $\lambda_{\mathsf{coop}}$, we offer practical examples of runners in action, a prototype implementation in OCaml, and a Haskell library built upon this calculus.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have emerged as a prevalent method for wireless localization utilizing channel state information (CSI). Typically, raw CSI is fed directly into the network to enable the automatic learning of channel representations for location mapping. However, existing research indicates that raw CSI is highly susceptible to system imperfections and minor environmental fluctuations. Conversely, manually engineered features may restrict the DNN's potential for learning optimal channel representations. This study introduces an attention-based CSI framework designed for robust feature learning. We assess the efficacy of these attended features within both centralized and distributed massive MIMO systems operating over ray-tracing channels across two non-stationary railway environments. Compared to a baseline DNN, our proposed approach delivers superior performance.

A primary obstacle in federated learning (FL) is the heterogeneity of local data distributions among clients, often leading to inconsistent feature spaces. To resolve this, we introduce FedFM, a novel approach that aligns each client's feature space by directing features toward shared, category-specific anchors. This alignment helps mitigate the adverse impacts of data heterogeneity. Furthermore, we address the challenge of varying objective functions by providing convergence guarantees for FedFM. Within this framework, we develop a more precise and effective loss function termed contrastive-guiding (CG). This loss enhances feature matching efficiency by ensuring local features align with their corresponding anchors while distancing themselves from non-matching ones. Additionally, to improve efficiency and flexibility, we present FedFM-Lite, a variant that reduces communication bandwidth and synchronization frequency between clients and the server. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedFM equipped with CG surpasses existing methods in both quantitative and qualitative metrics. Moreover, FedFM-Lite achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques while requiring five to ten times less communication cost.

Incorporating human explanations during model training can enhance both data efficiency and performance on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets. Beyond these empirical benefits, the resemblance between explanation-based learning and human cognition suggests that leveraging explanations is a promising avenue for fostering effective human-machine collaboration. While various methods have been developed to improve Natural Language Processing (NLP) models using different explanation types and integration mechanisms, they are seldom compared directly, creating challenges for practitioners seeking the optimal approach for specific applications. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of existing methods for learning from human explanations and examines key factors that can guide the selection of the most suitable method for a given use-case.

Superstring/M-theory offers a quantum gravity framework capable of completing viable inflation models in the ultraviolet regime. We extend the Starobinsky inflation model by incorporating the squared Bel-Robinson tensor, $T^{\mu\nu\lambda\rho}$, as a leading quantum correction motivated by superstring theory. The resulting model, expressed as $(R+\frac{1}{6m^2}R^2 -\frac{\beta}{8m^6}T^2)$, relies on two parameters: the inflaton mass $m$ and a string-inspired positive constant $\beta$. We derive the equations of motion within a Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker universe and analyze their solutions. By requiring the absence of ghost modes and ensuring that predicted inflationary observables align with cosmic microwave background measurements, we establish physical constraints on the parameter $\beta$.

We investigate the virtual transition of an atom-mirror system involving the simultaneous emission of two scalar photons, under conditions where the atom and mirror undergo relative acceleration. Regarding single photon emission, previous literature ({Phys. Rev. Lett. 121 (2018) 071301, https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.121.071301}) indicates that the transition probabilities for an atom accelerating relative to a mirror and its reverse scenario are equivalent when the frequencies of the atom and field are exchanged. That same literature also notes an observational feasibility for this excitation process, reporting a detectable probability of approximately $10^{-2}$. In contrast, our current findings demonstrate that the simultaneous emission of two photons, rather than one, breaks the equivalence between these transition probabilities previously reported. Furthermore, we compare these two-photon probabilities with those associated with single photon emission.

The early-type galaxy NGC 5195 (also designated M51b) exhibits extended gas structures across multiple wavelengths, which are believed to stem from past activity of its central supermassive black hole (SMBH). Through integral field spectroscopy obtained with the CFHT/SITELLE instrument, we identify a newly discovered large-scale ionized gas structure, marked by [O III], [N II], and H$\alpha$ emission, stretching approximately 10 kpc from NGC 5195's nucleus. Analysis of its bipolar shape, emission line ratios, and comparisons with Chandra X-ray and LOFAR low-frequency radio data suggest this feature is an outflow driven by a prior episode of heightened active galactic nucleus (AGN) activity. If this ionized gas is outflowing from the galaxy's center, the derived mass and energy outflow rates ($\dot{M}_{\rm out} = 3.5-27.9 \rm\, M_{\odot}\, yr^{-1}$ and $\dot{E}_{\rm out} = 0.98-7.9\times10^{40}\rm\, erg\, s^{-1}$, respectively) exceed what current star formation and the galaxy's low-luminosity nucleus can produce. Alternatively, given the gravitational history of the M51 pair and the presence of an HI tidal tail, the northern ionized gas structure is likely tidally stripped material that was once illuminated by a luminous AGN.

This study introduces a Hartree-Fock (HF) implementation designed to achieve robust convergence for arbitrary central potentials. By utilizing a B-spline basis within a finite box, the HF equations are reformulated as a generalized eigenvalue problem. Self-consistency convergence for occupied orbitals is secured through a gradual ramp-up of the electron-electron Coulomb interaction to its full strength. Results for atomic and negative ion systems under a Coulomb potential, including convergence behavior and energies, are benchmarked against prior calculations. The method's validity is further demonstrated through ground-state computations for an electron gas in a harmonic trap and within a uniformly charged sphere (the jellium model for alkali-metal clusters). For the harmonically confined electron gas, comparisons with the Thomas-Fermi approach and its analytical asymptotic limits reveal close agreement in electron energy and density for large systems. Excited state manifold accuracy and completeness are assessed by calculating static dipole polarizabilities at the HF level and applying the Random-Phase Approximation (RPA), which is essential for capturing electron screening effects in electron-gas and cluster models. These theoretical predictions are compared with experimental data for sodium clusters containing up to approximately 100 atoms.

We provide a comprehensive analysis of the short gamma-ray burst GRB 201221D, located at a redshift of $z=1.045$. Our investigation examines the burst's high-energy data in comparison to a sample of short gamma-ray bursts (SGRBs). While the prompt emission properties align with those typical of other SGRBs, the peak energy ($E_{\rm p}$) is notably softer, a trait more commonly associated with long bursts. Using the {\sc Python}-based tool {\sc Prospector}, we modeled the host galaxy's spectral energy distribution to determine its properties. This event stands out as having a high redshift relative to the SGRB sample, which has a median redshift of $z=0.47$. We compared the burst's characteristics with other SGRBs of known redshift, including GRB 200826A, which originated from a collapsar. A thorough examination of SGRBs across various redshifts suggests that some high-redshift events exhibit properties similar to long GRBs, implying a possible collapsar origin. Further research into these specific GRBs could illuminate the broader landscape of SGRB progenitor systems.

The primary objective of robust reinforcement learning (RL) is to develop a policy that withstands uncertainty in model parameters. Such parameter uncertainty frequently arises in practical RL scenarios due to simulator inaccuracies, shifting system dynamics in the real world, and adversarial disruptions. Typically, robust RL is framed as a max-min optimization problem, aiming to identify a policy that maximizes value against the worst-case models within a defined uncertainty set. This paper introduces Robust Fitted Q-Iteration (RFQI), a robust RL algorithm capable of deriving an optimal robust policy using solely offline data. Implementing robust RL with offline datasets presents significant difficulties compared to non-robust approaches, primarily due to the need to minimize across all models in the robust Bellman operator. These hurdles complicate data collection, model optimization, and unbiased estimation. To address these issues, we present a systematic methodology that culminates in the RFQI algorithm. We establish that RFQI converges to a near-optimal robust policy under standard assumptions and validate its enhanced performance on established benchmark tasks.

This study aims to explore a novel classification of embedded class-I solutions for compact stars within the context of $f(R)$ gravity, utilizing the Karmarkar condition. To accomplish this, we examine two distinct $f(R)$ gravity models applied to static, spherically symmetric spacetimes featuring anisotropic matter distributions. By applying the Karmarkar condition, we establish a relationship between the two metric potentials, $g_{rr}$ and $g_{tt}$; specifically, we derive one potential from a chosen model of the other. Using observational data from compact stars—namely $Vela~X-1$, $PSR~J1614-2230$, $4U~1608-52$, $Cen~X-3$, and $4U~1820-30$—we determine the values of constant parameters. Furthermore, we conduct various physical analyses, including the variability of energy density and pressure, stability and equilibrium conditions, energy constraints, mass functions, and adiabatic indices, to validate the $f(R)$ gravity models. These physical characteristics demonstrate consistent behavior for our proposed models. Consequently, our findings suggest that $f(R)$ gravity is a viable theory for describing a new classification of embedded class-I solutions for compact objects.

Intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) offer a promising solution for enhancing wireless powered communication networks (WPCNs) by intelligently reconfiguring signal propagation through smart reflection. Specifically, the substantial passive beamforming gain provided by IRS can markedly improve the efficiency of both downlink wireless power transfer (DL WPT) and uplink wireless information transmission (UL WIT) within these networks. While dynamic IRS beamforming—utilizing distinct phase shifts for DL WPT and UL WIT—is theoretically feasible, it introduces extra signaling overhead and computational complexity, leaving it uncertain whether such an approach yields tangible benefits. To address this, we examine an IRS-assisted WPCN where multiple devices utilize a hybrid access point (HAP) to harvest energy before transmitting data via non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA). Our objective is to maximize the total system throughput by jointly optimizing IRS phase shifts and resource allocation. In doing so, we first demonstrate that dynamic IRS beamforming is unnecessary for this specific scenario, thereby reducing the number of phase shifts requiring optimization. Subsequently, we develop both joint and alternating optimization algorithms to solve the resulting problem. Simulation outcomes confirm the superiority of our proposed designs compared to benchmark schemes and offer valuable insights into the critical role of IRS in achieving spectrally and energy-efficient WPCNs.

We present and examine an open quantum extension of the q-state Potts-Hopfield neural network, an associative memory system originally grounded in multi-level classical spins. The system's dynamics are described by a Lindblad-type Markovian master equation, enabling the simultaneous treatment of probabilistic classical and coherent quantum processes. Using a mean-field approach, we explore how temperature-induced classical fluctuations and coherent quantum fluctuations influence the network's capacity to recall stored patterns. Our resulting phase diagram reveals that, at low temperatures, the system exhibits pattern retrieval similar to its classical counterpart. However, as quantum fluctuations increase, a limit cycle phase emerges, a phenomenon absent in classical models. This demonstrates that quantum effects can fundamentally reshape the stationary state manifold compared to classical systems, potentially facilitating the encoding and retrieval of novel pattern types.

Security professionals concur that maintaining up-to-date systems is a vital defense strategy. Prior research indicates that users occasionally avoid timely updates, often due to adverse experiences, which compromises end-user security. However, a less-studied demographic—system administrators tasked with securing complex and diverse IT environments—has received limited attention. This study investigates administrators' attitudes, experiences, and behaviors concerning updates within corporate settings. Following an interview-based analysis, we designed an online survey to quantify prevalent practices and barriers, such as service downtime or insufficient information regarding updates. The results reveal that even seasoned administrators face challenges with update procedures, as the outcomes of these changes can be difficult to predict. Consequently, we contend that enhancing the usability of monitoring and update mechanisms is crucial for ensuring IT security on a large scale.

Perceptual hashing converts images sharing identical semantic meaning into the same $n$-bit hash, whereas images with different semantics receive distinct hashes. These algorithms are vital in cybersecurity for tasks like identifying copyright violations, content fingerprinting, and surveillance. Apple's NeuralHash is a notable example designed to detect illegal content on user devices while maintaining consumer privacy. We have unexpectedly found that NeuralHash operates approximately linearly, a characteristic that enables the creation of new black-box attacks. These attacks can (i) bypass detection of prohibited images, (ii) create near-collisions, and (iii) expose information about hashed content, all without requiring access to the model's internal parameters. Such vulnerabilities severely undermine NeuralHash's security objectives; consequently, we propose a straightforward remedy based on established classical cryptographic standards.

Direct numerical simulations and linear stability analysis are employed to examine mixed convection within a horizontal duct subjected to constant-rate bottom heating and a transverse horizontal magnetic field. A two-dimensional approximation, validated as the asymptotic limit for very strong magnetic fields, is utilized alongside full three-dimensional analysis to explore flow dynamics in previously uncharted control parameter ranges typical of nuclear fusion reactor liquid metal blankets (Hartmann numbers up to $10^4$ and Grashof numbers up to $10^{10}$). Results indicate that the instability toward quasi-two-dimensional rolls parallel to the magnetic field, previously identified at lower Hartmann and Grashof numbers, persists in this higher range. The transport of these rolls by the mean flow generates magnetoconvective temperature fluctuations with exceptionally large amplitudes. Furthermore, it is shown that the quasi-two-dimensional flow structure observed at very high Hartmann numbers does not ensure the accuracy of classical two-dimensional approximations; accuracy notably degrades at the highest Grashof numbers investigated.

Numerous studies ask participants to state their prior and posterior beliefs regarding a random variable to evaluate how information influences behavior. However, since beliefs are multi-dimensional, researchers frequently solicit only a single response. This paper examines how the incentives provided by experimenters determine how profit-maximizing subjects map their true belief distributions to their reported answers. Specifically, we demonstrate that minor variations in incentives can lead subjects to report the mean, mode, or median of their beliefs. When beliefs are asymmetric or non-unimodal, employing an elicitation method that does not align with the research question can alter both the magnitude and direction of the estimated effects, or even prevent identification entirely. As an illustration, we re-examine Cantoni et al.'s (2019) investigation into whether political protests act as strategic complements or substitutes. We find that their methodology elicits modal beliefs, whereas modal and mean beliefs may shift in opposing directions after the experiment. Consequently, the sign of the reported effects could reverse, supporting an alternative interpretation of their findings.

Accurately estimating post-click conversion rates (CVR) is vital for e-commerce, yet practical CVR prediction faces three significant hurdles: i) data sparsity, where conversion samples are far fewer than impressions; ii) sample selection bias, as models are typically trained on clicked impressions but must predict across the entire impression space; and iii) delayed feedback, where conversions are observed only after random, often long delays, leading to numerous false negatives during training. While prior research usually addresses only one or two of these issues in isolation, this paper introduces a new neural network framework called ESDF to handle all three challenges concurrently. Unlike previous approaches, ESDF models CVR prediction across the entire impression space, integrating user sequential behavior patterns with time delay factors. Specifically, ESDF mitigates sample selection bias by utilizing sequential user actions across the full space of all impressions and alleviates data sparsity by sharing embedding parameters between CTR and CVR networks. Distinct from traditional delayed feedback methods, ESDF imposes no specific assumptions regarding delay distributions. Instead, it discretizes delay time into daily slots and models the probability using survival analysis within a deep neural network, making it more practical for industrial applications. Extensive experiments validate the method's effectiveness. To our knowledge, ESDF represents the first unified attempt to address these three challenges simultaneously in the field of CVR prediction.

This study introduces an Energy Management System (EMS) designed for Multi-Microgrid (MMG) frameworks, managing power transactions between interconnected microgrids (MGs) and the main grid. Initially modeled as a centralized optimization task, the approach employs Lagrangian relaxation to decompose the problem into individual subproblems for each MG, which are then resolved via a distributed subgradient method. This framework minimizes operational costs for every MG while adhering to grid constraints and safeguarding privacy by keeping generation costs and demand data confidential. The distributed solution's validity is confirmed against the centralized model, and case studies illustrate its efficacy by comparing the costs of MGs operating in isolation versus cooperatively. Findings indicate that interconnecting MGs within the MMG system reduces costs for all participants through power exchanges, highlighting the benefits of such integration.

Object counting is dedicated to estimating the quantity of items within images, with current state-of-the-art methods primarily excelling in single-category tasks. However, real-world scenes often contain multiple object types, making multi-class counting a crucial extension of this field. While multi-target detection can address multi-class counting in specific contexts, it relies on bounding box annotations, which are significantly harder to acquire than the point-level annotations standard in mainstream counting problems. This paper introduces a simple yet efficient counting network designed for point-level data. Specifically, we adapt the traditional single-output channel to multiple channels corresponding to the number of categories to enable multi-class counting. Since our framework utilizes a shared feature extractor for all categories, features may interfere within the common feature space; consequently, we develop a multi-mask structure to mitigate this harmful interaction. Extensive experiments on challenging benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

This study addresses the challenge of reconstructing a partially observed, high-rank matrix where its columns follow a nonlinear structure, such as a union of subspaces, an algebraic variety, or cluster-based groupings. The recovery task is cast as minimizing the rank of a nonlinear feature map applied to the original matrix, which is subsequently approximated via a constrained non-convex optimization problem on the Grassmann manifold. We introduce two algorithmic frameworks: one based on Riemannian optimization and another utilizing an alternating minimization approach, each offering both first- and second-order variants. Both frameworks are supported by theoretical guarantees; specifically, for the alternating minimization scheme, we prove global convergence and worst-case complexity bounds. Furthermore, leveraging the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property, we demonstrate that this method converges to a unique limit point. Extensive numerical experiments validate our approach for subspace union recovery and clustering under both entry sampling and dense Gaussian sampling regimes. Our methods compete effectively with existing techniques, notably achieving high accuracy through the application of Riemannian second-order methods.

Force terms that switch stochastically are common in biological models involving active agents like proteins. The interplay between these switching forces and Brownian motion can establish an "effective thermal equilibrium," even when the system lacks a potential function. To broaden energy landscape analysis for assessing stability and transitions in such switching systems, we derive a quasipotential defining this effective equilibrium for a general overdamped Langevin system where forces switch according to a continuous-time Markov chain. By combining this with the string method for calculating most-probable transition paths, we apply our approach to an idealized system, revealing previously undocumented numerical difficulties. We introduce algorithmic modifications to address these challenges and validate our method by confirming that the computed quasipotential barrier aligns with asymptotic Monte Carlo transition times.

Current state-of-the-art object grasping techniques depend on depth sensing for robust planning, yet commercially available depth sensors struggle to detect transparent and specular objects. To enhance grasping performance on these challenging objects, we propose a method that learns a multi-modal perception model by bootstrapping from an existing uni-modal model. This transfer learning strategy requires only a pre-existing uni-modal grasping model and paired multi-modal image data for training, eliminating the need for ground-truth grasp success labels or actual grasp attempts. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach enables reliable grasping of transparent and reflective objects. Video and supplementary materials can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/transparent-specular-grasping.

Many three-dimensional (3D) crystal lattices are formed by stacking two-dimensional (2D) layers. However, it is still uncertain whether this geometric principle influences the stability of ordered compounds or if it can aid in computational materials design. In this study, we employ first-principles calculations to examine the dynamical stability of copper-based compounds (Cu$X$, where $X$ is a metal) within B$_h$ and L1$_1$ structures derived from buckled honeycomb (BHC) layers, as well as B2 and L1$_0$ structures derived from buckled square (BSQ) layers. We show that (i) dynamical stability in the BHC configuration implies stability in both the B$_h$ and L1$_1$ variants. Regarding the BSQ-derived structures, while the metastability link between the BSQ and 3D forms (B2 and L1$_0$) remains ambiguous, we observe that (ii) if the B2 (or L1$_0$) structure is dynamically stable, the corresponding L1$_0$ (or B2) structure is unstable, a pattern similar to the metastability relationship between bcc and fcc structures in elemental metals. Additionally, we analyze the total energy curves for Cu$X$ along both tetragonal and trigonal transformation paths.

**Context.** The evolutionary history of the dark matter halo in massive elliptical galaxies is tightly linked to that of their stellar populations. Analyzing the correlation between galaxy properties and halo mass provides insights into their evolution.

**Aims.** This study examines how the dark matter halo mass of elliptical galaxies varies with their intrinsic properties, utilizing weak gravitational lensing data. To avoid potential biases, we concentrate on robustly measurable attributes: surface brightness profiles and colour.

**Methods.** We analyzed 2,409 central massive elliptical galaxies from the SDSS spectroscopic catalog. Surface brightness profiles and colours were derived by fitting Sersic models to Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS) photometry. Using KiDS weak lensing measurements and a Bayesian hierarchical framework, we modeled the halo mass distribution as a function of redshift, rest-frame $r$-band luminosity, half-light radius, and rest-frame $u-g$ colour. To ensure robustness against assumptions regarding large-scale surface brightness behavior, we repeated the analysis substituting total luminosity and half-light radius with the luminosity within a 10 kpc aperture ($L_{r,10}$) and the light-weighted surface brightness slope ($\Gamma_{10}$).

**Results.** At fixed redshift and luminosity, we found no significant correlation between halo mass and either half-light radius or colour.

**Conclusions.** Our findings suggest that the average star formation efficiency in massive elliptical galaxies is largely independent of their final size or colour. This implies that the diversity observed in the size and colour distributions of these galaxies stems from factors other than halo mass.

We examine the physically relevant fully compressible framework of the Rayleigh-Bénard problem, involving a fluid sandwiched between two parallel plates, heated from below, and influenced by gravity. Assuming appropriate constraints on the constitutive relations, we demonstrate that this open system is dissipative according to Levinson's definition, which implies the existence of a bounded absorbing set for any global-in-time weak solution. Furthermore, global-in-time trajectories are asymptotically compact within suitable topologies, and the system features a global compact trajectory attractor, denoted as $\mathcal{A}$. Applying the standard Krylov-Bogolyubov technique establishes the existence of an invariant measure—a stationary statistical solution residing on $\mathcal{A}$. Additionally, the Birkhoff-Khinchin ergodic theorem ensures that ergodic averages of solutions within $\mathcal{A}$ converge almost surely with respect to this invariant measure.

This study explores whether a quark flavor model based on modular $A_4$ symmetry can explain both quark mass hierarchies and the CKM mixing matrix without requiring fine-tuning. The analysis focuses on the region near the fixed point $\tau = \omega = \exp(i\,2\pi/3)$, which represents the left cusp of the modular group's fundamental domain, where $\tau$ denotes the vacuum expectation value (VEV) of the modulus. The framework utilizes modular forms of level 3 with weights 6, 4, and 2, incorporating eight constants. Among these, only the VEV of the modulus, defined as $\tau = \omega + \epsilon$ with $(\epsilon)^* \neq \epsilon$ and $|\epsilon|\ll 1$, and two specific constants, $g_u$ and $g_d$, serve as sources of CP violation. We demonstrate that for real (CP-conserving) values of $g_u$ and $g_d$ and a shared $\tau$ ($\epsilon$) across both up- and down-quark sectors, the down-type quark mass hierarchies emerge naturally without fine-tuning, using $|\epsilon| \cong 0.03$ while keeping other constants at ${\cal O}(1)$. These hierarchies approximately follow the pattern $1 : |\epsilon| : |\epsilon|^2$. Similarly, the up-type quark mass hierarchies can be reproduced with the same $|\epsilon| \cong 0.03$, provided $g_u \sim {\cal O}(10)$, resulting in a hierarchy of $1 : |\epsilon|/|g_u| : |\epsilon|^2/|g_u|^2$. Within this context, the paper further examines CP violation and CKM quark mixing.

The ordered and disordered dynamics observed in large collections of coupled oscillators correspond to distinct functional states across various fields, such as the brain's active and resting modes or the stable and unstable configurations of power grids. Consequently, explosive synchronization transitions—enabling rapid, sudden shifts between these states—have recently attracted considerable research attention. Although prior studies have pinpointed specific properties of complex systems that enable explosive synchronization, these efforts have largely been conducted in an ad-hoc manner. In this work, we establish an exact criterion for explosive synchronization within coupled phase oscillator ensembles by examining the essential link between structural and dynamical disorder. This finding represents a pivotal advancement in disentangling the interconnected characteristics of complex systems that drive abrupt phase transitions and bistability in both biological and engineered contexts.

This paper offers a unified framework for various semantic approaches to modal logic found in existing literature by employing the language of topological categories over Set. Drawing parallels with categorical logic, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the relationship between the syntactic structure of (and various extensions of) the modal language and the semantic structures of topological categories within this framework. Consequently, this approach enables a conceptual grasp of the abstract architecture of modal logic.

This paper investigates a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite (PSD) constraint. By applying the Burer-Monteiro factorization within a specific Riemannian quotient geometry defined on a search space equipped with a Euclidean metric, we analyze the global landscape of the resulting factorized objective. Assuming the original objective function $f$ adheres to standard restricted strong convexity and smoothness conditions, we demonstrate that the entire search space partitions into three distinct regions: (R1) a neighborhood around the target parameter where the objective is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (R2) areas surrounding all strict saddle points; and (R3) remaining regions characterized by large gradients. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first global landscape analysis of the Burer-Monteiro factorized objective under this specific Riemannian quotient geometry. These findings offer a complete geometric rationale for the enhanced performance of vanilla gradient descent in this context. Furthermore, under a weaker restricted strict convexity assumption, we establish that geodesic convexity holds in a neighborhood of local minimizers. Our proofs rely on a detailed landscape analysis of a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, serving as a pivotal intermediate step. Additionally, our conclusions rest on a standalone result identifying that the geodesic ball centered at $Y$ with a radius equal to one-third of $Y$'s least singular value forms a geodesically convex set under the Riemannian quotient geometry; this result also yields a quantitative bound for the convexity radius in the Bures-Wasserstein space, which is proven to be sharp up to constant factors.

One-Shot Neural Architecture Search (NAS) offers a promising approach to drastically cut search times without requiring separate training phases. This process can be viewed as a network compression task applied to the architecture parameters of an over-parameterized network. However, conventional one-shot NAS methods face two primary challenges: first, they often neglect dependencies between nodes and their adjacent predecessors or successors, leading to mishandling of zero operations; second, pruning architecture parameters solely based on magnitude is problematic. To address these limitations, we utilize a classic Bayesian learning framework, specifically modeling architecture parameters with hierarchical automatic relevance determination (HARD) priors. Distinct from other NAS techniques, we train the over-parameterized network for just one epoch before updating the architecture. Remarkably, this strategy allowed us to identify an architecture for CIFAR-10 in merely 0.2 GPU days on a single GPU, while also delivering competitive results when transferred to ImageNet. Additionally, our method can be directly applied to compress convolutional neural networks by enforcing structural sparsity, resulting in highly sparse networks with no loss in accuracy.

Consider a Morita ring $\Delta =\left(\begin{smallmatrix} A & {_AN_B}\\ {_BM_A} & B
\\\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ satisfying the conditions $M\otimes_{A}N=0=N\otimes_{B}M$. This work first investigates the construction of (complete) duality pairs for $\Delta$-modules by utilizing (complete) duality pairs from $A$-modules and $B$-modules, thereby extending Mao's findings on duality pairs over triangular matrix rings (Comm. Algebra, 2020, 12: 5296--5310). Furthermore, we define Gorenstein projective modules relative to these complete duality pairs within the category of $\Delta$-modules. Finally, the study presents an application concerning Ding projective modules.

This work demonstrates the solution to the Merton optimal investment stochastic control problem within finance and insurance contexts utilizing Hawkes-based models. Specifically, it addresses a wealth portfolio $X(t)$ comprising a bond and a stock governed by a general compound Hawkes process (GCHP), alongside the capital $R(t)$ of an insurance firm modeled by claims driven by the same GCHP framework. The primary innovations lie in the introduction of these novel Hawkes-based models and the derivation of new optimal investment strategies for both financial and insurance applications.

Distributed quantum systems, and notably the Quantum Internet, hold growing promise for fully realizing the capabilities of quantum computation. This potential is significant because constructing a universal quantum computer is far more challenging than networking multiple small-scale quantum devices. A primary obstacle in realizing these distributed systems lies in programming them and ensuring their correctness. This paper introduces a Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP)-inspired distributed programming language designed to streamline the specification and verification of such systems. Following an exposition of its operational and denotational semantics, we construct a Hoare-style logic tailored for distributed quantum programs and prove its soundness and relative completeness regarding both partial and total correctness. The utility of this logic is validated through its application in verifying quantum teleportation and the local implementation of non-local CNOT gates, two critical algorithms prevalent in distributed quantum architectures.

The realization of quantum capabilities has triggered a fundamental transformation in how information is processed and computed. Among the well-investigated systems designed for these tasks, coupled cavity arrays stand out as a versatile platform for distributed information processing and communication within quantum networks. A key advantage of cavities is their ability to store photons for extended periods, allowing them to traverse the array coherently while minimizing losses due to dissipation. Numerous quantum information protocols have already been successfully executed in coupled cavity arrays. These developments underscore the potential of cavity arrays for large-scale quantum communication and computation. This article examines both theoretical proposals and experimental demonstrations of quantum information tasks implemented in such cavities.

Proteins that induce curvature and contain a Bin/Amphiphysin/Rvs (BAR) domain frequently feature intrinsically disordered regions, which recent studies have demonstrated enhance both curvature sensing and generation. This work utilizes meshless membrane simulations to investigate how these disordered chains alter protein-membrane interactions. In the models, the protein and its associated membrane are represented as a chiral crescent-shaped rod with two excluded-volume chains. Increasing chain length diminishes repulsion between chains, thereby reducing protein cluster sizes and triggering a transition from arc-shaped to circular assemblies on disk-shaped vesicles, while also promoting spindle-shaped vesicle formation. On flat membranes, intermediate chain lengths generate numerous tubules due to repulsion between protein clusters, whereas longer chains drive perpendicular tubule elongation. Additionally, rods with zero intrinsic curvature paired with sufficiently long chains stabilize spherical buds. Conversely, rods with negative curvature and intermediate chain lengths produce rugged membranes with branched protein assemblies, while longer chains lead to tubules featuring periodic concave-ring structures.

A strong edge-coloring $\varphi$ of a graph $G$ is a mapping of colors to the edges of $G$ where $\varphi(e_1) \neq \varphi(e_2)$ for any pair of edges $e_1$ and $e_2$ separated by a distance of at most 1; this concept is equivalent to a proper vertex coloring of the square of the line graph of $G$. In 1990, Faudree, Schelp, Gy\'arf\'as, and Tuza proposed that every bipartite graph with a maximum degree of 3 and sufficiently large girth admits a strong edge-coloring using no more than 5 colors. However, in 2021, Lu\v{z}ar, Ma\v{c}ajov\'{a}, \v{S}koviera, and Sot\'{a}k refuted this conjecture. This paper presents an alternative construction that also serves to disprove the conjecture.

The proliferation of defects serves as the mechanism driving topological phase transitions. In two dimensions, the XY-model exhibits such a transition within the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) universality class, a transition point identified via renormalization group (RG) analysis. By applying RG arguments to the three-dimensional plaquette-dimer model—a system characterized by fractonic mobility constraints—we determine the nature of its BKT transition. Our analysis reveals that a crucial component requires a modified dimensional approach, which alters how scaling dimensions are interpreted during coarse-graining. Leveraging this revised framework, we calculate the model's beta functions and predict a finite critical threshold above which the fractonic phase melts due to dipole proliferation. Notably, both the transition point and its specific value are rigorously established within the renormalization group formalism.

Let $q\ge3$ be an integer, let $\chi$ represent a Dirichlet character modulo $q$, and denote the associated Dirichlet $L$-functions by $L(s,\chi)$. In this work, we examine specific series of special functions and establish new identities for Dirichlet $L$-functions that involve Gauss sums. In particular, we derive explicit identities for $L(2,\chi)$.

This study addresses the linear least squares problem for $m\times n$ systems ($Ax = b$, with $m\geq n$) where the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ fluctuate within specified interval bounds. The primary objective is to determine the tightest possible interval enclosure for the set of all least squares solutions as $A$ and $b$ vary independently. We introduce PPS-methods (Partitioning of the Parameter Set) to tackle this challenge. By transforming the associated normal equations into a specialized extended matrix format, we derive a symmetric interval system equivalent to the original problem. To solve this symmetric system efficiently, we propose a novel PPS-based approach named ILSQ-PPS, which effectively estimates the solution set enclosure. Finally, we validate the ILSQ-PPS method through various numerical experiments and benchmark its performance against alternative techniques.

This study assesses the effectiveness of Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) trees and relations for evaluating discourse coherence. We demonstrate that integrating silver-standard RST features improves coherence classification accuracy. Using our tree-recursive neural architecture, RST-Recursive, which leverages features generated by a state-of-the-art RST parser, we achieve new state-of-the-art results on the Grammarly Corpus for Discourse Coherence (GCDC) when ensembled with existing methods. Additionally, RST-Recursive performs competitively as a standalone model while utilizing 62% fewer parameters.

While boosting weak learners has been extensively studied, there has been limited exploration of boosting strong learners, a paradigm that essentially functions as weighted voting based on learned weights. This study addresses the challenge of building an ensemble algorithm from 70 individual methods to predict sepsis early using clinical data. Our results demonstrate that this ensemble outperforms the individual algorithms, particularly on a hidden test set where most of them failed to generalize.

We introduce Quantum Brain Networks (QBraiNs) as an emerging interdisciplinary domain that synthesizes expertise and methodologies from neurotechnology, artificial intelligence, and quantum computing. Our primary goal is to establish superior connectivity between the human brain and quantum computers to enable a range of transformative applications. We anticipate the rise of hybrid networks comprising wetware and hardware nodes, facilitated by machine learning and brain-machine interfaces. QBraiNs has the potential to revolutionize arts, science, technology, and entrepreneurship in unprecedented ways, with significant implications for medicine, the Internet of Humans, intelligent devices, sensory experiences, gaming, the Internet of Things, cryptocurrency trading, and business operations.

We present the identification of four quasars at $z\sim5$ with absolute magnitudes $M_{1450} \gtrsim -25.0$ mag, including a supermassive black hole (SMBH) mass determination for one target. These objects were chosen as high-redshift quasar candidates using deep learning combined with the Bayesian information criterion, methods designed to effectively distinguish quasars from late-type stars and distant galaxies. Observations conducted with the Double Spectrograph on the Palomar 200-inch Hale Telescope revealed clear Ly$\alpha$ breaks between 7000-8000 \r{A}, confirming their redshifts in the range $4.7 < z < 5.6$. For HSC J233107-001014, we derived the SMBH mass via the C\Romannum{4}$\lambda 1549$ emission line, finding a mass of $\sim 10^8 M_{\odot}$ and an Eddington ratio of $\sim 0.6$. Despite its low bolometric luminosity ($L_{\rm Bol} < 10^{46}$ erg s$^{-1}$), this indicates the presence of a rapidly growing SMBH operating near the Eddington limit. The 100% success rate in quasar identification validates the efficiency of our selection techniques, suggesting their utility for expanding high-redshift quasar samples in future surveys.

Gait benchmarks enable the research community to develop and assess high-performance gait recognition systems. Despite increasing efforts toward cross-view recognition, academic progress is hindered by existing databases that are limited to controlled environments. This paper introduces a new benchmark, Gait REcognition in the Wild (GREW). The GREW dataset is built from natural videos featuring hundreds of cameras and thousands of hours of footage from open systems. With extensive manual annotations, it includes 26,000 identities and 128,000 sequences rich in attributes, designed for unconstrained gait recognition. Furthermore, an additional distractor set of over 233,000 sequences has been added to enhance its suitability for real-world scenarios. Unlike previous predefined cross-view datasets, GREW offers diverse, practical view variations along with more natural challenges. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first large-scale dataset dedicated to gait recognition in the wild. Using this benchmark, we analyze the unconstrained gait recognition problem by exploring representative appearance-based and model-based methods to establish comprehensive baselines. Experimental results demonstrate that: (1) the GREW benchmark is essential for training and evaluating wild gait recognizers; (2) significant room for improvement remains for state-of-the-art gait recognition approaches; and (3) GREW serves as an effective pre-training tool for controlled gait recognition. The benchmark website is available at https://www.grew-benchmark.org/.

Major corporations like Meta and Google have launched "data-for-good" initiatives that sanitize and publicly release aggregated location data, proving valuable for applications in transportation, public health (such as tracking COVID-19), and urban planning. Differential privacy (DP) serves as the primary framework to safeguard the privacy of individuals who provided the raw location data. However, existing methods struggle to maintain data utility when users contribute multiple location reports, necessitating user-level privacy. To mitigate this issue, Meta and Google currently employ high privacy budgets (e.g., $\epsilon$=10-100), which compromises privacy levels. We introduce a novel method for privately and accurately releasing spatio-temporal data by leveraging the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks, specifically variational auto-encoders (VAE). This approach reduces the noise introduced by DP mechanisms, thereby enhancing accuracy while maintaining privacy guarantees. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing benchmarks.

This paper investigates the (1+1)-dimensional higher-order Broer-Kaup (HBK) system using the consistent tanh expansion (CTE) method, demonstrating that the system is solvable via this approach. Explicit forms of exact interaction solutions involving various nonlinear excitations, including solitons, rational waves, periodic waves, and their corresponding images, are presented.

This study investigates the problem of minimizing average age, where only a subset of network users can transmit concurrently over unreliable channels. Determining the optimal scheduling strategy for this scenario is widely recognized as difficult; consequently, the Whittle's index policy has been suggested in existing literature as a low-complexity heuristic solution. While easy to implement, rigorously characterizing the performance of this policy remains a notoriously difficult challenge. In this work, we introduce a novel mathematical framework to prove its optimality within the many-users regime for particular network configurations. Our approach utilizes sophisticated techniques and, unlike prior studies, requires no mathematical assumptions. These results demonstrate that the Whittle's index policy possesses analytically provable asymptotic optimality for the Age of Information (AoI) minimization problem. Furthermore, we present numerical simulations that validate our theoretical conclusions and illustrate the policy's significant effectiveness in the many-users regime.

Learning by ignoring, a strategy that filters out less significant information to enhance focus, is a widely observed and effective aspect of human cognition. Psychological research confirms that the ability to disregard irrelevant stimuli significantly aids concentration. This paper investigates whether such a human learning principle can be adapted to enhance machine learning performance. We introduce a new machine learning approach called Learning by Ignoring (LBI). This framework automatically detects pretraining samples that exhibit substantial domain shifts relative to the target distribution by training a specific ignoring variable for each example, subsequently excluding these outliers from the pretraining phase. We define LBI as a three-stage optimization process: first, pretraining where losses are minimized using weights determined by the ignoring variables; second, finetuning; and third, updating the ignoring variables by minimizing validation loss. Furthermore, we develop a gradient-based algorithm to efficiently resolve this three-level optimization challenge. Empirical results across multiple datasets validate the efficacy of our proposed framework.

The chromosphere is a dynamic and complex layer where all relevant physical processes occur on very small spatio-temporal scales. A few spectral lines used for chromospheric diagnostics provide convoluted information that is difficult to interpret without realistic theoretical models. What are the key ingredients that these models need to contain? The magnetic field has a paramount effect on chromospheric structuring. This is evident from the ubiquitous presence of chromospheric dynamic fibrilar structures visible on the solar disk and at the limb. The numerical experiments presented in this manuscript illustrate the present state of modeling. They showcase to what extent our models reproduce various chromospheric features and their dynamics. The publication describes the effect different ingredients have on chromospheric models and provides a recipe for building one-to-one models. Combining these models with observations will provide insight into the physical processes that take place in the solar atmosphere.

Wasserstein dictionary learning is an unsupervised method designed to discover a set of probability distributions that produce observed data through Wasserstein barycentric combinations. Current techniques optimize objectives to find dictionaries capable of approximating training data via barycentric interpolation, yet they fail to enforce structural constraints on the associated coefficients. Consequently, these methods generate dictionaries that densely encode the data, rendering coefficient interpretation difficult and often resulting in suboptimal performance for downstream tasks. Drawing inspiration from sparse dictionary learning in Euclidean spaces, we introduce a geometrically sparse regularizer tailored for Wasserstein space, encouraging data representations to rely exclusively on proximal dictionary elements. This approach achieves sparse representations in Wasserstein space and resolves the issue of non-unique barycentric representations. Furthermore, when data originates as Wasserstein barycenters of fixed distributions, this regularizer aids in recovering the underlying generating distributions in scenarios that are ill-posed for unregularized learning. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that our geometrically regularized method produces sparser, more interpretable dictionaries that outperform existing approaches in downstream applications.

Probabilistic time-series forecasting supports robust decision-making across numerous fields. However, most forecasting tasks involve heterogeneous data with multiple modalities and structures, making it a significant challenge to effectively leverage both information and uncertainty from these sources to produce accurate and well-calibrated predictions. Existing multi-modal forecasting approaches typically aggregate intermediate representations from different data views using basic methods like summation or concatenation, often failing to explicitly model uncertainty for each view. We introduce CAMul, a general probabilistic multi-view forecasting framework capable of learning representations and uncertainty from diverse data sources. CAMul dynamically integrates knowledge and uncertainty from each view in a context-specific manner, prioritizing useful views to generate well-calibrated forecast distributions. Evaluated across multiple domains with varied sources and modalities, CAMul demonstrates superior performance, outperforming other state-of-the-art probabilistic forecasting models by more than 25% in both accuracy and calibration.

This paper investigates harmonic functions associated with general Dirichlet forms. We begin by examining the implications of Fukushima's ergodic theorem regarding harmonic functions within the domain of the $L^p$ generator. Subsequently, we establish analogues of Liouville's theorems, originally formulated by Yau and Karp, for weakly harmonic functions; both results assert that weakly harmonic functions adhering to specific $L^p$ growth conditions must be constant. As a result, we derive an integral criterion for recurrence.

The black hole information paradox stems from a conflict between general relativity and quantum mechanics regarding the radiation emitted by black holes. While Hawking's initial reasoning suggests that the radiation is thermal, leading to a monotonically increasing entropy as the black hole evaporates, quantum theory dictates that time evolution is reversible. Consequently, the Page curve predicts that radiation entropy should eventually begin to decline. Recent calculations utilizing the replica trick have validated this decrease and revealed its geometric basis: spacetime wormholes connecting the replicas. This analysis examines the divergence between Hawking's original findings and these newer conclusions through the lens of quantum information theory, specifically employing the quantum de Finetti theorem. This theorem posits the existence of additional information, $W$, which acts as a reference independent of both the black hole and the radiation. Under this framework, the entropy derived from the replica trick represents the conditional entropy $S(R|W)$ of the radiation given the reference $W$, whereas Hawking's result corresponds to the unconditional entropy $S(R)$. Mathematically an ensemble average, $S(R|W)$ acquires an operational significance in experiments involving $N$ independently prepared black holes; for large $N$, it matches the normalized joint entropy of their combined radiation, $S(R_1 \cdots R_N)/N$. The difference between this conditional entropy and the unconditional $S(R)$ indicates correlations among the black holes, suggesting that replica wormholes serve as the geometric manifestation of these correlations. Furthermore, these findings propose a many-black-hole extension of the standard random unitary model, a hypothesis supported by rigorous verification.

Unsteady pressure-sensitive paint (PSP) data, a type of time-series measurement, often contains substantial random noise. Consequently, this study examines a noise-reduction approach that integrates multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA) with low-dimensional data representation. MSSA functions as a state-space reconstruction technique based on time-delay embedding, while the low-dimensional representation is obtained by projecting data onto a basis derived from singular value decomposition (SVD). The efficacy of the proposed "projected MSSA" method for unsteady PSP data is evaluated against the truncated SVD method, a widely used noise-reduction technique. Results indicate that projected MSSA outperforms truncated SVD in mitigating random noise. Moreover, unlike truncated SVD, the performance of projected MSSA is less dependent on the chosen truncation rank. By effectively extracting smooth trajectories within a state space from noisy inputs, projected MSSA achieves successful denoising. It is anticipated that this method will prove effective for reducing random noise not only in PSP measurements but also across various high-dimensional time-series datasets.

The flow ansatz posits that the single-particle distribution for a specific event can be characterized by complex flow coefficients, denoted as $V_n$. Consequently, multi-particle distributions can be formulated as products of these single-particle coefficients, a concept known as factorization. However, event-by-event fluctuations in the amplitudes and phases of these coefficients may violate the factorization assumption when averaged over event samples, and non-flow phenomena, such as di-jets, can also disrupt it. Factorization breaking with respect to pseudorapidity ($\eta$) offers insights into initial condition fluctuations in heavy ion collisions and helps identify phase-space regions dominated by non-flow effects. This paper introduces a method to factorize the two-particle Fourier coefficients $V_{n\Delta}(\eta_a, \eta_b)$ with minimal dependence on detector effects. AMPT model simulations of Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\text{NN}}} = 5.02$ TeV are employed to determine the minimum $|\Delta\eta|$-gap required for factorization to remain valid. Additionally, a potential $\Delta\eta$-dependent decorrelation effect in the simulated data is quantified using the empirical parameter $F_2^\eta$. Finally, the decorrelation effect observed in these AMPT calculations is compared with CMS collaboration results for Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\text{NN}}} = 2.76$ TeV.

The rotation algebra $\mathcal A_{\theta}$ is defined as the universal $C^*$--algebra generated by unitary operators $U$ and $V$ that satisfy the commutation relation $UV = \omega V U$, where $\omega= e^{2\pi i \theta}$. These algebras are classified as rational when $\theta = p/q$ (with $1 \leq p \leq q-1$) and irrational otherwise. The operators within these algebras are significant in the study of the quantum Hall effect \cite{boca,rammal,simon}, kicked quantum systems \cite{lawton1, wang}, and the resolution of the Ten Martini problem \cite{avila}. While Brabanter \cite{brabanter} and Yin \cite{yin} provided a classification of rational rotation $C^*$--algebras up to $*$-isomorphism, and Stacey \cite{stacey} determined their automorphism groups, their approaches relied on advanced techniques familiar to specialists, including cocycles, crossed products, Dixmier-Douady classes, ergodic actions, K--theory, and Morita equivalence. This expository article introduces $\mathcal A_{p/q}$ as a $C^*$--algebra generated by two operators acting on a Hilbert space, employing linear algebra, Fourier series, and the Gelfand-Naimark-Segal construction \cite{gelfand} to establish its universality. Furthermore, it represents the algebra as the sections of a matrix bundle over a torus to determine its isomorphism class.
