The final section connects these ideas to broader operator algebra theory, targeting mathematicians who are not experts in $C^*$--algebras.

Experimentally inaccessible unstable heavy particles with masses far exceeding the TeV scale are currently constrained primarily by Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN), which limits their lifetimes to less than 0.1 seconds. We demonstrate that next-generation Gravitational-Wave (GW) interferometers could significantly tighten these bounds, extending sensitivity down to lifetimes of $10^{-16}$ seconds. The underlying mechanism involves these particles potentially dominating the universe's energy density, inducing an early period of matter domination that precedes BBN. This deviation from the standard single radiation era leaves distinct imprints on the stochastic background of primordial gravitational waves. Specifically, detecting the GW spectrum generated by persistent sources like cosmic strings offers a unique window into particle physics parameters. By analyzing these spectra within the context of specific early-universe production mechanisms, we can derive novel constraints on ultraviolet extensions of the Standard Model. We illustrate this approach with examples such as supersymmetric models, where scalar moduli and gravitino mass scales could be restricted up to $10^{10}$ GeV. Additionally, we establish tighter limits on the reheating temperature for models involving purely gravitationally interacting particles and constrain the kinetic mixing of heavy dark photons to the level of $10^{-18}$.

Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLTs) overseen by a limited set of trusted validators utilize most, though not all, of the infrastructure found in public DLTs. This paper investigates a method to leverage this environment by integrating a modified Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerant (PBFT) protocol with an updated Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold Signatures (FROST) scheme. The resulting proof-of-authority consensus mechanism is then embedded into Bitcoin, selected for its reliability, openness, and activity, to replace its proof-of-work system. This hybrid protocol is proposed as a secure, contemporary foundation for digital payment systems and Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs).

With the rapid evolution of quantum programming and the proliferation of new languages, the necessity for effective debugging and testing has grown significantly. Although classical software bug fixing has advanced considerably, research into quantum program errors remains limited. Addressing this gap, this paper offers a comprehensive analysis of bug fixing within quantum contexts. We gathered and examined 96 real-world bugs and their corresponding fixes across four prominent quantum languages: Qiskit, Cirq, Q#, and ProjectQ. Our investigation reveals that over 80% of these errors are specific to quantum computing, highlighting a critical need for further study in this domain. Furthermore, we summarize and expand upon existing bug patterns, specifically refining the most significant category—math-related bugs—to enhance their applicability to quantum research. Ultimately, our findings characterize the nature of bugs in quantum programs and establish a foundation for future work in testing and debugging.

Over the past few years, continuous-aperture multiple-input multiple-output (CAP-MIMO) has been revisited to enhance communication performance despite constraints on antenna aperture size. Distinct from classical MIMO systems that utilize discrete antennas, CAP-MIMO features a continuous antenna surface capable of generating arbitrary current distributions and inducing controllable spatial electromagnetic waves. This capability allows information to be modulated onto these waves, offering a promising path toward achieving the ultimate capacity limits of finite apertures. However, while pattern design is the critical determinant of CAP-MIMO performance, it remains underexplored in existing literature. This paper introduces pattern-division multiplexing as a solution for designing CAP-MIMO patterns. We begin by deriving a system model for a typical multi-user CAP-MIMO setup to formulate a sum-rate maximization problem. Subsequently, we propose a general pattern-division multiplexing technique that converts the design of continuous pattern functions into the optimization of their projection lengths onto finite orthogonal bases. Leveraging this method, we develop a specific pattern design scheme to address the sum-rate maximization problem. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves a sum-rate approximately 260% higher than that of the benchmark approach.

We introduce a streamlined method for actively managing Rabi oscillations within emitter-cavity hybrid systems by incorporating an optical gain element. Drawing on recent advancements in parity-time ($\mathcal{PT}$)-symmetry photonics, we demonstrate that nano- or micro-cavities, where intrinsic losses are counterbalanced by a tunable external gain, possess distinct advantages for steering emitter dynamics. Specifically, this approach allows for profound alterations to system behavior, including boosting overall occupation numbers, extending the duration of Rabi oscillations, and slowing them down to facilitate easier experimental detection. Additionally, we identify a critical gain threshold corresponding to an exceptional point; at this stage, both the emitter and cavity oscillate nearly in phase with occupation numbers that can far surpass unity. Finally, by re-examining a recently proposed metric for Rabi visibility, we establish reliable criteria for measuring coupling strength and attaining strong coupling with a tunable Rabi frequency through loss compensation.

A graph is termed "$\ell$-holed" when every induced cycle within it that has a length of four or greater possesses a length exactly equal to $\ell$. This work provides a comprehensive characterization of such $\ell$-holed graphs for all values of $\ell$ where $\ell \geq 7$.

We examine cluster formation in a non-ergodic stochastic system driven by counter-flow using an exactly solvable model. Specifically, we investigate a two-species asymmetric simple exclusion process on a periodic lattice containing impurities, which trigger flips between the two non-conserved species. Exact analytical solutions, corroborated by Monte Carlo simulations, reveal two distinct phases: a free-flowing phase and a clustering phase. In the clustering phase, the non-conserved species exhibit constant density and zero current, while the free-flowing phase is marked by non-monotonic density and finite, non-monotonic current. Within the clustering phase, the $n$-point spatial correlation among $n$ consecutive vacancies increases with $n$, signaling the emergence of two macroscopic clusters: one composed of vacancies and the other of all particles. We introduce a rearrangement parameter that alters the initial particle ordering while keeping input parameters constant, thereby highlighting the profound impact of non-ergodicity on clustering onset. Furthermore, for specific microscopic dynamics, we link this model to run-and-tumble active matter systems, where the two species with opposing biases correspond to run directions, and impurities function as tumbling agents facilitating direction changes.

Signed networks and balance theory offer a suitable framework for modeling real-world phenomena characterized by polarization, positive and negative ties, and political partisanship. These approaches have demonstrated effectiveness in analyzing the rising vote polarization within both chambers of the U.S. Congress since World War II. To deepen the analysis of this specific case, we introduce a methodology that leverages the spectral properties of a signed graph's Laplacian matrix to visualize and analyze network configurations. Although comparable to existing methods based on the frustration index, our approach offers two primary benefits: significantly reduced computational costs and the ability to quantitatively and visually assess how even minute subgraphs, down to individual nodes, contribute to the network's overall balance or imbalance. This pipeline enables an exploration of polarization dynamics in the American Congress from 1945 to 2020 across various resolution levels. Specifically, it allows for the identification of influential individuals or groups of congressmen regarding the network's balance and facilitates the observation of polarization evolution in both legislative chambers over time.

Over the past two decades, the intricate progression of the US opioid epidemic has driven extensive medical and pharmacological research, prompting multidisciplinary debates on implementing effective public health interventions. This study utilizes Reddit as a primary data source to examine the crisis. Our objectives were to identify a large cohort of users discussing opioid use, track the temporal shifts in this interest, and thoroughly characterize patterns of nonmedical consumption, specifically focusing on administration routes and drug tampering. Employing a semiautomatic information retrieval algorithm, we identified subreddits related to nonmedical opioid use, uncovering a potential cohort of over 86,000 firsthand users. We developed a word-embedding-based methodology to detect alternative colloquial and nonmedical terms for opioids, administration methods, and tampering techniques. By modeling preferences for specific substances and routes, we estimated their prevalence and temporal trends, noting significant increases in synthetic opioids like fentanyl and a growing interest in rectal administration. Furthermore, through odds ratio analysis of co-mentions, we assessed the associations between substances, routes, and tampering, revealing evidence of understudied abusive practices such as chewing fentanyl patches and dissolving buprenorphine sublingually. Ultimately, we believe this approach offers a novel perspective for comprehensively understanding nonmedical opioid abuse, thereby informing prevention, treatment, and control strategies for its public health impacts.

We introduce a unified framework for analyzing hierarchies of relaxations in Constraint Satisfaction Problems and their Promise variant. This approach decomposes the hierarchy description into an algebraic component, defined by a minion that establishes the "base level," and a geometric component, termed tensorisation, which draws inspiration from multilinear algebra. We demonstrate that minion test hierarchies generated by this method are sufficiently broad to encompass combinatorial bounded width, as well as the Sherali-Adams LP, Sum-of-Squares SDP, and affine IP hierarchies. By leveraging the geometric properties of the resulting tensor spaces, we establish general characteristics of these hierarchies. Furthermore, we define specific minion classes—linear and conic—whose associated hierarchies exhibit distinct, refined properties. Finally, to investigate the Sum-of-Squares SDP hierarchy, we characterize the solvability of the standard SDP relaxation via a newly identified minion.

This study examines the quantum dynamics of many-qubit systems strongly interacting with a quantized electromagnetic cavity, accounting for decoherence and dissipation affecting both fermions and cavity photons. The analysis incorporates variations in qubit-cavity coupling strengths and the distribution of transition frequencies. Using the stochastic Schrödinger equation approach within the Lindblad approximation, we derive compact analytic solutions for time-dependent quantum state amplitudes and observables across a wide range of open quantum systems. Our results demonstrate that, based on initial state preparation, an ensemble of qubits can evolve into diverse many-qubit entangled states characterized by constructive or destructive interference. Specifically, when only a small fraction of qubits are initially excited, cavity dissipation inevitably drives the system into robust dark states that are fully decoupled from the cavity and persist significantly longer than the cavity field's decay time. Furthermore, we identify the conditions under which coherent coupling to the quantized cavity field surpasses dephasing caused by frequency spread in multi-qubit systems, resulting in the formation of a decoupled dark state.

SND@LHC is a compact experiment designed to detect high-energy neutrinos generated by heavy flavor quarks at the LHC within the pseudo-rapidity range of 7.2 < η < 8.6. As a hybrid system integrating nuclear emulsions with electronic detectors, it enables the distinction of all three neutrino flavors, offering a unique opportunity to investigate charm production physics in the very forward region. The initial phase involves operating the detector during LHC Run 3 to accumulate a total integrated luminosity of 150 fb$^{-1}$. The electronic subdetectors were assembled in the summer and have recently undergone testing in beam experiments.

We present a strategy for indirectly measuring the spectrum of an electronic spin by transferring its polarization to surrounding nuclear spins. Because nuclear spins are more numerous and possess longer coherence times, they enable repeated accumulation of polarization, allowing subsequent nuclear measurements to reveal details about the electronic spectral density. We experimentally validate this approach by reading out the electron spin resonance (ESR) spectrum of Nitrogen Vacancy centers in diamond through the detection of lattice 13C nuclei. Implementing spin-lock control on the 13C nuclei significantly boosts the signal-to-noise ratio for this nuclear readout. This spectrally mapped method offers operational benefits, including immunity to crystal orientation and optical scattering, as well as a background-free signal. Leveraging these advantages, we demonstrate applications in underwater magnetometry. The underlying physical mechanism, a "one-to-many" spectral mapping, is conceptually fascinating; to explain its origin, we developed a theoretical model that maps the system's dynamics—specifically, traversal through a cascaded series of Landau-Zener anti-crossings—to the operation of a tilted Galton board. This research highlights new possibilities for "ESR-via-NMR" techniques in dilute electronic systems, as well as in hybrid electron-nuclear quantum memories and sensors.

Although Gaia is conducting an extensive survey of the Galaxy, photometric data from individual observation epochs has so far been made available for only a small subset of sources. We demonstrate that variable stars can be identified within Gaia Data Release 2 by selecting objects that exhibit unexpectedly high photometric uncertainties relative to their brightness and the count of their observations. By comparing our findings with established variable star catalogs, we reveal that details regarding variability amplitude are implicitly encoded in the Gaia photometric uncertainties. We introduce a catalog containing approximately 9.3 million candidate variable stars and outline its constraints alongside potential avenues for future validation and expansion.

Driven by the growing availability of uncertain event data from diverse sources, such as physical devices and sensors, this paper addresses the challenge of aligning stochastic process observations with models derived from datasets. Unlike prior studies that reduced stochastically known event logs into less informative uncertain logs defined by activity frequency bounds, this work focuses on integrating probabilistic knowledge into conformance checking methods. Utilizing a taxonomy that encompasses the range of conformance scenarios under stochastic observations, we identify three distinct challenges. The first involves checking the conformance of a stochastically known log against a specific process model. The second extends this by classifying a stochastically known log into one among several candidate models. The third expands further to scenarios where the process models themselves are only stochastically known. This problem formulation addresses the expanding array of applications where sensors deliver probabilistic process insights.

We build the spectrum for shift-invariant spaces defined on the Vilenkin group. Furthermore, we establish findings concerning both the spectrum and frame multiresolution analysis for the Cantor dyadic group and the Vilenkin group.

This study investigates the undetected error probability performance of the cyclic redundancy-check (CRC) codes proposed in the 5G New Radio technical specifications, specifically for fixed-length intervals. The authors suggest alternative CRC codes with 6, 11, and 16 check bits that offer superior error detection capabilities compared to those specified. For codes with 24 check bits, the three best-performing options are presented; however, no single optimal code was identified that performs best across the entire range of length intervals.

Relativistic electron components, though minor, can exist in both natural and laboratory plasmas. When high-atomic-number ions are present, the charge state distribution at low bulk electron temperatures may be dominated by these relativistic electrons, despite their density being orders of magnitude lower. This phenomenon occurs because relativistic effects significantly enhance collisional excitation and ionization cross sections. Consequently, this charge state effect can substantially influence the radiative power loss and the Bethe stopping power of relativistic electrons within a dilute plasma.

Two homogeneous pseudo-Riemannian manifolds $(G/H, ds^2)$ and $(G'/H', ds'^2)$ are considered part of the same {\it real form family} if their complexified counterparts, $(G_{\mathbb C}/H_{\mathbb C}, ds_{\mathbb C}^2)$ and $(G'_{\mathbb C}/H'_{\mathbb C}, ds'^2_{\mathbb C})$, are isometric. This classification is significant because specific properties of a given space $(G/H, ds^2)$ often extend to all spaces within its real form family. This work establishes that if a manifold $(G/H, ds^2)$ equipped with a reductive decomposition $\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{h} + \mathfrak{m}$ is a geodesic orbit space, then every member of its real form family shares this property. Consequently, insights into compact geodesic orbit Riemannian manifolds can be applied to geodesic orbit pseudo-Riemannian manifolds. Furthermore, analogous results are demonstrated for naturally reductive spaces, commutative spaces, and weakly symmetric spaces in most instances. The paper concludes by examining the inclusion relations among these real form families, analyzing D'Atri spaces, and presenting several open problems.

The prevalence of concave radial and orbital Regge trajectories among the majority of mesons, as demonstrated by fitted data, is a model-independent characteristic. In the absence of convex trajectories or those with inflection points, this concavity serves as a reliable criterion for identifying newly observed mesons or classifying particles within unwell-established states. Furthermore, the curvature of these trajectories offers a guiding principle for model construction, requiring appropriate theoretical frameworks to reproduce spectra that align with the observed concave nature of meson Regge trajectories. While most meson trajectories are concave, a few potential convex cases remain neither confirmed nor fully excluded; resolving this discrepancy will likely necessitate significant corrections or even a complete reconstruction of existing models, thereby advancing our understanding of meson dynamics.

Although propagating field squeezing can theoretically reach any strength, cavity-field squeezing is restricted by the well-known 3 dB limit, thereby limiting its utility. To overcome this barrier, we introduce a fully quantum degenerate parametric amplifier (DPA). Specifically, we demonstrate that by applying a two-tone drive to the signal mode, the pump mode can be driven by the signal's photon loss into a squeezed steady state with an arbitrarily high degree of squeezing, a result that is counterintuitive. Furthermore, we show that this intracavity squeezing can boost the signal-to-noise ratio for longitudinal qubit readout exponentially with respect to the squeezing level. Consequently, measurement errors can be reduced by many orders of magnitude even with modest system parameters. In sharp contrast, intracavity squeezing within a semiclassical DPA cannot practically enhance the signal-to-noise ratio or improve measurement precision. These findings broaden the application scope of DPAs and create new avenues for modern quantum technologies.

To assess the viability of using ESA's Ariel mission for ancillary target observations, we assembled a catalog of promising young stars, including FUors, systems with extreme debris discs, and a broader group of young stellar objects exhibiting strong near- and mid-infrared excess. These candidates are scheduled for observation during the intervals between planned exoplanet transit and occultation events. Following a review of the Ariel schedule, an algorithm was developed to identify the optimal target for each time gap. This selection process prioritized slew and stabilization durations required to observe the chosen young stellar object, while also weighing their scientific significance and prior observation status. Based on extensive simulation data, we determined that roughly 99.2% of available gaps (each lasting at least one hour) could be utilized effectively. Given an average slewing and stabilization time of approximately 16.7 minutes between exoplanet transits and ancillary targets, this yields an additional $2881 \pm 56$ hours of active observation time. Applying this extra time to our sample of 200 ancillary targets enables achieving a typical signal-to-noise ratio of $\sim$10$^4$ across Ariel's full spectral range.

We develop approximate iterative analytical solutions for the non-extensive Boltzmann transport equation under the relaxation time approximation. These solutions closely match the exact results across a broad spectrum of parameter values relevant to particle spectra generated in high-energy collisions. Additionally, we examine the Landau kinetic approximation of the non-extensive Boltzmann transport equation and the resulting non-extensive Fokker-Planck equation, utilizing this framework to estimate the drag and diffusion coefficients of high-energy light quarks traversing a gluonic plasma.

We introduce a novel, computationally efficient first-order approach to Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML). Our method hinges on framing MAML as a bilevel optimization (BLO) problem and employing sign-based stochastic gradient descent (signSGD) as the lower-level optimizer. By viewing MAML through the lens of signSGD-driven BLO, we derive a natural alternating optimization framework that relies solely on first-order gradients of the learned meta-model. We designate this approach as Sign-MAML. Unlike standard first-order MAML (FO-MAML), Sign-MAML is theoretically robust because it does not require assumptions regarding the non-existence of second-order derivatives during meta-training. Empirically, Sign-MAML surpasses FO-MAML across various few-shot image classification benchmarks and offers a significantly more favorable balance between computational efficiency and classification accuracy compared to traditional MAML.

Our comprehension of the visual environment extends beyond mere object identification to include the capacity to decompose objects into significant components, characteristics, and relationships. This study utilizes natural language descriptions across a varied collection of 2,000 procedurally generated objects to determine which parts individuals prioritize and the underlying principles driving these preferences. We frame this challenge as a search through a library of programs containing various part concepts, employing machine translation techniques to assess how well programs in each library correspond to human language. By integrating large-scale naturalistic language with structured program representations, we uncover a fundamental information-theoretic tradeoff in how people name part concepts: humans prefer a lexicon that enables concise descriptions for each object while simultaneously keeping the lexicon itself as small as possible.

Higher-order cumulants of conserved charges serve as sensitive indicators for detecting critical fluctuations near the QCD critical point in heavy-ion collisions. However, pileup events, arising from high interaction rates, constitute a significant background source in these measurements. This study investigates the impact of pileup on higher-order cumulants of proton multiplicity distributions using the UrQMD model. We find that the standard pileup correction method fails when its parameters are derived from Glauber fits of charged particle multiplicities, a common practice in actual heavy-ion experiments. To resolve this issue, we introduce a model-independent unfolding approach for determining the necessary correction parameters. This method is applicable to future pileup corrections for measuring higher-order cumulants in heavy-ion collision experiments.

Disordered dielectrics featuring structural correlations at scales similar to visible light wavelengths display intricate optical behaviors. Naturally occurring examples of these materials produce stunning, non-iridescent structural colors and are increasingly utilized as fundamental components for optical coatings and materials. This article investigates the single-scattering characteristics of micron-scale, disordered colloidal aggregates. These structures function as structurally colored supraparticles or as precursors for macroscopic photonic glasses. We provide experimental findings regarding differential scattering and transport cross-sections, demonstrating how established macroscopic models can be modified to accurately describe scattering from small colloidal assemblies beyond the weak-scattering limit and into the Lorentz-Mie regime.

We introduce the inaugural formalization and metatheory of soundness for language scheduling, specifically applied to Halide, a widely adopted array processing language. User-schedulable languages achieve a balance between abstraction and control in high-performance computing by decoupling the specification of computational results from the schedule determining how those results are computed. This approach entails a unique soundness claim: program outputs must remain consistent irrespective of the applied schedule. Providing this guarantee is complex because schedules can introduce redundant recomputation and operations on uninitialized data, going beyond simple statement reordering. Furthermore, Halide ensures memory safety via a compile-time bounds inference engine that calculates safe dimensions for all buffers and loops in generated code, posing a new challenge: formally specifying and analyzing a language whose definition relies on potentially unreliable program synthesis algorithms. Our formalization has uncovered defects and driven enhancements to the practical Halide system, while also establishing a foundation for designing new languages and tools that extend programmer-controlled scheduling to other domains.

Current denoising techniques typically generate clear outputs by aggregating pixels from noisy inputs. Rather than depending on manually designed aggregation schemes, we propose explicitly learning this process using deep neural networks. We introduce a spatial pixel aggregation network that learns sampling and averaging strategies for image denoising; this model naturally adapts to image structures and effectively enhances denoised results. Additionally, we develop a spatio-temporal pixel aggregation network for video denoising, enabling efficient pixel sampling across the spatio-temporal domain to address misalignment issues arising from significant motion in dynamic scenes. Furthermore, we incorporate a novel regularization term to facilitate effective training of the proposed video denoising model. Extensive analysis demonstrates that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art image and video denoising methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

Online experimentation platforms gather user feedback efficiently at scale, with some systems capable of real-time or near real-time processing to continuously update metrics like clicks and page views. However, critical signals often require hours or days to materialize, accumulating noise over time. When long-term outcomes depend on complex sequences of user-product interactions, identifying the specific drivers of those outcomes remains challenging due to a lack of clear attribution logic. Establishing such logic is essential for achieving finer-grained, targeted measurement, which is a prerequisite for fully leveraging reinforcement learning. This paper introduces the application of Causal Surrogacy to model long-term outcomes using incrementally available leading indicators, utilizing this model as a value function to track progress and attribute value to individual interaction steps. Applied to Airbnb's guest booking metric, this approach reduced variance by 50% to 85% while maintaining strong alignment with actual booking results. By enabling continuous attribution, the method assigns utility scores to each product page view, which can be flexibly aggregated across various units of interest, including searches and listings. The paper further demonstrates the approach's versatility through multiple real-world attribution applications.

We performed experiments using force-free, magnetically driven rigid helical swimmers in both Newtonian and viscoelastic (Boger) fluids. By altering the dimensions of the swimmer's body and helical tail, we demonstrated that the effect of viscoelasticity is highly dependent on the swimmer's geometry. This effect can result in a substantial increase in swimming speed (up to five times), a comparable decrease (also up to five times), or have negligible impact. Our analysis, combining experimental data with theoretical modeling, indicates that the influence of viscoelasticity on helical propulsion is governed by a "snowman-like" effect—previously observed in dumbbell swimmers—where the front-back asymmetry of the swimmer generates a non-Newtonian elastic force that may either enhance or impede locomotion.

We introduce a novel multi-task benchmark designed to evaluate text-to-image generation models. This benchmark was validated through a human evaluation comparing prominent open-source (Stable Diffusion) and commercial (DALL-E 2) models. The assessment involved twenty computer science graduate students who rated images across three tasks, three difficulty levels, and ten prompts each, resulting in 3,600 total ratings. While text-to-image generation has advanced rapidly, with recent models capable of producing realistic high-resolution images for various requests, existing methods and vision-language research still face challenges with intricate prompts involving multiple objects, attributes, and relationships. Our new benchmark addresses this by offering a suite of thirty-two tasks across multiple applications that test a model's ability to handle diverse prompt features, such as counting identical objects or correctly matching attributes to specific items. Unlike subjective evaluations based solely on a set of prompts, our multi-task framework includes challenge tasks at easy, medium, and hard difficulty levels, complete with human ratings for every generated image.

We examine various classes of combinatory structures associated with Krivine realizability. We demonstrate that, in the precise sense that they generate identical classes of triposes, these structures are equivalent for modeling higher-order logic. Our focus centers on a specific type of Ordered Combinatory Algebra, which we term "Krivine ordered combinatory algebras" ($\mathcal{KOCA}$s), proposing them as the foundational elements for the categorical view of Krivine's classical realizability as outlined by Streicher.

Our methodology proceeds as follows: we establish that each considered combinatory structure yields an indexed preorder and outline a transformation process between these structures that maintains the associated indexed preorders up to equivalence. Because all structures produce the same indexed preorders, we need only prove the existence of triposes once, specifically for the class of $\mathcal{KOCA}$s.

Finally, we demonstrate that within $\mathcal{KOCA}$s, realizability can be defined for every higher-order language, including higher-order arithmetic.

Large deviations theory typically involves a family of probability measures defined on a space $X$ equipped with a topology. This paper investigates the large deviation results achievable when the underlying measure space $X$ lacks a topological structure. The primary methodology employed is the duality theory of risk measures. We demonstrate that a monetary risk measure $\phi$ fulfills the Laplace principle, expressed as $\phi(f)={\rm ess.sup}_X(f-I)$ for a specific measurable function $I\colon X\to[0,\infty]$, if and only if $\phi$ is both maxitive and continuous from below. Regarding the asymptotic entropy $\psi(f)=\lim_{n\to\infty} \tfrac{1}{n}\log \int e^{n f} d\nu_n$, this finding serves as a non-topological counterpart to Varadhan's integral lemma. Following the approach of Bryc's theorem, we examine non-topological equivalents of exponential tightness that guarantee the Laplace principle established in our main result. Finally, we apply this framework to derive non-topological large deviation principles for sequences of sublinear expectations.

Resonant Inelastic X-ray Scattering (RIXS) stands as one of the most intricate and data-dense experimental methods used to explore electronic structures in physics, chemistry, and materials science by simultaneously probing occupied and unoccupied electronic subspaces. We present a precise and efficient *ab-initio* computational framework for simulating and analyzing RIXS spectra, which unites two distinct yet established methodologies for modeling electronic excited states. The Core-Hole Linear-Response RIXS (CleaRIXS) approach guarantees the accurate treatment of interactions between electrons and both core and valence holes, while automatically linking key RIXS spectral features to specific electronic excitations and de-excitations. By directly comparing our results with prior methanol C K-edge RIXS measurements [J. Phys. Chem. A 120, 2260 (2016)], we demonstrate the formalism's capability to model various regions of the RIXS spectrum and provide physical insights into their origins. Furthermore, we investigate the significance of incorporating valence electron-hole interactions and examine the relationship between CleaRIXS and determinant-based techniques for simulating X-ray absorption and non-resonant X-ray emission. Additionally, we offer a qualitative discussion of extra RIXS features potentially arising from vibrationally mediated processes. Ultimately, CleaRIXS establishes a robust and adaptable framework for predicting and interpreting RIXS phenomena and for simulating complex electronic excited states in general.

We introduce a theoretical framework for the $J/\psi\Lambda$ spectrum arising from $B^-\to J/\psi \Lambda\bar{p}$ decays, incorporating the recently identified $P_{\psi s}^\Lambda(4338)$ baryon by LHCb. Our approach posits production through triangle diagrams that connect to the final state via non-perturbative interactions, limited by heavy-quark and $SU_3$-flavor symmetries. The majority of the distribution stems from a triangle diagram with a color-favored electroweak vertex, whereas the distinct $P_{\psi s}^\Lambda(4338)$ peak results from a triangle singularity in a separate diagram involving a $1/2^-$ baryon compatible with $\Sigma_c(2800)$. We forecast a similar $P_{\psi s}^\Lambda(4338)$ signal in $\eta_c \Lambda$ channels and expect significant isospin mixing effects via decays into $J/\psi \Sigma^0$ and $\eta_c \Sigma^0$.

In massive stars undergoing slow neutron capture, reactions involving light elements can either generate or consume neutrons, thereby shaping the abundance of heavy elements. At low metallicities, the rapid neutron capture by 16-O can suppress s-process nucleosynthesis unless neutrons are recycled through the 17O(a,n)20Ne reaction. The effectiveness of this recycling hinges on the competition between the 17O(a,n)20Ne and 17O(a,g)21Ne pathways. While experimental data exist for the former, the radiative capture channel lacks data at the specific energies relevant to astrophysics. Consequently, the 17O(a,g)21Ne reaction was investigated directly using the DRAGON recoil separator at TRIUMF. The study determined the reaction cross section across energies from 0.6 to 1.6 MeV Ecm, extending into the Gamow window for core helium burning for the first time. Resonance strengths were extracted for peaks at 0.63, 0.721, 0.81, and 1.122 MeV Ecm. Although the experimentally derived reaction rate serves as a lower limit, it indicates that substantial s-process nucleosynthesis can still occur in low-metallicity massive stars.

This study details the kinematic and chemical characteristics of red giant stars from the APOGEE-2 survey within the Jhelum stellar stream, a Milky Way substructure situated in the inner halo approximately 13 kpc away. By analyzing data from six Jhelum pointings and selecting stars with log($g$) < 3.5, we obtained a sample of 289 red giants. Among these, seven stars matched the astrometric signature of the Jhelum stream in $Gaia$ DR2; one of these seven aligns with the red giant branch sequence previously defined by \cite{ji20}, representing a new Jhelum member with [Fe/H]=-2.2 located at the red giant branch tip. Additionally, by filtering for high orbital eccentricity and metal-rich stars, we identified red giants likely belonging to the $Gaia$-Enceladus-Sausage (GES) merger. Comparing the abundance profiles of Jhelum and GES stars reveals similar $\alpha$-element trends, consistent with low-metallicity populations, yet their orbits do not generally support a common origin. The chemical abundances of the new Jhelum member and other confirmed stream stars resemble those of known stellar streams, supporting an accreted dwarf galaxy origin for the stream's progenitor, though a globular cluster origin remains a possibility.

Conventional HEP analysis software relies on the ROOT framework to iterate through every event and object, adhering to an imperative paradigm where code execution is tightly coupled with the storage format. A preferable alternative is a declarative language that abstracts away both the storage medium and execution steps, a capability that will be crucial for handling the vast datasets generated by the LHC and HL-LHC. To address this, the Institute for Research and Innovation in Software for High Energy Physics (IRIS-HEP) developed FuncADL, a new analysis description language (ADL) built on Python and inspired by functional programming principles. The language's expressiveness was evaluated through example analysis tasks designed to benchmark ADL capabilities. FuncADL successfully handles many simple selections declaratively, serving as an interface to retrieve filtered data. Although certain limitations were noted, the language's architecture supports future extensions to incorporate missing features. As part of IRIS-HEP's suite of analysis tools, FuncADL will enable the development of highly scalable physics analyses for the LHC.

Quantum key distribution protocols are susceptible to side-channel attacks that leverage timing discrepancies in detector responses to extract key bits. The standard mitigation strategy involves employing a large time bin width rather than high-resolution timing data, operating on the assumption that reduced resolution limits information leakage to an eavesdropper. This study challenges that conventional wisdom by demonstrating that increasing bin width does not monotonically decrease the mutual information between the key bits and the eavesdropper's observations. Instead of arbitrarily expanding bin widths, they must be selected carefully, as mutual information fluctuates depending on the bin width. Additionally, the analysis reveals that decreasing the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of detector responses increases mutual information. Finally, the study highlights that the start time of the binning process is critical, showing that mutual information varies periodically with respect to this parameter.

Drawing inspiration from the studies by Cheskidov, Lopes Filho, Nussenzveig Lopes, and Shvydkoy [8] and those by Chen and Yu [5], this paper investigates the impact of $L^p$ bounds on vorticity regarding energy conservation in both homogeneous and nonhomogeneous incompressible Euler equations. For homogeneous flows within periodic domains or the entire space, we present a self-contained demonstration of the criterion $\omega=\text{curl}u\in L^{3}(0,T;L^{\frac{3n}{n+2}}(\Omega))\,(n=2,3)$, which extends the findings of [8] and aligns with Onsager's critical spatio-temporal spaces. Concerning nonhomogeneous flows, we establish that energy conservation holds provided the vorticity remains within the aforementioned space and $\nabla\sqrt{\rho}$ is in $L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{n}(\mathbb{T}^{n}))\,(n=2,3)$, thereby affirmatively resolving the question raised by Chen and Yu in [5].

This paper introduces a novel method for deriving constants of motion linked to scaling symmetries in dynamical systems. While scaling maps may constitute symmetries of the equations of motion, they do not necessarily preserve the associated Lagrangian action. To address this, we developed a Noether-inspired theorem within a vertical extended space, enabling the derivation of constants of motion for such symmetries; the standard Noether theorem emerges as a specific instance of our framework. To demonstrate the procedure, we provide two examples: a) Schwarzian Mechanics utilizing the Schwarzian derivative operator, and b) the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) nonlinear partial differential equation within the context of asymptotic General Relativity in AdS$_3$. Furthermore, we investigate the inverse of the Noether theorem for scaling symmetries, detailing how to construct and identify the generator of the scaling transformation and its application to the newly formulated vertical extended constant of motion. Our findings highlight a significant contribution regarding the symmetry arising from the fact that scaling symmetry does not qualify as a Noether symmetry of the action. Finally, we compare our results with recent analyses and prior attempts to identify constants of motion associated with these scaling laws.

Trustworthy machine learning relies heavily on privacy and interpretability. This paper examines the relationship between these two factors within graph machine learning by analyzing graph reconstruction attacks. In this scenario, an adversary attempts to recover the training graph's structure using access to model explanations. We introduce several such attacks, varying based on the auxiliary information available to the attacker, and demonstrate that post-hoc feature explanations significantly boost attack success rates. Furthermore, we analyze the performance differences among three classes of explanation methods for graph neural networks: gradient-based, perturbation-based, and surrogate model-based approaches. Although gradient-based methods reveal the most structural information, they do not always offer high utility. For the other two categories, there is a direct correlation where increased explanation utility leads to greater privacy leakage. Finally, we propose a defense strategy utilizing a randomized response mechanism for explanation release, which markedly lowers the success rate of these attacks. Our anonymized code is publicly accessible.

Nowcasting involves forecasting meteorological elements over short timeframes with high spatial precision, a task that has garnered significant attention due to its impact on various human activities. This study approaches nowcasting as an image-to-image translation task utilizing satellite imagery. We present Broad-UNet, a new architecture derived from the foundational UNet model, designed to tackle this challenge efficiently. Specifically, Broad-UNet incorporates asymmetric parallel convolutions and an Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) module. By integrating multi-scale features, the model captures complex patterns while utilizing fewer parameters than the original UNet. The Broad-UNet was tested on two distinct nowcasting tasks: precipitation mapping and cloud cover forecasting. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed Broad-UNet achieves superior prediction accuracy compared to other examined architectures.

By applying a homological linking theorem within variational theory alongside Maslov-type index iteration inequalities, we establish the existence of a sequence of subharmonic solutions for non-autonomous Hamiltonian systems where the Hamiltonian functions exhibit anisotropic growth conditions. Specifically, these functions may display superquadratic, subquadratic, and quadratic behaviors simultaneously across different components. Furthermore, we investigate the minimal period problem for certain autonomous Hamiltonian systems characterized by anisotropic growth.

We demonstrate that line defects within a non-Abelian Kitaev spin liquid support gapless one-dimensional Majorana modes when the interaction strength across the defect remains below a specific threshold. By applying a mean-field approximation to weak interactions at these line defects, we derive the critical interaction strength as a function of the external magnetic field. Furthermore, utilizing a low-energy effective field theory in the gapless regime, we calculate the spin-lattice relaxation rate for a nuclear spin situated near the defect, identifying a cubic temperature dependence that aligns with experimental observations in the Kitaev material $\alpha\text{-RuCl}_3$.

In Carry Propagate Adders, the primary source of delay stems from carry propagation. For the single-digit adders employed, the most effective approach involves generating two intermediate carries, $C_{out0}$ (where $C_{in}=0$) and $C_{out1}$ (where $C_{in}=1$), which are then multiplexed to yield the correct output based on the $C_{in}$ value. Regardless of the radix used, the carry output invariably assumes a logical value of either 0 or 1. This paper demonstrates that utilizing 0 and $V_{dd}$ levels for input and output carries in quaternary full adders—rather than the traditional 0 and $V_{dd}$/3 levels—significantly reduces carry propagation delays. Furthermore, we compare this quaternary full adder design against binary full adders when constructing N-digit carry propagate adders.

The VoicePrivacy Challenge seeks to advance privacy-preserving tools for speech technology by assembling a community to establish key tasks and evaluation methods, followed by benchmarking solutions via specific challenges. This document outlines the voice anonymization task chosen for the VoicePrivacy 2020 Challenge, detailing the datasets employed for system development and assessment. Additionally, it presents various attack models along with their corresponding objective and subjective evaluation metrics. Finally, the paper introduces two anonymization baselines and reports the resulting objective evaluation outcomes.

This study examines certain Bernstein-Gelfand-Gelfand (BGG) complexes defined on bounded Lipschitz domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$ using Sobolev spaces. Specifically, we calculate the cohomology for both the conformal deformation complex and the conformal Hessian complex within this Sobolev framework. Our approach does not rely on algebraic injectivity or surjectivity conditions between the input spaces and accommodates multiple input complexes. As applications, we prove a conformal Korn inequality in two dimensions involving the Cauchy-Riemann operator and an additional third-order operator set against a background of M\"obius geometry. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the linear Cosserat elasticity model constitutes a Hodge-Laplacian problem associated with a twisted de-Rham complex. From this cohomological standpoint, we suggest potential extensions to continuum models featuring microstructures.

To expedite the creation of new ion-conducting materials, we introduce a comprehensive graph-theoretic framework for analyzing ion migration across any crystalline lattice. In this model, graph nodes denote metastable positions of the moving ion, while edges signify discrete migration steps between neighboring sites. Beginning with a set of potential metastable locations, the system assigns edge weights by computing the specific energy barriers for migration between them. Macroscopic ion migration pathways within the periodic simulation cell are then identified by locating the lowest-cost cycle in the periodic migration graph. To demonstrate the framework's effectiveness, we performed automated analyses of lithium migration across various polymorphs of VO(PO4), successfully identifying two distinct crystal structures that feature simple migration routes with overall barriers below 300 meV.

This paper addresses synchronization challenges in heterogeneous networks of linear systems featuring nonlinear delayed diffusive coupling. By transforming the network into new coordinates representing mean-field dynamics and synchronization errors, the study reduces the synchronization problem to analyzing the stability of the synchronization-error system. The circle criterion for time-delay systems is employed to derive stability conditions for this error system. These findings are applied to a network of neural mass model populations to establish specific synchronization conditions, with simulation results provided to validate the analytical outcomes.

In the context of streaming Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), rows from a potentially infinite $d$-dimensional matrix arrive sequentially as points in $\mathbb{R}^d$. An $\epsilon$-coreset is defined as a significantly smaller matrix where the sum of squared distances from rows to any hyperplane approximates the original matrix's value within a $(1 \pm \epsilon)$ factor. Our primary contribution demonstrates that an $\epsilon$-coreset can be maintained using only $O(d \log^2 d / \epsilon^2)$ stored rows. Given that established lower bounds require at least $\Omega(d / \epsilon^2)$ rows, our approach is nearly optimal. Furthermore, each row in our coreset consists of a weighted subset of the input rows, which offers significant advantages: (1) it maintains sparsity, (2) ensures interpretability, (3) prevents precision errors, and (4) accommodates problems with specific input constraints. While prior streaming SVD methods returning input subsets required storing $\Omega(d \log^3 n / \epsilon^2)$ rows (where $n$ is the count of rows observed), our algorithm achieves storage independence from $n$. This marks the first result to utilize finite memory for infinite streams. We validate these findings through experiments on the Wikipedia dataset, benchmarking our approach against state-of-the-art algorithms.

Restricted mean survival time (RMST) offers a clinically intuitive metric that avoids assumptions regarding proportional hazards. This study examines two approaches for directly modeling survival time while adjusting for covariates. The first method involves calculating pseudo-survival times for each subject via a leave-one-out procedure, followed by a model analysis utilizing all pseudo-values to account for covariates; these pseudo-values effectively incorporate information from censored subjects. The second approach adjusts for covariates among subjects with observed event times while handling censored subjects through inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW). The paper assesses the performance of both methods in detecting group differences using a simple illustrative dataset and computer simulations. While the example demonstrates the intuitive mechanics of both approaches, it highlights that pseudo-survival times can be challenging to interpret. Furthermore, in a primary biliary cholangitis clinical trial, pseudo-survival times diverged from actual data due to the high volume of censored observations. Simulation results indicate that the IPCW method yields greater statistical power. Additionally, even when group differences exist regarding censoring incidence rates and covariates, the IPCW method preserves the nominal significance level for the type-1 error rate. Consequently, the study concludes that the IPCW method is preferable for estimating restricted mean survival time when covariate adjustment is required.

This paper presents a realistic and demanding multi-source, multi-room acoustic scenario alongside an enhanced algorithm for estimating source-dominant microphone clusters within acoustic sensor networks. Our suggested clustering technique relies on a single microphone per node and utilizes unsupervised clustered federated learning with a lightweight autoencoder model. We introduce an improved clustering control strategy that accommodates acoustic scene variability, enabling the estimation of a dynamic range of clusters with minimal training data. The approach is optimized through clustering-based metrics and validated using a network-wide classification task.

Spatial modulation (SM)-sparse code multiple access (SCMA) systems offer high spectral efficiency (SE) but require a large number of transmit antennas. To address this limitation, this letter introduces a novel uplink SM-SCMA system called rotational generalized SM-SCMA (RGSM-SCMA). The proposed system features three key contributions: a) the design and mathematical formulation of the transmitter, b) maximum likelihood and maximum a posteriori probability decoders, and c) a practical, low-complexity message passing algorithm accompanied by a complexity analysis. Simulation results and complexity evaluations demonstrate that the RGSM-SCMA system achieves the same spectral efficiency with a significant reduction in the number of transmit antennas, albeit with a slight degradation in bit error rate and a negligible increase in decoding complexity compared to standard SM-SCMA.

Typically, solving a reinforcement learning problem requires correctly defining the reward signal that guides the algorithm's learning. In this study, we tackle reward signal design by employing an evolutionary method to search the entire space of potential rewards. We present a general framework for optimizing $N$ objectives using $n$ reward signals. Experimental results show that this approach enables agents to learn high-level goals—such as winning, losing, and cooperating from scratch in the game of Pong—without any pre-specified reward signals. Notably, some solutions discovered by the algorithm are unexpected, as a human hand-coding a specific behavior would likely not have selected them. Additionally, the proposed method appears to offer greater stability in training performance compared to conventional score-based reward signals.

This text outlines the rationale for developing a quantum $S$-matrix framework for classical gravitational two-body scattering and briefly presents the derivation of black-hole metrics across different dimensions as an application.

A closed subspace remains invariant under the Cesàro operator $\mathcal{C}$ on the classical Hardy space $H^2(\mathbb D)$ if and only if its orthogonal complement is invariant under the $C_0$-semigroup of composition operators generated by the affine maps $\varphi_t(z)= e^{-t}z + 1 - e^{-t}$ for $t\geq 0$ and $z\in \mathbb D$. This finding extends to the Hardy spaces $H^p(\mathbb D)$ where $1<p<\infty$. In the Hilbert space context, we connect the invariant subspaces of $\mathcal{C}$ to the lattice of closed invariant subspaces of the standard right-shift semigroup acting on a specific weighted $L^2$-space over the line. This linkage yields a substantial collection of non-trivial closed invariant subspaces and offers a full characterization of those with finite codimension, thereby delineating the boundaries of this method for describing the entire lattice of $\mathcal{C}$'s invariant subspaces. Furthermore, utilizing a functional calculus approach, we generalize a recent theorem by Mashreghi, Ptak, and Ross concerning the square root of $\mathcal{C}$ and examine its invariant subspaces.

We introduce a hybrid superconducting-semiconducting design that links the flux degree of freedom of one mode with the charge degree of freedom of another. In the presence of external static magnetic fields, this setup generates nonreciprocity. We utilize this effect to create a passive on-chip gyrator, the essential two-port nonreciprocal component capable of enabling more complex devices like circulators. Through both analytical and numerical methods, we examine how the interaction's nonlinearity, circuit disorder, and parasitic couplings influence the gyrator's scattering response.

The Caccetta-H\"aggkvist conjecture represents a long-standing open question concerning the degree requirements necessary to ensure that an oriented graph contains a directed cycle of a specific bounded length. Driven by this conjecture, Kelly, K\"uhn, and Osthus began investigating degree conditions that guarantee the existence of directed cycles of a particular length. Specifically, they determined the optimal minimum semidegree—the lesser of the minimum indegree or outdegree—required to force a large oriented graph to contain a directed cycle of a length not divisible by 3, and they proposed a conjecture regarding the optimal semidegree for all other cycles, excluding the directed triangle. In this paper, we determine the precise minimum semidegree needed to force a large oriented graph to contain a directed cycle of a length divisible by 3 but greater than 3, thereby completely resolving the conjecture of Kelly, K\"uhn, and Osthus. Additionally, we establish an asymptotically optimal semidegree threshold for any cycle with a specified edge orientation, with the only exception being the directed triangle.

Prior to big-bang nucleosynthesis, as wavelengths corresponding to high-frequency gravitons re-enter the Hubble radius, they can be absorbed by the first and second viscosities of the post-inflationary plasma. Even when the medium's total sound speed is stiffer than that of radiation—causing the expansion rate to remain higher than the shear rate—the bulk viscosity remains significant. Depending on the entropy density at the conclusion of inflation, the spectral energy density of relic gravitons deviates from the inviscid prediction within the frequency range spanning from kHz to GHz. In the nHz domain, the spectrum retains the established suppression caused by neutrino free-streaming but may also exhibit a minor spike. This potential spike could result from an abrupt onset of bulk viscosity near the quark-hadron phase transition, a phenomenon hinted at by hadron spectra observed in heavy-ion collision experiments.

This study investigates how stochastic resetting influences the first-passage characteristics of the Feller process. Conceptually, the Feller process represents a diffusion with a space-dependent coefficient $D(x)=x$ within a potential $U(x)=x\left(\frac{x}{2}-\theta \right)$ that possesses a minimum at $\theta$. This confinement to the positive domain makes Feller diffusion an effective model for numerous biological and social phenomena where negative values are prohibited. In our analytically solvable framework, a particle experiencing Feller diffusion undergoes Poissonian resetting, meaning it is returned to its starting point at a constant rate $r$ following random time intervals. We examined two distinct scenarios based on the relative placement of the absorbing boundary ($x_a$) and the particle's initial position ($x_0$): (a) $x_0<x_a$ and (b) $x_a<x_0$. Our findings reveal that when $x_0<x_a$, resetting accelerates the first-passage time if $\theta<\theta_c$, where the critical $\theta_c$ diminishes as $x_a$ moves further from the origin. Conversely, when $x_a<x_0$, acceleration occurs when $\theta>\theta_c$, with $\theta_c$ increasing as $x_0$ recedes from the origin. This research paves the way for future investigations into more specialized Feller diffusion models incorporating resetting mechanisms.

In referential dialogue tasks, models are typically selected based on task success rates. However, we demonstrate that within the prevalent end-to-end framework, this selection criterion hinders the development of linguistically diverse dialogues because mastering language proficiency requires more time than simply learning to guess. Through a comparative analysis of models across various games—GuessWhat, GuessWhich, and Mutual Friends—we establish that this trade-off is independent of both the specific model and the task. Furthermore, we explore the conditions under which enhanced language quality might improve task performance. Our findings indicate that in the GuessWhat game, model accuracy can be boosted by training the system to ground, encode, and decode infrequent vocabulary found in the training set.

We present a novel approach for achieving time-quantitative density in flat dynamical systems. Initially, we provide a more concise and distinct proof of our previous finding: a half-infinite geodesic on any finite polysquare surface $P$ is superdense on $P$ whenever its slope is a badly approximable number. Subsequently, we modify this methodology to investigate the time-quantitative density of half-infinite geodesics on algebraic polyrectangle surfaces.

Conventional task-oriented dialog systems rely exclusively on structured knowledge sources to formulate responses. Yet, crucial information for generating answers often exists within unstructured sources like documents. Although recent advanced models such as HyKnow and SeKnow attempt to address these issues, they operate under restrictive assumptions regarding knowledge origins. For example, these systems presume that specific data types, like phone numbers, are invariably located in structured knowledge bases, whereas details such as entrance ticket prices are consistently found in documents. This paper introduces an adapted version of the MutliWOZ dataset, originally prepared by SeKnow, to illustrate how existing methods suffer significant performance drops when strict assumptions about information sources are lifted. Aligning with recent approaches leveraging pre-trained language models, we fine-tune a BART-based model using prompts for both querying knowledge sources and generating responses, without presupposing where specific information resides. Through various experiments, we demonstrate that our model remains robust against perturbations in knowledge modality and effectively integrates data from both structured and unstructured sources to produce responses.

**Context.** To create metre-sized pre-planetesimals within protoplanetary discs, growing grains must separate from the gas before being accreted by the central star during their rapid radial migration phase, thereby overcoming the so-called "radial-drift barrier" (often mistakenly termed the "metre-size barrier"). **Aims.** The study aims to forecast the radial trajectories of dust grains in protoplanetary discs characterized by surface density and temperature following power-law profiles with exponents $p$ and $q$, respectively. We examine both the Epstein and Stokes drag regimes that dictate dust motion. **Methods.** We analytically solve the equations of motion derived from perturbation analysis and compare these findings with results from direct numerical integration. Furthermore, utilizing data from observed discs, we predict the ultimate fate of dust grains in actual systems. **Results.** As dust grains reach the inner disc regions, the acceleration caused by the increasing pressure gradient is offset by the rising gas drag. We determine that most grains in the Epstein regime survive radial migration if $-p-q+1/2 \leq 0$ (and those in the Stokes regime if $q \leq 2/3$). Since the majority of observed discs satisfy both $-p-q+1/2 \leq 0$ and $q \leq 2/3$, a significant portion of both small and large grains remain within the disc, indicating that the radial drift barrier effectively does not exist for them.

Entanglement serves as the primary resource for adiabatic quantum transport. Dephasing impacts this resource by skewing trajectories and inducing transitions between successful and failed outcomes, a depletion of entanglement that holds significant implications for the practical deployment of quantum technologies. We offer a novel viewpoint on the breakdown of adiabatic computation by framing the failure of adiabatic transport as a dynamical phase transition. These concepts are illustrated using a simplified model of adiabatic transport involving a two-spin system.

Measuring contributions in cooperative game theory is a classic challenge, with the Shapley value being the most prominent solution. This paper investigates the convergence of the Shapley value within parametric Bayesian learning games, where players conduct joint Bayesian inference and the posterior-prior KL divergence serves as the characteristic function. Under specific regularity conditions, we demonstrate that for any pair of players, the difference in their Shapley values converges in probability to the difference in the Shapley values of a limiting game, where the characteristic function is proportional to the log-determinant of the joint Fisher information. We introduce an online collaborative learning framework that achieves asymptotic Shapley fairness as an application of this result. This approach eliminates the need for expensive calculations of posterior-prior KL divergences, requiring only a consistent estimator of the Fisher information. Experimental results using real-world data confirm the framework's effectiveness.

We demonstrate that massive Kalb-Ramond and Proca fields, both featuring quartic self-interactions, share an identical strong coupling scale. In the Proca framework, the longitudinal mode enters the strongly coupled regime once this scale is exceeded, whereas the two transverse modes continue to propagate and persist in the massless limit. Conversely, for the massive Kalb-Ramond field, the two transverse modes become strongly coupled beyond the Vainshtein scale, while the pseudo-scalar mode stays within the weak coupling regime and survives as the mass vanishes. These findings contradict widespread assertions in the literature claiming that these two theories are dual to one another.

Recently, machine learning has aided scientists in their research endeavors. Since human scientific theories rely on a sequence of concepts, understanding how machines derive these concepts from experimental data represents a crucial initial step. We introduce a hybrid approach designed to extract interpretable physical concepts via unsupervised machine learning. This two-stage method begins by calculating the Betti numbers of the experimental data. Subsequently, utilizing these Betti numbers, we employ a variational autoencoder network to identify significant physical variables. Finally, we validate this protocol using toy models to demonstrate its functionality.

We conducted a comprehensive modeling study of background counts in a phoswich scintillator X-ray detector deployed on a small scientific balloon for astronomical observations at balloon altitude. Utilizing the Geant4 simulation environment with Monte Carlo techniques, we estimated background contributions from various plausible sources. Under normal solar conditions, high-energy particles and radiation resulting from the interaction of Galactic Cosmic Rays with atmospheric nuclei constitute a primary source of background for such detectors. However, background levels are also significantly influenced by cosmogenic or induced radioactivity within detector materials caused by high-energy particle interactions, as well as by natural radioactive contamination present in the detector. To achieve this, we implemented detailed 3D models of the Earth's atmosphere and magnetosphere to determine the radiation environment at the balloon's altitude and employed an accurate mass model of the detector to compute background counts. These calculations successfully account for the observed background levels recorded at 30 km altitude (corresponding to an atmospheric depth of 11.5 $g/cm^{2}$) during a balloon flight experiment conducted near 14.5$^{\circ}$N geomagnetic latitude.

The Euclid imaging surveys are set to serve as a benchmark for galaxy morphology studies by providing high-resolution coverage of 15,000 square degrees. To evaluate the capabilities of measuring morphologies from Euclid-detected galaxies and to support pipeline implementation, we organized the Euclid Morphology Challenge, presented in two papers. While the companion study by Merlin et al. addresses photometry analysis, this paper focuses on the accuracy of parametric morphology measurements derived from the Euclid Wide Survey. We assessed five leading surface-brightness-fitting codes—DeepLeGATo, Galapagos-2, Morfometryka, Profit, and SourceXtractor++—using a dataset of approximately 1.5 million simulated galaxies that mimic reduced Euclid VIS and NIR observations. These simulations included both analytic S\'ersic profiles (single and two components) and more realistic galaxies generated via neural networks. Our findings indicate that, despite minor code-specific variations, all methods produce reliable structural measurements with a 10% scatter on ideal S\'ersic simulations down to an apparent magnitude of roughly 23 for single components and 21 for double components, corresponding to signal-to-noise ratios of about 1 and 5, respectively. Furthermore, we observe that testing on non-analytic profiles typically degrades results by a factor of three due to systematics. We conclude that Euclid's official Data Releases will provide robust structural parameters for at least 400 million galaxies in the Wide Survey by the mission's conclusion. Additionally, we identify that the primary factor explaining the differing behaviors of the codes at the faint end is the set of priors adopted for various structural parameters.

This study revisits the Salerno model as a representative system bridging the gap between the well-established integrable Ablowitz-Ladik lattice and the experimentally accessible, non-integrable discrete nonlinear Schrödinger model. We investigate how closely these two models align for generic initial conditions, specifically by assessing how well the conservation laws characteristic of the integrable system are maintained in the non-integrable regime. Our findings indicate that even minor departures from integrability in the Salerno model produce measurable effects on these formerly conserved quantities. However, since determining these quantities demands extensive physical and mathematical insight, we seek a more general diagnostic for detecting integrability breaking. Based on our computational results, we propose that the complete spectrum of Lyapunov exponents serves as a sensitive indicator of this phenomenon.

Nearly one hundred years after quantum mechanics emerged, a consensus on the mechanism of wavefunction collapse remains elusive. Existing theories vary widely, with some attributing collapse to conscious observation, others viewing it as a stochastic event, and the majority failing to uphold energy conservation. This paper posits that wavefunction collapse arises from interactions with other objects, whether microscopic or macroscopic, while strictly conserving energy. To evaluate competing hypotheses, we introduce a model system representing the quantum equivalent of a classical soft-impact oscillator. We further propose alternative postulates concerning the conditions and outcomes of collapse, deriving their implications for observable quantities that may be subject to experimental verification.

Ferrite is presented in this paper as a shallow embedding of session types within Rust. Unlike existing session type libraries or embeddings for mainstream languages, Ferrite uniquely supports both linear and shared session types. Shared session types enable channel sharing (aliasing) while maintaining session fidelity through type modalities that manage session acquisition and release. Utilizing a propositions-as-types approach, Ferrite encodes typing derivations as Rust functions, where a successful type-checking proof results in a valid Rust program. The authors evaluate Ferrite using Servo as a practical case study, demonstrating how Ferrite facilitates safe communication within the canvas component.

We utilize the recently generalized method of graphical functions, originally extended to six dimensions for scalar theories, to analyze $\phi^3$ theory. This approach enables us to calculate the $\beta$ function, the wave function anomalous dimension, and the mass anomalous dimension within the $\overline{\mbox{MS}}$ scheme up to five loops. Using these results, we derive the corresponding renormalization group functions for the Lee-Yang edge singularity and percolation theory. Following the determination of $\varepsilon$ expansions for the critical exponents up to $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^5)$, we employ recent resummation techniques to generate improved estimates for dimensions 3, 4, and 5. These findings align favorably with fixed-dimension numerical estimates and refine the existing four-loop results. To facilitate this comparison, we have compiled extensive data from numerical methods, organizing it into tables for each exponent.

We examine a dynamic public good contribution game in which players are naturally organized into groups. These groups are arranged in an exogenous sequence, with participants having only partial information regarding their specific position within this order. While players make their contribution choices simultaneously and independently, the aggregate contributions of the groups are revealed sequentially. Our framework aims to capture both intra-group and inter-group dynamics, specifically analyzing scenarios where players observe partial histories of total contributions from preceding groups. Within this structure, we demonstrate that a cooperative outcome remains achievable even if players witness a history of defection (zero contribution). This finding is especially significant when players observe only the contributions of their immediate predecessors, as we find that players play a crucial role in motivating others to contribute.

This work examines the semigroup produced by the hypoelliptic Laplacian on the circle and its maximal bounded holomorphic extension. By employing an orthogonal decomposition involving harmonic oscillators with complex shifts, we characterize the domain of this extension and demonstrate that boundedness within a half-plane is equivalent to the absolute convergence of the semigroup's expansion in eigenfunctions. This result depends on a new integral formula for spectral projections, which further provides asymptotic behavior for Laguerre polynomials in the large-parameter limit.

SaLinA is a straightforward library designed to simplify the implementation of intricate sequential learning models, such as reinforcement learning algorithms. Built as a PyTorch extension, it ensures that algorithms developed with \SALINA{} are easily comprehensible and modifiable for PyTorch users within minutes. Furthermore, SaLinA natively supports training and testing across multiple CPUs and GPUs, making it ideal for large-scale applications. Compared to other existing RL libraries, SaLinA offers a minimal adoption barrier while supporting a wide range of settings, including model-based, batch, hierarchical, and multi-agent RL. Beyond targeting RL practitioners, the library aims to equip any deep learning programmer with robust sequential learning capabilities.

Distribution testing involves drawing $q$ samples from an unknown distribution $P$ defined over a known domain $[n]$. Following the sampling phase, one must determine whether $P$ possesses a specific property or is significantly distant from it. The most prominent challenge in this field is uniformity testing, which requires distinguishing between a distribution $P$ that is uniform over $[n]$ and one that is $\epsilon$-far from uniform in the $\ell_1$ metric. In the standard setting, it is established that $\Theta\left(\sqrt{n}/\epsilon^2\right)$ samples are both necessary and sufficient for this task. Recent research has explored this problem under restricted models, such as those with communication or memory limitations. Frequently, the optimal solution in these scenarios involves counting collisions among the drawn samples—where each matching pair increments a counter—an approach originating from the first uniformity tester and termed the "collision-based tester."

This paper introduces the concept of comparison graphs to formally define a generalized collision-based tester. Conceptually, the graph's edges specify which pairs of samples the tester should compare, with the original tester corresponding to a clique where every pair is compared. We establish a structural theorem providing a sufficient condition for a comparison graph to yield an effective uniformity tester. As an application, we propose a generic framework for testing uniformity and construct nearly-optimal testers under diverse computational constraints. Our approach improves and simplifies several existing results and introduces a new constrained model where our method yields an efficient tester. The core methodology involves translating the computational constraints of a specific model into constraints on the comparison graph, thereby facilitating the identification of an optimal graph structure.

Low energy ion scattering (LEIS) is a method used to determine the energy of ions scattered off a surface. When utilizing noble gas ions, the technique is primarily sensitive to the outermost atomic layer because of efficient neutralization processes. However, depending on the specific projectile ion and target material, scattering spectra may also show contributions from multiple scattering events within deeper layers; this occurs when probing ions are re-ionized during their exit trajectory. Such events generate a distinct continuum extending toward lower scattering energies relative to the primary direct scattering peak. While a prior study by Nelson (1986) provided a semi-empirical formula for fitting spectra and extracting quantitative data, the current work derives an enhanced formula that reduces numerical artifacts and offers greater numerical stability.

We introduce a generalized Eulerian-Lagrangian (GEL) discontinuous Galerkin (DG) approach, extending the Eulerian-Lagrangian (EL) DG method for transport problems detailed in [arXiv preprint arXiv: 2002.02930 (2020)]. This extension tracks solutions along characteristic approximations within the DG framework, enabling enhanced stability with significantly larger time steps.
