Extensive experiments on the Stanford image-paragraph dataset demonstrate the method's effectiveness and efficiency, achieving a 38.4% performance improvement over state-of-the-art approaches.

We develop a unified framework for the ${\cal N}=1$ supersymmetric extension of Double Field Theory applicable to both Riemannian and non-Riemannian geometries. The necessity of incorporating fermions into double geometry compels the use of a generalized frame formalism to derive the corresponding generalized flux components. Our analysis centers on the most comprehensive prescription needed to formulate the $D=10$ minimal supergravity model. We investigate methods to consistently circumvent the gauge fixing of double Lorentz symmetry within the range $0\le n \le 5$ where $n=\bar n$, resulting in a bigravity structure characterized by a pair of vielbeins that yield identical non-Riemannian degrees of freedom. As a specific illustration, we demonstrate the inclusion of fermionic degrees of freedom within the type I torsional Newton-Cartan (TNC) theory ($n=\bar n=1$), which connects to Carrollian geometries and stringy Newton-Cartan via duality rotations and/or null reductions or uplifts.

DeepReg (https://github.com/DeepRegNet/DeepReg) is an open-source toolkit supported by the community, designed for research and educational purposes in medical image registration through the application of deep learning.

Strong-field photoemission from nanostructures and the resulting temporally modulated currents are pivotal for advancing ultrafast vacuum optoelectronics, with optical light fields potentially extending operational bandwidths into the petahertz regime. A crucial factor for their practical application is the influence of charge interactions, particularly space charge effects. This study examines photoemission and photocurrents generated by nanometric tungsten needle tips under carrier-envelope phase-controlled few-cycle laser fields. We observe a distinct step-wise rise in intensity-rescaled cutoff energies of emitted electrons above a specific intensity threshold. Comparing these findings with simulations allows us to attribute this phenomenon to the onset of photoemission dynamics dominated by charge interactions. These results are expected to hold significance for strong-field photoemission from other nanostructures, such as plasmonic nano-bowtie antennas utilized in carrier-envelope phase detection and petahertz-scale devices.

1. Inferring ecological interactions is challenging due to the frequent absence of appropriate parametric models. Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs) offer a nonparametric solution for estimating these interactions from time-series data; however, they suffer from slow training speeds and a lack of validation against ground truth.
2. We introduce Bayesian Neural Gradient Matching (BNGM), a rapid NODE fitting technique that interpolates time-series data using neural networks and applies Bayesian regularization to fit NODEs to the resulting dynamics. We evaluated this method's accuracy by inferring interactions in synthetic data generated by an ODE model with known parameters. Additionally, we applied BNGM to experimentally replicated time-series from a microcosm involving algae, flagellates, and rotifers, as well as the classic hare and lynx system.
3. Our BNGM approach reduces NODE fitting time to merely a few seconds. In artificial systems, the method yields accurate estimates of both linear and nonlinear interactions with minimal error. In real-world systems, dynamics arise from a mix of linear and nonlinear interactions, with only the most robust interactions remaining consistent across different experimental replicates.
4. In summary, NODEs eliminate the necessity for a pre-existing mechanistic understanding of interactions, while BNGM addresses their high computational cost. This advancement facilitates rapid NODE fitting, cross-validation, and uncertainty quantification, enabling a more objective estimation of interactions and their complex context-dependencies compared to traditional parametric models.

Quantum cellular automata (QCAs), characterized by unitary dynamics within a strict causal or "light cone," have been widely investigated, with a complete classification of one-dimensional QCAs established via index theory. Since physical systems typically display only approximate causal structures—where lattice Hamiltonian evolutions obey Lieb-Robinson bounds instead of strict locality—we investigate approximately locality preserving unitaries (ALPUs). We demonstrate that the index theory remains robust and fully applies to one-dimensional ALPUs. Consequently, we derive a converse to the Lieb-Robinson bounds: any ALPU with an index of zero can be precisely generated by a time-dependent, quasi-local Hamiltonian within a constant duration. Specifically, for finite chains with open boundaries, any unitary adhering to the Lieb-Robinson bound admits such a Hamiltonian generator. Additionally, we present findings regarding the stability of operator algebras, which may hold independent significance.

The paper presents simulation results detailing the performance and computational complexity of the sequential successive cancellation decoding algorithm, specifically for polar subcodes utilizing Arikan and large kernels, as well as extended BCH codes. A performance comparison is also provided against Arikan PAC and LDPC codes. Additionally, a comprehensive description of the decoding algorithm is included.

This paper investigates a dual-hop cooperative communication system linking a satellite (S) to a fleet of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) via cluster headers (CHs). These CHs, positioned alongside groups of uniformly distributed UAVs, function as aerial decode-and-forward relays to transmit data from the satellite. The architecture employs free-space optical (FSO) technology for the S-CH links to leverage high directivity over long distances, while radio frequency (RF) is utilized for CH-UAV links to ensure omnidirectional coverage. The spatial distribution of the CHs in three-dimensional space adheres to a Matern hard-core point process of type-II, ensuring a minimum separation distance between any two headers. The performance analysis models three distinct scenarios for the CH-UAV links: interference-free, interference-dominated, and combined interference-and-noise environments. Consequently, the study derives closed-form analytical expressions for the coverage probability (CP) of both the S-CH and CH-UAV links under these conditions, alongside asymptotic expressions for the interference-free scenario. Numerical simulations are presented to verify the proposed analytical models, leading to several meaningful conclusions.

For bounded Lebesgue measurable functions $f,g,\phi,$ and $\psi$ defined on the unit circle, the expression $P_{+}fP_{+}+P_{-}gP_{+} +P_{+}\phi P_{-}+P_{-}\psi P_{-}$ is termed a generalized singular integral operator (GSIO) on $L^{2}(\mathbb{T})$, where $P_{+}$ denotes the Riesz projection and $P_{-}=I-P_{+}$. This paper connects GSIOs to several other operators, such as the Cauchy singular integral operator, (dual) truncated Toeplitz operator, Foguel-Hankel operator, multiplication operator, and Toeplitz plus Hankel operator. We derive the short exact sequences linked to the $C^{*}$-algebras generated by GSIOs with bounded or quasi-continuous symbols. Consequently, we determine the spectra of various GSIO classes, establish the spectral inclusion theorem, and compute the Fredholm index for these operators. Furthermore, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the invertibility (and Fredholmness) of GSIOs utilizing Wiener-Hopf factorization.

The Gaia DR2 catalog currently represents the premier source for stellar astrometric and photometric information, effectively recording the Milky Way's evolutionary history. By analyzing parallaxes and photometry, astronomers can determine current stellar positions, formation epochs, and chemical compositions, thereby reconstructing the star formation history (SFH). We have constructed a Bayesian hierarchical model specifically designed to rebuild the SFH of resolved stellar populations. Focusing on stars brighter than $G=15$ within 100 parsecs of the Sun, we derived the SFH of the solar neighborhood. Our findings align with prior studies but offer improvements by accounting for chemical enrichment. The results indicate a peak in star formation activity approximately 10 billion years ago, generating numerous stars with sub-solar metallicity ($Z=0.014$), followed by a decline to a minimum around 8 billion years ago. Subsequent to a quiet interval, star formation surged to a second peak roughly 5 billion years ago, creating stars with solar metallicity ($Z=0.017$). Since then, star formation has gradually decreased to current residual levels, producing stars with $Z=0.03$. Additionally, we evaluated the impact of ignoring unresolved binary stars, lowering the limiting magnitude threshold, and altering the stellar initial mass function on the inferred SFH.

We introduce a novel architecture designed for forecasting human actions from video sequences. This system utilizes a temporal recurrent encoder to extract temporal information from input videos and incorporates a self-attention mechanism to focus on pertinent feature dimensions within the input space. To address temporal variations in the observed video data, we implement a feature masking technique. Additionally, an auxiliary classifier is employed to accurately classify observed actions, thereby enhancing the system's understanding of past events. Subsequently, the decoder predicts future actions by leveraging outputs from both the recurrent encoder and the self-attention model. Through experiments, we validate each component of our architecture, demonstrating the specific contributions of self-attention in identifying relevant features, the effectiveness of temporal masking, and the utility of the auxiliary classifier. Finally, our method is evaluated on two standard action forecasting benchmarks, yielding state-of-the-art performance.

We continue to investigate two-dimensional laterally propagating flames in type I X-ray bursts using fully compressible hydrodynamics simulations. In the current study we relax previous approximations where we artificially boosted the flames. We now use more physically realistic reaction rates, thermal conductivities, and rotation rates, exploring the effects of neutron star rotation rate and thermal structure on the flame. We find that at lower rotation rates the flame becomes harder to ignite, whereas at higher rotation rates the nuclear burning is enhanced by increased confinement from the Coriolis force and the flame propagates steadily. At higher crustal temperatures, the flame moves more quickly and accelerates as it propagates through the atmosphere. If the temperature is too high, instead of a flame propagating across the surface the entire atmosphere burns steadily. All of the software used for these simulations is freely available.

We introduce a composite layered architecture designed for tunable, low-loss plasmon resonances, comprising a noble-metal thin film encapsulated by graphene and resting on a hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) substrate. Through electron energy loss spectra (EELS) calculations, we numerically show that adding a graphene layer and an hBN substrate significantly suppresses bulk plasmon losses in noble-metal films while enhancing surface coupling. Specifically, silver films featuring a trilayer graphene coating and an hBN substrate exhibited surface-plasmon-dominated spectral profiles even for metallic layers up to 34 nm thick. To systematically illustrate plasmon peak tunability across various configurations, we employed a continued-fraction expression for the effective dielectric function, grounded in a specular reflection model that accounts for boundary interactions. These variations encompass changes in the substrate, plasmonic metal, and individual layer thicknesses. The mesoscale EELS calculations utilized individual layer dielectric functions as inputs for the effective dielectric function computation, directly yielding the resulting loss spectra.

Ultracold atoms and molecules confined within optical lattices are anticipated to function as simulators for strongly correlated systems and topological matter states. A particularly intriguing prospect involves employing ultracold polar molecules to realize the Kitaev quantum spin liquid. Although proposals exist for implementing Kitaev-type interactions experimentally, the stability of the resulting quantum spin liquid has not yet been thoroughly examined. In this study, we analyze a quantum spin model featuring long-range, angle-dependent Kitaev-type interactions suitable for polar molecules using the pseudofermion functional renormalization group method. Our findings indicate that the ground state exhibits magnetic ordering in both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic configurations, irrespective of the spatial anisotropy of the interactions, with the isotropic case presenting the highest level of frustration and coming closest to realizing the Kitaev quantum spin liquid. Additionally, by applying a cutoff to the interaction range, we demonstrate how long-range interactions disrupt the formation of the Kitaev quantum spin liquid. These results necessitate a reevaluation of the feasibility of achieving the Kitaev quantum spin liquid in systems of ultracold polar molecules.

Sound modelling involves creating algorithms capable of producing sound under parametric control. Historically, three primary approaches have emerged: simulating the physics of sound generation and propagation, combining signal processing and generation components to replicate acoustic characteristics, and manipulating collections of recorded audio samples. Although each method has successfully achieved high-quality synthesis and interaction for particular use cases, they remain labor-intensive and present unique challenges when designing flexible control strategies. Conversely, recent generative deep learning systems for audio synthesis can learn to navigate arbitrary sound spaces defined by their training data. Additionally, machine learning offers novel techniques for crafting control and navigation strategies for these models. This paper reviews how advancements in deep learning are transforming the practice of sound modelling.

The analysis determines the status and parameters of scalar, vector, and tensor mesonic resonances, comparing these findings with other studies. Additionally, the possible classification of these resonance states into SU(3) multiplets is examined.

Utilizing density functional theory combined with semi-classical Boltzmann transport theory, this study explores how strain and temperature modulate the thermoelectric characteristics of monolayer MoS$_2$. Increasing tensile strain narrows the electronic band gap, inducing a semiconductor-to-metal transition at $10\%$ biaxial strain. Generally, tensile strain diminishes thermopower and the power factor, particularly affecting p-type carriers more significantly. Furthermore, anharmonic phonon analysis reveals that tensile strain, especially uniaxial strain along the zig-zag direction, markedly lowers thermal conductivity in ML-MoS$_2$. This reduction is driven by decreased phonon relaxation times, a widened gap between ZA and optical phonon frequencies, and a shift in the Debye temperature. Consequently, the simultaneous decrease in thermal conductivity and increase in power factor under zig-zag tensile strain synergistically enhance efficiency and overall thermoelectric performance. Additionally, thermoelectric efficiency rises with temperature, indicating potential for high-temperature applications. Optimal doping concentrations can yield nearly a 75% boost in efficiency. Thus, in-plane tensile strain emerges as a critical factor for improving ML-MoS$_2$'s thermoelectric capabilities, offering promising prospects for future developments in 2D thermoelectrics.

Recommender systems are crucial for aiding information retrieval and decision-making in today's digital landscape, yet their widespread use raises significant data privacy concerns. These issues are mitigated by the European "General Data Protection Regulation" (GDPR), which mandates that companies erase personal data upon request under the "right to be forgotten." Many experts contend that this obligation extends beyond primary storage databases to include machine learning models trained on the data to be removed. This study investigates this requirement within the Next Basket Recommendation (NBR) framework, where the objective is to suggest items based on a user's purchase history. We develop efficient algorithms for both incrementally and decrementally updating a state-of-the-art NBR model in response to the addition or removal of user baskets and items. Additionally, we present an efficient, data-parallel implementation of our approach using Spark Structured Streaming. Evaluations on various real-world datasets reveal the impact of our update techniques on ranking metrics and the time required for model adjustments. Our findings demonstrate that the method achieves constant-time efficiency for incremental updates regarding new user baskets and linear efficiency for decremental updates involving basket deletion. With modest computational resources, we achieve a model update latency of approximately 0.2 milliseconds in the incremental case, independent of history size, and under one millisecond in the decremental case.

For decades, deciphering the microscopic characteristics of LiNiO$_2$, a Li-ion battery cathode material renowned for its exceptionally high reversible capacity, has proven to be a persistent challenge. Leveraging comprehensive electronic structure calculations that uncover numerous nearly degenerate phases—characterized by local Jahn-Teller effects and both bond and oxygen-based charge disproportionation—we suggest that LiNiO$_2$ resides in a high-entropy charge-glass-like state at and below ambient temperatures. Acknowledging the glassy nature of LiNiO$_2$ not only elucidates its primary experimental observations but also paves the way for developing entropy-stabilized battery cathodes with outstanding capacities.

Cooperative ad hoc unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) networks require critical security services to protect their communications, a task that relies heavily on cryptography and a robust key management system. However, the lack of infrastructure in these cooperative environments renders traditional key management schemes impractical. While key pre-distribution schemes have demonstrated promising performance in various cooperative networks due to their lightweight design, they are hindered by issues such as intermediate decryption-encryption (DE) steps and an inability to update keys. This paper introduces a simple and efficient key management algorithm inspired by pre-distribution concepts, which leverages the high mobility of UAV nodes in three-dimensional space to enable key updates and minimize intermediate DE operations. Although applicable to any mobile ad hoc network, we utilize UAV networks as a specific domain to demonstrate the model's efficiency under high mobility conditions. We define a communication density parameter to analytically prove that the algorithm remains effective regardless of highly dynamic random movement patterns. Using the ns-3 network simulator, we conducted an exhaustive analysis of the algorithm's security and performance within a UAV network context. The results confirm our analytical predictions and illustrate how the dynamic movement of UAVs facilitates key updates and optimizes the number of DE steps.

Assuming $0<t\le 1$ and a constant $C>0$, we demonstrate that for any $s$ satisfying $t/2\le s<t$, there exists a finite subset $\Omega\subset S^1$ with the following property: for every $t$-Ahlfors-David regular set $E\subset [0,1)^2$ having a regular constant no greater than $C$, the maximum of the upper box dimensions of the orthogonal projections $\pi_e(E)$ (where $e\in \Omega$) is at least $s$. While Orponen (2016) previously established this result for the case $t=1$, our findings extend its implications. Specifically, we prove the existence of a countable subset $\Omega\subset S^1$ such that for any $t$-Ahlfors-David regular set $E\subseteq [0,1)^2$ with $0<t\le 2$, the supremum of the upper box dimensions of the projections $\pi_e(E)$ over $e\in \Omega$ equals $\min\{t, 1\}$. Furthermore, when $0<t\le 1$, we show that there exist $t$-Ahlfors-David regular sets for which this supremum is not achieved.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are emerging as effective platforms for sensing and estimation across diverse fields such as disaster relief, search and rescue, and security surveillance. However, these sensing UAVs face constraints in battery life and computational power, necessitating data offloading to generate actionable insights. This study examines a computing infrastructure comprising a small fleet of well-equipped UAVs serving as mobile edge computing (MEC) servers to handle workloads locally. We introduce a novel distributed framework for collaborative processing that dynamically repositions MEC UAVs to adapt to workload fluctuations caused by both the movement of sensing UAVs and task generation. Our approach relies on two core components: (1) an efficient workload estimation mechanism that approximates the spatial distribution of pending tasks across the airspace, and (2) a distributed optimization strategy that partitions this task field to maximize system throughput. Using realistic simulations of surveillance UAV mobility, we demonstrate that our method yields up to a 28% throughput gain compared to a static, non-adaptive baseline.

Deep learning is transforming predictive healthcare, particularly in suggesting treatments for patients with complex conditions. While current methods typically predict all medications for a single visit—often duplicating prescriptions from prior visits—a more clinically meaningful objective is identifying specific medication changes. To address this, we introduce MICRON, a novel recurrent residual network designed for predicting medication adjustments. MICRON accepts changes in patient health records as input and recurrently updates a hidden medication vector and the medication set using a reconstruction mechanism. Functioning as a memory cell, this vector encodes the longitudinal history of medications. Unlike traditional approaches that necessitate full patient histories for prediction, MICRON employs residual-based inference to sequentially update based solely on new features, such as recent diagnoses, thereby enhancing efficiency. Evaluated on real-world inpatient and outpatient datasets, MICRON outperformed the best baseline models with relative F1 score improvements of 3.5% and 7.8%, respectively. Furthermore, by requiring fewer parameters, MICRON significantly accelerates training, reducing the time per epoch to 38.3 seconds, a 1.5x speed-up.

This study establishes bounds for the eigenvalues of saddle-point matrices featuring singular leading blocks, utilizing a proof strategy grounded in augmentation. The derived bounds are contingent upon the principal angles existing between the ranges or kernels of the constituent matrix blocks. Subsequent numerical experiments confirm the validity of these analytical results.

Grasping neutrino flavor transformation within dense settings like core-collapse supernovae (CCSN) is essential for deducing nucleosynthesis and analyzing detected neutrino signals. The impact of direction-altering collisions on the neutrino flavor field in these regions is significant yet inadequately understood, as it has not been addressed self-consistently. Although numerical integration has advanced the inclusion of collision effects in flavor dynamics, this method is constrained by the necessity of knowing complete initial conditions. Conversely, the feedback from collisions to the neutrino field constitutes a boundary value problem, which standard integration techniques struggle to resolve. This study demonstrates that an inference-based formulation can solve a simplified collision-only model of a CCSN core without requiring full prior knowledge of initial conditions. Instead, the approach resolves a two-point boundary value problem using partial information at the boundaries. Given the model's simplicity, physical reasoning can validate the inference-derived solution, which successfully recovers anticipated model dynamics. These findings indicate that inference can address challenges artificially obscured to integration methods—a key aspect of flavor evolution in dense environments—making it valuable to investigate augmenting current robust integration tools with inference-based strategies.

The Error-Related Potential (ErrP) serves as a distinct cortical marker linked to a Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) user's awareness of mistakes, and integrating ErrP detection can enhance BCI efficacy. This study pursues three objectives: first, assessing whether an ErrP classifier can be transferred from able-bodied individuals to those with spinal cord injuries (SCI); second, evaluating this generic classifier with both SCI and control subjects in an uncalibrated online setting; and third, analyzing the morphological characteristics of ErrPs across both groups. The research utilized pre-existing EEG data from able-bodied participants to train the classifier. This model was then tested asynchronously in an online experiment involving 16 new subjects (eight with SCI and eight able-bodied controls) without prior offline calibration. Throughout the session, participants received immediate feedback on ErrP detections, and while the classifier itself was not trained on individual brain signals, personalized decision thresholds were applied during the experiment to optimize performance. Results indicated that SCI participants exhibited non-homogeneous ErrP morphology, with four failing to show clear signals. The generic classifier performed above chance levels in participants displaying clear ErrP signals, regardless of SCI status (11 out of 16). Among the five participants achieving chance-level results with the generic model, three would likely not have gained advantages from a personalized classifier. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the feasibility of transferring ErrP classifiers from able-bodied users to SCI patients for asynchronous, uncalibrated online detection that provides immediate user feedback.

We introduce a Model Predictive Control (MPC) approach for collision-free navigation that leverages amortized variational inference to approximate the distribution of optimal control sequences. By training a normalizing flow conditioned on the start point, goal, and environment, this method captures robot dynamics and complex obstacle geometries. Sampling from this distribution within our proposed FlowMPPI framework yields control sequences that are both goal-oriented and collision-free. However, the robot may encounter out-of-distribution (OOD) environments that differ significantly from training data, rendering the learned flow unreliable for generating low-cost sequences. To address this, we present a generalization strategy that projects the environment representation during the MPC process, transforming it into a more in-distribution form while optimizing trajectory quality in the actual environment. Simulation results on a 2D double-integrator and a 3D 12DoF underactuated quadrotor demonstrate that FlowMPPI with projection surpasses state-of-the-art MPC baselines in both in-distribution and OOD settings, including those derived from real-world data.

We derive novel constraints on $f(T)$ gravity models by analyzing cosmological data, specifically focusing on gas mass fractions within galaxy clusters and transverse BAO measurements, both of which exhibit weak dependence on a fiducial cosmology. Our analysis further incorporates CMB temperature power spectrum data from the first peak, $H(z)$ measurements from cosmic chronometers, and Pantheon supernova data. Additionally, we project future constraints on the deviation of $f(T)$ models from the $\Lambda$CDM scenario based on the specifications of the J-PAS and Euclid surveys, revealing substantial improvements in the precision of the $b$-parameter constraints compared to current statistical analyses.

This study investigates coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy (CARS) within air-filled anti-resonance hollow-core photonic crystal fiber, commonly referred to as "revolver" fiber. We compare the CARS vibrational signal of N$_2$ at 2331 cm$^{-1}$ produced in ambient air without the fiber against the signal generated within a 2.96 cm section of revolver fiber. Our results demonstrate a 170-fold enhancement of the signal in the fiber, attributed to an extended interaction path. Notably, the N$_2$ signal from the revolver fiber exhibits a near-zero non-resonant background, resulting from minimal overlap between the laser field and the fiber cladding. Consequently, our findings indicate that revolver fibers are highly suitable for enhancing coherent Raman spectroscopy signals.

We identify and analyze self-similar solutions to the Airy equations, which correspond to the dispersionless nonlinear Schrödinger equation expressed in Madelung coordinates, focusing on their complete integrability and their function within the recurrence relation of a bi-Hamiltonian structure. This specific class of solutions transforms the partial differential equations into a finite system of ordinary differential equations that possesses multiple conserved quantities. These quantities enable the construction of explicit solutions via quadratures and yield a bi-Hamiltonian formulation for the resulting reduced ODEs.

We incorporate transient reductions in the inflaton's speed of sound into our search for features within the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) angular power spectrum, utilizing Planck 2018 data on temperature, polarization, and lensing. We introduce a novel methodology employing Gaussian Processes to test more flexible templates for reconstructing these speed-of-sound reductions. By applying a \textit{maximum-entropy} approach, we formally derive a dynamical prior for the reduction's shape to ensure adherence to physical model constraints. The resulting posterior analysis accommodates one or more consecutive reductions, effectively fitting apparent features across CMB power spectrum multipoles ranging from tens to $\ell\simeq 2000$. As anticipated, these fits do not demonstrate statistical preference over the $\Lambda$CDM model. However, the developed methodology facilitates the integration of additional datasets, particularly Large Scale Structure data, which could theoretically enhance the statistical significance of reconstructing the inflaton's speed of sound.

Data-driven methods have significantly enhanced oil and gas logging data processing, with deep learning further solidifying these gains. However, deep learning applications are often restricted to domains where researchers have access to vast quantities of high-quality data. To address this limitation, we propose a method that generates universal data representations adaptable to various oil fields and specific problems with minimal additional data. By employing a self-supervised approach for sequential logging data from well intervals, our method eliminates the initial need for labeled data. To validate the efficacy of these representations, we examined classification, clustering, and transfer learning scenarios. Our results indicate that a variational autoencoder yields the most reliable and accurate models. Furthermore, we found that researchers require only a small, separate dataset from the target oil field to solve specific problems when leveraging these universal representations.

This paper presents a boundary value problem linked to the difference equation with an advanced argument given by $\Delta\bigl (a_{n}\Phi(\Delta x_{n})\bigr)+b_{n}\Phi(x_{n+p} )=0$ for $n\geq1$, where $\Phi(u)=|u|^{\alpha}$sgn $u$, $\alpha>0$, $p$ is a positive integer, and the sequences $a$ and $b$ are positive. We focus on a specific class of decaying solutions for this equation, termed "intermediate solutions," and provide their definition later in the text. Specifically, we establish the existence of these solutions by transforming the original equation into an equivalent boundary value problem for a difference equation without deviating arguments. Our methodology relies on a fixed point theorem for difference equations, which is derived from analogous results in the continuous domain. The paper concludes with several examples and recommendations for future research.

This study investigates the transfer of $n$-qubit and $n$-photon states utilizing two-photon exchange interactions among $n$ coupled optical cavities, each hosting a single three-level atom. Extending the methodology of Ref.\cite{Alex1}, which originally addressed two cavities, we analyze the dynamics within an $n$-cavity system to generalize findings regarding quantum state transfer, inter-cavity photon transitions, and entanglement generation across $n$ atoms. Specifically, leveraging the symmetry of the Hamiltonian associated with photon number conservation, the system's Hamiltonian is reduced from a $3^n$-dimensional space to a $2n$-dimensional subspace. Furthermore, by defining a Fourier-transform-based basis for the atom-cavity state space, this reduced Hamiltonian is block-diagonalized into $2 \times 2$ blocks. Finally, the system's evolution under this Hamiltonian is examined to identify specific times $T$, dependent on the inter-cavity hopping strength $\xi$, at which initially unentangled atoms achieve maximal entanglement.

Concurrent time series frequently appear in diverse fields, ranging from environmental monitoring—such as air quality networks, weather stations, oceanographic buoys, and paleo-data like lake sediments, tree rings, ice cores, and coral isotopes—to other domains including stock prices, neurological signals, and quality control processes. In each of these scenarios, individual sites generate a time series, and the objective is to isolate a shared temporal trend or signal. To achieve this, we investigate the properties of Maximum Autocorrelation Factors (MAF), a technique that linearly combines multiple time series to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) when smooth signals are present. We demonstrate the equivalence between MAF and Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) within a regression framework, highlighting that MAF operates without requiring prior knowledge of the specific signal structure, unlike CCA. Furthermore, we derive the theoretical characteristics of MAF, quantify its SNR superiority over Principal Components Analysis (PCA)—a standard method for linearly combining time series—and compare their statistical properties based on samples. Finally, we apply both MAF and PCA to real and simulated datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of MAF.

If the Moon's rotation originated with faster prograde speeds, it might have settled into a spin-orbit resonance higher than the current 1:1 state. Given the present orbital eccentricity, the likelihood of locking into a 3:2 resonance reaches approximately 0.6, though this is heavily influenced by the interior's temperature and average viscosity. A warmer, less viscous Moon traveling a more eccentric path would be even more prone to capturing into supersynchronous resonances. We examine two probable explanations for its current spin-orbit configuration: a cold Moon on a low-eccentricity orbit or an initial retrograde rotation.

Since digital computers generally cannot compute elementary functions like sine and exponential exactly, they must rely on approximations. Standard library implementations often offer limited precision and insufficient efficiency for various applications. In contrast, polynomial approximations tailored to specific input domains and accuracy requirements can achieve superior performance. Although the Remez algorithm generates the optimal polynomial approximation for a given degree, it has not yet been formally verified. This paper introduces Dandelion, a fully verified automated certificate checker for polynomial approximations derived from Remez-like algorithms, implemented within the HOL4 theorem prover. Dandelion validates whether the discrepancy between a polynomial approximation and its target elementary function stays within a specified error bound across a defined set of constraints. By utilizing the CakeML compiler to extract a verified binary, Dandelion can validate these certificates efficiently, thereby fully automating processes that were previously handled through manual verification.

This study utilizes acoustic Doppler current profiler (ADCP) data collected by underwater gliders to estimate the glider's position, velocity, and subsurface currents. Since ADCPs do not directly measure these target quantities but rather the relative motion between the vehicle and the water column, we analyze the history of mathematical approaches applied to this challenge. Our review reveals an unstated yet erroneous assumption of independence in prior work. We reformulate a recent technique to establish a joint probability model linking current dynamics and vehicle navigation, thereby correcting this flaw and extending the classic Kalman smoothing framework. Comprehensive simulations validate the effectiveness of our method for generating accurate estimates and quantifying uncertainty. The resulting joint model provides a foundation for future research, enabling the integration of constraints, range measurements, and robust statistical modeling.

This study addresses the challenge of determining upper bounds for the dimension of Hilbert cubes within a finite field $\mathbb{F}_p$ that lacks primitive roots. We demonstrate that for any $\epsilon > 0$, the dimension of these cubes is bounded by $O_{\epsilon}(p^{1/8+\epsilon})$, a result that aligns with the classical Burgess estimate specifically when the Hilbert cube takes the form of an arithmetic progression. Furthermore, we examine the complementary problem of establishing bounds for the dimension of multiplicative Hilbert cubes that avoid a given interval.

The quasi-one-dimensional, narrow-gap semiconductor $\mathrm{Ta_2NiSe_5}$ is hypothesized to transition into an excitonic insulator at $T_\mathrm{c}=326$ K. Our findings reveal a distinct anomaly in the in-plane thermal conductivities, measured both parallel ($\parallel$ $a$) and perpendicular ($\parallel$ $c$) to the one-dimensional chains ($\kappa_\mathrm{a}$ and $\kappa_\mathrm{c}$), at this critical temperature. Specifically, $\kappa_\mathrm{a}$ exhibits a sharp decline below $T_\mathrm{c}$, whereas $\kappa_\mathrm{c}$ displays a prominent V-shaped reduction centered at $T_\mathrm{c}$. We attribute the drop in $\kappa_\mathrm{a}$ to the suppression of quasiparticle contributions resulting from excitonic condensation. Conversely, the V-shaped suppression in $\kappa_\mathrm{c}$ arises from enhanced phonon scattering driven by soft phonons linked to the monoclinic phase transition with momentum $\mathbf{q}\parallel c$. Furthermore, the fact that $\kappa_\mathrm{c}$ remains suppressed well above $T_\mathrm{c}$ indicates that phonon softening likely persists, potentially coupled to electronic, and presumably excitonic, fluctuations.
This paper introduces left ideal low-rank parity-check codes via group algebras and subsequently leverages them to extend the ROLLO-I KEM.

We demonstrate that difficult-to-detect characteristics of quadratic ODEs, such as specific conserved integrals and measures, can be largely derived algorithmically from their Kahan discretization by utilizing Darboux Polynomials. Comparable findings apply to ODEs of higher degree or order when employing particular birational discretization techniques.

Since mass loss is intrinsic to massive stars, interaction with circumstellar material (CSM) should be a universal characteristic of core-collapse supernovae (SNe). Focusing on CSM densities, extents, and masses typical of Type II SNe—excluding the extreme conditions found in Type IIn events—we examine the varied long-term radiative signatures resulting from the interaction between Type II ejecta and CSM with mass loss rates reaching $10^{-3} M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$. Given that this CSM is relatively tenuous and optically thin to electron scattering beyond a few stellar radii, radiation hydrodynamics is unnecessary; instead, the interaction can be modeled directly as an additional power source within a non-local thermodynamic equilibrium radiative transfer framework. The CSM accumulated prior to shock breakout creates a dense shell in the outer ejecta, generating high-velocity absorption features in spectral lines even when shock power is negligible. Beyond Balmer lines, such features can appear in NaID and HeI lines. Enhanced interaction intensifies the continuum flux (primarily in the UV), suppresses the absorption components of P-Cygni profiles, amplifies the MgII $\lambda\lambda$ 2795,2802 doublet, and promotes the formation of a broad, boxy H$\alpha$ emission component. Increased ionization in the outer ejecta may also extinguish certain lines, such as the CaII near-infrared triplet. The interaction power predominantly emerges in the UV, especially at later stages, shifting the optical color toward the blue while modestly boosting optical luminosity. However, strong thermalization and clumping appear necessary to render an interaction superluminous in the optical. The UV spectrum holds essential signatures that offer critical constraints for deducing the mass loss history and internal dynamics of core-collapse SN progenitors at the time of their death.

This study examines stochastic differential equations (SDEs) influenced by fractional Brownian motion, featuring a drift coefficient $b$ that can approach criticality in a scaling manner. We establish a robust solution framework encompassing strong existence, pathwise uniqueness, the existence of a diffeomorphic solution flow, Malliavin differentiability, and $\rho$-irregularity. These results yield significant implications for McKean-Vlasov, transport, and continuity equations.

This research investigates analogues of radial subalgebras in free group factors, known as class function algebras, within the framework of compact quantum groups. Specifically, for free orthogonal quantum groups, we demonstrate that these algebras fail to be maximal abelian subalgebras (MASAs) whenever the group is non-Kac. A central concept in this study is that of a (quasi-)split inclusion. We establish that the inclusion of class function algebras is quasi-split for certain unitary quantum groups; notably, in these instances, the subalgebra is non-abelian, and we derive a result regarding its relative commutant. Conversely, we construct specific bicrossed products based on the quantum group $SU_q(2)$ where the algebra of class functions does form a MASA.

Despite the superior performance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) "black box" systems in numerous real-world scenarios, their lack of explainability remains a significant barrier to adoption in high-stakes domains across various industries. Although numerous Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods exist to generate human-understandable explanations, each possesses distinct advantages and limitations, leaving many open challenges unresolved. This work demonstrates popular XAI techniques through a shared case study on credit default prediction, evaluates their competitive strengths from multiple angles (such as local and global perspectives), offers insights into quantifying explainability, and suggests pathways toward responsible or human-centered AI. Practitioners can utilize this study as a comprehensive catalog to comprehend, compare, and correlate the benefits of prevalent XAI methods. Furthermore, this survey outlines future research directions essential for developing responsible AI systems, a critical step for successfully integrating AI into high-risk applications.

We present a novel consensus-based optimization (CBO) approach in which an interacting particle system is governed by jump-diffusion stochastic differential equations. This work investigates the well-posedness of both the particle system and its mean-field limit. The primary contributions include establishing the convergence of the interacting particle system to its mean-field limit, as well as the mean-square convergence of a discretized particle system to the continuous-time dynamics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the mean-field jump-diffusion SDEs converge to the global minimizer across a broad class of objective functions. Numerical experiments on benchmark functions illustrate that the proposed CBO method outperforms earlier versions.

We define dispersion engineering principles that enable the regulation of the thermalization process and the resulting thermal state of an initial beam within a multimode nonlinear photonic circuit. To achieve this, we apply a kinetic equation (KE) framework to systems characterized by Bloch dispersion relations featuring bands and gaps. When the ratio of gap width to band width exceeds a specific critical threshold, the KE yields stationary solutions that deviate from the standard Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) distribution. Furthermore, the theory forecasts the relaxation times required for these non-conventional thermal states to emerge. We validated our findings using the prototype SSH model, where the connectivity of composite elements permits precise control over the band-gap structure. These spectral engineering guidelines are applicable to more intricate photonic networks that, despite lacking periodicity, possess spectra composed of mode groups separated by spectral gaps.

Recent research (Hirshberg et al., PNAS, 116, 21445 (2019)) has effectively utilized path integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) to simulate large bosonic systems. Building on this, the current study extends PIMD methodologies to investigate Green's functions within bosonic frameworks. We show that advancements to the foundational PIMD approach allow for the computation of Green's functions and the extraction of momentum distributions from simulation data. Furthermore, we apply this enhanced method to systems of identical interacting bosons to examine the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition near its critical temperature.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) are extensively utilized for semi-supervised learning on graphs, with the Graph Random Neural Network (GRAND) model recently achieving state-of-the-art results. However, GRAND struggles with large-scale graphs due to its reliance on computationally intensive data augmentation. To overcome this limitation, we introduce GRAND+, a scalable and high-performance GNN framework for semi-supervised graph learning. GRAND+ employs a Generalized Forward Push (GFPush) algorithm to pre-compute a general propagation matrix, enabling efficient mini-batch data augmentation. The low time and space complexities of GFPush allow GRAND+ to scale effectively to large graphs. Additionally, we incorporate a confidence-aware consistency loss into the optimization process, enhancing GRAND+'s generalization capabilities. Extensive experiments across seven public datasets of varying sizes demonstrate that GRAND+ not only scales to large graphs with lower running times than existing scalable GNNs but also consistently outperforms both full-batch and scalable GNNs in accuracy.

Consider a real $l$-dimensional minimal submanifold $M$ embedded in the Kaehler product manifold $\overline{M}^m \times \overline{M}^n$, where the normal connection of $M$ is flat. The factors $\overline{M}^m$ and $\overline{M}^n$ are complex manifolds of dimensions $m$ and $n$, respectively, each possessing constant holomorphic sectional curvatures $c_1$ and $c_2$. We derive an expression for the Laplacian of the second fundamental form of $M$. Specifically, we examine the case where $M$ is F-anti-invariant. Additionally, we present several applications of this derived formula.

We introduce an algorithm designed to generate strictly saturated random sequential adsorption (RSA) packings composed of rounded polygons. This method facilitates the investigation of various properties across diverse shapes and aids in modeling monolayers formed through the irreversible adsorption of complex molecules. In this study, we apply the algorithm to examine the densities of packings formed by rounded regular polygons. Unlike packings of sharp regular polygons, where the packing fraction increases as the number of sides grows, the packing fraction for rounded polygons peaks when the shapes are rounded regular triangles. As the number of sides and the rounding radius increase, the packing fractions approach the limit established by disk packings. Nevertheless, even for the rounded 25-gon—the polygon with the highest number of sides analyzed here—the resulting packings remain slightly denser than those of disks.

Entangled quantum networks offer significant flexibility and scalability for quantum information processing and the quantum Internet, though most existing research has concentrated on network nonlocalities. This work aims to establish new characterizations for networks with theory-independent configurations. We first demonstrate a configuration inequality applicable to any network by utilizing the fractional independent set of its associated graph; these inequalities can be constructed with polynomial-time complexity. This advancement enables the characterization of correlations in any classical network based solely on its topology. Analogous inequalities apply to all entangled quantum networks under local measurements, revealing an intrinsic property of quantum networks preserved by local unitary operations. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the verification of nearly all multipartite entangled pure states with linear complexity and allows for the witnessing of quantum network topology without requiring assumptions about inputs. The configuration theory is subsequently extended to encompass any no-signalling networks, with potential implications for entanglement theory, quantum information processing, and quantum networks.

We establish an upper bound for the reliability function of mismatched decoding in zero-rate coding scenarios. This bound relies on a theorem by Komlós, which demonstrates the existence of a subcode possessing specific symmetry characteristics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this bound matches the expurgated exponent at zero rate across a wide range of channel-decoding metric pairs.

Distributive laws serve as a conventional method for merging two monads, enabling a compositional strategy for analyzing computational effects within semantics. In cases where a strict distributive law is absent, a composite monad can still be obtained by adopting a weakened version of this law. Notably, Eugenia Cheng demonstrated that combining $n$ monads is achievable by iteratively applying distributive laws that adhere to the Yang-Baxter equation, a coherence condition that ensures the composition order is irrelevant, thereby establishing a form of associativity. This paper extends the associativity of iterated composition to scenarios involving weak distributive laws for $n = 3$ monads. To facilitate this, we employ string-diagrammatic notation, which greatly enhances the readability of increasingly intricate proofs. Additionally, we present examples of novel weak distributive laws generated through iteration.

Ensemble pruning involves selecting a subset of component classifiers from an ensemble that maintains performance comparable to the original while lowering storage and computational expenses. This technique remains largely underexplored within data stream environments, necessitating real-time analysis of ensemble components as they process streams to distinguish useful classifiers from redundant ones. We introduce CCRP, an on-the-fly pruning method for multi-class data stream classification that utilizes an imbalance-aware fusion of class-wise component rankings. CCRP aims to ensure the pruned ensemble includes the top-performing classifier for each target class, thereby mitigating class imbalance issues. Experimental results on both real-world and synthetic data streams show that various ensemble types integrating CCRP achieve performance equal to or better than their unpruned counterparts while reducing average memory consumption by 20% to 90%. Finally, we validate this pruning scheme by comparing it against approaches based on ensemble weights and basic rank fusion methods.

Extracting cuspidal automorphic representations from the entire automorphic spectrum remains a fundamental challenge within the trace formula methodology. For instance, matrix coefficients associated with supercuspidal representations serve as test functions that eliminate the continuous spectrum but inadvertently suppress a significant portion of the cuspidal automorphic representations. In the context of number fields, recent work [3] employs multipliers within the Schwartz algebra to isolate the full cuspidal spectrum, offering a sufficient set of test functions appropriate for comparing orbital integrals. These multipliers have subsequently been instrumental in proving the Gan-Gross-Prasad conjecture for unitary groups [3,2]. In this article, we establish a comparable result regarding the isolation of the cuspidal spectrum in the function field case, as outlined in [3].

Driven by the discovery of Kuiper belt objects and exoplanets, interest has surged regarding the internal structure of ice-rich planetary bodies, specifically distinguishing between rock and ice. Consequently, we conducted a parameter study across a mass range $M$, producing radii between 50 and 3000 km, and rock/ice mass ratios from 0.25 to 4. These bodies were evolved over 4.5 Gyr in a cold setting to determine their current configurations. Our thermal evolution model accounts for liquid and vapor flow within porous media, solving mass and energy conservation equations under hydrostatic equilibrium for a spherical body orbiting a central star. The framework incorporates pressure effects on porosity and melting points, heating from long-lived radioactive isotopes, and temperature-dependent serpentinization and dehydration processes. We identified the boundaries in parameter space (size versus rock content) separating differentiated bodies with rocky cores from undifferentiated ones; these include small bodies, those with low rock fractions, and the largest bodies considered, which experience high internal pressures that barely reach melting temperatures. The resulting differentiated structure features a rocky core, an ice-rich mantle, and a thin, dense surface crust. We also analyze and discuss the bulk density-radius relationship. Furthermore, investigating the impact of a very cold environment, we found that at ambient temperatures of approximately 20 K, small bodies retain ice in its amorphous form to the present day.

As search engine marketing scales, developing a robust bidding system has become essential for e-commerce success. Modern industrial bidding systems face two major challenges: the vast size of product catalogs leading to sparse bidding features, and the high volume of requests creating significant computational loads for both offline and online serving. To address sparsity, we utilize additional user-item data, specifically extracting natural language signals from user queries and contextual product knowledge. Our approach involves generating ad vector representations using a Transformer model and employing clustering to capture their geometric relationships for collaborative bidding predictions. This two-step process substantially lowers the computational strain on bid evaluation and optimization. This paper presents the end-to-end architecture of Walmart's search engine marketing bidding system, which effectively processes tens of millions of bids daily. We analyze the system's online and offline performance, demonstrating its effectiveness as a production-efficient solution.

Data preprocessing is essential for clustering, particularly when features describing entities operate on varying scales. To prevent any single feature from dominating the clustering algorithm's objective function, feature normalization is typically applied to rescale them. However, this paper argues that rescaling should not treat all features uniformly; rather, it should prioritize those more relevant to the clustering task. Consequently, we propose a feature rescaling method that incorporates the within-cluster relevance of each feature. Extensive simulations on both real and synthetic datasets, including scenarios with and without noise, demonstrate that clustering approaches utilizing this proposed normalization strategy significantly outperform those relying on traditional methods.

Gravity is a fundamental force in modern scientific inquiry and discovery, yet its origins extend far beyond the work of Newton and Einstein. The formulation of a complete theory of gravitation was the result of a long, evolving journey, incorporating contributions from various eras and global scholars, with significant insights provided by ancient Greeks. This three-part series traces the key milestones in the history of gravitational discovery. The initial article examines the ancient development of cosmic curiosity and the expansion of scientific understanding through early theories and observations.

Global optimization challenges in high- and infinite-dimensional spaces are prevalent across diverse fields, including engineering, economics, geophysics, biology, machine learning, and optimal control. Among stochastic global optimization techniques, bio-inspired methods are widely favored for their ability to mimic natural ecological and evolutionary processes, demonstrating efficiency in numerous practical scenarios. Nevertheless, these bio-inspired approaches suffer from significant limitations. Their semi-empirical foundation means they cannot always guarantee convergence to a global optimum and often struggle with high-dimensional spaces, resulting in slow convergence rates. In this work, we introduce the `Survival of the Fittest Algorithm' (SoFA), a bio-inspired stochastic global optimization method applicable within Hilbert function spaces. Rooted in Darwin's principle of "survival of the fittest," SoFA's convergence is mathematically grounded in the fundamental property of probabilistic measure localization in Hilbert spaces; we provide a rigorous proof of its convergence for a broad class of functionals. To demonstrate its utility, we apply SoFA to determine globally optimal trajectories for the daily vertical migrations of zooplankton in oceans and lakes—the largest synchronized biomass movement on Earth. By maximizing fitness within a function space derived from a von Foerster stage-structured population model using biologically realistic parameters, we show that SoFA outperforms other stochastic global optimization algorithms in high-dimensional fitness maximization problems. Furthermore, we elucidate the connections between this new algorithm and natural selection, specifically the gradual exclusion of competitive conspecific strains within ecosystems.

The temperature-dependent complex optical properties of the layered phosphide EuCd$_2$P$_2$ have been investigated across a broad frequency spectrum, both above and below the Néel temperature $T_{\rm N} \simeq 11.5$ K, for light polarized within the $a-b$ planes. At room temperature, optical conductivity is characterized by a weak free-carrier component with a Drude plasma frequency of approximately 1100 cm$^{-1}$ and a scattering rate of $1/\tau_D\simeq 700$ cm$^{-1}$, alongside interband absorption onsets above $\simeq 2000$ cm$^{-1}$. Two infrared-active $E_u$ modes appear at roughly 89 and 239 cm$^{-1}$. As temperature drops, the scattering rate diminishes and low-frequency conductivity rises slightly; however, below $\simeq 50$ K, conductivity declines until reaching a resistivity peak near 18 K (just below $2T_{\rm N}$), at which point spectral weight from free carriers shifts to a localized excitation around 500 cm$^{-1}$. Metallic characteristics are restored below $T_{\rm N}$. Notably, the $E_u$ modes remain largely stable, with only the high-frequency mode exhibiting slight anomalous shifts. Although multiple scenarios were evaluated, the dominant explanation attributes the resistivity maximum and carrier localization to the formation of ferromagnetic domains below $\simeq 2T_{\rm N}$, which generate spin-polarized clusters via spin-carrier coupling [1].

While blockchains rely on peer-to-peer networks for information dissemination, these networks currently lack provable guarantees for essential properties like Byzantine fault tolerance, strong connectivity, and small diameter. This is not merely a theoretical issue; recent attacks on Bitcoin have exploited insecure peer connection policies and weak synchronization to cause network partitions. Given that cryptocurrency blockchains are safety-critical, they require principled algorithms for network maintenance. Our core insight is leveraging the blockchain itself to facilitate peer communication, thereby simplifying network upkeep. Considering peers have limited computational resources and that at most a constant fraction are Byzantine, we present communication-efficient protocols to sustain a hypercubic network structure that supports dynamic peer joining and leaving. Notably, our design demonstrates the ability to recover from significant adversarial failures, even under high churn. A major contribution is a secure bootstrapping mechanism that utilizes the blockchain to assist new peers in connecting to the existing network. By analyzing this joining process, we establish a lower bound (up to logarithmic factors) showing that our network tolerates the maximum possible churn rate. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical lower bound on churn for any fully distributed service requiring connectivity.

Supersymmetric Twin Higgs frameworks alleviate the fine-tuning issues of the electroweak scale, which arise from the heavy scalar top partners necessitated by their non-observation at the Large Hadron Collider. If the Lightest Supersymmetric Particle belongs to the twin sector, it can serve as dark matter despite carrying charge under twin gauge interactions. We demonstrate that the twin stau constitutes a viable candidate for charged dark matter, even in scenarios where twin electromagnetic gauge symmetry remains unbroken, yielding a thermal relic density that naturally aligns with observed dark matter levels. A broad parameter space adheres to all experimental constraints, including limits on dark matter self-interactions. This twin stau dark matter could be detected in upcoming direct detection facilities like LUX-ZEPLIN. With masses between 300 and 500 GeV, the stau in minimal scenarios possesses a sufficiently long decay length to appear as a disappearing track or long-lived particle at the Large Hadron Collider.

We present GEM, a dynamic benchmark designed for Natural Language Generation (NLG), encompassing its evaluation methods and metrics. Assessing advancements in NLG depends on a continuously shifting landscape of automated metrics, datasets, and human evaluation protocols. Because of this volatility, newly developed models frequently rely on outdated, English-centric corpora and established yet imperfect metrics. This misalignment hinders the ability to pinpoint current model limitations and identify pathways for improvement. To resolve this issue, GEM offers a flexible environment where models can be applied across diverse tasks and where evaluation strategies can be rigorously tested. Through regular updates, the benchmark aims to make NLG research more multilingual and ensure the challenge evolves alongside emerging models. This paper outlines the dataset for a shared task organized at the ACL 2021 Workshop, inviting the entire NLG community to participate.

We calculate adjusted reflection coefficients for electromagnetic waves within the far-infrared and terahertz spectra, utilizing hydrodynamic boundary conditions for metallic conduction electrons. This approach allows us to assess the temperature-dependent component of the Casimir pressure acting between metal plates. These findings aim to clarify the "thermal anomaly," a phenomenon where experimental data diverge from predictions made by standard fluctuation electrodynamics for conductive metals.

To address image recovery, plug-and-play (PnP) approaches have emerged, substituting the proximal step of optimization algorithms with calls to application-specific denoisers, frequently realized via deep neural networks. Despite their success, these methods allow for further enhancement. A key limitation is that denoisers are typically trained on white Gaussian noise, whereas the actual input errors in PnP frameworks often deviate significantly from this distribution, exhibiting unpredictable statistics across iterations. While PnP methods grounded in approximate message passing (AMP) avoid this issue, they are restricted to scenarios where the forward operator resembles a large random matrix. This paper introduces a novel PnP framework leveraging the expectation consistent (EC) approximation algorithm, a broader extension of AMP, which ensures predictable error statistics at every iteration, thereby enabling the effective training of deep-network denoisers.

We present the first observation of direct CP violation in $B^0_s \to K^-\pi^+$ decays, achieving a significance greater than five standard deviations using 2011 LHCb $pp$ collision data with an integrated luminosity of $1.0\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ collected at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. The measured asymmetry is $A_{CP}(B^0_s \rightarrow K^- \pi^+)=0.27 \pm 0.04\,\mathrm{(stat)} \pm 0.01\,\mathrm{(syst)}$. Additionally, we report an updated, more precise determination of direct CP violation in $B^0 \to K^+\pi^-$ decays, finding $A_{CP}(B^0\rightarrow K^+ \pi^-)=-0.080 \pm 0.007\,\mathrm{(stat)} \pm 0.003\,\mathrm{(syst)}$.

This paper's investigations examine how cutoff dipole interaction radius and dilution affect the fundamental thermodynamic properties of kagome artificial spin ice under free boundary conditions. Our earlier work by Shevchenko et al. [JETP 124(6), 982-993 (2017)] demonstrated that phase transitions vanish at the limit of dipole interaction radius. Building on that study, this research addresses the necessary number of coordination spheres to preserve key collective phenomena. We conclude that at least three coordination spheres, encompassing 14 nearest neighbors, are required for kagome artificial spin ice. Limiting the cutoff radius to a smaller value induces significant alterations in the system's main thermodynamic characteristics. Conversely, expanding the interaction radius shifts the phase transition temperature toward lower values. Additionally, the effects of dilution were analyzed, revealing that the phase transition persists up to a dilution concentration of $p_c \approx 0.35$, which aligns well with Sykes and Essam theory. Beyond this threshold, the phase transition ceases to occur.

We examine the Wheeler-DeWitt equation in the vicinity of a black hole's horizon, adopting the static universe state as the entangled vacuum. Leveraging the entangled nature of this vacuum, we analyze the dynamical evolution of the subsystems located both inside and outside the horizon.

This paper explores new exact and analytic solutions to the Einstein-Maxwell field equations for Casimir wormholes, analyzing both scenarios with and without Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP) effects. By examining a particular GUP formulation, we study three specific redshift function models alongside two distinct equations of state. Our findings present a class of asymptotically flat, electrically charged Casimir wormhole solutions that include or exclude GUP corrections. We verify the null, weak, strong, and dominant energy conditions at the throat radius, demonstrating that classical energy conditions are violated by an arbitrarily small magnitude at this location. Additionally, we analyze the wormhole geometry incorporating semiclassical corrections via embedding diagrams. Using the volume integral quantifier, we measure the quantity of exotic matter near the throat, while further investigating the exotic fluid properties through the exoticity parameter and sound speed.

Rotation averaging serves as a synchronization technique for single or multiple rotation groups, acting as a core challenge in numerous computer vision applications, including multi-view structure from motion (SfM). Fundamentally, this process entails reconstructing global pose-graph consistency from pairwise relative camera orientations. Given pairwise rotations within groups, particularly within the 3-dimensional rotation group $\mathbb{SO}(3)$, the objective is to recover the original set of multiple rotations relative to a fixed coordinate frame. This paper introduces a robust framework designed to address the multiple rotation averaging problem, specifically under conditions with substantial noisy data. By incorporating an $\epsilon$-cycle consistency term into the solver, we facilitate a robust initialization scheme within the Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS) algorithm. Rather than performing expensive edge removal, we mitigate the impact of erroneous measurements through weight reduction, thereby effectively preventing IRLS failures stemming from poor initialization. Experimental results indicate that our proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art approaches across various benchmarks.

This study reports evidence for top quark production in heavy ion collisions, utilizing a dataset from 2018 lead-lead collisions recorded by the CMS experiment at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{_{\mathrm{NN}}}} = 5.02$ TeV, with an integrated luminosity of $1.7 \pm 0.1\,\mathrm{nb}^{-1}$. The measurement of top quark pair ($\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$) production focuses on events containing two opposite-sign, high-$p_\mathrm{T}$ isolated leptons ($\ell^\pm\ell^\mp =\,\mathrm{e}^{+} \mathrm{e}^{-},\,\mu^{+} \mu^{-},\,\mathrm{and}\,\mathrm{e}^{\pm} \mu^{\mp}$). Sensitivity to the $\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$ signal is evaluated both with and without the requirement of additional b-tagged jets, demonstrating the capability to identify top quark decay products regardless of whether they interact with the medium (as with bottom quarks) or do not (as with leptonically decaying W bosons). The inclusive cross section ($\sigma_\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$) is determined through likelihood fits to a multivariate discriminator that incorporates various leptonic kinematic variables, with and without b-tagged jet multiplicity data. For fits including and excluding b-jet multiplicity inputs, the observed (expected) significance of the $\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$ signal relative to the background-only hypothesis is 4.0 (5.8) and 3.8 (4.8) standard deviations, respectively. Following event reconstruction and background subtraction, the extracted cross sections are $\sigma_\mathrm{t\bar{t}} = 2.03 ^{+0.71}_{-0.64}$ and $2.54 ^{+0.84}_{-0.74}\,\mu\mathrm{b}$, respectively. These values are lower than, yet remain consistent with, expectations from scaled proton-proton data and perturbative quantum chromodynamics predictions. This measurement represents a pivotal initial step toward employing the top quark as a new probe for investigating strongly interacting matter.

Cloud-based data analysis has become standard practice due to reduced system management burdens and flexible pay-as-you-go pricing. However, this model can be problematic for query processing, as heavy usage leads to substantial expenses. For instance, in query-as-a-service environments where charges are based on processed bytes, frequently accessed data collections can become costly. This issue is further exacerbated by the limited optimization capabilities users have when relying on declarative interfaces like SQL. This paper demonstrates how to significantly lower overhead and costs in query-as-a-service systems without altering existing infrastructure or requiring cloud provider involvement. Our method utilizes query rewriting to merge multiple concurrent queries into a single execution. Experimental results indicate that the total computational work performed through shared execution is lower than that of a query-at-a-time strategy. Since billing is per byte, the cost of running a group of queries often equals the cost of running just one. As a demonstration, executing the TPC-H benchmark via shared queries was shown to be up to 100 times and 16 times cheaper in Amazon Athena and Google BigQuery, respectively, compared to the query-at-a-time approach, while also delivering higher throughput.

Accurately training Relation Extraction models necessitates a substantial volume of properly labeled data, yet acquiring such data is challenging and time-consuming; prior research indicates that achieving high accuracy often requires significant effort or compromises performance. We propose a method to rapidly generate high-quality datasets for Relation Extraction. When neural models are trained on these newly created datasets, they achieve strong performance and demonstrate excellent generalization across other datasets. In our study, we successfully annotated 10,022 sentences covering 19 relations within a reasonable timeframe and trained a standard baseline model for each relation.

Recent experiments have identified carbon-doped hexagonal boron nitride (C-doped hBN) as a potential candidate for both room-temperature ferromagnetism and the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), noting that carbon substitution can also induce graphene island formation. This study investigates these phenomena from first principles, confirming that the creation of graphene islands covering an unequal number of boron and nitrogen sites in hBN is energetically feasible. These asymmetric islands exhibit a net non-zero magnetic moment and demonstrate significantly higher chemical reactivity compared to their symmetric, non-magnetic counterparts. Furthermore, on-site Coulomb repulsion, a key factor in the magnetism of bipartite lattices like graphene and hBN, is shown to drive the chemical activation of carbon atoms at the zigzag interfaces of these magnetic islands and adjacent boron sites. However, while carbon substitution at boron sites is energetically favorable and activates these sites, such configurations have previously been deemed unsuitable for ORR. Fortunately, we observe that the activation of carbon at boron sites systematically decreases as the size of the graphene islands increases, thereby creating numerous efficient catalytic sites at the edges of larger magnetic islands that cover more boron than nitrogen sites. Consequently, we propose a class of metallic graphene-hBN hybrids featuring lattices of magnetic graphene islands embedded within hBN as a viable, precious-metal-free alternative for electrode applications.

Most differentially private (DP) approaches rely on either a central model, where a trusted third party adds noise to queries, or a local model, where users perturb their data individually. The central model suffers from a single point of failure, while the local model suffers from significantly reduced data utility. The recently introduced shuffle model offers an intermediate solution between these two paradigms. In this framework, users send locally privatized data to a server where messages are shuffled, severing the link between a specific message and its user. This shuffling amplifies privacy without requiring additional noise, thereby achieving a superior privacy-utility trade-off compared to the local model. This paper establishes the tightest known theoretical bound for DP guarantees in shuffle models utilizing $k$-Randomized Response local randomizers. Subsequently, we examine the utility of shuffle models for histogram queries. By applying the matrix inversion method to approximate the original distribution from the empirical output of the $k$-RR mechanism, we de-noise the histogram generated by the shuffle model to calculate the total variation distance from the true distribution, serving as our utility metric. We conducted experiments on both synthetic and real datasets to compare the privacy-utility trade-off of the shuffle model against the central model, which utilizes state-of-the-art Gaussian noise added to each bin. Although our experimental results align with existing literature that generally favors the central model, we observed that the difference in statistical utility between the two is minimal, indicating they are nearly comparable under identical levels of differential privacy.

Translucency has become a prevalent design feature in at least one major mobile operating system, introducing security risks by potentially obscuring trusted interaction elements for users. This paper illustrates such a vulnerability through the Safari browser in iOS 7 on Apple devices, examining both the technical hurdles of executing an attack and proposed countermeasures. We conclude with a survey-based user study designed to measure the security impact, which indicates that additional research is necessary.

VIRUP is an open-source C++ application that creates an interactive virtual reality environment for exploring extensive scientific astrophysical datasets derived from both simulations and observations. Optimized to render terabytes of data at 90 frames per second, it ensures a seamless immersive experience. Although originally built for gaming VR headsets, VIRUP also supports various modern immersive displays, including 3D screens, 180-degree domes, and 360-degree panoramas. The software is scriptable via Python, enabling the creation of pre-selected guided tours and pre-rendered cinematic sequences. Notably, a companion video for the 2020 SDSS release and the 21-minute documentary, "The Archaeology of Light," were produced entirely using VIRUP; links to these resources are available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KJJXbcf8kxA and https://go.epfl.ch/ArchaeologyofLight, respectively.

This study broadens the nonabelian Hodge correspondence, originally established for Kähler manifolds, to encompass a wider range of Hermitian metrics on complex manifolds known as balanced metrics of Hodge-Riemann type. By leveraging several fundamental insights, the work adapts established results—specifically the Donaldson-Uhlenbeck-Yau theorem and Corlette's theorem—to this new context. Furthermore, although these metrics are not necessarily Kähler, we demonstrate that the Sampson-Siu theorem, which asserts that harmonic maps are pluriharmonic, continues to hold for a slightly restricted subclass using existing arguments. Notable instances of such metrics include those derived from multipolarizations.

Three-dimensional Morphable Models (3DMMs) serve as potent statistical instruments for encoding the shapes and textures of object classes.
