This work introduces the most comprehensive human head 3DMM available, encompassing the face, cranium, ears, eyes, teeth, and tongue. We achieve this by proposing two strategies for merging existing 3DMMs of overlapping head regions: first, employing a regressor to fill missing segments of one model using another; second, utilizing the Gaussian Process framework to fuse covariance matrices from multiple sources. Consequently, we develop a novel combined face-and-head shape model that integrates the facial detail and variability of the LSFM face model with the full-head capabilities of the LYHM head model. Furthermore, we construct and integrate a highly detailed ear model to expand ear shape variation, while also incorporating eye and eye-region models alongside basic representations of the teeth, tongue, and inner mouth cavity. The resulting model attains state-of-the-art performance, enabling the reconstruction of complete head representations from single, unconstrained images. This allows for the parameterization of craniofacial shape and texture, ear geometry, eye gaze, and eye color.

This study reports on a search for pair-produced lightest bottom squarks ($\tilde{b}_{1}$) using 139 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV recorded by the ATLAS detector. The analyzed supersymmetric models assume that $\tilde{b}_{1}$ decays into a bottom quark and the second-lightest neutralino ($\tilde{\chi}^{0}_{2}$), which subsequently decays with 100% branching ratio into a Standard Model-like Higgs boson ($h$) and the stable, lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP), $\tilde{\chi}^{0}_{1}$. Two specific mass scenarios were investigated: one with a fixed LSP mass of 60 GeV, and another with a fixed mass difference of 130 GeV between the $\tilde{\chi}^{0}_{2}$ and $\tilde{\chi}^{0}_{1}$. The search targeted final states characterized by no charged leptons, at least three $b$-jets, and significant missing transverse momentum. No statistically significant excess of events above the Standard Model background was found in any signal region. Consequently, 95% confidence level limits were established, excluding bottom squarks with masses up to 1.5 TeV in the considered models.

We introduce a Krylov-Safonov framework to establish H\"older regularity for viscosity solutions of non-variational porous media equations. Our analysis highlights a key distinction in this class of problems: regularity is ensured either by a uniformly elliptic regime or by an eikonal mechanism. Our methodology relies on sliding paraboloids to derive an ABP-type measure estimate. Synthesizing these estimates yields a diminishing oscillation property, which ultimately guarantees control within H\"older spaces.

Geoscientists and researchers across various disciplines face the challenge of processing vast amounts of literature to locate, extract, and aggregate relevant data and findings for future studies or database construction, yet no current system adequately supports this workflow. Drawing on insights from a formative study regarding how geoscientists collaboratively annotate texts and extract information, we introduce DeepShovel, a publicly accessible AI-driven system designed to meet these needs. Utilizing state-of-the-art neural networks, DeepShovel facilitates a human-AI collaborative approach, enabling researchers to accurately annotate PDF documents and extract data from tables, figures, and maps with ease. A subsequent evaluation involving 14 researchers indicated that DeepShovel enhances data extraction efficiency for building scientific databases and fosters larger, more tightly integrated collaborative teams.

Experimentally accessing the universal low-temperature magnetic field scaling of Kondo-correlated quantum dots through electrical conductance has proven difficult. In this work, we demonstrate that nonlinear thermocurrent spectroscopy applied to a molecular quantum dot within the Kondo regime offers a viable solution. Our findings reveal that the bias-dependent thermocurrent serves as a sensitive indicator of universal Kondo physics, directly quantifies the magnetic-field-induced splitting of the Kondo resonance, and enables the study of nanosystems operating far from thermal and electrical equilibrium.

The ALICE collaboration has quantified inclusive J/$\psi$ production in Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}} = 2.76$ TeV, covering the full range down to zero transverse momentum within the rapidity interval $2.5 < y < 4$. A suppression of the J/$\psi$ yield in Pb-Pb relative to pp collisions, normalized by the number of binary nucleon-nucleon collisions, is observed. The nuclear modification factor, integrated across the 0–80% most central collisions, is determined to be $0.545 \pm 0.032 \rm{(stat.)} \pm 0.083 \rm{(syst.)}$, showing no significant variation with collision centrality. These observations differ markedly from results obtained at lower collision energies. The data are consistent with models that attribute J/$\psi$ production to charm quarks formed in a deconfined partonic phase.

A key advantage of stabilizer error-correcting codes is that stabilizer measurements project arbitrary errors into Pauli errors, which greatly simplifies both physical error correction and classical performance simulations. However, logical non-Clifford operations can transform Pauli errors into non-Pauli (Clifford) errors. Although subsequent stabilizer measurements eventually project these Clifford errors back to Pauli errors, the resulting error distributions acquire additional correlations dependent on the specific logical operation and the code's structure. Prior research examined these dynamics when applying a transversal $T$ gate to the three-dimensional color code, revealing a non-local "linking charge" phenomenon between intersecting error membranes. This work extends those findings to a $CCZ$ gate within the three-dimensional surface code, demonstrating that the problem is significantly more tractable in this context. Specifically, the emergence of linking charge manifests as a local rather than non-local effect. Leveraging the relative simplicity of Clifford errors in this setting, we simulate their impact on a single-shot magic state preparation process—marking the first simulation to fully account for these errors—and determine that their influence on the threshold is primarily governed by the probability of $X$ errors occurring immediately before the gate application, following the most recent stabilizer measurement.

Adversarial training (AT) stands as a highly dependable strategy for mitigating adversarial attacks in machine learning. This approach has been adapted as a regularization technique to achieve state-of-the-art performance on NLP benchmarks and proves beneficial for both transfer and continual learning. By comparing vanilla BERT models with those fine-tuned adversarially, we investigate the underlying causes of AT's efficacy. Our findings reveal that the primary factor behind AT's success is the partial retention of BERT's syntactic capabilities during fine-tuning. Specifically, adversarially fine-tuned models demonstrate greater fidelity to BERT's original language modeling behavior and exhibit heightened sensitivity to word order. As tangible illustrations of these syntactic strengths, adversarially fine-tuned models can improve anaphora agreement by up to 38% and dependency parsing by up to 11%. Our analysis indicates that standard fine-tuning often oversimplifies sentence representations by overemphasizing a limited subset of words. In contrast, AT tempers the impact of these dominant words and fosters representational diversity, thereby enabling a more hierarchical sentence representation and effectively preventing the loss of syntactic abilities observed in vanilla fine-tuning.

We introduce a resampling-based method for rapidly selecting significant Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) within multi-marker mixed effect models applied to twin studies. While current practices often limit analysis to individual SNPs due to computational constraints, jointly modeling variants within a gene or pathway offers superior power for detection; consequently, we adapt our recently developed $e$-value framework to this challenge. Our approach efficiently detects SNPs in families by leveraging multiple SNPs simultaneously through two key enhancements: first, unlike standard model selection techniques, it avoids the need to train models with all possible predictors; second, it employs a fast, scalable bootstrap procedure that relies solely on Monte-Carlo sampling to generate bootstrapped coefficient vectors. Using these samples, we calculate $e$-values for each SNP and select those falling below a specific threshold. Numerical studies demonstrate that our method outperforms both single-marker analyses on family data and model selection approaches that neglect familial dependency structures. Furthermore, we apply $e$-values to conduct gene-level analyses in nuclear families, successfully identifying several SNPs linked to alcohol consumption.

This study investigates the transit timing variations (TTVs) within the nearby, young (22 Myr) AU Mic planetary system. For AU Mic b, we report data from three Spitzer (4.5 $\mu$m), five TESS, eleven LCO, one PEST, and one Brierfield transit, along with two Rossiter-McLaughlin timing measurements; for AU Mic c, we add three TESS transits. We conduct two distinct TTV analyses: first, EXOFASTv2 is used to jointly model Spitzer and ground-based transits to derive midpoint times, followed by an O–C diagram constructed and modeled using Exo-Striker. Second, we validate these findings with an independent photodynamical approach. Our analysis yields a TTV-derived mass for AU Mic c of 10.8$^{+2.3}_{-2.2}$ M$_{E}$, which we compare against recent radial-velocity (RV) mass estimates. We detect excess TTVs inconsistent with the dynamical interactions of planets b and c alone, nor with stellar spots or flares. Consequently, we propose a hypothetical non-transiting "middle-d" exoplanet candidate that aligns with the observed TTVs and potential RV signals, suggesting the AU Mic system forms a compact resonant multi-planet chain with a 4:6:9 period commensurability. These findings confirm that the AU Mic system exhibits detectable TTVs driven by dynamic interactions, offering insights into its formation mechanisms. We recommend future RV and TTV observations of AU Mic b and c to refine mass constraints and verify the presence of any additional planets.

Instrumental variable techniques are frequently employed to estimate parameters when confounding exists and are also applicable to stochastic processes. By utilizing moment equations, these analyses derive estimators for causal effects. This work demonstrates that within stochastic processes, such moment equations can be identified through an integrated covariance matrix. Consequently, this approach introduces novel instrumental variable methods for continuous-time processes and offers a unified framework for handling both discrete- and continuous-time scenarios.

Although policy iteration converges locally at a quadratic rate, its computational cost becomes prohibitive for Markov decision processes (MDPs) with extensive state spaces. Leveraging the relationship between policy iteration and the semismooth Newton method, along with insights from inexact variants of the latter, we introduce \textit{inexact policy iteration}, a novel approach designed for large-scale finite MDPs that retains local contraction guarantees. We further develop a specific implementation utilizing GMRES for the approximate policy evaluation phase, termed inexact GMRES policy iteration. Experimental results on an MDP containing 10,000 states demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques, achieving a $5.8\times$ speedup over standard policy iteration and a $2.2\times$ speedup over optimistic policy iteration.

Let $P(z)$ be a polynomial of degree at most $n$ that has no zeros in the disk $|z| < 1$. Recently, Shah and Liman \cite[\textit{Integral estimates for the family of $B$-operators, Operators and Matrices,} \textbf{5}(2011), 79 - 87]{wl} proposed that for all $R\geq 1$ and $p\geq 1$,
\[\left\|B[P\circ\sigma](z)\right\|_p
\leq\frac{R^{n}|\Lambda_n|+|\lambda_{0}|}{\left\|1+z\right\|_p}\left\|P(z)\right\|_p,\]
where $B$ denotes a $\mathcal{B}_{n}$-operator with parameters $\lambda_{0}, \lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}$ defined by Rahman \cite{qir}, $\sigma(z)=Rz$, and $\Lambda_n=\lambda_{0}+\lambda_{1}\frac{n^{2}}{2}+\lambda_{2}\frac{n^{3}(n-1)}{8}$. However, the proof provided for this result contains errors. In this paper, we establish more general sharp $L_p$-inequalities for $\mathcal{B}_{n}$-operators that not only correct the aforementioned inequality as a specific instance but also extend its validity to the range $0 \leq p <1$.

Let $\mathcal{D}$ denote a weighted oriented graph with its corresponding edge ideal $I(\mathcal{D})$. This paper establishes that for a specific class of weighted oriented trees, the ordinary and symbolic powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$ are identical. Furthermore, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions under which the ordinary and symbolic powers coincide for naturally oriented lines.

Consider a sequence of independent and identically distributed non-negative random variables, $\xi_1, \xi_2, \dots$, whose tails exhibit regular variation with index $-1$. Let $S_n$ denote the sum and $M_n$ the maximum of the first $n$ variables. We determine the specific sequences $x_n \to \infty$ for which the probability $\mathbb P(S_n \ge x_n)$ is asymptotically equivalent to $\mathbb P(M_n \ge x_n)$ as $n \to \infty$. Beyond this specific regime, the typical magnitude of $S_n$ given that it exceeds $x_n$ cannot be fully characterized solely by the largest summand; instead, we introduce a necessary correction term that depends on the integrated tail of $\xi_1$.

The Data Bricks Space Mission serves as a prototype educational activity designed to introduce children to data through data physicalization. Grounded in a literature review and interviews with elementary educators, the program specifically targets students aged 10 to 12. By combining Lego bricks with a fictional space adventure narrative, teachers can utilize this activity to enable children to generate data, share their insights, and deepen their comprehension of how data connects to the world around them.

This report details findings from a broadband spectral and timing analysis of the transient X-ray pulsar GRO J2058+42 across a wide energy range, conducted at a low luminosity of approximately $2.5\times 10^{36}$ erg s$^{-1}$. The data indicate that both the pulse fraction and profile differ markedly from prior NuSTAR observations made when the source was ten times brighter. A cyclotron absorption line near 10 keV, observed within a narrow phase interval, aligns with findings from high-state observations. Spectral analysis reveals that at high luminosities ($L_{x}\simeq (2.7-3.2)\times 10^{37}$ erg s$^{-1}$), the spectrum exhibits a shape characteristic of accreting pulsars; however, when luminosity decreases by roughly an order of magnitude to $2.5\times 10^{36}$ erg s$^{-1}$, a two-component model becomes necessary to describe it. This behavior supports a model where the low-energy spectral component originates from a hot spot, while the high-energy component results from resonant Compton scattering of incident matter within an accretion channel above the neutron star's surface.

This paper introduces a method utilizing distributed traffic generation and monitoring to identify active data-paths within Software Defined Networking (SDN) data-planes. Under specific assumptions, we demonstrate that necessary and sufficient conditions exist to formally ensure the complete discovery of all operational paths via our approach. Ensuring reliable communication in SDN environments requires verifying that active data-paths align with intended configurations; this verification necessitates the discovery of actual running paths. In SDN, various applications may configure overlapping paths, potentially causing flows to traverse unintended routes, while SDN components themselves may suffer defects or compromise. Our work focuses on discovering operational paths in SDN-driven data-planes, though the proposed methodology applies broadly to any data-plane requiring path verification or certification. We have implemented a data-path discovery toolkit, detailing the associated tools and presenting experimental results that expose inconsistencies in established SDN applications.

We introduce a Nekrasov-type formula for the instanton partition functions of four-dimensional N=2 U(2) gauge theories coupled to (A_1,D_{2n}) Argyres-Douglas theories. This derivation involves extending the generalized AGT correspondence to the U(2) gauge group, a process that necessitates defining irregular states for the direct sum of Virasoro and Heisenberg algebras. Leveraging this formula allows for the calculation of the (A_1,D_{2n}) theory's contribution at every fixed point within the U(2) instanton moduli space. As a specific application, we compute the instanton partition function for the (A_3,A_3) theory, revealing a unique relationship with the SU(2) gauge theory featuring four fundamental flavors. Through this connection, we determine the action of the S-duality group on the UV gauge coupling of the (A_3,A_3) theory.

For a graph partitioned into connected components, a membership oracle determines whether any two vertices belong to the same component. We demonstrate that for $n \ge k \ge 2$, identifying the components of a hidden $n$-vertex graph with $k$ components necessitates at least $(k-1)n - \binom{k}{2}$ membership queries. This finding surpasses the existing information-theoretic lower bound of $\Omega(n \log k)$ and aligns precisely with the query complexity of the algorithm proposed by Reyzin and Srivastava (2007) for this task. Furthermore, we present an oracle that allows determining the number of components in $G$ with asymptotically fewer queries than required to learn the complete partition, thereby addressing another question raised by the same authors. Finally, we introduce a more practical variant of this oracle and establish asymptotically tight bounds of $\widetilde{\Theta}(m)$ queries for both learning and verifying an $m$-edge hidden graph $G$ when utilizing it.

We introduce a homotopy sampling method, loosely derived from importance sampling, which begins with a known probability distribution to determine the unknown normalization constant of a target distribution. Specifically, for stationary distributions linked to physical systems, this approach offers an alternative method for estimating the microcanonical ensemble. The iterative process not only computes the normalization but also yields samples from the target distribution. Although the homotopy method does not eliminate the need for sample averages when estimating the normalization constant, the procedure's accuracy relies on the errors inherent in these averages and the number of computational stages employed. We demonstrate that trading off the number of homotopy stages against the total sample count per stage can significantly improve computational efficiency. Furthermore, we derive error estimates as functions of both stages and sample averages, providing guidance for mapping calculations to specific computer architectures. The procedure is also adapted for Bayesian estimation, addressing both stationary and non-stationary problems, with a particular focus on sequential estimation via particle filtering. By integrating the homotopy process into the particle filter framework, we show enhanced computational robustness, specifically mitigating the issue of particle filter collapse that often occurs when the sample dimension is small relative to the state space dimensions.

Deep learning is increasingly replacing traditional Monte Carlo simulations in high energy physics, yet it currently demands substantial computational resources. A viable strategy to enhance efficiency involves quantizing neural network parameters to lower precision, a technique widely adopted in modern deep learning that reduces inference time, memory usage, and bandwidth requirements. This study examines the impact of low-precision inference on a complex deep generative adversarial network tailored for simulating subatomic particle interactions in accelerator-based calorimeter detectors. We utilize the innovative Intel low precision optimization tool (iLoT) for quantization and benchmark its performance against a TensorFlow Lite quantized model. Results on Intel hardware indicate a 1.73x speedup for the quantized iLoT model compared to its unquantized counterpart. Furthermore, using custom physics-inspired metrics, we confirm that the iLoT model maintains superior physical accuracy with less loss than the TensorFlow Lite alternative.

The healthcare sector is shifting from reactive symptom management toward proactive prevention, transitioning from generic approaches to personalized medicine, and moving from centralized to distributed models. Wearable IoT devices and advanced continuous monitoring algorithms are critical to this evolution. Hyperdimensional (HD) computing, an emerging machine learning paradigm inspired by neuroscience, holds significant promise for IoT and biomedical applications. This study investigates the previously unexplored area of optimally encoding spatio-temporal data, such as electroencephalogram (EEG) signals, into HD vectors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the HD computing framework can facilitate feature selection through the choice of appropriate encoding methods. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of using HD computing for feature selection in existing literature. Consequently, we anticipate that this approach will aid the machine learning community in advancing research into feature and channel selection, as well as enhancing model interpretability.

Autonomous vehicles represent an emerging technology poised to transform human life, yet their current reliance on optical sensor systems for perception faces significant limitations. Although deep neural networks excel at identifying objects using data from cameras and LiDAR, these optical methods struggle in adverse weather like rain, fog, and snow due to wavelength constraints. This thesis investigates alternative sensing modalities, specifically long-wave polarised infrared (IR) imagery and imaging radar, to enhance object recognition. First, we established a methodology utilizing Stokes parameters from polarised infrared data to identify vehicles via deep neural networks. Second, we assessed the viability of using solely the power spectrum from low-THz radar sensors for object recognition within controlled environments, employing a data-driven strategy that included a novel data augmentation technique addressing attenuation, range, and speckle noise. Finally, we constructed a large-scale "wild" dataset encompassing diverse weather conditions—including sunny, overcast, night, fog, rain, and snow—to demonstrate radar's robustness in detecting vehicles during severe weather. The study concludes that high-resolution radar and polarised IR imagery, when integrated with deep learning, offer a promising alternative to existing visible-spectrum optical automotive sensors by providing superior performance in harsh lighting and weather scenarios.

Hybrid fluid models, composed of two sectors featuring degrees of freedom that self-interact with varying strengths and are coupled consistently within a semi-holographic framework, demonstrate an attractor surface for Bjorken flow. By simplifying the description of both sectors to viscous fluids, we analytically confirm the universality of a key aspect of the bottom-up thermalization scenario: at sufficiently early times, the energy density of the weakly coupled (perturbative) sector surpasses that of the strongly coupled (holographic) sector, with the exponent governed by their respective viscosities and relaxation times. On this attractor surface, the hydrodynamization times for both subsectors follow a conformal scaling relative to the total energy density (scaled by a pre-factor), reaching a minimum before rising sharply. These minima occur when the energy densities approach the inverse of the dimensionful inter-system coupling. The pre-factor within the conformal window is universal and matches that of standard conformal attractors for the dominant sector; conversely, the pre-factor for the other sector grows with the ratio of the dominant to subdominant energy densities at early times. Investigating initial conditions inspired by saturation in $p$-$p$ and Pb-Pb collisions, we observe that the perturbative sector hydrodynamizes significantly later than the holographic sector in $p$-$p$ collisions, as the total energy densities at hydrodynamization fall inside and outside the conformal window for the two sectors, respectively.

Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models predicting molecular HOMO-LUMO gaps frequently face challenges with data efficiency, evidenced by slow reductions in prediction errors as training datasets expand. However, dividing training sets of organic molecules (specifically the QM7 and QM9 datasets) into three categories—systems with aromatic rings and carbonyls, those with single unsaturated bonds, and those with saturated bonds—before training yields independently trained QML models with enhanced learning rates. These selected models, evaluated at GW, B3LYP, and ZINDO theoretical levels, achieve mean absolute prediction errors of approximately 0.1 eV using up to ten times fewer training molecules compared to conventionally trained counterparts. Direct comparisons with $\Delta$-QML models indicate that this selected approach offers significantly superior data efficiency. Consequently, these findings imply that strategies like simple pre-training classifications could enable QML to effectively address demanding quantum property screening tasks across large libraries, ensuring high fidelity with reduced computational costs.

We present an enhancement to the standard Echo State Network (ESN), a model already known for competitive results in one-dimensional time series forecasting for dynamical systems. Our proposed architecture, a 20%-dense ESN utilizing reservoir weights sourced from a fruit fly connectome and its bootstrapped distribution, demonstrates superior accuracy in chaotic time series prediction while mitigating the high-variance issues typical of ESNs. We observe that random weight placement can harm both performance and variance, a drawback effectively addressed by adopting connectome-derived weight positions. This study evaluates four specific connectome characteristics—weight sparsity, positioning, distribution, and clustering—by constructing four distinct model classes (A, B, B₂, and C) based on a null-model ESN where the reservoir layer is substituted with a fruit fly connectivity matrix. Following hyperparameter optimization and selection of the optimal variant within each class, we trained and validated these models on size-variant subsets (50, 250, 500, and 750 steps) of the Mackey-Glass chaotic time series for multi-step prediction, calculating both Mean-Squared Error and variance across multiple train-validate trials.

This final project for CS254B, instructed by Li Yang Tan and Tom Knowles, explores Circuit Complexity, a field dedicated to analyzing Boolean Circuit Functions to derive insights into various complexity classes. Notably, the class $P / \text{Poly}$ has been pivotal in historical efforts to address the $P$ versus $NP$ problem, which concerns the equivalence of solution and verification. Although circuits offer a non-uniform computational model that can be more tractable than Turing Machines—since program size may vary with input size—establishing lower bounds for them remains exceptionally challenging. This report examines key results from Hastad, Sipser, and Razborov, illustrating the dynamic relationship between circuit complexity and core concepts in modern complexity theory, with a specific focus on the significance of Hastad's Switching Lemma.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as a potent solution for inference on graph-structured data. However, as real-world graphs grow larger, GNN training systems encounter significant scalability hurdles. While distributed training across multiple CPU nodes is a common remedy, there is limited focus on disk-based training, which offers a more cost-effective way to scale single-node systems by utilizing high-performance storage such as NVMe SSDs. Our analysis reveals that data transfer between main memory and disk is the primary bottleneck in SSD-based training, rendering conventional GNN pipelines sub-optimal when this overhead is ignored. Consequently, we introduce Ginex, the inaugural SSD-based GNN training system capable of processing billion-scale graph datasets on a single machine. Drawing inspiration from the inspector-executor model used in compiler optimization, Ginex restructures the training pipeline by decoupling the sample and gather stages. This separation allows Ginex to implement Belady's algorithm, a provably optimal replacement strategy for caching feature vectors, which constitute the majority of I/O accesses. Evaluation on four billion-scale datasets demonstrates that Ginex achieves an average training throughput 2.11x higher than SSD-extended PyTorch Geometric, with peak performance reaching up to 2.67x.

This work introduces a theory of logarithmic Chow rings and tautological subrings for logarithmically smooth algebraic stacks by extending the concept of piecewise-polynomial functions. Leveraging this framework, we demonstrate that the double-double ramification cycle resides within the tautological subring of the classical Chow ring of the moduli space of curves, and we confirm that the logarithmic double ramification cycle is divisorial, as previously conjectured by Molcho, Pandharipande, and Schmitt.

We demonstrate that point defects within two-dimensional photonic crystals can host bound states in the continuum (BICs). This confinement mechanism arises from a symmetry mismatch between the defect mode and the crystal's Bloch modes. Since these BICs exist without requiring bandgaps, they offer an alternative approach to light confinement. Additionally, we show that such BICs can propagate through fiber geometries, displaying arbitrarily low group velocities. This characteristic makes them a promising platform for amplifying non-linear effects and light-matter interactions within structured fibers.

An analytical formula for the orbital magnetization within a Floquet system is presented. This expression remains valid for clean systems under any driving scheme and arbitrary band occupations. The study demonstrates that orbital magnetization can be substantial not only in Chern insulators but also in anomalous phases where the Chern number alone fails to capture the full topology. Furthermore, significant orbital magnetization arises both from thermal equilibrium distributions in Floquet bands and from quantum quenches originating from an initial state with zero magnetization. In the context of quantum quenches, the orbital magnetization exhibits a strong dependence on the van Hove singularities present in the Floquet bands.

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, trained for next-word prediction, can effectively execute linguistic tasks involving long-distance syntactic dependencies, with accuracy on number agreement tasks nearing human levels (Gulordava et al., 2018). Despite this performance, the internal mechanisms driving these capabilities remain unclear: do LSTMs acquire abstract grammatical rules or depend on superficial heuristics? This study examines gender agreement in French, a task requiring the tracking of both hierarchical structure and lexical gender. Our results demonstrate that the model can reliably predict long-distance gender agreement in two subject-predicate contexts: noun-adjective and noun-passive-verb. However, the model exhibited higher error rates in plural noun phrases containing gender attractors compared to singular cases, indicating a dependence on cues from gendered articles. Collectively, these findings underscore specific deviations between LSTM behavior and human cognition, challenging the notion that LSTMs truly learn abstract syntactic rules and categories. Consequently, we propose gender agreement as a valuable probe for investigating the internal representations, mechanisms, and linguistic competencies of LSTM models.

Image cropping serves as a low-cost but potent method for maliciously modifying image content. Current detection mechanisms rely on analyzing inherent traces of cropping, such as chromatic aberration and vignetting, to identify attacks; however, these methods are vulnerable to common post-processing techniques that obscure these forensic cues. Furthermore, existing approaches overlook the potential of recovering discarded image regions to reveal the attacker's intent. This paper introduces CLR-Net, a novel robust watermarking framework designed for Image Cropping Localization and Recovery. The process begins by embedding imperceptible perturbations into the original image to protect it. Subsequently, various post-processing attacks are simulated to degrade the protected image. On the recipient's side, the system predicts the cropping mask and reconstructs the original image. To enhance real-world robustness, we propose two plug-and-play networks: the Fine-Grained generative JPEG simulator (FG-JPEG) and a Siamese image pre-processing network. To our knowledge, this work is the first to simultaneously address the challenges of localizing image cropping and fully recovering content from fragments. Experimental results confirm that CLR-Net can accurately pinpoint cropping boundaries and restore the details of missing regions with high quality and fidelity, even when subjected to diverse image processing attacks.

This work presents a non-trivial instance of elevating a "weak" eigenform to a genuine eigenform in characteristic 0. While the weak eigenform is intimately connected to Ramanujan's tau function, the resulting characteristic 0 eigenform corresponds to an elliptic curve defined over ${\mathbb Q}$. The lifting process is demonstrated by proving that the coefficients of the initial weak eigenform (for almost all indices) appear as traces of Frobenius within the Galois representation acting on the 4-torsion of the elliptic curve. Notably, this example is significant because the original form is known to be non-liftable to any characteristic 0 eigenform of level 1. Furthermore, we employ this case to illuminate recent inquiries in the theory of modular forms modulo prime powers and provide a concise overview of these emerging questions.

This study introduces a novel probabilistic post-processing approach for wind vectors within a distributional regression framework that utilizes a bivariate Gaussian distribution. Unlike prior research, this method simultaneously models all distribution parameters, including the means and variances for both wind components as well as their correlation coefficient, using flexible regression splines. To address potential discrepancies between predicted and observed wind directions, the approach incorporates ensemble forecasts of both wind components via flexible two-dimensional smooth functions, effectively allowing for a smooth rotation of wind direction conditional on the season and the forecasted ensemble direction. The method's efficacy was evaluated across stations in plains, mountain forelands, and an alpine valley, using ECMWF ensemble forecasts to explain all distribution parameters. Results indicate that the model permitting wind direction rotation significantly enhances predictive skill at all locations compared to a baseline that processes each wind component independently. Additionally, various correlation specifications were assessed, yielding minor performance gains over models with no estimated correlation specifically for stations situated in alpine valleys.

The share-of-choice product design (SOCPD) problem seeks to identify the optimal product configuration, defined by its attributes, that maximizes market share across various customer segments. When customer behavior adheres to a logit choice model, market share is calculated as a weighted sum of logistic probabilities, resulting in the logit-based SOCPD problem. Initially, this challenge seems intractable due to the need to optimize a non-convex, non-concave objective function over an exponentially large discrete space of attribute combinations. However, this paper introduces an exact solution methodology grounded in modern integer, convex, and conic optimization. Central to our approach is the counterintuitive finding that the logit-based SOCPD problem can be precisely reformulated as a mixed-integer convex program. Through testing on both synthetic data and real-world conjoint datasets, we demonstrate that our method can resolve large-scale instances to proven optimality or near-optimality within operationally feasible timeframes.

In 1990, Romero introduced an elegant formula for projecting onto the set of rectangular matrices with specified row and column sums. Variants of this formula were later rediscovered in 1998 by Khoury and by Glunt, Hayden, and Reams, specifically for bistochastic (square) matrices. These findings have inspired numerous generalizations and applications. This paper presents a formula for the broader problem of projecting onto rectangular matrices with prescribed scaled row and column sums. Our methodology relies on calculating the Moore-Penrose inverse of a specific linear operator linked to the problem. Furthermore, our analysis remains valid for Hilbert-Schmidt operators without requiring consistency assumptions, and we include numerical experiments demonstrating the new projection operator.

The classifying space for framed Haefliger structures of codimension $q$ and regularity class $C^r$ exhibits $(2q-1)$-connectivity for $1\le r\le\infty$. The derived corollaries address the existence of foliations, as well as properties concerning the homology and perfectness of diffeomorphism groups, alongside the existence of foliated products and foliated bundles.

A non-commutative Ulam quasimorphism is defined as a map $q$ from a group $\Gamma$ to a topological group $G$, where the deviation $q(xy)q(y)^{-1}q(x)^{-1}$ lies within a fixed compact subset of $G$. Extending the Barge and Ghys construction, we develop a family of such quasimorphisms on the fundamental group of a compact manifold $M$ with negative sectional curvature, with values in an arbitrary Lie group. This method, which generalizes the original Barge-Ghys approach, assigns a quasimorphism to every principal $G$-bundle equipped with a connection on $M$. While Kapovich and Fujiwara demonstrated that all quasimorphisms into a discrete group arise from group homomorphisms and those into commutative groups, we construct Barge-Ghys type quasimorphisms that take prescribed values on a specific subset of $\Gamma$, thereby providing counterexamples to the Kapovich-Fujiwara theorem for quasimorphisms valued in Lie groups. Furthermore, our work extends a result by D. Kazhdan from his paper "On $\epsilon$-representations." Kazhdan established that for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists an $\epsilon$-representation of the fundamental group of a genus 2 Riemann surface that cannot be approximated within $1/10$ by a representation. We prove this assertion holds for any compact manifold of negative sectional curvature.

The Educational Irish Research Satellite 1 (EIRSAT-1) is a 2U CubeSat developed within the ESA's "Fly Your Satellite!" initiative. While the project has a strong educational focus, it also aims to space-qualify novel detector technologies for gamma-ray astronomy, specifically for detecting gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). The primary payload, the Gamma-ray Module (GMOD), is a compact gamma-ray spectrometer featuring a 25 mm × 25 mm × 40 mm cerium bromide scintillator paired with an array of 16 silicon photomultipliers. Its readout system utilizes the IDE3380 (SIPHRA), a low-power, radiation-hardened ASIC. GMOD is designed to detect gamma-rays and measure their energies ranging from tens of keV to several MeV. Monte Carlo simulations conducted with the Medium Energy Gamma-ray Astronomy Library assessed GMOD's GRB detection capabilities in low Earth orbit, employing a detailed mass model of the spacecraft based on a high-fidelity 3D CAD design. These simulations determined that the sky-average effective area of GMOD on EIRSAT-1 is 10 cm² at 120 keV. The instrument is projected to detect between 11 and 14 GRBs with a significance exceeding 10σ (up to 32 at 5σ) over a nominal one-year mission. The GMOD scintillator's shape provides omni-directional sensitivity, enabling a nearly all-sky field of view.

This study employs the relativistic mean-field framework to analyze non-rotating, isotropic neutron stars containing dark matter (DM) admixture, utilizing the IOPB-I hadronic equation of state (EOS) under the assumption that fermionic DM from supersymmetric models has been accreted. The research examines how DM influences mass-radius relations and radial oscillations in pulsating DM-neutron stars, both with and without a crust. Results indicate that DM softens the EOS, thereby reducing both the maximum mass and its associated radius. Additionally, the inclusion of DM leads to higher oscillation frequencies, demonstrating a linear relationship between the fundamental mode frequency of canonical neutron stars and DM Fermi momentum. The study also validates the Sturm-Liouville boundary value problem by analyzing eigenfunction profiles. Furthermore, stellar stability is assessed through fundamental mode frequency variations with mass, confirming the stability criterion $\partial M/\partial\rho_c > 0$. Finally, the impact of the crust on large frequency separation across different DM Fermi momenta is investigated.

We introduce an open-access natural language processing toolkit designed for extracting medical information from Japanese sources. Initially, we propose a new annotation schema to examine relationships and temporal connections between medical entities within Japanese medical reports. To test practical annotation scenarios, we separately annotate two distinct report types. Our pipeline system comprises three modules responsible for identifying medical entities, classifying their modalities, and extracting relations. Empirical results demonstrate high analysis accuracy, indicating satisfactory annotation quality, an effective strategy for specific report types, and the advantage of using the latest contextual embedding models.

Building every extreme instance within the set of completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) maps, known as quantum channels, remains a difficult and significant open challenge in quantum information theory. This paper presents a systematic methodology capable of constructing precisely those extreme channels that exhibit covariance under either a finite discrete group or a compact connected Lie group. By innovatively labeling quantum channels using group representations, we isolate the subset of group-covariant channels composed of group-covariant generalized-extreme elements. Leveraging fundamental principles of group representation theory, we establish equivalence classes for these labels and partition the set of group-covariant channels, demonstrating that constructing a single representative from each partition is sufficient. We derive Kraus operators for group-covariant generalized-extreme channels by resolving systems of linear and quadratic equations for all candidates meeting the necessary conditions for such extremality. Determining whether these constructed instances are extreme or quasi-extreme is achieved by solving systems of linear equations. We formalize the problem of constructing and classifying group-covariant generalized extreme channels into an algorithmic framework, expressed as pseudocode. To demonstrate the utility of our approach, we compute explicit examples of group-covariant extreme channels. Provided with unbounded computational resources, our method guarantees a description of an extreme channel for any finite-dimensional Hilbert space and ensures the identification of a group-covariant extreme channel for any dimension and group type (finite-discrete or compact connected Lie group), provided such a channel exists.

Quantum state tomography, the process of determining the optimal description of a quantum state (the density matrix), serves as a fundamental component for quantum computation and communication. However, conventional tomography methods struggle to track evolving states and often yield poor results when environmental noise is present. While theoretical solutions exist for these challenges, experimental validations have been limited. Our proposed method, matrix-exponentiated gradient tomography, addresses these issues as an online technique capable of state tracking. It dynamically updates the estimated density matrix starting from the initial measurements, operates with high computational efficiency, and rapidly converges to an accurate estimate even under noisy conditions. The algorithm relies on a single learning rate parameter to control performance, which can be optimized for specific experimental setups through simulations. We demonstrate the experimental realization of this method on a qutrit system encoded within the transverse spatial modes of photons. By testing the method on both stationary and evolving states under significant environmental noise, we achieved fidelities of approximately 95% across all scenarios.

Cold start remains a critical and enduring challenge in recommender systems. Current state-of-the-art approaches typically train hybrid models using auxiliary information to address both cold-start and established user-item scenarios; however, these models often degrade performance for existing users and items, rendering them impractical for real-world applications where maintaining established user experiences is paramount. While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven effective for warm (non-cold-start) recommendations, they have not yet been applied to cold-start problems within user-item bipartite graphs. This presents a difficult yet valuable opportunity, given that cold-start entities lack interaction links. Furthermore, designing a GNN capable of handling cold-start recommendations without compromising performance for existing entities is a non-trivial task. To address this gap, we introduce GPatch, a specialized GNN-based framework comprising two interrelated yet distinct components. First, we develop an efficient GNN architecture, GWarmer, to model warm users and items. Second, we construct correlated Patching Networks that simulate and augment GWarmer to facilitate cold-start recommendations. Empirical results on both benchmark and large-scale commercial datasets demonstrate that GPatch significantly outperforms existing methods in delivering recommendations for both established and cold-start users and items.

We present a multi-epoch study of rapid optical and X-ray timing data from the exceptionally bright 2018 outburst of MAXI J1820+070, a black hole low-mass X-ray binary. Covering an initial 80-day hard-state period, the campaign utilized NTT/ULTRACAM and GTC/HiPERCAM for optical observations (ugriz filters, 8–300 Hz time resolution) alongside ISS/NICER for X-ray data. Our analysis reveals three key findings: (i) an increasing anti-correlation between optical and X-ray lightcurves; (ii) a consistent positive correlation with an optical lag of 0.2 s (increasing with wavelength) across all epochs; and (iii) a distinct positive correlation at negative optical lags during the final, X-ray softest epoch, where longer wavelengths exhibit stronger correlations and more negative lags. To account for these results, we propose a model involving two synchrotron-emitting components: a compact jet and a hot flow. In this scenario, the jet's contribution diminishes over the course of the outburst, while the hot flow remains constant, causing its relative significance to rise. Additionally, we examine a previously identified quasi-periodic oscillation and demonstrate how it generates coherent optical time lags that are wavelength-dependent during at least two epochs.

We have expanded upon the Paley constructions for Hadamard matrices, resulting in several new series of these matrices. While the standard Paley construction-II is limited to odd prime powers $q$ where $q \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$, our approach applies to any odd prime power. Furthermore, some of the resulting matrices are non-isomorphic to those generated by the Sylvester, Williamson, or combined Sylvester-Paley methods. Our innovation involves utilizing conference matrices of order prime power $q$ in a novel way, which is effective for any odd prime power or for the product of twin primes.

This study examines the transverse field Ising model under a two-step periodic driving scheme alongside quasiperiodic modulation of the Ising interactions. We present analytical findings regarding phase boundaries linked to Majorana edge modes, as well as numerical data on the localization of single-particle excitations. A region in the parameter space characterized by fully localized, domain-wall-like excitations is identified, which signifies eigenstate order and exact spectral pairing of Floquet eigenstates. Based on these features, we establish the existence of time crystals. Furthermore, we numerically analyze various correlation functions within the time crystal phase to substantiate its presence.

Computer simulators frequently serve as proxies for complex real-world phenomena that are either costly or impractical to study directly. This paper addresses the efficient resolution of the inverse problem for time series valued simulators that are expensive to evaluate. The study is driven by the need to calibrate a hydrological simulator capable of producing realistic rainfall-runoff data for Athens, Georgia, USA. Given that a simulator yields $g(x,t)$ across $L$ time points for an input $x$, the proposed methodology starts by constructing a discretization (time-) point set (DPS) of size $k \ll L$. This is accomplished through a regression spline approximation of the target response series at $k$ optimal knot locations $\{t^*_1, t^*_2, ..., t^*_k\}$. Following this, $k$ scalar-valued inverse problems for the simulator $g(x,t^*_j)$ are solved using the contour estimation method. The proposed approach, termed MSCE, also enables uncertainty quantification of the inverse solution. An extensive simulation study evaluates the performance of this method against popular competitors across several test-function based computer simulators and a real-life rainfall-runoff model.

This study examines the application of Koopman Operator theory to satellite motion around libration points within the Circular Restricted Three-Body Problem. Recently, the Koopman Operator has gained recognition as a valuable alternative to traditional geometric approaches for analyzing dynamical systems, defining them through observables. The paper investigates utilizing this operator to calculate 2D and 3D periodic orbits near these libration points. Additionally, simulation results demonstrate that the Koopman Operator yields highly accurate analytical solutions for both Lyapunov and Halo orbits, which are subsequently employed in a station-keeping scenario.

This paper generalizes prior convergence findings regarding the generalized alternating projection method for subspaces, originally detailed in [arXiv:1703.10547], to encompass smooth manifolds. We demonstrate that the algorithm exhibits comparable local behavior in both manifold and subspace contexts, yielding identical convergence rates. Furthermore, we establish convergence rate theorems for applications involving non-empty, closed, and convex sets. These outcomes rely on a finite identification property, which ensures that following an initial identification stage, the algorithm effectively solves a smooth manifold feasibility problem. Consequently, the derived rates apply asymptotically to problems satisfying this identification property. We provide several examples illustrating this condition alongside a counterexample where it does not hold.

Nonlinear balanced truncation is a model order reduction method that decreases the dimensionality of nonlinear systems while incorporating both open- and closed-loop controllability and observability characteristics. Two major computational hurdles have historically hindered its application to large-scale systems: (a) the necessity of solving high-dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations to define energy functions for controllability and observability, and (b) the need for efficient model reduction and simulation of reduced-order models (ROMs) on the resulting nonlinear balanced manifolds. This study introduces a unified, scalable solution to challenge (a) by employing a Taylor series-based method to address a specific class of parametrized Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations fundamental to balancing. A formulation parameter within this approach determines whether open-loop or various closed-loop balancing strategies are applied. To determine the coefficients for the Taylor series approximation of the energy functions, the proposed method constructs a linear tensor structure, leveraging it extensively to solve structured linear systems containing billions of unknowns. The algorithm's robustness and scalability are validated through applications to two semi-discretized partial differential equations: the Burgers equation and the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation.

Observational data regarding ultrahigh energy cosmic rays (UHECR), specifically their mass composition, strongly suggest that individual mass groups of cosmic ray nuclei exhibit extremely hard spectra upon reaching Earth. This study demonstrates that such hard spectra can arise from the finite lifetimes of UHECR sources, provided that a small number of individual sources dominate the flux at the highest energies. Under these conditions, time delays caused by deflections in the turbulent extragalactic magnetic field, as well as by diffusive or advective escape from the source environment, suppress low-energy cosmic rays, resulting in a steepening of the observed spectrum. Focusing on radio galaxies as the primary UHECR sources, we examine the requirements for a few individual sources to dominate over the cumulative contribution from the larger population of sources active in the past. We present two proof-of-principle scenarios indicating that for a turbulent extragalactic magnetic field with strength $B$ and coherence length $l_{\rm coh}$, the source lifetime at a distance $d_{\rm src}$ must satisfy ${t_{\rm act} \sim \left( B/1\,\text{nG} \right)^2\,\left( d_{\rm src}/10\,\text{Mpc} \right)^2\,\left( l_{\rm coh}/1\,\text{Mpc} \right)\,\text{Myr}}$ to achieve the necessary hardening of the cosmic ray spectrum observed at Earth.

This study examines the impact of $f(R,T)$ gravity on rapidly rotating neutron stars. We begin by outlining the fundamental principles of this modified gravitational framework, where the Lagrangian is defined as an arbitrary function of the Ricci scalar $R$ and the trace of the energy-momentum tensor $T$. Next, we derive the governing equations for neutron stars, incorporating the specific equations of state employed to model hadronic matter. Key physical parameters, including mass-radius relationships, moments of inertia, angular momentum, and compactness, are computed. By analyzing four distinct rotation regimes, our results demonstrate significant alterations in the physical characteristics of neutron stars under $f(R,T)$ gravity compared to general relativity. Specifically, the mass-radius sequences reveal that $f(R,T)$ gravity leads to an increase in both mass and equatorial radius for neutron stars rotating below the Keplerian limit.

For a directed graph $G$ and integers $k$ and $l$, a D-core is defined as the largest subgraph $H \subseteq G$ where every vertex in $H$ possesses an in-degree of at least $k$ and an out-degree of at least $l$. The task of D-core decomposition involves calculating the non-empty D-cores for all feasible pairs of $k$ and $l$. While various peeling-based algorithms exist in the literature, those operating sequentially with a need for global graph information are primarily tailored for centralized environments, making them unsuitable for efficiently processing large-scale graphs in distributed contexts. Addressing this limitation, this paper investigates distributed D-core decomposition. We introduce the concept of "anchored coreness" to develop a novel H-index-based algorithm for this problem. Additionally, we propose "skyline coreness," demonstrating that D-core decomposition is equivalent to computing skyline coreness values for all vertices. To facilitate distributed computation, we design an efficient D-index. The proposed algorithms are implemented within both vertex-centric and block-centric distributed graph processing frameworks. We also provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithms' message and time complexities. Extensive experiments on large real-world graphs containing billions of edges confirm the efficiency of our approaches regarding both execution time and communication costs.

Direct cross-section measurements in nuclear astrophysics require not only appropriate ion beams and detectors but also highly pure and stable targets. Utilizing a gas jet as a target provides a promising solution, offering exceptional stability under intense beam loads alongside superior purity and precise localization. Currently, such a target system is being constructed at the Felsenkeller underground ion accelerator laboratory in Dresden, Germany, dedicated to nuclear astrophysics. The target's thickness will be monitored via optical interferometry, enabling in-situ measurements that account for beam-induced effects. This contribution details the current status of the new system and discusses its potential applications within the field of nuclear astrophysics.
We examine the asymptotic behavior of a kernel-based nonparametric estimator for the linear multiplier within models defined by stochastic differential equations driven by a general Gaussian process.

The growing focus on explainable artificial intelligence has significantly elevated the interest in Explainable Recommendation. Among various strategies, post-hoc methods have emerged as the most practical solution for applying explanations to increasingly intricate recommendation systems, which are often treated as black boxes. However, recent studies indicate that post-hoc explanations relying on local surrogate models face inherent issues regarding their own robustness. This concern is particularly critical in human-centric domains like recommendation systems, where explanations must also work to bolster essential user experience factors such as transparency and trust. This paper demonstrates that classical post-hoc models based on surrogates are heavily dependent on the specific model being explained and ultimately fail to provide accountable justifications for the generated explanations.

Current software-based energy assessments for NLP models lack accuracy because they fail to account for the intricate interplay between energy usage and model execution. We introduce IrEne, an interpretable and extensible framework designed to precisely forecast the inference energy demands of diverse Transformer-based NLP architectures. IrEne builds a model tree graph that decomposes NLP models into modules, which are subsequently broken down into fundamental machine learning (ML) primitives. The system predicts the energy consumption of these primitives based on generalizable features and fine-grained runtime resource metrics. These low-level estimates are then aggregated recursively to determine the energy cost of each module and the model as a whole. Experiments spanning various Transformer models demonstrate that IrEne achieves an error rate of less than 7% against ground truth, significantly outperforming existing energy models that exhibit errors exceeding 50%. Additionally, we illustrate how IrEne facilitates energy bottleneck analysis and the evaluation of energy impacts from different architectural decisions. The source code and data are available at https://github.com/StonyBrookNLP/irene.

This paper establishes an energy conservation criterion for weak solutions of both homogeneous incompressible and general compressible Navier-Stokes equations, derived from a combination of velocity and its gradient. In the incompressible context, this framework encompasses most established results on periodic domains based on either velocity or its gradient, notably including Lions' famous energy conservation criterion. Regarding compressible flow, the approach extends prior energy conservation criteria from incompressible fluids to compressible regimes and refines recent findings by Nguyen-Nguyen-Tang and Liang.

Enforcing disentanglement within neural representations poses significant challenges. This difficulty may stem, in part, from a formalization that overly prioritizes isolating relevant factors of variation into single, distinct dimensions of the latent space. We contend that this restrictive definition is not necessarily advantageous for downstream applications. Instead, this work proposes an alternative perspective on learning (weakly) disentangled representations by drawing upon concepts from relational learning. We identify latent space regions corresponding to specific generative factor instances and learn the relationships between them to enable controlled modifications of latent codes. Furthermore, we introduce a compound generative model that realizes this weak disentanglement framework. Experimental results demonstrate that the learned representations can effectively separate relevant factors of variation while retaining the necessary information to generate high-quality data samples.

Variable selection in high-dimensional statistics is extensively researched because accurately determining the link between covariates and the response is critical across various scientific fields. Nevertheless, existing theoretical frameworks and methods for linear models typically rely on the assumption of independent and identically distributed (iid) sub-Gaussian covariates and errors. This study examines the theoretical behavior of Sure Independence Screening (SIS) within high-dimensional linear models featuring dependent and/or heavy-tailed covariates and errors. Furthermore, we propose a Generalized Least Squares Screening (GLSS) method that leverages serial correlation within the data. By incorporating this serial correlation to estimate marginal effects, GLSS demonstrates superior performance compared to SIS in numerous scenarios. We establish sure screening properties for both approaches, which hinge on moment conditions, the intensity of dependence in error and covariate processes, and other variables. Moreover, we analyze the integration of these screening techniques with adaptive Lasso. Dependence is measured using functional dependence metrics (Wu [Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 102 (2005) 14150-14154]), with results grounded in Nagaev-type and exponential inequalities for dependent random variables. Simulations are conducted to illustrate the finite-sample efficacy of these procedures, complemented by a real-world application forecasting the US inflation rate.

This study examines how speaker localization influences speech recognition performance within multispeaker, multichannel settings. Leveraging known speaker positions, speech separation is executed across three phases: first, a delay-and-sum (DS) beamformer enhances signals from the target location to generate a time-frequency mask via a neural network; this mask subsequently calculates second-order statistics to inform an adaptive beamformer in the final stage. We evaluated this pipeline on a multichannel, multispeaker, reverberant, and noisy dataset modeled after WSJ0-2mix, measuring outcomes via word error rate (WER). Results showed a $29.4\%$ average WER with ground-truth localization versus $42.4\%$ with GCC-PHAT estimated localization. Furthermore, the signal-to-interference ratio (SIR) between speakers significantly impacts ASR performance, with a $15$ dB SIR increase reducing WER by $59\%$ relative. In contrast, increasing spatial separation to $50^\circ$ or more yields a comparatively modest $23\%$ relative WER improvement.

Non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics plays a pivotal role in the formation of protoplanetary disks, specifically in controlling their dimensions. We present a simplified model to forecast disk size resulting from the interaction of ambipolar diffusion, the Hall effect, and Ohmic dissipation. This model predicts a compact disk size of approximately 20 AU for sub-Solar mass systems with moderate magnetization across various initial conditions; this size scales sub-linearly with disk parameters. The model successfully reproduces bimodal behaviors observed in numerical simulations regarding parallel and anti-parallel alignments between rotation and magnetic fields. In parallel configurations, the disk shrinks and vanishes, whereas in anti-parallel configurations, the disk forms a short-lived, flat, shrinking outer pseudo-disk alongside a slowly growing, long-lived inner region. Despite significant initial magnetization, the vertical field dominates only briefly during low-mass early stages, while the toroidal field eventually prevails in all disks.

Recent philosophical inquiry has highlighted the epistemological difficulties stemming from the opacity of deep neural networks, leading some to argue that conducting rigorous science with such models is nearly impossible. However, this pessimistic view clashes with the current surge of optimism in AI-driven scientific advancements and the wave of breakthroughs they have enabled. This paper contends that the rift between philosophical skepticism and scientific optimism arises from a neglect of how AI is practically employed in research. I argue that to grasp the epistemic validity of AI-fueled discoveries, philosophers must analyze deep learning not in isolation, but as an integral component of the broader discovery process. Utilizing the distinction between the 'context of discovery' and the 'context of justification' is crucial here. By examining two specific cases from the scientific literature, I demonstrate that paying attention to this distinction reveals that epistemic opacity does not necessarily undermine AI's ability to guide scientists toward significant and well-justified breakthroughs.

We utilize the Noether symmetry method to derive exact cosmological solutions within $f(T)$-gravity. Rather than relying on phenomenological models, we directly apply the Noether symmetry condition to $f(T)$ gravity. This approach identifies viable models and enables the solution of the equations of motion. Our results demonstrate that the resulting $f(T)$ models yield a power-law expansion for the cosmological scale factor.

Conformational changes in DNA molecules are common across various biological processes and are often modeled as a chain of strongly coupled oscillators featuring a nonlinear bistable potential. Although the mechanisms and properties of these changes have been studied, along with the development of several reduced-order models, the dynamics of conformational change relative to the oscillator chain's length remain poorly understood. To clarify this, we employed a modified Lindstedt-Poincare method alongside numerical simulations. By calculating a perturbation expansion for the frequency of the model's nonzero modes, we determined that approximating these modes with their unperturbed dynamics, as done in prior reduced-order models, becomes invalid as the DNA model lengthens. Investigating how conformational shifts respond to local perturbations in models of different lengths revealed two distinct regions based on input parameters and settings: initially, the minimum energy required for the transition increases with DNA length, followed by a region where this energy remains nearly independent of length. Furthermore, by introducing randomness to the local perturbation, we analyzed the system's stability, finding that the tendency to maintain a stable conformation diminishes as DNA length increases. These findings aim to enhance the understanding of how DNA length influences its conformational dynamics.

This work establishes comprehensive definitions for unramified and totally ramified maps across diverse mathematical frameworks, including commutative rings, schemes, ring spectra, and derived schemes. We demonstrate that these definitions align with classical notions when applied to rings of integers within number fields. Furthermore, this generalized approach yields a direct computation of topological Hochschild homology for such rings without relying on computational methods. Specifically, we establish that $THH(R)$ is the homotopy cofiber of a map $R[\Omega S^3]\otimes_R\Omega^1_{R/\mathbb{Z}}\to R[\Omega S^3\langle 3\rangle]$, resulting in the long exact sequence $\cdots\to H_\ast(\Omega S^3;\Omega^1_{R/\mathbb{Z}})\to H_\ast(\Omega S^3\langle 3\rangle;R)\to THH_\ast(R)\to\cdots$. Additionally, whenever an extension $Y/X$ comprises a composition of unramified and totally ramified extensions, our findings facilitate the analysis of $THH(X)$ relative to $THH(Y)$ through a mechanism akin to weak étale descent, or ramified descent.

The stacking sequences in hexagonal close-packed and related crystals typically generate steps on vicinal {0001} surfaces that alternate between A and B structures, each exhibiting distinct growth kinetics. However, the experimental difficulty in distinguishing which step corresponds to the A or B structure has previously prevented researchers from identifying which possesses faster adatom attachment rates. This study demonstrates that in situ microbeam surface X-ray scattering can resolve whether A or B steps exhibit superior kinetics under specific growth conditions. We apply this method to the organo-metallic vapor phase epitaxy of (0001) GaN, showing that X-ray measurements during growth reveal an increase in the average terrace width above A steps as the growth rate rises. This indicates that attachment rate constants are higher for A steps, contradicting most theoretical predictions. These findings provide direct insights into the atomic-scale mechanisms of GaN growth and are applicable to a broad range of related crystalline materials.

We present a classical algorithm capable of approximating the free energy of local, translation-invariant, one-dimensional quantum systems within the thermodynamic limit. Although finding the ground state (free energy at $T = 0$) for such systems is believed to be computationally intractable even for quantum computers, our method operates in subpolynomial time, $O((\frac{1}{\varepsilon})^{c})$ for any constant $c > 0$, for any fixed temperature $T > 0$, where $\varepsilon$ represents the additive approximation error. This represents a significant improvement over previous algorithms, which required polynomial time in $\frac{1}{\varepsilon}$ with a degree that was exponential in the inverse temperature $1/T$. Our approach is notably straightforward, reducing to the calculation of the spectral radius of a linear map. This map, interpretable as a noncommutative transfer matrix, has been previously utilized to establish findings regarding the analyticity of free energy and the decay of correlations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the corresponding eigenvector of this map provides an approximation of the Gibbs state's marginal, enabling the calculation of various thermodynamic properties of the quantum system.

This study examines third-order QCD corrections for various kinematic moments of inclusive semileptonic $B$ decays, calculated to first order in the $1/m_b$ expansion. Specifically, we analyze the first four moments of the charged-lepton energy spectrum ($E_\ell$), along with the total leptonic invariant mass ($q^2$) and the hadronic invariant mass ($M_X^2$), without applying any experimental cuts. Our analytical results are derived using an asymptotic expansion near the limit where $m_b \simeq m_c$. Following the conversion of the bottom mass scheme to the kinetic scheme, we compare the magnitude of higher-order QCD corrections against contributions from $1/m_b^2$ and $1/m_b^3$ power corrections, as well as their respective uncertainties.

Hybrid superconductor-semiconductor heterostructures represent a promising avenue for developing quantum devices rooted in mesoscopic and topological superconductivity. These systems require a semiconductor to be in intimate proximity to a superconductor while establishing an ohmic contact, a configuration well-suited for narrow band gap materials like InAs due to their surface Fermi levels residing near the conduction band. This study investigates the structural characteristics of near-surface InAs quantum wells, revealing a strong link between surface morphology and low-temperature transport properties, specifically how electron mobility depends on the growth temperature of the underlying graded buffer layer. Furthermore, by applying an In$_{0.81}$Al$_{0.19}$As capping layer, we demonstrate the ability to adjust surface Fermi level pinning within the top nanometer of the thin film. Experimental data align closely with Schr\"odinger-Poisson simulations of electron density, indicating that the conduction band edges at the surfaces of In$_{0.81}$Ga$_{0.19}$As and In$_{0.81}$Al$_{0.19}$As are pinned approximately \SI{40}{\milli eV} and \SI{309}{\milli eV} above the Fermi level, respectively.

Using the perturbative QCD framework with $k_T$ factorization, this study examines the decays of $B_{d,s}^0$ mesons into pairs of light scalar mesons ($\sigma$ and $f_0$), specifically the channels $\sigma\sigma$, $\sigma f_0$, and $f_0 f_0$, within the two-quark model where $\sigma$ and $f_0$ represent $f_0(500)$ and $f_0(980)$, respectively. Assuming a quark-flavor basis mixing angle of approximately $25^\circ$ between $\sigma$ and $f_0$, the analysis yields three key findings: (a) These neutral $B$-meson decays are predicted to possess substantial branching ratios ranging from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-4}$, suggesting constructive interference among decays with different flavor states, a phenomenon anticipated to be verified by future experiments at the LHCb and Belle-II facilities; (b) Significant direct CP violation is expected in the modes $B_d^0 \to \sigma\sigma, f_0 f_0$ and $B_{d,s}^0 \to \sigma f_0$, indicating strong interference between tree-level and penguin decay amplitudes across these four processes, which should be testable against upcoming data; (c) These decays can be investigated via the secondary decay chain $\sigma/f_0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-$, resulting in four-body final states such as $B_{d,s}^0 \to (\pi^+ \pi^-)_{\sigma(f_0)} (\pi^+ \pi^-)_{\sigma(f_0)}$. Additionally, other four-body decays like $B_d^0 \to (\pi^+ \pi^-)_{\sigma} (K^+ K^-)_{f_0}$, $B_s^0 \to (\pi^+ \pi^-)_{\sigma(f_0)} (K^+ K^-)_{f_0}$, and $B_s^0 \to (K^+ K^-)_{f_0} (K^+ K^-)_{f_0}$ may be observable at relevant experiments, provided that the $f_0 \to K^+ K^-$ signal can be distinguished from the background of $\phi \to K^+ K^-$.
We categorize homogeneous real (2,3,5) distributions that are multiply transitive, distinguishing them based on local diffeomorphism equivalence.

A key challenge in analyzing high-dimensional omics data involves identifying subsets of molecular variables linked to a specific phenotype. Tackling this requires overcoming issues related to high dimensionality, strong multicollinearity, and model uncertainty. We introduce STRANDS (STructural RANDomised Selection), a novel ensemble learning strategy designed to enhance sparse penalized regression methods. Building on the Random Lasso technique, STRANDS operates through two stages where dimensionality reduction is achieved via repeated variable subsampling. Penalized regression is applied to each subsampled dataset, and the outcomes are averaged. The first stage utilizes variable correlation structures to guide subsampling, while the second stage relies on importance metrics derived from the initial step. STRANDS functions as a wrapper for any sparse penalized regression method used as the base learner. Validation using both synthetic data and real biological datasets demonstrates that STRANDS generally outperforms its base learner, with the inclusion of correlation structure in the first step significantly improving the efficiency of model space exploration.

This paper investigates unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) outfitted with visible light communication (VLC) access points and coordinated multipoint (CoMP) capabilities, enabling users to connect to multiple UAVs simultaneously. These UAVs operate in three-dimensional (3D) space with constant acceleration, managed by a central server that oversees synchronization and collaboration. The study emphasizes the necessity of accounting for accelerated motion, distinguishing itself from prior research by analyzing how variable speed impacts kinetics and radio resource allocation. The proposed system model utilizes two distinct time frames: one for defining each UAV's acceleration and another for allocating radio resources within each slot. The primary objective is to formulate a multi-objective optimization problem that simultaneously maximizes total data rates and minimizes total communication power consumption. To address this, we employ a scalarization method followed by a multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG) algorithm, enhanced by the addition of two critic networks and a two-stage resource allocation strategy. Simulation results demonstrate that UAVs maintaining constant acceleration achieve approximately 8% better performance compared to conventional motion systems.

Recent advancements in neural rendering have achieved near-photorealistic image quality, yet the computational demands of these networks create high latency that hinders their use in low-latency, high-resolution applications like virtual reality and telepresence. The sequential nature of layers in deep networks further complicates optimization. To address this, we eliminate layer dependencies by caching data from the previous frame to accelerate current frame processing through an implicit warp. This shallow warping network significantly cuts latency, while the caching mechanism allows for parallelization to boost frame rates. Unlike existing temporal methods, our approach is specifically designed for rendering novel views of faces by conditioning on changes in the underlying surface mesh. We evaluate this method on view-dependent 3D portrait avatars using standard benchmark sequences.
