Results show that warping decreases latency by 70% (dropping from 49.4ms to 14.9ms on commodity GPUs) and scales effectively across multiple GPUs with only a 1% drop in image quality, making it ideal for end-to-end 3D teleconferencing. The project page is available at: https://yu-frank.github.io/lowlatency/.

Over the last ten years, the impact of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has extended well beyond computer science research and software development. Today, NLP techniques are employed across various academic fields, ranging from Asian Studies to Clinical Oncology. Furthermore, NLP has become a standard component in data science curricula, both within traditional universities and in alternative educational settings, attracting students from highly diverse backgrounds. Drawing on classroom experiences, this paper examines specific challenges associated with teaching NLP to such varied audiences, highlighting the difficulties instructors encounter—especially when no supporting ecosystem of related courses exists. Additionally, the study pinpoints key challenges for both NLP researchers and tool developers.

Trapdoor claw-free functions (TCFs) play a crucial role in cryptographic exchanges between classical clients and quantum servers. Standard protocols typically involve a quantum server generating a superposition of two-bit claw strings and subsequently measuring them via Pauli-$X$ or $Z$ operations. This paper introduces a novel method that leverages the full spectrum of qubit measurements within the $XY$-plane. We highlight the benefits of this strategy through two specific applications. First, extending the work of Brakerski et al. (2018) and Kalai et al. (2022), we present an optimized two-round proof of quantumness where security is directly tied to the hardness of the LWE (learning with errors) problem. Second, we develop a one-round protocol enabling blind remote preparation of any state on the $XY$-plane, subject only to a Pauli-$Z$ correction.

This overview covers the fundamental definitions of condensed categories and the internal Hom within condensed abelian groups. We also present a construction for the internal Hom of condensed sets, which we use to provide a novel proof of a theorem by Clausen and Scholze. Additionally, we offer a detailed explanation of how the real numbers can be constructed from discrete spaces, a key intermediate step in another theorem by Clausen and Scholze.

Let V be a total valuation ring within a division ring K, and let Q denote the additive group of rational numbers. Define Aut(K) as the group of automorphisms of K, and let sigma be a group homomorphism mapping Q to Aut(K). Considering the skew group ring K[Q, sigma] formed over K by Q, this paper classifies graded extensions of V within this ring into two distinct types and examines their structural properties.

Although research into scientific claim verification has produced powerful systems that nearly match human performance, these methods have not yet been rigorously tested against large-scale scientific literature in realistic settings. Transitioning to such open-domain evaluations presents distinct hurdles, most notably the impracticality of exhaustively annotating every evidence document. To address this, we introduce SciFact-Open, a new benchmark comprising 500,000 research abstracts designed to assess claim verification systems. Utilizing information retrieval pooling strategies, we gathered evidence by aggregating and annotating the top predictions from four state-of-the-art verification models. Our results indicate that systems trained on smaller datasets struggle to generalize to SciFact-Open, suffering performance declines of at least 15 F1 points. Furthermore, an analysis of the evidence within SciFact-Open uncovers intriguing patterns relevant to real-world deployment, such as instances where evidence supports only a specific subset of a claim. The dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/dwadden/scifact-open.

Transparency techniques, including model visualizations, offer insights that raw outputs often overlook by illuminating the internal workings of neural networks. However, the question remains whether these explanations accurately reflect model behavior, specifically regarding the detection of irregularities like backdoors or shape bias. To assess this, we classify a model as anomalous when it diverges from a reference set of normal models and examine whether transparency methods generate distinct explanations for anomalous versus normal models. Our findings indicate that while current approaches can identify obvious anomalies such as shape bias or adversarial training, they often fail to detect subtler issues, including models trained on incomplete datasets. Furthermore, these methods generally cannot pinpoint the specific inputs that trigger anomalous behavior, such as images containing backdoor triggers. These results highlight significant blind spots in existing explanation methods, underscoring the necessity for further development in this area.

Let $UVB_n$ and $UVP_n$ denote the unrestricted virtual braid group and the unrestricted virtual pure braid group on $n$ strands, respectively. This paper investigates these groups with the following primary findings: for $n \geq 5$, we provide a complete classification, up to conjugation, of all homomorphisms from $UVB_n$ to the symmetric group $S_n$. For $n \geq 3$, we characterize the possible images of $UVB_n$ under homomorphisms into any finite group $G$. Additionally, for $n \geq 5$, we establish that $UVP_n$ is a characteristic subgroup of $UVB_n$. We further determine the automorphism group of $UVB_n$ and demonstrate that $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ is a subgroup of the outer automorphism group of $UVB_n$. Moreover, we prove that both $UVB_n$ and $UVP_n$ are residually finite and Hopfian, yet not co-Hopfian. Finally, we note that several of these results extend to the welded braid group $WB_n$ and examine its automorphism group.

When lateral variations in topography, such as streamwise-aligned ridges, are introduced into a turbulent wall-bounded flow, secondary flows are produced. This results in a flow field characterized by streamwise-oriented vortical structures referred to as Prandtl's vortices of the second kind (Prandtl 1965). Previous experimental and numerical studies have shown that the organization and intensity of these turbulent structures vary according to the ridge's shape. This paper employs the linearised RANS-based model developed by Zampino (2022) to examine how ridge geometry influences secondary current generation. By analyzing symmetric channels containing rectangular, triangular, and elliptical ridges and comparing their resulting secondary flows, the study highlights key similarities and differences. The observed analogies in flow organization across these three geometries suggest that for small, isolated ridges, secondary currents are independent of ridge shape, with flow strength collapsing when scaled appropriately by the mean ridge height. Finally, the generation of secondary flows and the impact of ridge geometry on flow organization are investigated in detail for complex configurations. Specifically, regarding trapezoidal ridges, it was noted that tertiary flows emerge in cases where the established scaling behavior fails to hold.

This work extends the Seiberg-Witten invariant to families of smooth 4-manifolds where the fibers are diffeomorphic to a specific 4-manifold $X$. A key focus is the scenario where the family admits a smoothly varying Kähler structure. We derive a general formula for computing these invariants under the condition $b_1=0$, expressing them through characteristic classes of vector bundles linked to the cohomology groups of holomorphic line bundles within the family. Subsequently, we apply this formula to specific Kähler families to perform further explicit calculations. These examples include a family of $\mathbb{CP}^2$s derived from the projectivization of a rank 3 complex vector bundle, a family of $\mathbb{CP}^1\times\mathbb{CP}^1$s formed by the fiber product of the projectivizations of two rank 2 complex vector bundles, and the universal blowup family, which consists of blowups of a Kähler surface at a point.

This paper introduces NEREL, a Russian dataset designed for named entity recognition and relation extraction. Significantly larger than current Russian resources, NEREL includes 56,000 annotated named entities and 39,000 annotated relations. A key distinction from prior datasets is its annotation of nested named entities, along with relations occurring within those nested structures and at the discourse level. NEREL supports the development of new models capable of extracting relations between nested entities as well as those spanning sentences and documents. Additionally, the dataset features annotations for events involving named entities and their specific roles. The NEREL collection is accessible at https://github.com/nerel-ds/NEREL.

We address the challenge of determining the homogeneous coordinates of points within a zero-dimensional subscheme of a compact, complex toric variety $X$. Beginning with a homogeneous ideal $I$ defined in the Cox ring of $X$—which often results from homogenizing a sparse polynomial system—we establish a new eigenvalue theorem tailored to the toric compact setting. This theorem enables a fresh, robust numerical strategy for resolving the problem, specifically accommodating systems with isolated solutions of any multiplicity. The approach relies on the multigraded regularity characteristics of $I$, which we investigate further to derive bounds on the matrix dimensions required when $I$ constitutes a complete intersection.

This study extends the concept of SpaceX's Starlink satellite deployment to investigate the feasibility of Type-I civilizations constructing planetary megastructures, whether as solid entities or satellite networks, and the resulting techno-signatures they would emit. We demonstrate that the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) has the potential to detect the emission patterns of such massive constructions. Additionally, we highlight the effectiveness of the spectral variability method and examine the contribution of the FAST telescope.

Originally designed by Arpad Elo for chess, the Elo rating system has evolved into a pivotal metric across sports, economics, and gaming. Although its foundational framework assumes two-player zero-sum interactions, it has since been adapted for team-based and other contexts. In 2015, Junca and Jabin introduced a kinetic variant of the Elo model, demonstrating that ratings converge to player strength under specific conditions. This paper extends their model to accommodate variable performance among individual players or teams. We examine the core modeling assumptions, develop the corresponding formal mean-field model, and validate the system's dynamics through computational simulations.

This paper introduces a supervised learning framework for developing sparsity-promoting regularizers aimed at denoising signals and images. While sparsity-promoting regularization is fundamental to modern signal reconstruction, its underlying operators are typically manually crafted or learned unsupervised. Given the recent effectiveness of supervised learning, particularly convolutional neural networks, in image reconstruction, we posit that supervised approaches offer a promising avenue for designing these regularizers. Consequently, we propose a variational denoising formulation employing a parametric, sparsity-promoting regularizer, where the parameters are optimized via supervised learning to minimize mean squared error on training pairs of ground truth images and measurements. Addressing the resulting challenging bilevel optimization problem, we derive a gradient expression for the training loss based on the closed-form solution of the denoising task and implement a corresponding gradient descent algorithm. Experimental results on structured 1D signals and natural images demonstrate that our learned operator surpasses established methods, including total variation, DCT-sparsity, unsupervised dictionary learning, and collaborative filtering. Although currently tailored for denoising, this methodology is expected to be adaptable to a broader class of inverse problems involving linear measurement models, thereby extending its utility across diverse signal reconstruction applications.

The equations governing the motion of spinning density for extended bodies and their associated deviation equations are derived. Additionally, the dynamics of a spinning extended object with variable mass are established. Spinning fluids can be treated as a specific instance to describe the motion of spinning density within extended objects. Furthermore, the spinning density tensor is formulated using the tetrad formalism of General Relativity, framing it as a gauge theory of gravity. Finally, the equations for spinning and spinning deviation density tensors are derived through the application of a particular type of Bazanski Lagrangian.

This study theoretically investigates the optical characteristics of triptycene molecular membranes (TMMs) when exposed to both linearly and circularly polarized light. Given that TMMs feature a double-layered Kagome lattice structure for their $\pi$-electrons—composed of tiling trigonal and hexagonal-symmetric rings—their electronic band structures exhibit non-equivalent Dirac cones alongside perfectly flat bands. By developing a tight-binding model to characterize the $\pi$-electronic states, we calculated the optical absorption intensities and valley-selective excitation of TMMs using the Kubo formula. Our findings reveal that absorption intensity is critically influenced by both the light's polarization angle and the excitation position within momentum space, indicating momentum and valley-selective optical excitation. Furthermore, group theoretical analyses were employed to elucidate the polarization dependence and optical selection rules.

Universal hitting sets consist of words that are inescapable; specifically, every sufficiently long sequence contains at least one word from the set. These sets share a strong connection with minimizer schemes, where efficient schemes characterized by low density correspond to universal hitting sets of small cardinality. Local schemes extend the concept of minimizer schemes, offering a potentially much more efficient alternative. This work connects efficient local schemes to the minimum length required for a string to be hit by a universal hitting set. Furthermore, we provide bounds for the remaining path length of the Mykkeltveit universal hitting set and introduce a local scheme with the currently lowest known density, which is merely a logarithmic factor away from the theoretical lower bound.

Contextual bandits are extensively deployed in industrial personalization systems, where online learning frameworks determine treatment policies based on user-specific contextual features. While personalized experiences cater to individual interests, there is also value in shared community experiences that foster participation in the zeitgeist; these benefits arise from network effects and are often overlooked by standard regret metrics used in bandit evaluation. To address this trade-off, we introduce a novel online learning algorithm that maintains personalization advantages while enhancing treatment uniformity across users. Our method selectively interpolates between a contextual bandit and a context-free multi-arm bandit, utilizing contextual data for decision-making only when it offers substantial gains. Beyond balancing individualized and shared user experiences, simplifying the treatment policy by relying on context only when beneficial can accelerate learning rates in certain scenarios. We validate our hybrid approach in a classification setting using public datasets, demonstrating its advantages.

We establish the existence of ancient solutions to the rescaled mean curvature flow initiated from a specified asymptotically conical self-expander. These findings provide examples of mean curvature flows emerging from cones that are not self-similar. Furthermore, we demonstrate a robust uniqueness result for cases where the cone is generic, utilizing this theorem to classify mean curvature flows originating from generic cones with low entropy in lower dimensions.

Let $[n]=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ represent a finite chain, and let $\mathcal{CT}_{n}$ denote the semigroup of full contractions on $[n]$. We define $\mathcal{ORCT}_{n}$ and $\mathcal{OCT}_{n}$ as the subsemigroups consisting of order-reversing and order-preserving full contractions, respectively. As established in [17], the sets of regular elements (Reg$(\mathcal{ORCT}_{n})$ and Reg$(\mathcal{OCT}_{n}$)) and idempotent elements (E$(\mathcal{ORCT}_{n})$ and E$(\mathcal{OCT}_{n}$)) within these subsemigroups are themselves subsemigroups. This paper investigates various combinatorial and rank properties of these specific subsemigroups.

The velocity distribution function serves as a statistical bridge linking particle kinetics with macroscopic parameters in many-body systems. Laser-induced fluorescence (LIF) spectroscopy is employed to measure this function in spatially inhomogeneous plasmas; however, determining the appropriate analytic form remains challenging due to complex factors in non-equilibrium states. This study introduces a novel method to identify the valid velocity distribution function form using Bayesian statistics. We formulate a Bayesian inference framework for the ion velocity distribution function and apply it to LIF spectra collected locally at various positions within a linear magnetized plasma. By validating each analytic form of the local velocity distribution function, we demonstrate the evaluation of spatial inhomogeneity. This approach is broadly applicable for experimentally determining velocity distribution functions in plasmas and fluids, such as gases and liquids.

Process mining allows business leaders to examine and analyze their real-world workflows by leveraging event data readily found in information systems. Although this event data offers granular details that are highly insightful, it frequently encompasses sensitive and private information, making privacy and confidentiality concerns in process mining increasingly critical. Consequently, novel techniques are emerging to address these issues. To ensure these methods are accessible, new tools are required to consolidate these techniques and guide users toward suitable solutions based on their specific requirements. This paper introduces a Python-based infrastructure that implements and integrates leading privacy and confidentiality preservation methods within process mining. The proposed tool features a user-friendly web interface for publishing privacy-preserving data, conducting risk assessments, and evaluating data utility. It also offers a suite of anonymization operations to support the preservation of privacy and confidentiality. Furthermore, the tool handles both standard XES event logs and non-standard event data, while storing and managing privacy metadata to track modifications resulting from these preservation techniques.

This work describes integrated photonic circuits utilizing suspended rib waveguides capable of coherently trapping, guiding, and splitting ultra-cold neutral atoms within two-colour evanescent fields near their surfaces. The paper presents configurations for quantum inertial sensors built on these atomo-photonic waveguides, which facilitate the simultaneous propagation of both photons and atoms along identical paths. Furthermore, it elucidates the distinctions between guided and free-space atom interferometers when subjected to external forces. Finally, the theoretical and technological hurdles that must be addressed to realize this emerging platform for quantum technologies are examined.

We examine an axion cloud surrounding a black hole in the presence of background magnetic fields, calculating its decay rate driven by axion-photon conversion via the axion-photon coupling. For simplicity, we assume the axion configuration is dominated by an eigenvalue solution analogous to the Hydrogen atom, allowing the coupling term to be computed using successive perturbation theory. For a monopole background, the decay rate scales as $\sim q^2\kappa^2(GM)^5\mu^8$, where $\mu$, $M$, $G$, $\kappa$, and $q$ represent the axion mass, black hole mass, gravitational constant, axion-photon coupling constant, and monopole charge, respectively. In the case of a uniform background magnetic field, the decay rate is found to be $\sim B_0^2\kappa^2 (GM)^7\mu^6$, with $B_0$ denoting the magnetic field strength. When applying these formulas to the Milky Way's central black hole, the decay rate for a uniform magnetic field matches the growth rate of superradiant instability for parameters $\kappa\sim 10^{-12}{\rm GeV^{-1}}$, $B_0\sim 10^3{\rm G}$, and $\mu\sim 10^{-18}{\rm eV}$. However, this ratio increases by a factor of $10^5$ when considering a monopole magnetic field with identical parameter values.

We conduct a perturbative QCD study of the gravitational form factors (GFFs) of the nucleon at high momentum transfer, deriving an explicit factorization formula that expresses these GFFs through twist-3 and twist-4 light-cone distribution amplitudes. The power-law behaviors of these form factors are determined via leading-order calculations. Additionally, we provide numerical results for both quark and gluon contributions to various GFFs, utilizing existing model assumptions for the distribution amplitudes. Furthermore, we present perturbative computations for the scalar form factor $\langle P'|F^2| P\rangle$ of the pion and proton in the regime of large momentum transfer.

Gourdeau et al. (2019) established that distributional assumptions are essential for robustly learning concept classes when dealing with exact-in-the-ball robust risk and random example access. This paper investigates learning models enhanced by local queries, presenting the first distribution-free algorithms capable of robust empirical risk minimization (ERM) under this robustness definition. We first examine a model utilizing local membership queries (LMQ), allowing the learner to request labels for points proximate to the training set. Under a uniform distribution, we demonstrate that LMQs fail to improve the robustness threshold for conjunctions or their superclasses, such as decision lists and halfspaces. In response to this limitation, we propose the local equivalence query (LEQ) oracle, which determines agreement between a hypothesis and target concept within a perturbation region of a training point and provides a counterexample if disagreement exists. Our separation results indicate that if the query radius $\lambda$ is strictly less than the adversary's perturbation budget $\rho$, distribution-free robust learning remains impossible for many concept classes; conversely, setting $\lambda=\rho$ enables the development of robust ERM algorithms. We subsequently bound the query complexity of these algorithms using online learning guarantees, further refining these bounds for conjunctions. Finally, we present robust learning algorithms for halfspaces with margins applicable to both $\{0,1\}^n$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Recent Super-Resolution (SR) advancements have primarily been evaluated on general images like faces and landscapes, leaving Earth Observation (EO) applications underexplored. This study benchmarks top-tier SR algorithms across various EO datasets using both Full-Reference and No-Reference Image Quality Assessment (IQA) metrics. Additionally, we introduce a novel Quality Metric Regression Network (QMRNet), capable of predicting quality as a No-Reference metric by learning from specific image attributes such as resolution and distortions, while also optimizing SR algorithms for targeted metric objectives. This research supports the IQUAFLOW framework, designed to assess image quality, detect and classify objects, and handle image compression within EO contexts. Our experiments involved testing QMRNet on predicting features including blur, sharpness, SNR, RER, and Ground Sampling Distance (GSD), achieving validation median Rs below 1.0 (out of 50) and recall rates exceeding 95%. The overall benchmark highlights promising performance for LIIF, CAR, and MSRN, alongside the potential of QMRNet to serve as a loss function for optimizing SR predictions. Given its simplicity and fully scalable architecture and data processing, QMRNet is also well-suited for other image domains and use cases.

Despite decades of significant effort to enhance linear and nonlinear mixing models for hyperspectral unmixing, these methods still struggle to effectively handle diverse spectral variabilities while extracting physically meaningful endmembers, largely due to inadequate data fitting, poor reconstruction capabilities, and high sensitivity to spectral changes. Drawing inspiration from deep learning's robust learning potential, we propose a novel general approach termed the Endmember-Guided Unmixing Network (EGU-Net). Unlike standard autoencoder architectures, EGU-Net utilizes a two-stream Siamese structure that trains an auxiliary network on pure or near-pure endmembers to refine the weights of a primary unmixing network through shared parameters and the imposition of spectrally relevant constraints, such as non-negativity and sum-to-one conditions, thereby achieving more accurate and interpretable results. Moreover, this versatile framework extends beyond pixel-wise analysis to incorporate spatial information modeling via convolutional operators for spatial-spectral unmixing. Experiments on three distinct datasets, validated against ground-truth abundance maps, demonstrate that EGU-Net outperforms existing state-of-the-art unmixing algorithms. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/danfenghong/IEEE_TNNLS_EGU-Net.

Although cluster galaxies currently display significantly reduced star formation rates compared to their field counterparts, it is plausible that they hosted more vigorous star formation during the early universe. This study utilizes the Horizon-AGN large-scale cosmological hydrodynamic simulation to interpret the star formation history (SFH) of group and cluster galaxies. Our results indicate that massive galaxies generally possess short e-folding timescales for star formation decay—a phenomenon known as "mass quenching"—independent of their surroundings, whereas low-mass galaxies show a strong dependence on their environment. Specifically, within massive host halos (clusters), the e-folding timescales for low-mass galaxies diminish further if they remain within these halos for extended durations. This pattern of "environmental quenching" aligns with theoretical predictions regarding ram pressure stripping. Additionally, we define a "transition epoch" as the point at which cluster galaxies become less star-forming than field galaxies; this epoch varies based on both stellar mass and host cluster halo mass. Notably, low-mass galaxies in massive clusters exhibit the earliest transition, occurring approximately 7.6 billion years ago in lookback time, whereas massive galaxies in low-mass clusters show a later transition around 5.2 billion years ago. Ultimately, our findings allow us to characterize the SFH of cluster galaxies in relation to the ratio of cluster halo mass to stellar mass.

This study examines norm maps acting on algebraic even $K$-groups associated with finite extensions of number fields. We demonstrate that these maps are surjective in the majority of cases. When surjectivity fails, we provide a criterion to determine if an element in the even $K$-group of the base field originates from a norm of an element in the even $K$-groups of the extension field; this criterion depends exclusively on the real primes of the base field.

Multi-objective optimization involves simultaneously optimizing multiple objective functions, with various techniques available to address this challenge. This paper focuses on the primary methods for solving such problems within relational databases. Specifically, it investigates the Top-k query, which retrieves the $k$ best results from a dataset, and the Skyline query, which offers a broader overview of optimal outcomes. Additionally, the study explores Flexible-skyline, a novel approach engineered to enhance existing methods and overcome their limitations. For each technique, the paper outlines its key characteristics, reviews the algorithms that implement them, and compares their respective strengths and weaknesses.

Hydrokinetic energy harvesting can be achieved using oscillating foils undergoing synchronized pitch and heave movements. By analyzing the wake structure and its relationship with foil kinematics, predictive models for array configurations can be formulated. To define the link between wake characteristics and foil kinematics, a two-foil tandem setup was examined across a broad spectrum of motions, varying interfoil spacing from four to nine chord lengths and testing multiple phase shifts. Combining experimental and simulation data, a detailed wake analysis was conducted to quantify mean velocity and turbulent kinetic energy. This quantification adjusted trailing foil efficiency to consider both the mean flow and the energy carried by coherent leading edge vortices (LEVs) shed from the upstream foil. Utilizing mean wake velocity, a predictive model identified three distinct regimes by examining trailing foil efficiency profiles and the intensity of the primary LEV from the leading foil. Categorizing the wake into these regimes offers a valuable method for narrowing the scope of foil kinematics and configurations, thereby enhancing energy capture in two-tandem foil arrays.

This study focuses on defining the fundamental nature of super-resolution, with a primary emphasis on its stability and the diffraction limit. A key finding involves two location-amplitude identities that define the relationships between source positions and amplitudes within super-resolution challenges. These identities enable the direct derivation of super-resolution capabilities regarding the recovery of quantity, position, and amplitude, enhancing current state-of-the-art estimations to a practically significant degree. Although the nonlinear inverse problems addressed here are notoriously difficult and have only been partially resolved recently, this paper provides a clear, unified framework to solve them concisely.

The second major contribution is a theoretical proof of a two-point diffraction limit applicable to spaces of arbitrary dimensionality, contingent only on noise level assumptions. This limit is expressed as:
\[
\mathcal{R} = \frac{4\arcsin
\left(\left(\frac{\sigma}{m_{\min}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \right)}{\Omega}
\]
valid for $\frac{\sigma}{m_{\min}}\leq\frac{1}{2}$, where $\frac{\sigma}{m_{\min}}$ denotes the inverse of the signal-to-noise ratio ($SNR$) and $\Omega$ represents the cutoff frequency. When $\frac{\sigma}{m_{\min}}>\frac{1}{2}$, super-resolution is not achievable in certain scenarios. This work resolves long-standing debates regarding the diffraction limit for imaging and line spectral estimation under broad conditions. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that for distinguishing any two point sources, if $SNR>2$, the Rayleigh limit of $\frac{\pi}{\Omega}$ can definitely be surpassed. Finally, the paper identifies the optimal algorithm capable of achieving the best possible resolution when separating two sources.

Decoherence-induced leakage errors threaten physical and logical qubits by coupling them to other system levels. We present the first experimental realization of Leakage Elimination Operators (LEOs) designed to mitigate this issue while remaining compatible with universal quantum computing. By utilizing IBM's cloud quantum computer, we investigated three potential subspace configurations within two- and three-qubit Hilbert spaces, demonstrating that LEOs substantially suppress leakage.

This paper addresses the hop-constrained s-t path enumeration (HcPE) problem, which involves finding all paths between two distinct vertices, $s$ and $t$, in a graph $G$ with a length of at most $k$. Existing state-of-the-art methods struggle with significant performance bottlenecks due to expensive pruning operations during enumeration, particularly in scenarios with large search spaces, making them unsuitable for the real-time requirements of many online applications. To address this, we introduce PathEnum, an efficient index-based algorithm designed for real-time HcPE. For each query, PathEnum constructs a lightweight index to minimize the number of edges participating in the enumeration and employs two distinct index-based enumeration strategies: one utilizing depth-first search and the other based on joins. Additionally, we implement a query optimizer that uses a join-based cost model to determine the optimal search order. Experiments conducted on 15 real-world graphs demonstrate that PathEnum significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches, achieving orders of magnitude improvement in query time, throughput, and response time.

Graphs are categorized based on the characteristics of their data. Directed graphs indicate link directions, whereas signed graphs distinguish between positive and negative link types. Signed directed graphs, which incorporate both features, are the most intricate and informative. However, research on graph convolutions for these specific structures remains limited. While numerous graph convolution studies exist, the majority focus on undirected or unsigned graphs. This paper explores a spectral graph convolution network tailored for signed directed graphs. We introduce a novel complex Hermitian adjacency matrix that encodes graph information using complex numbers, where phases and magnitudes represent link direction, sign, and connectivity. Furthermore, we define a magnetic Laplacian based on this Hermitian matrix and demonstrate its positive semidefinite nature. Consequently, we present the Signed Directed Graph Convolution Network (SD-GCN). To our knowledge, this represents the first spectral convolution method for graphs with signs. Additionally, unlike existing models designed for specific graph types, our proposed approach offers generality, applicable to any graph structure, including undirected, directed, or signed ones. We evaluated the model's performance using four real-world datasets, and it outperforms all current state-of-the-art graph convolutions in link sign prediction tasks.

This study establishes a partial order on the maximal chains of any finite bounded poset $P$ equipped with a CL-labeling $\lambda$, termed the maximal chain descent order induced by $\lambda$ and denoted $P_{\lambda}(2)$. As an initial case, when $P$ is the Boolean lattice and $\lambda$ is its standard EL-labeling, $P_{\lambda}(2)$ becomes isomorphic to the weak order of type A. The paper further examines other well-structured instances: the max-min EL-labeling of the partition lattice results in a maximal chain descent order isomorphic to a partial order on specific labeled trees, while certain linear extension EL-labelings of finite distributive lattices yield orders isomorphic to those on standard Young tableaux. It is noted that the "polygon moves" defining the transitive closure of the maximal chain descent order do not always correspond to actual cover relations, a point illustrated by various examples. Despite this, the authors characterize the EL-labelings where every polygon move constitutes a cover relation and demonstrate that many standard EL-labelings satisfy this property. A primary motivation for $P_{\lambda}(2)$ lies in the fact that its linear extensions generate all shellings of the order complex of $P$ defined by $\lambda$-descent restrictions. This approach produces strictly more shellings than those derived lexicographically from $\lambda$, suggesting that $P_{\lambda}(2)$ effectively encodes the structure of the set of shellings induced by $\lambda$.

While the metastable liquid branch of hard spheres is well understood across dimensions from low $d$ to $d\to\infty$, their crystal counterparts remain largely unexplored for $d>3$. Specifically, it is uncertain whether the crystal phase remains thermodynamically stable in high dimensions, and consequently, whether a mean-field theory of crystals can be exact. To determine the stability range of hard sphere crystals, this study estimates their equation of state through numerical simulations and establishes fluid-crystal coexistence conditions by employing a generalized Frenkel-Ladd scheme to calculate absolute crystal free energies. The findings indicate that the crystal phase is stable at least up to $d=10$, with dimensional trends suggesting that stability likely extends well beyond this limit.

Contemporary structures are increasingly outfitted with intelligent energy meters that continuously produce vast volumes of time-series data, generating millions of data points daily. This rich dataset enables the extraction of hidden load signatures, the deduction of consumption patterns, the analysis of environmental interdependencies, and the characterization of building operations. Moreover, it facilitates the concurrent detection of irregularities in electricity usage, representing a significant stride toward energy conservation and global sustainability. Nevertheless, current research in anomaly detection is constrained by the scarcity of large-scale, annotated energy consumption datasets. To address this gap, we release a meticulously annotated subset of the public ASHRAE Great Energy Predictor III dataset, comprising 1,413 smart meter time series recorded over a year. Additionally, we evaluate and compare the efficacy of eight leading anomaly detection techniques using our dataset.

Building on our prior research [arXiv:2202.10042], which lowered Sinkhorn iteration complexity from $O(N^2)$ to the optimal $O(N)$ by exploiting kernel matrix structure, this paper investigates that structure through the definition and application of Lower-ColLinear Triangular (L-CoLT) and Upper-ColLinear Triangular (U-CoLT) matrices. We demonstrate that (1) vector multiplications with L/U-CoLT matrices require only $O(N)$ operations, and (2) these matrix families remain closed under Hadamard products and scaling. These characteristics address two major challenges in optimizing the Inexact Proximal point method (IPOT), enabling a reduction in iteration count to $O(N)$. Consequently, we introduce the Fast Sinkhorn II (FS-2) algorithm, which achieves accurate optimal transport computation with both low complexity and rapid convergence. Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness and efficiency of this method.

This study introduces a deep learning-based reduced order model (DL-ROM) designed to forecast fluid forces and unsteady vortex dynamics, validated through simulations of flow around a sphere. The approach utilizes a three-dimensional convolutional recurrent autoencoder network (3D CRAN) to distill low-dimensional flow characteristics from full-order data snapshots. A long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network then evolves these features temporally before reconstructing them into full-order flow voxels. By treating these 3D voxels as static, uniform query probes within a point cloud framework, the method simplifies unstructured mesh complexity and facilitates 3D CRAN training. We further detail a new technique for deriving interface descriptions and force metrics directly from these flow voxels. Initially, the 3D CRAN is tested on external flow over a stationary sphere at a Reynolds number of 300, accompanied by an evaluation of computational demands regarding memory, training expenses, and inference time. The framework is subsequently expanded to incorporate variable Reynolds number data, enabling a single 3D CRAN to learn a complex, symmetry-breaking flow regime between Re = 280 and Re = 460. Analysis of transfer learning reveals that training this intricate flow regime on a compact time series dataset is nearly 20 times faster than using a parallel full-order model, while maintaining excellent to good predictive accuracy. Specifically, the predicted flow fields yield an R² accuracy of 98.58% for drag and 76.43% for lift within the specified regime. Ultimately, this framework supports the creation of a digital twin for 3D unsteady flow fields that accounts for variable Reynolds number effects.

Electric Dipole Moments (EDMs) of subatomic particles are regarded as a premier method for investigating CP-violation beyond the Standard Model, a phenomenon sought to explain the universe's matter-antimatter asymmetry. This paper examines EDM searches for charged hadrons within storage rings. It highlights current activities at the COSY facility at Forschungszentrum J\"ulich, Germany, alongside the design of a prototype ring with a 100-meter circumference intended to validate essential technologies. These technologies include simultaneous clockwise and counter-clockwise beam operation using electrostatic bending elements and, when combined with a magnetic field, the frozen spin technique.

Living systems encompass a vast array of critical details that collectively sustain life. Despite this complexity, certain recurring structures and processes define them, including the homochirality of proteins and carbohydrates, along with metabolism and genetics. Regarding abiogenesis, or the origin of life, it is likely not the outcome of isolated incidents but rather a gradual progression characterized by increasing molecular and chemical complexity. Consequently, the prebiotic synthesis of molecules may not have left a discernible trace of how initial structures and reactions were established. However, it is possible to identify a sequence in the formation of the chemical building blocks of abiogenesis. This review examines experimental findings and proposes a model for the onset of abiogenesis, wherein the spontaneous emergence of protein homochirality serves as a prerequisite for the subsequent development of carbohydrate homochirality and metabolism at the dawn of life.

Over-the-air computation (AirComp) offers a promising solution for rapidly aggregating distributed data, yet its performance in long-distance scenarios remains uncertain due to distortions caused by channel fading and noise. To fully realize AirComp's potential, this paper introduces a low-cost unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) serving as a mobile base station to assist AirComp systems. Leveraging the UAV's controllable high mobility and altitude, it can position itself closely to sensors to establish line-of-sight links and dynamically adjust link distances. This approach improves signal magnitude alignment and noise suppression. The study aims to minimize the time-averaged mean-square error for AirComp by jointly optimizing the UAV's trajectory, the scaling factor at the UAV, and sensor transmit powers, subject to constraints on UAV location, flight speed, and sensor power limits. Given the non-convex nature of the resulting problem due to coupled variables and time-dependent constraints, we develop an efficient iterative algorithm using block coordinate descent and successive convex optimization. Simulation results confirm the algorithm's convergence and demonstrate that the proposed design achieves superior performance and robustness compared to benchmarks.

The combination of the recent Fermilab muon $g-2$ findings with the Brookhaven data strongly suggests new physics beyond the Standard Model, consistent with the electroweak sector of supersymmetry provided that sleptons and certain electroweak gauginos have masses in the few hundred GeV range. Conversely, the Higgs boson mass measurement of 125 GeV implies a squark mass scale in the few TeV region, suggesting a split spectrum between squarks and sleptons. This discrepancy is naturally resolved through gluino-driven radiative electroweak symmetry breaking, where a large gluino mass drives the radiative breaking process, and gluino color interactions generate significant splitting between squarks and sleptons. We demonstrate that an unbiased analysis utilizing an artificial neural network also points to gluino-driven radiative breaking. Furthermore, employing benchmark scenarios and a deep neural network approach, we evaluate the model's potential for discovering light sleptons and sneutrinos at the HL-LHC and HE-LHC.

We propose a general framework incorporating multiple methods to enhance the estimation of convex function or functional values, specifically when only noisy observations of the true inputs are accessible. Our approach technically identifies and eliminates the bias inherent to convexity by adjusting a baseline estimate. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that, under mild conditions, these methods strictly decrease the expected estimation error. The application of these methods requires no specific problem knowledge beyond convexity and the ability to evaluate the function, making them versatile, off-the-shelf tools for diverse applications. These include optimization problems involving random objectives or constraints, as well as functionals of probability distributions like entropy and Wasserstein distance. Numerical experiments across a broad spectrum of problems confirm that our methods significantly improve estimation quality compared to baseline approaches.

Theoretical analysis demonstrates that ferromagnetic superconductors UGe$_2$, URhGe, and UCoGe can be uniformly described using A-phase-like triplet pairing, analogous to superfluid $^3$He. This framework successfully accounts for their unique reentrant, S-shaped, or L-shaped $H_{\rm c2}$ curves. It further predicts an inevitable double transition between the A$_1$ and A$_2$ phases within the $H$-$T$ plane, where both phases exhibit a non-unitary state with broken time-reversal symmetry and a half-gap. The recently discovered spin-polarized superconductor UTe$_2$ is similarly examined through this lens, confirming that the anticipated A$_1$-A$_2$ transition is observed experimentally. Consequently, these four heavy fermion compounds are collectively recognized as topologically rich solid-state materials deserving of further investigation alongside the superfluid $^3$He A-phase.

Lately, diffusion models (DMs) have gained prominence in audio processing, particularly for speech super-resolution (SR), which focuses on recovering high-frequency details from low-resolution speech. Typically, this is done by conditioning a noise predictor on low-resolution audio. In this paper, we introduce a new sampling algorithm that conveys low-resolution audio information through the reverse sampling process of DMs. This approach serves as a direct replacement for standard sampling, significantly enhancing the performance of current methods. Furthermore, by integrating our sampling technique with an unconditional DM—one that lacks auxiliary inputs to its noise predictor—we can apply it across various SR configurations. Using this innovative framework, we achieved state-of-the-art results on the VCTK Multi-Speaker benchmark.

We extend Moore's nonstandard demonstration of the Spectral theorem, originally for bounded self-adjoint operators, to encompass unbounded operators. This extension relies crucially on employing Raab's definition of the nonstandard hull for internally bounded self-adjoint operators.

We employ an estimate from Aksoy Yazici, Murphy, Rudnev, and Shkredov (2016) regarding the number of solutions to specific equations involving set products and differences in prime finite fields. This approach yields an explicit upper bound for trilinear exponential sums that surpasses the earlier result by Bourgain and Garaev (2009). Additionally, we derive explicit bounds for quadrilinear exponential sums.

We investigate rigidity problems on $\mathbb{R}$ and $S^1$ outside of generic settings. Given $n$ distinct points $V = \{ v_1,...,v_n \}$ and a collection of mutual distances $\mathcal{P} \subseteq { V \choose 2}$, the question is whether $\mathcal{P}$ uniquely determines the configuration of $V$ up to isometry. We demonstrate that when $|\mathcal{P}| =\Omega(n^{3/2})$, the positions of a subset $V' \subseteq V$ with size $|V'| = \Omega(\frac{|\mathcal{P}|}{n})$ can be recovered. The core of our proof relies on establishing that dense graphs $G=(V,E)$, where any pair of non-adjacent vertices shares only a small number of common neighbors, necessarily contain large cliques. Additionally, we examine the case of random distance sets $\mathcal{P}$. If the distance between each pair of points is known with probability $p = \frac{C \ln(n)}{n}$ for a sufficiently large constant $C$, then $V$ can be reconstructed with high probability (w.h.p.). Furthermore, we provide a randomized algorithm with linear expected running time that outputs an embedding of the points onto the line w.h.p.

Fact verification remains a difficult endeavor because confirming a claim often involves extracting information from multiple sources that exhibit complex hierarchical semantic relationships. Prior research has predominantly relied on simply concatenating evidence sentences to determine claim validity, an approach that falls short given that evidence frequently contains hierarchical structures and dependencies. This study aims to verify facts using evidence selected from a list of Wikipedia articles. We employ pretrained language models like XLNET to create meaningful representations, while integrating graph-based attention and convolutions in a manner that allows the system to learn fact verification with minimal additional training.

We introduce a straightforward, easily implementable framework for a renormalon-free gluon condensate (GC) matrix element, mirroring established short-distance heavy-quark mass renormalization schemes found in existing literature. By relying on perturbative subtraction at the matrix element level with a flexible infrared factorization scale, this approach can be readily applied to any observable involving the GC with minimal effort. The method requires the independent determination of the GC's renormalon norm. We apply this framework to both fixed-order (FOPT) and contour-improved (CIPT) perturbative expansions of $\tau$ hadronic spectral function moments. These expansions have historically shown a persistent discrepancy in moments utilized for high-precision strong coupling determinations when using the conventional, non-renormalon-free GC scheme. Our results demonstrate that the new scheme successfully resolves the FOPT-CIPT discrepancy. Simultaneously, the perturbative behavior of moments that previously suffered from poor convergence and significant non-perturbative GC corrections is markedly enhanced. Consequently, this novel GC scheme offers a robust theoretical instrument for future phenomenological studies.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success across diverse fields, including speech recognition and synthesis, computer vision, machine translation, and game playing. However, these models are often computationally demanding and memory-intensive, which limits their deployment on resource-constrained devices or in latency-sensitive applications. Consequently, a logical approach is to compress and accelerate deep networks while maintaining performance, a process defined as complexity reduction. This work aims to reduce the complexity of state-of-the-art LSTM models for natural language tasks like text classification by distilling their knowledge into CNN-based architectures, thereby decreasing inference time and latency during testing.

We examine initial boundary value problems involving time-fractional advection-diffusion equations subject to zero Dirichlet boundary conditions, defined by $\partial_t^{\alpha} u(x,t) = -Au(x,t)$, where the operator $-A$ is given by $\sum_{i,j=1}^d \partial_i(a_{ij}(x)\partial_j) + \sum_{j=1}^d b_j(x)\partial_j + c(x)$. We demonstrate the uniqueness of an inverse problem aimed at identifying the fractional derivative order $\alpha$ using data $u(x_0,t)$ recorded at a single spatial point $x_0$ within the domain $\OOO$ for $0<t<T$. This uniqueness remains valid even when both the domain $\OOO$ and the operator $A$ are unknown, as long as the initial condition does not change sign and is not identically zero. The proof relies on eigenfunction expansions of finitely dimensional approximate solutions, a decay estimate, and the asymptotic behavior of Mittag-Leffler functions for large times.

Over time, populations accumulate neutral genetic substitutions driven by random drift. A foundational principle in population genetics states that the rate of substitution accumulation ($K$) matches the mutation rate ($u$) at which these changes originate in individuals, expressed as $K=u$. This equivalence allows genetic sequences to function as a "molecular clock" for dating evolutionary events. Although selection can disrupt this clock, the relationship $K=u$ is widely considered to hold generally under neutral evolution. This study demonstrates, however, that asymmetric spatial population structure can modify the molecular clock rate for neutral mutations, resulting in scenarios where $K<u$ or $K>u$. These deviations arise because mutations originate at varying frequencies across different sites and possess distinct fixation probabilities based on their location. Specifically, when birth rates are uniform across sites, $K$ remains less than or equal to $u$. Generally, $K$ can range from 0 to $Nu$. The proposed model is adaptable to diverse population structures. For instance, it is used to examine mutation accumulation in the small intestine and to analyze over 900 Twitter networks, investigating how network topology influences the fixation of neutral innovations in social evolution.

Recent advancements in semi-supervised learning have enabled performance levels comparable to state-of-the-art supervised learning techniques. In computer vision, the most effective semi-supervised methods typically exploit vast quantities of unlabeled data by employing data augmentation to learn general representations, generating pseudo-labels, utilizing diverse loss functions, and subsequently adapting this knowledge to smaller, task-specific models. This paper investigates three key dimensions of SimCLR, the leading semi-supervised framework for computer vision. First, we examine the properties of contrast learning during fine-tuning, recognizing it as the core driver of the method's success. Second, we explore knowledge distillation within a teacher-forcing framework, noting that performance improves when the teacher and student share the same base model. Finally, we analyze the mechanics of transfer learning and its correlation with the number of classes across various datasets. Our findings suggest that transfer learning yields superior results when the number of classes is lower.

The Vietnamese labor market suffers from uneven development, characterized by a surge in university graduates alongside rising unemployment. This disparity is frequently attributed to a lack of precise and up-to-date labor market data, resulting in a mismatch between available worker skills and actual market needs. To address this, a data monitoring and analytic platform is needed, with a key challenge being the automatic extraction of occupational skills from labor-related documents like resumes and job postings. Conventional methods depend on pre-existing taxonomies or extensive annotated datasets to train Named Entity Recognition (NER) models, which are costly and demand significant manual labor. This paper introduces a practical approach for identifying skills within Vietnamese job listings by reframing the task not as NER, but as a ranking problem. The proposed pipeline first extracts and ranks phrases based on their semantic similarity to the surrounding context, followed by a final classification step to identify skill phrases. After gathering three datasets and performing extensive experiments, the results show that this methodology outperforms NER models, particularly when working with limited data.

This study introduces a topology optimization (TO) framework designed to concurrently optimize the matrix topology and fiber distribution in functionally graded continuous fiber-reinforced composites (FRC). Existing density-based TO methods for FRC rely on the finite element mesh for both analysis and design representation, which creates significant challenges when enforcing sub-element fiber spacing and generating high-resolution continuous fibers. In contrast, we propose a mesh-independent approach utilizing a neural network (NN) to represent both the matrix topology and fiber distribution. This implicit NN-based representation allows for geometric and material queries at a resolution exceeding that of traditional mesh discretization, facilitating the precise extraction of functionally-graded continuous fibers. Additionally, by embedding finite element simulations within the NN computational framework, we employ automatic differentiation for end-to-end automated sensitivity analysis, eliminating the need to manually derive complex sensitivity expressions. The efficacy and computational efficiency of this proposed method are demonstrated through multiple numerical examples with diverse objective functions. Furthermore, we illustrate that the optimized continuous fiber-reinforced composites can be directly fabricated at high resolution via additive manufacturing.

We introduce a new queuing scenario in which a decision-maker must determine whether to accept or reject randomly arriving tasks into a bufferless system served by $N$ identical servers. Each task is characterized by a price (a positive real number) and a class; tasks within each class follow distinct price distributions and service rates, arriving via an inhomogeneous Poisson process. The goal is to select tasks for acceptance that maximize the total processed price over a finite horizon. We model this as a discrete-time Markov Decision Process (MDP) featuring a hybrid state space. By demonstrating that the optimal value function possesses a specific structure, we enable an exact solution to this hybrid MDP. Furthermore, we prove that as the time step diminishes, the discrete-time solution converges to the optimal solution of the underlying continuous-time problem. To enhance scalability for a larger number of task classes, we propose an approximation method utilizing state abstraction. Finally, we validate our approach using both synthetic data and a real-world financial fraud dataset, which serves as the primary motivation for this research.

Although passwords must be memorable, mandatory expiration policies force frequent changes, trapping users in a conflict that often leads them to employ creative strategies for making slight modifications. While these tactics successfully bypass basic similarity checks, they significantly weaken actual security because leaked expired passwords can still serve as effective seeds for cracking tools. This paper presents a method utilizing Bloom filters to identify password similarities, aiming to deter the habit of reusing passwords. Furthermore, the proposed scheme inherently obscures stored credentials to safeguard them during database breaches and can be configured to resist common cryptanalytic attacks, rendering it appropriate for deployment on exposed systems.

Prior research demonstrated that automated systems utilizing Deep Neural Networks (DNN) and commercial vision APIs could successfully bypass image challenges in reCAPTCHA v2. In response to these vulnerabilities, Google significantly updated its reCAPTCHA v2 image challenges, largely rendering previous methods ineffective. This paper evaluates the robustness of the latest reCAPTCHA v2 version against sophisticated object detection solvers. We introduce a fully automated object detection system that achieves an online success rate of 83.25%—the highest recorded to date—cracking the most advanced challenges in an average of 19.93 seconds, inclusive of network latency. Furthermore, we analyze updated security measures in reCAPTCHA v2, including anti-recognition mechanisms, enhanced anti-bot detection, and configurable security preferences. Our extensive experiments reveal that while these features offer some resistance, adversaries can still circumvent most of them. Our findings suggest that recent advancements in object detection technology pose a critical threat to image captcha designs that rely on simple object detection as their core AI task.

Multi-Access Edge Computing (MEC) represents a framework designed to support latency-sensitive services by executing computing and communication tasks at the access network level, specifically within Base Station (BS) sites where Virtual Machines (VMs) serve as computational resources. The integration of MEC with Energy Harvesting (EH) BSs is anticipated to be pivotal for next-generation mobile networks. EH systems are expected to reduce reliance on the electrical grid and enable the deployment of BSs in remote locations, thereby expanding network coverage and achieving energy self-sufficiency in rural areas. This paper introduces an online optimization algorithm named ENergy Aware and Adaptive Management (ENAAM), which manages remote BS sites using foresighted control policies that leverage short-term forecasts of traffic load and harvested energy. Numerical results demonstrate that ENAAM achieves energy savings between 56% and 66% compared to scenarios without energy management, while maintaining server utilization rates between 30% and 96% (averaging 75%) over time. Additionally, the algorithm shows significant advantages over heuristic energy management techniques.

We embark on a journey exploring four interconnected themes: the dual notions of independence and spanning within finite abelian groups, and their corresponding counterparts, designs and distance sets, on spheres. This overview examines key established results in each domain, highlights various open problems, and investigates the relationships linking these four compelling areas.

Large-scale beamforming in radio interferometers holds the promise of transforming pulsar and fast radio burst research by enhancing survey efficiency. We present a wide-field beamformer tailored for the MeerKAT radio telescope and detail strategies for optimizing such surveys. Additionally, we introduce ${\rm M{\small OSAIC}}$, a software implementation of these methods, and demonstrate its application within MeerKAT. Initial results from using this beamformer include observations of a globular cluster to track multiple pulsars at once, alongside evidence of the system's source localization capabilities.

We introduce a star formation rate function (SFRF) at $z\sim5.8$, derived from star formation rates (SFRs) obtained via spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting of galaxies across rest-frame UV to optical wavelengths in the CANDELS GOODS-South and North fields. This SFRF reveals an excess compared to earlier estimates based on rest-frame UV luminosity functions (LFs) corrected for dust extinction using the IRX-$\beta$ relation, aligning instead with values derived from far-infrared LFs. This discrepancy indicates that previous methods relying solely on rest-frame UV data underestimated the contribution of dust-obscured, intensely star-forming galaxies to total star formation at $z\sim6$. By fitting the SFRF with a Schechter function while fixing the faint-end slope and characteristic number density, we determined the characteristic SFR (${\rm SFR}^*$). The resulting ${\rm SFR}^*$ is comparable to that at $z\sim2$, the epoch of peak cosmic star formation. Combined with similar UV-to-optical SFRF estimates, ${\rm SFR}^*$ remains roughly constant from $z\sim2$ to $z\sim6$ but may decline at higher redshifts. Given that ${\rm SFR}^*$ reflects the high-SFR end of the distribution, its evolution implies that this end of the SFRF grew to levels similar to those at $z\sim2$ during the epoch of reionization.

Calculating distances between data points underpins numerous statistical methods, including clustering and dimensionality reduction. Yet, advancements in data acquisition have produced increasingly versatile structured datasets where conventional distance metrics often fail. This paper addresses the challenge of quantifying the distance between sequences and multisets of points within a metric space, driven by the need to analyze in-play football data. Synthesizing insights from time series analysis and optimal transport literature, we examine various applicable distance measures. For each metric, we establish and demonstrate theoretical properties, suggesting potential extensions for cases where limitations arise. Finally, we validate the practical utility of these distances through an empirical analysis of the football dataset.

I previously thought that my conventions for diagramming categorical statements could be fully documented on a single page, assuming the only difficulty lay in reconstructing objects from their names. However, I later discovered this assumption was incorrect. This work aims to explain, through motivations and examples, the conventions behind a specific diagram referred to as the "Basic Example" in the text. Once these conventions are grasped, the diagram serves as a "skeleton" for a particular lemma related to the Yoneda Lemma, allowing both its statement and proof to be derived from it. The final sections explore simple methods to extend these conventions, demonstrating how to diagram the "real" Yoneda Lemma and its corollary, define comma categories, and formalize the diagram for "geometric morphism for children."

Typically, researchers in Category Theory only share their visualization methods when their diagrams reach a threshold of mathematical significance—usually by proving new theorems or by translating complex calculations into much more intuitive visual forms. The diagrammatic language presented here falls below that threshold; therefore, it is a "private" language that I am making public to initiate a dialogue with others who have developed their own private diagrammatic systems.
New characterizations of real finite-dimensional unital algebras are presented, grounded in a functor derived from the methods used to uncurly the inverse operation within the units.

Abductive reasoning begins with observations and seeks the most plausible explanation for them. Humans typically rely on temporal and causal inferences, as well as knowledge regarding how hypothetical scenarios can lead to various outcomes, to perform abduction. This study presents the first investigation into how such knowledge influences the Abductive Natural Language Inference (NLI) task, which involves selecting the more probable explanation for a set of observations. We introduce a specialized language model, LMI, trained to generate potential subsequent events from a hypothetical scenario evolving from an initial event. Subsequently, we propose a multi-task model, MTL, designed to solve the Abductive NLI task by predicting a plausible explanation through two mechanisms: a) evaluating different possible events arising from candidate hypotheses—events produced by LMI—and b) identifying the option most similar to the observed outcome. Our results demonstrate that the MTL model outperforms previous vanilla pre-trained language models fine-tuned on Abductive NLI. Furthermore, our manual evaluation and analysis indicate that learning about potential next events from diverse hypothetical scenarios effectively supports abductive inference.

This note examines the statistical inference of input process parameters for a queue based on periodic workload data. The primary emphasis is on addressing the open challenge of developing statistically efficient estimators for a specific observation scheme, specifically by minimizing the asymptotic variance of the estimation error.

Calculating the dynamical characteristics of nuclear matter—spanning from nucleon and nuclear parton distribution functions to transport phenomena in the quark-gluon plasma—remains a primary objective in contemporary theoretical physics. Because this real-time physics frequently resists perturbative approaches, lattice QCD simulations represent the most effective current strategy. These numerical studies rely on Monte-Carlo sampling within an artificial Euclidean time framework. However, real-time physics is best described via spectral functions, which are obscured in lattice QCD by an ill-posed inverse problem. This presentation will examine state-of-the-art techniques for extracting these spectral functions from lattice QCD data using Bayesian inference, highlighting the critical role of prior domain knowledge in regularizing this inherently unstable task. By explicitly accounting for uncertainties in both observations and prior assumptions, Bayesian inference now enables a systematic quantification of total uncertainties in the derived spectral functions. I will present two implementations of the Bayesian Reconstruction (BR) method: one for Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) point estimates and another utilizing an open-access Monte-Carlo sampler. Additionally, I will briefly address the application of machine learning to spectral function reconstruction and the novel insights it has offered to the Bayesian community.

This study offers a reanalysis of Neptune's visible and near-infrared observations (480–930 nm) collected in 2018 using the MUSE instrument on the Very Large Telescope (VLT) in Narrow Field Adaptive Optics mode, originally reported by Irwin et al. in *Icarus* (311, 2019). Our investigation reveals that our prior analysis, which relied solely on central meridian data, underestimated retrieval errors regarding methane abundance variations with latitude when compared to a more comprehensive evaluation of Neptune's limb darkening. Furthermore, our previous work inadvertently introduced artificial latitudinal variability in both methane abundance and its associated uncertainty, which we now reevaluate. This reanalysis integrates limb-darkening effects derived from the Minnaert approximation, offering stronger constraints on cloud structure and methane mole fractions, while utilizing available data more effectively and with greater computational efficiency. Results indicate that, excluding discrete cloud features, the observed reflectivity spectrum between 800–900 nm is closely matched by a background cloud model that varies by latitude but remains zonally symmetric. This model comprises an H$_2$S cloud layer situated at 3.6–4.7 bar with variable opacity and scale height, alongside a stratospheric haze. The model successfully accounts for observed limb darkening across all wavelengths and latitudes. We determine that the methane mole fraction at 2–4 bar, located above the H$_2$S cloud but below the methane condensation level, ranges from 4–6% at the equator to 2–4% near the south pole, aligning with earlier findings and yielding an equator-to-pole ratio of $1.9 \pm 0.2$ for our assumed cloud and methane configuration. Additionally, the spectra of discrete cloudy regions are well approximated by adding a single, vertically thin methane ice cloud with opacities between 0 and 0.75 and pressures below approximately 0.4 bar.

Addressing the multi-scale nature of parton energy-momentum exchange with the quark-gluon plasma (QGP), this study computes charm quark interactions using the MATTER model under the higher twist formalism for high virtuality and energy regimes, while employing a linearized Boltzmann Transport (LBT) approach for the low virtuality, high-energy sector. The calculation incorporates coherence effects within the MATTER framework that suppress the medium-induced emission rate. We investigate the detailed interplay between these two formalisms to successfully reproduce the nuclear modification factor ($R_{AA}$) for D-mesons and charged hadrons across various centralities, with all computations executed via the JETSCAPE framework.

Representative datasets form the foundation for many successful artificial intelligence and machine learning models. Nevertheless, real-world applications often encounter scenarios that are poorly captured in the training data. This discrepancy stems from diverse factors, including time and cost limitations as well as ethical concerns. Consequently, ensuring the reliable deployment of these models, particularly in safety-critical contexts, presents a significant challenge. Integrating additional existing knowledge sources is essential to surpass the boundaries of purely data-driven methods and enhance model generalization. Moreover, ensuring predictions align with established knowledge is vital for making safe and trustworthy decisions, even in underrepresented situations. This work reviews literature techniques that fuse data-driven models with prior knowledge, categorizing identified approaches into integration, extraction, and conformity. Particular emphasis is placed on applications within autonomous driving.

Historically, transcribing spoken audio into the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) has been a task reserved for specialists. This study investigates an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) model named Generating IPA Pronunciation From Audio (GIPFA), designed to automatically derive the IPA phonemic representation of a word from its audio input. Trained on data from the French Wikimedia dictionary, the model achieved a 75% accuracy rate in predicting IPA pronunciations during testing. Furthermore, an analysis of the model's inference errors proved valuable for identifying potential inaccuracies within the dataset and determining the nearest phonemes in French.

Precise forecasting stands as a core priority within econometric time-series research. Frequently, practitioners and policymakers seek to predict outcomes across an entire future horizon rather than relying solely on single $k$-step-ahead forecasts. Such series often exhibit non-linear dependencies and are frequently driven by numerous external predictors. This paper develops prediction intervals for time-aggregated forecasts within a high-dimensional regression framework. Our methodology utilizes quantiles of residuals derived from the widely used LASSO algorithm. We accommodate general stationary error processes and stochastic predictors that may be heavy-tailed, possess long-memory characteristics, or display non-linearity. We establish theoretical guarantees for our proposed quantile-based approach through a sequence of consistency results covering all these scenarios. Following validation via simulations, we introduce a novel bootstrap technique designed to enhance the coverage of the theoretical intervals. Finally, by analyzing EPEX Spot data, we construct prediction intervals for hourly electricity prices over horizons extending up to 17 weeks and compare these results against selected Bayesian and bootstrap interval forecasts.

We demonstrate that any uniform state on the sphere can be fundamentally represented as a superposition of regular graphs. Furthermore, we introduce a graph-based ansatz for building trial FHQ ground states that exhibit the local characteristics of Jack polynomials. Specifically, these graphic states possess the $(k,r)$ clustering property. Additionally, a specific subset of our constructed states corresponds to the densest zero-energy state within a model that alters the projection Hamiltonian.

As one of the world's largest social networking platforms, Twitter boasted over 300 million active users in 2022. It has become a primary channel for consumers to voice opinions on various products and services, particularly commercial airline flights. This research aims to quantify customer satisfaction by applying machine learning techniques to analyze the sentiment of tweets mentioning airlines. Tweets are collected via the Twitter API, then processed through tokenization and vectorization before being fed into a pre-trained classifier to predict sentiment. Beyond sentiment analysis, the study conducts lexical analysis on the gathered tweets to model keyword frequencies, offering contextual insights that aid in interpreting sentiment. Furthermore, time series methods, specifically Bollinger Bands, are employed to identify anomalies within the sentiment data. Utilizing historical data from January to July 2022, the proposed approach successfully captured sudden and significant shifts in passenger sentiment. Ultimately, this research holds the potential to evolve into an application enabling airlines and other customer-facing businesses to efficiently detect abrupt changes in consumer sentiment and implement appropriate countermeasures.

This research investigates how quasidisorder and Anderson disorder influence a two-dimensional topological superconductor under an external magnetic field. Specifically, we examine both $p$-wave superconductors and noncentrosymmetric systems featuring mixed $p$ and $s$-wave pairings alongside Rashba spin-orbit coupling. Our findings indicate that under a perpendicular magnetic field, introducing quasidisorder generates topological phases in previously unoccupied regions, distinguished by integer Chern numbers. Conversely, with a parallel magnetic field, the addition of quasidisorder reveals regimes containing new Majorana flat bands and unidirectional Majorana edge states. We demonstrate that these Majorana flat bands possess a quantized Berry phase of $\pi$, which serves as a topological invariant. Furthermore, we identify two distinct topological transitions and determine the critical exponents $z$ and $\nu$. Finally, the fractal characteristics of the eigenstates are analyzed for both Anderson and Aubry-Andr\'e disorder scenarios.

Grasping the nature and likelihood of extreme events is fundamental to assessing climate change impacts, evaluating risks, planning adaptation strategies, and safeguarding life. This study introduces a methodology for constructing forecasting models specifically designed for extreme heatwaves. These models utilize convolutional neural networks trained on exceptionally long climate model datasets spanning 8,000 years. Given the inherently probabilistic relationship between extreme events, the approach prioritizes probabilistic forecasting and validation. We demonstrate that deep neural networks are effective for predicting prolonged 14-day heatwaves over France, achieving lead times of up to 15 days for fast dynamical drivers (500 hPa geopotential height) and even longer lead times for slow physical drivers like soil moisture. The method is both versatile and straightforward to implement. Our analysis reveals that deep neural networks identify extreme heatwaves linked to a North-Hemisphere wavenumber-3 pattern. Furthermore, we find that adding the 2-meter temperature field to the 500 hPa geopotential height and soil moisture data does not provide any additional statistical value for heatwave forecasting. The core scientific insight is that training deep neural networks to predict extreme heatwaves operates under a regime of severe data scarcity.
