This paper introduces, for the first time, a novel framework capable of generating action tube proposals from video streams via a single forward pass using a sparse-to-dense strategy. The framework features two primary innovations: (1) the explicit integration of both long-term and short-term sampled information within the spatiotemporal network, and (2) a newly designed Dynamic Feature Sampling (DTS) module that efficiently approximates tube outputs while maintaining system tractability. Evaluated on the UCF101-24, JHMDB-21, and UCFSports benchmark datasets, our model delivers competitive results against state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the proposed sparse-to-dense approach enhances efficiency by approximately 7.6 times compared to the closest competing method.

The proton's gluon radius is anticipated to expand at low gluon momentum fractions $x$, a phenomenon previously unaccounted for within the dipole model framework. This study examines the energy dependence of exclusive $J/\psi$, $\phi$, and $\rho$ production by implementing three distinct models for the $x$-dependence of the gluon thickness function. We permit the proton's transverse width to grow as $x$ diminishes, utilizing new parametrizations for both the spherical proton and hotspot models. These are contrasted with a scenario where the hotspot count rises as $x$ falls, with all models tested against HERA data. The models display distinct variations in the $t$-spectrum slopes and in the cross-section ratios between coherent and incoherent processes. Comparisons with $t$-slopes and $W_{\gamma p}$ measurements indicate a preference for models in which the proton's size increases as $x$ decreases.

Swarm behavior, where interacting particles or agents self-organize, is a subject of significant research across disciplines ranging from biology to physics and robotics. This paper presents a systematic investigation into how stable spatio-temporal patterns within a swarm are influenced by the number of agents, specifically when accounting for time-delayed interactions and agent heterogeneity. We demonstrate how coherent patterns evolve as agent count changes, including the convergence time from random initial states. Finally, we explore the practical implications of these findings for curve-tracking in autonomous robotic systems.

This paper constructs a representation of the virtual braid group $VB_n$ into the automorphism group of the free product of a free group and a free abelian group, which extends previously established representations. It verifies that these known representations are not faithful for $n \geq 4$. Leveraging representations of $VB_n$, the virtual link group is defined, and similarly, representations of the welded braid group $WB_n$ are constructed to define the welded link group.

This study expands upon the work of Adami and Ver Steeg [Class. Quantum Grav. \textbf{31}, 075015 (2014)] by modeling black hole particle emission as a quantum optical parametric down conversion (PDC) process. In this framework, the evaporating black hole is represented by a dynamical pump mode that can be either depleted or non-depleted. We analyze the quantum states in both short-time (non-depleted) and long-time (depleted) regimes to determine their impact on the Holevo channel capacity for transmitting information from the distant past to the far future amidst Hawking radiation. A novel contribution of this work is the coupling of emitted Hawking radiation modes through a shared black hole "source pump" mode, which phenomenologically embodies a quantized energy degree of freedom of the gravitational field. This zero-dimensional model provides a simplified setting to study black hole particle production, evaporation, and back-action effects under explicitly unitary evolution that enforces quantized energy and particle conservation. Within this analogous quantum optical model, we examine the entanglement between emitted particle-antiparticle and antiparticle-particle pairs linked by the black hole's evaporating pump source. Furthermore, we analytically and dynamically confirm the "Page information time" for our model, supporting the conventional view that information in black hole radiation becomes significant once half the initial energy has been radiated away. Finally, we investigate how black hole particle production and evaporation affect two initially maximally entangled exterior modes when one mode falls inward and interacts with the black hole while the other remains outside and non-interacting.

This paper details Galileo's performance in SemEval-2020 Task 12, which focuses on identifying and classifying offensive language in social media. For the offensive language identification sub-task, we introduced a multi-lingual approach leveraging pre-trained language models, specifically ERNIE and XLM-R. Regarding offensive language categorization, we employed a knowledge distillation technique trained on soft labels produced by multiple supervised models. Our team competed in all three sub-tasks. In Sub-task A (Offensive Language Identification), we achieved the highest average F1 scores across all languages, becoming the only team to place in the top three in every language. Additionally, we secured first place in Sub-task B (Automatic Categorization of Offense Types) and Sub-task C (Offence Target Identification).

We re-examine the derivation of the covariant scalar-fermion two-body equation involving a Coulomb interaction, previously discussed in another publication. We demonstrate that while this equation can be formally structured like a Dirac equation, it deviates because the eigenvalue appears within one of the coefficients, preventing linear inclusion. Consequently, the approach to the boundary value problem differs, though certain Dirac equation properties emerge in an approximation that recovers the concept of reduced mass. Furthermore, we explore a hybrid analytic-numerical solution method yielding highly precise results, using it to compute the lowest energy levels, states, and QED corrections for both pionic and kaonic atoms.

LiDAR technology has become integral to modern autonomous vehicles, offering essential 3D data about the environment and nearby objects. Nevertheless, adverse weather, particularly snowfall, presents substantial obstacles because captured point clouds are easily corrupted, leading to noise that degrades downstream applications like mapping. Current snow-corrupted point cloud denoising techniques rely on nearest-neighbor searches, which fail to scale effectively with contemporary LiDAR systems that generate 100,000 or more points per second at 10Hz frequencies. This paper presents LiSnowNet, an unsupervised denoising algorithm that operates 52 times faster than state-of-the-art methods while delivering superior denoising results. Unlike prior approaches, LiSnowNet utilizes a deep convolutional neural network, enabling efficient deployment on hardware accelerators such as GPUs. Furthermore, we illustrate how this method can be applied to mapping tasks even when point clouds are compromised by snow.

This study examines the joint distribution of area and perimeter statistics for the set $I_n$ of inversion sequences of length $n$, visualized as bargraphs. By utilizing recurrences satisfied by this distribution, we derive functional equations for both the ordinary and exponential generating functions. Explicit formulas are obtained for certain special cases, along with expressions for the cumulative totals of these statistics on $I_n$. A comparable analysis is conducted for the joint distribution on $I_n$ concerning the statistics of levels, descents, and ascents. Furthermore, relationships are established between specific instances of this latter distribution and the Stirling numbers of the first kind and Eulerian numbers.

Visual object tracking serves as a critical element in many emerging video applications. Although significant progress has been made in visual tracking, current deep trackers often struggle when objects undergo drastic appearance changes. This limitation arises because most deep trackers lack online update mechanisms or only update a single sub-branch, preventing them from adapting to such variations. Consequently, efficient updating strategies are essential; however, existing meta-updaters, which optimize trackers directly within the parameter space, are susceptible to overfitting and may even collapse on extended sequences. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a context-aware tracking model that optimizes the tracker in the representation space. This approach jointly meta-updates both branches by leveraging information across the entire sequence, thereby mitigating overfitting. Specifically, we observe that the embedded features of the localization branch and the box-estimation branch, which capture local and global target information respectively, act as effective complements. Building on this insight, we design a context-aggregation module to fuse data from historical frames, followed by a context-aware module that learns affinity vectors for both tracker branches. Additionally, we develop a specialized meta-learning scheme to ensure fast and stable updates with limited training data. On the VOT2018 benchmark, the proposed method achieves an EAO score of 0.514 at 40 FPS, demonstrating its ability to enhance the accuracy and robustness of the base tracker with minimal impact on speed.

We present and investigate families of finite index subgroups within the modular group that extend the concept of congruence subgroups. These groups, named $\phi$-congruence subgroups, are derived by reducing homomorphisms $\phi$ from the modular group into a linear algebraic group modulo integers. Specifically, we analyze two distinct families of examples: one stemming from a mapping into a quasi-unipotent group, and the other from mappings into symplectic groups of degree four. In the case involving the quasi-unipotent group, we offer an in-depth examination of the associated modular forms, leveraging the fact that the resulting tower of curves includes the tower of isogenies over the elliptic curve $y^2=x^3-1728$, which is defined by the commutator subgroup of the modular group.

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly advanced research in dialogue state tracking (DST), yet it contains substantial noise in its state annotations that hinders the robust training of DST models. Although refined versions (MultiWOZ 2.1–2.4) have recently emerged, they still suffer from numerous noisy labels, particularly within the training sets, and manually correcting these issues is expensive. Rather than focusing on further improving annotation quality, this paper introduces ASSIST (lAbel noiSe-robuSt dIalogue State Tracking), a general framework designed to train DST models robustly despite noisy labels. ASSIST operates by first generating pseudo-labels for training samples using an auxiliary model trained on a small clean dataset; these pseudo-labels are then combined with the original noisy labels to train the primary model. Theoretical analysis confirms the validity of ASSIST, and experimental results demonstrate that it boosts joint goal accuracy in DST by up to $28.16\%$ on MultiWOZ 2.0 and $8.41\%$ on MultiWOZ 2.4 compared to training solely on vanilla noisy labels.

The recent 4FGL-DR3 catalog from the $\textit{Fermi}$-LAT mission includes a significant number of unidentified sources (unIDs) lacking clear associations with known counterparts. This study employs machine learning algorithms, trained on the spectral features of identified sources, to classify these unIDs. Utilizing the state-of-the-art $\texttt{CatBoost}$ algorithm, which relies on gradient boosting decision trees, we achieved 67% accuracy across a 23-class dataset. Accuracy rises to 81% when excluding the "blazars of uncertain type" class, and reaches 99% for a binary distinction between AGNs and pulsars. Furthermore, we conducted an unsupervised search within both known and unidentified populations to predict the number of clusters of similar sources without prior class knowledge. The complete code used for all calculations is available as an interactive Python notebook.

This study examines scaling similarity solutions for two integrable PDEs featuring cubic nonlinearity and admitting peakon solutions: the modified Camassa-Holm (mCH) equation and Novikov's equation. By applying specific reciprocal transformations that convert the mCH and Novikov equations into negative mKdV and negative Sawada-Kotera flows, respectively, we demonstrate that each scaling reduction connects via a hodograph transformation to a Painlevé-type equation. Specifically, the mCH reduction yields a second-order, second-degree equation, whereas the Novikov reduction corresponds to a particular instance of Painlevé V. Additionally, we establish that these two Painlevé-type equations are linked to specific cases of Painlevé III derived from analogous similarity reductions of the Camassa-Holm and Degasperis-Procesi equations. For both cubic PDEs, we provide explicit parametric representations of their periodic traveling wave solutions using elliptic functions. We include parametric plots of these solutions and, utilizing explicit algebraic solutions of Painlevé III, generate similar plots for selected scaling similarity solutions, accompanied by descriptions of their leading-order asymptotic behavior.

In a quantum system defined by a Hilbert space, observables correspond to its orthogonal bases. Categorical Quantum Mechanics offers a higher-level abstraction of these observables, enabling a diagrammatic depiction of measurements that generalizes to broader quantum processes. This research investigates this abstraction, termed "classical structures," within a subtheory of quantum mechanics dedicated to qubit systems (2-dimensional systems and their composites). We developed a method to take the complementary classical structures of a single qubit and either compose them independently using the Kronecker product or "entangle" them via Bell states to generate complementary classical structures in $n$-qubit systems. This procedure was applied to two- and three-qubit systems as illustrative examples. Subsequently, utilizing ZX-calculus rewriting rules and graph-theoretic tools, we identified maximal complete sets of mutually complementary classical structures (the categorical equivalent of mutually unbiased bases) within the constructed composites. Our findings reveal 13 such maximal sets for two qubits and 32,448 for three qubits.

This work presents and examines a continuous-time, continuous-state model of opinion cascades within large-scale networks where agents evaluate multiple options. Building upon our previous findings regarding the emergence of agreement and disagreement states, we develop new analytical tools to manage and study these cascades. We demonstrate that novel centrality measures for agreement and disagreement, derived solely from network topology, are essential for characterizing the nonlinear dynamics of opinion formation and cascades. These findings hold significance for analyzing and controlling opinion cascades across biological, social, and artificial networks, as well as for engineering opinion-forming behaviors in robotic swarms. Furthermore, we apply the model to a multi-robot task allocation scenario and explore potential extensions and future research avenues enabled by this modeling framework.

The relaxation time approximation (RTA) is a widely used technique for modeling the temporal development of a statistical ensemble by connecting the distributions of key variables across different time points. We demonstrate that when every distribution within the RTA follows the same functional shape—a quasi-power Tsallis distribution—whose evolution is governed by its control parameter, nonextensivity $q(t)$, it becomes more advantageous to focus exclusively on the dynamics of this control parameter.

Current deep neural network methods for sound synthesis often lack controllability, particularly without fine-grained conditioning, which limits their utility for musicians. This paper reframes the creation of individual instrumental notes as an inpainting task, offering innovative methods for iteratively sculpting audio. Our proposed two-stage pipeline first adapts the VQ-VAE-2 image generation model for spectrograms, converting real-valued data into compact discrete codemaps, and subsequently employs token-masked Transformers to generate these codemaps via inpainting. We evaluate this architecture on the NSynth dataset using masked resampling tasks. Most significantly, we release an open-source interactive web interface that enables artists and practitioners to transform sounds through inpainting, facilitating new creative applications.

Tracking temporal shifts in COVID-19 transmission rates serves as a vital metric for assessing epidemic expansion. For policymakers and public health authorities responsible for determining lockdowns or permitting specific activities, near real-time surveillance of pandemic progression is essential. While the effective reproduction number ($R_t$) is widely adopted as the standard indicator for this purpose, its utility in decision-making is often constrained by lags between infection onset and case reporting. This paper introduces a novel near real-time metric, the COVINDEX, designed to monitor pandemic evolution. This index is derived from Generalized Additive Model (GAM) beta regression predictions that model the test positivity rate over time. The proposed approach is demonstrated using Italian COVID-19 data and benchmarked against $R_t$. Additionally, a straightforward charting method is suggested to assist officials in tracking both local and national outbreaks.

This paper introduces an action for nonrelativistic strings that remains invariant under general coordinate transformations on the worldsheet. We present the Hamiltonian formulation for such strings and derive specific solutions to the Euler-Lagrange equations within the time gauge.

Investigating the phase space of multidimensional systems represents a key unresolved challenge in the field of dynamical systems. Furthermore, distinguishing between chaotic and regular behaviors in nonlinear systems, alongside identifying specific regions within the phase space prone to instability, constitutes a vital area of research. To address these challenges, various chaos indicators have been created. The insights gained from these indicators are crucial for comprehending the dynamic behavior of numerous systems, ranging from celestial mechanics to, more recently, chemical reaction dynamics. This special issue presents novel findings centered on phase space structure, chaos indicators, and chemical reaction dynamics.

This study presents a visual SLAM framework that leverages both point and line clouds for robust camera localization, concurrently generating a structural map via an integrated piece-wise planar reconstruction (PPR) module. Addressing the challenges of scale ambiguity and graph optimization inherent in monocular systems, the proposed approach employs runtime optimizations on reconstructed lines and planes to ensure scale consistency during parallel tracking and mapping. Building on this monocular foundation, the system is extended to support depth and stereo sensors. Experimental results indicate that the framework effectively integrates semantic features to enhance both frontend tracking and backend optimization. The system has been rigorously evaluated across multiple datasets, and the source code is publicly available at (https://github.com/PeterFWS/Structure-PLP-SLAM).

Jet vetoes are crucial in numerous LHC analyses. While these are traditionally enforced by limiting the transverse momentum ($p_{Tj}$) of jets, an alternative approach utilizes jet observables where $p_{Tj}$ is weighted by a smooth function of jet rapidity ($y_j$) that approaches zero as $|y_j|$ becomes large. These rapidity-dependent observables effectively impose strict vetoes on central jets while allowing looser constraints at forward rapidities. This study examines two specific observables, $\mathcal{T}_{Bj}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{Cj}$, and calculates the necessary beam and dijet soft functions for the jet-vetoed color-singlet production cross section up to two-loop order. At this precision, clustering effects from the jet algorithm are significant; we compute the dominant contributions analytically and express subleading corrections, valid for small jet radii, as finite numerical integrals. Our findings facilitate full NNLL' resummation and represent a vital step toward achieving N3LL resummation for cross sections incorporating $\mathcal{T}_{Bj}$ or $\mathcal{T}_{Cj}$ jet vetoes.

Sudden camera movements or object shifts within a scene cause video blur, meaning that restoring high-quality footage necessitates two distinct improvements: visual enhancement and temporal upsampling. While extensive research has focused on deblurring image sequences or upscaling frames through interpolation, few studies address these challenges simultaneously. This paper introduces a novel, end-to-end framework capable of deblurring, interpolating, and extrapolating sharp frames from motion-blurred videos. Our approach first learns the pixel-level motion responsible for the blur using optical flow estimation, then predicts multiple clean frames by warping decoded features according to these estimated flows. To maintain temporal consistency and resolve potential ambiguities, we propose a straightforward yet effective flow-based rule. The superior performance and advantages of our method are demonstrated through comprehensive qualitative and quantitative assessments on motion-blurred datasets derived from high-speed video.

In the 1970s, Lovász and Cherkassky independently established that for a finite graph $G$ with a designated set $T$ of terminal vertices, where $G$ is inner Eulerian, the maximum number of edge-disjoint paths connecting distinct vertices in $T$ equals $\sum_{t\in T}\lambda(t, T-t)$, with $\lambda$ representing the local edge-connectivity function. Menger's theorem confirms the optimality of such a system of edge-disjoint $T$-paths through the existence of specific cuts. By combining the infinite generalization of Menger's theorem proposed by Aharoni and Berger (formerly the Erdős-Menger Conjecture) with Nash-Williams' characterization of infinite Eulerian graphs, the theorem can be extended to infinite graphs structurally. This paper aims to formulate and prove this generalization specifically for countable graphs.

A MasterFace is an image capable of matching a significant segment of the population, posing a security threat to widely adopted face recognition systems because its creation does not require data from enrolled individuals. Although prior research has demonstrated that generating such images can severely compromise recognition systems, those studies relied on outdated models, limited cross-dataset and cross-model evaluations, and small-scale testing data, making it difficult to assess the generalizability of these attacks. This work addresses those gaps through comprehensive empirical and theoretical analyses of MasterFace generalizability. The empirical study employs six state-of-the-art face recognition models, rigorous cross-dataset and cross-model protocols, and large, diverse testing datasets. Results reveal low generalizability when MasterFaces are trained on a different model than the one used for testing; in such scenarios, attack performance resembles that of zero-effort imposter attacks. Theoretically, we define and estimate face capacity and maximum MasterFace coverage under the assumption of well-separated identities within the face space. Given the industry trend toward improving fairness and generalizability in face recognition, the vulnerability of future systems is likely to diminish further. Future research should explore how MasterFaces can aid in understanding and enhancing the robustness of these models.

Over the past few years, the deployment of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), especially small-scale ones, has surged significantly thanks to their cost-effectiveness, accessibility, and user-friendly operation. Current and prospective uses for UAVs span remote surveillance, disaster relief, package delivery, and communication backhaul support, with the technology also poised to play a pivotal role in 5G and future wireless networks. These distinct operational contexts demand precise air-to-ground (AG) propagation channel models to effectively design and assess UAV communication links for both control/non-payload and payload data transfer. Unlike well-established terrestrial models, AG propagation models have received comparatively little detailed investigation. Consequently, this paper offers a comprehensive survey of existing AG channel measurement campaigns, reviews large- and small-scale fading models, outlines their limitations, and highlights future research avenues for UAV communication scenarios.

This paper investigates systems that are weighted homogeneous across multiple weight sets and analyzes their impact on Gröbner basis computation. We introduce several linear algebra algorithms designed to compute these bases, either directly or by leveraging existing structural reductions, alongside appropriate optimization strategies. Additionally, we offer preliminary insights into complexity analysis by defining potential notions of regularity and demonstrating that they are generic whenever non-empty. The study concludes with experimental results from a prototype implementation of these algorithms within SageMath.

Chimera states, characterized by the simultaneous presence of coherent and incoherent dynamics, have been investigated in complex networks but remain underexplored in modular architectures. This study examines the neural network of the *C. elegans* soil worm, which comprises six interconnected communities of neurons exhibiting chaotic bursting dynamics. Within these communities, neurons are linked via electrical synapses, whereas connections between communities rely on chemical synapses. Our numerical simulations demonstrate that the interplay between these two coupling mechanisms can induce chimera-like states. Specifically, these states feature a subset of synchronized neurons residing in larger communities alongside a subset of desynchronized neurons found in smaller ones. Beyond the standard Kuramoto order parameter ($\rho$), we utilize additional coherence metrics, including the chimera-like index ($\chi$) and metastability index ($\lambda$), to quantify synchronization levels both across communities and over time. We apply this analysis to other networks sharing structural similarities with the *C. elegans* system. Comparable outcomes indicate that, under specific conditions, chimera-like states are prevalent in modular networks, offering valuable insights into the behavior of more intricate modular systems.

Supernovae and their remnants deliver energetic feedback to the interstellar medium (ISM), which typically consists of multiple gas phases. Within this environment, warm molecular hydrogen (H$_2$) frequently governs the cooling of shocked molecular ISM, a phenomenon observable via H$_2$ emission lines in the near-infrared. Previous investigations, however, were constrained by narrow filter imaging or sparsely sampled mid-infrared spectroscopy with limited angular resolution. This study introduces near-infrared ($H$- and $K$-band) spectroscopic mosaic observations of the A, B, C, and G regions of the supernova remnant IC 443, conducted using the K-band Multi-Object Spectrograph (KMOS) on the Very Large Telescope (VLT). We identified 20 ro-vibrational transitions of H$_2$, one hydrogen line (Br$\gamma$), and two [Fe II] lines, all of which dominate the broadband images in both bands. The spatial distribution of H$_2$ lines across all regions reveals clumpy structures ranging from approximately 0.1 pc to 0.008 pc in scale. The derived excitation temperatures for H$_2$ fall between 1500 K and 2500 K, signifying warm shocked gas. A comparison of multiple gas phases indicates stratified shock structures in every region, accounting for the co-existence of various shock types. Finally, our spectroscopic data verify previously identified young stellar object candidates, revealing that none are associated with young stars. These findings challenge the earlier hypothesis that SNR shocks in IC~443 trigger star formation.

This study examines the dissipativity of a specific class of Duhem hysteresis operators exhibiting clockwise (CW) input-output behavior. We establish sufficient conditions for an operator to display CW characteristics and derive an explicit storage function that satisfies the associated dissipation inequality for CW systems. These findings are applied to assess the stability of a second-order system featuring hysteretic friction, modeled by the Dahl approach.

This study examines turbulent impurity transport in Deuterium tokamak plasmas, driven by Ion Temperature Gradient (ITG) and Trapped Electron (TE) modes, utilizing both fluid and gyrokinetic models. By calculating impurity diffusivity ($D_Z$) and convective velocity ($V_Z$), the zero-flux peaking factor ($PF_0$) is determined; this metric represents the impurity density gradient where diffusive and convective fluxes cancel each other out. The sign of $PF_0$ is particularly significant, as it indicates whether impurities experience an inward pinch ($PF_0 > 0$) or an outward pinch ($PF_0 < 0$).

We introduce the inaugural high-resolution abundance study of the globular cluster VVV~CL001, located in a zone characterized by significant interstellar reddening toward the Galactic Bulge. Leveraging \textit{H}-band spectra from the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE), we confirmed two likely cluster members and determined, via Fe I lines, a mean metallicity of [Fe/H] = $-2.45$ with a systematic uncertainty of 0.24 dex. Our analysis reveals that the light-element (N), $\alpha$-element (O, Mg, Si), and Odd-Z (Al) abundances in VVV~CL001 mirror trends observed in other metal-poor Galactic globular clusters. Consequently, VVV~CL001 stands as the most metal-poor globular cluster identified to date within the Sun's galactocentric radius and is arguably the second most metal-deficient cluster in the Galaxy, following ESO280-SC06. Through statistical isochrone fitting, we obtained consistent estimates for age, distance, and reddening, indicating an age of $11.9^{+3.12}_{-4.05}$ Gyr and a distance of $8.22^{+1.84}_{-1.93}$ kpc, thereby confirming VVV~CL001 as an ancient globular cluster in the inner Galaxy. The cluster's Galactic orbit suggests a highly eccentric, halo-like trajectory. Both its chemical composition and dynamical properties support the hypothesis that VVV~CL001 is an ancient fossil remnant from a massive merger event during the Galaxy's early evolution, potentially linked to either the Sequoia or the \textit{Gaia}-Enceladus-Sausage accretion structures.

This study presents the jet radial structure and the transverse momentum ($p_{\rm{T}}$) composition of particles within jets, specifically in centrality-selected Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 2.76 TeV. Charged jets, identified via tracks, were reconstructed using an $R=0.3$ resolution parameter at midrapidity ($|\eta_\mathrm{ch\,jet}|<0.6$) for transverse momenta ranging from 30 to 120 GeV/$c$. Measurements of jet-hadron correlations in relative azimuth and pseudorapidity ($\Delta\varphi$, $\Delta\eta$) were conducted to analyze the distribution of associated particles around the jet axis across $p_\rm{T, assoc}$ intervals of 1 to 20 GeV/$c$. Data from Pb-Pb collisions are compared against reference distributions from pp collisions derived from embedded PYTHIA simulations. Results indicate that the yield of high-$p_{\rm{T}}$ associated particles ($4<p_\rm{T, assoc}<20$ GeV/$c$) is suppressed in Pb-Pb collisions by 30% to 10% relative to the reference, with the suppression varying by centrality. The radial particle distribution relative to the jet axis exhibits moderate modifications in Pb-Pb collisions compared to PYTHIA predictions: high-$p_{\rm{T}}$ associates are slightly more collimated, whereas low-$p_{\rm{T}}$ associates tend to be broader. These findings, which extend measurements down to $p_\rm{T,\,ch\,jet}=30$ GeV/$c$ in Pb-Pb collisions for the first time, are consistent with prior jet-hadron measurements from the CMS Collaboration and jet shape data from the ALICE Collaboration at higher momenta, further reinforcing the established understanding of in-medium parton energy loss.

Spin waves represent a promising, chargeless medium for information transfer in future energy-efficient systems that surpass conventional CMOS technology. While their numerous benefits—including ease of nonlinearity generation, diverse interaction types, and various excitation methods—are well recognized, a significant research challenge remains: understanding multi-mode nonlinear effects, especially those involving propagating waves in nanoscale configurations. This study theoretically investigates the dynamic interactions between spin waves confined to the edge of a thin ferromagnetic film and an incident spin-wave beam. Our findings reveal inelastically scattered spin-wave beams with frequencies shifted up and down by the edge mode's frequency relative to the specularly reflected beam. We identified a strong correlation between the angular deviation of these scattered beams and the edge-mode frequency, enabling the proposal of a magnonic demultiplexing technique for signals encoded in edge-propagating spin waves. Since dynamic magnetostatic interactions are fundamental to this process and ubiquitous in spin-wave dynamics, these results suggest that the observed effects could be implemented in various other configurations within magnonic systems.

Quantum machine learning approaches have been suggested to potentially improve the performance of machine learning applications. This paper presents two novel quantum methodologies for neural networks. The first is a quantum orthogonal neural network, constructed using a quantum pyramidal circuit to execute orthogonal matrix multiplication. We offer an efficient training strategy for this architecture, detailing new algorithms for both classical and quantum hardware that demonstrate asymptotic scaling advantages over previously known methods. The second approach involves quantum-assisted neural networks, leveraging a quantum computer to estimate inner products during the inference and training of classical neural networks. Subsequently, we conduct extensive experiments on medical image classification using current state-of-the-art quantum hardware, comparing various quantum methods against classical ones on both real devices and simulators. Our findings indicate that quantum and classical neural networks achieve comparable accuracy, supporting the potential of quantum methods for visual tasks as quantum hardware capabilities advance.

Perpetual view generation, which involves creating new long-range perspectives by virtually flying through a provided image, represents a novel and promising field. We present DiffDreamer, an unsupervised framework designed to synthesize novel views along extended camera trajectories using only internet-sourced images of natural landscapes. Our results demonstrate that image-conditioned diffusion models excel at long-range scene extrapolation, maintaining significantly superior local and global consistency compared to previous GAN-based approaches. Project page: https://primecai.github.io/diffdreamer .

Networks serve as key indicators of complex phenomena, where interactions among various agents convert basic local rules into nonlinear emergent behaviors. Although recent research has highlighted links between network architecture and underlying dynamics, determining stochastic nonlinear dynamical processes remains a significant challenge. In this work, we introduce a straightforward, data-driven framework utilizing operator-theoretic methods to identify and regulate stochastic nonlinear dynamics across extensive networks. Our method necessitates no prior understanding of the network's topology, deriving the underlying dynamics exclusively from sets of two-step state snapshots. By employing the Koopman operator, we achieve this system identification by locating a low-dimensional representation where dynamical patterns evolve linearly. Furthermore, we leverage the global linear Koopman model to address critical control issues through model predictive control (MPC)—a task often difficult for large-scale networks. We demonstrate that our approach overcomes this difficulty by transforming the original nonlinear programming challenge into a more manageable optimization problem that is convex and involves significantly fewer variables.

Robot safety is paramount, particularly in collaborative environments where humans and robots share a space. However, testing physical systems requires more than just software validation. While simulators are widely used in robotic development for tasks such as navigation and manipulation, they struggle with vision systems because simulated data often diverges significantly from real camera inputs. This paper demonstrates the benefits of employing spherical cameras to capture test image sequences and outlines a method for integrating these sequences with current robotic simulators. Furthermore, the proposed system can be expanded to include rendered objects, thereby enhancing its overall utility.

This paper investigates the dynamics of a dumbbell satellite orbiting an oblate body within a gravity field, specifically accounting for the influence of the zonal harmonic parameter. We demonstrate that when this parameter is non-zero, the trajectory of the system's mass center is periodic yet distinct from the classical case. Furthermore, we extend the classical theory by showing that the equations of motion in the satellite approximation simplify to Beletsky's equation when the zonal harmonic parameter vanishes. The primary method employed to establish these findings is the Lindstedt-Poincaré technique.

The rapid evolution of the mobile app sector has produced a diverse ecosystem where each application caters to unique needs and specific user groups. As a result, individuals utilize different apps to fulfill their information-seeking tasks, often employing multiple applications simultaneously within a single session to accomplish a common objective. Recent research highlights the necessity for a unified mobile search platform functioning as a metasearch engine on personal devices; such a system would automatically determine relevant apps for a user's query, execute the search across them, and aggregate the results into a cohesive display. This study seeks to enhance our comprehension of mobile information access behaviors by performing a comprehensive analysis of the search process. Specifically, we examine how task categories and user demographics influence interactions with mobile applications. Our results uncover key trends and patterns that can guide the development of a more efficient mobile information retrieval environment.

Android has emerged as the dominant mobile operating system, leading to a surge in malware development designed to exfiltrate user data. A specific category of this threat, known as covert malware, disguises malicious intent within benign behaviors. In these applications, the malicious code constitutes only a small fraction of the total app but remains tightly integrated with the legitimate components. Consequently, standard detection methods that analyze entire applications often yield false negatives, as malicious indicators are obscured by benign features. While previous approaches attempted to segment apps to isolate malicious parts, they relied on the assumption that connections between normal and malicious sections are weak. This paper introduces the term "Android covert malware" and presents the inaugural dataset for this threat. To detect it, we perform static analysis to extract call graphs, observing that although correlations between normal and malicious parts are strong, these correlations follow a specific distribution. Leveraging this insight, we developed HomDroid, which identifies covert malware by analyzing the homophily of call graphs. Using a dataset comprising 4,840 benign and 3,385 covert malicious apps, we determined an optimal correlation threshold to distinguish between the two. Evaluation results indicate that HomDroid detects 96.8% of covert malware, significantly outperforming four state-of-the-art systems—PerDroid, Drebin, MaMaDroid, and IntDroid—which exhibited false negative rates of 30.7%, 16.3%, 15.2%, and 10.4%, respectively.

The concept of non-deterministic logical matrices, which interpret connectives as multi-functions, retains many advantageous properties of traditional matrix semantics (where connectives are functions) while finitely characterizing a broader range of logics; it has also been pivotal in numerous recent compositional developments in logic. Specifically, if a finite non-deterministic matrix satisfies monadicity—meaning distinct truth-values can be distinguished by unary formulas—an axiomatization for the induced logic can be automatically generated. Moreover, these resulting calculi are analytical, facilitating algorithmic proof search and the symbolic generation of counter-models. While it is established that checking monadicity is decidable for finite deterministic matrices, we demonstrate that this property becomes undecidable when non-determinism is introduced. Consequently, we conclude that no algorithm exists to compute the set of all multi-functions expressible within a given finite Nmatrix. This undecidability result is derived via reduction from the halting problem of deterministic counter machines.

This study examines edge-localized stationary states of the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation on a general quantum graph within the large-mass limit. Unlike prior research, we incorporate arbitrary multi-pulse positive states that asymptotically resemble a superposition of $N$ solitons, with each soliton located on a bounded edge (whether pendant, looping, or internal). We establish the existence of these states as the mass becomes large and calculate the precise Morse index, defined as the count of negative eigenvalues in the associated linearized operator. Specifically, for $N$-soliton states localized on pendant and looping edges, we demonstrate that the Morse index equals exactly $N$. The methodological innovation lies in bypassing elliptic functions and their associated exponentially small scalings, instead formulating existence proofs using Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps for the pertinent sections of the graph.

This paper introduces a generative model for controllable person image synthesis, illustrated in Figure , capable of performing both pose-guided and clothing-guided synthesis. In pose-guided synthesis, the model transfers the pose of a source image to a target configuration while maintaining the source's texture; in clothing-guided synthesis, it alters the source image's clothing texture to a desired style. By explicitly creating dense correspondences between the target pose and the source image, we mitigate misalignment issues inherent in pose transfer, resulting in high-quality outputs. Our approach begins by generating a target semantic map guided by the desired pose, offering precise structural constraints and pose representation during generation. Subsequently, a decomposed attribute encoder extracts component features, which enhances the accuracy of dense correspondence and enables clothing-guided generation. Following this, we establish dense correspondences within the sharded domain between the target pose and the source image, allowing the source image features to be warped to accommodate deformations flexibly. Finally, the network renders the output image using the warped source features and the target pose. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in pose-guided person generation and proves effective for clothing-guided person generation.

Advancements in medical imaging play a crucial role in deep learning research. A primary objective within computer vision is to create comprehensive models capable of detecting tumors in histology slides derived from biopsies. However, a significant obstacle is the scarcity of data for certain cancer types. This study demonstrates that employing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for data augmentation offers a viable strategy to address the imbalance in cancer type distribution within the dataset. Our results indicate that augmenting the dataset by 50% led to an improvement in tumor detection accuracy, rising from 80% to 87.5%.

An asymptotically Anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetime linking two or more boundaries corresponds to an entangled state, expandable within the product basis of the Hilbert spaces associated with the Conformal Field Theories (CFTs) residing on those boundaries. We establish a method to calculate this expansion for states representing spacetimes of arbitrary dimension and general spatial topology. In the large $N$ limit, this expansion aligns with the Schmidt decomposition, where the coefficients are determined by $n$-point correlation functions on a specific Euclidean geometry. We demonstrate that this framework applies to any spacetime admitting a Hartle-Hawking type wave functional; through a homological correspondence, these functionals map bijectively to CFT states defined at the asymptotic boundary. Furthermore, we observe that these states exhibit quantum coherence. Utilizing this approach for holographic engineering, one can construct an emergent space with a prescribed topology by preparing a corresponding entangled state in the dual quantum system. As a demonstration, we apply this technique to compute the expansion and characterize a spacetime whose initial spatial topology is a genus-one handlebody.

This study details a multi-wavelength analysis of a C-class flare event (C1.3) within active region NOAA 12734 on March 8, 2019. Data were collected using the SDO's AIA and HMI instruments alongside the Udaipur-CALLISTO solar radio spectrograph from the Physical Research Laboratory. Although of low intensity, the event exhibited characteristics typical of long-duration events (LDEs), including an extended flare arcade, extensive two-ribbon structures, and paired coronal dimmings. Occurring within a coronal sigmoid, the eruption demonstrated two distinct phases of energy release defined by their temporal and spatial evolution. The appearance of twin dimming regions supports the hypothesis of a large flux rope eruption, with footpoints anchored at the western and eastern margins of the sigmoid. Udaipur-CALLISTO metric radio data revealed a stationary plasma emission spanning approximately 50–180 MHz for about seven minutes during the second phase, resembling a type IV burst. This was preceded by approximately five minutes by decametre-hectometre type III radio bursts originating near 2.5 MHz. Combining multi-wavelength observations with Non-Linear Force Free Field (NLFFF) modeling and magnetic decay index analysis indicates that the sigmoid flux rope experienced a zipping-like uprooting from west to east, driven by asymmetric overlying magnetic confinement. This asymmetric eruption explains the observed large-scale features, such as the eastward displacement of flare ribbons and post-flare loops along the polarity inversion line (PIL), and offers evidence for the lateral progression of the magnetic reconnection site as the eruption advanced.

To ensure natural conversational flow, knowledge-grounded dialog systems must incorporate smooth transitions between selected knowledge. Document-grounded systems can model these flows by leveraging both inter- and intra-document knowledge relations. We introduce a novel Multi-Document Co-Referential Graph (Coref-MDG) that effectively captures inter-document relationships based on commonsense and similarity, alongside the intra-document co-referential structures within grounding documents. Additionally, we propose CorefDiffs, a method for managing Co-referential and Differential flows that linearizes the static Coref-MDG into conversational sequence logic. By considering contextual graph structures and knowledge difference sequences, CorefDiffs handles knowledge selection. This approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 9.5%, 7.4%, and 8.2% across three public benchmarks, demonstrating that effectively modeling co-reference and knowledge differences is critical for transitions in document-grounded conversations.

This work introduces a unified framework for mixed-space quantum representations in Condensed Matter Physics (CMP) and Quantum Field Theory (QFT). The formalism relies on expanding any quantum operator—whether for bosons, fermions, or spin systems—using a universal basis operator, Y(u,v), defined over mixed Hilbert spaces of position (Q) and momentum (P). In CMP, P and Q represent momentum and position operators, respectively, which can be viewed as a bosonization of free Bloch electrons that accounts for the Pauli exclusion principle and Fermi-Dirac statistics; these correspond to creation and annihilation operators in QFT via the relations ${\psi}^{{\dag}}=-iP$ and ${\psi}=Q$. The expansion coefficients correspond to the Fourier transform of the Wigner quantum distribution function (also known as the lattice Weyl transform or characteristic distribution function). Consequently, fermionization techniques like the Jordan-Wigner transformation for spin systems, as well as the Holstein--Primakoff transformation for converting bosons to spin operators, can be applied based on computational convenience. The framework also incorporates unitary transformations of creation and annihilation operators, such as the Bogoliubov transformation. Furthermore, when Y(u,v) is expressed in matrix form (e.g., Pauli spin matrices), the Jordan--Schwinger transformation maps these to bilinear expressions of creation and annihilation operators, streamlining representation calculations. We demonstrate that the standard coherent states formulation of quantum physics emerges as a specific instance of this unification. Additionally, a novel QFT formulation based on the Q-distribution of functional-field variables is proposed, with the appendix addressing nonequilibrium quantum transport physics, including non-Hermitian operators and time-reversal symmetry breaking.

The cosmological constant $\Lambda$ represents the vacuum's energy density; consequently, the characteristics of the energy within a metastable vacuum state mirror the properties of the time-dependent $\Lambda(t)$. We examine the energy $E(t)$ of a general quantum system in a metastable state across three stages of decay: the exponential phase, the transition phase between exponential and power-law decay, and the final phase. Our analysis reveals that the energy, initially approximated by the Weisskopf–Wigner theory during the exponential phase, diminishes rapidly during the transition phase to an asymptotic value in the late phase, described as $E(t) \simeq E_{min} + \alpha_{2}/t^{2}+\ldots$ (where $E_{min}$ denotes the system's minimal energy). This quantum mechanism lowers the energy of the unstable state by a factor ranging from a dozen to several dozen orders of magnitude. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if a universe originates in a metastable false vacuum, this mechanism allows the cosmological constant $\Lambda$ to start at a very large value predicted by quantum field theory during the inflationary era ($\Lambda \simeq \Lambda_{qft}$) and subsequently decrease rapidly to extremely small values.

This is an unstructured collection of notes on category theory, covering topics such as the definition of locally cartesian closed categories, the cartesian structure within slice categories, and the pseudo-cartesian structure on Eilenberg-Moore categories. References and proofs are occasionally included, which, to the author's knowledge, may be novel.

This paper develops parameterizations for elliptic curves over the rationals that possess numerous consecutive integral multiples. Leveraging these parameterizations, we conducted searches using GMP and Magma to identify curves with points of minimal height, those featuring many integral multiples of a point, instances where high multiples are integral, and over two hundred curves containing more than one hundred integral points. Furthermore, we established a new and comprehensive classification of "self-descriptive numbers" by determining the necessary lower bound on the count of zeros such numbers must contain.

Based on a data sample with an integrated luminosity of $2.0\,fb^{-1}$ gathered by the LHCb experiment, this study investigates the production of the $\eta_c(1S)$ state in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13 \text{ TeV}$, focusing on the rapidity interval ${2.0 < y < 4.5}$ and the transverse momentum range ${6.5 < p_{T} < 14.0\text{ GeV}}$. Utilizing the ${p\bar{p}}$ decay channel, the cross-section ratio for prompt $\eta_c(1S)$ production relative to $J/\psi$ mesons is measured as ${\sigma_{\eta_c(1S)}/\sigma_{J/\psi} = 1.69 \pm 0.15 \pm 0.10 \pm 0.18}$. These uncertainties correspond, respectively, to statistical errors, systematic errors, and uncertainties arising from the branching fractions of ${J/\psi\to p \bar{p}}$ and ${\eta_c\to p \bar{p}}$ decays. The absolute prompt $\eta_c(1S)$ production cross-section is calculated to be ${\sigma_{\eta_c(1S)} = 1.26 \pm 0.11\pm 0.08 \pm 0.14 \,\mu b}$, with the final uncertainty incorporating the error on the $J/\psi$ cross-section. Additionally, the ratio of branching fractions for $b$-hadron decays into $\eta_c(1S)$ versus $J/\psi$ final states is found to be ${\mathcal{B}_{b\to\eta_c X}/\mathcal{B}_{b\to J/\psi X} = 0.48 \pm 0.03 \pm 0.03 \pm 0.05}$, where the last error term reflects uncertainties in the ${J/\psi \to p \bar{p}}$ and ${\eta_c\to p \bar{p}}$ branching fractions. Finally, the mass difference between the $J/\psi$ and $\eta_c(1S)$ is determined to be ${113.0 \pm 0.7 \pm 0.1\text{ MeV}}$, representing the most precise single measurement of this parameter available to date.

The study investigates the photoproduction of the bottomonium-like states $Z_{b}(10610)$ and $Z_{b}(10650)$ through $\gamma p$ scattering using an effective Lagrangian framework and the vector-meson-dominance model. A Regge model is utilized to compute $t$-channel $\pi$ exchange contributions. Numerical findings indicate that at a center-of-mass energy of approximately 22 GeV, the total cross-sections for $Z_{b}(10610)$ and $Z_{b}(10650)$ reach roughly 0.09 nb and 0.02 nb, respectively. Consequently, experimental investigations in this energy range are recommended. Furthermore, utilizing the eSTARlight and STARlight codes, cross-sections and event yields for $Z_{b}(10610)$ production in electron-ion collisions (EIC) and ultraperipheral collisions (UPCs) are derived, revealing that a significant number of events are feasible. Additionally, rates and kinematic distributions for the process $\gamma p\rightarrow Z_{b}n$ in $ep$ and $pA$ collisions are calculated via EICs and UPCs, offering crucial references for future searches for $Z_{b}$ states at RHIC, LHC, EIC-US, LHeC, and FCC facilities.

We demonstrate rapid mixing and define the stationary distribution for the Langevin Algorithm applied to inverting random weighted deep neural network generators. This advances Hand and Voroninski's findings by extending efficient inversion to efficient posterior sampling. To enhance expressivity, we recommend performing posterior sampling within the latent space of a pre-trained generative model. Specifically, we train a score-based model within a StyleGAN-2 latent space to address inverse problems. Our proposed framework, Score-Guided Intermediate Layer Optimization (SGILO), builds on previous research by substituting sparsity regularization with a generative prior in the intermediate layer. Empirical results show substantial improvements over the current state-of-the-art, particularly under low measurement conditions.

Question-and-Answer (QA) sites have become highly effective venues for exchanging knowledge and resolving issues. Among these, Stack Exchange hosts some of the most prominent communities, including Stack Overflow. While initial assessments of these platforms rely on aggregate metrics such as the resolution rate or the average time required to obtain and verify correct answers, advanced longitudinal data analysis offers deeper insights into the QA process. This approach allows for the identification of key predictive variables and systematic performance comparisons across various communities. This paper applies survival analysis to selected Stack Exchange communities, demonstrating how this methodology can effectively characterize and evaluate community performance, while also highlighting implications for the design and management of QA platforms.

This study presents a model of a shell frictionally coupled to an elastic foundation. Utilizing Kikuchi and Oden's formulation of Coulomb's static friction law, we establish a displacement-based static-friction condition for the shell and demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions, drawing on the theoretical framework provided by Kinderlehrer and Stampacchia. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the inaugural derivation of such a displacement-based friction condition, as existing literature primarily relies on force- or stress-based formulations. For numerical investigation, we adapt Kikuchi and Oden's model to simulate a complete two-body contact problem within curvilinear coordinates. Our numerical findings suggest that the displacement fields of the foundation predicted by both models align more closely when the shell possesses a high Young's modulus or a high Poisson's ratio, and when the contact region exhibits either a high coefficient of friction or low curvature.

A learning approach is considered self-certified when it leverages the entire dataset to concurrently train a predictor and generate a precise statistical guarantee regarding its performance on unseen data. Recent studies indicate that neural networks optimized via PAC-Bayes bounds not only yield accurate models but also provide tight risk certificates, suggesting a promising path toward self-certified learning. These strategies are particularly appealing because they utilize all available information to derive a posterior distribution while simultaneously issuing a rigorous numerical bound on its risk. This paper evaluates advancements in self-certification within probabilistic neural networks trained using PAC-Bayes-inspired objectives. We conduct an empirical comparison across four classification datasets between traditional test set bounds for deterministic models and PAC-Bayes bounds for randomized, self-certified predictors. Our findings demonstrate that both generalization bounds remain closely aligned with out-of-sample test errors. Furthermore, we observe that in data-scarce scenarios, reserving data for classical test set bounds degrades generalization performance, whereas self-certified PAC-Bayes approaches avoid this limitation, highlighting their suitability for small-data regimes. Additionally, we discover that probabilistic neural networks trained with PAC-Bayes objectives produce certificates that are unexpectedly competitive with standard test set bounds.

The paper establishes several uniqueness theorems for non-compact, complete, stationary spacelike surfaces within an $n(\geq 3)$-dimensional Generalized Robertson Walker spacetime. To achieve this, we posit a natural inequality linking the surface's Gauss curvature, the warping function's restrictions, and the sectional curvature of the fiber restricted to the surface. This inequality ensures the surface is parabolic. Leveraging this property, we demonstrate that a specific non-negative superharmonic function on the surface must be constant, thereby proving that the stationary spacelike surface is totally geodesic. Additionally, we present non-trivial examples of such surfaces in four-dimensional Lorentz-Minkowski spacetime to illustrate that every assumption made is essential.

Effect algebras were originally developed as an abstract algebraic framework to model Hilbert space effects, which represent quantum mechanical measurements. This study investigates additional structures within an effect algebra $E$ that allow for the definition of spectrality and spectral resolutions for its elements, mirroring concepts found in self-adjoint operators. These structures, termed compression bases, consist of specific families of maps on $E$ that are analogous to compression sets in operator algebras, order unit spaces, or unital abelian groups. There is a one-to-one correspondence between elements of a compression base and specific elements of $E$ known as projections. An effect algebra is defined as spectral if it possesses a distinguished compression base satisfying two key conditions: the projection cover property, ensuring every element $a \in E$ has a minimal projection that majorizes it, and the $b$-comparability property, which parallels general comparability in operator algebras or unital abelian groups. It is demonstrated that in a spectral archimedean effect algebra $E$, every element $a$ admits a unique rational spectral resolution, and these properties are examined. Furthermore, if $E$ includes a separating set of states, then each element $a \in E$ is uniquely determined by its spectral resolution. Additionally, it is proven that for certain interval effect algebras (specifically those with RDP and being archimedean divisible), the spectrality of $E$ is equivalent to the spectrality of its universal group, with their corresponding rational spectral resolutions being identical. Notably, for convex archimedean effect algebras, spectral resolutions within $E$ align with those in the associated order unit space.

Doreian's (1989) Network Disturbance Model captures the interdependence among observations at network vertices by modeling correlations between adjacent nodes through a single parameter, $\rho$. It has been noted that estimating $\rho$ in dense graphs via Maximum Likelihood often yields results that are both biased and highly unstable. This paper outlines the reasons for this phenomenon, demonstrating that such variability is inescapable regardless of network size. Additionally, we introduce a more intuitive estimator for $\rho$ that exhibits minimal bias, and we briefly examine the related Network Effects Model.

Quality Estimation (QE) serves as a critical element within the machine translation pipeline by evaluating translated output quality without relying on reference translations. This paper presents our contribution to the WMT 2021 QE Shared Task, specifically addressing Task 2, the sentence-level sub-task, which requires predicting the HTER score for post-editing effort. Our system utilizes an ensemble of multilingual BERT (mBERT)-based regression models, developed through fine-tuning under various input configurations. This approach achieves performance comparable to the baseline in terms of Pearson's correlation and surpasses it in Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) for multiple language pairs. Furthermore, we extend our system to a zero-shot scenario by leveraging language pairs relevant to the target language and utilizing pseudo-reference translations.

We establish the stability, convergence, and consistency of the space-time Domain Decomposition approach for the 4DVAR Data Assimilation problem. Additionally, we define the problem's condition number and corroborate our theoretical findings with numerical experiments.

The primary function of a transport protocol is to facilitate communication between end-to-end entities, which may include hosts or network devices like routers and firewalls. These protocols establish a virtual circuit between such devices and are categorized into two types: connection-oriented and connectionless. As the names imply, connection-oriented protocols involve the overhead of establishing connections but offer reliability features such as packet reordering, congestion control, and guaranteed delivery. Conversely, connectionless protocols operate on a "send and forget" basis, focusing solely on delivering datagrams without tracking their successful arrival. The two principal protocols in this domain are TCP and UDP, which respectively support connection-oriented and connectionless services. Specifically, TCP ensures a reliable end-to-end connection and implements congestion control mechanisms to prevent receiver-side buffer overflow.

This study develops a compartmental stochastic model for SARS-CoV-2 transmission featuring distinct dynamics for mean and variance. By fitting the model to Washington state time series data from January 2020 to March 2021 using a deterministic, biologically-informed signal processing method, we demonstrate that hidden states, such as population prevalence, align with survey data and other estimates. The second half of the paper reframes this model as a branching process with a dynamic degree distribution, enabling the generation of approximate transmission trees and the estimation of higher-order statistics like case clustering. These findings regarding outbreak clustering are consistent with observations from contact tracing and phylogenetics.

Systematic design of low-friction surfaces for diverse technological applications necessitates the development of non-equilibrium thermodynamics for friction. Intuitively, the thermodynamic work generated when a material slides over a surface is anticipated to split between dissipation as heat and transformation into the system's internal energy. However, the general non-equilibrium thermodynamic principles dictating this separation remain unknown. We construct a theoretical framework integrating transition state theory with the standard Prandtl-Tomlinson model, enabling the derivation of explicit expressions for heat dissipation and internal energy changes during the stick-slip motion of an atomic force microscope tip. We apply this formalism to quantify heat dissipation across various parameters pertinent to materials used in practical nanoscale friction applications.

Recently, Artificial Neural-Network-based (ANN-based) lossy compressors have achieved remarkable performance across various sources, largely due to their capacity to detect the structure of low-dimensional manifolds embedded within high-dimensional spaces. Previous research has demonstrated that these compressors can attain the optimal entropy-distortion curve for certain such sources. Conversely, this study establishes the optimal entropy-distortion tradeoffs for two specific low-dimensional manifolds characterized by circular structures, revealing that current state-of-the-art ANN-based compressors are unable to optimally compress them.

Let $G$ denote a group where every non-trivial representation has a dimension of at least $d$. Consider distributions $X=(X_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{t})$ and $Y=(Y_{1},Y_{2},\ldots,Y_{t})$ defined over $G^{t}$, assuming $X$ and $Y$ are independent. We demonstrate that for any $g\in G$, the inequality $|\mathbb{P}[X_{1}Y_{1}X_{2}Y_{2}\cdots X_{t}Y_{t}=g]-1/|G||\le\frac{|G|^{2t-1}}{d^{t-1}}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{h\in G^{t}}X(h)^{2}}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{h\in G^{t}}Y(h)^{2}}$ holds. These findings extend, refine, and streamline earlier research.

This paper offers a thorough examination of the linear response of interacting underdamped Brownian particles subjected to simple shear flow. We detail six distinct approaches for calculating this response, two of which exploit the symmetry of the system and observables relative to the shear axes. Our work extends the Green-Kubo relation to underdamped scenarios, revealing two surprising additional terms. These six methods are utilized to analyze the relaxation of response toward the steady state across various observables, highlighting intriguing effects arising from interactions and finite particle mass. Furthermore, we evaluate the statistical efficiency of the different response relations, determining their relative requirements for experimental measurement duration or computational resources in simulations. Finally, we discuss several indicators of the breakdown of linear response theory at higher shear rates.

We report the inaugural measurement of differential cross sections for charged-current muon neutrino interactions on argon characterized by a final state containing one muon, two protons, and no pions. These events leave the target nucleus in a two-particle two-hole configuration, which is highly significant yet currently lacks substantial data regarding its production in neutrino-nucleus collisions. Rigorous studies of such states are essential for upcoming experiments investigating neutrino properties, a capability now enabled by the liquid-argon time-projection-chamber's ability to isolate these specific final states. Key observables, including the opening angle between the protons, the angle between the combined proton momentum and the muon, and the total transverse momentum of the system, offer sensitivity to underlying physics processes described by various models. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that realistic initial-state momentum distributions are crucial for accurately reproducing the experimental data.

The paper details the construction of HNN-extensions for involutive Hom-associative algebras and involutive Hom-Lie algebras. Subsequently, leveraging the validity of the Poincaré-Birkhoff-Witt theorem for involutive Hom-Lie algebras, an embedding theorem is established as an application of HNN-extensions.

The rising luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) presents significant challenges for primary vertex reconstruction within the ATLAS experiment. During the recently concluded Run 2, a rate of 70 or more inelastic proton-proton collisions per beam crossing was recorded, with even greater vertex density, known as pile-up, anticipated for Run 3. To address this, ATLAS has introduced two new tools: a Gaussian track density seed finder and an adaptive multi-vertex finder. The seed finder utilizes a straightforward yet robust analytic model of track density along the beam axis to identify candidate vertices, while the adaptive finder employs a global strategy for vertex discovery and fitting, enabling vertices to compete for nearby tracks. These proceedings outline the strategy, optimization, and preliminary performance of this updated vertex reconstruction software, emphasizing enhancements in vertex finding efficiency, purity, and spatial resolution under the expected pile-up conditions of Run 3.

Electroconvection promotes dendrite formation on battery electrodes. Introducing low molecular weight polymers into the electrolyte creates a concentrated polymer layer near the electrode surface, driven by van der Waals attractions between the metal and dissolved polymers. These forces function as a restoring body force that counteracts perturbation growth and inhibits electroconvective flow, as demonstrated through linear stability analysis. Consequently, the critical voltage needed to initiate electroconvection is raised.

Observations indicate that silicates in comets, which should originate from the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, exhibit a surprisingly high crystalline abundance of roughly 10–60%. This contradicts theoretical expectations, as crystalline silicates typically form through the annealing of amorphous precursors in the disk's inner region. To resolve this discrepancy, we conducted Monte Carlo simulations modeling the advection and diffusion of silicate particles within a turbulent disk under a pebble accretion framework. In this model, pebbles composed of numerous small amorphous silicates encased in ice form in the outer disk; silicate particles are liberated at the snow line, while crystalline variants emerge at the annealing line. These particles diffuse outward beyond the snow line before eventually re-attaching to drifting pebbles and returning inward. Our simulations and analytical results demonstrate that, in a simplified scenario lacking particle sticking with a steady pebble flux, the crystalline fraction beyond the snow line remains robustly and uniformly at approximately 5%. However, in a more realistic scenario incorporating sticking mechanisms and a decaying pebble flux, the crystalline abundance increases to roughly 20–25%, contingent upon the ratio of decay to diffusion timescales. This latter figure aligns well with observational data. While this study assumes a steady-state accretion disk, future work coupling simulations with disk evolution is necessary for a more detailed comparison with observed data.

Extensive surveys of star-forming regions have revealed power-law relationships between stellar mass and disc properties, specifically disc mass ($M_{\mathrm{d}} \propto {M_{\star}}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}$) and accretion rate ($\dot M \propto {M_{\star}}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{acc}}}$). Although observed slopes seem to rise over time, the underlying causes for these correlations and their evolution remain unclear. This study performs a theoretical analysis of how viscous evolution affects power-law initial conditions across a population of protoplanetary discs. Our findings indicate that for evolved populations, viscous evolution forces both correlations to converge to the same slope, $\lambda_{\mathrm{m}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{acc}}$, a limit uniquely set by the initial slopes $\lambda_{\mathrm{m}, 0}$ and $\lambda_{\mathrm{acc}, 0}$. We successfully reproduce the observed increasing trend when the initial difference $\delta_0 = \lambda_{\mathrm{m}, 0} - \lambda_{\mathrm{acc}, 0}$ exceeds $1/2$, attributing this trend to a positive correlation between the viscous timescale and stellar mass. Additionally, numerical simulations of disc population synthesis demonstrate good agreement with our analytical predictions while accounting for spreads and sampling effects. Finally, a preliminary comparison with observational data constrains the initial condition parameter space to $\lambda_{\mathrm{m}, 0} \in [1.2, 2.1]$ and $\lambda_{\mathrm{acc}, 0} \in [0.7, 1.5]$.

This paper investigates the $L_p$-Gaussian Minkowski problem within the framework of $L_p$-Brunn-Minkowski theory in a Gaussian probability space. By applying Aleksandrov's variational method utilizing Lagrange multipliers, we establish the existence of solutions to the logarithmic Gauss Minkowski problem. Furthermore, we develop a specific Gauss curvature flow for closed, convex hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, demonstrating its long-time existence and smooth convergence to a solution of the normalized $L_p$ Gaussian Minkowski problem for $p>0$ and $-n-1<p\leq 0$ under the condition of an even prescribed function. Additionally, we offer a parabolic proof within the smooth category for the $L_p$-Gaussian Minkowski problem when $p\geq n+1$ and $0<p<n+1$, also assuming an even prescribed function.

Machine learning (ML) is becoming increasingly pivotal in making decisions that impact diverse societal sectors, including criminal justice, banking credit extensions, and corporate hiring. This widespread influence underscores the necessity for model fairness, ensuring automated outcomes are equitable regarding protected attributes like race, gender, and age, which are frequently under-represented in datasets. We argue that this under-representation is intrinsically linked to the challenge of imbalanced data learning, where both class distributions and protected group representations are skewed. For instance, a dataset might over-represent approved loan applicants while under-representing women compared to men. A crucial component of achieving algorithmic fairness is simultaneously mitigating class imbalance and protected group disparity within the training data, a strategy that enhances both model accuracy and fairness. We explore the synergies between imbalanced learning and group fairness by highlighting their overlapping concepts, and we introduce a novel oversampling technique called "Fair Oversampling." This method effectively tackles skewed class distributions and protected feature imbalances. Our approach serves two main functions: (i) it acts as an efficient pre-processing step for standard ML algorithms to jointly address imbalance and equity, and (ii) it can be integrated with fairness-aware learning algorithms to bolster their robustness against varying degrees of class imbalance. Furthermore, we bridge the gap between fairness and imbalanced learning by proposing a new metric, "Fair Utility," which synthesizes balanced accuracy with fairness measures.

This work introduces a two-phase maximum-likelihood soft-decision decoding (tpMLSD) algorithm for binary linear block codes, grounded in the concept of supercodes. In the initial phase, the Viterbi algorithm is applied in reverse to a trellis constructed from the parity-check matrix of the code's supercode. Leveraging the data preserved from this stage, the second phase utilizes a priority-first search algorithm on the trellis associated with the linear block code itself, ensuring an optimal maximum-likelihood decision. Simulation results on Reed-Muller codes demonstrate that this two-phase approach reduces average decoding complexity by an order of magnitude compared to recursive maximum-likelihood decoding (RMLD) [1] at a signal-to-noise ratio per information bit of 4.5 dB.

This study investigates how Casual Affective Triggers (CAT)—objects embedded in survey invitations designed to evoke emotion—influence response rates. The core hypothesis posits that invitations containing CATs yield higher participation than those without. To test this, we compared a control group receiving standard invitations against an experimental group receiving CAT-enriched ones. Within the experimental group, we varied the trigger type: one-third of participants received a personalized invitation, another third received an image of the researcher's cat, and the final third received both. A subsequent survey validated these findings. The results indicate that CATs positively affect response rates and do not introduce response bias.

Recent research has shown that incorporating reconfigurable elements along the rim of a paraboloidal reflector antenna allows for sidelobe modification, including their cancellation. This study explores methods for calculating unit-magnitude weights—specifically those adjusting the phase of scattered signals—to achieve sidelobe cancellation at any angle relative to the reflector axis. It demonstrates that despite a vast search space and a non-convex cost function, weights with significant cancellation capabilities can be identified with manageable computational complexity.
