This work examines multiple deformations of the three-dimensional Skyrme model, specifically focusing on self-dual sectors with arbitrary baryonic charge. We demonstrate that for specific families of background metrics and field-dependent couplings, the model admits a single BPS sector capable of supporting any topological charge. Furthermore, we analyze the gravitating version of the model, showing that the inclusion of a cosmological constant results in an infinite number of BPS sectors.

u =  eta$), mechanisms like Faraday rotation or Lorentz violation suggest a dependence on frequency ($ eta_
u \propto 
u^n$). Our analysis samples the birefringence angle for each polarized HFI band and the 70 GHz LFI channel, and also fits a power-law model $ eta_
u= eta_0(
u/
u_0)^n$ where $
u_0 = 150$ GHz. For a nearly full-sky coverage ($f_{	ext{sky}}=0.93$), ignoring intrinsic foreground $EB$ correlations yields $ eta_0 = 0.26^{\circ}\pm0.11^\circ$ and $n=-0.45^{+0.61}_{-0.82}$, whereas using a filamentary dust model results in $ eta_0 = 0.33^\circ \pm 0.12^\circ$ and $n=-0.37^{+0.49}_{-0.64}$. Subsequently, we incorporate the 30 and 44 GHz bands, which have negligible polarized dust foregrounds, analyzing them separately. Without foreground modeling, including these lower frequencies generally increases the measured $ eta_
u$ values and tightens the constraints on $n$, leading to $ eta_0=0.29^{\circ+0.10^\circ}_{\phantom{\circ}-0.11^\circ}$ and $n=-0.35^{+0.48}_{-0.47}$ at nearly full-sky. Assuming no frequency dependence across all data, we measure $ eta=0.33^\circ \pm 0.10^\circ$. If foreground $EB$ effects are effectively mitigated, our results align with a primarily frequency-independent cosmic birefringence signal.

This work investigates $SU$-linear operations within complex cobordism, demonstrating that they are generated by the established geometric operations $\partial_i$. For $c_1$-spherical bordism theory $W$, we characterize all $SU$-linear multiplications on $W$ and the associated projections from $MU$ to $W$. Additionally, we examine complex orientations on $W$ and their corresponding formal group laws $F_W$. While Buchstaber (1972) previously explored the connection between these formal group laws and the coefficient ring $\varOmega^W$, we extend his findings by proving that for any $SU$-linear multiplication and orientation on $W$, the coefficients of $F_W$ fail to generate the ring $\varOmega^W$, a result that contrasts with the case of complex bordism.

Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) are essential instruments in Data Science and Statistics, primarily utilized for clustering and density estimation. Practically, estimating their parameters is often addressed using the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm, valued for its simplicity and minimal computational cost per iteration. However, EM suffers from slow convergence when dealing with significant hidden information or overlapping clusters. Recently, manifold optimization techniques for GMMs have garnered growing attention. This work presents an explicit formula for the Riemannian Hessian within GMMs and introduces a novel Riemannian Newton Trust-Region method that surpasses existing approaches in both runtime and iteration count. We evaluate this method on clustering and density approximation tasks, demonstrating its superior effectiveness compared to current methods, particularly for datasets containing a high proportion of hidden information.

Radio loud active galactic nuclei (RLAGNs) frequently exhibit complex morphologies, often comprising multiple spatially distinct components. While astronomers traditionally rely on visual inspection to link these radio components, applying this method to the hundreds of thousands of well-resolved RLAGNs in the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR) Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS) at $144$ MHz is an extremely labor-intensive and time-consuming task, even with significant human resources. To address this, we employed a machine learning strategy to automate the association of large ($> 15$ arcsec) radio components. By reframing the association task as a classification problem, we trained a modified region-based convolutional neural network to replicate expert annotations from the initial LoTSS data release. To mitigate overfitting and streamline the association process by filtering out unresolved sources likely unrelated to prominent components, we utilized rotation data augmentation alongside predictions from a pre-existing gradient boosting classifier. For large ($> 15$ arcsec) and bright ($> 10$ mJy) components within the LoTSS first data release, our model achieved agreement with manual astronomical associations in $85.3\%\pm0.6$ of cases, a result comparable to those obtained through public crowd-sourcing initiatives. This approach offers an efficient solution for manual component association in extensive radio surveys and can serve as a foundation for automated radio morphology classification or optical host identification. Consequently, this method facilitates a new avenue for investigating the completeness and reliability of samples featuring extended and complex radio source morphologies.

We introduce an open-source adaptive front-tracking solver designed for biological capsules within viscous flows. Membrane elastic and bending forces are resolved on a Lagrangian triangulation via a linear Finite Element Method combined with paraboloid fitting, while fluid dynamics are computed on an octree adaptive grid using the Basilisk platform. Communication between the Lagrangian and Eulerian grids is achieved through an Immersed Boundary Method employing Peskin-like regularized Dirac delta functions. The solver's accuracy is validated extensively against the Boundary Integral Method under Stokes conditions and compared with non-adaptive front-tracking solvers in inertial regimes, yielding excellent qualitative and quantitative agreement. Furthermore, we demonstrate the solver's robustness in scenarios involving extreme membrane deformation and its ability to simulate inertial flows of capsules within complex STL-defined geometries, thereby enabling bioengineering applications involving large three-dimensional channel structures. The source code and all associated test cases are freely accessible.

We examine a multi-agent framework where agents exchange information across a potentially time-varying network to minimize a separable objective function under specific constraints. To accomplish this, we introduce a new subgradient averaging algorithm capable of handling non-differentiable objectives and distinct constraint sets for individual agents. A unique aspect of our method is its ability to manage varying agent constraints alongside a dynamic communication topology, thereby extending prior work on distributed subgradient techniques. To underscore the importance of addressing heterogeneous constraints in distributed optimization, we analyze a specific problem instance where existing algorithms fail to converge when adapted to such scenarios. We demonstrate that our proposed iterative scheme achieves asymptotic convergence to an optimal solution for step sizes defined as $ \frac{\eta}{k+1} $ with $ \eta > 0 $. Furthermore, we evaluate the scheme using step sizes of $ \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{k+1}} $ ($ \eta > 0 $), proving an objective value convergence rate of $ \mathcal{O}(\frac{\ln k}{\sqrt{k}}) $. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of this approach through investigations into robust regression and $ \ell_2 $ regression with regularization.

Graph shotgun assembly involves reconstructing a graph from its local neighborhoods. This paper examines shotgun assembly for \ER random graphs $G(n, p_n)$ with $p_n = n^{-\alpha}$ where $0 < \alpha < 1$. We analyze both reconstruction up to isomorphism and exact reconstruction, which includes recovering vertex labels alongside the structure. Our findings indicate that given distance-$1$ neighborhoods, exact reconstruction of $G$ is possible for $0 < \alpha < \frac{1}{3}$, whereas it is impossible for $\frac{1}{2} < \alpha < 1$. Furthermore, when provided with distance-$2$ neighborhoods, exact reconstruction holds for $\alpha \in \left(0, \frac{1}{2}\right) \cup \left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{3}{5}\right)$, but fails for $\frac{3}{4} < \alpha < 1$.

We define a twisted Dirac structure on the space of irreducible connections for an SU(n)-bundle over a three-manifold, alongside a family of such structures on the space of irreducible connections for a trivial SU(n)-bundle over a four-manifold. This twisting is characterized by the Cartan 3-form defined on the connection space, which vanishes specifically over the subspace of flat connections. Consequently, the spaces of flat connections inherit non-twisted Dirac structures. Furthermore, the Dirac structure on flat connections over the three-manifold arises as the boundary restriction of the corresponding structure over the four-manifold. Finally, we examine the action of the gauge transformation group on these Dirac structures.

We derive a non-perturbative field redefinition linking a Gaussian random field to the actual non-Gaussian curvature perturbation within the framework of transient constant-roll inflation near a local maximum. Our findings reveal a new critical amplitude, $\zeta_*$, which signifies perturbations that stop the inflaton from overshooting the peak, thereby trapping it in the false minimum. For potentials exhibiting mild curvature at the maximum (resulting in low non-Gaussianity), our approach recovers the established perturbative field redefinition. We apply these insights to primordial black hole formation, specifically examining scenarios where $\zeta_*$ is comparable to or smaller than the critical threshold required for the collapse of spherically symmetric overdensities. In such cases, we introduce a simple potential model demonstrating that the power spectrum requires an amplitude ten times smaller than in the Gaussian scenario to generate a significant population of primordial black holes.

We examine the selfish scheduling problem within a decentralized environment comprising $m$ machines, where users strategically select machines to minimize their individual cost shares. Each machine's cost depends on its total load, distributed among users via a specific cost-sharing mechanism that defines the game dynamics. Our goal is to design a mechanism that minimizes the Price of Anarchy (PoA).

Recent studies have introduced \emph{resource-aware} cost-sharing mechanisms, which account for the system's machine configuration but remain independent of the total user count. While these mechanisms yield low PoA for instances with convex or concave cost functions, they often result in significantly high PoA for functions outside these categories.

This paper demonstrates that augmenting resource-aware mechanisms with limited prior knowledge about users enables them to achieve low PoA across a broader spectrum of cost functions. Specifically, we show that if the mechanism identifies just two participating users, it can assign them special roles to guarantee a constant PoA. Furthermore, we extend this approach to scenarios where the mechanism knows the probability of each user's presence, providing a mechanism that achieves an expected PoA logarithmic in the expected number of users for these cases.

Over the past five years, gravitational-wave astronomy has transitioned from a purely theoretical discipline to a flourishing experimental science. Numerous signals from stellar-mass binary black holes and binary neutron stars have already been detected, with even more anticipated in the future. Accurately observing these signals and characterizing their sources depends critically on precise models of the emitted gravitational waveforms. This thesis introduces an updated set of waveform models for spinning binary black holes based on the effective-one-body formalism. The key innovation of these models is the incorporation of higher-order multipole terms beyond the quadrupole. I initially develop the model for black holes with spins aligned to the binary's orbital angular momentum, subsequently extending it to cover generic spin orientations. Analyzing the source properties of gravitational-wave binaries necessitates generating $\mathcal{O}(10^7-10^9)$ distinct waveforms; given that standard models can take $\mathcal{O}(1-10)$ seconds per waveform, they pose significant challenges for data analysis. To address this computational bottleneck, I apply reduced-order modeling to create a more efficient version of the waveform model for aligned-spin systems. The models developed in this work have been utilized by the LIGO and Virgo collaborations to infer source parameters from signals detected during the second and third observing runs (O2 and O3). This thesis also includes a specific study on the source properties of GW170729 and GW190412, in which I played a direct role in the analysis.

We define a fifth force as an interaction that couples to matter with an intensity increasing in proportion to the number of atoms. Beyond competing with gravity, such a force can also lead to violations of the equivalence principle. Existing constraints on the strength and range of these forces over long distances are remarkably stringent. Potential candidates include forces coupling to lepton flavor charges such as $L_e-L_{\mu}$ or $L_e-L_{\tau}$, whose ranges and strengths are additionally limited by neutrino-matter interactions. This short note reviews current constraints on the parameter space for gauged $U(1)_{L_e-L_{\mu}, L_{\tau}}$ models. We identify two regions where neutrino oscillation experiments are currently at the limit of their sensitivity to detecting such a force. Specifically, we find an allowed parameter range where neutrino matter interactions, relevant for long-baseline oscillation studies, vary depending on the depth of the neutrino beam beneath the Earth's surface.

This paper examines the derivation of Quantized Inertia (QI) theory, previously termed MiHsC by McCulloch (2007, 2013), and identifies two significant errors in the initial formulation. We establish a discrete black-body radiation spectrum, which yields a revised expression for $F(a)$ distinct from the original theory. Furthermore, we provide numerical results for this new solution and compare them with the original predictions.

This study introduces a tidal framework for analyzing rotational evolution within the general three-body problem, accommodating arbitrary viscosities, extended masses, and mutual tidal interactions between all pairs. Grounded in creep tide theory, we derive a set of differential equations governing the rotation of each body, formulated in a manner easily adaptable to systems with N tidally interacting bodies. Applying this model to a circumbinary planet using a Kepler-38-like binary as a test case, we determine that, under low planetary eccentricity, the most probable final stationary state is a 1:1 spin-orbit resonance, provided the planetary viscosity falls within the range observed in solar system planets. We also derive analytical expressions for the mean rotational stationary state, utilizing high-order power series for the semimajor axis ratio ($a_1/a_2$) and low-order expansions for eccentricities. These expressions accurately replicate the mean behavior of low-eccentricity numerical integrations across arbitrary planetary relaxation factors, remaining valid up to $a_1/a_2 \sim 0.4$. Utilizing this analytical approach to predict the rotation of Kepler circumbinary planets, we conclude that most likely rotate in a sub-synchronous state, though the shift from synchrony is significantly smaller than previously estimated by Zoppetti et al. (2019, 2020). Finally, comparing our findings with those derived from the Constant Time Lag model reveals that, contrary to earlier assumptions, cross torques provide a non-negligible net secular contribution. Consequently, these torques must be included when calculating tides for each body in an N-extended-body system from an arbitrary reference frame, a factor naturally accounted for by the creep theory.

A four-dimensional special complex manifold with a Norden metric and constant holomorphic sectional curvature is constructed using a two-parameter family of solvable Lie algebras. The curvature characteristics of this manifold are analyzed, and the necessary and sufficient conditions for it to be an isotropic Kählerian manifold are established.

While Hawking radiation is typically linked to the event horizon of a black hole as a quantum effect, this paper demonstrates the existence of incoming Hawking-like radiation associated with the apparent horizon of the first cosmological black hole within Scalar-Tensor-Vector Gravity (STVG) theory, set against a Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) background. This radiation is also attributable to the cosmological apparent horizon of the FLRW universe and the cosmological event horizon of de Sitter spacetime. The study illustrates how STVG theory, effective for describing black holes across both local and global scales, influences the Hawking effect. Employing a semiclassical approximation, we utilize the Hamilton-Jacobi and Parikh-Wilczek tunneling methods, respectively, incorporating both back-reaction and non-back-reaction scenarios. Our findings indicate that back-reaction effects establish a correlation between emission modes in the Parikh-Wilczek formalism, offering a potential resolution to the information paradox. We derive the corresponding Hawking-like temperature as a function of the inverse powers of the apparent horizon radius of the cosmological black hole in STVG theory. Furthermore, we examine the impact of the STVG parameter, which signifies the deviation from General Relativity (GR), on both the apparent horizons and the Hawking-like temperature. We show that increasing the STVG parameter delays the emergence of the Hawking-like temperature to later cosmic epochs with reduced values. Additionally, we apply the Hamilton-Jacobi approach beyond the semiclassical limit to incorporate all quantum correction terms into the semiclassical results for the cosmological black hole in STVG theory.

The expansion of computational power has significantly broadened the reach of electronic structure simulations. Artificial intelligence and advanced data analysis offer the potential to accelerate both large-scale simulations and their analysis to previously impossible extents. As a rapidly evolving field for handling complex datasets, machine learning has recently gained significant traction in electronic structure simulations, where density functional theory (DFT) remains the dominant method. Consequently, DFT calculations impose some of the heaviest workloads on global academic high-performance computing systems. Utilizing machine learning to accelerate these processes can lower resource demands and facilitate the simulation of larger systems. Therefore, integrating DFT with machine learning holds the promise of rapidly advancing electronic structure applications, such as *in-silico* materials discovery and the exploration of new chemical reaction pathways. This paper presents an accessible theoretical overview of both DFT and machine learning, serving as the foundation for a comprehensive review of research articles from chemistry and materials science published up to December 2020 that utilize machine-learning techniques. Our analysis organizes the existing research into key themes and highlights significant findings. Finally, we conclude with an outlook on promising future research directions, supported by a citation analysis.

This study investigates the equation of state (EoS) and composition of dense, hot hypernuclear matter containing $\Delta$-resonance admixtures under conditions typical of supernovae and neutron star binary merger remnants. A cold, neutrino-free regime is also examined to serve as a reference for astrophysical EoS constraints. The formalism employed is the covariant density functional (CDF) theory, adapted to incorporate the full $J^P=1/2^+$ baryon octet and non-strange $J^P=3/2^+$ decuplet members using density-dependent couplings calibrated against laboratory and astrophysical data. At finite temperatures, $\Delta$-resonances soften the hypernuclear matter EoS at intermediate densities but stiffen it at high densities. At low temperatures, heavy baryons such as $\Lambda$, $\Delta^-$, $\Xi^-$, $\Xi^0$, and $\Delta^0$ emerge in that specific sequence if $\Delta$-meson couplings resemble nucleon-meson couplings. Similar to hyperons, increasing temperature lowers the density thresholds for $\Delta$-resonances, suggesting a substantial presence of $\Delta$'s in the low-density subnuclear regime. Results indicate that $\Delta$-resonances constitute a significant fraction of baryonic matter—approximately $10\%$ at temperatures of several tens of MeV in the neutrino-trapped regime. Consequently, they may influence supernova and binary neutron star dynamics by introducing new sources of neutrino opacity or bulk viscosity channels via direct Urca processes. Finally, the mass-radius relationship for isentropic, static, spherically symmetric hot compact stars is analyzed.

In December 2010, dust emissions were observed on main-belt asteroid 596 Scheila, attributed to an impact by a projectile measuring several tens of meters. Such collisions are expected to eject material primarily from the body's fresh, unweathered subsurface, suggesting that the asteroid's surface was partially or completely renewed by the 2010 event. By integrating existing literature spectra with our own observations, we demonstrate that this impact caused a significant shift in the asteroid's near-infrared (0.8 to 2.5 {\mu}m) spectral slope, transitioning from a moderately red (T-type) classification prior to the event to a red (D-type) classification afterward. This finding supports the hypothesis that red carbonaceous asteroids gradually lose their redness over time due to space weathering, aligning with laboratory predictions based on the primitive Tagish Lake meteorite, which shares spectral similarities with 596. This study marks the first telescopic confirmation of this weathering trend for asteroids analogous to Tagish Lake or anhydrous chondritic porous interplanetary dust particles. Furthermore, our results indicate that the population of implanted objects from the outer solar system within the main belt is far larger than previously estimated, with many of these bodies concealed beneath their space-weathered surfaces.

This study experimentally examines particle migration in non-Brownian suspensions subjected to shear within a Taylor-Couette device under vanishing Reynolds number conditions. Using highly resolved index-matching methods to determine local particulate volume fractions, we observe that for a broad range of bulk volume fractions ($\phi_b \in [20\% - 50\%]$) in this wide-gap setup, the fully developed concentration profiles align well with the Nott & Brady (J. Fluid Mech., vol. 275, 1994, pp. 157-199) suspension balance model. Furthermore, we present systematic measurements of both the migration strain scale and migration amplitude, which reveal the boundaries of the predictions made by the suspension balance model.

We begin by examining tree growth through the probabilistic attachment of new vertices to leaves, resulting in a model grounded in vertex clusters and assigned probabilities. This framework is easily extended to attachment at any tree depth, prompting a broader investigation into cluster-based tree growth. Drawing on the concept of intrinsic vertex fitness introduced by Bianconi and Barab\'asi, we define vertex mass as an additive intrinsic attribute. While Bianconi and Barab\'asi utilized fitness as a multiplier for vertex degree within preferential attachment, we treat vertex mass as a core probabilistic element where additivity is paramount. Specifically, independent mass distributions generate a distribution for their sums via Laplace convolution, allowing clusters to inherit mass distributions from their constituent vertices. Our primary contribution is a new theorem determining the joint distribution of cluster masses given their individual distributions. Echoing Ferguson and Kingman's work on general measures, we show that gamma conditioning distributions yield the Dirichlet distribution. Furthermore, our theorem accommodates other choices, including fat-tailed stable distributions with infinite means. We explore L\'evy conditioning distributions as an alternative to the gamma family, highlighting the L\'evy distribution as a key member of the stable family. Finally, we present a theorem providing the analytic marginals of the normalized distribution conditioned on the L\'evy distribution.

In recent years, researchers have increasingly focused on pre-training ever-larger language models to test the boundaries of deep learning capabilities. However, this approach demands substantial computational resources, and most models are trained from scratch without leveraging existing pre-trained knowledge, leading to inefficiency. To address this, we introduce bert2BERT, a method that effectively transfers knowledge from smaller pre-trained models (such as BERT_BASE) to larger ones (such as BERT_LARGE) via parameter initialization, thereby significantly enhancing pre-training efficiency. Specifically, we extend previous function-preserving techniques for Transformer-based language models and introduce advanced initialization strategies for large models. Additionally, we propose a two-stage pre-training approach to further accelerate the training process. Extensive experiments on representative pre-trained language models, including BERT and GPT, demonstrate that (1) our method reduces training costs significantly compared to baselines like training from scratch, StackBERT, and MSLT; and (2) the method is versatile and applicable across various pre-trained model types. Notably, bert2BERT reduces pre-training computational costs by approximately 45% for BERT_BASE and 47% for GPT_BASE when reusing models of nearly half their size. The source code will be made publicly available upon publication.

This study examines the convex set of $d$-dimensional unital quantum channels. Specifically, we define a parametrized family of maps to partially characterize the set of unital quantum maps relative to this family. Focusing on qutrit channels, we analyze extreme points and classify them based on Kraus rank, observing that our parametrized family corresponds to maps with a Kraus rank of three. Additionally, we introduce a new family of qutrit unital quantum channels with a Kraus rank of four to investigate extreme points across all possible Kraus ranks. We provide explicit examples for both families and evaluate whether they represent extreme points within the set of unital quantum channels. Finally, we illustrate the relationship between these examples and well-known channels.

This study theoretically examines how a rectangular barrier potential influences the quantum transport characteristics of silicene field-effect transistors. By deriving approximate analytical solutions to the Dirac equation, transmission and reflection probabilities are calculated. A custom computer program utilizing the Landauer-Büttiker formalism computes conductance based on various scattering parameters. The research indicates that a rectangular barrier effectively modulates these transport properties, revealing that transmission probability is highly sensitive to both barrier height and incident energy. Key phenomena such as Klein tunneling and resonant tunneling are observed, with their behavior strongly dictated by barrier width; notably, the barrier significantly amplifies Klein tunneling for Dirac electrons. Perfect transmission occurs across a range of oblique incidence angles, not merely at normal incidence. Furthermore, as barrier width increases, the transmission profile develops a more fragmented structure resembling Fabry-Pérot resonances. Conductance displays a non-monotonic dependence on Fermi energy, oscillating rapidly with increasing barrier height, though high Fermi energy values yield nearly identical conductance profiles at a fixed barrier height. Specifically, conductance reaches a local minimum when Fermi energy equals barrier height. Additionally, thin barriers cause a significant reduction in conductance, contrasting with the oscillatory behavior seen in thicker barriers. These findings advance the development of silicene field-effect transistors and provide new insights into the relativistic applications of tunneling within silicene.

By employing a scalar potential alongside a bivector potential, the vector field linked to diffusion drift is broken down into three components: a generalized gradient field, a field orthogonal to the gradient, and a divergence-free field. This decomposition is assigned a probabilistic meaning through the introduction of cycle velocity, derived from a bivectorial framework in nonequilibrium thermodynamics. The work also offers novel insights into the mean rates of thermodynamic variables. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that deterministic dynamical systems can be expressed in a generalized gradient form, where the resulting potential serves as a Lyapunov function, utilizing the method of random perturbations.

As causal inference gains prominence, the necessity for robust tools to assess causal effects grows. This study addresses the challenge of detecting causal effects that appear as distributional differences between treatment and control groups. Building upon existing kernel-based approaches to causality, particularly the Counterfactual Mean Embedding (CfME) framework, we introduce the Doubly Robust Counterfactual Mean Embedding (DR-CfME). By incorporating semiparametric theory, our proposed method offers superior theoretical properties compared to its predecessor. Consequently, we develop new kernel-based test statistics for distributional effects derived from doubly robust treatment effect estimators. We present two specific test statistics: one that directly enhances prior work and another capable of handling cases where the treatment arm's support is a subset of the control arm's. Finally, we validate our approach using both simulated and real-world datasets, including an application to off-policy evaluation.

Rapid domain adaptation is essential for expanding the applicability of reinforcement learning (RL) to real-world scenarios. While generalizing RL agents is crucial for success, zero-shot policy transfer remains difficult because even slight visual variations can cause a trained agent to fail entirely in new tasks. We introduce USRA (Unified State Representation Learning under Data Augmentation), a framework that enhances generalization to unseen domains by learning a latent unified state representation through data augmentation of observations. Our approach demonstrates significant success on the DeepMind Control Generalization Benchmark for the Walker environment, achieving superior sample efficiency and 14.3% better domain adaptation performance compared to the strongest baseline results.

This paper introduces DistSTN, a new framework designed for synthetic aperture radar (SAR) automatic target recognition (ATR). Unlike traditional SAR ATR methods, DistSTN addresses a more demanding practical scenario involving non-cooperative targets, where training data covers only a limited range of aspect angles, whereas testing samples may include unlimited angles. To overcome this challenge, DistSTN moves beyond learning pose-invariant features by employing an advanced feature disentangling model. This model separates pose-related factors from identity-specific ones, allowing them to independently regulate the target image representation. To explicitly disentangle these interpretable pose factors, a pose discrepancy spatial transformer module is integrated into DistSTN, utilizing an explicit geometric model to capture the intrinsic transformations between factors of different targets. Additionally, an amortized inference scheme is implemented, leveraging an encoder-decoder architecture to facilitate efficient feature extraction and recognition. Experimental validation on the Moving and Stationary Target Acquisition and Recognition (MSTAR) dataset confirms the approach's effectiveness, demonstrating that DistSTN outperforms other ATR algorithms in terms of recognition accuracy.

This paper investigates the position vectors of rectifying slant helices in $E^3$. We first derive the general equations for the curvature and torsion of these helices. Subsequently, we formulate and solve a second-order linear differential equation to generate a family of rectifying slant helices situated on cones.

Continual learning focuses on incrementally training models across a sequence of tasks while retaining prior knowledge. Although extensively researched in computer vision, applying these concepts to Vision+Language tasks is more complex due to the various ways settings can be defined based on input modalities. This paper offers a comprehensive analysis of how different configurations influence performance in Visual Question Answering. We introduce three distinct task formulations and illustrate their effects on continual learning algorithms. By dissecting various factors of task similarity, we reveal that both performance and sensitivity to task ordering are heavily influenced by shifts in the output distribution. Furthermore, we explore the efficacy of pretrained models and evaluate the robustness of transformer architectures using diverse visual embeddings. Finally, we present an analysis of model representations and their role in causing forgetting, with findings emphasizing the critical need to stabilize visual representations in deeper network layers.

Adversarial learning has proven highly effective for single-source Domain Adaptation (DA) and has recently been extended to Multi-source DA (MDA). However, while most current MDA approaches utilize multiple domain discriminators, the impact of this setup on latent space representations remains unclear. This work employs an information-theoretic framework to detect and address the detrimental consequences of using multiple discriminators in MDA, specifically: the fragmentation of domain-discriminative information, restricted computational scalability, and high variance in training loss gradients. By framing adversarial DA within the context of information regularization, we offer a theoretical basis for employing a single, unified domain discriminator. Building on this insight, we introduce Multi-source Information-regularized Adaptation Networks (MIAN), a novel neural architecture. Extensive large-scale experiments show that MIAN, despite its structural simplicity, consistently and significantly surpasses other state-of-the-art methods.

The flux-tube code $\texttt{stella}$ adopts a novel global gyrokinetic simulation strategy by applying a subsidiary expansion of the gyrokinetic equation based on the turbulence's perpendicular scale length. Originally formulated by Parra and Barnes [Plasma Phys. Controlled Fusion, $\textbf{57}$ 054003, 2015], this method facilitates the use of Fourier basis functions while incorporating radial profile variations perturbatively. To account for radial variations in magnetic geometry, the approach employs a global extension of the Miller equilibrium equations and the Grad-Shafranov equation, derived via Taylor expansion. Additionally, new radial boundary conditions have been developed that utilize multiple flux-tube simulations; these serve as a more physically grounded alternative to the standard Dirichlet conditions used in global simulations. These enhanced boundary conditions effectively reduce numerical artifacts near the radial edge that typically arise when representing non-periodic functions with spectral bases. The validity of this new methodology is demonstrated through both linear and nonlinear benchmarks against several standard test cases.

We present and address ten problems concerning partitions in triangle-free graphs within the context of Erdős' Sparse Half Conjecture. Among these, we establish a specific variant: for every sufficiently large even integer $n$, every triangle-free graph with $n$ vertices admits a partition $V(G)=A\cup B$ where $|A|=|B|=n/2$ and the sum of edges in the induced subgraphs $G[A]$ and $G[B]$ is at most $n^2/16$. This bound is tight, as demonstrated by the complete bipartite graph with part sizes $3n/4$ and $n/4$, which achieves equality when $n$ is a multiple of 4. Furthermore, we examine analogous problems for $K_4$-free graphs.

This paper introduces a variational framework for segmenting multichannel multiphase images, extending the Chan-Vese active contour model. The approach centers on determining a variable $u$ that represents the segmentation by minimizing a multichannel energy functional that integrates data from multiple images. The input data can be decomposed via multichannel filtering or directly utilized as is, such as standard RGB or medical images which inherently contain multiple channels. The proposed functional is then minimized simultaneously across all channels. The model satisfies the requisite assumptions, allowing for efficient resolution through optimization algorithms like the Chambolle-Pock method. We demonstrate that the energy functional possesses global minimizers and establish its stability and convergence properties in the presence of noise. Experimental evaluations confirm that the method effectively handles both single- and multichannel segmentation tasks, successfully applying to diverse image types including natural, texture, and medical images.

Mobile applications are essential to daily living. While automated GUI testing is prevalent, manual testing remains the final safeguard for app quality. Nevertheless, repetitive tasks and the potential to overlook features render manual testing inefficient and time-intensive. Drawing inspiration from the game Candy Crush, where colorful candies serve as move hints, we introduce NaviDroid, a method that guides testers by highlighting subsequent actions to enhance testing efficiency and effectiveness. NaviDroid builds an enriched state transition graph, using triggering actions as edges between states. Leveraging dynamic programming, it plans an exploration path and overlays visualized hints on the GUI, enabling testers to rapidly discover untested areas while preventing redundant explorations. Experimental results demonstrate NaviDroid's high coverage and efficient path planning, and a user study validates its practical utility. Ultimately, NaviDroid aids in creating more robust software for mission-critical environments by delivering more thorough testing within existing effort levels and by integrating these capabilities into various stages of the development pipeline.

In the scenario involving two light flavors, we introduce a stringy framework for a system comprising one heavy and one light quark-antiquark pair, aiming to investigate the two lowest-lying Born-Oppenheimer potentials as the separation of the heavy quark-antiquark pair varies. Our analysis identifies three critical separations associated with string reconnection, breaking, and junction annihilation. Specifically, for the ground state potential, only string reconnection plays a significant role. We observe that a tetraquark state provides the dominant contribution to the first excited state potential at small separations, marking a major distinction from the $QQ\bar q\bar q$ system, where this dominance occurs in the ground state potential. A further key difference is the emergence of a complete diquark configuration $[Qq][\bar Q\bar q]$ for the tetraquark state, rather than the partial configuration $QQ[\bar q\bar q]$. Conversely, the scales of string junction annihilation, below which the systems can be primarily regarded as compact tetraquarks, are nearly identical for both cases and become almost equal if the phenomenological rule $E_{QQ}=\frac{1}{2} E_{Q\bar Q}$ is satisfied. Similarly, the screening lengths align with each other and are consistent with lattice QCD results.

Domain-Specific Modelling Languages (DSMLs) enable practitioners to address domain-specific modelling challenges. However, as domains become increasingly complex and heterogeneous, industrial users often struggle with the usability of graphical DSMLs. Currently, there is a scarcity of guidelines for language engineers to enhance the user experience (UX) for these practitioners. Given that UX is a broad and subjective field, existing general definitions and guidelines are frequently too generic or restricted to specific technological contexts. To address this gap, we adapt established human-centred design and UX principles to define and propose guidelines for UX and User Experience Design (UXD) within graphical DSMLs. Drawing on our experience in building industrial DSMLs, this paper categorizes the essential UXD aspects that language engineers must consider during development. Ultimately, these guidelines aim to improve the overall usability of industrial DSMLs, assist engineers in creating tool-independent and widely adopted languages, and support the development of superior DSMLs.

The submitted letter serves as an executive summary of our prior paper, which proposes a self-consistent interpretation of quantum dynamics to resolve the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen paradox. A primary challenge in this framework is aligning it with classical physics; to prevent macroscopic backward causation, we formulate "corresponding transition rules" that define the necessary characteristics of macroscopic observations and manipulations. Understanding the classically unchosen options is essential to the apparent classical causal decision tree; these options are attributed to "incomplete knowledge" of boundary states common in macroscopic contexts. Consequently, precise boundary conditions with specific phases determine the actual measured path, though this selection is erroneously perceived as occurring at the moment of measurement. The perceived time direction of the decision tree stems from an assumed relative proximity to the initial state, whereas only a distant final state permits the selection of classically distinct options. On a cosmological scale, this model could align with a scenario featuring a Big Bang origin and a vastly extended final state, or potentially a Big Bang/Big Crunch universe. If this hypothesis holds, the Born probability postulate might gain a natural explanation if we exist within an expanding universe alongside a correlated, CPT-conjugate contracting one.

The NASA DART mission will strike the asteroid Dimorphos at an oblique angle that remains uncertain until impact. We conducted iSALE-3D simulations of DART-like collisions on asteroid surfaces across various impact angles, discovering that while the vertical momentum transfer efficiency ($\beta$) remains consistent regardless of the angle, the total imparted momentum decreases as the angle becomes more oblique. Specifically, a $45^\circ$ impact is expected to deliver up to 50% less momentum than a vertical strike. Although the direction of ejected momentum is not initially perpendicular to the surface, it tends to align more vertically as the crater expands. Complementary iSALE-2D simulations of vertical impacts provide context, revealing that the ejection angle depends on both target characteristics and crater development. While this angle is largely unaffected by target porosity, it can vary by up to $30^\circ$ based on the target's internal friction coefficient. These findings will aid in constraining target properties using the ejecta cone imaged by the LICIACube following the DART impact. Furthermore, our results establish an empirical scaling relationship for oblique impacts, offering a framework to analytically approximate the vertical component of ejecta momentum ($\beta-1$) when target properties are known.

Mathematical reasoning represents a critical frontier for advancing artificial intelligence. As research intensifies to resolve math word problems (MWPs) and enhance mathematical reasoning capabilities, this area will remain a central focus in the near future. This work examines both neural and non-neural techniques designed to solve natural language math word problems, emphasizing their generalizability, mathematical soundness, interpretability, and explainability. While neural approaches currently lead the state of the art, we survey them by categorizing three primary solving strategies: (1) direct answer generation, (2) expression tree generation to infer solutions, and (3) template retrieval for answer computation. Furthermore, we explore technological methodologies, trace the evolution of intuitive design choices for MWPs, and evaluate their mathematical reasoning proficiency. Finally, we pinpoint specific gaps that necessitate the integration of external knowledge and knowledge-infused learning, alongside other promising opportunities in this domain.

We utilize a local sample of 21 galaxies to compare $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ (Br$\gamma$) hydrogen recombination line observations with predictions generated by the Prospector Bayesian inference framework, which was previously applied to fit the broadband photometry of these systems. This serves as a robust validation of star formation rates (SFRs) derived from spectral-energy distributions, given that dust is likely optically thin at this wavelength for almost all galaxies. Consequently, unlike shorter-wavelength lines such as H$\alpha$, the conversion of SFR to predicted line luminosity relies minimally on specific dust models or posterior dust parameters. Our results indicate that Prospector predicts Br$\gamma$ luminosities and equivalent widths with minimal offsets ($\sim$0.05 dex) and scatter ($\sim$0.2 dex), both of which align with measurement uncertainties, although we note that the derived offset varies depending on the selected stellar isochrones. Furthermore, we show that even when Prospector-derived dust attenuation fails to accurately characterize H$\alpha$ line properties or observed reddening between H$\alpha$ and Br$\gamma$, the fundamental SFRs remain accurate, as confirmed by the dust-insensitive Br$\gamma$ comparison. Finally, we explore how Br$\gamma$ could assist in constraining model parameters when incorporated as an input and assess its viability as a precise monochromatic SFR indicator for the upcoming era of JWST multiobject near-infrared spectroscopy.

This article serves as the initial part of a two-part study dedicated to classifying numerous type $II$ quantum subgroups within the categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. Specifically, this work identifies the braided auto-equivalences of local module categories for all established type $I$ quantum subgroups of these categories. Our findings reveal that these symmetries are non-exceptional in every instance except for four specific cases (modulo level-rank duality). These exceptions correspond to the orbifolds $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{2},16)_{\operatorname{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_2)}$, $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{3},9)_{\operatorname{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_3)}$, $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{4},8)_{\operatorname{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_4)}$, and $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{5},5)_{\operatorname{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_5)}$.

Several technical instruments are introduced in this study. We provide a skein-theoretic characterization of orbifold quantum subgroups of $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$; these methods are broadly applicable and extend to generating skein theory for any orbifold of a braided tensor category. Additionally, we present a formulation of orthogonal level-rank duality for the type $D$-$D$ scenario, which aids in constructing one of the exceptional cases. Furthermore, we identify a surprising link between quadratic categories and the exceptional braided auto-equivalences of these orbifolds, utilizing this relationship to build two of the four exceptions.

The follow-up paper will employ the classified braided auto-equivalences to construct the associated type $II$ quantum subgroups of $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. Combined with Gannon's type $I$ classification for $r\leq 6$, this effort will finalize the type $II$ classification for those ranks. This paper also features an appendix by Terry Gannon, offering valuable insights into the dimensions of objects within the categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$.

After a parent body fragments, the Yarkovsky effect drives asteroid family members to disperse in their orbital semimajor axes at a rate typically inversely related to their size. This diameter-dependent drift creates V-shaped patterns in plots of semimajor axis versus inverse diameter. The V-shape method aims to identify the boundaries of these V-structures despite unknown centers and opening angles. While effective for locating ancient families in the inner main belt, the technique is highly sensitive to various parameters. In this study, we generated and evolved a synthetic asteroid family over billions of years, then added uncertainties to the semimajor axes and diameters of its members to create 99 additional, imperfectly V-shaped clones. We selected a low initial velocity dispersion of 20 m/s to facilitate a clearer correlation between semimajor axis spreading and family age (the slope of the evolving V). Additionally, we evolved a synthetic background of randomly distributed asteroids for 100 Myr. By varying the ratio of family to background asteroids, we mapped the detection efficiency of the V-shape method and assessed its sensitivity to signal-to-noise levels, ultimately identifying optimal parameter settings. Our findings indicate that families older than approximately 3 Gyr are likely undetectable, with efficiencies below 50%, whereas younger families aged between 0.5 and 2.5 Gyr are detected with efficiencies exceeding 80%.
Numerous demonstrations of the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra exist, with several relying on the theory of complex analytic functions. To our knowledge, this proof differs from all established ones.

This research investigates reward-poisoning attacks within offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), where an external adversary alters rewards in a static dataset prior to agent exposure. The attacker aims to steer agents toward a malicious target policy while minimizing the $L^p$ norm of these modifications. Contrasting with single-agent RL scenarios, we demonstrate that the adversary can establish the target policy as a Markov Perfect Dominant Strategy Equilibrium (MPDSE), ensuring compliance by rational agents. This approach proves significantly more cost-effective than executing separate attacks on individual agents. We confirm the attack's efficacy across various MARL algorithms, including those with uncertainty awareness, and provide linear programming formulations to solve the optimization problem efficiently. Additionally, we analyze how dataset structure influences the minimum attack cost, laying the groundwork for future defensive strategies in offline MARL.

While self-supervised learning allows training initiation using unlabeled data, existing generic methods for natural images fail to adequately integrate contextual information. In the domain of medical imaging, an effective approach must be highly sensitive to deviations from normal tissue within specific anatomical regions, where anatomy serves as the critical context. We propose a new framework featuring two-tiered self-supervised learning objectives: one focused on regional anatomy and another on the patient level. By employing graph neural networks, we capture relationships between various anatomical areas, with the graph structure derived from correspondences between individual patients and an anatomical atlas. Furthermore, this graph-based representation excels at processing images of any arbitrary size at full resolution. Experiments conducted on large-scale lung Computed Tomography (CT) datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms baseline approaches that ignore context. Finally, we apply the learned embeddings to stage lung tissue abnormalities associated with COVID-19.

Feature selection plays a crucial role in constructing machine learning models. By removing redundant or misleading attributes, this process enhances model performance while lowering computational demands. Although metaheuristic techniques, including swarm intelligence and evolutionary algorithms, are commonly employed for feature selection, they are often characterized by high complexity and slow execution speeds. This paper introduces a streamlined approach for universal feature selection that integrates filter and wrapper methods rather than simply combining them. The proposed technique preprocesses data using one-hot encoding and employs a random forest classifier. It assigns values to features based on normalized frequencies to identify the optimal subset. Additionally, a novel strategy is introduced to leverage mutual information outputs, providing a superior starting point for experimentation. The method was evaluated on two real-world intrusion detection datasets. Results indicate that the proposed approach surpasses several state-of-the-art related methods in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, F-score, and AUC.

Supersonic flows are frequently observed in molecular clouds, whereas (sub)sonic turbulence is typically found within dense cores and filaments. It remains uncertain whether such (sub)sonic motions occur at larger scales ($\gtrsim$1~pc) across various environments. Ophiuchus North 1 (Oph N1), situated approximately 110 pc away, represents one of the closest molecular clouds suitable for detailed turbulence analysis through large-scale mapping with single-dish telescopes. We conducted imaging observations of $^{12}$CO ($J=1-0$) and C$^{18}$O ($J=1-0$) toward Oph N1 using the 13.7 m telescope at the Purple Mountain Observatory, achieving an angular resolution of $\sim$55\arcsec (corresponding to 0.03~pc). The majority of the C$^{18}$O emitting regions exhibit Mach numbers of $\lesssim$1, indicating widespread (sub)sonic turbulence on large scales throughout Oph N1. Polarization data yield a magnetic field strength for the plane-of-sky component of $\gtrsim$9~$\mu$G. We conclude that Oph N1 is globally sub-Alfv{\'e}nic and is primarily supported against gravitational collapse by its magnetic field. The steep velocity structure function may result from the expansion of the Sh~2-27 H{\scriptsize II} region or the dissipative range of incompressible turbulence. These observations highlight a rare instance of a cloud defined by extensive subsonic turbulence and a steep size-linewidth relationship. Furthermore, the cloud is magnetized, suggesting that ion-neutral friction plays a significant role.

A significant challenge in deep learning is that models often acquire inappropriate biases, leading to poor performance on minority groups. While numerous algorithms have been developed to counteract this issue, their actual effectiveness remains unclear due to inconsistent study protocols, datasets that fail to cover diverse bias types, and systems that either access hidden information or are over-tuned to specific test sets. To resolve these ambiguities, we propose an enhanced evaluation framework, refined metrics, and a novel dataset. This setup allows us to rigorously interrogate bias mitigation algorithms. We benchmark seven state-of-the-art methods using a uniform network architecture and hyperparameter strategy across three datasets. Our new dataset, Biased MNIST, facilitates the assessment of robustness against various bias sources, while a visual question answering (VQA) benchmark evaluates resistance to hidden biases. Unlike previous approaches that tune solely to the test distribution, we examine performance across different tuning distributions, a crucial factor since the test distribution is often unknown during development. Our results indicate that current algorithms exploit hidden biases, struggle to handle multiple bias forms simultaneously, and are highly sensitive to the chosen tuning set. Consequently, we urge the research community to adopt more rigorous evaluation standards for future bias mitigation techniques. All data, code, and results are publicly available at: https://github.com/erobic/bias-mitigators.

To simulate laser-plasma interactions, we created YUNIC, a parallel, multi-dimensional, fully relativistic particle-in-cell (PIC) code. This paper details the core algorithm, encompassing the field solver, particle pusher, and interpolation methods for both fields and currents. Beyond classical electromagnetic interactions within plasmas, the code incorporates nonlinear Compton scattering and nonlinear Breit-Wheeler pair production using Monte-Carlo techniques to investigate quantum electrodynamics (QED) phenomena. We validated YUNIC by benchmarking it against theoretical predictions and other PIC codes across several representative scenarios. Consequently, YUNIC is applicable to diverse physical environments, ranging from relativistic laser-plasma interactions to astrophysical plasmas and strong-field QED physics.

The identification of many debris disks surrounding white dwarfs (WDs) has spurred significant research into how these disks contribute to WD pollution, yet their formation and evolution remain poorly understood. This study investigates the impact of aeolian (wind) erosion on the evolution of solids within WD debris disks. While aeolian erosion is a critical destructive mechanism that shapes the size distribution and properties of pebbles, boulders, and planetesimals in gaseous protoplanetary disks, our analysis reveals it similarly plays a vital role in WD environments. By examining aeolian erosion under various disk conditions and its effect on objects of differing sizes, we determined that solid bodies smaller than approximately 5 km will be eroded before the disk's lifetime concludes. When comparing aeolian erosion to other destructive mechanisms like collisional fragmentation and thermal ablation, we found that it is the dominant destructive process for objects with radii less than $\sim 10^3 \rm{cm}$ located within $\lesssim 0.6 R_\odot$ of the WD. Consequently, aeolian erosion serves as the primary destructive pathway connecting the fragmentation of large bodies via collisions with the sublimation of the smallest particles and Poynting-Robertson drag, ultimately facilitating the accretion of tiny particles onto the WD photosphere and resulting in polluted white dwarfs.

Assistive robots can aid individuals in completing daily activities, but they must first understand their users' intended goals. Training these robots is challenging for inexperienced, elderly, or physically disabled users, who often cannot physically demonstrate the desired actions. While inclusive learning principles suggest that teachers should be credited for actions they cannot show, current robots operate in reverse: they presume all users can perform any demonstration. Consequently, these systems mimic displayed behaviors even when those actions do not reflect the user's true intent. This paper proposes a novel reward learning strategy where robots analyze user demonstrations by considering similar or simpler alternatives. Unlike previous approaches that overestimate human capabilities, our method errs toward underestimating the range of actions a human can input. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that underestimating the user's choice set is a risk-averse strategy that yields superior worst-case performance compared to overestimation. We define three properties to generate these alternative actions, and both simulations and a user study confirm that our algorithm more accurately extrapolates the human's underlying objective. View the user study at: https://youtu.be/RgbH2YULVRo

Traffic forecasting serves as a critical component of mobility management and a driving force for the logistics sector. While extensive research has utilized time series and spatiotemporal dynamic forecasting methods, this paper investigates the application of Vision Transformers within a UNet architecture. Specifically, we eliminate all convolution-based components from the UNet, replacing them with 3D shifted window Transformers in both the encoder and decoder. Furthermore, we implement feature mixing prior to patch encoding to manage feature interrelationships without reducing the depth dimension of our spatiotemporal inputs. The proposed network was evaluated on the dataset from the Traffic Map Movie Forecasting Challenge 2021 (Traffic4cast2021) at the NeurIPS competition. This challenge requires predicting one hour of traffic conditions (volume and average speed) across 6 frames, based on one hour of input traffic states averaged into 12 frames over a 5-minute interval. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/bojesomo/Traffic4Cast2021-SwinUNet3D.

Tensor networks enable the concentration of computational and entanglement resources within specific regions of Hilbert space. When deployed on NISQ devices, they facilitate the simulation of quantum systems that significantly exceed the capacity of the underlying hardware, a feat accomplished through the parallelization of quantum simulations. This work demonstrates the approach using the most basic scenario: an infinite, translationally invariant quantum spin chain. We present Cirq and Qiskit implementations that convert infinite, translationally invariant matrix product state (iMPS) algorithms into finite-depth quantum circuits, thereby enabling the representation, optimization, and time evolution of arbitrary one-dimensional systems. Additionally, we provide illustrative simulation outputs showcasing the performance of these codes for achievable circuit dimensions.

Over recent years, the crowdsourced security sector, especially bug bounty programs, has expanded significantly, becoming the primary method for software security assessments for numerous organizations. Yet, academic research has largely overlooked security teams, particularly within crowdsourced work environments. Consequently, there is limited understanding of how these distributed teams organize, collaborate, and what technological requirements they face. This study addresses that gap by analyzing focus groups with the top five teams from a computer security Capture-the-Flag (CTF) competition, selected from 18,201 participating teams. Our findings reveal that these teams employed strategies based on specialized roles to mitigate challenges related to geographic dispersion, redundant efforts, and a lack of prior collaboration. By highlighting the limitations of current models that focus on individual workers in security crowdsourcing platforms, our case studies demonstrate that scaling security work to team-based structures is both feasible and advantageous. Finally, we pinpoint several areas requiring future research, including the role of social identity in high-skilled crowdsourced environments.

The electronic structure and transport properties of various MoS2 monolayer defects were investigated using a combination of the Density-Functional based Tight-Binding method and the Green's Function approach. Intrinsic defects within these monolayers profoundly impact their electronic characteristics; even at low concentrations, they significantly modify quantum conductance. Although electron transport in pristine MoS2 is nearly isotropic, the presence of defects introduces strong anisotropy. Localized mid-gap states appear in semiconducting MoS2, which, while not contributing to conductivity, scatter current in a direction-dependent manner. Consequently, conductivity is markedly diminished across line defects and specific grain boundary configurations.

The study introduces a physical model describing the non-perturbative parton distributions within the nucleon. This framework relies on quantum fluctuations where the nucleon transitions into baryon-meson pairs, combined with Gaussian momentum distributions for partons within hadrons. Developed using hadronic chiral perturbation theory, these fluctuations occur frequently, producing sea quarks and inducing dynamical effects on both valence quarks and gluons. The resulting parton momentum distributions, $f(x,Q_0^2)$, at low momentum transfers are subsequently evolved to higher scales using standard DGLAP equations from perturbative QCD. Consequently, this yields parton density functions for gluons and all quark flavors, characterized by just five physics-motivated parameters. Adjusting these parameters allows for the reproduction and interpretation of experimental deep inelastic structure function data. Specifically, the model attributes the observed $\bar{u}$-$\bar{d}$ asymmetry in the proton to sea quarks generated by hadronic fluctuations, while also accounting for the strong suppression of the strange-quark sea at low $Q^2$ as seen in observations.

Due to the exponentially large degrees of freedom associated with particle numbers, quantum systems exhibit complex dynamics that conventional computers cannot simulate. Quantum reservoir computing leverages this intricate behavior for temporal machine learning tasks. This chapter introduces quantum mechanics and machine learning pedagogically before explaining quantum reservoir computing, along with related methods such as quantum extreme learning machines and quantum circuit learning. These quantum machine learning techniques are both effective and experimentally viable on current state-of-the-art quantum hardware.

This study aims to address the existing gender wage gap by providing unbiased job recommendations derived from job seeker resumes. We utilize a generative adversarial network to eliminate gender bias from Word2Vec embeddings of 12 million job postings and 900,000 resumes. Our findings indicate that representations generated from recruitment texts harbor algorithmic bias, which leads to tangible negative outcomes in recommendation systems. Specifically, without bias mitigation, women are recommended positions with significantly lower salaries in our dataset. However, using adversarially fair representations causes this wage disparity to vanish, demonstrating that our debiased recommendations effectively reduce wage discrimination. We conclude that adversarial debiasing of word representations can enhance the real-world fairness of such systems and represents a viable component for developing fairness-aware recommendation frameworks.

Estimating Click-Through Rate (CTR) is a critical task in numerous real-world applications, necessitating that ranking models effectively learn complex high-order features. While shallow feed-forward networks are commonly employed in leading deep neural network architectures like FNN, DeepFM, and xDeepFM to implicitly model these interactions, prior research indicates that purely additive feature interactions within such networks struggle to capture common patterns efficiently. To address this limitation, we propose an instance-guided mask that introduces specific multiplicative operations into DNN ranking systems, performing element-wise products on both feature embeddings and feed-forward layers based on the input instance. Furthermore, we transform the feed-forward layer into a hybrid of additive and multiplicative interactions through a novel component called MaskBlock. This MaskBlock integrates layer normalization, the instance-guided mask, and the feed-forward layer, serving as a fundamental building block for constructing ranking models with various configurations. The resulting architecture, named MaskNet, includes two new variants designed to demonstrate the efficacy of MaskBlock as a core module for high-performance ranking systems. Experimental results across three real-world datasets show that our MaskNet models significantly outperform state-of-the-art approaches such as DeepFM and xDeepFM, confirming that MaskBlock is an effective unit for assembling advanced ranking models.

This study addresses the regularization of large-scale discrete inverse problems using inexact Krylov methods. We introduce two novel inexact Krylov approaches designed for both unregularized and Tikhonov-regularized least squares problems, analyzing their theoretical characteristics, connections to exact methods, and techniques for monitoring inexactness. These methods are subsequently applied to separable nonlinear inverse problems in blind deblurring, where uncertainty in blur parameters creates inherent inexactness. This uncertainty is managed via a variable projection method that establishes an inner-outer iteration framework: each cycle involves solving a linear deblurring subproblem for intermediate blur parameters generated by a nonlinear least squares solver. The proposed inexact solvers effectively accommodate fluctuating blur parameters during the resolution of linear subproblems, resulting in a significantly lower total iteration count and considerable computational efficiency compared to exact counterparts.

Recent research has presented a framework for fine-grained consent management in databases, integrating Boolean data provenance with interactive Boolean evaluation. This evaluation method seeks to reveal the truth value of a Boolean expression by efficiently querying individual variable values. The number of queries required varies based on the provenance structure and the unknown outcomes of these queries. While previous studies focused on optimizing the expected number of queries under a probabilistic model, this paper introduces a novel worst-case analysis inspired by the depth of decision trees for Boolean functions. Specifically, we define "evasive" provenance expressions, where determining the truth value may necessitate probing all variables in the worst-case scenario. We demonstrate that read-once expressions are evasive and identify a specific class—acyclic monotone 2-DNF—for which evasiveness can be determined in polynomial time. Regarding the search for optimal strategies, we prove that the general problem is coNP-hard. However, we also isolate a subclass of expressions that is "far from evasive," meaning an optimal worst-case strategy requires probing only $O(\log n)$ out of $n$ variables, a strategy that can be computed in polynomial time.

A recent study published in *Eur. Phys. J. Plus* (2022, 137:99) introduces a discrete, exact algorithm for constructing planetary systems. This method is applied to analyze systems governed by forces other than the standard Newtonian inverse-square law. While classical Newtonian systems feature stable, regular elliptical orbits, the study shows that systems with pure inverse forces remain stable with regular trajectories, whereas those with inverse cubic forces are unstable and lack regularity. Although the regular orbits in inverse-force systems are not standard ellipses but rather revolving paths tending toward three- or eight-loop configurations, the findings validate Newton's Proposition 45 from the *Principia* regarding the Moon's revolving orbits due to additional attraction. Specifically, additional inverse forces tend to stabilize the planetary system, while additional inverse cubic forces can destabilize it if their strength is sufficient.

The spectra of singly, doubly, and triply charmed baryons are examined across various temperatures utilizing anisotropic FASTSUM 'Generation 2L' ensembles. We analyze how these spectra evolve with temperature in both parity sectors, concentrating on the confining phase. Additionally, we explore the impact of chiral symmetry restoration in light quarks to better characterize the behavior of these states near the pseudocritical temperature. Our results indicate that the pseudocritical temperature can still be estimated from positive- and negative-parity charmed baryon correlators, even in scenarios where parity doubling is not clearly observable, as anticipated.

Standard General Relativity, without a cosmological constant, fails to account for the observed late-time acceleration of the universe. While introducing this constant into Einstein's field equations allows for such a description, it introduces a severe fine-tuning problem, motivating modifications to the theory's spacetime geometry. The $f(Q)$ gravity theory serves as an alternative, utilizing the non-metricity scalar $Q$ as the source of gravitational interaction. This study investigates a Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker cosmological model within $f(Q)$ gravity, dominated by a bulk viscous fluid, under the functional form $f(Q)=\alpha Q^n$, where $\alpha$ and $n$ are free parameters. The model is constrained using recent observational data, including 1048 Pantheon supernovae points, 31 Hubble data points, and six baryon acoustic oscillation points. Results indicate that for higher redshifts, the $f(Q)$ cosmology provides a superior fit compared to standard cosmology. The evolution of the deceleration parameter demonstrates a successful transition from decelerated to accelerated expansion phases. Additionally, the redshift evolution of density, bulk viscous pressure, and the effective equation of state parameter confirms that bulk viscosity can generate the negative pressure required to drive cosmic expansion efficiently. The viability of the model is further assessed by examining various energy conditions and statefinder diagnostics, which help distinguish this $f(Q)$ framework from other dark energy models.

This brief note examines a graph process recently proposed by Frieze, Krivelevich, and Michaeli. In this model, the edges of the complete graph $K_n$ are arranged in a uniformly random order and revealed sequentially to a player referred to as Builder. During each round, Builder must choose whether to accept the proposed edge or reject it. We demonstrate that for any $d \ge 2$, Builder can construct a spanning $d$-connected graph within $(1+o(1))n\log n$ rounds by accepting no more than $(1+o(1))dn/2$ edges, with the probability approaching 1 as $n$ grows large. This result confirms a conjecture made by Frieze, Krivelevich, and Michaeli.

Interaction frames are essential for characterizing and comprehending experimental designs in magnetic resonance. They frequently serve to remove dominant components of the spin Hamiltonian, such as the Zeeman Hamiltonian within the standard rotating frame or the radio-frequency (rf) Hamiltonian when analyzing decoupling and recoupling efficiency. Transitioning to an interaction frame can also render time-dependent Hamiltonian elements time-independent, as seen with the rf-field Hamiltonian in the conventional rotating frame. Removing the primary term often enhances the clarity of spin dynamics details. Additionally, this transition can decrease energy-level splitting in the Hamiltonian, thereby accelerating the convergence of perturbation expansions, average Hamiltonian theory, and Floquet theory. While there is no universally obvious choice for an interaction frame, certain options offer greater convenience than others. Using frequency-selective dipolar recoupling as a case study, we examine the distinctions, merits, and drawbacks of various interaction frame selections. These frames invariably encompass the full radio-frequency Hamiltonian but may also incorporate spin chemical shifts and either include or exclude effective fields averaged over a single pulse cycle.

The Gauss-Markov theorem establishes that the weighted least squares estimator serves as a linear minimum variance unbiased estimator (MVUE) within linear models. This paper initiates an extension of this finding to non-linear contexts by integrating deep learning with bias constraints. While classical methods for deriving non-linear MVUEs rely on maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)—a process often plagued by computationally intensive real-time optimizations—deep learning offers non-linear estimators with fixed computational costs. Although learning-based estimators achieve optimality on average relative to their training data, they can exhibit substantial bias regarding other parameters. To mitigate this, we introduce a straightforward bias constraint into the loss function, creating what we term the Bias Constrained Estimator (BCE). We demonstrate that this approach yields asymptotic MVUEs that mirror the behavior of classical MLEs and asymptotically reach the Cramér-Rao bound. We validate the benefits of our method in signal-to-noise ratio and covariance estimation scenarios. Additionally, BCE is motivated by applications requiring the averaging of multiple estimates for the same unknown to enhance performance, such as in distributed sensor networks and test-time data augmentation; in these contexts, we show that BCE produces asymptotically consistent estimators.

This work defines coherent states for equally spaced, homogeneous waveguide arrays across infinite, semi-infinite, and finite configurations, employing diverse methods to construct resolutions of the identity. The infinite case, equivalent to Euclidean coherent states, reviews an identity resolution on the circle that utilizes a nonlocal inner product. For the semi-infinite case, associated with London coherent states, several approaches are presented, including restricting to the circle with a non-local scalar product, rescaling or modifying the states, and utilizing a non-tight frame. In the finite case, a construction based on coherent states on the circle is provided, demonstrating that it serves as a regularization of both the infinite and semi-infinite scenarios.

In multilingual environments such as India, code-mixed social media content constitutes the bulk of online communication. Analyzing the sentiment of these mixed-language user opinions is vital for grasping social, economic, and political dynamics. This study introduces an ensemble approach combining a character-trigram-based Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model with a word-n-gram-based Multinomial Naive Bayes (MNB) classifier to detect sentiments in Hindi-English (Hi-En) code-mixed data. By merging the LSTM's ability to capture rich sequential patterns with the MNB's keyword polarity analysis, the ensemble effectively handles the sparsity and inconsistency typical of code-mixed inputs. Empirical results on real-world user data demonstrate that this method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to various baselines and other deep learning techniques.

The empirical distribution of the chiral index was simulated across different sample sizes for both uniform and normal distributions. The corresponding estimated quantiles $K_{0.90}$, $K_{0.95}$, $K_{0.98}$, and $K_{0.99}$ are presented in tables to facilitate symmetry testing under both the uniform and normal laws.

This paper investigates the exponentiation of monomial ideals. Although ideal exponentiation typically involves natural powers, we extend this concept to positive real exponents. Real powers of monomial ideals generalize the integral closure operation and reveal significant connections to convex polytope theory. We present several algorithms for calculating these real powers. A key finding is that for any monomial ideal $I$, the function mapping real numbers to the corresponding real power of $I$ is a step function with rational jump points.
