This property reduces the determination of real powers to the case of rational exponents.

Physicists are increasingly acknowledging the potential for laws that exist beyond the conventional model of forward time evolution; however, our current grasp of determinism relies heavily on this forward-moving framework, rendering it inadequate for addressing the varied research initiatives in contemporary physics. This article employs a constraint-based approach to propose a generalized form of determinism that does not assume a specific temporal direction, categorizing it into strong, weak, and delocalized holistic types. We examine the intriguing implications of these expanded concepts and demonstrate that this perspective offers fresh insights into the enduring debate concerning the essence of objective chance.

3D human pose estimation can be addressed by modeling geometric relationships among body parts and adhering to kinematic constraints. Recently, Transformers have been utilized to capture long-range dependencies between joints across both spatial and temporal dimensions. Although these models excel at handling long-range connections, research indicates a need to enhance the locality of Vision Transformers. To address this, we introduce a novel pose estimation Transformer that offers rich representations of body joints, which are essential for detecting subtle variations between frames (inter-feature representation). By employing two innovative interaction modules—Cross-Joint Interaction and Cross-Frame Interaction—the model explicitly captures both local and global dependencies among joints. Our proposed architecture, CrossFormer, achieves state-of-the-art results on two prominent 3D human pose estimation datasets, Human3.6 and MPI-INF-3DHP. Specifically, CrossFormer outperforms the closest competitor, PoseFormer, by 0.9% and 0.3% when using detected 2D poses and ground-truth settings, respectively.

We introduce a covariant version of refracted gravity (RG), a classical gravitational theory that modifies the standard Poisson equation by incorporating gravitational permittivity—a monotonic function of local mass density. This permittivity effectively reproduces dark matter phenomenology. Our covariant refracted gravity (CRG) framework fits within scalar-tensor theories, featuring a scalar field $\varphi$ governed by a self-interaction potential $\mathcal{V}(\varphi)=-\Xi\varphi$, where $\Xi$ is a normalization constant. In the weak-field limit, the scalar field corresponds to twice the gravitational permittivity. For a spherical mass distribution $\rho_s(r)$, the transition from Newtonian to RG dynamics occurs below the acceleration scale $a_\Xi=(2\Xi-8\pi G\rho/\varphi)^{1/2}$, where $\rho=\rho_s+\rho_\mathrm{bg}$ includes an isotropic, homogeneous background density $\rho_\mathrm{bg}$. Under the condition $2\Xi\gg 8\pi G\rho/\varphi$, this scale approaches $a_\Xi\sim 10^{-10}$~m~s$^{-2}$, a value comparable to the acceleration $a_0$ in Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND). Furthermore, CRG yields modified Friedmann equations for an expanding, homogeneous, and isotropic universe, revealing that the same scalar field responsible for mimicking dark matter also drives cosmic acceleration. Given that $\Xi$ plays a role analogous to the cosmological constant $\Lambda$ in standard cosmology and shares a similar magnitude, CRG offers a natural explanation for the observed relationship $a_0\sim \Lambda^{1/2}$. Consequently, CRG unifies the dynamics of cosmic structures and the universe's expansion through a single scalar field, aligning with models that merge the dark matter and dark energy sectors and suggesting a profound link between phenomena previously treated as separate.

This paper introduces a wavelet denoising technique for signals corrupted by Gaussian noise, specifically leveraging prior knowledge of the signal's $L^2$-energy. Under the independence model, which processes wavelet coefficients individually, we develop straightforward, level-dependent shrinkage rules that achieve $\Gamma$-minimax optimality for a specific class of priors. This approach proves especially effective for low signal-to-noise ratio scenarios, a finding supported by simulations across various standard test functions. Additionally, we compare the proposed method against commonly used wavelet shrinkage techniques.

Despite the widespread adoption of peer code review in both open-source and commercial development, current research indicates that many review comments lack utility. Unfortunately, no existing tools or techniques offer automatic support to enhance these non-useful comments. This paper presents a comparative analysis of useful versus non-useful comments, contrasting them based on textual features and reviewer experience. Leveraging these findings, we developed RevHelper, a prediction model designed to assist developers in refining their code review comments by automatically forecasting their usefulness upon submission. A comparative study of 1,116 comments revealed that useful comments share more vocabulary with the modified code, highlight relevant code elements, and are typically authored by more experienced reviewers. Furthermore, experiments involving 1,482 comments demonstrated that the model achieves a promising 66% accuracy in predicting comment usefulness. A case study comparing the model against three baseline variants further validated our empirical findings and highlighted the model's potential.

In a conventional two-level atom interacting with a resonant cavity's quantized field, thermal effects cause mode occupation that obscures the quantum characteristics of atom-light interactions. This study demonstrates that a hybrid setup comprising a superconducting cavity and a multi-level Rydberg atom allows for the observation of strong-coupling quantum phenomena even at finite temperatures. Furthermore, this coupling facilitates the cooling of the thermal microwave mode toward its ground state, enabling the detection of coherent vacuum Rabi oscillations at 4~K under realistic experimental conditions. The investigation also examines cooling across multiple atoms, revealing optimal performance for small ensembles, thereby establishing a viable method for cavity cooling with potential applications in the long-range coupling of superconducting qubits through thermal waveguides.

This research centers on the algebraic foundations governing the complexity and algorithms associated with the Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP). We consolidate, streamline, and expand upon three distinct methodologies developed for analyzing CSPs over finite templates: absorption theory, which characterizes problems solvable via local consistency (JACM'14), and the frameworks by Bulatov and Zhuk, which provided two separate proofs of the CSP Dichotomy Theorem (FOCS'17, JACM'20). Our first contribution introduces an elementary theorem regarding primitive positive definability, from which we derive the foundational elements of Bulatov's and Zhuk's proofs as corollaries. Second, we propose and begin a systematic investigation into minimal Taylor algebras. This class of algebras is sufficiently broad to verify the CSP Dichotomy Theorem exclusively within it, yet exhibits exceptional regularity. Notably, numerous concepts from the three original approaches converge within this class, a phenomenon that starkly contrasts with the general case. We anticipate that the theory established herein will ultimately yield a simpler, more natural proof of the Dichotomy Theorem utilizing a more efficient algorithm, while also aiding in addressing complexity issues in other CSP-related domains.

We introduce a semi-decision procedure for verifying generalized reachability properties on generalized Petri nets, utilizing the Property Directed Reachability (PDR) approach. This procedure comprises three distinct variants, differentiated by the abstraction techniques employed for identifying witnesses, enabling them to address challenges of escalating complexity. Implemented within a model-checker named SMPT, our methods provide empirical evidence that they can resolve problems that are currently difficult or intractable for state-of-the-art tools.

This paper investigates the time-dependent Lipschitz stability of $\alpha$-dissipative solutions to the Hunter-Saxton equation, with $\alpha$ being a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. By introducing metrics in both Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks, we prove Lipschitz stability for these respective metrics.

Stochastic Galerkin approaches applied to two-dimensional shallow water systems using random variables can compromise hyperbolicity, thereby altering the fundamental character of the original model. This study introduces a hyperbolicity-preserving stochastic Galerkin formulation by strategically selecting polynomial chaos expansions for the nonlinear terms within the shallow water equations. We establish a sufficient condition for maintaining hyperbolicity in the stochastic Galerkin system, which necessitates only a finite set of positivity constraints on the stochastic water height at specific quadrature points in the parameter space. Building on these theoretical findings, we construct a corresponding well-balanced, hyperbolicity-preserving central-upwind numerical scheme. Finally, we validate the accuracy and robustness of this new scheme through various demanding numerical experiments.

To enhance user comfort and mitigate virtual reality (VR) sickness in immersive telepresence, we propose a method that counteracts the rotational movements of the robot. In this setup, a 360-degree camera mounted on a mobile robot streams video and audio to a head-mounted display worn by a remote user, allowing them to feel present at the robot's location, survey their surroundings by turning their heads, and interact with nearby individuals. By effectively "unwinding" the camera's rotations, the user's visual perspective remains stable when the robot turns; the user must physically rotate their own body to shift their viewpoint. Since visual motion without corresponding vestibular input is a primary cause of VR sickness, we hypothesized that requiring physical rotation for viewpoint changes would alleviate these symptoms. We implemented this unwinding mechanism in a simulation of a robot navigating a virtual environment and conducted a user study (N=34) comparing the unwinding approach against traditional viewpoint rotation during robot turns. The results indicate that participants found the unwinding method more comfortable and preferable, and it significantly reduced their reported levels of VR sickness. Additionally, we report further findings regarding users' path integration abilities, viewing directions, and subjective perceptions of the robot's speed and distances to simulated people and objects.

Few-shot learning addresses the difficult challenge of acquiring knowledge from limited annotated examples while effectively generalizing to novel tasks. The core objective involves extracting prior knowledge from related tasks to facilitate rapid adaptation when data is scarce. This paper introduces MetaKernel, a meta-learning approach utilizing random Fourier features. Specifically, we develop a data-driven method to learn variational random features, generating task-specific kernels by harnessing shared insights from related tasks within a meta-learning framework. By treating the random feature basis as a latent variable estimated through variational inference, we integrate shared knowledge into the posterior context inference using a long-short term memory module. To enhance kernel expressiveness, we employ conditional normalizing flows with coupling layers to construct a more robust posterior distribution over random Fourier bases. These resulting kernels are more discriminative and informative, further boosting few-shot learning performance. Our method is rigorously evaluated on extensive few-shot image classification and regression experiments. A comprehensive ablation study confirms the efficacy of each proposed component, and benchmark results across fourteen datasets show that MetaKernel consistently matches or surpasses state-of-the-art alternatives.

This study details the SRIB-LEAP submission for the ConferencingSpeech challenge 2021, which focused on enhancing multi-channel speech to improve far-field audio quality from microphone arrays in video conferencing environments. The proposed two-stage approach combines a beamformer with single-channel enhancement. Specifically, the beamformer utilizes a filter-and-sum network (FaSNet) augmented with a self-attention mechanism for inter-channel processing, operating entirely in the time domain. Subsequently, single-channel enhancement is performed in the log spectral domain using a convolutional neural network (CNN) integrated with long short-term memory (LSTM). This method yielded a 0.5-point improvement in objective Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) on noisy data and achieved an absolute gain of 0.9 in the subjective Mean Opinion Score (MOS) compared to the original noisy audio.

Fluctuation-dissipation relations (FDRs) and time-reversal symmetry (TRS), fundamental principles of statistical mechanics, are violated in generic driven-dissipative systems, which typically result in non-equilibrium steady states distant from thermal equilibrium. Although driven-dissipative Ising-type models are generally thought to display effective thermal criticality near phase transitions, we demonstrate that both FDR and TRS are broken even on a macroscopic scale at or near criticality. This conclusion is drawn from examining various observables—both even and odd under time-reversal transformations—that overlap with the order parameter. Surprisingly, a modified version of the FDR and TRS persists, yet this yields profound implications for correlation and response functions as well as Onsager reciprocity relations. Furthermore, we establish that at criticality, TRS remains violated even within the weakly-dissipative limit.

Understanding how planets and disks form and evolve requires studying their dynamic interactions. Recently, two protoplanets were identified within the PDS 70 disk, alongside a northwest arm-like feature. Our objective is to determine this structure's morphology and origin, specifically evaluating if it represents a spiral density wave generated by the interaction between PDS 70c and the disk. We analyzed six years of polarized and angular differential imaging (PDI and ADI) data from VLT/SPHERE. PDI datasets were processed using the IRDAP pipeline, while ADI datasets were handled with MUSTARD, a new inverse problem algorithm designed to correct geometric biases that previously hampered this disk's analysis. The arm-like structure was confirmed across all PDI and ADI datasets. However, we did not detect a southeast arm symmetric to the disk's minor axis, which weakens the earlier hypothesis that the feature is a double-ring footprint. If the structure were a spiral density wave moving with PDS 70c, we would expect a rotation of $11\overset{\circ}{.}28^{+2\overset{\circ}{.}20}_{-0\overset{\circ}{.}86}$ over six years; yet, no significant movement was observed. Should the arm be a planet-driven spiral, this lack of rotation implies that rigid-body rotation may not apply to such structures. Instead, we propose that the feature is likely a vortex appearing as a one-armed spiral in scattered light due to projection effects. This vortex hypothesis explains both the absence of observed rotation and the nearby sub-mm continuum asymmetry detected by ALMA.

A family of sets is defined as star-shaped if every set within the family shares at least one common point. This paper aims to refute a question posed by James Aisenberg and colleagues regarding the Kneser-Lovász coloring principle, specifically addressing the case where k=2.

We introduce ShorTor, a protocol designed to decrease latency within the Tor network. By leveraging multi-hop overlay routing—a method commonly used in content delivery networks—ShorTor steers Tor traffic across the internet. Operating as an overlay atop onion routing, the Tor-native routing mechanism, ShorTor is executed by Tor relays rather than clients, ensuring it operates independently of client-side path selection. Consequently, ShorTor lowers latency without compromising Tor's established security features. Specifically, the routes selected by ShorTor remain uncorrelated with either the Tor user or their destination, including their geographic locations. Using the AnoA framework, we demonstrate that ShorTor upholds all of Tor's anonymity guarantees. We support these theoretical findings with empirical analysis, utilizing a real-world dataset comprising over 400,000 latency measurements between the 1,000 most active Tor relays, which handle the bulk of Tor traffic. This data allows us to identify relay pairs that would benefit from ShorTor by reducing latency through an additional intermediate hop compared to a direct connection. By applying ShorTor to two million Tor circuits based on Tor's specifications, we simulated its impact on end users. Results indicate that ShorTor reduces latency by 148 ms at the 99th percentile for relay pairs and by 122 ms at the 99th percentile for Tor circuits overall. Practically, this means ShorTor significantly cuts tail latencies in Tor, directly improving page load times and enhancing the user experience on the Tor browser.

Robots endowed with situational awareness can assist humans in efficiently locating lost items by utilizing spatial and temporal structures. However, current video and image retrieval methods fail to address the specific limitations of moving cameras that capture only partial environmental views. To address this, we introduce D3A, a Detection-based 3-level hierarchical Association framework, which generates an efficient, queryable spatial-temporal representation of unique object instances. D3A employs online incremental and hierarchical learning to pinpoint keyframes that best characterize objects within the environment, utilizing both spatial and temporal features. Once identified, the associated spatial-temporal data is structured within a key-value database. The system supports diverse query patterns, including searches for objects with or without: 1) specific attributes, 2) spatial relationships relative to other objects, and 3) temporal segments. Across a test set of 150 queries, D3A retrieves a minimal set of candidate keyframes—representing just 0.17% of the total sensory data—with an 81.98% mean accuracy in 11.7 milliseconds. This performance is 47 times faster and 33% more accurate than a baseline approach that naively stores object detections without integrating spatial-temporal associations.

Supported by advancements in computing and communication technologies, the Metaverse promises to deliver unprecedented service experiences to users. However, the growing user base imposes significant strain on network resources, particularly for graphical extended reality services that require rendering numerous virtual objects. To optimize network resource utilization and enhance Quality-of-Experience (QoE), we introduce an attention-aware network resource allocation scheme designed to provide customized Metaverse services. The primary objective is to direct greater network resources toward virtual objects that command higher user interest. We begin by examining key techniques essential to Metaverse services, such as QoE analysis, eye-tracking, and remote rendering. Following this, we review existing datasets and introduce the User-Object-Attention Level (UOAL) dataset, which provides ground-truth attention data for 30 users across 96 objects within 1,000 images, accompanied by a tutorial on its usage. Leveraging the UOAL dataset, we develop a two-step attention-aware resource allocation algorithm comprising attention prediction and QoE maximization. Specifically, we outline the designs for two attention prediction approaches: interest-aware and time-aware. By utilizing predicted user-object-attention values, the system optimally allocates network resources, such as edge device rendering capacity, to maximize QoE. Finally, we suggest promising future research directions for Metaverse services.

Few-shot learning (FSL) represents a significant and timely challenge in computer vision, driving extensive research across a spectrum of techniques ranging from complex meta-learning approaches to basic transfer learning baselines. Our objective is to advance a straightforward yet effective pipeline for more realistic and practical few-shot image classification scenarios. To achieve this, we examine FSL through the lens of neural network architecture and a three-stage update process adapted to varying data availability: utilizing unsupervised external data for pre-training, employing base categories to simulate few-shot tasks for meta-training, and leveraging sparsely labeled data from novel tasks for fine-tuning. We address key questions including: (1) the advantages of pre-training on external data for FSL, (2) the potential of state-of-the-art transformer architectures, and (3) the role of fine-tuning in mitigating domain shift. Ultimately, we demonstrate that a simple transformer-based pipeline achieves unexpectedly strong performance on standard benchmarks like Mini-ImageNet, CIFAR-FS, CDFSL, and Meta-Dataset. Our code and demonstration are accessible at https://hushell.github.io/pmf.

This article represents the initial installment of a research series examining the higher-order teleparallel gravity framework known as $f(T, B)$-theory. The study aims to elucidate the role of anisotropic spacetimes within this theory. We begin by reviewing prior analyses of $f(T, B)$-gravity and then explore global dynamics using a locally rotational Bianchi I background. Specifically, we examine the case where $f(T, B) = T + F(B)$ to establish the conditions under which this theory resolves the homogeneity problem. Furthermore, we analyze the integrability of the field equations through Painlevé analysis, with the resulting analytic solution expressed via a right Painlevé expansion.

We extend the Stein-Tomas $L^2$ restriction theorem [17] and the uniform Sobolev estimates established by Kenig, Ruiz, and the second author [11] to accommodate critically singular potentials. Additionally, we derive Strichartz estimates for Schrödinger and wave operators under these conditions. Since nontrivial eigenfunctions may exist, specific spectral assumptions are necessary, such as restricting solutions to sufficiently high frequencies.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), specifically Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) with numerous hidden layers, have recently demonstrated remarkable success across various speech applications, including recognition, verification, and synthesis. However, these techniques have not been adequately utilized for F0 modeling. This study employs Deep Belief Networks (DBNs), a subclass of DNNs, to model the F0 contours of speech synthesized using a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) system, focusing on the Bengali language. The research presents and evaluates several DBN-DNN architectures featuring four to seven hidden layers, each containing up to 200 hidden units. These results are benchmarked against clustering tree methods commonly used in statistical parametric speech synthesis. The findings indicate that DBN-DNNs can derive high-level structures from textual inputs, leading to improved F0 contours as validated by both objective and subjective evaluations.

This study examines how recent GRAAL Sigma-beam asymmetry data impact neutron multipole fits within the single-pion photoproduction database, and contrasts these findings with results derived from incorporating a double-polarization quantity linked to the sum rule.

We construct ancient solutions to Curve Shortening in the plane with total curvature uniformly bounded by stitching together an arbitrary sequence of specified Grim Reapers at their shared asymptotes.

This paper introduces an integral-based event-triggering controller designed to achieve bipartite consensus in multi-agent systems governed by general linear dynamics. We demonstrate that the system attains asymptotic bipartite consensus and ensures a positive minimum inter-event time (MIET) between consecutive triggering instants for every agent. The proof of asymptotic stability relies on a novel approach that bounds the norm of the discrepancy between the actual state and its estimate at any given time through the integration of its square. Numerical simulations are presented to validate the efficacy of the proposed controller.

Recent lattice calculations, incorporating perturbative and non-perturbative methods with nearly massless quarks, alongside thermal contributions from photons, neutrinos, leptons, electroweak particles, and Higgs bosons, have yielded various thermodynamic quantities—including pressure, energy density, bulk viscosity, relaxation time, and temperature—at zero net-baryon density. These results extend up to the TeV scale, encompassing the hadronic, quark-gluon plasma (QGP), and electroweak phases of the early Universe. This advancement motivated the current study to investigate the impact of bulk viscosity across different cosmic epochs. The analysis employed first-order (Eckart) and second-order (Israel-Stewart) relativistic fluid theories, integrating viscous equations of state into the Friedmann equations to derive analytical solutions for nonlinear, nonhomogeneous differential equations. While the Israel-Stewart equations are too complex to solve explicitly and are presented here as a roadmap for future research, the Eckart theory yields a functional relationship between the Hubble parameter $H$ and the scale factor $a(t)$; however, neither solution can yet be directly expressed in terms of proper or cosmic time $t$. In an Eckart-type viscous background with a finite cosmological constant, non-singular $H(t)$ and $a(t)$ are obtained, though $H(t)$ diverges for QCD/electroweak and asymptotic equations of state. In contrast, non-viscous and ideal equations of state exhibit a monotonic dependence of $H$ on $a(t)$. Furthermore, the rate at which $H(a(t))$ decreases as $a(t)$ increases varies across epochs, regardless of whether the cosmological constant is vanishing or finite. These findings significantly enhance our comprehension of nucleosynthesis and the formation of large-scale cosmological structures.

This paper demonstrates that in the planar circular restricted three-body problem, for all energies below the first critical threshold, there exist either infinitely many symmetric consecutive collision orbits or at least one periodic symmetric consecutive collision orbit. By employing Levi-Civita regularization, we differentiate between two distinct types of such orbits and establish the claim for each independently: one analogous to a solar eclipse and the other to a lunar eclipse. We interpret these orbits as Hamiltonian chords connecting two distinct Lagrangian submanifolds, utilizing a perturbed variant of $G$-equivariant Lagrangian Rabinowitz Floer homology to prove their existence. Furthermore, to compute this homology, we show that under specific conditions, the $G$-equivariant Lagrangian Rabinowitz Floer homology coincides with the Tate homology of $G$.

Discrete Weierstrass-type representations provide a construction technique within discrete differential geometry for specific classes of discrete surfaces. We demonstrate that existing discrete Weierstrass-type representations for particular surface categories can be understood as applications of the $\Omega$-dual transform to lightlike Gauss maps in Laguerre geometry. This approach generates additional Weierstrass-type representations. Furthermore, utilizing the developed techniques, we establish that all discrete linear Weingarten surfaces of Bryant or Bianchi type locally emerge via Weierstrass-type representations derived from discrete holomorphic maps.

This work focuses on Riemannian symmetric spaces $Z=G/K$ of non-compact type, specifically the Poisson transform $\mathcal{P}_\lambda$ that maps generalized functions on the boundary $\partial Z$ to $\lambda$-eigenfunctions on $Z$. A primary focus is the maximal unipotent subgroup $N<G$, which acts naturally on both $Z$ and $\partial Z$. The $N$-orbits in $Z$ are parameterized by a torus $A=(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^r<G$ (Iwasawa decomposition), and the limit $\lim_{a\to 0} Na$ along a ray yields $N$ as an open dense orbit in $\partial Z$ (Bruhat decomposition). For positive $\lambda$, the Poisson transform $\mathcal{P}_\lambda$ is injective on $L^2(N)$ functions. We provide a new characterization of $\mathcal{P}_\lambda(L^2(N))$ using complex analysis by viewing eigenfunctions $\phi = \mathcal{P}_\lambda(f)$ as families $(\phi_a)_{a\in A}$ of functions on $N$-orbits, where $\phi_a(n)= \phi(na)$ for $n\in N$. Theory dictates the existence of a tube domain $\mathcal{T}=N\exp(i\Lambda)\subset N_\mathbb{C}$ such that each $\phi_a$ extends holomorphically to a scaled tube $\mathcal{T}_a=N\exp(i\operatorname{Ad}(a)\Lambda)$. We define $N$-invariant weight functions ${\bf w}_\lambda$ on $\mathcal{T}$, rescale them to ${\bf w}_{\lambda, a}$ on $\mathcal{T}_a$, and demonstrate that each $\phi_a$ belongs to the $L^2$-weighted Bergman space $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{T}_a, {\bf w}_{\lambda, a}):=\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{T}_a)\cap L^2(\mathcal{T}_a, {\bf w}_{\lambda, a})$. The main result characterizes $\mathcal{P}_\lambda(L^2(N))$ as the set of eigenfunctions $\phi$ satisfying $\phi_a\in \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{T}_a, {\bf w}_{\lambda, a})$ and the boundedness condition $\|\phi\|:=\sup_{a\in A} a^{\operatorname{Re}\lambda -2\rho} \|\phi_a\|_{\mathcal{B}_{a,\lambda}}<\infty$.

Pre-training recognition models using contrastive learning on vast amounts of unlabeled data has proven highly effective for enhancing downstream tasks like image classification. However, acquiring such unlabeled data is often difficult and costly in fields like medical imaging. To address this, we propose adapting contrastive learning to leverage meta-label annotations, thereby improving medical image segmentation performance even without access to additional unlabeled data. Common meta-labels, such as the position of a 2D slice within a 3D MRI or the specific imaging device used, are typically obtained at no extra cost during data acquisition. We utilize these meta-labels to pre-train the image encoder and to regularize semi-supervised training, which relies on a limited set of fully annotated data. Furthermore, to maximize the utility of these weak annotations, we employ a self-paced learning strategy to facilitate learning and distinguish useful labels from noise. Experiments across three distinct medical image segmentation datasets demonstrate that our method: i) significantly improves model performance when trained on a small number of scans, ii) surpasses existing contrastive and semi-supervised techniques, and iii) achieves performance levels nearly equivalent to models trained on complete datasets.

Deep learning achievements typically depend on vast annotated datasets, yet curating them is particularly arduous for medical imagery. To alleviate this challenge in landmark detection, we investigate the viability of utilizing a single annotated image and introduce a novel framework called Cascade Comparing to Detect (CC2D) for one-shot landmark detection. CC2D operates through two phases: 1) Self-supervised learning (CC2D-SSL) and 2) Training with pseudo-labels (CC2D-TPL). The CC2D-SSL stage extracts consistent anatomical details in a coarse-to-fine manner by analyzing cascade feature representations to generate training set predictions. Subsequently, CC2D-TPL enhances performance by retraining a landmark detector using these predictions. Evaluated on a prominent public dataset for cephalometric landmark detection, CC2D demonstrates competitive accuracy, achieving 81.01% within a 4.0mm threshold, rivaling state-of-the-art fully-supervised methods that rely on significantly more training images.

This study evaluates the efficacy of multiple clustering methods within the domain of Cultural Heritage monitoring. Specifically, we assess the extent of decomposition and corrosion on the walls of the Saint Nicholas fort in Rhodes using hyperspectral imagery. Six distinct clustering algorithms—K-means, Spectral, Meanshift, DBSCAN, Birch, and OPTICS—were tested across 14 orthorectified hyperspectral datasets. Performance was quantified using the Calinski-Harabasz index, Davies-Bouldin index, and Silhouette score. To validate the results, we compared the clustering outputs against annotated ground-truth images detailing decomposition and corrosion zones. The findings indicate that several techniques achieved satisfactory accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 scores, ultimately demonstrating reliable detection of wall deterioration.

Most black holes and neutron stars are thought to be the ultimate remnants of massive stellar evolution. This study introduces a novel formation mechanism for black holes and unusual neutron stars, such as magnetars and Thorne-Żytkow objects (TŻOs), termed the core merger-induced collapse (CMIC) model. This process occurs when the core of a hydrogen- or helium-rich, non-degenerate star merges with an oxygen/neon/magnesium white dwarf at the conclusion of a common-envelope phase, resulting in unique celestial objects. Binary population synthesis simulations indicate that the CMIC channel significantly contributes to the populations of black holes, (millisecond) pulsars, TŻOs, and magnetars. Additionally, research is exploring whether TŻOs, magnetars, and CMIC-formed black holes can power superluminous supernovae. Furthermore, magnetars with immediate matter surroundings generated via the CMIC process may serve as promising sources for fast radio bursts.

Proto-neutron stars, which emerge a few seconds following core-collapse supernovae, represent hot and dense conditions conducive to the efficient production of hyperons via weak interactions. Utilizing advanced supernova simulations alongside updated equations of state that incorporate $\Lambda$ hyperons, we compute the cooling rates driven by dark boson $X^0$ emission resulting from the decay $\Lambda\to n X^0$. By comparing this novel energy-loss mechanism against the neutrino cooling observed in SN 1987A, we establish rigorous constraints on massless dark photons and axions possessing flavor-violating couplings to quarks. Our results indicate that these new supernova-derived limits on dark-sector models can be orders of magnitude more restrictive than existing bounds.

This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework for real-time 3D human action recognition using skeletal data, specifically designed to build a vision-based intelligent surveillance system. The proposed method encodes skeleton poses and their associated motions into a unified RGB image, upon which an Adaptive Histogram Equalization (AHE) algorithm is applied to amplify local patterns and produce more discriminative features. For feature extraction and classification, we utilize Deep Neural Networks built on the Densely Connected Convolutional Architecture (DenseNet). Experiments conducted on two challenging datasets demonstrate that this approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with minimal computational costs for both training and inference. Additionally, we present CEMEST, a new RGB-D dataset capturing passenger behaviors in public transport, comprising 203 untrimmed real-world surveillance videos featuring realistic normal and anomalous events. By leveraging data augmentation and transfer learning, we obtain promising results on this dataset under real-world conditions, paving the way for deep learning-based applications that enhance monitoring and security in public transport.

Recent years have seen a surge in interest for data-driven modeling approaches across various difficult meteorological domains, particularly in weather forecasting. This study presents a new predictive framework for precipitation nowcasting that leverages the TransUNet architecture. Originally developed for medical image segmentation by integrating Transformer and U-Net components, TransUNet serves as the foundational model in this work, enhanced further by Convolutional Block Attention Modules (CBAM) and Depthwise-separable Convolution (DSC). The resulting Attention Augmented TransUNet (AA-TransUNet) was assessed using two separate datasets: the Dutch precipitation map and the French cloud cover datasets. Evaluation results indicate that the proposed model surpasses other tested methods on both datasets. Additionally, an uncertainty analysis of the AA-TransUNet is included to provide deeper insights into its prediction capabilities.

This study calculates the bound-free pair production (BFPP) cross sections for the NICA collider. In the BFPP mechanism, a free electron produced in the pair production event is captured by one of the ions, leading to a reduction in the number of ions within the beam, a decrease in beam intensity, and an alteration of the beam lifetime. The calculations were performed for p-Au and p-Bi collisions at the NICA collider, with results indicating cross sections in the range of a few millibarns. The work employs lowest-order perturbation theory within the framework of Quantum Electrodynamics (QED).

This research examines how asymmetric bosonic dark matter influences neutron star characteristics, specifically alterations in maximum mass, radius, tidal deformability, and internal matter distribution. We outline the scenarios under which dark matter particles either condense in the stellar core or form an extended halo. Our findings indicate that core condensation reduces both the total gravitational mass and tidal deformability relative to a purely baryonic star, mimicking an effective softening of the equation of state. Conversely, a dark matter halo enhances these observable metrics. Consequently, accumulated dark matter can skew observational data on compact stars, thereby impacting constraints derived for strongly interacting matter at high densities. To verify dark matter's presence within compact stars and distinguish its effects from those of high-density matter properties, we propose several astrophysical and gravitational wave tests.

We present an exact correspondence between the high-temperature $(D+2)$-dimensional Tangherlini-AdS black hole and the low-temperature quantum phonon gas in $D$-dimensional nonmetallic crystals situated within $(D+1)$-dimensional flat spacetime. This equivalence is achieved through the application of the recently introduced restricted phase space formalism for black hole thermodynamics, offering a new quantitative insight into the AdS/CMT correspondence.

This document provides supplementary material for the paper titled "Passive controller realization of a biquadratic impedance with double poles and zeros as a seven-element Series-parallel network for effective mechanical control" [1].

Remote sensing and automated Earth monitoring are essential for addressing global issues like disaster mitigation, land use tracking, and climate change. Despite the abundance of remote sensing data, much of it remains unlabeled and unavailable for supervised learning. While transfer learning can reduce the data needs for deep learning, most existing methods rely on ImageNet pre-training and fail to generalize to remote sensing imagery due to domain differences. This paper introduces Seasonal Contrast (SeCo), a pipeline designed to utilize unlabeled data for in-domain pre-training of remote sensing representations. SeCo consists of two components: first, a systematic approach to aggregate large-scale, uncurated, unlabeled remote sensing datasets featuring images from various locations and timestamps; and second, a self-supervised algorithm that exploits invariance to time and position to learn transferable representations. Empirical results demonstrate that SeCo-trained models outperform both ImageNet pre-trained models and current state-of-the-art self-supervised methods across multiple downstream tasks. Furthermore, the datasets and models associated with SeCo will be released publicly to support transfer learning and accelerate advancements in remote sensing.

This study investigates $\bar{D}^\ast K^\ast$ interactions in both $S$- and $P$-wave channels using a coupled-channel approach to analyze the recently identified $X_0(2900)$ and $X_1(2900)$ states observed by LHCb. The experimental data distributions are accurately modeled, yielding two states with quantum numbers $I(J^P)=0(0^+)$ and $0(1^-)$ within a single theoretical framework. While the predicted masses for the $0^+$ and $1^-$ states align with experimental findings, the calculated width for the $0^+$ state exceeds that of the $1^-$ state. Within the hadronic molecular model, the $X_1(2900)$ is interpreted as the $P$-wave excitation of the ground-state $X_0(2900)$. Given the existence of numerous members in the $S$- and $P$-wave multiplets of the $\bar{D}^\ast K^\ast$ system, the current peak observed in the $D^-K^+$ invariant mass spectrum may actually comprise multiple subpeaks. To resolve these underlying fine structures and move beyond the single broad peak currently seen, more precise measurements in the $B^+\to D^+D^-K^+$ decay channel are required.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable advancements across numerous visual recognition tasks, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. While the evolution of convolutional architectures has improved performance, it has also introduced high computational costs. Furthermore, designing networks manually is labor-intensive and demands extensive domain expertise. To address these challenges, researchers have developed various Neural Architecture Search (NAS) methods that automatically discover optimal architectures, often surpassing the performance of human-designed models. This survey reviews existing research in this domain, with a specific focus on supernet optimization, which constructs a single neural network that incorporates multiple architectures as sub-models through weight sharing. We categorize supernet optimization approaches as solutions to common literature challenges, including data-side optimization, mitigating poor rank correlation, and enabling transferable NAS for diverse deployment scenarios.

Discourse parsing based on RST theory is a crucial NLP task with extensive downstream applications, including summarization, machine translation, and opinion mining. This paper presents a straightforward yet highly accurate discourse parser that integrates recent contextual language models. Our approach achieves new state-of-the-art performance for predicting both structure and nuclearity on two primary RST datasets, RST-DT and Instr-DT. Furthermore, we show that pretraining our parser on the recently released large-scale "silver-standard" discourse treebank, MEGA-DT, yields even greater performance improvements, indicating a novel and promising avenue for future research in discourse analysis.

This paper demonstrates that the DUNE experiment can determine the Earth's density profile by examining atmospheric neutrino oscillations. The key enabler for this measurement is the precise event reconstruction capability of liquid argon time projection chambers, which facilitates the study of the sub-GeV atmospheric neutrino sector. This sector exhibits complex oscillation behavior heavily influenced by the matter potential generated within the Earth. We offer a pedagogical overview of MSW and parametric resonances, highlighting their significance in probing core and mantle densities. Through comprehensive simulations that incorporate particle reconstruction at DUNE, nuclear physics effects in neutrino-argon interactions, and various uncertainties in the atmospheric neutrino flux, we derive a robust estimate of DUNE's sensitivity to the Earth's matter profile. Our findings indicate that DUNE can measure the Earth's total mass with 8.4% precision after an exposure of 400~kton-year. Leveraging existing data on the Earth's total mass and moment of inertia, the densities of the core, lower mantle, and upper mantle can be determined with precisions of 8.8%, 13%, and 22%, respectively, under the same exposure conditions. Furthermore, DUNE is capable of collecting atmospheric neutrino data during beam commissioning while far detector modules are operational. For a reduced exposure of 60~kton-year, corresponding to two far detectors running for three years, we estimate that DUNE could measure the core density with approximately 30% precision.

This paper examines physical layer security within the novel Alternate Rician Shadowed fading channel, specifically tailored for body-centric wireless links and land mobile satellite systems. We obtain exact closed-form expressions for the average secrecy capacity (ASC), secrecy outage probability (SOP), and probability of non-zero secrecy capacity (PNZ) across two scenarios: (i) when $m$, representing the line-of-sight fluctuation level, is a positive real number, and (ii) when $m$ is a positive integer. In the first scenario, SOP is expressed using the Meijer's G-function, whereas ASC and PNZ are formulated via the multivariate Fox's H-function. Conversely, in the second scenario, ASC relies on the Meijer's G-function, while SOP and PNZ are derived using elementary functions. Furthermore, we establish asymptotic expressions for ASC, SOP, and PNZ that align closely with the exact results at high signal-to-noise ratios. We also determine the capacity slope of the asymptotic ASC and the secrecy diversity order of the asymptotic SOP to offer deeper physical insights. Ultimately, the precision of these derived formulas is confirmed through Monte-Carlo simulations.

This paper aims to determine sharp bounds for the norm of the Schwarzian derivative regarding convex mappings of order $\alpha$, specifically expressed through the value of $f''(0)$, with a focus on the case where this value is zero. Furthermore, we derive sharp bounds for the distortion and growth of these mappings and extend the findings previously established by Suita and Yamashita for this specific scenario.

This paper introduces a refinement of Kool-Thomas invariants for local surfaces by utilizing the equivariant $K$-theoretic invariants developed by Nekrasov and Okounkov. Originally, Kool and Thomas formulated the reduced obstruction theory for the moduli space of stable pairs, denoted as $\mathcal{P}_{\chi}(X,i_{*}\beta)$, as the degree of the virtual class $\left[\mathcal{P}_{\chi}(S,\beta)\right]^{red}$ following the application of $\tau([pt])^{m}\in H^{*}(\mathcal{P}_{\chi}(X,i_{*}\beta),\mathbb{Z})$. The term $\tau([pt])$ encodes the incidence data between a point and a curve supporting a pair $(\mathcal{F},s)$.

**Keywords:** Kool-Thomas invariants, $K$-theoretic invariants, G\"ottsche Shende invariants

This study investigates the Bianchi-type-I cosmological model under the framework of holographic dark energy. By employing the generalized hybrid expansion law (HEL), we derive exact solutions to the associated field equations. The resulting equation of state (EoS) parameter $\omega$ for dark energy is determined to be dependent on both time and redshift, with its derived range aligning closely with current observational data. Furthermore, we utilize two mathematical diagnostics—the statefinder pair $\{r, s\}$ and the $\omega_{d}-\omega^{'}_{d}$ plane—to distinguish the HDE model from the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. Among these, the $\omega_{d}-\omega^{'}_{d}$ trajectories prove to be an effective tool for classifying dynamical dark energy models, revealing that our model occupies both thawing and freezing regions. Additionally, we construct the potential and dynamics for quintessence and tachyon scalar fields. A detailed discussion follows regarding the physical and geometric properties of the model, as well as the physical viability of the cosmological solution.

The aesthetic quality of a photograph is largely defined by its aspect ratio and spatial arrangement. However, integrating these elements into conventional convolution-based image aesthetics assessment models presents significant challenges. Resizing or cropping images to fixed dimensions for training often distorts the aspect ratio, while the localized nature of convolutional filters hinders their ability to capture the global spatial layout. To address these issues simultaneously, we introduce a two-stage framework utilizing graph neural networks. Initially, we develop a feature-graph representation that models the input image as a graph, thereby preserving its native aspect ratio and resolution. Subsequently, we employ a graph neural network architecture that leverages visual attention to model the semantic relationships between various image regions. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed framework outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in aesthetic score regression on the Aesthetic Visual Analysis (AVA) benchmark.

This study introduces an estimator for non-randomized experiments that infers heterogeneous treatment effects organized by pre-defined impact groups, a concept analogous to the broader aggregation of Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE) found in pre-analysis plans within economics. Given that observational studies are common in policy evaluations across labor markets, education, and other empirical fields, the authors address potential selection bias by implementing a doubly-robust estimator in the initial stage. Machine learning techniques are employed to model both the conditional mean functions and the propensity score. Subsequently, the average treatment effect for each group is estimated using a linear projection model. This linear approach offers interpretability, generates p-values and confidence intervals, and mitigates the risk of identifying spurious heterogeneity within small CATE subgroups. To manage confounding within the linear model, Neyman-orthogonal moments are utilized to isolate the influence of covariates on both treatment assignment and outcomes, resulting in a best linear predictor for effect heterogeneity based on impact groups. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed method yields lower absolute errors and reduced bias compared to standard doubly-robust estimators. Additionally, a bagging-style averaging process is introduced for the CATE function of each observation to prevent biases arising from sample splitting. Ultimately, the method's primary advantage lies in providing robust linear estimation of heterogeneous group treatment effects within observational studies.

We have developed a robust statistical framework to constrain chemical and dust evolution parameters in nearby late-type galaxies spanning a broad range of gas fractions ($3\%<f_g<94\%$). Utilizing a Bayesian Monte Carlo Markov Chain approach, we statistically evaluated parameters within chemical evolution models by comparing nearly one million one-zone models against data from 340 galaxies. Relative probabilities were derived from $\chi^2$ values between models and observations, marginalized over time steps, galaxy masses, and star formation histories. Initially, we identified 'best-fitting' metallicity-related parameters; these were then fixed to isolate constraints on dust parameters. For metallicity, we observed degeneracies involving the initial mass function, supernova metal yield tables, and outflow prescriptions. Regarding dust, uncertainties in best-fit values are typically substantial, with the exception of the fraction of metals available for grain growth, which is well-constrained. We identified several degeneracies among dust parameters that limit our capacity to distinguish between chemical models based solely on observations. Specifically, we demonstrate that the low dust content in low-metallicity galaxies can be explained by either lowering supernova dust yields or incorporating photo-fragmentation. Furthermore, we show that supernova dust production dominates in low-metallicity galaxies, while grain growth prevails in high-metallicity ones, with the transition occurring near $12+\log({\rm O/H})=7.75$—a value lower than those reported in most prior studies.

We examine the long-term asymptotic behavior of solutions to the heat equation involving the fractional Laplacian perturbed by subcritical or critical Hardy-type potentials. These asymptotics are determined by a self-similar solution, which arises as the normalized limit at the origin of the kernel associated with the corresponding Feynman-Kac semigroup.

This theoretical study examines how solutal free convection influences the diffusion of buoyant solutes at microfluidic scales, ranging from approximately 5 to 500 $\mu$m. Initially, we analyze a horizontal microfluidic slit where one half contains a binary solution and the other pure solvent; buoyant forces generate a gravity current that interacts with solute diffusion. Using numerical simulations of a 2D transport model, we identify distinct regimes governed by the Rayleigh number ($\text{Ra}$), which balances gravity-driven advection against solute diffusion. We derive asymptotic analytical solutions to determine the time-dependent width of the mixing zone across these regimes and construct a diagram to delineate conditions where buoyancy has no effect on diffusion. Subsequently, we apply numerical methods to the same model for a 3D microfluidic channel with a square cross-section, observing consistent regimes and focusing on the long-term dispersion regime. We derive the expression for the 1D dispersion coefficient in rectangular channels and evaluate the influence of transverse flow specifically for square sections. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the impact of this transverse flow on solute transport is negligible for most microfluidic experimental setups.

We demonstrate that within a specific semi-random framework, a Hamilton cycle can be constructed with high probability using at most $1.85 n$ rounds. In each round of this model, a uniformly random vertex $v \in [n]$ is provided, allowing the addition of an arbitrary edge $\{v,w\}$. This finding improves upon the recent result of $2.016 n$ established by Gao, MacRury, and Pralat.

A primary objective in human-robot interaction (HRI) is to enable machines to attain face perception capabilities comparable to those of humans. A key distinction between human intelligence and machine learning lies in the absence of compositionality in current systems. This paper presents a novel framework allowing generative adversarial networks to learn the distribution of face images constructed from constituent parts. This approach yields more flexible machine face perception and facilitates easier generalization to unseen training examples. We show that the model can generate realistic, high-quality face images by assembling these parts, and further demonstrate that it successfully learns the relationships between facial components and their distributions. Consequently, specific facial parts become interchangeable across different generated faces.

This paper presents RyanSpeech, a novel speech corpus designed to advance automated text-to-speech (TTS) research. Existing public TTS datasets frequently suffer from noise, include multiple speakers, or lack high-quality male audio. To address the demand for a reliable, publicly accessible male speech dataset for speech recognition, we developed RyanSpeech, which features textual data derived from authentic conversational environments. The collection comprises over 10 hours of recordings from a professional male voice actor, captured at a sampling rate of 44.1 kHz. RyanSpeech's specific design and processing pipeline render it particularly suitable for building TTS systems intended for real-world deployment. To establish a foundation for future studies, we trained four state-of-the-art speech models and a vocoder using this corpus, achieving a Mean Opinion Score (MOS) of 3.36 with the top-performing model. Both the dataset and the trained models are now available for public use.

This work offers a comprehensive investigation of a four-parameter family of elliptic weights defined on hexagonal tilings, originally introduced by Borodin, Gorin, and Rains, extending several of their findings. We establish a bridge between the model's combinatorial structure and the theory of elliptic special functions. By employing canonical coordinates for the hexagon, we demonstrate how $n$-point distribution functions and transition probabilities relate to $BC_n$-symmetric multivariate elliptic special functions and the elliptic difference operators proposed by Rains. Notably, these difference operators inherently encompass the entire combinatorial framework. Leveraging quasi-commutation relations among these operators, we develop natural measure-preserving Markov chains on such tilings, which facilitate an exact sampling algorithm for the corresponding elliptic distributions. We provide simulated random samples that reveal intriguing, potentially novel arctic boundary effects. Furthermore, we establish that the particle process linked to these tilings is determinantal, with a correlation kernel expressed through the univariate elliptic biorthogonal functions of Spiridonov and Zhedanov.

Neural methods for modeling coherence have recently reached state-of-the-art performance on various evaluation benchmarks. However, we demonstrate that many of these models struggle with more challenging tasks that reflect realistic application scenarios. Specifically, current models underperform when sensitivity to local context is required, such as in candidate ranking for conversational dialogue and machine translation. This paper introduces a unified coherence model that integrates sentence grammar, inter-sentence coherence relations, and global coherence patterns within a single neural framework. Through extensive experiments on both local and global discrimination tasks, we show that our model significantly outperforms existing approaches and establishes a new state-of-the-art.

We introduce a consistency condition for 8d ${\cal N} = 1$ supergravity theories featuring non-trivial global structures $G/Z$ within non-Abelian gauge groups, grounded in an anomaly associated with the $Z$ 1-form center symmetry. By integrating this condition with other Swampland criteria, we determine that most 8d theories possessing a gauge group $G/Z$ lack a string theory realization and are deemed inconsistent as quantum theories when coupled to gravity. Although this condition mirrors geometric features of elliptic K3 surfaces in F-theory compactifications, it also imposes constraints on the unexplored landscape of gauge groups in alternative 8d string models.

Existing correlation filter (CF)-based tracking techniques for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have predominantly concentrated on daytime operations. However, nighttime conditions present more challenging environments that often result in tracking failures. To address this limitation, we introduce ADTrack, a novel tracker featuring an anti-dark capability. This approach embeds an efficient low-light image enhancer within a CF-based framework. Additionally, the method generates a target-aware mask based on illumination variations, which is used to jointly train a target-focused filter that complements the context filter for enhanced robustness. Specifically, ADTrack employs dual regression, wherein the context and target-focused filters mutually constrain each other during the learning process. Extensive experiments were performed on a benchmark of typical dark scenarios, comprising 37 night sequences from authoritative datasets like UAVDark and our newly created UAVDark70. The results demonstrate that ADTrack surpasses other state-of-the-art trackers and operates in real-time at 34 frames/s on a single CPU, significantly expanding the scope of robust UAV tracking to night environments.

Selecting tuning parameters for penalized estimation is vital for achieving models that are both interpretable and predictive. However, widely used methods, such as cross-validation designed to minimize average squared prediction error, often result in the selection of models containing more predictors than required. This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective cross-validation approach that maximizes the squared correlation between observed and predicted values for support recovery, rather than minimizing squared error loss. This strategy is applicable to all penalized least-squares estimators; under specific conditions, it implicitly performs bias adjustment. The discussion focuses particularly on the Lasso estimator, where the proposed method aligns closely with the Relaxed Lasso. The approach is validated through a functional variable selection task aimed at determining the optimal placement of surface electromyogram sensors for controlling a robotic hand prosthesis.

Achieving top-tier performance on smaller datasets typically necessitates pre-training video transformers on massive-scale data. This paper demonstrates that Video Masked Autoencoders (VideoMAE) are highly data-efficient for self-supervised video pre-training (SSVP). Drawing inspiration from ImageMAE, we introduce a specialized video tube masking strategy with an exceptionally high ratio. This straightforward design complicates the video reconstruction task, thereby promoting the extraction of more potent video representations during pre-training. Our research on SSVP yields three key insights: (1) A very high masking ratio (90% to 95%) still produces strong VideoMAE performance; the temporal redundancy in video allows for higher masking rates compared to images. (2) VideoMAE delivers remarkable results on extremely small datasets (approximately 3k-4k videos) without requiring additional data. (3) For SSVP, data quality outweighs data quantity, and domain shifts between pre-training and target datasets are critical. Specifically, our VideoMAE implementation using a standard ViT attains 87.4% on Kinetics-400, 75.4% on Something-Something V2, 91.3% on UCF101, and 62.6% on HMDB51, all without extra data. The code is accessible at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/VideoMAE.

The second author previously established a characterization of Shimura subvarieties containing a Zariski dense set of weakly special subvarieties by merging o-minimality and functional transcendence. In this work, we present an alternative proof of this result utilizing dynamics on homogeneous spaces, inspired by the earlier contributions of Clozel and the second author. This approach integrates Ratner-style ergodic theory with a theorem concerning the dimension of Hausdorff limits of definable subsets within an o-minimal theory, derived from a definable family. Additionally, we derive general homogeneous dynamics statements applicable to arbitrary arithmetic quotients; these results are of independent interest and can be utilized in the analysis of variations of Hodge structures and their corresponding period domains.

The mass composition of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) can be deduced by fitting measured $X_{\rm max}$ distributions with Monte Carlo (MC) predictions for various primary nuclei across different energy intervals. Based on MC simulations, we demonstrate that an effective strategy involves fitting observed $X_{\rm max}$ distributions with all feasible combinations of elements from a comprehensive primary set (specifically p, He, C, N, O, Ne, Si, and Fe) to identify the "best combination" that most accurately describes the data. This method was applied to $X_{\rm max}$ distributions from the Pierre Auger (2014) and Telescope Array (TA) (2016) observatories within energy ranges of $\lg E (\rm eV) =$ [17.8 - 19.3] and $\lg E (\rm eV) =$ [18.2 - 19.0], respectively, utilizing QGSJETII-04 hadronic interaction model predictions. Results from both datasets indicate that UHECR mass composition is primarily dominated by protons and helium nuclei ($\gtrsim 70\%$), exhibiting energy-dependent abundance modulations while maintaining a relatively constant total sum. An indirect comparison between the two experiments revealed good compatibility in certain energy bins around and above the \textit{ankle} ($\lg E (\rm eV) \sim 18.7$), though agreement deteriorates at lower energies. We conclude that this approach, supplemented by predictions from various hadronic interaction models, can facilitate future research into mass composition, offering a more precise depiction of how individual nuclear fractions evolve with energy based on experimental $X_{\rm max}$ distributions.

Physics-constrained machine learning is becoming a vital area of study, particularly for applications in physics. A primary benefit of integrating physical constraints into machine learning models is the substantial reduction in the amount of training data required. By embedding physical laws directly into the model's formulation, predictions are guaranteed to align with physical reality. Among methods suitable for small datasets, Gaussian processes (GPs) are widely utilized. This paper examines the feasibility of enforcing monotonicity constraints within a GP framework across three material science datasets, comprising one experimental set and two computational sets. When compared to standard GPs, the monotonic variant demonstrates a marked decrease in posterior variance. While the model maintains strict monotonicity during interpolation, this effect diminishes during extrapolation as predictions move beyond the training range. Although imposing monotonicity incurs a minor penalty in accuracy relative to standard GPs, the approach is particularly advantageous for scenarios characterized by scarce and noisy data where monotonic behavior is strongly supported by physical principles.

Long-baseline accelerator experiments, such as NO$\nu$A, face challenges regarding octant degeneracy when measuring disappearance channels. In these setups, sensitivity to the mass hierarchy (MH) is contingent on the CP-violating phase $\delta_{CP}$, while the specific ordering of light neutrino masses remains undetermined and the fermion flavor structure is incompletely understood. This study addresses these challenges within a highly predictive, low-scale inverse seesaw (ISS) model based on $A_4$ flavor symmetry. Aligning with recent global analyses that favor normal hierarchy and a higher $\theta_{23}$ octant, we demonstrate that the vacuum alignment of the $A_4$ triplet flavon (1,-1,-1) supports these findings. Furthermore, we evaluate whether our precise predictions for the effective Majorana mass ($m_{ee}$) and the lightest neutrino mass fall within the detection range of neutrinoless double beta decay ($0\nu\beta\beta$) experiments. Ultimately, we show that once future measurements more accurately fix the MH and $\theta_{23}$ octant, our results will enable the precise identification of the favorable vacuum alignment for the $A_4$ triplet field as predicted by the model.

While highly excited eigenstates in quantum many-body systems generally resemble featureless thermal states, certain systems host a limited set of special, low-entanglement eigenstates called quantum scars. We present a quantum-inspired machine learning framework utilizing a Quantum Variational Autoencoder (QVAE) to identify families of scar states within many-body spectra. Distinct from classical autoencoders, the QVAE executes a parametrized unitary operation, enabling the compression of individual eigenstates into fewer qubits. Our results show that a QVAE trained on a specific scar state can successfully detect the entire family of scar states that share common characteristics with the input. Furthermore, we uncover new families of quantum many-body scars in the PXP model extending beyond the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_3$ classifications and identify dynamically decoupled subspaces within the Hilbert space of disordered, interacting spin ladder models. The capability for automated detection of these scar subspaces establishes novel avenues for investigating models exhibiting a weak breakdown of ergodicity and fragmented Hilbert spaces.

This study aims to establish a robust classification system for the variability of A-F stars brighter than magnitude 11 within the northern TESS continuous viewing zone. Our objectives include a detailed examination of classification challenges stemming from data characteristics and the ambiguity caused by similar light curve shapes produced by distinct physical mechanisms. Utilizing TESS long- and short-cadence photometry alongside Fourier transforms, we developed a clear and concise classification framework illustrated with numerous examples. Analysis revealed variability signs in 3025 of the 5923 surveyed stars (51%), with classifications provided for 1813 of these variable stars. Among the classified sample, 64.5% are pulsating stars of GDOR and DSCT types, including their hybrids. We observed that long- and short-cadence PDCSAP data can differ substantially in both amplitude and the presence of instrumental or reduction artifacts, rendering long-cadence data less reliable. Furthermore, we identified a new group of stars exhibiting stable light curves and characteristic frequency spectra (8.5% of classified stars); based on their location in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, these are likely GDOR stars that are, on average, 200 K cooler, with smaller amplitudes and longer periods. We demonstrated that distinguishing between ellipsoidal and rotational variability without spectroscopic data can be impossible. Additionally, applying our methodology to three prior studies highlighted significant discrepancies in their classifications, underscoring the inherent difficulties of classifying variable A-F stars using photometric data alone.

This paper investigates the boundary of the cone consisting of real polynomials expressible as sums of squares (SOS). While this SOS cone lies within the larger cone of nonnegative polynomials, they share a common boundary segment comprising polynomials with at least one zero; our focus is on the distinct boundary portion containing strictly positive polynomials. G. Blekherman recently provided a complete characterization for strictly positive cases involving degree-6 polynomials in three variables and degree-4 polynomials in four variables. However, extending these findings to higher degrees or greater numbers of variables remains complex, with limited existing examples or general results. Under the assumption of a conjecture by D. Eisenbud, M. Green, and J. Harris, we derive upper bounds for the maximum number of terms in an SOS decomposition and the maximum rank of matrices within the Gram spectrahedron. Specifically, for homogeneous quartics in five variables—a scenario where the relevant conjecture has recently been proven—we establish bounds that surpass current general limits. Furthermore, by integrating theoretical analysis with computational methods, we identify specific examples and counterexamples. These findings clarify the extent to which G. Blekherman's results can be generalized and demonstrate that the bounds predicted by our approach are achievable.

We present a motivic proof demonstrating that for non-singular real tropical complete intersections, the Euler characteristic of the real component equals the signature of the complex component. This result was first established by Itenberg for surfaces in $\mathbb{CP}^3$ and later extended by Bertrand, and subsequently by Bihan and Bertrand. Our approach, distinct from prior methods, utilizes the motivic nearby fiber of semi-stable degenerations. Notably, this work generalizes the original Itenberg-Bertrand-Bihan theorem to real analytic families that possess a $\mathbb{Q}$-non-singular tropical limit.

We present a novel approach to analyzing the Bose-Hubbard model for bosons with nearest-neighbor interactions, grounded in a number-theoretic formulation of the model's creation and annihilation operators. A key benefit of this method is its capacity for computations with arbitrary precision, allowing for highly accurate numerical simulations. Specifically, we offer a rigorous, computer-assisted demonstration of quantum phase transitions within finite systems of this kind. Additionally, we explore the characteristics of infinite arrays through harmonic analysis on the multiplicative group of positive rationals. This analysis establishes an isomorphism that reformulates the underlying Fock space as an infinite tensor product of Hecke spaces—defined as spaces of square-integrable periodic functions composed of non-negative frequency harmonics. Under this mapping, the number-theoretic operators correspond to the Kastrup model of the harmonic oscillator on a circle. Furthermore, this framework reveals a connection between the current model and an array of spin moments subject to a local anisotropy field, thereby identifying a distinct physical system that can be mapped onto the model in question.

Global analyses of current neutrino oscillation data support the standard $3+0$ framework, yet certain short-baseline anomalies suggest the potential existence of a fourth, eV-scale sterile neutrino. If such a sterile neutrino exists and is not adequately accounted for in data analyses, the interference terms generated by additional CP phases could significantly affect physics searches in long-baseline (LBL) oscillation experiments. This study examines the scenario of one light sterile neutrino, investigating all three CP phases ($\delta_{13}$, $\delta_{24}$, $\delta_{34}$) within the context of the upcoming Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). We also assess how incorporating data from NOvA, T2K, and T2HK would enhance these results. Furthermore, we present $\Delta \chi^2$ correlations among the CP phases and with the three active-sterile mixing angles, and briefly discuss how the parameter spaces relevant to neutrinoless double beta decay are altered by the constraints imposed by a light sterile neutrino.

Identifying top-quark jets that decay hadronically, or determining their total fraction within a jet sample, is a critical component for numerous LHC investigations into both Standard Model and Beyond Standard Model physics. While superior top-tagger algorithms currently exist, their development and projected performance depend on Monte Carlo simulations, which can introduce potential biases. To address this, we have created two straightforward unsupervised top-tagger algorithms utilizing Bayesian inference on mixture models. One algorithm employs a novel geometrically derived observable, $\tilde{A}_{3}$, whereas the other utilizes the conventional $\tau_{3}/\tau_{2}$ $N$-subjettiness ratio, which demonstrates superior performance. As anticipated, the unsupervised taggers exhibit lower performance than existing supervised methods, achieving expected Area Under Curve (AUC) values of approximately 0.80–0.81 and accuracies ranging from 69% to 75% across various sample purities. Nevertheless, these unsupervised approaches prove more resilient to potential Monte Carlo biases compared to their supervised counterparts. These results represent progress toward investigating and adopting simpler, unbiased tagging strategies.
There is further evidence supporting the claim that the microstates of Schwarzschild black holes in perturbative string theory correspond to the modes of long folded strings near the horizon.

This paper introduces ThielSort, a practical realization of the Diverting Fast Radix (DFR) Algorithm. It outlines theoretical enhancements compared to traditional radix sorts and details the implementation to demonstrate its competitiveness with current state-of-the-art methods. The efficacy of this DFR implementation is validated through evaluations across various standard data distributions and input sizes.

We introduce a straightforward architecture for deterministic quantum circuits utilizing single-photon qubits. This design requires minimal resources to execute two fundamental gates, which can then be reused for computations involving large qubit systems. Furthermore, this approach significantly streamlines the deterministic implementation of essential multi-qubit gates, including the Fredkin and Toffoli gates.

The Maier-Leibniz Doppler-Shift method stands as the most widely utilized and precise approach in fission experiments for distinguishing the gamma-ray yields of individual fission fragments. This method relies on the aberration effect, which refers to the alteration in the angular distribution of gamma rays emitted by a moving source. By utilizing a standard detector to ascertain the source's velocity and trajectory, alongside measuring gamma-ray yields at various angles relative to the direction of motion, researchers can calculate the mean multiplicities of gamma rays for each fragment. This study demonstrates that the technique can be expanded to measure second moments of the gamma radiation from each fragment. Specifically, addressing the current focus on fragment correlations in fission, we illustrate how the covariance of emission between the two fragments can be derived. Furthermore, the discussion covers experimental constraints and the convergence characteristics of this enhanced methodology.

In multivariate analysis, the precision matrix, which represents conditional linear dependencies among variables, is a key object of study. Sparse estimation methods like the graphical lasso (Glasso) have become popular due to their ability to enhance interpretability by distinguishing between variables that are conditionally dependent and those that are independent. However, Glasso is not robust to outliers. To address this, researchers typically employ a robust plug-in approach, calculating Glasso using a robust covariance estimate rather than the sample covariance to mitigate outlier effects. This paper investigates these estimators theoretically by deriving and comparing their influence functions, sensitivity curves, and asymptotic variances.

Emotion detection within text has grown increasingly vital across numerous disciplines. This study explores methods to enhance multi-label emotion recognition by leveraging label correlations. Initially, we propose two modeling strategies to capture associations among emotion terms: one incorporates emotions directly into the input, while the other utilizes Masked Language Modeling (MLM). Subsequently, we incorporate pairwise constraints on emotion representations as regularization terms alongside the standard classification loss, categorizing them into local and global types. Local constraints adapt dynamically according to gold labels, whereas global constraints remain fixed throughout training. Our monolingual BERT-based models achieve state-of-the-art results and demonstrate enhanced robustness across Spanish, English, and Arabic datasets in SemEval 2018 Task 1 E-c. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/gchochla/Demux-MEmo.

Investigating the formation of loosely bound states in high-energy hadronic collisions has been significantly advanced through the study of nucleus and antinuclei production.
