Detailed modeling and simulations of coded systems demonstrate that these proposed designs achieve superior bit error rate (BER) performance, along with reduced peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) and lower computational complexity compared to existing index-modulated systems.

This paper aims to establish the cohomology theory for $n$-Hom-Lie color algebras that governs one-parameter formal deformations. Subsequently, we examine formal deformations of these algebras and define the concept of a Nijenhuis operator on an $n$-Hom-Lie color algebra, which can generate infinitesimally trivial deformations of order $(n-1)$. Moreover, in relation to Nijenhuis operators, we introduce and explore the notion of a product structure within $n$-Hom-Lie color algebras.

While partial differential equations (PDEs) are standard for modeling physical phenomena and hold significant interest in image processing, conventional numerical solvers often demand extremely fine grid resolutions to maintain stability, leading to prohibitively high computational costs. This study integrates BLADE (Best Linear Adaptive Enhancement), a shallow learnable filtering framework, into PDE solving. The results demonstrate that this approach achieves both efficiency and accuracy, functioning more reliably at coarse grid resolutions compared to classical methods. Consequently, the model offers flexible applicability across a broad spectrum of imaging challenges.

Investigating higher-order topological insulators in bosonic systems, which exhibit gapless boundary states protected by topology with a codimension greater than one, has gained increasing attention. In this work, we introduce twisted bilayer honeycomb magnets as a novel platform for realizing second-order topological magnon insulators (SOTMIs) without requiring fine-tuning. Using a straightforward, minimal Heisenberg spin model, we analyze misaligned bilayer sheets of honeycomb ferromagnets with a substantial commensurate twist angle. Our results indicate that the higher-order topology in this bilayer configuration is highly sensitive to the interlayer exchange coupling. Specifically, ferromagnetic interlayer coupling supports an SOTMI characterized by topologically protected magnon corner states, whereas antiferromagnetic interlayer coupling leads to a nodal phase in the twisted bilayer system.

When implementing lambda-calculus evaluation strategies, ensuring both correctness and efficiency are paramount. While correctness is dictated by the chosen evaluation strategy, efficiency allows for a broader design space, particularly concerning the trade-off between time and space resources. To provide a unified framework for investigating this trade-off, we present an abstract machine inspired by Girard's Geometry of Interaction (GoI) that integrates token passing with graph rewriting. We establish the soundness and completeness of this machine, termed the \emph{Dynamic GoI Machine} (DGoIM), relative to three evaluation strategies: call-by-need, left-to-right call-by-value, and right-to-left call-by-value. Furthermore, our analysis of execution time costs categorizes the DGoIM as ``efficient'' according to Accattoli's taxonomy of abstract machines.

The evolving terrain of sequencing technologies offers fresh prospects for genomics research. The combination of extended read lengths, increased throughput, enhanced base accuracy, and reduced per-base costs now renders long reads ideal for investigating polymorphic regions of the human genome, including the human leucocyte antigen (HLA) complex. This work introduces a straightforward protocol for forecasting HLA signatures from whole genome shotgun (WGS) long reads by directly streaming alignments into HLAminer. The approach is as simple as executing minimap2, scales according to the number of sequences, and works with any aligner producing SAM format output, eliminating the need to store large alignment files. I demonstrate that these predictions remain robust even when using older, less accurate WGS nanopore datasets with relatively low (10X) coverage, and I provide a step-by-step guide for predicting HLA class I and II genes from long reads generated by modern third-generation sequencing platforms.

Reconstructing 3D objects from a single 2D image remains a persistent and difficult challenge. Existing methods often struggle to accurately model complex topologies, particularly those rich in detailed edges and corners. Furthermore, previous approaches relying on synthetic training data frequently suffer from domain adaptation issues when applied to real-world scenarios. To address these limitations, this paper introduces the Dynamic Multi-branch Information Fusion Network (DmifNet), capable of recovering high-fidelity 3D shapes with arbitrary topology from a single image. Specifically, the architecture incorporates multiple side branches originating from intermediate layers to generate diverse representations, thereby enhancing the network's generalization capabilities. Additionally, the method employs Difference of Gaussians (DoG) to extract edge and corner geometry from input images, feeding this information into a dedicated side branch network to better capture these specific features. Finally, the model dynamically fuses data from all branches to produce the final predicted probability. Extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations on a large-scale public dataset confirm the validity and efficiency of our approach. The code and models are accessible at https://github.com/leilimaster/DmifNet.

This paper introduces a novel approach to the containment problem for extended regular expressions, which incorporate intersection and complement operators, and for expressions defined over potentially infinite character sets. Unlike standard methods that fail to address extended operators or infinite alphabets, the proposed algorithm bypasses the conversion to equivalent automata. Instead, it employs a purely symbolic term rewriting system to resolve regular expression inequalities. The authors present a new symbolic decision procedure for containment, utilizing Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives alongside Antimirov's rewriting technique. Furthermore, they extend Brzozowski's syntactic derivative operator into two generalized versions capable of operating on representable, potentially infinite character sets.

**Background:** Although there is a long history of laws and regulations, research ethics often remains an uncomfortable subject for many software engineering scholars. Unethical research practices can result in a loss of trust in findings, funding cuts, and publication retractions. Confidentiality is a fundamental ethical principle, with anonymization serving as a primary method to ensure it. While various guidelines exist for qualitative software engineering and general qualitative research, they often fail to explain the specific methods and rationales for anonymizing interview data. **Aims:** This paper seeks to identify ethical guidelines specifically for software engineering interview studies involving industry practitioners. **Method:** Drawing on past experiences and consulting authoritative guidelines from the more established fields of medicine and software engineering, a comprehensive set of checklists for interview studies was developed. **Results:** Key components of interview studies were identified, along with ethical considerations and recommendations for each stage, with a specific focus on anonymization. Crucial ethical principles include consent, beneficence, confidentiality, scientific value, researcher competence, justice, adherence to the law, and ethical review. **Conclusions:** The study's primary contribution is the creation of checklists for ethical interview studies. Future research is required to further refine these guidelines regarding legal implications and ethical board requirements.

Elementary excitations simplify the complex many-body dynamics of interacting particles within condensed matter by utilizing a quasiparticle framework. In magnetic materials, the most recognized quasiparticles are magnons, which exist within ordered spin structures, and spinons, their fractional analogues found in disordered but correlated spin states. This study reports the discovery of a novel elementary excitation intrinsic to spin-stripe order, identified as a bound state of two phason quasiparticles that produces a wiggling motion of magnetic moments. We have observed these excitations, termed "wigglons," in the frustrated zigzag spin-1/2 chain compound $\beta$-TeVO$_4$, where they generate distinctive low-frequency spin dynamics within the spin-stripe phase. These findings offer valuable insights into the physics of stripes in strongly-correlated electron systems.

Identifying hate speech online has emerged as a critical endeavor, given that offensive language—including hurtful, obscene, and insulting material—can negatively impact marginalized individuals and communities. This paper details the experiments and outcomes from the TU Berlin team participating in the 2021 shared task on detecting hate speech and offensive content in Indo-European languages, specifically covering subtasks 1A and 1B. The study evaluates the performance of various Natural Language Processing models across these subtasks. The team experimented with recurrent neural networks at both word and character levels, as well as transfer learning methods utilizing BERT on the competition's dataset. Among the models assessed, those employing transfer learning yielded the highest performance in both subtasks.

This paper addresses the solvability of a non-convex regular polynomial vector optimization problem defined on a nonempty closed set. We propose regularity conditions for such problems, analyzing their properties and characterizations. Assuming these conditions hold, we examine the nonemptiness and boundedness of the solution sets. Consequently, we derive two Frank-Wolfe type theorems applicable to non-convex polynomial vector optimization. Finally, the study explores the stability of solutions for this class of problems.

A theorem established by Nail H. Ibragimov in 2007 establishes a relationship between symmetries and conservation laws applicable to any differential equation. This theorem holds for any system of differential equations, provided the count of equations matches the number of dependent variables. In this study, we apply the theorem to identify conservation laws for a nonlinear system of differential equations that models HIV transmission.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) architectures aim to train several subnetworks within a single base model and average their outputs to achieve ensembling without additional cost. Although these designs have shown some success, they are inefficient regarding parameter usage. This paper demonstrates that the learned subnetworks fail to share even basic features, which restricts their viability on resource-constrained mobile and AR/VR devices. We attribute this limitation to an ill-posed component within the MIMO framework. To address this, we introduce a novel unmixing step for MIMO architectures that enables proper feature sharing among subnetworks. Preliminary experiments on CIFAR-100 indicate that this modification facilitates feature sharing and enhances performance in compact models.

This study theoretically investigates Raman scattering induced by local optical excitation of Majorana edge modes in Kitaev spin liquids and topological superconductors. Despite sharing an effective one-dimensional model, the electromagnetic coupling differs between these systems. Results show that while the Raman spectrum at low energies scales with $\omega^3$ in Kitaev spin liquids, it exhibits a gap in topological superconductors. Conversely, infrared absorption reveals a gap in Kitaev spin liquids but follows a $\sim \omega^2$ dependence in topological superconductors. This contrast suggests that the electrodynamics of Majorana edge modes is contingent upon their higher-dimensional origins. Finally, a realistic estimation of the Raman scattering intensity is provided for $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$, a proposed candidate for a Kitaev spin liquid.

In recent years, machine learning has been extensively utilized to automate audio mixing, with systems now applied to various effects like gain adjustment, equalization, and reverb. These systems can be managed via visual interfaces, audio examples, physical knobs, or semantic descriptors. Among these, using semantic descriptors or text to guide the mixing process offers an effective means for artists to convey their creative intentions. This paper investigates the innovative approach of representing such descriptors through word embeddings, which are typically derived by training neural networks on extensive written corpora. These embeddings function as the input layer for a neural network designed to translate words into specific EQ configurations. This method allows the model to generate EQ settings for semantic descriptors it has never encountered before. To assess prediction quality, we compared human EQ settings against the neural network's outputs. The findings indicate that the embedding layer successfully enables the neural network to comprehend semantic descriptors. While models incorporating embedding layers outperform those without them, their accuracy still falls short of human-generated labels.

We investigate training Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) by treating them as a discrete variable inference problem within a factor graph framework. Focusing on under-parameterized BNNs, we introduce stochastic adaptations of Belief Propagation (BP) and Survey Propagation (SP) to address the computational intractability inherent in their standard formulations. Our findings demonstrate that, relative to conventional gradient-based optimization techniques for BNNs, both stochastic BP and SP successfully identify superior parameter configurations.

This study addresses Bayesian parameter estimation by introducing a general lower bound that encompasses a subset of $f$-Divergences. We apply these findings to specific scenarios and benchmark them against existing literature. Notably, we demonstrate that bounds based on Mutual Information can be enhanced by employing alternatives such as Maximal Leakage, Hellinger divergence, or broader versions of the Hockey-Stick divergence.

Creating visualizations for patient-collected health data to facilitate discussions during clinical visits presents a significant challenge due to the diverse stakeholders involved: patients, healthcare providers, and healthcare systems. Designers must satisfy the needs of all these parties, a complexity that prevents the existence of a single, universal solution applicable to every individual. Consequently, we frame this research challenge regarding patient data communication during visits as a "wicked problem." This article outlines how the characteristics of wicked problems apply to our specific research context. We then detail the methodologies used to investigate the design space for individualized patient data visualizations. Finally, we reflect on the insights and experiences derived from this exploratory design process and conclude by calling on researchers and visualization designers to prioritize the unique individualities of both patients and healthcare providers when developing these tools.

This paper introduces a randomized greedy algorithm designed to find independent sets in $r$-uniform, $d$-regular hypergraphs $G$ containing $n$ vertices and possessing a girth $g$. Through an analysis of the expected size of the independent sets produced by this method, we establish that $\alpha(G)\geq (f(d,r)-\epsilon(g,d,r))n$. In this inequality, $\epsilon(g,d,r)$ approaches $0$ as $g$ increases toward infinity for fixed values of $d$ and $r$, while $f(d,r)$ is defined by a specific differential equation. This work generalizes previous findings by Gamarnik and Goldberg, which were limited to graphs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that when the algorithm is applied to uniform linear hypergraphs with bounded degrees, the resulting independent sets concentrate around their mean value asymptotically almost surely.

A conjugation $C$ on a separable complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ is defined as an antilinear operator that is both isometric and involutive. These notes provide a characterization of all such conjugations on the Hardy-Hilbert space $H^{2}$ over the disk, and further characterize complex symmetric Toeplitz operators associated with a specific class of these conjugations.

This paper establishes a theoretical framework for ballistic SNS sandwiches where the Josephson effect occurs independently of the proximity effect. The model incorporates constraints derived from charge conservation and the mismatch between the superconducting gap and Andreev level energy spacing, leading to updated conclusions compared to prior studies. In one-dimensional systems, the ground-state Josephson phase is not fixed at zero but can assume any value between 0 and $\pi$. When this phase reaches $\pi$, it constitutes a $\pi$ junction, a phenomenon previously recognized. Contrary to earlier predictions, the suppression of supercurrent at temperatures comparable to or exceeding the Andreev level spacing does not occur in the one-dimensional regime. Furthermore, at absolute zero, ballistic SNS sandwiches of any dimensionality do not function as weak links, resulting in unique characteristics: the absence of a Josephson plasma mode localized within the normal layer and a Meissner effect characterized by identical London penetration depths in both the normal and superconducting layers.

A novel resistive plate chamber (RPC) utilizing diamond-like carbon (DLC) thin-film resistive electrodes is currently being developed for the MEG II experiment. Designed to operate within the high-intensity, low-momentum muon beam path, this detector must achieve ultra-low mass and high-rate capabilities. Performance studies were performed on a prototype measuring 2 cm × 2 cm with a material budget of 0.1% $X_0$, focusing on minimum ionizing particle (MIP) detection efficiency, timing resolution, and performance under high-rate conditions in a low-momentum muon beam. This paper details the measured results, including data from muon rates up to 1 MHz/cm², and discusses the anticipated performance of a full-scale detector for the MEG II experiment.

Reducing models for fluid flow simulations remains a significant focus in various scientific and engineering domains. This study investigates Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs)—a novel class of continuous-depth, differentiable networks introduced by Chen et al. in 2018—as a mechanism to propagate latent-space dynamics within reduced-order models. We evaluate their performance against two classical non-intrusive techniques: methods based on proper orthogonal decomposition with radial basis function interpolation and dynamic mode decomposition. The analysis covers test cases ranging from incompressible flow around a cylinder to real-world shallow water hydrodynamics in rivers and estuaries. Results demonstrate that Neural ODEs offer an elegant framework for the stable and accurate evolution of latent-space dynamics, showing promise for extrapolatory predictions. Nevertheless, to enable their broad application in large-scale systems, substantial effort is required to accelerate training times. Achieving this will allow for a more thorough exploration of the hyperparameter space, facilitating the development of generalizable Neural ODE approximations across diverse system dynamics.

This study re-examines the significance of individual units within Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for visual recognition tasks. Through ablation experiments on CNNs trained on large-scale image datasets, we find that while removing any single unit does not degrade overall classification accuracy, it significantly impairs the accuracy of specific classes. This indicates that individual units are specialized to encode information pertinent to a subset of classes. We analyzed the correlation between the drop in accuracy following unit ablation and various unit attributes, including class selectivity and weight L1 norm. Our findings confirm that attributes like class selectivity are poor predictors of a unit's impact on global accuracy, a conclusion consistent with recent literature \cite{morcos2018importance}. However, we demonstrate that combining class selectivity with other attributes provides a strong prediction of a unit's importance to individual classes. We further assessed the effects of random rotation, batch normalization, and dropout on unit importance for specific classes. The results highlight that highly selective units are crucial for the network's classification capabilities at the class level, making the interpretation of their behavior both necessary and meaningful.

This study presents preliminary findings from a search for time-integrated CP violation in D0 → h- h+ (where h = K, π) decays, utilizing 0.6 fb⁻¹ of 2011 LHCb data. The charm meson's flavor is identified via the charge of the slow pion within the D*⁺ → D0 π⁺ and D*⁻ → D̄0 π⁻ decay chains. The difference in CP asymmetry between the D0 → K⁻ K⁺ and D0 → π⁻ π⁺ modes, defined as ΔACP = ACP(K⁻ K⁺) - ACP(π⁻ π⁺), is measured to be ΔACP = [-0.82 ± 0.21 (stat.) ± 0.11 (syst.)] %. This result deviates from the CP conservation hypothesis by 3.5 sigma.

Representing articulated shapes as weighted graphs reduces the problem of matching voxel-sets to maximal sub-graph isomorphism. By applying spectral graph theory, these graphs can be mapped into lower-dimensional spaces, allowing shape matching through the alignment of embeddings that remain invariant to pose changes. While classical graph isomorphism methods, which depend on eigenvalue ordering to align eigenspaces, struggle with large or noisy datasets, we propose a new formulation. This approach identifies the optimal alignment between two congruent K-dimensional point sets by selecting the most suitable subset of Laplacian eigenfunctions. This selection utilizes histogram-based eigenfunction signatures, providing an intelligent initialization that significantly enhances overall performance. Consequently, dense shape matching, framed as graph matching, becomes a point registration task for embeddings under orthogonal transformations, solved via unsupervised clustering and the EM algorithm. Furthermore, matching non-identical shapes by finding maximal subsets is addressed by defining a specific outlier class. Experimental results on difficult cases demonstrate that the algorithm effectively handles topological changes, shape variations, and differing sampling densities.

We utilized the mlr machine learning package to implement various multilabel classification algorithms, including binary relevance, classifier chains, nested stacking, dependent binary relevance, and stacking. These methods are compatible with any base learner available within mlr, with additional access to the multilabel variants of randomForestSRC and rFerns. Within the standardized mlr framework, all these approaches can be readily compared using diverse multilabel performance metrics and resampling techniques. Furthermore, a benchmark study involving multiple multilabel datasets was conducted to evaluate the performance of these different methods.

We investigate a one-dimensional system of interacting particles governed by a tunable bistable potential, where the double-well geometry is adjusted using a shape deformability parameter. The primary goals are to analyze how this deformability influences the order of the quantum tunneling transition and to determine the conditions under which the system's transfer-integral operator admits exact solutions related to its partition function. The potential is modeled through three distinct families of parametrized double-wells, allowing independent tuning of barrier heights and minima. Our findings indicate that the additional degree of freedom provided by the shape parameter promotes a first-order transition in quantum tunneling, supplementing the second-order transition observed in the standard $\phi^4$ model. This first-order behavior aligns with Chudnovsky's conjecture regarding the impact of barrier shape on the order of thermally assisted transitions and occurs at a specific critical value of the deformability parameter that remains consistent across all three potential families. In terms of statistical mechanics, the partition function is transformed into a spectral problem via the transfer-integral formalism. We establish a criterion for the exact integrability of the partition function, which yields precise eigenvalues and eigenfunctions for the transfer-integral operator. We provide analytical expressions for certain exact eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, utilizing the resulting ground-state wavefunctions to calculate the probability density. This density is essential for deriving thermodynamic quantities, including correlation functions and correlation lengths.

This study addresses robust multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) within cooperative communication and coordination scenarios. MARL agents, particularly those trained centrally, often lack resilience because their policies assume specific behaviors from peers rather than reacting dynamically to them. Our goal is to steer the learning process toward strategies that maintain reactivity to others' actions. By introducing social empowerment—a metric quantifying the potential influence between agents' actions—as an auxiliary reward term, we enable agents to better adapt to one another. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach yields higher rewards more rapidly and achieves superior success rates across three cooperative communication and coordination tasks.

Reference [1] claims that [2] achieved EEG classification of visual stimuli responses solely through inherent temporal correlations in EEG data and the implementation of a block design. We demonstrate that this primary assertion is significantly exaggerated and that other analyses in [1] are critically flawed due to inappropriate methodological decisions. To substantiate our counterarguments, we assessed state-of-the-art methods on the dataset from [2], achieving approximately 50% classification accuracy across 40 classes; while this is lower than the results reported in [2], it remains statistically significant. Subsequently, we examined the impact of EEG temporal correlation on classification accuracy by applying the same models in two additional experimental configurations: one replicating [1]'s rapid-design protocol and another analyzing inter-block data during blank screen intervals. In both scenarios, classification accuracy approached chance levels, contradicting the findings in [1] and suggesting that temporal correlation contributes negligibly to classification performance. Conversely, we could only replicate [1]'s results by artificially introducing temporal correlation into our data. This indicates that Li et al. [1] effectively demonstrated that their data were heavily contaminated by temporal correlation and low signal-to-noise ratios. We argue that the unusually high correlation observed by Li et al. [1] stems from their unconventional experimental design and settings, which violate fundamental cognitive neuroscience design principles, particularly the recommendation to limit experiment duration, a constraint absent in [2]. Our analysis refutes the claims regarding the "perils and pitfalls of block-design" made in [1]. Finally, we conclude by addressing various other oversimplified statements, inconsistencies, misinterpretations of machine learning concepts, speculations, and misleading assertions found in [1].

We introduce the Adaptive Projection-Gradient Descent-Shrinkage-Splitting Method (APGDSSM), a technique that combines penalty-based channel pruning with quantization-aware training (QAT). APGDSSM simultaneously optimizes weights within both quantized and sparse subspaces. By employing a shrinkage operator alongside a splitting technique, the method generates sparse weights, while the Group Lasso penalty ensures these weights translate into channel-level sparsity. Furthermore, we propose a novel complementary transformed L1 penalty designed to stabilize training during extreme compression scenarios.

The Mpemba effect describes systems where the time required for thermal relaxation does not increase or decrease consistently with the starting temperature. Consequently, a system beginning at a high temperature may reach the bath's temperature faster than an identical system starting at a warmer, yet lower, temperature. Specifically, when system dynamics are modeled by a double-well potential featuring stable and metastable states, the process unfolds in two phases: a rapid shift to local equilibrium, succeeded by a gradual adjustment of population distributions across these coarse-grained states. We have recently detected the Mpemba effect experimentally in this context, using a colloidal particle suspended in water. In this study, we demonstrate that this metastable version of the effect stems from a non-monotonic relationship between temperature and the maximum extractable work from the local-equilibrium state achieved at the conclusion of Stage 1.

Optimal experimental design (OED) is crucial for addressing uncertainty identification when experimental data is scarce. In numerous applications, the objective is to reduce the uncertainty of a specific predicted quantity of interest (QoI) derived from an inverse problem solution, rather than focusing on the model parameters themselves. To address this, we introduce an efficient goal-oriented optimal experimental design (GOOED) method tailored for large-scale Bayesian linear inverse problems, specifically targeting sensor placement to maximize expected information gain (EIG) regarding a predicted QoI. By deriving a novel formula for EIG computation and leveraging the low-rank properties of two key operators, we implement an online-offline decomposition strategy alongside a swapping greedy algorithm. This approach maximizes EIG with a computational cost, measured in model solutions, that remains independent of problem dimensions. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive error analysis of the approximated EIG and validate the proposed algorithm's efficiency, accuracy, and independence from both data and parameter dimensions through a contaminant transport inverse problem featuring an infinite-dimensional parameter field.

The study employs inelastic neutron scattering alongside *ab-initio* lattice dynamical calculations to examine phonon renormalization during the semiconductor-to-metal transition in FeSi. Time-of-flight data, collected both above and below the crossover, map a substantial portion of reciprocal space, with emphasis on the 110–001 scattering plane, while individual momentum values are analyzed in detail across varying temperatures. The results indicate that the anomalous softening of phonons observed during metallization extends beyond the high-symmetry $R$ and $\Gamma$ points; similar softening with magnitudes comparable to those at the $R$-point occurs for various modes near the $R$-point, as well as at the $M$ and $X$ points of the Brillouin zone. Density functional perturbation theory-based lattice dynamical calculations successfully reproduce the momentum dependence of this softening. Finally, the findings are discussed in the context of the semiconductor-to-metal crossover in FeSi, evaluating competing microscopic explanations such as lattice thermal disorder and electronic correlation effects.

This paper establishes explicit lower and upper bounds for the cardinality of the set of polynomials $f\in k[x]$ with degree $r\geq 2$, under the assumption of Vojta's conjecture regarding bounded degree algebraic numbers over a number field $k$. The polynomials considered must have irreducible factors with multiplicity strictly less than $s$, and their evaluations at $M$ specific points, $f(b_1),\cdots, f(b_M)$, must be $s$-powerful elements in $k^*$. The points $b_i$ are drawn from an arbitrary sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $k$ that satisfy particular conditions.

Augmented Krylov subspace techniques enhance the convergence speed of standard Krylov methods by expanding the search space with extra vectors. Widely employed in High-Performance Computing (HPC), these approaches significantly lower the count of matrix-vector products needed to construct the Krylov basis. A recent survey on subspace recycling [Soodhalter et al., GAMM-Mitt. 2020] introduced a framework encompassing a broad spectrum of such augmented methods, characterized by a two-step procedure. First, a projected problem is solved using a standard Krylov subspace or another projection technique; second, an additional projection occurs into the augmentation subspace. This study demonstrates that the projected problem in the first step possesses an equivalent unprojected formulation. Leveraging this insight, we adapt the framework to describe *unprojected* augmented Krylov subspace methods. We illustrate this with two examples: first, recovering the R$^{3}$GMRES algorithm through this perspective, and second, deriving the inaugural unprojected augmented Full Orthogonalization Method (FOM). This new method enables the recycling of information from prior system solves, leading to its designation as *unproj rFOM* (unprojected recycled FOM).

This study integrates Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) with Simultaneous Wireless Information and Power Transfer (SWIPT) by examining a novel multi-functional MIMO architecture that combines wireless sensing, communication, and power delivery. In this configuration, a single multi-antenna hybrid access point (H-AP) simultaneously communicates with a multi-antenna information decoding (ID) receiver, wirelessly charges a multi-antenna energy harvesting (EH) receiver, and conducts radar sensing via echo signals. The primary objective is to determine the fundamental performance trade-offs among sensing, communication, and powering, quantified by the estimation Cramer-Rao bound (CRB), achievable data rate, and harvested energy levels. Specifically, the analysis covers two radar target models: point targets, where the goal is angle estimation, and extended targets, requiring the estimation of the full target response matrix. For both scenarios, the achievable CRB-rate-energy (C-R-E) region is defined, and its Pareto frontier is characterized by maximizing the ID receiver's rate while satisfying constraints on sensing CRB, EH energy requirements, and H-AP transmit power limits. By employing advanced convex optimization methods, well-structured optimal transmit covariance solutions are derived for these problems. Numerical simulations demonstrate the optimal C-R-E boundary achieved by the proposed design when compared against benchmark approaches utilizing time switching and eigenmode transmission (EMT).

This work presents the technique of generic chaining and majorizing measures to regulate sequential Rademacher complexity. We connect majorizing measures to fractional covering numbers, demonstrating that these are bounded by sequential scale-sensitive dimensions in a horizon-independent manner. Furthermore, under specific complexity constraints, we derive tight control over worst-case sequential Rademacher complexity using the integral of sequential scale-sensitive dimension. Additionally, we prove a tight contraction inequality for this worst-case complexity. These findings resolve several longstanding open issues regarding the extension of classical empirical process theory to sequential settings, thereby yielding sharp results for online learning.

Power exchanges between any element within an electric energy system and the remainder of the network occur naturally, dictated by the laws of energy conservation. However, instabilities arise when the power generated by a component via local energy conversion does not precisely match the power absorbed by the rest of the system. To address and manage these instabilities, this paper extends the concept of an interaction variable to characterize various system components uniformly. This variable encapsulates aggregate system-wide impacts and establishes reference points for multi-layered distributed output feedback control. Physically, it represents instantaneous and generalized reactive power. The higher-level design employs an interactive energy state-space model to generate intermediate reactive power control signals, which serve as commands for the lower-level physical model. These commands are executed using either Feedback Linearizing Control (FBLC) or Sliding Mode Control (SMC), with sufficient stability conditions provided for both. The authors assert that this proposed design is fundamental for aligning dynamic interactions between components to ensure stability and feasibility. For illustration purposes, a simple RLC circuit with a controllable voltage source is utilized; this serves as a generalized representation of any controllable component in microgrids.

Singing voice correction (SVC) holds significant appeal for amateur vocalists. However, commercial tools often automate this process by forcing pitch contours onto equal-tempered scales, resulting in robotic-sounding outputs. Furthermore, because these tools frequently overlook rhythmic inaccuracies, users still require extensive manual intervention. This paper introduces a streamlined framework designed to automate expressive SVC by addressing both pitch and rhythm errors. Building on prior research, we incorporate advanced singing voice separation (SVS) and vocal melody extraction techniques. The SVC process involves temporally aligning a source and target audio pair, then substituting the source's pitch and rhythm with those of the target. We assess this framework through a comparative study of melody extraction that includes both subjective and objective evaluations, using this context to examine the perceptual validity of standard metrics. Our findings indicate that while these metrics yield high pitch accuracy, this does not necessarily correlate with favorable perceptual scores.

Fine-tuning contextualized representations from pre-trained language models has become a standard practice in NLP. However, these representations are susceptible to degradation, known as representation collapse, during fine-tuning, which causes instability, suboptimal performance, and poor generalization. This paper introduces a new fine-tuning method that prevents representation collapse by discouraging undesirable changes in the representations. Our approach matches or surpasses the performance of existing regularization-based fine-tuning methods across 13 language understanding tasks, including the GLUE benchmark and six additional datasets. We also demonstrate its effectiveness in low-data scenarios and robustness against label perturbation. Additionally, we extend prior research on representation collapse by proposing several metrics to quantify it. Using these metrics and previous experiments, we show that our method significantly improves the retention of representation expressive power.

The elastocaloric effect (ECE) quantifies the relationship between entropy variations and applied strain in a material. Consequently, ECE measurements offer significant insights into the entropy landscape near strain-controlled phase transitions. In ordered states where only point symmetries are broken, the bilinear coupling between the order parameter and strain allows the ECE to expose fluctuations above the critical temperature, effectively serving as a thermodynamic indicator of susceptibility. To illustrate this, we employed ECE to detect nematic fluctuations in the prototypical Fe-based superconductor Ba(Fe$_{1-x}$Co$_{x}$)$_2$As$_2$. By conducting these measurements concurrently with elastoresistivity in a multimodal setup, we achieved a direct and clear comparison of these interrelated thermodynamic and transport properties, both of which respond to nematic fluctuations. This approach revealed an unexpected doping dependence regarding the strength of nemato-elastic coupling and the magnitude of low-energy quasi-particle scattering by nematic fluctuations: as doping increases, the coupling weakens while scattering intensifies dramatically.

A LieYRep pair is defined as a combination of a Lie-Yamaguti algebra and its corresponding representation. This paper develops a cohomology theory for these pairs and identifies their linear deformations through the second cohomology group. Subsequently, we define relative Rota-Baxter-Nijenhuis structures on LieYRep pairs, explore their characteristics, and demonstrate that such a structure yields a pair of compatible relative Rota-Baxter operators under specific conditions. Finally, we establish the equivalence between $r$-matrix-Nijenhuis structures and Rota-Baxter-Nijenhuis structures within the context of Lie-Yamaguti algebras.

This work investigates the decay of the lightest Higgs boson into a vector meson ($M$) and a Z boson ($hightarrow MZ$) within the $\mu$ from $
u$ supersymmetric standard model ($\mu
u$SSM), where $M$ represents vector mesons such as $ho$, $\omega$, $\phi$, $J/\Psi$, or $\Upsilon$. Unlike the minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM), the $\mu
u$SSM incorporates three right-handed neutrino superfields, resulting in mixing between the Higgs doublets and sneutrinos. This mixing modifies both the lightest Higgs boson mass and its couplings. Relative to the standard model, the $\mu
u$SSM can generate significant new physics contributions to the decay width of $hightarrow MZ$ within appropriate parameter regions, making these effects potentially observable at the HL-LHC or other future high-energy colliders.

A left brace is defined as a triple $(\mathcal{B},+,\cdot)$ consisting of an abelian group under addition, a group under multiplication, and a left-distributivity-like condition linking the two operations. By analogy, a left $\mathscr{M}$-brace is a triple $(\mathcal{B},+,\cdot)$ where $(\mathcal{B},+)$ forms a commutative monoid, $(\mathcal{B},\cdot)$ forms a monoid, and the left distributivity axiom is satisfied. An lcm-monoid $M$ is a left-cancellative monoid in which $1$ is the sole invertible element, and every pair of elements possesses a least common multiple relative to left-divisibility. This class of lcm-monoids encompasses Gaussian, quasi-Garside, and Garside monoids. We demonstrate that any lcm-monoid generates a left $\mathscr{M}$-brace, and additionally, that every Gaussian group gives rise to a partial left brace.

Multiple-choice machine reading comprehension is a challenging task that requires a system to identify the correct option from a set of candidates based on a provided passage and question. In this task, a human or machine must read a passage-question pair and choose the single best answer from $n$ available options. There are two primary strategies for determining the correct answer: selecting the option that best matches the passage or eliminating the least suitable options. This work proposes GenNet, a neural network-based model. The approach involves generating an answer directly from the passage and then comparing it against the provided options to select the best match. For the answer generation component, we utilize the S-net model (Tan et al., 2017), which was trained on the SQuAD dataset. Our model is evaluated using the Large-scale RACE dataset (Lai et al., 2017).

Local density fluctuations near the QCD critical point are hypothesized to display power-law behavior, detectable through intermittency analysis using scaled factorial moments (SFM) in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. This study systematically examines the dependence of second-order SFMs on collision energy and centrality within Au + Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ ranging from 7.7 to 200 GeV using the UrQMD model. We estimate the noncritical background inherent in intermittency measurements and introduce a cumulative variable method to effectively eliminate these background effects. Furthermore, we assess the impact of particle detection efficiency by incorporating RHIC (STAR) experimental tracking efficiencies into the UrQMD simulations. A cell-by-cell approach is proposed for applying efficiency corrections to SFMs in experimental settings. This research offers essential guidance for background subtraction and efficiency correction techniques in the experimental determination of intermittency during the search for the QCD critical point in heavy-ion collisions.

This study introduces two generalized algorithms designed to address the variational inequality problem within Banach spaces. We subsequently demonstrate the strong convergence of the sequences produced by these algorithms under appropriate conditions. Furthermore, numerical examples implemented via MATLAB software are presented to validate the theoretical findings.

Ever since Edwin Hubble and Georges Lemaître confirmed the universe's expansion roughly a hundred years ago, the Hubble constant ($H_0$), which quantifies this expansion rate, has remained a central focus for astronomers. Beyond its intrinsic scientific value, $H_0$ is essential for deducing fundamental properties of the cosmos. Over the past ten years, a notable discrepancy has arisen between measurement techniques: those relying on nearby cosmic distances versus those targeting cosmological scales. The SH0ES team determined a local value of $H_0 = 73.2 \pm 1.3$ km sec$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, contrasting sharply with the Planck Collaboration's early-universe estimate of $H_0 = 67.4 \pm 0.5$ km sec$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, derived from cosmic microwave background data. Does this divergence suggest the well-accepted $\Lambda$CDM model is incomplete, or does it stem from unknown systematic errors? Furthermore, how should astronomers navigate these conflicting values when a specific constant is required for their work? This article reviews the current findings and explores potential modifications to the cosmological model necessary to reconcile them. Additionally, we offer a concise summary for busy researchers and provide actionable recommendations.

This study presents techniques for establishing Lyapunov stability in dynamical systems affected by disturbances with unknown distributions. Under the assumption that only a finite collection of disturbance samples is accessible and that the actual online disturbance might follow a distribution distinct from these samples, we construct an optimization framework to identify a sum-of-squares (SOS) Lyapunov function. This approach incorporates a distributionally robust constraint on the derivative of the Lyapunov function, which can be transformed into multiple SOS constraints, thereby keeping the search within the realm of SOS polynomial optimization. Furthermore, for general systems, we propose a distributionally robust chance-constrained method for searching for neural network-based Lyapunov functions. Simulations confirm the effectiveness and computational efficiency of both formulations when applied to non-linear uncertain dynamical systems.

We examine a gauged B$-$L extension of the Standard Model that remains anomaly-free when incorporating three SM-singlet Right-Handed Neutrinos (RHNs). The breaking of the $U(1)_{\rm B-L}$ symmetry grants Majorana masses to the RHNs, while subsequent electroweak symmetry breaking naturally yields tiny Majorana masses for SM-like neutrinos via the seesaw mechanism. Consequently, the heavy mass eigenstates, predominantly composed of RHNs, exhibit suppressed electroweak interactions due to their small mixing with SM neutrinos. To explore this mechanism, we analyze the pair production of heavy Majorana neutrinos mediated by the $U(1)_{\rm B-L}$ gauge boson $Z^\prime$ at the 250 GeV and 500 GeV International Linear Collider (ILC). Taking into account existing and anticipated constraints on B$-$L model parameters from resonant $Z^\prime$ searches at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), we target a definitive signature of the Majorana nature of these neutrinos: a final state containing a pair of same-sign, same-flavor leptons, minimal missing momentum, and four hadronic jets. Finally, we calculate the projected significance of this signature at the ILC.

Extracting tabular data using computer assistance has historically been a difficult and error-prone endeavor, as it requires both spectral and spatial integrity within the data. This paper explores an approach to tabular data extraction within the domain of document understanding. Addressing the diverse formats of tables commonly encountered in various documents, we propose a novel method leveraging computer vision to extract tabular information from images or from vector PDFs converted into images.

Electrons situated at the boundary between localized and itinerant behaviors give rise to exotic matter states across diverse classes of strongly correlated and quantum materials. Heavy electron metals serve as a prime example, where magnetic interactions stem from the interplay between these opposing electron limits. This duality is closely linked to the emergence of various novel quantum phenomena, including unconventional superconductivity, electronic-nematic phases, hidden order, and recently identified topological states like topological Kondo insulators, Kondo semimetals, and potential chiral superconductors. However, a major challenge remains: the archetypal Kondo lattice model, which describes this electronic dichotomy, is notoriously difficult to solve for actual materials. In this study, we demonstrate using the prototypical antiferromagnet CeIn$_3$ that a multi-orbital periodic Anderson model, informed by *ab initio* bandstructure calculations, can be simplified into a tractable Kondo-Heisenberg model that quantitatively captures magnetic interactions. We validate this simplified Hamiltonian through high-resolution neutron spectroscopy, which accurately reproduces the magnetic soft modes in CeIn$_3$—modes believed to drive unconventional superconductivity. Our findings establish a foundation for the quantitative understanding of metallic quantum states, particularly unconventional superconductivity.

Continuous outcome regression models frequently necessitate transforming the outcome variable, a step that is either determined beforehand by the user or estimated from a specific parametric family. Cumulative probability models (CPMs) offer a flexible alternative by nonparametrically estimating this transformation; however, their asymptotic properties are challenging to establish because the transformation range can be unbounded. This paper demonstrates the asymptotic behavior of CPMs applied to slightly modified data where outcomes are censored at the extremes. We establish the uniform consistency of both the estimated regression coefficients and the transformation function within the non-censored region and characterize their joint asymptotic distribution. Simulation results indicate that when only a small proportion of data are censored, the findings from this censored approach closely mirror those obtained using CPMs on the original data. Finally, we reanalyze a dataset of HIV-positive patients using CPMs to demonstrate and compare these methodologies.

There has been a persistent belief that large, dense, and cosmopolitan regions foster diverse interactions and socioeconomic mixing. However, evaluating this hypothesis has been challenging because previous methods relied on static residential data rather than capturing real-world interactions occurring at work, leisure venues, and home neighborhoods. This study introduces a novel metric for interaction segregation (IS), which quantifies the economic diversity of individuals encountered in daily life. Utilizing cell phone mobility data representing 1.6 billion interactions among 9.6 million people across the United States, we analyzed interaction segregation in 382 Metropolitan Statistical Areas (MSAs) and 2,829 counties. On average, interaction segregation is 38% lower than conventional static estimates, indicating that people primarily meet diverse others outside their home neighborhoods. Nevertheless, interaction segregation is 67% higher in the ten largest MSAs compared to small MSAs with fewer than 100,000 residents. Our findings suggest that large cities, by offering a wider array of spaces targeted at specific socioeconomic groups, may inadvertently promote rather than reduce everyday economic segregation. Conversely, this segregation-increasing trend is mitigated when interaction hubs, such as shopping malls, are strategically placed to connect diverse neighborhoods and attract individuals from various socioeconomic backgrounds. Ultimately, these results challenge a longstanding assumption in human geography and urban design, demonstrating how the built environment can both hinder and facilitate diverse human interactions.

This study systematically investigates two-proton ($2p$) radioactivity half-lives using the two-potential method, where the nuclear potential is derived via the Skyrme-Hartree-Fock approach employing the {SLy8} effective interaction. For genuine $2p$ radioactivity cases (defined by $Q_{2p} > 0$ and $Q_p < 0$, with $Q_{2p}$ and $Q_p$ representing the released energies for two-proton and one-proton decay, respectively), the standard deviation between experimental half-lives and our theoretical predictions is {0.701}. Furthermore, we extend this model to forecast the half-lives of 15 potential $2p$ radioactivity candidates with $Q_{2p} > 0$ sourced from the AME2016 atomic mass evaluation. The findings reveal a distinct linear correlation between the logarithmic $2p$ radioactivity half-lives ($\rm{log}_{10}T_{1/2}$) and the Coulomb parameters [($Z_{d}^{0.8}$+$l^{0.25}$)$Q_{2p}^{-1/2}$], which incorporate the orbital angular momentum effects proposed by Liu et al. [Chin. Phys. C \textbf{45}, 024108 (2021)]. Additionally, we compared our results with those from the generalized liquid drop model (GLDM), the effective liquid drop model (ELDM), and the Gamow-like model, finding that our predictions align consistently with the outcomes of these other models.

Code comment generation seeks to produce natural language descriptions for source code. This task is addressed through two distinct, orthogonal strategies: information retrieval (IR) and neural-based methods. Recent research has attempted to merge the strengths of these approaches by feeding retrieved similar code snippets (via IR) into a neural model, aiming to boost the neural model's handling of low-frequency words and overall performance. However, our pilot study indicates that while progress has been made, this static combination lacks generalizability and can sometimes degrade performance. To address these limitations, we propose a simple yet effective dynamic integration strategy. Rather than statically binding the two methods, our approach dynamically selects the optimal technique for each input code snippet. First, an IR-based method retrieves a similar snippet from the corpus. Next, a Cross-Encoder classifier evaluates whether this retrieved snippet is semantically relevant (a true positive). If it is, the IR-based technique is used directly; otherwise, the input is passed to the neural-based model. Evaluated on a large-scale dataset of Java projects, our method achieves a BLEU score of 25.45, representing significant improvements of 41%, 26%, and 7% over the best existing IR-based, neural-based, and combined approaches, respectively.

Occupancy modeling is a widely used method for evaluating spatial and temporal species distribution patterns while explicitly addressing measurement errors inherent in detection-nondetection data. Although numerous extensions of the basic single-species model exist to handle dynamics, multiple species or states, interactions, false positives, autocorrelation, and data integration, specialized software that is both computationally efficient and capable of fitting spatial models to large datasets remains scarce. We present the spOccupancy R package, which facilitates the fitting of single-species, multi-species, and integrated spatially-explicit occupancy models. Employing a Bayesian framework, the package utilizes Polya-Gamma data augmentation and Nearest Neighbor Gaussian Processes to ensure computational efficiency even with massive datasets. spOccupancy offers user-friendly tools for data simulation, model fitting, validation through posterior predictive checks, model comparison using information criteria and k-fold cross-validation, and out-of-sample prediction. The package's capabilities are demonstrated through a vignette, simulated data analysis, and two bird case studies: estimating the occurrence of the Black-throated Green Warbler (*Setophaga virens*) across the eastern USA and assessing species richness of a foliage-gleaning bird community in the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest, New Hampshire. Ultimately, spOccupancy provides an accessible approach to fitting various single and multi-species occupancy models, simplifying the correction of detection biases and spatial autocorrelation in species distribution models for large-scale data.

Every established string theory model can be derived from the original, purely bosonic string theory through partial fermionization, projection, and specific background Ansatz choices. This foundational bosonic theory has recently been demonstrated to characterize a target spacetime that is chirally and non-commutatively doubled and explicitly T-dual. In this work, we demonstrate that this metastring theory inherently encompasses mirror symmetry.

We introduce a novel framework for investigating the non-thermal origins of the universe's baryon asymmetry (BAU) and dark matter (DM) arising from evaporating primordial black holes (PBHs) through stochastic gravitational waves (GW) generated by PBH density fluctuations. This model employs a baryogenesis mechanism where CP-violating, out-of-equilibrium decays of a colored scalar particle—produced non-thermally at late times via PBH evaporation—generate the BAU, while the same evaporation process accounts for the non-thermal creation of superheavy DM. Unlike leptogenesis-based baryogenesis, which restricts PBH masses to approximately $\mathcal{O}(1)$ g, our approach allows for PBH masses up to $\sim\mathcal{O}(10^7)$ g by producing BAU directly below the sphaleron decoupling temperature. Consequently, the larger permissible PBH mass enables observable gravitational waves in the mHz to kHz range, originating from PBH density fluctuations, making the model testable by current and upcoming experiments such as LIGO, BBO, DECIGO, CE, and ET. Furthermore, the inclusion of new colored particles and baryon number violation offers complementary detection opportunities at laboratory facilities.

This study examines $f(R)$ gravity within the Jordan frame applied to isotropic cosmic dynamics. The primary objective is to demonstrate that, based on recent analyses of the Pantheon supernovae Ia dataset, the effective redshift-dependence of the Hubble constant can be explained through the dynamics of a non-minimally coupled scalar field arising in $f(R)$ gravity. We address this issue using both analytical and purely numerical methods, adhering to a consistent technical framework. Our results confirm that the anticipated decline of the Hubble constant with increasing redshift $z$ is guaranteed by a specific form of the scalar field potential. This potential remains approximately constant for $z \lesssim 0.3$, a condition satisfied regardless of whether it is imposed a priori in the analytical derivation or derived a posteriori through numerical simulation. Consequently, we establish that an $f(R)$ dark energy model can successfully account for the apparent variation of the Hubble constant resulting from the rescaling of the Einstein constant by the $f(R)$ scalar mode.

Despite growing evidence, the specific characteristics of dark matter remain poorly understood. If dark matter consists of weakly interacting massive particles, it would accumulate around the galactic center's black hole, creating a dense, cuspy spike. The dynamical friction generated by this spike could produce observable consequences in binary systems. We investigate extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) involving massive black holes embedded in dark matter spikes and stellar-mass objects on elliptical orbits. Our findings reveal that gravitational-wave waveforms in the frequency domain can undergo significant modifications. Specifically, dark matter tends to suppress the characteristic strain of gravitational waves at low frequencies while amplifying it at higher frequencies, with these effects becoming more pronounced as dark matter density increases. Consequently, the signal-to-noise ratio for EMRIs may be markedly diminished near $10^{-3}$ to $0.3$ Hz but significantly enhanced near $1.0$ Hz, offering greater sensitivity for future space-based gravitational-wave observatories like LISA and TAIJI. These insights hold substantial implications for the detection and parameter estimation of EMRIs.

While classical physics dictates a fixed sequence of causality for physical events, recent discoveries in quantum mechanics demonstrate that events can exist with an indefinite causal order (ICO). This study leverages an optical quantum switch to experimentally explore ICO's utility in thermodynamic processes. We simulated a system interacting with two identical thermal reservoirs under ICO conditions, successfully extracting quantum heat despite the reservoirs being in thermal equilibrium—a scenario where conventional thermal contact yields no heat flow. Furthermore, we modeled an ICO-based refrigeration cycle to examine its characteristics. Our findings indicate that circulating the system through the ICO channel multiple times enhances heat extraction per cycle, thereby improving overall refrigeration efficiency. These results highlight causal nonseparability as a potent resource for advancing quantum thermodynamic tasks.

Convergence rates in both convex and non-convex optimization rely on various constants, such as step sizes, Lyapunov function parameters, and momentum coefficients. This study introduces factorial powers as a versatile mechanism for defining the constants utilized in convergence proofs. We outline several notable properties of these sequences and demonstrate their application in convergence analyses to streamline or enhance the performance of the momentum method, accelerated gradient, and stochastic variance reduced method (SVRG).

A recently developed technique known as Asymptotic Taylor expansion (ATEM) is utilized to derive analytical expressions for eigenfunctions and numerical values for eigenvalues within the Schrödinger equation for bistable potentials. By employing optimal truncation of the Taylor series, the method yields the most accurate analytical forms for eigenfunctions and numerical results for eigenvalues. The study demonstrates that these outcomes are achieved through a straightforward algorithm designed for computer systems capable of symbolic or numerical computation. Furthermore, it is noted that ATEM generates highly accurate results that align well with established literature.

We investigate the isoperimetric problem on the real line $\mathbb{R}^1$ using a prescribed density function $f$ that dictates the measurement of area and perimeter. The analysis focuses on density functions that are symmetric, radially increasing, possess a zero-density point at the origin, and adhere to a log-concavity condition ($\left[ \log f \right]'' \leq 0$). Under these constraints, we demonstrate that isoperimetric $n$-bubbles exhibit a regular structure and can be explicitly identified for any $n$. This result extends recent findings regarding the density function $|x|^p$ and contrasts sharply with log-convex density functions, which lack such regularity.

As the Milky Way's most luminous satellite galaxy, the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) serves as a prime laboratory for studying dwarf galaxy interactions, particularly with its companion, the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC). This study aims to examine the kinematics of the LMC's outer regions via stellar proper motions to assess the effects of past interactions, such as those occurring roughly 250 million years ago. We computed proper motions utilizing multi-epoch $K_\mathrm{s}$-band images from the VISTA survey of the Magellanic Clouds (VMC), covering a time baseline of 2–5 years. By integrating VMC data with Gaia early Data Release 3 observations, we developed a novel machine learning approach to differentiate between Magellanic and Milky Way stars. This technique facilitates a more extensive and cleaner selection of fainter sources, extending below the LMC's red clump. Our investigation into the SMC's impact on the LMC's rotational field reveals evidence of stripped SMC debris. Specifically, the southeast region of the LMC exhibits slower rotation than the galaxy's overall spin. $N$-body simulations indicate that this anomaly may result from a population of stripped SMC stars in that area moving counter to the expected rotational direction.

Addressing the substantial data requirements typically associated with supervised deep learning, we demonstrate an approach to mitigate this constraint within the FIRE2019 Arabic irony detection shared task (IDAT@FIRE2019). Our method involves fine-tuning pre-trained BERT bidirectional encoders on high-quality gold data using a multi-task framework. Additionally, we enhance model performance by further pre-training BERT on domain-specific data, effectively resolving dialect mismatches present in the Google-released version. Our top-performing model achieves a macro F1 score of 82.4 and distinguishes itself by being entirely feature-engineering-free, relying solely on deep learning techniques.

The first isodynamic point stands out as a significant center within triangle geometry, designated as X(15) in the Encyclopedia of Triangle Centers. This paper reviews established findings regarding this point and introduces new properties identified through computational methods.

To efficiently learn a dynamics model for a new environment, one can adapt a model trained in a similar source environment. However, current adaptation techniques often fail when the target dataset includes transitions with dynamics that differ significantly from the source. For instance, a model trained on a rope moving in free space may struggle to adapt to a target scenario involving collisions and deformations against obstacles. Our primary insight is to enhance data efficiency by restricting model adaptation to regions where source and target dynamics are alike. In the rope example, adapting only the free-space dynamics requires far less data than attempting to adapt free-space dynamics while simultaneously learning collision dynamics. We introduce a novel adaptation method effective for these similar-dynamics regions and integrate it with existing planning techniques for unreliable dynamics to create FOCUS, a framework for data-efficient online adaptation. First, we demonstrate that our adaptation method yields statistically significant reductions in prediction error within similar-dynamics regions on simulated rope manipulation and plant watering tasks. Subsequently, we show that FOCUS enables data-efficient online learning in both simulation and real-world settings through a bimanual rope manipulation task.

This study introduces the WRWACRTS, an adaptive cubature Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoother that integrates windowing and random weighting techniques. While the Unscented Kalman Filter (WRWUKF) already serves as a nonlinear smoothing alternative, the proposed method uniquely combines windowing and random weighted estimation to estimate noise statistics. Specifically, window weights are adjusted randomly at each epoch to update the process and measurement noise covariance matrices. This WRWACRTS algorithm addresses the limitations inherent in conventional CKS methods. Furthermore, a Lyapunov function-based approach is employed to validate the algorithm's convergence, and a numerical example illustrates its performance.

The formation of doubly and triply charged allene ions was examined using coincidence spectroscopies involving electron-electron, ion-ion, electron-electron-ion, and electron-electron-ion-ion interactions (ee, ii, eei, eeii) at specific photon energies. These findings offer corroborating support for a previously suggested roaming mechanism responsible for H$_3^+$ production during double ionization. The lowest vertical double ionization energy was determined to be 28.5 eV, whereas adiabatic double ionization was not reached through vertical ionization at the neutral molecular geometry. The triple ionization energy was measured near 50 eV, consistent with theoretical models. The doubly charged parent ion remains stable up to approximately 2 eV above the threshold; beyond this point, dissociation via charge separation and double charge retention occurs with similar intensities. Fragmentation into H$^+$ and C$_3$H$_3^+$ begins immediately above the threshold as a slow, metastable decay process characterized by a mean lifetime of 130 +/- 10 ns.

This research investigates large random partitions confined within a rectangle, originating from skew Howe duality or dual Schur measures. As the rectangle's dimensions expand indefinitely, we derive: 1) limit shape theorems for the profiles that extend the Vershik--Kerov--Logan--Shepp curve; and 2) universal edge asymptotics for the initial parts, characterized by the Tracy--Widom distribution, alongside less-universal critical regime findings by Gravner, Tracy, and Widom. These results apply to a broad spectrum of Schur parameters that surpasses the Plancherel or principal specializations found in prior work, defined by two real-valued functions $f$ and $g$. Additionally, we examine connections to a Bernoulli model of (last passage) percolation.

We introduce a novel, efficient methodology for conducting Bayesian global sensitivity analysis on large-scale multivariate datasets, specifically targeting computationally intensive models featuring correlated variables. To address high computational costs, a multivariate Gaussian process serves as a surrogate for the expensive original model. By employing compactly supported correlation functions, we enhance both efficiency and performance, facilitating the creation of sparse matrices that are particularly advantageous for handling large data volumes; the optimal sparsity level is determined via cross-validation. Furthermore, the approach integrates a robust adaptive Metropolis algorithm with a parallel implementation to accelerate convergence toward the target distribution. This framework was applied to a multivariate dataset from the IMPRESSIONS Integrated Assessment Platform (IAP2), an extension of the CLIMSAVE IAP widely utilized in climate change impact, adaptation, and vulnerability studies. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and IAP2 data demonstrate that the proposed method is both efficient and accurate for performing global sensitivity analysis on complex models.

The Neural Arithmetic Logic Unit (NALU) is a neural network layer designed to master exact arithmetic operations on hidden state elements. Its objective is to achieve perfect extrapolation by internalizing the precise logic of unseen arithmetic tasks. Assessing NALU performance is complex because a single arithmetic problem often admits multiple solutions; consequently, Mean Squared Error (MSE) on single instances has traditionally been used for comparison. However, interpreting the magnitude of MSE as a correct solution and understanding model sensitivity to initialization remain difficult. We introduce a success-criterion to determine whether and when a model converges. This approach allows us to aggregate success rates across numerous initialization seeds and compute confidence intervals. We also present a generalized version of the existing arithmetic benchmark to assess model sensitivity under varying conditions. To our knowledge, this marks the first extensive evaluation of NALU and its sub-units regarding convergence. Our analysis of 4,800 experiments using the success-criterion reveals that learning arithmetic extrapolation consistently proves challenging, especially for multiplication.

This paper introduces a new image inpainting approach that leverages frequency domain information. Previous methods rely solely on spatial domain data to predict missing pixels, yet they often fail to restore high-frequency details in complex scenes, resulting in color inconsistencies, boundary artifacts, distorted patterns, and blurry textures. To address these limitations, we explore whether incorporating frequency domain information (via Discrete Fourier Transform) alongside spatial data can enhance network performance. Consequently, we propose a frequency-based deconvolution module designed to enable the network to capture global context while selectively reconstructing high-frequency components. Our method is evaluated on the CelebA, Paris Streetview, and DTD texture datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art inpainting techniques in both qualitative and quantitative assessments.

We introduce a technique for certifying nonclassical features by correlating phase-space distributions, achieved by integrating concepts of quasiprobabilities and correlation function matrices. This approach builds upon and expands recent findings derived from Chebyshev's inequality [Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 133601 (2020)]. The proposed method establishes correlations between arbitrary phase-space functions at any location within phase space, accommodating multimode systems and higher-order correlations. Additionally, it offers necessary and sufficient criteria for nonclassicality, extends applicability beyond $s$-parametrized functions, and remains experimentally feasible. To illustrate the method's efficacy, we certify quantum properties across discrete- and continuous-variable, single- and multimode, and pure- and mixed-state scenarios using solely second-order correlations and Husimi functions—distributions that inherently mimic classical probabilities. We also investigate nonlinear extensions of this framework. Consequently, we have developed a flexible and widely applicable system for revealing quantum characteristics through matrices of phase-space distributions.

Precise and reliable localization is essential for mobile agents. Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) leverages data from cameras and inertial sensors to determine position and orientation. Recently, deep learning-based VIO approaches have gained significant interest because they derive pose information through data-driven methods, eliminating the need for manually designed algorithms. However, current learning-based VIO systems typically depend on recurrent models to integrate multimodal data and process sensor signals, which often struggle with training difficulties and lack sufficient efficiency. We introduce a novel learning-based VIO framework utilizing external memory attention, which effectively and efficiently fuses visual and inertial features for state estimation. This proposed model achieves accurate and robust pose estimation, even in challenging conditions such as overcast days and water-covered terrain—scenarios where traditional VIO algorithms fail to extract visual features. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses both conventional and existing learning-based VIO baselines across various scenes.

Conventional SLAM systems rely on artificial features that lack high-level context; incorporating semantic data enhances stability and robustness beyond what hand-crafted features can offer. However, the inherent uncertainty of semantic detection networks currently limits their practical utility. To address this, we introduce a novel probability map grounded in a Gaussian distribution assumption. This approach converts binary semantic object detection into probabilistic outputs, facilitating a probabilistic data association between artificial features and semantic information. By assigning higher weights to areas of greater confidence and lower weights to the detection boundaries, the proposed algorithm mitigates uncertainty, thereby reducing its impact on nonlinear optimization. Experimental evaluations on the TUM RGB-D dataset demonstrate that our method reduces indoor positioning errors by approximately 15% compared to ORB-SLAM2, confirming its effectiveness in dynamic environments.

This paper investigates $b_5(n)$, representing the $5$-regular partitions of $n$. Leveraging the theory of modular forms, we establish multiple theorems concerning the divisibility and distribution characteristics of $b_5(n)$ modulo primes $m \geq 5$. Specifically, we demonstrate the existence of infinitely many Ramanujan-type congruences for primes $m \geq 5$.

We conducted three-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations of a galaxy within an isolated dark matter halo to track the spin parameter $a$ of a black hole (BH) as it grows through super-Eddington phases. Although this regime is thought to generate powerful jet outflows that reduce BH spin, we found that such episodes occur infrequently. Consequently, relativistic jets cannot effectively lower the spin magnitude because thin disc accretion during quasar and radio (sub-Eddington) modes consistently increases it. The interplay between super- and sub-Eddington accretion prevents a straightforward analytical formula for spin evolution due to feedback from super-Eddington events; however, an approximate expression exists for $a\lesssim0.3$ if this feedback remains weak. Ultimately, BHs beginning with low spin can reach the maximum mass, and those initially misaligned with the galactic disc experience a slight accretion boost via retrograde accretion.

This paper generalizes the a posteriori bound for block Conjugate Gradients, which was previously established in [J. Comput. Applied Math., 48 (1993), pp. 327-341] to demonstrate superlinear convergence. While maintaining the same bound structure, we apply it specifically to the block variant. Furthermore, we provide computational experiments that validate both our newly derived bound and the one presented in [SIAM Review, 47 (2005), pp. 247-272], utilizing angles between subspaces for comparison. Leveraging these bounds, we analyze the emergence of superlinear convergence and examine its dependence on eigenvalue distribution and block size.

A primary obstacle in creating accurate and computationally feasible predictive models for turbulent flows involving numerous species is the computational burden of solving individual transport equations for each species. To address this, the paper introduces an on-the-fly reduced order modeling framework for both reactive and passive transport equations, aiming to significantly lower computational costs.
