This method achieves a low-rank decomposition of species data into three time-varying elements: (i) a collection of orthonormal spatial modes, (ii) a low-rank factorization of the instantaneous species correlation matrix, and (iii) a set of orthonormal species modes that define a low-dimensional, time-dependent manifold. Unlike traditional data-driven dimension reduction techniques like principal component analysis, which require solving full-dimensional species equations to generate high-fidelity data, this approach directly extracts low-rank components from the species transport equation itself. The evolution equations governing these three components are derived from the optimality conditions of a variational principle. Because these components evolve over time, the low-rank decomposition can adapt dynamically to transient changes in the species. The paper concludes by presenting several demonstration cases involving the reduced order modeling of passive and reactive transport equations.

This brief technical note introduces a baseline for decision-aware learning in contextual linear optimization, addressing stochastic linear optimization where cost coefficients are predicted using context data. We present a decision-aware variant of the predict-then-optimize framework. By reweighting prediction errors according to the decision regret caused by an unweighted pilot cost estimator, we construct a decision-aware predictor, which is then used for optimization. This method can be viewed as a finite-difference, iterate-independent approximation of the gradients found in prior end-to-end learning algorithms, aligning with existing intuitions for such approaches. It is computationally straightforward to implement using readily available reweighted prediction oracles and linear optimization, provided that the prediction error minimization is convex. Empirical results show that this approach outperforms standard predict-then-optimize frameworks in settings with misspecified models and remains competitive with other end-to-end methods. Consequently, given its simplicity and ease of use, we recommend it as a practical baseline for end-to-end and decision-aware learning.

This paper investigates the complexity of determining isomorphism between two matroids, a problem known to reside in $\Sigma_2^p$. For linear matroids defined over polynomially bounded fields, we observe that the problem is likely not $\Sigma_2^p$-complete but remains $\co\NP$-hard. We demonstrate that when the matroid rank is constant, both linear matroid isomorphism and general matroid isomorphism are polynomial time many-one equivalent to graph isomorphism. Furthermore, we provide a polynomial time Turing reduction from graphic matroid isomorphism to graph isomorphism, which enables a deterministic polynomial time solution for testing graphic matroid isomorphism in planar graphs. By establishing a polynomial time many-one reduction from the bounded rank matroid isomorphism problem to graphic matroid isomorphism, we prove that all these problems are polynomial time equivalent. Additionally, for both linear and graphic matroids, we establish that the automorphism problem is polynomial time equivalent to the respective isomorphism problems. Finally, we present a polynomial time algorithm to test membership in the automorphism group of a graphic matroid.

This paper aims to characterize $*$-$k$-Ricci-Yamabe solitons within the framework of Kenmotsu manifolds. We have examined the properties of these solitons and determined the scalar curvature for manifolds admitting them. Furthermore, we have characterized the associated vector fields and explored applications involving torse-forming vector fields in the context of $*$-$k$-Ricci-Yamabe solitons on Kenmotsu manifolds. Additionally, we investigated gradient $\ast$-$\eta$-Einstein solitons to reveal the nature of the Riemannian curvature tensor. Finally, we provided an example of a $*$-$k$-Ricci-Yamabe soliton on a 5-dimensional Kenmotsu manifold to validate our results.

We examine the three-dimensional Dirac operator $\mathfrak{D}_{\boldsymbol{A},\Phi,Q_{\sin}}$, which incorporates variable regular magnetic and electrostatic potentials $\boldsymbol{A}$ and $\Phi$, alongside singular potentials $Q_{\sin}$ supported on a smooth, unbounded surface $\Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^{3}$ that partitions $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ into two open regions, $\Omega_{\pm}$. We define an unbounded operator $\mathcal{D}_{\boldsymbol{A},\Phi,Q_{\sin}}$ in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{C}^{4})$ derived from the regular component of $\mathfrak{D}_{\boldsymbol{A},\Phi,Q_{\sin}}$, with a domain in $H^{1}(\Omega_{+},\mathbb{C}^{4})\oplus H^{1}(\Omega_{-},\mathbb{C}^{4})$ comprising functions that adhere to transmission conditions across $\Sigma$. We investigate the self-adjointness of $\mathcal{D}_{\boldsymbol{A},\Phi,Q_{\sin}}$ for unbounded surfaces $\Sigma$ that are $C^{2}$-uniformly regular, and analyze its essential spectrum when $\Sigma$ is a $C^{2}$-surface featuring conic exits to infinity. As an application, we explore electrostatic and Lorentz scalar $\delta_{\Sigma}$-shell interactions on unbounded surfaces $\Sigma$.

Inductive logic programming (ILP) aims to find a hypothesis that generalizes training examples alongside background knowledge (BK). To enhance performance, we propose a method that identifies regions to avoid searching before the hypothesis search begins. By leveraging provided BK to derive hypothesis constraints—such as the impossibility of a number being both even and odd—we bootstrap a constraint-driven ILP system. Experiments across various domains, including program synthesis and game playing, demonstrate that our approach can (i) significantly cut learning times by as much as 97% and (ii) scale effectively to domains containing millions of facts.

Silicon vacancies in silicon carbide (SiC) are promising candidates for quantum technologies, including quantum sensing and repeaters. Given that SiC comprises various polytypes with distinct stacking sequences, and vacancies can occupy multiple lattice sites within each, this study characterizes and identifies the three most significant charged silicon vacancies in the 6H-SiC polytype. By recording photoluminescence and continuous-wave optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectra across varying radio-frequency powers and temperatures, we individually isolate the zero-phonon lines of these vacancies at low temperatures to capture their corresponding ODMR spectra. This approach enables the correlation of optical and magnetic resonance data, effectively resolving a controversy from previous research.

We integrate molecular dynamics simulations with experimental data to determine the solubilities of organic salts within complex growth environments. By simulating the growth and dissolution of ions at crystal surface kink sites across varying solution concentrations, we predict solubility. Specifically, solubility is defined as the salt concentration where the energy of an ion pair in solution matches the energy of that pair crystallized at the kink sites. We demonstrate this simulation approach using anhydrous sodium acetate crystallizing from diverse solvent-antisolvent mixtures. To validate our predictions, we conducted in-house solubility measurements of sodium acetate using a specialized protocol that ensures moisture-free conditions, a critical requirement for this hygroscopic compound. Our results show excellent agreement between the experimental data and computationally derived solubilities across the tested mixtures. Leveraging this strong correlation and the extensive data generated by simulations, we can complement experimental efforts, thereby reducing both time and capital costs in designing industrial crystallization processes for organic salts.

We demonstrate that averaged Langevin Monte Carlo produces a sample with $\varepsilon$-relative Fisher information within $O( L^2 d^2/\varepsilon^2)$ steps when sampling from a density $\pi \propto \exp(-V)$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $V$ is $L$-gradient Lipschitz but potentially non-convex. This result mirrors complexity bounds for identifying $\varepsilon$-approximate first-order stationary points in non-convex optimization, marking an initial step toward a comprehensive theory for sampling from non-log-concave distributions. Furthermore, we explore various extensions and applications, notably establishing a new state-of-the-art guarantee for sampling from distributions that satisfy a Poincaré inequality.

Injecting spin polarization rapidly into a collection of nuclear spins is a critical challenge with wide-ranging implications, from dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) to quantum information science. This study presents a method to enhance the spin injection rate by utilizing electrons that can be quickly polarized through high-power optical pumping. We validate this approach using a nitrogen-vacancy center system in diamond, where electrons transfer polarization to a bath of 13C nuclei. By delivering more than 20 watts of continuous, nearly isotropic optical power to the sample—a level significantly exceeding prior experiments—we achieve spin injection rate improvements of over two orders of magnitude via a spin-ratchet polarization transfer mechanism. Our findings clarify bottlenecks in the DNP process related to electron polarization rates, transfer efficiency to nearby nuclei, and spin diffusion. This work highlights the potential for rapid spin injection using non-thermally generated electron polarization, offering relevance to diverse systems such as DNP, quantum sensing, and spin-based MASERs.

Driven granular media serve as representative systems for studying non-equilibrium statistical physics. By drawing an analogy between the motion of granular particles and atoms, one can derive macroscopic counterparts to phase transitions. This study examines fluid-like and crystal-like two-dimensional states within a driven granular material. In our experimental setup, a tunable magnetic field generates and regulates remote interactions among the particles. We analyze the velocity fluctuations of individual particles in a stationary state using high-speed video recordings. Through statistical averaging, we observe that particles self-organize into collective excitations defined by dispersion relations in frequency-wavenumber space. These results demonstrate that mechanical waves, analogous to phonons in condensed matter, propagate through driven granular media. Specifically, weak magnetic coupling yields longitudinal waves, consistent with a fluid-like phase, whereas stronger coupling allows for both longitudinal and transverse wave propagation, characteristic of solid-like phases. We model these dispersion relations based on the spatial particle distribution and their interaction potential. Finally, by deriving equivalent sound velocities, we determine the elastic parameters of the granular assembly, effectively performing spectroscopy on the material.

This study investigates a Bose-Einstein condensate of ultracold atoms under non-Hermitian spin-orbit coupling, which exhibits the non-Hermitian skin effect due to the combined influence of spin-orbit coupling and laser-induced atom loss. The existence of this effect is verified through its characteristic signatures: spectral winding under periodic boundary conditions, the localization of eigenstates at boundaries under open conditions, and directional bulk dynamics. Specifically, we highlight that bulk dynamics offer a practical indicator for experimental observation. Furthermore, we examine the effects of interactions and trapping potentials using non-Hermitian Gross-Pitaevskii equations. Our findings demonstrate that the non-Hermitian skin effect, along with its significant implications for topology and dynamics, is experimentally accessible within the realm of current cold-atom technologies.

Machine Learning (ML) has emerged as a rapidly expanding and highly popular methodology for developing practical solutions. As a subset of ML, Deep Learning (DL) utilizes deep neural networks to emulate human brain functions, employing computer algorithms to enable machines to independently acquire specific techniques and processes, a capability often associated with Artificial Intelligence (AI). This paper examines prevailing technical challenges within software development and delivery for organizations engaged in ML initiatives. Consequently, it highlights the significance of Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) as a concept capable of addressing these concerns. We also investigate commercially available MLOps tools within the software development landscape, comparing their performance and use cases. Furthermore, we analyze the features and usability of these tools to determine the most suitable support for specific scenarios. Ultimately, we conclude that there is a scarcity of fully functional MLOps platforms capable of automating processes by minimizing human intervention.

Single-stranded (ss) RNA viruses spontaneously self-assemble in solutions comprising their viral RNA genomes and capsid proteins. The formation of empty capsids can be explained by free energy minimization within relatively simple models. However, assembling complete viral particles within an infected cell's cytoplasm requires selecting specific viral genome molecules from a vast pool of highly similar host messenger RNAs. This process is characterized by the preferential heterogeneous nucleation of capsid proteins onto viral RNA, a phenomenon known as "selective nucleation." Recently, a straightforward mathematical model was introduced to describe the selective nucleation of small ssRNA viruses. In this paper, we provide a statistical physics analysis of the model's thermal equilibrium and kinetic properties, demonstrating that it qualitatively explains numerous observations regarding the self-assembly of small ssRNA viruses.

In the current era of Big Data, there is a critical need for computationally efficient and scalable techniques to facilitate timely insights and informed decision-making. One such technique is sub-sampling, which involves analyzing a subset of data to draw inferences rather than processing the entire dataset. A central challenge in applying sub-sampling is determining how to select an informative subset that aligns with specific data queries. While recent methods address this by calculating sub-sampling probabilities for individual data points, they are limited by their reliance on an assumed model for the Big Data. To overcome this, this article introduces a model-robust approach that evaluates a collection of models, deriving sub-sampling probabilities from a weighted average of the probabilities generated by each model individually. Theoretical backing for this method is provided, and it is tested through a simulation study and two real-world applications, comparing its performance against existing sub-sampling practices. The findings demonstrate that this model-robust approach surpasses alternative methods.

This study introduces an Exponential Transient Excision Algorithm (ETEA), designed for biomedical time series analysis such as in vivo neural recordings and electrocorticography (ECoG), where measurement artifacts often manifest as piecewise exponential transients. The method is formulated as an unconstrained convex optimization problem, incorporating a smoothed L1-norm penalty for regularization and solved via the majorization-minimization (MM) approach. With minor adjustments to the regularizer, ETEA effectively suppresses more irregular piecewise smooth artifacts, including ocular artifacts (OA) in electroencephalography (EEG) data. The proposed algorithms are demonstrated using examples from synthetic signals, EEG, and ECoG datasets.

Researchers consistently seek the most precise and pertinent responses within existing literature. However, conventional scholarly digital libraries merely list documents in search results, failing to deliver exact answers; their search capabilities are limited to metadata and, at best, full-text retrieval. We introduce a methodology to enhance faceted search systems on structured content by utilizing a federation of scholarly knowledge graphs. Implemented atop a scholarly knowledge graph, this system integrates content from third-party knowledge graphs to refine the exploration of academic materials. A key innovation of our approach is the use of dynamic facets across diverse data types, allowing facets to adapt based on user queries and enabling users to adjust their granularity. Furthermore, we leverage external knowledge graphs to significantly improve the discovery of scholarly knowledge.

Entropy metrics serve as nonlinear tools for quantifying time series complexity, with permutation entropy being widely adopted for its computational efficiency and robustness. To analyze data comprising multiple time series, specialized multivariate entropy methods are required. In response, we introduce $MPE_G$, a multivariate permutation entropy method grounded in a graph-based framework. The $MPE_G$ algorithm processes a multivariate signal through two primary stages: first, it constructs a graph $G$ as the Cartesian product of $G_1$ and $G_2$, where $G_1$ retains the temporal dynamics of individual series and $G_2$ captures inter-channel relationships; second, it treats the multivariate signal as samples distributed across this regular graph $G$ and applies recently developed graph permutation entropy. This graph-based methodology offers the adaptability to handle various signal types and cross-channel interactions, effectively addressing the constraints of existing multivariate permutation entropy techniques.

Gathering adequate labeled data for human activity recognition (HAR) models is both costly and time-intensive. Furthermore, training on existing datasets often results in models biased toward the training distribution, leading to poor performance on test data with different distributions. While transfer learning and domain adaptation address this issue, they typically require access to unlabeled target domain data, a condition often unattainable in real-world scenarios. Consequently, few approaches focus on developing models capable of generalizing to unseen target domains for HAR. This paper introduces a novel method, Semantic-Discriminative Mixup (SDMix), designed for generalizable cross-domain HAR. First, we implement semantic-aware Mixup to account for activity semantic ranges, thereby mitigating inconsistencies caused by domain differences. Second, we apply large margin loss to strengthen the discriminative power of Mixup samples, preventing misclassification due to noisy virtual labels. Extensive experiments across five public datasets confirm that SDMix significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 6% in cross-person, cross-dataset, and cross-position HAR tasks.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) are considered a groundbreaking and promising technology due to their ability to adaptively shape the wireless propagation environment. However, because RIS operates as a frequency-selective device, it can only effectively provide tunable phase shifts for signals within a specific frequency band. Consequently, establishing an optimal association between base stations (BS), RIS, and users is crucial for maximizing RIS efficiency and capability in cellular networks. This paper examines an RIS-aided cellular network with the goal of maximizing the downlink sum-rate by jointly designing BS-RIS-user association, active beamforming at the BS, and passive beamforming at the RIS. To achieve this, a dynamically successive access algorithm is introduced for user association, while an iterative algorithm is employed to alternately optimize active and passive beamforming during the access process. Ultimately, the optimal BS-RIS association is determined through an exhaustive search. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm for BS-RIS-user association and beamforming design yields significant performance improvements.

Although numerous techniques have been devised to facilitate lifelong learning in standard deep neural networks, they depend on accessing a "batch" of samples repeatedly, which limits their success. While effective in static environments, these methods struggle in realistic scenarios where data arrives via \emph{online streaming}. Empirical results indicate that existing approaches falter when inputs follow a streaming protocol with two key constraints: $(i)$ instances arrive sequentially and are viewable only once, and $(ii)$ the data violates the i.i.d. assumption, often exhibiting class-based correlations. To overcome these hurdles, we introduce CIOSL, a novel framework for class-incremental learning tailored to \emph{online streaming settings}. This method utilizes both implicit and explicit dual weight regularization alongside experience replay. Implicit regularization is achieved through knowledge distillation, whereas explicit regularization employs a new strategy for parameter regularization by modeling the joint distribution of replayed buffer data and current samples. Furthermore, we develop an efficient online memory replay and replacement buffer strategy that markedly enhances model performance. Comprehensive experiments and ablation studies on challenging datasets confirm the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) demonstrates significant potential for addressing graph theory challenges, such as identifying cliques within complex networks. Notably, molecular docking—a structural approach to drug design—can be modeled as a maximum weighted clique problem, suggesting that GBS could enhance this process. However, executing quantum molecular docking requires universally programmable, large-scale quantum hardware, a capability not yet fully realized by existing advanced GBS systems. In this study, we construct a universal, software-scalable, time-bin encoded GBS photonic processor featuring adjustable squeezing parameters and the ability to execute arbitrary unitary operations via an interferometer. Using this processor, we successfully solved a clique-finding problem on a 32-node graph, achieving a probability of success approximately double that of classical sampling. Additionally, we developed a quantum-based molecular docking platform that successfully docked two clinically promising target proteins—relevant to treating cancers, neurological conditions like Alzheimer's, and inflammatory diseases such as ischaemia—with their corresponding molecules. This processor represents the current state-of-the-art in GBS circuitry, distinguished by its unique universal and programmable architecture, thereby advancing GBS toward practical real-world applications.

Building on the univalence concept for (1-)categories established by Ahrens, Kapulkin, and Shulman, we advance bicategory theory within univalent foundations by defining and analyzing univalent bicategories. To facilitate the modular construction of examples, we introduce displayed bicategories, serving as an extension of the displayed 1-categories proposed by Ahrens and Lumsdaine. We validate the utility of this framework by proving the univalence of several key bicategories, including those of univalent categories with families and pseudofunctors between univalent bicategories. Additionally, we establish that any bicategory possessing univalent hom-categories is weakly equivalent to a univalent bicategory. All these results are formalized in Coq within the UniMath library.

This research investigates anomaly clustering, which organizes data into coherent groups based on anomaly types, distinguishing it from anomaly detection that separates anomalies from normal data. Unlike object-centered image clustering, anomaly clustering is notably difficult due to the subtle and local nature of anomalous patterns. We introduce a straightforward yet effective clustering framework that leverages patch-based pretrained deep embeddings combined with standard clustering techniques. Our approach defines an image distance metric by calculating the Euclidean distance between weighted averages of embeddings, where each image is treated as a bag of embeddings. These weights determine the significance of individual patch instances, potentially emphasizing defective areas. We derive these weights either unsupervised or semi-supervised when labeled normal data is accessible. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework and its novel distance function compared to existing multiple instance or deep clustering methods. Overall, the framework achieves normalized mutual information scores of 0.451 and 0.674 on the MVTec object and texture datasets, respectively. These results further improve to 0.577 and 0.669 with a small amount of labeled normal data, significantly outperforming both baseline methods (0.244, 0.273) and state-of-the-art deep clustering approaches (0.176, 0.277).

This study examines kink-antikink collisions within a two-dimensional Lorentz-violating $\phi^4$ framework. It demonstrates that the Lorentz-violating component does not alter the linear perturbation spectrum of the standard $\phi^4$ model, meaning only a single vibrational mode persists. However, this term does influence both the frequency and spatial wave function of that mode. Consequently, established findings regarding $\phi^4$ kink-antikink interactions are modified. Using the Fourier spectral method, simulations were conducted for kink-antikink pairs with varying initial velocities and Lorentz-violating parameters. The results show that models with higher Lorentz-violating parameters exhibit lower critical velocities ($v_c$) and narrower bounce windows. Additionally, fractal patterns within the curves of maximal scalar field energy densities were observed.

The second section of the review examines the utility of Herglotz-Nevanlinna functions within material sciences, showcasing a variety of applications with explicit details and clearly defining the functions' roles. The article concludes by surveying existing generalizations of this function class, which are driven by prospective applications.

Although explainable AI (XAI) methods have proliferated, there remains a significant lack of understanding regarding the specific needs of end-users. This knowledge gap is crucial because users may require explanations that current XAI methods fail to provide. To bridge this divide and explore how explainability can enhance human-AI interaction, we conducted a study involving interviews with 20 users of Merlin, a bird-identification application. Our findings reveal that users seek practically useful information to foster better collaboration with AI. They intend to utilize XAI explanations to calibrate their trust, refine their task skills, adjust their behavior to provide superior inputs, and offer constructive feedback to developers. Additionally, we evaluated users' perceptions of existing XAI approaches, noting a preference for part-based explanations. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results and offer recommendations for the future design of XAI, with a specific focus on supporting human-AI collaboration.

This white paper outlines a strategic roadmap for artificial intelligence research and development over the coming decade and beyond. The ultimate goal is a cyber-physical ecosystem integrating natural and synthetic sense-making, where humans serve as essential components in what we term "shared intelligence." This vision relies on active inference, a framework for adaptive behavior that functions as a physics of intelligence rooted in self-organization principles. Within this framework, intelligence is defined as the ability to gather evidence for a generative model of one's environment—a process known as self-evidencing. Mathematically, this involves maximizing Bayesian model evidence through belief updating across multiple scales, including inference, learning, and model selection. Practically, self-evidencing can be achieved through variational message passing or belief propagation on factor graphs. Importantly, active inference highlights an existential drive for intelligent systems: curiosity, or the drive to resolve uncertainty. This same drive supports belief sharing among agent ensembles, where specific factors of each agent's generative model create a common reference frame. Active inference is foundational to this ecology of shared beliefs, enabling a formal description of collective intelligence based on shared narratives and objectives. Furthermore, we examine the necessary communication protocols for such an ecosystem and advocate for the creation of a shared hyper-spatial modeling language and transaction protocol as a critical initial step toward realizing this collective intelligence.

Spin-1/2 nuclear pairs exist in one singlet and three triplet states. The nuclear singlet order, defined as the difference between the singlet population and the average triplet population, often constitutes a long-lived state in solution. Various techniques have been developed to generate this order from nuclear magnetization, typically requiring modulated radiofrequency fields to drive singlet-to-triplet transitions. We demonstrate that the PulsePol sequence (Schwartz *et al.*, Science Advances **4**, eaat8978 (2018); arXiv:1710.01508) is an effective method for converting magnetization into long-lived singlet order. By adapting symmetry-based recoupling theory from magic-angle-spinning solid-state NMR, we elucidate the operation of PulsePol; specifically, the concept of riffling allows this sequence to be interpreted through symmetry-based pulse sequence theory, accounting for its robustness. Utilizing this theoretical framework, we derive several new pulse sequences for singlet-triplet excitation and conversion in solution NMR and present schemes to further enhance the robustness of these transformations.

This paper introduces LT-IRKA, an interpolatory framework designed for time-limited $H_2$ optimal model order reduction. The algorithm generates high-fidelity reduced order models for linear time-invariant (LTI) systems across finite time intervals defined as $[0, \tau]$, where $\tau$ is finite. By employing the time-limited $H_2$ norm, we establish interpolation-based optimality conditions for $H_{2,\tau}$. LT-IRKA produces a reduced order system that is nearly optimal with respect to $H_2(\tau)$, with the degree of proximity to the exact optimum quantified by errors in these interpolation-based conditions. Numerical examples illustrate how the proposed method closely adheres to time-limited optimality criteria and compare its performance against the Time-Limited Two-sided Iteration Algorithm (TL-TSIA), Time-Limited Balanced Truncation (TL-BT), Iterative Rational Krylov Algorithm (IRKA), and Time-Limited Pseudo Optimal Rational Krylov (TL-PORK) Algorithm within a finite time horizon.

This research investigates the root cause of symmetry in the fluorescence spectrum of a two-level system under low-frequency periodic modulation and near-resonant high-frequency monochromatic excitation, utilizing both analytical and numerical approaches grounded in Floquet theory. We identify that the fundamental source of spectral symmetry lies in the generalized parity of Floquet states, a property contingent upon driving parameters. Conversely, the lack of this generalized parity results in spectral asymmetry. By leveraging the concept of generalized parity, we derive specific conditions for both symmetry and asymmetry, successfully predicting these behaviors across harmonic, biharmonic, and multiharmonic modulation scenarios. Furthermore, we observe that the secular approximation commonly employed in analytical calculations can induce artificial symmetry in the spectrum, an artifact that disappears when the approximation is bypassed. This study offers a crucial insight into the origins of spectral symmetry.

The Illinois Express Quantum Network (IEQNET) is an initiative designed to achieve metro-scale quantum networking over existing optical fiber infrastructure using present-day technology. Comprising several geographically distributed sites across the Chicago metropolitan area, the network features one or more quantum nodes (Q-nodes) at each location, which represent the communication entities. These nodes generate or measure quantum signals, such as entangled photons, and exchange outcomes through standard classical communication methods. Within IEQNET, entangled photons are produced at various wavelengths and routed to specific users via optical switches. This overview details the network architecture, highlighting an Internet-inspired layered hierarchy that utilizes software-defined networking (SDN) to manage traditional wavelength routing and assignment between Q-nodes. Specifically, SDN separates the control and data planes, with the control plane operating entirely in the classical domain. The discussion covers challenges related to synchronization, calibration, network monitoring, and scheduling. A primary objective of IEQNET is to demonstrate the feasibility of coexisting control and data planes on the same fiber lines, a goal supported by tunable narrow-band optical filtering at receivers and, in certain instances, significant wavelength separation between quantum and classical channels. Ultimately, IEQNET aims to foster the development of robust and practical quantum networks by validating metro-scale communication tasks like entanglement distribution and quantum-state teleportation.

A widely investigated topic concerns how well the confidence scores generated by machine learning algorithms align with ground truth probabilities. We begin with the premise that calibration appears fundamentally at odds with class weighting, a strategy frequently used to address class imbalance or to pursue specific external goals such as cost-sensitive learning. We offer a model-based rationale for this conflict and employ our anthropomorphic model to devise a straightforward method for recovering accurate likelihoods from algorithms that are miscalibrated due to class weighting. We validate this approach using the binary pneumonia detection task from Rajpurkar, Irvin, Zhu, et al. (2017).

Face anti-spoofing (FAS) is essential for protecting face recognition systems against presentation attacks (PAs). With the emergence of increasingly realistic and novel attack types, there is a critical need to develop robust algorithms capable of detecting unknown attacks in unseen scenarios. However, deep models trained with traditional binary loss (distinguishing between bonafide and PA samples) struggle to capture intrinsic and discriminative spoofing patterns. Recently, pixel-wise supervision has been introduced for FAS to offer finer-grained cues at the pixel or patch level. This paper first provides a comprehensive review and analysis of current pixel-wise supervision methods for FAS. We then introduce a novel pyramid supervision approach that guides deep models to learn both local details and global semantics by leveraging multi-scale spatial context. Extensive experiments across five FAS benchmark datasets demonstrate that, without complex auxiliary components, the proposed pyramid supervision not only surpasses existing pixel-wise frameworks in performance but also improves model interpretability by more accurately identifying patch-level attack locations. Additionally, detailed studies were conducted to evaluate the efficacy of various architectural configurations using two types of pixel-wise supervision (binary masks and depth maps), offering valuable insights for future designs in architecture and supervision strategies.

This paper investigates the Cauchy problem for the generalized Korteweg-de Vries equation and a one-dimensional fourth-order nonlinear Schrödinger equation, establishing the global well-posedness of solutions for small, rough initial data within a specific scaling limit of modulation spaces that includes cases where the $L^{2}$ norm is infinite.

Complex models like neural networks (NNs) consist of numerous interconnected elements, making it vital to define and describe the relationships between them. Consequently, diagrams, serving as "icons of relation," have become a dominant medium for representing these intricate structures. Given the current vast variety of diagrams used to depict NN architectures, the diversity in visual choices offers a unique chance to understand which specific aspects are prioritized for communication. This philosophical investigation into NN diagrams synthesizes theories of conceptual modeling, communication, and semiotics.

This study examines the use of widely linear (WL) receivers in uplink multi-user systems employing real-valued modulation, where a multi-antenna base station serves randomly distributed single-antenna users. The focus is on massive machine-type communication (mMTC) utilizing grant-free access, necessitating support for numerous low-data-rate devices transmitting uncoordinatedly. The research analyzes four WL receiver architectures: standard WL zero-forcing (ZF) and WL minimum mean-squared error (MMSE), alongside their enhanced variants that incorporate successive interference cancellation (SIC) with channel-dependent ordering, designated as WL-ZF-SIC and WL-MMSE-SIC. Analytical expressions for outage performance are derived for the high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regime and contrasted with conventional linear (CL) receivers designed for complex-valued modulation. Regarding non-SIC receivers, results indicate that WL counterparts achieve superior diversity gain compared to CL equivalents when decoding the same user count, while offering identical diversity gain but reduced coding gain when the user count is approximately doubled. The analysis of WL-SIC receivers leverages the marginal distribution of ordered eigenvalues from a real-valued Wishart matrix. Findings demonstrate that SIC with channel-dependent ordering does not enhance diversity gain for WL receivers but rather boosts coding gain. Furthermore, the coding gain of WL-SIC receivers improves with an increasing number of users and can surpass that of CL-SIC receivers under appropriate conditions.

We investigate the equilibria of a photoresponsive nematic elastomer ribbon using a continuum theory that extends the statistical mechanics framework established by Corbett and Warner [Phys. Rev. E 78, 061701 (2008)]. We demonstrate that the spontaneous deformation triggered by light is not monotonically related to the intensity $I$. While the ribbon's deflection initially rises with increasing $I$ as anticipated, it subsequently declines and abruptly stops at a critical intensity $I_\mathrm{e}$. This threshold $I_\mathrm{e}$, situated within a hysteresis loop, signifies a first-order shape transition. Furthermore, we identify a critical ribbon length, determined solely by the material's cross-linking density, below which no deflection occurs regardless of the light intensity applied.

Building on a previous study (Dunkl and Luque, SLC 2012) that applied the theory of nonsymmetric Macdonald polynomials within Hecke algebra modules of type $A$ to modules of anti-commuting variable polynomials, this work introduces nonsymmetric Macdonald superpolynomials. These objects, parameterized by $(q,t)$ and constructed via a Yang-Baxter graph, are the focus of the current investigation, which calculates their values at specific points such as $(1,t,t^{2},\ldots)$ or $(1,t^{-1},t^{-2},\ldots)$. The derivation relies on inductive arguments based on degree and calculations involving products of Hecke algebra generators, yielding formulas expressed through $(q,t)$-hook products. Additionally, evaluations are provided for Macdonald superpolynomials exhibiting restricted symmetry and antisymmetry.

This research employed the Imperialist Competitive Algorithm (ICA) to optimize the weights and biases of a neural network designed to predict earthquake intensity on the Richter scale. The model utilized input parameters including earthquake occurrence time, epicenter latitude and longitude, focal depth, and the distance from the seismological center to both the epicenter and the focal point, all sourced from the Berkeley database. The architecture comprised two hidden layers, containing 16 and 24 neurons respectively. Utilizing ICA for training, the model achieved an average testing error of 0.0007 with a variance of 0.318. In terms of Mean Squared Error (MSE) for earthquake prediction, ICA yielded a value of 0.101, outperforming the Genetic Algorithm (GA), which resulted in an MSE of 0.115.

Despite significant advancements in multi-view learning over recent decades, the field remains challenging due to the difficulty in modeling complex correlations among different views, particularly when views are missing. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel framework called Cross Partial Multi-View Networks (CPM-Nets), designed to fully and flexibly leverage multiple partial views. We begin by formally defining completeness and versatility in multi-view representation and provide a theoretical proof of the versatility of the learned latent representations. Regarding completeness, the task of learning latent multi-view representation is specifically framed as a degradation process that mimics data transmission, allowing the optimal tradeoff between consistency and complementarity across views to be implicitly achieved. By employing an adversarial strategy, our model stably imputes missing views, ensuring that information from all views for each sample is encoded into the latent representation to further enhance completeness. Additionally, a non-parametric classification loss is incorporated to generate structured representations and prevent overfitting, granting the algorithm strong generalization capabilities in scenarios involving missing views. Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared to existing state-of-the-art methods for classification, representation learning, and data imputation.

We calculate the branching ratios for lepton flavor violating Higgs decays, specifically $H^0 \to e^{\pm} \mu^{\pm}$, $H^0 \to e^{\pm} \tau^{\pm}$, and $H^0 \to \mu^{\pm} \tau^{\pm}$, under the scenario where lepton flavor violation is mediated by scalar unparticles. Our analysis reveals that these branching ratios exhibit significant sensitivity to the unparticle scaling dimension and may attain magnitudes on the order of $10^{-4}$, particularly for heavy lepton flavor scenarios and when the scaling dimension is small.

The primary objective of this paper is to compare two distinct methodologies for modeling the deck of a suspension bridge. The first approach treats the deck as a rectangular plate, whereas the second models it as a beam for vertical deflections and as a rod for torsional deformations; we refer to the latter as the \textit{beam-rod model}. Our analysis reveals that the beam-rod model possesses a higher number of \textit{degrees of freedom} compared to the isotropic plate model, making it arguably more suitable for capturing the behavior of a real suspension bridge. To enhance the efficiency of the plate model, one potential strategy involves replacing the isotropy assumption with a more general orthotropy condition, which would increase the degrees of freedom due to a greater number of elastic parameters, thereby enabling a direct comparison between the two frameworks. We establish fundamental results for this problem, covering solution existence, uniqueness, and spectral properties. By proposing realistic values for elastic parameters, we demonstrate that both approaches yield similar responses regarding the static and dynamic behavior of the deck. This work serves as a preliminary study, as significant further research is required to formulate comprehensive models for entire suspension bridges that account not only for the deck but also for the influences of cables and hangers. Consequently, a section is dedicated to outlining potential future developments in this direction.

Quantum computing poses a significant threat to numerous currently operational cryptographic protocols. It is projected that by 2035, quantum computers will possess the capability to compromise the critical RSA2048 encryption scheme. Since blockchain technologies depend heavily on cryptographic protocols for essential sub-routines, and some of these are susceptible to quantum attacks, this paper evaluates the risk exposure of major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, Litecoin, and ZCash. The analysis concludes with a comparative assessment of these digital currencies and their underlying blockchain frameworks, highlighting their varying degrees of vulnerability to quantum threats.

Following a quench, observables in integrable systems often fail to reach standard thermal equilibrium values, instead settling into predictions made by the generalized Gibbs ensemble (GGE) [M. Rigol et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 98, 050405 (2007)]. Although the GGE has proven effective in describing observables across various one-dimensional integrable systems, the underlying reason for its efficacy remains unclear. This work presents a microcanonical formulation of the GGE and offers a justification rooted in a generalized interpretation of the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis—a concept previously utilized to explain thermalization in nonintegrable systems. We examine post-quench relaxation in one-dimensional hard-core bosons within an optical lattice, utilizing exact numerical computations for systems comprising up to 10 particles on 50 lattice sites (involving approximately 10^10 eigenstates) to confirm the validity of our methodology.

Event-driven architecture (EDA) has become a popular alternative to REST-based enterprise application development. However, there is limited understanding of how EDA affects modularity as applications evolve. Consequently, practitioners often adopt EDA without empirical evidence regarding its impact on key indicators such as separation of concerns, coupling, cohesion, complexity, and size. This article presents an exploratory study comparing EDA and REST styles in terms of modularity. The study involved developing a real-world application using both approaches across five evolution scenarios, where a new feature was added in each iteration. The resulting versions were evaluated using ten metrics. Initial findings indicate that while EDA enhanced separation of concerns, it performed worse than REST in terms of coupling, cohesion, complexity, and size. These results are promising and represent a preliminary step toward a more comprehensive empirical evaluation of EDA's benefits relative to REST.

Our results demonstrate that incorporating subnucleon scale fluctuations, as constrained by HERA diffractive $J/\Psi$ production data, substantially impacts the incoherent diffractive $J/\Psi$ production cross section in ultraperipheral heavy ion collisions. Specifically, adding these fluctuations boosts the ratio of incoherent to coherent cross sections by roughly a factor of $2$ and alters the transverse momentum spectra of the generated $J/\Psi$ for momenta exceeding the scale associated with the subnucleonic distance. Furthermore, we provide predictions for $J/\Psi$ production in such collisions at the LHC ($\sqrt{s_{NN}}=5.02\,{\rm TeV}$) and RHIC ($200\,{\rm GeV}$).

**Context and Motivation:** To establish performance and safety guarantees for automated driving systems, the operational context must be understood. The Operational Design Domain (ODD) serves as an abstraction of this context, making its definition a critical component of system development. **Question/Problem:** Significant uncertainties remain regarding how to clearly define and document the operational context within the diverse and distributed environment of the automotive industry. This case study examines the specific challenges associated with context definitions when developing perception functions that rely on machine learning. **Principal Ideas/Results:** Through a qualitative analysis of semi-structured interview data, the study reveals a lack of industry-wide standardization for context definitions, ambiguities in the processes used to derive the ODD, insufficient documentation of assumptions regarding the operational context, and a lack of engagement from function developers in defining the context. **Contribution:** The findings highlight the challenges faced by an automotive supplier in defining the operational context for machine learning-based systems. Additionally, the study gathers potential solutions from the perspective of industry practitioners.

This paper re-evaluates the weak basis invariants at low energies, originally proposed by C. Jarlskog and Branco et al., by applying constraints derived from two zero entries and the equality of arbitrary non-zero elements within the Majorana neutrino mass matrix in the flavoured basis. Such a conjecture is deemed experimentally viable, as demonstrated by recent work from S. Dev and D. Raj. The current analysis seeks to establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for CP invariance under each experimentally viable ansatz relevant to this model, alongside highlighting key implications.

Recent advancements in machine learning have been significantly driven by the availability of challenging benchmarks. Within cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) has served as a prominent testbed for centralised training with decentralised execution. However, following years of continuous algorithmic improvement, performance on SMAC has plateaued near perfection. This study presents new analysis indicating that SMAC lacks sufficient stochasticity to necessitate complex closed-loop policies; specifically, we demonstrate that open-loop policies relying solely on the timestep can achieve non-trivial win rates across many scenarios. To overcome this limitation, we introduce SMACv2, a revised benchmark featuring procedurally generated scenarios that compel agents to generalise to unseen settings drawn from the same distribution during evaluation. Our findings show that these modifications ensure the benchmark effectively requires closed-loop policies. Furthermore, evaluating state-of-the-art algorithms on SMACv2 reveals significant challenges absent in the original version. Our analysis confirms that SMACv2 rectifies the identified shortcomings of SMAC and is poised to benchmark the next generation of MARL methods. Training videos are available at https://sites.google.com/view/smacv2.

We propose an extension of special relativity within $1+3$ dimensional spacetime to accommodate superluminal inertial observers. This extension demonstrates that conventional dynamics for mechanical point-like particles are invalid, necessitating a shift to a field-theoretic approach. Consequently, we establish that field theory emerges directly as a result of this extended special relativity.

This paper introduces the concept of the $\alpha$-fractal function and its application to fractal approximation for set-valued continuous maps defined on closed and bounded intervals of real numbers. We examine several properties of these fractal functions and estimate the perturbation error between the original continuous function and its $\alpha$-fractal counterpart. Furthermore, we propose a novel definition for the graph of a set-valued function that differs from standard literature definitions, establish bounds on the fractal dimension of this new graph for specific classes of set-valued functions, and illustrate the necessity of this definition through examples. Finally, we demonstrate that the graph of an $\alpha$-fractal function under this new definition serves as an attractor for an iterated function system.

Previously, under the grand desert hypothesis, we suggested investigating supersymmetric Grand Unified Theories (GUTs) using future proton-proton (pp) colliders and the Hyper-Kamiokande experiment. In this study, we provide a detailed analysis of supersymmetric GUTs featuring gravity-mediated supersymmetry breaking. First, by examining dimension-six proton decay mediated by heavy gauge bosons, we demonstrate that the Hyper-Kamiokande experiment can probe supersymmetric GUTs with a GUT scale ($M_{GUT}$) reaching up to $1.778 \times 10^{16}$ GeV. Second, for supersymmetric GUTs where $M_{GUT} \ge 1.0 \times 10^{16}$ GeV and $M_{GUT} \ge 1.2 \times 10^{16}$ GeV, we establish that the upper limits on universal gaugino mass are 7.2 TeV and 3.5 TeV, respectively, which correspond to gluino mass upper bounds of 15 TeV and 8 TeV. We also conduct a detailed investigation of the masses for charginos, neutralinos, squarks, sleptons, and Higgs particles. Specifically, supersymmetric GUTs with $M_{GUT} \le 1.2 \times 10^{16}$ GeV are accessible via Hyper-Kamiokande, while those with $M_{GUT} \ge 1.2 \times 10^{16}$ GeV can be detected at future 100 TeV pp colliders like the ${\rm FCC}_{\rm hh}$ and SppC through gluino searches. Consequently, the ${\rm FCC}_{\rm hh}$, SppC, and Hyper-Kamiokande experiments are capable of probing supersymmetric GUTs with gravity mediation. Our earlier work indicated that supersymmetric GUTs with anomaly and gauge-mediated supersymmetry breaking also fall within the reach of these facilities. Thus, our proposal defines a clear scientific objective for the ${\rm FCC}_{\rm hh}$, SppC, and Hyper-Kamiokande experiments: to probe supersymmetric GUTs.

This research employs modulation calorimetry to investigate the heat capacity of minute quantities (ranging from 30 nanograms to 10 micrograms) of the classical spin-ice materials Dy₂Ti₂O₇ and Ho₂Ti₂O₇ within the 0.5–3 K temperature range. By utilizing modulation frequencies between 0.1 and 200 Hz, we observed a pronounced frequency dependence in the heat capacity, enabling the analysis of thermal relaxation across various timescales. Dynamic Monte Carlo simulations confirm that this specific heat response stems from the slow magnetic monopole dynamics characteristic of spin ice. Our simulations yield a timescale of 20 ms per Monte Carlo step at 4 K, contrasting with the 2.5 ms reported in earlier studies by other methods. Consequently, this work demonstrates modulation calorimetry as a flexible experimental tool for probing dynamic phenomena in frustrated magnetic systems.

MPC-in-the-Head (MitH) serves as a versatile framework for building efficient Zero Knowledge protocols for general NP-relations based on secure multiparty computation (MPC). This paper presents the first machine-checked implementation of this transformation. We start with an EasyCrypt formalization of MitH that maintains its modular design and can be adapted to any MPC protocol adhering to standard security definitions, enabling the reuse of an existing machine-checked secret-sharing-based MPC protocol. The resulting concrete ZK protocol is proven secure and correct within EasyCrypt. By employing a recently developed code extraction mechanism for EasyCrypt, we generated a formally verified implementation of the protocol and benchmarked it to assess the performance overhead introduced by our formalization choices and code extraction approach.

This paper offers a broad survey of recent advancements in operator-valued $(L^{p},L^{q})$ Fourier multipliers and the stability theory governing evolution equations. Our objective is to present a relatively accessible introduction to the core concepts, highlighting the interplay between these two fields. Additionally, we outline the application of operator-valued $(L^{p},L^{q})$ Fourier multipliers within the framework of functional calculus theory.

While transformer-based models have transformed NLP, vision, and multimodal systems, the internal mechanisms of vision and multimodal transformers remain largely obscure despite the availability of interpretability tools for NLP. Understanding these black-box architectures is increasingly vital to developing more capable and trustworthy models. To address this need, we introduce VL-InterpreT, a novel, task-agnostic tool that offers interactive visualizations for analyzing attention mechanisms and hidden representations in multimodal transformers. VL-InterpreT integrates three core functionalities: (1) tracking diverse statistics across attention heads in all layers for both vision and language components, (2) displaying cross-modal and intra-modal attentions via clear heatmaps, and (3) plotting the trajectories of vision and language token representations through transformer layers. We demonstrate the tool's capabilities by analyzing KD-VLP, an end-to-end pretraining vision-language model, on Visual Commonsense Reasoning (VCR) and WebQA benchmarks. Additionally, we share several key insights regarding multimodal transformer behaviors uncovered through our analysis.

We demonstrate that when non-negative sectional curvature (or $2$-intermediate Ricci curvature) is combined with strictly positive scalar curvature, complete non-compact two-sided stable minimal hypersurfaces in a $4$-manifold of bounded curvature must be rigid. Specifically, this result proves that no such hypersurfaces exist within a closed $4$-manifold possessing positive sectional curvature. Furthermore, our research establishes novel comparison theorems and provides diverse examples illustrating that the rigidity of stable minimal hypersurfaces does not necessarily hold under alternative curvature assumptions.

The quantum confinement of Rydberg excitons (REs) within quantum structures enables the investigation of nonlinear interactions. We provide a theoretical analysis of optical properties for a nonlinear coupling between REs in a quantum well interacting with an electromagnetic wave. Employing the Real Density Matrix Approach (RDMA), we derive analytical formulas for both linear and nonlinear absorption, alongside numerical simulations for Cu$_2$O quantum wells. Our findings outline the conditions under which quantum well confinement states appear in linear and nonlinear optical spectra. Additionally, we examine Kerr nonlinearity and self-phase modulation within this system, while also discussing and comparing Rydberg blockade effects and associated optical bleaching with existing experimental data.

The adaptable choosability of a multigraph $G$, represented as $\mathrm{ch}_a(G)$, refers to the minimum integer $k$ ensuring that for any edge labeling $\tau$ and any list assignment of size $k$ to the vertices of $G$, a list coloring $\sigma$ exists such that no edge $e=uv$ satisfies $\tau(e) = \sigma(u) = \sigma(v)$. This paper demonstrates that for a multigraph $G$ with maximum degree $\Delta$ and no cycles of length 3 or 4, the bound $\mathrm{ch}_a(G) \leq (2\sqrt{2}+o(1))\sqrt{\Delta/\ln\Delta}$ holds. Furthermore, under appropriate constraints, this same bound applies to the conflict choosability of $G$, a related parameter introduced by Dvo\v{r}\'ak, Esperet, Kang, and Ozeki [arXiv:1803.10962].

This work introduces a single-beam atomic magnetometer designed for room-temperature detection of alternating magnetic fields, utilizing the non-linear magneto-optical rotation regime of $^{85}$Rb atomic vapour. The device achieves a sensitivity of approximately 0.9 pT$/\sqrt{Hz}$ at 2 kHz with a bandwidth extending to 24 kHz. With a dynamic range of $10^6$, the sensor remains effective even within Earth's magnetic field. We characterize the signal-to-noise ratio and bandwidth for both shielded and unshielded operational modes. Additionally, a theoretical analysis of the atom-light interaction in a single-beam configuration is provided, alongside experimental investigations into the impacts of light intensity and detuning, aimed at elucidating the method's capabilities and constraints.

We establish subexponential lower bounds, specifically $2^{\Omega (n^c)}$, regarding the smoothed complexity of Howard's Policy Iteration algorithm for Markov Decision Processes. These bounds apply to both total reward and average reward criteria. Our constructions are robust, as the subexponential limit persists not only under independent random perturbations of MDP parameters (transition probabilities and rewards) but also for all arbitrary perturbations within an inverse polynomial range. Additionally, we demonstrate an exponential lower bound on the worst-case complexity for the simple reachability objective.

The paper establishes the connection between the conserved quantum properties of elementary particles and the hidden symmetries inherent in six-dimensional pseudo-Euclidean space with a (+++--) signature. These hidden symmetries are revealed through diverse representations of the space's metric, utilizing spinors and hyperbolic complex numbers. By applying the resulting symmetry groups, one can identify conserved quantum characteristics such as spin, isospin, electric and baryon charges, hypercharge, color, and flavor. Furthermore, this framework allows for the precise prediction of the exact number of these conserved quantum attributes for quarks, specifically regarding color and flavor.

Real-world complex networks are typically represented as graphs, which assume binary relationships between node pairs. However, this limitation often fails to capture the intricacies of scenarios like peer-to-peer communication, co-authorship, or social interactions, where multi-relational structures are more naturally modeled using hypergraphs. As a generalization of standard graphs, a hypergraph allows a single edge to connect any number of vertices, offering a complete representation of many-to-many networks and enabling the discovery of subtle dependencies.

Manipulating hypergraphs necessitates specialized software libraries capable of handling operations ranging from basic traversal and search to complex tasks like community detection and measure computation. This paper introduces SimpleHypergraphs.jl, a high-performance library written in Julia, alongside two novel algorithms for analyzing hypergraph properties: s-betweenness and modified label propagation. Additionally, the tool integrates various visualization methods for hypergraphs. To demonstrate practical application, we present two case studies utilizing the 2019 Yelp Challenge dataset and a collaboration network derived from the *Game of Thrones* TV series. The findings are promising, confirming that hypergraphs yield deeper insights compared to traditional graph-based approaches.

With robots increasingly operating near humans and objects, ensuring their safe and efficient performance in real-world settings is critical, especially given that environments are rarely known with perfect accuracy. Sensor noise and actuation errors further compound uncertainties arising from environmental feature estimation. This work introduces a novel method that (1) integrates these uncertainties into robot state estimation and (2) calculates the collision probability for estimated robot configurations. We derive the collision probability as an infinite series and demonstrate its convergence, while also establishing an upper bound for truncation error. Furthermore, we analyze the convergence across various robot and obstacle setups to determine the necessary number of terms. Finally, we validate our approach within two simulation domains employing a roadmap-based strategy to generate trajectories that adhere to specified collision probability limits.

Pre-trained code models have proven effective across numerous critical software engineering tasks; however, they remain susceptible to adversarial attacks where minor input perturbations cause incorrect outputs. Existing research primarily targets code models using examples that maintain operational semantics but overlooks a key criterion for generating adversarial examples: the perturbations must appear natural to human evaluators, a concept termed the "naturalness requirement." This paper introduces ALERT (nAturaLnEss AwaRe ATtack), a black-box attack designed to modify inputs so that victim models generate erroneous results. Unlike previous approaches, ALERT simultaneously preserves the operational semantics of the original inputs and ensures the natural semantic quality of the generated examples. A user study confirms that human developers consistently find ALERT-generated adversarial examples more natural than those produced by the state-of-the-art method by Zhang et al., which neglects the naturalness requirement. When attacking CodeBERT, ALERT achieves success rates of 53.62%, 27.79%, and 35.78% on three downstream tasks: vulnerability prediction, clone detection, and code authorship attribution. Against GraphCodeBERT, the approach yields average success rates of 76.95%, 7.96%, and 61.47% for the same tasks. On average, these results surpass the baseline by 14.07% and 18.56% for the two models respectively. Furthermore, we evaluated the utility of these generated examples for hardening victim models via adversarial fine-tuning, demonstrating that the accuracy of both CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT against ALERT-generated attacks improved by 87.59% and 92.32%, respectively.

Large-scale electron microscopy (EM) datasets, produced via (semi-)automated microscopes, have become the norm in the field. Due to the immense volume of data, manual examination is impractical, making automated analysis essential. Key obstacles in this process involve the necessity of annotations for interpreting biomedical images while simultaneously maintaining high-throughput capabilities. This review examines the current state-of-the-art in automated computer techniques and identifies major hurdles in analyzing cellular EM structures. It discusses advanced computer vision, deep learning, and software tools developed over the past five years for automatic biomedical image analysis, focusing on annotation, segmentation, and scalability for EM data. Integrating automated image acquisition with analysis will enable the high-throughput processing of millimeter-scale datasets at nanometer resolution.

Identifying dynamic events, such as forest fires, landslides, and avalanches, is a core challenge in scene understanding. Although current methods prioritize the reliable extraction of both static and dynamic information, there is limited research on frame selection within dynamic scene sequences. This paper introduces a deep dual descriptor approach for dynamic scene recognition based on "key frames" and "key segments." Key frames, which are few in number, capture the salient static features of the sequence by reflecting its overall feature distribution. Conversely, key segments, extracted from the regions surrounding each key frame, enhance discrimination by utilizing dynamic patterns observed within short time intervals. Our methodology leverages two types of transferred convolutional neural network features: a fully connected layer handles the selection of key frames and segments, while a convolutional layer describes them. Experiments conducted on public datasets and a newly created dataset comprising 23 dynamic scene classes (10 videos per class) demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Database accesses occurring simultaneously are typically managed through transactions to ensure isolation from other concurrent processes and fault tolerance. Contemporary database systems offer transactions with diverse semantic guarantees, reflecting various trade-offs between consistency and availability. Because weaker consistency models generally yield superior performance, a critical challenge is determining the minimum consistency level required by a specific program to meet its specification. To address this, we examine whether a program exhibits identical behavioral sets when its consistency model is relaxed to a weaker one; this characteristic, termed robustness, ensures that program specifications remain valid under such relaxation. Our analysis focuses on robustness for consistency models weaker than standard serializability, specifically causal consistency, prefix consistency, and snapshot isolation. We demonstrate that verifying robustness between these models can be reduced in polynomial time to a state reachability problem under serializability. Leveraging this reduction, we develop a practical proof technique grounded in Lipton's reduction theory to establish program robustness. Furthermore, we have successfully applied these methods to several complex applications found in distributed systems and database literature.

As blockchain technology becomes increasingly integrated into enterprise systems, there is growing demand for specialized testing solutions tailored to blockchain-based software. With these applications moving into production environments, it is crucial to adhere to sound engineering practices, guarantee adequate testing coverage, and evaluate system readiness. Current research seeks to tackle the unique testing challenges inherent to blockchain software by offering appropriate methodologies and tools; however, given that this is an emerging field, robust best practices and testing instruments are not yet fully mature. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of testing for Blockchain-based Applications (BC-Apps). Initially, we examine the specific challenges associated with testing BC-Apps. Subsequently, employing a layered approach, we review state-of-the-art testing efforts within blockchain technology, outlining existing tools and techniques that address either individual components across various layers of the BC-App stack or the entire stack holistically. Furthermore, we propose future research directions derived from identified testing challenges and gaps in the current literature. Additionally, we reflect on the distinct nature of blockchain software development, noting why certain existing tools and techniques fall short, and advocate for the establishment of standardized testing procedures for BC-Apps. Ultimately, our study aims to underscore the significance of testing in blockchain software development and to establish a foundation for disciplined, testable, and verifiable practices.

We explore various graphical models to build optimal portfolios. Techniques including PCA-KMeans, autoencoders, dynamic clustering, and structural learning are capable of capturing time-varying patterns within the covariance matrix, thereby enabling the development of robust and optimal portfolios. Upon comparing the outcomes of these models against baseline approaches, we observed that, in numerous instances, our graphical strategies delivered consistent returns with reduced risk, ultimately surpassing the performance of the S&P 500 index. This study indicates that graphical models can effectively identify temporal dependencies in time series data and demonstrate significant utility in asset management.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), including architectures like ResNet and EfficientNet, have substantially advanced image processing tasks such as classification and object detection, often achieving top-tier performance on various datasets upon release. A pivotal element in training these networks is regularization, which mitigates overfitting. This study evaluates several regularization techniques introduced in recent years, demonstrating notable gains across different CNN models. These methods are categorized into three primary domains: "data augmentation," which modifies input data; "internal changes," which alter feature maps or kernels generated within the network; and "label," which involves transforming input labels. This survey distinguishes itself from existing reviews in two key ways: first, it exclusively includes papers published within the last five years, and second, it prioritizes reproducibility by featuring only those works where code is publicly available or has been implemented in frameworks like TensorFlow or PyTorch.

We present a robust numerical approach for second-order linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that exhibit solutions transitioning between highly oscillatory and slowly varying behaviors. Within oscillatory segments, the solution is constructed using a nonoscillatory phase function that satisfies a nonlinear Riccati equation. To approximate this phase function, we introduce a defect-correction iteration yielding an asymptotic series, which is then discretized on a Chebyshev grid using a minimal number of nodes. For analytic coefficients, we demonstrate that each iteration, up to a specific limit, decreases the residual by a factor proportional to the local frequency. The algorithm dynamically adjusts both step size and methodology, reverting to a standard spectral collocation technique in non-oscillatory areas. Numerical results indicate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art oscillatory solvers, particularly at low-to-intermediate frequencies and stringent tolerances, where it requires up to $10^6$ times fewer function evaluations. Furthermore, even in high-frequency scenarios, our implementation achieves an average speedup of tenfold compared to other specialized solvers.

We establish the existence of Ulrich line bundles on the plane $X_n$, blown up at $n$ general points, with respect to a line bundle defined by curves of degree $m$ that pass simply through these points, where $m\leq 2\sqrt{n}$ and the bundle is very ample on $X_n$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the count of such Ulrich line bundles grows without bound as $n$ increases. Additionally, we prove the existence of slope-stable rank-$r$ Ulrich vector bundles on $X_n$ for all $n\geq 2$ and any $r \geq 1$, and we calculate the dimensions of their corresponding moduli spaces. These results lead to the conclusion that $X_n$ is {Ulrich wild}.

The advancement of Web browsers is primarily driven by the growing demand for sophisticated Web applications. Contemporary needs for Rich Internet Applications, including data integration and background processing, highlight the necessity of treating Web applications as a coordinated effort across multiple browser execution contexts. Because developing such applications relies heavily on cross-context communication, numerous browser primitives and client-side frameworks have emerged to facilitate this interaction. This paper offers a systematic categorization of these cross-context communication systems within Web browsers. By analyzing prior research, the specific requirements of modern Web applications, and existing solutions, we derive a framework for classifying these communication mechanisms. Leveraging this framework, we assess the current landscape of cross-context communication and propose potential directions for future research and engineering in the Web domain.

Despite constraints such as a fixed camera view, body rate limitations, and response delays measured in hundreds of milliseconds, humans consistently outperform algorithms in drone racing. Gaining insight into how human pilots interpret dynamic visual cues to select motor commands could offer crucial solutions for vision-based autonomous navigation challenges. This study examines the link between eye movements, control actions, and flight performance within a drone racing context. Data was gathered from 21 seasoned pilots using a high-fidelity simulator, which was also employed to recruit professionals. The findings indicate that performance improves over time through task-specific adaptation. Specifically, eye gaze anticipates future waypoints (gates), with initial fixations averaging 1.5 seconds and 16 meters prior to arrival. Furthermore, pilots consistently direct their gaze toward the interior of the upcoming flight path to manage both lateral and vertical maneuvers. A strong correlation was observed between eye movements and commanded flight direction, with a mean visual-motor latency of 220 ms. These outcomes underscore the significance of coordinated eye movements in human-operated drone racing, and the dataset is now made publicly available.

J.-M. Hwang [8] previously employed the variety of minimal rational tangents linked to Hecke curves to establish the simplicity of the tangent bundle on the moduli space of vector bundles over a curve. This paper extends that approach by utilizing the tangent maps of symplectic and orthogonal Hecke curves to demonstrate an analogous result for symplectic and orthogonal bundles. Specifically, we prove the nondegeneracy of the associated variety of minimal rational tangents, which in turn implies the simplicity of the tangent bundle on the moduli spaces of these bundles over a curve. Furthermore, we show that for sufficiently large genus, the tangent map constitutes an embedding for a general symplectic or orthogonal bundle.

Accurately compiling statistics for vast amounts of IP address data is a critical component of network traffic measurement. These statistical findings are vital for assessing how user behaviors influence network loads, necessitating algorithms that can store and retrieve massive IP datasets within strict time and memory limits. This paper introduces two efficient algorithms designed to collect large-scale IP statistics while optimizing the trade-off between execution speed and memory usage. The proposed approaches leverage the sparsity inherent in IP statistics to construct hash functions and sustain a dynamic equilibrium among layered memory blocks. The first method utilizes two layers, each comprising a finite set of memory blocks; on a 64-bit system, every block holds 256 elements with a size of $256 \times 8$ bytes. Unlike standard hash mapping functions, these solutions eliminate costly hash collisions entirely while preserving linear time complexity. Furthermore, the mechanism adaptively adjusts hash index length based on the IP address range, effectively balancing temporal and spatial constraints. Additionally, an efficient parallel framework is introduced to accelerate statistical collection. Experimental evaluations on multiple synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed methods significantly surpass baseline approaches in both time and memory efficiency.

We introduce Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) architectures inspired by Echo State Networks (ESN), where specific recurrent neural network (RNN) layers are randomly initialized and remain untrained. Focusing on RNN-T and Conformer models, we demonstrate that model performance remains stable even when the decoder is fully randomized. Additionally, this approach allows for more efficient training since the decoder weights do not require updates. Conversely, randomizing the encoders degrades model quality, suggesting that optimizing encoders to learn effective acoustic representations is crucial for speech recognition. In summary, we question the standard practice of training every component of an ASR model, showing that ESN-based designs can match the performance of fully trainable counterparts while offering advantages in training efficiency and storage requirements.

This paper presents a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in microwave-based wireless energy transfer (WET) and their integration with wireless communications.
