Our analysis is structured into three main sections: first, we examine current WET technologies and the signal processing methods used to optimize energy transfer efficiency; second, we explore the concept of simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT), which enables the joint transmission of energy and data via a single radio waveform; and third, we review progress in wireless powered communication networks (WPCN), where devices operate using power harvested through WET. Additionally, we discuss potential extensions and future research directions for each of these domains.

Contemporary smart grids depend on advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) networks to handle monitoring and billing, yet this method remains vulnerable to cyberattacks involving electricity theft. Unlike prior studies that employ shallow, static, and customer-specific detection mechanisms, this paper introduces a generalized electricity theft detector based on deep recurrent neural networks (RNNs). By leveraging the time-series characteristics of customer consumption data through a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-RNN, the proposed model significantly enhances detection efficacy. Furthermore, during its training phase, the detector utilizes random search analysis to optimize hyper-parameters. Extensive evaluations using real-world data from 200 customers spanning 107,200 days of energy usage confirm that the proposed detector outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions.

High-fidelity partial differential equation (PDE) solvers are often impractical for time-sensitive tasks due to their extended runtimes. To address this, we introduce reduced-order modeling (ROM) to accelerate PDE solving. Unlike traditional ROM techniques that lower the dimensionality of discretized vector fields, our continuous reduced-order modeling (CROM) method constructs a smooth, low-dimensional manifold directly from the continuous vector fields, bypassing discretization entirely. We represent this reduced manifold using continuously differentiable neural fields capable of training on any available numerical solutions of the continuous system, regardless of the specific methods or discretizations used to generate them. We validated CROM across a broad spectrum of PDEs using training data derived from voxel grids, meshes, and point clouds. In comparison to previous discretization-dependent ROM approaches, such as linear subspace proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and nonlinear manifold neural-network-based autoencoders, CROM offers superior accuracy, reduced memory usage, dynamically adjustable resolutions, and universal applicability across any discretization scheme. For equivalent latent space dimensions, CROM achieves 79× and 49× higher accuracy, along with 39× and 132× smaller memory footprints, compared to POD and autoencoder methods, respectively. Furthermore, experiments indicate wall-clock speedups of 109× and 89× over unreduced models when running on CPUs and GPUs.

We examine the Langevin process defined by a vector of positions and momenta in $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^d$, where $\mathcal O$ denotes a bounded, connected, and $\mathcal{C}^2$ open subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$. Recent studies have established the existence and uniqueness of a quasi-stationary distribution (QSD) for this process on the domain $D:=\mathcal{O}\times\mathbb{R}^d$. This article investigates the overdamped limit of such a QSD, specifically as the friction coefficient approaches infinity. Our main result demonstrates that the position marginal of this limiting distribution corresponds to the QSD of the overdamped Langevin process restricted to the domain $\mathcal{O}$.

This study introduces a novel method for high-resolution, online isotopic analysis of liquid water, specifically designed for ice core research. The setup integrates a Wavelength Scanned Cavity Ring Down Spectrometer (WS-CRDS) from Picarro Inc. with a Continuous Flow Analysis (CFA) system. This configuration enables the simultaneous, continuous measurement of $\delta^{18}$O and $\delta$D in liquid water generated by melting an ice rod. Sub-microliter water samples are injected via a fused silica capillary and instantly vaporized with 100% efficiency in a custom-built oven. A specific calibration protocol ensures data reporting on the VSMOW–SLAP scale. Spectral analysis reveals combined system uncertainties below 0.1 permil for $\delta^{18}$O and 0.5 permil for $\delta$D, matching the precision of mass spectrometry. While sample dispersion in transfer lines restricts temporal resolution, an optimal filtering method is applied to correct smoothing effects in measured profiles. Given the technique's benefits—including simultaneous isotope and potential chemical analysis, reduced power consumption, and faster processing—it is proposed as a viable alternative to traditional isotope ratio mass spectrometry for field-based ice core studies. Field data collected during the 2010 NEEM deep ice core drilling project in North Greenland are presented as proof of concept.

This study reports a search for a heavy resonance decaying into a top quark and a W boson within proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. Utilizing data collected by the CMS detector at the LHC with an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$, the analysis reconstructs the top quark as a single jet and the W boson via its decay into an electron or muon paired with a neutrino. Identification of jets originating from the collimated top quark decay employs a tagging method combining variable-distance jet clustering with simultaneous grooming. Results are evaluated against two benchmark scenarios: an excited bottom quark ($b^*$) and a vector-like quark ($B$). By statistically combining these findings with a prior CMS search in the all-hadronic channel, upper limits on the cross sections for both models are established. This new analysis extends the sensitivity to lower resonance masses, reaching down to 0.7 TeV from the previous lower bound of 1.4 TeV. At a 95% confidence level, $b^*$ masses up to 3.0 TeV are excluded for left-handed and right-handed couplings, and up to 3.2 TeV for vector-like couplings. These observed limits constitute the tightest constraints to date on the $b^*$ model.

Sample-efficient generalization in reinforcement learning has long remained a challenge, particularly within complex environments containing numerous elements. This paper presents Plug and Play Markov Decision Processes, an object-centric framework enabling the zero-shot integration of novel objects from established classes. By decomposing global transition dynamics into a union of local functions—each corresponding to an active object—the system allows transition dynamics for specific object classes to be pre-learned and immediately deployed in new settings. Furthermore, each object possesses its own reward function; without a centralized reward structure, adding or removing objects is handled efficiently by updating only the relevant object-specific rewards, supported by a proposed transfer learning mechanism to adapt these rewards. Experimental results demonstrate that this representation achieves sample efficiency across diverse configurations.

The international Muon Ionization Cooling Experiment (MICE) will conduct a systematic study of ionization cooling using muon beams with momenta ranging from 140 to 240 MeV/c at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory's ISIS facility. To ensure the accuracy of these measurements, MICE requires a pure muon sample passing through the apparatus; consequently, the MICE Muon Beam is engineered to provide a beam with less than approximately 1% contamination. The final selection of muons is achieved through a particle-identification (PID) system positioned both upstream and downstream of the cooling cell, which comprises time-of-flight hodoscopes, threshold-Cherenkov counters, and calorimetry. This study establishes an upper limit for pion contamination of $f_\pi < 1.4\%$ at 90% C.L., accounting for systematic uncertainties. Thus, the MICE Muon Beam successfully satisfies the strict pion-contamination criteria necessary for investigating ionization cooling.

The emission of electromagnetic energy from electric or magnetic multipole sources can be altered by their immediate surroundings. This study demonstrates that a magneto-optical environment surrounding an unpolarized dipole source generates the emission of angular momentum into space, a process enhanced by the Purcell effect.

Azimuthal asymmetries, such as crescent-shaped dust rings in protoplanetary disks around young stars, are frequently interpreted as dust traps and potential sites for planetesimal and planet formation. However, it remains debated whether these traps effectively facilitate planetesimal formation around very-low-mass stars (VLMs, with masses $\lesssim$0.2~$M_\odot$), given the extended dynamical and grain growth timescales in these systems. To investigate grain growth in such environments, we observed the crescent dust ring around the VLM star ZZ~Tau~IRS using the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA) at centimeter wavelengths. Significant signals were detected around ZZ~Tau~IRS. By comparing the observed spectral energy distribution (SED) with models predicting SEDs for various maximum grain sizes ($a_{\rm max}$) derived from radiative transfer calculations, we estimated $a_{\rm max}$ to be $\gtrsim$~1~mm in the crescent and $\lesssim$~60~$\mu$m in the ring, although our modeling depends on uncertain dust properties. Our findings indicate that grain growth has occurred in the ZZ~Tau~IRS disk relative to the sub-micron-sized grains typical of the interstellar medium. Furthermore, planet formation within the crescent, containing mm-sized pebbles, may proceed more efficiently than in regions with only sub-millimeter-sized pebbles under pebble accretion scenarios.

This paper offers a systematic literature review of image datasets dedicated to document image analysis, with a specific emphasis on historical materials like handwritten manuscripts and early printed works. Locating suitable datasets is a vital prerequisite for advancing research utilizing various machine learning algorithms. However, the task is challenging due to the immense diversity in actual data (including scripts, tasks, dates, support systems, and deterioration levels), varied data and label formats, and inconsistent evaluation processes and benchmarks. This study addresses that gap through a meta-analysis of existing resources. Following a systematic selection process aligned with PRISMA guidelines, 65 studies were identified based on criteria such as publication year, number of implemented methods, algorithm reliability, dataset size, and journal venue. Each study is categorized into one of three pre-defined tasks: document classification, layout structure, or content analysis. The paper details statistics, document types, languages, tasks, input visual characteristics, and ground truth information for every dataset, alongside benchmark tasks and results from these papers or recent competitions. Furthermore, the authors discuss current gaps and challenges within the field. They recommend the development of conversion tools for common formats (e.g., COCO format for computer vision) and advocate for the provision of multiple evaluation metrics rather than a single one to ensure comparability across studies.

This study experimentally explores 2D phase transitions within a quasi-2D granular fluid. By employing a surface featuring periodically spaced dimples, we detected interfacial tension between coexisting liquid and crystal phases. Analysis of orientational and translational order parameters, along with their susceptibilities, reveals that surface topography shifts the phase transition from a two-step continuous process to a first-order liquid-crystal transition. The competition between boundary inelasticity and geometry, which can either facilitate or hinder ordering, governs the wetting behavior of the granular crystal/fluid system. This order-induced wetting mechanism has significant implications, dictating the spatial separation of coexisting phases.

Wave interference is a fundamental concept in physics, easily extended to scenarios involving more than two waves. The "order" of interference is determined by the number of interfering paths that cannot be simplified into lower-order patterns. For instance, second-order interference implies that in a triple-slit setup, the resulting pattern with all three slits open can be derived solely from the pairwise interference patterns of the individual slits. While quantum mechanics is frequently cited as exhibiting only second-order interference, this holds true only under specific conditions, such as single-particle systems undergoing linear evolution. This study experimentally demonstrates that nonlinear evolution can indeed produce higher-order interference. Within our experimental framework, this phenomenon is described simply by optical coherent states interacting within a nonlinear medium. Consequently, our findings suggest that nonlinear evolution may create a loophole for experiments designed to validate Born's rule by excluding higher-order interference.

This work investigates the complexity of computing edge connectivity in simple graphs using cut queries. We establish two main findings: first, a bounded-error randomized algorithm achieves this with $O(n)$ cut queries, and second, a bounded-error quantum algorithm accomplishes it with $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ queries. These results rely on a novel method termed "star contraction," which randomly contracts edges while maintaining non-trivial minimum cuts. Unlike the 2-out contraction technique proposed by Ghaffari, Nowicki, and Thorup [SODA'20], star contraction exclusively contracts vertex-disjoint star subgraphs, enabling efficient implementation through cut queries. The $O(n)$ randomized bound improves upon the previous $O(n\log^3 n)$ limit set by Rubinstein, Schramm, and Weinberg [ITCS'18] and was previously unknown even for basic connectivity. Under the conjecture that the randomized communication complexity of connectivity is $\Omega(n\log n)$—an open problem since Babai, Frankl, and Simon [FOCS'86]—this bound is tight. Furthermore, it rules out using edge connectivity on simple graphs to derive a superlinear randomized query lower bound for minimizing symmetric submodular functions. The quantum result provides a nearly-quadratic separation from randomized complexity, resolving an open question raised by Lee, Santha, and Zhang [SODA'21]. Additionally, the algorithm can be interpreted as performing $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ matrix-vector multiplication queries on the adjacency matrix. Finally, we apply star contraction beyond the cut query model by creating a one-pass semi-streaming algorithm for edge connectivity in the vertex arrival model, contrasting with the two-pass requirement for the edge arrival model.

We introduce a shared task focused on training instance selection for few-shot neural text generation. While large-scale pretrained language models have significantly advanced few-shot text generation capabilities, prior research has predominantly relied on random sampling to choose few-shot training examples, largely neglecting the impact of selection strategies on model performance. Investigating these strategies can optimize annotation budget utilization in downstream tasks and improve the benchmarking of few-shot generative models. We invite submissions that detail proposed selection strategies and analyze their effects on generation quality.

Building recommendation systems for fashion imagery is difficult because of the inherent ambiguity regarding the specific criteria users prioritize. One effective strategy to address this is to present multiple images, each matching the query based on a distinct feature or component. While existing fashion recommendation research has employed Siamese networks for similar pairs or Triplet networks for similar-dissimilar triplets, these approaches fail to provide fundamental insights, such as the degree of similarity between two clothing items or the specific parts responsible for that similarity. This paper introduces a method that explicitly learns and leverages part-based similarity. We propose a novel framework that extracts discriminative features from weakly-supervised data by integrating visual attention mechanisms over specific parts with a texture encoding network. Our results demonstrate that the learned features outperform state-of-the-art methods on retrieval tasks using the DeepFashion dataset. Furthermore, we apply this model to recommend fashion images that exhibit explicit variations based on the similarity of individual parts.

The LHCb experiment, utilizing 3.0 fb⁻¹ of proton-proton collision data collected in 2011 and 2012, has observed the $B^{-}\to D^{+}K^{-}\pi^{-}$ decay. The measured branching fraction is ${\cal B}(B^{-}\to D^{+}K^{-}\pi^{-}) = (7.31 \pm 0.19 \pm 0.22 \pm 0.39) \times 10^{-5}$, where the uncertainties correspond to statistical, systematic, and normalisation channel ($B^{-}\to D^{+}\pi^{-}\pi^{-}$) contributions, respectively. An amplitude analysis of the resonant structure within this decay quantifies the contributions from quasi-two-body processes involving $D_{0}^{*}(2400)^{0}$, $D_{2}^{*}(2460)^{0}$, and $D_{J}^{*}(2760)^{0}$ resonances alongside nonresonant sources. Furthermore, the analysis establishes that the $D_{J}^{*}(2760)^{0}$ resonance possesses a spin of 1.

We examined the pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) utilized within the Linux kernel, which also underpins Android, and established that it is cryptographically weak. The prandom PRNG serves numerous components across the kernel, with our analysis focusing on three specific network-level consumers: UDP source port generation, IPv6 flow label generation, and IPv4 identification (ID) generation. Because this flawed PRNG is shared among these consumers, it allows for "cross-layer attacks" targeting the Linux kernel. In such attacks, we deduce the internal state of the prandom PRNG from one OSI layer to either predict values generated by another layer or correlate them with states inferred from other protocols.

Leveraging this methodology, we developed a highly efficient DNS cache poisoning attack against Linux systems. By gathering TCP/IPv6 flow labels, UDP source ports, or TCP/IPv4 IP IDs, we reconstruct the internal PRNG state to predict outbound DNS query source ports, accelerating the attack by a factor of 3,000 to 6,000. This attack functions remotely and can also be executed locally across different Linux users and containers; depending on the resolver configuration, it can inject arbitrary DNS records into the cache. Furthermore, this approach enables the identification and tracking of Linux and Android devices. By collecting flow labels, source ports, and IP ID fields, we reconstruct the PRNG state and correlate it with previously extracted states to uniquely identify specific devices.

This study examines multiplication formulas for higher-order Apostol-Genocchi polynomials, deriving several explicit recursive relations. These results allow us to recover earlier findings by Carlitz and Howard concerning Genocchi numbers. We further define 2-variable Apostol-Genocchi polynomials and establish a multiplication theorem for them. Additionally, we introduce generalized Apostol-Genocchi polynomials characterized by parameters $a$, $b$, and $c$, and derive various identities associated with these generalized forms.

Siamese networks enhanced by Region Proposal Networks (RPN) have garnered significant interest in visual tracking owing to their superior accuracy and efficiency. Nevertheless, the RPN architecture relies on configuring anchor boxes regarding their quantity, scales, and aspect ratios, which impacts the model's practicality and ease of use. Additionally, these anchor boxes necessitate complex computations, such as determining their Intersection-over-Union (IoU) with ground truth bounding boxes. To address these anchor-related limitations, we present a straightforward yet potent anchor-free tracker called Siamese Corner Networks (SiamCorners), which undergoes end-to-end offline training on extensive image datasets. Specifically, we implement a refined corner pooling layer that transforms target bounding box estimates into predictions for two specific corners: the bottom-right and the top-left. By focusing on corner pairs rather than anchor boxes, the algorithm becomes more adaptable and streamlined compared to anchor-based methods. Our design further incorporates a layer-wise feature aggregation strategy, allowing the corner pooling module to forecast multiple corners for a target within deep network architectures. We also introduce a novel penalty term to identify the optimal tracking box among these candidates. Ultimately, SiamCorners delivers performance comparable to state-of-the-art trackers while sustaining high processing speeds; notably, it achieves a 53.7% AUC on NFS30 and a 61.4% AUC on UAV123, operating at 42 frames per second.

This study examines proximity-induced spin-orbit and exchange couplings in ABA and ABC trilayer graphene sandwiched between monolayers of semiconducting transition-metal dichalcogenides and the ferromagnetic semiconductor Cr$_2$Ge$_2$Te$_6$. Through first-principles calculations, we determine the electronic structures of these multilayer systems and derive key proximity-induced orbital and spin interaction parameters by fitting low-energy bands to model Hamiltonians. We further illustrate the tunability of these proximity effects via a transverse electric field. Additionally, we investigate mixed spin-orbit/exchange coupling configurations, which enable efficient tailoring of spin interactions through applied fields. Finally, we summarize the spin-orbit physics of bare ABA, ABC, and ABB trilayers, offering a qualitative understanding of observed behaviors alongside first-principles results on electronic band structures, density of states, spin splittings, and electric-field tunabilities. These realistic model parameters serve as a resource for simulating transport and correlation physics in trilayer graphene.

Numerous critical decisions operate within an "expert-in-the-loop" framework, where a human operator reviews algorithmic suggestions but retains final authority, often resulting in a gap between the recommended and actual actions. However, standard optimization methods typically assume perfect implementation of these recommendations. We introduce an adherence-aware optimization framework designed to address the discrepancy between suggested and executed policies, analyzing how partial compliance influences optimal recommendations. Our findings demonstrate that ignoring this partial adherence issue—a common practice in current recommendation systems—can cause performance to degrade arbitrarily, falling far below both human baseline capabilities and algorithmic expectations. Furthermore, our framework offers tools to examine policy structures and compute optimal recommendation strategies that are inherently resilient to human deviations, ensuring guaranteed improvements over baseline performance.

This paper presents a refined blow-up analysis of finite energy approximate solutions to a Nirenberg-type problem defined on half-spheres, which involves prescribing a given scalar curvature under minimal boundary conditions. We precisely determine the locations and rates of blow-up. This analysis reveals that the blow-up behavior for the Nirenberg problem on half-spheres is significantly more complex than on closed spheres. Beyond the combination of interior and boundary blow-ups, there exist non-simple blow-up points for subcritical solutions with zero or nonzero weak limits. The formation of these non-simple blow-ups is driven by a vortex problem, highlighting an unexpected connection to Euler equations in fluid dynamics and mean-field type equations in mathematical physics.

Deep learning model training demands significant computational resources, driving an industry-wide shift toward specialized hardware to enhance performance. To systematically evaluate deep learning platforms, we present ParaDnn, a parameterized benchmark suite that constructs end-to-end models for fully connected (FC), convolutional (CNN), and recurrent (RNN) neural networks. In addition to six real-world models, we assess Google's Cloud TPU v2/v3, NVIDIA's V100 GPU, and an Intel Skylake CPU platform. We conduct a detailed analysis of the TPU architecture, exposing its bottlenecks and offering key insights for designing future specialized systems. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive comparison of these platforms, demonstrating that each excels with specific model types. Finally, we measure the substantial performance gains achieved by specialized software stacks on both TPU and GPU architectures.

This study examines symmetric and antisymmetric structure functions derived from the electromagnetic deep inelastic scattering of charged leptons on spin-1/2 hadrons, utilizing a top-down holographic dual framework. The analysis incorporates scattering amplitudes from type IIB superstring theory and type IIB supergravity on AdS$_5 \times S^5$, alongside the BPST Pomeron, all employing the hard-wall prescription. We provide a detailed investigation of the proton's $F_2^P$ and $g_1^P$ structure functions across various kinematic regions of the Bjorken variable $x$ and the virtual photon's squared momentum $Q^2$. Additionally, the proton's virtual Compton scattering asymmetry, $A_1^P$, is analyzed. Our results are compared with data from multiple experimental collaborations. Furthermore, the holographic Pomeron offers predictions for these observables at very small $x$ values, specifically forecasting $g_1^P$ at $Q^2 \approx 10$ GeV$^2$ for anticipated measurements at a future electron-ion collider. Finally, the limitations inherent to this holographic dual approach are discussed.

Helmer first introduced the concept of adequate commutative domains in his 1943 paper published in the Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society. This article extends the definition of adequacy to noncommutative Bézout rings and demonstrates that the collection of nonsingular second-order matrices defined over a commutative principal ideal domain satisfies this property.

Tissue perfusion and oxygenation serve as vital indicators of organ viability during minimally invasive procedures, enabling real-time evaluation of blood flow and oxygen saturation. Multispectral imaging (MSI) offers a contactless optical approach to assess tissue perfusion across wide fields. This paper introduces a novel, rapid method that adapts standard RGB images for MSI; although this approach limits spectral resolution, it ensures compatibility with conventional laparoscopic systems. The technique leverages discrete Haar decomposition to partition video frames into low-pass and directional components, applying distinct multispectral estimation strategies to each. Acceleration is achieved by employing fast Tikhonov regularization on directional coefficients and more precise Bayesian estimation on the low-pass component. Implemented on a graphics processing unit (GPU), the pipeline operates at approximately 15 frames per second. The method's efficacy has been validated using both animal models and human data acquired via a da Vinci stereo laparoscope.

A Dyck sequence consists of balanced opening and closing parentheses of various types. The Dyck edit distance for a given parenthesis sequence $S$ represents the minimum number of edit operations—insertions, deletions, and substitutions—required to convert $S$ into a Dyck sequence. The threshold Dyck edit distance problem involves taking a sequence $S$ and a positive integer $k$ as input, with the objective of calculating the Dyck edit distance only if it does not exceed $k$; otherwise, it should be reported that the distance is greater than $k$. Backurs and Onak [PODS'16] demonstrated that this problem can be solved in $O(n+k^{16})$ time. In this study, we propose new algorithms for the threshold Dyck edit distance problem that run in $O(n+k^{4.544184})$ time with high probability or $O(n+k^{4.853059})$ time deterministically. These algorithms integrate several novel structural characteristics of the Dyck edit distance problem, an optimized method for fast $(\min,+)$ matrix multiplication, and a precise adaptation of concepts from Valiant's parsing algorithm.

Over two years ago, the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration released the first reconstructed image of the supermassive black hole in M87*, enabling an assessment of its shadow size. More recently, the collaboration has constrained the parameters of spherically symmetric black hole metrics by analyzing the allowed range for the shadow radius derived from their 2017 observations of M87*. Prior to this, analytical formulas for the shadow radius as a function of charge—including tidal charge—were derived for the Reissner–Nordström metric. Previously, Bin-Nun suggested using a Reissner–Nordström metric with a tidal charge as an alternative to the Schwarzschild metric for Sgr~A*. Assuming a Reissner–Nordström black hole with a tidal charge exists in M87*, we use the Event Horizon Telescope's shadow size measurements to constrain this tidal charge. Similarly, we evaluate the tidal charge based on shadow size estimates for Sgr~A*.

Various malicious activities have been detected across multiple permissionless blockchains, including Bitcoin and Ethereum. While some attacks exploit infrastructure vulnerabilities, others target users via social engineering. To combat these issues, we aim to automatically identify accounts that initiate such malicious exploitation of others. Specifically, we seek a robust supervised machine learning algorithm that remains resistant to biases caused by the over-representation of specific malicious activities in the dataset, as well as to adversarial attacks. Our findings indicate that most reported malicious behaviors, particularly within the Ethereum ecosystem, exhibit statistically similar patterns. Furthermore, existing ML algorithms for detecting malicious accounts often display bias toward the most frequent type of attack. Consequently, we determined that Neural Networks (NN) perform best in handling biased datasets while maintaining robustness against certain adversarial threats.

This work introduces a coherent microscopic framework for superconductivity in strongly correlated electronic systems. We derive the Dyson equation governing both normal and anomalous Green functions for projected (Hubbard) electronic operators. To evaluate different pairing mechanisms, we analyze an extended Hubbard model that incorporates intersite Coulomb repulsion alongside electron-phonon interactions. Our findings indicate that strong kinematical interactions between electrons and spin fluctuations drive $d$-wave pairing with high $T_c$, whereas both Coulomb repulsion and electron-phonon effects are suppressed in this pairing state. These outcomes corroborate the spin-fluctuation mechanism for high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates, a hypothesis previously suggested by phenomenological models.

The S-metric space was first introduced by Sedghi and colleagues in 2012. We establish several common fixed point theorems for self-mappings defined on complete S-metric spaces with vector-valued metrics. To validate these findings, we provide accompanying examples.

Langevin Monte Carlo (LMC) is a widely used technique for Bayesian sampling that exhibits exponential convergence for log-concave distributions, subject to a manageable discretization error. However, LMC necessitates computing a full gradient at every step, requiring $d$ partial derivative evaluations per iteration for problems in $\mathbb{R}^d$, which becomes prohibitively expensive when the dimension $d$ is large. This study explores improving computational efficiency by integrating Random Coordinate Descent (RCD) into LMC. The theoretical analysis considers two approaches: first, applying RCD directly to LMC replaces the full gradient with a randomly chosen directional derivative, lowering per-iteration costs but increasing the total iteration count to meet error tolerances, resulting in no net computational benefit. Second, incorporating variance reduction methods like SAGA and SVRG into the RCD-LMC framework reduces overall computational costs compared to standard LMC. Specifically, in the underdamped setting, convergence is achieved in the same number of iterations as classical LMC, but each iteration requires only a single directional derivative, yielding the optimal computational cost within the underdamped-LMC framework.

This study examines spontaneous breaking of scale invariance and its corresponding Goldstone boson, the dilaton, within renormalizable, unitary, non-supersymmetric scalar field theories in $4-\varepsilon$ dimensions. At the leading order, models can be constructed to exhibit classical spontaneous scale invariance breaking, allowing for the identification of a massless dilaton. However, beyond leading order, the absence of anomalous scale symmetry breaking in quantum field theory necessitates that the models reside at a Wilson-Fisher fixed point characterized by exact conformal symmetry. The analysis demonstrates that this condition on the couplings is incompatible with the existence of the flat direction required for an exactly massless dilaton. Consequently, spontaneous scale symmetry breaking accompanied by an exactly massless dilaton cannot occur in renormalizable, unitary $4-\varepsilon$ dimensional scalar QFTs. These findings also extend to $\phi^6$ theory in $3-\varepsilon$ dimensions.

Non-volatile main memory (NVM) that is byte-addressable requires transactional mechanisms to ensure atomic data access and manipulation. These mechanisms frequently rely on logging strategies, such as undo or redo logging. However, our evaluation reveals that such logging imposes significant runtime overhead, ranging from 8% to 49%, with 41% to 78% of this cost attributed to frequent cache-line flushing. This substantial overhead undermines the performance advantages of NVM. To address this, we propose a novel approach to minimize cache-line flushing overhead in logging-based transactions. Unlike traditional methods that operate at the program level by leveraging semantics, our solution utilizes architecture awareness. Specifically, we avoid flushing cache blocks that are predicted to be evicted by hardware caching mechanisms, such as replacement algorithms. Additionally, we merge cache blocks with low dirtiness to enhance flushing efficiency. We implemented Archapt, an architecture-aware, high-performance runtime system for persistent memory. Experimental results demonstrate that compared to undo logging (PMDK) and redo logging (Mnemosyne), Archapt reduces cache-line flushing by 66% and boosts system throughput by an average of 19% (up to 42%). Furthermore, crash tests across four hardware caching policies confirm that Archapt robustly guarantees crash consistency.

Visual embellishments serve as non-linguistic rhetorical devices designed to communicate abstract ideas or capture reader interest. However, crafting data visualizations with suitable and aesthetically pleasing enhancements remains difficult, as it heavily relies on a designer's expertise and taste. To support the ideation and creation process, we introduce VizBelle, a design space derived from an analysis of 361 categorized visualizations found online. This framework comprises four dimensions: communication goals to align with user intent, object selection to identify target areas, and strategies and techniques to suggest viable approaches. Additionally, we have developed a website offering detailed explanations and examples of these various techniques. A within-subject study involving 20 professional and amateur design enthusiasts was conducted to assess the tool's efficacy. The findings indicate that VizBelle provides valuable insights and assistance for designers aiming to create embellished data visualizations.

We present the concept of the $p$-adic quantum bit ($p$-qubit) within the framework of $p$-adic quantum mechanics, a field pioneered and expanded by Volovich and his colleagues. In this paradigm, physical phenomena occur in three-dimensional $p$-adic space instead of Euclidean space. Building on our previous research regarding the $p$-adic special orthogonal group, we propose a program to categorize its continuous unitary projective representations, a task interpretable as a theory of $p$-adic angular momentum. The $p$-adic quantum bit emerges from the irreducible representations of minimal nontrivial dimension two, for which we have constructed examples for every prime $p$.

Characterizations of t-normed integrals were derived in \cite{CLM} for finite compacta and in \cite{Rad} for the general case. These results establish a mapping between the space of capacities and homogeneous, t-norm-monotone, normed functionals that preserve the maximum operation for comonotone functions. Essentially, these theorems serve as non-additive and non-linear counterparts to the classic Riesz Theorem, which links $\sigma$-additive regular Borel measures with linear, positive functionals. We further examine the optimality of this characterization.

We present CoWeSe (the Corpus Web Salud Espa\~nol), currently the most extensive Spanish biomedical corpus, comprising 4.5GB of clean plain text (approximately 750 million tokens). Created in 2020 through a large-scale crawl of 3,000 Spanish domains, CoWeSe is openly accessible and fully preprocessed. This resource significantly supports biomedical and health-related natural language processing in Spanish and has already been utilized for training domain-specific language models and generating word embeddings. The corpus is released under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license and is available on Zenodo (\url{https://zenodo.org/record/4561971\#.YTI5SnVKiEA}).

1) Over the last century, local environments and land use have undergone significant transformations, making historical records essential for tracking these shifts. Consequently, these documents are vital for comprehending the impacts and consequences of altered land usage. Furthermore, this understanding is critical for identifying restoration initiatives aimed at mitigating the harmful and unsustainable effects resulting from such changes.

2) This study utilizes deep learning, specifically convolutional neural networks (CNNs), to extract data regarding the historical location and geographical spread of wetlands from hand-drawn maps. The CNN model was trained on a manually annotated dataset focusing on historical wetlands within Jönköping county, Sweden, derived from the "Generalstabskartan" historical map.

3) The proposed CNN demonstrates strong performance, achieving an F1-score of 0.886 when assessed via 10-fold cross-validation. Beyond evaluation, the trained models were employed to create a GIS layer depicting the probable historical distribution of wetlands across the southern collection of the Generalstabskartan, which covers southern Sweden. This GIS layer has been made available as an open resource for free use.

4) In summary, these results indicate that CNNs serve as an effective tool for extracting and digitizing non-textual information from historical documents, such as maps. Additionally, this research produces a modern GIS dataset that facilitates a deeper understanding of past land-use changes.

Recent years have seen significant interest in large-scale graph processing, which now underpins most modern datacenter workloads, including those handled by frameworks like MapReduce. This has spurred the development of numerous Domain-Specific Accelerators tailored for graph tasks, with Spatial Architectures emerging as a promising solution by partitioning graphs across nodes for parallel execution. Through experiments analyzing on-chip data movement within such architectures, we identified a critical bottleneck caused by high parallelism. To address this, we propose a novel power-law aware Graph Partitioning and Data Mapping scheme designed to minimize communication latency by reducing hop counts on a scalable network-on-chip. Experimental results on widely used graph algorithms demonstrate that our approach accelerates execution by 2-5x and improves energy efficiency by 2.7-4x compared to baseline implementations, primarily by cutting down data movement time.

This paper introduces a novel dynamic decision framework for blockchain selfish mining, leveraging sensitivity-based optimization theory. The primary objective is to determine the optimal dynamic policy for a dishonest mining pool that is pegged to the blockchain. To investigate selfish mining attacks, we design two competing mining pools with distinct criteria: the honest pool adheres to a standard two-block leading rule, whereas the dishonest pool employs a modified version of this criterion via a blockchain-pegged strategy. To identify the optimal policy, we establish a policy-driven continuous-time Markov process and examine critical influencing factors. Consequently, we analyze the monotonicity and optimality of long-run average profits relative to the blockchain-pegged reward and demonstrate the structural characteristics of the optimal policy. We believe the methodology and findings presented herein will offer valuable insights into future research on dynamic decision-making regarding blockchain selfish mining attacks.

We investigate an extremal problem regarding the degrees of link graphs within finite regular graphs, specifically the subgraphs formed by non-trivial spheres. Our findings demonstrate that for a connected, non-complete $d$-regular graph $G$, there exists a link graph with a minimum degree of at most $\lfloor 2d/3\rfloor-1$; furthermore, if $G$ is sufficiently large relative to $d$, some link graph will have a minimum degree no greater than $\lfloor d/2\rfloor-1$. Both of these bounds are optimal. Additionally, we present the corresponding best-possible results for the analogous problem involving subgraphs induced by balls instead of spheres. These inquiries are motivated by a conjecture on the expansion properties of link graphs in large bounded-degree graphs, supported by a heuristic justification.

The proliferation of grid resources on distribution networks, coupled with inaccurate forecasting capabilities, makes current grid operation and control methodologies unsustainable in the future. Consequently, a more distributed yet coordinated strategy will emerge, utilizing a larger footprint and deeper hierarchy to unify the control of diverse transmission and distribution (T&D) resources within a single framework. This approach necessitates Alternating Current State Estimation (ACSE) for integrated T&D networks. Currently, no practical method exists for implementing combined T&D ACSE. This paper addresses this gap from a circuit-theoretic perspective by developing a combined T&D ACSE solution that is fast, convex, and robust against bad data. To tackle challenges related to massive problem sizes (involving millions of variables) and data privacy, the proposed approach distributes both memory and computing resources. To ensure timely convergence, the method constructs a distributed circuit model for combined T&D networks and employs node-tearing techniques to enable efficient parallelism. To validate the approach's effectiveness, the combined T&D ACSE algorithm was executed on large test networks comprising multiple T&D feeders. The results demonstrate the accuracy of the estimates, measured by root mean-square error, and the algorithm's scalability in terms of wall-clock time.

Sparse multichannel blind deconvolution (S-MBD) is a prevalent challenge in various engineering fields, including radar, sonar, and ultrasound imaging. To mitigate the associated computational and implementation expenses, we introduce a compression technique that facilitates blind recovery from a significantly reduced number of time-domain measurements compared to the full received signal. This approach involves filtering the signal followed by subsampling, thereby substantially lowering implementation costs. We establish theoretical guarantees regarding the identifiability and recovery of sparse filters from these compressed measurements, which supports the design of a broad range of compression filters. Subsequently, we develop a data-driven unrolled learning framework to optimize the compression filter and address the S-MBD problem. The encoder utilizes a recurrent inference network to map compressed measurements to estimates of sparse filters. Our results demonstrate that this unrolled learning method exhibits greater robustness to variations in source shapes and achieves superior recovery performance relative to optimization-based approaches. Furthermore, in scenarios with limited data (few-shot learning), we show that unrolled learning offers enhanced generalization capabilities compared to conventional deep learning methods.

Recent adversarial attack studies have highlighted the susceptibility of learning-based classifiers to meticulously engineered perturbations. Nevertheless, most current attack techniques struggle with cross-dataset generalization because they depend on a classification layer restricted to a fixed set of categories. Moreover, the perturbations produced by these methods often fall within regions easily detected by the human visual system (HVS). To address these issues, we introduce a novel algorithm that targets semantic similarity within feature representations, enabling us to deceive classifiers without being confined to a specific dataset. To ensure imperceptibility, we implement a low-frequency constraint that restricts perturbations to high-frequency components, thereby maintaining perceptual similarity between the original images and the adversarial examples. Comprehensive experiments conducted on three datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1K) and three public online platforms demonstrate that our approach generates misleading and transferable adversarial examples across various architectures and datasets. Furthermore, visualization results and quantitative evaluations using four distinct metrics reveal that the proposed algorithm produces more imperceptible perturbations than existing state-of-the-art methods. The source code is publicly available.

High-dimensional entanglement provides significant benefits for both theoretical research and practical applications within quantum information science. A key component enabling these uses is a programmable processor capable of managing entangled states, which is essential for certifying, manipulating, and distributing high-dimensional entanglement. While integrated multiport interferometers are currently the dominant technology for photon processing, they struggle to handle structured light and face difficulties regarding scalability. This study overcomes these barriers by presenting a reconfigurable processor for high-dimensional entangled photons based on multi-plane light conversion (MPLC), a technique recently advanced for multiplexing numerous spatial modes in classical communication. Utilizing this programmable MPLC platform, we successfully certify three-dimensional entanglement across two mutually unbiased bases, execute 400 arbitrary random transformations on entangled photons, and facilitate entanglement distribution by converting the mode basis of these photons.

Domain adaptation seeks to bridge the gap between a source domain with labeled data and a target domain. However, current disentanglement-based approaches fail to adequately separate domain-invariant from domain-specific features, resulting in non-discriminative invariant features, and they underutilize reconstructed features during training. To address this, we introduce a novel Enhanced Separable Disentanglement (ESD) model. First, a disentangler extracts both domain-invariant and domain-specific features. Next, we implement feature separation enhancement to reduce contamination between these two feature types. Finally, our model reconstructs complete feature vectors to facilitate further disentanglement throughout the training process. Extensive experiments across three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in challenging cross-domain scenarios.

The Minkowski problem concerning electrostatic capacity identifies measures arising from this capacity, representing a recognized variant of the classical Minkowski problem. This concept has been extended to the $L_p$ Minkowski problem involving $\mathfrak{p}$-capacity, where the specific logarithmic case ($p=0$) connects to cone-volumes, underscoring its geometric importance. In this work, we resolve the discrete logarithmic Minkowski problem for $1<\mathfrak{p}<n$ under the condition that the support of the provided measure lies in general position.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as powerful instruments for representing and analyzing graph data. Their application in software engineering is growing, playing a vital role in areas such as program analysis, type inference, and code representation. This paper presents GraphGallery, a platform designed to streamline the development and rapid benchmarking of GNN-based software. GraphGallery simplifies the deployment of GNNs, enabling developers with limited domain expertise to utilize them effectively. The platform provides implementations of common GNN models using major deep learning frameworks and easily integrates existing toolboxes like PyG and DGL. Experiments confirm the reliability of these implementations and their advantages in accelerating coding workflows. The official source code for GraphGallery can be accessed at https://github.com/EdisonLeeeee/GraphGallery, and a demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/mv7Zs1YeaYo.

We investigate the transient dynamics of two weakly coupled, parallel quantum dots interacting with macroscopic leads, specifically focusing on quantum coherence effects. The stationary particle current in this system is highly sensitive to perturbations that are significantly smaller than the system-lead coupling strength or the temperature. We demonstrate that this sensitivity arises from a parity-like symmetry in the dynamics, which gives rise to two distinct stationary states. When small perturbations break this symmetry, the system exhibits metastability with two phases that can be approximated as combinations of the stationary states found in the unperturbed limit. Additionally, long-time dynamics can be modeled as classical transitions between these phases, ultimately converging to a unique stationary state. Specifically, the competition between these two metastable phases accounts for the current's extreme sensitivity to minor perturbations. We further show that this behavior offers the potential to utilize the parallel dots as a charge sensor leveraging quantum coherence to achieve a signal-to-noise ratio independent of temperature constraints. Consequently, this parallel-dot configuration outperforms analogous single-dot charge sensors across a broad temperature range.

Training massive models such as BERT and GPT-3 across hundreds of GPUs often faces significant communication bottlenecks, particularly on commodity systems constrained by low-bandwidth TCP networks. While large-batch optimization techniques like LAMB aim to decrease communication frequency and compression methods like 1-bit Adam seek to shrink communication volume, relying on either approach alone is insufficient, especially when network bandwidth is limited. Driven by this limitation, we propose combining large-batch optimization with communication compression. However, we observed that standard compression strategies fail when applied directly to LAMB due to its distinctive adaptive layerwise learning rates. To address this, we developed 1-bit LAMB, a new communication-efficient algorithm that enables adaptive layerwise learning rates under compression. Additionally, we implemented a novel system using PyTorch's distributed NCCL backend to enhance both usability and performance. Evaluations on up to 256 GPUs for BERT-Large pre-training with batch sizes ranging from 8K to 64K demonstrate that our NCCL-based 1-bit LAMB achieves up to a 4.6x reduction in communication volume and a 2.8x end-to-end speedup, while maintaining identical sample-wise convergence rates and fine-tuning accuracy compared to uncompressed LAMB.

Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) facilitates the lateral edge epitaxy of transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures, which hold promise for optoelectronic applications. The performance of carrier and exciton transport relies heavily on the quality of the constituent monolayers and the characteristics of their lateral heterojunctions. Previously, large inhomogeneous broadening in as-grown samples obscured key details of their optical properties. This study employs optical spectroscopy at both 4 K and 300 K to investigate CVD-grown MoSe₂-WSe₂ lateral heterostructures that have been transferred from the growth substrate and encapsulated in hBN. Photoluminescence (PL), reflectance contrast, and Raman spectroscopy demonstrate that these samples exhibit significantly narrowed optical transition linewidths, comparable to high-quality exfoliated monolayers. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) reveals near-atomically sharp junctions with a covalent bonding extent of approximately 3 nm. Furthermore, PL imaging shows that at low temperatures (4 K), the excitonic diffusion length is greater in WSe₂ than in MoSe₂, a trend that reverses at 300 K.

**Context:** Experimental research is fundamental to machine learning, serving as the primary means to benchmark, evaluate, and compare learning algorithms; therefore, ensuring the reliability and trustworthiness of these experiments is crucial. **Objective:** This study examines the frequency of errors within a subset of machine learning experiments focused on software defect prediction, specifically targeting simple arithmetic and statistical mistakes. **Method:** We analyzed 49 papers comprising 2,456 individual experimental results from a prior systematic review comparing supervised and unsupervised defect prediction classifiers. Our analysis involved extracting confusion matrices to verify constraints, such as ensuring marginal probabilities sum to one, and screening for errors in multiple statistical significance tests. **Results:** We identified errors in 22 of the 49 papers. Among these, 16 involved inconsistencies in confusion matrices, 7 were statistical errors, and one paper exhibited both types of issues. **Conclusions:** Although some mistakes, such as transcription errors, may be minor, their existence undermines confidence in the findings. We strongly advocate for researchers to adhere to open science principles to facilitate easier detection and correction of errors, thereby helping the community address this alarmingly high rate of inaccuracies in computational experiments.

Entanglement serves as a vital resource for quantum tasks. Recently, Yang et al. [arXiv:2205.08801] introduced entanglement polygon inequalities (EPI) based on specific entanglement measures for $n$-qudit pure states. Building on this, we further investigate EPIs by demonstrating their validity for $n$-qudit pure states using the geometric entanglement measure (GEM). We then examine residual entanglement via GEM within three-qubit systems. Finally, we provide counterexamples indicating that EPIs fail for higher-dimensional systems when measured by negativity, while also identifying a class of non-qubit states that do satisfy EPIs under negativity.

We have evaluated and adjusted CAMS air quality multi-model forecasts for PM10, PM2.5, O3, NO2, and CO using observational data from Liguria's Regional Monitoring Network (northwestern Italy) during 2019 and 2020. Our calibration approach builds upon the established Ensemble Model Output Statistics (EMOS), which effectively converts raw ensemble forecasts into predictive probability density functions while simultaneously correcting for biases and dispersion errors; this method also generates calibrated estimates of model uncertainty. Our analysis highlights the critical importance of ingesting real-time pollutant observations, particularly for short-term forecasts, revealing that our dynamic calibration strategy outperforms analogous methods that do not incorporate such data. The optimal strategy identified enhances the reliability of the CAMS multi-model system compared to other raw air quality models operating at higher spatial resolutions that rely on more detailed emission inventory information. We anticipate that our research will positively contribute to the development of cost-effective and reliable early warning systems for air pollution.

Industrial robots lacking precision-enhancing measures are only marginally suitable for machining tasks due to their inherently compliant structures. Beyond structural, thermal, and bearing deformations, the primary source of this compliance is backlash within transmission drives. This study introduces a method to enhance trajectory tracking accuracy by integrating secondary encoders with a control strategy combining feedback and flatness-based feedforward techniques. To achieve this, a new nonlinear, continuously differentiable dynamical model for flexible robot joints is developed. This model represents the joint as a two-mass oscillator featuring pose-dependent inertia, nonlinear friction, nonlinear stiffness, and backlash. A flatness-based feedforward controller is designed to optimize guiding behavior, while a feedback controller utilizing secondary encoders compensates for disturbances. Leveraging Automatic Differentiation, the nonlinear feedforward controller can be calculated online within a few microseconds. Ultimately, the proposed algorithms are validated through simulations and experimental testing on a real KUKA Quantec KR300 Ultra SE robot.

We propose that the core degenerate (CD) scenario for type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) successfully accounts for the compact, helium-rich circumstellar material (CSM) observed in SN 2020eyj. Our newly suggested channel within the CD framework involves two distinct common envelope evolution (CEE) phases. Following the white dwarf (WD) companion's removal of the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star's hydrogen-rich envelope, the spiraling-in process halts at a few solar radii from the core, diverging from the hydrogen-rich SNe Ia-CSM CD scenario where it continues to the carbon-oxygen (CO) core. Only after hundreds to tens of thousands of years, once the helium-rich core expands, does the WD engage in a second CEE phase with this helium-rich layer. By this stage, the hydrogen-rich envelope has been pushed far from the center. During this second phase, the WD merges with the CO core; subsequent to a merger-to-explosion delay (MED) spanning weeks to tens of years, the merger remnant detonates. The resulting SN Ia ejecta then collide with the helium-rich CSM located at tens to hundreds of AU. We tracked the evolution of two stellar models with initial masses of 5M☉ and 7M☉ up to their AGB phase, where they were expected to engulf the WD companion. Our findings confirm the presence of a sufficiently massive CO core to merge with the WD under the CD scenario, alongside a substantial helium-rich layer of 0.3–1M☉, which explains the helium-rich CSM of SN 2020eyj.

We present multiple novel reformulations of the covariant holographic entanglement entropy formula originally proposed by Hubeny, Rangamani, and Takayanagi. These new expressions include: (1) a minimax approach requiring the identification of a maximal-area achronal surface on a timelike hypersurface homologous to $D(A)$—the causal boundary of the region $A$—followed by minimization over possible hypersurfaces; (2) a max V-flow formulation that maximizes the flux of a divergenceless bulk 1-form $V$ through $D(A)$, constrained by a norm upper bound that is non-local in time; and (3) a min U-flow formulation that minimizes the flux of a divergenceless timelike 1-form $U$ over a bulk Cauchy slice, subject to a norm lower bound that is non-local in space. The two flow-based formulas constitute convex programs linked by Lagrange duality. In each case, the optimal configurations dynamically identify the HRT surface along with the entanglement wedges for $A$ and its complement. The V-flow formula serves as the covariant extension of the Freedman-Headrick bit thread reformulation of the Ryu-Takayanagi formula. Furthermore, we introduce a measure-theoretic notion of a "thread distribution" and demonstrate how Riemannian flows, V-flows, and U-flows can be represented using these distributions.

Sorting is essential across numerous application fields. Traditionally, data is fetched from memory, processed by general-purpose processors or specialized hardware, and then written back, a workflow that incurs substantial latency and energy costs due to data transfer between memory and processing units. This study introduces, to our knowledge, the first architectures designed for in-memory sorting. We propose two distinct approaches: the first handles conventional weighted binary radix data formats, while the second targets emerging unary processing systems where data is encoded as uniform unary bitstreams. Although each architecture offers unique trade-offs making them better suited for specific applications, both significantly outperform previous sorting designs in terms of processing speed. Our evaluations demonstrate average energy reductions of 37x for binary designs and 138x for unary designs compared to traditional off-memory CMOS sorting systems.

To date, the life course epidemiology of chronic diseases has been primarily guided by an environmental framework. Whether examining early-life exposures or later lifestyle choices, this perspective posits that prior experiences interact across life stages to influence future health pathways. Drawing inspiration from social trajectory analysis—which examines transitions between various states across multiple dimensions of social experience—this paper introduces a new empirical method for handling multiple time-to-event health data, termed "multiple state analysis." Similar to state sequence analysis, this approach aims to generate typologies of primary life course trajectories. The method is demonstrated using data from a South London general practice electronic health record, analyzing multiple long-term conditions linked to myocardial infarction. Beyond anticipated findings such as the recurring impact of hypertension, multiple state analysis reveals that distinct patterns of long-term conditions, encompassing both physical and mental health issues, correlate with the timing of myocardial infarction onset as well as socio-demographic factors like sex and ethnicity.

Electron production originating from beauty-hadron decays was investigated at midrapidity in both proton-proton (pp) and central lead-lead (Pb-Pb) collisions at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV using the ALICE detector at the LHC. In pp collisions, the cross section within the transverse momentum range $2 < p_{\rm T} < 8$ GeV/$c$ was evaluated against perturbative quantum chromodynamics models. For the 10% most central Pb-Pb collisions, the yield in the interval $2 < p_{\rm T} < 26$ GeV/$c$ was utilized to calculate the nuclear modification factor $R_{\rm AA}$, extending the pp reference cross section to $p_{\rm T}$ values exceeding 8 GeV/$c$. The resulting $R_{\rm AA}$ indicates substantial suppression of high-$p_{\rm T}$ electrons from beauty-hadron decays, with no significant $p_{\rm T}$ dependence observed above 8 GeV/$c$ given the uncertainties. These findings align with various theoretical frameworks depicting heavy quark interactions with the quark-gluon plasma, which anticipate reduced energy loss for beauty quarks relative to light and charm quarks.

This paper presents the design, implementation, and field testing of WiMesh, a resilient Wireless Mesh Network (WMN) disaster communication system specifically tailored for underdeveloped and rural regions. Since mesh networking is a well-established field, this work does not propose new models or protocols; rather, it highlights critical design considerations and justifies specific trade-offs for deploying mesh networks in resource-constrained disaster scenarios. These decisions are evaluated against essential attributes such as security, affordability, power efficiency, compactness, availability, customizability, portability, ease of deployment, and coverage. The study details the development and real-world performance of WiMesh, which allows users across vast areas to communicate despite the absence of cellular networks, electricity, or traditional infrastructure by utilizing multi-hop mesh networking and Wi-Fi-enabled handheld devices. Additionally, the paper shares practical lessons and results from a deployment in a remote, mountainous village in Pakistan, and the source code is made available to the research community.

Recent studies have highlighted inherent constraints within text-only pretraining. This paper identifies reporting bias—the tendency to omit obvious information—as a primary driver of this limitation and examines how multimodal training can alleviate it. Our approach involves three steps: first, creating the Color Dataset (CoDa), which captures human-perceived color distributions for 521 common objects; second, using CoDa to contrast color distributions in text, within language models, and as perceived by humans; and third, evaluating performance gaps between text-only and multimodal models on this dataset. Our findings reveal that the color distributions recovered by language models align more closely with the inaccurate textual distributions than with ground-truth human perception, confirming that reporting bias negatively constrains text-only training. Furthermore, we show that multimodal models can utilize visual training to counteract these biases, offering a promising direction for future research.

Due to the significant influence of language models on Natural Language Processing, numerous Spanish encoder-only masked language models (BERTs) have been developed and released. These models originate from either large-scale projects utilizing extensive private datasets or smaller academic initiatives relying on publicly available data. This paper offers a comprehensive head-to-head comparison of Spanish language models, yielding two key findings: (i) Multilingual models from major corporations, which were previously overlooked, outperform monolingual models, thereby reshaping the evaluation landscape for Spanish NLP; (ii) Results among monolingual models remain inconclusive, with some smaller or ostensibly inferior models demonstrating competitive performance. Based on these empirical findings, we advocate for further research to understand the underlying factors. Specifically, the impact of corpus size, quality, and pre-training techniques requires additional investigation to develop Spanish monolingual models that surpass those released by large private companies, especially given the field's rapid advancement. While the recent surge in Spanish language technology development is positive, our results indicate that constructing language models remains an open, resource-intensive challenge that demands combining financial and computational resources with top-tier research expertise and practical experience.

Multiple nucleosynthesis investigations suggest that r-process elements in very metal-poor (VMP) halo stars may originate from distinct sources. Utilizing standard statistical methods—such as correlation analysis, clustering, and rank tests of elemental abundances—we identify causally linked abundance patterns to associate them with specific astrophysical events. These events either produce r-process elements alongside iron or do so without significant iron contribution. During the early evolution of the Galaxy, at least three distinct r-process nucleosynthesis sites were active. The first two sites generate both iron and most lighter r-process elements; we classify these as two varieties of core-collapse events that differ from standard core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe), which typically yield only light trans-iron elements. The third category is defined by a robust r-process signature and accounts for the bulk of heavy main r-process elements without substantial iron co-production. This site does not appear linked to CCSNe; consequently, the iron observed in r-process-enriched stars associated with this category must stem from earlier CCSNe. The presence of actinide-boost stars reveals a further subdivision among strong r-process sites. We attribute these two strong r-process sources to neutron star mergers lacking fast black hole formation and to events dominated by black hole accretion disk outflows. Evidence from the lowest-metallicity stars also points toward a connection with massive single stars (collapsars) that formed black holes in the early Galaxy.

This study introduces a privacy-preserving algorithm designed to address the average consensus problem using Shamir's secret sharing scheme, enabling a network of agents to converge on a shared state while keeping individual data concealed until consensus is achieved. Distinct from existing approaches, the proposed method ensures the network remains secure against collusion by any subset of neighbors, including scenarios where all neighbors collude. Additionally, this approach safeguards the consensus process from eavesdropping.

In the last twenty years, there has been an exponential rise in the collection of irregularly shaped point clouds across diverse fields. Driven by the critical role of solid modeling in this context, we introduce a new and efficient smoothing technique utilizing multivariate splines on tetrahedral partitions. This approach extracts the underlying signal to construct a 3D solid model from point cloud data. The proposed method effectively denoises or deblurs point clouds and delivers multi-resolution reconstructions of the actual signal. Moreover, it is capable of processing sparse and irregularly distributed point clouds to recover the underlying trajectory. Additionally, this smoothing and interpolation framework offers a natural mechanism for data reduction. We also provide theoretical assurances for the method by deriving the convergence rate and asymptotic normality of the estimator, demonstrating that the convergence rate reaches the optimal nonparametric standard. Finally, extensive simulations and a real-world data example illustrate that our method surpasses traditional smoothing techniques in both estimation accuracy and data reduction efficiency.

The coalescence model posits that bound states form instantaneously from unbound particles when their states overlap in spatial and momentum domains, as well as in quantum numbers. Consequently, when applied to parton hadronization, it captures a snapshot of the Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP) immediately preceding hadronization. In this study, the coalescence model is utilized for creating the ground state of open heavy flavors, while the statistical model handles heavier states. Under the assumption that all heavy flavors in thermal equilibrium undergo hadronization via coalescence, we conclude that the QGP just before hadronization does not consist of fully randomized partons; rather, it must exhibit strong correlations in color charges, as well as in momentum and/or coordinate spaces, between heavy quarks and light (anti-)quarks.

Detecting text with arbitrary shapes presents significant challenges, primarily due to diverse sizes and aspect ratios, unpredictable orientations, and imprecise annotations. While segmentation-based approaches have gained attention for their ability to handle varied text shapes through pixel-level prediction, they struggle because obtaining accurate pixel-level labels is difficult; existing scene text datasets typically offer only coarse-grained boundary annotations. This lack of precision leads to numerous misclassified pixels—both text pixels incorrectly labeled as background and background pixels included within annotations—which degrades the performance of segmentation-based detectors. Observing that a pixel's classification is strongly influenced by its distance to the nearest annotation boundary, this paper introduces a robust, segmentation-based detection method utilizing probability maps. Specifically, we employ a Sigmoid Alpha Function (SAF) to convert distances from boundaries to internal pixels into a probability map. However, a single probability map fails to capture complex distributions arising from the uncertainty of coarse boundaries. To address this, we utilize a set of probability maps generated by multiple SAFs to represent potential distributions. Furthermore, we develop an iterative model designed to predict and refine these probability maps, ensuring sufficient information to reconstruct text instances. Finally, simple region growth algorithms aggregate these maps to complete the text instances. Experimental results confirm that our approach achieves state-of-the-art detection accuracy across several benchmarks.

A scarcity of dermatologists results in prolonged waiting periods for patients seeking skin care, while studies indicate that general practitioners' diagnostic accuracy is often inferior to that of artificial intelligence. This article details the Skincare project (H2020, EIT Digital), which delivers interactive machine learning (IML) technology for clinical decision support, a reference architecture for a Digital European Healthcare Infrastructure (aligned with EIT MCPS), tools for aggregating digitized patient data, and the integration of decision support into clinical test environments. The primary achievement is a dermatology-specific diagnostic and decision support system designed for both patients and physicians, featuring an interactive deep learning approach for differentiating malignant skin lesions. The article outlines the system's functionalities and user interfaces, which are engineered to facilitate machine learning through human feedback. The foundational deep learning model, capable of achieving state-of-the-art results and augmenting the capabilities of general practitioners and dermatologists, was developed and validated using approximately 20,000 de-identified cases from the ISIC dermatology image database. These cases were curated by board-certified dermatologists who established the reference standard for each entry. The ISIC system supports differential diagnosis by providing a ranked list of eight potential conditions, a feature particularly valuable for treatment planning in scenarios of diagnostic uncertainty. The article provides a comprehensive overview of the Skincare project's outcomes, with a specific focus on the steps required to enhance communication and coordination between humans and machines within the IML framework. This aspect is crucial for advancing future cognitive assistants in healthcare, and the text describes the necessary intelligent user interfaces to support this evolution.

Text recognition is a cornerstone of computer vision, driven by its vast commercial potential. However, the problem's complexity has historically led to a split in research into Scene Text Recognition (STR) for everyday environments and Handwriting Text Recognition (HTR) for handwritten input. This paper proposes, for the first time, unifying these domains into a single model that rivals the performance of separate state-of-the-art STR and HTR systems. We demonstrate that directly merging STR and HTR models causes significant performance degradation due to their distinct inherent challenges. To address this, we introduce a knowledge distillation (KD) framework, which is non-trivial because standard KD techniques rely on fixed-length global data and fail to accommodate the variable-length, sequential nature of text. Consequently, we develop three specialized distillation losses tailored to these unique text characteristics. Empirical results indicate that our unified model performs comparably to, and in some instances exceeds, individual models. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that naive baselines, including two-stage frameworks and domain adaptation/generalization methods, are less effective, validating the suitability of our proposed design.

Machine learning offers significant potential for enhancing event generation and simulations. We are currently exploring the application of neural networks to approximate matrix elements in high-multiplicity scattering scenarios, specifically targeting loop-induced diphoton production via gluon fusion. This study develops a practical simulation approach applicable to hadron collider observables. The neural networks are trained on one-loop amplitudes from the NJet C++ library and integrated with the Sherpa Monte Carlo event generator to conduct an in-depth analysis of $2\to3$ and $2\to4$ scattering processes. Furthermore, we examine the performance of these trained networks under varying kinematic cuts that influence the phase space, as well as the overall reliability of the neural network-based simulations.

The Max $r$-SAT problem involves finding an assignment that maximizes the number of satisfied clauses in a CNF formula with $n$ variables, where each clause contains at most $r$ literals. Although many polynomial-time approximation algorithms exist for this task, this work adopts the perspective of space complexity, drawing on [Biswas et al., Algorithmica 2021], to develop sublinear-space approximation methods. We demonstrate that the classical approach by [Lieberherr and Specker, JACM 1981] can be executed in $n^{O(1)}$ time with only $(\log{n})$ bits of space. In contrast, advanced techniques relying on linear or semi-definite programming appear difficult to adapt for sublinear space. Furthermore, we show that a more recent algorithm achieving an approximation ratio of $\sqrt{2}/2$ [Chou et al., FOCS 2020], originally intended for the streaming model, can be implemented in $n^{O(r)}$ time using $O(r \log{n})$ bits of space. Unlike existing streaming algorithms that are randomized and approximate optimal values, our proposed algorithms are deterministic and produce approximately optimal assignments within sublinear space. Finally, for Max $r$-SAT instances featuring planar incidence graphs, we introduce a factor-$(1 - \epsilon)$ approximation scheme that runs in $n^{O(r / \epsilon)}$ time and requires $\max\{\sqrt{n} \log{n}, (r / \epsilon) \log^2{n}\}$ bits of space.

This document serves as a brief, informal guide to computing phase diagrams using the ATAT tools emc2 and phb, as well as generating cluster expansions with maps. It is neither comprehensive nor an official publication; rather, it consists primarily of personal notes gathered during my experimentation with ATAT.
