For linear maps, we explicitly characterize their covariance using Kraus, Stinespring, and Choi representations, while systematically analyzing standard attributes such as positivity, decomposability, and complete positivity. Furthermore, we identify the invariant subspaces of these maps and leverage their structural properties to establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the separability of the related invariant bipartite states.

Term clustering plays a crucial role in building biomedical knowledge graphs, and leveraging term embedding similarities is an effective approach for this task. Current state-of-the-art embeddings utilize pretrained language models to encode terms, incorporating synonym and relation data from knowledge graphs to guide contrastive learning; this process ensures that terms sharing the same concept have similar representations. However, our probing experiments reveal that these embeddings lack sensitivity to minor textual variations, causing failures in biomedical term clustering. To address this issue, we refine the pretraining sampling strategy by introducing dynamic hard positive and negative samples during contrastive learning, enabling the model to learn fine-grained representations that enhance clustering performance. We have named this proposed method CODER++, and it has been successfully applied to cluster biomedical concepts in the recently launched Biomedical Knowledge Graph, BIOS.

This study introduces an analytical framework for characterizing domain wall structures in ultrathin films featuring a perpendicular easy axis and interfacial Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, specifically under arbitrary in-plane magnetic fields. The model's solution is streamlined into the numerical minimization of a single-variable analytic function. When compared against numerical micromagnetic simulations using parameters from established samples, the model demonstrates strong agreement; any discrepancies are analyzed and partially rectified. The text also highlights distinctions from the simplest literature model, which restricts variation solely to the in-plane orientation of the domain wall moment. Ultimately, the proposed model enables precise calculations of domain wall tension and width as functions of in-plane field magnitude and direction, providing critical insights into the creep motion of domain walls in these films.

The superconductor-insulator transition (SIT) in disordered thin-film superconductors stands as a quintessential example of a quantum phase transition. Although recognized for over three decades, its fundamental nature remains a subject of intense debate. A particularly fascinating aspect involves the insulating regime, which displays anomalous characteristics. Notably, its current-voltage ($I-V$) relationship features: (1) a conductance that shifts abruptly by multiple orders of magnitude as voltage increases, (2) hysteretic effects, and (3) numerous smaller current jumps (often exceeding one hundred) near the transition point. While various models have been proposed, none have fully captured this observed behavior. A prevalent method involves representing the disordered sample as a two-dimensional grid of conducting islands where charge carriers tunnel between adjacent sites. These models typically assume rapid relaxation, treating the system as perpetually in electrostatic and thermal equilibrium. While they successfully explain certain measurements, including the phase transition itself, they fail to generate the hysteresis seen in experimental $I-V$ curves. In this work, we propose integrating a finite relaxation time into an array-based model. We demonstrate that under slow relaxation conditions, our model can replicate both hysteresis and the multiple jumps observed in the $I-V$ curve. Consequently, we argue that analogous behavior should manifest in two-dimensional normal (non-superconducting) arrays, a hypothesis supported by historical data. Furthermore, we examine the influence of various parameters within our model, identify the relevant time scales, and compare our findings with specific experimental measurements.

This paper introduces a method for probabilistically forecasting the trajectories of vulnerable road users (VRUs) by integrating historical motion data and environmental context. Historical movements are captured through 3D poses that depict individual body postures and dynamics, while the environment is represented via semantic maps detailing infrastructure like sidewalks and streets, as well as obstacles. The resulting forecasts are produced as arbitrary discrete probability distributions over spatial grids, which are assessed based on reliability, sharpness, and positional accuracy. We contrast our approach with methods utilizing Gaussian distributions, examining the specific benefits and drawbacks of each, while also analyzing the influence of pose data and semantic maps. By employing spatial label smoothing, our method generates reliable predictions. The analysis reveals that pose data significantly enhances forecast quality, whereas semantic maps allow for situational adaptation of probability distributions; however, within the 2.52-second forecast horizon, their impact is secondary to the VRU's past movements. The proposed method is validated using a dataset collected from inner-city traffic with a research vehicle, which is now publicly released.

Anonymization and data sharing are vital for safeguarding privacy and gathering extensive datasets for medical image analysis, presenting a significant challenge in neuroimaging where the brain's distinct structure facilitates re-identification, necessitating unconventional anonymization methods. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) offer a promising solution to create anonymous images while maintaining predictive capabilities. In this study, we trained three GAN architectures—Deep Convolutional GAN, Wasserstein-GAN with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP), and WGAN-GP with Spectral Normalization (WGAN-GP-SN)—on time-of-flight (TOF) magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) patches to generate image-label pairs. These synthetic data were used to train U-net models for vessel segmentation, which were then tested against real data. Additionally, we employed a transfer learning strategy using our synthetic patches on a separate dataset. We evaluated model performance on real data from one to fifteen patients, comparing scenarios with and without pre-training. Performance was measured using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and the 95th percentile of the Hausdorff Distance (95HD). Among the models, the U-net trained on WGAN-GP-SN generated synthetic data achieved the highest vessel prediction performance (DSC/95HD: 0.82/28.97), though it still trailed the U-net trained directly on real data (0.89/26.61). Transfer learning demonstrated superior results for the same GAN compared to no pre-training, particularly when limited to a single patient (0.91/25.68 vs. 0.85/27.36). This work confirms that synthetic image-label pairs retain generalizable information and yield robust vessel segmentation results. Furthermore, we demonstrated the efficacy of using synthetic patches in a transfer learning framework with independent datasets, offering a potential pathway to address the dual challenges of data scarcity and anonymization in medical imaging.

Over the last few decades, visual localization and odometry for autonomous robots and virtual reality have been subjects of extensive study. Traditionally, these tasks relied on costly hardware like LiDARs. Currently, research priorities have shifted toward achieving robust localization using more affordable sensors, specifically cameras and IMUs. While geometric visual localization techniques have improved in accuracy over time, they remain prone to significant errors and divergence in difficult scenarios, such as rooms filled with moving people. To address this, researchers began integrating deep neural networks (DNNs). The core objective of employing DNNs is to better interpret complex data and handle challenging conditions, including full-field-of-view occlusions by dynamic objects, extreme lighting, and high camera speeds. Although prior end-to-end DNN approaches have addressed some of these issues, a comprehensive and robust framework capable of handling all such challenges simultaneously has yet to be established. This paper presents a hybrid approach that merges geometric and DNN-based methods, leveraging the speed and generality of geometric SLAM while using DNNs to overcome most adverse conditions, thereby creating the most robust solution to date. Our proposed framework, built upon Vins-Mono, demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on the TUM-Dynamic, TUM-VI, ADVIO, and EuRoC datasets when compared to both geometric and end-to-end DNN-based SLAMs. Furthermore, the framework yields exceptional results in extreme simulated scenarios that mimic the aforementioned challenges.

HIV-1 protease is an ideal candidate for directed enzyme redesign due to its well-documented nature, simple structure, and diverse endogenous targets. Building on a computational algorithm recently introduced by Chaudhury and Gray (Structure, 2009) to identify specificity-determining residues, this study introduces two computational tools designed for HIV-1 protease redesign. The first tool employs an energy-based approach to distinguish between cleavable and non-cleavable peptides for both wild-type and mutant proteases. The second is an algorithm developed to forecast mutant proteases capable of cleaving novel substrate peptides distinct from the enzyme's natural targets. These predicted *in silico* mutants were subsequently evaluated for cleavability and specificity toward the target peptide using the energy-only methodology. Ultimately, two mutant proteases emerged as the optimal candidates regarding specificity and cleavability for the target sequence.

Symplectic maps are commonly employed to model single-particle dynamics within circular accelerators. For linear accelerator maps, the rotation number, equivalent to the betatron frequency, can be readily derived directly from the map. Conversely, with nonlinear maps, this value is typically determined numerically by iterating the map with specific initial conditions or via normal form analysis, which serves as a perturbation theory for maps. Integrable maps, a subset of symplectic maps, permit an analytic calculation of their rotation numbers. This paper introduces an analytic formula to compute the rotation number for integrable symplectic maps in the plane and illustrates the approach with several accelerator-relevant examples. These findings enable the analysis of accelerator Hamiltonian topology and provide a foundation for developing a perturbation theory for maps.
We offer a concise and self-contained demonstration of the choosability variant of Brooks' theorem.

The future aircraft industry now deems it essential to rely on a "smart sky" to manage air traffic and an "Internet above the clouds" for in-flight entertainment. Aeronautical Ad Hoc Networking (AANET) represents a promising approach to delivering broadband connectivity above the clouds by expanding Air-to-Ground (A2G) network coverage into oceanic and remote regions through autonomous, self-configuring wireless links between commercial passenger aircraft. Conceptually, AANET functions as a specialized type of Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) operating in the airspace. However, AANETs face distinct difficulties compared to ground-based networks, including highly dynamic topologies, vast and fluctuating geographic scales, stringent security needs, and adverse transmission environments. These unique traits create significant hurdles in modeling aircraft mobility and aeronautical channels, mitigating interference, and managing network scheduling and routing. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of AANET solutions by defining the relevant scenarios, requirements, and challenges. Specifically, it reviews research on core AANET techniques, encompassing mobility models, scheduling, routing, security, and interference management. Additionally, the study highlights outstanding challenges in AANET development, proposes potential solutions, and addresses open issues. The analysis examines the design framework of AANETs alongside key technical problems and recent findings. Finally, the paper outlines various performance metrics optimized for AANET design and presents several representative multi-objective optimization algorithms.

We establish a Leray model for discrete polymatroids featuring any arbitrary building set and demonstrate a generalized Goresky-MacPherson formula. The initial row of this model corresponds to the polymatroid's Chow ring, for which we prove the Poincaré duality, Hard Lefschetz, and Hodge-Riemann theorems. Additionally, we present a relative Lefschetz decomposition in relation to the deletion of an element.

Although quantum mechanics relies fundamentally on linear algebra, the application of nonlinear operators can yield remarkable discoveries under specific conditions. This Letter introduces a square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal (SHOWS) model by adapting characteristics from its parent Hamiltonians. Our findings reveal that SHOWS supports both "Fermi-arc" surface states and hinge states linking the projections of Weyl points. We successfully constructed this exotic SHOWS state theoretically and observed it experimentally in three-dimensional (3D) stacked electric circuits featuring honeycomb-kagome hybridizations and double-helix interlayer couplings. These results pave the way for achieving square-root topology within 3D solid-state systems.

The extended Bondi-Metzner-Sachs (BMS) group comprises supertranslations, dual supertranslations, and Lorentz transformations. These symmetry generators can be categorized by parity into "electric" and "magnetic" classes. By applying a multipole expansion of gravitational sources within the Newman-Penrose formalism, we link each charge to a specific moment. At the leading order, the "electric" and "magnetic" monopole moments map directly to supertranslations and dual supertranslations, respectively. Moving to the first subleading order, the "electric" and "magnetic" dipole moments correspond to boosts and rotations, thereby encompassing the full Lorentz group. Furthermore, electric-magnetic duality facilitates the rotation of boost and rotation generators into one another.

Daichi Oka et al. (Commun. Phys. 4, 269 (2021)) recently investigated the metal-insulator transition (MIT) in disordered crystalline SrNbO$_{3-x}$N$_x$, basing their analysis on the Al'tshuler-Aronov theory regarding electron-electron interference and elastic impurity scattering. This comment argues that such an evaluation method is unsuitable. To demonstrate this, we re-examine data for samples with $x = 0.96$ and $x = 1.02$ through three distinct lenses: (i) analyzing the logarithmic temperature derivative of conductivity, (ii) assessing deviations of measured conductivity from the Al'tshuler-Aronov temperature dependence approximation, and (iii) comparing experimental temperature data against values derived by treating the sample as a secondary thermometer within that framework. Consequently, for the $x = 0.96$ sample—labeled metallic by Oka et al.—we reveal qualitative discrepancies between measurements and the zero-temperature extrapolation predicted by the Al'tshuler-Aronov theory, suggesting the material likely undergoes activated rather than metallic conduction. These results thereby challenge the continuity of the MIT as derived from the widely cited scaling theory of localization.

We perform numerical simulations of classical particle motion within Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}^{4}$, restricted to the interior of a bag. Specifically, we examine the trajectory structures resulting from the breaking of dilatation symmetry, conformal symmetry, and their combined effect. These confining forces originate directly from the associated nonconserved currents. Our simulations demonstrate that, under specific initial conditions, these particles migrate toward the bag's interior.

For each proper geodesic space $X$, we define its quasi-geometric boundary $\partial_{QG}X$, characterized by six key properties: 1. Every geodesic ray in $X$ converges to a point in $\partial_{QG}X$, and conversely, every point in $\partial_{QG}X$ is the limit of some geodesic ray in $X$; 2. The boundary $\partial_{QG}X$ is a compact metric space; 3. It remains invariant under quasi-isometric equivalences; 4. Any quasi-isometric embedding induces a continuous mapping between the corresponding quasi-geometric boundaries; 5. When $X$ is Gromov hyperbolic, $\partial_{QG}X$ coincides with the Gromov boundary of $X$; 6. If $X$ is a Croke-Kleiner space, then $\partial_{QG}X$ consists of a single point.

The origins of fast radio bursts (FRBs)—astronomical transients lasting only milliseconds—are currently unidentified. A significant challenge lies in the potential heterogeneity of their sources, evidenced by the fact that some FRBs repeat while others do not. Given constraints in observing duration and telescope sensitivity, certain bursts may be erroneously categorized as non-repeaters; thus, accurately distinguishing between repeaters and non-repeaters is crucial for understanding their origins. This study employs unsupervised machine learning to classify these populations without the need for costly monitoring campaigns. We introduce a repeating FRB identification technique utilizing Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP). The primary objectives are: (i) to demonstrate that unsupervised UMAP can classify repeating FRBs without prior knowledge of their repetition patterns, (ii) to assess the hypothesis that non-repeating FRBs are contaminated by repeating ones, and (iii) to identify repeater candidates and generate a catalogue using only single-epoch observations. Applying this method to the CHIME/FRB database, we achieved 95% completeness in detecting repeating FRBs and identified 188 repeater candidates among 474 non-repeater sources. These findings establish a foundation for a new classification system for FRBs based on single-epoch data.

Topological photonics has garnered significant research interest due to its ability to introduce novel physical principles for controlling light. The band topology of optical materials is typically characterized by the Berry phase associated with Bloch states. However, within topological physics, there has been a notable scarcity of criteria for experimentally detecting phase transitions in band topology. Additionally, radiation topology arises from the far-field polarizations of radiating Bloch states and is described by the Stokes phase. Despite both band and radiation topologies being linked to Bloch states on the band structure, their development has remained largely independent. This work reveals that the phase transition of band topology can be investigated through radiation topology. We both theoretically design and experimentally verify this phenomenon by constructing photonic crystals that exhibit optical analogs of the quantum spin Hall effect. Our results demonstrate that as band topology shifts from trivial to non-trivial, the topological charge of the far-field polarization vortex transitions between +1 and -2 (or vice versa), offering a new method to probe band topology phase transitions using radiation topology. These findings provide deep insights into the relationship between band and radiation topologies and open a novel pathway for manipulating both near and far fields of light.

This paper aims to establish modified q-Genocchi numbers and polynomials incorporating weights ({\alpha},{\beta}). We examine special generalized q-Genocchi polynomials by employing the generating function method to derive new classes of q-Genocchi polynomials and develop associated q-Genocchi numbers. Utilizing the Laplace-Mellin transformation integral, we define a q-Zeta function with weight ({\alpha},{\beta}) and establish a connection between this function and q-Genocchi numbers with weight ({\alpha},{\beta}) to derive an interpolation formula. Furthermore, we obtain a distribution formula (Multiplication Theorem) and a Witt's type formula for these modified entities, providing deeper insight into the efficacy of such generalizations for q-Genocchi numbers and polynomials. Additionally, we highlight several interesting properties of our newly introduced generating function.

This study characterizes breaking wave field statistics using a novel multi-layer framework that extends the single-layer Saint-Venant system into a non-hydrostatic, multi-layer Navier-Stokes formulation. We simulate an ensemble of phase-resolved surface waves in physical space, capturing strong nonlinearities such as wave breaking (excluding surface overturning) for freely evolving fields initialized with typical wind wave spectra. By identifying breaking fronts and their velocities, we extract the kinematics of wave breaking. The $\Lambda(c)$ distribution—defined per Phillips (1985) as the length of breaking fronts per unit area moving at speeds between $c$ and $c+dc$—is reported across a wide range of conditions. For sufficiently steep wave fields, we recover the $\Lambda(c) \propto c^{-6}$ scaling without explicit wind forcing. Furthermore, a scaling of $\Lambda(c)$ derived solely from the mean square slope and peak wave phase speed effectively describes the modeled breaking distributions. These results align well with field measurements and are consistent with prior empirical formulations. This work establishes a foundation for directly simulating the turbulent upper ocean coupled with realistic breaking wave dynamics, including Langmuir turbulence and other sub-mesoscale processes.

Astroaccesible is an outreach initiative by the Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía - CSIC, led by a blind astronomer, dedicated to promoting astronomy and astrophysics for both disabled and non-disabled audiences. While audio description is a well-established and accessible method for conveying information in films and museums to those who are blind or partially sighted, it has not yet been widely adopted for describing astronomical images. This contribution introduces "The Universe in Words," a series of videos that provide audio descriptions of popular objects from the Messier catalogue. These descriptions serve a dual purpose: they enhance inclusivity and foster a deeper understanding of the images for everyone. Utilizing inclusive resources not only broadens accessibility but also significantly improves the efficiency of information transmission for all viewers. Furthermore, these videos can function as supplementary materials for in-person events and complement other resources, such as sonifications or physical models of similar astronomical objects.

The recent surge in AI sophistication has led to increasingly complex models, driving a significant demand for computational resources that is now becoming a major hurdle. While this demand is addressed by deploying more powerful accelerators and large-scale compute clusters, the resulting improvements in prediction accuracy come at the cost of substantially higher energy usage, prompting concerns about the environmental sustainability of large-scale AI. Consequently, energy efficiency has become a critical priority for both AI model developers and infrastructure operators. Since energy consumption varies based on model implementation and hardware choices, accurately measuring the power draw of AI workflows across different compute nodes is essential for optimizing algorithms and designing future hardware and clusters. In this study, we present energy consumption measurements for two typical deep learning applications across various compute nodes. Our findings reveal that: 1) calculating energy usage directly from runtime is inaccurate, necessitating an analysis of the compute node's overall composition; 2) ignoring accelerator hardware on mixed nodes leads to disproportionately high energy inefficiency; and 3) training and inference energy consumption must be evaluated separately, as GPU-based training outperforms other node types in both speed and efficiency, whereas CPU-based inference can achieve comparable efficiency. A key benefit of our approach is that making energy consumption data accessible to all supercomputer users facilitates the application of these insights to other workloads and enhances user awareness of energy usage.

We introduce an algorithm for determining connectivity in hypergraphs that operates in time $\hat O_r(p + \min\{\lambda^{\frac{r-3}{r-1}} n^2, n^r/\lambda^{r/(r-1)}\})$, where the $\hat O_r(\cdot)$ notation conceals terms subpolynomial in the primary parameter and those dependent solely on $r$. In this context, $p$ denotes the size, $n$ the vertex count, and $r$ the rank of the hypergraph. This approach surpasses current methods when the rank is constant and the connectivity $\lambda$ grows asymptotically faster than one. Central to our solution is a structural finding about min-cuts in simple hypergraphs, which establishes a trade-off between the count of hyperedges involved in every min-cut and the magnitude of the smaller partition within such a cut. This result generalizes a celebrated structural theorem for simple graphs by Kawarabayashi and Thorup (JACM 2019). Furthermore, we adapt the expander decomposition framework to simple hypergraphs to substantiate this structural insight. By rendering the proof of this result constructive, we derive the aforementioned accelerated algorithm for hypergraph connectivity.

The asteroidal main belt is traversed by a network of mean-motion and secular resonances, which arise from commensurabilities between the fundamental frequencies of asteroids and planets. Historically, these objects were identified through visual analysis of their resonant arguments—combinations of orbital elements involving the asteroid and perturbing planet(s). However, as the population of affected asteroids can number in the thousands, this manual process has become increasingly burdensome. Recent studies have employed Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to automate this task. This paper compares the results of such models against some of the most advanced and publicly available CNN architectures, including VGG, Inception, and ResNet. Initially, model performance was tested and optimized to address overfitting using validation sets and regularization techniques such as data augmentation, dropout, and batch normalization. The three top-performing models were subsequently applied to predict labels for larger testing databases comprising thousands of images. Results indicate that the VGG model, both with and without regularizations, proved to be the most efficient method for labeling large datasets. Given that the Vera C. Rubin Observatory is expected to discover up to four million new asteroids in the coming years, these models may prove highly valuable for identifying populations of resonant minor bodies.

This work theoretically investigates the conditions enabling Coherent Perfect Absorption (CPA) for two laser fields incident on a single-mode bidirectional optical cavity coupled to two two-level quantum emitters (such as atoms, quantum dots, or qubits). Beyond indirect coupling via the cavity-mediated field, our Tavis-Cummings model incorporates direct dipole-dipole interactions (DDI) between the quantum emitters. Utilizing the mean-field approximation and assuming low excitation, we specifically examine how DDI influences CPA existence amidst decoherence mechanisms, including spontaneous emission and photon leakage from the cavity. We further provide a dressed-state analysis to elucidate the underlying physics of polariton state transitions within the Jaynes-Tavis-Cummings ladder. A key finding is that in the strong-coupling regime of cavity quantum electrodynamics, strong DDI combined with emitter-cavity detuning can facilitate CPA at two laser frequencies tunable by inter-atomic distance—outcomes unattainable with a single quantum emitter under detuning. These CPA results hold potential for constructing quantum memories, a critical element for long-distance quantum networking.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) currently represent the leading approach for processing image data. Nevertheless, emerging research indicates that these networks often exhibit biases toward texture and color rather than the shapes of objects, which contradicts the assumption that they mimic human biological learning by focusing on form. Consequently, recent studies have sought to enhance shape bias within CNNs to improve robustness and accuracy. One specific strategy involves utilizing style transfer to eliminate texture cues from the input data. This study replicates that technique across four image classification datasets and further expands the approach by incorporating domain-adversarial training to amplify the shape bias in the learned representations. The findings demonstrate that the proposed method successfully increases both robustness and shape bias, although it does not yield improvements in overall accuracy.

Accurate segmentation of land cover in spectral imagery is a complex task that has garnered significant interest within the remote sensing community. While numerous supervised approaches have been developed, unsupervised subspace clustering techniques, particularly Sparse Subspace Clustering (SSC), have emerged as high-performing alternatives. However, SSC faces two main limitations: its high computational cost renders it unsuitable for large spectral datasets, and its neglect of spatial information restricts its discriminative power, thereby compromising the spatial homogeneity of clustering outcomes. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces a rapid algorithm that first identifies a minimal set of representative pixels for their neighborhoods to derive a sparse coefficient matrix. It subsequently applies spatial filtering to ensure pixel connectivity and employs fast spectral clustering for the final segmentation. Extensive simulations confirm the method's efficacy, yielding superior clustering performance compared to both advanced SSC-based algorithms and recent unsupervised deep-learning techniques. Additionally, the proposed approach achieves a speedup of up to three orders of magnitude over SSC when processing datasets with more than $2 \times 10^4$ spectral pixels.

The page number of a directed acyclic graph $G$ is defined as the smallest integer $k$ such that $G$ admits a topological ordering alongside a $k$-edge coloring where no two edges of the same color cross, meaning their endpoints do not alternate in the ordering. This text tackles a longstanding open question regarding the maximum page number found in upward planar graphs. We enhance the existing lower bound to $5$ and introduce the first asymptotic improvement upon the trivial $O(n)$ upper bound, where $n$ represents the vertex count. Our approach initially establishes that the page number of any upward planar graph is constrained by both its width and height. Subsequently, by integrating these two strategies, we demonstrate that the page number for every upward planar graph with $n$ vertices is $O(n^{2/3} \log(n)^{2/3})$.

We examine the Hamilton-Jacobi equation governing a probe particle traversing a d-dimensional generalized Lense-Thirring metric, which distinguishes itself from the slowly rotating Myers-Perry black hole at the second order of rotation parameters. Our analysis demonstrates that the probe's dynamics along time-like geodesics in this generalized Lense-Thirring space-time are super-integrable and possess a greater number of constants of motion compared to the corresponding dynamics on a Myers-Perry black hole. Furthermore, we explore the second-rank Killing tensors linked to the generalized Lense-Thirring metric.

The relaxed galaxy cluster Zwicky 3146 has been analyzed using SuperModel, a tool validated on numerous clusters since 2009. This study specifically examines X-ray temperature data of the intracluster medium from XMM-Newton, extending to r_{500}, following a prior analysis based on pressure data from the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect. The gas mass fraction (f_{gas}) is derived from the SuperModel temperature profile extrapolated to the virial radius (R); this result aligns with steep temperature profiles observed by Suzaku and the gas density profile from XMM-Newton. Comparing f_{gas} to the universal value suggests a non-thermal pressure component (p_{nth}) in the cluster's outskirts. The SuperModel analysis indicates that the ratio of p_{nth} to total pressure, alpha(R), is approximately 50%, exceeding simulation values and implying accreting substructures and gas density inhomogeneities. After correcting the profile for clumpiness, the p_{nth} level decreases significantly, yet notable turbulence (alpha(R) around 20%) and entropy flattening remain in the cluster's outskirts.

This study addresses the numerical solution of a data completion problem for time-harmonic Maxwell equations regarding the electric field. The objective involves reconstructing missing information on the inaccessible portion of the boundary of a bounded domain using measurements obtained from the accessible part. The paper investigates the non-iterative quasi-reversibility method and introduces several mixed variational formulations. Proofs are provided for well-posedness, convergence, and regularity. Furthermore, edge finite elements are employed for discretization. Numerical simulations conducted in both two and three dimensions demonstrate the method's efficiency, particularly when dealing with noisy data.

We address signal estimation within generalized linear models featuring rotationally invariant design matrices. Given that these matrices support arbitrary spectral distributions, the framework effectively captures complex correlation patterns frequently encountered in practical applications. We introduce a new class of approximate message passing (AMP) algorithms for this purpose and rigorously analyze their asymptotic performance in high-dimensional settings using state evolution recursion. This rotationally invariant AMP matches the computational complexity of existing AMP methods developed under the restrictive Gaussian design assumption, while also subsuming that existing method as a special case. Numerical experiments demonstrate performance comparable to Vector AMP—a method conjectured to be Bayes-optimal in certain contexts—but with significantly reduced complexity, as our approach avoids the need for computationally intensive singular value decomposition.

A comprehensive investigation into chaos and thermalization is conducted for a disordered linear chain of trapped bosonic atoms. At high disorder levels, the system remains regular and localized, whereas weak disorder reveals chaos and validates the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH) for most eigenstates, except for those at the energy spectrum's extremes, which stay regular and non-thermalizing. The study analyzes the temporal evolution of experimentally accessible occupation basis states, classifying them by maximum occupation and a crowding parameter linearly correlated with average energy. States within the chaotic energy range display significantly larger participation ratios in the eigenbasis compared to the noticeably smaller ratios of regular states. Furthermore, chaotic states with the highest participation ratios exhibit the characteristic random matrix correlation hole in their survival probability, while regular states lack this feature and demonstrate long-lasting revivals.

When two layers in a twisted moiré system experience unequal strain, the resulting effect is magnified by the inverse twist angle; for instance, in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (TBG), this amplification reaches a factor of 50. TBG samples typically exhibit heterostrain ranging from 0.1% to 0.7%, which can expand the bandwidth of "flat" bands up to ten times, thereby positioning TBG within an intermediate coupling regime. In this study, we investigate the phase diagram of TBG under heterostrain using unbiased, large-scale density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations with a bond dimension of $\chi=24576$, accounting for all spin and valley degrees of freedom. At a filling of $\nu = -3$, we observe that a strain of $0.05\%$ induces a transition from a quantized anomalous Hall insulator to an incommensurate-Kekulé spiral (IKS) phase. This unique order, previously explored at the mean-field level by Kwan et al. (PRX 11, 041063), violates both valley conservation and standard translation symmetry $\hat{T}$, yet maintains a modified translation symmetry $\hat{T}'$ featuring moiré-incommensurate phase modulation. Strains exceeding this threshold further drive the system into a fully symmetric metal.

We introduce a second-order ensemble approach utilizing a blended three-step backward differentiation formula (BDF) for time-stepping to solve a collection of Navier-Stokes equations. In contrast to the sole existing second-order ensemble method—which merges a two-step BDF scheme with a specialized explicit second-order Adams-Bashforth treatment for the advection term—our proposed technique achieves superior accuracy with only a marginal rise in computational expense. We provide a thorough analysis of the method's stability and error characteristics. Furthermore, numerical experiments are presented to validate the theoretical findings and illustrate the enhanced precision of this approach.

While Xu et al. (2020) recently proposed that numeral systems across languages evolve to meet functional demands for efficient communication within an information-theoretic framework, this study adopts a learning-theoretic perspective to demonstrate how such efficiency arises through reinforcement learning. In our model, two artificial agents engage in a Lewis signaling game aimed at conveying numeral concepts. As the agents progressively refine their communication strategies via reinforcement learning, the emergent numeral systems prove to be information-theoretically efficient according to the criteria established by Regier et al. (2015) and Gibson et al. (2017) and closely resemble human numeral systems of the same category. Consequently, our findings offer a mechanistic reinforcement learning-based explanation for the results reported by Xu et al. (2020) and suggest potential applicability to other semantic domains.

**Context.** Stellar parameters are fundamental to traditional star studies, which rely on atmospheric models; however, spectral observations are often hindered by high time costs and brightness constraints. The J-PLUS observational campaign addresses this by capturing photometry across 12 bands, creating a valuable dataset for stellar research. Machine learning offers efficient tools to analyze such large-scale data, enabling expanded investigations into stellar parameters.

**Aims.** This study aims to develop a Support Vector Regression (SVR) algorithm to estimate stellar parameters for the first data release of the J-PLUS campaign.

**Methods.** The training dataset combines 12-band J-PLUS photometry with spectra-based catalogs from LAMOST, APOGEE, and SEGUE, labeling the entries with effective temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity. Ten percent of the sample is reserved for a blind test. To comprehensively account for uncertainties in both magnitudes and stellar parameters, a novel multi-model approach is employed, utilizing over two hundred models for uncertainty analysis.

**Results.** The study presents a catalog of 2,493,424 stars, achieving a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 160 K for effective temperature, 0.35 for surface gravity, and 0.25 for metallicity. Additionally, the advantages of this multi-model approach are discussed and compared against other machine-learning techniques.

This paper investigates the relationship between entropic optimal transport and the entropy power inequality (EPI). Initially, we establish an HWI-type inequality by leveraging the infinitesimal displacement convexity of the optimal transport map. Subsequently, we derive two Talagrand-type inequalities based on the saturation of EPI, which yields a specific numerical term within our formulation. We evaluate this term across a broad range of distributions, obtaining explicit forms for Gaussian and i.i.d. Cauchy cases. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our findings generalize prior results regarding the Gaussian Talagrand inequality for Sinkhorn distance to the strongly log-concave setting.

We employ numerical renormalization group theory to examine the Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) bound state characteristics of isolated magnetic molecules embedded in an s-wave superconducting substrate. The molecular system comprises a large core spin and a single orbital interacting through an exchange coupling. Our findings indicate that the critical Coulomb interaction required for the singlet-to-doublet transition diminishes when this exchange interaction is present, regardless of whether the coupling is ferro- or anti-ferromagnetic. Additionally, the number of YSR states rises to two pairs; however, within the singlet phase, one of these pairs exhibits zero spectral weight. By utilizing the Anderson model, we investigate the evolution of these in-gap states. Deviating from particle-hole symmetry, the results reveal a doublet-singlet-doublet transition as the on-site energy decreases while the Coulomb interaction remains constant. To interpret these phenomena, we construct an effective model for the molecule under the assumption of a large superconducting order parameter, which qualitatively accounts for the observed phase transitions and the spectral properties of the in-gap states. Furthermore, we assess the impact of magnetic anisotropic fields acting on the core spin. Given the internal degrees of freedom associated with excited spin states, a variety of new states appear within the gap. Depending on the magnitude and sign of the uniaxial anisotropic field, up to three pairs of YSR states can emerge.

This article examines the iteration of the function $f_\lambda(z)=\lambda + z+\tan z$ for $z \in \mathbb{C}$. It is demonstrated that for any $\lambda$, the Fatou set of $f_\lambda$ contains a completely invariant Baker domain $B$, termed the primary Fatou component. Subsequent results focus on cases where $f_\lambda$ is topologically hyperbolic. Specifically, for all real $\lambda$ or $\lambda=\pi k +i \lambda_2$ (where $k$ is an integer and $0 < \lambda_2<1$), the sole additional Fatou component is another completely invariant Baker domain.

The study proves that when $|2+\lambda^2|<1$, the Fatou set comprises $B$ and an infinite collection of invariant attracting domains. Each such domain $U$ features exactly one invariant access to infinity and exhibits a specific unboundedness: while the set of imaginary parts $\{\Im(z): z\in U\}$ is unbounded, the set of real parts $\{\Re(z): z\in U\}$ remains bounded.

Furthermore, if $\Im(\lambda)> \sqrt{2}+ \sinh^{-1}1$, it is established that the primary Fatou component is the unique Fatou component, resulting in a disconnected Julia set. For every natural number $k$, the Fatou set of $f_\lambda$ with $\lambda=k\pi+i\frac{\pi}{2}$ is shown to include $k$ wandering domains possessing distinct grand orbits; these domains are identified as escaping. In this scenario, the Fatou set consists of $B$, these wandering domains, and their pre-images.

Recent deep learning architectures have proven highly effective for crowd counting, a vital task with broad industrial relevance. However, despite these advancements, data-dependent models often fail to generalize to unseen environments due to inherent domain shifts. To address this challenge, we introduce Adversarial Scoring Network (ASNet), a novel framework designed to bridge the domain gap through a coarse-to-fine approach. At the coarse-grained level, a dual-discriminator strategy leverages adversarial learning to align source and target domains by matching their global and local feature distributions. Subsequently, at the fine-grained level, the model evaluates the similarity between source and target samples across multiple levels using generative probabilities derived from the initial stage. These hierarchical scores guide the selection of transferable source features, thereby enhancing knowledge transfer during adaptation. This hierarchical design effectively mitigates the generalization bottleneck caused by domain discrepancies. Empirical results from three migration experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art counting performance compared to leading unsupervised techniques.

Compressed sensing fluorescence microscopy (CS-FM) utilizes a framework where fewer measurements are gathered during sensing, followed by reconstruction to retrieve the image. While significant research has focused on optimizing the sensing and reconstruction stages independently, we introduce a method for end-to-end joint optimization of both components under a fixed total measurement limit. This approach simultaneously learns the ideal sensing strategy and the parameters of a neural network-based reconstruction model. Our model is trained on a comprehensive dataset of confocal, two-photon, and wide-field microscopy images featuring diverse biological specimens. We demonstrate that our method surpasses various baseline sensing protocols and a regularized regression reconstruction algorithm in performance.

This study examines a nearest-neighbor solid-on-solid (SOS) model featuring spin values ranging from $0$ to $m$ ($m\geq2$) in the presence of a nonzero external field, defined on a Cayley tree with degree $k$ ($k+1$ neighbors). Our objective is to extend findings from \cite{rs}, which primarily analyzed an SOS model with three spin values and no external field. Notably, the SOS model serves as a natural generalization of the Ising model, which corresponds to the case $m=1$. We focus mainly on the scenario where $m=2$ (three spin values) to investigate translation-invariant (TI) and splitting (S) Gibbs measures (GMs); splitting GMs possess a specific Markov-type property characteristic of tree structures. For $m=2$ under antiferromagnetic (AFM) conditions, a translation-invariant splitting Gibbs measure (TISGM) is proven to be unique across all temperatures and external field strengths. Conversely, in the ferromagnetic (FM) case with $m=2$, the count of TISGMs fluctuates based on temperature and external field, providing a compelling example of phase transitions. A secondary result offers a complete classification of all TISGMs for the Three-State SOS-Model on a degree-two Cayley tree with an external field. We demonstrate uniqueness for AFM interactions and establish that FM interactions can yield up to seven TISGMs, where the number of distinct phases is contingent upon the interaction strength and external field.

We present the discovery of a massive neutral gas outflow in the gravitationally lensed, dust-obscured star-forming galaxy HATLASJ085358.9+015537 (G09v1.40) at z=2.09. Detected via absorption in the OH+(1_1-1_0) transition, this outflow was mapped using spatially resolved ALMA observations (0.5"x0.4"). The blueshifted OH+ line was observed concurrently with CO(9-8) emission and the dust continuum, while complementary high-resolution ALMA data (0.17"x0.13") captured CH+(1-0) and the continuum, alongside Keck 2.2 micron imaging of stellar light. Spatial offsets were identified between the outflow, dust, dense molecular gas, and stars. The outflow's total atomic gas mass reaches 6.7x10^9 M_sun, surpassing 25% of the galaxy's total gas mass. A conical geometry best fits the OH+ kinematics and morphology, allowing for deprojected outflow properties across inclination angles ranging from 0.38 to 64 degrees. The neutral gas mass outflow rate spans 83–25400 M_sun/yr; if the inclination exceeds 3.6 degrees, this rate surpasses the star formation rate (788±300 M_sun/yr), yielding a mass-loading factor of 0.3–4.7. Kinetic energy and momentum fluxes range from 4.4–290x10^9 L_sun and 0.1–3.7x10^37 dyne, respectively (energy-loading factor = 0.013–16), suggesting that the feedback mechanisms driving the outflow vary with assumed inclination. We calculated a gas depletion time of 29–1 Myr, concluding that the outflow likely remains gravitationally bound to the galaxy unless the inclination is low, and could potentially be re-accreted if further feedback processes are absent.

We examine anomalous dissipation from a microscopic perspective. Following the work of Drivas, Elgindi, Iyer, and Jeong (2022), the phenomenon of anomalous dissipation ensures the existence of non-unique weak solutions for a transport equation governed by a singular velocity field. This paper revisits that solution through the lens of kinetic theory to elucidate its microscopic characteristics. As a result, energy loss is shown to arise from non-vanishing microscopic advection.

Bounded stochastic dominance orders play a pivotal role in risk management and decision-making under uncertainty. We introduce a new characterization of the $n$-th degree bounded stochastic dominance order, which evaluates the $n$-th lower partial moments of random variables within a bounded range. This framework links the risk tolerance of decision-makers to these stochastic orders, offering a decision-theoretic interpretation for them. Additionally, our findings yield non-trivial inequalities for $n$-convex functions and establish lottery rankings for agents possessing a globally bounded Arrow-Pratt measure of risk aversion.

Although the ether concept was long discarded and later revived by Dirac between 1951 and 1953, it has recently become a prominent topic in theoretical physics, often referred to as the Einstein-Dirac ether. This framework designates a unique inertial frame as the "rest frame." The current note highlights that this idea naturally arises within the covariant theory of quantum electrodynamics in media when the refractive index is set to unity. The author previously addressed this specific case in a 1971 preprint series; the present work offers a concise summary of that formalism, linking back to the original publication. We consider this to be among the earliest treatises on modern ether theory.

Let $H$ and $G$ be graphs. An $H$-colouring of $G$ is defined as a mapping $f:E(G)\rightarrow E(H)$ where, for every vertex $u \in V(G)$, there is a vertex $v \in V(H)$ such that the set of edges incident to $u$ in $G$ maps exactly to the set of edges incident to $v$ in $H$ (denoted as $\partial_G(u)$ and $\partial_H(v)$, respectively). If such a mapping exists, $H$ is said to colour $G$. The Petersen Colouring Conjecture directly addresses whether a specific graph $H$ exists that can colour every bridgeless cubic graph $G$, proposing that the Petersen graph itself fulfills this role. In 2012, Mkrtchyan demonstrated that if the conjecture holds, the Petersen graph is the only connected, bridgeless cubic graph $H$ capable of colouring all such graphs $G$. This paper extends that finding by removing degree constraints on $H$, revealing that the only graph (other than the Petersen graph) that can colour every bridgeless cubic graph $G$ is the unique subcubic multigraph $S_{4}$ on four vertices. Similar results are also presented under weaker assumptions regarding $G$. Furthermore, the second part of the paper examines $H$-colourings of regular graphs $G$ with degrees strictly greater than 3, proving two key points: (i) for any integer $r > 3$, no graph $H$ (even one allowing parallel edges) can colour every $r$-regular multigraph $G$, and (ii) for every integer $r > 1$, no graph $H$ (allowing parallel edges) can colour every $2r$-regular simple graph $G$.

Recent studies have firmly established that incorporating a restart mechanism can significantly and beneficially modify the first-passage statistics of stochastic processes. While various mechanisms have been explored previously, this work derives a probability generating function for a discrete-time first-passage process under restart, applying it to analyze two specific cases, one of which involves a biased random walk on the non-negative integers.

This study examines the extension of the Standard Model lepton sector by introducing three right-handed Majorana neutrinos with masses reaching up to the $10^2$ MeV scale. In this framework, the lightest heavy neutral lepton serves as a dark matter candidate with a mass around 10 keV, while the other two leptons generate standard active neutrino masses via the type I see-saw mechanism. Beyond lepton flavor violation, these heavy neutral leptons can also induce violations of lepton universality in charged meson decays, with such deviations potentially being detectable experimentally. The analysis evaluates the magnitude of these universality violations under two natural mixing scenarios, incorporating three-particle decays into the calculation of the total meson width. Furthermore, the discussion highlights the strong dependence of lepton universality violation on the specific mixing scenario adopted.

Observations indicate that protoplanetary disks exhibit less turbulence than predicted by their accretion rates, suggesting that magnetized disk winds are the primary drivers of angular momentum transport. This hypothesis has significant consequences for planet formation. We modeled the physical and chemical evolution of disks, along with planet formation and migration, incorporating both turbulent viscosity and disk winds. Our simulations accounted for planet traps that restrict Type I migration, generating thousands of evolutionary tracks for single planets across a range of initial disk conditions and turbulence levels, while excluding multi-planet systems and N-body interactions. Our results show that assuming constant turbulence and wind strengths yields mass-semimajor axis distributions with too little scatter to match observations. In contrast, models that sample disks with varying relative strengths of turbulence and winds align much better with data. These scenarios successfully produce a significant population of super-Earths between 0.03 and 2 AU, clearly distinguish hot Jupiters from warm Jupiters, and accurately reproduce the observed mass-radius distribution of exoplanets once post-disk photoevaporation is considered.

Nickel-carbon based multi-layers represent a promising approach for developing future hard X-ray and soft $\gamma$-ray focusing telescopes. This study investigates the pulsed laser deposition conditions required to grow such bilayers, utilizing Reflective High Energy Electron Diffraction, X-ray Reflectivity and Diffraction, Atomic Force Microscopy, X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy, and cross-sectional Transmission Electron Microscopy. The analysis focuses on optimizing process pressure and substrate temperature. The thin multi-layers were fabricated on a treated SiO substrate, achieving Ni and C layers with surface roughnesses (RMS) of $\leq$0.2 nm. Although small droplets formed during target surface melting increase roughness, they are unavoidable. Furthermore, sequential processing at temperatures exceeding 300$^\circ$C causes intermixing between the layers, which degrades the multi-layer's reflectivity.

This paper examines the structure of the parafermion vertex operator algebra linked to an integrable highest weight module of the simple affine Lie superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, with a specific focus on identifying the generators of this algebra.

The inclusion of erodible substrate material by geophysical flows can substantially increase the mass of the moving debris and expand the area of final deposition. The dimensions of both the flowing particles and the erodible bed govern the entrainment processes and dictate the broader flow behavior. This study investigates these mechanisms through laboratory experiments using an inclined flume, where particles of varying sizes move over an erodible base. Dynamic X-ray radiography was employed to visualize the interaction at the flow-bed interface. Results indicate that maximum downslope velocity is a function of the ratio between flow particle size and bed particle size, with larger ratios resulting in higher velocities. Two distinct approaches were utilized to estimate evolving erosion depth: a conventional critical velocity method and a newly developed particle-size-based method. When calculating erosion rates using both techniques, the findings presented conflicting trends. Specifically, the critical-velocity method showed that normalized erosion rates increase as the ratio of flow to bed grain size grows, while the particle-size-based approach revealed the opposite relationship. We address this inconsistency by analyzing the physical basis of each measurement technique, offering guidance for future modeling to integrate both complementary metrics. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that estimated erosion rates are entirely contingent upon the specific method used to determine erosion depth and the chosen measurement technique.

Accurate segmentation of live cell images holds significant value in both clinical and research settings. Although deep learning techniques can achieve high precision in cell segmentation, developing such models typically necessitates access to high-fidelity live cell images. This requirement is frequently unmet due to resource limitations, such as restricted access to high-performance microscopes or the inherent characteristics of the organisms under study. Consequently, segmenting low-resolution live cell images presents a considerable challenge. This paper introduces a method to address this issue by integrating super-resolution as a pre-processing step within the segmentation pipeline.

We introduce a novel class of quantum Weyl algebras, wherein the polynomial component serves as a quantum analogue to functions defined on homogeneous spaces associated with symmetric matrices, skew-symmetric matrices, and the full matrix space of a specified dimension. This framework is built upon twisted tensor products and their deformations, leveraging invariance properties from quantum symmetric pairs. These algebras possess $U_q(\mathfrak{gl}_N)$-module algebra structures that align with standard ones on the polynomial section, feature relations elegantly formulated through matrices, and maintain a close connection to an algebra emerging within the theory of quantum bounded symmetric domains.

Fe$_{3}$Ga$_{4}$ exhibits a sophisticated magnetic phase diagram that responds sensitively and can be adjusted through modifications to both its crystallographic and electronic structures. To investigate this tunability, researchers synthesized and analyzed vanadium-doped (Fe$_{1-x}$V$_{x}$)$_{3}$Ga$_{4}$. High-resolution synchrotron X-ray diffraction coupled with Rietveld refinement indicates that samples containing up to 20% vanadium maintain the same crystal structure as Fe$_{3}$Ga$_{4}$ and exhibit a linear expansion of the unit cell volume as the doping level rises. Magnetic analysis demonstrates that vanadium doping suppresses the antiferromagnetic helical spin-density wave (SDW), evidenced by shifts in both the low-temperature ferromagnetic-antiferromagnetic (FM-AFM) transition (T$_{1}$) and the high-temperature AFM-FM transition (T$_{2}$). Specifically, at 7.5% V-doping, the metamagnetic characteristics of the helical AFM SDW phase disappear. These findings provide a pathway for effectively controlling magnetic order in Fe$_{3}$Ga$_{4}$ for technological applications and deepen the understanding of magnetism within this system.

Splash bridges form when two gas-rich disk galaxies collide directly, often ejecting gas masses comparable to \SI{e10} Msun from their stellar disks. The Taffy Galaxy system (UGC 1294/5) serves as a classic example of such a system; CO observations indicate its bridge holds a molecular hydrogen ($H_2$) mass equal to that of the Milky Way. Despite this immense reservoir, the minimal visible star formation observed in the bridge underscores the necessity for improved models of direct gas-rich disk collisions. Another potential example is the Arp 194 system, which exhibits a splash bridge between two disk galaxies containing bright clumps of active star formation. To better understand the conditions triggering star formation in these bridges, we apply the Jeans criterion to identify regions of gravitational instability within the shocked and cooling gas of colliding disks. Building on previous work using a sticky particle code, our post-processed results demonstrate that the inclination between gas disks and the collision velocity significantly influence the fraction of gas becoming gravitationally unstable. Specifically, low inclinations lead to starbursts, while high inclinations produce steady-rate star formation. Conversely, the offset of the gas disks at impact affects the number of directly colliding gas elements but does not strongly alter the resulting star formation activity.

Homogeneous two-phase cavitation models are the preferred choice for simulating cavitating flows within large-scale computational fluid dynamics frameworks, utilizing the computationally efficient volume-of-fluids method for multiphase issues. Since cavitation phenomena occur on spatial and temporal scales significantly smaller than the macroscopic bulk flow, the primary challenge for homogeneous models is accurately representing these sub-scale effects. This review examines how phase transitions and bubble dynamics are modeled at these sub-scales, emphasizing that the specific assumptions underpinning a model dictate its resulting formulation. The article identifies twelve distinct approaches to homogeneous cavitating flow modeling, detailing their methodologies and derived outcomes. By fostering a deeper understanding of these models, the review clarifies the inherent limitations of the homogeneous approach based on their fundamental assumptions. Consequently, it establishes a unified theoretical foundation for these models, setting the stage for future investigations into their accuracy and performance.

Functional data analysis has gained significant attention and is encountering new hurdles, particularly the rise of streaming data. This article introduces an online nonparametric approach to dynamically update estimates of mean and covariance functions for functional data. The kernel-based estimators can be broken down into two sufficient statistics based on data-driven bandwidths. We suggest approximating future optimal bandwidths using a sequence of dynamically evolving candidates and aggregating the associated statistics across data blocks to generate updated estimates. This proposed online method is computationally efficient, relying only on stored sufficient statistics and the current data block. We establish the asymptotic normality of the online estimates and, crucially, derive lower bounds for their relative efficiency. These results offer insights into the trade-off between estimation accuracy and computational cost, which is influenced by the length of the candidate bandwidth sequence. Additionally, simulations and real-world data examples are presented to validate these findings.

We introduce a highly sensitive mid-infrared (mid-IR) photodetector designed for the mid-wavelength (MWIR) and long-wavelength (LWIR) infrared spectra. This device utilizes a hybrid heterostructure combining nanopatterned graphene (NPG) and vanadium dioxide (VO$_2$), leveraging the phase transition of a thin VO$_2$ film to achieve exceptional performance near room temperature. The photodetector demonstrates a responsivity of approximately $R\sim 10^4$ V/W, a detectivity surpassing $D^*\sim 10^{10}$ J, and a noise-equivalent power (NEP) sensitivity of about $100$ fW/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$. Nearly 100% absorption in monolayer graphene is realized through localized surface plasmons (LSPs) generated around patterned circular holes. Furthermore, the absorption peak within the 3 to 12 $\mu$m mid-IR range can be tuned by adjusting the nanopattern geometry and applying an electrostatic gate potential. Upon photon absorption by the NPG and the subsequent insulator-to-metal phase change in VO$_2$, an applied bias voltage ($V_b$) induces a detectable current within roughly 1 ms, a response time faster than that of existing VO$_2$ bolometers. Ultimately, this proposed mid-IR photodetector matches the detectivity of cryogenically cooled HgCdTe devices and exceeds the sensitivity of VO$_2$ microbolometers while operating close to ambient conditions.

This research focuses on developing signal processing algorithms to unlock the capabilities of the PICOSEC-MicroMegas detector, enabling precise online timing. As a new type of gaseous detector, the PICOSEC-MicroMegas device is designed to achieve high timing resolution in experimental settings. The proposed algorithms were assessed through various tests using experimental data collected during a Laser Beam Test at CEA/IRAMIS-SACLAY. The study utilized two distinct datasets: the SPE-set, consisting of single photoelectron waveforms, and the EXP-set, comprising waveforms averaging 7.8 photoelectrons. Full analysis of the EXP-set yielded a timing resolution of $18.3 \pm 0.2$ ps. The work also details and evaluates alternative algorithms based on Constant Threshold Discrimination, which employ multi-charge measurements above the threshold to correct systematic timing errors. Additionally, a timing technique utilizing Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) was advanced and assessed. To create a suitable training dataset for the ANN, a new simulation model was developed. Using the EXP-set waveforms to verify accuracy, the results demonstrated that the proposed methods achieve the same timing precision as full signal processing analysis. Furthermore, it was proven that the estimated Signal Arrival Time is consistent and unbiased. Finally, a key advantage of these newly developed techniques is their ability to operate during data acquisition, providing rapid particle arrival timing for triggering and event selection.

This study extends the authors' previous work on noninvasive model-reference adaptive control for continuing periodic orbits in periodically excited linear systems with matched uncertainties to a broader class of periodically excited nonlinear systems sharing similar uncertainty characteristics and known structural properties. Additionally, a candidate adaptive feedback approach is introduced for scalar systems featuring unmodeled nonlinearities. In the primary scenario, rigorous analysis establishes guaranteed bounds for prediction and estimation errors. Combined with a persistent excitation assumption, this ensures asymptotic convergence to periodic responses uniquely defined by an a priori unknown periodic reference input and independent of initial conditions, fulfilling the requirements of the control-based continuation framework. Specifically, when the reference input matches the desired periodic response, the steady-state control input becomes zero. Similar conclusions apply to scalar dynamics with unmodeled nonlinearities, though convergence occurs at a slower rate. Numerical simulations confirm these theoretical findings for specific parameter sets. Furthermore, integration with the COCO software package demonstrates successful continuation along families of both stable and unstable periodic orbits with minimal parameter tuning. These outcomes broaden the scope of known noninvasive feedback strategies applicable to experimental model validation and engineering design.

This research investigates learning-based controllers as an alternative to model predictive control (MPC) for autonomous vehicles, focusing experiments on the simple yet representative bicycle model. We evaluate training methods using both supervised and reinforcement learning, while also analyzing neural network architectures to achieve high performance with compact models. The primary goal is to develop controllers that are suitable for real-time embedded systems and capable of formal verification.

For a graph $G$, a subset $S \subseteq V(G)$ is defined as a \emph{resolving set} if, for every pair of distinct vertices $u, v \in V(G)$, there is a vertex $w \in S$ such that $d(w,u) \neq d(w,v)$. The {\sc Metric Dimension} problem involves determining whether a graph $G$ possesses a resolving set of size at most $k$. First introduced in the 1970s, this problem is established as NP-hard~[GT~61 in Garey and Johnson's book]. In the context of parameterized complexity, Hartung and Nichterlein~[CCC~2013] demonstrated that the problem is W[2]-hard when parameterized by $k$. They further noted that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) when parameterized by the vertex cover number, prompting an inquiry into its complexity under even smaller parameters, specifically the feedback vertex set number. We address this by proving that {\sc Metric Dimension} is W[1]-hard when parameterized by the feedback vertex set number, a finding that strengthens the result by Bonnet and Purohit~[IPEC 2019], which showed W[1]-hardness with respect to treewidth. Concerning the vertex cover number, we establish that {\sc Metric Dimension} lacks a polynomial kernel unless $NP\subseteq coNP/poly$, a conclusion that also applies to the distance to clique parameter. Conversely, we demonstrate that {\sc Metric Dimension} is FPT when parameterized by the distance to cluster or the distance to co-cluster, both of which are more restrictive than the vertex cover number.

Global leadership computing centers enable advanced scientific inquiry across diverse fields, ranging from climate change analysis and opioid addiction research to neutron decay simulations. Although rising computational power has enhanced scientists' ability to validate models, the expanding scale of these projects now necessitates a dedicated framework to manage workflows effectively. A standard scientific computing workflow entails defining input parameters for each computational step, establishing task dependencies, storing output data, conducting post-processing, and performing data analysis. EspressoDB is a Python-based, object-relational data management system built upon the Django web framework. Developed to optimize data management processes, ensure data integrity, and offer flexibility with ease of use, the EspressoDB framework is designed to address the growing complexity of scientific workflows at major computing facilities. Its primary objective is to minimize the human effort required for job management, thereby allowing researchers to dedicate more time to their scientific investigations.

Scattering amplitudes at tree level can be geometrically characterized by the intersection numbers of twisted differential form pairs defined on the moduli space of punctured Riemann spheres. We have compiled a catalog of these twisted differential forms, incorporating both established and newly discovered examples. By pairing elements from this collection, one can calculate intersection numbers to determine scattering amplitudes for various theories; while some results align with the known CHY framework, others remain previously unknown. Similarly, specific pairings yield both familiar and innovative double-copy constructions for spin-two theories. Through this approach, we derive double-copy structures for numerous models, including higher-derivative gravity, (partially massless) bimetric gravity, and other exotic theories. Additionally, we provide a derivation of amplitude relations within the context of intersection theory.

The Kremer-Grest (KG) polymer model is a widely used framework in Molecular Dynamics simulations for investigating general polymer characteristics. Its enduring popularity stems from its computational efficiency and simplicity, rather than its capacity to replicate specific polymer species or conditions. In this work, we demonstrate that by adjusting chain stiffness, the KG model can be adapted to simulate melts of real-world polymers. Specifically, we establish mapping relations between KG parameters and SI units applicable to a broad spectrum of commodity polymers. This connection between experimental data and KG simulations is anchored at the Kuhn scale, representing the transition from chemistry-dependent small-scale behavior to universal large-scale dynamics. We anticipate that Kuhn-scale-mapped KG models will accurately capture universal properties driven by the large-scale conformational statistics and dynamics of flexible polymers. Notably, we observe excellent agreement between the entanglement moduli predicted by our KG models and those measured experimentally for the target polymers.

Theoretical predictions suggest that itinerant spin polarons and metallic ferromagnetism can exist in Mott insulators within semiconductor moiré superlattices, specifically when doped with electrons or holes, respectively.

Generalized parton distributions (GPDs) offer a unified framework for investigating hadronic form factors, parton distribution amplitudes, and parton densities. At low-x with finite skewness, these distributions are primarily governed by Pomeron and Reggeon exchanges. Within the large-$N_c$ limit, we propose that the leading twist Gegenbauer (conformal) moments at low resolution scales can be determined from leading Witten diagrams in holographic QCD. We explicitly calculate these moments for several exclusive processes, focusing on photon and meson electroproduction. Subsequently, these moments are evolved to higher resolution scales using established leading-order QCD evolution equations. Utilizing our explicit results for evolved singlet, non-singlet, and gluon GPDs, we analyze the electroproduction of longitudinal $\rho^{0,+}$ and $\phi$ mesons, comparing our findings with existing data. These explicit holographic predictions are expected to facilitate the extraction of GPDs from current and future global analyses of photon and meson electroproduction.

A numerical model, building upon the advanced framework by Hazenberg and van Oijen (PCI, 2021) to incorporate unsteady effects, was employed to simulate pulsed iron flames stabilized within a multidimensional hot counterflow burner. These simulations were validated against experimental data from McRae et al. (PCI, 2019), encompassing particle image velocimetry, direct flame imagery, flow velocity profiles, and flame speeds across varying iron and oxygen concentrations. The study demonstrates that the model accurately predicts particle dynamics and flame morphology, while also achieving quantitative agreement with experimental measurements regarding flow velocity and flame propagation. Utilizing these validated results, the investigation analyzes iron combustion characteristics, including thermal structures and multidimensional phenomena, under diverse oxidizer conditions. The findings reveal that iron particles transition from a kinetic-controlled regime prior to ignition to a diffusion-controlled regime during burning along the central axis in both environments. This transition is characterized by the Damköhler number and a particle temperature exceeding the gas temperature at the flame front. Furthermore, the hot counterflow burner exhibits multidimensional effects, evidenced by radial variations in both temperature and the Damköhler number.

In the realm of rapid, hyperconnected parcel logistics, intermediate hubs are essential for achieving economies of scale by aggregating scattered cargo flows. However, resorting small parcels at each hub consumes significant resources, potentially increasing operational workload and extending total delivery times. This process can be minimized through smart containerized consolidation, which groups parcels sharing both service levels and final destinations. This study presents an optimization model designed to evaluate how such consolidation reduces expected total pickup-to-delivery times across a parcel logistics network and its effects on the sustainability of urban logistics operations. We present empirical findings from a synthetic urban setting, comparing consolidation performance across various operational and tactical capabilities, network structures, and demand scenarios.

Observing gravitational waves from merging compact binaries enables us to investigate the dynamical, nonlinear aspects of general relativity and restrict potential modifications. Certain events detected by the LIGO-Virgo Collaboration possess a high signal-to-noise ratio during the merger phase, permitting an analysis of the remnant black hole's relaxation into its final stationary state, known as the ringdown. This phenomenon is defined by a spectrum of quasinormal modes. The central question is whether the ringdown can be utilized to limit deviations from general relativity as proposed by various alternative theories. In this study, we address this by employing an inspiral-merger-ringdown waveform model grounded in the effective-one-body formalism, enhanced with a spin-based expansion for the ringdown. We outline a method for incorporating quasinormal mode frequencies computed for specific theories into this model. Specifically, we examine theories that introduce higher-order curvature corrections to general relativity, including Einstein-dilaton-Gauss-Bonnet (EdGB), dynamical Chern-Simons (dCS), and cubic- and quartic-order effective-field theories (EFT). Applying this parametrized model to the two most prominent ringdown signals to date, GW150914 and GW200129, we find that while EdGB remains unconstrained, we establish upper limits on the fundamental length scales for cubic- ($\ell_{\rm cEFT} \leqslant 38.2$ km) and quartic-order ($\ell_{\rm qEFT} \leqslant 51.3$ km) EFTs, as well as dCS gravity ($\ell_{\rm dCS} \leqslant 38.7$ km). The constraint on dCS gravity serves as a concrete instance of a theory that has eluded detection through inspiral-only analyses but is now restricted by merger-ringdown investigations using current gravitational-wave data.

We have constructed a microscopic model for the recently realized double quantum dot (DQD) maser. Upon analyzing the device's gain, we discovered that alongside direct photon stimulation, there is a significant contribution from the concurrent emission of a photon and a phonon, known as the phonon sideband. Our findings indicate that this phonon-assisted gain usually surpasses the total gain responsible for the maser effect. Furthermore, our model accurately reproduces recent experimental results.

This study examines the two-time correlation functions of a dichotomously driven two-level system interacting with a thermal bath, incorporating corrections that extend beyond the quantum regression theorem. Within the regime of strong system-environment coupling, we find that noise parameters can be adjusted to regulate the magnitude of these corrections at low temperatures. Additionally, the external noise induces motional averaging and narrowing effects on the absorption and emission spectra of the two-state system. Finally, the dynamics of the two-time correlations exhibit phenomena analogous to tunneling destruction and noise-enhanced transport.
