By integrating experimental data with micromagnetic simulations, we reveal that the interplay between exchange and magnetostatic energies within these domain walls significantly impacts the resulting magnetic domain configuration.

This research investigates enumerative problems concerning the moduli space $\mathcal{M}(L)$ of hyperplane arrangements defined by a specific intersection lattice $L$. Mn\"ev's universality theorem indicates that these spaces may exhibit arbitrary complexity, making the computation of their dimension $D =\dim \mathcal{M}(L)$ challenging. By embedding $\mathcal{M}(L)$ into a product of projective spaces, we analyze its degree $N=\mathrm{deg} \mathcal{M}(L)$, which represents the count of arrangements in $\mathcal{M}(L)$ intersecting $D$ points in general position. For generic cases, $N$ admits a combinatorial calculation and is significant in the study of the Chow variety of zero-dimensional cycles. Utilizing Schubert calculus, we determine both $D$ and $N$ when $L$ corresponds to the intersection lattice of multiple cones over a generic arrangement. Furthermore, we derive characteristic numbers for families of generic arrangements in $\mathbb{P}^2$ consisting of 3 and 4 lines.

This study introduces techniques for determining optimal configurations and actuator forces or torques to maximize contact wrenches in a specific direction for Underwater Vehicle Manipulator Systems (UVMS). The wrench maximization challenge is modeled as a linear programming problem, with the optimal configuration derived through bi-level optimization within a parameterized redundancy space. The research further addresses scenarios involving one or more manipulators subject to multiple contact forces, aiming to enhance wrench capability during trajectory tracking and to generate substantial wrench impulses via dynamic movements. Specific applications examined include maximizing force to lift heavy loads and maximizing torque for valve turning operations. Extensive experimental validation using an underwater robotic platform with a 4DOF manipulator demonstrates significant improvements in wrench capability compared to existing UVMS methods.

In an edge-colored graph $G$, a tree $T$ is termed a {\em rainbow tree} when all its edges possess distinct colors. For any subset of vertices $S \subseteq V(G)$, a tree linking the vertices in $S$ is referred to as an $S$-tree. A {\em $k$-rainbow coloring} of $G$ is an edge coloring scheme where, for every set $S$ comprising $k$ vertices of $G$, there exists a rainbow $S$-tree within $G$. The {\em $k$-rainbow index} of $G$, symbolized by $rx_k(G)$, represents the smallest number of colors required for such a $k$-rainbow coloring. This paper determines the precise values of $rx_3(K_{2,t})$ for all $t\geq 1$.

Lithium-ion batteries are essential in contemporary applications, spanning from portable devices to electric vehicles. Regardless of the specific use case, accurately estimating the battery's state of health (SOH) in real-time via onboard systems is vital for ensuring safe operation and protecting asset integrity. This study presents and assesses a machine learning framework designed to predict battery capacity fade—a key indicator of health—across 179 cells subjected to diverse cycling conditions. The proposed pipeline utilizes two parametric and two non-parametric algorithms to estimate SOH along with confidence intervals. By extracting 30 features from segments of charge voltage and current curves, the system performs automated feature selection and algorithm calibration. When applied to cells undergoing fast-charging protocols, the optimal model achieves a root mean squared percent error of 0.45%. This research offers valuable insights into creating scalable, data-driven models for SOH estimation, highlighting the significance of providing prediction confidence bounds. Furthermore, the methodology, which integrates experimental data with machine learning, is adaptable for estimating SOH in other critical components requiring real-time monitoring.

Geometric reasoning demonstrates the existence of families of inflationary cosmologies that are homospectral, meaning distinct expansion histories yield identical spectra of comoving curvature perturbations. We formulate a general algorithm to derive the potential of minimally-coupled single scalar fields from any given expansion history. Applying this method to homospectral scenarios produces the corresponding potentials, illustrated through both numerical and analytical cases. This infinite set of homospectral potentials relies on two free parameters: the initial energy scale and the initial field value. Consequently, a unique potential cannot be reconstructed from the curvature spectrum alone unless these initial conditions are determined, potentially via observations of primordial gravitational waves.

In 2020, Cameron et al. proposed the restricted numerical range of a digraph as a framework for analyzing algebraic connectivity and characterizing these graphs. Specifically, they identified that digraphs with restricted numerical ranges corresponding to a single point, a horizontal line segment, and a vertical line segment are $k$-imploding stars, directed joins of bidirectional digraphs, and regular tournaments, respectively. This paper extends those findings by examining digraphs whose restricted numerical ranges form convex polygons within the complex plane. We introduce computational techniques to identify such polygonal digraphs and demonstrate that they fall into three mutually exclusive categories: normal, restricted-normal, and pseudo-normal digraphs, each of which remains closed under complementation. Furthermore, we establish sufficient conditions for normal digraphs and prove that the directed join of two normal digraphs yields a restricted-normal digraph. We also show that when the graph order is square-free or twice a square-free number, directed joins are the exclusive form of restricted-normal digraphs. Finally, for orders that are neither square-free nor twice a square-free, we present methods to construct restricted-normal digraphs that do not arise as directed joins.

Thixotropy, anti-thixotropy, and viscoelasticity represent three distinct time-dependent behaviors driven by different physical mechanisms, yet their differentiation remains difficult, complicating the study of structure-property relationships. This study demonstrates that hysteresis offers a robust method for distinguishing these dynamics by analyzing the signatures of fundamental models for each. By employing shear-rate ramps that start and finish at high rates, two key distinguishing characteristics within hysteresis loops were identified. First, the loop direction varies: thixotropy produces a clockwise loop, whereas viscoelasticity and anti-thixotropy yield counterclockwise loops. Second, at high ramping speeds where hysteresis vanishes, the viscoelastic response exhibits a stress plateau at low shear rates due to a lack of stress relaxation, while thixotropic and anti-thixotropic responses behave purely viscously with negligible shear thinning or thickening. These features remain consistent regardless of specific model details. Further validation was achieved through experimental hysteresis measurements on thixotropic Laponite suspensions, anti-thixotropic carbon black suspensions, and viscoelastic poly(ethylene oxide) solutions. These protocols provide a reliable means to differentiate the three dynamics, thereby illuminating the microstructural physics governing complex fluids.

This paper investigates the credit assignment challenge within reward augmented maximum likelihood (RAML) learning, demonstrating a theoretical equivalence between the token-level variant of RAML and entropy-regularized reinforcement learning. Leveraging this relationship, we introduce two sequence prediction methods: one that enhances RAML through fine-grained credit assignment and another that refines Actor-Critic via systematic entropy regularization. Experiments on two benchmark datasets reveal that our proposed algorithms surpass RAML and Actor-Critic individually, offering novel alternatives for sequence prediction tasks.

Hairstyle transfer involves adapting a source hairstyle to match a target style. Despite recent advancements capable of capturing intricate hair details, current models face two significant challenges. First, they struggle to transfer hairstyles when the source and target images differ in pose, such as viewing angle or face scale, a common scenario in real-world applications. Second, these models often produce unrealistic results when substantial portions of the source image are occluded by the original hair; for instance, inpainting is required to reconstruct shoulders or backgrounds hidden beneath long hair during a transition to a short style. To overcome these limitations, we introduce HairFIT, a novel framework for pose-invariant hairstyle transfer. Our approach comprises two phases: flow-based hair alignment and hair synthesis. In the alignment phase, we employ a keypoint-based optical flow estimator to align a target hairstyle with the source's pose. Subsequently, the synthesis phase generates the final transferred image using a Semantic-region-aware Inpainting Mask (SIM) estimator. This SIM estimator segments occluded areas in the source image into distinct semantic regions to better capture their unique characteristics during the inpainting process. We validate our model's effectiveness through both quantitative and qualitative assessments on multi-view datasets, specifically K-hairstyle and VoxCeleb. The results demonstrate that HairFIT achieves state-of-the-art performance by successfully transferring hairstyles between images of varying poses, a capability not previously realized.

We present the Convex Hull of Admissible Modularity Partitions (CHAMP) algorithm, designed to filter and rank network community structures discovered through various computational heuristics across multiple runs. CHAMP determines the modularity optimization domain for each partition—the parameter space where it exhibits the highest modularity relative to the input set—thereby eliminating partitions with empty domains to isolate "admissible" candidates that remain potentially optimal within specific parameter ranges. Notably, CHAMP accommodates multi-dimensional parameter spaces, such as those found in multilayer networks involving resolution parameters and interlayer coupling. By leveraging CHAMP's output, users can effectively select robust community structures by evaluating the size of optimization domains and conducting pairwise comparisons among admissible partitions. Our demonstration using several example networks highlights CHAMP's utility, showing that it narrows the focus to pruned subsets of admissible partitions that are 20-to-1785 times smaller than the unique partition sets generated by the input community detection heuristics.

We demonstrate that any completely regular code possessing a minimum eigenvalue within an arbitrary geometric graph $G$ maps to a completely regular code in the clique graph of $G$. By analyzing the relationship between these codes, we achieve a full characterization of completely regular codes in Johnson graphs $J(n,w)$ that have a covering radius of $w-1$ and strength 1. Notably, this finding completes the characterization for Johnson graphs $J(n,3)$. Furthermore, we classify completely regular codes of strength 1 in Johnson graphs $J(n,4)$, leaving open only a single case regarding their eigenvalues.

Recent gamma-ray data indicate that cosmic ray (CR) diffusion within the interstellar medium (ISM) is inhomogeneous, a phenomenon anticipated given that CR diffusion relies on turbulence properties that vary across the ISM's multiple phases. This study examines mirror diffusion generated by highly compressible turbulence in molecular clouds (MCs) surrounding supernova remnants (SNRs), where magnetic mirroring significantly inhibits CR diffusion near their sources. The resulting slow diffusion causes substantial energy loss from proton-proton interactions, flattening the low-energy CR spectrum, whereas the high-energy spectrum becomes steeper due to the strong energy dependence of mirror diffusion. Consequently, the resulting broken power-law CR spectrum aligns closely with gamma-ray observations from SNR/MC systems, such as IC443 and W44.

We introduce two concepts of partial sums for a Riordan array, representing the partial sums of its rows and columns respectively. We identify the matrices resulting from these operations: one yields a new Riordan array, while the other produces a rectangular array whose inverse is a lower Hessenberg matrix. We analyze the structure of these Hessenberg matrices and conclude with a generalization related to Fibonacci numbers and phyllotaxis.

We aim to characterize surface defects in smectic A thin films by establishing a free discontinuity problem, defined as a variational framework where the order parameter can exhibit jump discontinuities across an unspecified set. The free energy functional incorporates an interfacial energy term that penalizes the dislocation of smectic layers occurring at these jumps. Furthermore, we address mathematical concerns regarding the existence of minimizers and present specific examples of minimizers within simplified contexts.

The Levenshtein distance, commonly referred to as edit distance, is a fundamental metric for comparing strings, widely utilized in natural language processing and genetic sequence analysis. However, its nature as a discrete function makes optimization difficult, which limits its applicability in machine learning. For instance, even basic algorithms like K-means struggle to cluster sequences of varying lengths and frequencies when relying on edit distance. To address this, we introduce a new metric called soft edit distance (SED), a smooth approximation of the traditional edit distance. Because SED is differentiable, it can be optimized using gradient-based methods. Like the original metric, SED and its derivatives can be computed efficiently in polynomial time using recurrence relations. We demonstrate the utility of SED through experiments on synthetic datasets and the clustering of biological sequences.

This work investigates the quantity of connected components within non-Gaussian random spherical harmonics defined on the two-dimensional sphere $\mathbb{S}^2$. We establish that the expected number of nodal domains remains constant regardless of the coefficient distribution, as long as it possesses a finite second moment.

We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, an optical field within a two-mode squeezed vacuum (TMSV) state can travel through a lossy atomic medium without undergoing degradation or evolution. Furthermore, these losses can generate this specific state even when a different initial state is injected. This phenomenon occurs in a $\Lambda$-type atomic system where both optical transitions are driven by strong laser fields that are two-photon resonant with the respective signal modes. In this setup, the interactions between the two signal modes and the ground-state atomic coherence interfere destructively, thereby ensuring the preservation of the TMSV with a specific squeezing parameter. This mechanism offers a unified explanation for recent experimental findings and predicts new phenomena.

This study introduces two greedy sampling rules tailored for the Sketch & Project method, which addresses linear feasibility problems. These rules extend the traditional max-distance and uniform sampling approaches, resulting in accelerated variants of Sketch & Project. Additionally, we propose improved greedy capped sampling rules that enhance existing capped methods. By integrating a heavy ball momentum technique into these greedy frameworks, we derive several established algorithms—including Randomized Kaczmarz (RK), Motzkin Relaxation (MR), and Sampling Kaczmarz Motzkin (SKM)—as specific instances through parameter adjustments regarding sampling rules and sketching vectors. Furthermore, we derive novel techniques such as Randomized Coordinate Descent, Sampling Coordinate Descent, and Capped Coordinate Descent for solving linear feasibility issues. We establish global linear convergence for both the fundamental greedy approach and its momentum-enhanced counterpart, and under less restrictive conditions, demonstrate an $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{k})$ convergence rate for the Cesaro averages of sequences produced by these methods. We also broaden the certificate of feasibility results for the proposed momentum method, encompassing multiple prior findings. Extensive numerical experiments on both randomly generated and sparse real-world datasets validate our theoretical claims, revealing that the proposed greedy sampling strategies significantly surpass existing methods. Finally, the momentum variants developed here enhance the computational efficiency of Sketch & Project methods across all sampling rules.

We announce the identification of a rare close binary system, SMSS J160639.78-100010.7, consisting of a magnetic white dwarf with a field strength of approximately 30 MG and a brown dwarf. Our measurements indicate an orbital period of 92 minutes, which aligns with the photometric period. Minimum and maximum light are observed at the orbital quadratures (Phi=0.25 and 0.75, respectively); these variations are not due to reflection from the brown dwarf but rather stem from a spot on the synchronously rotating magnetic white dwarf. The brown dwarf does not fill its Roche lobe, suggesting the system is likely in a detached state following past mass transfer episodes, or possibly in a low-accretion state. SMSS J160639.78-100010.7 represents the nearest known system of a magnetic white dwarf paired with a brown dwarf.

Most current deep neural networks for automatic facial expression recognition rely on predefined emotion classes, where performance heavily depends on the volume of training data. However, standard over-parameterized networks struggle with few-shot learning, often leading to rapid overfitting. Furthermore, these methods lack the robust generalization required to identify new categories characterized by limited data and significant intra-class expression variations. Addressing these challenges, we frame the task as low-shot learning, requiring a base classifier to swiftly adapt to novel classes using minimal samples. This paper re-evaluates and compares existing few-shot learning techniques for low-shot facial expression recognition, specifically assessing their generalization capabilities through episode-based training. We further extend this analysis to cross-domain generalization, where training and testing tasks originate from different distributions, demonstrating the effectiveness of these methods through extensive experimentation.

Imaging markers for cerebral small vessel disease offer critical insights into brain health, yet their manual evaluation is labor-intensive and suffers from significant variability between and within raters. Although automated assessment could enhance both clinical practice and biomedical research, the reliability of current algorithms remains uncertain. This study reports on the *VAscular Lesions DetectiOn and Segmentation* (\textit{Where is VALDO?}) challenge, held as a satellite event at MICCAI 2021. The initiative sought to advance automated detection and segmentation of sparse cerebral small vessel disease markers—specifically enlarged perivascular spaces (EPVS) in Task 1, cerebral microbleeds in Task 2, and lacunes of presumed vascular origin in Task 3—using weak and noisy labels. Twelve teams submitted solutions for one or more tasks, with nine focusing on microbleeds, six on lacunes, and four on EPVS. Training and evaluation utilized multi-cohort data. Performance varied widely across tasks and teams; while Task 1 (EPVS) and Task 2 (Microbleeds) yielded promising results, Task 3 (Lacunes) produced outcomes not yet practical for use. Furthermore, the results revealed performance inconsistencies across individual cases that may limit individual-level application, though the data remains valuable for population-level analysis.

This study examines the electronic behavior of bilayer graphene containing both a magnetic quantum dot and a magnetic quantum ring. Analytical solutions for the eigenenergies and wavefunctions of quasiparticle states are derived by resolving decoupled fourth-order differential equations. Regarding the magnetic quantum dot, when subjected to a negative inner magnetic field, two distinct features emerge in the evolution of eigenenergies: (i) energy eigenstates shift in discrete steps due to anticrossing phenomena, and (ii) quantum states converge toward zero energy. In the case of the magnetic quantum ring, varying the inner radius induces a transition in the angular momentum of the eigenenergy, while the Aharonov–Bohm effect manifests within the eigenenergy spectra for both positive and negative magnetic fields located inside the inner radius.

The projective variety formed by square-zero elements within the six-dimensional minimal supersymmetry algebra is isomorphic to $\mathbb{P}^1 \times \mathbb{P}^3$. Leveraging this result alongside the pure spinor superfield formalism, we investigate supermultiplets in six dimensions by beginning with vector bundles defined on projective spaces. Our classification focuses on all multiplets where the derived invariants for the supertranslation algebra constitute a line bundle over the nilpotence variety; conceptually, these are multiplets whose holomorphic twists possess rank one relative to Dolbeault forms on spacetime. Furthermore, we explicitly construct multiplets corresponding to natural higher-rank equivariant vector bundles, such as the tangent and normal bundles and their respective duals. The resulting constructions include the vector and hypermultiplets, the family of $\mathcal{O}(n)$-multiplets, as well as the supergravity and gravitino multiplets. Throughout this process, we address several theoretical issues inherent to the pure spinor superfield formalism. Specifically, we provide a general discussion regarding the connection between the projective nilpotence variety and multiplets, and we establish general theorems concerning short exact sequences and sheaf dualities within this formalism.

Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), a technology that transforms audio into text, has recently garnered significant interest within the machine learning field, leading to the release of numerous models on HuggingFace. However, the majority of these models are English-based, with only a small fraction supporting Thai. Furthermore, most existing Thai ASR models are proprietary, and the few open-source options available often lack robustness. To overcome these limitations, we developed a new ASR model by fine-tuning a pre-trained XLSR-Wav2Vec architecture on the Thai CommonVoice corpus V8 and integrated a trigram language model to enhance performance. We anticipate that our contributions will prove valuable to both individuals and the broader ASR community in Thailand.

Surface energy represents a fundamental nuclear property, first appearing in the simplest version of the semi-empirical mass formula. It significantly influences nuclear shape and deformability, factors that are expected to impact fusion reactions near the Coulomb barrier where dynamical processes like neck formation occur. To investigate this, Frozen Hartree-Fock and Time-Dependent Hartree-Fock calculations were performed on various effective interactions with systematically adjusted surface energies, using the $^{40}$Ca + $^{48}$Ca system as a test case. Contrary to naive expectations, the dynamical reduction of the barrier was most pronounced with the highest surface energy. We speculate that this result may stem from variations in other nuclear matter properties associated with these specific effective interactions.

Digital holography captures the complex optical field and a device's transfer matrix, with polarization diversity typically realized via spatial multiplexing. We propose angular multiplexing to enhance the flexibility of the optical configuration. In comparison, a photonic lantern exhibits comparable cross-talk and mode-dependent loss values.

The FCC-ee proposed $e^+e^-$ collider targets an exceptional level of precision for measuring fermion pair production from $e^+e^-$ collisions near the $Z$ resonance, utilizing approximately $10^{13}$ events. By employing the S-matrix method to characterize the $Z$ boson line shape, one can achieve a model-independent, quantitative analysis of the $e^+e^- \to {\bar f}f$ process around the $Z$ peak using a minimal set of parameters, including the $Z$-boson mass $M_Z$ and width $\Gamma_Z$. Although weak and strong corrections remain complex and effectively "black," a rigorous theoretical treatment of photonic interactions is essential. This work presents the methodology, details its applications, and introduces the analysis tool SMATASY/ZFITTER.

Because of the open-world assumption, Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are inherently incomplete. To tackle this limitation, numerous Link Prediction (LP) approaches have been developed, including inductive LP models that can generate representations for entities encountered only during testing. However, to the best of our knowledge, no current inductive LP model addresses the challenge of learning representations for unseen relations. This paper introduces Relation Aware Inductive Link Prediction (RAILD), a novel framework for KG completion designed to handle both unseen entities and unseen relations. Beyond utilizing language models to incorporate textual literals from entities and relations, RAILD employs a new graph-based method to extract relation features. Extensive experiments across various challenging benchmark datasets demonstrate that RAILD surpasses state-of-the-art models in performance. Furthermore, as no existing inductive LP models handle unseen relations, we established custom baselines, against which RAILD also shows superior results.

We introduce the inverse Penrose transform, which maps spacetime to twistor space, for self-dual Yang-Mills (SDYM) theory and its higher-spin extensions on a flat background. The twistor action corresponding to the higher-spin extension of SDYM (HS-SDYM) belongs to the BF-type. By deforming the higher-spin extension of SDYM away from its self-dual sector, we identify a novel action describing a higher-spin extension of Yang-Mills theory (HS-YM). The twistor action for HS-YM represents a direct generalization of the standard Yang-Mills action.

The coexistence of semiconducting (2H) and metallic (1T) phases in MoS$_{2}$ monolayers has significantly enhanced their potential for next-generation electronic devices utilizing two-dimensional lateral heterojunctions. Structural defects play a crucial role in determining the performance of these 2D devices, particularly since phase-engineering techniques, such as electron beam irradiation, often create numerous vacancies at the imperfect interfaces between phases. This study investigates the transport characteristics of these heterojunctions containing point defects using first-principles calculations combined with the non-equilibrium Green's function approach. Results indicate that while vacancies in semiconducting MoS$_{2}$ function as scattering centers, their presence at the interface actually facilitates charge carrier flow. Specifically, molybdenum vacancies ($V_{Mo}$) increase the current by two orders of magnitude compared to a perfect device. This transmission enhancement is attributed to modifications in electronic density at the T-H interface, which open new channels for electron conduction.

This letter presents a comparative analysis of outdoor Urban Microcell (UMi) large-scale path loss models, along with root mean square (RMS) delay spreads (DS), angular spreads (AS), and the count of spatial beams, based on extensive measurements taken at 28, 38, 73, and 142 GHz. These measurement campaigns, conducted between 2011 and 2020, covered communication ranges up to 930 meters in downtown Austin, Texas, as well as Manhattan and Brooklyn, New York. By examining channel statistics across a broad spectrum from millimeter-wave to sub-terahertz bands, the study identifies key similarities and differences in outdoor wireless channels. Notably, path loss exponents (PLEs) remain remarkably consistent across all measured frequencies when normalized to the first meter free space path loss, while both RMS DS and AS decrease as frequency rises. The consistency of PLEs from millimeter-wave to THz frequencies suggests that the spacing between cellular base stations need not be altered as carrier frequencies approach the THz range. This is because, with constant physical antenna area, antenna gains increase quadratically with frequency; consequently, the wider bandwidths available at sub-THz or THz frequencies allow them to cover comparable distances.

This study examines the higher-order buckling eigenvalues associated with the Dirichlet poly-Laplacian in the unit sphere, defined by $(-\Delta)^p u = \Lambda (-\Delta) u$ for an order $p \geq 2$. We derive universal bounds for the $(k+1)$th eigenvalue based on the first $k$ eigenvalues, where these bounds hold independently of the specific domains. Notably, when $p=2$, our findings provide sharper estimates for buckling problem eigenvalues than those previously established by Wang and Xia.

Over-the-air computation (AirComp), which exploits the superposition characteristic of the wireless multiple-access channel (MAC), offers a promising approach for efficiently collecting data and performing computations on large-scale sensor measurements within Internet of Things environments. While most prior AirComp research has focused on spatial and temporally independent signals, real-world sensor data typically exhibits correlations. This letter introduces an AirComp system designed to handle spatial and temporally correlated signals, formulating an optimization problem to minimize computation mean-squared error (MSE). We derive an optimal policy that achieves the minimum MSE at each time step by incorporating both current and previously received signals. Additionally, we present and optimize a closed-form, low-complexity AirComp policy whose performance closely approximates that of the optimal solution.

Recent anomalies observed in lepton pair transitions within $^8$Be$^*$ and $^4$He nuclei could be explained by the presence of a feebly interacting light vector boson, $X17$. This study investigates the impact of this hypothetical particle on semileptonic $H^* \to H e^+e^-$ decays (where $H$ represents a $Q\bar{q}$ meson) using the HQET+VMD framework. By applying current experimental limits and assuming universality for the $X17$ boson's coupling to quarks, we demonstrate that decays involving $D^{*+}$ and $D_s^{*+}$ mesons could be significantly amplified compared to standard photon-mediated processes. Consequently, specialized experiments at existing heavy meson facilities could either validate the existence of this light boson or establish tighter constraints on its interactions with ordinary matter.

We examine specific infectious logics (Sfde, dSfde, K3w, and PWK) alongside various non-infectious variants, including two novel systems. For these logics, we either reconstruct existing natural deduction frameworks or develop them anew for the innovative cases, ensuring that a proof of the normalisation theorem becomes feasible. Consequently, we provide this proof and demonstrate the negation subformula property for the logics under study.

We introduce PreQuEL, or Pre-(Quality-Estimation) Learning, a task where a system forecasts the translation quality of a sentence without generating the translation itself. This approach avoids wasting computational resources on sentences likely to yield poor results. PreQuEL can be evaluated against a specific machine translation (MT) system, such as an industry service, or broadly compared to the state-of-the-art. Theoretically, PreQuEL centers on the source text, identifying characteristics or linguistic features that hinder machine translation. We established a baseline model for this task and evaluated its performance, while also creating a data augmentation technique derived from parallel corpora that significantly enhances results. Furthermore, we demonstrated that this augmentation method boosts performance in the Quality-Estimation task itself. By testing on challenge sets and various languages, we examined the input text properties to which the model is sensitive. Our findings indicate that the model recognizes syntactic and semantic distinctions and correlates with, and even over-prioritizes, standard NLP features.

A cograph is defined as a graph where every connected induced subgraph possesses a disconnected complement; equivalently, these are exactly the graphs that do not contain the 4-vertex path as an induced subgraph. We introduce the concept of a $2$-cograph as a graph in which the complement of every $2$-connected induced subgraph fails to be $2$-connected. Similar to cographs, $2$-cographs admit a recursive definition, yet unlike cographs, they remain closed under induced minors. This work characterizes the specific class of non-$2$-cographs such that every proper induced minor within them is a $2$-cograph. Additionally, we identify the finite set of members within this class whose complements are also induced-minor-minimal non-$2$-cographs.

Contracting systems cause the lengths of line segments (1-dimensional parallelotopes) to shrink exponentially. A key advantage of these systems is that connecting multiple contracting subsystems often results in a larger, overall contracting system. This concept extends to $k$-contracting systems, where $k$ ranges from 1 to $n$. In these generalized systems, the volume of $k$-dimensional parallelotopes contracts exponentially; notably, when $k=1$, they revert to standard contracting systems. Muldowney and Li demonstrated that time-invariant $2$-contracting systems exhibit well-ordered asymptotic behavior, meaning all bounded trajectories eventually converge to the set of equilibria. In this work, we establish a sufficient condition ensuring that the series interconnection of two subsystems yields a $k$-contracting system. This derivation relies on a novel formula for the $k$th multiplicative and additive compounds of a block-diagonal matrix, which holds independent interest. Furthermore, we apply these findings to identify conditions under which $2$-contracting systems with exponentially decaying inputs maintain the well-ordered asymptotic properties characteristic of time-invariant $2$-contracting systems.

This study examines how public blacklists report malicious internet activity (mal-activity), aiming to systematically characterize historical reports and analyze their evolution. By starting with a seed of 22 blacklists spanning from January 2007 to June 2017, the authors gathered over 51 million mal-activity reports concerning 662,000 unique IP addresses globally. To enrich this data with historical metadata—including geographic locations, autonomous system (AS) numbers, and mal-activity types—the researchers integrated the Wayback Machine, antivirus tool reports, and other public datasets like BGP Route Views and Internet registries. Additionally, a machine learning classifier was trained on an initial labeled set of approximately 1.57 million mal-activities derived from public blacklists to categorize the remaining 44 million unlabeled entries from supplementary sources. The authors have made both the unique dataset and the associated scripts publicly accessible for further research.

The paper's primary contributions include a novel report collection method, a machine learning approach for classifying reported activities, a detailed dataset characterization, and a crucial temporal analysis of mal-activity reporting patterns. Drawing inspiration from P2P behavior modeling, the analysis reveals that certain mal-activity classes (such as phishing) and a limited number of sources remain persistent. This suggests that blacklist-based prevention systems may be ineffective or suffer from excessively long update cycles. Furthermore, the findings indicate that resource allocation can be optimized by targeting heavy contributors, which account for the majority of mal-activities.

For the last three years, Pinterest has tested multiple visual search and recommendation tools, namely Related Pins (2014), Similar Looks (2015), Flashlight (2016), and Lens (2017). This article provides an overview of the visual discovery engine that drives these services, detailing the reasoning behind our technical and product choices, such as employing object detection and interactive interfaces. We find that this engine substantially boosts engagement for both search and recommendation functions.

We continue our initiative to publish all planets (and potential candidates) identified visually from the 2021 Korea Microlensing Telescope Network (KMTNet) online dataset. In this release, we present four planets—KMT-2021-BLG-0712Lb, KMT-2021-BLG-0909Lb, KMT-2021-BLG-2478Lb, and KMT-2021-BLG-1105Lb—with mass ratios falling within the range of -3.3 < log q < -2.2. This addition brings the cumulative count of secure, visually detected 2021 KMTNet planets to 16, with eight belonging to this specific series. The visual detection sample serves as a crucial validation for the completeness of semi-automated detections, which underpin statistical analyses. Notably, KMT-2021-BLG-1105Lb is blended with a relatively bright star, with magnitudes (I,V) approximately (18.9,21.6), which could be the host. This hypothesis can be immediately confirmed via high-resolution imaging. If confirmed, the host would be an early G dwarf, allowing the planet to be characterized through radial-velocity observations using 30-meter class telescopes.

Determining causal effects represents a cornerstone of causal inference. This paper addresses an identifiability challenge where both experimental and observational data exist, yet neither dataset independently suffices to identify the target causal effect. In these experiments, surrogate outcomes are recorded rather than the outcomes of interest. We frame this issue as a generalization of identifiability via surrogate experiments, designating it as "surrogate outcome identifiability." Furthermore, we demonstrate that the concept of transportability offers a sufficient condition for establishing surrogate outcome identifiability across a broad range of queries.

This note introduces a unified framework for determining the existence of a potential in optimal transport problems involving non-traditional cost functions that may take infinite values. We develop a novel method based on establishing the solvability of a specific family of linear inequalities, which can include infinite values. We provide a necessary and sufficient condition on the coefficients guaranteeing a solution, termed $c$-path-boundedness within transport theory. This condition completely characterizes sets admitting a potential and serves as the counterpart to $c$-cyclic monotonicity found in classical theory for real-valued costs. Furthermore, our approach yields a new, elementary proof for the classical results established by Rockafellar, Rochet, and R\"uschendorf.

This study constructs a first-stage linear regression framework for instrumental variables (IV) quantile regression (QR) models. Similar to the least squares approach, the quantile first-stage represents a linear projection of endogenous variables onto instruments and other exogenous covariates; however, unlike the standard case, it utilizes a weighted projection. These weights are determined by the conditional density function of the innovation term within the QR structural model, given the endogenous and exogenous covariates and the instruments at a specific quantile. We demonstrate that the necessary Jacobian identification conditions for IVQR models are inherently contained within this quantile first-stage. Furthermore, we propose inference procedures to assess instrument adequacy by testing their statistical significance based on the first-stage results. This test is formulated within an over-identification context, as consistent weight estimation for the first-stage implementation necessitates at least one valid instrument. Monte Carlo simulations provide numerical evidence that the proposed tests perform as anticipated regarding empirical size and power in finite samples. An empirical application highlights the importance of evaluating instrument significance across different quantiles. The suggested procedures are particularly valuable in QR contexts, where instruments may exhibit relevance at certain quantiles while remaining ineffective at others.

This work investigates how acceleration influences genuine tripartite entanglement in a system where one or two detectors couple to a vacuum field. Surprisingly, the observed increases and decreases in entanglement do not strictly correspond to the Unruh or anti-Unruh effects. Specifically, the Unruh effect can both diminish and amplify the tripartite entanglement between detectors, while the anti-Unruh effect can similarly either enhance or reduce it. We provide an explanation for this behavior and extend the analysis from tripartite to N-partite systems.

While rapid, user-controllable music generation offers innovative possibilities for composition and performance, current state-of-the-art systems are hindered by their heavy data and computational requirements during training, as well as their slow inference speeds, rendering them unsuitable for real-time interaction. To address these limitations, we present Musika, a system capable of training on hundreds of hours of audio using just one consumer GPU and generating music of any length on a consumer CPU at speeds exceeding real-time. Our approach involves first learning a compact, invertible representation of spectrogram magnitudes and phases via adversarial autoencoders, followed by training a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) on this representation for specific music genres. A latent coordinate system facilitates the parallel generation of arbitrarily long sequences, while a global context vector ensures stylistic consistency over time. We provide quantitative evaluations of sample quality and demonstrate user control features for piano and techno music. Additionally, we release the source code and pretrained autoencoder weights at github.com/marcoppasini/musika, enabling researchers to train a GAN for a new music domain on a single GPU within hours.

Recent studies have demonstrated that introducing a single unit with specific parameterization can eliminate all bad local minima from neural network loss landscapes. We demonstrate that the fundamental technique underlying these papers extends to any loss landscape—provided the global minimum achieves a loss of zero—to remove all such bad local minima. This approach does not necessitate the addition of auxiliary units nor does it require the loss function to be tied to a neural network. Instead, the mechanism functions by transforming all bad local minima into bad non-local minima at infinity regarding auxiliary parameters.

We recently created an automated theorem prover for projective incidence geometry that employs a combinatorial method based on matroids, operating through saturation with matroid rules. Built as an independent C-based tool, it accepts a geometric configuration and generates Coq proof scripts, including the theorem statement, the proof itself, and any necessary auxiliary lemmas. This document demonstrates how to integrate this external tool as a Coq plugin, enabling its use as a straightforward tactic.

This study employs the string-melting version of the AMPT model to examine how nuclear structure influences charged-particle multiplicity ($N_{ch}$) and anisotropic flow coefficients ($v_{2}$ and $v_{3}$) during the isobaric collisions of $^{96}_{44}$Ru + $^{96}_{44}$Ru and $^{96}_{40}$Zr + $^{96}_{40}$Zr at center-of-mass energies ($\sqrt{s_{NN}}$) of 7.7, 27, 62.4, and 200 GeV. Comparisons with recent STAR collaboration data reveal that the quadrupole deformation ($\beta_{2}$) primarily affects the $v_{2}$ difference in most central collisions, whereas octupole deformation ($\beta_{3}$) plays a dominant role in near-central collisions. Additionally, the neutron skin effect is the prevailing factor in mid-central collisions. These structural effects become more pronounced at lower collision energies.

Algebro-geometric solutions for the lattice potential modified Kadomtsev-Petviashvili (lpmKP) equation are derived. By utilizing a Darboux transformation of the Kaup-Newell spectral problem, a Lax triad for the lpmKP equation is constructed, alongside the definition of commutative integrable symplectic maps that produce discrete eigenfunction flows. These maps possess integrals identical to those of the finite-dimensional Hamiltonian system linked to the Kaup-Newell spectral problem. The asymptotic properties of Baker-Akhiezer functions are examined, yielding their representation via Riemann theta functions. Subsequently, algebro-geometric solutions for the lpmKP equation are recovered from these Baker-Akhiezer functions.

Multi-speaker speech synthesis involves modeling the voices of various speakers within a unified framework. While numerous deep neural network (DNN) approaches exist, they are susceptible to overfitting when training data is scarce. This study introduces a multi-speaker synthesis framework utilizing deep Gaussian processes (DGPs), which employ a deep architecture of Bayesian kernel regressions to ensure robustness against overfitting. In this setup, speaker codes are provided to both duration and acoustic models. Additionally, we explore deep Gaussian process latent variable models (DGPLVMs), where speaker representations are learned concurrently with other parameters, allowing for efficient assessment of speaker similarity or dissimilarity. Experimental evaluations were conducted under two conditions: one with balanced data per speaker and another with limited data for specific speakers. Subjective and objective assessments revealed that both DGP and DGPLVM methods outperformed DNNs in the speaker-balanced scenario. Furthermore, the DGPLVM demonstrated significant superiority over the DGP in the speaker-imbalanced scenario.

To tackle computational efficiency challenges in modeling blood flow within complex networks, we develop a family of nonlinear lumped-parameter (0D) models derived from established one-dimensional (1D) frameworks. These 0D models are designed to retain key nonlinear features of the original 1D system, specifically the nonlinear pressure-area relationship and pressure-dependent parameters for resistance ($R$) and inductance ($L$), which are defined based on a time-varying cross-sectional area influenced by pressure fluctuations. We establish appropriate coupling conditions to connect 0D vessels via 0D junctions, thereby constructing 0D networks that maintain the topology of the original 1D networks. The newly formulated nonlinear 0D models are subsequently applied to various arterial networks, with results compared against (i) reference 1D simulations to validate the models and demonstrate their capacity to accurately approximate pressure and flow waveforms across all vessels at significantly reduced computational costs (CPU time), and (ii) linear 0D simulations to quantify the benefits of incorporating specific nonlinearities by assessing their alignment with the 1D results.

The statistical power of weak lensing is primarily determined by the quantity of high-redshift galaxies with resolved shapes. It is generally believed, based on physical intuition, that deep imaging in the red and near-infrared optimizes this power, thereby preventing the loss of redshifted Balmer and Lyman break galaxies. Using the synthetic Emission Line EL-COSMOS catalogue, we simulated lensing observations across various filters and altitudes to forecast the number of exposures needed to reach a target source density for z > 0.3, employing both standard and custom filters. Our results indicate that ground-based telescopes are superior at red wavelengths, a trend that also applies narrowly to space-based instruments. Conversely, we find that SuperBIT, a diffraction-limited observatory operating in the stratosphere, should conduct its lensing-quality observations at blue wavelengths.

Accurately tracking body and hand movements within three-dimensional space is crucial for establishing social and self-presence in virtual and augmented reality. Contrary to standard 3D pose estimation, this challenge is typically addressed through inside-out tracking that relies on embodied perception, such as data from egocentric cameras or handheld sensors. This paper introduces a novel data-driven framework for inside-out body tracking designed to overcome the limitations of occlusion inherent in optimization-based approaches like inverse kinematics solvers. We begin by compiling a large-scale motion capture dataset featuring both body and finger movements, recorded via optical markers and inertial sensors. This dataset specifically targets social interactions, capturing ground truth poses during self-occlusions and body-hand interactions. Subsequently, we simulate occlusion patterns typical of head-mounted displays on this ground truth using a ray casting algorithm to train a deep neural network capable of inferring hidden body parts. Experimental results demonstrate that our method successfully generates high-fidelity embodied poses when applied to real-time inside-out body tracking, finger motion synthesis, and three-point inverse kinematics tasks.

Tremor serves as a critical diagnostic indicator for Parkinson's Disease (PD), Essential Tremor (ET), and various other central nervous system (CNS) conditions. Currently, clinicians or trained evaluators determine tremor severity using TETRAS scores through direct observation. However, the absence of quantitative metrics makes inter- and intra-observer variability nearly unavoidable, as distinguishing between adjacent score levels is often subtle. Furthermore, the requirement for in-person patient visits restricts how frequently disease progression can be monitored. Consequently, developing an automated, remote, and repeatable assessment method that allows for continuous monitoring at the patient's convenience is highly advantageous. This study proposes training a deep neural network (DNN) utilizing rank-consistent ordinal regression on 276 clinical videos from 36 patients with essential tremor. These videos are paired with clinician-assigned TETRAS scores, which serve as ground truth labels for the DNN. To address the scarcity of training data, optical flow is employed to filter out irrelevant background elements and static objects from RGB frames. Additionally, transfer learning is implemented to utilize pre-trained weights from a related task involving tremor frequency estimation. The approach was evaluated by dividing the dataset into training (67%) and testing (33%) subsets. The mean absolute error on the TETRAS score for the testing set was 0.45, suggesting that most discrepancies arose from adjacent label mismatches, a result that is both expected and acceptable. The model's predictions align closely with clinical ratings. Furthermore, the model was applied to smartphone videos from a PD patient with an implanted device capable of switching tremor "On" or "Off," yielding outputs consistent with the patient's tremor states. These findings demonstrate that the trained model can effectively assess and track tremor severity.

We investigate the resurgence structure of a quantum field theory undergoing a phase transition to reveal the connections between these two concepts. Specifically, we examine three-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric quantum electrodynamics (SQED) containing multiple hypermultiplets, focusing on a recently proposed second-order quantum phase transition within the large-flavor limit. By analyzing the Lefschetz thimble structure and the large-flavor expansion of the partition function derived via supersymmetric localization, we interpret this phase transition through the lenses of Lefschetz thimbles and resurgence. Our findings demonstrate that the second-order transition arises from the simultaneous occurrence of Stokes and anti-Stokes phenomena, with the transition's order dictated by the collision of saddles at the critical point. Furthermore, supersymmetry ensures that this transition is accompanied by an infinite series of Stokes phenomena, which align precisely with the Borel plane structures anticipated by resurgence theory. Building on insights from SQED, we offer a broader discussion on the interplay between resurgence and phase transitions, specifically illustrating how Borel resummation techniques can decode information regarding phase transitions.

We examine the area-preserving Willmore flow for surfaces near a small-radius hemisphere that slide along the boundary $S$ of a domain while maintaining orthogonality. We demonstrate that this flow persists for all time and retains its "half-spherical" geometry. Furthermore, we analyze the flow's long-term behavior, proving that for large times, the surface barycenter approximately satisfies a specific ordinary differential equation. By imposing extra constraints on the mean curvature of $S$, we subsequently establish the convergence of the flow.

Public and privately deployed serverless computing systems strive to create an illusion of limitless resources, shielding users from allocation complexities. By targeting low costs and high Quality of Service (QoS), the serverless paradigm offers avenues to achieve these objectives. This dissertation proposes a strategy to eliminate redundant computation, particularly for similar independent task requests or futile processing attempts. We investigate two primary methods: (A) reusing partial computations for service processing and (B) proactively discarding tasks with low success probabilities to enhance overall QoS. Regarding the first method, we introduce a mechanism to detect various "mergeable" tasks that can benefit from shared execution. We extensively evaluate task merging configurations by quantifying resource savings and using experimental data to build a predictive model for these savings. We analyze multiple merging strategies suitable for different workloads to determine optimal aggregation points and allocation methods that minimize QoS impacts on other tasks. For the second method, we developed mechanisms to skip tasks unlikely to complete on time by dropping or deferring them. We established minimum success probability thresholds required for task scheduling and dynamically adjusted these thresholds based on workload characteristics and system status. Additionally, we utilized approximate computing to reduce the computational overhead of the pruning mechanism, ensuring its practical applicability.

A proposed noise reduction strategy for future aircraft involves shielding propulsion noise by positioning the source over a wing or similar surface. This paper presents an approximate analysis of the acoustic field in the far field from a small circular source located near the edge of a semi-infinite plate, a model used to simulate wing-based noise shielding and trailing edge scattering. The derived approximation, applicable to sources with a small radius, demonstrates high accuracy when compared against full numerical evaluations of the field.

Model checking has emerged as a vital instrument for verifying the correctness of multi-threaded programs, surpassing the limitations of unit and functional tests which often fail to detect race conditions. McMini is an extensible model checker grounded in Dynamic Partial Order Reduction (DPOR), featuring a mechanism that enables users to define new primitive thread operations in under 100 lines of C code. This mechanism was expanded to support custom thread wakeup policies, such as spurious wakeups from condition variables. Users specify three key aspects: the enabling conditions for an operation, the independence between thread operations, and the criteria for co-enabled operations. Additionally, an optional wakeup policy is defined by specifying when wait operations on semaphores or condition variables are enabled. A new enqueue operation was introduced to allow users to declare alternative wakeup policies. Initial validation confirmed McMini's efficiency and correctness as an extensible model checker for standard synchronization primitives like mutexes, semaphores, condition variables, and reader-writer locks. Its extensibility was subsequently demonstrated through novel primitives representing other multithreading paradigms, such as readers-and-two-writers, which proved to be at least five times faster than traditional condition variable-based implementations. Finally, alternative wakeup policies (e.g., FIFO, LIFO, arbitrary) were evaluated using the enqueue operation, and the system's ability to handle spurious wakeups was verified by testing a program that exposes a bug specifically under those conditions.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) can produce highly realistic images that are nearly impossible to distinguish from genuine photographs. However, these systems depend on extensive datasets to accurately replicate specific domains. This limitation becomes critical when the goal extends beyond creating random images to modeling specific continuous features. A significant application within Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) research involves generating human facial images that convey emotion, which supports tasks like automatic avatar creation. The primary obstacle in this area is the scarcity of appropriate training data; most relevant datasets utilize categorical emotion models with discrete labels, thereby impeding the learning of smooth transitions between affective states. To address this, we investigate how label interpolation can enable networks trained on categorical data to generate images conditioned on continuous features.

This study examines the rank growth of elliptic curves over quartic $S_4$ and $A_4$ extensions $K/\mathbb{Q}$, specifically focusing on the difference $\mathrm{rk}(E/K) - \mathrm{rk}(E/\mathbb{Q})$ for a fixed curve $E$ as the field $K$ varies. Assuming $\mathrm{rk}(E/\mathbb{Q}) \leq 1$ and imposing additional constraints on $E$, we demonstrate that there exist infinitely many $S_4$ quartic extensions where the rank does not increase, meaning $\mathrm{rk}(E/K) - \mathrm{rk}(E/\mathbb{Q}) = 0$. Our approach involves controlling the 2-Selmer rank of $E$ within specific quadratic extensions, a method that facilitates the regulation of rank behavior across families of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$.

The federated learning (FL) paradigm trains machine learning models by periodically aggregating locally trained models from edge devices holding decentralized data. While popular FL optimization algorithms typically employ vanilla (stochastic) gradient descent for both client-side local updates and server-side global aggregation, recent research has explored adaptive methods like AdaGrad for server updates. However, the impact of applying adaptive optimization to local client updates remains unclear. This work demonstrates through both theoretical analysis and empirical results that although local adaptive methods can speed up convergence, they may introduce a non-vanishing solution bias, causing the final converged solution to diverge from the stationary point of the global objective. To address this inconsistency, we propose correction techniques that enhance local adaptive methods within the FL context. Extensive experiments on realistic federated training tasks confirm that these proposed algorithms outperform baselines lacking local adaptivity, achieving both faster convergence and higher test accuracy.

We have compiled data for 4,615 star-forming early-type galaxies (ETGs) by cross-referencing the $Galaxy~Zoo~1$ dataset with MPA-JHU emission-line measurements from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 7. The sample primarily spans a star formation rate (SFR) range of $\rm -0.7<log(SFR[M_{\sun}yr^{-1}])<1.2$, with a median SFR slightly exceeding that reported by Davis & Young. We observe a clear trend where both lower and higher stellar mass ETGs exhibit correspondingly lower and higher SFRs, respectively. Our best-fit relation, $\rm log(SFR)=(0.74\pm0.01)log(M_{*}/M_{\sun})-(7.64\pm0.10)$, yields the same slope as that determined by Cano-D\'{i}az et al. Furthermore, we explicitly demonstrate the stellar mass–metallicity (MZ) correlation within this star-forming ETG population. We note that diffuse ionized gas can artificially elevate metallicity measurements when using the D16, Sanch18, and Sander18 calibration indicators. Finally, we examine the relationships between SFR and 12+log(O/H) across various metallicity estimators, suggesting these correlations likely stem from the underlying SFR–stellar mass and MZ relations in ETGs.

For integers $n$ and $k$ satisfying $n \geq 2k$, the Kneser graph $K(n,k)$ is constructed with vertices representing all $k$-element subsets of $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$, where adjacency denotes disjointness. Lovász's classical theorem establishes that the chromatic number of $K(n,k)$ equals $n-2k+2$. The computational Kneser problem involves using an oracle for a coloring of $K(n,k)$ with $n-2k+1$ colors to identify a monochromatic edge. We introduce a randomized algorithm solving this problem in time $n^{O(1)} \cdot k^{O(k)}$, demonstrating its fixed-parameter tractability relative to $k$. This analysis relies on structural properties of intersecting families and induced subgraphs within Kneser graphs. Additionally, we examine the Agreeable-Set problem, which seeks a small subset of $m$ items assigned to $\ell$ agents such that every agent values the subset at least as highly as its complement. Leveraging our Kneser algorithm, we derive a randomized polynomial-time solution for Agreeable-Set instances where $\ell \geq m - O(\frac{\log m}{\log \log m})$. Finally, we establish that the Agreeable-Set problem is at least as difficult as a variant of the Kneser problem featuring extended access to the input coloring.

Although cryptocurrencies have seen remarkable adoption over the past ten years, detecting fraud within this sector remains a severely under-explored field. Among various crypto-related scams, "pump and dump" schemes are particularly prevalent. While research on such fraud exists for stock markets, the scarcity of labeled data and the distinct volatility of cryptocurrencies limit the transferability of those stock market findings. Moreover, prior work in this specific domain has relied exclusively on statistical methods or classical machine learning algorithms like random forests. This study introduces the innovative application of two neural network architectures to address this issue, demonstrating that deep learning approaches significantly surpass all current methods for detecting pump and dump activities in cryptocurrencies.

The progress in artificial intelligence and machine learning is accelerating the testing and public deployment of autonomous vehicles (AVs). In response, the California Department of Motor Vehicles (CA DMV) initiated the Autonomous Vehicle Tester Program to gather and publish reports on Autonomous Vehicle Disengagements (AVDs). Analyzing the root causes of AVDs is essential for enhancing system safety and stability, as well as guiding future testing and deployment strategies. This study establishes a scalable, end-to-end pipeline that utilizes natural language processing and deep transfer learning to collect, process, model, and analyze disengagement reports spanning from 2014 to 2020. Through the application of taxonomy, visualization, and statistical testing, the research identified trends in AV testing, categorized the frequency of causes, and uncovered significant correlations between disengagement initiators and their underlying causes. Key findings include: (1) manufacturers conducted intensive testing during spring and/or winter seasons; (2) test drivers triggered over 80% of disengagements, with more than 75% attributed to errors in the AV system's perception, localization, mapping, planning, and control; and (3) a strong relationship exists between who initiates an AVD and the specific cause category. Ultimately, this work demonstrates an effective application of deep transfer learning with pre-trained models and creates a consolidated disengagement database to facilitate further research.

Although end-to-end neural networks have advanced significantly over the past decade for both task-oriented and chit-chat dialogue systems, most current implementations still utilize hybrid architectures combining rule-based, retrieval, and generative methods to produce ranked responses. These systems typically depend on fallback mechanisms to handle out-of-domain or novel queries that fall outside their operational scope. While existing fallback responses are often static and unnatural, such as "I don't know the answer," we propose a neural approach capable of generating context-aware refusals tailored to the specific user query. These customized responses enhance interaction by improving paraphrasing and contextualization, thereby reducing dialogue monotony. Our straightforward method leverages rules based on dependency parsing and a text-to-text transformer fine-tuned on synthetic question-response pairs to generate highly relevant, grammatically correct, and diverse outputs. We validate the system's effectiveness through both automatic and manual evaluations.

Recent galaxy imaging surveys have achieved $2-3\%$ precision in constraining cosmological parameters. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory's upcoming Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) promises sub-percent accuracy, offering a critical test of the $\Lambda$CDM model. To prepare for LSST analysis, it is essential to thoroughly evaluate and compare the results from recent surveys. This study conducts a unified reanalysis at the catalog level of three cosmic shear datasets: the first year of Dark Energy Survey data (DES-Y1), the 1,000 deg$^{2}$ Kilo-Degree Survey data (KiDS-1000), and the first year of Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program data (HSC-Y1). We employ a pipeline developed and validated by the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration to ensure robustness against various analysis choices. Our findings indicate that the $S_8$ constraint remains stable across different small-scale modeling methods and cosmological priors. This unified approach rigorously tests survey consistency, revealing that all three surveys are statistically compatible. Given the partial overlap in their observational footprints, we approximate the cross-covariance between KiDS-1000 and HSC-Y1 when combining datasets, yielding an $S_8$ constraint of $1.6-1.9\%$ under varying assumptions regarding this covariance.

League of Legends (LoL) stands as the world's most popular multiplayer online battle arena (MOBA), relying heavily on competitive ranked play that employs skill-based matchmaking to assemble balanced teams. However, player proficiency fluctuates significantly based on the specific champion selected. This paper introduces a method to forecast outcomes in ranked LoL matches by analyzing players' experience with their chosen champions. Utilizing a deep neural network, we achieved 75.1% prediction accuracy immediately after champion selection, prior to the start of gameplay. These findings offer critical insights for both gameplay strategy and matchmaking: individual champion mastery heavily influences match results irrespective of team composition; despite skill-based matchmaking, substantial disparities in team skill remain before games begin; and players seeking victories should focus exclusively on champions they have mastered.
An algorithm with linear time complexity for identifying a set of closest elements within a mesh.

JavaScript (JS) remains a leading programming language owing to its adaptability, yet its codebase is often difficult to maintain and prone to errors. Our research employed an empirical study to analyze the relationships among co-changed software entities, such as functions and variables, and developed a machine learning (ML) system to suggest additional entities for modification based on developer changes. We initiated this by crawling 14,747 commits across 10 open-source projects, constructing change dependency graphs (CDGs) for each to map the referencer-referencee interactions between co-changed items. Subsequently, we identified common subgraphs within these CDGs to detect recurring co-change patterns. Leveraging these patterns, we extracted code features and trained an ML model to recommend entities for updating within a given program commit. Our investigation revealed that: (1) three specific patterns recur across all projects; (2) 80% to 90% of co-changed function pairs either share invoked functions, access identical variables, or contain similar statements; and (3) our ML-driven tool, CoRec, achieved high accuracy (73%–78%) in recommending entity changes. CoRec distinguishes itself from prior work by integrating program syntax, textual similarity, and software history, ultimately outperforming two existing tools in our evaluation.

This study introduces a family of quantum potentials representing non-rational extensions of the harmonic oscillator, derived through two distinct yet equivalent supersymmetric transformations. We define ladder operators for these extensions by combining the intertwining operators from both transformations. Furthermore, we construct Barut-Girardello coherent states for this family and examine their characteristics, including temporal stability, continuity with respect to the label, and completeness relations. Additionally, we compute mean-energy values, time-dependent probability densities, Wigner functions, and the Mandel Q-parameter to reveal the inherent non-classical behavior of these states.

WhatsApp stands as the world's leading messaging application, distinguished by its closed ecosystem and the ease of sharing multimedia and information within large groups. These features allow anonymous, encrypted messages to go viral rapidly, reaching many users quickly. However, the immediacy and personal nature of direct phone notifications have been extensively exploited to disseminate baseless rumors and misinformation campaigns, particularly during recent elections in Brazil and India. Although WhatsApp has implemented countermeasures, such as capping message forwarding to five recipients at a time, there is currently no empirical evidence regarding the actual efficacy of these restrictions. This study proposes a methodology to assess the impact of such virality limits on misinformation propagation using an epidemiological model and real-world data from WhatsApp in Brazil, India, and Indonesia. Our findings indicate that while WhatsApp's current efforts can significantly delay the spread of information, they remain ineffective at blocking misinformation campaigns within public groups when the content possesses high viral potential.

Although deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are highly effective for various computer vision tasks, their immense scale makes interpreting the image filtering mechanisms they employ challenging. This study presents a technique to extract "feature-preserving circuits" from deep CNNs by adapting saliency-based neural network pruning methods. These circuits function as modular sub-processes embedded within the network, comprising only the specific convolutional kernels necessary to identify a target feature. We evaluate three different saliency criteria for isolating these sparse circuits and demonstrate how "sub-feature" circuits can be derived to maintain feature responses to specific images, thereby decomposing features into even more granular filtering operations. Additionally, we created a tool to visualize "circuit diagrams," which depict the complete image filtering logic executed by these circuits in a machine-readable format.

Traditional statistics-driven approaches for joint Chinese word segmentation and part-of-speech tagging (S&T) possess generalization capabilities that allow them to identify novel words absent from training data; however, this often leads to the erroneous creation of numerous nonsensical words. We present an effective and efficient S&T framework that incorporates specific features to substantially minimize the generation of such meaningless words. This system leverages a general lexicon, Wikipedia, and a massive raw corpus of 200 billion characters to construct wordhood-based features. The proposed word-lattice architecture integrates both character-based and word-based models to utilize these word-level features. Experiments conducted on the Penn Chinese Treebank 5 demonstrate that this approach reduces the generation of meaningless words by 62.9% compared to the baseline, resulting in a segmentation F1 score of 0.984.

This paper examines recent advancements in the theoretical understanding of electroweak radiative corrections within semileptonic decay processes. By revitalizing Sirlin's representation, which relies on current algebra relations, we achieve a distinct separation between perturbatively calculable and non-calculable components of the $\mathcal{O}(G_F\alpha)$ corrections. The latter are formulated as concise hadronic matrix elements, facilitating systematic non-perturbative investigations through methods like dispersion relations and lattice QCD. This approach significantly enhances the precision of electroweak radiative corrections for semileptonic decays involving pions, kaons, free neutrons, and $J^P=0^+$ nuclei, providing crucial theoretical inputs for precision Standard Model tests. The discussion concludes with an overview of remaining challenges and future directions.

This paper offers a comprehensive investigation into the phase diagrams of superconducting topological surface states, with a specific focus on how crystalline symmetry interacts with the topology of the effective BdG Hamiltonian. We demonstrate that for the $4\times 4$ normal-state kinematic Hamiltonian, a mirror symmetry $\mathcal{M}$ can be established. Under $\mathcal{M}$-odd pairings, the classification of the resulting $8\times8$ BdG Hamiltonian is $\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}$, and time-reversal symmetry is broken intrinsically. Furthermore, the topologically non-trivial phase supports chiral Majorana edge modes and can be achieved in thin films of iron-based superconductors, such as FeSeTe.

Content creators and translators require unified access to up-to-date, reliable terminology across various disciplines and languages. Furthermore, such resources are essential for AI applications, including machine translation, speech recognition, information extraction, and other natural language processing systems. This project enables standards-compliant sharing and administration of terminology resources through the EuroTermBank Toolkit, an open-source management solution. It empowers organizations to organize, search, and build term collections, while facilitating both internal and external sharing via a network of federated databases. Data maintained in these federated databases is automatically synchronized with EuroTermBank, Europe's largest multilingual terminology repository. Consequently, translators, language service providers, researchers, and students can access the most current versions of these terminology resources.

Unlike Anti-de Sitter (AdS) black holes, where the isochoric heat capacity vanishes while the isobaric capacity remains non-zero, this specific dynamic does not apply to de Sitter (dS) black holes. This study investigates the phase transitions of Reissner-Nordstr\"om-de Sitter (RNdS) spacetime incorporating quintessence by accounting for interactions between the black hole horizon and the cosmological horizon. The findings indicate that this spacetime exhibits phase transition behavior analogous to the Van der Waals (VdW) system, with a non-vanishing isochoric heat capacity that satisfies the entire thermodynamic framework. Furthermore, by analyzing the entropic force acting between the two horizons, we elucidate its role in spacetime evolution. Additionally, we examine how various parameters influence both the phase transition and the entropic force, offering a novel micro-perspective approach to exploring interactions among black hole molecules.

Kagome crystal structure materials display complex physical phenomena, including frustrated magnetism, skyrmion creation, topological flat bands, and Dirac/Weyl points. Historically, research on kagome magnets has primarily focused on bulk crystals or polycrystalline films. In this work, we present the synthesis of high-quality thin films of the topological kagome magnet Fe$_3$Sn$_2$ using atomic layer molecular beam epitaxy. Characterization of Fe$_3$Sn$_2$ grown on epitaxial Pt(111) confirms the formation of highly ordered films with c-plane orientation and an in-plane magnetic easy axis. Anomalous Nernst effect imaging of the local magnetic structure uncovers micrometer-scale domains aligned in-plane. Furthermore, superlattice structures comprising both Fe$_3$Sn$_2$ and Fe$_3$Sn have been fabricated via atomic layer molecular beam epitaxy, showcasing the capacity to engineer sample structures at the atomic scale. Achieving high-quality films through this method paves the way for investigating the intricate physics of this system and exploring new spintronic effects by interfacing Fe$_3$Sn$_2$ with other materials.

The vocabulary size represents a fundamental design decision in large pretrained language models, impacting both performance and memory usage. Standard subword tokenization methods like Byte Pair Encoding and WordPiece are commonly employed. This study examines the compatibility of tokenization schemes across multilingual static and contextualized embedding spaces and introduces a metric to evaluate cross-linguistic tokenization alignment. Our objective is to avoid incompatible tokenizations—such as representing "wine" as a single word in English versus "v i n" at the character level in French—which hinder the learning of effective multilingual semantic representations. We demonstrate that this compatibility metric enables system designers to construct cross-lingual vocabularies that are mutually compatible, addressing a gap previously overlooked in multilingual modeling.

We introduce a moduli space of rational curves featuring finite-order automorphisms and weighted orbits, demonstrating that the combinatorial structure of its boundary strata is represented by a specific polytopal complex. This complex also encapsulates the algebraic properties of a complex reflection group acting on the moduli space.
