This demonstration paper introduces StreamSide, an open-source toolkit designed for annotating diverse meaning representations. It accommodates both frame-based schemes, such as Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR), and frameless approaches like Widely Interpretable Semantic Representation (WISeR). StreamSide facilitates sentence-level and document-level annotation by enabling the creation of multi-rooted graphs. The tool can open and automatically convert various input formats, including plain text, Penman notation, and its proprietary JSON format, to support enhanced annotation capabilities. It includes reference frames for AMR predicate argument structures and offers concept-to-text alignment. Released under the Apache 2.0 license, StreamSide is fully open-source, allowing customization for enriched meaning representations across different languages, such as Uniform Meaning Representations. All resources are publicly available via the project repository at https://github.com/emorynlp/StreamSide.

Voice production disorders significantly impact the quality of life for those affected. This study employs a simulation approach to explore the cause-effect mechanisms in voice generation, highlighting typical features like sub-glottal pressure and specific functional disorders such as glottal closure insufficiency and left-right asymmetry. Using a previously published hybrid aeroacoustic model, a parameter study simulated 24 distinct voice configurations. By correlating selected acoustic parameters (e.g., HNR, CPP) at evaluation points with these configuration details, the research aims to gain deeper insights into flow-induced sound generation during human phonation. Building on recent institutional studies that correlated experimental flow and acoustic data with healthy and disordered voice signals, this work advances toward a detailed dataset definition. Although the dataset is small, the methodology of simVoice ensures precise characterization of relevant features. Correlation analysis and a Support Vector Machine classifier with an RBF kernel were used to classify the data representations. Additionally, Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) was applied to visualize the dimensions of the individual studies, enabling the identification of key features from acoustic signals measured at the mouth. The Glottal Closure (GC) type was best distinguished using CPP and boxplot visualizations. Furthermore, utilizing the LDA-reduced feature space, subglottal pressure could be classified with 91.7% accuracy, regardless of whether the voice simulation parameters represented healthy or disordered states.

Utilizing interior-point methods on central-path conditions is a standard technique for addressing quadratic programs. Recasting these conditions into the log-domain represents a novel variation of this approach, to the best of our knowledge, that has not been previously investigated. This paper examines log-domain interior-point methods and demonstrates their polynomial-time convergence. Furthermore, we establish that these methods approximate classical barrier methods in a rigorous manner and present straightforward computational experiments highlighting their enhanced performance.

Offline policy learning (OPL) utilizes pre-collected data to optimize policies without active exploration. Although this area has gained significant attention, its theoretical and algorithmic underpinnings within function approximation frameworks remain insufficiently developed. This paper addresses distributional shift, optimization, and generalization in offline contextual bandits employing neural networks. Specifically, we introduce a provably efficient offline contextual bandit algorithm using neural network function approximation that makes no functional assumptions regarding rewards. We demonstrate that our approach achieves provable generalization over unseen contexts under a distributional shift condition that is less stringent than those in existing OPL literature. Distinctively, our method learns from offline data in an online fashion via stochastic gradient descent, thereby integrating the advantages of online learning into an offline context. Furthermore, we establish that our approach offers superior computational efficiency and a more favorable dependence on the effective dimension of the neural network compared to online alternatives. Finally, we validate the empirical performance of our method across various synthetic and real-world offline policy learning scenarios.

On an almost complex manifold, a quasi-Kähler metric possessing a canonical connection within the c-projective class of a specific minimal complex connection corresponds to a non-degenerate solution of the c-projectively invariant metrizability equation. By substituting the maximal rank condition for solutions with a non-degeneracy condition on the prolonged system, we obtain a strictly broader set of solutions characterized by non-vanishing (generalized) scalar curvature. This study examines the geometries arising from this expanded class of solutions. For every solution, the strict point-wise signature divides the underlying manifold into strata, extending the model's decomposition of $\mathbb{CP}^m$ into certain Lie group orbits. We detail the smooth properties and geometric structure of each stratum, generalizing the geometries of the embedded orbits in the model. This includes a quasi-Kähler metric defined on the open strata that becomes singular at their boundaries. The closed strata inherit almost CR-structures and can be interpreted as a c-projective infinity for the associated quasi-Kähler metric.

This work introduces the "twinning field," defined as an electromagnetic pulse that elicits an identical optical response from two different materials. We demonstrate that for any pair of generic many-body systems, such a field capable of rendering the systems \emph{optically indistinguishable} invariably exists. We derive the conditions governing the uniqueness of this field and support our analysis with numerical computations of twinning fields applied to the Fermi-Hubbard model. The universal existence of these fields suggests promising avenues for future research in non-linear optics, materials science, and quantum technologies.

The recently introduced E(xplicit)I(implicit)N(null) method addresses numerical instability in PDEs by adding and subtracting an operator $\mathcal{D}$ with arbitrary structure, applying it explicitly in one instance and implicitly in another. This work extends that concept by creating an adaptive process to determine an optimal approximation for $\mathcal{D}$. We introduce a numerical error metric capable of identifying instabilities across all wavelengths, adjusting each Fourier component of $\mathcal{D}$ to its minimum necessary value to suppress these instabilities. We demonstrate that for various nonlinear and non-local PDEs in both one and two dimensions, the spectrum of $\mathcal{D}$ dynamically and automatically aligns with the theoretical predictions for marginal stability. Consequently, our approach offers the stability characteristics of a fully implicit scheme while incurring computational costs similar to an explicit solver. Furthermore, because the adaptive implicit component is diagonal in Fourier space, it introduces minimal overhead relative to the explicit method.

We analyzed extensive citizen science datasets to identify eight Hot Jupiter systems exhibiting deviations from constant orbital periods: HAT-P-19 b, HAT-P-32 b, TrES-1 b, TrES-2 b, TrES-5 b, WASP-4 b, WASP-10 b, and WASP-12 b. The latter system is already recognized for strong tidal orbital decay, serving as a key control for our research. Several other identified systems have previously reported disputed period drifts, enabling an independent verification of these findings. The data originate from the Exoplanet Transit Database (ETD), a global initiative launched in 2008 by the Variable Star and Exoplanet Section of the Czech Astronomical Society. With over 400 planets and 12,000 observations spanning 15 years, the ETD offers significant potential for investigating the long-term orbital evolution of close-in Hot Jupiters. Our findings will inform the prioritization of targets for follow-up studies, which are essential to confirm the observed period drifts and determine their underlying causes.

This study explores the self-organization of ferrofluid droplets suspended in a wall-bounded shear flow under an external magnetic field. By adjusting the magnetic field's strength, we observe that droplets arrange into chains aligned with the flow under weak fields, whereas strong fields induce a crystal-like pattern. Utilizing both numerical simulations and analytic calculations, we establish the phase diagram and critical thresholds for this transition from chains to crystals. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these organized structures can be manipulated by altering the magnetic field's orientation. These findings highlight the potential of field-controllable ferrofluid droplets as a versatile, reconfigurable, and reproducible metamaterial.

This paper addresses a question raised jointly by A. A. Klyachko and N. M. Luneva regarding the optimality of an estimate for the cost of symmetry in graphs. The original estimate posits that if $n$ vertices can be removed from a connected graph to eliminate any connected subgraph isomorphic to $\Gamma$, then there exists a set of at most $n|V(\Gamma)|$ invariant vertices under all graph automorphisms such that the graph contains no subgraph isomorphic to $\Gamma$. We demonstrate that this estimate is not optimal by proving the existence of a graph $\Gamma$ for which it fails.

Structural glasses created by rapid cooling of a melt are recognized for containing low-energy, quasilocalized excitations (nonphononic modes) whose frequencies $\omega$ adhere to a universal $\sim\!\omega^4$ distribution as $\omega\!\to\!0$, regardless of formation history, interparticle potentials, or spatial dimensions. This study demonstrates that this universal quartic behavior also applies to disordered crystals with finite long-range order—a feature missing in their glassy equivalents. Consequently, we confirm that the universality of the quartic law extends beyond quenched structural glasses. Furthermore, we observe that disordered crystals, which allow for continuous control over disorder levels, contain significantly more quasilocalized excitations than predicted based on their mechanical disorder (measured by shear modulus fluctuations), especially when compared to structural glasses with similar mechanical disorder. Additionally, we verify that the stability bound for nonlinear quasilocalized excitations, previously identified in structural glasses, remains valid in disordered crystals. These findings connect to glass-like anomalies experimentally detected in disordered crystals and represent a significant advancement in identifying the key factors required for the emergence of universal nonphononic excitations in disordered solids.

Plankton blooms represent intricate nonlinear phenomena that can be modeled using the fast-slow phytoplankton-zooplankton framework introduced by Truscott and Brindley in 1994. Their research demonstrated that a rapid increase in water temperature triggers a critical shift from low phytoplankton levels to a single, intense outburst known as a bloom; however, the specific dynamical mechanism behind this transition remained unidentified until now. By applying geometric singular perturbation theory, we have revealed an overlooked rate-sensitive quasithreshold composed of special trajectories called canards. This transition occurs when the quasithreshold, which is sensitive to the warming rate, crosses the current state of the plankton system within a narrow range of warming speeds. Consequently, we have identified rate-induced tipping as the fundamental mechanism driving this change. These findings not only clarify previously reported shifts toward single blooms but also predict a novel transition pattern involving sequences of blooms under higher warming rates, potentially explaining the rising frequency of harmful algal blooms observed in nature.

The $\alpha$-emitting isotope $^{214}$U was discovered using the gas-filled recoil separator SHANS and the recoil-$\alpha$ correlation method, resulting from the fusion-evaporation reaction $^{182}$W($^{36}$Ar, 4n)$^{214}$U. Additionally, more accurate $\alpha$-decay characteristics for the even-even nuclei $^{216,218}$U were determined through reactions involving $^{40}$Ar and $^{40}$Ca beams on $^{180, 182, 184}$W targets. By integrating these experimental results, refined $\alpha$-decay reduced widths ($\delta^2$) were calculated for even-even Po–Pu nuclei near the magic neutron number $N=126$. These trends were analyzed using the $N_{p}N_{n}$ scheme to investigate how proton-neutron interactions affect $\alpha$ decay in this region. Notably, the reduced widths for $^{214,216}$U are approximately doubled compared to the $N_{p}N_{n}$ systematics observed in even-even nuclei where $84 \leq Z \leq 90$ and $N<126$. This anomalous enhancement is attributed to a robust monopole interaction between valence protons in the $\pi 1f_{7/2}$ orbit and neutrons in the $\nu 1f_{5/2}$ spin-orbit partner orbit, a finding corroborated by large-scale shell model calculations.

This research investigates the criteria required for fluorescent beads to effectively mimic single fluorescent molecules during the calibration of optical microscopes. While beads are commonly employed for their high brightness and ease of handling, their point spread functions (PSFs) often differ significantly from those of single-molecule fluorophores due to variations in emission patterns and physical size. We theoretically analyze these discrepancies across different scenarios, including those with and without polarization channel splitting, to identify when beads serve as valid models for single molecules. Additionally, we introduce techniques to model and correct blurring caused by size differences, thereby generating PSFs that more closely resemble those of single molecules.

This study demonstrates the existence of unique, global-in-time classical solutions for the multi-component BGK model proposed in \cite{mixmodel}, provided the initial data represents a minor perturbation of global equilibrium. To achieve this, we rigorously examine the dissipative characteristics of the linearized multi-component relaxation operator. We find that the partial dissipation arising from both intra-species and inter-species linearized relaxation operators complements one another, yielding the necessary dissipation estimate for the model. Furthermore, we note that the convergence rate of the distribution function accelerates as the momentum-energy interchange rate among the various gas components increases.

The integration of residential electric vehicle (EV) charging has transformed households into active participants within the power distribution grid, presenting a significant challenge for operators to deliver electricity reliably through current infrastructure. This paper tackles the issue of scheduling EV charging for multiple households while ensuring network stability. A key difficulty lies in limited information exchange, as consumers lack access to grid data and operators do not know individual consumer load parameters. To address this, we introduce a distributed framework that creates optimal charging schedules based on user preferences, iteratively refining them until operator-defined reliability constraints are met. We validate this method using a synthetic digital twin of a real distribution network across various EV adoption rates. Results indicate that the proposed approach achieves superior network reliability compared to scenarios where consumers charge solely based on personal preferences, offering a viable solution for the existing grid to accommodate rising EV adoption without substantial upgrades to grid capacity.

While the ringdown of a perturbed black hole is conventionally modeled using first-order perturbation theory, this Letter demonstrates that second-order effects are essential for accurately simulating ringdowns from black hole mergers. Focusing on the $(\ell,m)=(4,4)$ angular harmonic of the strain, we identify a quadratic effect consistent with theoretical predictions across various binary mass ratios. Specifically, the amplitude of this nonlinear $(4,4)$ mode scales quadratically with its parent, the fundamental $(2,2)$ mode, and can be comparable to or even exceed the amplitude of the linear $(4,4)$ component. Consequently, to properly model the ringdown and reduce mismatches by an order of magnitude, it is necessary to incorporate these nonlinear effects.

Identifying and segmenting objects within images based on their content remains a primary focus in computer vision research. Currently, this challenge is commonly tackled using deep learning frameworks like Faster R-CNN and YOLO, among others. This study examines the performance of various RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, and Mask R-CNN configurations available in the Detectron2 library. We first assess the pre-trained models both qualitatively and quantitatively (measuring AP) on the KITTI-MOTS and MOTSChallenge datasets. Our findings indicate substantial performance gains following fine-tuning on specific datasets and hyperparameter optimization. Furthermore, we conduct inference tests on out-of-context datasets to explore edge cases, yielding insights that enhance our understanding of these network behaviors.

This paper introduces a new safe screening test for Lasso. Our approach utilizes a safe region with a dome-shaped geometry and leverages a canonical representation of the dual feasible set, termed "dual cutting half-spaces." We demonstrate that this proposed region is always contained within the state-of-the-art "GAP Sphere" and "GAP Dome" methods introduced by Fercoq et al., with strict inclusion under very mild conditions, all while maintaining identical computational costs. Numerical experiments validate that our dome-based method yields more powerful screening tests than GAP regions and significantly accelerates the solution of Lasso problems.

This study reports a collection of highly precise excited-state properties derived from high-order coupled-cluster (CC) calculations utilizing diffuse-enriched basis sets, accompanied by comprehensive comparisons against experimental data. Specifically, we calculated key ground-to-excited transition characteristics, including oscillator strengths and dipole moments for both ground and excited states, across thirteen small molecules: hydridoboron, hydrogen chloride, water, hydrogen sulfide, boron fluoride, carbon monoxide, dinitrogen, ethylene, formaldehyde, thioformaldehyde, nitroxyl, fluorocarbene, and silylidene. Our approach systematically incorporates corrections up to the quintuple excitation level (CCSDTQP) within the CC expansion and extrapolates results to the complete basis set limit. In cases where consistent experimental data are available, theoretical values consistently fall within the experimental error margins for excited-state properties. Beyond extending our prior research on transition energies (see *J. Chem. Theory Comput.* 14 (2018) 4360–4379, 15 (2019) 1939–1956, 16 (2020) 1711–1741, and 16 (2020) 3720–3736), this work delivers ultra-accurate dipole moments and oscillator strengths suitable for future theoretical benchmarks.

This study explores the construction of Gabor and wavelet frames for the Weyl-Heisenberg and extended affine groups by leveraging the contraction between these groups, as established by Subag, Baruch, Birman, and Mann. Initially, we present the construction of multi-generator Gabor frames derived from a unitary irreducible representation linked to the Weyl-Heisenberg group. Subsequently, we derive multi-generator wavelet frames associated with the extended affine group and examine the relationship between frames in both groups. Finally, we demonstrate that Gabor and wavelet frame structures remain stable under minor perturbations.

Let $\mathcal{K}$ represent a nonsingular conic within the complex projective plane. According to Pascal's theorem, for any six distinct points $A, B, C, D, E, F$ lying on $\mathcal{K}$, the three intersection points formed by $(AE \cap BF)$, $(AD \cap CF)$, and $(BD \cap CE)$ are collinear; the line passing through these points is known as the Pascal line of the sextuple. Nevertheless, this construction breaks down when some of the six points coincide. This paper identifies the indeterminacy locus where the Pascal line becomes undefined and employs blow-ups along polydiagonals to resolve this issue. We further examine the geometry of Pascal's theorem in these degenerate scenarios and conclude with observations regarding the indeterminacy of other geometric components within Pascal's hexagrammum mysticum.

With the increasing prevalence of edge devices, deploying Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) has become a pressing challenge, primarily due to the high computational demands that often exceed the limited resources available on these devices. To address this, we introduce PQK, a novel model compression technique tailored for resource-constrained environments, which integrates pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation (KD). Distinct from conventional approaches, PQK leverages the unimportant weights identified during pruning to construct a teacher network for training an enhanced student network, eliminating the need for a separately pre-trained teacher. The method operates in two phases: Phase 1 utilizes iterative pruning and quantization-aware training to produce a lightweight, power-efficient model. In Phase 2, a teacher network is created by reintegrating the pruned, unused weights into the pruned architecture. This teacher then guides the training of the pruned network as a student, removing the requirement for an external pre-trained teacher since both networks exist within the same structure. We validated PQK on recognition models, demonstrating its effectiveness in both keyword spotting (KWS) and image recognition tasks.

Monocular depth estimation serves as a foundational task in computer vision, witnessing significant advancement over the past decade driven by deep learning. However, blurred boundaries in generated depth maps remain a critical issue. Research identifies two primary causes: first, low-level features carrying boundary and structural details often degrade during convolution in deeper network layers; second, models overlook errors in boundary regions because these areas occupy a small fraction of the total image during backpropagation. To address this, we target these two factors. We introduce a scene understanding module that integrates global information from both low- and high-level features, which is then adapted to varying scales via our proposed scale transform module at different decoder stages. Additionally, we develop a boundary-aware depth loss function to emphasize the importance of boundary depth values. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach yields depth maps with sharper boundaries and achieves competitive accuracy on the NYU-depth v2 and SUN RGB-D datasets.

We investigate spherically symmetric spacetimes within Einstein-aether theory across three coordinate systems—Schwarzschild, Painlevé-Gullstrand, and isotropic—in which the aether field remains comoving. Our work introduces both time-independent and time-dependent exact vacuum solutions. Specifically, within isotropic coordinates, we identify a family of exact static solutions defined by a single parameter, $c_{14}$, expressed in closed form. These solutions adhere to all existing observational constraints and revert to the standard Schwarzschild vacuum black hole when the decoupling limit is applied ($c_{14} = 0$). Nevertheless, whenever $c_{14} \neq 0$, a marginally trapped throat with a finite, non-zero radius invariably appears. On one side of this throat, the spacetime remains asymptotically flat, whereas on the other side, it develops a singularity at a finite proper distance from the throat, despite the geometric area remaining infinite at the singular point. Furthermore, this singularity is strong and involves spacetime curvature, causing both the Ricci and Kretschmann scalars to diverge to infinity.

Sparse neural networks have experienced significant expansion recently, especially within computer vision, driven by their lower parameter requirements for training and storage and enhanced learning efficiency. Contrary to expectations, their application in Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has remained largely unexplored. This study conducts a systematic examination of applying various existing sparse training methods across diverse DRL agents and environments. Our findings align with observations from the computer vision field, confirming that sparse networks outperform dense networks when parameter counts are equal within the DRL context. We offer a detailed analysis of how different DRL components are impacted by sparse networks and conclude by proposing fruitful directions for enhancing sparse training effectiveness and promoting its adoption in DRL.

Circumcenters are pivotal in the design and analysis of iterative optimization methods that aim for acceleration. This study introduces Bregman (pseudo-)circumcenters defined for finite sets. We demonstrate their existence and provide explicit formulas for the unique backward and forward Bregman pseudo-circumcenters. Furthermore, leveraging duality, we establish the relationships between backward and forward Bregman (pseudo-)circumcenters. Several examples are provided to illustrate these concepts. Our general framework for circumcenters lays the foundation for developing accelerated iterative methods utilizing Bregman circumcenters.

This paper addresses the challenge of efficiently and equitably distributing a collection of indivisible items among agents who share identical, additive valuations, with the goal of maximizing Nash social welfare—the geometric mean of individual valuations. Although finding the exact maximum is NP-hard, Nguyen and Rothe previously introduced a PTAS for this scenario. Our primary contribution is the development of the first additive PTAS for this problem: a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves a Nash social welfare within an additive error of $\varepsilon v_{\rm max}$, where $\varepsilon$ is any positive constant and $v_{\rm max}$ represents the highest single-good utility. Our algorithm's approximation quality surpasses that of existing PTAS methods. The approach is straightforward, involving a preprocessing step followed by the application of a recently developed additive PTAS for the target load balancing problem by Buchem et al.; however, calculating the additive error of the final output requires significant nontrivial effort.

This research introduces a novel approach to domain translation, converting semantic label maps and Computer Graphics (CG) simulation edge maps into photo-realistic imagery. By employing a conditionally trained Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), we generate photorealistic renditions of specific CG scenes. Current GAN architectures often fail to provide the level of photo-realism required for training deep neural networks in computer vision; we resolve this by integrating edge maps and utilizing adversarial training. Furthermore, we present an extension of this model that leverages the GAN framework to produce visually attractive and temporally consistent videos.

While the human brain can learn tasks sequentially with minimal forgetting, deep neural networks (DNNs) typically experience catastrophic forgetting when trained on successive tasks. This study tackles this issue within a class-incremental learning framework, where the DNN must classify test data without prior knowledge of the specific task origin. The proposed method, Continual-Prune-and-Select (CP&S), operates by identifying a subnetwork within the DNN dedicated to a specific task during training. At inference time, CP&S activates the appropriate subnetwork to generate predictions. To learn a new task, the method trains previously unused connections in the DNN to form a new subnetwork through pruning; notably, this process avoids updating shared connections, allowing it to repurpose links from other subnetworks. This approach eliminates catastrophic forgetting by establishing specialized, non-conflicting regions within the DNN while facilitating knowledge transfer between them. Implemented with various subnetwork selection strategies, CP&S outperforms state-of-the-art continual learning methods across multiple datasets (CIFAR-100, CUB-200-2011, ImageNet-100, and ImageNet-1000). Specifically, CP&S successfully learns 10 sequential tasks from ImageNet-1000 while maintaining approximately 94% accuracy with negligible forgetting—a groundbreaking result for class-incremental learning. To the authors' knowledge, this achieves an accuracy improvement of over 20% compared to the leading alternative method.

How do living systems achieve the flexibility required to respond rapidly and adapt readily to shifting environments? This inquiry has captivated biologists for many years and holds significant interest for computer scientists and engineers seeking to enhance the adaptability of artificial systems like machine learning models, robotics, and manufacturing processes by drawing inspiration from nature. This paper presents a comprehensive overview of the design characteristics in living organisms that foster flexibility, which we term the "elements of flexibility." Furthermore, to support interdisciplinary, bio-inspired research aimed at integrating these elements into human-made task-executing systems, we propose a general formalism for optimizing system flexibility. This framework is designed to (i) establish a shared vocabulary for discussing flexibility across researchers from diverse backgrounds, (ii) aid in analyzing and comparing existing studies on flexibility, such as those in transfer learning or manufacturing, and (iii) lay the groundwork for a comprehensive theory of system flexibility optimization.

This study examines the constraints of transferability in deep learning models designed for semantic segmentation of pneumonia in CT scans. The methodology employs a four-channel input consisting of three Hounsfield unit channels and a binary channel representing the lung region. The research leverages three distinct, publicly accessible CT datasets. In instances where lung masks are absent, a deep learning model generates a proxy image. Experimental findings indicate that transferability requires caution when developing COVID segmentation models, as retraining the model multiple times on extensive datasets leads to a decline in segmentation accuracy.

Predicting the spread of infectious diseases, particularly those transmitted by vectors, presents distinct difficulties for researchers. The transmission dynamics are shaped by the complex behaviors and interactions among viruses, vectors, hosts, and the environment. While public health surveillance and other data sources offer valuable information for accurately forecasting disease incidence, these datasets often suffer from imperfections. Common issues include reporting delays or missing cases, a lack of vector data, and insufficient geographical or temporal resolution in case reports. To address these gaps, researchers must make assumptions when building either mechanistic models that account for underlying processes or statistical models that justify their exclusion. Regardless of the modeling approach, scientists should assess their work using established best practices from the growing field of infectious disease forecasting, alongside conventions from other disciplines with decades of forecasting experience. Carefully managing assumptions and rigorously evaluating models will enable researchers to produce forecasts that offer significant insights to public health officials. This chapter offers an overview of general forecasting practices, examines the biological and statistical models applied to infectious disease prediction, details the technical aspects of constructing and evaluating these models, and investigates the challenges of communicating forecast results within a public health framework.

We present the Merkel Podcast Corpus, a German audio-visual-text dataset derived from nearly 16 years of almost weekly internet podcasts featuring former Chancellor Angela Merkel. To our knowledge, this marks the first single-speaker corpus in German that combines audio, visual, and textual modalities of comparable magnitude and temporal scope. We detail the collection and editing methodologies, which encompass downloading videos, transcripts, and metadata; executing forced alignment; performing active speaker recognition and face detection; and ultimately curating a single-speaker dataset of Merkel's utterances. This proposed pipeline is versatile and applicable to curating similar datasets, such as those from talk shows. Through various statistical analyses and applications in talking face generation and text-to-speech (TTS), we demonstrate the dataset's utility. We contend that it offers a significant contribution to the research community, particularly because of its realistic and challenging content situated at the intersection of prepared and spontaneous speech.

This paper examines the interaction between the totally positive monoid $G_{\ge 0}$, associated with a connected reductive group $G$ equipped with a pinning, and the conjugacy classes within $G$. Specifically, we analyze the intersection of conjugacy classes with the distinct cells of $G_{\ge 0}$. Furthermore, we propose a conjectural Jordan decomposition for $G_{\ge 0}$ and demonstrate its validity in several special instances.

The lazy algorithm, originally defined for real bases $\beta$, is extended to the context of Cantor bases $\boldsymbol{\beta}=(\beta_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$, a concept recently proposed by Charlier and the author. Let $x_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ denote the largest real number admitting a $\boldsymbol{\beta}$-representation $a_0a_1a_2\cdots$ where every digit $a_n$ satisfies $a_n \in \{0,\ldots,\lceil \beta_n \rceil -1\}$. This work investigates the combinatorial characteristics of lazy $\boldsymbol{\beta}$-expansions, which exist provided $x_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is finite. As a specific example, the study examines Cantor bases derived from the Thue-Morse sequence and establishes a formula for the associated value of $x_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$. Initially, it is demonstrated that lazy $\boldsymbol{\beta}$-expansions result from "flipping" the digits of greedy $\boldsymbol{\beta}$-expansions. Subsequently, a Parry-like criterion is proven to characterize the sequences of non-negative integers constituting lazy $\boldsymbol{\beta}$-expansions for real numbers within the interval $(x_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-1,x_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]$. Furthermore, the lazy $\boldsymbol{\beta}$-shift is analyzed; specifically, for alternate bases (periodic Cantor bases), an analogue of Bertrand-Mathis' theorem is established within the lazy framework: the lazy $\boldsymbol{\beta}$-shift is sofic if and only if all quasi-lazy $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(i)}$-expansions of $x_{\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(i)}}-1$ are ultimately periodic, where $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(i)}$ represents the $i$-th shift of the alternate base $\boldsymbol{\beta}$.

This research examines generalized theta lifting within the double covers of split special orthogonal groups, utilizing the non-minimal theta representations developed by Bump, Friedberg, and Ginzburg. We concentrate on the theta liftings associated with non-generic representations and propose a conjecture that establishes an upper bound for the initial non-zero occurrence of these liftings based solely on the unipotent orbit. Furthermore, we provide both global and local results that lend support to this conjecture.

Given the widespread adoption of deep neural networks (DNNs), particularly in safety-critical domains, and their opaque nature, verifying their properties and interpreting their behavior is a crucial endeavor. We introduce an automata-theoretic methodology to address challenges in DNN analysis. We demonstrate that a DNN's input-output behavior can be exactly represented by a specialized weak Büchi automaton, albeit one of exponential size. Furthermore, we illustrate how these automata facilitate common verification and interpretability tasks, such as assessing adversarial robustness and identifying minimal sufficient reasons. Finally, we present a proof-of-concept system that translates DNNs into automata over finite words to enhance computational efficiency, accepting a trade-off in analytical precision.

Octave equivalence acts as essential domain knowledge for various Music Information Retrieval (MIR) systems, such as chromagrams, harmonic CQT, and spiral convolutional networks. Previous studies utilized the Isomap manifold learning algorithm on unlabeled audio to map frequency sub-bands into a 3-D space where Euclidean distances reflect the inverse strength of Pearson correlations. However, relying on visual inspection to identify octave equivalence through Isomap limits scalability. To overcome this limitation, we introduce "helicality," defined as how well a 3-D Isomap embedding conforms to a Shepherd-Risset helix. Our unsupervised approach employs a custom Frank-Wolfe algorithm to minimize a least-squares objective within a convex hull. Numerical results demonstrate that isolated musical notes exhibit higher helicality than speech, with drum hits ranking next.

We report initial findings on the morphological and structural characteristics of galaxies at $z > 3$, observed via the James Webb Space Telescope during the Early Release Observations of the SMACS 0723 galaxy cluster ($z=0.39$). For the first time, we analyze the optical structures of numerous high-redshift galaxies with precise photometric redshifts to characterize galaxy formation in the early universe. By combining visual assessments with \textsc{Morfometryka} metrics, we conduct quantitative morphology analysis using both parametric methods (S\'ersic indices via light profile fitting) and non-parametric approaches (CAS values). These techniques allow us to determine the relative proportions of disk, spheroidal, and peculiar galaxies between $3 < z < 8$. Our analysis reveals the unexpected finding that disk galaxies dominate the morphological population at $z > 1.5$, outnumbering those detected by the Hubble Space Telescope at these redshifts by a factor of approximately ten. Furthermore, our visual classifications show strong agreement with galaxy positions in CAS parameter space and their corresponding S\'ersic indices.

For Kahler 4-manifolds that are not necessarily compact or of finite topological type, we establish connections between the fundamental groups of compact embedded Levi-flat or pseudoconvex submanifolds and the ambient manifold $M^4$. Specifically, if a Levi-flat submanifold $V^3$ possesses a finite fundamental group, then $\pi_1(M^4)$ equals the image of $\pi_1(V^3)$ under the inclusion map; conversely, if a non-separating pseudoconvex submanifold $V^3$ has a finite fundamental group, then $\pi_1(M^4)$ is isomorphic to the semidirect product $\iota_*\pi_1(V^3)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}$. As applications, we demonstrate that a Kahler manifold (compact or non-compact) containing an embedded holomorphic $\mathbb{P}^1$ with positive self-intersection must intersect every other holomorphic $\mathbb{P}^1$ of non-negative self-intersection, implying that $\pi_1(M^4)$ is trivial and that no ALE or ALF ends are present. Furthermore, if both a Levi-flat submanifold and an embedded holomorphic $\mathbb{P}^1$ of positive self-intersection exist, they must intersect. Regardless of the types of ends present, the total count of ALE and ALF ends is either zero or one. We also present examples, including a 2-ended scalar-flat Kahler metric conformal to the Taub-NUT solution.

The South Pole Telescope (SPT-3G) utilizes a detector array consisting of 16,000 millimeter-wave bolometers mounted on the 10-meter diameter South Pole Telescope to conduct a deep survey of the Cosmic Microwave Background in the Southern sky. This article details the geometry of the telescope's secondary mirror, which is shaped as a segment of a prolate spheroid, expressed across multiple coordinate systems, with broader applications to off-axis mirrors. Furthermore, the paper proves a geometric theorem concerning the Dragone condition: it establishes that the intersection of a prolate spheroid with any plane forms an ellipse, and the lines drawn from the ellipse's points to either focus create right circular cones whose central axes intersect outside the spheroid's interior.

Precise detection and localization of anomalies in radiological images are vital for computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems. Developing highly generalizable models typically demands extensive datasets with high-quality annotations, encompassing both global disease context and specific localization details. Nevertheless, medical imaging faces a scarcity of such high-quality data and annotations due to the high costs associated with labeling. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a novel method for generating diseased X-rays using conditional generative adversarial networks. Specifically, we synthesize a corresponding radiology image in a target domain from a source domain chest X-ray while maintaining patient identity. These generated images are then employed to augment training data in the target domain, thereby enhancing detection performance. Furthermore, we propose a unified framework that concurrently executes disease generation and localization. Our approach is evaluated on the dataset from the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), demonstrating superior results compared to current state-of-the-art detection algorithms.

Detecting lymph nodes (LN) automatically is a critical yet difficult clinical task in Computed Tomography (CT) imaging, primarily due to poor contrast with surrounding tissues and the nodes' diverse sizes, orientations, shapes, and sparse distribution. Current state-of-the-art methods, which rely on one-shot boosting of 3D HAAR features, achieve sensitivities of 52.9% (at 3.1 false positives per volume) or 60.9% (at 6.1 false positives per volume) for mediastinal lymph nodes. This paper introduces a two-stage approach: first, a preliminary candidate generation phase targets 100% sensitivity despite generating high false positive rates (40 per patient) to isolate volumes of interest (VOI). Subsequently, a 2.5D method processes each 3D VOI by resampling it into 2D orthogonal views multiple times, applying random scales, translations, and rotations relative to the VOI centroid. These varied views train a deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) classifier. During testing, the CNN evaluates probabilities across all generated views, which are averaged to determine the final classification probability for each VOI. Validation on two datasets—90 CT volumes containing 388 mediastinal LNs and 86 patients with 595 abdominal LNs—demonstrated sensitivities of 70% and 83% at 3 false positives per volume, and 84% and 90% at 6 false positives per volume for the mediastinum and abdomen, respectively, representing a significant improvement over prior state-of-the-art results.

This study characterizes domain wall solutions that emerge as minimizers of an energy functional derived from the asymptotic regime of micromagnetics, specifically for infinitely long, thin ferromagnetic strips with in-plane magnetization. For this energy functional, we establish the existence, uniqueness, monotonicity, and symmetry of 180° and 360° wall magnetization profiles. Furthermore, we illustrate how this energy arises as the $\Gamma$-limit of a reduced two-dimensional thin-film micromagnetic energy that accounts for non-local stray field effects, and we characterize the minimizers associated with this limit.

Extracting maximal learning signals from trajectory data remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL), where sample inefficiency hinders practical deployment. Recent advancements indicate that leveraging expressive policy approximators and conditioning on future trajectory information—such as future states in hindsight experience replay or returns-to-go in the Decision Transformer (DT)—facilitates efficient multi-task policy learning, sometimes replacing online RL entirely with offline behavioral cloning akin to sequence modeling. We demonstrate that these methods fundamentally perform Hindsight Information Matching (HIM), training policies to generate trajectory continuations that align with specific future state statistics. We introduce the Generalized Decision Transformer (GDT) to solve any HIM problem, illustrating how varying feature functions and anti-causal aggregators not only recovers DT as a specific instance but also yields novel variants: Categorical DT (CDT) and Bi-directional DT (BDT) for matching distinct future statistics. To evaluate CDT and BDT, we define offline multi-task state-marginal matching (SMM) and imitation learning (IL) as two generic HIM problems, propose Wasserstein distance as a unified metric, and empirically assess them on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. CDT, which substitutes anti-causal summation with anti-causal binning in DT, enables the first effective offline multi-task SMM algorithm that robustly generalizes to unseen and synthetic multi-modal state-feature distributions. BDT, utilizing an anti-causal second transformer as its aggregator, learns to model any future statistics and surpasses DT variants in offline multi-task IL. Our generalized HIM framework and GDT significantly broaden the applicability of advanced sequence modeling architectures in contemporary RL.

Ride-hailing, a novel travel mode facilitated by online platforms connecting passengers with private car drivers, has gained widespread popularity globally in the mobile internet era. Despite significant practical and theoretical interest, current understanding remains constrained due to a scarcity of relevant data. This study addresses this gap by presenting, for the first time, multi-day trip order data from ride-hailing drivers to illustrate mobility patterns in Beijing, China, through regional and driver-centric lenses. Regional analyses elucidate the spatiotemporal dynamics of ride-hailing demand, while driver-focused insights characterize service provision preferences. Key findings include observations of the city's spatiotemporal rhythm regarding ride-hailing usage and the identification of two distinct driver categories based on the relationship between their activity spaces and working hours. These results advance the comprehension of ride-hailing activities, enhance demand forecasting, refine models of driver preferences, and support the management of ride-hailing services.

We conducted general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations of merging binary neutron stars that include both neutrino transport and magnetic fields. Our implementation features a novel radiative transport module for neutrinos based on a general relativistic, truncated-moment (M1) formalism. The simulated binaries comprise two identical, irrotational stars described by the SLy nuclear equation of state, initially orbiting in a quasicircular configuration and threaded by a poloidal magnetic field extending from the stellar interiors outward, similar to pulsars. Neutrino processes were introduced shortly post-merger, with a specific focus on their role in initiating a jet after the hypermassive neutron star (HMNS) remnant collapses into a spinning black hole (BH). We examined two microphysical scenarios: a "warm-up" model evolving a single neutrino species with charged-current interactions only, and a more comprehensive model evolving three species ($
u_e,  ar{
u}_e, 
u_{m x}$) and their associated processes. The simulations tracked the system's evolution until it settled into a quasiequilibrium state following black hole formation. Our results indicate that the BH plus disk remnant eventually generates an incipient jet with an electromagnetic Poynting luminosity of approximately $10^{53} m \, erg\, s^{-1}$, aligning with typical short gamma-ray bursts (sGRBs). Neutrino cooling was found to shorten the HMNS lifetime and slightly reduce the amplitude of the primary peak in the gravitational wave power spectrum. Post-BH formation, neutrinos assist in evacuating matter near the black hole poles, leading to reduced baryon-loaded debris. Once quasiequilibrium is reached, the neutrino luminosity falls within the range of $\sim 10^{52-53} m \,erg\,s^{-1}$. Compared to models without neutrinos, we observed that including them results in similar ejecta masses and proves inefficient at removing additional angular momentum.

Building machine learning (ML) systems necessitates statistical oversight across their entire lifecycle. Thoroughly quantifying business needs and pinpointing critical factors that influence these needs helps mitigate the risk of project failure. Defining business requirements leads to the establishment of random variables that represent key performance indicators (KPIs), which are then examined via statistical experiments. Furthermore, both the data available for training and the outcomes of experiments shape the system's architecture. After development, the system undergoes testing and ongoing monitoring to verify compliance with business goals, achieved by continuously applying statistical experiments to analyze and regulate KPIs. This book guides the creation and development of ML systems, promoting an "experiment first" methodology that emphasizes defining statistical experiments from the project's inception. Additionally, it provides a detailed examination of how to maintain statistical control over ML systems throughout their lifespan.

Networks effectively model complex phenomena across diverse fields. While their capacity to represent complexity is advantageous, it is often beneficial to isolate a simplified structure comprising only the most critical edges, known as the backbone. This paper presents and illustrates the `backbone` package for R, which provides methods to extract backbones from weighted networks, weighted bipartite projections, and unweighted networks. For each network type, fully replicable code is demonstrated using small toy datasets followed by comprehensive empirical analyses of transportation, political, and social networks. Additionally, the study explores the statistical inference challenges inherent in backbone extraction. The work concludes with a review of current applications of the `backbone` package and outlines future research directions in network backbone extraction.

We introduce a superspace framework for two-dimensional conformal $(p,q)$ supergravity, formulated as a gauge theory based on the superconformal group $\mathsf{OSp}_0 (p|2; {\mathbb R} ) \times \mathsf{OSp}_0 (q|2; {\mathbb R} )$ utilizing a flat connection. By gauging away specific local symmetries, this conformal superspace simplifies into a conformally flat $\mathsf{SO}(p) \times \mathsf{SO}(q)$ superspace characterized by two key features: (i) a structure group comprising the direct product of the Lorentz group and $\mathsf{SO}(p) \times \mathsf{SO}(q)$, and (ii) a residual local scale symmetry implemented via super-Weyl transformations with an unrestricted real parameter. Applying this formalism, we characterize ${\cal N}$-extended AdS superspace as a maximally symmetric supergeometry when $p=q \equiv {\cal N}$. Furthermore, if at least one parameter ($p$ or $q$) is even, distinct superconformal groups and associated conformal superspaces become available; specifically, for $p = 2n$, the superconformal group may be chosen as $\mathsf{SU}(1,1|n) \times \mathsf{OSp}_0 (q|2; {\mathbb R} )$ when $n \neq 2$, or $\mathsf{PSU}(1,1|2) \times \mathsf{OSp}_0 (q|2; {\mathbb R} )$ when $n=2$. Generally, a conformal superspace formulation corresponds to a supergroup $G = G_L \times G_R$, where $G_L$ and $G_R$ represent any extended superconformal groups identified by G\"unaydin, Sierra, and Townsend. Degauging the resulting conformal superspace yields a conformally flat $H_L \times H_R$ superspace, with $H_L$ ($H_R$) serving as the $R$-symmetry subgroup of $G_L$ ($G_R$). Finally, for cases where $p,q \leq 2$, we propose composite primary multiplets that generate the Gauss-Bonnet invariant along with supersymmetric extensions of the Fradkin-Tseytlin term.

Meta-analysis serves as a systematic method for comprehending a phenomenon by synthesizing findings from numerous prior experimental studies. It plays a pivotal role in determining the aggregate effects of treatments and interventions across medicine, poverty reduction, and other socially impactful domains. However, traditional meta-analysis demands significant manual labor, making the process highly inefficient and susceptible to human bias. To address these challenges, we aim to automate meta-analysis with a specific emphasis on mitigating bias risks. Our approach begins by extracting data from natural language scientific literature. Adopting a novel causal learning framework, we conceptualize automated meta-analysis as a multiple causal inference problem, where the summary effect is derived via intervention. Leveraging existing tools that automate the initial stages of meta-analysis, our method achieves full automation and substantially decreases the required human effort. Evaluations conducted on both synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets indicate that this approach yields promising outcomes.

A central objective in quantum parameter estimation and quantum metrology is to develop strategies that maximize precision within available resources. Conventional models typically assume fixed dynamics, where peak precision is attained solely through optimal probe preparation and measurement. However, many practical scenarios allow for additional controls that can modify the system's evolution. We propose leveraging optimal control techniques to surpass the precision limits of quantum parameter estimation. By utilizing the extra degrees of freedom provided by these controls, we demonstrate that higher precision bounds are achievable. Specifically, we show that controlled schemes can exceed the precision constraints imposed by the coherent time, a limitation that invariably restricts the standard approach.

This study presents a radio continuum analysis utilizing both new and archival data from the Australia Telescope Compact Array focused on N 103B. Located in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), N 103B is a young (<=1000 years) spectroscopically confirmed type Ia supernova remnant (SNR) hypothesized to stem from a single degenerate progenitor. The remnant exhibits asymmetrical radio morphology, characterized by two bright regions situated to the north-west and south-west of the central emission source. Key features of N 103B include a radio spectral index of -0.75 +/- 0.01, which aligns with other young Galactic type Ia SNRs, and a bulk expansion rate comparable to X-ray observations. Additionally, morphology and polarized electric field vector measurements reveal a peak in radial polarization towards the north-west at both 5500 and 9000 MHz. The spectrum displays a concave-up shape, likely resulting from non-linear diffusive shock acceleration or the presence of two distinct populations of ultra-relativistic electrons; this hypothesis is supported by the observation of unpolarized clumps in the south-west region. We calculate a typical magnetic field strength of 16.4 microG based on an average rotation measure of 200 rad m^-2, whereas the equipartition field is estimated at approximately 235 microG, corresponding to a minimum energy of 6.3*10^48 erg. Given the remnant's close (~0.5 degree) proximity to the LMC mid-plane, an early interaction with a dense interstellar medium may significantly constrain its evolutionary path. Finally, we compare N 103B's characteristics with six other young type Ia SNRs in the LMC and Galaxy across various proposed degeneracy scenarios to underscore potential model-dependent differences. We propose that the single degenerate scenario may account for the morphological asymmetry observed in type Ia supernova explosions.

The non-exponential nature of structural relaxation is a defining feature of glassy dynamics, and the unique shape detected by dielectric methods has long captivated researchers. Specifically, the unusually narrow dielectric response in polar glass-forming materials has traditionally been linked to dipolar cross-correlations. In this work, we demonstrate that dipole interactions can couple with shear stress, altering flow behavior and inhibiting the emergence of simple liquid characteristics. We contextualize these results within the broader framework of glassy dynamics and the significance of intermolecular interactions.

This study investigates how gravitational settling influences the concentration of inertial particles within a wall-bounded turbulent flow. Although it might be assumed that settling effects are negligible when the settling parameter ($Sv \equiv v_s/u_\tau$) is small—where $v_s$ represents the Stokes settling velocity and $u_\tau$ the fluid friction velocity—we demonstrate that settling can still exert a leading-order influence on concentration profiles even in this regime. This occurs because the significance of settling depends not on the magnitude of $v_s$ relative to $u_\tau$ or other fluid velocity scales, but rather on $v_s$ compared to other mechanisms governing vertical particle velocity and concentration distribution. Analyzing the particle mean-momentum equation reveals that, generally, there exists a region within the boundary layer where settling cannot be ignored, regardless of how small $Sv$ is (as long as it remains finite). Direct numerical simulations support these findings, indicating that near-wall concentration is strongly dependent on $Sv$ even when $Sv \ll 1$, potentially decreasing by an order of magnitude as $Sv$ increases from $O(10^{-4})$ to $O(10^{-2})$. Furthermore, the results show that the preferential sampling of ejection events by inertial particles in the boundary layer (observed when $Sv=0$) is significantly modified as $Sv$ increases, shifting toward a preferential sampling of sweep events driven by the onset of the preferential sweeping mechanism.

Paraphrase generation represents a compelling yet difficult natural language processing task with many real-world uses. This paper examines datasets frequently utilized in paraphrase research and demonstrates that merely repeating input sentences outperforms state-of-the-art models when assessed using standard metrics. Our results indicate that a model may appear proficient at creating paraphrases even when it makes only trivial modifications to the input or produces no changes whatsoever.

Image classification stands as a primary challenge within computer vision and machine learning. Because real-world applications often lack control over image acquisition, there is a significant risk that captured images will contain noise, such as sensor artifacts from low-quality surveillance devices. This paper examines how three distinct noise types affect descriptors generated by two prominent feature extraction techniques—LBP and HOG—and evaluates the efficacy of denoising in alleviating these issues. Through experiments on two datasets, varying noise types and intensities, and testing multiple denoising approaches, the study demonstrates that noise can substantially degrade classification performance and obscure class boundaries. While denoising methods failed to match the accuracy of noise-free conditions, they successfully enhanced classification outcomes for noisy data.

This work addresses predictive monitoring (PM), which involves forecasting the satisfaction of a target property based on a system's current runtime state. Given PM's critical role in ensuring runtime safety and enabling online control, these methods must be efficient enough to facilitate timely responses to predicted violations while maintaining correctness guarantees. We present *quantitative predictive monitoring (QPM)*, the inaugural PM approach capable of handling stochastic processes and complex specifications defined in Signal Temporal Logic (STL). In contrast to most existing PM techniques that merely predict binary satisfaction of a property $\phi$, QPM delivers a quantitative assessment by forecasting the robust STL semantics of $\phi$. Specifically, QPM generates highly efficient prediction intervals with probabilistic assurances, ensuring these intervals capture the STL robustness values relative to the system's stochastic behavior with an arbitrary confidence level. Achieving this, we employ a machine-learning strategy that utilizes recent advancements in conformal inference for quantile regression, thus eliminating the need for costly Monte-Carlo simulations at runtime to estimate intervals. Furthermore, we demonstrate how our monitors can be compositionally combined to manage composite formulas without requiring retraining or compromising guarantees. Finally, we validate the effectiveness and scalability of QPM across a benchmark comprising four discrete-time stochastic processes with varying levels of complexity.

This paper examines the ACC and LSC conjectures concerning the minimal log discrepancies of generalized pairs, demonstrating that established results for standard pairs extend to this broader context. Additionally, it explores the theory of complements within the framework of generalized pairs.

Simulating condensed-matter systems on engineered quantum platforms offers a promising avenue for research, though achieving the precision required to surpass classical methods has remained a significant hurdle. In this study, we present an experimental framework using eighteen superconducting qubits to build an accurate condensed-matter simulator and investigate fundamental electronic characteristics. By reconstructing the single-particle band structure of a one-dimensional wire, we benchmark our approach, demonstrating near-total mitigation of decoherence and readout errors. This allows us to measure energy eigenvalues with an error of approximately 0.01 rad, compared to typical energy scales of order 1 rad. We attribute this unprecedented algorithmic fidelity to robust properties of the Fourier transform, which enables resolving eigenenergies with a statistical uncertainty as low as 1e-4 rad. Additionally, we synthesize magnetic flux and disordered local potentials, two essential components of condensed-matter systems. As we vary the magnetic flux, we detect avoided level crossings in the spectrum, serving as a precise indicator of local disorder distribution. By integrating these techniques, we reconstruct the electronic properties of eigenstates, revealing persistent currents and a marked suppression of conductance in the presence of disorder. This work establishes an accurate method for quantum simulation and opens new possibilities for studying novel quantum materials using superconducting qubits.

In fixed-target scattering experiments, interaction cross-section measurements are usually conducted by observing the attenuation of a particle beam as it passes through a target slab. However, fully active sampling calorimeters, such as time projection chambers, function as larger-volume targets that can be modeled as a sequence of smaller slabs. This paper introduces a robust method for calculating hadron-nucleus interaction cross-sections using data from these fully active calorimeters, ensuring accuracy even when the target consists of many slabs with varying thicknesses.

Traditional ICP algorithms typically rely on a static selection of both the data association method and the error metric. This paper introduces Hybrid ICP, a novel and adaptable variant that dynamically optimizes both the data association technique and the error metric by analyzing the live object image alongside the current ICP estimate. We demonstrate that, for object pose estimation, Hybrid ICP achieves higher accuracy and greater robustness against noise compared to other standard ICP variants. Additionally, we examine scenarios where ICP operates sequentially with a moving camera, investigating the trade-off between the precision of individual estimates and the total number of estimates achievable within a fixed time frame.

This study investigates the nonlinear evolution of two-fluid interfacial structures, such as spikes and bubbles, driven by the combined effects of Rayleigh-Taylor and Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities or those resulting from the interaction of Richtmyer-Meshkov and Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities induced by oblique shocks. Analytic expressions for the asymptotic combined growth rates of these features are derived using Layzer's model for both scenarios. However, when the overlying fluid is less dense, the interface perturbation exhibits distinct behaviors: depending on the magnitude of the velocity shear from the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, both bubble and spike amplitudes may grow monotonically (instability), oscillate over time, or display coupled dynamics where spike steepening coincides with bubble undulation. In the case of an oblique shock, which triggers combined Richtmyer-Meshkov instability (via the shock's normal component) and Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (via velocity shear from the parallel component), the instability growth rate does not decay as $1/t$ as $t \rightarrow \infty$ like it does for normal shocks. Instead, it asymptotically approaches a spike peak height growth velocity of $\sim \sqrt{\frac{5(1+A_{T})}{16(1-A_{T})}(\Delta v)^2}$, where $\Delta v$ represents the velocity shear and $A_T$ is the Atwood number. The implications of these findings regarding the generation of spiky fluid jets in astrophysical contexts are also discussed.

Although interdependence is a critical factor for analyzing the stability of real-world complex systems with functional links, the physical mechanisms underlying such coupling remain elusive due to an absence of theoretical frameworks. To bridge this gap, we introduce an interdependent magnetization framework, demonstrating that dependency links among $K-1$ pairwise networks of Ising spins can be rigorously translated into directed $K$-spin interactions or adaptive thermal couplings. Utilizing the thermal portrait, we analytically derive the phase diagram for various structural configurations and validate our findings through extensive simulations. Our results indicate that interdependence functions as an entropic force that magnifies site-to-site thermal fluctuations, creating unique vulnerability patterns that often render system recovery impossible. Furthermore, we identify an isomorphism between the ground states of random multi-spin models and interdependent percolation on randomly coupled networks. This insight opens new avenues for cross-disciplinary exchange, offering novel methodologies with significant implications for understanding constraint satisfaction and the functional robustness of interdependent systems.

Obtaining extensive, high-quality ground truth data remains a significant hurdle for developing supervised machine learning models in healthcare. While digital data within clinical workflows is growing, it is largely fragmented across various sites and restricted to maintain patient privacy. Processing radiological records and managing large-scale clinical datasets place a heavy strain on resources, a challenge where machine learning and artificial intelligence are essential. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) for musculoskeletal (MSK) diagnosis exemplifies this; although these scans contain rich information, they demand considerable time to interpret and label. Self-supervised learning (SSL) offers a pathway to address the scarcity of labeled data but typically necessitates vast amounts of training data during the pretraining phase. In this study, we introduce Slice-based Self-supervised Deep Learning (SB-SSL), a novel approach for classifying abnormalities in knee MRI scans. Our results demonstrate that with fewer than 1,000 cases, the proposed framework can detect anterior cruciate ligament tears with 89.17% accuracy and an AUC of 0.954, surpassing state-of-the-art methods without relying on external pretraining data. This confirms that our framework is well-suited for self-supervised learning in data-limited scenarios.

We introduce the first semi-streaming PTAS for the minimum feedback arc set problem on directed tournaments, achieving this in a small number of passes. Specifically, our approach delivers a $(1 + \varepsilon)$-approximation within polynomial time $O \left( \text{poly}(n) 2^{\text{poly}(1/\varepsilon)} \right)$, utilizing $p$ passes and $n^{1+1/p} \cdot \text{poly}\left(\frac{\log n}{\varepsilon}\right)$ space. The prior algorithm sharing this pass/space efficiency only achieved a $3$-approximation (SODA, 2020), while other polynomial-time methods reaching a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation required either quadratic memory or a linear number of passes. Additionally, we propose a novel time/space trade-off for 1-pass algorithms addressing the tournament feedback arc set problem, an issue with significant applications in machine learning, including the development of linear classifiers and Bayesian inference. Furthermore, we offer several new algorithms and lower bounds for related streaming problems on directed graphs, an area that remains largely unexplored.

This study investigates the behavior of holographic entanglement entropy (HEE) in near-equilibrium thermal states, which are macroscopically modeled by conformal relativistic hydrodynamic flows dual to dynamical black brane geometries. We calculate HEE for strip-shaped subsystems in boundary dimensions $d=2, 3, 4$ to derive general qualitative insights into the interaction between fluid flows and entanglement dynamics. Initially, examining the zeroth order of the hydrodynamic derivative expansion via stationary boosted black branes, we work non-perturbatively in fluid velocity. Our findings indicate that as fluid velocity approaches its relativistic maximum, the UV-regulated HEE diverges at any temperature. Furthermore, the holographic mutual information between two nearby subsystems drops to zero at a specific critical fluid velocity and stays zero thereafter. Subsequently, we compute HEE for an excited fluid state containing a sound mode at the first order of the derivative expansion. As a simplified case, we first analyze non-dissipative dynamics in $d=2$, studying HEE time evolution under a sound mode and a propagating pressure pulse. In $d=4$, we observe that dissipative sound modes generate an additional dynamical UV divergence, which is subleading relative to the standard 'area law divergence.' Conversely, no such divergence appears for dissipative sound modes in $d=3$.

Data from the Rosetta orbiter and the Philae lander have significantly advanced our understanding of the composition of cometary nuclei. This text examines the properties of the 67P/CG nucleus, comparing them with those of other comets previously studied by space missions. Cometary nuclei consist of a mixture of ices, minerals, organic compounds, and salts, creating surfaces that are notably dark and red. At distances far from the Sun, exposed water and carbon dioxide ices are scarce on 67P/CG, appearing only in specific areas where pristine subsurface layers are exposed or where volatile recondensation, driven by solar heating and local topography, allows their temporary persistence. The nucleus surface is largely covered by a dust layer of varying thickness; these dust grains are primarily dehydrated and composed of minerals, organics, and salts. Spectral analysis indicates that the mineral component is dominated by silicates, fine-grained opaque materials, and ammoniated salts. Organic matter contains both aliphatic and aromatic groups, alongside a prominent hydroxyl group. The surface composition of cometary nuclei changes in response to heliocentric distance and seasonal cycles: as the comet approaches perihelion, increased solar flux enhances activity through volatile sublimation, leading to the erosion of surface layers, the exposure of ices, activity within cliffs and pits, the collapse of overhangs and walls, and the mobilization and redistribution of dust. These color, compositional, and textural changes across different morphological regions are linked to these processes. This chapter explores the composition and evolutionary processes of the 67P/CG nucleus as observed by Rosetta, contextualizing them within findings from other comets explored by space missions or observed from Earth.

The article introduces integrable delay variants of the two-dimensional Toda lattice equation and derives their multi-soliton solutions by utilizing the delay reduction method on the Gram determinant solution.

This study examines asymmetry monotone-based limits on the shortest duration needed for an initial qubit state to transform into a final state that can be probabilistically distinguished with a fixed minimal error rate, known as the distinguishability time. For unitary evolution driven by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition involving two asymmetry monotones that ensures any state of a two-level system or a separable state of $N$ two-level systems can evolve unitarily into a distinguishable state with a fixed minimal error probability $\delta \in [0,1/2]$. This condition facilitates ordering qubit states by their distinguishability time and determines the optimal release time for driven two-level systems, such as those found in the Landau-Zener scenario. Regarding non-unitary dynamics, we evaluate three lower bounds for the distinguishability time, introducing a novel bound defined by the asymmetry of the uniformly time-twirled initial system-plus-environment state relative to the generator $H_{SE}$ of the Stinespring isometry. Specifically, this new bound is expressed as $\Vert [H_{SE},\rho_{\text{av}}(\tau)]\Vert_{1}$, where $\rho_{\text{av}}(\tau):={1\over \tau}\int_{0}^{\tau}dt\, e^{-iH_{SE}t}\rho \otimes \vert 0\rangle_{E}\langle 0\vert_{E} e^{iH_{SE}t}$.

Data augmentation is a validated method for building machine learning models resilient to specific distributional shifts, such as image rotations, while alignment regularization is frequently paired with augmentation to enhance representation invariance. Motivated by the growing variety of alignment regularization options, this paper evaluates popular design choices regarding robustness and invariance by introducing a novel testing framework. Our synthetic experiments highlight the advantages of squared L2 norm regularization, and we complement our empirical findings with a formal analysis of alignment regularization behavior under realistic assumptions. Furthermore, we validate a simple yet effective technique—worst-case data augmentation combined with squared L2 norm alignment regularization—demonstrating that its benefits surpass those of specially designed methods. Additionally, we provide an open-source implementation in both TensorFlow and PyTorch, available with minimal setup at https://github.com/jyanln/AlignReg.

Feature selection is a critical challenge in machine learning, dedicated to identifying variables that construct optimal predictive models. This paper addresses feature selection specifically for forecasting post-intervention outcomes using pre-intervention data. Inspired by healthcare contexts where the objective is often to choose a treatment that maximizes a specific patient's result, we note that randomized control trial data is frequently insufficient to accurately estimate conditional treatment effects. We demonstrate how observational data can enhance both feature selection and effect estimation in two scenarios: (a) when the causal graph is known, and (b) when the causal graph is unknown but observational data exists alongside limited experimental data. Our work extends the concept of the Markov boundary to apply to treatment-outcome pairs and offers theoretical assurances for our proposed methods. Finally, experiments with simulated data confirm that integrating observational and experimental data yields improvements in feature selection and effect estimation.

The Item Details Page (IDP) is a web page on an e-commerce site that displays details about a specific product, typically followed by sections recommending other relevant items. These recommendations are usually organized into modules or carousels, each presenting a curated set of suggested products. The arrangement and selection of these modules aim to enhance item discoverability, boost user engagement, showcase inventory diversity, and meet broader business goals. However, IDP recommendation modules are frequently manually curated and statically configured for all users, neglecting the potential for personalization. This paper introduces a scalable, end-to-end production system designed to optimize the real-time, personalized selection and ordering of these recommendation modules using deep neural networks. Extensive offline experiments and online A/B testing demonstrate that this system significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of click-through and conversion rates. Specifically, our online A/B test revealed that the proposed framework increased the click-through rate by 2.48% and the purchase-through rate by 7.34% compared to static configurations.

Solitons within liquid crystals have attracted significant attention, yet no consensus exists regarding the underlying forces governing their structure or formation, despite various hypotheses of differing complexities. This study introduces a minimal model for soliton structures in achiral nematic liquid crystals, identifying the essential conditions for generating traveling solitons without added charges. These conditions include surface imperfections or inhomogeneities that induce twist, flexoelectricity, dielectric contrast, and an applied AC electric field coupled to the director's orientation. Based on a tensorial representation of a confined liquid crystal, the model predicts the emergence of quadrupolar "butterfly" structures in slit channel regions where the surface imperfection twists the director. As the electric field strength increases, solitons (referred to as "bullets") detach from the butterfly wings and propagate rapidly across the system. The model's key predictions—including the formation and architecture of butterflies, bullets, and stripes, along with the influence of surface imperfections and field strength—align with experimental findings presented here for nematic LCs confined between two chemically treated parallel plates.

Glaucoma stands as a primary cause of blindness, yet it poses significant detection challenges because it often remains asymptomatic until damage becomes severe. Consequently, diagnosis frequently occurs only after pathological markers are evident.
