While early detection typically relies on functional, structural, and clinical evaluations, researchers continue to debate which specific markers serve as consistent metrics for the disease. Deep learning approaches have partially addressed this issue by bypassing the need for explicit marker identification and directly analyzing high-level information to classify data. However, despite their effectiveness, these methods hinder expert interpretation by offering no insight into the model's discrimination logic. This paper proposes a solution using deep generative networks, which are capable of learning complex, high-dimensional probability distributions. Specifically, we trained a Deep Feature Consistent Variational Autoencoder (DFC-VAE) to reconstruct optic disc images. Our findings demonstrate that a compact latent space derived from the DFC-VAE can effectively capture the high-dimensional distribution of glaucoma data and provide clear discriminatory evidence between normal and glaucomatous eyes. Notably, latent representations with a dimensionality as low as 128 achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.885 when paired with a Support Vector Classifier.

The academic community has extensively investigated computer-assisted pronunciation training (CAPT) for non-native speakers, examining various model architectures like Bayesian networks and deep learning, as well as different speech signal representations. Despite recent advancements, current CAPT methods struggle to detect pronunciation errors with high accuracy, achieving only 60% precision within 40%-80% recall. A primary obstacle is the scarcity of mispronounced speech data required for robustly training error-detection models. If a generative model could emulate non-native speech and produce unlimited training data, error detection would become significantly more feasible. This work introduces three novel techniques utilizing phoneme-to-phoneme (P2P), text-to-speech (T2S), and speech-to-speech (S2S) conversion to synthesize both correctly and mispronounced speech. We demonstrate that these methods enhance the accuracy of three machine learning models for error detection and establish a new state-of-the-art in the field. While prior studies employed simple generation techniques like P2P merely as supplementary mechanisms to boost detection accuracy, our approach treats speech generation as a primary method for identifying pronunciation errors. Effectiveness was evaluated on detecting pronunciation and lexical stress errors using non-native English corpora from German, Italian, and Polish speakers. The top-performing S2S technique improved pronunciation error detection accuracy by 41% on the AUC metric, rising from 0.528 to 0.749 compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Introductory courses on linear state-space control primarily address time-invariant systems, dedicating significant effort to system realizations that help students master core concepts such as controllability, observability, and the design of controllers and observers. This note introduces a graphical method for converting a system from observability form to observer form using basic block diagram manipulations, a technique often underutilized in teaching. Leveraging the well-established duality principle regarding controllability and observability in linear systems, this graphical approach can also be applied to transform a system from controllability form to controller realization.

The basic knapsack problem involves maximizing the total value of selected items without exceeding a weight constraint. This study transitions from computer science to physics by modeling the knapsack problem as a statistical physics system and calculating its partition function. By approximating the solution for a large number of items, we derive a novel algorithm. When compared to existing approximation methods, this new approach demonstrates superior speed while maintaining high accuracy. Based on this balance between speed and precision, we characterize the algorithm as a manifestation of a greedy strategy. Finally, we explore potential extensions to rigorously formalize the underlying heuristics or apply this framework to other combinatorial optimization challenges. Overall, this work bridges computer science and statistical physics, offering a fresh analytical perspective for solving problems in the former using techniques from the latter.

A primary obstacle in the real-time detection and parameter estimation of gravitational waves from compact binary mergers is the high computational demand of traditional matched-filtering and Bayesian inference techniques. Specifically, applying these methods across the full parameter space accessible to gravitational-wave detectors or performing real-time estimation is computationally infeasible. Conversely, swift detection and inference are essential for the immediate follow-up of electromagnetic and astroparticle counterparts associated with significant transients, such as binary neutron-star and black-hole–neutron-star mergers. By training deep neural networks to recognize specific signals and learn an efficient representation of the mapping between gravitational-wave signals and their parameters, both detection and inference can be executed rapidly and reliably with high sensitivity and accuracy. This study applies a deep-learning approach to quickly identify and characterize transient gravitational-wave signals from binary neutron-star mergers within real LIGO data. We demonstrate, for the first time, that artificial neural networks can promptly detect and characterize binary neutron star gravitational-wave signals in actual LIGO data, effectively distinguishing them from noise and signals arising from coalescing black-hole binaries. We substantiate this finding by showing that our deep-learning framework correctly classifies all gravitational-wave events in the Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog, GWTC-1 [Phys. Rev. X 9 (2019), 031040]. These outcomes highlight the necessity of utilizing realistic gravitational-wave detector data in machine learning methodologies and mark progress toward achieving real-time detection and inference of gravitational waves.

Question Answering (QA) systems depend heavily on extensive annotated data, which is expensive and labor-intensive to collect. Transforming existing QA benchmark datasets is difficult because of varying formats and inherent complexities. To overcome these hurdles, we introduce an algorithm that automatically creates shorter, more natural questions from longer trivia items by adapting the style between the Natural Questions (NQ) and Quizbowl (QB) datasets. This approach offers an automated method for expanding data availability for QA systems. To maintain both the quantity and quality of the generated data, we employ a neural classifier to identify and eliminate ill-formed questions. Our results demonstrate that in low-resource scenarios, incorporating this synthetic data enhances QA performance compared to baseline systems on both NQ and QB datasets. Ultimately, our algorithm increases the scalability of training data without compromising data quality.

This overview presents the most recent findings from the PHENIX experiment at RHIC concerning hard probes. Data obtained from measuring high-$p_{T}$ hadrons, hadron-hadron correlations, open heavy flavor, quarkonia, and direct photons across a spectrum of collision systems—ranging from large (Au+Au) to small ($p$+Al and $p/d/^3$He+Au)—offer enhanced understanding of the medium formed in large systems and the potential emergence of QGP-like properties during the transition from small to large systems.

A standard approach to investigating quantum systems involves manipulating their electronic or magnetic characteristics through external variables like temperature, magnetic fields, or pressure. Among these, applying hydrostatic pressure via a specialized cell is a prevalent technique; however, this method introduces significant challenges for Muon Spin Rotation/Relaxation ($\mu^+$SR) experiments. Specifically, a substantial fraction of implanted muons end up in the pressure cell rather than the sample, generating an elevated background signal. This problem is exacerbated when the sample's temperature-dependent response is negligible compared to that of the cell, potentially obscuring the sample's signal and complicating sample alignment within the beam. To address this, we developed pySRIM, a practical simulation tool utilizing TRIM to calculate muon stopping fractions for the pressure cell setup at the $\mu$E1 beamline's GPD spectrometer at the Paul Scherrer Institute. This program estimates muon stops in both the sample and the cell at specific momentum levels. By integrating the tool into a graphical user interface (GUI), researchers can easily approximate the relative stopping fractions in their fitting procedures before conducting experiments at GPD.

This study examines the magnetic ground state of Sm$_3$BWO$_9$, which features a distorted kagome lattice. A magnetic phase transition occurs at $T_N=0.75$ K, as evidenced by the specific heat's temperature dependence. $^{11}$B nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) measurements reveal incommensurate magnetic ordering through double-horn spectra when a magnetic field is applied along the $c$-axis. Conversely, the lack of line splitting for fields oriented within the $ab$-plane suggests that the incommensurate modulation of the internal field is strictly confined to the $c$-axis. Regarding spin dynamics, critical slowing down is observed in the $1/T_1$ temperature dependence when $\mu_0H\perp c$-axis, a phenomenon entirely absent when $\mu_0H||c$-axis. Leveraging the local symmetry of $^{11}$B sites, we analyzed the hyperfine coupling tensors and established two constraints on the feasible magnetic structure. Furthermore, we propose that single-ion anisotropy is pivotal in explaining the contrasting ground states of Sm$_3$BWO$_9$ and Pr$_3$BWO$_9$.

This study investigates whether the widely separated double quasar Q2138-431 is a gravitational lens. While early research established that the two quasar images share nearly identical spectra and redshifts, no lensing galaxy had previously been identified. Utilizing recent deep surveys across infrared and optical wavelengths, we searched for a galaxy matching the expected characteristics of a gravitational lens. The search yielded a $5 \sigma$ detection of a faint galaxy situated between the two quasar images in a deep $J$-band frame from the VISTA Science Archive, with an apparent magnitude of $J = 20.68$. The non-detection in the $I$-band suggests a redshift of $z > 0.6$, and mass modeling of the system indicates the lensing galaxy has a mass of $1.31 \times 10^{12} M_\odot$ and a mass-to-light ratio of $M_{\odot}/L_{\odot} = 9.0$. Additionally, archival photographic data from the UK 1.2m Schmidt telescope spanning 25 years were utilized to generate light curves for both quasar images, which were cross-correlated to determine any time lag. The results show that image B leads image A by approximately one year, aligning with the 410 days predicted by the mass model. Although the spectral similarity and the identification of the lensing galaxy are the strongest evidence for classifying Q2138-431 as a gravitational lens, the time delay and mass-to-light ratio offer a consistent framework supporting this conclusion. Furthermore, the large separation between the quasar images and the simplicity of the mass model render Q2138-431 an ideal system for measuring the Hubble constant.

While pure Vision Transformer models excel at short video classification and action recognition, their quadratic self-attention complexity and absence of inductive bias make them resource-heavy and data-inefficient. These limitations are exacerbated in long-form video understanding, rendering current methods impractical for domains with strict memory or data constraints. To address this, we present the Spatio-Temporal Attention Network (STAN), an efficient architecture employing a two-stream transformer to capture dependencies between static image and temporal context features. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on various long video tasks, is highly data-efficient, and can process videos up to two minutes long using a single GPU.

A novel class of dynamical black holes is introduced within manifolds that feature flat spatial sections and exhibit asymptotic behavior consistent with spatially flat Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) spacetimes. Unlike previous solutions, these black holes are not vacuum solutions to the Einstein equations, yet they maintain the isotropy characteristic of the flat spatial sections in the asymptotic FLRW geometry.

This study aims to demonstrate fundamental results regarding $\mathbf{E}$-compact extensions of $\mathbf{E}$-completely regular spaces, specifically focusing on Hewitt realcompactifications and Banaschewski compactifications, within the framework where the Axiom of Choice is not assumed. The work introduces original findings concerning a specific subring of the ring of continuous real-valued functions defined on a zero-dimensional $T_1$-space. Additionally, it presents new insights into $P$-spaces, Baire topologies, and $G_{\delta}$-topologies. While some statements examined here lack proofs within $\mathbf{ZF}$, others are proven equivalent to the Boolean Prime ideal Theorem, and still others are consequences of the Axiom of Countable Multiple Choices.

Swimming bacteria in dense suspensions display collective behavior driven by the combination of steric and hydrodynamic interactions. While unconfined groups show fleeting vortices and jets, and those in circular domains may form spiral vortices, we demonstrate that restricting them to a long, narrow "racetrack" geometry stabilizes their movement into a steady, unidirectional circulation. Simulations of discrete swimmers confirm this phenomenon and highlight the pivotal role of bacteria-generated fluid flows in the dynamics. Specifically, cells near the channel walls generate strong flows that propel bulk cells against their swimming direction. We analyze the transition from disorder to persistent directed motion as a function of channel width, finding that the crossover width matches the typical correlation length of swirls observed in unbounded systems. These findings clarify the mechanisms behind collective behavior in bacteria and other active matter systems, emphasizing the significance of ubiquitous boundaries present in natural environments.

For an extended period, tracking-by-detection (TbD) remained the dominant paradigm in Multi-Object Tracking, involving initial object detection followed by frame-to-frame association. Traditional models typically relied on motion and appearance cues, such as re-identification networks, whereas recent attention-based approaches have achieved impressive results by learning these cues in a data-driven fashion. This paper investigates whether standard TbD methods can match the performance of end-to-end models. We introduce two key components that enable conventional re-identification networks to excel in appearance-based tracking. Through extensive analysis of failure cases, we demonstrate that combining our proposed appearance features with a simple motion model yields robust tracking outcomes. Our tracker achieves state-of-the-art performance across four public datasets—MOT17, MOT20, BDD100k, and DanceTrack—and the associated code and models will be made available.

Recently, Kayumov \cite{K} established a sharp estimate for the $n$-th truncated area functional of normalized Bloch space functions when $n \le 5$, later extending this result to $n=6$ in collaboration with Wirths \cite{KW1}. We demonstrate that for functions possessing non-negative Taylor coefficients, this same sharp estimate holds for all $n$. In the case of arbitrary functions, we derive an estimate that is asymptotically of the same order but marginally larger (approximately by a factor of $4/e$). Furthermore, we examine related weighted estimates involving functionals with powers $n^t$ where $t>0$, revealing that the exponent $t=1$ constitutes the critical case for achieving the expected sharp estimate.

Over the last ten years, Ising machines designed to solve difficult combinatorial optimization problems have emerged, utilizing spins modeled as continuous dynamical variables to minimize the Ising Hamiltonian. Nevertheless, the potential of these systems at larger scales remains largely unexplored. This study examines an Ising machine constructed from a network of nearly linearly coupled analog spins. We demonstrate that these networks exploit a computational resource analogous to the semidefinite positive relaxation of the Ising model. By evaluating the anticipated performance of this nearly linear machine against a collection of {0,1}-weighted graphs, we find that its execution time scales polynomially, specifically growing linearly with the number of edges in the connectivity graph. Furthermore, we provide a physical realization of this machine through a CMOS-compatible design featuring an array of vertices that store continuous spins on charged capacitors and communicate externally via analog currents.

Measurements of anisotropic flow coefficients ($v_n$), non-linear flow mode coefficients ($\chi_{n,mk}$), and correlations between various symmetry planes ($\rho_{n,mk}$) have been conducted in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_\rm{NN}}=5.02$ TeV. Utilizing multi-particle correlation techniques, results are presented for the transverse momentum range $0.2<p_\rm{T}<5.0$ GeV/$c$ and the pseudorapidity interval $0.4<|\eta|<0.8$, analyzed across different collision centralities. These data extend the $v_n$ coefficients to the ninth harmonic order, while $\chi_{n,mk}$ and $\rho_{n,mk}$ reach up to the seventh and ninth harmonic orders, respectively. Theoretical calculations indicate that both the non-linear flow modes and inter-plane correlations rely on the shear and bulk viscosity-to-entropy ratios of the quark-gluon plasma formed in heavy-ion collisions. By comparing these findings with lower-energy measurements and hydrodynamic model predictions, stringent constraints are placed on the system's initial conditions and transport properties.

Reservoir simulation-based optimization is employed to make oilfield development decisions by evaluating various production scenarios and well controls. Because these simulations are computationally intensive, surrogate models are utilized to speed up the process. While deep learning has previously been applied to create such surrogates, these models often struggle with interpretability and fail to quantify prediction uncertainty. This study proposes a beta-VAE based regression approach to generate simulation surrogates within an optimization workflow. The beta-VAE provides an interpretable, factorized representation of decision variables in the latent space, which serves as the basis for regression. Probabilistic dense layers are incorporated to quantify prediction uncertainty and facilitate approximate Bayesian inference. The resulting surrogate model, built via beta-VAE regression, yields a latent representation that is both interpretable and relevant. An appropriate beta value strikes a balance between factor disentanglement and reconstruction fidelity. Furthermore, the probabilistic dense layer enables the quantification of uncertainty for the objective function, informing the decision on whether a full-physics simulation is necessary for a specific case.

Document Layout Analysis (DLA) seeks to segment document images into distinct regions of interest and interpret their functions, a capability essential for applications like optical character recognition (OCR) and document retrieval. Nevertheless, constructing a DLA system remains difficult due to scarce training data and the absence of efficient models. To address this, we introduce an end-to-end unified architecture called the Dynamic Residual Fusion Network (DRFN) specifically for DLA tasks. Notably, we developed a dynamic residual feature fusion module capable of leveraging low-dimensional information while preserving high-dimensional category details. Furthermore, to mitigate overfitting arising from data scarcity, we implemented a dynamic selection mechanism designed for efficient fine-tuning with limited training sets. Experiments conducted on two challenging datasets confirm the efficacy of our proposed module.

This study examines the nonlinear interaction between Weyl semimetals (WSM) and intense electromagnetic driving fields. Utilizing a structure-gauge invariant low-energy nonlinear electrodynamic framework, the research analyzes polarization-resolved high-order harmonic generation spectra. The findings reveal that WSM spectra differ entirely from those of 2D graphene. Specifically, when the electric field and the momentum separation vector of Weyl nodes are non-collinear, anomalous harmonics emerge, polarized perpendicular to the pump wave's electric field. The intensity of these anomalous harmonics scales quadratically with the momentum space separation between the Weyl nodes. However, if the right and left Weyl fermions merge to form a 4-component trivial massless Dirac fermion, these anomalous harmonics disappear. Conversely, the intensities of normal harmonics remain independent of the Weyl nodes' momentum separation, and their spectral characteristics resemble those of a massless 3D Dirac fermion.

A single-balanced mixer operating at 2.4 GHz for Wi-Fi applications was designed in ADS and fabricated on a Rogers 4350B substrate, utilizing the HSMS-281x diode model. The study involved measuring isolation across all ports and evaluating the conversion loss. Additionally, non-linear characteristics, specifically IM3 versus frequency, were analyzed. The resulting performance metrics were compared against the manufacturer's datasheet values, with any discrepancies discussed.

Boson sampling, a task believed to be difficult for classical computers to simulate, offers a promising avenue for experimentally demonstrating quantum advantage using bosons. However, inherent experimental imperfections, such as interferometer loss and random detector counts, may prevent the process from reaching the noise threshold required for quantum advantage. This study introduces higher-order non-linearities to boost the problem's computational complexity and enhance the protocol's resilience to noise, effectively raising the limit for efficient classical simulation. By employing a phase-space approach centered on the negativity volume of relevant quasi-probability distributions, we derive a necessary condition for non-classicality that any proof of quantum advantage must meet. Our findings suggest that incorporating single-mode Kerr non-linearity during input state preparation, while maintaining linear-optical evolution, significantly improves the noise robustness of the Boson sampling protocol, thereby relaxing the strict noise constraints needed to achieve quantum advantage.

This study utilizes phase field simulations to investigate the coarsening dynamics of morphologically intricate two-phase microstructures where phase mobilities are highly dissimilar, mirroring conditions in experimental solid-liquid systems. Specifically, a two-phase system at the critical composition (50% volume fraction) is examined, featuring a mobility ratio of 100 between the phases. Simulations are conducted in both two and three dimensions using the Cahn-Hilliard model with concentration-dependent mobility, and the outcomes are contrasted with those derived from constant mobility assumptions. In the two-dimensional case (representing a thin film), a morphological transition occurs during coarsening in systems with disparate mobilities, leading to nearly circular particles of the high-mobility phase dispersed within a low-mobility matrix. This transition causes the coarsening rate constant to diminish over time, accounting for the lack of alignment with the theoretical $t^{1/3}$ power law observed in prior research. Conversely, three-dimensional systems with unequal mobilities develop bicontinuous microstructures that evolve self-similarly, as confirmed by quantitative analysis of interfacial shape distributions. Following an initial transient phase, the coarsening kinetics in three dimensions align closely with the $t^{1/3}$ power law. Furthermore, a model is formulated to elucidate the nearly linear correlation between the coarsening rate constant and the variance of the scaled mean curvature observed during this transient period.

Hilbert's 13th Problem in algebraic form seeks the resolvent degree $\text{rd}(n)$ for the general polynomial $f(x) = x^n + a_1 x^{n-1} + \ldots + a_n$ of degree $n$, where $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ serve as independent variables. This degree represents the smallest integer $d$ ensuring that all roots of $f(x)$ can be derived through a finite sequence of steps, beginning with $\mathbb C(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ and successively adjoining algebraic functions dependent on at most $d$ variables. Recently, Farb and Wolfson introduced the concept of resolvent degree $\text{rd}_k(G)$ for any finite group $G$ and any base field $k$ of characteristic 0, noting that $\text{rd}(n) = \text{rd}_{\mathbb C}(S_n)$ when $S_n$ is the symmetric group. This paper extends the definition of $\text{rd}_k(G)$ to arbitrary algebraic groups $G$ over any field $k$, examines how this value depends on $k$, and demonstrates that $\text{rd}_k(G) \leq 5$ for all fields $k$ and any connected group $G$. It remains an open question whether $\text{rd}_k(G)$ can exceed $1$ for any field $k$ and any algebraic group $G$ over $k$, even if the group is not necessarily connected.

The tail process $\bY=(Y_{\bi})_{\bi\in\Z^d}$ of a stationary regularly varying time series or random field $\bX=(X_{\bi})_{\bi\in\Z^d}$ captures the asymptotic local distribution of $\bX$ conditioned on a typical exceedance over a threshold $u$ as $u\to\infty$. Drawing inspiration from standard Palm theory, we demonstrate that every tail process possesses an invariance property known as exceedance-stationarity; combined with the polar decomposition of the tail process, this property fully characterizes the class of all such processes. We then focus on the scenario where $Y_{\bi}\to 0$ as $|\bi|\to\infty$, establishing several Palm-like dualities between the tail process and the anchored tail process, which, under appropriate conditions, describes the asymptotic distribution of a typical cluster of extremes for $\bX$. The primary finding is that the tail process distribution exhibits a bias toward clusters containing a higher number of exceedances. Finally, we apply these results to derive the distribution of the typical cluster of extremes for moving average processes featuring random coefficients and heavy-tailed innovations.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis relies on identifying opinion target expressions (OTEs), which are typically extracted using supervised learning algorithms trained on manually annotated corpora. However, creating these corpora is labor-intensive, resulting in large datasets being available only for a limited range of languages and domains. To overcome the scarcity of annotated data for specific languages, this study proposes a zero-shot cross-lingual method for OTE extraction. This approach utilizes multilingual word embeddings that share a common vector space across different languages, integrating them into a convolutional neural network architecture designed for OTE detection. Experiments conducted across five languages yield promising results, demonstrating the ability to train a model on annotated data from a source language and achieve accurate predictions on a target language without utilizing any annotated samples from that target language. Depending on the specific source-target language pairs, the model reaches up to 77% of the performance of a model trained directly on target language data in a zero-shot setting. Additionally, by incorporating cross-lingual learning from multiple source languages, this performance can be improved to up to 87% of the baseline model trained on target language data.

We present a novel proof establishing logarithmic bounds for Roth's theorem regarding arithmetic progressions, specifically showing that if $A \subset \{1,2,\ldots,N\}$ contains no three-term progressions, then $\lvert A\rvert \leq N/(\log N)^{1-o(1)}$. Distinct from earlier approaches, this proof relies almost exclusively on physical space techniques grounded in almost-periodicity.

Over the last few years, object detection has gained significant traction within human-robot collaboration and Industry 5.0, driven by substantial advancements in deep learning. In numerous scenarios, these detection models must rapidly adapt to evolving environments by learning new objects. However, a critical yet difficult requirement for this adaptability is the automatic creation of new training data, which currently hinders the widespread adoption of object detection in industrial manufacturing. This paper explores the adaptation of leading object detection techniques for automatic bounding box annotation, specifically for cases involving a homogeneous background and human-provided object labels. We evaluate an adapted Faster R-CNN model against the Scaled Yolov4-p5 architecture, demonstrating that both can be effectively trained to differentiate unknown objects from complex but uniform backgrounds using minimal training data.

This work investigates the detailed dynamics of unstable two-level quantum systems using the qubit Bloch-sphere formalism. By applying the Bloch-vector representation to these unstable qubits, we identify a new category of critical scenarios where the energy-level vector (${\bf E}$) and decay-width vector (${\bf\Gamma}$) are orthogonal, and the parameter $r = |{\bf \Gamma}|/(2|{\bf E}|)$ is less than unity. Notably, our analysis in a suitably defined co-decaying frame reveals that critical unstable qubits display atypical behaviors, such as coherence--decoherence oscillations. Within this frame, a unit Bloch vector ${\bf b}$ representing a pure critical qubit rotates around ${\bf E}$, sweeping out unequal areas over equal time intervals. These phenomena arise beyond standard oscillatory patterns due to the system's energy-level splitting. Furthermore, we observe that these distinctive features endure even in quasi-critical cases where ${\bf E}$ and ${\bf\Gamma}$ are not strictly orthogonal. The implications of these findings for quantum information science, as well as for unstable meson--antimeson and similar systems, are also explored.

Time-to-Digital Converters (TDCs) serve as critical elements for measuring time intervals. Recent advancements in Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGA) now allow for the implementation of high-performance TDCs, a capability previously restricted to dedicated hardware. To address issues like empty histogram bins and improve linearity, conventional FPGA-based TDCs often employ compensation techniques involving multiple delay lines that consume significant resources or post-processing, which results in a permanent loss of temporal data. We introduce a novel TDC architecture featuring a single delay line and no compensation, achieving high linearity by encoding delay line states rather than using the thermometer code standard in traditional designs. Experimental results demonstrate that this state-based approach yields an improved Differential Non-Linearity (DNL) across various time resolutions: [-0.998, -1.533] at 5.00 ps, [-0.44, 0.49] at 10.04 ps, [-0.16, 0.19] at 21.65 ps, [-0.10, 0.11] at 43.87 ps, [-0.06, 0.07] at 64.12 ps, and [-0.07, 0.05] at 87.73 ps, with no observed empty bins. To our knowledge, this combination of raw linearity, zero empty bins, and a simplified single delay line structure surpasses previously reported performance in FPGA-based TDCs.

This study investigates lepton flavour violating decays of the Higgs boson, specifically targeting the $\mu\tau$ and e$\tau$ channels. The analysis utilizes a dataset of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded by the CMS detector in 2016 at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. No significant deviation from standard model predictions is found. Consequently, the 95% confidence level upper limits on the lepton flavour violating branching fractions are established as $\mathcal{B}$(H$\to\mu\tau$) < 0.25% (0.25%) and $\mathcal{B}$(H$\to$e$\tau$) < 0.61% (0.37%). These findings further constrain the off-diagonal $\mu\tau$ and e$\tau$ Yukawa couplings to $\sqrt{|{Y_{\mu\tau}}|^{2}+|{Y_{\tau\mu}}|^{2}} < 1.43 \times 10^{-3}$ and $\sqrt{|{Y_{\mathrm{e}\tau}}|^{2}+|{Y_{\tau\mathrm{e}}}|^{2}} < 2.26 \times 10^{-3}$ at the same confidence level. To date, these represent the most restrictive limits on both the lepton flavour violating branching fractions of the Higgs boson and the corresponding Yukawa couplings.

We introduce a novel method for generating low-rank matrix approximations used in machine learning kernel techniques. Our strategy combines a newly developed, automatically generated analytic expansion of the kernel function with a data-driven compression step to enhance the approximation. This process operates in linear time and applies to any isotropic kernel. Unlike existing approaches that require the rank as input, our method accepts a target error tolerance. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our technique outperforms the widely used Nyström method in both accuracy for a fixed rank and computational efficiency for a fixed accuracy across various kernels, dimensions, and datasets. In numerous scenarios, our approach yields near-optimal low-rank approximations. Additionally, we offer an efficient open-source implementation of this technique to support our theoretical findings and empirical results.

The weak decays of ${\Upsilon}(nS)$ into $B_{c}D_{s}$ and $B_{c}D_{d}$ are initially investigated using the pQCD method. The results indicate that the branching ratios ${\cal B}r({\Upsilon}(nS){\to}B_{c}D_{s})$ are on the order of $10^{-10}$, while ${\cal B}r({\Upsilon}(nS){\to}B_{c}D_{d})$ are on the order of $10^{-11}$, suggesting these processes could be detectable in upcoming experiments.

This paper establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of the Moore-Penrose inverse of a product of two matrices within an indefinite inner product space (IIPS) where the reverse order law is valid. Additionally, it presents rank equivalence formulas specific to IIPS and concludes by addressing an open problem.

This study introduces a self-supervised data augmentation method designed to enhance model performance in scenarios with limited labeled data. The process begins by training multiple copies of the original model on the downstream task, which then generate predictions to annotate a substantial volume of unlabeled examples. Subsequently, the training set undergoes multi-task training using these parallel annotations, with final scores derived by averaging the predictions from each annotator-specific head. When applied to fine-tune neural language models for the AcCompl-it shared task at EVALITA 2020, this approach yielded significant improvements in prediction quality.

In recent times, there has been increasing enthusiasm for applying machine learning to forecast and detect phase transitions across diverse systems. This study employs convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to analyze phase transitions within the Vicsek model, addressing limitations where conventional order parameters prove inadequate. Extensive simulations reveal four distinct phases, and we verify that transitions between adjacent phases are first-order. Our CNN-based approach successfully classifies these phases with high precision and pinpoints transition points, whereas traditional methods relying on various order parameters fail to achieve this. These findings highlight the significant potential of machine learning for deciphering the complexities of collective behaviors and related complex systems in general.

The most general concept regarding the quasi-coincidence of a fuzzy point with a fuzzy subset is examined, alongside a discussion on generalizing fuzzy fated structures within $R_0$-algebras. An $(\epsilon , \epsilon \vee q_k)$-fuzzy fated filter in an $R_0$-algebra is defined, and various properties of this filter are explored. Additionally, characterizations of such filters are provided, and the construction of an $(\epsilon , \epsilon \vee q_k)$-fuzzy fated filter is achieved through the utilization of a set of fated filters.

Few-shot font generation (FFG), which creates new fonts using only a few examples, is increasingly popular because it significantly lowers labor costs. Typical FFG pipelines treat characters from standard libraries as content glyphs and transfer them to a new font by extracting style information from reference glyphs. Most current methods explicitly separate content and style either globally or on a component-by-component basis. However, glyph style is primarily embedded in local details, where the combination of radicals, components, and strokes defines the overall look. Consequently, even a single character can exhibit varying styles distributed across different spatial locations. This paper introduces a novel font generation approach that learns 1) fine-grained local styles from references and 2) the spatial correspondence between content and reference glyphs. This allows each spatial location in the content glyph to be assigned the appropriate fine-grained style. To achieve this, we utilize cross-attention, using content glyph representations as queries and reference glyph representations as keys and values. Rather than relying on explicit global or component-wise disentanglement, this mechanism selectively attends to relevant local styles in the references and aggregates them into a fine-grained style representation for the target content. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art FFG approaches, with user studies further confirming that our approach significantly surpasses previous methods in terms of style consistency.

Quandles are defined as algebras that are self-distributive, right-invertible, and idempotent, with groups equipped with the conjugation operation serving as a primary example. For any quandle $(Q, \ast)$ and a positive integer $n$, we define the operation $a\ast_n b$ as the result of applying $\ast$ iteratively $n$ times with $b$. This new operation $(Q, \ast_n)$ also forms a quandle. The central problem addressed here is to identify a quandle $(Q, \ast)$ where the resulting sequence of quandles $\{(Q, \ast_n) \mid n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\}$ consists entirely of pairwise non-isomorphic structures. This article successfully constructs such a quandle. The study focuses on the general linear group of $2 \times 2$ complex matrices under conjugation, examining its conjugacy classes as subquandles. It is demonstrated that these subquandles are connected, and rigidity properties are established, such as the fact that the dihedral quandle of order 3 is generally not a subquandle of these classes. Furthermore, the projective linear group of $2 \times 2$ complex matrices under conjugation is shown to solve the stated problem. Additionally, a necessary and sufficient condition for a quandle to be latin is proven, which substantially simplifies the computational complexity of verifying this property.
We present a novel elementary proof demonstrating that closed orientable 3-manifolds are parallelizable.

Let $u(t,x)$ denote the solution to the stochastic heat equation
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}u=\frac12\frac{\partial^2}{\partial
x^2}u+\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t\partial x}X(t,x),\quad t\geq 0, x\in
{\mathbb R}
$$
subject to the initial condition $u(0,x)\equiv 0$, where $X$ represents a time-space white noise. This work investigates stochastic analysis problems concerning $u(t,x)$. Specifically, $u(t,x)$ is a Gaussian process where the mapping $t\mapsto u(t,\cdot)$ behaves like a bi-fractional Brownian motion (resembling a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index $H=\frac14$) for any fixed $x \in \mathbb{R}$. However, the characteristics of the spatial process $x\mapsto u(\cdot,x)$ remain unexplored. In this paper, we analyze the quadratic covariations between the processes $x\mapsto u(\cdot,x)$ and $t\mapsto u(t,\cdot)$. We demonstrate that $x\mapsto u(\cdot,x)$ possesses a nontrivial finite quadratic variation; its forward integral of certain adapted processes aligns with the Itô integral, yet it does not constitute a semimartingale. Furthermore, we derive several generalized Itô formulas and Bouleau-Yor identities.

Let $Q_n = [0,1]^n$ denote the unit cube in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $C(Q_n)$ represent the space of continuous functions $f: Q_n \to \mathbb{R}$ equipped with the supremum norm $\|f\|_{C(Q_n)} := \max_{x \in Q_n} |f(x)|$. We denote by $\Pi_1(\mathbb{R}^n)$ the set of polynomials of degree at most 1, which corresponds to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Consider the interpolation projector $P: C(Q_n) \to \Pi_1(\mathbb{R}^n)$ defined by $n+1$ nodes $x^{(j)} \in Q_n$ such that $Pf(x^{(j)}) = f(x^{(j)})$ for $j=1, \dots, n+1$. Let $\|P\|_{Q_n}$ denote the operator norm of $P$ mapping $C(Q_n)$ to itself. When $n+1$ is an Hadamard number, a nondegenerate regular simplex with vertices located at the corners of $Q_n$ exists. This text explores various methods to establish inequalities of the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c\sqrt{n}$ for the norm of the associated projector $P$.

We numerically resolve the large $N$ Dyson-Schwinger equations for the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model using Legendre polynomial decomposition, achieving an accuracy of $10^{-36}$. This approach allows us to calculate the energy of the SYK model at low temperatures ($T\ll J$) and derive a series expansion up to order $T^{7.54}$. Contrary to previous suggestions of terms like $T^{3.77}$ and $T^{5.68}$, we identify the first non-integer power of temperature as $T^{6.54}$. This term originates from the two-point function of the fermion bilinear operator $O_{h_{1}}=\chi \partial_{\tau}^{3}\chi$, which has a scaling dimension of $h_{1}\approx 3.77$. The coefficient of the $T^{6.54}$ term aligns well with predictions from conformal perturbation theory. Consequently, we conclude that conformal perturbation theory remains applicable even though the SYK model is not strictly conformal.

Automatically producing coherent and semantically rich text is crucial for various machine learning applications, including machine translation, dialogue systems, and image captioning. Recently, integrating policy gradient with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)—where a discriminative model guides the generative model's training via reinforcement learning—has yielded promising results in text generation. However, the scalar feedback signal provided by this approach is only available after the full text is generated, lacking intermediate insights into text structure during the process. Consequently, this limitation hinders success in generating longer texts (exceeding 20 words). To address this, we introduce LeakGAN, a novel framework designed for long text generation. In LeakGAN, the discriminative network shares its high-level extracted features with the generative network to enhance guidance. The generator integrates these informative signals at every generation step through a dedicated Manager module, which processes the features of currently generated words to produce a latent vector that guides the Worker module in generating the next word. Extensive experiments on synthetic data and diverse real-world tasks, validated by Turing tests, demonstrate that LeakGAN is highly effective for long text generation and also improves performance in short text scenarios. Most significantly, without any supervision, LeakGAN can implicitly learn sentence structures solely through the interaction between the Manager and Worker modules.

This paper establishes a relationship between the special values of Dirichlet $L$-functions and those of spectral zeta functions or $L$-functions associated with cycle graphs, revealing that these values naturally determine one another. This connection is achieved through a combinatorial derivative formula derived from an investigation into the spectral zeta functions of first-order self-adjoint differential operators defined on the unit circle.

Biological cells employ droplets to compartmentalize and spatially regulate their internal contents. Experimental evidence indicates that the intricate, crowded cellular milieu influences droplet size and arrangement. To elucidate this phenomenon, we develop a theoretical framework describing droplet growth within an elastic matrix, inspired by synthetic experiments where monodisperse emulsions emerge upon cooling. We demonstrate that large droplets arise exclusively when they induce cavitation in the surrounding matrix. The energy barrier linked to cavitation stabilizes small droplets comparable to the mesh size and reduces stochastic nucleation effects. As a result, cavitated droplets exhibit uniform sizes and highly correlated positions. Specifically, our model predicts a droplet density that rises with faster cooling rates, mirroring experimental observations. Furthermore, the theory offers insights into how modifying cooling protocols and nucleation site density impacts droplet size distributions. In conclusion, our approach clarifies the influence of elastic matrices on droplets in synthetic systems and establishes a foundation for interpreting biological scenarios.

We employ a double Gaussian approximation to model the wavefunction of twin photons (biphotons) generated through a type-I spontaneous parametric downconversion (SPDC) process in a nonlinear crystal. Our analysis reveals that as these photons propagate, the wavefunction accumulates a Gouy phase that relies on two-photon correlations and the Rayleigh length. By evaluating the covariance matrix, we demonstrate that while the logarithmic negativity—used to quantify entanglement in Gaussian states—varies with the Rayleigh length, it remains independent of the propagation distance. Furthermore, we establish a connection between biphoton Gouy phase and two-photon entanglement, noting that both are linked to the Rayleigh length. Finally, we apply a thin lens to focus the double Gaussian biphoton wavefunction and compute a Gouy phase that aligns reasonably well with experimental results reported by D. Kawase et al. in Ref. [1].

Maps depicting albedo, spectral slopes, and water ice band depths for the five mid-sized Saturnian moons—Mimas, Enceladus, Tethys, Dione, and Rhea—have been generated using Cassini VIMS data. These maps are constructed systematically from photometrically corrected data utilizing the Kaasalainen-Shkuratov model (Kaasalainen et al., 2001; Shkuratov et al., 2011). In this study, a quadratic function fits phase curves derived from observations meeting specific criteria: incidence angles ($i$) $\le 70^\circ$, emission angles ($e$) $\le 70^\circ$, phase angles ($g$) between $10^\circ$ and $120^\circ$, and a Cassini-satellite distance ($D$) $\le 100,000$ km. This procedure is applied consistently across a subset of 65 visible and near-infrared wavelengths for each moon. The resulting average photometric parameters facilitate comparisons of satellite properties and investigations into variability under changing illumination conditions. We calculated equigonal albedo values extrapolated to $g=0^\circ$ and excluding the opposition effect at $0.55 \, \mu\text{m}$: $0.63 \pm 0.02$ for Mimas, $0.89 \pm 0.03$ for Enceladus, $0.74 \pm 0.03$ for Tethys, $0.65 \pm 0.03$ for Dione, and $0.60 \pm 0.05$ for Rhea. Knowledge of the photometric spectral response enables the correction of individual VIMS spectra via geolocation for map construction. The final maps are rendered at a fixed resolution of $0.5^\circ \times 0.5^\circ$ bins on a longitude-latitude grid, yielding spatial resolutions of 1.7 km/bin for Mimas, 2.2 km/bin for Enceladus, 4.7 km/bin for Tethys, 4.5 km/bin for Dione, and 6.7 km/bin for Rhea. These spectral maps establish connections between surface properties and morphological features, as well as endogenic and exogenic processes that modify the moons' surfaces through various mechanisms.

This study introduces a novel method for determining effective fracture toughness in heterogeneous materials, utilizing a process-dependent temporal averaging technique that accounts for both crack velocity and material toughness. The approach is evaluated within the framework of hydraulic fracturing in heterogeneous rock featuring periodic toughness variations. To facilitate the analysis of distinct toughness-to-viscosity regimes, the investigation employs a plane strain model that excludes fluid leak-off. Numerical simulations, executed via a highly efficient custom-built time-space adaptive solver, assess the new homogenization strategy by comparing it with a recently proposed maximum toughness method. Ultimately, the specific conditions under which each strategy performs effectively are identified.

By exploiting the analogy between spacetime torsion and axial gauge couplings, we investigate torsional contributions to the equilibrium partition function within a stationary background. For a charged fluid minimally coupled to torsion, we identify linear torsional magnetic and vortical effects; however, the axial-vector current and spin energy potential remain uncorrected at linear order. Conversely, the covariant energy-momentum tensor includes terms linear in the torsion tensor. We also examine a two-flavor hadronic superfluid, calculating the resulting torsional contributions to its constitutive relations. Our findings indicate a torsional electric chiral effect mediated by charged pions.

Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSP) are widely employed to model and resolve numerous intricate real-world challenges; however, creating efficient solvers for CSP, particularly at large scales, remains a significant difficulty. Consequently, most existing complete solving methods are often inadequate, which has driven growing interest in hybrid CSP-based approaches over recent decades. This study introduces a novel framework that integrates incomplete and complete CSP techniques. Leveraging the Group Search Optimization (GSO) algorithm alongside constraint propagation (CP), the proposed method addresses problems within the remote sensing domain. To our knowledge, this is the inaugural work to hybridize an enhanced GSO variant with CP for tackling complex constraint-based issues. Experiments focused on object recognition in satellite imagery demonstrate that the proposed CSP-based approach achieves superior performance in both convergence speed and execution time compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

The intrinsic properties of dark matter remain completely unidentified, with Twin Higgs mirror matter emerging as a strong candidate; these are invisible counterparts to Standard Model particles and forces residing in a hidden sector. This framework generally forecasts the existence of mirror neutron stars, which are degenerate entities composed solely of mirror nuclear matter. By applying realistic equations of state that are rigorously adjusted using first-principles quantum chromodynamic calculations, we have determined their internal structure. Furthermore, we project their observability through gravitational waves and binary pulsar systems, indicating a significant potential for discovery and the capacity to investigate the dark sector.

One-dimensional quasicrystals modeled by the nearest-neighbor Aubry-Andr\'{e}-Harper (AAH) Hamiltonian for non-interacting spinless electrons exhibit a metal-insulator transition (MIT) driven by a critical quasi-periodic potential strength, a phenomenon rooted in the Hamiltonian's self-duality. At this critical, or self-dual, point, single-particle wave functions display multifractal and non-ergodic characteristics, contrasting with the ergodic and delocalized states found below the critical threshold and the localized states above it. This study investigates the one-dimensional quasi-periodic AAH system incorporating Rashba-type spin-orbit (SO) coupling, which adds both spin-conserving complex hopping and spin-flip hopping terms. Our findings indicate that while the intrinsic self-dual nature of the AAH Hamiltonian persists, the location of the self-dual point shifts significantly; furthermore, the impacts of complex and spin-flip hoppings are equivalent. We accurately identified the critical point by extending Kohn's localization tensor calculations to quasi-particles. Subsequent detailed multifractal analyses, utilizing inverse participation ratios and von Neumann entropy, confirm that quasi-particle eigenstates remain multifractal and non-ergodic at the critical point. Finally, we constructed the phase diagram within the parameter space defined by the quasi-periodic potential and SO coupling strength.

This paper outlines our method for integrating pre-trained BERT models with Convolutional Neural Networks to address sub-task A of the Multilingual Offensive Language Identification shared task (OffensEval 2020), a component of SemEval 2020. We demonstrate that the hybrid CNN-BERT architecture outperforms BERT used in isolation and highlight the critical role of pre-trained language models in downstream applications. Our system achieved 4th place with a macro-averaged F1-Score of 0.897 in Arabic, 4th place with a score of 0.843 in Greek, and 3rd place with a score of 0.814 in Turkish. Furthermore, we introduce ArabicBERT, a collection of pre-trained transformer language models for Arabic, which we have made available to the community.

We investigate the Lyapunov exponent $\lambda_L$ within quantum field theories featuring spacetime-independent disorder. Typically, $\lambda_L$ is calculable only at specific points in parameter space, leaving the evolution of chaos under deformations from weak coupling largely unknown. This paper presents families of theories where the disorder coupling acts as an exactly marginal deformation, enabling the tracking of $\lambda_L$ from weak to strong coupling regimes. Our analysis reveals unexpected phenomena in certain instances, such as a discontinuous onset of chaos. Additionally, we establish self-consistency equations for two- and four-point functions associated with products of $N$ nontrivial CFTs subjected to disorder, accurate to leading order in the $1/N$ expansion.

This study evaluates the viability of detecting axions through X-ray spectroscopy of the Sun. We examine axion-photon mode conversion theory, focusing specifically on axions generated by the 14.4 keV M1 transition of 57Fe at the solar core. These axions can convert into photons within the Sun's outer envelope, potentially appearing as detectable X-rays. However, for axion masses exceeding approximately 10^-4 eV, resonant conversion is required at a depth where the local electron plasma frequency matches the axion mass. If the mass surpasses roughly 10^-2 eV, this conversion happens too deep for the resulting photons to escape the solar surface before being obscured by Compton scattering. Conversely, for masses below this threshold where detection might be possible, the predicted photon flux from axion models seems too weak for current instruments to detect. While nonresonant conversion for masses under 10^-4 eV is theoretically plausible, the expected flux remains even lower due to the relationship between the axion coupling constant and its mass. Consequently, obtaining meaningful constraints on massive axion parameters via solar X-ray observations of this transition appears unlikely. Nevertheless, such observations could still yield results regarding massless counterparts, such as the "arion," which may convert in the solar atmosphere without being constrained by a small coupling constant.

A defining feature of human intelligence is the capacity to adjust to novel scenarios by utilizing learned rules on new information (systematicity), which facilitates an unlimited range of inferences and actions (generativity). We suggest that the human brain achieves this via parietal cortical pathways encoding the abstract structure of space, events, and tasks, alongside temporal cortical pathways encoding details about specific entities, locations, and objects (content). Recent neural network models demonstrate how architectural biases and learning can produce a separation between structure and content, resulting in significant enhancements in modeling systematic and generative behaviors. Finally, we examine the role of the hippocampal formation in creating integrative memories that support the rapid acquisition of new structural and content-based representations.

Iron (Fe), magnesium (Mg), and oxygen (O) constitute some of the most plentiful elements in terrestrial planets. Although the pressure behaviors of the Fe-O, Mg-O, and Fe-Mg binary systems have been explored, research on the Fe-Mg-O ternary system at pressures relevant to Earth's core and super-Earth mantles remains scarce. In this study, we employ the adaptive genetic algorithm (AGA) to investigate ternary Fe$_x$Mg$_y$O$_z$ phases across various stoichiometries at 200 GPa and 350 GPa. We identified three dynamically stable phases—FeMg$_2$O$_4$, Fe$_2$MgO$_4$, and FeMg$_3$O$_4$—which exhibit lower enthalpy than any previously known Fe-Mg-O high-pressure compound combination at 350 GPa. Leveraging these discoveries, we constructed the Fe-Mg-O ternary convex hull. Furthermore, by analyzing both the stable and metastable structures identified by the AGA, we clarified how structural motifs depend on composition and pressure. Analysis of both binary and ternary stable phases indicates that oxygen, magnesium, or both could stabilize a body-centered cubic (BCC) iron alloy under inner core pressures.

We explore the use of efficient recursive numerical integration methods for lattice gauge theory models within quantum field theory. Leveraging the coupling structure of these physical problems alongside the group structure inherent in lattice cubature rules, we demonstrate how Fast Fourier Transform techniques can solve these challenges efficiently. Specifically, we examine applications to the quantum mechanical rotor and compact U(1) lattice gauge theory in two and three physical dimensions. This proceedings article summarizes our findings, which were originally published in J. Comput. Phys 443 (2021) 110527.

This letter models a residential household's day-ahead price-based demand response, incorporating battery energy storage and other controllable loads, as a convex optimization problem. By applying duality theory and Karush-Kuhn-Tucker optimality conditions, we establish a sufficient criterion that ensures the battery does not charge and discharge simultaneously, achieving this without explicitly formulating it as a constraint.

The Hamiltonian cycle (HC) problem, a notorious NP-complete challenge in graph theory, is addressed via a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lattice gauge theory (LGT) formulated on a lattice dual to the graph. When the coupling parameter $g$ falls below the critical threshold $g_c$, the ground state emerges as a superposition of all configurations featuring closed spin strings in a uniform single-spin state. This state can be reached using an adiabatic quantum algorithm with a time complexity of $O(\frac{1}{g_c^2} \sqrt{ \frac{1}{\varepsilon} N_e^{3/2}(N_v^3 + \frac{N_e}{g_c}}))$, where $N_v$ and $N_e$ denote the vertex and edge counts, respectively. Solving the HC problem involves subsequently searching for a Hamiltonian cycle within these closed-string configurations. Empirical analysis on small random graphs reveals a linear relationship between the average $g_c$ and $\sqrt{N_{hc}}$ (where $N_{hc}$ represents the number of Hamiltonian cycles), as well as between the average $1/g_c$ and $N_e$. These findings suggest that the HC problem could be solvable in polynomial time for certain graphs, and a potential quantum algorithm leveraging $g_c$ to estimate $N_{hc}$ is also explored.

We introduce a new neural architecture designed for generating French poetry, which integrates two pretrained models fine-tuned for this specific task. The system employs a RoBERTa-based encoder to leverage advanced natural language understanding and a GPT-2-based decoder to capitalize on strong generation capabilities. Evaluation results demonstrate the model's success in producing French poetry, with human judges awarding a typicality and emotionality score of 3.57/5 and an understandability score of 3.79/5.

This study investigates the dynamics of heavy quarks within a thermalized quark-gluon plasma subject to time-correlated thermal noise, $\eta$, which possesses memory. We employ an integro-differential Langevin equation where both the dissipative force and the thermal noise incorporate this memory effect. The noise time correlations are assumed to decay exponentially with a characteristic time scale, $\tau$, treated as a free parameter. We analyze how $\tau \neq 0$ influences heavy quark thermalization time, momentum broadening, and the nuclear modification factor ($R_{AA}$). Our results indicate that memory generally retards the momentum evolution of heavy quarks: specifically, transverse momentum broadening and $R_{AA}$ formation are delayed, leading to an increased thermalization time. We also briefly discuss the potential implications for other observables.

We investigate how recent discrepancies in the $W$-boson mass and the muon's anomalous magnetic moment impact the $U(1)_{L_\mu-L_\tau}$ framework. Our findings indicate that incorporating vector-like leptons that mix with the muon can simultaneously address both anomalies. Furthermore, contrary to established beliefs, the presence of an electroweak-scale $Z'$-boson remains viable without contradicting experimental results from trident neutrino production.

Breast cancer is the most prevalent malignant tumor in women, representing 30% of all new malignant cases. While its global incidence remains high, mortality rates have steadily declined, largely attributed to advancements in molecular biology, enhanced comprehensive diagnostics, and standardized treatments. Mammography plays a crucial role in this early detection process, which primarily identifies masses and calcifications as indicators of breast cancer. Although previous detection methods often achieved high sensitivity, they suffered from unsatisfactory specificity. This study investigates an approach utilizing discrete wavelet and Fourier transforms to analyze images and extract statistical features, such as mean intensity and intensity skewness. A naive Bayesian classifier will then use these features for image classification, with the goal of achieving optimal high specificity.

Federated Learning (FL) represents a decentralized machine learning framework where a central server iteratively averages model parameters from local clients without accessing their raw data. However, user heterogeneity presents substantial challenges to this paradigm, often resulting in global models that drift and converge slowly. Recently, Knowledge Distillation has been introduced to mitigate these issues by refining the server model through aggregated knowledge from diverse users, rather than simply averaging their parameters. Nevertheless, this method relies on a proxy dataset, rendering it impractical when such data is unavailable. Furthermore, existing approaches fail to fully leverage ensemble knowledge to guide local learning, potentially compromising the quality of the final aggregated model. Drawing inspiration from previous work, we propose a data-free knowledge distillation strategy for heterogeneous FL. In this approach, the server trains a lightweight generator to synthesize user information without requiring data, broadcasts this generator to the clients, and uses the resulting knowledge as an inductive bias to regulate local training. Empirical results, supported by theoretical analysis, demonstrate that our method enhances FL generalization performance and reduces the number of communication rounds required compared to state-of-the-art solutions.

This paper introduces an offline/online computational framework for determining the dual norm of parameterized linear functionals. The methodology relies on two core components: (i) an empirical test space tailored to the manifold of Riesz elements linked to the functional, and (ii) an empirical quadrature method designed to handle parametrically non-affine terms efficiently. We provide several theoretical findings to pinpoint various error sources and justify the proposed technique. Furthermore, we demonstrate the approach's efficacy in minimizing both offline and online computational expenses related to calculating the time-averaged residual indicator introduced in [Fick, Maday, Patera, Taddei, Journal of Computational Physics, 2018 (accepted)].

We examine a general branching population where individual lifetimes follow independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) laws with arbitrary distributions, and each individual reproduces at independent Poisson times. Furthermore, individuals undergo mutations at a Poisson rate $\theta$ under the infinitely many alleles model, with types inherited from parents to offspring. This mechanism generates a partition of the population by type, known as the allelic partition. The central focus of this study is the frequency spectrum $A(k,t)$, which represents the count of families of size $k$ at time $t$. The process $(A(k,t), t\in\mathbb{R}_+)$ constitutes a non-Markovian branching process within the class of general branching processes counted by random characteristics. In this work, we introduce approximation methods to substitute the frequency spectrum with simpler metrics. Our primary objective is to analyze the asymptotic error introduced by these approximations via central limit theorems. Finally, we conduct numerical analyses using this model, specifically to evaluate the behavior of one approximation relative to Sabeti's Extended Haplotype Homozygosity [18].

More than two decades ago, Abadi and colleagues introduced the Dependency Core Calculus (DCC), a versatile framework for analyzing dependencies within typed programming languages. Since its inception, dependency analysis has proven highly beneficial for language design, aiding users and compilers in enforcing security protocols and removing dead code, among other uses. This paper presents the Dependent Dependency Calculus (DDC), which adapts these principles for dependently-typed languages. By leveraging this calculus to monitor both compile-time and run-time irrelevance, we achieve accelerated type-checking and program execution.

Non-standard neutrino self-interactions (NSSI) might exceed the strength of Fermi interactions. This study examines how galactic supernova neutrino fluxes can be used to limit these four-neutrino interactions. Within the dense environment of a core-collapse supernova, such new self-interactions can substantially alter neutrino oscillations, affecting both flavor evolution and spectral distributions. Our approach involves simulating the neutrino flux from a 13 solar mass supernova located 10 kpc away and numerically propagating these neutrinos through the stellar medium, incorporating vacuum and MSW oscillations, Standard Model $
u-
u$ scattering, and NSSI-driven $
u-
u$ interactions. The resulting flux is then input into a simulation of the future Hyper-Kamiokande detector to determine potential constraints on NSSI parameters upon the next galactic supernova's detection. Our results indicate that these constraints are highly sensitive to the neutrino mass hierarchy and whether the NSSI preserves or violates flavor. While sensitivity in the normal hierarchy (NH) at Hyper-K is restricted by the experiment's efficiency in detecting $
u_{e}$, significant deviations from the no-NSSI scenario could still be observed if the interactions are sufficiently strong. Conversely, in the inverted hierarchy (IH) case, Hyper-K could markedly tighten constraints on flavor-violating NSSI, reaching down to $\mathcal{O}(10^{-1})G_{F}$.

The Journalistic Voting System functions as a proxy voting mechanism where journalists cast votes on behalf of citizens within a Western democratic framework. This paper introduces the system, examining both its potential benefits and drawbacks. Specifically, it analyzes the advantages for key stakeholders—voters, journalists, and politicians—and evaluates the system's impact against major election security threats, including cybersecurity risks, social media influence, big data, artificial intelligence, and gerrymandering. The model draws upon its predecessor, the Valence Voting System, which is also reviewed.

The upcoming COMET experiment at J-PARC and Mu2e at Fermilab aim to measure the $\mu-e$ conversion rate with high sensitivity around $\mathcal{O}(10^{-17})$ using an aluminum target. Within the minimal supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model featuring local $B-L$ gauge symmetry (B-LSSM), we investigate the lepton flavor violating (LFV) process of $\mu-e$ conversion in nuclei. Given the experimental upper limits on the LFV rare decay $\mu\rightarrow e\gamma$, the predicted $\mu-e$ conversion rates in the B-LSSM framework reach $\mathcal{O}(10^{-12})$. This value exceeds the anticipated sensitivity of future Mu2e and COMET experiments by five orders of magnitude, suggesting the signal could be detected soon.

Climbing grades serve to categorize routes according to their perceived difficulty and are fundamental to rock climbing. This paper details the application of a recently developed, statistically rigorous method for estimating these grades from complete ascent histories, utilizing a dynamic Bradley-Terry model designed for players with fluctuating skills. By employing Markov chain Monte Carlo inference on a dataset of regular climbers, we calculated the model's scale parameter *m*, which represents the proportional difficulty increase per grade step. Our analysis confirms that the climbing grade system operates as a logarithmic scale of difficulty, analogous to decibels or stellar magnitudes. Specifically, under a logistic success probability model, a single grade increment corresponds to a 2.1-fold increase in difficulty for the Ewbank system, 2.09 for French, and 2.13 for UIAA, whereas the bouldering V-scale reflects a 3.17-fold increase. Furthermore, we explore potential links between these logarithmic characteristics and the psychophysical principles established by Weber and Fechner.

Deep neural networks have rightfully established themselves as one of the most accurate analysis tools in high-energy physics. This paper examines several methods for enhancing the performance of deep neural networks in a classification task within top quark analysis. The discussed approaches and recommendations include hyperparameter tuning, error boosting, and the application of AutoML algorithms to collider physics.

Recent research in recommendation systems has prioritized diversity as a key indicator of quality. However, this work contends that post-processing techniques designed solely to enhance recommendation diversity inadvertently cause user discrimination. We introduce the previously neglected concept of user fairness and propose metrics to measure it. Experimental results on two diversification algorithms demonstrate that boosting aggregate diversity leads to greater disparity among users.

We introduce a correlated random walk (CRW) derived from the time evolution matrix, specifically the Grover matrix, associated with a graph $G$. By utilizing a determinant formulation for the generalized weighted zeta function of $G$, we derive an expression for the characteristic polynomial of the transition probability matrix of this CRW. In applications, we determine the spectra of the transition probability matrices for CRWs generated by the Grover matrices of regular graphs and semiregular bipartite graphs. Additionally, we examine a distinct type of CRW defined on a graph.

Over millions of years, the mammalian adaptive immune system has developed into a highly effective mechanism for combating foreign antigens. Within this system, the humoral response generates plasma B cells and memory B cells, each serving distinct immunological purposes. While affinity maturation is traditionally considered a heuristic approach to solve the global optimization problem of identifying B cells with the highest antigen affinity, evidence suggests that memory B cells are actually selected earlier in this process and possess lower affinity. We hypothesize that the selection of memory B cells represents an approximate solution to two specific optimization challenges: ensuring high affinity for similar antigens encountered in the future despite mutations or minor variations, and enabling a "warm start" for the generation of plasma B cells during subsequent immune responses. Using simulations that incorporate data on the probability of specific B cell mutations, we provide support for our hypothesis that memory B cells exhibit high affinity toward mutated antigens. However, our findings do not offer strong evidence that memory B cells are more effective than selected naive B cells for seeding secondary germinal centers.

Deep learning (DL) approaches for denoising hyperspectral images (HSIs) directly learn the nonlinear transformation from noisy observations to clean targets. However, these methods often ignore the physical properties of HSIs, resulting in a lack of interpretability, which is essential for understanding their denoising mechanisms. To address this limitation, we propose a novel model-guided interpretable network for HSI denoising. By fully accounting for the spatial redundancy, spectral low-rankness, and spectral-spatial characteristics of HSIs, we first construct a subspace-based multi-dimensional sparse model. This model projects observed HSIs into a low-dimensional orthogonal subspace and represents the resulting image using a multidimensional dictionary. Subsequently, the model is unfolded into an end-to-end network called SMDS-Net, whose core modules are seamlessly integrated with the denoising process and model optimization. This integration ensures that SMDS-Net conveys clear physical meanings, specifically by learning the low-rankness and sparsity inherent in HSIs. Finally, all critical variables, including dictionaries and thresholding parameters, are acquired through end-to-end training. Extensive experiments and comprehensive analyses demonstrate that our method achieves superior denoising performance and interpretability compared to state-of-the-art HSI denoising techniques.

The classical Hard Lefschetz theorem (HLT), Hodge-Riemann bilinear relation theorem (HRR), and Lefschetz decomposition theorem (LD) are valid only for powers of a Kähler class on a compact Kähler manifold; they do not hold for arbitrary classes, even those admitting smooth, strictly positive representatives. Counterexamples in dimension 4 involving bidegree $(2,2)$ classes were identified by Timorin (1998) and Berndtsson-Sibony (2002). However, Gromov (1990), Timorin (1998), and Dinh-Nguyen (2006, 2013) established the mixed versions of HLT, HRR, and LD for products of arbitrary Kähler classes. Dinh-Nguyen (2013) further conjectured that determinants of Griffiths positive $k \times k$ matrices with $(1,1)$ form entries in $\mathbb{C}^n$ satisfy these theorems in the linear setting. This paper confirms Dinh-Nguyen's conjecture for $k=2$ when $n=2$ and $n=3$. Additionally, if the matrix entries are diagonalized, the determinant satisfies HLT for bidegrees $(n-2,0)$, $(n-3,1)$, $(1,n-3)$, and $(0,n-2)$ when $k=2$ and $n \geqslant 4$. Consequently, under this diagonalization assumption, the conjecture holds true for $k=2$ and $n=4,5$.

The primary motivation for the increasing interest in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model stems from its short-time (high-energy) dynamics. True chaotic behavior emerges at the Thouless time, a value derivable from the energy spectrum. To extract this, the spectrum must be unfolded to remove global trends; however, employing a simple ensemble average for this unfolding yields a parametrically low estimate of the Thouless energy. By analyzing how the spectrum behaves when matrix element distributions shift to log-normal, it is demonstrated that the sample-to-sample variance in level spacing dictates this low estimate. Conversely, utilizing Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to filter out these sample-to-sample fluctuations results in a parametrically larger Thouless energy, on the order of the bandwidth. Furthermore, it is established that the SYK model exhibits non-self-averaging behavior even in the thermodynamic limit, a characteristic that must be accounted for when analyzing its short-time properties.

We report a measurement of relativistic corrections to the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) effect spectrum, known as the rSZ effect, directed at the massive galaxy cluster RX J1347.5-1145. This analysis combines sub-millimeter images from Herschel-SPIRE with millimeter-wave maps from Bolocam. Our method simultaneously models the SZ signal, the population of cosmic infrared background (CIB) galaxies, and galactic cirrus dust emission, fully accounting for their spatial and frequency-dependent correlations. Furthermore, our methodology incorporates gravitational lensing of background galaxies by the cluster, utilizing a mass model derived from Hubble Space Telescope (HST) observations. Using realistic mock observations, we apply a forward modeling approach that considers non-Gaussian covariances between astrophysical components to derive the posterior distribution of SZ brightness values consistent with the data. We find a maximum a posteriori (MAP) value for the average Comptonization parameter of the intra-cluster medium (ICM) within $R_{2500}$ of $\langle y \rangle_{2500} = 1.56 \times 10^{-4}$, with a 68% credible interval of $[1.42, 1.63] \times 10^{-4}$. The corresponding MAP ICM electron temperature is $\langle \textrm{T}_{\textrm{sz}} \rangle_{2500} = 22.4$~keV, with a 68% credible interval of $[10.4, 33.0]$~keV. These results align well with the pressure-weighted temperature from {\it Chandra} X-ray observations, which yields $\langle \textrm{T}_{\textrm{x,pw}}\rangle_{2500} = 17.4 \pm 2.3$~keV. We intend to extend this methodology to a sample of 39 galaxy clusters using comparable existing data, estimating an uncertainty on the ensemble mean $\langle \textrm{T}_{\textrm{sz}} \rangle_{2500}$ of approximately 1~keV. This precision is sufficient to investigate ICM physics and refine X-ray temperature calibrations.

An increasing number of RNA sequences are recognized as having multiple stable structural distributions. Current algorithms leverage nucleotide sequences alongside auxiliary experimental data to forecast these distributions. While these methods are generally effective at identifying the structures within a distribution, accurately determining their relative weights remains a significant challenge.
