Furthermore, we establish a representability theorem that characterizes the motivic space of twisted $K$-theory as an extension of the twisted Grassmannian by the sheaf of "twisted integers." These developments facilitate a proof of both cdh descent and Milnor excision for twisted homotopy $K$-theory.

We introduce a parameter-efficient Bayesian layer for hierarchical convolutional Gaussian Processes, integrating Gaussian Processes within Wasserstein-2 space to ensure reliable uncertainty propagation. This approach substitutes the conventional convolution of Gaussian Processes with a distance-preserving affine operator acting on distributions. Experimental results on brain tissue segmentation demonstrate that this architecture achieves performance comparable to established deterministic methods like U-Net, a milestone previously unattained by hierarchical Gaussian Processes. Furthermore, when applied to out-of-distribution data—specifically images containing pathologies such as brain tumors—our uncertainty estimates enable superior out-of-distribution detection compared to prior Bayesian networks and reconstruction-based techniques that learn normative distributions.

The objective of text generation is to enable machines to communicate in human language, representing a pivotal yet demanding challenge within natural language processing (NLP). Since 2014, the field has seen the emergence of various neural encoder-decoder models, initially pioneered by Seq2Seq, designed to achieve this by learning mappings from input to output text. Nevertheless, input text alone often offers insufficient context for generating optimal outputs, resulting in performance that falls short of expectations in many real-world applications. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored integrating diverse knowledge sources beyond the input text into generation models, a field known as knowledge-enhanced text generation. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of research in this area conducted over the last five years. The content is structured into two main sections: (i) general methodologies and architectures for embedding knowledge into text generation, and (ii) specific techniques and applications tailored to different types of knowledge data. This survey is intended for a broad audience, including both researchers and practitioners in academia and industry.

Commodity Trading Advisors (CTAs), primarily engaged in commodity futures, achieved strong returns during the 2000s but have struggled since the 2010s. One hypothesized cause for this decline is the rise of short-term reversal traders (STRTs), who are thought to exploit CTAs for profit. This study constructed an artificial market model by introducing a CTA agent (CTAA) and an STRT agent (STRTA) into an existing framework to examine whether the presence of STRTAs reduces CTAA earnings. Contrary to the hypothesis, the findings indicate that CTAs and STRTs are more likely to engage in trading and generate higher returns when both are present, suggesting a potentially mutually beneficial relationship rather than predatory behavior.

The Computational Paninian Grammar (CPG) model aids in decoding natural language expressions into sequences of modifier-modified relations, thereby enabling the identification of dependency relations that align more closely with linguistic semantics than standard Stanford dependencies. Despite this, the significance of the CPG dependency scheme has not yet been investigated within multi-modal vision and language applications. At IIIT Hyderabad, we intend to conduct a novel study to examine the potential benefits and drawbacks of the CPG framework in the context of vision-language navigation, a prominent and demanding multi-modal grounding task.

Utilizing occupation measures to analyze stochastic processes has emerged as a highly effective strategy for both theoretical and computational investigations into various stochastic optimal control problems. We introduce a streamlined adaptation of the conventional occupation measure framework by resolving these measures locally across a partition of the state space and control horizon. This adjustment connects discretization-based methods for solving Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellmann equations with convex optimization techniques grounded in the moment-sum-of-squares hierarchy. When integrated with this hierarchy, local occupation measures enable precise control over the development of highly structured semidefinite programming relaxations for a broad spectrum of stochastic optimal control problems featuring embedded diffusion and jump components. We detail the construction of these relaxations, examine their advantageous characteristics, and illustrate through examples that they offer the capacity to compute significantly tighter bounds orders of magnitude faster than the naive combination of the moment-sum-of-squares hierarchy with the traditional occupation measure framework.

A finite set of integers $A$ is said to tile the integers by translations if $\mathbb{Z}$ can be partitioned into disjoint translated copies of $A$. Focusing on a single tiling period, this condition is equivalent to $A \oplus B = \mathbb{Z}_M$ for some natural number $M$ and subset $B \subset \mathbb{Z}$, a relationship also expressible via the cyclotomic divisibility of the associated mask polynomials $A(X)$ and $B(X)$. This paper presents a novel framework for systematically investigating such tilings, introducing key tools including the box product, multiscale cuboids, and saturating spaces, which synthesize harmonic-analytic and combinatorial techniques. We establish new criteria for tiling and cyclotomic divisibility based on these concepts. Applications include determining whether a set $A$ containing specific configurations can tile a cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_M$ and reconstructing a tiling set from partial data. Furthermore, we develop reduction methods that replace a given tiling with simpler ones. These tools are essential to our subsequent proof demonstrating that all tilings of period $(pqr)^2$, where $p, q,$ and $r$ are distinct odd primes, satisfy the tiling condition proposed by Coven and Meyerowitz.

This study introduces a comprehensive method for obtaining exact, analytical, and numerically stable expressions regarding the characteristic equations and eigenmodes of both Euler-Bernoulli and Timoshenko beam models. It extends the approach recently outlined by Goncalves et al. (2018), adapting it to ensure numerical stability for the Timoshenko beam formulation. Consequently, our findings facilitate the reliable calculation of eigenvalues and eigenmodes for both models across any number of vibration modes. Beyond detailing the mechanisms for stabilizing solutions to the eigenvalue problem for these two models, we provide tabulated results covering a wide range of common boundary conditions. A key contribution of this work is the unified presentation of both traditional and novel, numerically stabilized results for the Euler-Bernoulli and Timoshenko beam models within a single manuscript, utilizing consistent notation for prevalent boundary conditions. Furthermore, code implementing the stabilized Timoshenko expressions and finite element verification is accessible via the Mendeley Data repository at http://dx.doi.org/10.17632/r275tx2yp8.1.

In Cost-Per-Click (CPC) or Cost-Per-Impression (CPM) campaigns, advertisers frequently face the risk of exhausting their budgets without achieving sufficient conversions. Furthermore, traditional bidding strategies for ad inventory often lack the necessary linkage to propensity models required to meet target Cost-Per-Acquisition (tCPA) objectives. To resolve this issue, this paper introduces a bid optimization framework designed to help advertisers achieve their desired tCPA goals. Specifically, we developed an optimization engine that makes decisions by solving a rigorously defined constrained optimization problem. This approach utilizes a bid landscape model derived from extensive historical auction data through non-parametric learning. The proposed model naturally suggests bids that align with advertiser expectations by inferring patterns from past auction behaviors, effectively addressing common data challenges in bid landscape modeling, such as incomplete auction logs and uncertainties arising from fluctuating bidding behaviors. On real-world campaigns, this bid optimization model outperforms baseline methods and has been successfully deployed across diverse scenarios to enhance performance and increase revenue.

Researchers across various disciplines seek to identify influential features from a vast pool while managing the rate of false discoveries. To address this, we introduce the Bayesian Knockoff Filter (BKF) by integrating the knockoff procedure within a Bayesian framework, enabling the selection of features with significant effects on the response. Unlike frequentist methods that rely on fixed knockoff variables, our approach allows these variables to be dynamically updated via Markov chain Monte Carlo. Leveraging posterior samples and refined greedy selection algorithms, the BKF effectively identifies truly important features while maintaining the Bayesian false discovery rate at an acceptable level. Empirical evaluations using both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the method's superiority over existing knockoff techniques and Bayesian variable selection approaches, demonstrating higher statistical power and a reduced false discovery rate.

Localized residual stresses and elastic strain concentrations in microelectronic devices frequently impact electronic performance, resistance to thermomechanical damage, and potentially radiation tolerance. A major challenge in characterizing these concentrations is their existence at sub-micrometer length scales, which limits the effectiveness of conventional residual stress measurement methods. This study demonstrates that synchrotron X-ray-based differential aperture X-ray microscopy (DAXM) serves as a viable, non-destructive technique for depth-resolved characterization of such stress and strain concentrations. DAXM was employed to map two-dimensional strain fields between source and drain regions within the gallium nitride (GaN) layer of high electron mobility transistors (HEMTs) with sub-micrometer spatial resolution. The study presents strain field data from various locations in both pristine and irradiated HEMT specimens, alongside a preliminary stress analysis to estimate the distribution of different stress components within the GaN layer. Results indicate that $\gamma$-irradiation significantly decreases lattice plane spacing in the GaN along the sample normal direction, a phenomenon attributed to radiation damage affecting transistor components bonded to the GaN.

We present a technique for identifying independent invariant tensors within a gauge theory. This approach relies on a theorem connecting invariant tensors to constant configurations in field space. By applying this method to an $SU(3)$ gauge theory featuring matter in the adjoint representation, we determine the independent invariant tensors for this specific model.

Systematic full configuration-interaction (FCI) calculations applied to the microscopic many-body Hamiltonian successfully predict the spectra of three-electron hybrid qubits based on GaAs asymmetric double quantum dots as a function of detuning. These calculations reveal that strong inter-electron correlations cause the observed spectroscopic patterns—specifically avoided crossings between states with different electron occupancies in the left and right wells—to be intrinsically linked to the formation of Wigner molecules. Such physical entities elude capture by previously used independent-particle or Hubbard-type models. The findings show remarkable agreement with recent experimental data. Furthermore, this FCI approach for multi-well quantum dots can be readily extended to Si/SiGe hybrid qubits, where the pivotal role of Wigner molecules has also been experimentally verified.

For decades, researchers have been fascinated by the challenge of seamlessly integrating logics to allow connectives from both classical and intuitionistic systems to coexist harmoniously. In 2015, Dag Prawitz introduced a natural deduction framework for an ecumenical first-order logic. This paper initiates by developing a {\em pure} sequent calculus counterpart to his system, meaning that connectives are introduced independently of others. To achieve this, we augment sequents with an additional context known as the stoup and establish an ecumenical definition of polarities. Furthermore, we extend these concepts to accommodate modalities, offering pure labeled and nested systems designed for ecumenical modal logics.

This paper investigates the long-term dynamics of nonnegative solutions to the Cauchy problem for a nonlocal heat equation featuring a nonlinear convection term. The diffusion operator corresponds to the infinitesimal generator of a stable Lévy process, potentially exhibiting significant anisotropy. Under the assumption that initial data are bounded and integrable, the solution's mass remains conserved throughout the evolution. The asymptotic behavior is characterized by a source-type solution derived from a limit equation, where the specific form depends on the balance between convection and diffusion strengths. If diffusion dominates convection, the equation asymptotically reduces to a purely diffusive nonlocal heat equation. Conversely, when convection is dominant, its influence is restricted to the convection direction; however, diffusion persists in the orthogonal subspace, governed by a limit equation where the diffusion operator is a "projection" of the original operator onto that subspace. Determining this projection constitutes a central challenge of the study. In the scenario where convection and diffusion are of comparable magnitude, the limit equation is identical to the original equation. Notably, many of these findings are novel even in the isotropic case involving the fractional Laplacian. While the convection nonlinearity is generally assumed to be locally Lipschitz, the analysis also extends to cases where it is merely locally Hölder continuous, a setting previously unexplored in nonlocal diffusion contexts.

This study employs two-phase flow calculations to examine the thermo-hydraulic impacts of 300 kJ, 2 ms, 1.3 GeV proton pulses interacting with a closed mercury loop, serving as a model for the planned European Spallation Source (ESS) target. The analysis utilizes a two-fluid model comprising six first-order partial differential equations that resolve one-dimensional mass, momentum, and energy balances for both liquid and mercury vapor phases, enabling the description of rapid transients such as shock waves and cavitation. Proton beam absorption is modeled as an instantaneous heat source within the energy balance equations. Mercury liquid-vapor density and internal energy are derived using the van der Waals equation, with the general methodology for obtaining these properties also detailed. A second-order accurate, high-resolution shock-capturing numerical scheme, employing various limiters, is applied to the calculations. The analysis indicates that even 75-degree temperature heat shocks do not induce significant cavitation effects in mercury during 2 ms pulses.

Understanding the magnetic fields within supernova remnants (SNRs) is critical for refining Galactic cosmic ray acceleration theories and can also offer indirect insights into interstellar magnetic fields. This study presents the first predictions of Faraday dispersion functions (FDFs) for SNRs. Utilizing three-dimensional (3D) ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of SNRs expanding into a weak, regular magnetic field, we analyze the intrinsic FDFs of the shocked regions across various viewing angles. Our findings indicate that these FDFs are generally Faraday complex, suggesting that traditional rotation measure analyses are inadequate for characterizing magnetic fields in shocked regions and that Faraday tomography is essential. Additionally, we demonstrate that FDFs can be used to determine the physical-depth distribution of polarization intensity when the line of sight aligns with the initial magnetic field orientation. Finally, we show that the radial profile of the FDF width allows for the identification of the contact discontinuity location with an accuracy ranging from 0.1 to 0.2 parsecs.

The integrability characteristics of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) can be clarified through the presence of second integrals, referred to as weak integrals or Darboux polynomials in the context of polynomial ODEs. Yet, their preservation under numerical schemes remains largely unexplored. This work demonstrates that, generally, all Runge-Kutta methods maintain affine second integrals but fail to preserve irreducible quadratic second integrals. Several significant corollaries are examined, including the retention of specific rational integrals by any Runge-Kutta method. Additionally, the study addresses the scenario of affine second integrals featuring constant cofactors and investigates the conservation of affine higher-order integrals.

The sodium monoxide radical (NaO) appears in the Earth's mesosphere as part of night glow and holds significant astronomical relevance. This research focuses on optical transitions between the ground X $^2\Pi$ state and the low-lying excited A $^2\Sigma^+$ state ($T_{\textrm e}\approx 2000$ cm$^{-1}$). Utilizing the \Duo program to solve coupled-channel Schr\"{o}dinger equations via a variational approach, we generated a comprehensive line list containing rovibronic term values, allowed electric dipole transitions, Einstein coefficients, and temperature-dependent partition functions. Integral to constructing the final deperturbation model were MRCI \textit{ab initio} calculations describing the potential energy curves of both states, spin-orbit and $L$-uncoupling non-adiabatic matrix elements, and both permanent and transition dipole moments. These \textit{ab initio} potential energy curves, modeled using the analytical Extended-Morse-Oscillator form, were refined alongside spin-orbit and $L$-uncoupling functions through least-squares fitting to existing spectroscopic data. The experimental input comprised pure rotational transitions within the fine structure components of the X $^2\Pi$ state for vibrational levels $v''\in [0,3]$, as well as rovibronic A $^2\Sigma^+(v'=0) \leftarrow$ X $^2\Pi(v''=0)$ transitions, both of which exhibit limited rotational coverage. Due to the scarcity of data regarding the vibrational structure of both states, further experimental investigation of higher excited levels is recommended to establish a robust spectroscopic model. The NaO NaOUCMe line list can be accessed through www.exomol.com and the CDS database.

This article applies concepts from complexity science to re-examine classical fluid mechanics. For nearly a century, the mathematical self-consistency of the Navier-Stokes equations has eluded functional analysts, leading to its designation as one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems at the start of the 21st century. The paper traces the historical evolution of fluid mechanics and elucidates the implications of failing to rationalize a foundational tenet: the continuum hypothesis. It argues that fluids should be viewed as emergent phenomena, where atoms and molecules at the nanometer scale can be correlated with continuum physics at the microscale. If this holds true, a new theoretical framework could model how fluids emerge from atomic structures, effectively resolving the multi-scale problem within a single abstract system. The article proposes the Cantor set, with layers $N$ (where $N$ can reach up to two orders of magnitude), as a promising analytical framework to bridge molecular-level energy $C_{1}$ at length scale $l_{cut}$ with continuum-level energy $C_N$ at length scale $L$. Beyond fluid mechanics, the Cantor set is demonstrated to offer a conceptual model for VLSI hardware design (where $N=5$). Additionally, the text highlights an experimental approach to architecting metafluids as a method to empirically solve emergence by connecting physics across specific lower and higher scales.

The characteristics of Pastro polynomials defined on the real line are analyzed using a set of three $q$-difference operators. It is demonstrated that the $q$-difference equation and recurrence relation satisfied by these polynomials correspond to generalized eigenvalue problems involving this operator triplet, for which the Pastro polynomials serve as solutions. Additionally, a discrete biorthogonality relation on the real line is derived and interpreted through the lens of adjoint operators, while the algebra generated by the triplet of $q$-difference operators is also examined.

A fault diagnostic model developed for a laboratory machine struggles to perform effectively on industrial machines subjected to variable operating conditions. Consequently, training a new diagnostic model for every distinct operating condition is both time-consuming and economically inefficient. To address this, we propose a rapid learning mechanism capable of adapting an existing diagnostic model to suit industrial machines under diverse conditions. This approach employs the Net2Net transformation followed by fine-tuning to minimize the maximum mean discrepancy between new and historical data. The proposed method requires only a minimal number of labeled target samples and training iterations for fine-tuning, enabling it to quickly learn new data patterns. The efficacy of this fault diagnosis technique has been validated using datasets from Case Western Reserve University, Intelligent Maintenance Systems, and Paderborn University under significant operational variations. Furthermore, it has been confirmed that models trained on artificially damaged data can be rapidly adapted to handle real-world damage datasets.

In the realm of network security monitoring, protocol detection involves identifying the application layer protocol to facilitate timely and accurate protocol-specific deep packet inspection. This challenge is significant because relying solely on isolated features, such as port numbers, is insufficient for reliably distinguishing application layer protocols. Consequently, dynamic detection methods have emerged. This paper examines the dynamic protocol detection mechanisms utilized by prominent open-source network monitoring tools. Using HTTP as a case study, we demonstrate that all evaluated detection mechanisms are susceptible to evasion attacks, presenting a critical risk to practical monitoring operations. Our analysis reveals that the fundamental issue of protocol disambiguation remains inadequately resolved in two out of the three systems reviewed. To support effective operational decisions, this work underscores the inherent trade-offs associated with Dynamic Protocol Detection.

This research investigates wireless power transmission from an energy source to multiple harvesting nodes, aiming to maximize energy efficiency. The source selects a transmit power level from a set of options for each time slot, while nodes use harvested energy to send information back to the source. Lacking channel state information, the source only receives binary feedback indicating whether a node's codeword was successfully decoded. Under these constraints, the source must identify the optimal power level to maximize network efficiency. We formulate this as a stochastic Multi-Armed Bandits problem and propose an Upper Confidence Bound-based algorithm that learns the power level yielding maximum energy efficiency. Numerical results confirm the algorithm's performance guarantees and demonstrate substantial improvements over benchmark schemes.

Neutrino interaction lengths increase with energy, reaching scales comparable to Earth's diameter at energies exceeding 10's of TeV. Consequently, over terrestrial distances, the brief lifetime of the tau lepton generates a flux of regenerated tau neutrinos (via $\nu_\tau \to \tau \to \nu_\tau$) within the Earth. Upcoming neutrino experiments targeting ultra-high energy neutrinos often rely on detecting these regenerated tau neutrinos or the resulting tau decay showers. However, both signatures are influenced by tau polarization, which affects the energy distribution of secondary particles produced during decay. Although taus generated via weak interactions are nearly 100% polarized, electromagnetic interactions within the Earth are expected to cause some depolarization. This paper presents the first quantification of tau depolarization due to electromagnetic energy loss. Our findings indicate that this depolarization has only a minor impact on the final energy of tau neutrinos or taus produced by high-energy incident tau neutrinos. Furthermore, tau depolarization effects can be directly incorporated into Monte Carlo simulations such as nuPyProp and TauRunner.

Sumset estimates, which establish bounds on the cardinality of sumsets for finite sets within a group, constitute a fundamental component of additive combinatorics. Recently, probabilistic and entropic counterparts to many of these inequalities have been developed. This paper investigates analogous sumset estimates within convex geometry and Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$. First, we demonstrate that volume exhibits supermodularity to arbitrary orders regarding Minkowski summation across the space of convex bodies. Second, we examine sharp constants associated with convex geometry analogues of various Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality variants. Finally, the paper concludes by establishing links between these inequalities and the classical Rogers-Shephard inequality.

For every $\lambda \in \left]0,1\right]$, we construct an uncountable collection of compact quantum groups $\mathbb{G}$ whose associated von Neumann algebra $\mathsf{L}^{\!\infty}(\mathbb{G})$ constitutes a separable predual injective factor of type $\mathrm{III}_\lambda$. Additionally, we demonstrate that uncountably many injective factors of type $\mathrm{III}_0$ emerge as $\mathsf{L}^{\!\infty}(\mathbb{G})$ for certain compact quantum groups. To differentiate these instances, we define invariants inspired by the Connes invariant $T$ for von Neumann algebras, specifically modeling them on the scaling group, and explore the relationship between these invariants for $\mathbb{G}$ and the Connes invariants $T(\mathsf{L}^{\!\infty}(\mathbb{G}))$ and $S(\mathsf{L}^{\!\infty}(\mathbb{G}))$. Finally, we establish that type $\mathrm{I}$ factors cannot be realized as $\mathsf{L}^{\!\infty}(\mathbb{G})$ for any non-trivial compact quantum group $\mathbb{G}$.

Current research indicates that node embeddings produced by graph neural networks (GNNs) are susceptible to adversarial threats, including subtle modifications to adjacency matrices and node attributes. Consequently, developing robust representations within GNNs is essential. To enhance the resilience of graph representation learning, we introduce a new Graph Adversarial Contrastive Learning framework (GraphACL) that integrates adversarial augmentations into graph self-supervised learning. This approach maximizes the mutual information between local and global representations derived from perturbed graphs and their adversarial variants, which can be generated through either supervised or unsupervised methods. Grounded in the Information Bottleneck Principle, we provide a theoretical proof that our method yields a significantly tighter bound, thereby bolstering the robustness of graph representation learning. Empirical evaluations across various node classification benchmarks demonstrate that GraphACL achieves accuracy comparable to existing supervised methods.

Supermassive black hole (SMBH) mergers, potent sources of gravitational waves (GW), may generate relativistic jets capable of producing observable electromagnetic (EM) radiation. Our study simulates the propagation of these post-merger jets within the circumnuclear disk wind environment existing prior to the merger and computes multi-wavelength EM spectra originating from the forward shock. We demonstrate that non-thermal EM signals from such mergers remain detectable out to the range of upcoming GW observatories like the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). Furthermore, our model predicts slowly fading transients occurring with time delays ranging from days to months post-coalescence, offering significant implications for electromagnetic follow-up efforts following a GW detection.

To expand upon existing centered Gaussian processes, we present a novel centered mixed self-similar Gaussian process termed the mixed generalized fractional Brownian motion, offering a robust model for a broader range of natural phenomena. This process extends both the mixed fractional Brownian motion by Cheridito [10] and the generalized fractional Brownian motion by Zili [31]. We examine its primary stochastic attributes, including its non-Markovian and non-stationary nature, as well as the criteria under which it fails to be a semimartingale. Furthermore, we demonstrate the long-range dependence characteristics of this process.

This paper addresses the optimal beamformer design for rate splitting multiple access (RSMA)-assisted multiple-input single-output (MISO) visible light communication (VLC) systems. Initially, we establish closed-form lower bounds for the achievable rate of each user, marking the first theoretical limits for RSMA-aided VLC networks. Subsequently, we examine the optimal beamforming strategy to maximize the sum rate within optical and electrical power constraints. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed RSMA-aided networks outperform both space-division multiple access (SDMA) and nonorthogonal multiple access (NOMA) in terms of performance.

We introduce single-cell entropy (scEntropy) as a metric to quantify the order within cellular transcriptome profiles derived from single-cell RNA-seq data, enabling an unsupervised cell type classification approach termed scEGMM. This method combines scEntropy with a Gaussian mixture model. scEntropy effectively defines a cell's intrinsic transcriptional state, while scEGMM offers a coherent, parameter-free, and clustering-free classification framework. Despite lacking these components, scEGMM performs comparably to established machine learning methods in benchmarking and supports clearer biological interpretation.

Thermal transport across a metal-insulator interface can be described by electron-phonon interactions, which couple an electron lead to a phonon lead when phonon-phonon coupling at the boundary is negligible. We examine the thermal conductance and rectification between the electron and phonon components using the nonequilibrium Green's function approach. Our findings reveal that thermal conductance exhibits nonmonotonic behavior as a function of average temperature or the coupling strength between the phonon leads in the metal and insulator regions. Furthermore, the metal-insulator interface demonstrates significant thermal rectification, an effect that can be reversed by altering the average temperature or the electron-phonon coupling.

This study evaluates the viability of galaxy cluster edges as a standard ruler for cosmological distance measurements and the investigation of exotic physics. By testing five alternative cosmological models against predictions from the upcoming Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument survey, we determine that cluster edges offer a promising method for constraining theories beyond the $\Lambda$CDM framework. Specifically, the precision with which cluster edges can constrain the dark energy equation of state is approximately double that of the Pantheon Type Ia supernovae sample. Our results indicate that the constraining power of cluster edges is significantly enhanced when combined with other cosmological probes. When paired with cosmic microwave background data, baryon acoustic oscillations, Type Ia supernovae, cosmic chronometers, and simulated gravitational-wave events from the space-based Einstein Telescope, cluster edges help refine $\Lambda$CDM constraints. Notably, the combination of cosmic microwave background and cluster edges yields the tightest constraints on the Hubble constant ($H_0$) at $0.5\%$ precision and the matter density ratio ($\Omega_m$) at $1.6\%$ precision among the five pairings, while the pairing of gravitational waves with cluster edges achieves constraining power nearly equivalent to that of Type Ia supernovae and cluster edges. Furthermore, we establish the most stringent limits on $\Lambda$CDM by integrating cluster edges with all available cosmological datasets. Ultimately, leveraging additional probes allows galaxy cluster edges to provide novel insights into exotic physics across cosmological scales.

New radio detection methods are currently under investigation to identify astrophysical neutrinos with energies exceeding the PeV scale interacting within polar ice. Given the substantial attenuation length of radio waves in such media, these instruments are anticipated to also detect radio emissions from cosmic ray air showers. Additionally, when cosmic ray air showers strike a high-altitude ice layer, they trigger an in-ice particle cascade that generates radio emission. This study presents initial findings from detailed simulations of these cosmic-ray-induced in-ice cascades, utilizing a combined approach of the CORSIKA Monte Carlo code and the Geant4 simulation toolkit. We outline the general characteristics of these particle cascades and provide a parameterization of their longitudinal and lateral distributions based on $X_{max}$. Furthermore, we evaluate the feasibility of observing these in-ice cascades via both Askaryan radio emission detection and the RADAR reflection technique. Based on our results, the expected signals from the continuation of these cosmic-ray-induced in-ice cascades closely resemble neutrino signals. Consequently, a comprehensive understanding of these events is essential for distinguishing neutrino candidates, while simultaneously offering a valuable in-situ natural calibration source.

This study introduces an efficient technique for calculating inner and outer approximations of forward reachable sets in nonlinear control systems experiencing altered dynamics and reduced control authority, utilizing a precomputed reachable set from a nominal system. The approach adjusts a pre-existing reachable set by expanding or contracting it according to prior understanding of how trajectory deviations evolve, depending on whether an inner or outer approximation is needed. These evolution dynamics establish an upper limit on the minimum divergence between trajectories starting from the same point: one generated by the nominal system under standard controls, and the other by the compromised system under restricted controls. Such dynamics are determined by the specified Hausdorff distance between the nominal and potentially unknown impaired control sets, as well as the rate of change between nominal and off-nominal dynamics. Given its superior computational efficiency over directly calculating off-nominal reachable sets, this method is well-suited for on-board fault-tolerant path planning and failure recovery. Furthermore, unlike previous research, the proposed algorithm does not mandate that reachable sets be convex, enhancing its applicability to general scenarios. The authors outline several implementation considerations and provide three illustrative examples: heading dynamics for a ship, a lower triangular dynamical system, and a system of coupled linear subsystems.

This paper introduces a new advancement in entropy-stable finite-volume and finite-difference schemes. The first section addresses the construction of high-order entropy-conservative fluxes. While [LMR2002] extended Tadmor's second-order accurate fluxes to high-order ($2p$) using a simple centered linear combination, we further generalize this approach to non-centered flux combinations, which are particularly advantageous for handling non-periodic boundary conditions. In the second section, we establish a Lax-Wendroff theorem for these combined fluxes and the entropy dissipation steering method from [Klein2022]. Finally, numerical simulations confirm all theoretical results.

Skeleton-based action recognition remains a central challenge in human-centric scene understanding due to the diverse granularities and significant variability in human movement. Current methods typically rely on a single neural representation for varying motion patterns, often struggling to identify fine-grained action classes when training data is limited. To overcome these issues, we introduce a novel multi-granular spatio-temporal graph network designed for skeleton-based action classification, which simultaneously models both coarse and fine-grained motion patterns. This approach utilizes a dual-head graph network with two interleaved branches, allowing for the effective and efficient extraction of features at two distinct spatio-temporal resolutions. Furthermore, our network employs a cross-head communication strategy to mutually enhance the representations generated by both heads. We conducted extensive experiments across three large-scale datasets—NTU RGB+D 60, NTU RGB+D 120, and Kinetics-Skeleton—and achieved state-of-the-art results on all benchmarks, demonstrating the efficacy of our proposed method.

Electrostatic gating currently regulates electron transport in integrated circuits, yet magnons—the quanta of spin waves associated with magnetic order—remain challenging to control despite their potential as alternative information carriers. This study demonstrates that placing superconducting strips atop thin magnetic films enables total magnon reflection through the strips' diamagnetic response to stray magnon fields. These interactions induce significant frequency shifts that unidirectionally block magnon propagation perpendicular to the magnetization. Furthermore, arranging two such superconducting gates parallel to the magnetization forms a magnonic cavity. The ability to coherently gate magnons enhances magnonic device capabilities, enabling features like reprogrammable logic and stronger coupling to other physical degrees of freedom.

UCLID5 serves as a comprehensive tool for the multi-modal formal modeling, verification, and synthesis of complex systems. It addresses verification challenges in heterogeneous environments, including hybrid hardware-software combinations, systems with diverse specifications, and those requiring mixed modeling approaches. A key innovation of UCLID is its focus on leveraging syntax-guided and inductive synthesis to automate modeling and verification processes. This paper details recent advancements in the tool, featuring new language capabilities, enhanced integration with syntax-guided synthesis and satisfiability solving techniques, support for hyperproperties and a blend of axiomatic and operational modeling, demonstrations across novel problem classes, and a strengthened implementation.

Upcoming large-scale sky surveys aim to observe billions of galaxies, necessitating the determination of fundamental structural parameters to track their evolution. This endeavor is particularly difficult for ground-based telescopes due to the seeing-limited point-spread function (PSF). To enable rapid and precise analysis of galaxy surface brightness, we created a suite of supervised Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) designed to extract Sersic profile parameters. This study introduces the first two members of this family, the Galaxy Light profile CNNs (GaLNets): GaLNet-1, which utilizes only galaxy images, and GaLNet-2, which incorporates both images and the local PSF. We evaluated these networks against the 2DPHOT tool, a standard PSF-convolved fitting method applied to galaxies from the Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS). The results indicate that GaLNet-2 achieves accuracy comparable to 2DPHOT, whereas GaLNet-1 underperforms due to the absence of local PSF data. Furthermore, both GaLNets are approximately three orders of magnitude faster than conventional methods. This initial application of CNNs to ground-based surface photometry demonstrates their potential for analyzing massive galaxy samples anticipated from surveys like Vera Rubin/LSST. Additionally, these networks can be readily adapted for space-based missions, including Euclid and the China Space Station Telescope.

The global integration of artificial intelligence has significantly increased its potential influence in low-resource areas of the Global South. Major tech corporations such as Microsoft, Google, and IBM have established substantial research operations in nations like India, Ghana, and South Africa. Although the work conducted by these labs is frequently driven by the desire to benefit local populations, the implementation of their tools has not always proceeded without complications. This paper offers a case study on the deployment of AI by large industry labs in resource-constrained settings, identifies factors leading to unanticipated rollouts, and reflects on the current landscape of AI in the Global South. It concludes by proposing recommendations for inclusive design methodologies that prioritize the needs of marginalized communities, ensuring they are viewed not merely as beneficiaries but as primary stakeholders in AI development.

We developed a family of marginally-rigid (isostatic) spring networks featuring a fractal structure extending to a controllable length and computed their viscoelastic spectra, $G^{*}(\omega)$. Two distinct scaling regimes were identified: (i) at low frequencies, $G^{\prime}\approx G^{\prime\prime}\propto\omega^{\Delta}$, aligning with $\Delta=1/2$; and (ii) at intermediate frequencies, $G^{\prime}\propto G^{\prime\prime}\propto\omega^{\Delta^{\prime}}$, which corresponds to the fractal structure and matches the theoretical prediction $\Delta^{\prime}=(\ln3-\ln2)/(\ln3+\ln2)$. The transition between these regimes shifted to lower frequencies as the fractal size increased, a behavior indicative of diffusive-like dispersion. Furthermore, solid gels created by introducing internal stresses demonstrated comparable dynamics above a low-frequency cutoff, highlighting the practical significance of these results.

Anti-de Sitter space is defined as the Lorentzian space form characterized by negative curvature. This paper examines lightlike hypersurfaces situated along spacelike submanifolds within anti-de Sitter space, accommodating general codimensions. Specifically, we explore the singularities of these lightlike hypersurfaces by applying the theory of Legendrian singularities.

This study investigates the first-order confinement-deconfinement phase transition in $SU(N)$ pure Yang-Mills theory using Polyakov loop models (PLMs), specifically analyzing the resulting gravitational wave (GW) spectra. We find that PLMs incorporating the Haar measure term, which successfully describe QCD for $N=3$, may conflict with large $N$ scaling predictions for thermodynamic quantities and latent heat near the criticality of the first-order phase transition, as observed in lattice simulations. To address this, we introduce polynomial models termed the 4-6 PLM (featuring four- and six-point interactions among basic PL fields with center charge 1) and the 4-8 PLM (featuring four- and eight-point interactions). We explain how these models can naturally emerge when a heavy PL with charge 2 is present. Our results demonstrate that these proposed models yield consistent thermodynamic and large $N$ properties around the criticality. Furthermore, the predicted GW spectra exhibit sufficient sensitivity to be detected by future interferometers, including LISA, BBO, DICIGO, and TianQin.

We investigate the creation of intensity quantum correlations through four-wave mixing within a rubidium vapor. The lack of a cavity in these setups enables the simultaneous handling of multiple spatial modes. In the conventional amplifying configuration, we observe relative intensity squeezing reaching 9.2 dB below the standard quantum limit. Furthermore, we both theoretically identify and experimentally validate a novel regime where quantum correlations emerge despite the absence of net amplification. In this scenario, a four-wave mixing arrangement functions as a photonic beam splitter with non-classical characteristics, effectively dividing a coherent state input into two beams exhibiting quantum correlations.

Machine learning, satellite imagery, and local sensors are essential for achieving sustainable and resource-efficient agricultural optimization, demonstrating their significant value in land management. Historically, efforts have prioritized expanding datasets analyzed through supervised learning; however, the dependency on labeled data remains a time-consuming constraint. Conversely, rapid technological advancements are generating vast quantities of unlabeled data. Self-supervised learning (SSL) offers a solution to this bottleneck by effectively integrating existing unlabeled datasets. Consequently, a crop type dataset spanning 2016 to 2018 was employed to experiment with SSL and benchmark it against supervised approaches. A distinctive characteristic of this dataset was the divergent climatic conditions in 2018, which lowered yields and altered plant spectral signatures. The study aimed to predict the 2018 season using SSL with either no labels or minimal labels to determine if new data collection was necessary for unknown years. Despite these challenging conditions, the findings indicated that SSL achieved higher accuracy. These results are expected to stimulate further advancements in precision farming, prompting the publication of the SSL framework and associated data (Marszalek, 2021).

Simulating three-dimensional (3D) turbulence using neural networks presents significant challenges due to the field's extreme nonlinearity, vast degrees of freedom, and the high memory demands of traditional simulations. While the attention mechanism has emerged as a promising method to enhance turbulence modeling performance, the standard self-attention approach is hindered by quadratic $O(n^2)$ complexity in both time and space relative to the input dimension $n$, creating a major bottleneck for 3D applications. This study addresses that limitation by introducing a linear attention network, which approximates standard attention through two linear projections, thereby reducing computational and spatial complexity from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$. We developed the Linear Attention-coupled Fourier Neural Operator (LAFNO) specifically for 3D turbulence simulation. Numerical results demonstrate that the linear attention mechanism achieves a 40% reduction in error at equivalent computational costs, enabling LAFNO to accurately reconstruct diverse statistical properties and instantaneous spatial structures of 3D turbulence. Furthermore, this linear attention approach holds potential for advancing neural network models addressing other high-dimensional, nonlinear scientific problems across various domains.

This study investigates the three-body systems $\eta K^*\bar{K}^*$, $\pi K^*\bar{K}^*$, and $KK^*\bar{K}^*$ using the fixed-center approximation of the Faddeev equations, with the $K^*\bar{K}^*$ pair modeled as the scalar meson $f_0(1710)$. The interactions among $\pi$, $\eta$, $K$, and $K^*$ are derived from the chiral unitary approach. Scattering the $\eta$ meson off the clustered $(K^*\bar{K}^*)_{f_0(1710)}$ system reveals a peak in the squared modulus of the three-body scattering amplitude, identified as a bound state with quantum numbers $I^G(J^{PC})=0^+(0^{-+})$, possessing a mass and width of approximately 2054 MeV and 60 MeV, respectively; this state may correspond to the $\eta(2100)$ meson. In the $\pi (K^*\bar{K}^*)_{f_0(1710)}$ scattering process, a bump structure emerges around 1900–2000 MeV with quantum numbers $1^-({0^{-+}})$. For the $K K^* \bar{K}^*)_{f_0(1710)}$ system, three structures are observed, one of which is notably stable with a mass near 2130 MeV. These theoretical findings are anticipated to be verified by upcoming experimental data from collaborations such as BESIII, BelleII, and LHCb.

Collaborative settings, such as programming labs, are essential for developing experiential skills like critical thinking, problem-solving, and peer dialogue. While traditional, in-person labs facilitate these abilities through natural verbal and physical interactions, the global pandemic has rendered such gatherings unsafe, necessitating a reimagining of these practices for remote contexts. As the educational community seeks effective remote strategies, there is an urgent need to identify the distinct requirements of both students and instructors across different learning modes. This study addresses how to design accessible remote learning by adapting in-person practices alongside digital solutions. Specifically, we analyze observations from two introductory programming courses offered before and during the COVID-19 pandemic in both physical and online formats. Our findings highlight five unique themes regarding user needs and interaction practices tied to students' prior curriculum experience and academic level. We observe that current video-conferencing tools fail to support peer collaboration, lack a conducive learning atmosphere, and hinder spontaneous engagement between learners and educators. Consequently, we propose design recommendations and intervention strategies to enhance synchronous remote learning, specifically aiming to create a superior environment for introductory lab courses.

A recent study \cite{Temme:2021:AKH} introduced new asymptotic expansions for the Kummer functions $M(a,b,z)$ and $U(a,b+1,z)$, focusing on large positive $a$ and $b$ with fixed $z$, particularly when $a\sim b$. This work extends that methodology to accommodate large values of $z$, yielding expansions valid whenever at least one of the parameters $a$, $b$, or $z$ is large. Numerical tables are included to demonstrate the accuracy of these expansions.

A two-electron temperature plasma is generated by diffusing two separate plasmas that possess distinct densities and temperatures. This straightforward approach allows for sufficient regulation of plasma parameters. The research demonstrates that the temperature and density of both electron populations can be precisely managed by adjusting the discharge currents of each plasma. An ion-acoustic wave is induced within the plasma and detected via a planar Langmuir probe; by measuring the wave's damped amplitude, researchers can confirm the existence of two distinct electron components. This production technique offers a valuable method for controlling hot electron density and temperature, with significant applications in plasma processing industries.

Following the 2017 introduction of the Transformer for translation tasks, attention-based architectures gained significant prominence. Subsequently, the development of BERT, which enhanced the NLU-oriented encoder component of the Transformer, and GPT, which optimized the NLG-focused decoder component, catalyzed the emergence of diverse methodologies, datasets, and models for pretrained language learning. Moreover, over the last three years, numerous pretrained language models tailored specifically for Korean have been introduced. This study aims to conduct both quantitative and qualitative comparisons and analyses of the publicly available Korean PLMs.

The primary goal of Galactic archeology is to trace the formation and assembly of the Galaxy's stellar components over time by analyzing the properties of its stars. Recently, the launch of the ESA Gaia mission and advances in spectroscopic surveys have enabled researchers to explore the Galaxy's deep past for the first time. Globular clusters (GCs) are pivotal to this field as some of the Milky Way's oldest systems, preserving a record of its entire history. In recent years, numerous studies have attempted to determine whether clusters are accreted or formed in situ by analyzing kinematic spaces to reconstruct the Milky Way's past accretion events. This work tests the common assumption regarding the clustering of accreted GC populations in integrals of motion space. By analyzing dissipation-less N-body simulations modeling the accretion of one or two satellite systems with their GC populations onto a Milky Way-like galaxy, we find that for mass ratios of 1:10, significant overlap is expected between accreted GCs and "kinematically-heated" in-situ GCs in kinematic spaces. Contrary to standard literature assumptions, our results indicate that accreted GCs lack dynamical coherence and do not cluster in these spaces. Furthermore, GCs can appear in regions dominated by stars of different origins, challenging the widespread practice of associating GCs with field stars to assign a common origin. These findings cast serious doubt on the recovery of the Milky Way's accretion history based on phase-space clustering of the GC population.

Parkinson's disease (PD) ranks as the second most prevalent neurodegenerative condition globally, impacting approximately 1% of the elderly population (aged 60 and above) in industrialized countries. Over 80% of those affected experience motor symptoms, which could be effectively managed through tailored medication schedules and dosages. Achieving such personalization, however, demands the continuous, objective, and precise monitoring of motor symptoms during patients' daily routines. This study proposes utilizing a wrist-worn smartwatch equipped with 3D motion sensors to assess the severity of motor fluctuations in PD patients within a free-living context. Furthermore, we present a new network architecture, a post-training strategy, and a specialized loss function designed to handle label noise, aiming to enhance outcomes from our prior research and set a new benchmark for estimating nine-level PD motor states.

We introduce a new framework termed Dynamical Dimension Reduction (DDR) for learning low-dimensional data representations through nonlinear dynamical systems. In the DDR model, data points evolve via a nonlinear flow toward a lower-dimensional subspace, with the final embedding derived from the projection onto this subspace. The training process focuses on identifying both the nonlinear flow and the target subspace. Adopting an equation discovery approach, the vector field governing the flow is expressed as a linear combination of pre-specified linear or nonlinear candidate functions from a dictionary. Additionally, a regularization term based on average total kinetic energy is incorporated, grounded in optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that the resulting optimization problem is well-posed and outline several key properties of the DDR method. Furthermore, we detail a gradient-based training strategy where gradients are calculated using the adjoint method from optimal control theory. Finally, the DDR method is implemented and evaluated on synthetic and real-world datasets, with performance compared against other dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP.

Multistage decision policies offer valuable control strategies for high-dimensional state spaces, especially in intricate control tasks; however, they suffer from weak performance guarantees when faced with disturbances, model mismatches, or uncertainties, making them unsuitable for high-risk scenarios. We demonstrate how to quantify the sensitivity of these policies to assess their robustness capabilities and introduce a minimax iterative dynamic game framework for designing policies that remain effective under disturbances and uncertainties. We validate our quantification approach using a carefully constructed deep neural network policy and employ the minimax iterative dynamic game (iDG) framework to enhance policy robustness against adversarial disturbances. Our evaluation on a mecanum-wheeled robot aims to identify a locally optimal, robust multistage policy for a goal-reaching task. The proposed algorithm is straightforward and adaptable for creating robust meta-learning or deep policies that can withstand disturbances, model mismatches, and uncertainties up to a specific bound. Result videos are available at http://ecs.utdallas.edu/~opo140030/iros18/iros2018.html, code for reproducing experiments can be found at https://github.com/lakehanne/youbot/tree/rilqg, and a self-contained Docker environment is accessible at https://hub.docker.com/r/lakehanne/youbotbuntu14/.

Comparing athletes from vastly different eras using statistical models is a complicated endeavor, often hindered by societal and sporting shifts as well as the reliance on flawed traditional metrics. This study examines cricket by ranking Test match bowlers using data spanning from the inaugural Test in 1877. To address the under- and overdispersion inherent in small count data, we developed a truncated, mean-parameterised Conway-Maxwell-Poisson model designed to isolate individual bowlers' innate abilities. Employing a Bayesian framework with Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms, we derived parameter estimates and confidence intervals. The resulting model demonstrates a strong fit and reveals that the conventional bowling average is a deficient metric.

Using MasterCode, we conducted a frequentist analysis of constraints on the pMSSM11, a phenomenological MSSM model defined by 11 parameters. Our analysis incorporates data from approximately 36/fb of LHC collisions at 13 TeV, alongside results from PICO, XENON1T, and PandaX-II dark matter scattering experiments, as well as prior accelerator and astrophysical measurements. We present fits both with and without the $(g-2)_{\mu}$ constraint. The pMSSM11 is characterized by three gaugino masses ($M_{1,2,3}$), distinct masses for first/second-generation squarks ($m_{\tilde{q}}$) versus third-generation squarks ($m_{\tilde{q}_3}$), distinct masses for first/second-generation sleptons ($m_{\tilde{l}}$) versus third-generation sleptons ($m_{\tilde{\tau}}$), a universal trilinear mixing parameter $A$, the Higgs mixing parameter $\mu$, the pseudoscalar Higgs mass $M_A$, and $\tan\beta$. When the $(g-2)_{\mu}$ constraint is included, a Bino-like lightest neutralino ($\tilde\chi^0_1$) is favored; however, removing this constraint shifts preference toward a Higgsino-like $\tilde \chi^0_1$. We also identified the mechanisms within various regions of the pMSSM11 parameter space that adjust the $\tilde\chi^0_1$ relic density to align with cosmological observations. In the fit with the $(g-2)_{\mu}$ constraint, favored mechanisms involve coannihilation with $\tilde \chi^0_2$ and the Wino-like $\tilde\chi^{\pm}_1$, or with nearly degenerate first/second-generation sleptons. Conversely, dropping the $(g-2)_{\mu}$ constraint makes coannihilation with $\tilde \chi^0_2$ and the Higgsino-like $\tilde\chi^{\pm}_1$, or with first/second-generation squarks, potentially significant. Future prospects include the discovery of strongly interacting sparticles at the LHC and electroweakly interacting sparticles at future linear $e^+ e^-$ colliders like the ILC or CLIC.

Managing the influx of social web data at the start of a disaster is difficult because relevant information is scarce and labeling datasets for active crises presents practical constraints. This paper proposes that unsupervised domain adaptation combined with multi-task learning offers a robust framework to utilize historical crisis data for training efficient filtering models during the sudden emergence of new events. We introduce a novel approach to categorize pertinent tweets during an unfolding crisis without requiring any new labeled examples, utilizing the publicly available TREC incident streams dataset. Specifically, we develop a customized multi-task architecture featuring a multi-domain discriminator for crisis analytics, termed the Multi-Task Domain Adversarial Attention Network. This model incorporates dedicated attention layers for each task to ensure interpretability, a crucial factor for real-world deployment. Addressing the challenge of deep networks performing poorly on sparse data, we demonstrate that performance improves by sharing a base layer through multi-task learning and domain adversarial training. To evaluate domain adaptation, we treat a specific target event as the test set while training on the remaining data. Our findings indicate that the multi-task model surpasses its single-task equivalent. Regarding qualitative interpretability, we show that the attention layers serve as an explanatory guide for model predictions, enabling emergency services to assess model accountability by identifying the specific words in tweets deemed significant for classification. Finally, we illustrate the practical utility of our work through a use-case application for the COVID-19 pandemic.

The study of the numerical range and numerical radius for tensors remains a largely unexplored area in the literature. Although Ke et al. (2016) were the first to define the numerical range of a tensor using the $k$-mode product in *Linear Algebra Appl.*, they did not establish its convexity. This paper introduces the concepts of numerical range and numerical radius for even-order square tensors based on the inner product via the Einstein product. We derive sufficient conditions involving the numerical radius for a tensor to be unitary and prove the convexity of the numerical range. Additionally, an algorithm is presented for plotting the numerical range of a tensor, and we examine properties related to the Moore-Penrose inverse of a tensor.

We show that discontinuous shear thickening (DST) can occur in dilute or moderately dense inertial suspensions composed of frictionless soft particles. This phenomenon can be understood as an ignited-quenched transition within inertial suspensions. An approximate kinetic theory aligns closely with Langevin simulation results across a broad spectrum of volume fractions, requiring no fitting parameters.

Gravitational wave detections from LIGO/Virgo of compact star inspirals offer a crucial means to investigate the poorly constrained equation of state (EOS) of dense matter within these objects. The nature of merging stars—whether they are neutron stars or quark stars composed of self-bound quark matter—remains ambiguous. This study examines EOSs based on the bag model by assuming the merging stars are strange quark stars (SQSs), utilizing Bayesian analysis of tidal deformability data from the GW170817 and GW190425 binary mergers. We analyze two extreme configurations of strange quark matter: non-superfluid and color-flavor locked (CFL) phases, finding that the outcomes in both scenarios are essentially consistent. Specifically, our findings suggest that the sound speed within SQS matter remains nearly constant, approaching the conformal limit of $c/\sqrt{3}$. We establish universal relationships linking mass, tidal deformability, and compactness for SQSs. The analysis yields the most probable maximum masses of $M_{\rm TOV}=2.10_{-0.12}^{+0.12}~(2.15_{-0.14}^{+0.16})\,M_{\odot}$ for normal (CFL) SQSs at a 90% confidence level. Corresponding radii and tidal deformabilities for a $1.4\,M_{\odot}$ star are determined to be $R_{\rm 1.4}= 11.50_{-0.55}^{+0.52}~({11.42}_{-0.44}^{+0.52})~\rm km$ and $\Lambda_{1.4}= {650}_{-190}^{+230}~({630}_{-150}^{+220})$, respectively. Furthermore, we assess the likelihood that the secondary component ($m_2$) of GW190814, with a mass of $2.59_{-0.09}^{+0.08}\,M_{\odot}$, is an SQS. Our results indicate it could be a CFL SQS, provided the pairing gap $\Delta$ exceeds $244~\rm MeV$ and the effective bag parameter $B_{\rm eff}^{1/4}$ falls between 170 and 192 MeV, all at a 90% confidence level.

In far-field speaker verification, speaker embeddings often suffer performance degradation due to mismatches between enrollment and test conditions. To address this, we introduce a teacher-student framework incorporating both feature-level and instance-level transfer learning to construct a domain-invariant embedding space. For feature-level knowledge transfer, we employ a contrastive loss function to guide the student model using the teacher, effectively reducing intra-class distances while expanding inter-class distances. Additionally, we propose an instance-level pairwise distance transfer approach that compels the student model to maintain the pairwise instance distances found in the teacher's optimized embedding space. Evaluation on the FFSVC 2020 dataset shows that our method achieves a 13.9% relative reduction in EER on Full-eval trials compared to the fusion system's Partial-eval results in Task 2. In Task 1, our minDCF on Full-eval trials is reduced by 6.3% relative to the winner's DenseNet results from Partial-eval trials. For Task 3, our proposed method's EER and minDCF on Full-eval trials closely match the fusion system's Partial-eval performance. Furthermore, our results surpass other competitive domain adaptation techniques.

Accurately estimating depth is vital for autonomous systems to understand their surroundings and gauge the distance of key objects. A prominent recent approach involves monocular depth estimation, which derives a depth map from a single image. This paper enhances self-supervised deep learning methods to achieve more accurate and generalized monocular depth estimation. The core strategy involves training a deep model to process sequences of frames, each geotagged with location data. This enables the model to refine depth predictions by incorporating area semantics. We demonstrate that our model effectively improves depth estimation outcomes. Trained in a realistic setting, the results indicate that integrating location information during the training phase yields superior depth maps.

This research centers on embodied agents capable of executing complex tasks within visually observed settings by following natural language commands. Current approaches depend heavily on extensive datasets of (instruction, gold trajectory) pairs to train effective policies; however, the resulting high data requirements and low sample efficiency hinder the creation of versatile agents that can rapidly acquire new skills. To address this, we introduce LLM-Planner, a novel framework that leverages large language models like GPT-3 to perform few-shot planning for embodied agents. Additionally, we present a straightforward yet effective technique to physically ground these LLMs, ensuring their generated plans align with the immediate environment. Evaluations on the ALFRED dataset demonstrate that our approach achieves highly competitive few-shot performance, surpassing several recent baselines trained on full datasets while utilizing less than 0.5% of the paired training data. In contrast, existing methods struggle to complete tasks successfully under identical few-shot conditions. This work paves the way for developing embodied agents that are both versatile and sample-efficient, enabling them to quickly master a wide range of tasks.

Federated learning offers a robust method for deriving insights from diverse user devices while maintaining user privacy. Nevertheless, federated environments often encounter novel classes characterized by entirely unseen data distributions that are inaccessible to the global server or other participants. To address this, we introduce a unified zero-shot framework designed to manage these challenges within federated learning. We evaluate two specific scenarios: first, a traditional setup where users do not report new class labels, and second, a scenario where users do report these labels, allowing us to generate Anonymized Data Impressions. This involves computing class similarity matrices for each device's new classes and applying unsupervised clustering to differentiate new classes across users. Additionally, our framework accommodates statistical heterogeneities in both labels and models among participating users. We empirically assess the framework on-device across varying communication rounds (FL iterations), incorporating new classes in both local and global updates alongside heterogeneous labels and models. Using two prominent audio classification tasks—keyword spotting and urban sound classification—we observe average deterministic accuracy improvements of approximately 4.041% and 4.258%, respectively.

We explore galaxy clustering within an expanding universe governed by a modified theory of gravity, utilizing principles from thermodynamics and statistical mechanics. A modified general relativity (MGR) framework is constructed by employing a regular line element field to define a symmetric tensor representing the gravitational field's energy-momentum. This approach yields a modified gravitational potential that incorporates dark matter and dark energy effects without explicitly invoking them. Using this potential, we determine the galaxy distribution function and derive various thermodynamic equations of state. Furthermore, we analyze data from the SDSS-III survey to evaluate the viability of the theoretical model describing the probability distribution of galaxies in the universe.

We introduce SpeechMatrix, a comprehensive multilingual corpus of speech-to-speech translations derived from real-world recordings of the European Parliament. This dataset features speech alignments across 136 language pairs, encompassing a total of 418,000 hours of audio. To assess the quality of this parallel speech data, we trained bilingual speech-to-speech translation models exclusively on the mined corpus and established extensive baseline performance on the EuroParl-ST, VoxPopuli, and FLEURS test sets. Leveraging the multilingual nature of SpeechMatrix, we investigated multilingual speech-to-speech translation, an area that has received limited attention in previous research. Furthermore, we demonstrated that model pre-training combined with sparse scaling via Mixture-of-Experts significantly enhances translation performance. The dataset and associated models are publicly accessible.

This research introduces a novel protocol combining cooperative non-orthogonal multiple access (CNOMA) with an improved hybrid simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (IHS SWIPT) approach, designated as CNOMA-IHS. Designed to boost the spectral efficiency (SE) of downlink CNOMA systems, this scheme increases both ergodic sum capacity (ESC) and energy efficiency (EE) by transmitting extra symbols to users and powering relay operations, all without consuming additional resources like time slots, frequencies, or codes. Analytical and simulation findings demonstrate that the CNOMA-IHS scheme surpasses other established SWIPT methods—including those utilizing hybrid SWIPT, power-splitting, time switching, or wireless powering, as well as orthogonal multiple access with IHS SWIPT—in terms of ESC. Furthermore, simulations confirm that CNOMA-IHS achieves superior energy efficiency compared to conventional time-switching SWIPT-based schemes. Additionally, when applied with an EE optimization technique, the CNOMA-IHS scheme outperforms both its non-optimized variant and other existing time-switching SWIPT approaches regarding energy efficiency.

This study presents the BLCU-ICALL system for SemEval-2022 Task 1, focusing on the Definition Modeling subtrack of the Comparing Dictionaries and Word Embeddings competition, where it secured 1st place in Italian, 2nd in Spanish and Russian, and 3rd in English and French. We introduce a transformer-based multitasking framework designed to address this task, which combines various embedding architectures via a cross-attention mechanism and models gloss structure using a masking language model objective. Furthermore, we examine a straightforward yet effective model ensembling strategy to enhance robustness. The evaluation outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, and the code is publicly available at: https://github.com/blcuicall/SemEval2022-Task1-DM.

The core objective of Human-Object Interaction (HOI) recognition is to determine the relationship between humans and objects. While HOI detection in images has advanced significantly, video-based HOI detection still requires improvement. Current one-stage approaches utilize end-to-end networks to identify video segments and directly infer interactions, which complicates model training and optimization. This paper presents the Spatial Parsing and Dynamic Temporal Pooling (SPDTP) network, which treats the entire video as a spatio-temporal graph where humans and objects serve as nodes. Distinct from existing methods, our network explicitly parses spatial data to distinguish between interactive and non-interactive pairs before performing interaction recognition. Additionally, we introduce a learnable, differentiable Dynamic Temporal Module (DTM) that highlights critical video frames while filtering out redundant ones. Experimental results demonstrate that SPDTP effectively focuses on active human-object pairs and valid keyframes, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the CAD-120 and Something-Else datasets.

This paper addresses the inverse problem of reconstructing a sound-soft scatterer from measured scattered field data, assuming the field is generated by a point source located on a known curve or surface. We propose and analyze novel direct sampling methods for this task. The first approach employs a far-field transformation of near-field data to establish explicit resolution bounds for the imaging functional of the direct sampling method. Two direct sampling methods utilizing this far-field transformation are examined, with resolution analysis conducted via Funk-Hecke identities. Additionally, we investigate a direct sampling method applicable to given Cauchy data. Numerical examples in 2D demonstrate the effectiveness of these new imaging functionals in recovering sound-soft scatterers.

Ensuring publication quality relies heavily on the review process. However, the surge in submissions to leading machine learning and NLP venues has created an excessive workload for reviewers, raising concerns about potential quality degradation. An automated system could help alleviate this issue. This paper investigates automatic review summary generation for scientific manuscripts, hypothesizing that neural language models are well-suited for this task. To test this, we introduce a novel dataset comprising scientific papers and their reviews from the NeurIPS conference between 2013 and 2020. We evaluate leading neural summarization models, demonstrate the initial feasibility of generating automatic review summaries, and outline future research directions.

Although communication is recognized as a facilitator of cooperation in multi-agent environments, designing artificial agents that can learn to communicate effectively and efficiently remains an open challenge. Much of the existing research on the emergence of communication relies on reinforcement learning (RL) and investigates unsituated communication within one-step referential tasks. These tasks lack temporal interaction and the time pressures inherent in natural communication. While agents can successfully learn to communicate in these settings, they often fail to exchange information concisely, tending instead toward over-communication and inefficient encoding. This study examines situated communication within a multi-step task, requiring the acting agent to forgo an environmental action to communicate. By imposing an opportunity cost on communication, we mimic the real-world pressure of time passing. We compare communication emergence under this temporal pressure against learning to communicate with a cost on articulation effort, implemented as a fixed and progressively increasing per-message penalty. Our findings indicate that while all tested pressures can discourage over-communication, situated communication achieves this most effectively and, unlike effort-based penalties, does not hinder the emergence of communication. Implementing an opportunity cost in a temporally extended environment represents a step toward embodiment and may serve as a prerequisite for incentivizing efficient, human-like communication.

This paper addresses the question of determining for which pairs $(g, n)$ the rational Chow or cohomology ring of $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}$ is generated by tautological classes. This problem has been completely resolved for genus $0$ by Keel, where the rings are tautological for all $n$, and for genus $1$ by Belorousski, who established that the rings are tautological if and only if $n \leq 10$. For $g \geq 2$, van Zelm demonstrated that the Chow and cohomology rings are not tautological when $2g + n \geq 24$, leaving only a finite number of cases unresolved. In this work, we prove that for $g = 2$ and $n \leq 9$, as well as for $3 \leq g \leq 7$ with $2g + n \leq 14$, the Chow and cohomology rings of $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}$ are isomorphic and generated by tautological classes. For these specific $(g, n)$ values, this result implies that the tautological ring is Gorenstein and that $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}$ exhibits polynomial point counts.

Radio maps are widely utilized in wireless communications and mobile robotics for tasks such as interference coordination, resource allocation, and mission planning. While existing methods generate these maps from spatially distributed data, they typically assume measurement locations are fixed in advance. Conversely, this paper introduces spectrum surveying, a method where a mobile robot, like a UAV, actively selects measurement locations to generate high-quality map estimates efficiently. The approach consists of two stages. First, two new algorithms—a model-based online Bayesian estimator and a data-driven deep learning method—are developed to update map estimates and calculate an uncertainty metric that identifies the most informative locations; both algorithms offer complementary advantages with constant computational complexity per measurement. Second, this uncertainty metric guides the UAV's trajectory to collect data from the most valuable spots. To address the combinatorial complexity of trajectory planning, a dynamic programming method is proposed to generate linear-time lists of waypoints targeting high-uncertainty areas. Numerical experiments using realistic datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework constructs accurate radio maps rapidly.

This study investigates how user attitudes regarding privacy and security on mobile devices influence the robustness of unlock authentication, specifically focusing on Android graphical unlock patterns. We carried out an online survey via Amazon Mechanical Turk involving 750 participants ($N=750$), collecting data on self-reported unlock choices and Likert-scale responses to seven privacy and security prompts. The responses were analyzed across multiple dimensions, including calculating the average Likert scores and applying Principal Component Analysis to uncover latent factors. Our analysis revealed that only two of the seven questions yielded significant results: those addressing general concern for data stored on mobile devices and worries about unauthorized access by known entities.
