Although the Reduced Basis (RB) method has previously accelerated fine-scale computations, the coarse system remained unoptimized, thereby restricting overall performance gains. To overcome this limitation, we apply RB techniques to a novel two-scale LOD formulation. The resulting Two-Scale Reduced Basis LOD (TSRBLOD) reduces the entire two-scale system, producing order-reduced models that are independent of the coarse mesh size. This enables efficient solution approximation for parameterized multiscale problems even over extensive domains. Furthermore, a rigorous and efficient a posteriori estimator is developed to bound the model reduction error, accounting for approximation errors in both the local fine-scale problems and the global coarse-scale system.

Unitary braiding operators serve as resilient entangling quantum gates. We present a solution-generating method to address the $(d,m,l)$-generalized Yang-Baxter equation within the range $m/2\leq l \leq m$, enabling the systematic construction of these operators. This approach relies on partition algebras, which extend the Temperley-Lieb algebra known from statistical mechanics. Our results include families of both unitary and non-unitary braiding operators that generate the complete braid group. Furthermore, we provide explicit instances for 2-, 3-, and 4-qubit systems, alongside a classification of the resulting entangled states according to Stochastic Local Operations and Classical Communication.

The $LU$ factorization, also known as Gauss-Borel factorization, of Gram matrices associated with bilinear forms serves as a central component in the theory of biorthogonal polynomials. From this perspective, the text examines the construction of biorthogonal polynomial families and their functions of the second kind, along with spectral matrices representing multiplication by the variable $x$, the Christoffel-Darboux kernel, and its projection characteristics. The discussion then shifts to the Hankel case, detailing specific properties such as three-term recurrence relations, Heine formulas, Gauss quadrature, and the Christoffel-Darboux formula. Within this framework, classical orthogonal polynomials of Hermite, Laguerre, and Jacobi types are analyzed and characterized. Ultimately, the approach demonstrates its utility in deriving Christoffel formulas for general perturbations of bilinear forms, including those of Christoffel and Geronimus types.

Two-dimensional (2D) materials have gained prominence as highly functional substances for applications ranging from semiconductors to photovoltaics, driven by their distinctive optoelectronic characteristics. Although existing databases have screened thousands of 2D candidates, identifying novel 2D materials remains a significant challenge. This study introduces a deep learning generative model for creating chemical compositions, integrated with a random forest-based classifier to identify new hypothetical 2D materials. Additionally, we developed a template-driven element substitution method to predict crystal structures for a subset of these new formulas, enabling stability verification through DFT calculations. To date, this approach has identified 267,489 potential 2D material compositions, with twelve 2D or layered materials confirmed via DFT formation energy analysis. These findings demonstrate that generative machine learning offers a powerful strategy for exploring the extensive chemical design space required for discovering new 2D materials.

We demonstrate that Gibbs distributions for two-state spin systems (binary Markov random fields) without hard constraints on trees exhibit strong spatial mixing (strong correlation decay). This holds under the condition that, for any external field, the absolute value of the inverse temperature is small, or the external field is uniformly large or small. The constraint on the inverse temperature is tight when restricted to ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic Ising models. Leveraging Weitz's self-avoiding walk, we extend this result to sparse graphs on average, generalizing aspects of recent work by Mossel and Sly \cite{MS08}, who established strong spatial mixing for ferromagnetic Ising models. Our proof offers a distinct approach that meticulously utilizes the monotonicity of local recursions. To our knowledge, this paper is the first to consider and state the second condition regarding the external field for strong spatial mixing in terms of maximum average degree and interaction energy. As an application, we provide a Fully Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (FPTAS) for the partition functions of two-state spin models without hard constraints under these assumptions, applicable to a broad family of graphs, including notable bounded-degree graphs.

Dunhuang murals represent a self-contained collection of Chinese and national styles, constituting a unique form of Buddhist art with profound historical, cultural, and research value. Within these murals, the line work is notably versatile and expressive, effectively capturing both distinct character traits and complex inner emotions; consequently, the study of mural outlines is vital for understanding Dunhuang culture. Technically, generating these contours involves image edge detection, a key area of computer vision aimed at extracting salient boundary information. While convolution-based deep learning networks have achieved success in edge extraction by leveraging contextual and semantic features, their reliance on expanding receptive fields often results in the loss of local details, hindering the creation of accurate mural outlines. To address this, we introduce a novel edge detector that combines self-attention mechanisms with convolution specifically for generating Dunhuang mural line drawings. Our approach offers two main advancements: first, a new Residual Attention and Mixed Convolution (Ramix) module that fuses local and global features within feature maps; and second, a novel densely connected backbone network designed to efficiently propagate rich edge information from shallow to deep layers. Experiments on various public datasets demonstrate that our method produces sharper and more detailed edge maps compared to existing techniques. Furthermore, testing on the Dunhuang mural dataset confirms that our approach achieves highly competitive performance.

Stock Movement Prediction (SMP) involves forecasting the future price trends of publicly traded companies, a difficult endeavor given the inherent volatility of financial markets. Recent research indicates that momentum spillover effects are crucial in driving stock fluctuations. Nevertheless, prior studies often rely on learning only basic connections between related firms, which hinders their ability to capture the intricate relationships found in real-world financial markets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a comprehensive Market Knowledge Graph (MKG) featuring two types of entities—listed companies and their associated executives—and hybrid relations encompassing both explicit and implicit links. Subsequently, we present DanSmp, a novel Dual Attention Network designed to learn momentum spillover signals based on the MKG for enhanced stock prediction. Empirical evaluations on our datasets against nine state-of-the-art baselines demonstrate that DanSmp effectively improves stock prediction performance by leveraging the constructed MKG.

This paper introduces the inaugural automatic lexical simplification system designed for Turkish. While recent advancements in text simplification depend on manually created simplified corpora and robust NLP tools capable of analyzing text at both the word and sentence levels, Turkish presents unique challenges. As a morphologically rich agglutinative language, it necessitates specific handling of inflectional cases. Furthermore, the scarcity of available resources and industrial-grade tools classifies Turkish as a low-resource language, thereby complicating the text simplification task. To address this, we propose a novel simplification pipeline that combines the pretrained BERT model with morphological features to produce word-level simplifications that are both grammatically correct and semantically appropriate.

Although commodity GPUs offer an expanding array of sophisticated features to accelerate compute tasks, many cutting-edge point cloud rendering techniques still depend on standard graphics API point primitives (e.g., GL_POINTS) for image generation. This paper introduces several compute-driven rendering methods that surpass the hardware pipeline by up to tenfold and deliver significantly improved frame rates compared to prior compute-based approaches. Extending beyond basic closest-point rendering, we propose a rapid, high-quality variant specifically designed to minimize aliasing. We evaluate multiple optimized versions of these methods across various platforms and architectures to ensure broad applicability and peak performance despite differing levels of support for new GPU features. Experimental results demonstrate that an RTX 3090 can render 796 million points (12.7GB) at 62–64 frames per second (equivalent to 50 billion points per second or 802GB/s) without utilizing level-of-detail structures. Additionally, we introduce an optimized vertex ordering strategy that enhances the efficiency of GL_POINTS by a factor of five when hardware rendering is required. Our analysis of different ordering schemes reveals that Morton-sorted buffers excel at certain viewpoints, whereas shuffled buffers perform better in others. However, a hybrid approach that first sorts vertices by Morton code and then shuffles the sequence in batches of 128 points yields a vertex buffer layout that combines high rendering performance with low sensitivity to viewpoint variations.

Multi-jet production rates at hadron colliders offer a distinct avenue for investigating Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the framework describing strong interactions. By juxtaposing theoretical predictions with experimental data, researchers can rigorously test perturbative QCD, determine fundamental constants such as the strong coupling $\alpha_s$, and hunt for phenomena extending beyond the Standard Model. This study presents, for the first time, the calculation of next-to-next-to-leading (NNLO) QCD corrections applied to standard three-jet observables and differential three-to-two jet ratios. We show that incorporating these NNLO corrections markedly diminishes the sensitivity of these observables to variations in factorization and renormalization scales. Beyond its immediate phenomenological utility, this proof-of-principle calculation marks a significant milestone in the development of perturbative QCD.

This study examines the influence of neutrino phenomenology and associated cosmological factors on an $A_{4}\otimes Z_{8}$ symmetric $\nu$2HDM extended by a new gauge singlet ($S$). Identified as a sterile neutrino, this additional particle serves as a potential dark matter candidate. Assuming a sterile neutrino mass within the keV range, we calculate the active-DM mixing angle, decay rate, and relic abundance while adhering to various cosmological constraints. Concurrently, we conduct a thorough investigation into baryogenesis and neutrinoless double beta decay scenarios involving low-scale right-handed neutrino masses. To ensure the model's validity regarding these phenomena, we incorporate experimental limits from Lyman-$\alpha$ data, X-ray observations, Planck results, and KamLAND-Zen constraints.

Viewing the Standard Model as the leading term of an effective field theory requires that anomaly-cancellation conditions be satisfied at every order of the expansion. This work highlights this necessity and provides a detailed examination of a specific subset of anomalies relevant to the electroweak scale. The analysis yields a set of sum rules governing operator coefficients; these rules are essential for the theory's internal consistency. When applied to experimental data analysis, they produce significant phenomenological outcomes: they reduce the number of free parameters across various physical processes and can link processes involving different flavor structures. Conversely, any violation of these sum rules would definitively signal the presence of undetected, non-decoupling new physics at the electroweak energy scale.

This work presents a probabilistic examination of inductive knowledge and belief, investigating its implications for predictions regarding future events, natural laws, and the values of imprecisely measured quantities. The approach integrates a theory of knowledge and belief based on comparative normality relations with a probabilistic framework for those relations. Consequently, it predicts that belief is reserved only for propositions with high probability and that numerous widely accepted principles of belief revision are incorrect.

The promise of compressive sensing (CS) has generated significant interest and rapid growth within the research community. However, translating CS theory into practical hardware that offers clear advantages over conventional imaging techniques remains limited. This article aims to guide researchers in identifying niche applications where CS delivers substantial improvements, using sea-skimming missile detection as a case study to illustrate key lessons learned. As a proof of concept, a simplified CS architecture and algorithm for missile detection are shown to achieve results comparable to conventional imaging while utilizing a smaller focal plane array (FPA). The central takeaway is that while the enthusiasm for CS is justified for fostering creativity, researchers must also set aside optimism and critically evaluate their ideas, methods, and outcomes against established conventional imaging standards.

Privacy has emerged as a critical issue in machine learning, serving as the primary motivation for federated learning, which restricts data transmission to only intermediate updates rather than raw private data. Nevertheless, federated learning does not inherently ensure privacy, as these intermediate updates can inadvertently expose sensitive information. This paper presents an explicit information-theoretic analysis of a federated expectation-maximization algorithm for Gaussian mixture models, demonstrating that such updates can lead to significant privacy breaches. To mitigate this risk, we propose a fully decentralized, privacy-preserving framework capable of securely computing updates during each maximization step. Furthermore, we evaluate the approach against two adversary models: honest-but-curious and eavesdropping. Numerical results indicate that our proposed method outperforms existing solutions in both accuracy and privacy protection.

Majorana corner modes emerging in two-dimensional second-order topological superconductors hold significant promise for fault-tolerant topological quantum computing. We show that when subjected to an in-plane magnetic field, two-dimensional ($s+p$)-wave superconductors support Majorana corner modes whose positions can be controlled by adjusting the magnetic field's orientation. Furthermore, we examine how edge imperfections influence these modes. We detail how variations in edge geometry and disorder impact the quantity and tunability of the Majorana corner modes, factors crucial for realizing topological quantum computations. Additionally, we analyze tunneling spectroscopy with a lead wire connected to the corner of a noncentrosymmetric superconductor. The resulting zero-bias differential conductance exhibits a clear periodicity dependent on the magnetic field direction, confirming the high controllability of these modes in this configuration. These findings establish the theoretical foundation necessary for experimentally observing and tuning Majorana corner modes in ($s+p$)-wave superconductors.

The Mpemba Effect, characterized by a system farther from equilibrium relaxing more rapidly than one closer to it, can be investigated using Markovian dynamics within a non-equilibrium thermodynamic framework. This phenomenon has been observed across various systems, including the Ising model. We show that the Markovian Mpemba Effect in the Ising model can be forecasted using multiple machine learning techniques: decision trees, neural networks, linear regression, and LASSO-based non-linear regression. We compare the performance of these methods and find that they can accurately extrapolate predictions to data beyond their training range. Notably, neural networks can predict the presence of the Mpemba Effect even when trained exclusively on data where the effect is absent, suggesting that signatures of the effect exist even in systems where it does not manifest. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the Mpemba Effect can be predicted in complex, computationally intensive systems without requiring full-scale calculations.

The variance of the position operator reflects the width or narrowness of a wave-packet, while momentum variance correlates with the spread of a wave-packet in momentum space; similarly, angular-momentum variance measures the degree to which a wave-packet deviates from spherical symmetry. We analyze an interacting three-dimensional trapped Bose-Einstein condensate in the limit of an infinite particle number, focusing on position, momentum, and angular-momentum anisotropies. By calculating the variances of the three Cartesian components for these operators, we demonstrate simple scenarios where the anisotropy of a Bose-Einstein condensate differs between many-body and mean-field theories, even when the densities per particle are identical at both levels. This approach offers a method for classifying correlations based on the morphology of 100% condensed bosons in a three-dimensional trap at the infinite particle limit. Brief implications are discussed.

The Independent Causal Mechanisms (ICM) principle posits that real-world data generation arises from independent modules that neither influence nor inform one another. Although this concept has driven significant progress in causal inference, it remains underappreciated within the NLP community. This paper argues that the causal direction inherent in data collection offers nontrivial insights capable of explaining various established NLP results, including performance variations in semi-supervised learning (SSL) and domain adaptation (DA) across different scenarios. We classify standard NLP tasks based on their causal orientation and empirically evaluate the ICM principle for text data using minimum description length. Furthermore, we perform a comprehensive meta-analysis of over 100 SSL studies and 30 DA studies, confirming that the findings align with our causal hypotheses. This work marks the inaugural effort to apply the ICM principle to NLP and offers constructive guidance for future modeling strategies. Code is accessible at https://github.com/zhijing-jin/icm4nlp.

This paper examines the singular values and vectors arising from low-rank perturbations of large rectangular random matrices within the "long" regime, where the count of rows (or columns) increases polynomially relative to the columns (or rows). We establish the existence of a critical signal-to-noise ratio, contingent upon matrix dimensions, which triggers a BBP-type phase transition in the behavior of extreme singular values and vectors. As a primary application, we analyze the tensor unfolding algorithm applied to the asymmetric rank-one spiked tensor model, deriving an exact detection threshold that remains independent of the unfolding procedure. Specifically, if the signal-to-noise ratio exceeds this threshold, the algorithm successfully identifies the signals; conversely, it fails to detect them when the ratio falls below it.

This study evaluates various oversampling techniques for multi-class topic classification, focusing on the SMOTE algorithm, a widely adopted method that creates new minority class instances by interpolating between two existing examples. The authors contrast the standard SMOTE approach with its variants—Borderline SMOTE and ADASYN—as well as random oversampling, using a specific text classification task as a testbed. The research examines the performance of several machine learning models, including k-nearest neighbors (KNN), support vector machines (SVM), and three neural network architectures: feedforward networks, long short-term memory (LSTM), and bidirectional LSTM. By integrating these algorithms with diverse text representations, the study assesses the impact of synthetic oversampling methods. Results indicate that oversampling generally enhances classification quality significantly. Furthermore, the authors conclude that for this specific task, class imbalance has a more pronounced effect on the performance of KNN and SVM algorithms compared to neural networks.

We investigate the four standard capacities of a two-parameter family of qubit Pauli channels, which are SO(2) covariant and include the depolarizing channel as a specific instance. We derive exact formulas for both the classical and entanglement-assisted capacities, and analytically identify the parameter regions where the quantum capacity becomes zero. Furthermore, utilizing a flag extension, we establish upper bounds for the quantum and private capacities across the entire parameter space, while also computing a lower bound for the quantum capacity via single-shot numerical methods. Combined with prior findings on depolarizing channels, our work advances the determination of capacities for the complete class of Pauli channels.

By definition, a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model is unconstrained; however, this characteristic is suboptimal when a solution of a specific, fixed binary vector size is required. This paper demonstrates a method for incorporating a constraint into a QUBO to enforce a solution of a particular magnitude.

A novel upper limit for the count of neighborly boxes in R^d is established by utilizing a well-known theorem by Kleitman regarding the maximum cardinality of sets with a fixed diameter within discrete hypercubes. The work further includes findings from computational experiments and introduces a developing conjecture.

We examine the merger history of primordial black holes (PBHs) under the assumption that they constitute the primary dark matter component within the cores of typical dwarf galaxies. Our analysis explores whether a series of collisions leads to hierarchical mergers and investigates the resulting mass spectrum of these {\it clusters}, which begin as a monochromatic (single-mass) PBH population. Our findings indicate that the merging process transfers approximately $40\%$ of the core's total mass into merger products, independent of the initial PBH mass, while radiating about $5\%$ of the energy as gravitational waves. Furthermore, in the limit of lighter masses, black holes up to eight times the original population's mass can form within a Hubble time.

Assessing inter-annotator agreement is crucial for annotation tasks, yet many existing metrics depend on fully-annotated datasets where every annotator labels every sample. We introduce Sparse Probability of Agreement (SPA), a method that estimates the probability of agreement even when no complete annotator-item pairs are available. Under specific assumptions, we demonstrate that SPA serves as an unbiased estimator and offer various weighting schemes to address samples with varying numbers of annotations, validated across multiple datasets.

This study introduces a fractional differential equation of order one-half designed to model the temporal dynamics of contaminant accumulation and elimination in human organisms with compromised immune systems, particularly following repeated ingestion of contaminated food. The framework quantifies toxin exposure for vulnerable populations with comorbidities, such as unweaned infants, the elderly, and pregnant women, regarding food-borne illnesses. The modeling approach employs the Adomian Decomposition Method alongside Riemann-Liouville fractional integration.

This text explores the post-World War II history of scientific computing within the University of Cambridge's Cavendish Laboratory, specifically focusing on its role in Radio Astronomy. It details the evolution of the aperture synthesis technique and its reliance on pioneering computing systems developed by the Mathematical Laboratory, namely EDSAC, EDSAC 2, and TITAN. The narrative highlights scientific breakthroughs by the Radio Astronomy team, including the gathering of data that refuted the Steady State Hypothesis. Furthermore, it investigates software innovations—such as the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and the degridding algorithm—that facilitated the construction of larger telescopes. Finally, the work uncovers the significant contributions of women, ranging from creating diagrams for publications and programming/operating computers to authoring scientific papers.

Multivariate point processes are extensively utilized to model event-type data, including natural disasters, online communications, financial trades, and neuronal spikes. Among these, the Hawkes process is particularly popular due to its ability to define the probability of new events based on the process's history. This study focuses on the nonlinear Hawkes process, which effectively captures excitation and inhibition dynamics between different dimensions. Within a nonparametric Bayesian estimation framework, we derive concentration rates for the posterior distribution regarding the parameters, assuming only mild conditions on the prior and the model. These findings also establish convergence rates for Bayesian estimators. Additionally, a key aspect of event-data modeling is reconstructing the interaction graph, or Granger connectivity graph. We demonstrate consistency guarantees for Bayesian approaches in estimating this structure, specifically proving that the posterior distribution remains consistent for the process's graph adjacency matrix and that a Bayesian estimator using an appropriate loss function achieves consistency.

Expectiles have recently gained significant traction in risk management due to their robust axiomatic and probabilistic characteristics. Although estimating expectiles at central levels is well-established, their estimation at extreme levels has primarily been addressed only for distributions with heavy right tails. This paper addresses the more difficult scenario of short-tailed distributions, specifically where the variable of interest has a negative extreme value index and is bounded above. We establish an asymptotic expansion for extreme expectiles under a general second-order extreme value condition. This expansion enables the analysis of two semiparametric estimators for extreme expectiles, deriving their asymptotic properties within a broad framework of strictly stationary yet weakly dependent observations. Finally, a simulation study and an analysis of real-world data demonstrate the efficacy of these proposed statistical methods.

This study utilizes data from a real-time monitoring system to examine online local news coverage in the United States. It investigates the connections between COVID-19 reporting, regional case and death counts, and the characteristics of news organizations and their audiences. The analysis is based on a distinctive dataset comprising over 750,000 articles from more than 300 local outlets, collected between April 2020 and February 2021. Our findings indicate that while local news coverage of COVID was initially driven by national death rates, this correlation weakened over time as pandemic reporting gave way to sociopolitical issues, particularly the 2020 U.S. elections. Additionally, we observed that both the quantity and nature of COVID coverage varied according to local political landscapes and outlet audience size, alongside evidence suggesting that more vulnerable populations received less pandemic-related information.

This letter introduces a direct method for constructing cross Z-complementary sequence sets (CZCSSs), characterized by aperiodic correlation sums that maintain zero correlation zones at both the leading and trailing shifts. CZCSSs can be viewed as an extension of the symmetrical Z-complementary code set (SZCCS); however, existing SZCCS constructions are limited to a maximum set size of 8. In contrast, the proposed generalized Boolean function-based approach generates CZCSSs of non-power-of-two lengths with a variable set size of $2^{n+1}$, where each code comprises $2^{n+1}$ constituent sequences. Furthermore, this construction produces cross Z-complementary pairs and sets containing a significantly larger number of constituent sequences than previous methods.

The Independent Cascade (IC) model is a prevalent framework for influence propagation in social networks. This paper integrates causal inference concepts and techniques to examine parameter identifiability from observational data within an extended IC model that accounts for unobserved confounding factors. This extension captures more realistic propagation scenarios but has previously received little attention in influence modeling. We establish conditions determining whether parameters are identifiable or unidentifiable across several specific structures, including the Markovian IC model, the semi-Markovian IC model, and the IC model featuring a global unobserved variable. Establishing parameter identifiability is crucial for related tasks, such as influence maximization in diffusion networks affected by unobserved confounders.

The widespread integration of large language models has ushered in a new age of efficient knowledge transfer across numerous natural language processing tasks. Nevertheless, these models pose a significant risk to user trust by potentially exposing sensitive data about individuals, which malicious actors might extract via adversarial attacks. This study empirically examines the degree to which personal information is embedded within the pre-trained representations of various popular models, revealing a direct correlation between model complexity, the volume of pre-training data, and data leakage. Furthermore, we offer the first comprehensive evaluation and comparison of leading privacy-preserving algorithms using a large, multi-lingual sentiment analysis dataset annotated with demographic details such as location, age, and gender. Our findings indicate that larger, more complex models are more susceptible to leaking private information, making the adoption of privacy-preserving methods essential. Additionally, we observe that highly effective privacy techniques, such as differential privacy (DP), can severely impact model utility; however, this trade-off can be mitigated through the use of hybrid or metric-DP approaches.

This research establishes novel probability bounds for the summation of random, independent Hermitian tensors, specifically characterizing the large-deviation behavior of their extreme eigenvalues. By extending the Laplace transform method and Lieb's concavity theorem from matrices to tensors, the study generalizes classical scalar bounds attributed to Chernoff, Bennett, and Bernstein into the tensor domain. Additionally, tail bounds for the norm of sums of random rectangular tensors are derived as corollaries of the results for Hermitian tensors. The underlying proof techniques are further applicable to tensor-valued martingales, leading to the formulation of tensor-based Azuma, Hoeffding, and McDiarmid inequalities.

Null findings from new physics searches at the LHC do not rule out an intermediate-mass new particle if it exhibits fermiophobia. Within the Type-I two-Higgs-doublet model, a fermiophobic light Higgs boson ($h_{\rm f}$) exists when $\alpha=\pi/2$, while the heavier $CP$-even Higgs boson accounts for the observed 125 GeV Higgs. We first determine the remaining valid parameter space that satisfies theoretical constraints, flavor-changing neutral currents in $B$ physics, a cutoff scale exceeding 1 TeV, Higgs precision measurements, and direct collider search limits. Additionally, we examine the high-energy scale behavior through renormalization group equation analysis. A key finding is that the fermiophobic Type-I model can maintain scalar potential stability up to the Planck scale provided the mass of $h_{\rm f}$ exceeds half the observed Higgs mass. Due to the severely restricted parameter space, particularly regarding the high cutoff scale, signal rates for multi-photon states of the new Higgs boson at the LHC are well predicted. Consequently, we propose $4\gamma+VV'$ ($V^{(\prime)}=Z, W^\pm$) as ideal discovery channels, as these processes benefit from a nearly background-free environment and high selection efficiencies for four photons.

Given a set $P$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and a positive integer $w < n$, the goal is to identify a subset $C \subset P$ with $|C| \leq n-w$ such that the convex hull of the remaining points, $CH(P \setminus C)$, contains the minimum number of vertices. We present a dynamic programming approach for monotone decomposable functions (MDF)—previously established for determining optimal convex $w$-gons with vertices from $P$—originally running in $O(wn^3)$ time, and enhance it to $O(n^3 \log w)$ time. This improvement specifically benefits the existing MDF algorithm when the input is a convex polygon.

The latency inherent in speech processing algorithms is primarily governed by the frame length utilized for Fourier analysis, a factor that constrains the efficacy of magnitude-based methods. Given that prior research indicates phase importance increases as frame length decreases, this study systematically examines the roles of phase and magnitude in contemporary Deep Neural Network (DNN)-driven speech enhancement across varying frame lengths. The findings reveal that DNNs are capable of accurately estimating phase with short frames, achieving performance that matches or surpasses that of longer frames. Consequently, modern phase-aware DNNs enable high-quality, low-latency speech enhancement.

Over the past ten years, the exponential expansion of data has enhanced the capabilities of machine learning algorithms and facilitated their integration into everyday activities. This advancement is partly attributed to the rise of deep learning techniques, which stack simple architectures to form increasingly complex models. While these factors yield remarkable results, they also present challenges, as training intricate models on vast datasets is both costly and time-intensive. These issues are particularly pronounced in video analysis. Although some research has employed transfer learning or domain adaptation to mitigate training difficulties, most methods operate on individual frames or small sequences. This paper introduces a novel approach to transfer knowledge from action recognition to event recognition using an energy-based model called the Spectral Deep Belief Network. This model processes all frames simultaneously, effectively capturing both spatial and temporal information during learning. Experimental results on two public datasets, HMDB-51 and UCF-101, demonstrate the model's efficacy and highlight its reduced computational burden compared to traditional energy-based models like Restricted Boltzmann Machines and Deep Belief Networks.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) is renowned for its ideal conservation properties, guaranteeing exact preservation of total mass, energy, and both linear and angular momentum up to machine precision when correctly implemented. This feature is crucial for computational astrophysics applications involving binary dynamics, mergers, and the accretion of compact objects like neutron stars, black holes, and white dwarfs. However, in scenarios requiring gravity, the computational cost of calculating pairwise particle interactions becomes prohibitive. The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) addresses this by substituting these interactions with symmetric forces between distant particle clusters organized in tree nodes. While standard FMM conserves linear momentum, it generates spurious torques that compromise angular momentum conservation. This paper introduces a modified FMM that eliminates these spurious torques and ensures explicit angular momentum conservation, all with negligible computational overhead compared to the conventional approach.

This study aims to develop a machine learning counterpart to the Optimal Power Flow (OPF) optimization, a critical component in wholesale electricity market-clearing processes. The proposed method addresses the requirement for a digital twin that offers superior speed compared to traditional approaches while maintaining high accuracy and generating consistent results for both primal variables (generation dispatches) and dual variables (Locational Marginal Prices or LMPs). By enabling computationally efficient evaluation of various dispatch scenarios under fixed unit commitments, this approach facilitates the deployment of advanced market-clearing tools. Instead of solving the OPF problem directly, the research formulates the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions and expresses generator and load LMPs using OPF Lagrangian multipliers. Leveraging the practical observation that many line-related multipliers are zero (indicating non-binding thermal limits), the authors construct and train a machine learning framework that maps flexible resources to binding lines. This is supplemented by an efficient, grid-aware linear mapping to derive optimal dispatch and LMPs. The proposed scheme is validated using IEEE models, and a trade-off analysis is presented regarding the relationship between reconstruction quality and the number of training samples required.

Over recent years, the Lightning Network (LN) has experienced rapid expansion, emerging as the leading scaling solution for the Bitcoin blockchain. LN security fundamentally relies on nodes' ability to settle channel balances by confirming transactions on the Bitcoin blockchain within a specific timeframe. This inherent timing constraint makes the network vulnerable to attacks designed to congest the blockchain and disrupt proper protocol execution. This study investigates the LN's susceptibility to \emph{mass exit} attacks launched by a small group of adversarial nodes. In such scenarios, an adversary compels a large number of honest participants to engage with the blockchain. We examine two specific attack vectors: (i) a \emph{zombie} attack, where $k$ nodes become unresponsive to lock funds across numerous channels for longer than the protocol allows, and (ii) a \emph{mass double-spend} attack, where $k$ nodes attempt to steal funds by submitting multiple closing transactions based on expired states, forcing honest nodes to rapidly counter with invalidating transactions. Our simulations demonstrate that, under historically realistic congestion levels and with modest statistical assumptions regarding channel balances, both attacks can be executed by a very small coalition. To identify the worst-case coalition of $k$ adversarial nodes, we modeled the problem as a graph cut problem. These experimental results are further validated by theoretical analysis grounded in the scale-free topology of the LN.

A re-examination of the work by Jaffe, Jenkins, and Kimchi [Phys. Rev. D79, 065014 (2009)] investigates whether the region of congeniality identified in their analysis withstands additional constraints from nucleosynthesis. It is noted that a significant portion of this congenial region vanishes when conditions are applied to generate the correct primordial element abundances and to ensure that stars can initiate stellar nucleosynthesis by burning hydrogen into helium. The surviving region is reduced to a very narrow slit, with the range for the difference between nucleon and quark masses shrinking from approximately 29 MeV to just about 2.2 MeV. Furthermore, additional bounds on $\delta m_q /m_q$ appear to constrain this narrow slit down to the physical point itself.

We investigate the extragalactic HII region Ha luminosity function (LF) using a unique dataset of approximately 23,000 HII regions from the PHANGS-MUSE survey, resolved at an average physical scale of 67 pc. This sample targets the star-forming disks of 19 nearby, low-inclination spiral galaxies that lie near the star formation main sequence at redshift z=0. The mean LF slope ($\alpha$) across our sample is 1.73 ($\sigma$ = 0.15). We observe that $\alpha$ declines as the galaxy's star formation rate surface density increases, attributing this trend to stronger clustering of young stars in regions with high gas surface densities. On an intra-galactic scale, we detect no significant differences in the LF between the inner and outer disk regions; however, for 13 galaxies with distinct spiral arms, the LF slope is shallower within spiral arms compared to inter-arm regions in six cases. We ascribe these spatial variations to spiral arms enhancing the mass contrast between molecular clouds in arm and inter-arm zones, with effects appearing more pronounced in galaxies possessing stronger spiral structures. Finally, we identify systematic shifts in $\alpha$ between HII region samples characterized by high and low ionization parameters ($q$), suggesting these differences arise from the aging process of HII regions.

Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached state-of-the-art levels in medical image segmentation, they depend heavily on extensive manual annotations for training. While Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) offers a path to reduce annotation needs, its effectiveness remains constrained when datasets are small or contain few labeled images. Utilizing pre-annotated datasets featuring similar anatomical structures holds promise for enhancing model performance; however, this approach faces significant hurdles due to cross-anatomy domain shifts caused by variations in appearance and imaging modalities between target and source structures. To address these challenges, we introduce Contrastive Semi-supervised learning for Cross Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA). This method adapts a model to segment analogous structures in a target domain, requiring only minimal target annotations by leveraging a source domain dataset of similar anatomy. Our approach employs Domain-Specific Batch Normalization (DSBN) to normalize feature maps separately for each anatomical domain and proposes a cross-domain contrastive learning strategy to foster the extraction of domain-invariant features. These components are integrated within a Self-Ensembling Mean-Teacher (SE-MT) framework to maximize the utility of unlabeled target images through prediction consistency constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CS-CADA successfully mitigates the challenging cross-anatomy domain shift, enabling accurate segmentation of coronary arteries in X-rays using retinal vessel data, and cardiac MR images using fundus data, even with limited target domain annotations.

This study introduces a diffuse interface framework for compressible multicomponent flows incorporating mass, momentum, and energy transport phenomena, specifically mass diffusion, viscous dissipation, and heat conduction. Derived from the seven-equation Baer-Nunziato model through asymptotic analysis of instantaneous mechanical relaxation limits, the approach distinguishes itself from Kapila's five-equation model by assuming distinct time scales for pressure and velocity relaxations, where the pressure scale is significantly shorter. This assumption preserves velocity disequilibrium to represent the mass diffusion process. Guided by diffusion laws, the resulting system formally comprises five equations. The model satisfies two key criteria: adherence to thermodynamic laws and the elimination of spurious oscillations near the diffused interface. Mass diffusion, viscous dissipation, and heat conduction yield parabolic partial differential equations solved via the Chebyshev local iteration method. Numerical results confirm that the model sustains pressure, velocity, and temperature equilibrium within the diffused interface region. Convergence tests indicate that the numerical scheme achieves second-order accuracy in both space and time. Furthermore, applications to simulating laser-driven Richtmyer-Meshkov instability in inertial confinement fusion demonstrate strong agreement with experimental data.

The $Q^2$ dependence of the cross-section ratio involving proton spin flips, alongside the polarization asymmetry in $e\vec{p} \to e\vec{p}$ scattering, has been numerically evaluated based on JLab polarization data regarding Sachs form factor ratios. These computations assume fully polarized initial (at rest) and final protons sharing a common spin quantization axis aligned with the final proton's momentum. Additionally, longitudinal polarization transfer to the proton was calculated for a partially polarized initial proton within the kinematics of the experiment by Liyanage et al. (SANE Collaboration, Phys. Rev. C 101, 035206 (2020)), which measured double spin asymmetry in the $\vec{e}\vec{p} \to ep$ process. Significant sensitivity of the proton's polarization transfer to the specific form of the $Q^2$ dependence of the $\mu_p G_E/G_M$ ratio was identified. This sensitivity suggests the potential for a new independent experiment to determine this dependence in the $e\vec{p} \to e\vec{p}$ channel. Furthermore, a criterion for evaluating the reliability of Rosenbluth technique measurements of the Sachs form factor ratio was proposed and applied to analyze two experimental results.

This study introduces a new transformer-based architecture designed for medical imaging tasks focused on vertebrae. The model addresses two specific applications using MR images: (a) identifying spinal metastases along with associated conditions like vertebral fractures and metastatic cord compression, and (b) assessing the radiological grading of degenerative changes in intervertebral discs. The key contributions include: (i) the development of the Spinal Context Transformer (SCT), a deep-learning framework optimized for analyzing repeated anatomical structures such as vertebral bodies. Distinct from prior methods, SCT integrates all vertebral bodies across every available imaging modality simultaneously, generating predictions for each vertebra based on contextual information from the entire spinal column and all modalities. (ii) The application of this architecture to a novel task: detecting spinal metastases, cord compression, and vertebral fractures/collapse from multi-series spinal MR scans. This approach utilizes annotations derived from free-text radiological reports rather than custom-made labels, yet the model demonstrates strong concordance with bespoke radiologist annotations at the vertebral level on the test set. (iii) The deployment of SCT to an established problem: radiological grading of intervertebral discs (IVDs) in lumbar MR scans for common degenerative changes. Results indicate that by incorporating the context of vertebral bodies, SCT achieves higher accuracy in several grading metrics compared to previously published models.

Cyclists navigating urban environments face heightened risks from emissions due to their close proximity to vehicles and elevated breathing rates. This paper introduces a routing framework designed to mitigate pollution exposure for cyclists. Unlike traditional studies that rely solely on ambient pollution levels and travel duration, our approach integrates individualized fitness and physiological data. A significant finding from analyzing random synthetic commutes in London is that street-level pollution disproportionately affects individuals with lower fitness levels. Furthermore, our research indicates that inhalation of pollutants in high-risk areas can be reduced by increasing cycling speed. These results demonstrate that personalized travel optimization is a viable strategy for minimizing pollution risks and enhancing the overall benefits of active commuting.

Graphs serve as ubiquitous tools for encoding information, particularly in diverse research domains where data must be modeled through local and spatial relationships. This paper introduces and examines the Attributed Relational SIFT-based Regions Graph (ARSRG), a previously proposed structure for digital image representation that has not been thoroughly investigated in prior literature. The objective is to explore its under-explored characteristics. The study comprises two components: a theoretical section that establishes new formal definitions to clarify the structure's configuration, and an experimental section that evaluates its adaptability and flexibility across various applications. By combining these theoretical and experimental perspectives, the research demonstrates the ARSRG's capacity to adapt to diverse image representations, regardless of content nature.

We derive a Chung-type law of the iterated logarithm, along with exact local and uniform moduli of continuity, for a broad category of anisotropic Gaussian random fields characterized by a harmonizable-type integral representation and strong local nondeterminism. In contrast to prior literature, our findings eliminate the need for the assumption of stationary increments and offer sharper upper and lower bounds for the limiting constants. Furthermore, these results apply to solutions of specific linear stochastic partial differential equations driven by fractional-colored Gaussian noise, such as the stochastic heat equation.

Deep neural networks are found to be vulnerable to imperceptible adversarial attacks, posing significant risks for their deployment in medical diagnostic systems where high reliability is paramount. However, defense strategies effective for natural images often fail in medical contexts; preprocessing techniques like random resizing or compression can erase critical small lesion details, and retraining on augmented data is impractical for models already deployed online. Consequently, there is an urgent need for an efficient, deployable defense framework tailored for medical diagnostics. This paper introduces MedRDF (Robust and Retrain-Less Diagnostic Framework), designed to protect pretrained medical models during inference. For every test image, MedRDF generates numerous noisy variants, collects the predictions from the pretrained model for each variant, and determines the final robust diagnosis through majority voting. Additionally, MedRDF calculates a Robust Metric (RM) to serve as a confidence indicator for the result. This approach offers a convenient and reliable method to transform non-robust pretrained models into robust ones. Experimental evaluations on the COVID-19 and DermaMNIST datasets confirm that MedRDF effectively enhances the robustness of medical diagnostic models.

Deformed relativistic kinematics provides a framework for modeling the effective behavior of particles and fields moving through quantum spacetime. This approach is defined by a modified dispersion relation and an altered momentum conservation law. In this study, we employ Finsler geometry to express deformed relativistic kinematics via particle velocities. By establishing the connection between this velocity-dependent Finsler formulation and the traditional momentum-dependent version, we derive deformed Lorentz transformations applicable to arbitrary reference frames. Furthermore, we determine the corresponding momentum conservation equation, accurate to the first order in the Planck-scale deformation of special relativity based on the $\kappa$-Poincar\'e algebra in the bicrossproduct basis. Our findings indicate that both the deformed Lorentz transformations and the time dilation factor include terms proportional to the fourth power of the particle's energy. We also analyze how the distributions of decay products change under the deformed relativity principle, specifically observing that for a pion decaying into a muon and a neutrino, the ratio of expected neutrinos to muons at a specific energy is only marginally altered compared to standard special relativity predictions. Finally, we examine the phenomenological implications of this framework regarding cosmic-ray showers in the atmosphere.

This work details the theoretical framework and numerical analysis of backscattering rates caused by acceptor holes or Mn spins within HgTe and (Hg,Mn)Te quantum wells operating in the quantum spin Hall regime. We quantify the contributions of anisotropic s-p and sp-d exchange interactions, Kondo coupling, Luttinger liquid effects, precessional dephasing, and bound magnetic polarons. The predicted conductance values and their temperature dependence align with experimental findings for these quantum well systems.

For a finitely presented group $G = F/R$, Hopf's formula relates the second integral homology of $G$ to $F$ and $R$. Building on earlier research, we detail the method for determining generators of $H_2(G;\mathbb{F}_p)$. We also provide the relevant background, which connects to a conjecture by Quillen, along with illustrative computations.

Multimodal object recognition remains an emerging domain, resulting in a scarcity of publicly available datasets that are often limited in size. This dataset was created to address this gap by providing multimodal information for 63 objects, including instances with visual and haptic ambiguity. It comprises visual, kinesthetic, and tactile (audio and vibration) data. While sensory integration or fusion is necessary to fully resolve sensory ambiguity, this report details the dataset's creation and organization. The first section outlines the methodology used to capture visual and haptic characteristics, the second covers the technical requirements and experimental setup for data collection, the third introduces the objects involved, and the final section describes the dataset's structure and contents.

We investigate specific representations of the quantum toroidal $\mathfrak{gl}_1$ algebra under the condition $q=t$. We establish an explicit bosonization for the Fock modules $\mathcal{F}_u^{(n',n)}$, characterized by a nontrivial slope $n'/n$. As a vector space, these modules correspond naturally to the basic level 1 representation of affine $\mathfrak{gl}_n$. Furthermore, we examine twisted $W$-algebras of $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ acting on these Fock modules. As an application, we demonstrate the relationship regarding $q$-deformed conformal blocks, a connection previously conjectured within the context of the $q$-deformation of the isomonodromy/CFT correspondence.

This work investigates weighted Sobolev spaces defined on the half-space $\mathbb{R}^{N+1}_+=\{(x,y): x \in \mathbb{R}^N, y>0\}$, specifically tailored to singular elliptic operators of the form \begin{equation*} \mathcal L =y^{\alpha_1}\Delta_{x} +y^{\alpha_2}\left(D_{yy}+\frac{c}{y}D_y -\frac{b}{y^2}\right). \end{equation*}

Morphological segmentation is the process of breaking words down into morphemes, the smallest units of language that carry meaning. This task is crucial for NLP applications involving morphologically complex agglutinative languages, particularly the Southern African Nguni language group. This paper examines both supervised and unsupervised models for two types of segmentation: canonical and surface segmentation. We employ sequence-to-sequence models for canonical segmentation, where the morphemes differ from the word's surface form, and use Conditional Random Fields (CRF) for surface segmentation. On canonical segmentation, Transformers surpass LSTMs with attention, achieving an average F1 score of 72.5% across four languages. For surface segmentation, feature-based CRFs exceed bidirectional LSTM-CRFs, reaching an average F1 score of 97.1%. In the unsupervised context, an entropy-based method utilizing a character-level LSTM language model fails to beat a Morfessor baseline, and on certain languages, neither method significantly outperforms a random baseline. We anticipate that the high performance of our supervised segmentation models will aid in creating more effective NLP tools for Nguni languages.

Using 2016 CMS data from proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$, the fiducial cross section for producing $\Upsilon$(1S) pairs was measured in the region where both mesons have $|y| < 2.0$. Assuming unpolarized production, the result is $79 \pm 11 \text{ (stat)} \pm 6 \text{ (syst)} \pm 3 \text{ ($\mathcal{B}$)}$ pb, where the final uncertainty reflects the error in the $\Upsilon$(1S) dimuon branching fraction. This measurement, based on the four-muon final state, provides a Standard Model benchmark for searching for narrow resonances decaying into $\Upsilon$(1S)$\mu^+\mu^-$. Such a resonance might signify a $bb\bar{b}\bar{b}$ tetraquark. The search covers a mass range of 17.5–19.5 GeV for potential tetraquarks and 16.5–27 GeV for generic resonances. No significant event excess compatible with a narrow resonance was observed, leading to mass-dependent limits on the cross section times branching fraction for intermediate $\Upsilon$(1S) resonances decaying to four muons.

This paper addresses the reconstruction of a compact Riemannian manifold with a strictly convex boundary using partial travel time data. This dataset assumes the existence of an open measurement region on the boundary, where the distance function from every point within the manifold to the points in this region is known. This geometric inverse problem holds significant relevance to seismology, particularly regarding micro-seismicity. The reconstruction methodology involves embedding the manifold into a function space, a process that necessitates differentiating the distance functions. Consequently, the paper also investigates certain global regularity properties of the distance function on a compact Riemannian manifold featuring a strictly convex boundary.

This study examines the information acquired by a convolutional neural network (CNN) when trained to map synthetic Ca II intensity spectra from a database to the corresponding vertical temperature stratifications of their source atmospheres. Specifically, we assess the network's capacity to discern how the sensitivity of spectral lines to temperature varies with altitude. By training the CNN on narrow wavelength intervals within Ca II spectral profiles, we observe that the temperature prediction error is inversely proportional to the spectral line's temperature response function; consequently, specific spectral regions yield more accurate temperature predictions at their respective expected formation heights. These results demonstrate that the mapping function learned by the CNN during training establishes a physically meaningful connection between wavelength and atmospheric height.

We introduce a variational Bayesian inference framework designed for online identification of nonlinear systems. Upon receiving each output observation, we update a collection of parameter posterior distributions to generate a posterior predictive distribution for subsequent outputs. Our approach targets polynomial NARMAX models, reformulating them into a probabilistic structure represented by a Forney-style factor graph. Efficient inference within this graph is achieved using a variational message passing algorithm. Empirical results demonstrate that our variational Bayesian estimator surpasses online recursive least-squares methods, particularly in scenarios with limited data and low noise, while achieving performance comparable to an iterative least-squares estimator trained offline.

Kidney tumor segmentation has become a significant new area within medical image computer vision, driven by the difficulties of manual annotation and its substantial clinical value. Focusing on the Kidney Tumor Segmentation Challenge 2019, which targets simultaneous segmentation of kidneys and tumors, this study introduces TuNet, an innovative framework that integrates multiple 3D U-Nets to leverage kidney masks for subsequent tumor segmentation. Evaluated via five-fold cross-validation on a dataset of 210 patients, the proposed method achieved Sørensen-Dice coefficients of 0.902 for kidney segmentation and 0.408 for tumor segmentation.

The Farkas lemma is established and utilized to derive a structure theorem for polyhedra. These notes originate from a presentation delivered at the New York Number Theory Seminar on October 20, 2022.

We introduce a straightforward yet potent data-augmentation method designed to facilitate data-efficient learning from parametric experts in reinforcement and imitation learning. Our focus lies in the "policy cloning" scenario, where online or offline expert queries guide a student policy's behavior. This scenario is fundamental to various applications, ranging from behavior cloning variants to components of algorithms like DAGGER, policy distillation, and KL-regularized RL. Our proposed approach, Augmented Policy Cloning (APC), employs synthetic states to generate feedback sensitivity near sampled trajectories, thereby significantly cutting down the environment interactions needed for successful expert cloning. We demonstrate highly data-efficient behavior transfer from experts to student policies, particularly in high-degrees-of-freedom control tasks. Furthermore, we validate our method's advantages within several established algorithms that incorporate policy cloning. Finally, we underscore the utility of APC in two practical contexts: (a) expert compression, involving transfer to a student with fewer parameters, and (b) transfer from privileged experts, where the expert possesses a different, often richer, observation space than the student.

This study examines abstract Cauchy problems involving the Caputo fractional time derivative of order $\alpha\in(0,1]$, focusing on the continuity of their solutions with respect to the parameter $\alpha$. Additionally, I analyze the continuity of Mittag-Leffler families of operators, generated by sectorial operators for $\alpha\in(0,1]$.

We establish the invariance of plurigenera for generalized polarized pairs featuring abundant nef components and generalized canonical singularities. This result is achieved by examining a specific class of newly defined multiplier ideal sheaves that exhibit bimeromorphic properties.

Since the era of Pythagoras, the relationship between mathematics and the physical universe has sparked extensive speculation. Various perspectives on the nature of mathematics have emerged, including Realism (mathematics exists and is discovered), Logicism (mathematics can be deduced solely through pure logic), Formalism (mathematics is merely the manipulation of invented rules and formulas), and Intuitionism (mathematics consists of mental constructs based on self-evident rules). This ongoing debate among these schools is central to understanding Eugene Wigner's concept of "The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences." Conversely, this very effectiveness hints at a resolution favoring Realism. The key factor lies in the remarkable predictive power of mathematical structures that describe physical theories.

We investigate the origin of dynamical friction through a non-perturbative, orbit-focused method. Contrary to the conventional perturbative view, which attributes friction to the Lynden-Bell-Black (LBK) torque from pure resonances, this complementary perspective clarifies how a massive object alters the energy and angular momentum of field particles on near-resonant trajectories, generating friction via an imbalance between energy gainers and losers. By modeling dynamical friction within a spherical host as a restricted three-body problem, we address the "slow" regime where the perturber sinks gradually and non-linearities render standard perturbative methods ineffective. This approach is particularly valuable for studying core-stalling, defined as the halt of dynamical friction within central constant-density cores. We identify three distinct families of near-co-rotation-resonant orbits that primarily drive dynamical friction, with their relative significance determined by Lagrange points (fixed points in the co-rotating frame). Notably, one family, termed "Pac-Man orbits" due to their visual appearance in the co-rotating frame, exists exclusively in cored density distributions. Upon the perturber entering a central core, a bifurcation of the Lagrange points drastically alters the orbital composition, causing Pac-Man orbits to dominate. Furthermore, the relatively shallow gradients of the distribution function within a core result in a net positive torque from these Pac-Man orbits, creating a dynamical buoyancy. We conclude that core stalling occurs at the equilibrium point where this buoyancy counteracts the friction.

Parameterized synthesis addresses the challenge of generating verified, correct controllers for parameterized systems, which frequently arise in practical scenarios such as distributed protocols where the number of processes is undetermined during design and must remain valid regardless of scale. This paper introduces a new learning-based methodology for synthesizing reactive controllers from safety specifications within the context of parameterized systems. By employing regular model checking, we frame the synthesis task as an infinite-duration two-player game and demonstrate how Angluin's renowned L* algorithm can be leveraged to derive correct-by-design controllers. This method yields a synthesis procedure that is conceptually more straightforward than current techniques while offering a completeness guarantee for cases where a winning strategy can be represented by a regular set. We have developed a tool named L*-PSynth to implement this algorithm and evaluated it across various benchmarks, including robotic motion planning and distributed protocols. Despite its conceptual simplicity, L*-PSynth performs competitively against, and in several instances surpasses, leading tools for synthesizing parameterized systems.

A three-dimensional acoustic Luneburg meta-lens offers the benefit of refracting sound waves across all incident angles and generating higher sound pressure levels compared to two-dimensional lenses. Constructed from plastic with a 120 mm diameter, the lens incorporates thousands of lattice column-shaped meta-atoms to sustain its spherical geometry. Its three-dimensional focusing capabilities and acoustic imaging were both simulated and experimentally measured within a frequency range of 5 kHz to 20 kHz. The omnidirectional nature of the device was verified by rotating the lens to vary the angle of incidence while recording sound pressure. Ultimately, the advancement of these spherical Luneburg meta-lenses is anticipated to enhance the performance of applications requiring precise acoustic focusing.

Researchers frequently aim to quantify the impact of consistent pharmacological treatment on health outcomes. However, strict adherence to treatment regimens is often difficult for patients, rendering estimates based on sustained use potentially unhelpful for decision-making when non-adherence is anticipated. As a solution, pragmatic randomized trials and observational studies have explored more flexible protocols that incorporate "grace periods," allowing for intermittent breaks in treatment. This paper examines the interpretation, identification, and estimation of such strategies involving grace periods. We compare natural grace period approaches, which permit individuals to use treatment according to their own patterns, with stochastic strategies where researchers define the distribution of treatment usage. Specifically, we assessed the effects of initiating thiazide diuretics or angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) in hypertensive patients under various strategies with grace periods. Our findings indicate that the risk of adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events is greater with ACEI treatment, and this disparity widens under grace period strategies that result in lower overall drug utilization.

Historically, it was believed that all coronal loops existed in static equilibrium; however, advancements in observation and modeling over the last ten years have disproven this notion. Current understanding indicates that warm (~1 MK) loops detected in the EUV consist of unresolved strand bundles heated impulsively by nanoflare storms. The ongoing debate regarding whether these loops are multi-thermal or isothermal can be resolved by considering storm duration: short storms generate narrow thermal distributions, whereas long storms produce broad ones. We also investigated whether thermal nonequilibrium—where concentrated heating near footpoints creates dynamic behavior under steady heating—could explain warm loops. Our findings suggest this mechanism is not viable for monolithic loops under the conditions studied, though it may apply to multi-stranded loops. Nevertheless, significant questions remain.

Reactor-based experiments offer an ideal framework for investigating potential coherence loss in neutrino oscillations caused by wave-packet separation. By integrating results from the short-baseline Daya Bay and RENO experiments with data from the long-baseline KamLAND experiment, we establish the most stringent current constraint on the reactor antineutrino wave-packet width, finding $\sigma > 2.1 \times 10^{-4}$ nm at 90% confidence level. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the extraction of standard oscillation parameters remains robust; specifically, these determinations are largely unaffected by hypothetical decoherence effects when combining outcomes from the various reactor neutrino experiments.

This study details a search for Higgs boson pair ($hh$) production in conjunction with a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$), utilizing 139 $fb^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected at $\sqrt{s}=$ 13 TeV by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis focuses on final states where the vector boson undergoes leptonic decay ($W	o\ell
u, Z	o\ell\ell,
u
u$, with $\ell=e, \mu$) and each Higgs boson decays into a $b$-quark pair. The investigation targets $Vhh$ signals arising from both Standard Model (SM) non-resonant $hh$ production and resonant $hh$ production predicted by certain SM extensions. An observed 95% confidence-level upper limit of 183 (87) times the SM cross-section was established for non-resonant $Vhh$ production under the assumption of SM kinematics. Additionally, limits were set on Higgs boson coupling modifiers. For the resonant search, upper limits on production cross-sections were determined for two specific scenarios: the production of a vector boson with a neutral heavy scalar resonance $H$ (mass 260–1000 GeV) decaying into $hh$, and the production of a heavier neutral pseudoscalar resonance $A$ (mass 360–800 GeV) decaying into a $Z$ boson and an $H$ boson (mass 260–400 GeV). Furthermore, constraints were derived within the parameter space of two-Higgs-doublet models.

Prior theoretical studies anticipated Ag3AuSe2 to function as a semiconductor with a band gap near 1 eV. This work details the synthesis of single-crystal Ag3AuSe2 and investigates its optical and transport characteristics. The crystals were produced via slow cooling from a melt, with electron backscatter diffraction confirming grain dimensions exceeding 2 mm. Experimental data indicate that Ag3AuSe2 is a highly resistive semiconductor possessing a band gap and activation energy of approximately 0.3 eV. First-principles calculations demonstrate that the observed experimental band gap falls between values predicted by GGA and hybrid functionals. We propose that band inversion could be achieved through the application of tensile strain. Furthermore, the influence of Ag/Au ordering, chemical substitution, and heat treatment on the band gap warrants additional study.

This paper presents our contribution to the IWSLT-2021 offline speech translation challenge. Our architecture follows a cascaded design, comprising speaker diarization, Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), and Machine Translation (MT) components. We employed the LIUM SpkDiarization tool for the diarization stage. The ASR component utilizes a modified Transformer encoder trained via multi-source learning on three datasets from diverse origins. The MT component was initialized with pretraining on the extensive WMT news dataset and subsequently fine-tuned using the TED corpus. This approach yielded a BLEU score of 24.6 on the 2021 evaluation set.

Grasping the ultrafast transport characteristics of hot charge carriers holds both fundamental and practical significance for technologies such as solar cells and transistors; however, directly measuring this transport at nanometer scales remains difficult, with only limited experimental techniques available. This study presents molecular nanoprobe experiments conducted on Si(111)-7x7 at room temperature, demonstrating that charge injected from a scanning tunnelling microscope (STM) tip travels laterally across the surface, inducing reactions in individual toluene adatoms over distances spanning tens of nanometers. We propose a straightforward model to calculate the fraction of tunnelling current captured by each surface electronic band, relying solely on high-resolution scanning tunnelling spectroscopy (STS) data from the clean Si(111)-7x7 surface. This model is quantitatively connected to the voltage dependence of the nanoprobe results via a single manipulation probability per state, serving as the sole fitting parameter. The model successfully aligns with experimental data, explaining observed voltage onsets, the exponential rise in manipulation probabilities, and the subsequent plateau at higher voltages. Furthermore, it validates an ultrafast relaxation of injected charge to the bottom of a surface band immediately after injection and prior to its nonlocal spread.

NeRF generates high-fidelity novel views by modeling scenes with a neural radiance field fitted to RGB images, but its reliance on querying a massive Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) millions of times results in prohibitively slow rendering, even on contemporary GPUs. This paper proposes achieving real-time performance by replacing a single large MLP with thousands of smaller ones. In this approach, each tiny MLP represents only a specific portion of the scene, enabling faster evaluation. By integrating this divide-and-conquer methodology with additional optimizations, rendering speeds increase by three orders of magnitude relative to the original NeRF, all without significantly increasing storage requirements. Furthermore, through teacher-student distillation during training, we demonstrate that these performance gains can be realized without compromising visual quality.

We examine interacting quark matter (IQM), incorporating perturbative QCD corrections and color superconductivity, for both up-down ($ud$QM) and strange quark matter (SQM). By unifying all scenarios through a simple reparametrization and rescaling, we derive an equation of state (EOS) that minimizes the degrees of freedom. Contrary to the standard EOS $p=1/3(\rho-4B_{\rm eff})$ for non-interacting quarks, the extreme strongly interacting limit of our unified IQM EOS yields $p=\rho-2B_{\rm eff}$, where $B_{\rm eff}$ represents the effective bag constant. Utilizing this unified EOS, we investigate the characteristics of pure interacting quark stars (IQSs). Recent astrophysical data, including pulsar mass measurements, NICER analyses, and gravitational-wave events from binary mergers (GW170817, GW190425, and GW190814), are used to further restrict the parameter space. Our analysis establishes an upper limit for the maximum mass of IQSs at $M_{\rm TOV}\lesssim 3.23 M_{\odot}$. Furthermore, our results suggest a novel possibility that observed compact stars, such as the secondary component of GW190814 ($M=2.59^{+0.08}_{-0.09}\, M_{\odot}$), may consist of interacting quark matter.

This work provides a comprehensive, self-contained overview of various approaches to globally describing the geometry of double field theory. Following a review of Courant algebroid geometry and its realization within the AKSZ framework, we establish the theory of metric algebroids and their associated graded geometry. Leveraging metric algebroids, we present a global formulation of doubled geometry that integrates the section constraint and offers an AKSZ-based construction of topological doubled sigma-models. By combining these concepts with elements of para-Hermitian geometry, we show how kinematical aspects of double field theory emerge globally, covering solutions to the section constraint on Riemannian foliated doubled manifolds and a natural definition of generalized T-duality for polarized doubled manifolds. Furthermore, we outline the $L_\infty$-algebras governing the symmetries of doubled geometry and briefly examine other proposals for global doubled geometry found in existing literature.

We report the findings of applying a grammatical test suite to German-to-English machine translation systems from WMT19, featuring a detailed examination of 107 phenomena across 14 categories. On average, these systems still incorrectly translate one out of every four test items. Performance remains particularly low for idioms, modals, pseudo-clefts, multi-word expressions, and verb valency. Compared to the previous year, improvements have been observed in function words, non-verbal agreement, and punctuation. Additionally, we provide more specific conclusions regarding individual systems and particular phenomena.

The Wellington port, known as CentrePort, sustained substantial damage during the $M_w$ 7.8 Kaikoura earthquake due to soil liquefaction, lateral spreading, and structural failures caused by shaking. To understand these impacts and suggest strategies for preventing future occurrences, it was necessary to quantify spatial variations in bedrock depth, shear stiffness, and the fundamental site period ($T_0$) throughout the port area. To characterize $T_0$ and generate shear wave velocity (Vs) profiles for seismic site response modeling, researchers conducted horizontal-to-vertical (H/V) spectral ratio measurements alongside active-source (MASW) and passive-wavefield (MAM) surface wave testing. A map of site periods derived from 114 H/V measurements revealed zones with complex, rapidly changing subsurface structures. Additionally, deep Vs profiles (exceeding 200 meters) established at six reference points were utilized to estimate the depth to soft (Vs > 760 m/s) and hard (Vs > 1500 m/s) rock. Analysis of $T_{0,H/V}$ estimates from these six locations demonstrated a relationship with hard rock depth based on linear viscoelastic transfer functions computed from Vs profiles truncated at various depths. Furthermore, $T_{0,H/V}$ values recorded at two ground motion stations near the port showed reasonable agreement with the predominant periods of maximum spectral amplification observed during the 2016 Kaikoura and 2013 Cook Strait earthquakes, even accounting for soil nonlinearity and potential 3D basin edge effects at these sites.

With the rising frequency of cyber attacks driving up insurance premiums, there is a growing necessity for improved cyber risk modeling.
