Addressing this, Jevtić and Lanchier (2020) introduced a dynamic structural model for the aggregate loss distribution of small and medium-sized enterprises, based on a tree-based local-area-network topology integrating Poisson processes, homogeneous random trees, bond percolation, and cost topology. Their framework assumes contagion spreads across network edges with a fixed, symmetric probability, thereby neglecting the dynamic security realities of most networks; consequently, while they derived an exact formula for the mean aggregate loss, their estimate for the variance remains only a rough upper bound. In contrast, this paper proposes a bidirectional extension of their percolation model where contagion propagates toward lower-level assets with one probability and toward higher-level assets with another, creating a more realistic representation of cyber security environments. Furthermore, our distinct mathematical approach yields exact expressions for both the mean and variance of the aggregate loss, thereby enabling the precise calculation of insurance premiums.

This study introduces an adapted gyrokinetic framework designed to forecast the critical gradient triggering the linear onset of ion temperature gradient (ITG) modes in stellarator plasmas. By applying a coarse-graining method to the drift curvature within standard gyrokinetic equations near local minima, this new formalism offers a simple approach. Its computational efficiency allows for practical use in stellarator optimization. Comparisons with a gyrokinetic solver reveal strong agreement across various stellarator configurations. The physical insights gained regarding ITG instability onset facilitate the design of a compact stellarator, akin to Wendelstein 7-X, that achieves nearly double the linear ITG critical gradient, enhanced nonlinear critical gradients, and diminished ITG mode transport beyond the nonlinear threshold.

Preliminary findings regarding J/psi spectra at elevated transverse momentum (5 < p_T < 14 GeV/c) are presented for both p+p and Cu+Cu collisions at s_NN = 200 GeV. A nuclear modification factor of 0.9 +/- 0.2 is determined for p_T > 5 GeV/c. Additionally, correlations between J/psi and charged hadrons are examined in p+p collisions to elucidate the high p_T J/psi production mechanism.

Decentralized Finance (DeFi) applications form a comprehensive financial ecosystem operating on blockchains, relying on intricate protocols and incentive structures that make assessing their financial safety challenging. Given the rapid expansion of DeFi adoption, which exposes ever-increasing amounts of assets to risk, precise formalization and verification of these applications are crucial for evaluating their security. We have created a tool designed for the formal analysis of Lending Pools (LP), one of the most prevalent DeFi applications. This development utilized an established formal model for LPs, the Maude verification environment, and the MultiVeStA statistical analyser. The tool facilitates various analyses, including reachability, LTL model checking, and statistical model checking. This paper demonstrates how the tool can examine key parameters within LPs to assess and forecast their behavior. Specifically, we employ statistical analysis to identify optimal threshold and reward parameters that reduce the risk of unrecoverable loans.

This study employs large eddy simulations of propane/air jet flames operating in the wrinkled flamelets regime of the Borghi diagram to evaluate a newly developed consumption speed correction model for premixed combustion. The combustion process utilizes flamelet tabulation combined with a presumed probability density function. The examined flame, situated outside the shear layer and undergoing self-driven oscillations, provides an optimal scenario for assessing the model's efficacy. Initial analysis relies on an accurate simulation conducted on a refined mesh without any corrections. In contrast, applying the same modelling framework to a coarser mesh results in an overestimation of the consumption speed and a consequent reduction in flame length. Implementing the consumption speed correction successfully restores the flame length and width observed in the refined mesh simulation, thereby validating its effectiveness. Furthermore, an extended model designed for partially-premixed combustion is introduced and preliminarily evaluated using a high-pressure combustor.

We investigate false vacuum decay processes catalyzed by magnetic monopoles, which function as tunneling portals with exponentially accelerated rates. Unlike the standard $O(3)/O(4)$ symmetric field profiles, these decays exhibit different symmetries, necessitating an expanded approach to calculating decay rates. To numerically identify the saddle point solutions characterizing the tunneling event, we employ a novel algorithm grounded in the mountain pass theorem. This technique is broadly applicable to phase transitions involving reduced symmetry, including scenarios far from zero and infinite temperature limits. Our findings indicate that monopole-catalyzed tunneling can surpass homogeneous false vacuum decay across a broad parameter range, substantially altering gravitational wave signatures or initiating phase transitions that would otherwise remain incomplete. Consequently, a solitary monopole within our Hubble volume could dictate the stability and lifetime of the Standard Model vacuum.

This paper introduces a scalable neural network hardware architecture designed for image segmentation. By utilizing shared computing resources, both convolution and deconvolution operations are executed by the same process element array. Furthermore, memory access to both on-chip and off-chip storage is optimized to mitigate the overhead caused by partial sums. As a demonstration, SegNet-Basic was implemented on a Xilinx ZC706 FPGA using this unified architecture, achieving performance rates of 151.5 GOPS for convolution and 94.3 GOPS for deconvolution. This unified design is suitable for other CNNs that incorporate deconvolution layers.

Camera-trap image label distributions are characterized by significant imbalance and a long-tail pattern, causing neural networks to favor frequent head-classes. While long-tail learning has been extensively investigated to mitigate data imbalance, few studies have addressed specific camera-trap characteristics, such as multi-domain and multi-frame configurations. In this work, we introduce a unified framework and two novel datasets tailored for long-tailed camera-trap recognition. First, we develop domain experts that individually learn to correct decision boundaries distorted by data imbalance, thereby collectively generating balanced boundaries. Additionally, we propose a flow consistency loss that prioritizes moving objects by ensuring class activation maps across multiple frames align with optical flow maps. To validate our approach, we present the WCS-LT and DMZ-LT datasets. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's efficacy, with our proposed methods outperforming previous approaches, particularly on samples from recessive domains.

The ability to determine the path of a quantum particle within an interferometer is fundamental to inferring its history, a concept that has sparked extensive debate regarding quantum complementarity and the relationship between path and visibility. These discussions fundamentally rely on the description, detection, and manipulation of which-path information. This study investigates multidimensional which-path information within a nested Mach-Zehnder interferometer. We derive a general expression for this information, which can be partially extracted through various detection techniques. Further analysis demonstrates that such information can be regulated by adjusting phase differences and beam splitting ratios between the interferometer's arms. Additionally, we predict and experimentally verify a novel phenomenon involving the elimination of which-path information. Our findings enhance the understanding of quantum particle physics and hold potential applications for quantum information processing and metrology.

A Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) was employed to analyze the statistical characteristics and properties of voids within a $\Lambda$CDM universe. The total count of voids and the size distribution are comparable between the generated and simulated image sets, and the average void properties align within formal error margins. However, the generated images contain a slightly reduced number of small voids and significantly fewer voids with a central density contrast of approximately $-1$. Consequently, the distribution of mean interior density contrasts for generated voids is systematically higher than that of simulated voids due to the scarcity of the emptiest voids in the generated set. While the mean radial underdensity profiles for the largest voids are broadly similar, systematic deviations exist: on small scales ($r < 0.5r_{v}$), generated voids exhibit stronger underdensities, whereas simulated voids show greater underdensity on large scales ($r > 0.5r_{v}$). These discrepancies arise from the GAN's difficulty in capturing absolute data patterns, specifically manifesting as an underproduction of pixels with density contrasts near $-1$ and an overproduction of pixels with contrasts between $-0.88$ and $-0.63$.

Traditionally, optimal screening designs for any run size are generated using the D-criterion with factor levels fixed at ±1, even for continuous factors defined within the [-1, 1] range. This paper highlights undesirable variance characteristics in such D-optimal designs and contends that A-optimal designs generally yield variances closer to their theoretical minimum. By analyzing the coordinate-exchange formulas for these criteria, new insights into their behavior are revealed. The study confirms that D-optimal designs consisting solely of ±1 settings exist for both main effect and interaction models in blocked and unblocked experiments. Furthermore, specific scenarios are identified where arbitrarily adjusting a coordinate within [-1, 1] results in infinitely many D-optimal designs with varying variance properties; under these same conditions, the A-criterion yields a unique optimal coordinate value for improvement. Additionally, the paper compares Bayesian versions of the A- and D-criteria regarding their trade-offs between minimizing estimation variance and bias, supported by multiple examples of screening designs across various models under both Bayesian and non-Bayesian frameworks for these criteria.

Luminescent solar concentrators (LSCs) function by capturing a segment of the solar spectrum and directing it toward photon harvesting units. However, modeling these devices at a quantum chemical level presents significant challenges due to the intricate dynamics of excitons and photons. This research investigates singlet exciton behavior within a standard LSC configuration. Utilizing a rejection-free kinetic Monte Carlo approach, the study predicts diffusion lengths, coefficients, substrate anisotropy, and average exciton lifetimes for perylene diimide (PDI) and tetracene substrates under low-concentration conditions. Rate constants are derived using time-dependent density functional theory based on *ab initio* calculations. Results indicate that PDI substrates exhibit superior singlet exciton transport characteristics compared to tetracene. Furthermore, simulations reveal that substrates featuring dipole-aligned chromophores display anisotropic exciton diffusion with marginally enhanced transport capabilities. Finally, a PDI-tetracene hybrid substrate was modeled in both disordered and dipole-aligned states; in this multi-dopant system, transport is primarily governed by PDI due to the disparity in transport rates between the two dyes. The study concludes by analyzing the properties of multi-dopant substrates and their potential influence on the design of future-generation LSCs.

Although applying formal privacy-preserving methods such as Differential Privacy (DP) to machine learning enables the extraction of valuable insights from sensitive medical imaging data while safeguarding patient privacy, it typically results in a significant privacy-utility trade-off. This study introduces the use of steerable equivariant convolutional networks for medical image analysis under DP constraints. By leveraging their enhanced feature quality and parameter efficiency, these networks achieve notable accuracy improvements that substantially narrow the gap between privacy and utility.

Following recent observations of anomalies in semileptonic decays across multiple collider experiments that suggest potential lepton universality violation, we present a concise overview of the theoretical underpinnings of tree- and loop-level b-hadron decays alongside their experimental contexts. We re-examine the global averages for $R_{D(D^*)}$, $R_{K(K^*)}$, $R_{J/\psi}$, and $R_{\eta_c}$, offering predictions based on the relativistic independent quark model in conjunction with model-independent analyses. A confirmation of these findings would constitute the first evidence of physics beyond the Standard Model, thereby broadening our perspective on new physics and enhancing our understanding of it.

We examine a scenario where an agent repeatedly selects actions to maximize cumulative payoff, which depends on both the chosen action and an evolving, unknown state of the world. Prior to each decision, the agent may spend from a limited budget to acquire noisy observations of this state, with the freedom to allocate funds across rounds as they see fit. We analyze the problem of identifying a sampling strategy that maximizes total expected payoff, specifically comparing steady sampling against batched acquisition. We derive the optimal policy, demonstrating that it naturally favors batched sampling. Furthermore, under a generalized framework incorporating fixed costs per round, we prove that a modified version of this batching approach achieves a 2-approximation.

This paper introduces an intelligent algorithm for unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs) specifically designed to mitigate the impact of ocean currents during optimal pathfinding. The methodology comprises two key components: a neural network module responsible for calculating the shortest collision-free route, and an adjustment mechanism that compensates for deviations caused by current forces. The study provides a detailed analysis of the algorithm's optimization results and compares them against traditional path planning methods that ignore current effects. The comparative analysis confirms the superior effectiveness of the proposed approach when navigating currents of varying directions and speeds.

Lanconelli and Scorolli (2021) recently generalized a Wong-Zakai-type approximation for Itô stochastic differential equations, originally proposed by \Oksendal and Hu (1996), to a multidimensional setting. This paper aims to further extend that result to systems of Itô-type stochastic differential equations driven by fractional Brownian motion (fBm), similar to those analyzed by Hu (2018). Due to the specific covariance structure of fBm, the methodology employed by Lanconelli and Scorolli cannot be applied; instead, we utilize a truncated Cameron-Martin expansion to approximate the fBm. This approach necessitates the study of a semilinear hyperbolic system of evolution equations across multiple spatial variables, which we employ to construct solutions for the Wong-Zakai approximated systems. We demonstrate that the probability law of each component in the approximating sequence satisfies a Fokker-Planck equation in the distributional sense, and that the sequence converges to the solution of the Itô equation as the number of terms in the expansion approaches infinity.

Continuous-time quantum walks (CTQWs) serve as a significant framework for quantum transport, universal quantum computation, and spatial search, among other applications. Recent research has highlighted the utility of incorporating new degrees of freedom—specifically, complex phases along the loops of the underlying graph—into the Hamiltonian generator of CTQWs to optimize or suppress transport across various topologies. We propose that the quantum-classical distance, a metric designed to quantify the dynamical divergence between a CTQW and its classical stochastic equivalent, acts as a guiding figure of merit. This metric facilitates the optimization of Hamiltonian parameters to enhance quantum transport on cycle graphs and to achieve the quantum speed limit for spatial search on complete graphs without an oracle, a result that also ensures rapid uniform mixing. By comparing fluctuations in this distance against the 1-norm of coherence and the Inverse Participation Ratio, we demonstrate that the quantum-classical distance is connected to both, albeit through topology-dependent relationships that are essential for identifying the most significant quantum evolutions in specific contexts.

Recent initiatives aim to boost machine learning performance in collider physics by aggregating multiple distinct events into unified ensemble features. To assess these approaches, we examine the relationship between single-event and multi-event classifiers under the assumption that collider events are independent and identically distributed (IID). We demonstrate methods for constructing optimal multi-event classifiers from single-event ones and vice versa. These concepts are illustrated using a Gaussian example and classification tasks pertinent to searches and measurements at the Large Hadron Collider. Furthermore, we extend the discussion to regression by framing it within parametrized classifiers. Empirical results indicate that training a single-event (per-instance) classifier is more effective than training a multi-event (per-ensemble) classifier for the scenarios analyzed, a finding linked to the properties of the loss function gradient in both cases. Although no clear advantage was found for multi-event classifiers in this specific collider context, we speculate on their potential utility in situations involving approximate independence, such as those encountered in jet substructure studies.

Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy (CRES) measures the kinetic energy of charged particles by precisely analyzing the frequency of cyclotron radiation emitted as they move within a magnetic field. The Project 8 collaboration is leveraging this technique to develop an advanced experiment for determining neutrino mass. One proposed method involves a phased antenna array enclosing a volume of tritium gas to detect and quantify the cyclotron radiation from $\beta$-decay electrons. To verify the viability of this approach, Project 8 established a test stand to evaluate how well an antenna array can reconstruct signals simulating authentic CRES events. A new probe antenna was created to generate these synthetic events, emitting radiation that closely mimics the cyclotron radiation of charged particles in magnetic fields. This paper details the design, assembly, and characterization of the Synthetic Cyclotron Antenna (SYNCA). Additionally, we conducted a series of measurements using the SYNCA to assess the position reconstruction abilities of the digital beamforming technique. Our results indicate that the SYNCA generates radiation characteristics that align closely with expected cyclotron radiation and successfully replicates the experimental phenomenology observed in digital beamforming simulations of true CRES signals.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a potent method for deriving predictions from biological datasets, yet their use with neuroimaging data, particularly functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), remains underexplored. Despite this limitation, leveraging GNNs for fMRI analysis promises to significantly enhance predictive accuracy and potentially aid future clinical diagnostics. This study introduces a new framework for encoding resting-state fMRI data into a graph structure of nodes and edges that retains all voxels, thereby minimizing information loss. By evaluating various GNN architectures, we demonstrate their capability to accurately predict both disease status and sex. We aim to establish a foundation for future research that harnesses the full potential of GNNs in brain imaging applications.

To assist development teams in prioritizing Software Quality Assurance (SQA) efforts based on the probability of defects, defect prediction models have been introduced. However, developers often expend unnecessary resources on entire files when only a small portion contains errors; our findings indicate that defective lines constitute merely 1% to 3% of a file's total code. Consequently, this work introduces LINE-DP, a novel framework designed to pinpoint defective lines using a model-agnostic, Explainable AI approach that elucidates the reasoning behind model predictions. Specifically, LINE-DP first constructs a file-level defect model utilizing code token features. It then employs the state-of-the-art LIME technique to identify "risky tokens"—specific code tokens that drive the model's prediction of file-level defects. Lines containing these risky tokens are subsequently classified as defective. A case study involving 32 releases from nine Java open-source systems demonstrates that LINE-DP outperforms six baseline methods, achieving an average recall of 0.61, a false alarm rate of 0.47, a top 20% LOC recall of 0.27, and an initial false alarm count of 16. Furthermore, the framework requires an average computation time of 10 seconds for both model construction and defective line identification. Additionally, 63% of the identified defective lines correspond to common defects, such as argument or condition changes. These results suggest that LINE-DP effectively locates defective lines associated with common issues while minimizing inspection effort and maintaining a manageable computational cost.

This note demonstrates that $\mathcal{Q}$-groups, as defined in [H. Heineken and F.G. Russo, Groups described by element numbers, Forum Math. 27 (2015), 1961--1977], are solvable groups (though not necessarily nilpotent) satisfying the equation $T_G(r,s)=0$.

Session types offer a flexible approach to structuring interactions and ensuring the safe, consistent composition of distributed processes. However, traditional session types rely solely on one-directional input and output guarded choices, which limits their ability to match the full expressive power of the pi-calculus, where mixed choices are demonstrably more powerful. To address this limitation, Casal, Mordido, and Vasconcelos recently introduced binary session types with mixed choices (CMV+). This paper presents a surprising and unfortunate finding regarding CMV+: despite incorporating unrestricted channels with mixed choice, the system's mixed choice mechanism remains effectively separate rather than truly mixed. We demonstrate this negative result through two distinct methodologies—utilizing either the leader election problem or a specific synchronization pattern as distinguishing criteria—to prove that no good encoding exists from the pi-calculus into CMV+ that preserves distribution. Furthermore, we resolve an open problem posed by the authors concerning the encoding from CMV+ to CMV (which lacks mixed choice), establishing its soundness and confirming that the encoding is valid up to coupled similarity.

We introduce a technique to produce multi-mode entangled catalysis squeezed vacuum states (MECSVS) by integrating a cross-Kerr nonlinear medium within a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. This approach facilitates the exchange of quantum states across different modes via the Fredkin gate. Furthermore, we investigate the application of MECSVS as a probe state in multi-arm optical interferometers for the simultaneous estimation of multiple phases. Our findings indicate that the Quantum Cramer-Rao bound (QCRB) for phase estimation improves by either increasing the count of catalytic photons or reducing the transmissivity of the optical beam splitter employed in the photon catalysis process. Additionally, we demonstrate that despite photon loss, the QCRB of our photon catalysis scheme remains lower than that of ideal entangled squeezed vacuum states (ESVS), highlighting that the photon catalytic operation offers greater robustness against photon loss compared to schemes without catalysis. These results hold significant potential for applications in quantum metrology concerning multiparameter estimation.

We investigate two-dimensional eternal black holes possessing non-zero mass, where each asymptotic boundary interfaces with a CFT on a circle, adhering to the doubly holographic braneworld frameworks outlined in [arXiv:2006.04851, arXiv:2010.00018, arXiv:2010.16398]. Our analysis calculates the Page curve for the black hole or the bath CFTs by identifying distinct geodesics within the bulk BTZ geometry featuring a Randall-Sundrum brane descending into the black hole. We further examine the potential inclusion of an intrinsic JT gravity action on the brane. Consistent with expectations, the generalized entropy increases linearly during early times. Subsequently, a transition occurs to a late-time regime where the entropy stabilizes. This late-time entropy value is contingent upon the dimensions of the thermal baths: for small baths, it matches their thermal entropy, whereas for large baths, it equals twice the black hole's horizon entropy. The critical size and Page time are directly proportional to the ratio of the central charges of the conformal defect and the bath CFT.

Feynman's circuit-to-Hamiltonian construction serves as a bridge between quantum computation and the ground states of many-body quantum systems. Kitaev utilized this framework to prove the QMA-completeness of the local Hamiltonian problem, while Aharanov and colleagues employed it to establish the equivalence between adiabatic computation and the quantum circuit model. This study examines the low-energy characteristics of a specific class of modified circuit Hamiltonians, incorporating elements such as complex weights and branching transitions. For systems featuring linear clocks and complex weights, we devise a technique to adjust the circuit propagation Hamiltonian, enabling any desired distribution over time steps within a frustration-free ground state. We demonstrate that this approach facilitates a constant output probability for universal adiabatic computation while maintaining the $\Omega(T^{-2})$ spectral gap scaling, all without increasing the qubit count. Additionally, we delineate constraints on ground energy increases caused by input and output penalty terms in modified tridiagonal clocks with non-uniform time-step distributions by proving a tight $O(T^{-2})$ upper bound on the product of the spectral gap and ground state overlap at computation endpoints. By employing variational methods that surpass the $\Omega(T^{-3})$ scaling derived from standard geometrical lemmas, we show that the conventional Feynman-Kitaev Hamiltonian already reaches this bound. We also review the formalism of unitary labeled graphs, which substitute linear clocks with structures permitting branching and loops, and extend the $O(T^{-2})$ bound from linear clocks to this broader context. To accomplish this, we utilize Chebyshev polynomials to generalize an upper bound on the spectral gap—originally based on graph diameter—to the domain of arbitrary Hermitian matrices.

Mastering counting serves as a key illustration of the human ability to generalize systematically, a developmental process typically marked by a rapid surge in proficiency known as an inflection point. This study sought to replicate such a trajectory by training a reinforcement learning agent on the give-$N$ task, which involves selecting $N$ items from a binary vector upon instruction. Our results indicate that a memory-augmented modular network, built upon the recently introduced Emergent Symbol Binding Network (ESBN), displayed a learning inflection mirroring human development. Furthermore, this model demonstrated systematic extrapolation beyond its training limits; for instance, after being trained only to choose between 1 and 10 items, it successfully handled requests for 11 to 15 items, provided it could access an arbitrary count sequence of sufficient length. These strong parallels to child development and the model's capacity for extrapolation imply that this architecture may offer valuable insights into how systematicity emerges in humans.

Within the Stueckelberg-Wheeler-Feynman "one-electron Universe" framework, we examine a worldline implicitly characterized by a system of algebraic (specifically polynomial) equations. Pointlike "particles" of two distinct types are located along this worldline (or its complex extension) at the real (or complex conjugate) roots of the polynomial system, identified by an external inertial observer via light cone connections. Consequently, the collective dynamics of this particle ensemble generally adheres to several Lorentz invariant conservation laws. Notably, this characteristic arises directly from Vieta's formulas applied to the generating polynomial system. At specific discrete intervals of the observer's proper time, pairs of particle-roots merge and undergo transmutation, thereby simulating particle/antiparticle annihilation and creation processes.

Bloom filters offer rapid approximate set membership with minimal memory usage, making them popular among engineers for bypassing slow disk or network operations. In contrast, Cuckoo filters can be faster and require less space than Bloom filters. Chazelle and colleagues introduced the Bloomier filter as a generalization of the Bloom filter, while Dietzfelbinger and Pagh proposed a variation suitable for approximate membership queries that, to our knowledge, has never been empirically tested. This paper reviews an efficient implementation of their method, termed the xor filter. Our findings indicate that xor filters outperform both Bloom and Cuckoo filters in speed while consuming less memory. Additionally, we demonstrate that a more compact variant, the xor+ filter, occupies even less space than highly compressed alternatives like Golomb-compressed sequences, while maintaining speed comparable to standard Bloom filters.

We examine the well-known challenge of agnostically learning intersections of halfspaces under the Gaussian distribution. While Diakonikolas et al. (2021) previously demonstrated that any Statistical Query (SQ) algorithm achieving constant excess error for this class over $\mathbb{R}^n$ must either use queries with tolerance as low as $n^{-\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{\log k})}$ or perform $2^{n^{\Omega(1)}}$ queries, we improve this bound by raising the tolerance requirement to $n^{-\tilde{\Omega}(\log k)}$. This new lower bound is nearly tight, as Klivans et al. (2008) established an SQ algorithm that learns the same class with $n^{O(\log k)}$ queries and tolerance $n^{-O(\log k)}$. Our proof presents two variants, each merging components from Diakonikolas et al. (2021) with an extension of Dachman-Soled et al.'s (2014) earlier Boolean-setting approach. Furthermore, our method derives lower bounds for agnostically SQ learning "convex subspace juntas" (Vempala, 2010) and sets with bounded Gaussian surface area; these results are also nearly optimal because they align closely with the upper bounds provided by Klivans et al. (2008).

This paper demonstrates that on triangular rings, without the assumption of unity, every Jordan centralizer and every Jordan two-sided centralizer functions as a standard centralizer. As an application, we establish that every Jordan generalized derivation on a triangular ring is necessarily a two-sided generalized derivation. Additionally, other related findings are examined.

Recent Early Release Observations by JWST have captured deep images and near-infrared spectra of galaxies within the lensing cluster SMACS J0723.3-7327. Notably, this data includes two NIRSpec spectra of galaxies at redshift $z=7.7$ and one at $z=8.5$, marking the first-ever detection of rest-frame optical emission lines from the epoch of reionization, including the crucial [OIII]4363 auroral line (refer to JWST PR 2022-035). Our analysis of these emission lines reveals characteristics typical of low-metallicity star-forming galaxies, such as high excitation ratios ([OIII]/[OII], [NeIII]/[OII]), elevated [OIII]4363/H$\gamma$ ratios, and high equivalent widths. Applying the direct method, we calculated oxygen abundances of $12+\log(O/H)=7.9$ for the two $z=7.7$ galaxies, while strong line methods yielded a lower metallicity of $12+\log(O/H)\approx 7.4-7.5$ for the $z=8.5$ galaxy; however, more precise metallicity estimates will depend on improved data. Based on stellar masses derived from spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting, these three galaxies align closely with or fall below the $z \sim 2$ mass-metallicity relation. In summary, these initial JWST spectra at $z \sim 8$ demonstrate that the emission line properties of reionization-era galaxies strongly resemble those of rare local analogues previously identified in SDSS surveys. These early observations underscore the remarkable capability of spectroscopy to uncover the properties of galaxies in the early Universe.

Constellations serve as asymmetric generalizations of categories. While they do not inherently require a range concept, numerous natural instances do exhibit this property. These include constellations linked to concrete categories—which model surjective morphisms—as well as those derived from distinct origins, such as specific classes of semigroups. We demonstrate that constellations equipped with a well-behaved range operation are essentially ordered categories with restrictions. Furthermore, we abstractly characterize categories that act as canonical extensions of constellations with range, defining them as IS-categories. These categories feature distinguished subcategories of insertions (monomorphisms) and surjections (distinct from epimorphisms), ensuring every morphism admits a unique factorization into a surjection followed by an insertion. Most standard concrete categories qualify as IS-categories, and we illustrate how key properties of these categories stem from this classification. Finally, by selecting appropriate morphisms, we establish that the category of IS-categories is equivalent to the category of constellations with range.

Predictive recursion (PR) is a rapid recursive method that provides a smooth estimate of the mixing distribution within the general mixture model framework. However, the PR algorithm necessitates the calculation of a normalizing constant at every iteration. When the mixing distribution's support has low dimensionality, this is manageable using efficient quadrature methods. Conversely, in higher-dimensional settings, quadrature becomes inefficient, and no clear Monte Carlo alternative exists. To address this, we introduce a novel approach called the PRticle filter. This method enhances the standard PR algorithm by incorporating a filtering mechanism that adaptively reweights an initial particle set along the update sequence, thereby generating Monte Carlo approximations for the normalizing constants. We establish the convergence properties of this PRticle filter approximation and validate its empirical accuracy through simulation studies and an analysis of marked spatial point process data.

Motifs are unique, recurring components within folklore that function as meaningful communicative tools in news, literature, press releases, and propaganda. By briefly encapsulating a vast array of culturally significant information, their widespread use highlights their cognitive role as anchors of cultural knowledge, thereby making their identification a valuable objective for culturally aware natural language processing. Historically, folklorists and researchers have relied solely on manual extraction to identify these motifs from narratives. This paper presents a preliminary account of a system designed for the automatic detection of motifs. We outline an ongoing annotation initiative intended to generate training data and provide a detailed overview of our current architecture, which seeks to model the human process of determining if a motif candidate is being employed in a "motific" manner. This description includes an evaluation of a commercial metaphor detector as a feature for motif detection, yielding an F1 score of 0.35 for motifs and a macro-average F1 of 0.21 across four assigned categories of motif candidates.

Panoptic segmentation seeks to unify semantic and instance segmentation within a single framework, yet finding an efficient solution for applications such as autonomous driving remains an unsolved challenge. To address this, we introduce SMAC-Seg, a novel LiDAR-based panoptic system. Our approach employs a learnable sparse multi-directional attention clustering mechanism to handle multi-scale foreground instances. As a real-time, clustering-driven method, SMAC-Seg eliminates the need for complex proposal networks typically used for instance segmentation. While most existing clustering methods rely solely on the offset between predicted and ground truth centers to supervise centroid regression, this strategy overlooks the relative spatial relationships between neighboring objects during clustering. Consequently, we introduce a novel centroid-aware repel loss as an additional supervision term to effectively distinguish each object cluster from its neighbors. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that SMAC-Seg achieves state-of-the-art performance among all real-time deployable networks on the SemanticKITTI and nuScenes panoptic segmentation benchmarks.

We introduce a novel wavelet-based approach for density estimation tailored to size-biased data. Specifically, this method focuses on estimating a power of the target density, where the exponent is greater than 1/2. The approach utilizes warped wavelet bases, achieved through a continuous cumulative distribution function (c.d.f.). This framework encompasses conventional orthonormal wavelet estimation as a specific instance where the warping c.d.f. is the standard uniform distribution. We demonstrate that both linear and nonlinear wavelet estimators within this framework are consistent, achieving optimal or near-optimal convergence rates. Monte Carlo simulations compare four practical, easily interpretable scenarios, and a real-world application involving fatal traffic accidents related to alcohol usage illustrates the method's utility. Results indicate that warped bases yield more flexible and superior estimates for both simulated and real data. Furthermore, estimating a power of the density (such as its square root) leads to additional improvements in performance.

Phase-change memory (PCM) represents a scalable, low-latency non-volatile memory (NVM) technology designed to function as storage class memory (SCM). It offers access speeds comparable to DRAM while often surpassing the capacity of SSDs. Additionally, PCM's multilevel capability makes it suitable for neuromorphic applications, enabling the creation of high-density synaptic storage. This study examines and outlines two primary limitations within PCM systems: first, writing operations entail substantially greater latency and energy costs compared to reading; second, the high operating voltages required can compromise reliable operation. To address these challenges, we propose specific methodologies aimed at enhancing the performance, reliability, energy efficiency, and sustainability of PCM systems.

Nodal loop semimetals exhibit a torus-shaped, highly anisotropic Fermi surface near the Fermi energy, which significantly influences their transport characteristics. This study explores the non-equilibrium dynamics of these materials by moving beyond linear response theory to analyze the time-dependent current following the application of a uniform electric field. When the field is oriented perpendicular to the nodal loop plane, the current increases monotonically over time; conversely, fields aligned within the plane induce non-monotonic behavior. Following an initial non-universal growth phase proportional to $Et$, the current reaches a plateau scaling with $E$. For perpendicular fields, the current subsequently rises, whereas for in-plane fields, it declines to a second plateau, also scaling with $E$. These dynamics originate from interband processes. At long durations or under strong electric fields, the current follows growth laws of $\sim E^{3/2}t$ for perpendicular fields and $\sim E^3t^2$ for parallel fields. This nonlinear response stems from an intraband effect driven by a large population of excited quasiparticles reacting to the field. The analytical findings are validated through numerical calculations of the current using both continuum and tight-binding models of nodal loop semimetals.

Sequential Recommendation encompasses techniques designed to capture dynamic user behavior for predicting future interactions within sequential data. Fundamentally, these methods model the transition probabilities between items using Markov chains, recurrent networks, or Transformers. Despite these advancements, challenges such as data sparsity and noise persist, often degrading performance in complex, parameter-intensive models. This paper explores applying contrastive Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) to sequential recommendation to mitigate these problems. By generating augmentations from unlabeled instances and maximizing agreement among positive pairs, contrastive SSL faces significant hurdles when adapted to sequential recommendation due to the discrete nature of items, inter-item correlations, and skewed length distributions. To address this, we introduce CoSeRec, a novel framework for Contrastive Self-supervised Learning in sequential Recommendation. This approach utilizes two informative augmentation operators that leverage item correlations to generate high-quality views for contrastive learning. Experiments across three real-world datasets confirm that CoSeRec enhances model performance and robustness against sparse and noisy data. The code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/YChen1993/CoSeRec}.

We have generalized Expanded Wang-Landau (EWL) simulations from classical systems to those governed by a tight-binding Hamiltonian, enabling the calculation of partition functions and all associated thermodynamic properties, such as entropy and Gibbs free energy, for silicon fluid phases. Our analysis compares quantum many-body (QMB) tight-binding models, which explicitly compute orbital overlaps between neighboring atoms, against classical many-body force fields (CMB) that replicate the tetrahedral structure of condensed silicon via repulsive three-body terms. Along the vapor-liquid coexistence curve between 3000K and 6000K, densities in the coexisting phases exhibit significant variation—changing by five orders of magnitude for the vapor and up to 25% for the liquid—offering a rigorous test for both modeling approaches. Vapor-to-liquid transitions are predicted at chemical potentials approximately 10–15% higher for CMB models compared to QMB models, while force field rankings are established by evaluating vapor pressure predictions against experimental data. Furthermore, QMB models demonstrate the emergence of a gap in the electronic density of states within the coexisting liquid at elevated temperatures. Nanoscopic confinement drastically alters the phase diagram; for instance, at 6000K, liquid densities decrease by roughly 50% in both models, whereas vapor densities increase by 90% (CMB) to 170% (QMB). These findings comprehensively illustrate how the choice between CMB and QMB strategies to represent many-body effects influences the thermodynamic behavior of silicon fluids.

This paper establishes a unified framework for $U_q(sl(2))$ quantum invariants by utilizing intersections of embedded Lagrangians within configuration spaces. Specifically, we develop a state sum defined by Lagrangian intersections in the configuration space of a punctured disc, resulting in a polynomial involving three variables. This construction yields the coloured Jones polynomial and the coloured Alexander polynomial via specific coefficient specializations. The formula applies to oriented links colored with identical representations of the quantum group and remains valid at roots of unity. Consequently, both the Jones and Alexander polynomials emerge as special cases of an intersection pairing between embedded Lagrangians in configuration spaces, offering a method well-suited for computation. Notably, we derive the first intersection model for the Jones polynomial from intersections between submanifolds represented by arcs and circles within the punctured disc.

We have accurately determined the lifetime of the cesium $6P_{3/2}$ excited state by leveraging the intrinsic timing stability of pulses from a mode-locked laser. The experiment involves exciting cesium atoms in two opposing beams to the $6P_{3/2}$ level using an initial pump pulse. A synchronized probe pulse subsequently ionizes any atoms remaining in the excited state, and these photo-ions are collected and counted. By varying the temporal delay between pump and probe pulses, we sampled the excited state population over time, yielding a lifetime of 30.462(46) ns. The resulting measurement uncertainty of 0.15% exceeds the 0.12% reported in our previous study [Phys. Rev. A 84, 010501(R) (2011]) because of the inclusion of additional data and systematic error sources. This follow-up work details the primary systematic errors identified, specifically atomic motion within laser beam intensity profiles, quantum beating in the photo-ion signal, and radiation trapping, while also discussing strategies to further reduce experimental uncertainty.

This study investigates the reconstruction of an inflationary universe within the framework of one $f(\phi)T$ gravity, where $T$ represents the trace of the energy-momentum tensor. To achieve this reconstruction during the inflationary epoch, we adopt the scalar spectral index $n_s$ as an attractor, expressed as a function of the number of $e$-folds $N$, utilizing the slow-roll approximation. By specifying a particular form for $f(\phi)$ alongside a basic attractor $n_s(N)$, we derive various expressions for the reconstructed effective potential $V(\phi)$. Furthermore, we examine the subsequent reheating era following the inflationary reconstruction. In this scenario, we calculate the duration and temperature of the reheating phase based on the equation of state parameter and observational data. Finally, within this context, the parameters characterizing the reconstructed model are constrained during both inflation and reheating by incorporating recent astronomical observations.

This study examines the existence and multiplicity of solutions for the system
$$ \begin{cases} -\Delta_p u-\Delta_q u = g(x, u)\quad & \mbox{in } \Omega,\\
\displaystyle{u=0} & \mbox{on } \partial\Omega, \end{cases} $$
where $\Omega$ denotes a smooth, bounded domain in $\mathbb R^N$, satisfying $1<p<q<\infty$, and the nonlinearity $g$ exhibits $u^{q-1}$ behavior at infinity. Employing variational techniques, we identify multiple solutions as minimax critical points of the corresponding energy functional. Additionally, under appropriate conditions on the nonlinearity, the analysis extends to the resonant scenario.

Container technologies, such as Docker, are increasingly used to deploy software applications and infrastructures via container images, making security flaws within these images a critical concern. Exploiting these vulnerabilities can lead to severe consequences, including the compromise of confidentiality, integrity, and availability. While understanding the exploitability and impact of such flaws is essential for securing containerized environments, there is a notable gap in empirical research regarding these aspects. To address this, we conducted an empirical study examining the exploitability, impact, and prevalence of security vulnerabilities in base images within open-source containerized software. Base images were selected as the focal point because they supply the fundamental functionalities required to construct and run containerized applications. Our analysis identified and characterized 1,384 unique security vulnerabilities across 261 base images, which serve as the foundation for 4,681 actively maintained official images on Docker Hub, the largest container registry. Furthermore, to assess the prevalence of these vulnerable base images in practical settings, we analyzed 64,579 containerized projects on GitHub. This investigation yielded 13 novel findings, offering developers valuable insights into potential security risks associated with base images and encouraging a more rigorous security-oriented evaluation of these components during application development.

Python has quickly emerged as the dominant language for scientific computing and machine learning. Leveraging extensive frameworks like Numpy, SciPy, and TensorFlow, these fields have achieved significant productivity gains on existing systems without compromising performance. Although high-performance libraries suffice for single-node operations, distributed computing is essential to scale Python across multiple nodes, making it truly competitive in large-scale high-performance computing environments. Various frameworks—including Charm4Py, DaCe, Dask, Legate Numpy, mpi4py, and Ray—enable this cross-node scaling. Nevertheless, there remains a lack of understanding regarding the relative strengths and weaknesses of these tools, leaving practitioners and researchers uncertain about which framework best fits their specific needs. This paper aims to address that gap by evaluating the performance of two such frameworks: Charm4Py and mpi4py. We conduct a comparative performance analysis using CPU and GPU microbenchmarks, along with representative mini-applications typical of scientific computing.

Traditionally, human sciences have depended on human intellect to derive knowledge from diverse sources like oral histories, written accounts, and traditions. This study extends classical social network analysis by integrating the concept of meaning for each actor, enabling the quantification and inference of additional insights directly from the network's source data. This extension relies on a novel "semantic affinity" function, which establishes fuzzy relationships among network actors through combinations of affinity functions. Additionally, we introduce a new heuristic algorithm grounded in the shortest capacity problem to calculate this affinity. Applying these concepts of meaning and semantic affinity, we analyze and compare deities and heroes across three distinct classical mythologies: Greek, Celtic, and Nordic. Our examination covers both the internal structures of each mythology and the overarching patterns emerging when all three are fused. The results reveal a strong correlation between Celtic and Nordic gods, while indicating that Greek narratives place greater emphasis on heroic figures than on deities. Ultimately, our approach offers a method to identify and quantify significant relationships within the original network domain that cannot be inferred solely from structural properties.

Conceptual blending serves as a potent mechanism for computational creativity, capable of merging properties from two harmonic spaces to generate a new, coherent harmonic space in a consistent way. Nevertheless, determining which property features are significant within input spaces and assessing the outcomes of conceptual blending remains a complex challenge. Specifically within musical harmony, identifying the crucial characteristics of chord transitions and judging the validity of newly created harmonic spaces demands extensive expertise in musicology. This paper introduces a creative instrument designed to assist musicologists in both evaluating and refining harmonic innovation. The system enables music experts to define arguments regarding specific transition properties; these inputs guide the system's feature combination process during an idiom-blending operation. Experts can then determine if the resulting harmonic idom aligns with musicological principles and modify their feature selections to investigate alternative blends that may yield superior harmonic spaces. The paper concludes by outlining future directions aimed at further automating the harmonization process.

We introduce NaturalCC, a streamlined and adaptable toolkit designed to connect natural language and programming languages, thereby advancing research in large-scale code analysis. Leveraging NaturalCC, scholars from either domain can effortlessly replicate state-of-the-art baselines and develop new approaches. Built on Fairseq and PyTorch, the toolkit offers: (1) high-performance computation via multi-GPU and mixed-precision processing for rapid model training; (2) a modular, extensible architecture that simplifies the reproduction and implementation of big code analysis methods; and (3) both command-line and graphical interfaces to showcase model performance. To date, we have integrated several state-of-the-art baselines covering various tasks, such as code completion, comment generation, and code retrieval. A demonstration video is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q4W5VSI-u3E&t=25s.

We establish the Manin-Peyre conjecture regarding the count of rational points with bounded height, excluding a thin set, for a family of Fano threefolds with bidegree (1,2). This proof combines the circle method with methods derived from the geometry of numbers.

In recent times, machine learning-powered personal devices utilizing acoustics have gained significant traction. However, these machine learning systems are susceptible to adversarial attacks. Consequently, many modern systems defend themselves by targeting the artificial nature of these attacks, employing mechanisms to detect the absence of human involvement in their generation. These defenses, however, implicitly rely on the flawed assumption that humans cannot create meaningful or targeted adversarial examples. This paper challenges that premise, demonstrating that for tasks such as speaker identification, humans can generate analog adversarial examples with minimal cost and supervision. Specifically, by speaking through a tube, an adversary can reliably impersonate other speakers to ML models designed for speaker identification. These findings also apply to various other acoustic biometric tasks, including liveness detection, thereby casting doubt on their suitability for security-critical real-world applications like phone banking.

This review addresses the challenge of creating machine learning models that are both interpretable and explainable. These concepts are fundamental to numerous applications across medicine, economics, law, and the natural sciences. While a universally accepted definition for interpretability and explainability remains elusive, significant techniques have emerged over the past three decades, with current attention increasingly directed toward deep learning approaches. We highlight the distinction between these two concepts and demonstrate their divergent research trajectories using concrete examples of state-of-the-art methods. Targeted at a general machine learning audience, this review explores interpretability and explanation issues that extend beyond standard tools like logistic regression or random forest variable importance. Rather than serving as an exhaustive literature survey, this work functions as a selective primer, focusing on specific research avenues deemed particularly interesting and informative by the authors.

Throughout film production, directors meticulously control where the audience's gaze falls on the screen, utilizing shot composition, framing, camera movement, and editing to guide attention. To quantitatively analyze the connection between these cinematic tools and viewer gaze patterns, we introduce a novel eye-tracking database featuring gaze data from movie sequences alongside detailed editing annotations. We demonstrate how current computational saliency methods perform on this dataset, revealing robust correlations between film editing and spectator scanpaths. Furthermore, we highlight how incorporating editing knowledge can enhance visual attention modeling for cinematic material. The dataset and analysis generated for this study are accessible at https://github.com/abruckert/eye_tracking_filmmaking.

Fast yellow pulsating supergiants (FYPS) represent a newly identified category of evolved massive pulsators, serving as potential post-red supergiant candidates. As one of the limited classes of pulsating evolved massive stars, they hold significant promise for reshaping our comprehension of massive stellar structure and evolution. This study analyzes the light curves of 126 cool supergiants in the Magellanic Clouds, observed by the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), to detect pulsating stars. Following quality control and the removal of contaminants, we investigated the distribution of these pulsators within the Hertzprung-Russell (HR) diagram. Our findings indicate that FYPS reside in a region where $\log L/L_\odot \gtrsim 5.0$. This luminosity limit aligns with progenitor stars of initial masses between $\sim$18 and 20 $M_\odot$, matching the most massive red supergiant precursors to Type II-P supernovae and the observed characteristics of Type IIb supernova progenitors. This threshold supports the hypothesis that FYPS are post-red supergiant stars. Furthermore, we characterized FYPS pulsational behavior relative to their positions in the HR diagram, observing low-frequency pulsations at higher effective temperatures and high-frequency pulsations at lower temperatures, with a transition occurring at intermediate temperatures. Given their distinct properties, FYPS are compelling subjects for future theoretical investigation.

This paper introduces and evaluates two novel approaches derived from the additive average Schwarz (AAS) method, specifically tailored for elliptic problems featuring highly heterogeneous coefficients. Both techniques employ a non-overlapping strategy where subdomain interactions are managed through a coarse space. The first approach, the Minimum Energy Schwarz (MES) method, utilizes a coarse space with constant extensions within each subdomain, ensuring the lowest possible energy and yielding a condition number that consistently outperforms that of the standard AAS method. The second approach comprises non-overlapping spectral additive Schwarz (NOSAS) methods, which rely on low-rank discrete energy harmonic extensions. To achieve this low-rank property, a generalized eigenvalue problem is solved in every subdomain. NOSAS methods minimize energy for a specified coarse space rank, and their condition number remains independent of the coefficients. Furthermore, these methods exhibit favorable parallelization characteristics, with the global problem size determined solely by the total count of selected eigenvalues per subdomain, which correlates directly to the number of high-permeability islands contacting the subdomain interfaces.

Determining the lane number is a critical component in intelligent vehicle systems. While numerous lane detection algorithms have been developed, they are not always flawless; however, if lane detection were perfect, the lane number could be derived directly from those results. Since detection algorithms sometimes fail, we introduce a novel method that predicts the lane number by integrating drive recorder images with lane detection outputs. Experimental results on our proprietary dataset demonstrate that this approach achieves superior performance without incurring a significant increase in computational cost.

This study investigates zero-temperature condensates within a tunable binary Bose-Einstein condensate system, focusing on Rabi transitions between atomic hyperfine states. The system is modeled as coupled two-field dynamics involving both gapless and gapped excitations. We establish a configuration featuring an acoustic horizon separating subsonic and supersonic regimes in elongated two-component condensates to simulate Hawking radiation, specifically arising from gapped excitations. To ensure analytical tractability, a simplified step-like variation in sound speed is applied to the transition between these regimes. The effective energy gap in the dispersion relation of gapped excitations imposes a threshold frequency, $\omega_\text{min}$, in the subsonic region; propagating modes cannot exist below this frequency. Consequently, the Hawking mode particle spectrum diverges significantly from gapless cases near $\omega_\text{min}$ due to a modified grey-body factor that vanishes for frequencies below the threshold. Furthermore, we examine the impact of gapped excitations on the quantum entanglement between Hawking modes and their gapless partners using the Peres-Horodecki-Simon (PHS) criterion. Results indicate that gapped excitations degrade the quantumness of gapless pair modes, particularly when their frequency approaches $\omega \sim \omega_\text{min}$. Additionally, a sufficiently large coupling constant between gapless and gapped excitations leads to a high particle density of gapped modes at low frequencies, which substantially disentangles the gapless pair modes. The analysis further addresses the detailed time-dependent PHS criterion.

Spatial small area estimation models have gained significant traction in fields like disease mapping, where data typically consist of exhaustive registers capturing every observable event. Conversely, many small area investigations rely on non-exhaustive data, such as surveys that employ specific sampling designs and subsequently extrapolate findings to the broader population. This paper introduces a spatial model tailored for small area survey studies, leveraging spatial dependence between units—a core assumption in exhaustive data analyses. Furthermore, unlike most existing spatial survey methodologies, our approach integrates sampling design details and supplementary variables to generate small area estimates. This strategy enables the synthesis of spatial and sampling-based techniques into a unified framework.

Value-at-Risk (VaR) serves as a preferred institutional risk metric endorsed by financial regulators, often interpreted as the 95th percentile of future portfolio values given current information. This study introduces Conditional Autoregressive Value at Risk (CAViaR), originally proposed by Engle and Manganelli (2001), which posits that returns are not independent and identically distributed and exhibit notable autocorrelation. The model was evaluated using data from 1986–1999 and 1999–2009 covering GM, IBM, XOM, and the SPX, with validity confirmed through dynamic quantile testing. The findings indicate that the tails of the return distribution function differently compared to the central portion.

A significant challenge in quantum error correction is identifying a physical system that supports a "passively-protected quantum memory," an encoded qubit naturally coupled to an environment that corrects errors without active intervention. While stable quantum memories against finite-temperature effects have only been established in four or more spatial dimensions, this work proposes an alternative approach utilizing a driven-dissipative environment. We introduce a new model capable of passively correcting both bit-flip and phase-flip errors in two dimensions: a square lattice of photonic "cat qubits" connected through dissipative terms that locally fix errors. Drawing inspiration from two distinct $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetry-broken phases, the scheme employs Ising-like dissipators to guard against bit flips and a driven-dissipative photonic environment to shield against phase flips.

For decades, the duality between the mechanical equilibrium of elastic bodies and non-inertial flow in viscous liquids has served as a fundamental research principle. However, this correspondence breaks down when the Gaussian curvature of viscous films changes rapidly over time. Under these conditions, the film undergoes a geometrically nonlinear, non-inertial surface dynamics that has been largely unexamined. We identify the driver of this behavior as the flow of Gaussian curvature currents across the evolving surface, contrasting with the elastic analogue, which relies on an energetically favored target metric. Using the collapse of a bubble following rapid depressurization as a prototypical example, we demonstrate that a spherically shaped viscous film evolves through a topological instability—an event prohibited in the elastic case by an energy barrier. This topological transition induces compression within the film, triggering a subsequent symmetry-breaking instability that generates radial wrinkles; these wrinkles increase in amplitude and spread across the flattening film. Leveraging an analogy between surface currents of Gaussian curvature and polarization in electrostatic conductors, we derive quantitative predictions for the film's evolution. Furthermore, we suggest that this classical dynamics holds implications for the emerging field of viscous hydrodynamics concerning strongly correlated electrons in two-dimensional materials.

Three-dimensional Particle-in-Cell simulations of Laser Wakefield Acceleration are essential for realistic predictions and future experimental design, despite their significant resource demands. The upcoming Apollon laser experiments involve two-stage plasma acceleration with total lengths ranging from tens of millimeters to centimeters. Given that conventional 3D numerical simulations are impractical in this context, we present findings from applying a recently developed envelope method. This approach models the laser pulse and its plasma interaction without resolving high-frequency oscillations. We detail the implementation of this model within the Smilei code, alongside benchmark results comparing it to standard laser simulations and its application in designing two-stage Apollon experiments.

The theory of generalized locally Toeplitz (GLT) sequences serves as a robust tool for determining the asymptotic spectral distribution of square matrices $A_n$ generated by the discretization of differential equations. Specifically, as the mesh refinement parameter $n$ approaches infinity, the sequence $\{A_n\}_n$ frequently constitutes a GLT sequence. Driven by recent applications, this paper extends the classical square GLT framework by establishing a comprehensive theory for rectangular GLT sequences. Furthermore, we provide a concrete application example to demonstrate the theory's potential significance.

A probabilistic classifier featuring dependable predictive uncertainties must successfully adapt to target domain data, offer well-calibrated class probabilities in challenging areas (such as class overlaps), and accurately detect and reject out-of-distribution queries. We present a novel integration of Evidential Deep Learning, Neural Processes, and Neural Turing Machines designed to deliver these three critical capabilities for comprehensive uncertainty quantification. Across five classification benchmarks, our approach stands as the sole standalone predictor capable of excelling in all three dimensions of total calibration. This unified framework offers a practical, computationally efficient solution for safety assurance and enhances the intellectual efficiency of exploring the algorithmic foundations of epistemic awareness in deep neural networks.

This research examines how adolescent sports involvement influences health in early adulthood, utilizing longitudinal data from the National Survey of Youth and Religion. We analyze two key outcomes recorded between ages 23 and 28: self-rated health and the total PHQ-9 depression score, while adjusting for various demographic and socioeconomic confounders. While a simple comparison between sports participants and matched non-participants is feasible, such a broad approach fails to determine if specific sport types—such as high-contact activities like football or soccer—exert greater negative effects than others. To address this, we propose a tiered hierarchy of exposure definitions, spanning from broad categories (any after-school organized activity) to narrow ones (limited-contact sports). We will conduct separate matched observational analyses for each definition to assess health impacts across different participation levels. To maintain a fixed family-wise error rate while performing these multiple tests, we have developed an ordered testing strategy that leverages the logical connections between the exposure categories. Additionally, the study will evaluate secondary outcomes such as body mass index, life satisfaction, and problematic drinking behaviors.

To address classification challenges, we introduce a novel evolutionary learning algorithm called the Multi-Output Neural Tree (MONT), trained using the Non-Dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm (NSGA)-III. Because evolutionary learning involves stochastic processes, each execution of the algorithm generates a unique MONT hypothesis, resulting in trees with distinct properties across both topological and parameter spaces. This creates an optimization challenge aimed at simultaneously minimizing tree size and maximizing classification accuracy. To address this, we employed hypervolume indicator analysis to ensure Pareto-optimality. The MONT was evaluated on nine benchmark classification tasks, yielding models capable of solving these problems with high accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that MOUT outperforms several established classifiers, including multilayer perceptrons, reduced-error pruning trees, naive Bayes, standard decision trees, and support vector machines. Furthermore, comparing three training variants—genetic programming, NSGA-II, and NSGA-III—indicates that NSGA-III produces the superior Pareto-optimal solution.

Using an integrated luminosity of $3.19$ fb$^{-1}$ recorded by the BESIII detector at a center-of-mass energy of 4.178 GeV, we conduct an amplitude analysis of the $D_s^+\to\pi^+\pi^-\pi^+$ decay. The analysis includes a sample of 13,797 candidates with approximately 80% signal purity. Based on a quasi-model-independent method, we determine the amplitude and phase of the contributing $\pi\pi$ ${\cal S}$ wave, as well as the amplitudes and phases of the ${\cal P}$ and ${\cal D}$ waves, which are modeled using Breit-Wigner functions. Additionally, the fit fractions for various intermediate decay channels are presented.

The spatial and dynamical architecture of star-forming regions offers valuable insights into stellar formation patterns. Given the vast data volumes from existing and future surveys, there is a need for robust, objective methods to identify structures that allow for statistical analysis and inter-regional comparison. We present a tool designed to detect significant small-scale structures above random expectations, which may reflect the imprint of the stellar formation process. This tool utilizes the one-point correlation function and nearest-neighbor statistics to calibrate the DBSCAN algorithm. It successfully identifies significant small-scale substructures within heterogeneous regions, meeting its design objectives and yielding highly reliable results. However, analysis of regions near complete spatial randomness ($Q \in [0.7, 0.87]$) indicates that even when structure is recovered, it is difficult to distinguish from spurious detections in homogeneous areas caused by projection effects, necessitating cautious interpretation. In concentrated regions, the tool detects a primary structure surrounded by smaller ones, representing the core plus Poisson fluctuations, which we argue do not match the small compact regions of interest. For realistic scenarios, a more comprehensive hierarchical, multi-scale analysis may be required to fully capture regional complexity. We have developed implementations of this procedure and made publicly available a catalogue of Nested Elementary Structures (NESTs) detected in four star-forming regions (Taurus, IC 348, Upper Scorpius, and Carina). Additionally, 3D and up to 6D versions incorporating proper motions are currently under development and will be released in future work.

This paper presents our submission to the DISRPT2021 Shared Task, focusing on Discourse Unit Segmentation, Connective Detection, and Relation Classification. Our system, named DisCoDisCo, utilizes a Transformer-based neural classifier that augments contextualized word embeddings with hand-crafted features. It employs tokenwise sequence tagging for discourse segmentation and connective detection, alongside a feature-rich, encoder-less sentence pair classifier for relation classification. Our results for the first two tasks surpass the state-of-the-art scores achieved in the 2019 shared task, while the relation classification results indicate strong performance on the 2021 benchmark. Ablation studies demonstrate that incorporating features beyond CWEs benefits both tasks, and a partial evaluation of various pre-trained Transformer-based language models suggests that those pre-trained on the Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) task yield optimal results for relation classification.

We introduce and validate a new approach that merges Raman scattering with optical cycling in molecules featuring diagonal Franck-Condon factors. This resonance Raman optical cycling method induces molecular behavior akin to efficient fluorophores, characterized by distinct absorption and emission profiles that can be easily separated for sensitive fluorescence detection even under high background light conditions. Employing a molecular beam of SrF as a test species, we achieved an average of approximately 20 spontaneously emitted photons per molecule, constrained by interaction duration, while utilizing a bandpass filter to attenuate scattered laser light by roughly $10^6$. This versatile technique serves as a potent instrument for high-fidelity fluorescence detection of molecules in diverse environments and is especially advantageous for molecular laser cooling and trapping experiments.

Lad, Sanfilippo, and Agr\`o recently introduced Extropy as a dual complement to Shannon Entropy. This paper presents dynamic formulations of Extropy tailored for doubly truncated random variables, defining them as Interval Extropy and Weighted Interval Extropy to quantify uncertainty. We provide various characterizations of random variables in relation to these novel measures and illustrate them with multiple examples. Furthermore, we analyze how these measures behave under linear transformations and conclude by establishing specific bounds for them.

Future 6G and beyond networks are anticipated to fulfill the unrealized objectives of 5G, enabling technologies like the Internet of Skills and Industry 4.0 to become stable and viable through sustained, reliable mobile performance. However, the primary hurdles for these future technologies extend beyond low latency and high bandwidth. A more critical challenge for Mobile Service Providers (MSPs) will be balancing the surge in network connection demands with customer trust, specifically by interconnecting billions of unique devices while strictly adhering to Service Level Agreements (SLAs). To achieve these goals, MSPs must move beyond isolated operations and foster cooperation that ensures trust both among themselves and with their customers.

This study introduces the BEAT (Blockchain-Enabled Accountable and Transparent) Infrastructure Sharing architecture. Leveraging the inherent attributes of permissioned distributed ledger technology, BEAT ensures accountability and transparency when infrastructure is shared between providers. Additionally, we propose a lightweight mechanism for device-level accountability. Designed for easy deployment requiring only minor software upgrades to network equipment like routers, our simulations on resource-constrained devices indicate that BEAT introduces only a few seconds of processing overhead; with modern state-of-the-art devices, we expect this overhead to be significantly lower.

This work explores multiple parallels between convex geometry and the theory of holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or Kähler manifolds. We examine the connection between positive products and mixed volumes, introduce and analyze a Blaschke addition for both divisor and mixed divisor classes, and establish new geometric inequalities concerning these classes. Furthermore, we reframe several foundational results from convex geometry within algebraic geometry: the Alexandrov body construction corresponds to the convex geometry analogue of divisorial Zariski decomposition, while Minkowski's existence theorem represents the convex geometry counterpart to the duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves.

We compare the mean atomic gas mass ($\langle M_{Atom}\rangle$, comprising HI and He), mean molecular gas mass ($\langle M_{Mol}\rangle$), and mean stellar mass ($\langle M_*\rangle$) for a sample of star-forming galaxies at $z\approx0.75-1.45$ to investigate baryonic composition during the universe's peak star-formation era. Using HI 21cm signal stacking from the GMRT-CAT$z1$ survey, we derived $\langle M_{Atom}\rangle$ for two stellar-mass matched samples spanning $z=0.74-1.25$ and $z=1.25-1.45$. Our results reveal a stark contrast in the baryonic makeup of star-forming galaxies at $z\gtrsim 1$ compared to $z\approx0$. For galaxies with $\langle M_*\rangle\approx10^{10} M_\odot$, stars account for roughly $61\%$ of the total baryonic mass ($M_{Baryon}$) at $z\approx0$, dropping to only $16\%$ at $z\approx1.3$. Conversely, molecular gas represents about $6\%$ of $M_{Baryon}$ locally but rises to $14\%$ at $z\approx1.3$. Notably, atomic gas dominates the baryonic mass, comprising approximately $70\%$ at $z\approx1.3$. The $\langle M_{Atom}\rangle/\langle M_*\rangle$ ratio is significantly elevated at both $z\approx1.0$ and $z\approx1.3$ relative to the local Universe, reaching $\approx1.4$ and $\approx4.4$, respectively, compared to $\approx0.5$ today. Additionally, for galaxies with $\langle M_*\rangle\approx10^{10} M_\odot$, the $\langle M_{Atom}\rangle/\langle M_{Mol}\rangle$ ratio is $\approx2.3$ at $z\approx1.0$ and $\approx5.0$ at $z\approx1.3$. In summary, atomic gas is the primary baryonic component of star-forming galaxies at $z\approx1.3$, coinciding with the epoch of peak cosmic star formation.

Recent cyber incidents have highlighted credential theft as a dominant method for initial system access. Once attackers establish a foothold, they employ techniques like token manipulation to escalate privileges and access sensitive resources, underscoring the necessity of robust authentication and token-based authorization for secure, resilient systems. This paper outlines the design principles for an adaptive authentication and authorization framework that adjusts dynamically based on risk scores and trust profiles.
