Under this weak learnability assumption, we present an efficient algorithm that iteratively enhances the accuracy of these weak methods until global optimality is achieved. We establish bounds on both sample complexity and runtime that are polynomial in the problem's natural parameters—specifically the approximation guarantee, discount factor, distribution mismatch, and number of actions—without dependence on the number of states.

A key challenge in applying existing boosting results is the non-convexity of the value function across the policy space. To address this, we employ a non-convex variant of the Frank-Wolfe method, integrated with recent advancements in gradient boosting that support weak learners with multiplicative approximation guarantees. This approach successfully overcomes non-convexity and ensures global convergence.

Over the past twenty years, substantial methodological advancements have been made in simultaneously analyzing both simple and complex randomized designs, especially when proportions serve as endpoints. These developments encompass: i) the novel Tukey trend test methodology, ii) multiple contrast tests for binomial proportions, iii) multiple contrast tests for poly-k estimates, and iv) the Add-1 approximation for one-sided inference. This report specifically examines a new Tukey-type trend test designed for evaluating repeated long-term carcinogenicity bioassays, a development inspired by multiple glyphosate studies. Please note that the objective is not to contribute to the assessment of glyphosate or the surrounding controversies. Using the CRAN packages tukeytrend, MCPAN, and multcomp, conducting real data analysis becomes straightforward.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) provide a real-time method for inverting borehole resistivity data to model both forward and inverse operators. While extremely large DNNs can approximate these operators effectively, they necessitate extensive training durations and consume substantial memory and processing resources during evaluation. Furthermore, there is a risk of overfitting with such large models. This study introduces a scoring function that balances DNN accuracy against network size relative to a reference DNN known for high approximation quality. By applying this scoring function within DNN architecture search algorithms, we identify a quasi-optimal network that is smaller than the reference model, thereby reducing computational demands for both training and inference while maintaining accuracy comparable to the original large DNN.

Building language resources is essential for language processing, yet it is expensive, requires extensive interdisciplinary research, and demands continuous updates. This paper outlines the cross-lingual framework employed to create the Multilingual Central Repository (MCR), a multilingual knowledge base encompassing wordnets for Basque, Catalan, English, Galician, Portuguese, and Spanish, along with several ontologies: Base Concepts, Top Ontology, WordNet Domains, and the Suggested Upper Merged Ontology. We detail the history of the MCR, its status as of 2017, and the tools developed for it.

Inspired by recent experimental data on various alkali metals and alkali-like ions, we conducted an in-depth investigation of electric dipole (E1) transition amplitudes in K, Ca+, Rb, Sr+, Cs, Ba+, Fr, and Ra+. These elements are crucial for research into atomic parity violation, electric dipole moments, polarizabilities, and atomic clocks. Employing the all-orders correlation potential method, we executed high-precision calculations of E1 transition amplitudes involving low-lying s, p, and d states. We implemented a rigorous error analysis and compared our findings with numerous experimentally determined amplitudes of high precision. Our results show excellent agreement, with deviations no greater than 0.1%. Additionally, we benchmarked our results against other theoretical evaluations and examined the implications for uncertainty assessments of theoretical approaches. Furthermore, by integrating our branching ratio calculations with recent measurements, we derived high-precision experimental values for several E1 amplitudes in Ca+, Sr+, Cs, Fr, and Ra+.

The BumpHunter algorithm is a standard tool for discovering new particles in High Energy Physics, distinguished by its ability to calculate both local and global p-values for localized data deviations without requiring assumptions about the signal's nature. Driven by Python's growing prominence, a new public version named pyBumpHunter was developed, introducing enhancements and extra capabilities; notably, it is the first BumpHunter implementation to be integrated into Scikit-HEP. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the BumpHunter algorithm and the specific features introduced by this implementation, with all features undergoing rigorous testing to validate their behavior and performance.

Approximate query processing (AQP) for dynamic databases, which handle insertions and deletions, is vital for applications such as high-frequency trading and IoT analytics. We introduce JanusAQP, a novel dynamic AQP system capable of executing SUM, COUNT, AVG, MIN, and MAX queries amidst dataset modifications. By adapting static partition tree synopses—hierarchical dataset aggregations—for dynamic environments, JanusAQP offers three key innovations: (1) efficient synopsis initialization upon data arrival, (2) robust maintenance of the synopsis during updates, and (3) partition re-optimization to minimize approximation error. Experimental results show that JanusAQP lowers the error of a state-of-the-art baseline by over 60% while consuming only 10% of the storage. Furthermore, the system achieves a throughput of more than 100,000 updates per second on a single node, maintaining query latency in the millisecond range.

We introduce a novel method for identifying deepfake images by leveraging inconsistencies in source features inherent to forged content. This approach relies on the premise that distinct source characteristics remain intact and extractable even after advanced deepfake generation. To achieve this, we propose a new representation learning technique known as Pair-wise Self-Consistency Learning (PCL), which trains ConvNets to isolate these source features and detect fakes. Additionally, we developed the Inconsistency Image Generator (I2G), a synthesis method designed to create richly annotated training data for PCL. Evaluations across seven widely used datasets demonstrate that our models significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods, raising the average AUC from 96.45% to 98.05% in in-dataset tests and from 86.03% to 92.18% in cross-dataset tests.

This study examines how a brane and a magnetic-flux-carrying cosmic string influence the vacuum expectation value (VEV) of the current density for a charged fermionic field within a 4+1 dimensional anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetime. The brane lies parallel to the AdS boundary, while the cosmic string stands orthogonal to it. We analyze two specific boundary conditions on the brane: the MIT bag condition and those applicable to Z2-symmetric braneworld models. The brane partitions the space into two regions characterized by distinct vacuum properties. The current density possesses only a nonzero component in the azimuthal direction, and its VEV in both regions is split into brane-free and brane-induced parts. The brane-induced contribution disappears on the string; however, near the string, the total current is primarily dominated by the brane-free component. At large distances from the string, specifically in the region between the brane and the AdS horizon, the brane-induced current density decays according to a power law with respect to proper distance for both massive and massless fields. For massive fields, this decay behavior differs significantly from that observed in a Minkowski bulk. Conversely, in the region between the brane and the AdS boundary, the large-distance decay of the current density is exponential. Depending on the chosen boundary condition, the brane-induced contribution either dominates or remains subdominant in the total current density at large distances from the string. Furthermore, using fields that correspond to two inequivalent irreducible representations of the Clifford algebra, we investigate the vacuum current density within C- and P-symmetric fermionic models. Finally, we apply these findings to a cosmic string situated in a Randall-Sundrum-type braneworld model featuring a single brane.

**Background:** Building upon our prior investigation [Phys. Rev. C 104, 055804 (2021)], which examined the surface characteristics of neutron stars modeled as large finite nuclei composed of protons, neutrons, electrons, and muons for several representative masses, this paper provides a comprehensive analysis to establish definitive conclusions. **Method:** Extending our previous approach, the energy density functional of neutron star matter in momentum space is transformed into coordinate space under the local density approximation. This functional is then applied within the coherent density fluctuation model to derive surface properties, utilizing a weight function derived from the neutron star's density profile. The calculations employ the G3 parameter set, alongside the widely utilized NL3 and IU-FSU sets, within the relativistic mean-field framework. **Results:** We systematically compute surface properties including incompressibility, symmetry energy, the slope parameter, and the curvature coefficient. The total symmetry energy is decomposed into volume and surface components using the $\kappa$ factor, derived from the volume-to-surface ratio of symmetry energies in the Danielewicz liquid drop limit. The calculated magnitudes of these surface quantities exhibit an increase with the neutron star's mass. **Conclusion:** An analysis of the incompressibility ($K^{\rm star}$), symmetry energy ($S^{\rm star}$), slope parameter ($L_{\rm sym}^{\rm star}$), and curvature coefficient ($K_{\rm sym}^{\rm star}$) across neutron stars of varying masses reveals a dependence on the chosen model. Specifically, the NL3 parameter set yields the stiffest equation of state, resulting in higher magnitudes for surface quantities compared to the G3 and IU-FSU interactions.

Polymer-grafted nanoparticles (PGNPs), characterized by a rigid core and a flexible corona, self-assemble into diverse superlattice structures where each particle adopts the geometry of its corresponding Wigner-Seitz (or Voronoi) cell. While traditional perspectives attribute the stability of these lattices to mean-field principles like surface area minimization or corona entropy maximization—approaches lacking a molecular basis—we have developed a simulation technique to compute the free energy penalty required to deform spherical PGNPs into Wigner-Seitz polyhedra within specific crystalline superlattices. Using this approach, we quantified the free energy variations among model BCC, FCC, and A15 PGNP systems, identifying BCC as the predominant stable structure in most scenarios. Furthermore, examining polymer configurations within the corona, whose boundaries are indistinct due to chain interpenetration, reveals that the radial distribution of grafted chains and their associated entropy remain nearly identical in both BCC and FCC arrangements. Consequently, the superior stability of the BCC structure cannot be attributed to a mean-field description of corona shape.

Although population-wide tobacco control measures have significantly lowered global smoking rates, the pace of this decline is decelerating, necessitating models that fully capture the epidemic's complexity. Such models can serve as platforms for designing new strategies to curb smoking spread. However, existing approaches primarily rely on ordinary differential equation (ODE) models, which struggle to account for individual contact networks and often overlook critical interpersonal interactions driving behavioral changes. To address these gaps, we developed, calibrated, and validated an agent-based model (ABM) using historical data from the US and UK. This ABM incorporates spontaneous factors, agent interactions, and contact networks. We evaluated the model across six networks—both synthetic and real-world—and compared its performance against an ODE model. Our findings indicate that ODE dynamics align with the ABM only in fully connected (FC) networks, yet FC networks fail to replicate empirical trends as effectively as real-world networks do. When real-world network data is inaccessible, our ABM applied to Lancichinetti-Fortunato-Radicchi benchmark networks (or those with similar average degrees) offers a viable alternative for modeling smoking behavior. These results underscore the importance of network structures in tobacco modeling and demonstrate that our ABM can inform the development of network-based interventions and policies for tobacco control.

This study demonstrates that for a code randomly selected from a pairwise independent ensemble, the probability that its error exponent falls below a specific lower bound of the typical random-coding exponent approaches zero as the codeword length increases indefinitely. This lower bound has previously been established as tight for i.i.d. ensembles on binary symmetric channels and for constant-composition codes on memoryless channels. The findings encompass both scenarios as special cases and extend validity to any alphabet, any channel—including finite-state channels with memory—and any pairwise-independent ensemble. Furthermore, the results are applied specifically to i.i.d., constant-composition, and cost-constrained ensembles over discrete memoryless channels, as well as to ensembles defined over finite-state channels.

Fine-grained visual classification (FGVC) has emerged as a critical research area driven by its extensive applications and the swift advancement of computer vision. Current state-of-the-art FGVC methods typically utilize attention mechanisms to identify semantic components and discern their subtle variations across different classes. Specifically, channel-spatial attention mechanisms, which simultaneously target discriminative channels and regions, have markedly enhanced classification accuracy. Nevertheless, existing attention modules lack adequate guidance because part-based detectors in FGVC rely on the network's intrinsic learning capabilities without supervision from part annotations. Since acquiring such annotations is labor-intensive, visual localization and explanation techniques like gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) can be leveraged to supervise the attention mechanism. We introduce a Grad-CAM guided channel-spatial attention module for FGVC, which uses Grad-CAM to generate coarse localization maps that supervise and constrain attention weights. To validate the method's efficacy, we performed comprehensive experiments on three prominent FGVC datasets: CUB-200-2011, Stanford Cars, and FGVC-Aircraft. Our approach surpasses state-of-the-art attention modules in FGVC tasks, and visualizations of feature maps further illustrate its superiority over existing approaches.

Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) datasets leverage highly precise measurements of large-scale spatial distributions as a distance ladder to constrain cosmological parameters. In a recent publication \cite{Benisty:2020otr}, we integrated 17 uncorrelated BAO measurements spanning the effective redshift range $0.106 \le z \le 2.36$ with Cosmic Chronometers, Pantheon Type Ia supernova data, and a Hubble Diagram comprising Gamma Ray Bursts and Quasars. This combination yielded $\Lambda$CDM model constraints of $H_0 = 69.85 \pm 1.27 \, \text{km/s/Mpc}$ and $r_s = 146.1 \pm 2.15 \, \text{Mpc}$. Furthermore, we examined alternative models, specifically $\Omega_k$CDM and $w$CDM, deriving results of $\Omega_k = -0.076 \pm 0.012$ and $w = -0.989 \pm 0.049$, respectively. In this proceeding, we elaborate on these findings and compare them with other recent literature.

The objective of image style transfer is to apply artistic characteristics from a reference style to an image while preserving its original content. However, due to the local nature of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), capturing and retaining global image information remains challenging, leading to biased content representations in traditional neural style transfer methods. To overcome this limitation, we introduce StyTr$^2$, a transformer-based framework that incorporates long-range dependencies. Unlike visual transformers used for other tasks, StyTr$^2$ employs two distinct transformer encoders to create domain-specific sequences for content and style, followed by a multi-layer transformer decoder that applies the style sequence to the content sequence. Additionally, we identify shortcomings in current positional encoding techniques and propose Content-Aware Positional Encoding (CAPE), which is scale-invariant and better suited for style transfer. Both qualitative and quantitative experiments confirm that StyTr$^2$ outperforms existing state-of-the-art CNN-based and flow-based methods. The code and models can be accessed at https://github.com/diyiiyiii/StyTR-2.

The validity of the weak cosmic censorship conjecture regarding near-extremal BTZ black holes has been investigated using test particles and fields, with some studies suggesting the possibility of overspinning. This paper reviews the thermodynamics and the weak cosmic censorship conjecture for BTZ black holes through the lens of scalar field scattering. While the first law of thermodynamics is successfully recovered for non-extremal BTZ black holes, the analysis of extremal and near-extremal cases encounters a divergence in entropy variation. Consequently, the conjecture is tested by calculating the minimum values of the function $f$. The results indicate that neither extremal nor near-extremal BTZ black holes can be overspun.

This work presents four case studies leveraging Bayesian methods to facilitate inductive reasoning. Our primary aim is to demonstrate scenarios where the Bayesian framework excels in handling complex analytical tasks, including description, testing, estimation, and prediction. We do not intend this as a comprehensive survey or reference text for Bayesian statistical inference; rather, our objective is to offer illustrative examples of Bayesian methodology applied to data-driven challenges. The selected topics encompass Bayesian nonparametrics, time series analysis, and spatial data analysis.

We examine the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model in the absence of an external field, with an inverse temperature $\beta<1$, and demonstrate that the expected operator norm of the Gibbs measure's covariance matrix is bounded by a constant determined solely by $\beta$. This resolves an open question posed by Talagrand, who had previously established a bound of $C(\beta) (\log n)^8$. Our finding is achieved by deriving an approximate expression for the covariance matrix through the differentiation of the TAP equations, followed by the optimal control of the resulting error terms. Additionally, we provide diverging lower bounds for the operator norm at both the critical and low-temperature regimes.

We investigate whether Natural Language Inference (NLI) neural models can acquire the compositional interplay between lexical entailment and negation. This inquiry utilizes four distinct evaluation approaches: behavioral methods involving challenge test sets and systematic generalization tasks, alongside structural methods comprising probes and interventions. To support this comprehensive assessment, we introduce Monotonicity NLI (MoNLI), a novel dataset centered on lexical entailment and negation within a naturalistic context. Our behavioral analysis reveals that models trained on standard NLI corpora systematically fail on MoNLI instances featuring negation, yet fine-tuning on MoNLI resolves this issue. In our structural analysis, we examine whether our top-performing BERT-based model has internalized the monotonicity algorithm underlying MoNLI. Probe results provide evidence aligning with this hypothesis, while intervention experiments further substantiate it by demonstrating that the model's causal dynamics mirror those of the algorithm across subsets of MoNLI. Consequently, this indicates that the BERT model partially embeds a theory of lexical entailment and negation at an algorithmic level.
